projectDetails.name: FireTrack - Platform for monitoring fire hotspots and identifying historical patterns
projectDetails.summary:
FireTrack is a web-based platform designed to harmonize fire hotspot data from NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS satellite sensors, addressing inconsistencies between different datasets and providing a more consistent historical overview of fire activity. Through the integration of historical records dating back to 2003, spatial and temporal data processing, and sensor calibration, the platform aims to reduce duplicate detections and improve data comparability. Its features include an interactive map with filters by region, period, and fire intensity based on Fire Radiative Power (FRP), a historical fire activity calendar, and an analytical dashboard displaying hotspot totals, historical averages, and anomalies. Users can also export filtered datasets for further analysis.
FireTrack transforms complex satellite observations into accessible information to support environmental monitoring, early warning strategies, and emergency response. Rather than predicting fires, the platform serves as a preventive tool by identifying critical periods, highlighting unusual fire activity, and providing valuable information that enables authorities and environmental managers to anticipate risks, plan interventions, and strengthen preparedness. By connecting historical fire patterns with intuitive data visualizations, the project aims to promote more informed decision-making, improve data literacy, and contribute to wildfire prevention and environmental protection.

projectDetails.name: SPHEREye
projectDetails.summary:
We developed an interactive web explorer that lets anyone search the infrared sky for objects that move or change brightness, using real data from NASA's SPHEREx mission. The user enters a position in the sky; the tool retrieves two cutouts of the same field from the NASA/IPAC IRSA archive, taken months apart, aligns them on the same sky grid, applies a common contrast, and lets the user switch between the images and compare them. A pre-processed example keeps the site working if the data service is down.

The project addresses the challenge by turning public but hard-to-use data into a simple visual search for hidden or moving objects, the same principle used to find cold brown dwarfs such as WISE 0855 and in the search for the hypothetical Planet X. In a first test with Barnard's Star, one source shifted about 1.5 pixels (roughly 10 arcseconds) over about 12 months, while the reference stars stayed nearly fixed. This validates the method; it is not a discovery.

This matters because it opens SPHEREx data to students, teachers and amateur astronomers, with nothing to install.
projectDetails.details:
Our project is a public web explorer for SPHEREx, NASA's all-sky near-infrared spectral survey (0.75-5.0 micrometers). The user enters a sky position (right ascension and declination in degrees). The backend queries the NASA/IPAC IRSA archive (SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 collections, through the IVOA SIA2 protocol and the IRSA IBE cutout service), selects two exposures of the same field taken months apart by the same detector, downloads small FITS cutouts, masks invalid pixels, reprojects both images onto the same sky grid using their WCS, and applies one shared contrast scale.

The frontend then lets the user switch between the two epochs to spot sources that moved or changed brightness, and shows the provenance of each frame (collection, observation date, detector and source link). If the data service is unavailable, a pre-processed real example keeps the site working. SPHEREx data are public, but using them requires knowledge of FITS files, coordinate systems and archive protocols. Our tool removes that barrier: nothing to install, no coding, and every image is traceable to its source. We want students, teachers and amateur astronomers to explore real infrared survey data and learn how moving objects are found, the same principle used to discover cold brown dwarfs such as WISE 0855 and in searches for the hypothetical Planet X. It can be used in classrooms and outreach.

We use the following programming tools:

Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript.

Backend: Python 3.12, FastAPI, Pydantic, Uvicorn (Render).

Scientific processing: Astropy, NumPy, reproject, Pillow, Requests.

Data: NASA/IPAC IRSA (SPHEREx DR1 and QR3).

Version control and hosting: GitHub.

No special hardware; development was done on the team's personal computers. We brought the classical blink-comparison technique to the browser and paired it with a guided experience for non-experts: one input, two real frames, one clear question ("what moved?"). The explicit provenance panel and the offline example make it both educational and trustworthy.

Scientific validity: same detector, epochs separated by months, shared contrast and masks, so apparent changes are comparable. -

Honest limits: in a first test on a high-proper-motion star (Barnard's Star), one source shifted about 1.5 pixels (roughly 10 arcseconds) over about 12 months while reference stars stayed nearly fixed. This validates the method; it is not a discovery.

We also saw isolated bright pixels appear in only one frame, which are detector artifacts, not motion. The archive returned intermittent errors (HTTP 503) during testing, and our free-tier server can sleep, so the app handles failures and offers a ready example. Works in a browser, runs on free hosting.

Credits and openness: data credited to NASA/IPAC IRSA (DOIs 10.26131/IRSA678 and 10.26131/IRSA662); the code is public. AI USE AI assistance (Claude, by Anthropic) was used to help draft code, documentation and text.

projectDetails.name: SpaceAtlas: Mission Control
projectDetails.summary: SpaceAtlas: Mission Control is a free browser game that puts players in charge of a real space mission, from the first requirement to the final debrief. Players sign a mission contract, choose a target (Earth observation, the Moon's south pole, a real near-Earth asteroid or Mars), design the spacecraft and its science payload, pick the orbit and the rocket, and balance cost, mass, power, data and lifetime. Every choice is explained in plain words and checked with the same first-order rules engineers use in early studies. The mission is then flown in 3D, with events driven by real NASA data such as space weather and asteroid close approaches. The debrief traces every lost point to a number, compares the design with hundreds of other valid spacecraft, and lets players rerun the mission changing one decision. It runs on phones and desktops, in English, Portuguese and Spanish, solo or with up to four players.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

SpaceAtlas turns the full mission-design loop into a 10-minute game:

1. Contract: the player sets the minimum and full success goals the mission will be judged against.

2. Design: ten guided questions (objective, duration, instruments, orbit, size, power, battery, propulsion, communications, rocket). Each answer shows the numbers it changed. Secondary decisions (thermal, computer, redundancy, shielding, radio band, ground network) are settled automatically, and a hint shows the smallest change that fixes a failing check.

3. Go/No-Go: every budget (mass, power, energy, data, delta-v, cost, margins) is checked before launch.

4. Flight: a cinematic 3D launch and mission. Two or three events arrive (13 kinds, such as coronal mass ejections, a stuck solar wing, micrometeoroids, debris conjunctions, budget cuts or an unexpected discovery), and the player decides how to respond. The outcome depends on the design and on the decision.

5. Board of Investigation: the verdict against the player's own goals, a waterfall of where the science came from, a comparison with 100–400 other valid designs (value for money as distance to the science-versus-cost Pareto frontier), and a one-change rerun that keeps the same random seed, so the comparison is fair.

The physics engine is deterministic and separate from the interface. It includes the rocket equation (Tsiolkovsky), solar power falling with distance squared plus cell degradation and eclipse or night fractions, battery depth of discharge against the longest dark period, radioisotope power with decay, a simplified link budget (data rate falls with distance squared; data per day = rate × contact time), and design margins of 10, 15 or 20 % by difficulty, following ESA's margin philosophy for early studies.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Mission design is usually taught as isolated formulas. SpaceAtlas shows how every decision pulls on every other one: a bigger camera needs more power, which needs bigger solar panels, which adds mass, which needs a bigger rocket and a bigger budget. It targets high-school and early university students, and the general public. It is free, needs no install or account, and works on low-end phones and in three languages, so it can be used in classrooms with few resources. Because the debrief explains failures with numbers instead of a score alone, players learn why engineers keep margins, why Mars missions need larger solar panels, and why a light-delay of minutes requires autonomy. The team mode (Systems & Budget, Spacecraft, Science, Comms & Ops) reproduces the trade-offs between subsystems that real mission teams negotiate.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE

- Languages: TypeScript, Python (asset build scripts), Node.js scripts.

- Interface: Preact, Vite, three.js (3D scenes, launch films, an exploded view of spacecraft and rocket parts), sounds synthesised in the browser with the Web Audio API.

- Quality: Vitest (physics, sizing model, simulation, translations with identical keys), Playwright with Chromium (end-to-end play-through of every mission, screenshots at 390 px and 1440 px, performance measurements).

- Data: NASA open APIs (DONKI, NeoWs, EONET), JPL CNEOS NHATS and the Close-Approach Data API, NASA SVS and NASA 3D Resources.

- Hosting: Vercel (static web build); the same build also runs as a one-file page.

- Trailer: Remotion (React video), FFmpeg (mix and loudness), Kokoro-82M text-to-speech for the narration.

- Hardware: no special hardware; it runs in any modern browser.

CREATIVITY

The game uses mission-control roles instead of a sandbox: players sign a contract and are later judged by it. Space weather is shown as it is really observed (flare, particle tracks on the camera sensor, the plasma cloud, aurora), not as explosions. Every spacecraft and rocket part can be tapped for a plain-language explanation, and "Separate parts" opens an exploded view of the stages, boosters and fairing. The four playable crew members are fictional pixel-art characters whose paths are inspired by real NASA astronauts.

FACTORS THE TEAM CONSIDERED

- Scientific honesty: first-order models, clearly labelled as for learning trade-offs, not for flight; every constant has a cited source; no purely random failures, so outcomes always come from the design and the decisions.

- Fairness: a shared seed for the whole team, and reruns that keep the seed.

- Accessibility: keyboard navigation, visible focus, a reduced-motion setting, mute, readable contrast, responsive layouts for phones and desktops, and quality tiers that adapt to weaker devices.

- Reach: three languages, no account, small first download (about 0.7 MB), and an offline data snapshot when live APIs cannot be reached.

- Brand rules: no NASA logos or insignia are used, and the game states that NASA does not endorse it.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project GURIS
projectDetails.summary:
1. O que você desenvolveu?
Criamos o PERIAPSIS, um jogo de navegador em 3D em que o jogador é o diretor de uma missão espacial e cuida de tudo, do começo ao fim. Primeiro escolhe um destino (Marte, Europa, Lua, Bennu, Mercúrio ou Titã). Depois monta a nave num hangar 3D, escolhe a órbita e o foguete e lança. Na viagem, enfrenta falhas e imprevistos. Quando chega, desce ao planeta como astronauta, em primeira pessoa, e cumpre os objetivos de lá. No fim recebe uma pontuação e uma explicação do que deu certo e do que deu errado.

2. Como ele aborda o desafio escolhido?
O desafio pede um jogo em que as decisões de uma missão se conectam. No nosso jogo, cada peça escolhida muda massa, energia, dados, custo e vida útil ao mesmo tempo. Mais massa pede um foguete maior e mais caro. Painéis solares rendem menos longe do Sol. Instrumentos potentes geram mais dados e pedem antenas melhores.  Os eventos durante o voo testam o que o jogador construiu, e no final o jogo explica o resultado.
3. Por que é importante?
Quase ninguém tem a chance de viver uma missão espacial inteira. Em geral aprende-se cada assunto separado e não se vê como eles pesam uns contra os outros. O jogo deixa a pessoa errar, ver o motivo e tentar de novo, sem precisar saber nada antes. Roda no navegador e pode ser usado em sala de aula. A ideia é mostrar que engenharia espacial é feita de escolhas e compromissos, e despertar o interesse de quem está começando.
projectDetails.details:
Descrição detalhada do projeto

O que ele faz?

O jogador passa por cinco etapas. No briefing, escolhe o contrato e o nível de dificuldade (Iniciante, Engenheiro ou Diretor), ou joga no modo sandbox, sem limite de orçamento. Na engenharia, monta a nave com chassi, painéis solares, baterias, RTG, instrumentos, antenas, propulsores e computador de bordo, e escolhe a órbita e o foguete. No voo, decide como reagir a anomalias como tempestade solar, micrometeoroide e eclipse. Na superfície, anda pelo planeta e cumpre objetivos como coletar amostras, instalar um robô ou montar uma base. No debriefing, vê a pontuação e a análise da missão.

Como funciona?

Por trás do hangar há um motor que soma massa, custo, energia, dados e comunicação de tudo o que foi escolhido e confere se a missão fecha. Ele considera que os painéis solares perdem força com a distância ao Sol, que o sinal enfraquece longe da Terra e que o foguete precisa de margem de massa. Considera também o delta-v exigido, a órbita escolhida e a vida útil. Se algo não fecha, o jogo explica o porquê e bloqueia o lançamento. Durante o voo, as opções disponíveis dependem do que foi instalado: com baterias, computador redundante ou chassi reforçado, o jogador ganha escolhas mais seguras. A pontuação junta o valor científico, a economia de orçamento e os objetivos cumpridos no planeta. Também dá para salvar um projeto, compartilhar por código e comparar com o melhor resultado anterior.

Quais são os benefícios?

O jogador aprende vendo o sistema inteiro funcionar junto, e pode refazer o projeto quantas vezes quiser. Os níveis, as dicas e o tutorial ajudam quem está começando, e o sandbox serve para quem quer experimentar sem limite. Não precisa instalar nada, então é fácil usar em aula.

O que esperamos alcançar?

Queremos que as pessoas percebam que projetar uma missão é equilibrar várias coisas ao mesmo tempo, e que isso desperte curiosidade pela área. Daqui para frente, queremos testar o jogo com mais gente, fazer um modo para até quatro jogadores, desafios diários, medalhas e uma versão em inglês.

Ferramentas, linguagens e software

Fizemos o jogo em HTML, CSS e JavaScript, num único arquivo que roda direto no navegador. Os gráficos 3D usam a biblioteca Three.js, com formas geradas por código em vez de modelos prontos. As fontes vêm do Google Fonts, e o ranking e os projetos salvos ficam no armazenamento do navegador. Também criamos um protótipo de servidor em Python (Flask) para um futuro modo cooperativo. Basta um navegador com WebGL, no computador ou no celular. Os números do jogo (massa, custo, energia, delta-v) são simplificados e inventados, feitos para ensinar o raciocínio de uma missão.

projectDetails.name: Project SOLARS
projectDetails.summary:
"**Solars — Aprender explorando. Evoluir decidindo.**

O Solars é um jogo educativo de simulação espacial que transforma os desafios da exploração lunar em uma experiência interativa para crianças de 7 a 12 anos.

Durante uma missão de 10 dias, os jogadores assumem o controle de uma base lunar e precisam gerenciar recursos essenciais, como energia e oxigênio, realizar pesquisas científicas e proteger dois astronautas dos riscos da radiação e das tempestades solares.

O projeto aborda o desafio de tornar conhecimentos científicos sobre exploração espacial mais acessíveis, traduzindo situações complexas em decisões práticas e consequências compreensíveis.

Sua importância está em aproximar crianças da ciência e da exploração espacial por meio da experimentação, estimulando o raciocínio lógico, o planejamento, a resolução de problemas e a curiosidade científica.
projectDetails.details:
O que é o Solars?

O Solars é um protótipo de jogo educativo para navegador que simula os desafios de administrar uma base lunar. A experiência combina estratégia, gerenciamento de recursos e conceitos científicos para aproximar crianças de 7 a 12 anos da exploração espacial.

Como funciona?

O jogador assume a responsabilidade por uma missão de 10 dias com dois astronautas. A cada dia, precisa avaliar as condições da base, planejar atividades e tomar decisões que afetam os recursos disponíveis e a segurança da tripulação.

A experiência está organizada em cinco mecânicas principais:

- Gestão de recursos: acompanhar energia e oxigênio e planejar sua utilização.
- Planejamento diário: escolher atividades e avaliar os custos de cada decisão.
- Eventos solares: interpretar previsões e decidir quando utilizar o abrigo de proteção.
- Pesquisa científica: realizar experimentos para alcançar a meta de 20 pontos científicos.
- Feedback e aprendizado: consultar os resultados de cada dia e compreender as consequências das escolhas.

O objetivo é completar os 10 dias, manter a tripulação segura e atingir a meta científica.

Quais são os benefícios?

O Solars permite explorar conceitos que normalmente são apresentados de maneira teórica, transformando-os em situações práticas de tomada de decisão.

A proposta busca desenvolver raciocínio lógico, pensamento crítico, planejamento, resolução de problemas e interesse por ciência, tecnologia e exploração espacial.

O que esperamos alcançar?

Queremos demonstrar como jogos educativos podem tornar conhecimentos científicos complexos mais acessíveis e envolventes, incentivando crianças a aprender por meio da experimentação.

Como evolução, o projeto poderá incorporar novos cenários, níveis de dificuldade, conteúdos científicos e recursos educacionais para utilização em ambientes escolares.

Tecnologias e ferramentas

O projeto foi concebido como uma aplicação web responsiva, sem necessidade de hardware específico ou integrações externas.

A arquitetura proposta utiliza React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, componentes reutilizáveis e um motor de simulação local, com eventos predefinidos e cálculos executados no navegador.

As ferramentas de apoio incluem ChatGPT para concepção, documentação e desenvolvimento da proposta, geração de imagens por IA para os assets visuais e Lovable como plataforma planejada para implementação.

projectDetails.name: Horus Nasa TimeLine
projectDetails.summary:
Horus NASA Timeline is a bilingual (EN / PT-BR) interactive web platform that transforms the history of spacecraft hardware left behind by NASA since the 1960s into an engaging visual and audio experience for school-age students.
To connect this engineering hardware with the science it enabled, we built a navigable 3D Solar System observatory featuring planetary surface maps and markers anchored to official landing and trajectory coordinates across the Moon, Mars, Asteroids 433 Eros and 4 Vesta, Dwarf Planet 1 Ceres, heliocentric orbit, and interstellar space, alongside Earth's permanent NSSDCA archive. The platform combines a chronological timeline of 64 milestones (1966–2026) — tracking each mission from launch to its current operational or dormant state — with an auto-advancing Guided Tour synchronized to spatial soundscapes and authentic NASA recordings, official NASA/USGS 3D spacecraft models, 2.5D archival photo galleries, and an interactive 72-flight telemetry explorer for the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter.
By replacing static lists of facts with a browser-based interactive exploration, the project helps spark scientific curiosity in young learners and brings students closer to aerospace engineering and planetary science. 
Built strictly from verified NASA and NSSDCA datasets and media — with zero fabricated 3D meshes or data — it ensures scientific integrity while remaining freely accessible worldwide in English and Portuguese.

projectDetails.name: HemoSpaceApp
projectDetails.summary:
The conditions of the space environment, to which the human body is not naturally adapted, pose a challenge to astronauts' health. Exposure to microgravity causes changes in cardiovascular system functioning, which can become more pronounced during long-duration missions.

In response to this challenge, we developed a system focused on monitoring astronauts' cardiovascular health, using data from medical examinations they already undergo daily. Based on these data, we created an intuitive, organized, and easy-to-understand interface.

The project's main innovation lies in how information is presented. Although health data is already collected and made available to astronauts, it is often displayed through extensive charts containing large amounts of information. Considering the number of health indicators astronauts must monitor during their missions, we aim to make this analysis more straightforward and accessible.

Our solution organizes health indicators into different body systems, using visual elements and a color-coded system to facilitate the identification of potential health changes.

The prototype also has the potential to expand to monitoring other human body systems and can be adapted for applications on Earth, making health monitoring more accessible and easier to understand.

projectDetails.name: Lunar Landing Site Navigator
projectDetails.summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator helps mission planners choose where and when to land near the lunar south pole. It shows, hour by hour, when the Sun is up for power and when Earth is in view for a direct radio link, over the real terrain horizon of each site.

- Sun and Earth positions come from NASA's SPICE ephemerides.
- The terrain comes from LRO's LOLA elevation model.
- Comparison: you can compare up to three sites.
- Any point: you can click any point on a 3D map and get results in under a second.

Our results match JPL Horizons to within 0.005° and NASA's PGDA illumination maps to within 1.5 percentage points on average.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

Near the lunar south pole the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon, and Earth wobbles above and below it. A hill 10 km away can decide whether a lander has power or can talk to Earth, so flat-horizon estimates are not enough. Our tool builds the real 360° horizon of each site from NASA's LOLA terrain (including the Moon's curvature), tracks the Sun and Earth every hour from November 2026 to December 2028, and reports what a planner needs: how much of the Sun's disk is visible, whether Earth is in view, when the next sunset or Earthset comes, and how long the longest night lasts.

You can pick one of 10 candidate sites, search a crater name, type coordinates or click the 3D map. You can compare up to three sites for the next 30 days from any date. A month-by-month strip shows the share of hours with Sun, with Earth and with both for every month, so if a launch slips you see which month still works: at Malapert Massif, Sun and Earth together go from 37% of hours in April 2028 to 80% in October 2028. For students and the public, a four-step tour, "Why the south pole is hard", explains the physics with "Show me" buttons that set the app to the case that proves each point.

WHAT WE LEARNED

More sunlight does not always mean a better site. For a landing on 14 November 2026, Shackleton Rim is sunlit 87% of the time overall but has only 13 days with both Sun and Earth in the next 30 days. Malapert Massif has 22 days with both, because Earth stays in view much longer. The Shackleton crater floor, only about 10 km from the rim, gets 0% Sun and 0% Earth in two years: a permanently shadowed region where water ice may exist.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Terrain: the LRO LOLA polar elevation model (120 m per pixel) is used to cast 720 rays from each site, up to 150 km. The highest terrain angle in each direction is the horizon.

2. Sun and Earth: NASA/NAIF SPICE kernels (DE440) give their direction from the site every hour.

3. Visibility: we compare the Sun and Earth with the horizon (fraction of the Sun's disk above it; whether Earth's center is above it).

4. Browser: a static web app (Svelte, D3, three.js). For custom points it repeats the same calculation in the browser on a 240 m version of the terrain.

HOW WE KNOW IT IS RIGHT

Sun and Earth positions match JPL Horizons within 0.005° (automated tests). The sunlit share matches NASA's PGDA average illumination maps within 1.5 percentage points on average across the 10 sites. The horizon code is tested on two cases with exact answers (a smooth sphere and a wall of known height). Limits are stated in the app: 120 m terrain resolution (240 m for custom points), no atmosphere or refraction, and Earth counts as visible when its center is above the horizon.

WHY IT MATTERS

Artemis missions plan to land near the south pole. A planner can use this tool to choose a landing date with the most days of both power and a direct link, see the exact hour when the Sun or Earth will disappear, and check any spot in seconds without installing software.

CODE

https://github.com/marcelin1555/lunar-landing-site-navigator

USE OF AI

We used an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) for research, discussing the architecture, generating and reviewing code, and helping translate this written submission from Portuguese to English. The author made all design decisions, checked the data and results against NASA references (JPL Horizons and PGDA maps), and reviewed the final work. No images, video or audio in this project were generated by AI: the demo is a screen recording of the real app.

projectDetails.name: SPHEREx Viewer
projectDetails.summary:
SPHEREx Viewer is a free public website that turns NASA's SPHEREx archive into a short movie of the sky. Pick a challenge target or type any coordinate, and it shows real SPHEREx images of that patch of sky epoch by epoch, aligned on a common grid. Blink and Difference modes, like the comparator that found Pluto, make whatever moved or changed brightness stand out while the static sky disappears.

A Python pipeline queries IRSA, removes zodiacal light, discards bad pixels, aligns hundreds of exposures and stacks them per epoch. The site also builds each target's 0.75-5 µm spectrum from individual exposures, overlays Gaia DR3 and AllWISE on an all-sky map, and offers false color, shareable links and a Portuguese/English interface.

All five challenge targets pass an automated science validation against SIMBAD and Gaia: WISE 0855 appears only at 4-5 µm and moves as predicted, Barnard's Star's motion is measured to 0.02 pixel, and both variable stars change brightness at over 12 sigma. Data refresh every three days and are published only if validation passes.

SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months, but comparing its images takes expert skills. SPHEREx Viewer lets anyone look for the next moving dot.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

SPHEREx Viewer turns NASA's SPHEREx archive into a short movie of the sky. You pick one of the challenge targets or type any coordinate (degrees or sexagesimal) or an object name, and the site shows real SPHEREx images of that patch of sky, one frame per epoch, aligned on a common grid. A fixed crosshair and a circle at the catalog-predicted position guide the eye. Four modes help you compare: Play (the epochs in order), Blink (two epochs back and forth, like the comparator Clyde Tombaugh used to find Pluto), Difference (one epoch minus another, in units of noise, so the static sky disappears and only what changed remains) and Sum (all epochs stacked for depth). You can switch between the six detectors (0.75 to 5 µm), use false color (D6, D3, D1 as red, green, blue), mark unreliable pixels, choose a 6′ or 10′ field, and share the exact view through the URL or embed it in another page.

For each challenge target the site also shows a 0.75 to 5 µm spectrum built from individual exposures (each SPHEREx exposure sees the target through a different part of its linear variable filter) and warns when a neighbor star falls inside the measurement aperture. An all-sky SPHEREx map, with Gaia DR3 and AllWISE overlays, answers "is this dot already known?" and opens any spot in the viewer.

How it works

A Python pipeline queries the IRSA archive (TAP, with SIA as a fallback), downloads a cutout of every exposure, subtracts the zodiacal light, discards bad pixels using the quality flags in two levels, reprojects everything onto one tangent-plane grid with normalized interpolation, groups exposures into epochs and stacks each epoch with inverse-variance weights. The output is a small, formal data contract (JSON Schema): a field.json plus float32 frames of about 14 KB each. The browser does contrast, blinking, differencing and stacking locally, so changing modes needs no new requests.

The five challenge targets are pre-processed in 6′ and 10′ and published as static files, so they open instantly. Any other coordinate goes to a FastAPI service that processes the field on demand and reports progress while it downloads. A GitHub Actions workflow refreshes the targets every three days with new SPHEREx data, runs a scientific validation against independent catalogs, and publishes only if it passes.

Results and benefits

All five challenge targets pass the automated validation (16 tests on real data, checked against SIMBAD and Gaia DR3):

  • WISE 0855 appears only at 4 to 5 µm, at the predicted position (0.12 to 0.19 px).
  • Barnard's Star moves about 11″ north in a year, measured to about 0.02 px.
  • Epsilon Indi B is detected at S/N 250 to 640, and its motion matches.
  • RW Aurigae brightens 1.35× between epochs (12σ), and R Draconis fades to 0.46× (15σ).
  • Field stars stay put to 0.02 to 0.04 px: the alignment is about 25 times better than a pixel.

The benefit is access. Seeing what moved in SPHEREx data used to require querying an archive, reading FITS files and aligning hundreds of rotated images. Now it takes a browser and a few seconds, for a student, an amateur astronomer or a researcher who wants a quick look.

Intended impact

SPHEREx maps the whole sky every six months, which is far more sky than professional astronomers can inspect by eye. Citizen-science projects such as Backyard Worlds have shown that volunteers comparing images find real brown dwarfs and moving objects. SPHEREx Viewer brings that method to a new mission in the infrared, where cold, nearby objects shine, and makes it easy to share a candidate with a single link. It is also a teaching tool: Pluto's discovery method, live, with today's data.

Tools and technologies

  • Python 3.12 with Astropy, reproject and NumPy (pipeline); FastAPI (API); uv for environments.
  • TypeScript with Vite, no UI framework; Vitest for tests; Aladin Lite for the all-sky map.
  • JSON Schema as the contract between backend and frontend.
  • GitHub Pages (site), Render free tier (API), GitHub Actions (automatic updates and tests).
  • Data: SPHEREx DR1 and QR3 images and the all-sky HiPS cube from NASA/IPAC IRSA; SIMBAD; Gaia DR3 and AllWISE via VizieR.
  • Development was test-driven: 192 automated tests, including the scientific validation. AI assistance (Claude Code) was used for coding, documentation and review.
  • No special hardware: a laptop and free cloud services.

What makes it creative

  • It treats the archive as a time-lapse, in the spirit of Tombaugh's blink comparator, and keeps that metaphor in the design: epochs are shown like glass photographic plates, with red pencil marks for the predicted position.
  • It uses the 102 bands creatively: stacking all exposures of a detector per epoch for depth, false color from three detectors, and a spectrum assembled from exposures that each sample a different wavelength.
  • The Difference mode is expressed in units of noise, not raw brightness, so what stands out is statistically real change.
  • Coordinates from another epoch (like the 2010 position of WISE 0855 in the challenge text) are recognized and open the object where it is today.

Factors we considered

  • People without astronomy training: a plain-language introduction and "how to read" steps at the top, target descriptions written for non-experts with a "what to look for" hint, a dark-sky default, and the interface in English and Portuguese.
  • Scientific honesty: positions propagated by proper motion, quality flags shown instead of hidden, warnings when a neighbor star contaminates the spectrum, and a validation that blocks publication if the science fails.
  • Reliability: the IRSA services went down during the hackathon, so the pipeline falls back from TAP to SIA, retries with backoff, skips and reports single failed exposures, and never caches a transient error.
  • Cost and maintenance: everything runs on free tiers, with no database; new SPHEREx releases are a configuration change.
  • Speed: challenge targets are pre-processed and served as static files; the browser handles all interaction.
  • Openness: open source under GPL-3.0, shareable links and embed mode so results can be cited and reused.

projectDetails.details:
ECOBEATS – EARTH JUKEBOX 3D

Listen to Our Planet. Discover Earth Through Music.

EcoBeats – Earth Jukebox 3D is an interactive web experience that transforms Earth's environmental and climate information into a dynamic symphonic musical experience. Inspired by the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, The Earth Information Jukebox, the project explores an innovative way to connect science, technology, music, and environmental awareness by allowing people to not only see our planet's changes but also hear them.

At the heart of EcoBeats is an interactive 3D representation of Earth, designed as a digital planetary instrument. Users can explore the globe, observe environmental indicators, and experience how different regions and natural phenomena can be translated into musical elements.

HOW THE INTERFACE WORKS

The interface features a rotating 3D Earth with environmental visualization layers representing important planetary processes, including temperature variations, atmospheric conditions, winds, ocean currents, vegetation, and biomass indicators.

A vertical scanning line moves across the rotating planet, progressively reading the visual indicators and creating a continuous connection between the geographical information and the musical composition. As users select different regions or environmental layers, the musical experience changes, reflecting the characteristics and variations represented by the selected data.

FROM SCIENTIFIC DATA TO SYMPHONIC MUSIC

EcoBeats uses the concept of data sonification: translating scientific information into sound through musical parameters.

Environmental variables can influence different musical characteristics, such as:

  • Temperature: influences musical pitch and tonal variation.
  • Wind and atmospheric movement: inspires dynamic textures and rhythmic patterns.
  • Ocean currents: influences rhythmic sequences and melodic movement.
  • Vegetation and biomass: contributes to harmonic layers and musical density.
  • Environmental variations: create changes in intensity, rhythm, and orchestral composition.

The result is an evolving instrumental soundtrack inspired by the complexity and interconnectedness of Earth's natural systems.

The musical experience is designed around a symphonic orchestral aesthetic, transforming environmental information into an engaging and emotionally meaningful listening experience rather than presenting scientific data exclusively through charts and numerical indicators.

INTERACTIVE EXPERIENCE

The platform combines visual exploration and audio interaction through an intuitive interface featuring:

  • Interactive 3D planetary navigation.
  • Environmental visualization layers.
  • Selection of geographical regions and environmental indicators.
  • Dynamic musical changes associated with the selected information.
  • Play, pause, and stop controls.
  • A visual audio experience that connects sound and planetary information.

This approach encourages users to explore the planet actively, discover environmental patterns, and understand how different Earth systems interact.

SCIENTIFIC FOUNDATION AND NASA DATA

The project is inspired by NASA's Earth Information Center (EIC) visualizations and the scientific resources made available through NASA's Earth observation programs.

Its proposed data framework includes environmental information related to surface temperature, atmospheric processes, ocean dynamics, vegetation, biomass, and other indicators of planetary change.

By connecting scientific visualization with musical interpretation, EcoBeats offers a new way to communicate the value of Earth observation data and encourage curiosity about our planet.

INNOVATION, ACCESSIBILITY, AND IMPACT

One of EcoBeats' central ideas is that scientific information can be experienced through more than one sense. By combining visual and auditory representations, the project explores opportunities to make Earth science more engaging and potentially more accessible to people with different ways of perceiving and interacting with information.

Beyond its technological approach, EcoBeats aims to inspire environmental awareness. It transforms abstract scientific indicators into an experience that can be explored, heard, and remembered.

OUR VISION

What if we could listen to the Earth?

What if rising temperatures, moving ocean currents, changing vegetation, and atmospheric dynamics could become part of a musical composition?

EcoBeats turns this question into an interactive experience, connecting planetary science and artistic expression.

Our goal is to transform Earth's scientific information into a living symphony — where every region, every environmental signal, and every planetary change can contribute to a new way of understanding our world.

EcoBeats – Listen to Our Planet. Science has a sound.

projectDetails.name: Data trends and floods
projectDetails.summary:
Hydrological Trends and Flood Risk Through NASA Earth 

Using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), Mann-Kendall, and trend analysis, the tool investigates statistically significant environmental changes that may influence flood generation. It integrates NASA Earth science data to analyze long-term trends in precipitation, soil moisture, evapotranspiration, and atmospheric conditions.

Rather than examining rainfall independently, the platform evaluates interactions between atmospheric water input and terrestrial water storage to identify changes in flood susceptibility.

Historical data are retrieved through NASA POWER, primarily using MERRA-2 reanalysis. The application calculates accumulated rainfall, antecedent precipitation, soil wetness, and compound conditions involving heavy rainfall and elevated soil moisture.

By integrating NASA Earth science data, hydrological indicators, and statistical methods, Earth Science Data Analysis transforms complex environmental datasets into accessible scientific information. The platform aims to support researchers, students, environmental professionals, and local decision-makers in understanding regional environmental changes and identifying conditions that may contribute to flood susceptibility.
projectDetails.details:
Hydrological Trends and Flood Risk Through NASA Earth Observation Data With Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), Mann-Kendall, and trend analysis

The tool is designed to investigate whether flood-prone regions are experiencing statistically significant changes in environmental conditions that influence flood generation. It integrates Earth science variables provided by NASA to investigate long-term trends in precipitation, soil moisture, evapotranspiration, and atmospheric conditions.

NASA provides gridded datasets covering areas of approximately 50 × 60 km, containing environmental variables that may influence flood risk. Trends in these variables are analyzed to identify environmental changes that could affect flood susceptibility.

The tool addresses an important challenge in Earth science: environmental variables do not necessarily follow the same trends across different geographical regions.

Even when driven by the same large-scale climate processes, precipitation, soil moisture, and atmospheric conditions may exhibit opposite trends depending on regional characteristics.

For example, a region may experience increasing precipitation while simultaneously experiencing decreasing soil moisture due to increased evapotranspiration. These opposing trends can significantly influence the hydrological response of a watershed.

Rather than analyzing precipitation independently, the platform investigates the interaction between atmospheric water input and terrestrial water storage to identify environmental changes that may influence flood susceptibility.

Flood generation is influenced by multiple interconnected environmental processes.

Precipitation provides the immediate water input, while soil moisture represents the antecedent hydrological condition of the terrain. When soil moisture is already high, the available capacity for additional infiltration may be reduced, increasing the potential for surface runoff.

Conversely, when soil moisture decreases, a larger proportion of rainfall may infiltrate into the soil, potentially reducing runoff under certain conditions. This relationship means that changes in rainfall alone cannot fully explain changes in flood behavior.

Wasko and Nathan (2019), in *Influence of changes in rainfall and soil moisture on trends in flooding*, demonstrated that increasing rainfall extremes can coexist with decreasing flood magnitudes when soil moisture trends move in the opposite direction. This finding provides the scientific foundation for analyzing precipitation and soil moisture together rather than treating them as independent indicators.

**Research question:**

Are historical flood-prone regions experiencing statistically significant changes in precipitation, soil moisture, and atmospheric conditions that could explain changes in their hydrological behavior?

The main objective is to develop an accessible analytical platform capable of identifying and evaluating long-term environmental trends using NASA Earth science datasets.

1. Retrieve historical Earth science variables from NASA POWER.

2. Identify long-term trends in precipitation and soil moisture.

3. Investigate relationships between rainfall and antecedent soil moisture.

4. Calculate accumulated precipitation and antecedent precipitation indices.

5. Identify periods of simultaneous heavy rainfall and elevated soil moisture.

6. Quantify the magnitude and direction of environmental trends.

7. Evaluate statistical significance using complementary statistical methods.

8. Compare environmental trends across geographically distinct regions.

The selection of environmental variables is based on their relevance to the hydrological processes associated with flood generation.

The challenge is not simply to retrieve as many Earth science variables as possible, but to identify a scientifically meaningful combination of variables that allows the investigation of environmental changes.

- Atmospheric water input: precipitation.

- Terrestrial water storage: soil moisture.

- Land-atmosphere exchange: evapotranspiration.

Additional atmospheric variables provide context for understanding environmental conditions that influence water availability and surface processes.

The selection is supported by hydrological research demonstrating that flood magnitude depends on the interaction between precipitation characteristics and antecedent catchment conditions.

SCIENTIFIC REFERENCES

Wasko, C., & Nathan, R. (2019). Influence of changes in rainfall and soil moisture on trends in flooding. Journal of Hydrology, 575, 432–441. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhydrol.2019.05.054

Simpson, I. R., et al. (2025). Confronting Earth System Model trends with observations. Science Advances, 11, eadt8035. https://doi.org/10.1126/sciadv.adt8035

NASA POWER. Prediction of Worldwide Energy Resources — Data Sources and Methodology. https://power.larc.nasa.gov/docs/methodology/data/sources_hydrology/

NASA POWER. Daily API Documentation. https://power.larc.nasa.gov/docs/services/api/temporal/daily/

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: for_ecastBR
projectDetails.summary: We developed for_ecastBR, an interactive climate analytics platform that enables users to inspect, analyze, and forecast precipitation dynamics across Brazil's states and the Federal District. It directly addresses the challenge by providing state-by-state time series visualization and monthly anomaly classification, but it goes further: the system calculates non-parametric Mann-Kendall trend statistics and executes short-term machine learning forecasts, delivering instant feedback on historical climate shifts and near-future rainfall estimates. Its importance lies in being more than a visualization tool; it is a climate diagnostic and validation framework. Through its integration of the Meteomatics Weather API via spatial polygon queries, for_ecastBR benchmarks machine learning predictions against a strict seasonal baseline using zero-leakage temporal validation. It doesn't just answer how much it rained in the past, but whether predictive models genuinely outperform simple historical patterns, making scientific transparency and evidence-based planning a fundamental priority.
projectDetails.details:
The for_ecast ingests daily accumulated rainfall from the Meteomatics Weather API using spatial polygon queries for state boundaries, aggregating daily values into monthly state-wide time series.

The system operates through dual analytical engines:

Statistical: Computes localized monthly anomaly categories (relative to historical baseline calendar months for each state) and applies non-parametric Mann-Kendall trend tests to detect statistically significant long-term climate shifts and trend magnitudes.

Machine Learning: Utilizes a Random Forest Regressor trained on historical data from 2006 to 2025. By leveraging temporal cyclical features (sine/cosine month encoding), historical lags (1, 2, 3, and 12 months), and rolling averages (3 and 12 months) constructed strictly from past observations, the model accurately forecasts weather conditions for the upcoming month or year. The ML framework operates recursively to project multi-step forecasts and estimate future precipitation thresholds across a 12-month experimental horizon. Crucially, for_ecastBR empowers users to compare and decide which model best meets their operational needs—either the baseline Seasonal model or the Random Forest Regressor—based on state-specific MAE and RMSE metrics.

for_ecast: Data for Tomorrow

The for_ecast gives hydrologists, agricultural planners, disaster management teams, and climate researchers all over Brazil easy access to solid, evidence-based data. By turning complex weather API streams into state-by-state trend insights and reliable short-term forecasts, it supports regional risk planning and climate adaptation.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

The project was developed using a combination of Python for data processing, statistical analysis, and machine learning, and web technologies for the interactive dashboard.

  • Programming languages: Python 3, JavaScript, HTML5, and CSS3. SVG was also used for charts and editable visual elements.
  • Python libraries and tools: Pandas and NumPy, data cleaning, manipulation, and numerical calculations; SciPy, statistical analysis and tests; Matplotlib, data visualization and statistical charts; Scikit-learn, machine learning models, including Random Forest and model evaluation; Requests, API data collection; Pytest, automated testing.
  • Data sources and APIs: The project includes precipitation data collected through the Meteomatics API, along with historical datasets organized in CSV files.
  • Software and development tools: Git for version control, Python's built-in HTTP server for running the dashboard locally, and a web browser to access and interact with the dashboard. Figma is included in the dashboard documentation as a design and implementation reference.
  • Dashboard technologies: Vanilla JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and inline SVG. The dashboard uses locally generated JSON data and does not require a hosted database, external browser APIs, or third-party JavaScript frameworks.
  • Hardware: The project was developed as a software-based workflow on a standard computer. No specialized hardware, such as GPUs, servers, or dedicated scientific equipment, is documented as a requirement.

projectDetails.name: Astro Health
projectDetails.summary:
Imagine it is day od a 900-day mission, on the way to Mars. Earth is up to 22 minutes away, so Dr. Okafor, the crew medical officer, leads every medical decision on board.
Commander Silva wakes up with a body temperature of 37.6 °C. Astro Health marks it "Watch" and tells her what to do: drink 250 ml of water and rest for 30 minutes. Once she ticks both steps, her Astroskin shirt takes a new reading on its own.
Her other readings arrive live, with nothing to type: 7 h 10 min of sleep, 116/76 mmHg, 98% SpO₂ and 1.9 of 2.5 L of water. A 3D astronaut shows each one on the suit. Her readiness is 86/100, down 3 points since yesterday but still above the 80 needed for a spacewalk. When she asks "How is my health today?", the assistant answers with these exact numbers and shows where to see them. At 08:00 UTC, the chat reminds her to take vitamin D.
Meanwhile, Dr. Okafor's panel puts Eng. Tanaka first: readiness 58 and a fever. If any reading reaches "Act now", a voice guides the rescue step by step and alerts the crew with the location.
Offline, free and accessible, Astro Health turns data into decisions when Earth is too far away.
projectDetails.details:
Astro Health is a web app for astronauts and the crew medical officer. It tracks health before, during and after missions to the space station, the Moon and Mars. Each screen shows only what matters in that phase.

Continuous monitoring.

  • No typing: the Astroskin shirt (heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, breathing, temperature and sleep), the water dispenser and the exercise machines (ARED, treadmill and cycle) send data on their own. The app updates numbers and charts every 5 seconds.
  • The only vital sign typed by hand: blood glucose, and only when the glucometer is not connected over Bluetooth. Mood and symptoms are logged by the astronaut.

3D astronaut.

  • Sensor points: NASA's EMU suit shows 8 points colored by status. Tapping a point opens its current value, the last 24 hours and what to do.
  • Symptoms: tapping a body region logs a symptom with a 1–5 intensity, and each level comes with fixed guidance.

Nausea mode.

  • When nausea or vomiting is logged, the screen shows only the essentials, with no animation and a "what helps now" bar.

Voice-guided emergency.

  • How it starts: when a vital sign reaches "Act now", or with the SOS button.
  • What happens: the voice reads the values and each step of the guide, alerts the crew in real time and shows where the emergency is on the habitat map and accepts the commands "next", "repeat" and "help".
  • CPR: includes a metronome set to 110 compressions per minute and a timer

"Ask" assistant.

  • How to ask: pick a suggestion, type or speak.
  • What it answers:What it answers: it uses real data (health today, weekly trends, readiness, sleep, tasks, medication) and passages from the app’s guides, always with ‘where to see it in the app'.

Messages and goals.

  • Health chat: reminders for tasks, medication (vitamin D and the contraceptive pill) and exams arrive as messages, with no pop-ups.
  • Daily goals: water, exercise, sleep and a mood check-in, with private achievements.

Doctor's panel.

  • Crew: health records, alerts sorted by urgency with decision guides, and review of the neck ultrasound the astronaut sends.
  • Before flight: scheduling of pre-flight exams.

Modules by sex.

  • Women's health: cycle plan, pill and its supply, urinary symptoms and preparation for the flight.
  • Men's health: early alerts for vision problems (SANS), noise exposure and hearing tests, and radiation and fertility.

Fine-grained privacy.

  • Choice by data type: each person decides who sees each type of data: flight surgeon, crew medical officer or researchers (with consent).
  • Mission control: only sees whether each astronaut is ‘fit for duty’ or not.

Benefits that solve current problems

  • Autonomy far from Earth: with up to 22 minutes of delay, the app gives immediate guidance that is offline and deterministic.
  • No manual logging of vital signs: data comes from the sensors, so astronauts neither lose time nor make typing errors.
  • Every status says how to get back to normal: each "Watch" shows "Back to normal when…" and the steps to follow.
  • Hands-free emergency: voice, captions and spoken commands, with an automatic alert to the crew.
  • The gap in women's data: only about 75 women have flown to space. The women's module addresses their needs and lets them donate anonymous data to research.
  • Less visual clutter: notifications in a chat, nausea mode, and one test for every element on screen: "does it help the person act on their own health in this phase?".

Intended impact

  • Medical autonomy: support crews on long missions such as Artemis and Mars, in line with NASA's Human Research Program.
  • Early detection: Early detection: help flag the first signs of risks such as SANS (Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome), jugular vein thrombosis, bone loss and radiation effects.
  • More inclusive science: collect more data on women’s health in space.
  • Use on Earth: the same model (sensors, offline guidance and accessibility) serves isolated places such as offshore platforms, Antarctic stations and remote areas.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: vanilla JavaScript (no frameworks), HTML5 and CSS3, with the BEM methodology and design tokens.
    • Three.js r170 (3D, with GLTFLoader, DRACOLoader and RoomEnvironment);
    • Firebase JS SDK (Firestore and anonymous Auth, for real-time alerts).
  • Hardware considered: Astroskin shirt, radiation and acoustic dosimeters, Bluetooth glucometer, portable ultrasound, OCT, SLAMMD (mass measurement without gravity) and the ARED, T2 and CEVIS machines.
  • Infrastructure: Firebase Hosting (free Spark plan) and a back end modeled in Supabase/PostgreSQL. The App.records layer already uses the database tables and columns.
  • Quality: Playwright (regression tests at 414 and 1280 px) and axe-core (zero accessibility violations in light and dark themes).
  • Design: Figma/FigJam (UX research) and the official Space Apps 2026 visual standards.

Creative aspects

  • A clickable 3D astronaut as the interface for the body, with regions that light up when touched or hovered over.
  • Nausea mode as "space accessibility".
  • A voice-driven emergency guide that does not mistake its own speech for a command.
  • An assistant that answers with real numbers without generative AI: safe, predictable and offline.
  • A health chat instead of pop-ups.
  • Surface contexts: base and rover on the Moon and Mars, with a higher readiness score required on the rover (85 instead of 80), because help from the base is 40 minutes away.

Factors the team considered

Research came first. Before writing any code, we researched the whole picture:

  • how astronauts train before a mission;
  • how pre-flight, in-flight and post-flight exams are done today, and how health is monitored on board now;
  • what causes the most problems for astronauts (the pain points);
  • how the body reacts differently in women and men;
  • how life and medical support change between Earth, the space station, the Moon and Mars.

We mapped these findings in a UX study in FigJam. They decided which screens exist and what each one shows.

We put accessibility and usability first. We designed the interface for WCAG 2.2 AA and Nielsen's 10 heuristics from the start, not as a final check:

  • status shown with icons and text, never color alone;
  • full keyboard navigation;
  • large touch targets;
  • captions for every spoken word.

We also created a "nausea mode" for space sickness, and made sure every warning tells the astronaut how to get back to normal.

We worked in a clear front-end, back-end and QA flow:

  • Front end: pure JavaScript with the BEM methodology and a design system based on the official Space Apps brand, built mobile first and offline first. We added only a few free, locally hosted libraries (Three.js for the 3D astronaut, Firebase for real-time crew alerts).
  • Back end: we modeled the database in Supabase/PostgreSQL, and the app saves data with the same tables and columns.
  • QA: the main features were covered by automated tests on phone and desktop screen sizes, including accessibility checks in light and dark themes.

We defined a file architecture for performance. Shared code lives in assets/, each page in its own folder, and common parts are generated by one script. This keeps the code lean and reusable, loads heavy parts only when needed, and targets a PageSpeed score of 90 or higher.

We prioritized safety. No AI decides on medical care. The assistant and the emergency voice use fixed, verified texts with the real measured values, always show where the information comes from, and display "Not a medical device".

We worked as a team. We split the tasks so no one carried too much, and every member of the team contributed equally.

challengeDetails.title: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
challengeDetails.excerpt: Long-duration missions expose astronauts to space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment, which can bring immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events, and behavioral health problems. node.title: KATION
node.excerpt: We are a team of Computer Science and Computer Engineering students who developed Lunite, a web-based platform that simplifies the selection and comparison of potential lunar landing sites through interactive visualizations and mission-specific data.

projectDetails.name: Lunite
projectDetails.summary:
Lunite is a web platform that lets mission planners, educators, and the public compare lunar landing sites and dates in seconds. Why did we build it? Because the information needed to evaluate a landing site is scattered across different tools and the existing tools for planning a lunar landing have a structure that makes them slow to use and hard to share beyond specialist teams. The result? the process becomes inefficient, and the decision-making process slows down.

Lunite closes that gap. It brings that information together in one place. With a simple, intuitive interface, users go from accessible mission planning, through unique 3D visualizations of relevant data to be compared, to comparisons and results that can be shared easily.

Our vision is a platform where planners, educators, and the public analyze and compare landing sites using the same data and the same visual language. We stay close to our users, which is why simplicity, organization, and creativity drive our design: not just faster site evaluation, but wider access to lunar knowledge for everyone.
projectDetails.details:
THE PROBLEM

The tools available today for evaluating lunar landing sites, such as Quickmap, Moon Trek, and JPL Horizons, were built for detailed analysis, but their results are locked behind complex interfaces that make them hard to use whether for specialists or for the general public.

The main obstacle is that the information is scattered: to evaluate each combination of site and date, a planner has to navigate several interfaces, extract raw data from each one, and cross-reference it manually. Ephemeris and topographic data arrive untranslated, rather than as clear, comparable visualizations, which slows down scenario comparison exactly when it is needed most. Schedules shift and hardware gets delayed, and teams must reassess sites and dates quickly, yet there is no accessible tool to support that kind of agile planning.

The result is a gap between the abundance of technical data and the real ability to use it for decision-making, one that also keeps educators and the general public from understanding how a lunar landing is planned. That gap weighs even more heavily at the Moon's south pole, where many future missions are planned because of the presence of water ice. There, the terrain's geometry produces extreme variations in lighting and Earth visibility across lunar days and seasons, so small changes in site or date dramatically alter the available power and the communication windows.

WHAT OUR SOLUTION DOES

Lunite is a web tool that turns raw lunar data into an answer to one question: where, and when, can we land? The planner describes the mission once, choosing a curated site or any point on a 3D globe of the Moon, then setting probe parameters, dates, mission duration, allowed launch delay and tolerances for sunlight and communication. For each candidate point around the site, Lunite uses NASA's LOLA terrain and JPL Horizons positions of the Sun and Earth to compute the share of time in sunlight, the share with direct Earth communication, the longest darkness and the longest blackout. Valid points appear as vertical bars over the real 3D terrain, filtered and compared side by side, and the best candidates can be exported in a PDF report to share with the team.

This solves the problem by putting terrain and ephemeris in one place and translating them into percentages, hours and bars that specialists and non-specialists can read. When the schedule slips, Lunite slides the mission window day by day, fixes the best one and says which requirement to relax if nothing works. It also respects the south pole's sensitivity, with terrain resolution down to 10–40 m, real horizons that include the Moon's curvature, and landing precision as a parameter.

OUR DIFFERENTIALS

Lunite lets users compare periods and see how viable each site is in each one, while choosing only the metrics they care about. The data is shown in an intuitive way, through vertical bars that represent each site’s information.

What does that mean in practice?

Periods, not just places.

Launch dates change, and a site that works today may not work two weeks later. Lunite is built to answer “what if we land later?” as easily as “what if we land somewhere else?”. Users can see how the same site performs across different dates, and not only how one site compares with another. 

The user is in control, the visualization is unique and the data explains itself.

When the viable landing sites for a region are loaded, the user chooses one or more metrics that matter for the mission, such as sunlight duration or Earth visibility windows. Lunite displays vertical bars, one for each site, that show at a glance how well each one satisfies the selected metric (or set of metrics). Instead of opening several tools and cross-referencing numbers by hand, the planner quickly sees which sites stand out, and even non-specialists can interpret the chart.

From this overview, filters narrow the list of candidates further, discarding sites that fail requirements such as a minimum of power generation or Earth communication, which speeds up decision-making and avoids wasting time on unviable options. Finally, the user compares two sites side by side, fixing one and choosing another, or sequentially, stepping through the sites as a list. In both cases, the data is handpicked, only what truly matters for the decision, which makes the process much easier and more efficient.

Everything in one place: a simple and intuitive interface. 

Lunite brings together the data of all landing sites on a single platform, with a simple and intuitive interface. Users do not need to cross-reference information manually across different tools, which makes assessing viability and selecting the most suitable site less complex and more efficient. 

Shareable

Upon completing the analysis, users can generate a report detailing the specifics of the selected landing sites. This document allows a quick comparison of the strongest candidates and can be shared with the rest of the team, supporting the final decision on the landing site.

OUR IMPACT

Our mission starts from a simple observation: the solutions available today for choosing a landing site are too complex and too scattered. Lunite’s impact comes from reversing that, in three ways.

  • For mission planners, Lunite shortens the path between a changed constraint and a new decision. When a launch slips or hardware changes, teams can quickly identify a viable alternative site or date, and science and engineering teams can discuss the same visual evidence instead of translating between different tools.
  • For educators and students, Lunite turns ephemeris and topographic data into something that can be seen and explored. Rather than explaining in the abstract why the Moon’s south pole is so demanding, a teacher can show the Sun and Earth over the horizon and let students change the date themselves.
  • For the general public, Lunite lowers the barrier to understanding lunar exploration. Anyone can ask where and when a landing could work and receive an answer they can read, without specialist training.

As a result, Lunite leaves a clear legacy: solving the decentralization of lunar knowledge. By bringing it together in one place, with the same data and the same visual language for everyone, it allows more people to access it. Simplicity, organization, and creativity guide how we get there, and staying close to our users keeps us moving in the right direction.

projectDetails.name: Project Kbool4_on
projectDetails.summary:
The Kbool4_on Project 
Focuses on developing a Python-based platform for analyzing flame behavior in microgravity environments. The system combines image processing, computer vision, data analysis, and scientific visualization techniques to monitor and characterize combustion phenomena under reduced-gravity conditions. Using tools such as OpenCV, NumPy, Pandas, and Matplotlib, the platform automatically detects flame contours and extracts key parameters including diameter, area, brightness, and shape. The collected data are processed into graphs and statistical reports, providing a more accurate and efficient alternative to manual analysis methods. By improving the understanding of combustion dynamics in microgravity, the project contributes to spacecraft fire safety, future space exploration missions, and the advancement of combustion technologies. Its modular architecture also enables future integration of machine learning and predictive modeling techniques, creating a foundation for advanced research on fire behavior and safety in space environments.

Reference

NASA. NASA Studies Fire in Microgravity. NASA Scientific Visualization Studio. Available at: https://svs.gsfc.nasa.gov/31394. Accessed: November 14, 2026.
projectDetails.details:
Project Description

Kbool4_on is a Python-based platform designed to analyze flame behavior in microgravity environments using computer vision, image processing, and data analytics. The system processes images and videos of combustion experiments to automatically detect flame contours and extract key parameters such as diameter, area, brightness, and shape. These measurements are then analyzed and presented through graphs, statistics, and visual reports, enabling researchers to better understand combustion dynamics under reduced-gravity conditions.

The project addresses the challenge of studying fire behavior in space, where the absence of gravity significantly changes flame structure, heat transfer, and combustion efficiency. Traditional manual analysis methods are time-consuming and susceptible to measurement errors. By automating data extraction and analysis, our solution improves accuracy, efficiency, and reproducibility.

The intended impact of the project is to contribute to spacecraft fire safety, support future human space exploration missions, and advance scientific knowledge of combustion processes in microgravity. Understanding how flames behave in space can help engineers design safer spacecraft systems and develop innovative combustion technologies.

To develop the project, we used Python along with OpenCV for image processing and computer vision, NumPy for numerical computation, Pandas for data management, and Matplotlib for scientific visualization. The platform was developed on standard computer hardware and designed with a modular architecture that supports future integration of machine learning and predictive modeling techniques.

The creativity of the project lies in combining automated visual analysis with scientific data processing to create an accessible and scalable research tool for space-related combustion studies. Our team considered factors such as measurement accuracy, automation, usability, scientific relevance, scalability, and the potential for future enhancements, ensuring that the platform can evolve alongside emerging research needs in space science and fire safety.

projectDetails.name: LIASTRA AEROSPACE INNOVATION CENTER
projectDetails.summary:
The Aerospace Innovation Center (AIC) is an interactive 3D astronaut mission simulator developed by the LIASTRA Institute for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the challenge of creating a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. The project allows users of all ages to experience space exploration through realistic missions on Mars, the Moon, and aboard a replica of the International Space Station.

Players perform scientific experiments, manage life-support systems, cultivate plants, operate equipment, explore extraterrestrial environments, and respond to challenges such as solar storms and radiation exposure. The simulator integrates real scientific data from NASA, including solar activity, radiation measurements, and planetary orbital calculations.

By transforming complex scientific concepts into interactive missions, AIC makes aerospace education more accessible and engaging. It encourages critical thinking, problem-solving, and interest in STEM fields while helping users understand the scientific, technological, and human challenges of space exploration. Its importance lies in connecting real space research with hands-on learning, inspiring the next generation of scientists, engineers, and explorers.
projectDetails.details:
The Aerospace Innovation Center (AIC) is an interactive 3D space exploration and astronaut training simulator developed by the LIASTRA Institute for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It allows players of all ages to experience realistic space missions across Mars, the Moon, and a replica of the International Space Station.

Players complete missions involving resource management, space agriculture, scientific experiments, radiation protection, life-support systems, engineering, and survival challenges. The simulator incorporates real NASA scientific data, including solar activity from the DONKI API, radiation measurements, and planetary orbital calculations, connecting gameplay to actual space research.

The project promotes STEM education, scientific literacy, critical thinking, and problem-solving while making aerospace knowledge more accessible. Its main innovation is transforming real scientific research and historical space missions into interactive experiences that allow users to learn by doing.

It was developed using HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and Three.js (r128), with NASA APIs, scientific datasets, and 3D rendering technologies. The team prioritized scientific accuracy, accessibility, browser compatibility, educational value, and reliable data integration.

Our goal is to inspire future scientists, engineers, and explorers by demonstrating how science and technology can make space exploration accessible to everyone. The project is an independent educational initiative and is not an official NASA product.

projectDetails.name: Project MARSPIRE
projectDetails.summary:
Mars on Everyone – Explore Mars

The "Mars on Everyone" project is an interactive educational platform designed to bring people closer to space exploration and facilitate learning about the planet Mars. The platform features a character named Marti, who guides users through a journey of discovery. It includes an interactive map that integrates various layers of scientific data, such as optical characteristics, topography, temperature, mineral composition, atmospheric conditions, and radiation levels.

In addition to educational content, the project offers games, quizzes, and interactive activities—including a rover exploration experience inspired by NASA missions. A key objective is to contribute to the future of human exploration on Mars by developing resources that can help astronauts navigate, explore, and map the planet more safely and efficiently.

The project’s significance lies in making science more accessible and engaging, fostering curiosity, scientific thinking, and a deeper understanding of Mars. Our goal is to demonstrate that space exploration can be open to everyone, by bridging the gap between technology, education, and innovation.
projectDetails.details:
Marspire – Marti on Mars

"Marti on Mars" is a project developed with the goal of contributing to the future of human exploration on Mars. Our vision is to leverage technology, creativity, and innovation to bring people closer to space exploration—and, most importantly, to help find solutions that facilitate how astronauts move across the Martian surface.

A primary objective is to help astronauts walk and navigate on Mars with greater safety, efficiency, and ease, taking into account the challenges of that environment—such as low gravity, uneven terrain, Martian dust, and the planet's extreme conditions. We also aim to contribute to the mapping of the Martian surface, assisting in the understanding of the terrain and the identification of potential routes for exploration.

The project seeks to provide benefits both for science outreach and for the development of concepts related to space exploration. We intend to spark interest in science, encourage new technological solutions, and foster reflection on the challenges that future explorers of Mars may encounter.

To develop Marspire, we utilized various technological tools and artificial intelligence resources. These include ChatGPT and Claude AI, which assisted us in brainstorming ideas, organizing information, and developing the project; Lovable, used to build and structure the digital application; and GitHub, employed to store, organize, and manage the project’s files and code.

The creative aspect of the project lies in transforming curiosity about Mars into an initiative with a practical purpose: devising ways to assist humans in exploring the Red Planet. Beyond simply imagining what life on Mars might be like, we aim to contribute ideas that can help astronauts navigate the real-world challenges of its surface.

Throughout the development process, we took into account factors such as astronaut safety, the environmental conditions of Mars, mobility, accessibility, technological innovation, ease of use, and the scientific potential of the proposal. Our mission with Marspire is to help ensure that walking on and exploring Mars evolve from mere challenges of space exploration into increasingly safe and accessible possibilities. We want to be part of the generation that not only dreams of exploring other planets but also works to make such exploration a reality.
