projectDetails.name: Earth Sleuth
projectDetails.summary: "Earth-Sleuth is a climate intelligence platform that transforms NASA's open Earth observation data into accessible investigations. We help students, governments, and businesses understand what is changing in their environment, where it's changing, and whether the change is statistically significant, bridging the gap between raw scientific data and actionable decision-making."
projectDetails.details:
What exactly does it do and how does it work? Earth-Sleuth is a climate intelligence and science education web application that transforms open Earth observation data into accessible, investigative dossiers. Instead of overwhelming non-specialists with raw datasets, our platform guides users through a 6-step investigative journey:

  1. Case: The user asks a question (e.g., "Is it getting drier in Ceará?").
  2. Case File: The app proposes the region, variable, and period for the user to validate.
  3. Scene: A map displays the geographical context and scale.
  4. Report: The system generates a time series, calculates anomalies, and measures the rate of change per decade.
  5. Verdict: A deterministic statistical engine classifies the event as a "Real Trend" (p < 0.05), "Possible Noise," or "Insufficient Data."
  6. Board: The user receives a transparent, verifiable dashboard that cites the data source and methodology, ready to be shared.

What benefits does it offer? Earth-Sleuth democratizes environmental science by removing three major barriers: variable overload, spatial complexity, and statistical misinterpretation. It allows citizens, teachers, public managers, and businesses to explore environmental trends without needing advanced programming or climate science degrees. The main benefit is delivering clear, evidence-based answers to four critical questions: What is changing? Where is it changing? By how much? And is it statistically significant?

What is the intended impact of the project? Our intended impact aligns directly with the UN Sustainable Development Goals, specifically SDG 4 (Quality Education), SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation), and SDG 13 (Climate Action). By transforming raw satellite data into actionable insights, we aim to improve climate literacy in schools, support local governments (like Civil Defense) in urban and water planning, and help businesses (agriculture, insurance) mitigate climate-related economic risks. We want to prove that preparation begins with data.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use? We built a modern, hybrid architecture to ensure performance and reliability:

  • Frontend: Built with React, Next.js, and TypeScript, hosted on Vercel for a seamless, responsive user experience ([https://earthsleuth.lovable.app/](https://earthsleuth.lovable.app/)).
  • Visualizations: React-Leaflet for mapping coordinates and Recharts/Plotly.js for rendering time series and confidence intervals.
  • Backend & Analytics: A Python Serverless API handles data validation and the statistical engine (Mann-Kendall test, Sen’s Slope, and seasonal adjustments).
  • Data Sources: We integrated data derived from NASA POWER, Giovanni, and AppEEARS (including MODIS, GPM, and GLDAS missions).
  • Version Control: Managed via GitHub ([https://github.com/KarineDuarte15/earth-sleuth.git](https://github.com/KarineDuarte15/earth-sleuth.git)).

What is the creative aspect of your project? Our biggest creative differentiator is the "Two Scenes Mode" and the "Investigative Storytelling." Instead of a standard dashboard, the user acts as a "detective" gathering clues. The Two Scenes Mode allows users to compare the exact same variable over the same period in two completely different regions. This visually demonstrates how the same global environmental shift can produce dramatically different—and sometimes opposite—local trends, educating users against false geographic generalizations.

What factors did your team consider? Our team prioritized Scientific Validity and Trust. We heavily considered the risks of AI hallucinations in data analysis. To mitigate this, we established a strict architectural rule: AI (LLMs) is only used to interpret the user's initial question and to translate the final mathematical results into plain language. AI does not choose variables randomly, plot coordinates, or calculate statistics. All p-values, trends, and confidence intervals are calculated deterministically by our Python engine. We also considered scalability, designing a multi-tiered business model (Community, Education, Municipality, Enterprise API) to ensure the project's long-term financial sustainability.

projectDetails.name: Echoes in the Cosmos (E'k-os z'kik C'os)
projectDetails.summary:
"Echoes in the Cosmos" is an interactive, multilingual web experience that gives a voice to the 17 machines NASA left behind on the Moon and Mars. To address the "Abandoned, but Not Forgotten" challenge, we transformed raw NASA/JPL and NSSDCA data into an engaging educational journey for young space enthusiasts.

Users can pick a world, locate a relic on an interactive map, read its "logbook," and test their knowledge through gamified quizzes to earn XP. What makes our project unique is how we humanize telemetry—turning the dry engineering metric that the Opportunity rover was designed for 90 sols but survived 5,111 into an inspiring story of resilience.

By combining verified historical mission data with narrative gamification, we make space exploration accessible and exciting. This matters because it not only preserves the legacy of pioneering missions but actively inspires the next generation of STEM explorers, proving that human curiosity can outlast the harshest environments.
projectDetails.details:
Overview

"Echoes in the Cosmos" is an interactive, multilingual web experience that gives a voice to the 17 machines NASA left behind on the Moon and Mars. Addressing the "Abandoned, but Not Forgotten" challenge, we transformed raw NASA/JPL and NSSDCA data into an engaging educational journey for young space enthusiasts.

How It Works & Features

Users can select a world, locate a relic on an interactive map, read its digital "logbook," and test their knowledge through gamified quizzes to earn XP. What makes our project unique is how we humanize telemetry—turning dry engineering metrics (such as the Opportunity rover surviving 5,111 sols instead of its designed 90) into inspiring narratives of resilience.

Technology Stack & Architecture

Built with an open-source, high-performance web architecture, leveraging modern frontend frameworks, local-first workflows, and structured JSON telemetry datasets directly mapped from authentic NASA mission archives.

Creative Aspect & Impact

By blending verified historical mission data with narrative gamification and Yautja-inspired linguistic ciphers, we make space exploration accessible and exciting. It preserves the legacy of pioneering missions while actively inspiring the next generation of STEM explorers, proving that human curiosity outlast harsh environments.

projectDetails.name: LA-IRA
projectDetails.summary:
LA-IRA (LunarAres - Integrated Route Assistant) is an offline-capable EVA planning and navigation web tool for Martian astronauts exploring Gale Crater.

It translates raw NASA planetary data for field safety by combining high-resolution mapping, mineral targets, thermal sand masks, and radiation estimates. The system computes optimal, terrain-aware walking routes and dynamic timelines using an advanced A* pathfinding algorithm.

On Mars, improper route planning or unexpected hazards can put an astronaut's life at risk. A-IRA provides real-time, self-contained decision support in the field without needing cloud connectivity, maximizing both scientific discovery and crew safety during complex surface explorations.
projectDetails.details:
LA-IRA (LunarAres – Integrated Route Assistant) is an Extravehicular Activity (EVA) route-planning web tool built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It currently maps two target sites: a 2.46 × 2.46 km region around the Mount Sharp boxwork formations in Gale Crater on Mars (explored by Curiosity), and the Apollo 17 landing site in the Taurus-Littrow valley on the Moon.

The application runs on a modular data pipeline and a two-stage interface:

  1. Source Verification & Startup Gate: When you select a celestial body on startup, the app runs live health checks (OK / FAIL) against each configured NASA endpoint. You can toggle which data layers feed into the planner or plug in a custom ArcGIS ImageServer or WMTS URL. Only topography is strictly required—if optional layers are disabled or an endpoint goes down, the planner falls back and continues with the available data.
  2. Multi-Layer Terrain Modeling & Route Planning: All layers are aligned onto a 1000 × 1000 grid (~2.4 m per cell) to calculate traversal costs and routes:
    • Topography & Slope (HiRISE 1 m DTM / LROC NAC 5 m DTM): Calculates terrain gradients using the Horn method (3×3 window), blocking cells that exceed maximum forward or cross-slope limits and adding a cost penalty to caution slopes (greater than 15°).
    • Optical Imagery & Relief: Stitches 15×15 WMTS tiles from the HiRISE (~0.6 m/px) or LROC NAC mosaics into a 3840×3840 base map, layered with a server-rendered DTM hillshade.
    • Thermal Sand Proxy (THEMIS Night IR, ~100 m/px): Flags the coldest 30% of the region at night—where low thermal inertia indicates loose sand and dust—and applies an adjustable walking-time penalty.
    • Mineralogy & Target Suggestions (CRISM MTRDR, 18 m/px): Georeferences CRISM spectral browse products (sulfates, clays, carbonates, and true color) using PDS3 labels, then automatically picks up to 6 scientific points of interest based on the strongest sulfate signals located on walkable slopes.
    • Sky-View Radiation Estimate (Curiosity RAD / LRO CRaTER + DTM): Pulls a reference dose rate—including live HTTP Range reads of the latest 5 sols from the ~70 MB/sol Curiosity RAD archive paired with recent MSL waypoints—and scales it by the visible sky fraction (cos⁡2\cos^2cos2 of the horizon angle across 16 directions out to ~390 m). This highlights where surrounding topography provides natural radiation shielding.
    • Pathfinding & Emergency Return Map: Estimates walking speed with an adapted Tobler function and computes paths using A*, Dijkstra, or D* Lite. It optimizes stop order (caching previously solved legs so only modified segments are recalculated) and runs a reversed Dijkstra search from the Habitat to map 30-, 60-, and 90-minute emergency return boundaries across the map.

What benefits does it have and what is the intended impact?

  • EVA Safety & Life-Support Budgeting: Astronauts and mission planners can immediately track total travel time, science time per stop, worst-case return time to the habitat, cumulative elevation gain/loss, sand traversal distance, and estimated radiation exposure (µGy) against suit limits and safety reserves.
  • Offline Reliability: Once loaded, the app works fully offline by caching terrain packages in the browser's IndexedDB and verifying data integrity with SHA-256 hashes. In live Vercel deployments, it queries NASA endpoints on demand and automatically falls back to packaged snapshots if any external service is unreachable.
  • Easy Expansion to New Sites: Any planetary region can be added without changing core code by supplying a JSON body profile or a Schema 1 data package (meta.json + base64 float32 elev.txt).

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Frontend: Vanilla JavaScript (ES Modules), HTML5 (using <canvas> for dynamic layer rendering, pixel extraction, and elevation profiles), CSS3, and Leaflet 1.9.4 (EPSG:4326), built with zero bundlers or build steps.
  • Backend & Data Pipeline: Python 3.12 (managed with uv), using Pillow (PIL) and requests for WMTS tile stitching, ArcGIS ImageServer float32 DEM exports, PDS3 label parsing, and HTTP Range requests.
  • Deployment & Testing: Vercel (Python serverless functions in api/), Node.js built-in test runner (node:test), and Python unittest.
  • NASA Data Sources: NASA Mars Trek, NASA Moon Trek, NASA Planetary Data System (PDS Geosciences & PPI), HiRISE, CRISM, THEMIS, MSL Curiosity RAD & MMGIS waypoints, and LRO LROC & CRaTER.

How is your project creative and what factors did your team consider?

  • Targeted HTTP Range Reads for Live Radiation Data: Rather than downloading massive ~70 MB PDS tables in full, the backend uses byte-range requests to fetch only the latest Curiosity RAD measurements, combining them with a DTM-based horizon model to map terrain radiation shelter in real time.
  • Asymmetric Reversed Dijkstra Return Map: Because walking uphill and downhill have different Tobler speeds and slope limits, simply reversing a forward path gives the wrong return time. Our emergency return map reverses edge directions (v→uv \to uv→u) when expanding outward from the habitat, showing the actual time needed to get back to safety from any point on the grid.
  • Suit Mobility Constraints: The pathfinding model accounts for both forward slope and sideways cross-slope limits, slowdowns in loose sand, and an equipment-carrying mode that tightens slope limits by 5° and reduces walking speed by 20%.
  • Transparent Model Limitations: Because planetary datasets vary widely in scale, the UI explicitly displays the resolution and constraints of every active layer—noting, for example, that ~2.4 m cells cannot resolve meter-scale boulders, CRISM alignment is approximate at ~18 m/px, THEMIS night IR is a ~100 m regional heuristic, and Tobler's function is an Earth-derived hiking model. Missing data is always flagged as unavailable rather than silently defaulted to zero.

projectDetails.name: Surviving In Mars
projectDetails.summary: Surviving in Mars is an interactive simulator that places players in charge of a Martian outpost. Players make decisions to keep the outpost running while balancing essential mission needs such as life support, power and ratiation protection. The game addresses the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by turning these competing demands into a hands-on experience: players can see how resource choices affect the outpost and the success of its mission. This project is important because it makes the engineering trade-offs of living on Mars accessible to young learners and encourages them to think like mission planners.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do and how does it work ?

Surviving in Mars is a mission-management simulator about operating a Martian outpost. It is designed to help young players explore how life support, power, food production, radiation protection, and local resources affect one another. Players make mission decisions and see how limited resources and environmental conditions can influence the outpost and the mission’s chances of success.

The game is supported by a data pipeline that collects, preserves, standardizes, and packages selected data for local use. The pipeline includes weather feeds for NASA’s Curiosity and Perseverance rovers; InSight TWINS wind data; Mars dust-opacity and radiation measurements; solar events from NASA’s DONKI database; MOLA topography; Mars reference facts; and NASA technical references on crew needs, life support, agriculture, power systems, in-situ resource use, and radiation shielding. It organizes selected information into local database tables, JSON data, and raster map products, with source information retained for traceability. This approach allows the web game to use a prepared local data package without relying on a live NASA connection during every play session.

The project’s benefit is that it turns space exploration concepts into decisions players can explore. Instead of presenting Mars survival only as facts, the simulator encourages systems thinking: a choice that helps one part of the outpost may place pressure on another. Its intended impact is to build curiosity about space science and engineering, and to help young learners understand why planning a real mission involves trade-offs.

A key factor in development was scientific transparency. The collected datasets come from different missions, locations, time periods, and measurement systems, so they cannot automatically be treated as simultaneous observations of one outpost. The project also distinguishes measured data from simplified game values. For example, RAD measurements are detector readings rather than a direct measure of human health risk, and ice-consistency maps are evidence maps rather than estimates of extractable water. The simulator is an educational model, not a validated engineering design for a Mars habitat.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did we use to develop our project?

Assets tools

  • Audio: Itch.io
  • 2D Models: Itch.io
  • Images: Pinterest, ChatGPT

Development tools

  • Data collection and pipeline: Python, SQLite, JSON and raster data;
  • Web game: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, NodeJS, GoDaddy domain.
  • AI tools: Claude Code and Copilot as a coding assistant and ChatGPT for research, writing and image generation.
  • Design and collaboration: Figma, Google Docs, Discord, Git.

projectDetails.name: Project Via Lunae
projectDetails.summary:
ViaLunae is a web-based lunar surface simulator that helps mission planners compare landing and operation sites by sunlight, terrain and solar power. The user picks a location, a start time and a duration. The tool computes sunlight over time using the real terrain horizon up to 150 km and estimates, in kW, the output of a solar panel the user configures: area, efficiency and orientation. Scenarios can be added to a comparison table, sorted by any column and exported as CSV. The interface is available in Portuguese and English.

Lunar missions have been cut short by power, communication, illumination and landing-site constraints; for example, IM-2 Athena operated about 12 of its 240 planned hours. ViaLunae does not predict landing failures: it supports the evaluation of operating conditions at a given site and date before a mission. It uses NASA Moon Trek imagery.
projectDetails.details:
1. DETAILED PROJECT DESCRIPTION

WHY VIALUNAE EXISTS

The lunar south pole is the hardest place to land and the most wanted: the Sun skims the horizon, crater floors stay in shadow, and the Earth sits low in the sky and can drop out of view. Recent landers show how little margin there is:

  • SLIM (JAXA, Jan 2024): lost an engine on descent and landed nose-down with its solar panels facing west. It shut down about 3 hours after landing with 12% battery, and recovered days later when the Sun direction changed.
  • IM-1 Odysseus (Intuitive Machines, Feb 2024): caught a foot on the surface and tipped over onto a rock, which made it hard to point its antennas at the Earth. It operated about 6 days against about a week planned.
  • IM-2 Athena (Intuitive Machines, Mar 2025): landed on its side inside a crater near Mons Mouton, roughly 250 m from target by the company's figure and more than 400 m by NASA's. It operated about 12 h 45 min against 10 days planned.
  • VIPER (NASA, not flown): designed to survive at most about 50 hours of darkness, and at the pole the Earth can be out of sight for about two weeks of every month.

In the three flights, the trigger was landing and attitude, and the consequence was power and communication. Planning tools exist, but 3D line-of-sight analysis lives in specialist software, while the public maps (QuickMap, Moon Trek) are 2D. ViaLunae puts site, date, horizon, power and communication in one page that anyone can open.

WHAT VIALUNAE DOES

  • 3D globe of the Moon (CesiumJS) with the south pole view, fixed sites (six Apollo sites, Mons Mouton and Malapert A) and free coordinates by typing or clicking.
  • Sun and Earth on the real horizon: azimuth and elevation of both for any date, with the terrain profile deciding what is visible.
  • Metrics per scenario: sunlight percentage and longest lit period, time to next sunset or sunrise, Earth-visible windows and signal delay, solar power in kW and energy in kWh, ground irradiance, estimated surface temperature.
  • Conditions at the site at any instant of a timeline, with animation and speed control, plus charts of Sun/Earth elevation, irradiance and temperature.
  • Ground view: a camera 2 m above the surface with real relief, with the Sun and Earth placed in the sky by the timeline.
  • Comparison table for up to 12 scenarios: sort by any column, best value highlighted in green, CSV export.
  • PT/EN interface and a public codebase with automated tests.

Figure 1: globe at the south pole with Mons Mouton selected and the scenario results panel (14 Nov 2026, 30 days, panel set to 12.6 m², relief on).

Figure 2: "Conditions at the site" card with the horizon panorama (relief in grey, Sun and Earth paths), the Sun and Earth elevation chart, and the irradiance and temperature chart.

HOW IT WORKS: KEY TECHNICAL DECISIONS

  • Ephemerides, not approximations. Sun and Earth positions come from NASA/JPL Horizons (DE441). The browser cannot call Horizons directly (no CORS), so two serverless functions on Vercel act as a validated, cached proxy. Fixed sites ship with 12 months of hourly data pre-computed (1 Nov 2026 to 1 Nov 2027); any other site or period is fetched live.
  • A real horizon up to 150 km. The pole's light depends on mountains tens of kilometres away, so a smooth-sphere horizon is wrong. For each site the app samples the Cesium Moon terrain (NASA and USGS data) in 180 directions and 27 distances out to 150 km, in two passes (near and far), and builds a horizon profile. The Sun or the Earth only counts as visible above that profile. Fixed sites have the profile pre-computed; free coordinates are computed in the browser (about 30 to 70 seconds) and cached.
  • Power model. Irradiance is 1361 W/m² divided by the squared Sun distance (from Horizons), times the cosine of the incidence angle on the panel. Three panel modes: vertical rotating to follow the Sun (default), two-axis tracking, fixed tilt and azimuth. Area and efficiency are editable and the result recalculates instantly. Anything behind the relief produces zero.
  • Temperature model (estimate). Radiative equilibrium by day (albedo 0.12, emissivity 0.95) and a night floor by latitude. The screen says it is an estimate.
  • Comparison by design. Every metric is computed by pure functions shared by the screen, the table and the CSV, so the three cannot disagree. The suite has 21 automated tests (metrics, power, conditions, comparison).
  • Credits on every layer: NASA/JPL Horizons, Cesium Moon Terrain, LROC WAC imagery via NASA Moon Trek.

Figure 3: ground view, 2 m above Mons Mouton, looking at the Sun on 22 Nov 2026 at 02:00 UTC, with relief on the horizon.

2. CASE STUDY: REPLAYING IM-2 ATHENA'S SITE

We asked ViaLunae what the target site looked like during the 10 days Athena was planned to operate, starting 6 March 2025 at 17:00 UTC (approximately its landing time) at Mons Mouton (84.79 S, 29.20 E), with the real horizon on.

  • Sun above the terrain horizon: 100% of the 10 planned days.
  • Sun elevation: 2.4 to 5.4 degrees (mean 4.4).
  • Earth above the terrain horizon: 100% of the 10 planned days.

What it says. At the target coordinates, the Sun and the Earth were both above the horizon for the whole planned mission, so illumination and communication geometry at the site were not the limit. Sources report that Athena instead stopped after about 12 h 45 min after landing on its side inside a crater, with the Sun direction, the panel orientation and the cold preventing it from recharging. With the Sun only 2 to 5 degrees above the horizon, a few degrees of tilt or a crater wall around the real landing spot is enough to remove nearly all light.

What it does not say. The model sees a 150 km horizon at the target coordinates. It does not see crater-scale shadows 250 to 400 m away, where Athena actually stopped, nor the lander's tilt. That gap is the next feature on our roadmap, and it is why ViaLunae treats its result as "is this site worth considering", not "this landing will succeed".

3. COMPARING SITES AND DATES

The same engine, 30 days from 1 Nov 2026, default panel (10 m², 30% efficiency, vertical rotating):

  • Mons Mouton (IM-2 Athena): sun 59.2% on a smooth sphere and 53.3% with real relief; longest lit period 377 h; Earth visible 74.1% (smooth) and 88.9% (relief); mean power 2.20 kW; ground irradiance 58 W/m²; temperature -219 to -46 °C.
  • Malapert A (IM-1 Odysseus): sun 55.6% smooth and 47.9% with relief; longest lit period 316 h; Earth visible 100%; mean power 1.97 kW; ground irradiance 92 W/m²; temperature -215 to -14 °C.
  • Apollo 11 (equator): sun 49.4% smooth and 49.2% with relief; longest lit period 354 h; Earth visible 100%; mean power 1.31 kW; ground irradiance 436 W/m²; temperature -178 to 115 °C.

Three things this comparison shows that a smooth sphere hides:

  1. Relief changes the answer in both directions. At Mons Mouton the terrain takes sunlight from 59% to 53%, and at Malapert A from 56% to 48%, but it raises Earth visibility at Mons Mouton from 74% to 89%, because the massif sits above the surrounding ground and sees below the smooth-sphere horizon.
  2. The pole's mean power can beat the equator's while its light is much weaker. With a vertical panel that follows the Sun, a low Sun still lights the panel face-on, so mean power is higher at the pole than at Apollo 11 (2.20 versus 1.31 kW) even though ground irradiance is 58 versus 436 W/m². The temperature range shows the cost: the pole never warms past -14 °C.
  3. Over a full year the picture shifts. With relief on, sunlight falls to 44.7% (Mons Mouton) and 41.7% (Malapert A), against 48.6% at Apollo 11, and Earth visibility at Mons Mouton drops to 86.6%.

Figure 4: the comparison table with Mons Mouton, Malapert A and Apollo 11 loaded (panel set to 12.6 m² in this screenshot, so its kW and kWh are higher than the figures above).

How the numbers were produced. The figures above come from the project's own pre-computed ephemerides and horizon profiles (and, for March 2025, from the app's live /api/sky function), run through the same metrics, power and conditions code the app uses. They are model outputs, not flight telemetry.

4. LIMITS WE STATE ON PURPOSE

  • No validation against flight data yet. We replay Athena's site but we do not claim that the model predicts its outcome.
  • Horizon resolution: 2 degree steps in azimuth and terrain out to 150 km, with no crater-scale shadows and no lander tilt.
  • Temperature is an equilibrium estimate with a night floor by latitude, not a thermal simulation.
  • Panel model: no dust, degradation or self-shadowing by the lander.
  • Pre-computed window: fixed sites cover 1 Nov 2026 to 1 Nov 2027. Other periods use the live API (up to 400 days).
  • 3D terrain uses a Cesium ion token.

5. ROADMAP

Done: globe, horizon, power, conditions, ground view, comparison, CSV, PT/EN, tests. Planned, not built yet:

  1. Educational mode: short "?" cards on each metric, a first-visit tour, and cards on why the pole is hard.
  2. Traffic-light filters per variable (solar energy, relief and shadow, Earth communication, available time). Each filter shows red, yellow or green, filters stack, and any can be switched off. Open design question we want to test with users: equal weights, user-set weights, or filters that can veto a site outright.
  3. Landing-risk parameters taken from what actually went wrong: panel orientation, tilt at landing, terrain slope, landing precision (distance from target), crater cold, night length, Earth visibility, and rocks near the pad.
  4. Crater-scale shadows from high-resolution LOLA relief around candidate sites, which would close the gap shown in the Athena case study.
  5. Replay mode for past missions so each failure can be loaded with the conditions it landed in.

6. RECOMMENDATIONS AND VISION

  • Treat the site and the date as one decision. The same coordinates give very different light and Earth contact on different weeks.
  • Plan with the real horizon, not a smooth sphere. Differences of several percentage points of sunlight, in either direction, are common (see section 3).
  • Design for tilt. Three recent landers ended up tilted or on their side. Power and antenna margins at a given tilt should be a standard input to site selection.
  • Share the same open data. Everything in ViaLunae comes from public NASA and USGS data, so a student team and a mission team can look at the same numbers.

Sources for the mission facts: SLIM, JAXA statements reported by AFP and Reuters; IM-1, AP and Gizmodo; IM-2, Intuitive Machines and NASA as reported by Spaceflight Now and SpacePolicyOnline; VIPER, NASA.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

projectDetails.name: Project EarthSound
projectDetails.summary: EarthSound is an accessible, bilingual web app inspired by NASA’s The Earth Information Jukebox challenge. It turns environmental observations into sound, allowing users to explore data visually and listen to patterns through interactive sonification. The MVP includes a 2021 global temperature-anomaly experience, an Antarctic ozone timeline spanning 1983–2018, and a library of nine NASA audiovisual resources. Using the Web Audio API, verified numerical data are mapped to sound features such as pitch and rhythm. When a source provides only visual categories, the sound is clearly labeled as a qualitative interpretation—not a measurement. The app supports Portuguese and English, keyboard navigation, spoken guidance, and text alternatives for browsers without voice recognition. EarthSound makes open Earth science more approachable, supports multimodal learning, and aims to broaden participation in understanding environmental change.
projectDetails.details:
Project Description

EarthSound turns environmental data into accessible audiovisual experiences. Inspired by the NASA Space Apps Challenge The Earth Information Jukebox, it lets people explore NASA visualizations and hear interpretations of the data. The MVP includes an exploration of 2021 global temperature anomalies, Antarctic ozone maps from 1983 to 2018, and a library of nine NASA audiovisual resources.

Where reliable numerical data are available, values are mapped to sound characteristics such as pitch and rhythm while the related visualization remains on screen. When a source provides only visual categories or states, the sound is identified as qualitative, not as a measurement. This helps prevent invented values or misinterpretations—for example, treating temperature anomalies as absolute temperatures. The experience also explains key references and limits: GISTEMP anomalies are relative to the 1951–1980 mean, and the ozone materials identify the 220 DU threshold.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Audio provides another way to perceive environmental patterns. It can make data exploration more accessible to people who are blind or have low vision, and support educators and audiences without a technical background. The project aims to bring people closer to open scientific data, encourage climate literacy, and show how environmental information can be understood through multiple senses. These are intended outcomes, not measured impact results.

Tools and Technologies

The MVP was built with React, TypeScript, Vite, and CSS. It uses the Web Audio API to generate sound from data and the Web Speech API for spoken guidance and, where supported, voice commands. Sources include NASA Earth Information Center and Scientific Visualization Studio materials, NASA GISTEMP data, and resources from NASA Ozone Watch and NOAA. GitHub is used for version control.

No specialized hardware is required: the app runs in a browser on a computer or phone with audio. A microphone is optional; conventional controls and text alternatives allow people to use the app without voice commands.

Creativity and Design Considerations

Sonification is treated as a way to represent data—not as background music. The interface explains how data relate to sound and pairs audio with visual and textual information. The project also considers accessibility, keyboard navigation, screen readers, contrast, Portuguese and English support, and browser compatibility—including a text alternative when voice recognition is unavailable.

The team prioritized traceable sources, units, and scientific references, clear distinctions between measurements and qualitative interpretations, and preservation of NASA’s original visualizations.

Team: Anny Karoline, Isabella Marques, and Ana Luiza.

projectDetails.name: Project Outpost Commander
projectDetails.summary:
Outpost Commander — Project Summary
Outpost Commander is an interactive survival simulation where students manage a lunar or Martian outpost across multiple sols. Players balance six critical resources — power, oxygen, water, food, shielding, and crew health — each depleting in real time, with any one hitting zero ending the mission. Gameplay blends real-time resource depletion, skill-based astronomy puzzles, timed mid-sol events, adaptive difficulty, and a certificate reward system.

What makes it fun and educational is the fusion of mechanics and meaning. To power solar arrays or tend the greenhouse, players solve astronomy quizzes and classification puzzles drawn from a pool of hundreds of questions — so progress rewards genuine learning, not luck. The adaptive difficulty scales with performance, and a persistent leaderboard drives replay. A companion Astronomy Academy study hub reinforces concepts with on-demand explanations of every answer, connecting each challenge to real science.

This matters for the NASA Space Apps Challenge because it turns passive space knowledge into active decision-making under pressure, mirroring the tradeoffs real mission controllers face. By grounding survival mechanics in authentic planetary science and NASA imagery, Outpost Commander cultivates systems thinking, scientific literacy, and curiosity about space exploration — empowering the next generation to engage meaningfully with humanity's future beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Outpost Commander is an interactive survival simulation that teaches space science through real stakes. Players manage a lunar or Martian outpost across multiple sols, balancing six critical resources — power, oxygen, water, food, shielding, and crew health — each depleting in real time. Any single resource hitting zero ends the mission, so every decision carries weight. To perform operations like deploying solar arrays or reinforcing shielding, players solve timed astronomy puzzles from a pool of hundreds of questions; fail the puzzle and you waste precious oxygen, tying learning directly to survival. The game works through a clean separation: a pure game engine handles state and logic, while the React interface renders resource meters, action cards, event modals, and a mission log. Adaptive difficulty scales resource drain and puzzle timers to each player's performance, mid-sol random events mimic the pressure of real mission control, and a persistent leaderboard with mission certificates drives replay and mastery.

Its benefits are both educational and motivational: it turns passive space knowledge into active decision-making, rewards genuine scientific understanding, and builds systems thinking and curiosity about space exploration. The intended impact is to inspire the next generation to engage meaningfully with humanity's future beyond Earth — students don't just read about radiation on Mars, they feel what happens when shielding fails. To build it, we used React, Framer Motion for animations, Tailwind CSS for styling, the Base44 platform for backend and persistence, and AI-generated explanations that clarify every correct answer. The project is creative because it fuses survival-game tension with a curriculum — gameplay literally cannot progress without learning the science. Key factors we considered included scientific accuracy, engaging yet fair difficulty curves, accessibility for classroom use, replayability, and tying every mechanic to authentic planetary science so the fun and the learning never separate.

projectDetails.name: Sky Spotter
projectDetails.summary:
Sky Spotter is a citizen science and astrometric intelligence web platform that democratizes celestial anomaly detection using open NASA data. We developed a full-stack digital observatory built with Angular, Python FastAPI, and Supabase, featuring a flicker-free, dual-layer Blink Comparator and a real-time Collective Intelligence dashboard.

Modern all-sky surveys like WISE and SPHEREx generate petabytes of imaging data far beyond the manual inspection capacity of professional teams. Sky Spotter addresses this bottleneck by querying the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) via the IVOA SIA v2 protocol and delivering fast, georeferenced multi-epoch sky cutouts. Users visually inspect alternating exposures to pinpoint and classify transient moving objects, variable stars, and sensor noise with exact Right Ascension and Declination coordinates.

This platform is vital because it bridges the gap between raw space telemetry and public participation, accelerating the discovery of Near-Earth Objects while sustaining long-term astronomical research through a scalable citizen science and institutional SaaS model.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works

Sky Spotter is a citizen science and astrometric intelligence web platform that democratizes celestial anomaly detection using open NASA data. The system transforms complex astronomical surveys modeled after the WISE and SPHEREx missions into an interactive digital observatory accessible directly from any web browser.

The platform operates through a four-stage integrated pipeline:

  1. Astronomical Querying (IVOA SIA v2): The back-end queries the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) (irsa.ipac.caltech.edu/SIA, wise_allwise_p3am_cdd collection) using standardized spatial cone searches (POS=CIRCLE) to retrieve metadata for cataloged deep-sky sectors.
  2. High-Speed Cutout Proxy (/api/sky-cutout): A dedicated FastAPI proxy integrates with the IVOA HiPS2FITS protocol to deliver $500 \times 500$ pixel tangential (TAN) projections ($0.25^\circ \times 0.25^\circ$ field of view) across distinct epochs and spectral bands (DSS2/red and DSS2/blue), backed by a deterministic SVG starfield fallback generator.
  3. Dual-Layer Blink Comparator: On the front-end, both epochs are preloaded into superimposed layers with automated opacity toggling every 800ms. This allows the human eye to immediately spot objects that shift position or brightness between exposures.
  4. Classification & Collective Intelligence: Upon spotting an anomaly, users click directly on the target to log normalized (X, Y) screen vectors mapped to real celestial coordinates (Right Ascension RA and Declination Dec), classifying the signature as a Transient (Motion), Variable (Brightness), or Artifact (Sensor Noise). Records are persisted in real time on Supabase, feeding an analytical dashboard with automated scientific recommendations (such as orbit cross-referencing with the Minor Planet Center).

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Scientific Accessibility: Removes the technical barrier of handling heavy multi-extension FITS files and specialized desktop software, empowering anyone to contribute to astronomical discovery via a web browser.
  • Accelerated Data Triage: Wide-field sky surveys produce petabytes of imaging data that exceed the manual inspection capacity of science teams. Sky Spotter scales human-in-the-loop pre-screening to filter out sensor artifacts and prioritize genuine transient candidates.
  • Educational, Scientific, and Sustainable Impact: Connects students and enthusiasts with real space research, supports Near-Earth Object (NEO / Planetary Defense) monitoring initiatives, and ensures long-term financial viability through a hybrid Freemium & B2B/B2G SaaS model (free access for citizen scientists, institutional licensing for universities, and high-throughput APIs for observatories).

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Coding Languages: TypeScript, Python, HTML5, CSS3, and SQL.
  • Front-end Software: Angular (Standalone Components, RxJS, HttpClient, NgZone, and ChangeDetectorRef).
  • Back-end Software: Python FastAPI, Uvicorn, HTTPX, and Pydantic.
  • Database & Cloud Infrastructure: Supabase (PostgreSQL), Vercel (serverless hosting and CI/CD), Git, and GitHub.
  • Astronomical Protocols & Catalogs: NASA/IPAC IRSA (IVOA SIA v2), CDS IVOA HiPS2FITS, Digitized Sky Survey 2 (DSS2), 2MASS, and methodological integration with the IAU Minor Planet Center (MPC).
  • Hardware & Environment: Standard developer workstations for full-stack engineering and cloud-native serverless compute, requiring zero specialized hardware from end users.

Creativity & Innovation

  • Reimagining a Classic Astronomical Instrument: We took the concept of the 20th-century optical Blink Comparator (used to discover Pluto) and reimagined it as a modern Command Center / HUD interface with glassmorphism, live telemetry, and visual radar feedback.
  • Resilient Image Engineering: Rather than overloading the browser with repetitive requests to slow external academic servers or running into CORS blocks, we engineered a lightweight pipeline combining a FastAPI proxy, HTTP caching, dual-layer opacity preloading, and a deterministic SVG starfield fallback.
  • Bridging Open Science and Sustainability: We paired open-access citizen science with a structured institutional SaaS business model designed to sustain cloud operations well beyond the hackathon.

Key Factors Considered by the Team

  • Human Visual Perception & UX: We calibrated the 800ms blink interval and smooth opacity transitions to prevent visual flickering, optimizing the human eye's ability to detect subtle motion against static background stars.
  • Network Latency & High Availability: Accounting for external astronomical server latency and browser Cross-Origin policies, we built caching and fallback layers to guarantee uninterrupted operation during live scans.
  • Astrometric Standardization & Scalability: We structured our database schema around standard equatorial coordinates (RA/Dec) and clean categorical labels so community-validated annotations can train future Computer Vision models and scale natively to SPHEREx's 102-band near-infrared spectral cubes.

PORTUGUÊS

O que o projeto faz e como funciona

O Sky Spotter é uma plataforma web de ciência cidadã e inteligência astrométrica que democratiza a detecção de anomalias celestes utilizando dados abertos da NASA. O sistema transforma levantamentos astronômicos complexos — modelados sobre o legado das missões WISE e SPHEREx — em um observatório digital interativo acessível diretamente pelo navegador.

Na prática, o fluxo opera em quatro etapas integradas:

  1. Consulta Astronômica (IVOA SIA v2): O back-end consulta o arquivo NASA/IPAC IRSA (irsa.ipac.caltech.edu/SIA, coleção wise_allwise_p3am_cdd) por meio de buscas espaciais padronizadas (POS=CIRCLE) para obter metadados de setores celestes catalogados.
  2. Proxy de Recortes de Alta Velocidade (/api/sky-cutout): Um servidor dedicado em FastAPI integra-se ao protocolo IVOA HiPS2FITS para entregar projeções tangenciais (TAN) de $500 \times 500$ pixels ($0,25^\circ \times 0,25^\circ$ de campo de visão) em diferentes épocas e bandas espectrais (DSS2/red e DSS2/blue), contando com um gerador determinístico de campo estelar em SVG como contingência.
  3. Blink Comparator de Dupla Camada: No front-end, as duas épocas são pré-carregadas em camadas sobrepostas com alternância automática de opacidade a cada 800ms. Isso permite que o olho humano identifique instantaneamente objetos que mudaram de posição ou brilho entre exposições.
  4. Classificação e Inteligência Coletiva: Ao detectar uma anomalia, o usuário clica sobre o alvo para registrar vetores percentuais (X, Y) vinculados às coordenadas celestes reais (Ascensão Reta RA e Declinação Dec), classificando o achado em Transiente (Movimento), Variável (Brilho) ou Artefato (Ruído do Sensor). Os dados são gravados em tempo real no Supabase e alimentam um painel analítico com recomendações científicas automatizadas (como cruzamento de órbitas com o Minor Planet Center).

Benefícios e Impacto Pretendido

  • Acessibilidade Científica: Elimina a barreira técnica de manipular arquivos científicos pesados (como cubos espectrais FITS) e softwares especializados, permitindo que qualquer pessoa contribua para a astronomia pelo navegador.
  • Aceleração da Triagem de Dados: Missões de varredura de céu inteiro geram petabytes de imagens, superando a capacidade de revisão manual das equipes científicas. O Sky Spotter escala a pré-triagem humana para filtrar ruídos de sensores e priorizar candidatos reais.
  • Impacto Educacional, Científico e Sustentável: O projeto aproxima estudantes e entusiastas da pesquisa espacial real, apoia programas de monitoramento de Objetos Próximos à Terra (NEOs / Defesa Planetária) e garante longevidade financeira por meio de um modelo híbrido Freemium & SaaS B2B/B2G (acesso gratuito para ciência cidadã, pacotes institucionais para universidades e APIs de alta vazão para observatórios).

Ferramentas, Linguagens e Softwares Utilizados

  • Linguagens de Programação: TypeScript, Python, HTML5, CSS3 e SQL.
  • Front-end: Angular (Standalone Components, RxJS, HttpClient, NgZone e ChangeDetectorRef).
  • Back-end: Python FastAPI, Uvicorn, HTTPX e Pydantic.
  • Banco de Dados e Infraestrutura Cloud: Supabase (PostgreSQL), Vercel (hospedagem e deploy contínuo), Git e GitHub.
  • Protocolos e Catálogos Astronômicos: NASA/IPAC IRSA (IVOA SIA v2), CDS IVOA HiPS2FITS, Digitized Sky Survey 2 (DSS2), 2MASS e referência metodológica ao IAU Minor Planet Center (MPC).
  • Hardware e Ambiente de Desenvolvimento: Estações de trabalho padrão para desenvolvimento full-stack e infraestrutura serverless em nuvem (eliminando a necessidade de hardware especializado por parte do usuário final).

Criatividade e Diferenciais

  • Releitura Moderna de um Instrumento Histórico: Resgatamos o conceito clássico do Blink Comparator óptico (usado no século XX para descobrir Plutão) e o reinventamos como uma interface futurista de Command Center / HUD com glassmorphism, radar visual e telemetria ao vivo.
  • Engenharia Resiliente de Imagem: Em vez de sobrecarregar o navegador com requisições repetitivas a servidores acadêmicos lentos ou bloqueados por CORS, criamos uma arquitetura que combina proxy em FastAPI, cache HTTP, pré-carregamento em dupla camada e fallback determinístico em SVG.
  • Ponte entre Ciência Aberta e Viabilidade de Negócio: Unimos engajamento comunitário gratuito com um modelo de monetização institucional estruturado para manter a infraestrutura ativa após o hackathon.

Fatores Considerados pela Equipe

  • Percepção Visual Humana e UX: Ajustamos a cadência de alternância (800ms) e a transição suave de opacidade para evitar cintilação (flicker), maximizando a capacidade do olho humano de captar deslocamentos sutis entre estrelas estáticas.
  • Latência de Rede e Disponibilidade: Consideramos a instabilidade e as restrições de Cross-Origin de APIs astronômicas externas, projetando camadas de cache e contingência para que a plataforma nunca trave durante varreduras ao vivo.
  • Padronização Astrométrica e Escalabilidade: Estruturamos o banco de dados com coordenadas equatoriais (RA/Dec) e categorização limpa para que o conjunto de dados gerado pela comunidade possa treinar modelos futuros de Visão Computacional e suportar os cubos espectrais de 102 bandas do telescópio SPHEREx.

projectDetails.name: Project Echoes of Space
projectDetails.summary:
Echoes of Space is an interactive virtual memorial honoring spacecraft and equipment that remained beyond Earth after helping humanity explore. Visitors walk beneath a futuristic dome, discover paintings and sculptures inspired by space missions, and learn about the discoveries and people behind them.

The memorial uses NASA mission resources to present facts about the missions and compare where their hardware remained. A central InSight station invites visitors to experience the sound of Martian wind through a NASA video.

By combining verified mission information with art and storytelling, Echoes of Space gives a voice to machines that could not return, but whose discoveries came home. It invites visitors to reflect on humanity’s achievements and our responsibility for the traces we leave beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Echoes of Space is an interactive virtual memorial dedicated to spacecraft and equipment that remained beyond Earth. It invites visitors to explore the stories of these machines and reflect on how their discoveries continue to shape life on Earth.

Visitors enter a fictional futuristic memorial beneath a star-filled dome. They can move through the space using a keyboard or on-screen controls, look around with a mouse or touch, and select an artwork to explore its mission story and NASA sources. The collection menu helps visitors walk to a chosen exhibit. Paintings and sculptures offer artistic interpretations of the missions, while the exhibit text distinguishes those interpretations from documented facts.

NASA mission resources are used throughout the memorial. Information from the records is organized into mission facts and used in a comparison showing where the featured hardware remained, such as on a planetary surface, in orbit, or traveling outward. A central InSight station gives visitors access to a NASA video featuring the sound of Martian wind and links to the official mission page.

The memorial was built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using Three.js for the interactive 3D environment. The team used generative AI to create illustrations and assist with code and text. The soundtrack was generated with Suno AI. AI-generated visuals are identified in the experience, and credits and source links are provided.

Our creative approach combines a walkable environment, art, sound, and reliable mission information to make overlooked space hardware more meaningful to a broad audience. We considered accessibility for visitors unfamiliar with 3D navigation, clear controls, mobile use, source transparency, and the distinction between a fictional setting and real mission history.

We hope visitors leave with a deeper appreciation for the people and machines behind space exploration and with a thoughtful question about the traces humanity leaves beyond Earth.

projectDetails.name: BRAVEN - Survival on the Moon
projectDetails.summary: [What we built] We developed BRAVEN – Survival on the Moon, an interactive lunar expedition simulator designed for children aged 7 to 12 to experience managing an off-world colony. [How it answers the challenge] It directly addresses the challenge by transforming complex lunar survival concepts and authentic space data into intuitive, hands-on decision scenarios where young players balance vital resources like oxygen, energy, and scientific research. [Why it matters] This project is vital because it fosters critical thinking, problem-solving, and STEM curiosity, empowering the Artemis generation to realize that a sustainable human presence on the Moon is achievable through thoughtful planning.
projectDetails.details:
Our project empowers children to manage a simulated lunar base through an interactive, event-driven Python application deployed via Streamlit. By processing player decisions in real time, the simulator calculates immediate consequences on base survival and resource stability. Incorporating authentic lunar conditions and data, the game fosters critical thinking, problem-solving, and scientific curiosity in young learners—equipping the next generation with the foundational skills to envision and support future space exploration.

To build this project, we leveraged state-of-the-art Artificial Intelligence within Google Antigravity—utilizing advanced models such as Gemini 3.8 Flash and GPT-OSS 120B for development and problem-solving—alongside HeyGen for dynamic avatar video generation and Streamlit for an accessible web experience. Our creativity lies in bridging complex NASA telemetry and educational gaming: through intuitive mechanics, immersive audio-visual assets, and engaging storylines, we transform raw space science into an inspiring, hands-on learning adventure.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Space Mission – Destiny Is in Your Hands
projectDetails.summary:
Space Mission – Destiny Is in Your Hands is an educational, interactive game for children aged 7 to 12 that puts players in the role of space mission commanders. Their goal is to plan and carry out a journey to the Moon or Mars, using reasoning, strategy, and decision-making to overcome each challenge. Through a fun and accessible adventure, the game introduces concepts of space exploration, engineering, science, and resource management, showing how every choice can affect the success of the mission.

The adventure starts with choosing a destination and receiving a budget of 5,000 coins, to be spent on essentials such as oxygen, water, food, thermal clothing, and medicine. Players then customize the rocket and the astronaut and prepare for launch by connecting electrical wires and refueling the spacecraft. During the six-day journey, they track resource consumption, monitor equipment, and handle unexpected events such as technical failures and meteor showers.

Upon arrival, players carry out scientific activities, collect samples, answer educational questions, and help repair an exploration robot. In the final stage, an emergency damages the spacecraft and players must find parts to repair it, then manage their resources again on the trip back to Earth.

Along the way, participants develop logical reasoning, planning, problem solving, creativity, and decision-making, while learning how real space missions work and why planning and teamwork matter.
projectDetails.details:
Space Mission – Destiny Is in Your Hands! is an educational, interactive game designed for children aged 7 to 12. Players act as commanders of a mission to the Moon or Mars. They choose a destination and receive a budget of 5,000 coins. They spend it on oxygen, water, food, thermal clothing, and medicine, then customize the rocket and the astronaut.

Before launch, they complete tasks such as connecting electrical wires and refueling the spacecraft. The six-day journey requires tracking supplies, monitoring equipment, and handling technical failures and meteor showers. Upon arrival, players collect samples, complete science challenges, answer educational questions, and help repair an exploration robot. In the final stage, an emergency damages the spacecraft, requiring players to find replacement parts, repair it, and manage their resources again on the journey back to Earth.

What benefits does it offer?

The game transforms space-mission planning into a fun, accessible learning experience. Children practice logical reasoning, planning, problem-solving, creativity, and decision-making. They also explore fundamental concepts in science, engineering, and technology, discovering how real space missions depend on careful preparation, scientific knowledge, and resource management.

What is the intended impact?

We aim to spark children's curiosity about science and space exploration. By making different choices and experiencing their consequences, players learn that a successful mission depends on planning, organization, knowledge, and teamwork, not only on advanced technology. The game also encourages an early interest in STEM fields (Science, Technology, Engineering, and Mathematics).

What tools, languages, hardware, or software were used?

The game was developed with the assistance of Claude, an artificial intelligence tool used to support the programming and development process. Scientific research and educational content were informed by resources from the NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), helping connect the game to real scientific data and space research.

The game is built as a single, self-contained web page using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, without external libraries. The scenes are rendered using the browser's Canvas technology, while the rocket and astronaut are created with vector (SVG) graphics.

It runs in a standard web browser on computers, tablets, and smartphones, supporting keyboard, mouse, and touchscreen controls. No special hardware or software installation is required.

What is the creative aspect?

  • Players are commanders rather than spectators, and every decision has visible consequences.
  • A limited budget forces players to make strategic trade-offs between essential supplies.
  • Players can personalize their own rocket and astronaut.
  • Mini-games, a walkable 360° spacecraft cabin, and surface exploration make the experience feel like a real space adventure.
  • Educational fact cards connect gameplay to real space science, including Apollo Moon samples, NASA's DONKI space-weather records, the Perseverance rover, and Olympus Mons.
  • The integration of AI-assisted development and NASA scientific resources combines accessible game design with authentic scientific references.

What factors did the team consider?

  • Age-appropriateness: Simple language, large buttons, and a friendly tone designed for children aged 7 to 12.
  • Balance of fun and learning: Every challenge incorporates a specific educational objective.
  • Accessibility: The game works across different screen sizes and input methods, includes a sound on/off button, and respects reduced-motion settings.
  • Realistic constraints: Limited resources, equipment failures, and emergencies reflect the real challenges of space missions.
  • Scientific accuracy: NASA-related scientific resources were considered to bring authentic space exploration concepts into the gameplay and encourage curiosity about real scientific discoveries.

projectDetails.name: Project tellai
projectDetails.summary:
Project tellai is an AI-augmented decision-support platform developed to help smallholder farmers and extensionists transition from vulnerable monocultures to resilient, regenerative crop rotations and polycultures. 
Addressing the "Field Shift" challenge, tellai integrates 24 years of NASA Earth Observations—including NASA POWER agroclimatology (precipitation, temperature, and clear-sky solar radiation), SMAP root-zone soil moisture, MODIS vegetation persistence, and SRTM topography—with local soil data, ZARC agroclimatic risk zoning, and municipal agricultural statistics from IBGE. 
By calculating the Land Equivalent Ratio (LER > 1.35) and modeling multi-season rotations through mixed-integer optimization, tellai evaluates soil cover during the dry season, mitigates thermal stress, and recommends companion planting strategies that biologically fix nitrogen. 
tellai is vital because smallholder farmers produce over 70% of Brazil’s staple food, yet only 8.2% in the semi-arid region receive regular technical assistance. Under erratic rainfall and extreme heat, monoculture failure threatens community food security. tellai bridges cutting-edge space science with traditional agroecological wisdom, empowering farmers to conserve up to 45% of soil moisture, restore soil organic carbon, and safeguard livelihoods against climate change (directly advancing UN SDGs 2, 6, 12, 13, and 15).
projectDetails.details:
🛰️ What does tellai do and how does it work?

tellai is an open-source, intelligent decision-support platform designed to help smallholder farmers and agricultural extensionists in semi-arid and drought-prone regions transition from vulnerable monocultures to climate-resilient, regenerative crop rotations and polycultures.

Operating under the guiding philosophy "supports, does not decide", tellai works by harmonizing 24 years of NASA Earth Observations across 195 semi-arid locations with local soil parameters, official Brazilian agricultural statistics (IBGE), and agroclimatic risk zoning (ZARC):

1. Satellite Diagnostic Pipeline: Ingests daily NASA POWER agroclimatology (rainfall, extreme temperatures, and all-sky vs. clear-sky solar irradiance), NASA SMAP root-zone soil moisture, NASA SRTM topographical slope, and MODIS vegetation indices (NDVI) to identify historical dry spells (veranicos) and critical bare-soil exposure windows (Campo Nu).

2. Machine Learning & Uncertainty Modeling: Deploys an XGBoost predictive model calibrated with Adaptive Conformal Inference (ACI 80% and 90% coverage), achieving a 28% error reduction over historical climatology in forecasting vegetation anomalies.

3. Agroecological Optimization: Uses multi-criteria stochastic sorting (SMAA-O) and Mixed-Integer Linear Programming (MILP) to generate multi-season crop rotation plans and intercropping strategies based on peer-reviewed Land Equivalent Ratio (LER > 1.35) studies.

4. Accessible Interfaces: Delivers insights through two tailored interfaces: an interactive diagnostic dashboard (Streamlit) for detailed technical simulation, and Maíra, anaccessible, voice-enabled conversational AI (React 19 + FastAPI + DeepSeek) grounded in a strict Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system with automated fact-checking guardrails.

🌱 What benefits does it have?

* Food & Income Security: Replaces single-crop failure risks with diversified year-round harvests (proteins from cowpea/pigeon pea, energy from corn/cassava, and forage from spineless cactus).

* Soil Water Conservation: Living mulches (such as squash and spreading legumes) cut direct soil evaporation by 40% to 60% under intense solar radiation (>20 MJ/m²/day).

* Zero Synthetic Nitrogen Dependency: Integrates biological nitrogen fixation (BNF) through symbiotic Rhizobium legumes, reducing costly and polluting fossil-fuel fertilizers.

* Extensionist Empowerment: Empowers local extension agents with automated, longitudinal environmental profiles for farms, preparing high-quality on-field technical recommendations.

🎯 What is the intended impact of the project?

In the Brazilian Semi-Arid region, smallholder farming accounts for more than 70% of staple food production, yet only 8.2% of rural establishments receive regular technical

assistance (IBGE Agricultural Census). Climate change has intensified rainfall irregularities and topsoil degradation, pushing vulnerable communities toward food insecurity.

tellai directly addresses this crisis by advancing five UN Sustainable Development Goals:

* SDG 2 (Zero Hunger - Target 2.4): Increases harvest yield per hectare with Land Equivalent Ratio (LER > 1.35) without requiring deforestation.

* SDG 6 (Clean Water - Target 6.4): Preserves precious root-zone moisture measured by NASA SMAP and relieves pressure on regional aquifers.

* SDG 12 (Responsible Production - Target 12.4): Eliminates chemical fertilizer runoff and promotes closed-loop organic cycling.

* SDG 13 (Climate Action - Target 13.1): Sequesters Soil Organic Carbon (SOC) and buffers canopy temperatures by up to 3.8°C (monitored by ECOSTRESS).

* SDG 15 (Life on Land - Target 15.3): Halts Caatinga desertification and topsoil runoff on fragile slopes.

💻 What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

* Backend & Scientific Computing: Python 3.14, FastAPI, Uvicorn, XGBoost, Scikit-learn, Scipy, Pandas, NumPy, PyArrow, PyTorch (CPU).

* Machine Learning & Time Series: Adaptive Conformal Inference (ACI), GroupKFold cross-validation by geographic cell, and walk-forward backtesting.

* Natural Language Processing & RAG: DeepSeek LLM, Hugging Face transformers (multilingual-e5-small), custom hybrid semantic-lexical search (BM25) over 50 regional agronomic manuals, and strict anti-hallucination verification filters.

* Frontend Web & UI: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, TanStack Router & Query, Tailwind CSS v4, Three.js / React Three Fiber (3D interactive field and topographical scenes), and Streamlit.

* Platform Engineering, SRE & GitOps: Multi-stage Docker builds, Nginx Alpine, Docker Compose, automated pre-commit security pipelines, and non-root read-only container hardening.

* Data Sources & APIs: NASA POWER API, NASA SMAP, NASA/USGS MODIS (ORNL DAAC), NASA SRTM, ISRIC SoilGrids, Brazilian IBGE SIDRA (PAM API), and MAPA ZARC.

💡 How is tellai creative?

* Prescriptive, Not Just Descriptive: Most environmental tools are passive data viewers. tellai acts as a prescriptive recommendation engine that translates orbital physics into actionable farming practices.

* Fusing Orbital Tech with Ancestral Knowledge: It unites modern satellite radiometry with proven indigenous polyculture systems (such as the 4,000-year-old Milpa and Cactus CAM metabolism).

* Radical Scientific Honesty: In an era of black-box AI, tellai refuses to hallucinate precision. It transparently communicates data resolution limits, highlights empirical ties, and explicitly lists data gaps (e.g., market price volatility or seed availability).

* Voice-First Rural Accessibility: By integrating natural voice interaction in local Brazilian Portuguese, tellai removes technological barriers for farmers with limited literacy.

🔍 What factors did your team consider?

1. Semi-Arid Biophysical Constraints: The strict 4-month wet season (Quadra Chuvosa, Feb–May), unpredictable multi-week dry spells (veranicos), and the severe Campo Nu dry period.

2. Edaphic Heterogeneity: Marked soil contrasts across the Cariri region—from shallow, rocky Neossolos susceptible to rapid erosion to deeper Latossolos on the Araripe Plateau.

3. Socioeconomic Reality: Low capital reserves of smallholders, making expensive synthetic inputs unviable and multi-functional crops (food + animal forage) essential.

4. Data Sovereignty & Offline Resilience: Ensuring all algorithms can run locally inside containerized environments without perpetual internet dependencies.

projectDetails.name: Cultiva.io
projectDetails.summary:
Cultiva.io is a free web platform that helps farmers choose the crop rotation that protects their soil and holds up against the climate ahead. Farmers mark their land on the map, tell us what they grow today and, in under a minute, see their current rotation side by side with three alternatives. Each option is compared on water security, soil health, income, resilience and soil loss.

To do this, we combine open NASA data (30 years of daily climate from POWER, soil moisture from SMAP, rainfall from GPM, vegetation from MODIS, groundwater from GRACE and terrain from SRTM) with NOAA's El Niño data, SoilGrids soil data and actual crop production figures from IBGE. We simulate each crop at 36 planting dates across all 30 years using the FAO water balance model. We estimate erosion with RUSLE.

This matters because the old planting calendar no longer holds. In Sorriso, Mato Grosso, the number of days above 35 °C a year rose from 55 to 93 in 20 years. The data farmers need to adapt already exists, but it isn't reaching them. Cultiva.io turns that data into plain farm language, with no sign-up, on any phone, in Portuguese and English.
projectDetails.details:
Cultiva.io answers the central question of the Field Shift challenge: which crop rotation will make my farm more resilient to a changing climate?

Farmers mark their land on the map (by GPS, by tapping, or by searching a place name). They choose their farm profile (smallholder/family farm, medium or large) and tell us what they currently grow each season.

The system then reads that location from open data sources:

  • NASA POWER: 30 years of daily rainfall and temperature;
  • NASA SMAP: current soil moisture;
  • NASA GPM IMERG: recent rainfall;
  • NASA MODIS: vegetation vigor (NDVI);
  • NASA GRACE: the trend in regional water storage;
  • NASA SRTM: terrain and slope;
  • NOAA: El Niño phase;
  • SoilGrids: soil properties;
  • IBGE: what the municipality actually harvests.

The engine simulates each of 21 crops at 36 planting dates in each of the 30 years. It uses the FAO-56 daily water balance and the FAO-33 yield response to water stress. That adds up to more than 20,000 simulated seasons per analysis. From them come the planting calendar, the yield potential in a typical year and the risk of crop failure.

The farmer's current rotation is compared with three alternatives, using the same data and the farmer's own priorities: water security, soil health, income and resilience. Soil loss is estimated month by month with the RUSLE equation, depending on whether the soil is covered or bare.

As the challenge asks, each alternative comes with five sections: why it was suggested, evidence (the data behind it), benefits, information gaps, and risks to review with an agronomist.

Real example: in Juazeiro do Norte, Ceará, the system confirmed that traditional corn with beans is the best of the rotations compared. It also showed that switching from common beans to cowpea eliminates the risk of crop failure on the best planting date and widens the planting window. And it warned that in El Niño years, the local rainy season had about 20% less rain.

Benefits

  • Decide before planting instead of counting losses afterwards: the right planting window, a safe date for the start of the rains, and the effect of El Niño measured on the farm itself.
  • Healthier soil: farmers see how many tonnes of soil per hectare the rain carries away, and how many months the soil stays bare, in their current rotation and in each alternative.
  • Estimated yields in kg/ha, calibrated against actual production in the municipality.
  • "What if the climate changes?" simulator: tests drought and heat scenarios and reruns every simulation instantly.
  • No barriers to access: free, no sign-up, works on a phone, shares the plan via WhatsApp, and available in Portuguese and English.

Intended impact
We want to bring satellite data that already exists, free of charge, to the people who need it most: small and medium farmers who still plant by a calendar from years ago. In Sorriso, Mato Grosso, for example, the number of days above 35 °C a year rose from 55 to 93 in 20 years. The goal is to reduce crop losses and erosion and to help farmers adapt to the climate. Extension agents and cooperatives can serve more farmers with a ready-made analysis that shows the source of every number.

Tools and technologies

  • Analysis engine: Python 3.12, FastAPI and NumPy (vectorized simulation of all dates and years at once).
  • Web application: Laravel (PHP 8.4), Blade, Alpine.js and Leaflet, as an installable app (PWA).
  • Database: PostgreSQL 17.
  • Infrastructure: Docker Compose, with a Caddy proxy for HTTP and HTTPS.
  • Data sources: NASA POWER, SMAP, GPM IMERG and GRACE (via NASA GIBS), MODIS (ORNL DAAC), SRTM, NOAA CPC, SoilGrids/ISRIC, IBGE SIDRA, Open-Meteo and OpenStreetMap.
  • Scientific methods: FAO-56 water balance and the WRSI index, FAO-33, RUSLE, Saxton & Rawls pedotransfer functions, and cross-validated regression.
  • Hardware: none. It runs on any standard server and on the farmer's phone.

Creative aspects

  • Starts from what the farmer already does: instead of prescribing a rotation, it compares the farmer's own rotation with alternatives and respects local knowledge. When the traditional rotation is already the best, the system says so.
  • El Niño measured, not assumed: instead of using a generic map, we classify each of the 30 years by ONI phase and compare rainfall and simulated harvests at the farm's exact location.
  • Linked rotations: the second crop starts when the first is harvested, and the first planting date is adjusted so the second crop still gets rain.
  • "The farm's story": four sentences that say where the land is, how it is doing today, what the best change would be, and what to expect this season.

Factors the team considered

Scientific honesty:

  • the yield model has a single climate parameter, so it doesn't memorize noise from just a few seasons;
  • climate is only added to the forecast when it beats the trend in out-of-sample validation;
  • model accuracy is published on the Transparency page.

Data limitations:

  • every number shows its source;
  • satellites measure averages over kilometer-wide areas, so the system accepts the farmer's own soil test;
  • every recommendation reminds the farmer to check it with an agronomist and against Brazil's official agricultural climate risk zoning (ZARC).

Field realities:

  • plain language, plus a glossary that explains terms with a tap;
  • works on slow connections and without a login;
  • if one data source fails, the analysis continues with the others.

Accessibility: calendar colors always come with a text label, and the interface is bilingual.
