projectDetails.name: Entressafra: Crop-Rotation Planner for the Fields Between Harvests
projectDetails.summary: Entressafra (Portuguese for the interval between one harvest and the next planting) is a decision-support web tool that helps farmers compare crop-rotation strategies using NASA Earth observation data. A user marks a field on the map, says what is currently grown, and sets priorities such as saving water, adding extra income, or improving soil. The tool then compares at least three rotation strategies, including the current one, and explains why each was suggested, what evidence supports it, what benefits it may bring, where data is missing, and which risks need review by local farmers or agronomists. We use the semi-arid region of Ceará, Brazil, as our case study. Rain there is concentrated in a short season and varies strongly from year to year, so choosing what to plant next is a high-stakes decision. Entressafra supports farmers’ judgment; it does not replace it, and it presents results as risk indicators, not yield forecasts.
projectDetails.details:
O QUE FAZ E COMO FUNCIONA
Entressafra é uma ferramenta web gratuita que ajuda os agricultores a decidir o que plantar após a colheita. O usuário marca um campo em um mapa e escolhe a cultura atual, a estação chuvosa e o que mais importa: resiliência hídrica, saúde do solo, interrupção do ciclo de pragas, forragem ou renda. A ferramenta extrai até 30 anos de precipitação diária e temperatura máxima do NASA POWER (20 anos por padrão) para esse ponto exato. Transforma-os em indicadores climáticos simples: precipitação sazonal, variação anual, período de seca mais longo, dias quentes e meses com pouca chuva para cultivar sem irrigação (a "janela entresafra"). Em seguida, compara três estratégias de rotação: a atual mais as duas melhores alternativas. Para cada opção, a ferramenta mostra uma pontuação, por que ela foi sugerida e o que observar. As evidências da NASA e as lacunas de informação são listadas uma vez, para todas as opções. A pontuação é uma média ponderada transparente, e as prioridades do próprio agricultor definem os pesos.

BENEFÍCIOS
Os agricultores obtêm uma comparação clara e explicada em vez de um palpite, em linguagem simples, em inglês ou português. Cada resultado também indica o que os dados não podem dizer. A mesma ferramenta funciona para um pequeno agricultor e para uma fazenda comercial, porque o usuário escolhe as prioridades. Ele roda em um telefone, sem conta ou instalação.

IMPACTO PRETENDIDO
Na agricultura de sequeiro no semiárido brasileiro, a precipitação se concentra em poucos meses e muda muito de ano para ano, portanto a escolha da próxima cultura é uma decisão de risco. Em Cedro, Ceará, onde mora nossa equipe, a temporada fevereiro-maio trouxe 795 mm em 2009, mas apenas 382 mm em 2012. Em Petrolina, Pernambuco, a temporada novembro-abril variou de 120 mm a 593 mm nas últimas 19 temporadas. Queremos tornar a escolha da próxima cultura mais bem informada e mais resiliente à seca, protegendo ao mesmo tempo o solo e quebrando os ciclos de pragas. A Entressafra apoia o julgamento do agricultor e nunca o substitui. O próximo passo é um piloto no Ceará com agricultores e agrônomos.

FERRAMENTAS E TECNOLOGIA

  • HTML, CSS e JavaScript, sem framework e sem backend
  • Folheto com OpenStreetMap para o mapa
  • NASA POWER Daily API, comunidade de agroclimatologia, variáveis PRECTOTCORR e T2M_MAX
  • Testes unitários com o executor de testes Node.js
  • Páginas do GitHub para hospedagem
  • Código fonte aberto (licença MIT)

    Demonstração ao vivo: https://teogenes18.github.io/entressafra/
    Código: https://github.com/Teogenes18/entressafra

COMO É CRIATIVO
Tratamos o intervalo entre as colheitas como a janela de decisão, o que dá nome à ferramenta: "entressafra" é a palavra portuguesa para ela. Em vez de uma previsão de caixa preta, a ferramenta mostra uma pontuação transparente com razões, evidências, lacunas e riscos para cada opção. Cada pontuação é dividida por prioridade, para que o agricultor veja exatamente quantos pontos cada escolha adicionou, e a classificação é atualizada instantaneamente conforme as prioridades mudam. Diferentes tipos de fazendas podem usar a mesma lógica mudando as prioridades. A ferramenta funciona para qualquer ponto da Terra, em inglês ou português, no navegador.


FATORES QUE CONSIDERAMOS

  • Apoio à decisão, não um veredito: o resultado é um indicador de risco climático, não uma previsão de rendimento ou lucro.
  • Limites honestos: NASA POWER são dados em grade que descrevem uma área, não um campo. A tabela de características das culturas e os limites são provisórios e devem ser validados com fontes como a Embrapa e com agrônomos locais. Esta versão não modela solo local, preços de mercado, irrigação, mão de obra ou acesso a sementes.
  • Usuários: pequenos agricultores e fazendas comerciais que enfrentam o mesmo clima instável.
  • Acesso: um layout mobile-first, linguagem simples, cores seguras e daltônicas com uma tabela atrás de cada gráfico e dados salvos do NASA POWER como alternativa quando a API está lenta.
  • Transparência: todas as fórmulas e fontes de dados estão documentadas no repositório.
  • Próximos passos: adicionar dados de umidade do solo, precipitação e vegetação da NASA (como SMAP, GPM, MODIS ou Landsat) e validar com os agricultores.

ASSISTÊNCIA DE IA

Partes do código, testes e documentação foram escritas com a assistência de Claude (Anthropic), uma IA projetada para programação, seguindo a orientação da equipe. A equipe definiu o desafio e o problema, tomou decisões de design e testou a ferramenta em computadores e dispositivos móveis, relatando problemas que foram posteriormente corrigidos. Todos os dados climáticos são provenientes da NASA POWER; nenhum dado foi gerado por IA.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: Project Capivara Astronauta
projectDetails.summary: Antarctic Ice Mass Trend Detective is an interactive 3D platform that uses NASA satellite data to investigate where, how much, and since when Antarctica is losing ice. By processing GRACE and GRACE-FO observations, our open-source pipeline analyzes monthly ice-mass changes across West Antarctica, East Antarctica, and the Antarctic Peninsula. We apply statistical methods to distinguish long-term trends from natural variability and identify when the evidence becomes statistically significant. Through interactive visualizations, 3D exploration, time-series charts, and a detection timeline, users can explore regional differences, uncertainties, and the influence of snowfall. The platform also connects Antarctic ice loss to projected sea-level rise in 17 coastal cities. By making complex scientific data accessible, transparent, and explorable, Trend Detective helps students, researchers, and the public understand how Antarctica is changing and why long-term satellite observations matter.
projectDetails.details:
Antarctic Ice Mass Trend Detective is a web-based interactive 3D expedition that answers one question about our planet: is Antarctica losing its ice, where, by how much, and since when can we say so with statistical confidence? Most reports give a single number for the whole continent. Our platform opens that number up, sector by sector and month by month, and adds the piece that is usually missing: the moment when the evidence became strong enough to rule out natural variability.

How it works:

Trend Detective ingests the NASA/JPL GRACE and GRACE Follow-On mascon solution (RL06.3 CRI, April 2002 to July 2026) and sums the ice-mass signal over the Antarctic drainage-system sectors defined by Zwally et al. (West, East, Peninsula). Each sector's monthly series is deseasonalised, its trend is estimated with Theil-Sen (95% confidence interval) and tested with Mann-Kendall using an effective sample size that corrects autocorrelation. An expanding window then finds the first year from which the trend stays statistically significant, and we compare that with the analytical years-to-detect of Weatherhead et al. (1998). NASA's MERRA-2 reanalysis puts snowfall variability in context, because snow is the main natural noise hiding the signal. A stress-test lab shows how the answers change with start date, mission gap and instrument splice.

What it finds (all computed from NASA data by our open pipeline):

- Antarctica as a whole: about −128 Gt/year, detectable since 2008.

- West Antarctica: about −160 Gt/year, detectable since 2016.

- Antarctic Peninsula: about −29 Gt/year, not yet detectable (roughly 17 years of record needed).

- East Antarctica: about +61 Gt/year, a gain, detectable since 2009.

Key Benefits & Impact:

- Shows scientists and students that "Antarctica is losing ice, but not everywhere", and how long a record must be before a trend can be trusted.

- Helps researchers prioritise sectors where the signal is still hidden in the noise.

- Connects the ice sheet to people: using IPCC AR6 projections, it shows how much of the sea-level rise at 17 coastal cities comes from Antarctica alone, across three emissions scenarios and four dates.

- Gives non-programmers visual, no-code access to a large satellite dataset, with uncertainty stated openly (including NASA's published ±39 Gt/year, which also covers the glacial isostatic adjustment model).

- Fully open: every number on the site comes from a tested pipeline in our public repository.

Tools & Technologies:

- Python (NumPy, SciPy, pandas, xarray, netCDF4) for preprocessing, trend statistics, sector masks and tests (pytest)

- React 19, TanStack Start and TypeScript for the web app, with Zod validating the data contract

- Three.js / React Three Fiber for the 3D globe and ice-sheet scenes, Recharts for the time series and detection charts

- Vitest for front-end tests, GitHub for collaboration, Vercel for hosting

- Data: NASA/JPL GRACE and GRACE-FO, NASA GMAO MERRA-2, IPCC AR6 sea-level projections, NASA Blue Marble

Creative Elements:

- A nine-chapter "expedition" from orbit to the ice sheet, built around the three questions of the challenge: where, how much, and since when.

- A hands-on "since when?" scrubber: the viewer drags an expanding window and watches the trend lock in against the snow noise.

- A heat map that follows the real continent outline, with live telemetry under the cursor.

- Everyday comparisons (tonnes of ice per second, school buses, a 16 m cube of ice) next to the sea-level conversion, so the numbers can be felt.

- A "cities nearest to me" option that makes sea-level rise personal; location is requested only after a click.

- Works with wheel, swipe or arrow keys, with sound off by default and reduced-motion support.

Use of Artificial Intelligence (AI)

We used AI tools to speed up development and documentation.

- AI-assisted code autocomplete and coding assistants helped write code, tests and documentation throughout the repository.

- An AI assistant (Claude code) helped us assemble the website: the interface, the 3D scenes, the charts and the data-processing scripts, always from our own data choices, method and design decisions. Everything was reviewed and edited by the team.

- Lovable.dev: To prototype page structure and layout faster.

- No NASA logos or branding were generated or imitated by AI.

AI helped accelerate the process, but the scientific question, the statistical method, the choice of datasets, the sector definitions and the interpretation of results were team-led. Every figure shown comes from NASA data processed by our own tested code.

Team Capivara Astronauta: Priscilla Leandro, Alexandre Moreira, Matheus Oliveira and Maria Eduarda Ishimaru.

Live site: https://capivaraastronauta.patitow.dev · Code: https://github.com/patitow/nasa-space-apps-2026

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

challengeDetails.title: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
challengeDetails.excerpt: Space-themed STEM content often oversimplifies the engineering trade-offs that define a real mission or presents them at a level too complex to hold a young learner's attention. Few tools make those trade-offs both tangible and fun. Your challenge is to design and build an interactive game or app that lets students run a lunar or Martian outpost, balancing competing demands like life support, radiation shielding, power, and food production, so they experience firsthand the decisions that determine whether a mission fails or succeeds.

projectDetails.name: Project LâmpadaCareca
projectDetails.summary: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive, deterministic 2D space simulation developed with Godot 4 and a high-performance, test-driven Rust core (GDExtension). Players command an experimental lunar spacecraft, "Lata de Sardinha", guiding astronaut Neil Armstrong through a 7-day translunar journey to establish humanity's first permanent Moon base. To address the challenge, the game bridges authentic NASA datasets with accessible youth gameplay (ages 7–12). It integrates real Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) imagery, NOAA/SWPC proton flux records, and CCMC DONKI solar flare catalogs from the historic September 2017 solar storms. Players navigate critical trade-offs under a strict 5-block zero-sum energy economy—balancing life support, radiation shielding, and hydroponics—while repairing system faults and managing realistic light-time telemetry delays with Houston and the Recife tracking station. This project is important because it transforms complex astrophysics into intuitive cause-and-effect learning. By demonstrating how real space weather impacts spacecraft survival, it fosters genuine scientific literacy, engineering problem-solving, and systems thinking, inspiring the Artemis generation of future explorers.
projectDetails.details:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a 2D spaceflight simulation developed in Godot 4 with a deterministic Rust simulation core (via GDExtension). Players guide astronaut Neil Armstrong through a 7-day translunar crossing aboard the experimental spacecraft Lata de Sardinha to establish humanity's first lunar base. Each turn (Sol), players allocate a strict 5-block energy budget across life support, deflector shields, and hydroponics, where deficits carry over into future turns. Players examine real NASA Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO) spectroscopy and NOAA proton flux data to predict space weather, repair hull faults with a MultiTool, and transmit telemetry to Houston and Recife under simulated light-delay latency (3–20 minutes).

Benefits & Impact

• Root-cause feedback: Decisions yield immediate, deterministic reports on hull damage, crew radiation dose (mSv), and food reserves.

• Scientific accuracy: Translates historical NASA CCMC DONKI flare catalogs and NOAA solar proton peaks into concrete engineering constraints without exaggerated medical claims.

• STEM literacy: Replaces guesswork with hypothesis testing; children aged 7–12 learn that deep-space habitats require constant resource trade-offs.

Tools & Technologies

• Engine: Godot Engine 4 (GDScript, 2D physics, UI, CRT shaders).

• Simulation Core: Pure Rust 2021 (rust_core), isolated from engine dependencies for memory safety and zero runtime panics.

• Datasets: NASA CCMC DONKI, NOAA SWPC, and NASA OSDR research contexts validated via serde_json.

• Quality Gate: Automated CI script (build_and_verify.sh) verifying JSON schemas, asset paths, Rust unit tests (cargo test), strict linter rules (cargo clippy), and headless Godot boots.

Creativity & Design Factors

• Replaces combat mechanics with non-violent systems engineering and historical space operations.

• Pairs the Apollo 11 lunar module aesthetic with September 2017 solar flare records (region AR 12673).

• Implements dual-channel visual accessibility (symbols paired with high-contrast colors) and single-command offline launchers (jogar.sh and jogar.bat) for school computers.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Speculum
projectDetails.summary: Speculum is an interactive web tool for choosing where on Earth to test a rover, drill, habitat, or power system before it flies to the Moon or Mars. Its catalog has 89 locations: 23 backed by published analog literature and 66 candidates scored on climate alone, 61 of which came from a global climate scan of places outside the catalog. All sites are scored against lunar, Martian, and Europan targets. Users describe their project and get a ranked list that shows why each site scored as it did, how complete its data is, and where the analogy breaks down. All climate values come from 25 years of NASA POWER data, and the planetary reference values come from the NASA NSSDC Moon and Mars Fact Sheets.
projectDetails.details:
What Speculum does

Speculum has three tools, available at https://gpradines.github.io/speculum/.

Map: An interactive map of documented analog sites and climate-only candidates. Each site’s panel lists its climate values with confidence levels, its strengths and weaknesses, how testing there helps exploration, and access and permit warnings. It also has a “where the analogy breaks down” section, which compares the site with Moon and Mars reference values in plain language, for example how many times the site’s air pressure exceeds Mars’s.

Finder: The user picks a project type (wheeled rover, ice drilling, habitat and ISRU, power and communications, and others), a target environment (lunar south pole, lunar lava tubes, equatorial Mars, Mars mid-latitudes with ice, and others), logistics filters, and optional parameter weights. The tool returns the top 10 sites, split into Tier A (published analog evidence) and Tier B (climate similarity only). Each result has a per-parameter breakdown, and the list can be exported as CSV.

Methods: A page with the scoring method, a worked example, all 29 parameters, confidence rules, known limitations, and the full source list.

The problem

Teams preparing hardware for the Moon or Mars need field sites on Earth that stress their equipment realistically. Published analog studies are scattered across decades of papers, and no Earth location reproduces every condition of another world. Teams often fall back on a few famous sites without a systematic comparison.

How it works

Ranking is relative. No place on Earth reaches the absolute temperature, pressure, or dryness of Mars or the Moon. Each target defines a direction (equatorial Mars is colder, drier, and thinner-aired than most of Earth), and each site gets a percentile position among all other sites along those directions.

Each project type has its own parameter weights: a drilling project values ground ice and cold, a rover values terrain and dryness. Weights are scaled by data confidence, and users can adjust them.

Only parameters that have data are scored. Each result shows its coverage, such as “based on 7 of 12 parameters with data”, plus low-confidence warnings. Of the 29 parameters in the schema, only 12 currently have data. The rest (slope, rock abundance, soil bearing strength, radiation, and others) are listed as limitations and future work.

When a published paper and NASA POWER give different values for the same parameter, the paper wins. Where the coarse grid clearly misrepresents a mountain or island site, we removed the grid values instead of keeping misleading numbers.

To look beyond known analog sites, we scanned 64 regions not in the catalog, including the Gobi, Taklamakan, Pamir, Altiplano, Antarctic and Greenland ice domes, and Kamchatka. This produced candidates such as the Pamir Plateau and Altun Shan for equatorial Mars rovers, and Dome A and Axel Heiberg for the lunar south pole. They are labeled as hypotheses from climate data only, with no literature behind them.

The method re-ranks known analogs highly (Concordia for ice and cold, Atacama for astrobiology). We also built reference test cases with expected rankings and checked the site’s output against them, for example wheeled rover for equatorial Mars: Qaidam 74.0, MDRS 67.7, Death Valley 60.1, Atacama 54.2.

Where the analogy fails

Earth analogs never reproduce reduced gravity, lunar vacuum, the Martian atmosphere, or the radiation environment. Concordia ranks high for ice and cold, but it is an analog for isolation and extreme cold, and says little about terrain. Climate-only candidates have low confidence and need local verification before any real test campaign. Many coordinates are approximate.

Why it matters

Speculum puts scattered analog knowledge into one ranking tool and shows the uncertainty behind each result. The discovery scan points to less-studied regions that deserve a closer look.

Next steps

A continuous global grid scan instead of hand-picked regions, elevation-based slope and roughness from NASA and other agencies’ terrain data, ice and permafrost layers, local field-station verification, and more Europa and lunar-polar analogs.

Team

High school students from Recife, Brazil: Elias Cassemiro de Lucena Junior, Guilherme Pradines Falcão, Pedro Endry Garmes Veras, Victor Germano Peregrino, and Vinicius Soares Campelo.

Links

Website: https://gpradines.github.io/speculum/
Repository: https://github.com/gpradines/speculum

projectDetails.summary: Aqui está o resumo ajustado para atender ao limite de caracteres (com contagem otimizada):Flame Atlas é um painel digital interativo e protótipo independente para explorar pesquisas sobre fogo em microgravidade e segurança espacial.   O Problema: Evidências dispersas. Comparar estudos exige contexto, pois a ausência de gravidade altera o transporte de calor, a forma das chamas e o escopo dos experimentos.   A Solução: Plataforma com catálogo de 6 investigações (FLEX, BASS-II, Saffire-VI, SoFIE-GEL, SAME, ACME-BRE). Permite busca por material/tema, filtros por plataforma, comparação cruzada de até 3 estudos e exportação de sínteses.   Exemplo: O estudo FLEX revelou chamas frias invisíveis após o término da chama visível, enquanto o SAME caracterizou partículas de fumaça, provando que a detecção precisa ir além da luz visível.   Evolução: Conta com catálogo curado e análise por regras. Os próximos passos incluem integrar medições e avaliar IA com recuperação de fontes. Nota: É uma ferramenta exploratória e educacional, sem cálculo de risco em tempo real.
projectDetails.details:
O Flame Atlas é um painel interativo em português que facilita a exploração de pesquisas da NASA sobre combustão em microgravidade. Nosso objetivo é tornar essas informações mais acessíveis, ajudando estudantes, pesquisadores e participantes do desafio a compreender descobertas relevantes para a segurança contra incêndios na exploração espacial.

O protótipo reúne resumos de seis investigações: FLEX, BASS-II, Saffire-VI, SoFIE-GEL, SAME e ACME-BRE. O usuário pode buscar estudos, filtrar por tema e plataforma, comparar até três investigações e consultar suas fontes originais. Também pode exportar o catálogo e baixar uma síntese com referências.

Organizamos as informações por temas como detecção, extinção, propagação e materiais. Cada estudo apresenta o que a fonte informa, uma interpretação editorial e suas limitações. A interface distingue resultados relatados, descrições de ensaios e objetivos de pesquisa, evitando apresentar expectativas como descobertas comprovadas.

Desenvolvemos o painel com HTML, CSS e JavaScript, com apoio do OpenAI Codex na programação e na organização do conteúdo. A aplicação funciona no navegador, sem hardware específico ou chave de API. Utilizamos fontes públicas da NASA, incluindo páginas de experimentos, o NASA Technical Reports Server e o catálogo NASA PSI.

O diferencial do projeto é permitir que o usuário acompanhe o caminho entre a evidência e sua interpretação. Consideramos a clareza da linguagem, a rastreabilidade das fontes e as diferenças entre materiais e condições experimentais.

Nesta versão, a síntese usa regras determinísticas e conteúdo editorial. Não implementamos IA generativa ou superinteligência, nem importamos séries de medições experimentais. Como próximos passos, propomos integrar esses dados e avaliar um assistente de IA que recupere evidências e apresente respostas com citações, com validação por especialistas.

O impacto pretendido é facilitar o acesso à literatura e apoiar a formulação de perguntas de pesquisa. O painel não calcula riscos nem define procedimentos de emergência. Também reconhece que resultados em microgravidade não se aplicam automaticamente às condições de gravidade parcial da Lua ou de Marte.

challengeDetails.title: Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data
challengeDetails.excerpt: For decades, NASA has studied how flames and fire behave in microgravity, gathering a trove of experimental data along the way. Your challenge is to create an interactive, super intelligence (SI) powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets those findings to deliver fire safety insights for human space exploration.

projectDetails.name: Project M.A.P.S = Moon and Mars Analog Planetary Scouts
projectDetails.summary:
M.A.P.S. (Mission Analog Planning System) is a planetary analog investigation platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It helps mission teams identify and investigate terrestrial locations that may serve as analogs for lunar and Martian environments, supporting equipment testing, operational research, and mission planning.

Its first functional workflow focuses on Mars, analyzing local terrain morphology around a selected point within a crater or crater rim. Using planetary elevation datasets, the system calculates terrain characteristics on demand, identifies potential terrestrial candidates, and provides evidence for comparative investigation.

Beyond terrain analysis, M.A.P.S. supports independent scientific evidence, multiscale comparisons, auditable candidate shortlists, and downloadable reports in PDF and JSON formats.

By connecting planetary datasets with interactive geospatial analysis, M.A.P.S. aims to make the investigation of terrestrial analog environments more accessible, transparent, and reproducible for future planetary exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview

M.A.P.S. (Mission Analog Planning System) is an interactive planetary analog investigation platform developed to support the identification and study of terrestrial environments that may resemble specific locations on the Moon and Mars.

The platform addresses the challenge of finding suitable Earth analog sites for planetary research, equipment testing, operational simulations, and mission preparation.

How It Works

The first functional workflow focuses on Mars. Users select a point within a Martian crater or crater rim, and the system retrieves planetary elevation data to calculate local terrain morphology on demand.

Based on this analysis, M.A.P.S. identifies and ranks potential terrestrial candidates using a seeded catalog of Earth locations. Users can then investigate the candidates through comparative evidence, multiscale terrain analysis, and individual candidate dossiers.

The platform also supports independent thermal and mineralogical evidence where available. These evidence layers complement the investigation but do not modify the topographic ranking.

Users can create an auditable shortlist of up to three candidates, add human annotations, compare locations, and export investigation reports in PDF or JSON formats.

Scientific Foundation and Data

M.A.P.S. integrates planetary and terrestrial datasets, including NASA's Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA), the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM), and additional planetary and environmental data sources.

The architecture supports independent evidence retrieval, data provenance tracking, and explicit handling of unavailable datasets.

Technology

The platform is developed using React, Vite, and CesiumJS for the frontend, with Python and FastAPI powering the backend. Docker Compose supports the development environment and service orchestration.

Innovation and Expected Impact

M.A.P.S. connects planetary topography with terrestrial site investigation through an interactive and reproducible workflow.

Rather than treating visual similarity as scientific equivalence, the system provides structured evidence that researchers and mission teams can inspect, compare, annotate, and preserve for further investigation.

Its goal is to support more informed exploration of terrestrial analog environments and contribute to research, technology testing, and future Moon and Mars mission planning.

projectDetails.name: MARSYNC🚀
projectDetails.summary:
MARSYNC is an educational website that shows the real Mars using NASA and ESA data. We explain Gale Crater, Mount Sharp, and the Boxwork formations studied by the Curiosity rover in a simple and visual way for students.
 Our project includes an interactive exploration map where users can mark points, analyze simulated altitude, slope and radiation, and create a route A → B → C to plan a mission base. MARSYNC helps young people understand how we could survive on Mars.
projectDetails.details: MARSYNC is a website built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. It presents real information about Mars: distance from Earth, temperature, Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris, Gale Crater, Curiosity, Perseverance and Ingenuity. The main feature is the Boxwork Mission Map. The user can click on the map to create custom points, see simulated altitude, slope, radiation index and risk classification, and calculate an estimated EVA walking route. The map uses a mathematical illustrative model, not official NASA elevation data, and we clearly explain this limitation. The benefit is to make space science accessible and easy to understand for students, using simple language and visual explanations. The creative aspect is combining storytelling, real data and an interactive planning tool in one mobile-friendly site. Our team considered education, simplicity and scientific honesty.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: WHERE EXPLORERS REST: STORIES OF MACHINES THAT CROSSED THE SILENCE TO BRING US CLOSER TO THE STARS
projectDetails.summary:
The project Where Explorers Rest tells the stories of space probes, rovers, and equipment that, after completing their missions, remained on other worlds or continued traveling through deep space. Through an illustrated narrative for young audiences, readers discover these silent explorers and their contributions to space exploration.
Guided by Linaria, the journey explores the Moon, Mars, and distant regions of the Solar System, revealing technological achievements and the human stories behind each mission. The book aims to inspire scientific curiosity and celebrate humanity's desire to explore and understand the unknown.
projectDetails.details:
Introduction

Space exploration is marked by great discoveries, technological advancements, and missions that have expanded our understanding of the Universe. Throughout this journey, numerous machines have been sent to explore other worlds, collect information, and reach distant regions of the Solar System.

However, not all of them remain operational. Some rest on the surfaces of the Moon and Mars, others completed their missions in the depths of giant planets, while some continue traveling through space, even after decades of activity.

Where Explorers Rest is an illustrated book that brings these stories back to life, introducing young readers to the machines that have shaped space exploration and the scientific legacy they have left for humanity.

Objectives

The main objective of this project is to bring young audiences closer to the history of space exploration, inspiring curiosity about the technologies, missions, and discoveries that have contributed to our understanding of the Solar System.

  • Specific objectives include:
  • Introducing probes, landers, rovers, and other equipment used in space exploration.
  • Explaining, in a simple and accessible way, the scientific importance of these missions.
  • Highlighting the legacy of equipment that has ceased operating or remains in distant locations.
  • Encouraging interest in astronomy, technology, and scientific research.
  • Demonstrating that even after a mission ends, its discoveries continue to contribute to human knowledge.

Development

The project was developed as an illustrated book, organized into chapters that follow different stages of space exploration.

The narrative begins on the Moon, moves on to the machines that explored Mars, and continues with missions that met their final destinations on planets such as Jupiter, Saturn, and Mercury. It then introduces probes that continue traveling through the most distant regions of the Solar System.

Among the explorers featured are the modules and instruments from the Apollo missions, the Viking landers, the Sojourner, Spirit, and Opportunity rovers, as well as the Cassini, Galileo, MESSENGER, Pioneer, and Voyager probes.

The book uses an educational and narrative approach, guided by the character Linaria, who accompanies readers throughout the journey and introduces the stories of each explorer. Scientific information is based on official NASA materials and records, while the illustrations and visual identity were designed to convey a science fiction atmosphere inspired by the aesthetics of the 1960s.

Impact

The project seeks to transform scientific information into a more engaging, visual, and accessible reading experience for young audiences.

By presenting space missions through stories, illustrations, and accessible explanations, the book aims to encourage scientific curiosity and demonstrate that space exploration is about more than astronauts and major discoveries.

Every piece of equipment sent into space represents years of research, planning, and human effort. Even those that no longer function remain part of scientific history, as the data they collected helps us better understand planets, moons, and the very origins of the Solar System.

In this way, the project also seeks to highlight engineering, scientific research, and collaboration across different fields of knowledge.

Conclusion

Throughout history, machines built by humanity have traveled vast distances to explore places we once knew very little about. Some have remained on distant worlds; others have disappeared into the depths of planets or continued their journeys toward interstellar space.

Although many of these missions have come to an end, their contributions remain. Every transmitted image, every measurement taken, and every discovery represents an important step in humanity's attempt to understand the Universe.

Where Explorers Rest is, above all, a tribute to these silent explorers and to the people who made their journeys possible. After all, a mission may end, but the knowledge it leaves behind continues to travel.

Use of Artificial Intelligence

Artificial intelligence was used as a supporting tool throughout the development of this project, contributing to the organization of ideas, the drafting and revision of texts, and the creation of visual concepts for the character Linaria and the book's illustrative identity.

AI tools assisted in the creative process, particularly in developing an aesthetic inspired by 1960s science fiction and in visually representing the journey through space.

projectDetails.name: Project STRATA
projectDetails.summary:
Hello! I’m Enzo, and these are Mel and our teacher, Gisele.

We’re here to present our project for the 2026 Challenge! We are team STRATA (Health, Technology, Tracking, Environment, Territory, and Analysis), and our challenge is: “Become a detective of Earth system trends!”

We analyzed environmental changes from 1970 to 2026, looking at ten-year intervals. We observed that precipitation increased from 990 to 1,015 millimeters per year (an increase of 0.5% every 10 years), alongside shifts in vegetation indices and solar reflection.
What can STRATA uncover by cross-referencing these indicators?
The great advantage lies in analyzing these indicators together.

For example:
- Rising temperature + decreasing NDVI: could indicate vegetation stress.
- Decreasing precipitation + decreasing air humidity: could indicate drier conditions.
- Increasing albedo + changes in vegetation cover: could indicate surface transformation.
- Decreasing EVI + decreasing NDVI: could indicate a loss of vegetation vigor.
These relationships serve as analytical hypotheses, not as definitive proof of causality.

Our goal is to investigate the transformations of our planet over time!
projectDetails.details:
What is STRATA?
STRATA is essentially a dashboard that displays the state of the Earth in real time. It is referred to as "Earth Intelligence"—a way of capturing the "intelligence" of our planet. Although it is a school project using demonstration data, the concept behind it is very real: helping us better understand the place where we live. In the example shown on the screen, it displays the Cerrado region here in Brazil. At a glance, it provides key data: the temperature is 26.8°C, soil moisture is at 60%, there has been no rainfall (0.0 mm), and the air quality index is 48—indicating good, breathable air. It also highlights three active alerts that require attention.

What does it contain?
Think of it as a control center for a given territory. The menu covers a wide range of categories: maps, soil, climate, topography, agriculture, rivers, the atmosphere, satellite data, vegetation, air quality—even the solar system and alerts. In short, it doesn’t just present isolated figures; it aggregates everything to provide a comprehensive summary of a territory, allowing us to grasp the full story of that place. And how does this benefit humanity? In very practical ways: if a farmer knows that the soil is already moist and no rain is expected, they can avoid wasting water—leading to more food on the table and less waste. If a parent sees that air quality is poor on a given day, they know it’s better for their child to limit outdoor play—a way of safeguarding health. If a city receives an alert about an approaching storm or drought, there is time to prepare—and preparation can save lives. Furthermore, if we notice vegetation disappearing, we can identify environmental issues before it’s too late. Ultimately, STRATA is more than just a website packed with data. It’s a way for us to look at the Earth with greater care, understand what it’s trying to tell us, and make better decisions. It represents science and technology working together to look after both people and the planet. And for us at school, it’s even better—because we get to learn physics, mathematics, and geography by seeing all of this unfold in the real world.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project AstroKali
projectDetails.summary: Our project explores the science and safety of combustion in microgravity aboard the International Space Station (ISS). To address the challenge of understanding fire behavior and improving energy efficiency, we developed a dashboard based on experimental ISS combustion data. Studying flames without the interference of gravity and turbulence allows scientists to observe combustion with high precision, revealing that fire in space can burn at lower temperatures and spread invisibly depending on spacecraft ventilation. This work is vital because its findings directly improve safety and sustainability: on Earth, it supports cleaner fuel burning and has inspired life-saving technologies like smoke detectors and firefighter oxygen tanks, while in space, accurate fire-behavior data is essential to protect astronauts on future long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars.
projectDetails.dataReferences: [Physical Sciences Informatics Database](https://psi.nasa.gov/physci/repo/search?q=combustion&data_source=psi&data_type=investigation)

challengeDetails.title: Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data

Your challenge is to create an interactive, super intelligence (SI) powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets those findings to deliver fire safety insights for human space exploration.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: AstroCare
projectDetails.summary: O AstroCare é um projeto de óculos inteligentes desenvolvido para monitorar a saúde dos astronautas durante missões espaciais. Por meio de tecnologias avançadas, os óculos poderão acompanhar sinais vitais, como frequência cardíaca e temperatura corporal, além de identificar sinais de cansaço. O projeto busca solucionar os desafios do monitoramento da saúde no espaço, emitindo alertas sobre possíveis alterações no organismo. Sua importância está em prevenir problemas de saúde, proporcionar mais segurança aos astronautas e contribuir para missões espaciais mais seguras e eficientes.
projectDetails.details:
Projeto AstroCare: Sistema Integrado de Monitoramento Biométrico e Preditivo de Saúde Mental para Atividades Extraveiculares

O AstroCare é uma solução tecnológica desenvolvida para integrar e processar, em tempo real, os dados de telemetria biomédica captados pelos sistemas de suporte à vida da NASA, exibindo indicadores críticos de saúde diretamente nos dispositivos de exibição já utilizados pela agência, como visores de capacetes e óculos de realidade mista. Esta inovação resolve uma lacuna crítica na exploração espacial contemporânea, caracterizada pela impossibilidade de gerenciar e analisar ativamente as condições de saúde do astronauta durante Atividades Extraveiculares. Durante essas missões fora da espaçonave, a equipe de solo e o próprio operador carecem de ferramentas centralizadas que transformem dados brutos de sensores em tomadas de decisão imediatas, o que se torna ainda mais grave quando somado aos riscos da fadiga cognitiva e do isolamento social. O confinamento prolongado e o convívio restrito representam gatilhos severos para o esgotamento mental, aumentando a probabilidade de erros humanos catastróficos que comprometem a segurança de toda a tripulação, conforme o BMed-102.

No mapeamento de riscos para o desenvolvimento de soluções de saúde mental em ambiente espacial, identificou-se que os métodos tradicionais sofrem com um ponto de falha potencial devido à dependência de dados de entrada subjetivos e não auditáveis. Diagnósticos baseados em questionários autodeclarativos frequentemente falham, pois os indivíduos tendem a omitir ou mascarar sintomas psicológicos quando interagem com interfaces computacionais frias e automatizadas. Para mitigar esse viés de auto-relato, o AstroCare implementa uma interface conversacional personalizada, configurada para mimetizar o tom de voz, o acolhimento, a proximidade e a identidade visual de um familiar do astronauta. Essa abordagem estabelece um vínculo de confiança que estimula respostas mais fidedignas e transparentes, potencializando a precisão das análises automatizadas sem violar a percepção de segurança do usuário.

A partir desse canal de comunicação humanizado, o software opera por meio de um modelo preditivo que monitora continuamente parâmetros biológicos e executa o processamento de linguagem natural para analisar metadados da fala, como variações de tom, ritmo, pausas e escolhas semânticas. Esses dados são cruzados por algoritmos de aprendizado de máquina para antecipar picos de estresse e fadiga cognitiva antes que afetem o desempenho operacional. O sistema atua de maneira escalonada e governada por níveis de risco bem definidos. Em condições nominais, sob o nível verde, o AstroCare restringe-se ao monitoramento passivo e rotinas casuais. Caso detecte desvios leves no comportamento ou na fisiologia, o nível amarelo é acionado, fazendo com que a interface sugira intervenções preventivas discretas, como exercícios de respiração e pausas guiadas. Por fim, ao atingir o nível vermelho, que indica sobrecarga mental iminente, o software projeta alertas visuais urgentes nos visores de realidade mista, notifica simultaneamente o controle da missão na Terra e recomenda a interrupção imediata da atividade para aplicação dos protocolos de descompressão e segurança.

projectDetails.name: Project Star Promises
projectDetails.summary: Star Promises: Earth-to-Mars and Moon Analog Atlas is an interactive 3D Google Earth (KML) expedition connecting extreme terrestrial environments to Moon and Mars exploration sites. Starting from dual Ground Zeros at the Sorocaba Technology Park in Brazil and the Kennedy Space Center in the USA, our crew and five original characters guide users through 11 global and Brazilian planetary analogs. Powered by open NASA satellite datasets (Landsat, MODIS, ASTER, SRTM, ICESat-2, and LRO) and bilingual vertical video guides, the project combines remote sensing, pop-culture storytelling, and space education to support future Artemis and Mars missions.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: Project Agrolynx
projectDetails.summary:
Agrolynx is a digital platform developed to bring space technology closer to agriculture, helping farmers and agricultural professionals organize information and make more informed and sustainable decisions.

The project brings together agricultural management tools, geographic mapping of farms and fields, and information about soil, climate, crops, and irrigation. It also incorporates NASA data sources and scientific resources, including NASA POWER, NASA Earthdata CMR, and MODIS, making it possible to relate meteorological information and satellite observations of the Earth's surface to agricultural needs.

Agrolynx aims to contribute to more efficient and sustainable agriculture that is better prepared to face environmental and climate challenges. Its purpose is to transform scientific and geospatial data into useful information for people working in agriculture, bringing Earth observation closer to everyday farming decisions.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details — AGROLYNX

Agrolynx is a smart agriculture digital platform designed to connect space technology with the everyday needs of farmers. Its goal is to facilitate agricultural management and transform environmental, geographic, and meteorological information into useful knowledge to support decision-making in the field.

The platform brings together features for registering and managing rural properties, mapping agricultural fields, monitoring crops and growing seasons, organizing soil, climate, and irrigation information, as well as agricultural monitoring and planning.

One of the project's main differentiators is its use of scientific Earth observation resources. Agrolynx works with NASA data sources, including NASA POWER, NASA Earthdata CMR, and MODIS observation data, to relate climate information and satellite observations to agricultural needs. These resources expand the possibilities for monitoring environmental conditions and vegetation.

The intended impact is to contribute to more efficient and sustainable agriculture by helping farmers and agricultural professionals better understand the conditions of their properties, plan activities, and use natural resources more responsibly. The project also aims to bring space technologies closer to small and medium-sized farmers, making scientific information more accessible.

The project was developed using React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS for the user interface, along with Node.js and Express for the server infrastructure. It also uses georeferencing concepts and geographic data to represent agricultural areas.

Its creative aspect lies in integrating farm management and satellite observation into a single modular platform. Rather than keeping information about climate, soil, vegetation, and properties separate, Agrolynx proposes bringing these elements together in an organized environment designed for future expansion.

The team prioritized accessibility, information organization, ease of use, visual identity, and the ability to incorporate new scientific data sources. Some integrations and advanced features are still under development, allowing the platform to evolve progressively.

Agrolynx represents an initiative to bring together space science, technology, and agriculture, demonstrating how Earth observation data can help address real-world challenges in agricultural production.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project impere
projectDetails.summary: A map created using imagery captured by a NASA space probe, the Odyssey. This map was designed to assist astronauts on Mars by identifying safe and unsafe areas for them to visit. It incorporates data sourced from NASA, including optical, thermal, spectral, topographical, geophysical, atmospheric, radiation, and chemical information.
projectDetails.details:
Project Name
Mars Mission: Survival Map

High-Level Project Summary
Mars Mission: Survival Map is an interactive web atlas that helps future explorers judge where to land and move safely on Mars. It combines eight layers of NASA data for Ares Vallis into a simple green and red safety map. An astronaut guide explains the results.

Detailed Project Description
Mars Mission: Survival Map is an interactive web guide built around Ares Vallis, one of the largest outflow channels on Mars. It stretches about 1,600 to 2,000 km, from the highlands of Margaritifer Terra to the plains of Chryse Planitia.

The site has four screens:

  1. A landing page with a GO button.
  2. An introduction to Ares Vallis.
  3. A multilayer atlas on a Mars Odyssey (THEMIS) base image (about 100 m/pixel). It overlays eight data layers: topography, temperature, spectral data, optical imagery, geophysics, atmosphere, radiation and surface chemistry.
  4. A “safezone map” that turns the data into a safety overlay.

On the safezone map:

  • Green areas are flatter regions with fewer obstacles. They make landing and astronaut movement easier and lower the risk of accidents.
  • Red areas have craters, slopes and uneven terrain. They need caution.

A friendly astronaut guide explains the map in plain language, so students and the general public can understand it. Its conclusion is that green areas are only potential candidates for exploration. No region is completely safe without detailed studies.

We built it to turn complex planetary data into something anyone can read at a glance. It supports the idea that careful site selection is the first step of survival on another planet.

NASA Data

  • Mars Odyssey THEMIS (base imagery, thermal, optical)
  • Mars Global Surveyor MOLA (topography)
  • Mars Global Surveyor (geophysical layer)
  • Mars Climate Sounder, MCS (atmosphere)
  • MARIE (radiation)
  • CRISM (spectral and chemical)
  • Gamma Ray Spectrometer, GRS (chemistry)
  • NASA Planetary Data System (PDS)

challengeDetails.title: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

projectDetails.name: FarmStar
projectDetails.summary:
Farmstar is a digital platform that combines NASA Earth observation data, climate information, and agricultural data to support more informed farming decisions. Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data,” the platform helps users monitor environmental conditions, explore vegetation and climate information, and compare crop rotation strategies.

By integrating satellite imagery, meteorological information, and agricultural statistics, Farmstar aims to connect environmental monitoring with practical agricultural planning. Its crop rotation comparison feature allows users to explore different cultivation strategies and consider their potential benefits and risks.

The project is important because climate variability and environmental changes can directly affect agricultural production. Farmstar seeks to make Earth observation data more accessible and useful, helping farmers evaluate alternatives and plan their next growing seasons with greater awareness.
projectDetails.details:
1. Project Overview

Farmstar is a web-based agricultural decision-support platform developed to help users understand environmental conditions and explore crop rotation strategies using satellite observations, climate information, and agricultural data.

2. Data Integration and Technology

The platform integrates multiple data sources to provide different perspectives on agricultural areas. NASA POWER provides meteorological and climatological information, while NASA GIBS enables the visualization of satellite imagery and environmental layers, including vegetation, precipitation, land surface temperature, and soil moisture. Additional NASA resources include FIRMS, HLS, and GEDI L4B.

The platform also uses Sentinel-2 imagery to calculate vegetation indices, Open-Meteo climate data, and IBGE agricultural and territorial information.

3. Main Features and Functionality

One of the project's main features is its crop rotation comparison functionality. It allows users to explore different cultivation strategies and consider how environmental conditions and agricultural context may influence their decisions. The goal is to make complex environmental information easier to interpret and connect it to practical agricultural planning.

4. Benefits and Intended Impact

Farmstar was designed around accessibility, integration of diverse datasets, and the practical use of Earth observation information. It aims to support more informed decisions, encourage climate-aware agricultural planning, and help users identify potential opportunities and risks before the next growing season.

5. Development Tools and AI Assistance

The project was developed using Node.js, Java, HTML, and Next.js, with README documentation. AI-assisted tools, including Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Grok, supported coding, research, technical problem-solving, and documentation. The team remained responsible for the project's concept, design choices, implementation, and final decisions.

6. Current Limitations

The platform has not yet been tested with farmers. Its recommendations should therefore be treated as decision-support information that requires local assessment, rather than as validated agronomic prescriptions.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project GUMA
projectDetails.summary:
GUMA — Earth Intelligence is an independent platform designed to help users investigate environmental trends through Earth science data and statistical analysis.

Building on an existing project, we developed an interactive Trend Detective that retrieves the NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 global temperature record and allows users to upload their own environmental datasets. It applies the Mann–Kendall trend test with Hamed–Rao autocorrelation correction, Sen's slope estimation, and bootstrap confidence intervals. Users can also compare regional trends, explore spatial autocorrelation, and examine relationships between environmental variables.

GUMA addresses the challenge by helping users investigate what is changing, how much it is changing, and whether observed trends are statistically significant. Its broader research prototype explores additional Earth observation and agricultural data sources.

Our goal is to make scientific methods more accessible, encourage evidence-based environmental research, and support a deeper understanding of our changing planet.
projectDetails.details:
GUMA — Earth Intelligence

Project Description | NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 — Challenge 02: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!

GUMA is an independent Earth-intelligence platform designed to connect climate data, Earth observation, agricultural systems, and collaborative environmental research. Its goal is to make complex environmental information more accessible, understandable, and useful for exploring the relationships between climate, ecosystems, and human activities.

What does it do and how does it work?

GUMA brings together environmental datasets from multiple scientific and public sources in an interactive platform. Users can explore climate indicators, vegetation observations, geographic information, and agricultural variables, while examining historical patterns and comparing environmental conditions.

For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, GUMA's primary focus is its Earth System Trend Detective module. It uses NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 global temperature-anomaly data or annual datasets uploaded by users. The module allows users to select a time period, visualize a time series, and investigate long-term trends using statistical methods such as the Mann–Kendall test and Sen's slope estimator.

Beyond trend analysis, the broader platform includes:

  • Global climate indicators, including temperature anomalies and atmospheric greenhouse-gas measurements.
  • NASA POWER climate data and MODIS vegetation-index observations.
  • Global satellite-scene discovery through the Earth Search STAC API.
  • Active-fire observations from NASA FIRMS.
  • Agricultural climate screening and crop-cycle analysis.
  • FAO-56 reference evapotranspiration estimates and a simplified root-zone water-balance scenario.
  • Geographic exploration, data exports, and PDF reporting.
  • Community research features for sharing hypotheses and contributor-reported observations.

The platform is designed to make data provenance, methodological choices, and scientific limitations visible to users.

What benefits does it have?

Environmental information is often distributed across different institutions, datasets, and technical platforms. GUMA seeks to reduce this fragmentation by bringing complementary information into one accessible environment.

Its main benefits include:

  • Making scientific environmental data easier to explore without requiring advanced programming skills.
  • Helping users identify historical patterns and investigate possible environmental changes.
  • Connecting global climate indicators with agricultural and territorial contexts.
  • Supporting exploratory research, education, and evidence-informed discussions.
  • Encouraging transparency through source references, data-quality information, and explicit methodological limitations.
  • Providing tools for researchers, students, educators, agricultural professionals, and interested communities.

What is the intended impact?

GUMA aims to contribute to a more accessible and collaborative understanding of the Earth system.

Its long-term vision is to become a global platform where climate information, Earth-observation data, agricultural knowledge, and local research can be explored together. By connecting different scales of environmental information, GUMA hopes to help people ask better questions about climate change, land use, vegetation, water, and agricultural resilience.

The project is being developed in Brazil, but its architecture and vision are global. It is intended to support collaboration across countries and regions, rather than focus on a single territory.

GUMA does not claim to predict climate events, establish causal relationships, or replace scientific and professional assessment. Its purpose is to support exploration, transparency, and better-informed research.

What tools, programming languages, and software were used?

GUMA was developed primarily with:

  • Python: data processing, scientific calculations, environmental analysis, and application logic.
  • Streamlit: interactive web application and dashboard development.
  • Pandas and NumPy: data organization, numerical operations, and time-series processing.
  • Requests: communication with public data APIs.
  • Folium and Streamlit-Folium: interactive geographic visualization.
  • ReportLab: generation of PDF reports.
  • Supabase: authentication and optional user-project persistence.
  • Git and GitHub: source-code management, version control, and collaborative development.

The platform connects to public scientific and institutional data sources, including NASA GISS GISTEMP, NASA POWER, NASA FIRMS, MODIS, Earth Search, NOAA, IBGE, and Brazilian agricultural information resources. It also incorporates methodological references from FAO and Embrapa.

No specialized hardware or physical sensors were required for the current prototype. The project relies on public datasets, satellite-derived observations, computational methods, and web technologies.

How is the project creative and innovative?

GUMA's creativity lies in connecting areas that are often explored separately: global climate trends, satellite observations, agricultural systems, geographic context, and community research.

Instead of presenting environmental indicators as isolated numbers, it creates an exploratory environment where users can move between datasets, investigate patterns, compare evidence, and understand the limitations of each analysis.

Another distinctive aspect is its combination of global environmental intelligence with practical agricultural questions. It seeks to connect large-scale Earth-system observations with the territorial and agricultural contexts in which environmental changes are experienced.

The project also has an original visual identity inspired by the relationship between people, territory, the sea, and the horizon in Brazilian visual culture. Its name, GUMA, references the character from Jorge Amado's Mar Morto. This cultural foundation gives the platform a recognizable identity while keeping its scientific ambition international.

What factors did the team consider?

The development process considered several important factors:

  1. Scientific reliability: choosing recognized data sources and documented analytical methods.
  2. Transparency: identifying data sources, units, reference periods, assumptions, and limitations.
  3. Global applicability: designing the platform to work with environmental information beyond Brazil.
  4. Accessibility: making complex datasets easier to explore through an interactive interface.
  5. Agricultural relevance: connecting climate and vegetation information with agricultural systems and water-balance concepts.
  6. Data quality: considering missing observations, spatial resolution, temporal coverage, and differences between datasets.
  7. Responsible interpretation: avoiding unsupported causal claims, false precision, and unverified agricultural recommendations.
  8. Scalability and collaboration: creating a foundation that can evolve through partnerships, additional datasets, and community contributions.

GUMA is an evolving independent prototype. Its scientific methods and data integrations are subject to continued testing and validation. The project is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.

GUMA — Earth Intelligence
Territory • Climate • Future

projectDetails.name: BioOrbit — Astronaut Health OS
projectDetails.summary: BioOrbit is an offline-first health monitoring and decision-support app for astronauts on long-duration missions. Astronauts log vital signs, sleep, mood and symptoms. They can also measure heart rate with a phone camera and take a 3-minute reaction test that screens for fatigue. BioOrbit turns these data into a colour-coded interactive body map, a readiness score and clear actions. It compares every value with the astronaut's personal baseline to catch problems early, and it combines signals into insights such as fatigue or possible infection. Escalation advice adapts to the communication delay of each environment, from the ISS to Mars. A compact report can be sent to the flight surgeon. Because crews on Mars cannot rely on real-time help from Earth, BioOrbit gives them the knowledge and autonomy to assess and act on their own health. The same tool serves remote communities on Earth.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

BioOrbit is a "health bridge" for each crew member:

  • Readiness score and duty status (Mission ready, Ready with caution, Limited duty, Medical attention), calculated from 14 indicators, symptoms and baseline changes.
  • Interactive body map: eight body systems (brain & behaviour, eyes/SANS, heart, lungs, metabolism, immune, muscles, skeleton). Each one is colour-coded, clickable and explains its function, what spaceflight does to it, the latest values and what to do now.
  • Guided logging: fields turn green, amber or red while you type, and explain why each indicator matters in space and how to measure it with onboard equipment.
  • Camera heart rate (photoplethysmography): a fingertip over the camera is enough, with no extra hardware. Tap-to-the-beat fallback.
  • Psychomotor Vigilance Test (PVT-B): the brief vigilance test validated for spaceflight, to detect fatigue before critical operations.
  • Personal-baseline drift detection: flags meaningful change even when values are still "normal".
  • Multi-signal insights: sleep debt + slower reactions → fatigue; fever + elevated heart rate/rash → possible infection; persistent low mood → behavioural health; vision change → possible SANS. Each comes with concrete onboard actions.
  • Mission environments: Space Station, Lunar Base, Mars Transit, Mars Surface and Earth Remote Care. Radiation dose rate (cumulative dose vs. the 600 mSv career limit), gravity, communication delay and escalation rules adapt to each one.
  • Delay-tolerant downlink: a structured TXT/JSON report with findings, actions and 7-day trends, showing the real arrival time at Earth.
  • Crew overview, mission routine with gamification (XP, levels, streaks, badges) and a knowledge library on the five NASA HRP hazards.

HOW IT WORKS

Values are classified against reference ranges. A personal-baseline model compares each person's last three days with their own previous 18 days (z-score plus a clinically meaningful minimum change), and rule-based patterns combine several signals. The camera pulse algorithm averages the red channel of the fingertip image, resamples it to 30 Hz, removes the slow trend and estimates heart rate by autocorrelation, with protection against octave errors (within ±3 bpm from 42 to 178 bpm on synthetic test signals). The PVT follows the PVT-B protocol (1–4 s intervals, lapses > 355 ms, false starts < 100 ms).

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

It helps astronauts who are not doctors understand and act on their own health far from Earth, detects early change instead of waiting for a critical value, works fully offline on any phone or laptop, and keeps data private on the device. On Earth, it fits remote care: isolated and riverside communities, Antarctic stations, ships and home monitoring. Next steps: wearable/Bluetooth sensors, ultrasound guidance, machine-learning baselines from analog-mission data and validation with health professionals.

TOOLS

HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript with no frameworks or external libraries (so it works offline); Canvas and SVG APIs for charts and the body map; MediaDevices/getUserMedia for the camera; localStorage for data; hosted on GitHub Pages.

projectDetails.summary:
Analog Atlas is an interactive platform designed to identify, map, and catalog terrestrial environments that resemble the geological and environmental conditions of the Moon and Mars.

Our project features interactive maps with geographically located analog sites, organized into lunar and Martian categories. It also provides information about their geological characteristics, soil types, environmental conditions, and visual landscapes. These include volcanic terrains, regolith-like soils, arid deserts, and polar environments.

By addressing the challenge of identifying Earth locations analogous to the Moon and Mars, Analog Atlas creates an accessible resource for exploring potential research environments. These locations can support scientific studies, equipment testing, and the development of protocols for future space missions.

Our goal is to connect planetary exploration with terrestrial research, making relevant information easier to discover and understand.

With Analog Atlas, Earth becomes a starting point for exploring new worlds.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Analog Atlas is an interactive web platform designed to identify, map, and catalog terrestrial locations that share geological and environmental characteristics with the Moon and Mars.

The website uses Google Maps to display the geographical locations of terrestrial analogues, allowing users to explore different regions and discover information about their geological formations, soil characteristics, environmental conditions, and landscapes.

The platform organizes locations into lunar and Martian analogues, presenting categories such as basaltic terrains, regolith-like soils, high plateaus, arid deserts, and polar environments.

Additionally, users can submit data and register new locations, allowing the platform to expand through new contributions.

What benefits does it offer?

Analog Atlas centralizes geographical and scientific information in an accessible, interactive environment. It helps researchers, students, and space enthusiasts discover potential terrestrial analogues that may be useful for geological research, equipment testing, and the preparation of future space missions.

What is its intended impact?

Our goal is to support planetary exploration by connecting Earth-based research with future lunar and Martian missions. By making terrestrial analogue locations easier to identify and study, the platform aims to contribute to scientific research and the development of technologies and protocols for space exploration.

What tools and technologies were used?

The website was developed using Wix as its website-building platform, with Google Maps integrated to provide interactive geographical visualization and location mapping.

For scientific research and content development, we consulted NASA's scientific resources and information about planetary environments and terrestrial analogues. We also used visual resources and organized geographical information to present the locations and their characteristics.

What makes the project creative?

The main creative aspect of Analog Atlas is combining interactive geographical mapping, geological classification, scientific information, and collaborative data submission in one platform.

Rather than simply listing locations, the project connects each terrestrial environment to the planetary characteristics it resembles. Its contribution system also allows users to register new locations, making the platform expandable and open to further discoveries.

What factors did our team consider?

Our team considered geological similarities, soil composition, terrain characteristics, environmental conditions, geographical distribution, and scientific relevance when organizing the locations.

We also prioritized accessibility, intuitive navigation, clear scientific communication, visual organization, and the possibility of continuous expansion through user contributions.
