challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: Smart Earth - From Space to Your Field
projectDetails.summary:
Smart Earth is a decision-support tool that helps farmers in Brazil adapt to climate change using NASA Earth observation data.

On a global satellite map, each field plot shows NDVI, soil moisture, and temperature, with green for healthy, yellow for attention, and red for alert.

The app uses NASA POWER for rainfall and solar radiation, and NASA FIRMS for fire alerts. Farmers can manage their plots, like Talhao Pioneiro in Sorriso-MT, and track water and crop health without walking the whole farm.

A Smart AI assistant answers questions about irrigation, planting, pests, and satellite data in simple language. Our goal is to help small farmers save water, protect soil, prevent fires, and make better decisions. From space, to your field!
projectDetails.details:
Smart Earth is a decision-support tool that helps farmers adapt to climate change using NASA Earth observation data.

What does it do?

On an interactive map, the farm is divided into plots. Each plot has a color based on satellite data: Green means healthy, Yellow means needs attention, and Red means alert for water stress, low vegetation, or pests. When the farmer clicks on a plot, they can see NDVI, soil moisture, and temperature.

How does it work?

We use NASA Landsat to measure NDVI (how green and healthy the plants are) and NASA SMAP to measure soil moisture. The app translates this complex satellite data into a simple color and a simple tip, like "Water this plot" or "Rest this soil and rotate crop."

Benefits and Impact:

Our goal is to help small farmers in Brazil save water, protect soil health, and choose the best crop rotation without needing to walk the whole farm every day. This makes farming cheaper, easier, and more sustainable.

Tools we used:

We built the app prototype with Google Gemini and Canva for the presentation. We used NASA Landsat and SMAP data as our main source.

Why is it creative?

Most satellite tools are too difficult for small farmers. Smart Earth is creative because it turns space data into traffic-light colors that any farmer can understand in 5 seconds. From space, to your field!

projectDetails.name: Incredible stories of NASA space equipment on the Moon and Mars
projectDetails.summary:
The project transforms hardware left by NASA in a captivating story. The main proposal is to transform those machines in characters that guide the public on their missions

Each equipment represents a new engineering approach made to gather knowledge about the Moon or Mars, the user discovers why the hardware was sent to its mission and what it contributed to space exploration.

The project’s distinguishing feature lies in its combination of narrative and scientific information: creativity serves as a gateway to knowledge, not as a substitute for it. 
Thus, the experience seeks to spark interest in science and engineering by showcasing the historical and scientific significance of various NASA hardware.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IS OUR PROJECT?

Incredible stories of NASA space equipment on the Moon and Mars is a digital storytelling project that shows the story of the multiple hardware that NASA left across the moon and mars. The main objective of our project is to provide in a accessible way, using interactive language, captivating characters and thrilling imagery, helping kids and adults understand how important each equipment was to science.

WHY IS IT RELEVANT?

The relevance of the project comes from the fact that, even if all of the information is public, most people are unable to understand it, either because the language is to complex, or simply due to lack of interest. Incredible stories of NASA space equipment on the Moon and Mars tries to solve both problems, using a simple language and combining it with amazing storytelling.

TARGET AUDIENCE AND STORY ORGANIZATION

The target audience is 5-12 years old children, and the stories are organized with that in mind. Each story has a didactic way of teaching, where we accompany the hardwares into their objectives. At the end of each story, there always is: a question, to instigate the reader to search for more and a curiosity, to fixate the new knowledge.

WHAT ARE THE STORIES ABOUT?

There are 8 stories on our demonstration, 4 of them being from hardware left on the Moon (RANGER 7, SURVEYOR 3, retroreflector apollo 11 and seismometer apollo 12), and 4 of them being from hardware left on Mars (Sojourner, Viking 1, Spirit and Opportunity).

WHAT TOOLS WHERE USED ON THE CREATION OF THE DEMO?

The entire project is made using Canva, the specific Canva tools that where used, aside from the basic slide creation tools, are:

  • Canva AI;
  • Background remover;
  • Hyperlinks between pages.

projectDetails.name: RainShift
projectDetails.summary:
RainShift is a web tool that lets anyone check whether rainfall and air temperature have really changed on the northern coast of Rio de Janeiro state, Brazil, from the Macaé River headwaters to Campos dos Goytacazes. It takes two NASA records, GPM IMERG precipitation and MERRA-2 air temperature, and shows for the whole region and for every grid cell what changed, where, by how much, and how strong the statistical evidence is.

The problem it addresses is that a trend line is easy to draw and easy to over-read. RainShift reports every trend with its 95% confidence interval drawn against zero and gives one of three plain labels: increase, decrease, or insufficient evidence of a trend. With real data the two variables tell different stories. The region warmed by about 0.22 °C per decade (95% CI 0.12 to 0.32), close to 1 °C in 45 years. Rainfall shows an estimated decline of 76 mm per decade, but the interval runs from −218 to +76, so 26 years of data cannot tell a decline from no change, and the estimate nearly doubles if the record starts in 2001 instead of 1999.

This matters because students, teachers and people who manage water in the region need to know not only what the data suggest but how far the data can be trusted. Four guided cases, a period selector that recomputes the trend live, and a plain-language glossary turn a statistics lesson into a detective exercise on real NASA data.
projectDetails.details:
What exactly does it do?

  • Shows a full-screen map of grid cells coloured by the estimated trend, and a time series with its trend line for the region average or any cell you click.
  • Covers two variables with four yearly metrics each. Precipitation: annual, wet-season and dry-season totals, and the wet-season share. Air temperature: annual, wet-season and dry-season means, and the wet-minus-dry contrast.
  • For every series, reports the trend per decade, the 95% confidence interval, the number of years, the period, the source and the unit, and one label: Increase, Decrease, or Insufficient evidence of a trend.
  • Lets you change the start and end year and recomputes the trend in the browser, so you can see how much an answer depends on the years chosen.
  • Offers four guided cases that set the controls and explain what to look at: "Getting warmer?", "Less rain?", "Does the start year matter?" and "Do the seasons differ?".
  • Includes a glossary, a one-sentence reading "in plain words" for every result, and CSV download of every series.

How does it work?

  • A Python pipeline downloads bounding-box subsets from NASA GES DISC through Harmony, checks units, coordinates, dates and missing values, and converts the monthly values (rain rate in mm/hr × hours in the month; temperature in K to °C).
  • The region average weights each cell by the geodesic area that lies inside the region.
  • The wet season is defined from the rainfall record itself (the run of months rainier than the average month: November to March). Years run from November to October so that a wet season is never split in two.
  • Trends use the Theil–Sen slope with Sen's 95% confidence interval and the Mann–Kendall test, with the Hamed–Rao correction when neighbouring years resemble each other. The map applies a Benjamini–Hochberg correction for testing many cells at once and is labelled exploratory.
  • The pipeline writes small JSON and GeoJSON files. The website is static: it needs no server and no NASA login, so it keeps working during judging.

What did we find?

  • Air temperature (MERRA-2, 1981–2025): +0.22 °C per decade, 95% CI +0.12 to +0.32. All 16 cells pass the many-tests correction. Both seasons warmed, but the data cannot tell whether one warms faster than the other: the wet-minus-dry contrast is −0.10 °C per decade, CI −0.25 to +0.04.
  • Precipitation (IMERG, 1999–2024): −76 mm per decade, 95% CI −218 to +76. None of the 204 cells passes the correction for the annual total. Starting the record in 2001 changes the estimate to −133 mm per decade, with the same label.
  • Two "significant" labels are not a comparison. To test whether seasons differ, RainShift fits the trend of the paired difference instead of comparing labels.

What benefits does it have?

  • It teaches how a trend is estimated and tested, with a real case where the answer is clear and a real case where it is not.
  • It keeps two things apart that are often mixed up: statistical uncertainty (how much the values jump from year to year) and the limits of the data products themselves.
  • Every series can be downloaded as CSV from the app, and the method page documents each step, so the numbers can be checked independently.

What do we hope to achieve?

A tool that classrooms and local water and climate groups can use to ask "has the climate here really changed?" and get an honest answer, and a pipeline that can be pointed at other regions and other NASA variables.

Limits

  • The region is a rectangular box aligned to the IMERG grid, not a watershed boundary.
  • IMERG is a merged satellite and rain-gauge estimate; MERRA-2 is a model reconstruction on cells of about 55 × 65 km that mix land, mountains and ocean.
  • The confidence interval covers year-to-year variability only. Trends are linear; the rainfall series looks more like a rise followed by a fall.
  • The period selector uses the same estimator in the browser without the Hamed–Rao correction and shows a caution note when it would matter.

Tools, languages and software

A Python pipeline for the data and the statistics, and a static website built with Next.js, React and CesiumJS. The project is licensed under Apache-2.0.

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

Yes. An SI/AI coding assistant (Claude Code, Anthropic) was used throughout:

  • Planning: it helped turn the idea into a technical plan and checked the official rules and data catalogues.
  • Code: it wrote most of the Python pipeline, the tests and the web application, under the author's direction and review.

The project idea, the research question, the choice of region, data and methods, and all decisions were made by the author. No images, video or audio were generated with SI. No data values were generated: every number comes from the NASA products listed below. SI use is acknowledged in the application's "Method & credits" page, in the metadata file published with each dataset (`meta.json`, field `si_note`) and in the project's source files.

NASA Data

  • GPM IMERG Final Precipitation L3 1 month 0.1 degree x 0.1 degree V07 (GPM_3IMERGM), NASA GES DISC. DOI: 10.5067/GPM/IMERG/3B-MONTH/07. Variable `precipitation`, January 1998 to September 2025, 204 grid cells. Used for all rainfall series, maps and for defining the wet season.
  • MERRA-2 tavgM_2d_slv_Nx, monthly mean single-level diagnostics V5.12.4 (M2TMNXSLV), NASA GMAO / GES DISC. DOI: 10.5067/AP1B0BA5PD2K. Variable `T2M` (2-metre air temperature), January 1980 to September 2026, 16 grid cells. Used for all temperature series and maps.
  • NASA Earthdata Login, Harmony and the Common Metadata Repository (CMR): used to find the collections and to download bounding-box subsets.
  • NASA `earthaccess` and `harmony-py` Python libraries: used for authentication and downloads.

Space Agency Partner Data and Other References

No Space Agency Partner data were used.

  • OpenStreetMap map tiles, OpenStreetMap contributors, ODbL: base map, loaded at view time.
  • CesiumJS: map engine.
  • NASA earthaccess and harmony-py: data access.
  • Open-source software: Python scientific libraries (xarray, SciPy, pymannkendall, statsmodels) for the analysis; Next.js, React and Recharts for the website.

Methods

  • Sen, P. K. (1968). Estimates of the regression coefficient based on Kendall's tau. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 63(324), 1379–1389.
  • Mann, H. B. (1945). Nonparametric tests against trend. Econometrica, 13(3), 245–259.
  • Hamed, K. H., & Rao, A. R. (1998). A modified Mann–Kendall trend test for autocorrelated data. Journal of Hydrology, 204(1–4), 182–196.
  • Benjamini, Y., & Hochberg, Y. (1995). Controlling the false discovery rate. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society B, 57(1), 289–300.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Sertão Vivo
projectDetails.summary: Sertão Vivo helps learners investigate how rainfall and temperature have changed near Açude Cedro in Brazil’s semiarid Ceará. For Be An Earth System Trend Detective!, users select a variable and time window, explore 45 years of NASA POWER / MERRA-2 data, and inspect the rate of change and its uncertainty. Daily Funceme rainfall adds observed dry spells; NASA daily temperatures show whether selected spells were hotter than usual. The working browser prototype preserves missing observations, provides guided examples and exports data. Its value is making local evidence understandable and checkable before preparedness discussions—not forecasting drought or claiming proven mitigation.
projectDetails.details:
The question

How can we better understand dry periods in the sertão so that communities can discuss ways to reduce drought consequences? We start with a bounded historical question: what do rainfall and air-temperature records near Açude Cedro reveal about seasonal variability, unusual years and trends? The intended users are learners and people discussing water preparedness with local specialists. This prototype has not been tested with those users.

How it addresses the challenge

What: corrected rainfall and 2 m air temperature. Where: the NASA grid near Açude Cedro, Quixadá. How much: Sen change per decade. How certain: nominal Mann–Kendall tests plus block-resampling sensitivity intervals. Users select either variable and one of three time windows. This is a bounded single-location demonstration, with regional expansion left for future work.

Our solution

The English browser explorer contains NASA POWER monthly corrected precipitation and 2 m air temperature for 1981–2025, requested at 4.9799°S, 39.0800°W near Quixadá. Users can choose a variable, compare three documented analysis windows, inspect annual values and uncertainty, compare any year with the 1991–2020 monthly reference, and download a CSV. Two short guided investigations explain variable units and lead users from trends to a daily case. The interface also counts daily station dry spells in complete windows and compares five selected zero-rain cases with NASA daily temperatures relative to the same calendar dates in 1991–2020. It works offline, without installation, an account or a server.

What we built during the event

Using existing local-data preparation, we acquired the long NASA POWER series, audited calendar coverage and units, calculated annual and seasonal summaries, implemented trend and uncertainty analysis, built the interactive explorer, added daily dry-spell and temperature comparisons, and prepared seven English slides. The participant provided the underlying question; earlier data collection is distinguished from the analysis and prototype developed during the hackathon.

Methods

NASA POWER precipitation is a mean daily rate in mm/day, multiplied by the number of calendar days in each month. Annual temperature is weighted by days. Annual summary keys ending in 13 are excluded. Sen slopes and nominal two-sided Mann–Kendall p-values are calculated for 1981–2025, 2001–2025 and 2007–2025. The p-values assume independent years. We also report exploratory residual-block bootstrap intervals using 3- and 5-year blocks, 2,000 replicates and a fixed seed. These checks address some short-range dependence and do not establish climate attribution. No multiple-testing correction is applied across the exploratory windows.

Daily comparisons

Station sequences preserve missing readings. Within-window comparisons require every day observed: 16 complete February–May seasons are available. For temperature, we use NASA POWER daily T2M and T2M_MAX from Jan 1981 through Jul 2026, rather than deriving daily values from monthly means. Calendar-date departures use the 1991–2020 reference. Gauge intervals end at 07:00 GMT−3; NASA uses local-solar days. Matching dates is descriptive; a preceding-day match is reported as a sensitivity check.

What the results show

At this source grid in 1981–2025, the estimated rainfall slope is −12.2 mm/decade, with nominal p=0.681 and a 5-year block sensitivity interval from −77.1 to +55.9 mm/decade. The uncertain annual slope does not imply an absence of drought risk or of changes within seasons. Annual mean temperature has an estimated slope of +0.22 °C/decade, nominal p=0.010, and a 5-year block interval of +0.08 to +0.34 °C/decade. The shorter 2007–2025 temperature interval includes zero, demonstrating window sensitivity. In 2012, annual rainfall was 315.5 mm, 54.7% below the 1991–2020 reference. These are historical patterns and descriptive departures, not an official drought class or evidence of a particular cause.

During 2012, 44 zero-rain intervals from March 31 to May 13 had mean NASA temperature 2.06 °C above the same-date reference. After 8 mm on May 14, another 39 zero-rain intervals on May 15–June 22 averaged 2.30 °C above reference. Previous-day matches give 2.03 and 2.35 °C. In contrast, the 229-day zero-rain case in 1991–1992 averaged near the thermal reference (−0.16 °C departure). Selected-case duration does not identify thermal severity by itself. These are temporal associations, not causal effects.

Why local data quality matters

The archived Funceme AC. CEDRO file contains 239 of 463 possible months between Jan 1988 and Jul 2026. Only 212 months and 11 full years have complete daily coverage. Missing 999 codes and absent months are never treated as zero rainfall; partial monthly sums remain partial. COGERH Pedras Brancas records are shown separately as published storage context. Repeated published values are not assumed to be new measurements, interpolations or genuine stability. Reading rules, quality, revisions and the storage-curve version remain unresolved. Cedro rainfall is not a catchment mean for Pedras Brancas and cannot establish storage causality.

Limits and future value

This is one gridded reference location, not a regional diagnosis. The NASA monthly archive ends in 2025; the new daily archive ends in July 2026. Neither is a current alert. Daily station counts supplement the monthly analysis; their incomplete coverage does not support a historical trend. We have not estimated water demand, linked rainfall causally to reservoir storage, or demonstrated a mitigation effect. Future work should expand regional coverage, validate daily dry-spell findings and established drought indices, incorporate water use and reservoir operations, and validate the interpretation and proposed actions with local users and domain experts. The present contribution is a transparent, reproducible way to inspect evidence before making such claims.

AI assistance and originality

The participant supplied the question about understanding dry periods to help reduce drought consequences. Codex assisted with selecting sources, writing Python and browser code, exploratory calculations including the participant-requested daily dry-spell and temperature comparisons, data checks, English writing and slide preparation. Provider data were preserved; missing observations were not imputed. Charts use source data, and no generated photographs, audio or videos are included. The AI disclosure is also visible in the interface and slides. Participant review and independent scientific validation remain necessary. We do not claim autonomous scientific discovery or demonstrated mitigation effects.

Implementation tools

Python, NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib and HTML/CSS/JavaScript. Source snapshots, dependency versions, code and methods are available through the final-project link. All charts use the cited provider data. No NASA logos or generated photographs, audio or video are used.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Location on Mars: The best guide for the astronauts
projectDetails.summary: Research conducted during the Perseverance rover expedition has revealed several similarities between Mars and Earth. However, certain obstacles to the existence of life on Mars have also been identified. For this reason, we have developed a project designed to assist astronauts in navigating their expeditions, helping them avoid any unforeseen issues that might arise.
projectDetails.details:
NASA’s Mars 2020 mission sent the Perseverance rover to Mars with the goal of exploring its surface, studying its environment, and investigating potential signs of past life.

The rover was launched on July 30, 2020, and landed in Jezero Crater—a region that, according to scientific studies, once held a large lake fed by rivers billions of years ago.

Throughout its exploration, Perseverance has traveled over 45 kilometers, collected various rock and soil samples, and analyzed geological formations that help us understand the planet’s history.

Among its discoveries are signs of an ancient lake and delta system, as well as rocks with chemical characteristics that could be linked to the existence of microbial life in the past.

The rover also recorded dust devils and electrical discharges in the Martian atmosphere, illustrating just how extreme the planet’s environment can be.

Another significant finding was the identification of potential organic compounds and chemical signatures that require further study to determine their origin.

Furthermore, the mission conducted experiments demonstrating that it is possible to produce oxygen from the carbon dioxide present in the Martian atmosphere.

All of this information is essential for understanding Mars’ past, identifying areas of scientific interest, and assisting NASA in planning future human missions—ultimately making the exploration of the planet safer and more efficient.

projectDetails.name: biosphere // mars
projectDetails.summary:
Imagine being stranded on Mars. 
How would you survive? 
What would happen if your habitat lost pressure, your food supply ran low, or you were exposed to dangerous levels of radiation?

These are some of the questions behind our project: an interactive 3D Mars survival simulator that helps young students discover what it takes to live on another planet.

Built with Three.js and Blender, the simulator lets players explore a Martian habitat, run experiments, and face challenges inspired by real NASA research. Instead of simply reading about atmospheric pressure, radiation, protective shielding, or food production, students can see how these factors affect survival and experiment with different solutions.

The simulator has two modes. 
In Experiments, players explore scientific concepts by changing conditions and observing what happens. In Missions, they put that knowledge to use, solving problems involving habitat safety, limited resources, and astronaut protection.

Our goal is to make space science something students can experience, not just study. By combining realistic scenarios, interactive experiments, and gameplay, we hope to spark curiosity, encourage problem-solving, and inspire more young people to explore science, engineering, and space exploration.

projectDetails.name: A Space Voyage
projectDetails.summary: The project is a comic book that playfully addresses the interaction between three young astronauts and equipment left on Mars during different NASA missions. Upon coming into contact with the Curiosity rover, the story of this and other space exploration equipment is told so that children aged 9 to 12 can become familiar with what has already been accomplished in the search for knowledge about space, stimulating their interest in the subject. The comic book presented is intended to be the first in a series that will cover a wide variety of artifacts sent into space by humankind.
projectDetails.details:
The team's proposal for the challenge was the creation of a comic book that uses fiction, based on the journey of three young astronauts to Mars, to present to a children's audience, preferably from 9 to 12 years old, the history and information about the equipment sent for space exploration and reconnaissance. The option was made to present both the equipment still in operation and those that are already inactive.

The team believes that the format chosen to tell these stories is easily accepted by children and has the potential to encourage the search for more information about the equipment and missions presented.

The creativity of the project consists of the graphic and playful representation of a scientific and technological theme, with the creation of original characters and storyline, created by three 9-year-old boys, and integrated with real information about Mars exploration equipment.

The team considered, in choosing the challenge and the solution, factors such as: the age of the child participants, their knowledge and skills in drawing and writing, their interest in arts, astronomy and science in general, and the time available to carry out the Hackathon.

Tool: Adobe Express
Use of SI: none

projectDetails.name: ASTRA Health — Autonomous Space Health Decision Support
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRA Health is an autonomous space health decision-support prototype developed by Team ANGARIS to help astronauts monitor their health and respond to potential medical concerns during deep-space missions, where communication with Earth may be delayed or unavailable.

The platform combines simulated vital-sign monitoring, symptom assessment, daily health journals, nine space-health domains, and guided response workflows. It identifies abnormal patterns, distinguishes possible sensor failures from physiological changes, presents scientific evidence, and proposes transparent, rule-based actions for human review.

ASTRA Health also supports extravehicular activity (EVA) decisions, offline operation, and prioritized communication with Earth. Its scientific foundation includes NASA Human Research Program resources and the NASA Open Science Data Repository.

The prototype has documented automated, end-to-end, and scientific verification tests. All physiological data are simulated, and its decision rules and procedures are provisional, not clinically validated.

ASTRA Health demonstrates how evidence-based, human-supervised technology could strengthen astronaut autonomy and health management beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRA Health — Project Details

The Problem

During deep-space missions, astronauts may experience communication delays of 3–22 minutes each way between Mars and Earth. Medical emergencies, physiological changes, equipment failures, and extravehicular activities (EVAs) can require decisions before guidance from Earth becomes available.

ASTRA Health addresses this challenge by demonstrating how astronauts can monitor their health, understand potential risks, and receive structured decision support while operating independently of real-time ground communication.

Our Solution

ASTRA Health is an offline-first, autonomous space health decision-support prototype developed by Team ANGARIS.

The platform follows four core stages:

1. MEASURE — Health Monitoring

Monitors simulated heart rate, oxygen saturation (SpO₂), body temperature, and sensor reliability. It identifies abnormal patterns and distinguishes potential sensor failures from physiological deviations.

2. UNDERSTAND — Health Assessment

Uses transparent, deterministic rules to analyze measurements, assess reported symptoms, identify warning signs, and explain findings in accessible language.

The system displays uncertainty, references scientific evidence, and avoids presenting provisional findings as medical diagnoses.

3. ACT — Guided Response

Provides structured demonstration checklists, requests human confirmation, records actions, and proposes escalation when predefined conditions are met.

During EVAs, it supports pre-activity checks, equipment-failure alternatives, incident response, and commander-reviewed decisions.

4. COMMUNICATE — Earth Link

Simulates Earth–Mars communication delays, prioritizes urgent medical reports, stores messages during communication outages, and transmits them when connectivity returns.

Advanced Health Platform — FUTURE Modules

We extended the original prototype with five integrated modules:

  • F01 — Health Journal: Daily astronaut check-ins, symptoms, sleep, hydration, fatigue, scheduled examinations, and longitudinal trends.
  • F02 — Symptom Assessment: Structured symptom evaluation, versioned decision rules, scientific references, uncertainty reporting, and human review.
  • F03 — Space Health Profile: Nine health domains covering neuro-ocular, cardiovascular, renal, radiation, bone/mineral, vascular, immunological, emotional/cognitive, and sleep-related monitoring.
  • F04 — EVA & Autonomous Response: Mission checklists, equipment-aware alternatives, incident management, commander decisions, and priority reporting.
  • F05 — Readiness & Trace: Data-completeness monitoring, system checks, versioned rules, and exportable audit trails.

Unavailable measurements, such as intracranial pressure or bone density, are explicitly identified as missing rather than artificially generated.

Technology and Scientific Resources

ASTRA Health was developed using Next.js, React, TypeScript, and JavaScript, with automated testing through Vitest and Playwright.

The platform uses local browser storage and offline application capabilities to preserve records and support continued operation during simulated communication interruptions.

Its scientific foundation includes NASA Human Research Program publications, Human Research Roadmap resources, and NASA Open Science Data Repository dataset OSD-575, containing cardiovascular biomarker measurements from the Inspiration4 mission.

Scientific research data remain separate from simulated astronaut vital signs. NASA references provide scientific context and do not validate the application's provisional clinical rules.

AI-assisted development tools supported engineering, testing, documentation, and presentation. Medical decision proposals in the demonstrated system are generated by deterministic rules rather than generative AI.

Testing and Validation

The team documented the following successful software verification results:

  • 184/184 automated tests passed, combining original and FUTURE suites.
  • 31/31 end-to-end browser checks passed, including regression tests.
  • 32/32 scientific source-verification checks passed.
  • Zero violations detected in the automated accessibility audit across 29 checks.

The platform also demonstrates offline operation, prioritized message synchronization, human decision logging, and detection of alterations to its audit trail.

These results verify specified software behavior; they do not constitute clinical validation.

Innovation and Impact

ASTRA Health's key innovation is combining continuous health monitoring, longitudinal astronaut records, evidence-based context, structured symptom assessment, autonomous offline workflows, and human-supervised operational decisions in one integrated platform.

Rather than relying on continuous communication with Earth, the system demonstrates how crews could maintain situational awareness and follow transparent decision-support workflows during communication delays or outages.

The concept may inform future research into medical autonomy for lunar and Martian missions, remote expeditions, and other environments with limited access to healthcare professionals.

Safety and Limitations

ASTRA Health is a research and demonstration prototype, not a medical device.

All astronaut physiological data are simulated or entered during demonstrations. Medical thresholds, decision rules, and response procedures are provisional, have not been clinically validated, and are not endorsed by NASA.

Human crew members remain responsible for operational decisions.

Project Access

Live demonstration: https://astrahealth.angaris.com.br

Team: ANGARIS

Event: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

projectDetails.name: Beyond Horizons
projectDetails.summary:
Beyond Horizons is a holographic health-monitoring console for astronauts on long missions. On one screen it tracks vital signs (heart rate, SpO₂, temperature, blood pressure, breathing), the habitat (O₂, CO₂, pressure, temperature, radiation) and long-term spaceflight risks. In Scan mode the suit becomes a 3D hologram that shows where in the body a problem is: the affected organs glow and are labelled. Every alert is checked against NASA limits and linked to its NASA source.

It goes beyond monitoring. Astronauts can log their own vitals and history, simulate how radiation changes their genes and career dose against NASA's 600 mSv limit, follow a Mars mission day by day, see their own risk inside a four-person crew, and compare options for a critical spacewalk with an auditable debate between mission roles. An AI assistant explains everything in plain language.

Far from Earth, help can be 20+ minutes away. Beyond Horizons helps a crew catch problems early, understand them, and decide with evidence.

For the best experience with the interactive 3D dashboard, use a desktop or laptop browser.
projectDetails.details:
What it does Beyond Horizons is a health-monitoring console for astronauts on long-duration missions, built as one mission-control screen with nine tabs:

  • Overview: live vital signs with waveforms, habitat environment against NASA-STD-3001 limits, systems status, genetic overview and AI insights. Readings turn amber (watch) or red (alert) outside their limits.
  • Astronaut mode / Scan mode: the suit turns into a translucent 3D hologram; a scan line reveals skeleton, vessels, lungs, a beating heart, digestive organs and brain. Affected systems glow and are labelled, so anyone on the crew can see in seconds where the problem is.
  • Scenarios: hypoxia, arrhythmia, solar particle event, heat stress, bone loss, SANS, plus scenarios the user creates (with a live preview and an optional mission day).
  • My Vitals: the astronaut enters their own readings; they are evaluated, saved to a history, charted, shown on the hologram and explained by the AI (value, normal range, meaning, affected organ, what to do).
  • Genetics: a radiation → gene-alteration simulator. Choose the situation (ISS, one-year mission, Mars transit), days, previous dose, a solar event and a vitamin A countermeasure, and see the dose, the career total against NASA's 600 mSv limit, the added cancer risk, which genes change (published NASA-funded data) and the consequences NASA found. The effects also appear on the astronaut's body scan.
  • Mission: follow a mission day by day; events (solar storm, exercise-machine failure, spacewalk) change the astronaut's status automatically.
  • Crew Risk: a day-by-day simulation of a four-person, 180-day Mars-transit crew in which the user takes a seat under their own name; crew traits, events and countermeasures are customizable.
  • EVA Decision: three options for a critical spacewalk after a solar storm (keep, delay, reassign) compared on success chance and risk, plus a Debate Chamber where commander, flight surgeon, science officer and a skeptic each apply one transparent formula.
  • Research: an evidence graph (14 factors, 13 links) where every link shows its evidence level and NASA source, plus a ranking of the next experiments worth doing.
  • Beyond AI: an assistant that answers questions about the crew, the scan and the user's own vitals, with care and in the user's language.

How it works A static three.js front end (GitHub Pages) talks to a FastAPI back end (Render) through a Next.js proxy (Vercel). The back end runs a deterministic simulation engine, the counterfactual EVA comparison, the evidence graph and the vitals evaluation. If the server is asleep, the app keeps working on a stored snapshot of the real API outputs and says so on screen.

Built-in guide (?): the "?" button in the top-right corner opens a guide to the whole app. It explains, in plain language, what each tab is for, what the colors and labels mean (SIMULATED, WATCH, ALERT, NASA source tags), how to switch between Astronaut and Scan mode, and how to customize the astronaut, the mission and the crew. Together with the A−/A+ text-size buttons, it makes the app usable by anyone, not only experts.

Benefits and impact Far from Earth, the crew cannot wait 20+ minutes for an answer from the ground. Beyond Horizons helps them detect problems earlier, understand them visually, and make decisions (for example, who should do a spacewalk) with evidence instead of guesswork. It is also a clear way to explain spaceflight health risks to students and the public.

Tools and languages JavaScript, HTML/CSS, three.js (WebGL, custom hologram shader, bloom), Python (FastAPI, Pydantic, pytest), TypeScript (Next.js, Tailwind), Jupyter notebooks, gltf-transform for 3D-model compression, GitHub Pages, Vercel and Render.

What makes it creative The suit becomes a hologram that shows where the body is in trouble; everything is connected (a solar storm in the mission changes the scan, the genetics simulator lights up the body, the user's own name appears in the crew and in the spacewalk decision); and every number is honest: simulated data is labelled SIMULATED, hypotheses are labelled as hypotheses, and every limit links to its NASA source.

Factors we considered Scientific honesty (no invented numbers, evidence levels on every link), clarity for non-experts (built-in guide, text-size controls, plain-language AI), the communication delay on deep-space missions, privacy (history stays in the user's browser) and resilience (offline snapshot). It is a research prototype, not a medical device.

Links:

Live app: https://estercpaulino2007.github.io/beyond-horizons/

Source code: https://github.com/estercpaulino2007/beyond-horizons

Use of Super Intelligence (SI) tools:

Claude supported code development, debugging, translating and interface refinement. Project direction, feature selection and final integration remained the creator's responsibility. Beyond AI is the project's user-facing assistant, helping users understand the information presented by the platform. Simulation outputs are generated by the project's deterministic engine, not by the AI assistant.

- Beyond AI, the project's user-facing assistant, uses an Anthropic API integrated through the project's backend. It helps users understand and navigate the information presented by the platform. Simulation outputs are generated by the project's deterministic engine, not by the AI assistant.

The application is deployed using GitHub Pages for the frontend, Vercel for the proxy layer, and Render for the backend services.

No NASA logos or branding were used or generated.

Recommended Viewing:

For the best experience with the interactive 3D dashboard, use a desktop or laptop browser.

projectDetails.name: Fire Mok
projectDetails.summary:
Fire Mok is an intelligent flood monitoring platform designed to help communities and public authorities prepare for and respond to floods. Inspired by the devastating May 2024 floods in the Guaíba River Basin, in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, the project transforms satellite data into clear and useful information for disaster response.

Using radar images from NASA and ESA satellites, Fire Mok can detect flooded areas even when heavy clouds make it difficult for traditional satellites to capture images. The platform combines this information with weather forecasts, terrain data, and population information to identify areas at greater risk and understand which communities may need help first.

Fire Mok turns complex environmental data into easy-to-understand flood maps, before-and-after comparisons, and risk assessments for each municipality. It also provides practical recommendations to help public authorities prioritize emergency actions and protect the most vulnerable populations.

Our goal is to make satellite technology more accessible and useful, helping communities make faster, better-informed decisions and reduce the impact of future floods.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

What does it do and how does it work?

Fire Mok is an intelligent flood monitoring and triage platform designed for environmental disaster management, anchored on the May 2024 Guaíba basin flood in Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil.

The platform automatically ingests day-and-night, all-weather Sentinel-1 Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery—which is NISAR-ready—to detect surface water extent through dense cloud cover.

The data pipeline processes SAR radar backscatter (σ), applies context masks to eliminate false positives, and integrates topographic terrain susceptibility using Copernicus DEM and the Height Above Nearest Drainage (HAND) model. It combines these physical layers with weather observations and forecasts from Open-Meteo and NASA POWER, alongside demographic vulnerability metrics from the IBGE 2022 Census and WorldPop exposure data.

The system outputs a municipal risk index (choropleth map) and generates data-traceable emergency action plans. Users interact with the platform through a React web application featuring interactive map layers, backscatter threshold adjustments, a before-and-after flood swipe tool, and municipal triage summary panels.

What benefits does it have and what is its intended impact?

The main benefit of Fire Mok is providing public managers and emergency responders with rapid, objective situational awareness during extreme rainfall events.

Because extreme storms bring heavy cloud cover that blinds conventional optical satellites, Fire Mok’s active microwave sensing ensures uninterrupted monitoring day and night.

Its intended impact is to empower local authorities to identify vulnerable communities early, prioritize rescue and relief logistics, and make data-driven policy decisions to protect human lives and critical infrastructure.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Programming Languages: Python 3.13 (69.4%), TypeScript (27.1%), and CSS.
  • Backend & Data Engineering: Python with uv package manager, FastAPI, rio-tiler for dynamic COG raster tile rendering, STAC API via Planetary Computer, ASF DAAC for NISAR HDF5 conversion, and Docker for containerization.
  • Frontend Development: React, Vite, MapLibre GL for web mapping, and static deployment via GitHub Pages.
  • Testing & Automation: GitHub Actions (daily scheduled data ingestion pipeline), pytest (87 pipeline tests, 9 API tests), and Vitest (20 frontend tests).
  • Datasets & External APIs: Sentinel-1 SAR (RTC), Copernicus DEM (HAND model), Open-Meteo API, NASA POWER, IBGE 2022 Census, WorldPop, ESA WorldCover 10m, and Sentinel-2 NDWI (for chip validation).

How is your project creative and what factors did your team consider?

  • Creativity: Fire Mok bridges advanced radar remote sensing physics with granular socio-demographic census data, turning complex satellite backscatter into automated, human-readable municipal triage scores and data-backed action plans.
  • Factors Considered:
    1. Optical Blindness: Traditional optical imagery fails during heavy rain; radar SAR was selected because its active microwave signals penetrate clouds day and night.
    2. Noise & False Positive Reduction: Radar signals suffer from urban corner-reflection and permanent water ambiguity; our team implemented ESA WorldCover 10m masks to clean the flood extents.
    3. Statistical Validation: SAR water extents were rigorously validated against Sentinel-2 NDWI chips using confusion matrices, F1 scores, IoU, and Cohen’s kappa with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals.
    4. Accessibility: To guarantee resilience, the system was designed with both a lightweight static web demo (mirrored pre-rendered tiles and JSON endpoints) and a full microservice API.

projectDetails.name: Body in Orbit
projectDetails.summary:
Body in Orbit is a portable crew health dashboard that runs offline on any computer with a modern browser, with no installation and no server. All data stays on the onboard computer, in the browser’s own database. A backup file and a smaller “Send data to Earth” package can travel through whatever link the mission has.

The dashboard follows six body systems that NASA lists among the main health risks of spaceflight: bone, muscles, heart, eyes and brain (SANS), sleep and radiation. Each crew member signs in to a short daily check-in, and resting heart rate can come straight from a Bluetooth chest strap. Rules turn the numbers into an analysis of the day. An optional onboard superintelligence, a language model running locally on the same computer, writes a short summary, and every number in it is checked against the measurements. To keep the crew answering, a mission capsule unlocks photos and messages from home every few answered days.

On a long mission, the crew can’t rely on the internet or on Earth to keep track of their health. Body in Orbit helps them follow their own health day by day, with private data and analysis that never needs a connection.
projectDetails.details:
# Body in Orbit

https://github.com/faustinopsy/Body-in-Orbit/

Onboard crew health dashboard for the **NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026**, challenge

"Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions".

Body in Orbit is designed as a **portable, embedded dashboard**: one web app that runs on any

computer with a modern browser, with no installation, no server and no internet connection after

the first load. It follows six body systems that NASA lists among the main health risks of

spaceflight (bone, muscles and fitness, heart and vessels, eyes and brain/SANS, sleep and

workload, radiation), collects a short daily check-in from each crew member (resting heart rate can come straight from a

common Bluetooth chest strap), and explains the day

with rules and with an **onboard superintelligence** that also runs offline, on the same computer.

> All data in the demo is simulated or projected from public NASA information. This is not a

> medical device, it does not diagnose, and it must not be used for health decisions about real

> people.

## Design choices

| Choice | Why |

|---|---|

| **Front end only, no backend** | A spacecraft, a remote base or a field station cannot depend on a server or on the internet. The whole app is static files that any computer can serve or open. |

| **Database in the browser (IndexedDB)** | Every mission, crew member, check-in, password hash and capsule item is stored locally, on the machine where the dashboard runs. It keeps working when the link to Earth is down. |

| **Backup and "Send data to Earth" as files** | Communication happens in windows. A full backup (JSON) restores the mission on another computer, and a smaller downlink package (no age, weight, height or personal capsule) can travel by any channel the mission has: file transfer, ground link, USB drive. |

| **Onboard superintelligence** | Analysis must not need the internet either. The app talks only to a local language model (Ollama at `http://127.0.0.1:11434`) on the same computer, and only after the administrator turns it on. |

| **Rules first, model second** | The app builds the analysis of the day with fixed rules. The model only rewrites those facts as a short summary, in a fixed JSON format, and every number in its answer is compared with the measurements. A failed check discards the answer. The screen always says where the text came from. |

| **Profiles on a shared device** | One computer serves the whole crew. The administrator sets up the mission; each crew member signs in with a password and sees only their own data. Sessions end after 3 minutes without activity. |

| **A common chest strap, read straight from the browser** | Resting heart rate can come from a consumer Bluetooth chest strap (the team uses a **Geoid HS500**). The app reads the standard Heart Rate service (0x180D) through Web Bluetooth: no driver, no vendor app, no cloud account, and the readings never leave the computer. Any strap that offers the standard service should work. Only a rest measurement is kept: 2 minutes still, median of the last minute, and the app asks to repeat when the readings do not settle. |

| **A mission capsule that rewards answering** | A health log is only useful if the crew keeps answering it, and on a long mission a daily questionnaire is easy to skip. So each crew member gets a personal capsule of photos and messages (from family, friends or the ground team), loaded by the administrator before launch. Items stay locked and open one by one: one every 3 answered days by default, from 1 to 30 as the administrator sets. The screen shows the streak of days in a row, the days answered and how many are left for the next item, and a card announces each new one. The reward is for answering, never for the answer: a bad night unlocks the capsule just like a good one, so nobody is pushed to report better numbers. |

## Technology choices

The team put its time into the features that matter on a mission (the onboard superintelligence,

the daily check-in and its gamification, the heart strap) and chose plain, long-lived web

technology for everything else.

| Layer | Choice | Why |

|---|---|---|

| Structure, style, logic | **HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript** (ES modules, ES2022), no framework | Only web standards: nothing to upgrade in the middle of a mission, a small bundle, and any developer can read it. |

| CSS | Cascade layers (`tokens`, `base`, `ui`, `features`), design tokens as custom properties, one CSS file per component | Light and dark themes and the text size (A- / A+) change only tokens; a component's style lives next to its code. |

| Build | **Vite** | Fast development server and a production build of static files in `dist/`. `base: './'` lets the build open from any folder or static host. |

| Storage | **IndexedDB** through `idb` (a small promise wrapper) | A real database inside the browser, with versioned migrations. |

| Browser APIs | Web Crypto (PBKDF2), Web Bluetooth, `fetch` to the local Ollama | Passwords, the heart strap and the onboard model need no backend. |

| Avatar | **SVG drawn with AI assistance** | 3D modelling software is heavy and slow to learn, and the focus was the onboard AI and gamification. SVG is light, sharp at any size, takes the theme colours from CSS, makes every body region clickable and accessible, and zooms with a simple `viewBox` animation. |

| Icons and fonts | Lucide icons; Barlow Condensed and IBM Plex fonts stored in the project | No request to outside servers, even for fonts. |

| Quality | **ESLint** (file and function size limits, complexity limit) and **Vitest** with happy-dom and fake-indexeddb | Every change runs `npm run check`: lint, tests and build. |

## Two ways to use it

### Demo mission (for evaluators)

Built so judges can see everything in a few clicks. The welcome dialog opens a 180-day simulated

mission with three crew members, and the sign-in dialog offers one-click shortcuts (administrator,

C01, C02, C03), with no passwords.

In the demo, **both the data and the analyses are mocked**: the measurements are a simulated series,

the crew already has a few days of check-ins, the mission capsule comes with fictional images and

messages (C01, C02 and C03 start with 8, 5 and 2 answered days, so each shows a different stage of

the capsule), and the onboard superintelligence uses analyses prepared by the app (no model is called),

which still pass the same checks. The heart strap is simulated too, and the 2-minute rest

measurement takes 12 seconds.

### Real mission (fully functional)

Without the demo, every feature works with your own data: create the administrator password,

register a mission and its crew, set each crew member's password, answer the daily check-in, close

the day, load the mission capsule, read the analysis of the day, back up and restore, and export

the package for Earth.

The only extra requirement is for the onboard superintelligence: **Ollama and a model must be

installed on the same computer that runs the dashboard** (for example `ollama pull llama3.2`), and

the administrator turns it on in Settings. Without it, the analysis by rules keeps working.

## What you can do

- **Sign in by profile.** Administrator (mission, crew, passwords, capsule, data, settings) or crew

member (Dashboard, Today and Help, own data only). Passwords are stored as PBKDF2-SHA-256 hashes

with 600,000 iterations and a random salt, following OWASP.

- **Register a mission and its crew.** One of the eight NASA Design Reference Mission categories,

its length, and up to six crew members (role, age, weight, height). Members get codes (C01,

C02...); no names are stored.

- **Answer the daily check-in (Today).** Hours and quality of sleep, what disturbed it, and resting

heart rate. Answers update the dashboard for that day. The administrator closes the day.

- **Measure resting heart rate with a chest strap.** From the heart rate question, connect the

strap, stay still for 2 minutes and use the median of the last minute as the answer. The value

only goes in when the crew member confirms it, and is kept only when the check-in is saved.

- **Read the analysis of the day.** Up to six points, the worst first: measurements past their

limits, resting heart rate above the weekly average, short or poor sleep, and measurements that

will cross a limit within 30 days, each with what can help.

- **Ask the onboard superintelligence.** A short summary with up to three habits, the main points

highlighted, and "numbers checked against the measurements".

- **Unlock the mission capsule.** Images and messages sent with the mission open one by one, every

3 answered days by default (the administrator can change it), to keep the crew answering. Each

crew member sees their streak, the days answered, a countdown to the next item and the locked

items still waiting. The personal capsule never goes into the package for Earth.

- **Follow the timeline.** Six body layers, an SVG anatomical avatar that zooms into the region you

click, metric cards, a chart with limits, a table, countermeasures, and a Play button.

- **Learn why.** The Help screen explains every risk, the NASA ratings, how the timeline is

projected, and the onboard technology.

- **Use it your way.** English, Spanish and Portuguese, text size (A− / A+), light and dark themes,

full screen.

## Limitations

- **The heart strap works only in Chrome and Edge.** Web Bluetooth works only in **Google Chrome**

and other Chromium-based browsers (such as Microsoft Edge) on desktop, with the app opened on

localhost or HTTPS; **Firefox and Safari do not support it**, and on Linux Chrome needs an

experimental flag. In other browsers the value is typed by hand.

- **Resting heart rate only, no heart rate variability.** The RR interval the Geoid HS500 sends is

always 60000/bpm, repeated across packets, so it is not a real beat-to-beat measure. The strap

needs wet electrodes and connects to one device at a time. The rest criteria (15 bpm spread, 30

readings) are the app's own, not scientifically validated.

- **Not yet tested with the real strap.** So far the measurement was tested with a simulated

sensor. **[VERIFY]**

- **The onboard superintelligence needs Ollama on the same computer.** The quality of the summary

depends on the model; the app discards any answer that fails the checks.

- **Passwords separate profiles on a shared device.** They do not protect the data from someone

with technical access to the browser.

- **Limits are provisional.** Warning and critical limits are demo values, not NASA medical

standards. **[VERIFY]**

- **Demo data and demo analyses are simulated**, as described above.

## How it works

```

mission type + length + crew (age, weight, height)

-> risk weights per mission type (NASA LxC ratings)

-> weight factor x personal factor x expected monthly change

-> projected daily series per crew member and metric

-> daily check-ins replace the projected values of that day

-> 7-day mean, status (normal / warning / critical), 60-day trend, projected crossing day

-> dashboard, avatar, analysis of the day, onboard superintelligence, help screen

```

### Risk weights

For every risk and mission type, NASA's Human System Risk Board gives two ratings: operations

(during the mission) and long-term health. Each is a likelihood times a consequence (LxC) on a 5x5

matrix (older ratings use 3x4).

- score = (L x C) / (maximum of the matrix: 25 or 12)

- weight = the larger of the two scores

- level: below 30% low, 30-59% moderate, 60% or more high

- timeline factor = weight of the mission / weight of a long low-orbit mission (the ISS-like

reference where most measured data comes from), limited between 0.4x and 2x

| Mission type | Bone | Muscles | Heart | SANS | Sleep | Radiation |

|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

| Low Earth orbit, short | 50% | 50% | 36% | 16% | 40% | 25% |

| Low Earth orbit, long | 50% | 50% | 48% | 48% | 40% | 50% |

| Lunar orbit (or orbit + surface), short | 33% | 33% | 36% | 16% | 40% | 25% |

| Lunar orbit (or orbit + surface), long | 50% | 50% | 48% | 48% | 40% | 50% |

| Mars preparatory | 50% | 50% | 48% | 48% | 40% | 75% |

| Mars planetary | 75% | 75% | 64% | 80% | 40% | 75% |

Notes: the bone rating dates from 2017 and used older mission categories, mapped by the team.

Our sources have no LxC table for muscles and fitness, so it reuses the bone weight. The radiation

rating still uses the older 3x4 matrix.

### Crew factors

- **Age** (heart metrics only): +1% of expected change per year above 40, -1% per year below,

limited to 0.85x-1.25x. Basis: the NASA cardiovascular report lists age, sleep, exercise, diet

and stress as known contributors to cardiovascular disease.

- **Body mass index** from weight and height (heart metrics only): +1% per BMI unit outside

18.5-25, up to +15%. **[VERIFY]** illustrative team choice, not from NASA.

- Radiation dose and SANS do not use personal factors (see the Help screen for why).

### Expected monthly change (reference: long low-orbit mission)

| Metric | Change | Basis |

|---|---|---|

| Spine and hip bone density | -1.25% per month | NASA: 1-1.5% per month in 4-6 month missions |

| Tibia bone density | -0.75% per month | **[VERIFY]** team assumption |

| Core, thigh, calf strength | -1.5%, -2%, -2.5% per month | NASA: 10-12% average loss of strength and aerobic fitness on ISS missions |

| Resting heart rate / recovery | +1 / -0.8 bpm per month | **[VERIFY]** team assumption |

| Sleep hours / quality | -1.5 h / -0.6 over the first 14 days | NASA: crews sleep about 6 h per night in flight |

| SANS signs (0-4) | +0.2 per month | NASA: about 70% of crew on 4-6 month missions show early optic disc edema |

| Radiation dose | 0.5 (LEO), 1.4 (lunar), 1.8 (deep space), 1.5 (Mars mission) mSv per day | **[VERIFY]** order of magnitude, not in the reports used |

### Analysis of the day and onboard superintelligence

- **Rules (always on):** reads the same numbers the dashboard shows plus the check-in of the day and

fills fixed sentences in English, Spanish and Portuguese. It never diagnoses.

- **Onboard superintelligence (optional, off by default):** receives only crew codes, day, level and

the facts found by the rules (no names, age, weight or height), must answer in JSON (summary,

focus, tips), and every number it writes must match the analysis. In the demo, the summary is

prepared by the app and no model is called.

## Privacy and safety

- No server and no account in the cloud: data lives in the browser's IndexedDB, on the onboard

computer.

- No requests outside the app's own origin, except the optional local Ollama after it is turned on.

- Crew members are codes; passwords are stored only as salted PBKDF2 hashes.

- The package for Earth never includes age, weight, height or the personal mission capsule.

- Texts from data files are inserted with `textContent`, never as HTML.

- No NASA logo is used.

## Architecture and SOLID

The code follows the SOLID principles in plain JavaScript, with functions and modules instead of

classes.

| Principle | How it shows in the code |

|---|---|

| Single responsibility | One job per file: a component, a command, a repository, a rule. ESLint enforces it: at most 200 lines per file, 60 per function, complexity 10. |

| Open/closed | A new feature is new files: a folder in `src/features` with its components and its texts (found automatically), plus its commands. Existing screens barely change. |

| Liskov substitution | Parts with the same contract can replace each other: the real Bluetooth strap, the demo simulator and the test fake; the real IndexedDB and fake-indexeddb; the local Ollama and the test fake. |

| Interface segregation | Services are small and focused (preferences, datasets, accounts, capsule, hasher, session, ollama, heart sensor), and each command uses only the ones it needs. |

| Dependency inversion | Commands and screens depend on services handed to them at start: `createServices` in the browser, `createTestServices` in the tests. The domain (`src/domain`) is pure calculation and never touches the screen, the database or a device. |

The state changes only inside commands, and screens only read the state and call commands, so the

data flows in one direction.

Why this way: a hackathon team works in parallel and fast, much of the code was drafted with AI

help, and every piece had to be easy to review, to test alone and to replace. Small, independent

parts also make the future ports below possible.

## Tests

**50 test files and 224 tests**, mirroring `src`. Line coverage of `src` is **96.6%**

(statements 94.5%, branches 86.6%, functions 93.5%): domain 100%, data 97.9%, screens 98.7%, app

88.3%, where the lower part is the thin adapters that talk to real devices. Measured on

2026-11-15 with `@vitest/coverage-v8`, which is not a project dependency.

Why tests matter here:

- The app shows health numbers and analyses; a wrong mean, limit or trend would mislead the crew.

- The onboard superintelligence check compares the model's numbers with the analysis, so the

analysis itself must be right.

- Fakes let every feature be tested without Bluetooth, Ollama or a real browser database.

- AI-assisted code is accepted only when `npm run check` (lint, tests, build) passes.

## Run it

```bash

npm ci # install the exact versions locked in package-lock.json

npm run dev # development server

npm run check # lint + tests + build

npm run data:generate # rebuild public/data/sample-dataset.json

npm run deploy # check, then publish dist/ to the producao branch (GitHub Pages)

```

Requirements: Node.js 22.12 or newer. For the onboard superintelligence: Ollama and one model on

the same computer. For the heart strap: Google Chrome or another Chromium-based browser, and a strap with the

standard Heart Rate service (the team uses a Geoid HS500).

## Project structure

| Folder | Content |

|---|---|

| `src/domain` | Pure calculation: metrics, status, trend, missions, check-in, capsule rules, access rules, rest heart rate measurement, analysis and its checks |

| `src/data` | IndexedDB: migrations and repositories (missions, datasets, accounts, capsule, backup) |

| `src/app` | Store, i18n, commands, services, adapters (Ollama, Bluetooth heart strap and its demo simulator, password hashing, session, image files) |

| `src/features` | Screens: shell, access, welcome, dashboard (avatar), today, heart sensor, analysis, capsule, missions, settings, help, datasets |

| `src/ui` | Small DOM and SVG helpers |

| `tests` | Vitest + happy-dom + fake-indexeddb, mirrors `src` |

## Future work

- **Desktop and mobile apps from the same code.** The app is static files, and the parts that

depend on the platform (Bluetooth, files, the local model, the session) are isolated in

- **Test with the real strap** and add straps that send real beat-to-beat intervals, to measure

heart rate variability.

- **Review the limits with flight surgeons**, replacing the provisional values marked

projectDetails.name: Make it Mars: Mars Survival Guide
projectDetails.summary: Armstrong Maps is a prototype of the mission-planning tool a crew would use aboard the spacecraft before an astronaut goes down to the surface of Mars. On the ship's console, the crew picks a landing site on a 3D globe, stacks real NASA data over it and draws the route of the walk. The plan is checked before anyone steps outside and returns a go, caution or no-go verdict with its reasons: life support, the distance to walk back, the radiation dose measured by Curiosity, space weather forecast by NASA's DONKI, daylight from NASA/JPL Horizons, and ground too steep to walk from NASA elevation models. The prototype also shows how the astronaut's helmet visor would carry that same plan on the surface: heading, next waypoint, life support left, time to turn back, dose and a map of the route, over real rover panoramas, in step with the ship. Everything is built on NASA open data, and every number carries its source or a label saying it is simulated or assumed. Its purpose is simple: the success and the safety of every walk on Mars.
projectDetails.details:
Summary

Armstrong Maps is a layered map of Mars that integrates data from multiple NASA sources into an all-in-one platform designed to guide astronauts during their missions.

The platform is built as a web application that astronauts can use aboard their spacecraft to plan exploration routes and visualize data. It is also accessible on mobile devices that astronauts can carry during surface exploration. Finally, the Astronaut Visor view simulates a helmet display, showing essential information while an astronaut carries out a mission. (More information in Astronaut Visor section).

Expected Impact

Armstrong Maps aims to make Mars exploration safer and more accessible by bringing NASA data available for selected exploration sites into a single, interactive platform. Its spacecraft view helps crew members visualize terrain, plan routes, and assess potential hazards, while its Astronaut Visor view provides essential mission information during surface exploration. Communication features connect the astronaut in the field with the spacecraft crew, allowing them to exchange messages and flags to coordinate activities. By combining these tools with Go, No-Go, and Caution risk assessments, the project demonstrates how scientific data can support informed decisions before and during a mission.

Features

The features available in the project can be described in the following sections: Mars Globe, Visiting a Site and Astronaut Visor.

Mars Globe

The landing page features an interactive Mars globe highlighting exploration sites. These locations were selected based on previous exploration sites and the availability of data in NASA Mars Trek.


Visiting a Site

Selecting a site opens a detailed map of the area. From this view, users can explore data and access mission tools through panels on the left and right sides of the screen.

In the left panel, users can toggle map layers to display topography, terrain relief, and other information, providing an overview of the exploration site. The available layers and their data sources are described in the Map Layers section.

The right panel contains four tabs: Walk, Link, Site, and Photos.


Walk

The Walk tab allows users to plan an exploration route by selecting points on the map. It displays the distance from the base, the total distance along the selected route, and a Go, No-Go, or Caution recommendation for the planned walk.

This tab also provides access to the Astronaut Visor view, which simulates the information an astronaut would see during a mission.

Route planning and the criteria behind these recommendations are explained in the Plan a Walk section. The visor interface is described in the Astronaut Visor section.

Link

The Link tab displays mission progress and allows crew members aboard the spacecraft to send messages and flags to the astronaut exploring the surface. These updates appear in the astronaut’s helmet display.


Site

The Site tab displays key information about the selected location, including the Mars clock, weather conditions, radiation, and Curiosity’s route, where applicable. It also shows air temperature and atmospheric pressure over the past 30 days, along with wind information. The data sources for each element are described in the Site section.


Photos

The Photos tab retrieves mission images related to the selected site from the NASA Image and Video Library.

Astronaut Visor

The Astronaut Visor simulates a 360° view from inside an astronaut’s helmet while following the planned exploration route. It uses images of the selected site from the NASA Image and Video Library to create a visual representation of the surroundings. If 360° images from the site are not available, the app uses a vision from another location, to simulate the environment. This information can be retrieved in the “Sources” button, available on the Visor page.

The interface also displays life-support information, mission progress (such as the number of waypoints visited) and environmental data, including radiation, air temperature, and atmospheric pressure, when available.

Data Source and Assumptions

The full documentation of the project is also available on https://www.armstrongmaps.us/docs

projectDetails.name: LunarSight
projectDetails.summary: LunarSight is a free interactive website that helps compare landing sites and dates near the Moon’s south pole. It features a 3D Moon with ten sites and real, hourly Sun and Earth positions from NASA’s JPL Horizons System over 30 days. Users can compare two sites and dates, visualize sunlight and Earth visibility, estimate sunset and Earthset times, and assess power and communication conditions. A heat map highlights alternative sites and dates if mission schedules are delayed. LunarSight makes complex lunar landing conditions easier to understand, helping mission planners, educators, and the public explore critical trade-offs.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does the project do?

LunarSight is a website that compares different landing sites at the Moon’s South Pole. Users can explore a 3D Moon, select two locations and compare sunlight, communication with Earth and energy availability. They can also change the landing date and see how delays affect each location.

2. What benefits does it have?

The website makes complex scientific data easier and faster to understand. It helps compare locations, plan for possible delays and provides reliable information from NASA/JPL. It is also useful for scientists, students and the general public.

3. What is its intended impact?

Our goal is to make lunar mission planning easier and help scientists choose better landing locations. We also want to educate people about the challenges of exploring the Moon, especially its South Pole.

4. What tools did we use?

We used React, Vite and Three.js to develop the website, Python to download data, and NASA/JPL Horizons for scientific information. We also used AI (Claude) to help with coding, calculations and website content. The website is hosted on Netlify.

5. How is the project creative?

LunarSight combines real scientific data with an interactive 3D Moon. It uses realistic sunlight, interactive comparisons and a heat map showing how conditions change over 30 days. Its design and visual elements were created using our own code.

6. What factors did our team consider?

Energy: We analyzed sunlight availability for solar panels.

Communication: We checked when Earth is visible from each location.

Cost: We used free tools and hosting.

Accessibility: The website works in normal browsers, requires no installation and has simple controls.

Accuracy: We used official NASA and scientific data, while explaining the limitations of our calculations.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”
