PROJECT ATLAS - Abandoned, but not forgotten.

ATLAS is an inventory of objects launched to the Moon, Mars, and Space.

What does it do and how does it work?
ATLAS organizes all human-made objects left in space in one simple, searchable place. Each object is classified as Active, Deactivated, or Lost. The user can search by name, location - Moon, Mars, or Earth Orbit - and status, and quickly see what it is, where it is, and what happened to it.

What benefits does it offer?
It transforms complex space data into a simple consultation for study in any situation - from a young student to an astronaut. Anyone can learn, in seconds, what humanity has left in space.

What is the intended impact?
To create awareness about space debris, preserve the history of space exploration, and help future missions plan more sustainably, avoiding new collisions and pollution in orbit.

What tools did we use?
We used NASA open data, web research, HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the website, and AI tools for research, organization of data, design and video creation.

What is the creative aspect?
The concept "Abandoned, but not forgotten" - every object has a story. ATLAS does not show just trash in space, it shows the legacy of humanity.

What factors did the team consider?
Simplicity, education, accessibility for all ages, and the use of reliable data for a real problem: the growing amount of objects left in space.
projectDetails.details:
PROJECT ATLAS - Abandoned, but not forgotten.

ATLAS is an inventory of objects launched to the Moon, Mars, and Space.

What does it do and how does it work?

ATLAS is a digital archive and interactive inventory that catalogs human-made objects left in space and on other worlds. From rovers and landers to flags, tools, satellites and even small personal items, ATLAS records what was sent, when, by which mission and agency, where it is now, and what its current status is.

The user can search by destination, mission, year, agency, type of object and status. Each object has a profile with its history, photos, location and its scientific or historical importance. The platform also shows a timeline and a map view, so people can explore the journey of humanity beyond Earth in a simple and visual way.

What benefits does it offer?

ATLAS turns scattered mission data into one accessible place. It helps students, researchers, space enthusiasts and the general public understand how much we have already sent to space. For education, it is a powerful tool to teach history, science and exploration. For future missions, it helps avoid confusion about what is already on the Moon and Mars and supports responsible exploration.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to preserve space heritage. These objects are not just trash. They are proof of human curiosity, courage and innovation. ATLAS wants to create awareness about space debris, sustainability and planetary protection, and inspire new generations to care about how we explore.

What tools, languages and software did we use?

We used HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the front end, with a responsive and accessible design. For data organization we used JavaScript and JSON, and Python for data cleaning and validation. We used NASA Open Data, mission archives and public space databases as sources. For design and prototyping we used Figma and Canva. For collaboration we used GitHub, Google Docs and WhatsApp.

What is the creative aspect?

Instead of a boring list, ATLAS tells stories. Each object has a story, like it was abandoned, but not forgotten. We use visual storytelling, timelines and a museum-like experience to make users feel like they are visiting a space museum. The design mixes science with emotion and memory.

What factors did our team consider?

We considered accuracy of data, accessibility for all users, simplicity for non-experts, and respect for space heritage. We also thought about sustainability, planetary protection, and the ethical question of what we leave behind on other worlds. Our team worked to make ATLAS clear, reliable, inclusive and inspiring for everyone.

projectDetails.name: Project SYMBIOCORE
projectDetails.summary:
Symbiocore Outpost is an educational space mission training game developed by Nicolas Augusto Paixão, a 9-year-old Brazilian student and young inventor, with parental support.

Created for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, the project introduces young learners to the challenges of managing a lunar or Martian habitat, including waste management, resource conservation, sustainability, and life-support systems.

The game introduces Symbiocore, an original scientific concept exploring how microorganisms and microscopic robots might one day transform human waste into useful mineral panels for space habitats.

Currently classified as Technology Readiness Level 1 (TRL 1), Symbiocore is a theoretical proposal, not a tested technology. Its potential applications would require extensive scientific research and experimentation.

The project addresses the challenge by combining interactive learning, scientific imagination, and real space exploration problems.

Nicolas dreams of studying science and engineering, transforming his concept into a real technology one day, and working at NASA to contribute to humanity's future in space.
projectDetails.details:
Symbiocore Concept Proposal

November 15, 2026

Young Inventor: Nicolas Augusto Paixão
Age: 9 years old
Country: Brazil
Project: Symbiocore Outpost
NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026
Challenge: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
Technology Readiness Level: TRL 1 — Basic Principles and Conceptual Exploration

1. Summary

Symbiocore is an early-stage scientific concept for a system that would use living microorganisms and microscopic robots to transform human waste into solid mineral panels during long-duration space missions.

The proposed technology aims to explore how biological processes, mineral formation, and robotic assembly might eventually contribute to more sustainable living environments beyond Earth.

Symbiocore is currently a theoretical concept, not a working device. It is classified as Technology Readiness Level 1 (TRL 1), meaning that the underlying scientific ideas are being explored, but the proposed integrated system has not been built, experimentally validated, or tested.

The concept originated from the imagination and scientific curiosity of Nicolas Augusto Paixão, a nine-year-old Brazilian inventor, and was developed with parental support.

It is presented through Symbiocore Outpost, an educational game created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, under the challenge Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer.

Within the game, players unlock Symbiocore as an experimental technology while learning about resource management, waste recycling, sustainability, and the challenges of living in space.

However, the project represents more than a fictional technology developed for a game.

Nicolas hopes that, through years of education, scientific research, experimentation, and collaboration, the concept might one day inspire a real technological solution for future space missions.

His personal ambition is to become a scientist or engineer and work at NASA, contributing to humanity's exploration of space.

2. The Problem: Waste During Long-Duration Space Missions

On the International Space Station, solid waste is generally collected, stored, and loaded into cargo spacecraft that burn up during atmospheric reentry.

This approach is possible for missions operating relatively close to Earth. However, missions to the Moon, Mars, and other distant destinations introduce significant logistical challenges.

Resupply missions are expensive, transportation capacity is limited, and waste cannot always be returned to Earth.

According to NASA, a crew of four astronauts could generate more than 2,100 kilograms of single-use waste in one year, including food packaging, plastic films, foam, and clothing.

Source: NASA — Sustainability Solutions for Lunar Missions

Human waste represents an additional challenge that requires safe collection, treatment, and management.

Symbiocore focuses specifically on the possibility of processing human waste into potentially useful mineral materials.

A system capable of converting waste into valuable resources could help reduce storage requirements, improve resource efficiency, and support more sustainable space habitats.

3. The Concept: Five Steps From Waste to Mineral Panels

Symbiocore is envisioned as a sealed processing unit installed inside a spacecraft or extraterrestrial habitat.

The conceptual system would operate through five interconnected stages.

Step 1 — Intake Chamber

Human waste would be collected inside a sealed chamber designed to prevent contamination of the spacecraft environment.

The chamber would isolate the material from the crew and prepare it for subsequent processing.

Step 2 — Light Reactor

A controlled lighting system would support selected microorganisms associated with the internal surfaces of the reactor.

The concept proposes investigating whether light-dependent biological processes could contribute to waste treatment or mineral production.

Step 3 — Mineralization Chamber

Microorganisms would participate in a biological mineralization process intended to produce useful mineral materials.

One proposed material is silica, a mineral compound associated with naturally occurring biological structures.

Water would be separated where technically feasible and directed toward the spacecraft's water recovery system.

The conversion of human waste into usable silica panels remains an unproven hypothesis requiring extensive scientific investigation.

Step 4 — Robotic Assembly

Microscopic robots controlled through magnetic fields would hypothetically transport, organize, and compact mineral particles.

Their purpose would be to assist in forming solid structures from the processed mineral material.

The ability of such robots to perform this function in a space environment has not been demonstrated.

Step 5 — Mineral Panels

The final stage would produce sealed mineral panels.

If future testing demonstrated appropriate material properties, these panels might be investigated for applications such as:

  • Additional radiation shielding.
  • Thermal insulation.
  • Nonstructural habitat components.
  • Resource reuse within spacecraft or planetary habitats.

Their suitability for any of these applications would require experimental validation, including testing for strength, contamination, durability, and radiation-related properties.

Throughout the process, sensors would monitor parameters such as acidity, humidity, and gas concentrations.

4. The Science Behind Symbiocore

The Symbiocore concept draws inspiration from existing scientific research in microbiology, biomineralization, regenerative life-support systems, and magnetic microrobotics.

Although these fields are real, their proposed combination into a functioning waste-to-panel system has not been demonstrated.

4.1 Mineral-Producing Microorganisms

What exists today

Diatoms are microscopic organisms capable of producing intricate silica structures.

Certain bacteria can also precipitate calcium carbonate through biochemical processes involving the enzyme urease.

These mechanisms are studied in biomineralization and biocementation research on Earth.

What remains unproven

The controlled conversion of human waste into silica-based construction panels, particularly under microgravity conditions.

4.2 Microorganisms for Life-Support Systems

What exists today

NASA-supported research and the European Space Agency's MELiSSA project investigate biological systems that could help recycle waste and recover resources needed for human life.

Such research includes the use of microorganisms and algae in regenerative life-support systems.

What remains unproven

The integration of a reliable mineral-producing process into a closed-loop system that converts human waste into usable habitat materials.

4.3 Magnetic Microrobots

What exists today

Scientific research has demonstrated microscopic robotic systems that can be moved or guided through fluids using magnetic fields.

Many of these technologies are being investigated for biomedical applications.

What remains unproven

Their ability to collect and assemble mineral particles into solid panels while operating reliably for extended periods in spacecraft environments exposed to radiation and microgravity.

5. Scientific Challenges and Future Research

Transforming Symbiocore from a conceptual idea into a functional technology would require extensive scientific research.

Important questions include:

  1. Which microorganisms could safely process human waste under controlled conditions?
  2. Could biological processes produce sufficient mineral material for practical applications?
  3. Would silica production require additional mineral sources or chemical inputs?
  4. How could water be safely separated, treated, and recovered?
  5. Could magnetic microrobots manipulate mineral particles effectively in microgravity?
  6. What energy, water, nutrients, and maintenance would the system require?
  7. How could harmful microorganisms, gases, and contaminants be contained?
  8. Would the resulting panels provide meaningful insulation or radiation protection?
  9. Could the system operate safely over long periods without introducing risks to astronauts?
  10. Would the benefits justify the mass, energy consumption, and complexity of the equipment?

These questions demonstrate why Symbiocore remains a TRL 1 concept.

Any future development would require controlled laboratory experiments, scientific supervision, engineering analysis, and extensive safety testing.

6. Symbiocore Outpost: The Educational Game

Symbiocore Outpost introduces the concept through an interactive learning experience.

The game is designed to encourage young players to think about the scientific and engineering challenges associated with human space exploration.

Players encounter situations involving resource management, waste processing, habitat sustainability, and technological decision-making.

As they progress, they unlock the fictional Symbiocore system as a possible future technology.

The game aims to encourage:

  • Scientific curiosity and creative problem-solving.
  • Awareness of sustainability in space.
  • Interest in biology, engineering, and robotics.
  • Understanding of resource limitations during long-duration missions.
  • Critical thinking about emerging technologies.
  • Recognition of the difference between scientific concepts and experimentally validated inventions.

The educational purpose is not to suggest that Symbiocore already exists.

Instead, the game invites young learners to imagine how scientific discoveries might eventually help address real challenges faced by astronauts.

7. From Imagination to Reality: Nicolas's Vision

Symbiocore was born from the imagination and scientific curiosity of Nicolas Augusto Paixão, a nine-year-old Brazilian inventor who dreams of working at NASA one day.

Although Symbiocore is currently a conceptual proposal presented through the educational game Symbiocore Outpost, Nicolas hopes that, with sufficient scientific research and technological development, this idea could one day move beyond simulation and become a real solution for space exploration.

He understands that transforming a scientific idea into a functional technology requires much more than imagination.

It demands years of education, dedication, experimentation, critical thinking, and collaboration with researchers and specialists.

Nicolas hopes to deepen his knowledge of mathematics, physics, biology, engineering, robotics, and space science as he grows.

His long-term goal is to develop the skills necessary to contribute to scientific discoveries and technological innovations that could support future astronauts.

Working at NASA represents one of his greatest dreams.

Through Symbiocore, Nicolas wants to demonstrate that even a young student can begin exploring important scientific questions.

The project does not claim to have solved the problem of waste management in space.

Instead, it presents a possible direction for future investigation and reflects a commitment to learning.

For Nicolas, Symbiocore Outpost is more than a game.

It is the first step toward a scientific ambition that he hopes to pursue through knowledge, perseverance, creativity, and discovery.

8. Long-Term Development Goals

If Nicolas chooses to continue developing the concept in the future, possible research stages could include:

Stage 1 — Scientific Education

Study the fundamentals of microbiology, chemistry, physics, robotics, and space engineering.

Stage 2 — Literature Research

Investigate existing scientific studies on biomineralization, biological waste treatment, closed-loop life-support systems, and microrobotics.

Stage 3 — Preliminary Experiments

With qualified scientific supervision, investigate safe model systems using nonhazardous materials and appropriate laboratory procedures.

Stage 4 — Engineering Feasibility

Evaluate whether the proposed biological and robotic processes could realistically be combined into a single system.

Stage 5 — Prototype Development

If supported by experimental evidence, develop and test preliminary components under controlled laboratory conditions.

Stage 6 — Space-Relevant Research

Only after successful earlier stages, investigate potential applications under simulated space conditions and assess whether further development is scientifically and economically justified.

These stages are long-term aspirations, not completed research activities or guaranteed development milestones.

9. Expected Educational and Scientific Impact

The immediate contribution of Symbiocore is educational.

Through Symbiocore Outpost, the concept introduces young learners to scientific challenges associated with sustainable space exploration.

Its potential future scientific contribution remains hypothetical.

If research eventually established a feasible biological mineralization process, the underlying ideas might contribute to new approaches for resource recovery and waste management.

However, the project's present value lies in encouraging curiosity, scientific literacy, and responsible innovation.

Symbiocore illustrates how an imaginative question can become the starting point for structured scientific investigation.

10. Conclusion

Symbiocore is an early-stage concept that explores the possibility of transforming human waste into useful mineral materials through biological processes and microscopic robotic systems.

The technology has not been constructed or experimentally validated, and substantial scientific challenges remain.

Its presentation through Symbiocore Outpost provides an educational opportunity to explore sustainability, engineering, and resource management in space.

For its young creator, Nicolas Augusto Paixão, the project also represents a personal commitment to a future in science.

His dream is to study, develop his knowledge, and one day work at NASA, contributing to technologies that may help humanity explore space more sustainably.

Symbiocore begins as an idea inside a game, but its greatest purpose is to inspire the scientific learning that could one day turn imagination into discovery.

Educational Game: Symbiocore Outpost
Young Inventor: Nicolas Augusto Paixão
Developed with parental support
Brazil — November 15, 2026
Technology Readiness Level: TRL 1

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: SpaceCare
projectDetails.summary: Space-Care is a Body-Area Network (BAN) software with a decentralized, distributed architecture, integrated with NASA’s back-end platform, GHP-IDSP, designed to monitor and guide astronauts in situations that could compromise their physical or psychological health during long-duration space missions. Our solution addresses the challenge because its decentralized architecture ensures data scalability and reliability in low-latency environments. The clinical support provided by the software—covering medical exams, sample collection, and various activities—along with the preliminary analysis of conditions and the gathering of statistics from sensors, enables astronauts to evaluate the best courses of action during the mission to ensure the well-being of the crew.
projectDetails.details:
A pervasive distributed system for health monitoring that incorporates a Body Area Network (BAN), connecting sensors for radiation (dosimeters), heart rate, carbon dioxide (via an acoustic sensor within the spacecraft), and light levels received by the body. This system processes the information through a central hub and transmits it to an available external server.

However, continuous data transmission can lead to information loss and excessive power consumption by the sensors; therefore, data should be transmitted based on specific triggers—such as the detection of anomalies that threaten the well-being of the crew—or at predetermined time intervals.

The software will operate via a decentralized architecture, in which individual servers manage health indicators for a subset of the astronauts. These servers can communicate with one another to request services or information, ultimately generating a comprehensive, global view of the data to be presented to medical personnel. Detailed analysis of the environment in which the astronauts are located (such as a planet or other celestial body), providing data—including gravity and pressure levels—to highlight potential health risks and necessary precautions, such as medical procedures, equipment usage, or the procurement of medication.

Comparison of samples and baseline data collected on Earth with data gathered during the mission to identify changes in the astronaut's health status.

An interface displaying the astronaut’s body, highlighting areas that require closer monitoring (e.g., bones, heart, brain, etc.).

A color-coded system indicating the urgency of medical evaluation for specific body parts: green (low urgency), yellow (moderate), and red (high urgency).

The ability to click on a specific body part to access a detailed report, including the history of previous examinations, recommended follow-up tests, and health metrics (such as heart rate, cell counts, or bone/muscle density).

Suggestions for adjustments to the astronaut’s daily routine—such as modifications to diet, self-care time, physical exercise, or rest periods—based on the collected data.

Identification of the equipment required to perform medical examinations, cross-referenced with the spacecraft’s onboard inventory.

An automated diagnostic assistant to guide astronauts — who are trained to perform self-assessments during the mission— ensuring they follow the correct procedures.

Analysis of saliva samples (liquid or dried) to detect changes in the immune system, specifically assessing the risk of the reactivation of, or exposure to, dormant viruses. (As seen in the "Artemis II" mission, where astronauts provided saliva samples before and after the flight to monitor shifts in immune biomarkers over time.)

Collection of behavioral data to develop a personalized profile for the astronaut regarding health issues that may arise and the measures to be taken by the astronaut throughout the mission.

For the purpose of automation, the system will use previously collected data to draw inferences about factors such as sleep regularity, work overload, and changes in body temperature or heart rate, in order to suggest actions the astronaut can take (such as resting or engaging in self-care).

projectDetails.name: Astra Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
projectDetails.summary:
Astra Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive educational game designed to transform children's recreational screen time into a high-quality, engaging learning experience. The platform immerses young players in simulated space environments—such as the Moon—where they manage critical life-support resources like water, oxygen, energy, and food, alongside interactive mission tasks.

How it addresses the challenge: The project anchors gameplay in real NASA space weather datasets, directly linking critical decisions (such as radiation protection) to actual environmental conditions to ensure scientific traceability and verifiability. It features balanced mechanics that avoid overly safe choices or system overload, requiring genuine trade-offs that mirror real space mission planning.

Why it is important: It bridges the gap between entertainment and education, fostering early interest in STEM and space careers. By incorporating AI-driven mascots, accessibility features, and a second-screen parental control dashboard, the project ensures safety, visibility, and measurable educational impact.
projectDetails.details:
How It Works and What It Does

The Astra Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive educational game where children step into the role of junior astronauts exploring simulated environments like the Moon. The player manages essential life-support resources—such as water, oxygen, energy, and food—while completing mission tasks.

The game is directly anchored in real NASA space weather datasets, linking critical survival decisions (such as radiation protection) to actual environmental conditions. Key features include:

  • An AI-driven interactive mascot that users can customize using a photo.
  • Dynamic environmental hazards, such as dust storms equipped with visual freezing effects and mission timers.
  • A second-screen parental control dashboard that allows supervisors to monitor progress.
  • Visual evolution updates as items and habitats are repaired or upgraded.

Project Benefits

  • High-Quality Screen Time: Transforms low-quality recreational screen time into a productive, engaging educational experience.
  • Balanced Cognitive Load: Avoids overwhelming young players by focusing on four essential resources (oxygen, energy, food and water) rather than complex, cluttered systems.
  • Non-Punitive Replayability: Utilizes variable mechanics and events between playthroughs to encourage children to learn from failure without feeling discouraged.
  • Accessibility and Safety: Features built-in accessibility options and a parental control system to ensure a secure, inclusive environment.

Intended Impact

The primary goal of the project is to ignite early interest in STEM and space exploration, guided by the vision that "the person who will step on the moon might be taking their first steps in our game". It addresses children's feelings of isolation in digital spaces by providing meaningful, interactive companionship through AI mascots and collaborative tasks, helping shape the next generation of scientifically literate explorers.

Tools and Technologies Used

  • NASA Data & Science Datasets: Utilizes official NASA space weather data and lunar trivia to guarantee scientific traceability and verifiability.
  • Artificial Intelligence (AI): Powers the interactive companion mascot and Face ID personalization features.
  • Development Software: Built using modern web and software frameworks supporting multi-phase level design, timer progress trackers, and second-screen parental dashboards.

Creativity and Innovation

The project stands out by treating content as the primary attraction rather than relying solely on superficial visual polish. Its creative highlights include:

  • Real-World Science Integration: Tying in-game survival choices directly to live, current space weather metrics.
  • Personalized AI Companion: Enabling players to generate a custom mascot using Face ID.
  • Authentic Trade-offs: Eschewing "safe choices" that lack educational depth, ensuring every decision reflects genuine mission planning constraints.

Key Design Factors Considered

  • Simplicity and Focus: Ensuring young players are not overloaded with too many simultaneous systems.
  • Mechanical Precision: Valuing functional, accurate game mechanics over superficial visual effects.
  • Pedagogical Approach: Grounding interactions in positive reinforcement and educational frameworks.
  • Verifiable Transparency: Ensuring prototypes clearly explain which NASA datasets were used and why, making the science fully traceable for judges and educators.

projectDetails.name: S.O.L. — Satellite-Oriented LLM
projectDetails.summary:
Climate volatility, water scarcity, and soil degradation are invalidating traditional farming calendars worldwide. Yet, existing precision agriculture tools require high digital literacy, complex dashboards, and stable broadband — excluding the smallholder and family farmers who need them most.

S.O.L. (Satellite-Oriented LLM) solves this by turning NASA’s Earth observation fleet into a 100% Voice-First field partner. By simply speaking in natural language and local rural units, farmers share their plot size, crop, and main challenge (drought, pests, soil exhaustion, or market prices). S.O.L. fuses data from seven NASA missions (POWER, SMAP, GPM, MODIS, ECOSTRESS, Landsat, and SRTM) with scientific agronomy (FAO/Embrapa), computer vision, and IoT telemetry to deliver clear spoken guidance. It compares three actionable scenario — Current Practice, Regenerative Crop Rotation, and Green Manure/Low-Water Management — 
showing real impacts on water, soil health, cost, and yield, displaying visual charts only when requested by voice.

Designed for offline resilience and omnichannel scale (Web, 2G phone calls, SMS, community radio, and enterprise APIs), S.O.L. democratizes climate adaptation from family farms to large cooperatives.
projectDetails.details:
THE PAIN WE SOLVE
Farmers today fight on two fronts: extreme climate unpredictability (irregular rain, heatwaves, exhausted soils) and digital exclusion. Millions of producers cannot use traditional ag-tech platforms because those tools demand reading fluency, complex registration, and high-speed internet. When a farmer makes a blind decision on planting windows or crop choice, they risk losing their entire livelihood.

WHAT S.O.L. DOES & HOW IT WORKS
S.O.L. (Satellite-Oriented LLM) is an intelligent, 100% Voice-First agricultural advisor that puts orbital intelligence directly into the farmer’s hands through natural conversation.
1. Zero-Friction Voice Dialogue: With a single tap, the farmer talks to S.O.L. as they would to a trusted neighbor — using regional land units (hectares, "alqueires", or square meters) and everyday terms.
2. Multimodal Satellite & Field Fusion: Using geolocation, S.O.L. combines seven NASA Earth Observation datasets (POWER, SMAP, GPM, MODIS, ECOSTRESS, Landsat, and SRTM) with verified agronomic literature (FAO/UN, Embrapa, SciELO), field computer vision (diagnosing crop pests, nutrient deficiencies, and straw cover from a quick photo or video), and local IoT soil/weather sensors.
3. Three Actionable Scenarios: Instead of overwhelming the user with raw data, S.O.L. delivers a clear spoken diagnosis and simulates three practical paths: Current Management, Regenerative Crop Rotation, and Green Manure / Water-Saving Management. For each option, the farmer hears the expected harvest yield alongside Water savings, Soil recovery, and Cost/Simplicity.
4. On-Demand Visuals: Built for bright sunlight and working hands in the field, the screen stays clean and only displays comparative charts when requested by voice.

BENEFITS & INTENDED IMPACT (FROM SMALLHOLDERS TO AGRIBUSINESS)
- Cognitive Adaptation (Personas N1 to N4): S.O.L. automatically adapts its language. It speaks in warm, jargon-free analogies for smallholder farmers without formal schooling (N1/N2), and dynamically shifts to high-precision technical metrics (NDVI, SMAP root-zone moisture, evapotranspiration, ZARC windows) for extension technicians (N3), cooperatives, and corporate agronomists (N4).
- Omnichannel & Offline-First Reach: To ensure no farmer is left behind due to lack of connectivity, S.O.L. scales across an offline-capable Web App (PWA), toll-free 2G voice calls (IVR/URA), USSD menus, SMS alerts, automated daily bulletins for rural community radios, and REST/GraphQL APIs for cooperatives, ERPs, and agricultural insurance.
- Sustainable Social & Environmental Impact: S.O.L. operates on a B2B2C impact model — 100% free for family farmers, sustained by SaaS/API licensing for large agribusinesses, cooperatives, and public extension programs. It directly advances UN SDGs 2 (Zero Hunger), 6 (Clean Water), 13 (Climate Action), and 15 (Life on Land).

HOW OUR PROJECT IS CREATIVE & FACTORS CONSIDERED
- Grounded AI ("Zero Numeric Hallucination"): In farming, a hallucinated number can ruin a harvest. S.O.L. separates reasoning from calculation: every spoken number is strictly grounded in deterministic predictive models and verified before reaching the farmer's ears.
- Biological & Human Safety: S.O.L. prioritizes regenerative soil practices, blocks chemical pesticide dosage prescriptions, and always reinforces collaboration with local agricultural technicians and rural extension services.
- Data Sovereignty & Privacy (LGPD): Sensitive farm coordinates and production histories remain encrypted locally on the farmer’s device (AES-256), while regional crop models improve across harvests using Federated Learning and differential privacy.

TOOLS, SOFTWARE & HARDWARE ECOSYSTEM
- Earth Observation & Science: NASA POWER, SMAP, GPM, MODIS, ECOSTRESS, Landsat, SRTM (geospatial harmonization via STAC, COG, and Zarr), combined with RAG over FAO/UN and Embrapa knowledge bases.
- AI, Voice & Vision: Multi-model LLM routing (Google Gemini, OpenAI, local Ollama with offline fallback), ElevenLabs & Web Speech API for natural voice interaction, and edge-ready Computer Vision.

projectDetails.summary:
NEXUS — From Earth Observation to Action

NEXUS is an interactive institutional platform designed to make complex Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) and Earth observation data easier to understand and use.

The platform aims to transform satellite observations into accessible geographic information through interactive maps, event records, document organization, and activity tracking.

By combining Earth observation data with an AI-powered institutional assistant, NEXUS aims to help organizations interpret potential environmental changes, identify areas that require further investigation, and coordinate their responses.

For example, satellite observations indicating surface water can help civil defense agencies investigate potential flood risks, while agricultural and infrastructure departments can assess possible impacts on crops, roads, and nearby communities.

NEXUS connects satellite data, artificial intelligence, and institutional collaboration to turn complex scientific information into practical insights that can support better decision-making and environmental monitoring.

**Our goal is simple: make Earth observation data more accessible, understandable, and useful for protecting people and our planet.

projectDetails.name: Inspot
projectDetails.summary:
Inspot is a mobile app that helps people anywhere check what they hear about the climate of the place where they live. The user writes what they noticed, for example “it is raining less in my city”. The app turns that sentence into a question, looks for the answer in four public datasets with global or near-global coverage (NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, CHIRPS and ERA5) and calculates the trend in each one. The result is a verdict in plain language, such as “probable decrease”, that shows how many sources agree.

Because the data covers the planet, the same method works for any city. We started with three cities in the interior of Bahia, Brazil, where the app showed that temperature has risen in all of them, while the drop in rainfall people talk about is confirmed by only one source.

This addresses the challenge because the app selects the variables, gets regional data, uses long time series and measures the rate of change with a significance test. NASA data is public and global, but hard to use. Our goal is for students and communities in any country to verify things by themselves instead of repeating what they heard.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

The user starts with an everyday statement. The app identifies the place and the variable, and asks the same question to several datasets. For each dataset we use one value per year and calculate the rate of change per decade (Theil-Sen slope) and its significance (Mann-Kendall test). Then we compare the sources. If two or more confirm the change, there is consensus. If they only point in the same direction, the result is “probable”. If they disagree, the app says so.

We tested it with real data for three cities in Bahia, Brazil, and for twelve points across the region. One example: in Barreiras, one source shows rainfall falling by 42 mm per decade, but the other three do not confirm it. Temperature, on the other hand, rose in all three cities according to both sources we used.

Benefits and impact

In the interior of Bahia, a late or weak rainy season decides what a family plants, how much water a town stores and whether a harvest pays off. People there hear every year that the climate has changed, but they have no way to check it. inspot gives them that way. In a few seconds, anyone can see whether a change is confirmed by several sources, only probable, or not supported by the data at all.

This changes three things. Farmers and local managers can tell a real trend from a bad year before making long-term decisions. Students learn to check a claim with evidence instead of accepting or rejecting it by opinion. And news about the climate can be compared with the record by any reader, which makes exaggeration and denial equally easy to spot.

The impact also reaches NASA. Every question asked and every local report sent shows what people notice on the ground and what they want to know, something satellites cannot measure. Because the datasets cover the planet, the same benefit applies to any city, not only to the ones we tested.

People can understand the result without knowing statistics, and they can see which years were analysed. We also designed a community area for local reports and a field mode where the user photographs what they see.

Learning

inspot is also a place to learn. A detective character guides the student through five short missions, each one built on a real case from the data: why one source is not enough, what a trend is, how to read a line chart, how to check a headline against the record, and how different datasets measure the same thing. In the “climate court”, two AI agents argue for and against a statement using only the calculated numbers, and the student gives the verdict before seeing what the sources say. Every explanation can be read at three levels, from elementary school to university. Students earn badges and a free certificate. We want them to leave knowing how to question a claim about the climate, not only what the answer was.

Tools

Python to download and process the data. HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the prototype. Data: NASA POWER, GPM IMERG and CHIRPS (through ClimateSERV), ERA5 (through Open-Meteo) and NOAA’s ONI index. We used AI assistants such as Claude Code and Codex to support coding and text review. We used Photoshop for the initial asset concepts of the visual identity, and ChatGPT for image generation and video editing.

Creativity

We treat the analysis as an investigation. The user brings the case, the app is the detective and the datasets are the witnesses. Showing when sources disagree, instead of hiding it, is the core of the idea.

What we considered

We do not forecast and we do not assign causes. The verdict is an estimate, not a final answer. We know the sources are not fully independent. Three cities are a start, but the datasets cover the planet, so the same method can be applied anywhere. We have not yet measured the impact with real users; that is the next step.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Echoes
projectDetails.summary:
Echoes is an interactive web platform that lets students explore what NASA has found on Mars and the Moon, including discoveries from before they were even born. It uses real NASA data and images, and it’s simple enough that kids can start exploring with almost no instructions.

Along the way, each discovery is tied to ideas from Physics, Chemistry and Biology. A rover’s tools, the water ice on the Moon or the dust on Mars become a way into the science students already study in class, explained in a light and visual way. Many of these stories come from missions that have ended, like Opportunity, but whose findings still matter. That’s the idea behind the name: when a signal goes quiet, its echoes keep reaching us.

We’re building Echoes so schools, education networks and city governments can use it to bring quality science content to more students and support teachers in the classroom.
projectDetails.details:
Echoes: “Abandoned, but not forgotten.”

What it does and how it works

Echoes is a prototype of an interactive space museum that runs in the browser. It’s made for kids between 8 and 13, ideally explored with a teacher or another adult nearby, and we’re building it so schools and city education programs can use it too. We made it for the challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten: NASA’s Discarded Equipment Storytelling.”

The main story is about Opportunity, the Mars rover that was supposed to work for 90 days and ended up exploring Mars for more than 14 years. Visitors start in a 3D Solar System, pick a world, and scroll through the story. They see the original mission plan, a real NASA map of the rover’s final route, and an official 3D model they can poke at, including a “teardown” view where kids can look at the rover’s parts. Four short chapters tell what the mission was, what it found, and how it ended. We also show the real, incomplete image Opportunity sent back at the end, and then a short quiz and a final screen about what the rover left behind.

There’s a second journey on the Moon, with Apollo 11, the lunar exosphere, regolith, water ice and Artemis. And because not every school computer can handle 3D, we also made an Archive Mode: a plain, linear, text version that works without WebGL or animations.

Benefits

Most space content for kids ends up as a pile of facts. We wanted the images, maps and 3D models to work together as one story, so kids can see the evidence behind what they’re reading.

We also built it thinking about who actually gets to use it. It works with a keyboard, has captions, respects reduced-motion settings, offers optional narration, adapts to phones, and comes in Portuguese and English. Nothing essential depends on sound or 3D, and it runs in a browser with no installation, which matters for public-school computer labs. The story, the quiz and the Archive Mode also leave natural pauses where a teacher can stop and talk with the class.

Finally, you can always see where things come from. Every important image, model, map and fact shows its source, and we mark what is real NASA material and what is an artistic reconstruction. We chose not to present Opportunity’s last transmission as a “final message” or to invent a farewell for it.

Intended impact

We want kids to understand that a mission doesn’t stop mattering when its signal goes quiet. We’d like them to leave knowing not just what Opportunity did, but what it discovered and what it left for everyone.

Beyond that, we hope Echoes sparks interest in space and engineering, helps build the habit of looking at evidence, and makes NASA’s public archives feel closer to public-school students. For schools and city governments, we want it to be a low-cost, ready-to-use tool that supports teachers rather than replacing them. And since the format isn’t tied to one rover, it could be reused for other retired missions. Because Echoes is still a prototype, our next step is to test it in real classrooms.

Tools

We built it as a responsive web app with React 19, TypeScript, HTML and CSS, using Vite for builds. The 3D parts run on Three.js with React Three Fiber and Drei, animations use Motion, and Zustand handles the app’s state. We tested with Vitest, React Testing Library, Playwright and axe-core, and used the browser’s SpeechSynthesis for narration. The content comes from official NASA/JPL-Caltech resources: the Opportunity 3D model, the Mars texture, the final traverse map, mission photos and historical data. We also used Codex as an AI tool to help with development and quality checks.

How is the project creative?

An echo is what’s left after a sound stops. When Opportunity went silent, its echoes kept reaching us as discoveries and data that still shape how we understand Mars. That’s where the name comes from, and it’s the idea behind the whole project.

Instead of treating a retired rover as a list of facts, we treat it as a character with a journey, from a 90-day plan to more than 14 years on Mars. We tell the ending with the real incomplete image instead of an invented goodbye, because we think that honesty is part of the story.

What our team considered

We thought about who would use it: kids of 8 to 13, usually with an adult, in schools that may not have powerful computers. That’s why we focused on accessibility, a no-3D fallback and no installation. We also cared about scientific honesty, so we kept real and reconstructed material clearly separate, and about making the format easy to extend to other missions. We tested the code and accessibility as we went, and we were open about using AI tools.

projectDetails.name: SEDE – The Invisible Thirst of the Atmosphere
projectDetails.summary: Be An Earth System Trend Detective! Wildfire response is still mostly reactive: resources move after ignition. SEDE ("thirst" in Portuguese) moves the decision before the fire. Using NASA Earth-observation data, it computes Vapor Pressure Deficit (VPD), the measure of how thirsty the atmosphere is and how fast it pulls water from soil and plants, to flag vegetation that is drying into fuel. A retrospective module links past VPD patterns to past ignitions, and a predictive module projects short- and medium-term VPD trends to map rising desiccation risk. The method works in any biome, from the Brazilian Cerrado to temperate forests. It matters because wildfires drive smoke-related health risks, biodiversity loss and food and commodity price volatility. An alert before the fire lets civil defense, brigades and environmental agencies place prevention resources where they matter most.
projectDetails.details: How it works: air temperature and relative humidity give VPD (VPD = es − ea; es = 0.6108·exp[17.27·T/(T+237.3)] kPa; ea = es·RH/100). SEDE adds evapotranspiration and vegetation context and compares each region with its own history. Retrospective module: identifies the climate patterns and exact conditions that preceded past ignitions. Predictive module: projects short- and medium-term VPD trends to map desiccation risk before fires appear. Output: a ranked list of critical regions with VPD level, trend and alert level (Critical, Attention, Monitored). Benefits: lead time for prevention, a region-agnostic method, and an accessible tool for civil defense, fire brigades, environmental managers, government agencies and researchers. Tools: NASA data, an interactive project page (HTML/CSS/JavaScript) and a concept interface prototype.

projectDetails.name: AstroByte
projectDetails.summary:
AstroByte bridges the gap between complex NASA data and the public by transforming technical information into accessible, engaging experiences directly on smartphones. The project offers a two-pronged approach:
 Augmented Reality (AR) Platform: A browser-based platform featuring 10 animated AR experiences, allowing users to explore concepts from the SPHEREx mission to the hypothetical Planet X.

 Space Race Educational Game: A browser-based game where players dodge asteroids and collect real stars, integrating factual information into gameplay.

How it Works (Technical Prototype)
AstroByte utilizes real NASA images and data. Python scripts generate animated 3D models incorporating NASA textures, the Tycho star map, and Kepler's laws of planetary motion. The AR experiences run directly in the mobile browser (Android and iPhone) using WebXR and AR Quick Look, supporting glTF and USDZ file formats, eliminating the need to install a dedicated app.

Key Differentiators
  Accessibility: Functions entirely within the mobile browser (iOS and Android) without requiring app installation.
 Real-time Data: Leverages real-time data from NASA.
  Educational Impact: Delivers accessible and educational content designed for all levels, combining technical accuracy with gamification.
projectDetails.details:
The Problem We Are Solving

The SPHEREx telescope is designed to photograph the entire sky every six months, cataloging over a billion objects and tracking how the cosmos changes over time. However, this massive amount of technical data is difficult to translate into accessible formats that can reach classrooms and the general public. For many students, the universe remains an abstract concept; they may dream of being astronauts, but they have never looked through a physical telescope.

Furthermore, educational gaps remain a significant hurdle. In Brazil, for example, students scored an average of 403 points in science on the 2022 PISA test, falling short of the OECD average of 485. Yet, there are more active smartphones in the country than inhabitants. Our goal was to bridge this gap by transforming the device already in students' hands into a powerful window to the universe.

Our Solution: AstroByte

AstroByte is a web-based educational platform that brings complex astronomical data to life through gamification and Augmented Reality (AR). We designed the platform to be entirely accessible directly from mobile browsers, requiring zero app installations. The project is divided into two core experiences:

* Augmented Reality (AR) Platform: We created 10 fully animated AR experiences. Users can project 3D models into their own physical space—exploring the SPHEREx telescope, comparing the sizes of planets, and visualizing the hypothetical orbit of Planet X.

* "Space Race" Browser Game: An interactive 2D pixel-art game where players control an astronaut, dodge asteroids, and collect "cards" containing factual information about real stars and space missions.

Technical Implementation

AstroByte was built with accessibility and scientific accuracy in mind:

* Data Processing & Modeling: We used Python to generate and animate 3D models based on real NASA images and data. Planetary movements in our models are accurately simulated using Kepler's laws of planetary motion, meaning the passage of time reflects real physics.

* Web-Native AR: To ensure cross-platform compatibility, we exported our 3D models in both glTF (for Android) and USDZ (for iPhone) formats.

* Seamless Integration: By utilizing WebXR and AR Quick Look technologies, the browser securely opens the device's camera without forcing the user to download a heavy application.

Use of Space Agency Data

AstroByte relies heavily on real astronomical data to ensure an educational experience. Our 3D models use authentic NASA textures, and our starry backgrounds are generated using the Tycho star map. The core narrative and educational content are directly inspired by the SPHEREx mission parameters (mapping the sky in 102 infrared colors every six months) and the search for Planet X.

Impact and Differentiators

AstroByte stands out because it removes the friction of traditional educational software. It works instantly on Android and iPhone browsers and uses real-time NASA data to unite technical research with gamified learning. Designed for students, researchers, and space enthusiasts of all levels, AstroByte proves that you don't need an observatory to explore the stars—the universe can fit right in the palm of your hand.

projectDetails.name: MFIEC-AI: Effective Contribution Analysis for Complex Systems
projectDetails.summary:
MFIEC-AI is an experimental research framework designed to investigate adaptation, resilience, recovery, and structural reorganization in complex systems.

The project explores how variables contribute to system adaptation beyond traditional correlation-based analysis. Instead of focusing only on statistical relationships, MFIEC-AI analyzes dynamic state transitions, temporal continuity, and reorganization processes to identify potential effective contributors to change.

For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, the framework is applied to astronaut health monitoring, where adaptation, recovery, and stability are critical in long-duration space missions.

The project aims to provide a complementary analytical perspective for understanding how complex systems maintain functionality, recover from disturbances, and adapt under changing conditions.
projectDetails.details:
MFIEC-AI is an experimental framework designed to investigate adaptation, resilience, recovery, and structural reorganization in complex systems.

The project introduces the concept of Effective Contribution Analysis, which seeks to distinguish variables that may actively contribute to adaptation and recovery from variables that merely exhibit statistical correlation with observed outcomes.

The framework combines dynamic state representation, temporal monitoring, reorganization analysis, and Effective Contribution Assessment (ECM). Instead of analyzing isolated observations, MFIEC-AI evaluates how system states evolve over time and how specific factors participate in transitions associated with stability, recovery, and adaptation.

As a proof of concept, the project uses computational models, Python-based analytical pipelines, and publicly available scientific datasets. The initial application focuses on astronaut health monitoring and adaptation during long-duration space missions.

The expected impact is to provide a complementary analytical perspective for studying complex systems in aerospace, environmental science, and technology. The project emphasizes dynamic behavior, temporal continuity, and adaptive processes, offering a framework that may support future research on resilience and system stability under changing conditions.

projectDetails.name: Project IBI
projectDetails.summary: IBI is an integrated technological solution designed to address agricultural challenges related to climate change, crop losses, and food waste. The project was developed in response to the difficulties many farmers face in anticipating changes in soil and climate conditions, identifying risks to their crops, and planning their production.
projectDetails.details:
IBI — Intelligence for More Resilient Agriculture

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

IBI is an integrated technological solution designed to address agricultural challenges related to climate change, crop losses, and food waste. The project was developed in response to the difficulties many farmers face in anticipating changes in soil and climate conditions, identifying risks to their crops, and planning their production.

IBI works by combining a physical device installed directly in the soil with environmental information obtained from satellite data. The device monitors soil conditions in real time, while satellite data provides additional information about the surrounding environment, such as rainfall, temperature, evapotranspiration, and vegetation development.

By collecting and analyzing these different sources of information, IBI aims to identify changes and potential risks, transforming technical data into simple alerts and guidance through an accessible application for farmers.

For example, in a corn plantation, the device may detect a decrease in soil moisture while satellite data indicates high temperatures and low rainfall in the region. By combining these observations, the system can alert the farmer to potentially unfavorable conditions, helping them evaluate and adopt preventive measures before further damage occurs.

In addition to monitoring agricultural conditions, IBI aims to support harvest forecasting. By analyzing soil, environmental, and vegetation data, the system seeks to help farmers estimate their production, identify potential surpluses, and plan their harvest more efficiently.

2. What benefits does it offer?

IBI offers several potential benefits:

- Preventive agricultural management: Helps farmers identify potential risks earlier and make more informed decisions.

- Improved production planning: Supports estimates of agricultural production and helps identify possible variations and surpluses.

- Reduced food waste: Encourages better planning for the use and distribution of surplus food, including potential partnerships with schools and NGOs.

- Accessible information: Transforms complex scientific and environmental data into simple, understandable alerts.

- More efficient use of resources: Supports decisions that may help reduce losses associated with unfavorable soil and climate conditions.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

IBI aims to contribute to a more resilient, sustainable, and socially responsible agricultural system.

Its intended impact goes beyond helping farmers monitor their crops. By supporting preventive decisions and better harvest planning, the project seeks to reduce agricultural losses, minimize food waste, and encourage the more efficient use of natural and productive resources.

The project also has a social dimension: by identifying potential food surpluses and creating opportunities for connections between producers and institutions such as schools and NGOs, IBI seeks to contribute to a more efficient food distribution system and improve access to food.

Another important objective is to democratize access to scientific information, making technological resources more accessible to small and medium-sized farmers.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software were used?

During the development and planning of the project, our team used digital tools to support research, idea development, content creation, and the presentation of the solution.

The tools used included:

- ChatGPT: Used to support research, organize ideas, develop the project description, and explore possible solutions.

- Claude: Used as an additional artificial intelligence tool to support analysis and idea development.

- Canva: Used to create and design the project's visual presentation and materials.

- Gemini: Used to assist with research, information organization, and project development.

The proposed hardware consists of a physical soil-monitoring device designed to collect real-time information about soil conditions. The project also incorporates satellite data sources, including NASA datasets, to complement the measurements collected by the device.

The software component is an application designed to present the collected and analyzed information through an accessible interface.

5. What is the creative aspect of the project?

The creative aspect of IBI lies in integrating physical soil monitoring, satellite data, agricultural analysis, and food waste reduction into a single solution.

Rather than relying exclusively on satellite information or creating another standalone agricultural application, IBI combines direct measurements from a device installed in the soil with broader environmental data. This integration aims to provide a more comprehensive understanding of agricultural conditions.

Another distinctive aspect is connecting agricultural monitoring with harvest planning and the potential distribution of surplus food. In this way, the project brings together technological innovation, environmental sustainability, and social responsibility.

6. What factors did the team consider?

In developing IBI, our team considered several important factors:

- Climate variability: The effects of phenomena such as El Niño on rainfall, temperature, soil moisture, and agricultural productivity.

- Farmers' needs: The importance of providing useful information in a simple and accessible format, especially for small and medium-sized producers.

- Technical feasibility: The integration of physical monitoring equipment with satellite data and an accessible software interface.

- Data accessibility: The use of scientific and environmental information that can support agricultural analysis and decision-making.

- Economic viability: The importance of developing a solution that can be practical and useful in the daily lives of farmers.

- Environmental and social impact: The potential to reduce agricultural losses, prevent food waste, and encourage the distribution of surplus food to institutions in need.

Our purpose

With IBI, we aim to turn information into prevention, technology into opportunities, and agricultural production into social impact.

Because producing better is not enough: we must be prepared for climate challenges, reduce losses in the field, and help ensure that the food produced reaches those who need it.

projectDetails.name: Project OPP Team
projectDetails.summary:
BRASA (Bahia's Fire Calendar) answers NASA's 2026 challenge, Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots, by turning two incompatible satellite fire-detection records into one honest, decision-ready history for Bahia's 417 municipalities.

MODIS and VIIRS detect wildfires at different pixel resolutions (1 km vs 375 m), so VIIRS registers up to 4x more detections for the same fire. Simply adding the sensors together creates a false jump in activity exactly when VIIRS launched. BRASA calibrates a monthly conversion factor from their overlap period (2012-2021) and builds a single harmonized series, in equivalent-MODIS detections, from 2003 to today.

The web app lets technicians, fire brigades, and researchers select any municipality, see its weekly fire calendar against a 23-year historical baseline, compare raw MODIS/VIIRS records side by side, and export the filtered data as CSV with full source and sensor provenance.

Every number states its source, sensor, and limitation: detections are not burned area, and the current year's data is preliminary.
projectDetails.details:
How it works: BRASA ingests raw NASA FIRMS hotspot detections (MODIS C6.1 and VIIRS C2, from Terra/Aqua, S-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21) and IBGE's municipal boundaries for Bahia. A Python pipeline (pandas, GeoPandas, PyArrow) filters detections to vegetation fires inside Bahia, aggregates them daily by municipality and by a 0.1° grid cell, then harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS into a single "equivalent-MODIS" series using a monthly calibration factor, fitted on the 2012-2021 overlap period and validated with leave-one-year-out cross-validation (mean annual error 2.2%). The output is static JSON served to a React + TypeScript + Vite front end.

The interface (a MapLibre GL JS map of all 417 municipalities, weekly and monthly calendars, an annual series with uncertainty bands, and a MODIS-vs-VIIRS comparison with an experimental harmonization toggle) lets anyone pick a place and period, see whether current activity is above or below the 23-year normal, read the critical fire window for that place, and export the exact filtered rows as CSV.

Benefits: municipal environmental technicians and fire brigades get a clear, sourced answer to "is this unusual?" instead of raw satellite noise, without needing to know anything about sensor physics. Every claim links back to its source, sensor, and stated limitation.

Creativity: BRASA's core contribution is the harmonization itself — converting two physically different sensors (1 km vs 375 m pixels, ~4x detection-count gap) into one continuous, honest timeline, including a measured correction for MODIS orbital drift after Terra and Aqua ran out of station-keeping fuel.

Tools: Python (pandas, GeoPandas, PyArrow, NumPy), React, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, deployed as a static site on Vercel.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

projectDetails.name: Project ISIS
projectDetails.summary:
Developed for deep space exploration, ISIS (Integração de Softwares de Indicadores de Saúde) is a 100% offline assistive executive support ecosystem. It addresses the severe challenges of astronaut isolation, communication delays of up to 20 minutes, chronic sleep deprivation, and cognitive overload by integrating advanced health hardware (Bio-Monitor, MicroPREP, Tempus Pro) with environmental computer vision and the local ISIS IA neuro-specialist chatbot.

To overcome decision paralysis and operational stress, ISIS uses a strict cognitive load filter aligned with W3C COGA guidelines, delivering one primary action per screen, alongside an automated Manchester-protocol triage system. Furthermore, its neuroscience-based anti-punishment architecture rewards honest symptom reporting and utilizes flexible streaks to prevent anxiety and symptom concealment.   

This project is vital because it guarantees absolute operational autonomy for crews beyond Earth, protecting mental and physical health, preventing performance degradation, and safeguarding mission success in extreme deep-space environments.
projectDetails.details:
ISIS (Integration of Health Indicators Software) is a 100% offline executive support ecosystem developed for deep space missions, such as crewed journeys to Mars. The solution was designed to mitigate the critical impacts of isolation, communication delays of up to 20 minutes with Earth, sleep deprivation, and decision collapse.

The fundamental pillars of the solution include:

  • Integrated Technological Ecosystem: Combines continuous telemetry from advanced aerospace hardware (such as the Bio-Monitor and MicroPREP), environmental computer vision for passive monitoring, and the ISIS AI chatbot operating in an isolated local core.
  • Cognitive Load Filter (W3C COGA): Adapts to crew fatigue and stress by displaying only one primary action per screen, while automated clinical triage (Manchester Protocol) immediately forwards critical alerts to the onboard medical officer, reinforcing that artificial intelligence acts strictly as support and never replaces human clinical judgment.
  • Neuroscience-Based Anti-Punishment Architecture: Encourages continuous adherence by rewarding the act of logging (where reporting a negative state scores the same as well-being to prevent symptom concealment) and replacing punitive metrics with self-care constellations and evolving 3D avatars.
  • Impact and Autonomy: Guarantees crew operational sovereignty in extreme environments, enables prolonged stays with total safety, and generates valuable terrestrial spin-offs for isolated bases and support for neurodivergent individuals.

projectDetails.name: Ciclus
projectDetails.summary: Ciclus is a revolutionary decision-making tool built to support millions of small and medium farmers. It delivers tailored crop rotation plans and future scenarios, empowering producers to adapt proactively to evolving climate challenges and market uncertainties.
projectDetails.details:
• What it does and how it works: Ciclus is an intelligent decision-support system designed for farmers, built upon a robust 30-year historical series of Earth observation data collected by NASA satellites (such as NASA POWER, GPM, and SMAP), combined with agricultural research, climate variability models, and market intelligence. It works by translating complex satellite telemetry and soil properties (such as data from SoilGrids) into practical, intelligible insights. The system features a temporal timeline simulation ("time travel") where users input their location, farm area, and soil type to receive a customized 1-to-5-year crop rotation plan. It is guided by a friendly AI assistant personified by our mascot, "Raul", which translates technical data into simple, accessible language for everyday producers.
  • What are the benefits of this: The core benefit is providing small and medium-scale farmers with clear, actionable guidance on crop rotation (such as alternating cash crops with soil-regenerating cover crops like Urochloa or legumes) to enhance soil health, retain moisture during dry spells, and prevent erosion. Unlike conventional platforms that only focus on future risks, Ciclus empowers producers with a concrete understanding of how past management decisions impacted their land, optimizing both biological resilience and economic stability.
  • What is the intended impact of the project: The intended impact is to scale support for millions of small and medium producers who historically lack technical expertise and financial resources to navigate unpredictable climate shifts and market volatility. By offering this guidance for free and making physical kits accessible via logistics channels like Mercado Livre, Ciclus aims to secure long-term food security, climate resilience, and financial sustainability for vulnerable agricultural communities in regions like the Brazilian Cerrado.
  • What tools, programming languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project: The platform was built utilizing Claude Code as the core development environment, powered by VS Code as the software engine. The application architecture integrates front-end and back-end development using Java and React, coupled with geospatial APIs and datasets including NASA POWER, SoilGrids (ISRIC), FAO EcoCrop, CONAB, and IBGE (SIDRA).
  • How your project is creative: Ciclus’s creative peak lies in its "time travel" feature. While existing tools (such as ZARC or Broto) only evaluate immediate future sowing risks, and others (like ABC-MAP) focus exclusively on long-term projections, Ciclus uniquely allows producers to look backward into concrete historical data and ask: "What if I had planted crop X instead?". By pairing retrospective counterfactual analysis with forward-looking 1-to-5-year rotation scenarios and an engaging agricultural mascot ("Raul"), the tool turns abstract climate data into an intuitive, storytelling-driven experience.
  • What factors your team considered: The team carefully balanced high scientific rigor with extreme practical usability. We considered the socioeconomic constraints and limited technological resources of our target audience (small/medium farmers), ensuring the interface remains intuitive and leigo-friendly (layman-friendly). Furthermore, we factored in local agronomic realities (such as the vulnerability of Cerrado soils to dry spells and erosion), combining environmental sustainability, economic viability, and regional crop compatibility (using Embrapa guidelines) into a single cohesive solution.
