projectDetails.name: Project Salus
projectDetails.summary:
Project Salus is a health monitoring platform designed to help protect astronauts on long-duration space missions, where distance from Earth makes reactive care too slow.

We developed a web application (FastAPI, PostgreSQL and React) that brings together each astronaut’s physiological data (heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, temperature, sleep, fatigue and mood), medical history, medications and pre-flight baselines. Each crew member is compared with their own baseline rather than a population average. Versioned clinical rules generate alerts that the medical team reviews. We also integrated NASA’s DONKI API to track solar flares, coronal mass ejections and solar energetic particle events, linking them to mission timelines and radiation exposure records.

Our approach is predictive: by combining mission profile, crew health and space environment data, Project Salus is designed to learn from every mission and anticipate risks before they become emergencies, giving health professionals time to act. AI supports decisions; it never replaces the medical team.

Project Salus: predict to protect.
projectDetails.details:
Project Salus is a health monitoring platform for astronauts on long-duration missions. It brings together, in one place, each crew member’s physiological data, mental health indicators, medical history, the mission context and space weather events. The goal is to help health professionals spot risks early instead of reacting after a problem appears.

The current prototype includes:

  • Crew and mission management, with role-based access for astronauts, flight surgeons and mission administrators.
  • Health observations for 12 indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, level of consciousness, sleep duration and quality, fatigue, mood, attention and blood glucose. They are shown on an interactive 3D body map and in charts over time.
  • Personal baselines: each astronaut’s readings are compared with their own pre-mission reference, not only with population averages.
  • Deterministic, versioned alert rules that classify readings as caution or critical. Alerts have a full lifecycle (active, acknowledged, resolved) with an audit trail, and critical alerts notify the medical team.
  • Pre-flight screening, medications, allergies and nutrition records.
  • A space weather module that imports solar flares, coronal mass ejections and solar energetic particle events from NASA’s DONKI API, links them into cause-and-effect chains, and relates them to mission timelines. It also includes data models for crew activity (inside the spacecraft, spacewalk or storm shelter), radiation dose records, exposure limits and a 48-hour follow-up after solar particle events, based on NASA’s Human Research Program evidence.
  • A prototype AI assistant that turns free-text symptom reports into structured assessments, grounded in a curated knowledge base of NASA sources.

Benefits

  • Physical, mental, environmental and space weather data in a single view, instead of separate systems.
  • Alerts tailored to each astronaut through personal baselines.
  • Transparent, versioned rules: every alert can be traced to the rule and data that triggered it.
  • Clinical decisions stay with health professionals. The system supports them and never diagnoses.

Intended impact

As missions go farther from Earth, communication delays grow and ground support becomes more limited. Project Salus aims to move astronaut health care from reactive to preventive. The next step is a predictive layer that combines mission profile (destination, duration, phase), crew health trends and space environment data to anticipate risk periods and alert professionals in advance. The system is designed to learn from every mission, so its alerts become more accurate over time and more risks can be prevented.

Tools and technologies

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, SQLModel, Alembic and PostgreSQL.
  • Frontend: React 19, Vite, TypeScript, Recharts for charts, Three.js for the 3D body map, and Lucide icons.
  • Infrastructure: Docker Compose.
  • Testing: pytest and Playwright.
  • Scientific basis: NASA Human Research Program materials, including Human Health and Performance Risks of Space Exploration Missions (NASA SP-2009-3405).
  • AI: an OpenAI-compatible model provider for the assessment prototype. Claude (Anthropic) assisted with development, research and video production.
  • Hardware: It runs on any computer with Docker and Ollama (or any other local AI).

Creativity

Most health dashboards show vital signs in isolation. Project Salus treats the astronaut’s health in context. For example, a solar flare is shown as a precursor and a solar particle event as an exposure risk, following NASA’s own classification. A spacewalk during such an event raises the level of attention. Our goal is to bring the same idea behind recommendation algorithms (learning from past patterns to anticipate what comes next) to astronaut health. Instead of recommending content, the system recommends attention.

Factors our team considered

  • Scientific grounding: features were mapped to risks documented by NASA’s Human Research Program.
  • Safety and responsibility: the system does not diagnose, rules are explainable, and the medical team makes every decision.
  • Privacy: role-based access and audit logs for every action on health data.
  • Real-world constraints: limited communication far from Earth, a small number of past missions, and the need to compare each person with their own baseline.
  • Honesty about data: the prototype uses fictitious demonstration data, clearly labeled, and keeps simulated data separate from real data.
  • Licensing: we chose free, validated instruments and avoided licensed questionnaires.

projectDetails.name: Project Xandar
projectDetails.summary:
Desenvolvido pela equipe Xandar para o desafio Dancing with the SARs do NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, o projeto consiste em uma plataforma de inteligência preditiva de riscos geológicos e hidrológicos alimentada pelos dados em Banda L do satélite NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar).

A solução aborda o desafio ao utilizar interferometria diferencial (InSAR)—aproveitando a capacidade da Banda L de penetrar nuvens espessas e vegetação densa a cada 12 dias—para detectar deformações milimétricas no solo e em encostas antes de rupturas catastróficas, substituindo sistemas reativos de última hora por janelas de evacuação planejada.

Isso é fundamental porque, como demonstrado no colapso glacial de Rasuwa (Nepal), desastres geram prejuízos bilionários e perda de vidas quando há falha de alerta precoce. A plataforma comprova que investir em prevenção orbital reduz custos de reconstrução, blinda o Estado contra a responsabilidade civil por omissão e preserva vidas humanas.
projectDetails.details:
DANÇANDO COM OS SARS (XANDAR)

Detalhes do projeto

O QUE FAZ E COMO FUNÇÃO

Dançando com os SARs é uma aplicação web interativa que transforma observações do radar NISAR em uma forma acessível de explorar mudanças na superfídia da Terra. Desenvolvido para o NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, o painel organiza locais monitorados, imagens de radar de diferentes dados e informações sobre áreas estudadas. A pessoa usuária pode explorar casos, comparar observações e acompanhar explicações visuais. Entre os recursos estão o globo interativo, comparações de cenas e uma visualização 3D do relevo de Langtang, no Nepal.

O radar SAR é um sensor ativo: emite micro-ondas e registra a energia que retorna da superfície. Pode colecionar dados de dia ou de noite e atrair novos. Suas imagens respondem a fatores como rugosidade, unidade e geometria da superfície; portanto, não são fotografias comuns. Legendas e contexto ajudam a interpretar como cenas, e a aplicação informa quando a cobertura é parcial.

BENEFICIÁRIOS

• Facilita a compreensão de dados de radar para pessoas sem formação especializada.

• Reúne imagens, dados, contexto geográfico e explicações em uma experiência interativa.

• Ajuda a comparar observações e explorar possíveis mudanças ambientais e geográficas.

• Explicações limitadas para evitar que uma imagem isolada seja tratada como prova conclusiva.

• Pode aprender educação, comunicação científica e exploração inicial por pesquisadores, gestos e público interessado.

IMPACTO PRETENDIDO

O projeto busca aproximar dados de observação da Terra das comunidades que podem se beneficiar deles, apoiando a compreensão de fenômenos como deformação do terreno, deslizações, subsídios e mudanças ambientais. Pretende facilitar a comunicação de evidências e incentivar o uso responsável de dados de radar em investigações futuras.

Como visualizações são ferramentas de exploração e comunicação. Não comprovam, por si só, a causa de uma mudança, não são um sistema de alerta e não prevemos desastres. O deslocamento observado pelo radar pode corresponder à linha de visão do sensor, não necessariamente ao movimento vertical. Conclusões exigem contexto, validação e fontes complementares.

FERRAMENTAS, LINGUAGENS E SOFTWARE

• Linguagens: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, CSS e Python em scripts de preparação.

• Interface: React 18 e React Router.

• Visualização 3D: Three.js.

• Estilo e componentes: CSS, Tailwind CSS, Radix UI e componentes anteriores.

• Desenvolvimento: Vite, Node.js e npm.

• Qualidade: ESLint, TypeScript, Vitest e Testing Library.

• Dados: arquivos JSON, cenas SAR preparadas anteriormente e Copernicus DEM GLO-30 para o alívio de Langtang.

• Hardware: computador para desenvolvimento e dispositivo com navegador para acessar a aplicação; não é necessário hardware especializado.

CRIATIVIDADE

O projeto combina dados científicos com narrativa visual para mais como observações feitas em dados diferentes a julgar a contar uma história sobre a superficie terrestre. O caso de Langtang, no Nepal, destaca a comparação temporal em torno do evento documentado em 26 de agosto de 2026. Cenas de radar e relevo 3D situam a área, enquanto o globo conecta diferentes locais monitorados.

A proposta fez uma tecnologia muito familiar em comparações, lendas e controles que convidam à exploração sem transformar os dados de radar em uma fotografia ou afirmar mais do que eles permitem concluir.

FATORES CONSIDERADOS PELA EQUIPE

• Clareza: explique conceitos de radar em linguagem acessível.

• Rigor científico: separar observação, interpretação e hipótese e evitar alegações causais sem evidências.

• Transparência: indicar dados, cobertura, fontes e limitações.

• Contexto: relacional como cenas ao relevo e à história do local.

• Usabilidade: criar uma interface navegável para diferentes números de familiaridade técnica.

• Desempenho e disponibilidade: preparar dados previamente para evitar processamento pesado e dependência de serviços externos durante o uso.

• Responsabilidade: comunicar que o painel apoia a exploração, mas não substitui validação científica ou sistemas oficiais de alerta.

projectDetails.name: Project 14hrsamoeba
projectDetails.summary:
# Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an educational space-exploration simulation designed to introduce students, especially those aged 8–14, to the challenges of living and working beyond Earth.
The project allows users to explore the concept of establishing a research outpost on the Moon or Mars and understand the importance of resources, infrastructure, and survival systems in space.
### Problem Statement
Space exploration involves complex challenges such as limited water, oxygen and energy, extreme environmental conditions, and the need for safe habitats. These concepts can be difficult for young learners to understand through textbooks alone.
### Proposed Solution
The project presents these challenges through an interactive, game-inspired mission experience. Users are introduced to planetary environments, mission briefings, resource management concepts, and the infrastructure needed to support a future space outpost.
### Key Features in the Current Prototype- Moon and Mars mission concepts.- Mission briefing interface.- 3D planetary environment.- Space-outpost construction concepts.- Resource indicators for oxygen, water, food, and energy.- Camera viewing options.

Current Development Status
This is an early-stage working prototype. The main interface and initial simulation elements have been developed. Some navigation, interaction, and gameplay features remain incomplete and require further development and testing.

I reviewed the suggestions and adapted them to my project requirements. AI tools were used as development assistance, while the project idea, feature selection, and final decisions were guided by my own understanding and objectives.

projectDetails.name: MV-Sat: Harmonized MODIS-VIIRS Satellite Fire Detection System
projectDetails.summary: MV-Sat harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS satellite data to create a continuous, sensor-agnostic record of wildfire activity from 2001 to 2025 for Canada and the US. By correcting the 6x detection bias between the two sensors, we provide a seamless timeline for emergency responders and scientists. The interactive web application features an interactive satellite hotspot map, a GitHub-style burning activity calendar, and anomaly charts comparing current data against multi-year averages. This tool empowers users to analyze historical fire patterns, track critical deviations, and make data-driven decisions for fire management.
projectDetails.details:
What it does: MV-Sat is a web application that visualizes harmonized historical wildfire data for Canada and the US (2001-2025). It features an interactive satellite map, a GitHub-style contribution calendar for fire intensity, and an analytics dashboard that charts historical anomalies against the 25-year average.
Intended Impact: This tool enables emergency managers, scientists, and land managers to understand long-term fire trends, identify unusually severe fire seasons, and use historical context to prepare for current and future wildfire threats.
Tools & Languages: Python, Streamlit, Pandas, Plotly, Folium, PyArrow, NumPy, Docker, GitHub.
Creativity: We successfully solved the sensor bias between MODIS (1km) and VIIRS (375m) by calculating an overlap ratio (6.00) and applying a bias correction to the historical data. The UI was designed with a custom glassmorphism aesthetic and an accessible color ramp.

projectDetails.name: PROJECT PYROS
projectDetails.summary:
PROJECT PYROS (Predictive Yield & Risk in Orbital Spacefire) is an SI-powered, web-based dashboard and 3D WebGL simulation platform that transforms NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion database into actionable fire safety intelligence for human space exploration.

The platform summarizes, ranks, and interprets all 22 relevant PSI combustion investigations — spanning gaseous (ACME/BRE, E-FIELD, CFI-G), liquid (FLEX, FLEX-2, CFI), solid (BASS, BASS-II, Saffire I–III), and aerosol (SAME, SAME-R, DAFT, DAFT-2) experiments — across four interactive 3D environments: an ISS orbital laboratory, an Artemis lunar base, a Martian pressurized rover, and a Mars surface outpost. Users can explore investigation dossiers, compare experimental variables side-by-side, and trace hardware lineages (CIR → ACME/MDCA, MSG → SPICE duct, SAME → DAFT instrument repurposing).

Because no partial-gravity combustion data yet exists in PSI, PROJECT PYROS implements deterministic physics bounding - Roper flame-height scaling, Grash of convection velocity, and Dalton oxygen partial-pressure laws — to extrapolate flammability between 0g (ISS) and 1g (Earth) for lunar (0.166g, 34% O₂, 10.2 psi) and Martian (0.38g) regimes. The platform also highlights terrestrial spinoffs including fine-water-mist extinguishers, dual-wavelength smoke detectors, and firefighter protective gear derived directly from spaceflight research.
projectDetails.details:
What does our project do?

When we first looked at NASA's PSI combustion database, we understood the challenge immediately — there's an incredible wealth of microgravity fire research spanning two decades, but it's scattered across dozens of investigations, different hardware platforms, and varying test conditions. A researcher trying to figure out "what happens if a fire starts inside an Artemis lunar habitat?" would have to manually dig through experiments that used completely different fuels, sensors, and atmospheric setups. We wanted to change that.

So we built PROJECT PYROS — a web-based dashboard paired with four immersive 3D simulation environments that take all 22 relevant PSI combustion investigations and make them searchable, comparable, and genuinely understandable.

On the dashboard side, users can browse every investigation with rich detail cards showing what fuels were tested, what shapes and sizes the samples were, what oxygen levels and pressures were used, what sensors captured the data, and what the scientists actually found. You can pull up any two investigations side by side and instantly see what they share, where they differ, and how they connect through shared hardware — like how the same smoke detection instrument from the SAME experiment was later repurposed to measure lunar dust in the DAFT studies. That kind of connection is nearly impossible to spot when you're reading individual papers, but our knowledge graph (which maps 352 relationships between investigations) surfaces it automatically.

The really fun part is the 3D simulations. We built four interactive environments in Three.js that let you actually experience fire behavior in the places astronauts will live and work:

  • Inside the ISS, you can watch a candle flame transform from its normal flickering teardrop shape into the eerie blue sphere that forms in microgravity — and it's not just an animation. There's a real Navier-Stokes fluid solver running on your GPU computing how removing gravity eliminates buoyant convection and forces combustion to rely purely on molecular diffusion. You can adjust the oxygen level, cabin pressure, and airflow speed with sliders and see the flame respond in real time.
  • On the Moon, we modeled an Artemis base camp at Shackleton Crater with habitation modules, solar arrays, and fuel cells. The challenge specifically mentions that the Moon Base will operate at roughly 10.2 psi and 34% oxygen to reduce spacesuit pre-breathing time — so we built that exact atmosphere into the simulation. You can toggle between five viewing modes including a thermal camera view and an emergency power failure scenario.
  • Inside a Mars rover, we recreated the Warm Electronics Box — the sealed avionics bay where a circuit failure could spark a fire under Martian partial gravity (0.38g). A guided 7-stage timeline walks you through how thermal overstress leads to micro-arcing, then polymer ignition, and finally autonomous safe mode shutdown.
  • On the Martian surface, you can trigger an emergency hypoxic venting protocol — dumping the habitat's breathable atmosphere into Mars's near-vacuum (0.13% oxygen) and watching the flame extinguish in under 2.5 seconds. It's a vivid demonstration of how Mars's hostile atmosphere could actually be used as a fire suppression tool.

How does it address the challenge?

The challenge says PSI data is "hard to find, harder to compare, and harder yet to interpret." We tackled all three directly.

Finding is solved by our Investigation Explorer — search by fuel type, hardware facility, fire safety pillar (prevention, detection, or suppression), or just scroll through organized dossier cards. No more hunting through NASA's raw database.

Comparing is solved by our cross-investigation comparison engine and knowledge graph. Select any two experiments and get an instant breakdown: shared hardware lineage, overlapping test conditions, differing fuel types, and synthesized scientific insights. The graph captures every connection the challenge mentions — ACME's six gaseous fuel experiments sharing CIR hardware, FLEX/FLEX-2/CFI sharing the MDCA droplet apparatus, BASS/BASS-II/SPICE/SLICE sharing the MSG flow duct, and the SAME-to-DAFT instrument evolution.

Interpreting is solved by our deterministic physics engine. The challenge notes that no partial-gravity combustion data currently exists in PSI, but suggests that microgravity and normal-gravity results could bound intermediate gravity levels. That's exactly what we implemented. Using Roper flame-height scaling, Grashof convection analysis, and Dalton's partial pressure law, our engine calculates what happens to flame height, spread rate, and convection velocity at any gravity between 0g and 1g — with honest confidence levels that flag where predictions need future LUCI and FM2 data to be refined.

Users can type natural scenario queries like "What happens during a fabric fire in a lunar habitat at 34% O₂?" and get a ranked list of the most relevant PSI investigations, computed physics bounds, and specific safety recommendations — all grounded in real NASA data with zero hallucinated content.

Why does this matter?

Fire in space is not a theoretical concern — it's a documented killer. The Apollo 1 crew died in a pure-oxygen fire. Apollo 13 nearly lost its crew to an oxygen tank explosion. The Mir station crew survived a terrifying chemical fire that filled their station with toxic smoke. As we prepare to send astronauts back to the Moon and eventually to Mars, understanding fire behavior in these alien environments isn't just academic — it's life or death.

The twist is that lunar and Martian habitats will operate at elevated oxygen concentrations (30-34% O₂) to make spacesuit pre-breathing practical, which means materials that are perfectly safe on Earth become significantly more flammable. Our platform helps researchers, engineers, and students quickly understand which NASA experiments are most relevant to these new environments and what the physics tells us about fire risks we haven't directly tested yet.

We also highlight how space fire research has already saved lives on Earth — lightweight composite breathing tanks that replaced 35-pound steel cylinders for firefighters, dual-wavelength smoke detectors that cut false alarms in mines by 85%, and heat-resistant Nomex and PBI fabrics used in every modern firefighter's turnout coat. These spinoffs deserve to be visible and accessible.

What did we build it with?

We kept the frontend deliberately simple — vanilla JavaScript with ES modules, no React, no build tools, no npm install required. The 3D scenes run on Three.js 0.170.0 with a custom GPU-accelerated fluid physics solver that auto-detects WebGPU support and falls back to WebGL2 so it works on any modern browser. The entire frontend, including the complete 22-investigation dataset, is embedded and works fully offline — no server required.

The backend is Python with FastAPI serving a RESTful API, NetworkX for the knowledge graph, NumPy for physics computations, and an optional LangChain + FAISS RAG pipeline for enhanced natural language queries (with Google Gemini or OpenAI). Pydantic enforces strict data validation on every investigation record.

What makes it creative?

Honestly, we're most proud of the "zero mockup" principle. Every single number in the platform — every oxygen percentage, every flame height prediction, every sensor name, every atmospheric test condition — comes from authentic NASA PSI data or verified physics equations. We built an autonomous fallback system so that even if the LLM is unavailable, the dashboard still delivers scientifically accurate, peer-reviewed answers through a grounded cache and deterministic solver. A built-in Criteria Audit modal lets anyone verify this with a single click.

We also thought carefully about accessibility. A professor can use the Investigation Explorer as a teaching tool. A graduate student can run scenario queries to scope their thesis research. An aerospace engineer can compute physics bounds for habitat design. And anyone can just explore the 3D environments and develop an intuitive feel for why fire behaves so differently without gravity — something that's almost impossible to convey through papers and data tables alone.

projectDetails.name: ASTRA-MONITOR: Astronaut Health Monitoring and Alert System
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRA-MONITOR is a health-monitoring support system designed to help track astronaut health parameters and identify potentially concerning changes during space missions. The application allows authorized personnel to register astronauts, manage mission information, manually enter health measurements, and import readings through CSV files.

It monitors parameters such as heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), body temperature, blood pressure, and respiratory rate. Configurable, mission-specific threshold rules are used to identify readings that require attention and automatically generate alerts with severity levels and explanations. The system also supports historical health tracking, statistical anomaly detection when sufficient data is available, and human review of generated alerts.

Built using React, TypeScript, Python, FastAPI, and a database backend, ASTRA-MONITOR aims to provide a structured, transparent, and data-driven approach to astronaut health monitoring. It is designed as a decision-support tool, not a medical diagnostic system, and does not assume access to live spacecraft sensors.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRA-MONITOR is a web-based astronaut health monitoring and analysis platform designed to support the monitoring of crew members during space missions. It allows authorized personnel to register astronauts, manage mission information, manually enter health measurements, and import health records through CSV files.

The system monitors important physiological parameters, including heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), body temperature, blood pressure, and respiratory rate. It evaluates recorded measurements using configurable, mission-specific threshold rules and identifies potential health concerns through warning and critical alerts. It also provides historical measurement records, health trends, personalized baseline comparisons, and statistical anomaly detection when sufficient genuine data is available.

The platform uses statistical methods such as baseline analysis, Z-score-based deviation detection, and the Isolation Forest algorithm for identifying unusual patterns when the required data is available. Alerts are designed to support human review by authorized personnel rather than provide medical diagnoses.

ASTRA-MONITOR was developed using Python, FastAPI, React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and a database backend using SQLAlchemy with PostgreSQL support and SQLite for local development. Additional technologies include Pandas, NumPy, and Scikit-learn for data processing and statistical analysis. JWT authentication and role-based access control help protect sensitive information and restrict actions according to user permissions.

The creativity of the project lies in bringing astronaut health records, configurable monitoring rules, statistical analysis, historical trends, and alert management together in one platform. Instead of relying on a single measurement, the system supports the examination of health patterns over time and highlights unusual readings for further investigation.

During development, we considered data integrity, privacy, secure access, measurement validation, scalability, reliability, and the importance of avoiding unsupported medical conclusions. The platform does not claim to connect to live medical sensors; it works with manually entered and CSV-imported records.

The intended impact of ASTRA-MONITOR is to provide a structured and accessible health-monitoring support system that can help mission personnel organize astronaut health information, identify unusual changes earlier, and make more informed decisions during space missions.

NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) was consulted as a reference for spaceflight-related biological and physiological research. ASTRA-MONITOR does not directly ingest OSDR datasets; it currently works with manually entered and CSV-imported health records.

projectDetails.name: Project Aero.Vision - Comprehensive Fire and Combustion Analysis.
projectDetails.summary:
Flame in Freefall – AI-Powered Fire and Combustion Analysis

Aero.Vision is an AI-powered research platform investigating fire behaviour, combustion, and flame dynamics in aerospace and microgravity environments.

Project Goal: To create an accessible, evidence-driven platform that brings together scientific research, AI-powered analysis, and data visualisation to better understand combustion in space and identify gaps in existing research.

Our platform features Ember, an interactive AI assistant with two modes:

Project Evidence Mode: Analyses curated research on experiments like Saffire-IV, FLEX, and BASS-II, providing source-linked answers and identifying evidence gaps.

General AI Mode: Answers broader scientific questions with automatic AI provider fallback.

Research Database: Organises experimental data on fuel properties, oxygen, pressure, airflow, and gravity.

Data Visualisation: Presents interactive charts for scientific analysis.

Evidence Gap Identification: Highlights areas requiring further research.

Interactive Dashboard: Offers chat history, intuitive navigation, and a floating AI assistant.

Aero.Vision addresses the challenge of understanding combustion under varying environmental conditions, supporting aerospace safety, fire prevention, and safer future space missions. It is important because reliable fire research is essential for aerospace safety, fire prevention, and the development of safer future space missions.
projectDetails.details:
Flame in Freefall – AI-Powered Fire and Combustion Analysis

Developed by Aero.Vision | AI Assistant: Ember

1. Project Overview and Objective

Flame in Freefall is an AI-powered scientific research and analysis platform developed to investigate combustion behaviour, flame dynamics, and fire safety in aerospace environments, particularly under microgravity conditions.

The central goal of our project is to make existing scientific research on combustion in space more accessible, organised, and understandable while identifying gaps in current experimental knowledge. Fire behaves differently in microgravity than it does under Earth's gravity, making conventional assumptions about flame behaviour and fire safety insufficient for certain space environments.

Our platform, Aero.Vision, addresses this challenge by integrating a structured scientific research database, AI-assisted investigation, interactive data visualisation, and evidence-based analysis into one unified dashboard.

2. What Does the Project Do and How Does It Work?

Aero.Vision works as an integrated research environment with several interconnected modules.

A. Ember – AI Research Assistant

Ember is the platform's AI-powered assistant, designed with two specialised modes:

1. Project Evidence Mode

This mode focuses exclusively on our curated scientific research records. It analyses experimental information from studies such as NASA's Saffire-IV, FLEX, and BASS-II.

Its capabilities include:

  • Answering questions using available project research records.
  • Providing source-linked scientific information.
  • Identifying missing experimental parameters.
  • Distinguishing established findings from incomplete or uncertain evidence.
  • Highlighting research gaps instead of presenting unsupported conclusions.

A key restriction is that Ember must not invent experimental findings or treat missing information as proof of a scientific conclusion.

2. General AI Mode

This mode provides broader scientific explanations and answers questions beyond the curated research database. It uses external AI providers, with automatic fallback between Google Gemini and Groq if a provider encounters an error.

This ensures users can explore scientific concepts, ask follow-up questions, and understand complex combustion-related topics.

B. Scientific Research Database

We developed a structured database containing experimental records and relevant scientific parameters.

The database considers:

  • Fuel type and physical phase.
  • Sample shape and dimensions.
  • Oxygen availability and concentration.
  • Environmental pressure.
  • Airflow conditions.
  • Gravity conditions.
  • Experimental apparatus.
  • Sensors and measurement methods.
  • Evidence levels and original research sources.

This allows users to investigate how different environmental and experimental conditions relate to combustion behaviour.

C. Interactive Data Visualisation

The platform includes interactive charts that help users explore scientific information more effectively.

Features include:

  • Comparing oxygen and pressure conditions.
  • Exploring experimental records.
  • Comparing two research studies.
  • Examining relationships between recorded environmental parameters.

These visualisations transform structured experimental data into more understandable representations.

D. Evidence Gap Identification

One of the important features of Aero.Vision is its emphasis on identifying limitations in existing research.

Instead of assuming that all scientific parameters are available, the platform highlights missing measurements, incomplete records, and areas requiring further investigation.

It also distinguishes experimental observations from exploratory assessments, preventing preliminary interpretations from being mistaken for established scientific predictions.

E. Interactive Dashboard

The application is organised into dedicated sections:

  • Home: Introduces the project and its objectives.
  • Explore: Allows users to browse and filter research records.
  • Evidence: Presents scientific evidence and experimental sources.
  • Analyze: Provides interactive comparisons and visualisations.
  • Mission: Explores the relevance of research to aerospace environments.
  • About: Provides project and team information.

The interface also includes chat history, intuitive navigation, and a floating Ember assistant.

3. Benefits of the Project

Aero.Vision offers several advantages:

  1. Centralised Research: Brings multiple scientific experimental records into one organised platform.
  2. Evidence-Based Investigation: Encourages conclusions supported by actual research rather than assumptions.
  3. Time Efficiency: Makes it easier to locate, compare, and understand relevant scientific information.
  4. Scientific Transparency: Clearly identifies missing data and limitations in available evidence.
  5. Interactive Learning: Uses AI explanations and visualisations to make complex scientific concepts more accessible.
  6. Research Expansion: Helps identify questions that existing experiments may not have sufficiently addressed.

4. Intended Impact

The long-term intention of Flame in Freefall is to contribute to a better understanding of fire behaviour in environments beyond Earth.

As space exploration expands, fire safety becomes an increasingly important consideration aboard spacecraft, space stations, and future space habitats.

Our platform aims to support:

  • Improved understanding of combustion under microgravity conditions.
  • Research into spacecraft fire prevention and safety.
  • Identification of limitations in existing experimental research.
  • More accessible scientific investigation for students and researchers.
  • Future research into combustion under different environmental conditions.

The project is a research-support tool, not a certified spacecraft fire-safety system or a replacement for physical experiments.

5. Technologies, Programming Languages and Tools Used

We developed Aero.Vision primarily using Python and modern web technologies.

Programming language:

  • Python – Core application logic, data processing, AI integration, and backend functionality.

Framework and libraries:

  • Streamlit – Interactive web application and dashboard development.
  • Pandas – Scientific dataset organisation, processing, and analysis.
  • Plotly – Interactive charts and data visualisation.
  • Google GenAI SDK – Integration with Google Gemini.
  • Groq SDK – Integration with Groq AI services.
  • Streamlit Components – Additional interactive interface functionality.
  • Python libraries including pathlib, base64, re, and os – File handling, application utilities, and supporting functionality.

AI technologies:

  • Google Gemini – General AI assistance.
  • Groq – Alternative AI provider for automatic fallback.
  • Ember – Our integrated AI assistant with specialised research and general-purpose modes.

Data management:

  • CSV-based research datasets.
  • Structured experimental records and source references.
  • Separate catalogue and experimental-conditions datasets.

Development and deployment:

  • GitHub – Source-code management and version control.
  • Render – Cloud application hosting and deployment.
  • GoDaddy – Custom domain management.
  • Environment variables and deployment secrets – Secure API-key configuration.

Hardware:

The project was developed using a standard computer for programming, testing, and deployment. No specialised combustion apparatus or custom physical hardware was required to build the software platform.

6. Creativity and Innovation

The creativity of Flame in Freefall lies in combining scientific research, artificial intelligence, and interactive analysis into a single specialised platform.

Rather than developing another general-purpose chatbot, we designed Ember with two distinct operating modes to separate curated scientific evidence from broader AI-generated explanations.

Another important innovation is our emphasis on scientific limitations. Many digital research tools focus on presenting available information, whereas Aero.Vision also draws attention to what is missing, unverified, or insufficiently investigated.

The combination of a structured experimental database, source-linked AI responses, evidence-gap identification, and interactive comparisons creates a more responsible approach to AI-assisted scientific research.

We also designed the platform around a specific scientific challenge rather than simply integrating AI for general information retrieval.

7. Factors Considered During Development

Several scientific and technical considerations influenced our design:

Scientific factors:

  • Differences between terrestrial gravity and microgravity.
  • Fuel composition, physical state, and sample geometry.
  • Oxygen concentration and availability.
  • Environmental pressure and airflow.
  • Differences between experimental setups.
  • Reliability and completeness of scientific measurements.
  • Distinction between observed results and theoretical explanations.

Technical factors:

  • Accuracy and traceability of AI-generated responses.
  • Reliability of external AI providers.
  • Handling incomplete or unavailable research data.
  • Accessibility and ease of navigation.
  • Efficient organisation of scientific records.
  • Clarity of charts and experimental comparisons.
  • Secure management of API credentials.
  • Scalability and accessibility through cloud deployment.

We particularly prioritised preventing unsupported scientific claims. Missing experimental information is explicitly treated as an evidence limitation rather than an opportunity for the AI to guess.

8. Conclusion

Flame in Freefall represents our attempt to bring together aerospace research, artificial intelligence, and scientific data analysis to address an important challenge in future space exploration.

Through Aero.Vision and its AI assistant Ember, we have developed a platform that does more than retrieve information: it organises experimental evidence, facilitates comparisons, highlights research limitations, and makes complex scientific investigations more accessible.

Our ultimate vision is to support more informed research into combustion beyond Earth and contribute to the broader goal of making future space missions safer.

Agri Space AI 

Agri Space AI – Space-to-Soil Intelligence is a web-based agricultural platform designed to bridge the gap between satellite technology and everyday farming. Farmers often face challenges in understanding crop health, soil conditions, rainfall patterns and changing climate conditions. Our project aims to make this information more accessible through a single, farmer-friendly platform.

The website consists of eight modules: Dashboard, Farm Profile, Satellite Intelligence, Crop Recommendation, Crop Rotation, Climate Risk Analysis, AI Farming Assistant and About Agri Space. It is designed to combine farmer-provided information, NASA Earth observation datasets and machine learning techniques to support informed agricultural decisions.

The proposed system uses satellite data sources such as NASA POWER, MODIS, SMAP and GPM IMERG to analyze environmental indicators, including vegetation, temperature, rainfall and soil moisture. Machine learning models are intended to support suitable crop recommendations, while crop rotation and climate analysis modules assist with long-term farm planning.

Built using React.js and Tailwind CSS, with a planned Python Fast API backend, Agri Space AI aims to make space-based agricultural intelligence easier to understand and use, encouraging climate-aware and sustainable farming practices.
projectDetails.details:
Agri Space AI – Space-to-Soil Intelligence

Agri Space AI is a web-based agricultural intelligence platform designed to connect satellite technology, artificial intelligence and farming. Our project addresses the challenges farmers face in understanding crop health, soil conditions, rainfall patterns and changing climate conditions.

What does it do and how does it work?

Agri Space AI brings together farmer-provided information, satellite-based environmental observations and machine learning to support better-informed agricultural decisions. The platform consists of eight modules: Dashboard, Farm Profile, Satellite Intelligence, Crop Recommendation, Crop Rotation, Climate Risk Analysis, AI Farming Assistant and About Agri Space AI. Farmers can enter their farm details, explore agricultural indicators, access crop-planning tools and interact with a farmer-friendly assistant. Our planned data integrations include NASA POWER, MODIS MOD13Q1, NASA SMAP and GPM IMERG for meteorological conditions, vegetation indices, soil moisture and precipitation information. Machine learning models are intended to support crop recommendations.

What are its benefits and intended impact?

The project aims to make complex satellite information easier to understand, improve awareness of crop and environmental conditions, support informed crop selection and rotation planning, and help farmers consider climate-related risks. Our long-term vision is to encourage accessible, climate-aware and sustainable agriculture, particularly for farmers who may not have access to advanced agricultural technology.

What tools and technologies did we use?

We developed the frontend using React.js, JavaScript and Tailwind CSS. Recharts is used for data visualization, while React Leaflet provides geographical mapping. Our planned backend uses Python and Fast API to connect the website with machine learning models and external data sources. Python-based machine learning tools and Joblib/Pickle are used for model development and storage. NASA Earth observation datasets are identified for integration. The current prototype uses illustrative data in sections where live integrations are pending.

What makes our project creative?

The creativity of Agri Space AI lies in bringing multiple agricultural intelligence capabilities into one platform. Instead of presenting satellite information as complicated scientific data, we aim to translate it into farmer-friendly dashboards, visual indicators, crop-planning support and conversational assistance. Combining space-based observations with farm-specific information creates an opportunity for more relevant agricultural insights.

What factors did our team consider?

Our team considered farmers' accessibility, ease of use, soil characteristics, geographical location, crop history, water availability, seasonal requirements, climate variability and the importance of understandable recommendations. We also considered the reliability, coverage and relevance of satellite datasets, machine learning model inputs, and the need to distinguish actual observations from illustrative information.

Through Agri Space AI, our team aims to bring the benefits of space technology closer to the agricultural community and contribute to a more informed and sustainable farming future.

The platform includes interactive 3D visualisations, a space equipment explorer, mission timelines, scientific discoveries, mission comparisons and quizzes. We also developed an AI Space Historian that answers questions using verified NASA mission records and provides source references.

Our project addresses the challenge of making the history of retired and inactive space equipment more interesting and easier to understand, especially for students and young space enthusiasts. projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Echoes of Space

1. What the Project Does

Echoes of Space is an interactive 3D digital museum that preserves and showcases the history of NASA's robotic explorers and lunar equipment. Users can explore Earth, Mars and the Moon, discover forgotten spacecraft, rovers and landers, and learn about the missions and scientific discoveries associated with them.

2. How It Works

The platform brings NASA mission information together in one place and presents it through interactive features.

  • 3D Planetary Exploration: Explore realistic 3D models of Earth, Mars and the Moon.
  • Space Equipment Explorer: Search, filter and explore 12 historical spacecraft and hardware relics.
  • Interactive Hardware Inspector: Examine detailed 3D spacecraft models and their components.
  • Mission Timeline: Follow 24 important milestones in space exploration.
  • Scientific Discoveries Archive: Explore six major scientific discoveries.
  • Mission Comparison: Compare spacecraft, their engineering specifications and instruments.
  • AI Space Historian: Ask questions and receive answers grounded in verified NASA mission records, with source citations.
  • Mission Detective Quiz: Solve five interactive mystery cases and earn NASA Curator Ranks.

3. Benefits and Intended Impact

The project makes space exploration easier and more interesting for students, educators and space enthusiasts. It converts complex technical information into an interactive learning experience, encourages scientific curiosity and helps preserve the history of machines whose missions have ended.

Our aim is to help younger audiences understand not just what NASA explored, but also how these machines contributed to scientific discoveries.

4. Tools and Technologies

Software-based project (No hardware required).

  • 3D Graphics: Three.js (r128)
  • Rendering: WebGL 2.0
  • Frontend: HTML5 and Tailwind CSS
  • Programming: JavaScript
  • Icons: Lucide Icons
  • Data Storage: JSON datasets and browser LocalStorage
  • AI Component: RAG Query Engine / AI Space Historian
  • Modular Architecture: React and TypeScript-ready source

5. Creativity and Innovation

What makes Echoes of Space different is the way it turns forgotten space equipment into something people can actively explore. Instead of presenting mission information as ordinary articles, it combines 3D planetary environments, interactive spacecraft models, historical timelines, scientific discoveries and an AI-based space historian.

The platform also connects individual discoveries back to the spacecraft responsible for them, helping users understand the relationship between engineering and scientific progress.

6. Technical and Educational Factors

The project follows a modular, frontend-first architecture. Its mission data is organised into eight structured datasets containing 12 hardware records, eight historical programs, 22 scientific instruments, six discoveries, 24 timeline milestones and 13 verified NASA source registries.

The platform uses open-source web technologies and browser-based rendering, making it accessible without specialised hardware.

Overall, Echoes of Space aims to turn the forgotten history of space exploration into an experience that people can explore, learn from and remember.

projectDetails.details:
ROOTWISE – NASA-Powered Climate-Adaptive Crop Rotation Intelligence Platform

ROOTWISE is a web platform designed to help farmers plan and compare crop rotations across three growing seasons. It brings together farm details, soil records, previous crop history, environmental data and farmer preferences to suggest suitable crop sequences.

How It Works:
Farmers can add their farm and field details, record soil samples and maintain their crop history. ROOTWISE uses this information along with tested NASA POWER climatology data to explore different crop rotations. It offers three planning strategies: Soil Guardian, Water Saver and Balanced Return, each focusing on different farming priorities.

Key Features:

  • Three-Season Rotation: Compare crop sequences across three growing seasons.
  • Planning Strategies: Choose between soil-focused, water-saving and balanced approaches.
  • Risk Radar: Highlights possible issues such as water stress, repeated crop-family use, seasonal mismatch and missing data.
  • Explainable Recommendations: Shows why a crop sequence is suggested and highlights data limitations.
  • Farm Management: Manage farm, field, soil-sample and crop-history records.

Technology Used:

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS v4, HTML and CSS.
  • Backend & Database: Supabase, PostgreSQL, Supabase Auth, JavaScript Client, PostgreSQL Functions/RPC and Row Level Security (RLS).
  • Development Tools: Node.js, npm, Git, GitHub, VS Code and PowerShell.
  • Deployment: Vercel (intended hosting platform).

NASA Data:
We tested NASA POWER climatology data, including temperature, precipitation, root-zone wetness, surface wetness and solar radiation, to bring environmental information into crop-rotation planning.

What Makes It Different:
Instead of focusing on just the next crop, ROOTWISE looks at how crop choices can affect the following growing seasons. Farmers can compare different strategies and understand the reasons behind the suggested rotations.

Factors Considered:
We considered soil conditions, water requirements, previous crops, crop-family compatibility, seasonal suitability, climate conditions, economic returns and farmer preferences while developing the platform.

Intended Impact:
Through ROOTWISE, we want to help farmers make better-informed crop decisions, plan water use more carefully, maintain soil health and adapt their farming choices to changing environmental conditions.

projectDetails.name: Orbitcare
projectDetails.summary: OrbitCare (Orbitspace) is an offline-first health dashboard for astronauts on long-duration missions, where Earth is minutes away by radio and there is no hospital. It follows three astronauts across a simulated 180-day mission, comparing each day's resting heart rate, heart-rate variability, sleep, blood oxygen and bone density against that astronaut's own first-21-day baseline. Direction-aware anomaly scores feed four domain scores — Heart, Bone & Muscle, Sleep & Mind, Immune/Radiation — the crew view always shows the worst-off astronaut first, every flag carries its evidence and a plain-language action plan, and a PDF health report can be handed over to Earth. On Day 63, Kenji declines to Watch (79/100) and recovers to Nominal (95/100) by Day 90. All data is simulated and clearly labelled; OrbitCare is decision support only, not a medical device.
projectDetails.details:
OrbitCare is a working web app. The Crew View ranks the three astronauts worst-first by overall health score, with Nominal / Watch / Alert status chips. The Astronaut Dashboard shows each day's vitals against the astronaut's personal 21-day baseline, the four domain scores, and every active flag with its evidence. Trends charts show vitals against the normal band with a mission-day slider (1-180) and Play. The Action Plan turns each flag into plain-language steps and a downloadable health report. A daily self-check (sleep, mood, stress, symptoms) feeds the Sleep & Mind score. Everything works offline from a local cache, and a one-tap Emergency Guide covers six situations with a 110 bpm CPR metronome.

How it works: 540 simulated daily readings (3 crew x 180 days) with injected events, including Kenji's Day-63 infection. Each indicator gets a direction-aware z-score against the personal baseline, smoothed over 3 days into domain scores; Watch starts at 1, Alert at 2. Flags are rule-based and auditable, so every recommendation can be traced to its numbers.

Impact: on a Mars mission, early warning matters more than treatment — OrbitCare helps a crew spot a decline days before it becomes an emergency, and gives Earth a clean handover report.

Built with: HTML/CSS/JavaScript frontend, Node.js backend, Supabase (PostgreSQL), hosted on Vercel. The backend is tested with 64 automated tests, all passing. All health data is simulated. AI tools (Muse) helped write code and text, and this is disclosed in the project README. The full 12-slide deck is in the GitHub repo.

**ALUNA: An Immersive 3D Space Exploration and Autonomous Satellite Operations Game**

ALUNA is an interactive, space-themed 3D platform developed to make space exploration and satellite operations more engaging, accessible, and educational. It combines an immersive 3D space headquarters, mission-based gameplay, spacecraft design, satellite fleet management, and autonomous intelligence systems. The platform features 25 solo campaign levels, 25 squad campaign levels, and four multiplayer modes, encouraging both individual learning and teamwork.

ALUNA addresses the challenge by transforming complex space concepts into interactive missions and simulations. Players can explore different facilities, coordinate with teammates, manage spacecraft and satellites, and experience scenarios inspired by real-world space operations. Its autonomous systems aim to help users understand satellite coordination, orbital safety, and potential close-approach risks.

The project is important because satellites support communication, navigation, weather forecasting, and scientific research. As space becomes increasingly crowded, understanding responsible satellite operations and orbital safety is essential. ALUNA makes these topics more approachable while inspiring interest in space science, technology, and future space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
ALUNA – Project Details

ALUNA is an immersive 3D space exploration and autonomous satellite operations platform that combines gaming, space science, simulation, and teamwork. It is designed to help users understand space missions and the challenges of managing satellites through interactive experiences.

1. What does it do and how does it work?

ALUNA features an interactive 3D space headquarters that acts as the central hub. Users can explore different facilities, including Mission Control, Satellite Operations, Spacecraft Design, Autonomous Intelligence, Training and Simulation, and Squad Coordination.

The platform includes:

  • 25 Solo Campaign Levels for individual space missions.
  • 25 Squad Campaign Levels for cooperative missions.
  • 4 Multiplayer Modes to encourage teamwork and coordination.
  • Satellite Fleet Management to monitor and manage satellite operations.
  • Orbital Safety Simulation to understand satellite close approaches and collision risks.
  • Autonomous Intelligence Systems to support monitoring, decision-making, and mission coordination.
  • Spacecraft Design and Mission Planning to make space operations interactive.

Players navigate a 3D environment, enter facilities, select missions, operate spacecraft, and collaborate with teammates to complete objectives.

2. What are its benefits?

  • Makes complex space science concepts easier to understand.
  • Encourages STEM learning through interactive gameplay.
  • Builds teamwork, communication, and problem-solving skills.
  • Introduces satellite management and orbital safety concepts.
  • Promotes awareness of responsible space operations.
  • Makes learning about space more engaging and accessible.

3. What is the intended impact?

ALUNA aims to inspire students and young innovators to explore space science, aerospace engineering, satellite technology, and autonomous systems. It also highlights the importance of orbital safety and responsible satellite operations as the number of objects in Earth's orbit increases.

4. What tools and technologies were used?

The project uses modern web and 3D development technologies, including:

  • Frontend: React, JavaScript, HTML, CSS
  • 3D Environment: Three.js, React Three Fiber
  • 3D Modelling and Animation: Blender
  • Backend: Python
  • Database: SQLite
  • Simulation: Orbital simulation and satellite close-approach screening
  • Development Tools: Visual Studio Code and web development tools

5. How is the project creative?

ALUNA combines the immersive experience of a 3D video game with educational space simulations. Instead of presenting space concepts through ordinary text or videos, it allows users to explore a virtual space headquarters, undertake missions, manage satellite systems, and work together as a squad. Cinematic character introductions, interactive facilities, realistic space environments, and autonomous mission systems create a distinctive learning experience.

6. What factors did the team consider?

The team considered:

  • Scientific relevance: Keeping missions connected to real space-operation concepts.
  • Orbital safety: Highlighting satellite collision risks and responsible operations.
  • User experience: Making controls, navigation, and missions understandable.
  • Team collaboration: Supporting squad coordination and multiplayer interaction.
  • Performance: Optimising 3D graphics and gameplay for smooth operation.
  • Scalability: Designing the platform to support additional missions and features.
  • Accessibility: Making space education engaging for a broad audience.

Keywords: Space Exploration, Satellite Operations, Autonomous Intelligence, Orbital Mechanics, Orbital Safety, Collision Risk Detection, 3D Simulation, STEM Education, Space Technology, Mission Control, Satellite Fleet Management, Three.js, React, React Three Fiber, Blender, Python, Multiplayer Gaming, Team Collaboration, Aerospace Innovation.

projectDetails.name: ANANT — Interactive Deep-Space Exoplanet & Orbital Reconnaissance Simulator
projectDetails.summary:
ANANT is a zero-install, browser-based 3D exoplanet exploration and orbital reconnaissance simulator developed by Team Ananth Tandav. Built using WebGL and procedural planetary generation, ANANT allows users to pilot the DSN reconnaissance probe ANANT-01 across real-scale star systems modeled after confirmed NASA mission targets, including the TRAPPIST-1 system, Kepler-452b, and Proxima Centauri b.

Traditional exoplanet catalogs present discovery metrics as static tables, making it difficult for students and the public to grasp orbital scale, atmospheric scattering, and planetary scale. ANANT transforms NASA Exoplanet Archive parameters and JPL Horizons ephemeris concepts into an interactive, real-time flight experience complete with Deep Space Network telemetry overlays and surface flyby missions. By running directly in any modern web browser without heavy downloads, ANANT democratizes access to realistic exoplanetary science and space mission simulation.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works

ANANT is an interactive 3D spaceflight and planetary survey simulation accessible directly through a web browser. Players command the ANANT-01 reconnaissance probe across multi-body star systems, executing orbital insertions, atmospheric grazing maneuvers, and low-altitude surface inspections. The simulation renders real-time planetary terrain, atmospheric Rayleigh/Mie scattering horizons, and orbital trajectories paired with a NASA Deep Space Network (DSN) telemetry HUD.

Tools, Languages & Architecture

  • Core Engine & Rendering: TypeScript, WebGL / Babylon.js procedural planetary and shader pipeline.
  • UI & Telemetry Layer: HTML5, CSS3, custom high-contrast monospace telemetry overlay modeled after JPL flight instrumentation.
  • Deployment: Static web bundle hosted for instant, zero-install browser access across desktop devices.

Intended Impact & Creativity Rather than treating exoplanet discovery as passive data visualization, ANANT bridges scientific catalog parameters with tactile spatial exploration. Users experience the true scale difference between red dwarf habitable-zone worlds (such as TRAPPIST-1e and TRAPPIST-1f) and super-Earths (Kepler-452b). Because it requires zero installation and runs smoothly on standard laptops, educators, students, and space enthusiasts can immediately explore distant worlds and understand orbital mechanics firsthand.

Design Considerations Our team prioritized zero-friction accessibility, visual clarity, and scientific grounding—stripping away cluttered controls in favor of clean telemetry readouts and curated mission scenarios (Project Lazarus: Habitable Zone Recon, TRAPPIST-1e Atmospheric Survey, and Europa Cryo-Surface Scan).

projectDetails.summary:
EarthPulse is an AI-powered satellite monitoring platform designed to visualize, analyze, and understand changes occurring across Earth's surface. Inspired by NASA's NISAR mission, EarthPulse explores the potential of Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) technology to monitor environmental and human-induced changes, even through clouds and during nighttime.

The platform aims to support monitoring across six major areas: forest and wetland changes, agricultural activities, wildfires, earthquakes and ground movement, glaciers, and other environmental transformations.

By combining satellite observations, AI-assisted analysis, geospatial visualization, and interactive dashboards, EarthPulse transforms complex Earth observation information into meaningful insights. Users can explore locations, compare changes over time, identify potential environmental risks, and better understand how our planet is evolving.

Our goal is to make satellite-based Earth monitoring more accessible, understandable, and useful for environmental awareness, research, and informed decision-making.
projectDetails.details:
EarthPulse – Project Details

1. What Does Our Project Do?

EarthPulse is an AI-powered Earth observation and satellite monitoring platform designed to help users understand how Earth's surface changes over time. It brings multiple environmental monitoring applications together in one interactive platform, inspired by NASA's NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) mission.

The platform focuses on six major areas: forest and wetland monitoring, agricultural changes, wildfire impacts, earthquake-related ground movement, glacier monitoring, and other environmental transformations.

2. How Does It Work?

EarthPulse is designed to combine satellite observations, geospatial information, AI-assisted analysis, and interactive visualizations. Users can explore geographical regions, understand environmental changes, and view monitoring insights through an accessible dashboard.

The project is inspired by NISAR's Synthetic Aperture Radar technology, which uses microwave signals instead of relying on sunlight to observe Earth's surface. This allows radar observations during both day and night and through many cloud conditions.

3. Benefits and Intended Impact

  • Makes complex satellite observation concepts easier to understand.
  • Supports environmental awareness and monitoring.
  • Helps users explore potential environmental changes.
  • Brings multiple Earth observation applications into one platform.
  • Demonstrates how AI and satellite technology can support environmental research and informed decision-making.

4. Technologies Used

Frontend: React.js, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS.

Development Tools: Visual Studio Code, Git and GitHub.

Deployment: Cloud-based web hosting.

AI Assistance: AI tools were used to support development, problem-solving, code assistance, and project documentation.

5. What Makes EarthPulse Creative?

The key innovation is bringing six different Earth monitoring applications into one unified interactive experience. Instead of presenting satellite information as complicated scientific data, EarthPulse aims to make it understandable through visual exploration, interactive dashboards, and AI-assisted insights.

The platform connects the potential of NASA's NISAR mission with practical environmental monitoring applications.

6. Factors Considered

Our team considered accessibility, usability, environmental relevance, scalability, data visualization, and the importance of reliable satellite observations. We also considered how to make complex scientific information understandable to students, researchers, and the general public.

Our Vision

EarthPulse aims to turn satellite observations into meaningful environmental insights and help people better understand our changing planet.

One Earth. Countless Changes. One Platform to Understand Them.

projectDetails.summary:
Our approach: We started from NASA's challenge and its five spaceflight hazards: radiation, isolation, distance from Earth, gravity, and closed environments. We asked how an astronaut could check their own health when ground replies take up to 22 minutes, and designed the tool around that.
What we're building: A digital twin of the astronaut's body. A 60-second daily check-in logs heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, sleep and mood. projectDetails.details:
Health Max AI: Your Body's Digital Twin for Deep Space

Health Max AI is health monitoring software that gives astronauts a living digital twin of their own body. On long missions to the Moon and Mars, ground replies can take up to 22 minutes, so astronauts must assess and treat themselves. Health Max AI makes that simple.

Our team, APEX CODERZ, developed an AI-driven health intelligence system at the core of the app. In a 60-second daily check-in, astronauts log heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, sleep and mood. The AI analyzes these readings and their trends, then lights up a clickable 3D body in green, yellow or red. Each alert is linked to one of NASA's five spaceflight hazards, so the astronaut learns why the body is changing, not just that it is.

A smart escalation engine decides the next step: keep going, retest in six hours, or contact the flight surgeon with an auto-generated report. A mind companion tracks mood and sleep to catch isolation stress early. Mission Mode adapts advice for a spacecraft, Moon base or Mars rover, and gamified streaks keep astronauts engaged.

Health Max AI turns raw numbers into clear, explainable guidance, helping crews stay healthy when help is far away.

projectDetails.name: Red Planet Rescue
projectDetails.summary:
Red Planet Rescue is an interactive Mars outpost survival simulator built for the challenge “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer”. Students act as Mission Commander and run an outpost of six astronauts for 30 Martian days (sols), balancing oxygen, water, food and power against Martian weather.

It addresses the challenge by making engineering trade-offs tangible. Every decision has a cost: rationing water adds supply but raises crew stress, and the emergency oxygen generator saves air but drains the battery. Dust storms cut solar power, and a cascade failure map shows how one problem spreads to others, such as a storm leading to a water shortage. Four rule-based advisors (Chief Engineer, Medical Officer, Mission Commander, Risk Analyst) explain their recommendations and risk levels, so players learn why, not just what. Crew, Explore and Mission Report pages track astronaut health, explain real Martian conditions and score the final outcome.

It matters because young learners often meet space engineering as oversimplified or too complex. This simulator lets them experience why missions succeed or fail by making the decisions themselves.
projectDetails.details:
Challenge
Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

1. What it does and how it works
Red Planet Rescue is a web-based Mars outpost survival simulator. The player takes the role of Mission Commander and manages six astronauts for 30 Martian days (sols). Four critical resources are tracked: oxygen, water, food and battery power. Each sol, these resources decrease according to crew consumption and Martian weather, which ranges from normal conditions to a severe dust storm that cuts solar output to 15%. The player makes one decision per sol from six options, such as rationing water, repairing solar panels or giving the crew a rest day. Every option improves one area and has a cost in another. A cascade failure map shows how one event spreads: a dust storm lowers solar power, the battery drains, water recycling slows and the risk of a water shortage rises. Four rule-based advisors (Chief Engineer, Medical Officer, Mission Commander and Risk Analyst) give recommendations with reasons and risk levels. At the end of the mission, a report presents the survival rate, score, grade and a timeline of key events.

2. Benefits
The simulator makes engineering trade-offs tangible for young learners. Students see cause and effect directly, and because every advisor explains its reasoning, they learn why a decision is made and not only what to choose. It runs in a standard web browser on laptops and phones, so no installation or special hardware is needed.

3. Intended impact
Space-themed STEM content is often oversimplified or too complex for young learners. Our aim is for students to finish a mission understanding why real missions succeed or fail, because they experienced the consequences of their own decisions. The weather schedule is fixed, so every run is repeatable and a class can compare strategies and discuss which choices worked best.

4. Tools and technologies

  • Frontend: React, Vite, JavaScript, HTML and CSS
  • Backend and data: Python Flask with a REST API (JSON)
  • Development: Git, GitHub and Visual Studio Code
  • Hardware: standard laptops, no special equipment

5. How the project is creative
Our cascade failure map explains each step of a failure with a stated reason, which turns the game into a reasoning exercise. Crew health, fatigue, stress and morale respond to supplies, weather and the player’s choices, so decisions have human consequences. A resource forecast shows when each supply would run out if nothing changes, which encourages planning ahead. An Explore page links seven real Martian conditions, such as thin atmosphere, extreme cold, low gravity and communication delay, to the rules of the game.

6. Factors our team considered
We designed rules simple enough for young learners yet realistic enough to teach genuine trade-offs. We kept the advisors rule-based so every recommendation can be traced to a clear reason. We built a working simulator first and added visual features afterwards, and we made the layout responsive for laptop, tablet and phone screens.

projectDetails.name: AETHER-QKD
projectDetails.summary: AETHER-QKD is an interplanetary command and cryptography hub built by Team Aracus for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, combining futuristic Deep-Space Quantum Key Distribution (BB84) with historical Enigma code-breaking simulation suites. To address deep-space communication security, the platform simulates polarized photon transmission between deep-space probes and ground stations while integrating real-time atmospheric telemetry from the Meteomatics Weather API to dynamically model quantum channel noise and QBER safety thresholds. Furthermore, it features a dual-layer Enigma intercept and code-breaking lab to demonstrate robust encryption and signal decryption. This project is vital for advancing unhackable quantum communication architectures for future space missions.
projectDetails.details:
Aether-Net Interplanetary Command & Cryptography Hub (AETHER-QKD) is an advanced dual-layer security platform engineered for future interplanetary missions. It bridges futuristic Quantum Key Distribution (BB84) with historical Enigma-based code-breaking cipher suites, dynamically audited against real-time ground-station environmental data.

WHAT IT DOES & HOW IT WORKS:

- BB84 Quantum Protocol & Basis Sifting: Simulates Alice (deep-space probe) transmitting polarized photon streams across interplanetary distances to Bob (ground station), performing real-time basis sifting to generate secure cryptographic keys.

- Real-Time QBER Security Auditing: Integrates live meteorological data from the Meteomatics Weather API (/now/ endpoint) to dynamically evaluate the Quantum Bit Error Rate (QBER) against real-world environmental noise factors (ground temperature, humidity, and wind speed) to ensure channel security remains below the critical 11% threshold.

- Enigma Intercept & Code-Breaking Lab: Provides a dual-mode rotor-based cipher interface for encrypting deep-space telemetry and decrypting intercepted operational intelligence.

- Interplanetary Telemetry Dashboard: A high-visibility, cinematic deep-space command interface featuring live atmospheric metrics, high-contrast typography, and atmospheric link status monitors.

BENEFITS & INTENDED IMPACT:

As humanity reaches deeper into the cosmos, secure communication across interplanetary distances becomes paramount. Traditional encryption remains vulnerable to quantum computing advancements. AETHER-QKD ensures that deep-space probes and ground stations can establish unbreakable, error-audited quantum links while maintaining absolute operational readiness under varying atmospheric conditions.

TECHNOLOGY STACK:

- Frontend & UI: Python Streamlit (Community Cloud Deployed), Custom CSS High-Contrast Deep-Space UI Styling.

- Backend Logic: Python, Random, Pandas.

- API Integration: Meteomatics Weather API (/now/t_2m:C,relative_humidity_2m:p,wind_speed_10m:ms/) for real-time atmospheric auditing.

- Version Control & Deployment: Git, GitHub, Streamlit Cloud.
