projectDetails.summary:
MarsWalk Planner is an integrated mission planning system designed to reduce risks for astronauts conducting Extravehicular Activities (EVAs) on the Martian surface. We developed an end-to-end telemetry pipeline and interactive visual interface. The system ingests Digital Elevation Models (DEMs) and environmental datasets (radiation, thermal) and processes them through a custom Multi-Layer Cost Fusion engine, applying strict physiological constraints—such as limiting safe slopes to under 15 degrees. A core A* pathfinding algorithm uses this consolidated cost matrix to calculate the safest, most efficient route.

The resulting plan is visualized in a localized, dark-mode Mission Control interface with interactive layer toggles and real-time readouts, including projected EVA duration, suit oxygen utilization, and total mSv radiation dose. This is critical for crewed Mars exploration, where topographic instability and radiation exposure present severe safety challenges. MarsWalk Planner addresses these challenges by empowering planners with immediate, science-grounded, and customizable terrain risk assessment and optimized routing.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do, and how does it work?

MarsWalk Planner is an end-to-end mission planning and navigation system for Martian extravehicular activities (EVAs).

  • The Backend Pipeline: It ingests elevation and environmental data (such as Digital Elevation Models, thermal inertia, and radiation flux) into a 2D grid structure. It calculates surface elevation gradients using NumPy (np.gradient), converts them into slope angles in degrees (θ=arctan⁡(dx2+dy2)\theta = \arctan(\sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2})θ=arctan(dx2+dy2
    [IMAGE ID NOT FOUND title:"" ]
    ​)), and applies strict physiological thresholds—locking impassable cliffs or steep slopes (>15∘>15^\circ>15∘) with infinite barriers (np.inf).
    WhatsApp Image 2026-11-14 at 19.01.01.jpeg+ 3
  • Cost Fusion & Pathfinding: It merges multiple environmental layers through a weighted summation formula(Ctotal=(w1.slope cost)+(w2.Radiation Cost)). A core A pathfinding algorithm* processes this consolidated cost matrix to calculate the safest, most efficient traverse route.
  • The Frontend Handoff: The path and telemetry are serialized into JSON (route.json) and handed off to an interactive, dark-mode Mission Control web interface.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Automated Risk Mitigation: Automatically detects and routes around life-threatening hazards like extreme grades and radiation hot spots.
  • Real-Time Telemetry Readouts: Instantly computes and displays crucial mission metrics, including total distance, estimated EVA duration, suit oxygen consumption, and cumulative radiation dosage (mSv\text{mSv}mSv).
  • Seamless Full-Stack Integration: Bridges advanced geospatial backend analytics with a user-friendly, interactive frontend map viewer complete with layer toggles and alternative route comparisons.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The project aims to enhance astronaut safety and mission success during future crewed surface operations on Mars. By providing planners with an immediate, science-grounded tool to visualize terrain risks and optimize EVA routes, MarsWalk Planner minimizes human error, reduces radiation exposure, and serves as a scalable concept demonstrator for planetary exploration software.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Programming Languages: Python (for backend data processing, cost matrix math, and pathfinding logic) and JavaScript/HTML/CSS (for the frontend mapping interface).
  • Libraries & Frameworks: NumPy (for high-performance 2D array operations and gradient calculations), Leaflet.js (for interactive map rendering and coordinate overlays).
  • Development Environment: Visual Studio Code (VS Code), Git, and custom simulation datasets modeled after real Martian topography (e.g., Gale Crater sub-grids and NASA Mars Trek tiles).

5. How is your project creative?

MarsWalk Planner creatively bridges the gap between raw planetary science data and actionable human operations. Instead of treating pathfinding as a purely abstract math problem, it fuses multiple physical layers—slope mechanics, radiation exposure, and spatial boundaries—into a unified cost function. Furthermore, wrapping this complex scientific pipeline into a sleek, functional Mission Control interface gives it the polish and usability of a real aerospace deployment tool.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Human Physiology & Safety Limits: Factoring in astronaut physical constraints, such as a maximum safe slope threshold (≤15∘\le 15^\circ≤15∘) and cumulative radiation limits (mSv\text{mSv}mSv).
  • Topographical Reality: Accounting for severe Martian hazards like cliff drop-offs by utilizing mathematical barriers (np.inf) that force absolute avoidance
  • System Modularity & Handoff: Designing clean interfaces between the science/data lead, the backend engineering pipeline, and the frontend developer via serialized JSON telemetry hand-offs.

projectDetails.name: Hear Earth’s Forests
projectDetails.summary:
EarthEcho is an interactive Earth Jukebox that pairs NASA Earth Information Center visualizations with sound generated during playback. Built by ARTICXCODERS, it lets users explore GEDI forest-height visualizations from California, Florida, and Senegal and compare two selected image areas through stereo or alternating audio.

The application estimates canopy height from each visualization’s color scale and maps those estimates to pitch. Soft ticks indicate increasing matched-pixel coverage. A sound legend, narrated explanations, numeric readouts, and listening challenges help users interpret the experience.

EarthEcho explores how sound can provide another way to engage with Earth science. It includes keyboard controls, audio-only viewing, adjustable sound layers, and downloadable sound postcards. The interface explains that rendered-image estimates are approximate and affected by lighting, perspective, and camera movement.
projectDetails.details:
What we built

EarthEcho is a browser-based application that combines NASA Earth Information Center imagery with interactive sonification. Users select a GEDI close-up visualization from California, Florida, or Senegal and compare two image areas.

How it works

The application samples the currently displayed video frame using Canvas. It compares selected pixels with a palette sampled from the corresponding NASA colorbar, rejects background and ambiguous colors, and calculates an approximate median color-derived height.

Each visualization has its own source scale. EarthEcho converts the resulting estimates into a shared audio range, mapping 0–50 meters to 180–720 hertz at the default sensitivity. Higher estimates produce higher tones, with values above 50 meters capped. Pitch smoothing reduces abrupt changes.

Area A and Area B can play through separate stereo channels, alternate, or play individually. Soft ticks indicate an increase in matched-pixel coverage. Areas with insufficient matching pixels become silent.

Interaction and learning

Users can choose preset areas, draw custom image selections, inspect numeric estimates and charts, and explore an interactive sound legend. Narrated explanations, listening challenges, and science questions explain the relationship between imagery and sound.

The application supports keyboard operation, audio-only viewing, high contrast, frozen visual motion, and adjustable sound layers. Users can save bookmarks and export screenshots, comparison reports, audio snapshots, and video postcards.

Tools and implementation

EarthEcho uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript modules, Canvas, Web Audio, browser speech synthesis, MediaRecorder, and a service worker for optional offline caching. Node.js provides the local demonstration server. NASA media assets are bundled with the project.

Scientific considerations

Rendered colors provide approximate estimates, affected by lighting, compression, perspective, and masking. Matching-pixel coverage represents a visualization proxy rather than counted GEDI observations. Screen selections do not track fixed geographic plots, and the sequence reveals observation coverage rather than forest growth.

Intended impact

EarthEcho aims to make Earth science more engaging through combined visual, auditory, and textual exploration. Testing with intended users remains necessary to evaluate accessibility and learning benefits

projectDetails.name: Project ASTERA-X
projectDetails.summary:
ASTERA is a space exploration and learning platform that I developed to tell the stories of human-made equipment left behind during space missions. Inspired by NASA's “Abandoned but not Forgotten” challenge, the project focuses on preserving the history of these objects and helping people understand why they were sent, what they accomplished, and what remains of them today.

Through ASTERA, users can explore an interactive 3D solar system, discover historic Moon and Mars missions, learn about spacecraft and scientific equipment, and understand what happened to them after their missions ended. I have also incorporated educational content, mission timelines, planetary exploration views, and interactive simulations to make learning more engaging.

I wanted to build ASTERA because space exploration is not just about successful launches or major discoveries. Every mission leaves behind a story, whether it is a rover that completed its journey, equipment that continues to travel through space, or scientific instruments that helped us understand another world. ASTERA brings these stories together in one place and makes them easier for students and space enthusiasts to discover and appreciate.
projectDetails.details:
ASTERA — Every Mission Leaves a Mark

ASTERA is an interactive space exploration and educational platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, inspired by the challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars.” The project focuses on documenting the stories of human-made spacecraft, landers, rovers, scientific instruments, and other mission equipment that remain on the Moon, Mars, or continue travelling through space.

What does the project do, and how does it work?

ASTERA brings space mission information together in an interactive digital archive. Users can explore a stylized 3D solar system, discover historical space missions, learn about equipment left behind after mission completion, and understand the purpose and contributions of these objects.

The platform includes a searchable mission archive, individual mission information pages, mission timelines, a schematic Moon and Mars exploration atlas, and interactive educational features. It also provides a Space Academy for learning, an educational mission calculator, and a simulated science workbench.

A key aspect of ASTERA is its approach to mission lifecycle classification. Instead of treating every inactive spacecraft as abandoned, the platform distinguishes between equipment remaining on planetary surfaces, spacecraft still travelling through space, decommissioned or inactive hardware, and missions that ended through loss of contact or impact. This helps users understand what actually happened to each mission asset.

What benefits does it offer?

ASTERA makes space exploration history more accessible and engaging. Information about historic missions and their equipment is often spread across different scientific archives and mission websites. ASTERA provides a more approachable way to discover these stories in one place.

Its interactive visualizations and educational activities help students, educators, and space enthusiasts understand complex space missions without needing advanced technical knowledge. It also encourages curiosity about planetary exploration, space science, engineering, and the long-term legacy of human exploration.

What is the intended impact?

The main goal of ASTERA is to preserve the history and significance of human-made objects beyond Earth. Space missions are usually remembered for their launches, discoveries, and achievements, but the equipment that remains after a mission also represents an important part of that history.

Through ASTERA, I want to encourage people to look beyond mission success and understand the scientific, technological, and historical value of these objects. The project aims to make space heritage easier to explore, support space education, and inspire students to learn more about humanity's exploration of the solar system.

What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software were used?

The project was developed using the following technologies:

  • Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS.
  • 3D visualization: Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Drei.
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI.
  • Database: PostgreSQL with pgvector.
  • Additional services: Redis.
  • Mobile development: React Native and Expo.
  • Data and infrastructure: SQLAlchemy, Alembic, and Docker.

For research and mission information, I used NASA and NSSDCA resources, including official mission pages and the supplementary catalogue of human-made material on the Moon. The platform includes a source registry and a NASA page retrieval workflow, with extracted information intended for human review.

How is the project creative and innovative?

The creative aspect of ASTERA is the way it transforms space mission records into an exploratory experience. Rather than presenting information only through conventional articles or tables, it allows users to navigate a stylized 3D solar system and discover the stories of mission equipment through interactive visual elements.

I also wanted to make the experience meaningful beyond visual exploration. The mission archive, lifecycle classifications, educational activities, timelines, and simulations connect the historical, scientific, and educational aspects of space exploration.

The central idea behind ASTERA is that a mission does not lose its significance when communication ends or its hardware stops functioning. Every piece of equipment has a story, and those stories deserve to be documented.

What factors were considered during development?

I considered several factors while designing and developing ASTERA:

  1. Scientific accuracy: Mission information should be based on NASA and NSSDCA references. Unverified details should not be presented as established facts.
  2. Correct lifecycle classification: Surface equipment, inactive spacecraft, travelling probes, and crashed or lost hardware should not all be labelled as abandoned.
  3. Accessibility: The platform should make technical space exploration information understandable to students and general audiences.
  4. User experience: Navigation, visualizations, and learning features should make exploration engaging without overwhelming users.
  5. Data transparency: The distinction between sourced mission information, educational simulations, and illustrative visualizations should remain clear.
  6. Scalability: The architecture should support adding more missions, artifacts, scientific references, and educational features over time.
  7. Responsible representation: ASTERA is an independent educational project and does not claim NASA endorsement or represent its visual simulations as official NASA data.

Ultimately, ASTERA was built around one simple idea: Every mission leaves a mark, and every mark has a story worth remembering.

projectDetails.name: LunaSight — Lunar Landing Site Navigator
projectDetails.summary:
LunaSight is an open-source, interactive web application engineered to solve the complex lighting and communication constraints of missions targeting the Moon’s south pole. Mission planners, educators, and the public can rapidly compare 44+ curated landing sites (including Artemis candidate sites, CLPS targets, Apollo landmarks, and international missions) or any custom lunar coordinates across arbitrary mission epochs.

Powered by sub-arcminute analytical ephemeris and high-resolution LOLA lunar topographic horizon modeling, LunaSight visualizes real-time Sun and Earth azimuth-elevation paths, 360-degree lunar horizon panoramas with local terrain masking, and solar power flux efficiency. An automated Launch Window Finder ranks optimal landing windows based on simultaneous sunlight availability and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) line-of-sight communication. 

By bridging the gap between raw planetary ephemerides and agile decision-making, LunaSight accelerates mission trade-off studies when launch dates shift or hardware constraints evolve.
projectDetails.details:
LunaSight evaluates lunar landing site viability through an integrated browser-based suite:

1. High-Precision Ephemeris Engine: Implements Meeus and Brown-Chapront lunar and solar analytical ephemeris models verified against NASA JPL Horizons vectors (sub-arcminute accuracy), computing topocentric Sun and Earth azimuths, elevations, lunar librations, sub-solar/sub-Earth latitudes, and lunar phases.

2. Topographic Horizon Masking: Integrates LOLA (Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter) elevation profiles to project true 360-degree local terrain horizons, accurately identifying when mountain ridges block sunlight or Direct-to-Earth communication links.

3. Multi-Site Side-by-Side Comparator: Allows simultaneous evaluation of up to 4 sites across custom mission time windows (from 1 to 30 lunar days).

4. Automated Window Finder: Algorithms scan time horizons at selectable intervals (1 hr to 1 day) to score and rank optimal landing epochs based on minimum continuous sunlight and unobstructed Earth elevation.

5. Deep-Linkable Scenario URLs: All selected sites, coordinate overrides, mission epochs, and UI display preferences serialize directly into URL fragment hashes, enabling instant collaboration between distributed engineering teams.

- Benefits: Replaces tedious multi-tool data workflows (navigating JPL Horizons CLI, Moon Trek, and QuickMap separately) with a single, responsive cockpit that renders comparisons in seconds.

- Mission Impact: When launch delays occur or payload landing parameters change, mission planners and CLPS commercial providers can instantly determine whether alternative landing sites offer viable power and communication windows without having to regenerate complex orbital ephemeris scripts.

- Educational Impact: Provides educators and STEM students with an intuitive, visually engaging portal to explore real lunar polar geometry, crater shadows, and orbital mechanics.

- AI, Agentic Development & Intelligence Platforms:

• Google Antigravity: Multi-agent orchestration, automated testing workflows, and rapid system synthesis platform.

• Google Gemini & Anthropic Claude: Advanced reasoning models utilized for mathematical validation of ephemeris equations, algorithm optimization for window searches, and documentation architecture.

• Carbon: Elegant code snippet visualization, documentation asset creation, and technical showcase rendering.

- Version Control, CI/CD & Cloud Infrastructure:

• GitHub & GitHub Actions: Git source code management, automated continuous integration (CI) test workflows, and static deployment pipelines.

• GitHub Pages: Edge-hosted static PWA distribution platform.

• Vercel: Serverless API execution runtime with dynamic Gzip compression, HTTP ETag caching, and CORS handling.

- Languages & Runtimes:

• Modern JavaScript (ES Modules, ES2022+), Node.js (v20+ LTS engine), semantic HTML5, and CSS3 with responsive custom design tokens and media queries.

- Web & Visualization Frameworks:

• HTML5 Canvas 2D API: High-performance 360-degree local terrain horizon projection and lunar south pole stereographic radar map.

• Chart.js: Dynamic multi-series elevation, line-of-sight, and solar flux timelines.

• Lucide Icons: Accessible, lightweight SVG icon system.

- Astronomical & Data Libraries:

• Astronomy Engine (Don Cross, MIT): Rigorous topocentric ephemeris cross-verification against NASA JPL Horizons vectors.

• NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) & LOLA Altimetry: High-resolution lunar digital elevation models.

• NASA APOD API: Live space imagery data feed.

- Testing, Quality Assurance & Security:

• Node.js Native Test Runner (`node --test`), automated syntax checkers, strict Content Security Policies (CSP), and a comprehensive 20/20 passing test suite.

projectDetails.summary:
Here is your **Project Summary** tailored for the NASA Space Apps submission form (178 words, within the recommended 50–200 word limit):

---

**Sol Survivor** is an AI-powered Mars mission digital twin, closed-loop survival simulator, and interactive Space Academy engineered for students aged 8 to 16. Developing a full-stack flight control center with Python, Django, and HTML5 Canvas, we placed learners into the seat of a NASA Flight Director managing seven interdependent life-support subsystems—including MOXIE oxygen generation, hydroponics, and thermal grids—alongside eight physics-driven educational mini-games.

The platform directly addresses the challenge by transforming complex aerospace engineering, astrodynamics, and planetary science into an intuitive, cause-and-effect learning experience. Grounding its diurnal cycles and environmental crises in authentic NASA telemetry from the Perseverance MEDA, Curiosity REMS, and MOXIE missions, Sol Survivor demystifies space science through age-adaptive cognitive calibration and an onboard AI Flight Copilot.

Sol Survivor is important because it inspires the Artemis and Mars generation through "Stealth Learning." By navigating cascading thermodynamic failures and extreme resource scarcity on the Red Planet, young minds develop critical systems-thinking skills and a profound appreciation for closed-loop sustainability, renewable energy, and ecological stewardship on our home planet Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Sol Survivor is an educational, turn-based Mars habitat simulator, interactive digital twin, and virtual space academy engineered specifically for students aged eight to sixteen. Created for the NASA International Space Apps Challenge, the project transforms complex aerospace engineering, planetary meteorology, orbital mechanics, and closed-loop life-support physics into an immersive, narrative-driven space exploration command center. Rather than approaching science education through passive reading or abstract problem sets, Sol Survivor immerses students directly into the high-stakes role of a Mars Mission Flight Director. Players assume command of an operational Martian surface outpost, navigating environmental hazards, balancing delicate life-support thermodynamics, deploying exploration rovers, and resolving compounding mechanical emergencies across four escalating mission tiers. The application integrates two seamlessly connected educational platforms within a unified software ecosystem: a turn-based Mars Mission Control digital twin and the NASA Space Academy, an interactive flight school featuring eight fully playable, physics-driven educational mini-games. Supported by an atmospheric outer-space aesthetic, authentic procedural audio synthesis, and real planetary telemetry from NASA robotic missions, Sol Survivor provides an engaging, scientifically rigorous entry point into humanity’s next giant leap.

1. What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

Sol Survivor operates as a turn-based simulation engine where each turn corresponds to one Martian Sol. The core engine models seven interdependent environmental subsystems: the primary electrical power grid, solid-oxide electrolysis oxygen production, hydroponic food biomass, closed-loop water reclamation, thermal regulation, active magnetic radiation shielding, and structural habitat integrity. In the Martian environment, no subsystem functions in isolation; resource generation and consumption operate under strict physical trade-offs. For example, overcharging the Mars Oxygen ISRU Experiment (MOXIE) replenishes breathable air for the habitat crew, but demands a massive draw from the primary electrical bus that can leave thermal heating elements underpowered during the freezing Martian night.

The engine introduces realistic cascading failures to teach students the critical importance of systems engineering. If a cadet opts to dim habitat heaters to preserve battery storage during a regional dust squall, the immediate power surge prevents a total blackout; however, if heating coils remain unpowered for two consecutive Sols, sub-zero ambient temperatures cause water reclamation pipes to freeze, triggering a pipe rupture that immediately destroys thirty-five percent of the habitat's hydroponic crops. The game progresses across four escalating operational tiers: Level 1 (Touchdown) introduces basic diurnal energy cycles; Level 2 (Red Dust) incorporates atmospheric dust squalls modeled after empirical Martian optical depth dynamics; Level 3 (Solar Storm) unleashes Coronal Mass Ejections that bombard surface assets with dangerous radiation doses; and Level 4 (Apocalypse Protocol) challenges advanced students with multiple simultaneous system failures. An interactive Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) digital twin of the habitat serves as the central visual schematic, dynamically pulsing amber and red as individual modules incur stress. By clicking on any habitat component, students can inspect live telemetry, power routing diagrams, and authentic engineering schematics of the underlying NASA hardware.

To assist young flight directors through these engineering crises, Sol Survivor incorporates the Houston AI Flight Copilot. Functioning as a virtual flight director, the Copilot analyzes current environmental parameters and active crises by executing a forward simulation tree. It evaluates all candidate actions one Sol in advance, calculating risk scores, highlighting trade-offs, and recommending the safest course of action accompanied by clear pros-and-cons comparisons. Crucially, the AI Copilot operates via a deterministic, rule-based expert system that runs entirely offline without requiring external API keys, while also supporting optional Large Language Model integrations for natural language flight advisory chats. Complementing this advisory system is a predictive survival analytics suite powered by Chart.js graphs, which visually projects resource depletion curves three to five Sols into the future, enabling cadets to identify life-support bottlenecks before they reach catastrophic failure thresholds.

Alongside Mission Control, the NASA Space Academy provides eight interactive physics mini-games: Planet Explorer (ordering the eight planets and comparing planetary atmospheres), Zero Gravity Challenge (navigating a spacewalking astronaut with nitrogen thrusters according to Newton’s First Law), Rocket Builder (balancing staging, engines, and Thrust-to-Weight Ratio to achieve orbital velocity), Mars Rover Adventure (driving the Perseverance rover across Jezero Crater to collect rock samples with authentic rocker-bogie suspension), Asteroid Defender (launching kinetic impactors to alter asteroid trajectories, inspired by NASA's DART mission), Save The Astronaut (solving environmental life-support emergencies involving CO2 scrubbers and hull breaches), Gravity & Orbit Lab (adjusting velocity and altitude to visualize circular, elliptical, and escape Keplerian orbits), and Space Quiz Battle (a timed trivia arena covering universe IQ and spaceflight history).

2. What Benefits Does It Have?

Sol Survivor delivers deep educational value through "Stealth Learning"—the pedagogical principle that deep, lasting comprehension occurs when learners are actively immersed in problem-solving rather than memorizing isolated formulas. By placing scientific phenomena directly into the context of Mars exploration, abstract principles such as electrolysis, the Beer-Lambert law of atmospheric extinction, Keplerian orbital mechanics, and thermal dissipation become intuitive, practical tools for survival.

The platform provides a dynamic three-tier age calibration system: Junior Cadet (ages 8–10), Flight Specialist (ages 11–13), and Mission Commander (ages 14–16). Younger players receive simplified language, forgiving timers, and plain-English button subtitles like "Make Breathing Air" and "Save Battery Power." Older students experience full technical realism, quantitative equations, Astronomical Units, and unassisted life-support telemetry. This adaptive approach ensures that younger children are not intimidated, while older teenagers are intellectually challenged by genuine engineering trade-offs.

Furthermore, Sol Survivor features a comprehensive, exploit-resistant gamification architecture. Cadets earn experience points (XP) synchronized between Mission Control and the Space Academy, unlocking nine NASA STEM achievement badges, daily flight challenges, personal best tracking, and a printable Junior Commander Certificate of Completion complete with an automated cryptographic verification hash and a dynamic QR code. Built as a Progressive Web App (PWA) with zero mandatory installation or sign-up hurdles, it features an instant One-Click Guest Launch, making it accessible to any classroom or competition judge within seconds.

3. What Is the Intended Impact of the Project?

The primary impact of Sol Survivor is democratizing hands-on aerospace and planetary science education for students worldwide. Many schools lack specialized aerospace curricula or laboratory equipment; Sol Survivor bridges this gap by turning any standard web browser, Chromebook, tablet, or smartphone into a functional NASA mission control terminal. It connects NASA’s flagship missions—such as Artemis, Perseverance, and DART—directly to everyday learners, demystifying space technology and inspiring underrepresented youth to pursue careers in STEM, computer science, and engineering.

Equally important is the project's contribution to environmental stewardship. Living on Mars requires an absolute circular economy where water is perpetually recycled, carbon dioxide is scrubbed, and every watt of solar power is accounted for. By experiencing firsthand how fragile closed-loop life support is on the Red Planet, students develop a profound respect for Earth's ecological systems, gaining an intuitive appreciation for renewable energy, resource conservation, and terrestrial climate resilience.

4. Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, and Software Used

Sol Survivor is built upon a robust, scalable full-stack software architecture engineered for cross-platform responsiveness and reliability. The backend is powered by Python 3.10+ and the Django 6.0 web framework, which enforces server-side game state integrity, handles session authentication, processes deterministic turn-based state machines, and manages a relational SQLite database. The database records comprehensive session profiles, student quiz attempts, and immutable step-by-step replay logs that store complete resource states before and after every single Sol action, providing students and educators with an exhaustive post-mission flight telemetry record for retrospectives.

The frontend presentation tier is crafted using semantic HTML5, CSS3, and Tailwind CSS, styled to evoke the sleek aesthetic of a modern space agency operations console. High-performance interactive elements—including the gravity sandbox, the lunar/Martian rover driving terrain, the microgravity spacewalk simulation, and the animated cosmic starfield—are rendered directly via the HTML5 2D Canvas API without reliance on heavy third-party gaming frameworks. Data visualization is powered by Chart.js, rendering multi-series forecasting graphs with dynamic color-coded safety thresholds.

Procedural auditory synthesis is accomplished through the browser-native Web Audio API, which generates real-time audio oscillations for Martian wind drones, two-tone emergency sirens, and Geiger counter clicks directly in memory without streaming heavy audio assets. The Web Speech API provides synthesized voice comms from Houston Flight Control, while Service Workers (sw.js) and a Web App Manifest (manifest.json) enable Progressive Web App offline caching. Rather than relying on static or synthetic background data, the system incorporates a dedicated NASA Data Center that integrates curated archives from the Mars Science Laboratory Curiosity Rover Environmental Monitoring Station (REMS), the Mars 2020 Perseverance Rover Environmental Dynamics Analyzer (MEDA), the NASA Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, and Information (DONKI), and Planetary Data System (PDS) benchmarks for MOXIE. Deployment and public access are facilitated through automated Cloudflare edge tunnels, providing global SSL/TLS encryption.

5. How Is Your Project Creative?

Sol Survivor demonstrates exceptional creativity through its dual-engine synergy, sensory immersion, and adaptive interface design:

First, it unites a serious closed-loop survival digital twin with an accessible physics arcade, sharing unified XP, ranks, and achievements between both worlds. Second, rather than relying on static, looping sound files, the application uses real-time Web Audio mathematical oscillators to synthesize procedural Martian wind that dynamically alters pitch based on atmospheric dust opacity (tau), alongside authentic emergency klaxons and synthesized voice radio communications from Houston.

Third, crises emerge naturally through thermodynamics rather than arbitrary random penalties; neglecting thermal coils causes water pipes to physically freeze, and dust storms attenuate photovoltaic output according to the Beer-Lambert law (I=I0e−τ/cos⁡θI = I_0 e^{-\tau / \cos\theta}I=I0​e−τ/cosθ), requiring robotic rover dust-brushing sorties. Fourth, the "Stealth Subtitles" system creatively bridges age demographics: an eight-year-old child and a sixteen-year-old high schooler can play the exact same simulation side-by-side, with the younger seeing intuitive labels like "Make Breathing Air" while the older sees "SOEC Electrolysis (12g/h)." Finally, the interactive SVG habitat turns passive graphics into an active technical blueprint, allowing students to click any module to inspect authentic NASA engineering schematics.

6. What Factors Did Your Team Consider?

Throughout development, our team prioritized five core non-functional requirements to ensure the platform’s accessibility, robustness, and ethical integrity:

  1. Scientific Accuracy vs. Cognitive Playability: A fundamental engineering challenge was balancing physical fidelity with child-friendly gameplay. Modeling exact partial differential equations for fluid dynamics or thermal radiation would quickly alienate an eight-year-old. Our team resolved this by preserving accurate scientific relationships under the hood—such as modeling solar flux attenuation via the Beer-Lambert law and orbital periods via Keplerian dynamics—while expressing these systems through intuitive visual gauges, percentage thresholds, and immediate cause-and-effect feedback.
  2. Universal Accessibility and Inclusivity: We recognized that visual motion can trigger discomfort in users with vestibular sensitivity. To address this, Sol Survivor includes a prominent Reduced-Motion toggle (✨ MOTION: [ON/OFF]) that instantly halts starfield drifts, spinning galaxies, and pulsing glows, defaulting to a tranquil static starry backdrop while maintaining full functional readability. The color palette adheres to high-contrast WCAG guidelines, and all touch controls are optimized for mobile screens.
  3. Graceful Offline Fallback and Zero-Key Reliability: Web-based hackathon applications frequently break during judging when third-party cloud APIs fail or exhaust billing quotas. Sol Survivor was engineered with zero external dependencies. The core game engine, the AI Flight Copilot, the predictive analytics, and all eight Space Academy mini-games operate completely autonomously offline on the local Django server, ensuring seamless reliability under any evaluation conditions.
  4. Data Privacy and Child Safety: Designed for elementary and secondary school students, Sol Survivor strictly adheres to modern child data protection standards. No personally identifiable information (PII), email addresses, or social logins are collected. Cadets authenticate using lighthearted astronaut callsigns and simple four-digit clearance PINs stored in localized session tables, accompanied by an instant one-click guest bypass.
  5. Data Provenance Ethics: We strictly adhered to NASA guidelines by never fabricating synthetic values as "real telemetry." Every piece of space weather data is labeled with its exact instrument, Martian Sol, terrestrial date, and source classification (OBSERVED, DERIVED, or SIMULATED).

projectDetails.name: Mangalverse
projectDetails.summary:
The 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge focuses on using science and technology to address real challenges in understanding and exploring space. MARS EXPLORER addresses the challenge of making complex, scattered Mars exploration data easier to access, understand, and use.

Scientific information about Mars including terrain elevation, geological formations, environmental conditions, and rover exploration history comes from different datasets and sources. Understanding how these elements relate to one another can be difficult, especially for students, educators, and people without specialized scientific tools.

We developed an interactive exploration platform focused on Jezero Crater that brings authentic NASA and USGS data together in one place. It allows users to investigate geological features, explore scientific discoveries, examine terrain conditions, visualize the Perseverance rover's traverse, and compare terrain-aware routes.

By connecting diverse scientific datasets through an accessible, interactive experience, MARS EXPLORER helps bridge the gap between raw planetary data and meaningful exploration. It makes Mars science easier to understand while encouraging curiosity, discovery, and informed exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview

What it does

MARS EXPLORER transforms authentic NASA and USGS planetary datasets into an interactive, objective-driven exploration and mission-planning platform focused on Jezero Crater, Mars. It enables users to select scientific objectives, investigate rover discoveries, explore geological formations, examine terrain and historical environmental conditions, and generate terrain-aware rover routes. By incorporating elevation, slope constraints, distance, and sand-hazard avoidance, the platform offers three route strategies: shortest, safest, and balanced. Its Explorer Mode features ARES, a virtual exploration companion that provides contextual explanations and guides users through locations and waypoints, creating a more immersive and accessible way to investigate Mars.

Benefits and intended impact

The project bridges the gap between complex planetary science data and meaningful exploration. It makes Mars research more accessible to students, educators, researchers, and space enthusiasts while demonstrating how scientific priorities, terrain characteristics, and environmental context can inform robotic exploration. Its terrain-aware route analysis provides an experimental decision-support approach for evaluating potential rover paths. Ultimately, MARS EXPLORER aims to turn fragmented scientific information into a connected exploration experience, encouraging scientific curiosity and supporting a deeper understanding of the Martian environment.

Technology

The backend is powered by Python and FastAPI, with Rasterio and NumPy for geospatial data processing, SQLite for scientific records, and terrain-aware A* pathfinding for route generation. The frontend combines React and JavaScript with Leaflet for interactive planetary mapping, Tailwind CSS for interface design, Vite for development and builds, SVG-based visualizations, and browser speech synthesis for guided narration. Designed to run through ordinary laptops and web browsers, the platform makes advanced geospatial exploration accessible without requiring specialized hardware.

Creativity, innovation and considerations

MARS EXPLORER brings together two complementary experiences: a tactical Mission Control interface for objective-driven exploration and a narrative Explorer Mode that makes scientific investigation more engaging through ARES. Its distinctive strength lies in integrating real mission-derived datasets with interactive geological exploration and terrain-aware route analysis. Scientific provenance, coordinate accuracy, terrain coverage limitations, rover safety constraints, accessibility, and uncertainty are treated as essential considerations rather than afterthoughts. The platform also distinguishes project-generated analyses from certified mission decisions, reinforcing a responsible approach to using planetary science data.

projectDetails.name: Mission-Architect
projectDetails.summary:
Mission Architect is a free, browser-based game, in which everyone may design, launch and run an entire space mission without needing to sign up or download anything. Users pick a scenario, then create their spaceship, instruments, orbit and launch vehicle, and ground communications. Real-time dashboard measures mass, power, budget, data, communications and time. After a review of the design, users launch their mission and get the simulation. Finally, they receive a report on whether their mission was successful or not.

The solution to this problem demonstrates how every decision leads to a consequence – adding a new instrument adds to power, data, mass and cost, and therefore, a bigger rocket is needed. Students form teams of up to four people and assume different roles to discuss these trade-offs.

It is important because designing a mission as a whole system is difficult to grasp for a beginner. This game allows students to see how real engineers solve these problems.
projectDetails.details:
Mission Architect is a web-based game, where the player designs and flies their space mission, using the same steps as NASA does. The player selects a mission scenario (CubeSat Earth observation, space telescope, lunar orbiter or Mars mission) and designs the spacecraft – bus, solar panels, batteries, antenna, attitude control and scientific payload. Then, the player selects the orbit and the launcher, and establishes the ground communications network. The dashboard shows the status of six resources – mass, power, budget, data, communications and time. The design review lists all the constraints the player violates – for instance, a battery too small to survive eclipse. Finally, the player launches and simulates the mission, which is impacted by some unpredictable events like solar flares or ground-station outage. The player receives the final score and a report of the success or failure reasons.

A rule engine ties all the subsystems together, so any change affects other subsystems. Adding an instrument means more power, data, mass and budget, leading to the need of a larger solar panel, heavier spacecraft and launcher. The game won't let the player to launch the mission if the spacecraft is too massive

Benefits

  • It is free, needs no install or login, and works on desktop and mobile.
  • Beginners can play with hints, while experienced players get tighter margins.
  • It explains why a decision works or fails, instead of only marking it right or wrong.
  • There is no single correct design, so players can try many solutions.

Intended impact

We want students and first-time learners to understand mission design as a connected system, so they see why real engineers constantly balance competing demands. It can be used in classrooms, clubs and outreach events, solo or in teams of up to four.

Tools and technology

  • Development: Google Antigravity
  • Frontend: [e.g. React, TypeScript, Vite]
  • 3D visualization: [e.g. three.js]
  • Team rooms: [e.g. Supabase or Firebase]
  • Hosting: [e.g. Netlify or Vercel]

projectDetails.name: FireChronicle | Harmonized MODIS–VIIRS Burning Calendar
projectDetails.summary: FireChronicle turns NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS hotspot observations into a burning activity calendar. Land managers, researchers, and emergency response teams can compare fire activity across sensor eras, identify unusually active months, and find recurring peak seasons. The long records for California and Assam span November 2000 to June 2026. Users can draw an area, trace trends back to archived detections, compare recent activity with the same dates in prior years, and export results. In California, calibration lowered mean absolute error from 1,271 to 414 active grid-cell days per month on held-out overlap years.
projectDetails.details:
What FireChronicle does

Satellite sensors see the same landscape at different resolutions and sensitivities. FireChronicle makes their hotspot records more comparable so land managers, researchers, and responders can investigate when activity tends to peak and which months are unusual. The long California and Assam records span November 2000 to June 2026. Thailand and the Laos study area offer shorter monthly records.

How we harmonize the records

The Python and DuckDB pipeline filters NASA FIRMS detections and aggregates unique active 1 km grid cells by UTC day. Overlapping Terra and Aqua detections count once per cell-day in the combined MODIS series. We calibrate eligible platforms against VIIRS Suomi-NPP using seasonal ratios learned from overlapping observations. The calendar distinguishes observed, calibrated, and unavailable months and provides the raw series for comparison.

How we tested it

We hold out each overlap year in turn and evaluate predictions against observed Suomi-NPP activity. MODIS mean absolute error fell from 1,271 to 414 active cell-days per month in California and from 593 to 137 in Assam across 157 overlap months per region. These tests cover years with both instruments operating. Estimates earlier in the archive remain uncertain, and hotspots measure detected activity, not incidents or burned area.

What users can do

The Next.js and TypeScript app uses MapLibre for the hotspot map and Apache ECharts for charts. Users can compare raw and harmonized calendars, see peak seasons and outliers, inspect archived points, draw an area for a local timeline in California or Assam, and compare a recent FIRMS snapshot with matching dates in previous years. The app exports CSV data and PNG calendars. Explicit gaps and provisional feed labels show where coverage limits a comparison.

AI/SI disclosure

OpenAI Codex assisted with planning, code, testing, and drafting the demo script and submission text. Microsoft Edge neural text-to-speech generated the English narration. The video shows captures of the working app and credits NASA FIRMS. Analytics are computed from the cited observed satellite data using the described pipeline.

projectDetails.name: Earth-Jukebox_Aura-X
projectDetails.summary: Earth Jukebox is a browser app that lets people hear NASA’s pictures of Earth. It takes visualizations from NASA’s Earth Information Center and Worldview and plays them as live music. A playhead sweeps across each image from west to east, reading it as eight horizontal bands: higher in the picture is a higher note, brighter is louder, and warmer colour sounds brighter, with notes kept inside a chosen musical scale. A 3D globe turns under the playhead while eight spikes show each band’s loudness, and a flat map offers the same information. Thirteen tracks cover phenomena such as ocean currents, aerosols, carbon dioxide, night lights and forest height, and NASA’s Caldwell 73 serves as a listening reference. Extras: touch-to-hear probe, guided tour, WAV export. It runs locally in the browser with no logins or API keys, supports keyboard use, screen-reader announcements and reduced motion, and credits every NASA source on screen. The sound comes from the colour and brightness of rendered images
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES:

Earth Jukebox lets people hear NASA's pictures of Earth. It plays visualizations from NASA's Earth Information Center and Worldview as live music in the browser. A playhead sweeps across the image and reads it as eight horizontal bands: higher in the picture is a higher note, brighter is louder, warmer color sounds brighter. Notes stay inside a musical scale. A 3D globe turns under the playhead, and a flat map shows the same information.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT:

NASA's Earth visuals leave out blind and low-vision people. Earth Jukebox gives them, and anyone who learns by listening, another way to explore oceans, air, forests and city lights, and works as a classroom and outreach tool.

TOOLS:

React, Vite, JavaScript, Three.js and the Web Audio API. Free tools only, running in the browser with no logins or API keys. NASA media is downloaded ahead of time. Parts of the code were written with AI assistance (Claude, Google Antigravity) and reviewed by the team.

CREATIVITY:

The picture is the score: you watch a planet turn under a playhead and hear what you see. The team chose the mapping, scales and looks.

FACTORS CONSIDERED:

The sound comes from colour and brightness in NASA's rendered images, not raw measurements, and the app says so. Globe view is only used for full-world flat maps. Keyboard, screen-reader and reduced-motion support. Every NASA source is credited on screen.

projectDetails.summary:
**ORBITERRA ATLAS – From Space to the Soil**

ORBITERRA ATLAS is an Earth observation and agricultural decision-support platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It focuses on the Northern Transition Zone of Karnataka, India, bringing Earth data, climate information and crop-water scenario analysis into one workspace.

The platform includes an interactive dashboard for exploring environmental conditions, a Crop Resilience & Scenario Lab for comparing crop water requirements, and an ORBITERRA AI section for agricultural decision support. Its scenario modelling allows users to examine how rainfall, evapotranspiration, soil-water storage, crop coefficients and irrigation influence the soil-water balance.

ORBITERRA ATLAS addresses the challenge by making Earth and climate information easier to understand and explore in an agricultural context. It is important because changing rainfall patterns and limited water availability make crop planning increasingly difficult. By helping users explore crop-water scenarios and understand environmental conditions, the platform aims to support more informed and climate-resilient agricultural decisions.
projectDetails.details:
ORBITERRA ATLAS – From Space to the Soil

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

ORBITERRA ATLAS is an Earth observation and agricultural decision-support platform designed for the Northern Transition Zone of Karnataka, India. It brings environmental information, climate conditions and crop-water scenario analysis into one digital workspace.

The application has five main navigation areas: Home, Dashboard, Crop Resilience Analysis, ORBITERRA AI, and Data & Methodology.

The Dashboard provides an overview of environmental conditions and satellite-informed soil-moisture estimates. The Crop Resilience & Scenario Lab allows users to explore different crop-water scenarios by adjusting parameters such as initial soil-water storage, soil-water capacity, rainfall, reference evapotranspiration, crop coefficients, irrigation and scenario duration.

The model uses these inputs to explore how water availability changes under different conditions, helping users understand potential agricultural challenges.

2. What are the benefits?

  • Brings Earth observation, climate and agricultural information together.
  • Helps users understand crop-water requirements.
  • Allows comparison of different rainfall and irrigation scenarios.
  • Makes environmental and agricultural concepts easier to explore.
  • Encourages informed water-management and crop-planning decisions.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our aim is to support more climate-resilient agriculture by making environmental information understandable and useful for agricultural planning. ORBITERRA ATLAS can help farmers, students and agricultural researchers explore how changing rainfall and water availability may affect crop decisions.

In the future, the platform can be expanded with locally validated agricultural information and stronger decision-support capabilities.

4. What tools and technologies were used?

  • Programming language: Python.
  • Application framework: Streamlit.
  • Deployment: Streamlit Community Cloud.
  • Software: Visual Studio Code and web-based development tools.
  • Application components: Interactive dashboards, user-adjustable scenario inputs, charts and analytical visualisations.
  • Hardware: A standard computer and internet connection for development and access.

No specialised agricultural hardware or field sensors are required for the current software prototype.

5. What makes the project creative?

The creative aspect of ORBITERRA ATLAS is its approach of connecting information from Earth observation and climate science with a practical crop-water scenario explorer.

Instead of simply displaying environmental information, the platform allows users to experiment with different conditions and understand how rainfall, evapotranspiration, soil-water storage and irrigation influence agricultural water availability.

Its central concept is to translate complex environmental information into an accessible agricultural decision-support experience.

6. What factors did the team consider?

The project focuses on the Northern Transition Zone of Karnataka and considers:

  • Regional climate and rainfall variability.
  • Soil-water storage and water-holding capacity.
  • Crop water requirements and crop coefficients.
  • Reference evapotranspiration.
  • Irrigation availability and water-management scenarios.
  • The importance of clear data sources and transparent assumptions.
  • The need for local agricultural validation before using model outputs for actual farm decisions.

The current Crop Resilience Lab clearly identifies its default rainfall, evapotranspiration and crop-coefficient profiles as illustrative inputs rather than verified local farm observations.

ORBITERRA ATLAS aims to turn Earth data into understandable agricultural insights and encourage smarter, more resilient crop-water planning.

projectDetails.name: MODIS–VIIRS Hotspot Harmonization Platform
projectDetails.summary: Our project, built by Team BlackCat, is a web application that harmonizes active-fire hotspot records from two NASA satellite sensors — MODIS and VIIRS — into one unified, analyzable record of burning activity. The two sensors differ in spatial resolution, confidence reporting, and overpass times, so their data cannot be compared directly. Our platform ingests NASA FIRMS observations from both sensors, preserves every original record, and maps them into a common schema. It then links candidate cross-sensor detections of the same burning, groups related observations into candidate clusters with DBSCAN, flags statistically unusual activity with Isolation Forest, and presents the result as an interactive burning activity calendar, fire map, and intelligence dashboard. By turning fragmented sensor records into a consistent historical picture, the platform helps early warning and emergency responders, scientists, land managers, and firefighters examine fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

The platform takes active-fire hotspot observations recorded by two different NASA satellite instruments — MODIS (aboard Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS (aboard Suomi NPP) — and harmonizes them into a single, consistent burning activity picture. Instead of being just another map of raw hotspots, its core is an intelligence pipeline that finds relationships between the two sensors' records, groups related observations, and identifies statistically unusual burning activity, all presented through a burning activity calendar, an interactive fire map, and an intelligence dashboard.

How it works

1. Ingestion — NASA FIRMS observations are loaded from archive files (CSV or GeoJSON) or, by design, from the FIRMS area API. Every original record and its sensor-specific fields are preserved.

2. Validation and harmonization — Records are normalized into one unified schema: latitude/longitude, UTC observation datetime, sensor, satellite, fire radiative power (FRP), day/night flag, and a documented harmonized confidence scale that maps MODIS percentage confidence and VIIRS low/nominal/high categories onto a common ordinal scale without hiding the original values or the sensors' differences.

3. Cross-sensor candidate matching — A MODIS and a VIIRS observation within 1.5 km and 3 hours of each other are recorded as a candidate link: a possible co-detection of the same burning. Both original observations are always kept; nothing is merged away or deleted.

4. DBSCAN clustering — Observations are grouped per UTC day using DBSCAN with a haversine distance metric (eps 2.5 km, min_samples 3), producing candidate activity clusters. Clusters that contain observations from both sensors are highlighted — they are the strongest evidence that the harmonization is working.

5. Isolation Forest anomaly detection — Observations are aggregated to 0.25° grid cells per day (observation count, mean and maximum FRP, VIIRS share, night share). An Isolation Forest model flags statistically unusual grid-days, and every flag carries a plain-language, percentile-based explanation.

6. Burning activity calendar and insights — Daily, per-sensor activity is shown as a calendar heatmap and charts, and a set of insights is generated from the computed results only — totals, mixed-sensor cluster counts, peak activity day, and unusual periods.

7. Area selection and export — On the fire map, users filter by date range, sensor, and a latitude/longitude area of interest, and can download the hotspot rows matching their search as a CSV file (in addition to a regional summary report).

Demonstrated results (bundled demo dataset)

Our submitted demo runs on real archived NASA FIRMS data — not simulated data — for a selected area of interest in the Chhattisgarh–Odisha fire belt, India (longitude 80.5–83.5 E, latitude 20–23 N), covering 2025-02-01 to 2025-04-30:

- 30,951 harmonized observations (MODIS 2,440 · VIIRS S-NPP 28,511)

- 3,262 cross-sensor candidate links

- 2,944 candidate clusters, of which 906 contain observations from both sensors

- 301 anomalous grid-days flagged with explanations

- Peak activity day: 2025-03-06, with 2,061 observations

Benefits and what we hope to achieve

Fire managers today must work with fragmented records that cannot be compared directly across sensors. Our platform gives early warning and emergency responders, scientists, land managers, and firefighters one consistent historical record for a selected area of interest, so they can examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods — for example, spotting the days and places where burning activity was statistically exceptional during a fire season. This matters now because MODIS, aboard Terra and Aqua, is approaching the end of its operational life after more than two decades of observations, while VIIRS provides the continuing record at finer spatial resolution — a harmonized series is the only way the long MODIS archive and the VIIRS era can be read as one consistent history. We hope to show that scientifically careful multi-sensor harmonization, combined with transparent machine learning, can turn two incompatible satellite archives into a single trustworthy picture of burning activity, and that this approach can be extended to more regions, more seasons, and live data.

Tools, languages and software used

Frontend: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, React Leaflet (Leaflet / OpenStreetMap), Recharts

Backend: Python, FastAPI, pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn (DBSCAN, Isolation Forest)

Database: SQLite

Data formats: CSV, GeoJSON

Development: Git/GitHub, VS Code, pytest automated tests (17 backend tests)

Scientific honesty — the limits we state openly

- Satellite hotspots are detected thermal anomalies, not confirmed ground-truth wildfires.

- A DBSCAN cluster is a group of candidate related observations, not one confirmed wildfire, and a candidate link is a possible co-detection, not a proven duplicate.

- An anomaly is a statistically unusual grid-cell day within this dataset — it is not a new fire and not a prediction of future fires.

- MODIS and VIIRS have different spatial resolutions and sensor characteristics; we preserve and surface those differences rather than pretending the datasets are identical.

projectDetails.name: HydroWaltz: NASA NISAR 3D Hydrological Digital Twin & Deep Polarimetric Intelligence
projectDetails.summary:
During intense monsoon surges across the Brahmaputra River Basin in Assam, India, optical Earth-observation satellites are blinded by perpetual storm clouds. HydroWaltz leverages penetrating L-band (24 cm) Synthetic Aperture Radar from the joint NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission to peer through cloud cover and track sub-surface hydrological change at centimeter resolution.

Our project addresses the "Dancing with the SARs" challenge by resolving a notorious radar paradox: the 99.8% Transitional Fringe Illusion. By pairing dual-polarization (HH/HV) threshold sweeps with a 20-pixel spatial-shift null test and Dual-Pol Radar Vegetation Index (DpRVI) physics, HydroWaltz proves that while headline flood water fluctuated by -4.15 km², the core navigation thalweg remained dynamically invariant (-0.62 km², within null spread [-0.67, +0.02] km²).

HydroWaltz packages these discoveries into an interactive WebGL 3D Digital Twin featuring real-time river flow and erosion particle physics, coupled with an autonomous disaster response AI Copilot powered by NVIDIA NIM that synthesizes instant UN-SPIDER situation reports for humanitarian responders.
projectDetails.details:
### 1. What does it do and how does it work?

HydroWaltz is a spaceborne hydrological decision-support platform and 3D digital twin built on provisional Level-2 Ground Projected Covariance (GCOV) radar products from the joint NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission. Operating in L-band microwave radar (24 cm wavelength), it penetrates thick monsoon storm cloud cover over the Brahmaputra River Valley in Assam, India (Relative Orbit 91, Frame 76, common footprint: 1,480.43 km²).

The platform operates through a 4-stage pipeline:

1. Scientific Radar Conditioning: Ingests raw dual-polarization (HH & HV) backscatter, rejects radio frequency interference and power artifacts (< -40 dB, > +10 dB), applies 2x2 linear spatial averaging (10m native to 20m grid), and performs 5x5 boxcar speckle suppression (ENL = 18.42, suppressing speckle variance below ±0.21 dB).

2. Dual-Pol Core vs. Fringe Physical Modeling: Decomposes backscatter into Core Open Water (HH < -20 dB, HV < -23 dB, specular bounce) and Transitional Reeds (HH in [-20, -15] dB, dihedral double-bounce). It executes a 19-step sensitivity sweep (-21 dB to -12 dB) and a 20-pixel Monte Carlo spatial translation null test.

3. 3D WebGL Digital Twin: Renders dynamic river flow (2.35 m/s) and riverbank soil erosion particles (~2.15M tons/day) draped over a 3D digital elevation model with 1.8x vertical exaggeration, accompanied by Esri cartographic labels, a 60-second guided audio tour, and an IEEE scientific whitepaper viewer.

4. Autonomous AI Intelligence Copilot: Embedded NVIDIA NIM serverless microservice (nemotron-3.5-bolt-e4b) grounded strictly on verified project metrics, providing natural language radar interrogation and instant UN-SPIDER / CWC disaster Situation Reports (SitReps).

### 2. What benefits does it have?

- Eliminates False Alarm Flood Alerts: Traditional single-polarization SAR algorithms mistake wind-roughened water or emergent reed fringes for massive flood shifts. HydroWaltz proves that 99.8% of new and 99.5% of receded water occurs strictly in the ambiguous transitional reed band.

- Confirms Navigation Stability: Demonstrates that the deep core braided navigation channel changed by only -0.62 km² (indistinguishable from zero vs spatial null spread [-0.67, +0.02] km²), reassuring inland water transit and ferry operations.

- Zero-Latency Disaster Synthesis: Generates complete district-level humanitarian situation reports in under 2 seconds.

### 3. What is the intended impact?

HydroWaltz bridges the gap between complex radar astrophysics and front-line humanitarian action. Floods in Assam displace hundreds of thousands of people across volatile sandbars (chars) every year. By delivering an accessible 3D visual digital twin coupled with an authoritative AI copilot, state disaster management authorities (ASDMA), the Central Water Commission (CWC), and UN-SPIDER emergency taskforces can direct boat rescue operations and emergency food relief with pinpoint precision.

### 4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

- Languages: Python 3.11 (Scientific Pipeline & Serverless Functions), JavaScript ES6+ / HTML5 Canvas / CSS3 (Frontend).

- Radar & Geospatial: rasterio, numpy, scipy, h5py, pyproj, GDAL, MapLibre GL JS v4, AWS Terrarium Global Elevation RGB DEM tiles, Esri World Imagery & Cartographic Places.

- Generative AI & Microservices: NVIDIA NIM (nvidia/nemotron-3.5-bolt-e4b) deployed on Vercel Serverless Functions.

- Hosting & Deployment: Vercel Edge Network (Production), GitHub (Source Control).

- Open-Source Code Repository: https://github.com/Thouseef68/nasa-spaceapps-dancing-with-the-sars

### 5. How is your project creative?

- Kinetic Hydrological Particle System: Rather than showing static colored polygons, our engine calculates real-time hydrodynamic vectors, animating glowing water currents and silt erosion plumes that reactively surge upon user interaction.

- Space-to-Valley Cinematic Cam: Users smoothly descend from a planetary orbit down into the Brahmaputra riverbed with dynamic camera pitch, terrain shadowing, and radar cross-examination lenses.

- Integrated Peer-Reviewed Whitepaper: The application embeds a complete IEEE/AGU-formatted scientific paper directly into the interactive dashboard.

### 6. What factors did your team consider?

- Radiometric Calibration & Noise Floor: Accounted for NISAR L-band NESZ (-26 dB) and cross-talk suppression.

- Inundated Vegetation Scattering: Modeled dihedral corner-reflector bounce where flooded reeds produce anomalously bright backscatter, resolving the classical SAR edge-inversion illusion.

- Low-Bandwidth Resilience: Optimized 20 GB of satellite rasters into sub-megabyte, lossless web-optimized PNG overlays and lightweight JSON data vectors so field responders on 3G mobile networks can operate the platform smoothly.

projectDetails.name: Project SpaceHealth
projectDetails.summary: SpaceHealth is an educational web-based astronaut health monitoring dashboard designed to demonstrate how crew health information can be organised and monitored during long-duration space missions. It allows users to enter health measurements, view health indicators, track historical readings through charts, receive illustrative health status alerts, and record psychological wellness check-ins. The goal is to demonstrate how a centralised digital dashboard could support awareness of astronaut health during space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
SpaceHealth – Astronaut Health Monitoring Dashboard

The Problem

Astronauts on long-duration space missions face several health challenges due to the space environment. Monitoring their physical and psychological well-being is important for supporting crew health and mission safety.

Our Solution

SpaceHealth is an educational web-based dashboard that demonstrates how astronaut health information can be monitored and organised in one place.

The dashboard allows users to:

  • Enter heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature and glucose readings.
  • View health indicators classified as Normal, Get Checked or Critical.
  • Monitor health trends using interactive charts.
  • View previous health readings in an activity history.
  • Receive alerts when readings cross illustrative thresholds.
  • Record psychological wellness through mood check-ins.
  • View crew member profile and mission progress information.

How It Works

Users enter health measurements through a form. JavaScript processes the readings and updates the dashboard, charts, status indicators and health history. Browser local storage helps retain the information between visits.

Technology Used

HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Chart.js and browser local storage.

Creativity and Impact

SpaceHealth combines physical health indicators, historical trends, alerts and psychological wellness in a single dashboard. It demonstrates how a centralised monitoring interface could help organise crew health information during future space missions.

Limitations

This is an educational prototype. Its thresholds and sample readings are illustrative, not official NASA medical standards. It is not a medically validated device and does not diagnose health conditions.

projectDetails.name: BYTE BEBELS
projectDetails.summary:
1. What have we developed?
Earth Trends (Data Detective) is a web app for investigating climate change anywhere on Earth. Users search or click a place on a NASA-layer map, choose a variable (temperature, rainfall, clouds, humidity, sunlight or wind), and the app fetches real NASA POWER data. It then removes seasonal cycles, fits a trend, runs a robust Mann-Kendall test, and gives a plain-English verdict with the p-value. It is built with React, Fast API and SQLite.

2. How does it address the challenge?
It lets anyone be an Earth system trend detective. A guided wizard walks users through finding a variable, detecting a trend and judging whether it is significant. It also explains why a trend may happen (urban heat, deforestation, drought), compares two places, and shows how many more years of data are needed to be sure.

3. Why is it important?
NASA data is open but hard to interpret. Our app turns it into trustworthy, understandable evidence for students, citizens, journalists and planners. It is honest about limits: a trend shows change, not its cause.🚀
projectDetails.details:
NASA Data

Our project uses NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources), which provides satellite and model-based data from MERRA-2 and CERES for any latitude and longitude. We use six variables: air temperature (T2M), rainfall (PRECTOTCORR), cloud cover (CLOUD_AMT), relative humidity (RH2M), sunlight (ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN) and wind speed (WS2M). We fetch monthly and daily time series from 1984 to the last full year and use them to detect long-term trends. We also show NASA GIBS satellite layers on the map: satellite photo, cloud fraction, land-surface temperature and IMERG rain rate. NASA data is the core of the project: every trend, p-value and verdict comes from real NASA data.

I also wrote a fuller Project Details answer, in case it needs more detail:

What does it do / how does it work?

Earth Trends (Data Detective) is a web app that helps anyone find out whether the climate of a place is really changing. The user searches for a place or clicks it on a full-screen Earth map and chooses a variable: temperature, rainfall, clouds, humidity, sunlight or wind. Our Python backend fetches real NASA POWER data and stores it in a database so repeat requests are instant. The app removes the seasonal cycle, fits a trend line, and reports the change per decade with a p-value. It also runs a robust Mann-Kendall test with Sen’s slope as a second check. The result becomes a plain-English verdict: significant trend, not yet significant, or inconclusive. A slider shows how many more years of data are needed to be sure.

Benefits

It makes NASA climate data easy for people with no statistics background. It gives a clear answer in seconds for any place on Earth, explains why a change may happen (for example urban heat or deforestation), and is honest about its limits.

Intended impact

To improve climate and data literacy for students and citizens, and to give journalists, teachers and local planners quick, evidence-based answers about local change.

Tools and technology

JavaScript (React, Vite, Chart.js, MapLibre GL), Python (FastAPI), SQLite, NASA POWER and NASA GIBS data, and OpenStreetMap. No special hardware was needed. It runs on a normal laptop and browser.

How is it creative?

It works like a detective story: ask a question, test the evidence, then deliver a verdict. It has a “how many more years of data do we need?” slider and uses two statistical methods to cross-check results. It also puts real NASA satellite layers on an Earth-themed map.

Factors considered

Scientific honesty (seasonal noise, and a trend is not a cause), ease of use for non-experts, reliability (caching and fallbacks if NASA is down), and the 50 km resolution of the data.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”
