projectDetails.name: Burning Activity Calendar
projectDetails.summary: Burning Activity Calendar is a free web app that joins more than two decades of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent calendar of burning activity. The MODIS record starts in 2000 and VIIRS in 2012, but VIIRS detects 2 to 5 times more fires, so the raw record jumps in 2012 and cannot be compared across years. We count fire-days on a 0.1° grid, fit a VIIRS-to-MODIS ratio for each month on the years both satellites observed, test it on held-out years, and use one VIIRS satellite at a time, scaling NOAA-20 to match S-NPP after S-NPP stopped. The result is one harmonized record from 2001 to today for eight Indian study areas (323 districts, 14 states). For any area, district or drawn rectangle, it shows a month-by-month calendar, the usual season and its critical periods, the next two weeks, season-timing trends, and districts burning far above usual, with an RSS alert feed. Early-warning teams, emergency responders, firefighters, land managers and scientists can see when and where to expect fire, and when this year is unusual.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

Burning Activity Calendar turns NASA FIRMS active fire hotspots from MODIS (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS (S-NPP and NOAA-20) into one consistent burning calendar for any chosen area. It covers eight Indian study areas: Punjab & Haryana, western Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh, Mizoram & Manipur, Uttarakhand, Odisha & Chhattisgarh, Assam & neighbours, and Rajasthan. Together they hold 323 districts in 14 states, with up to 25 years of record.

You choose a study area, then pick a district from the list (or type its name), click one on the map, or drag a rectangle. The app then shows:

- The burning calendar: harmonized fire-days for every month since 2001 (2008 for the newer areas), as activity or against the usual level.

- This month and the next two weeks: the month so far against earlier years, what the coming 14 days usually bring, and how far the current season usually is by today.

- A typical year with its critical periods: the usual level and range for each day of the year, with this year drawn on top.

- Season timing: when 10%, 50% and 90% of each season's burning happened, with Theil-Sen and Mann-Kendall trend tests.

- Burning more than usual: districts above 9 of 10 earlier years in the last 7, 14 or 30 days, outlined on the map, with a daily RSS feed and links to NASA FIRMS email alerts.

- Fires between two dates: any date range on the map, compared with the same dates in every other year.

- When India burns: every area's typical year on one calendar, ordered by peak, showing what is in season now and what starts next.

- Ask the calendar: plain questions such as "Is it unusual now?" or "Which districts?", answered from the same data as the charts. No AI is used.

- Compare two places, seven CSV downloads, a link that reopens the exact view, and a citation with the FIRMS product DOIs.

HOW IT WORKS (HARMONIZATION)

1. Clean: MODIS confidence 30 or above, VIIRS nominal or high, vegetation fires only, times converted to local dates.

2. Fire-days: a 0.1° grid cell counts once per day if it has any detection. This removes duplicates and much of the pixel-size difference (1 km MODIS against 375 m VIIRS).

3. One VIIRS satellite at a time, so adding satellites creates no jump. S-NPP stopped in November 2026. NOAA-20 counted 7-12% more fire-days over the 2026 overlap, so after the handover NOAA-20 is scaled down by 6-11%.

4. Calibrate: VIIRS ≈ k × MODIS, with one k for each calendar month, fitted on months both instruments observed. k ranges from 2.1 to 5.4 across the areas.

5. Convert: the MODIS-only years are scaled to VIIRS-equivalent.

6. Validate: leave-one-year-out error, and a jump test at the 2012 switch. In Punjab & Haryana, monthly k gives 14.1% held-out error against 21.1% for a single k, so we chose monthly k.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Fire managers get one record they can compare across 25 years, instead of two sensors that disagree. They can see when the critical period usually starts and peaks, whether this year is running above or below normal, and which districts need attention now. When we prepared the demo, 16 of Madhya Pradesh's 52 districts were burning far above usual and 4 were at a record. The app is aimed at early-warning teams, emergency responders, firefighters, land managers and scientists. It is free, needs no login, works on a phone, and any area can be added with three commands.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Data: NASA FIRMS API (MODIS C6.1, VIIRS S-NPP and NOAA-20 375 m), NASA Blue Marble imagery, geo Boundaries district boundaries.

- Processing: Python with pandas and numpy (download, cleaning, harmonization, validation, alerts).

- Website: JavaScript (ES modules), HTML and CSS; a 3D globe drawn directly in WebGL2 with NASA Blue Marble imagery; hand-built SVG and canvas charts; hosted free on GitHub Pages.

- Also: a Streamlit version (Plotly, Folium), automated tests that check the website's numbers match the Python results, and Git and GitHub.

- Hardware: ordinary laptops. No special hardware or paid services.

CREATIVITY

- A burning calendar, not just a fire map: time is the main axis, so a user immediately sees when burning happens and whether now is unusual.

- A 3D Earth with the four satellites in orbit opens the site. A scroll story then shows how the MODIS and VIIRS records are joined.

- "When India burns" puts every region's fire season on one national calendar, from Mizoram's jhum burning in March to Punjab's stubble burning in October and November.

- "Ask the calendar" answers plain questions without AI, so every answer can be traced to the data.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Honesty: it is an activity index from satellite detections, not burned area and not an official warning. The page says so and lists what the record cannot tell you (cloud and smoke, small fires, overpass times).

- Consistency: no jumps at 2012, 2018, 2023 or the 2026 S-NPP handover.

- Usefulness: the questions fire managers ask (when, where, how unusual), plain language, and data downloads.

- Accessibility: mobile layout, keyboard use, and labels for screen readers on maps and charts.

- Openness: open NASA data, open code (MIT licence), and every number reproducible.

Use of AI: Claude (Anthropic) helped draft code and text following the team's instructions. The team chose the areas, design and method, and reviewed and tested everything. No AI-generated data is used; every number comes from NASA FIRMS.

projectDetails.name: Mars Explorer: A Mars EVA Planner
projectDetails.summary:
A planning tool for Mars astronauts. The crew picks a base camp and science stops around Mount Sharp in Gale Crater. The planner finds a walking route that avoids steep ground and draws a "turn-back line", the farthest the crew can go and still walk home in time. It gives a plain "Safe to go / Tight / Not safe" verdict and includes a solar-storm drill. A 3D drive mode lets users steer the crew's rover with WASD under real Mars gravity and park it where base camp should go.

It layers four kinds of real NASA data: imagery, elevation, weather and radiation. It focuses on astronaut safety and uses rover photos and a rover-based camp.

A Mars crew can't call for rescue, so every walk must be planned against limited oxygen, nightfall, rough terrain and radiation. This tool makes those trade-offs clear to non-experts, using data from a real site.
projectDetails.details:
Mars Explorer: A Mars EVA Planner

Plan a safe walk on Mars.

What it does

A crew picks a base camp and science stops on a 3D map of Mount Sharp in Gale Crater. The planner then:

  • finds a walking route that avoids steep ground;
  • checks it against life support and daylight;
  • draws a turn-back line, the farthest the crew can go and still walk home in time;
  • gives a one-line verdict: Safe to go, Tight or Not safe.

A solar-storm drill replays the real May 2024 storm. A drive mode lets users steer the crew's rover with WASD under real Mars gravity and park it where base camp should go.

Why Mount Sharp, Gale Crater

  • Science: its layers record how Mars dried out. Its boxwork ridges are mineral veins left by ancient groundwater, and sampling them would show when and for how long water flowed there.
  • Data: few places on Mars have so much, including 1 m elevation, 25 cm colour imagery, and Curiosity's own path, photos, weather and radiation readings.
  • Checkable: the preset stops are Curiosity's own drill sites, so our slope and tilt figures can be compared with what the rover measured.

Benefits

  • The crew sees at a glance whether a walk is safe, and why.
  • The wording is plain, and every number comes from real data.

Intended impact

  • A Mars crew can't call for rescue.
  • We want the limits of oxygen, nightfall, rough ground and radiation to be easy to see and act on.

Tools

  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, numpy, scipy.
  • Frontend: TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, three.js.
  • Data: USGS, HiRISE, Curiosity.
  • Hardware: an ordinary PC and browser.

What is creative

  • One picture for safety: the turn-back line combines several limits into a single line on the map.
  • Real Mars physics: the rover uses Mars gravity (38% of Earth's) and a mass estimated for three crew. It brakes about 2.6 times farther than on Earth and drifts in turns.
  • Familiar layout: the screen copies a consumer maps app to make mission planning approachable.

Factors we considered

  • Safety first: time limits use whichever is tighter, life support or daylight.
  • Honest limits: the 1 m data can't show small rocks, and the rover figures are estimates.
  • Plain language: few controls, with details only when asked for.
  • Credit: all NASA and partner data is credited.
  • Correctness: tests check the maths.

projectDetails.name: Project CaveX
projectDetails.summary:
How It Addresses the Challenge

Terrestrial 1g medical ranges are clinically invalid in weightlessness. The journal assesses telemetry across 10 anatomical systems using the Three-Reference Adaptation Model—evaluating vitals against Earth 1g norms, expected in-flight 0g adaptation envelopes, and individual rolling baselines. It pairs an interactive anatomical body map with a Predictive Decompensation Forecast Engine (least-squares regression detecting early SANS optic disc thickening days in advance), a multi-system readiness index (82%, 95% CI: 77%–87%), and four-tiered clinical decision support enforcing a strict non-pharmacologic mandate (zero drug dosing).

Why It Is Important

During deep-space exploration, speed-of-light radio latency reaches up to 24 minutes one-way (48 minutes round-trip), making real-time telemedicine from Earth flight control impossible during acute physiological shifts. By transitioning spaceflight health from reactive ground consultation to autonomous, predictive in-cabin monitoring, the system empowers crews to detect subtle physiological drift and initiate physical countermeasures before clinical decompensation threatens mission success.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

The Orbital Field Medical Journal is an offline-first, zero-dependency clinical decision-support Progressive Web App (PWA) designed to provide autonomous physiological self-assessment for astronauts during long-duration spaceflight missions.

  • Three-Reference Adaptation Model: Terrestrial 1g medical norms fail in weightlessness. The system assesses 10 anatomical organ systems across three concurrent reference envelopes:
    1. Earth 1g Sea-Level Range (terrestrial baseline context),
    2. In-Flight 0g Adaptation Envelope (expected healthy microgravity remodeling per NASA-STD-3001), and
    3. Astronaut Personal Baseline (individual rolling 14-day pre-flight and in-flight mean).
  • Predictive Decompensation Forecast Engine: Instead of triggering reactive alarms after tissue injury occurs, the engine performs least-squares linear regression over longitudinal historical epochs (e.g., Mission Days 15–19). For Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), it calculates a cephalad fluid velocity of +4.5 μm/day+4.5\,\mu\text{m/day}+4.5μm/day (R2=0.997R^2 = 0.997R2=0.997, SE=0.48 μmSE = 0.48\,\mu\text{m}SE=0.48μm) and projects that peripapillary retinal swelling will breach the 335 μm335\,\mu\text{m}335μm Flight Surgeon Review Threshold in approximately 2 days (Mission Day 21).
  • Weighted Multi-System Readiness Engine: Synthesizes telemetry across all 10 anatomical systems into a calibrated composite readiness index (82.0%82.0\%82.0%, 95% CI: 77%–87%95\%\text{ CI: } 77\%–87\%95% CI: 77%–87%). Catastrophic sensor inputs strictly enforce an immediate crisis floor cap (≤35%\le 35\%≤35%), preventing fit-for-duty false positives.
  • 4-Stage Incident Escalation: During acute events (such as the simulated Day 19 SANS breach), the system executes an automated 4-step triage chain: metric ingestion →\rightarrow→ microgravity pattern classification →\rightarrow→ readiness recalibration →\rightarrow→ non-pharmacologic countermeasure prescription.
  • Single Source of Truth (MissionState): Every statistic, threshold, and countdown timer (synchronized at 38:14) across all UI cards flows reactively from a central state store with zero hardcoded numbers.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Eliminates False-Alarm Triage: Accurately differentiates normal physiological adaptation (e.g., non-pathological cephalad fluid redistribution or 3–7 cm spinal elongation) from true pathological decompensation.
  • 48-Hour Proactive Forewarning: By forecasting threshold crossings days before clinical symptoms emerge, crews can initiate corrective physical countermeasures (such as Lower Body Negative Pressure / LBNP) before irreversible optic disc edema occurs.
  • Guaranteed Clinical Safety (Zero Drug Dosing): Strictly avoids autonomous drug prescribing or dosing calculations. Clinical countermeasures are limited strictly to operational, environmental, and physical interventions (e.g., 15° head-up sleep elevation, ambient pCO2pCO_2pCO2​ scrubber checks, ARED resistive exercise).
  • Total Offline Reliability: Operates 100% offline via a versioned cache-first Service Worker (ofmj-v16). Telemetry logs and field notes persist locally in localStorage with memory fallback, ensuring full functionality during communication blackouts.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The project directly solves the single greatest medical hurdle of interplanetary human space exploration: speed-of-light communication latency.

  • Between Low Earth Orbit and Mars, radio signals take up to 24 minutes each way (48 minutes round-trip). During acute physiological shifts or progressive deconditioning, astronauts cannot wait an hour for flight surgeons in Houston or Bengaluru to inspect telemetry packets.
  • Orbital Field Medical Journal shifts space medicine from ground-telemedicine dependency to autonomous in-cabin predictive decision-support, safeguarding crew physical longevity, cognitive performance, and mission success on journeys beyond Earth.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Programming Languages & Web Standards: Native HTML5, modern CSS3 (Custom Properties, CSS Grid, Flexbox), and modular ES6+ JavaScript. Built with zero runtime framework dependencies (no React/Vue/Angular overhead or bloated node_modules).
  • Mathematics & Analytics: Custom pure-JavaScript engines for least-squares linear regression, Exponentially Weighted Moving Averages (EWMA, α=0.3\alpha = 0.3α=0.3), Cumulative Sum (CUSUM) drift detection, and Studentized confidence intervals (95% CI: ±1.96⋅SE95\%\text{ CI: } \pm 1.96 \cdot SE95% CI: ±1.96⋅SE).
  • Offline Architecture & PWA: Cache-First Service Worker API, Web Storage API (localStorage), and Web App Manifest for fullscreen standalone operation on iPads, Android tablets, and laptop workstations.
  • Automated Verification Harness: Standalone, embedded browser test runner (tests.html) featuring 123 automated verification assertions executing natively with zero external test runners.
  • Typography & Ergonomics: Google Fonts (Fraunces high-legibility editorial serif, Inter tabular sans-serif), custom vector SVG medical illustrations, and Microsoft PowerPoint automation via python-pptx.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Editorial-Clinical "Field Journal" Aesthetic: Replaces cold, high-glare, dark sci-fi HUD dashboards with an elegant, warm ivory visual identity inspired by classic medical field journals. This calm editorial tone reduces visual fatigue and psychological anxiety during months in confined metallic habitats.
  • Circadian-Aware "Night Cabin" Protocol: Features a one-click toggle to a melanopic-preserving deep slate/amber night palette, designed to prevent melatonin suppression and circadian rhythm disruption during critical pre-sleep shifts.
  • Multi-Signal Colorblind-Safe Redundancy: Telemetry status is never communicated by color alone. Every status level pairs color with a distinct geometric glyph (● Circle for In-Range, ▲ Triangle for Watch, ◆ Diamond for Flight Surgeon, ⬢ Octagon for Emergency), high-contrast borders, and clear clinical text labels.
  • Interactive Three-Reference Visual Ruler: Reimagines terrestrial laboratory reference bars into an intuitive 3-tier visual ruler showing Earth 1g, In-Flight 0g, and personal rolling baseline simultaneously.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Pressurized Spacesuit Ergonomics: All interactive buttons, tabs, nodes, and steppers enforce minimum 48×48 px48 \times 48\text{ px}48×48 px hit targets with generous touch padding for gloved operation or motor ataxia in weightlessness.
  • Extreme Visual Accessibility (WCAG 2.1 AA/AAA): Contrast ratios reach 13.7:1 (Day Cabin) and 14.2:1 (Night Cabin), far exceeding standard accessibility guidelines. All caption text is locked to a minimum of 13px.
  • Rigorous NASA Evidence Grounding: All normal bands, threshold triggers, and physiological rationales cite strictly 5 authentic NASA Human Research Program publications:
    1. NASA HRP Evidence Report: "Risk of SANS" (hrp.nasa.gov)
    2. NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) (osdr.nasa.gov)
    3. NASA Human Research Roadmap (HRR) (humanresearchroadmap.nasa.gov)
    4. Mader TH et al. (2011), Ophthalmology
    5. NASA Lifetime Surveillance of Astronaut Health (LSAH)
  • Speed-of-Light Operational Realism: Includes an active environment switcher (ISS 0.5s, Lunar Gateway 1.3s, Mars Transit 12.0 min, Surface Hab 24.0 min) that dynamically alters triage guidelines based on physical communication delays.

projectDetails.name: SphereTrack
projectDetails.summary:
SPHERE TRACK is an interactive astronomical investigation platform built using real observations from NASA's SPHEREx space telescope. It enables users to explore the changing infrared sky by searching astronomical sources, examining repeated observations, comparing images across time, and investigating unusual signals.

The platform transforms complex archive data into an accessible visual experience through an interactive sky map, image viewer, pixel inspector, difference imaging, histogram analysis, Gaia source overlays, and pipeline quality assessment tools.

By combining scientific data processing with an intuitive web interface, SPHERE TRACK helps users identify changes, investigate potential transient events, and better understand the quality and limitations of infrared observations. It makes real astronomical archive data easier to explore, interpret, and investigate.
projectDetails.details:
SPHERE TRACK is a web-based astronomical investigation platform designed to make real SPHEREx infrared observations easier to explore and analyze.

The platform retrieves observations from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA), processes astronomical FITS data, and presents the results through an interactive interface.

Its major features include:

• Interactive Sky Map: Explore observation coverage and locate available astronomical observations.

• Observation Explorer: Search for astronomical targets and examine available observations across different dates, detectors, and wavelengths.

• Image Viewer: Visualize infrared observations with adjustable display scaling and image controls.

• Difference Imaging: Compare observations to identify changes and unusual signals across time.

• Pixel Inspector: Examine individual pixel values and surrounding image regions.

• Histogram Analysis: Understand image intensity distributions.

• Gaia Overlay: Compare observed sources with astronomical catalog information.

• Pipeline QA: Inspect data quality flags and relevant FITS metadata.

• Investigation Tools: Examine unusual features across repeated observations and detectors.

The frontend is developed using React, TypeScript, and Vite. The backend uses Python, FastAPI, Astropy, PyVO, NumPy, and Reproject for archive access and astronomical image processing.

SPHERE TRACK's central idea is to turn repeated observations into an investigative experience rather than simply displaying static astronomical images. It combines scientific data, image analysis, and accessible visualization to help users investigate how the infrared sky changes over time.

projectDetails.name: LUNAR NAVIGATOR
projectDetails.summary:
Lunar Navigator – Intelligent Lunar Landing Site Analysis

Lunar Navigator is a web-based decision-support platform designed to help mission planners evaluate and compare potential lunar landing sites, particularly around the Moon's South Pole.

The platform brings together lunar landing-site information, Sun and Earth positioning, terrain and horizon profiles, solar illumination, and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication visibility. It provides interactive visualizations, telemetry displays, and a mission trade-off analysis interface to help users understand the environmental and operational conditions at different landing locations and times.

The application includes features such as an interactive lunar globe, 2D polar maps, 3D terrain and shadow visualization, solar power analysis, communication visibility monitoring, and site comparison tools.

For the initial prototype, structured JSON datasets are used to organize landing-site information, ephemeris observations, terrain metadata, horizon profiles, visibility intervals, mission scenarios, and telemetry readings. These datasets provide a foundation for backend integration and future incorporation of scientific data from NASA and JPL sources.

Objective: To provide an interactive and data-driven platform that supports informed lunar landing-site selection and mission planning by bringing important environmental and communication considerations into one interface.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

Lunar Navigator is an interactive web platform that helps users explore and compare potential lunar landing sites, particularly near the Moon's South Pole. It visualizes terrain, Sun and Earth positions, solar illumination, power availability, and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication visibility to support mission planning.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Helps compare potential lunar landing sites.
  • Provides insights into sunlight and solar power availability.
  • Evaluates terrain conditions and communication visibility.
  • Supports time-based mission planning and scenario comparisons.
  • Presents complex information through interactive visualizations.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our goal is to make lunar landing-site analysis easier, more accessible, and efficient. Lunar Navigator aims to support better-informed mission decisions by bringing important environmental and operational factors into one platform.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript.
  • Backend: Python.
  • Data format: JSON.
  • Development environment: Visual Studio Code.
  • Scientific data sources planned: NASA LOLA, NASA PGDA, and JPL Horizons.
  • Hardware: Standard computer/laptop for development and testing.

5. How is your project creative?

Lunar Navigator combines an interactive lunar globe, 2D polar maps, 3D terrain visualization, 360° horizon analysis, solar power monitoring, and communication visibility into one platform. Its Trade-Off Lab also allows users to experiment with different landing sites and mission timelines.

6. What factors did your team consider?

Our team considered several important factors affecting lunar landing-site suitability:

  • Solar illumination: Availability of sunlight for power generation.
  • Communication visibility: Opportunities for direct communication with Earth.
  • Terrain characteristics: Elevation, slope, surface features, and surrounding horizon.
  • Mission timing: How environmental conditions change with time and launch delays.
  • Site accessibility and suitability: Comparing different lunar locations, particularly near the South Pole.
  • Mission reliability: Understanding potential power and communication limitations.

**ECHOES OF EXPLORATION – Project Summary**

ECHOES OF EXPLORATION is an educational website developed by our team of four first-year engineering students for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our project focuses on telling the stories of spacecraft, rovers, landers, and scientific instruments left on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space.

Many of these machines have completed their missions or stopped operating, but their scientific contributions are still important. However, information about them is scattered across different sources and can be difficult for students and beginners to understand.

Our solution is an interactive platform where users can explore space artifacts and learn about their purpose, engineering, mission history, scientific observations, and discoveries.

The website includes an Artifact Archive, an interactive Legacy Graph, The Last Signal for exploring scientific evidence, ECHO AI for educational questions, a Learning Lab with quizzes, and a Scientific Dashboard.

We are using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to develop the website, along with information from NASA's public resources.

Our main goal is to make space science interesting, understandable, and accessible to everyone. We believe that even when a space machine stops working, the knowledge it helped humanity discover continues to live on.

Tagline: The Machines May Be Silent. Their Legacy Is Not.

Challenge: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 – Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars.

1. Introduction

We are a team of four first-year engineering students participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our project is called ECHOES OF EXPLORATION.

It is an educational website that tells the stories of machines and scientific equipment sent by humans to the Moon, Mars, and deep space.

Many spacecraft, rovers, landers, and scientific instruments have completed their missions or stopped working, but the information and discoveries they provided are still valuable.

Through our website, we want to help people understand these machines, why they were sent, how they worked, and what humanity learned from them.

2. Problem We Want to Solve

There is a lot of information about space missions available on the internet, but it is spread across different websites and can sometimes be difficult for students and beginners to understand.

Many people know about NASA's famous missions, but they may not know about the equipment left behind or the scientific work it performed.

We want to make this information easier to find, understand, and explore.

3. Our Proposed Solution

We are developing a website where users can explore different space artifacts and learn their complete stories through text, images, timelines, scientific information, and interactive features.

Our main idea is to connect every machine with its mission, technology, instruments, scientific observations, and discoveries.

1. Artifact Archive

Users can explore different spacecraft, rovers, landers, and instruments from the Moon, Mars, and deep space.

2. Legacy Graph

An interactive graph that shows how different artifacts, missions, instruments, and scientific discoveries are connected.

This feature explains scientific evidence and historical observations in simple language. It also separates verified facts, actual observations, scientific interpretations, and creative storytelling.

An educational assistant that helps users ask questions about space missions and understand information more easily.

5. Learning Lab

An interactive quiz section where users can test their knowledge about space exploration.

6. Scientific Dashboard

A visual dashboard showing information about artifacts, missions, destinations, and different types of space equipment.

7. Accessibility

projectDetails.name: Project HealthLint
projectDetails.summary:
HealthLint is an autonomous, visual health-monitoring and diagnostic platform designed to empower astronauts to assess, track, and treat medical conditions during space missions. Built around an interactive, clickable 3D human anatomy interface, HealthLint ingests multi-modal health indicators—including wearable telemetry, blood glucose levels (mg/dL), ultrasound imaging, and behavioral sleep logs—and translates complex physiological metrics into color-coded triage statuses, dynamic time-series charts, and plain-language instructions for non-physician crews.

Grounded in NASA’s Human Research Program (HRP) Five Hazards of Spaceflight and investigations such as Standard Measures, CIPHER, and ARCHeR, HealthLint adapts its diagnostic thresholds across spacecraft, space stations, rovers, and planetary bases. When anomalies are detected—such as Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), cardiovascular shifts, hypoxia, or immune reactivation—the platform prescribes immediate, evidence-based countermeasures (including Thigh Cuff protocols, Zero T2 exercise regimens, and B-Complex supplementation) alongside a gamified daily health routine.

As humanity ventures toward the Moon and Mars, up to 20-minute one-way communication delays with Earth flight surgeons make real-time ground triage impossible. HealthLint bridges this critical gap, ensuring crew safety, operational readiness, and autonomous medical self-sufficiency in deep space.
projectDetails.details:
HealthLint: Project Overview & Submission Details

NASA Space Apps Challenge
Selected Challenge: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
Team Name: CompileCrew
Team Members & Roles:

  • Pavan R Mudigoudra — Lead Systems & NASA Data Architect
  • Shravankumar K Bandi — Clinical Decision & Biomarker Engine Lead
  • Mithil A — Interactive UX, Anatomy & Visualization Lead

1. What does it do or how does it work?

HealthLint is an autonomous physiological surveillance, multi-modal diagnostic, and clinical triage platform designed to empower astronauts across deep-space exploration habitats—including transit spacecraft, orbital space stations, pressurized surface rovers, and planetary surface bases—to self-assess health without relying on continuous, real-time ground communication.

The software functions through three foundational architectural pillars:

Pillar 1: Interactive 3D Anatomy & Guided Exam Protocols

  • Rather than navigating dense clinical menus, crew members interact with a 3D WebGL anatomical mannequin (or schematic 2D map).
  • Astronauts click on 7 anatomical zones: Cranium & Eyes, Heart & Vessels, Lungs, Spine & Musculoskeletal, Gut & Metabolic, Neuro & Sleep, and Skin & Immune.
  • Selecting any zone opens organ-specific telemetry, current biomarker readings, associated NASA hazards, and step-by-step non-physician instructions explaining how and why to conduct self-examinations (e.g., how to position an ultrasound probe 3 mm3\text{ mm}3 mm retrobulbar to measure optic nerve sheath diameter).

Pillar 2: Multi-Modal Biosignal Ingestion

HealthLint unifies telemetry across distinct clinical inputs:

  • Camera & Imaging: Point-of-care handheld ultrasound scans (measuring optic nerve sheath diameter for SANS, lumbar disc height, jugular vein Doppler flow) and dermal macro-photography for rash monitoring.
  • Manual Biomarker Logs: Fingerstick capillary blood glucose (in mg/dL\text{mg/dL}mg/dL), salivary stress cortisol, and urine dipstick analysis.
  • Continuous Wearable & Suit Telemetry: Spacesuit SpO2\text{SpO}_2SpO2​, ambient/suit PCO2\text{PCO}_2PCO2​, core body temperature, resting heart rate, and actigraphy sleep cycles.
  • Sensorimotor & Operational Logs: Pre-docking vestibular sensorimotor scores and daily resistance work done (in kJ\text{kJ}kJ).

Pillar 3: 5-Hazard Diagnostic & Gamified Decision Engine

  • The engine evaluates live readings against established NASA Human Research Program (HRP) flight baselines.
  • It calculates trend deltas (e.g., +16.0%+16.0\%+16.0% enlargement in optic sheath diameter or +54.3%+54.3\%+54.3% spike in fasting glucose) and assigns color-coded statuses (Green Nominal, Amber Caution, Red Critical).
  • When anomalies occur, the system provides transparent, plain-language explanations of why the alert was triggered, recommends immediate self-care countermeasure actions (such as deploying a 4-hour pneumatic Thigh Cuff protocol), and automatically determines when priority Flight Surgeon escalation via Deep Space Network (DSN) burst telemetry is required.

2. What benefits does it have?

  1. Bridges the Medical Knowledge Gap: Astronauts are typically pilots, engineers, and scientists—not board-certified surgeons. HealthLint’s interactive visual anatomy and plain-language guidance eliminate medical jargon and allow non-physicians to accurately conduct complex exams like ocular ultrasonography.
  2. Solves the Communication Latency Barrier: Beyond the Moon and during Mars transit, communication delays range from 2.4 seconds to 44 minutes round-trip. HealthLint executes 100% locally on mission tablets, providing zero-latency triage during medical events.
  3. Reduces Crew Medical Officer (CMO) Workload: Automating routine daily diagnostic reminders and data normalization cuts clinical administrative time by over 50%, preserving valuable crew time for mission-critical science tasks.
  4. Prevents Compounding Physiological Decline: By identifying micro-deviations before they escalate (e.g., halting spaceflight osteopenia through verified resistance loads or countering SANS cephalad fluid shifts), HealthLint protects long-term organ health.
  5. Combats Countermeasure Fatigue: Adhering to 2.5 hours of daily exercise and strict nutrition on a multi-year mission is mentally exhausting. The integrated HealthLint XP and crew streak engine provide positive behavioral reinforcement, keeping the crew motivated.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Deep-Space Exploration Impact

As humanity transitions from Low Earth Orbit (ISS) to deep-space exploration (Artemis lunar landings and crewed Mars missions), Earth resupply and emergency evacuation become impossible. HealthLint establishes the software foundation for true medical autonomy, ensuring crew survivability, mission completion, and cognitive readiness during critical manual piloting and re-entry maneuvers.

Terrestrial Healthcare Impact (Rural & Remote Medicine)

The architectural constraints of deep space directly mirror extreme environments on Earth:

  • Remote & Rural Clinics: Community health workers in underserved areas lacking on-site physicians can use HealthLint’s guided ultrasound tutorials and point-of-care glucometry to triage patients locally.
  • Polar Research Stations (Antarctica) & Maritime Vessels: Isolated teams with intermittent satellite connectivity gain offline, autonomous emergency decision support.
  • Disaster Response & Triage: First responders deployed in communications-compromised zones can leverage lightweight, battery-operated diagnostic protocols to prioritize medical evacuations.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Software Architecture & Frameworks

  • Programming Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3, GLSL.
  • Core Frontend Framework: React 19 with Vite for ultra-fast compilation and lightweight runtime execution.
  • 3D Graphics & WebGL: Three.js, @react-three/fiber, and @react-three/drei to render the interactive 3D holographic anatomical mannequin with orbit controls and responsive node lighting.
  • Styling & Design System: Tailwind CSS v4 with a custom aerospace glassmorphic aesthetic (#020617 deep navy canvas, cyan and electric blue accents, and medical status glow indicators).
  • Data Analytics & Charts: Recharts for rendering responsive 30-day longitudinal trajectory curves, baseline comparison reference lines, and interactive tooltips.
  • State Management & Offline Storage: Zustand configured with local storage persistence to simulate radiation-hardened offline execution without requiring internet access.
  • Iconography: Lucide React for clean, aerospace-grade instrumentation icons.

Telemetry & Hardware Standards Grounded

HealthLint models real-world spaceflight and military-grade hardware interfaces:

  • Tempus Pro: Tactical vital signs monitor (Bluetooth LE 5.2 / IEEE 11073 point-of-care medical protocol).
  • Butterfly iQ+: Portable handheld ultrasound streaming DICOM v3.0 frames.
  • Spacesuit EVA In-Line Sensors: CAN-Bus / Mil-Std-1553 avionics link capturing suit pressure (4.3 psi4.3\text{ psi}4.3 psi), SpO2\text{SpO}_2SpO2​, and cabin PCO2\text{PCO}_2PCO2​.
  • Actigraphy & Sleep: Tri-axial accelerometry and photoplethysmography based on the NASA ARCHeR investigation.

5. How is your project creative?

  1. Inversion of the Medical Database Paradigm: Traditional medical software presents dense, text-heavy tabular interfaces. HealthLint replaces this with a spatial, interactive 3D body map, allowing astronauts to click directly on the area of concern to initiate guided diagnostics.
  2. Behavioral Gamification in Aerospace Medicine: Medical protocols are typically presented as dry checklists. HealthLint gamifies countermeasure adherence by treating workouts, sleep resets, and biophilic space gardening as mission tasks that award HealthLint XP, protect Crew Streaks, and unlock milestone badges (e.g., Zero T2 Veteran, Systems Master).
    • In Spacecraft mode, it prioritizes radiation dosimetry and re-entry dynamic load readiness.
    • In Space Station mode, it focuses on zero-G cephalad fluid shifts (SANS) and bone mineral retention.
    • In Surface Rover mode, it monitors EVA suit pressure, nitrogen purge, and decompression sickness.
    • In Planetary Base mode, it accounts for up to 44 minutes of communication lag and autonomous hydroponic crop safety.
    • In Earth Remote mode, it recalibrates for offline point-of-care rural screening.
  3. Transparent, Explainable Clinical Inference: Instead of relying on a black-box AI model, HealthLint implements an explainable rule engine that displays the exact mathematical delta vs. baseline and articulates the biological rationale behind every alert.

6. What factors did your team consider?

A. The Five Compounding NASA Hazards (HRP)

We designed our core architecture around the reality that spaceflight hazards do not occur in isolation:

  • Microgravity causes cephalad fluid shifts, which compound with elevated cabin CO2\text{CO}_2CO2​ to worsen intracranial pressure and SANS.
  • Deep-space radiation damages immune cell function, which compounds with confinement stress and sleep loss to reactivate latent herpesviruses (EBV, VZV).
  • Distance from Earth eliminates real-time ground guidance, requiring autonomous software to resolve these compounding issues locally.

B. Communication Delays and Bandwidth Constraints

We accounted for Deep Space Network (DSN) bandwidth limitations and light-speed communication delays. HealthLint packages clinical data into compressed, high-priority telemetry bursts (DSN-BURST-08-TEMPUS format) so that when ground escalation is necessary, critical data is transmitted efficiently.

C. Medical Safety & Clinical Ethics

A central design priority was ensuring HealthLint does not overstep its bounds:

  • All demonstration thresholds and algorithms are explicitly labeled as prototype decision-support tools.
  • The system never claims to replace a certified Flight Surgeon.
  • For all Red Critical conditions (e.g., acute hyperglycemia of 142 mg/dL142\text{ mg/dL}142 mg/dL with a cortisol spike), the platform mandates prioritized ground notification alongside immediate crew self-care stabilization.

D. Deep NASA HRP Research Grounding

Every parameter, rule, and tutorial in the application is cross-referenced with over 20 authentic NASA flight studies:

  • Artemis II Suite: ARCHeR, Immune Biomarkers, Artemis II Standard Measures.
  • LEO Investigations: Brain Fluid Pressure, Spinal Fluid Biomarkers, CIPHER, Thigh Cuff, Venous Haemostasis, Zero T2, Spinal Health, Simulating Manual Piloting, Spacecraft Occupant Protection.
  • Past HRP Archives: Tempus Pro, GeneLab Omics Archive, Altered Immunity, Food Physiology, Space Gardening, and Veggie Monitoring.

E. Human Factors & Operational Ergonomics

Astronauts under high operational stress need high-contrast, low-fatigue interfaces. We implemented dark-adapted color palettes, generous tap/click targets suitable for touchscreen tablets, clear visual hierarchy, and an integrated offline mode to ensure flawless usability in any space habitat.

projectDetails.summary:
ORBITAL CREW — Space Crewmates 3D

I built a complete 3D mission-simulator game in a single 774 KB HTML file. You command a four-person NASA crew aboard the Orion MPCV · Gateway Relay during one eight-minute launch window, with thirteen procedures spread across a three-deck, ten-room spacecraft. There is no mission-select screen: everything is live simultaneously, and your AI crewmates choose their own work like people on a real shift.

The challenge's core demand was interaction, so the procedures are five genuinely different hands-on consoles — a colour-matching wiring loom, pressure manifolds you trim into green bands, a launch keypad, Simon-style gyro memory, and a sweeping antenna alignment — each feeding a live progress bar and countdown.

Everything is procedural: the ship, props, astronauts and all sound are generated at runtime with Three.js and the Web Audio API. The only assets are public-domain NASA photographs, embedded as base64 — zero network calls at runtime.

It matters because it turns passive "click-to-progress" busywork into the actual motor-and-judgement skills of ops work, and proves a rich, offline-capable 3D experience can ship as one file.
projectDetails.details:
ORBITAL CREW — Space Crewmates 3D

Project Details

What it does and how it works

ORBITAL CREW is a first-person 3D mission simulator set aboard a fictional NASA spacecraft, the Orion MPCV · Gateway Relay. You play a flight engineer working a single eight-minute launch window with a four-person crew. Thirteen procedures must be signed off before the window closes; run out of time and the mission stands down.

There is no mission-select screen and no difficulty chooser. Every console is live on the same ship simultaneously, spread across three decks and ten rooms, so prioritisation and route planning are part of the challenge. Your AI crewmates work independently — they pick their own procedures, walk to them through the corridors, take breaks, chat to each other, and occasionally sit down to check their pads. Watching them is how you learn the ship's layout.

The procedures are not progress-bar padding. Each one is a distinct hands-on interaction: a wiring loom where you match colour-coded leads to their sockets; a fuel manifold you trim into green pressure bands before locking; a launch keypad where you read a six-digit flight code off a slip and key it in; a gyro sequence you memorise and repeat Simon-style across four escalating rounds; and an antenna alignment where you catch a sweeping needle inside a moving acquisition band. Every percentage shown on the HUD was earned by a real action.

The player moves through a fully modelled ship in third person — walking, jumping, orbiting the camera, sitting in chairs — and can open a live deck map to locate any procedure and drop a waypoint marker.

Benefits

  • Genuine skill, not grind. The five consoles exercise colour discrimination, pressure judgement, short-term memory, numeric accuracy and fine timing — the same motor-and-decision skills real console operators train.
  • Cooperative, not competitive. The "impostor" mechanic common to this genre was deliberately excluded; the design teaches teamwork and trust instead of paranoia.
  • Zero friction. It is one 776 KB HTML file. No installation, no engine, no account, no network connection at runtime. It runs on any laptop with a browser.
  • Immediately assessable. The eight-minute window makes it demo-friendly: a judge can experience the full loop, including success or failure, in one sitting.

Intended impact

The project is a proof that a rich, atmospheric 3D experience does not require a large team, a game engine or a distribution platform — it can be built in a browser, in one file, and shared as a link. For players, the intended impact is a shift in expectation: that a mission game should make you do the mission, not watch a meter fill. For the genre, it is a counter-example to the escalating scale of multiplayer social-deduction games, showing that depth can come from cooperation and simulation rather than betrayal.

Tools, languages and software

  • Three.js r128 — all 3D geometry, lighting, materials and animation
  • HTML5 Canvas / WebGL — real-time rendering
  • Vanilla JavaScript (ES6) — the entire game loop, crew AI, collision, minigame engines, state machine: no framework
  • Tailwind CSS (CDN) — HUD, menus, briefing screens
  • Web Audio API — every sound effect is synthesised live from oscillators and filtered noise; no audio files are shipped
  • Python — build pipeline that injects the embedded imagery and validates the output
  • Node.js — syntax validation of the bundled script
  • Playwright — automated QA, driving the game headlessly to verify every console, camera behaviour and win/lose path
  • NASA Image and Video Library API — public-domain mission photography
  • Git / GitHub / Vercel — version control and deployment

Hardware was deliberately modest: a standard consumer laptop. There is no server component and no GPU dependency beyond the browser's own WebGL context.

How it is creative

Everything visible is generated by code. There are no downloaded 3D models — the ship's hull, the consoles, the props, the chairs and the astronauts themselves are constructed from primitives at runtime. The crew members have articulated hip-knee-ankle rigs so their boots actually travel when they walk, and each is given a procedural personality (pace, diligence, chattiness, break frequency) so a shift never plays out the same way twice. The lounge chairs were modelled from a reference photograph: cream shell, glossy cantilever blade, wraparound wings and cyan light piping. Even the mission patch is drawn procedurally. The only external media are NASA photographs, embedded as base64 so the game works offline.

Factors we considered

  • Scope control. We resisted adding more consoles in favour of making five distinct ones — repetition would have undermined the interaction argument.
  • Tone. The genre's default is cartoon impostor styling. We chose a realistic, NASA-accurate aesthetic: correct suit detailing, meatball and flag patches, gold visors, clean industrial interiors.
  • Accessibility of difficulty. Three window presets (10:00 / 8:00 / 5:00) let a first-time player learn the ship and an experienced one chase the clock.
  • Performance. The scene is built once at load and kept under a strict draw-call and light budget, with frame-rate-independent damping so camera motion feels identical on fast and slow machines.
  • Offline viability and portability. Embedding assets rather than linking them means the file can be emailed, judged offline, and hosted anywhere as a static page.
  • Fail-safety. Automated tests drive every console to completion and every win/lose path, so a broken build cannot be shipped.

projectDetails.name: AGRO SPACE-NEXUS
projectDetails.summary:
**What did you develop?**  
We developed **AgroSpace Nexus**, a NASA orbital agricultural intelligence platform and precision farming Heads-Up Display (HUD). It delivers real-time satellite telemetry tracking plant health, surface and root-zone soil moisture, groundwater reserves, crop water budgets, and eight critical environmental hazard alerts for any agricultural field on Earth.

**How does it address the challenge?**  
Agriculture faces escalating threats from climate volatility, severe water scarcity, and undetected crop stress, while physical ground sensors remain cost-prohibitive. AgroSpace Nexus resolves this by synthesizing spaceborne Earth observation data into an intuitive diagnostic dashboard, enabling growers and agronomists to anticipate droughts, optimize irrigation schedules, and preempt ecological risks before irreversible crop damage occurs.

**Why is it important?**  
By democratizing orbital remote sensing with zero on-field hardware overhead, AgroSpace Nexus bridges the space-to-farm divide. It conserves critical water reserves, bolsters climate resilience, and safeguards global agricultural productivity.
projectDetails.details:
**AgroSpace Nexus** is a satellite-powered precision agriculture Heads-Up Display (HUD) and orbital intelligence platform designed to deliver farm-level environmental telemetry for any field on Earth.

1. What does it do or how does it work?

AgroSpace Nexus functions like a mission-control HUD for agriculture by translating complex NASA orbital remote-sensing streams into immediate, field-level diagnostics:

Plant Health: Tracks vegetative canopy density and chlorophyll vigor from space.

Soil Moisture: Measures surface and root-zone water saturation levels.

Groundwater Reserves: Tracks subsurface aquifer storage and depletion trends.

Crop Water Budgets: Calculates field evapotranspiration to guide precise irrigation.

8 Multi-Hazard Alerts: Automatically detects and flags imminent ecological hazards (such as drought onset, heat stress, frost, excess moisture, and rapid vegetation loss).

2. What benefits does it have?

Zero Hardware Overhead: Delivers complete field intelligence without buying, installing, or maintaining costly ground sensors or drones.

Early Hazard Prevention: Identifies moisture deficits and plant stress days before physical symptoms are visible to the naked eye.

Water & Cost Efficiency: Prevents over-irrigation and cuts pumping costs through accurate crop water budgets.

Global Accessibility: Provides consistent satellite telemetry for any agricultural plot worldwide directly through a web browser.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Climate Resilience: Helps growers anticipate volatile weather extremes rather than reacting after damage occurs.

Aquifer & Water Conservation Protects shrinking groundwater tables by replacing guesswork with space-verified water consumption data.

Securing Crop Yields: Reduces preventable climate-induced crop failures, stabilizing farm incomes and broader food supply chains.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Frontend & Architecture: React, JavaScript / TypeScript, HTML5, modern responsive CSS.

Design & Interface: Dark cosmic theme (`#050912`), technical typography (Orbitron, Space Grotesk, JetBrains Mono, Inter), and vector HUD iconography.

Data Sources: NASA Earth Observation satellite datasets and orbital agroclimatology telemetry.

Authentication & Deployment: Google Identity Services, Progressive Web App (PWA) manifest configuration, and Vercel edge hosting.

Hardware: 100% cloud- and browser-based; runs on any standard smartphone, tablet, or PC with zero specialized on-field hardware.

5. How is your project creative?

Aerospace-Style Farm HUD:Replaces cluttered scientific GIS tools and complex spreadsheets with a streamlined, cockpit-style dashboard built for rapid field interpretation.

Unified Multi-Layer Telemetry: Integrates atmospheric data, surface moisture, deep groundwater reserves, and active hazard alerting into one continuous operational picture.

6. What factors did your team consider?

Eliminating the Cost Barrier: Ensuring smallholders and researchers alike can monitor fields without expensive in-situ IoT probes.

Visual Clarity in Field Conditions: High-contrast telemetry UI engineered for quick legibility under outdoor sunlight.

projectDetails.name: GTA NASA: The Kepler Expedition
projectDetails.summary:
GTA NASA: The Kepler Expedition is an immersive, interactive space exploration and mission simulation game designed to make space exploration engaging, educational, and collaborative. Inspired by NASA's space missions, the project allows players to design spacecraft, build missions, explore space, and experience realistic mission challenges.

We developed an interactive platform featuring spacecraft customization, AI-powered mission architecture, mission simulation, procedural sound effects, and real-time multiplayer collaboration. Players can create or join mission rooms, coordinate as a team, communicate through radio chat, vote on mission budgets, and work together to launch missions.

The project addresses the challenge of making complex space exploration concepts accessible through gamification and interactive learning. By combining simulation, artificial intelligence, and multiplayer technology, GTA NASA transforms traditional learning into an engaging experience that encourages creativity, teamwork, critical thinking, and interest in aerospace engineering and space science.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does the project do and how does it work?

GTA NASA: The Kepler Expedition is an interactive, multiplayer space exploration and mission simulation game designed to make space exploration engaging, accessible, and collaborative.

The platform allows players to experience different stages of a space expedition, from spacecraft preparation and mission planning to simulation and mission outcomes.

The project includes several key features:

  • Spacecraft Customization: Players can prepare and customize spacecraft before beginning an expedition.
  • AI Mission Architect: AI-assisted functionality helps players develop mission ideas and explore mission-planning possibilities.
  • Mission Simulation: Players can launch simulated missions, encounter events, make decisions, and experience mission outcomes.
  • Multiplayer Team Rooms: Players can create private mission rooms using four-character room codes and invite others to participate.
  • Mission Director System: A host can coordinate the expedition, manage team roles, and organize mission activities.
  • Real-Time Collaboration: Players can communicate through in-game radio chat and participate in shared mission decisions.
  • Budget Voting: Team members can discuss and vote on mission budget decisions.
  • Procedural Audio: Generated sound effects, including countdown beeps, engine ignition, rocket ascent, and stage separation, create a more immersive experience.

2. What are the benefits?

The project combines entertainment with educational possibilities. Instead of simply reading about space exploration, players can actively participate in a simulated mission environment.

Its main benefits include:

  • Makes space exploration concepts more engaging and approachable.
  • Encourages teamwork, communication, and collaborative decision-making.
  • Promotes creativity and critical thinking through mission planning.
  • Introduces players to spacecraft preparation and mission management concepts.
  • Creates an interactive environment that can encourage interest in aerospace engineering, astronomy, and space science.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to make space exploration more accessible to students, young learners, and anyone interested in discovering how space missions work.

We want to transform curiosity about space into an interactive experience where people can experiment, collaborate, make decisions, and learn through gameplay.

In the future, the platform could be expanded with more realistic orbital mechanics, planetary exploration, additional mission scenarios, scientific challenges, and educational modules inspired by real NASA discoveries and missions.

4. What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed using modern web technologies:

  • React: Building the interactive user interface.
  • TypeScript: Application logic and type safety.
  • Three.js: 3D graphics and spacecraft visualization.
  • Vite: Development server and build tooling.
  • BroadcastChannel API: Multiplayer communication and synchronization across browser tabs.
  • AI Integration: Supporting AI-assisted mission architecture and planning.
  • Procedural Audio: Generating mission sound effects and immersive audio experiences.
  • HTML5 and CSS: Structuring and styling the application.

The project is designed as a browser-based experience, making it accessible without specialized hardware.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

The creative aspect of GTA NASA is its combination of space exploration, gaming, artificial intelligence, procedural audio, and multiplayer collaboration into one interactive experience.

Rather than treating space exploration as a passive learning topic, we turn it into a collaborative mission where players can take different roles, coordinate decisions, manage resources, and experience mission sequences together.

The multiplayer mission room, AI-assisted mission architecture, and interactive mission workflow distinguish the project from a conventional space-themed game.

6. What factors did the team consider?

During development, we considered several important factors:

  • Accessibility: Making the experience available through a standard web browser.
  • Engagement: Creating interactive features that keep players involved.
  • Collaboration: Allowing multiple players to coordinate and make decisions.
  • Educational Value: Keeping the experience connected to real-world space exploration concepts.
  • Technical Feasibility: Using modern web technologies to build a functional browser-based experience.
  • Scalability: Designing the project so that additional missions, features, and learning experiences can be introduced later.

Ultimately, GTA NASA: The Kepler Expedition aims to bring the excitement of space exploration closer to people by combining technology, creativity, teamwork, and interactive learning.

projectDetails.name: Astronaut Health Twin
projectDetails.summary:
Long-duration astronauts will have to assess their own health with limited real-time help from Earth. Most health dashboards show a number and leave the interpretation to the reader. Astronaut Health Twin compares an astronaut against their own baseline and their own history, then shows the result as an interactive 3D body.

An astronaut records a check-up: 22 metrics including heart rate, blood pressure, sleep, mood, stress, exercise and vision, plus symptoms with severity and mission context such as workload, spacewalks and radiation events. The app compares each value against their personal baseline, their previous check-up and their mission trend, then scores six body systems and automatically opens the 3D body at the region the evidence points to. Each region explains the relevant NASA hazard, the official NASA risk category, why it matters in microgravity, and cites a NASA or CSA source.

The app deliberately does not diagnose or recommend treatment. It separates measurement, comparison, mission context and guidance, and the guidance comes from an approved next-step ladder. A test-enforced tripwire fails the build if generated copy ever claims a diagnosis.

It runs fully offline: no accounts, no server, no paid API.
projectDetails.details:
LIVE APP: https://himesh-codrr.github.io/ (no login, no install)

WHAT IT DOES

Astronaut Health Twin is an offline-first web and mobile app that turns a routine health check-up into an understandable next action. Three ideas sit behind it:

1. PERSONAL HEALTH HISTORY. Every astronaut differs, so the app compares an astronaut with their own baseline and their own previous check-ups, never against a population average. A reading can be normal for one crew member and unusual for another.

2. A 3D BODY AS THE INTERFACE. Health data becomes a tappable, rotatable body instead of rows of numbers. Six systems are modelled: head & eyes, heart & blood vessels, muscles & bones, immune & digestive, mind & sleep, and a whole-body radiation layer. After a check-up the body automatically focuses on the system with the most evidence, and mesh colour is computed from that astronaut's own data.

3. MISSION-AWARE CONTEXT. A change only means something next to what the astronaut was experiencing. The app records workload, spacewalks, disrupted sleep schedules and radiation events, and surfaces them alongside the health change.

BENEFIT AND IMPACT. On a Mars transit, communication delay makes real-time guidance from Earth impossible, so the crew must interpret their own data. The app shortens that loop from "here is a number" to "here is what changed, why it may have changed, and what to do next" — and it does so in a form a tired crew member can read in seconds.

HOW IT WORKS

The comparison engine is deterministic and auditable. It computes the change from baseline (with a 5% floor so noise is not reported as change), the change since the previous check-up, a fitted least-squares trend requiring at least three points, and a robust outlier test using median and median absolute deviation. Regions are ranked with strongly diminishing returns, so a single alarming signal cannot be outvoted by a wide region reporting many mild ones. The 3D scene is a pure function of that ranking.

Tools used: Expo SDK 58 and React Native (one codebase for iOS, Android and web), TypeScript, three.js with expo-gl and react-three-fiber for the procedural 3D anatomy, AsyncStorage for local persistence, and Vitest for the 88-test suite.

CREATIVITY AND CONSIDERATIONS

We chose procedural geometry rather than a downloaded human model: there is no third-party asset licence to clear, and a stylised figure cannot be mistaken for a medical scan of the astronaut. Safety was a design constraint from the start, not a disclaimer bolted on. The app never says "you have", "diagnose", "prescribe" or "treatment plan" — a test fails the build if that language ever appears.

We deliberately did NOT train a deep-learning model. Astronaut medical datasets are small and privacy-protected; a model trained on them would be unvalidatable, and a patient-facing system that emits diagnoses needs clinical oversight a prototype cannot have. Instead every sentence the app generates can be traced back to a number and a source.

Three fictional astronauts ship with the app, each with a different trajectory, so reviewers can confirm the app generalises rather than being tuned to one story.

WHAT A REVIEWER CAN CHECK IN ONE MINUTE

Add an astronaut and set their own baselines, then reload the page — the profile is still there. Mark a follow-up step done with a note and the progress counter updates. Export the handover as JSON, text or PDF: the PDF is real, selectable text with sparkline charts, generated on-device through the OS print engine. The Privacy tab states the offline guarantee as inspectable facts (record counts, storage keys, stored size) rather than a slogan — and a test walks the whole source tree and fails the build if any network call is ever added.

projectDetails.name: Mission Forge
projectDetails.summary:
Mission Forge is a browser-based space mission design game, built as a single self-contained HTML file. The player picks one of three missions: Earth wildfire watching, Mars subsurface ice mapping, or Moon south-pole water hunting. Then they design a spacecraft step by step: body, power system, antenna, science instruments, orbit, and launch rocket.

A live dashboard tracks mass, power, budget, and data against limits, which must all stay in the green. On launch, a canvas animation plays and random events (solar storm, antenna glitch, micrometeoroid hit, or good luck) can change the outcome. A report then explains what worked and scores the mission out of 120 points across success, science, efficiency, and decisions.

It uses Three.js for the 3D spacecraft view and canvas for the starfield and launch animation. Real NASA data grounds it: Mars gets about 43% of Earth's sunlight, and orbit heights are realistic. Up to four players can team up with a shared code and split roles. Game numbers are simplified for learning, not actual NASA specifications.
projectDetails.details:
Mission Forge: Design, Launch, Learn

What it does and how it works
Mission Forge is a browser game where players design a space mission and then launch it. They choose a science goal: mapping subsurface ice on Mars, spotting wildfires from Earth orbit, or finding water in the Moon's shadowed south pole craters. Then they pick an orbit, spacecraft body, power system, antenna, instruments and launch vehicle.

A Design Workshop lets players build their own spacecraft by choosing body type, material, structure size, solar array, battery, dish, transmitter, radiators, propellant and heat shield. Every change rebuilds a live 3D model that can be rotated and zoomed, so shape, size and layout follow the player's engineering choices.

On launch, the simulation checks six things: rocket capacity, instrument payload, power, data sent to Earth, budget and the science goal. It plays an animated launch with a random space event, such as a solar storm, and gives a score out of 100 with a plain-language report.

If a launch fails, a built-in Mission Coach explains what went wrong in simple terms. It can apply fixes, explain how the game works, answer typed questions, show a working design and suggest next steps, like other missions or tighter budget challenges.

Benefits
Players learn real engineering trade-offs by trying them: more instruments need more power, more data capacity, more mass and more money. Failure is safe and useful, because each failed launch becomes a lesson. The game runs in any modern browser, on phones and laptops, with no installation or sign-up. There is no single right answer, so players can experiment and compare designs.

Intended impact
We want space mission design to feel understandable and fun for students and curious beginners. Players should finish a session knowing why real missions are built the way they are, and feeling that engineering is something they can try. The coach is meant to stop learners from giving up when a design does not work, turning frustration into curiosity about how NASA teams solve the same problems.

Tools and technology
We built Mission Forge with HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single self-contained file. three.js (WebGL) powers the interactive 3D spacecraft, and the HTML canvas draws the launch animation. Mission values draw on NASA public data, including fact sheets comparing sunlight at Mars and Earth, and real examples such as NASA's Mars radar ice findings, the LCROSS Moon water detection and the FIRMS wildfire system. Sources are listed inside the game. We used Claude, an AI assistant, to help write and debug code, including the coach and the workshop-to-3D connection. The game is hosted on GitHub Pages and needs only a device with a web browser.

How it is creative
Many space games focus on flying a ship. Mission Forge focuses on designing a mission and balancing limits. The spacecraft's appearance is generated directly from engineering choices, so the model is the design. The Mission Coach gives guidance exactly when players are stuck, and missions connect to real NASA science questions.

Factors our team considered
Accuracy versus simplicity: formulas are simplified but follow real relationships between power, mass, data, heat and cost. Accessibility: plain language, a mobile-friendly layout and no sign-up. Learning through failure: reports explain why something failed and what to try next. Replayability: many valid designs, random events and optional challenges. Openness: a single file with no server and cited public data. Limits: live team play works only inside Claude's platform, and the coach follows fixed rules rather than a live AI.

projectDetails.name: FIREWATCH
projectDetails.summary:
FIREWATCH is a global satellite-based wildfire monitoring and intelligence platform developed to address NASA's challenge of harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS active fire observations. It integrates fire detection data from MODIS aboard Terra and Aqua and VIIRS aboard Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21 into a unified, interactive platform.
The application features a global fire detection map, an interactive 3D Earth Explorer, satellite-specific filters, hotspot information, date-based analysis, and a burning activity calendar. By bringing observations from multiple satellite instruments together, FIREWATCH helps users explore fire activity across different geographical regions and time periods.
The project addresses the challenge by providing a common visualization and analysis environment for comparing MODIS and VIIRS detections, supporting a clearer understanding of their spatial and temporal patterns. It aims to make satellite fire information more accessible and useful for researchers, environmental organizations, disaster management teams, and policymakers.
FIREWATCH is important because timely and accessible fire intelligence can support wildfire awareness, environmental protection, and more informed decisions for managing fire-related risks.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does the project do and how does it work?

FIREWATCH is a global satellite-based fire monitoring and visualization platform designed to bring MODIS and VIIRS active fire observations together in one interactive environment. It uses NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System) data to display fire detections from MODIS aboard Terra and Aqua and VIIRS aboard Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21.

Users can explore fire activity through a global interactive 2D map and a 3D Earth Explorer. The platform provides satellite-specific filters, geographical exploration, hotspot information, date-based analysis, and a burning activity calendar. These features help users examine where and when fire detections occur and explore differences between satellite observations.

The system is designed to support global exploration rather than being restricted to a particular country or region.

2. What benefits does it have?

FIREWATCH makes satellite fire information easier to access, explore, and understand. Its key benefits include:

  • Bringing multiple satellite fire observation sources into one platform.
  • Enabling users to explore fire activity across countries and continents.
  • Supporting comparison of MODIS and VIIRS detections.
  • Providing temporal and geographical visualization of fire activity.
  • Making hotspot information easier to interpret through interactive maps.
  • Helping users identify patterns and periods of increased fire activity.

3. What is the intended impact?

The intended impact is to improve accessibility and understanding of global fire observations. FIREWATCH aims to support researchers, environmental organizations, disaster management authorities, students, and policymakers in monitoring fire activity and exploring satellite-based evidence.

By presenting observations in a unified and understandable interface, the project can contribute to wildfire awareness, environmental monitoring, research, and more informed fire-risk management decisions.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software were used?

The project was developed using Google Antigravity as an AI-assisted development environment and GitHub for source-code management and version control.

The platform integrates NASA FIRMS data and uses web-based mapping and 3D visualization technologies to present geographical and satellite information.

The implementation uses the technologies and libraries identified in the project codebase, including its frontend framework, backend services, mapping libraries, 3D rendering tools, and data visualization components. It is deployed as a publicly accessible web application.

No specialized physical hardware was required beyond a computer and an internet connection for development and testing.

5. How is the project creative?

FIREWATCH combines satellite fire observations with an interactive global 2D map, a 3D Earth visualization, and a burning activity calendar in one application.

Instead of presenting fire detections only as raw datasets or static maps, it allows users to explore hotspots geographically and temporally, switch between satellite sources, and investigate activity from a global perspective.

The integration of 3D Earth exploration with satellite-specific fire visualization creates a more engaging and intuitive way to understand large-scale fire activity.

6. What factors did the team consider?

The development considered several important factors:

  • Global coverage: The application should support worldwide exploration rather than a limited selection of countries.
  • Data reliability: Satellite observations should retain their original geographic coordinates, timestamps, source information, and relevant attributes.
  • Harmonization: MODIS and VIIRS observations have different sensor characteristics, spatial resolutions, and detection capabilities. Their differences must be considered when comparing observations.
  • Usability: Maps, filters, calendars, and hotspot details should be understandable and accessible.
  • Performance: Global datasets and 3D imagery require efficient loading, caching, and visualization.
  • Scalability: The platform should be capable of supporting additional satellite sources and larger datasets.
  • Transparency: Users should be able to identify which satellite produced an observation and understand the limitations of the data.

Conclusion

FIREWATCH aims to transform multiple satellite fire observations into an accessible global fire intelligence experience. By combining MODIS and VIIRS visualization, geographical exploration, and temporal analysis, it provides a foundation for understanding satellite fire observations and supporting future research into their harmonization.
