projectDetails.name: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
projectDetails.summary:
AURA-MED: Autonomous Astronaut Health & Multi-Hazard Clinical Decision Support System

Our Solution: 
We built an autonomous AURA-MED, the clinical decision support platform for deep space that employs edge computing to support medical diagnostics and treatments with up to 20-min latencies for communications with Earth.

Why Is Our Solution a Game-Changer?  
AURA-MED creates an autonomous "Gather → Evaluate → Act" system, in compliance with NASA-STD-3001 Medical Level of Care V. AURA-MED takes biometric telemetry data, habitat life-support metrics, and diagnostic tools' results. Our major innovation, the Cross-Hazard Synergistic Threat Engine, analyses correlation between environmental hazards (such as increased cabin CO2) levels or radiation exposure) and astronaut's physiological data to detect early-stage compound threats of cardiovascular deconditioning, SANS, bone resorption, immune suppression, and cognitive fatigue, providing instant closed-loop actions (Lower Body Negative Pressure exercise, dynamic ARED resistance changes, and circadian lighting adjustment).

Why Does It Matter? 
With AURA-MED, there is no need for real-time telemedical diagnostics from the Earth; it allows non-medical personnel to safely diagnose and treat astronauts during the mission. In addition, its ability to operate autonomously in offline mode gives immediate application of the platform in isolation environments on Earth (for example, Antarctic stations or rural clinics).
projectDetails.details:
Project Details: AURA-MED (Autonomous Astronaut Health & Multi-Hazard Clinical Decision Support System)

1. What does it do or how does it work?

AURA-MED is an offline-first, edge-computed clinical decision support platform engineered for deep-space missions—such as transit to Mars—where communication latencies reach up to 20 minutes one-way (40 minutes round-trip) and real-time telemedicine from Earth is impossible.

The software operates through a closed "Gather → Evaluate → Act" loop:

  • Gather (Tri-Tier Telemetry Ingestion): Ingests continuous vitals from wearable smart garments (ECG, photoplethysmography, respiration rate, skin temperature, actigraphy, and heart rate variability), real-time environmental life-support data from spacecraft systems (cabin ambient CO2), atmospheric pressure, and active dosimeter radiation flux), and episodic diagnostics (point-of-care ultrasound and cognitive performance tests).
  • Evaluate (Cross-Hazard Synergistic Threat Engine): Rather than analyzing health indicators in silos, the engine correlates environmental stressors with physiological signals. For example, it detects when microgravity cephalad fluid shifts combine with elevated cabin (CO2) ((>3.0mmHg)) and expanding Optic Nerve Sheath Diameter (ONSD> 5.82mm), pre-symptomatically flagging Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) before visual impairment occurs.
  • Act (Closed-Loop Countermeasures & AI Guidance): Automatically transitions from diagnosis to actionable execution cards. It prescribes and timers targeted countermeasures—such as Lower Body Negative Pressure (LBNP at (-30mmHg)) to draw pooled fluids toward the legs, dynamic (+15%) resistance increases on the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED) to prevent bone mineral density loss, and habitat-wide routing to water-wall storm shelters during acute Solar Particle Events (SPEs).

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Enables Medical Self-Reliance (Level of Care V): Fulfills NASA-STD-3001 Level of Care V requirements, allowing non-physician astronauts to diagnose and treat complex medical conditions without ground intervention.
  • Pre-Symptomatic Detection: Spots compounded, multi-hazard risks early, intervening before irreversible tissue remodeling, bone mineral loss, or operational error takes place.
  • Zero Automation Paralysis & Alarm Fatigue: Emphasizes context-aware triaging (Green/Yellow/Red) with dynamic alert shelving, preventing nuisance alarms from waking or overwhelming crew during high-stress flight maneuvers.
  • Eliminates Human Error in Clinical Exams: Provides real-time AI augmented-reality guidance during point-of-care ultrasound examinations, ensuring non-specialist crew capture diagnostic-grade imaging.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • For Deep-Space Exploration: Eliminates the critical "distance from Earth" hazard, safeguarding crew health and mission success during multi-year expeditions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.
  • Galactic Impact (Terrestrial Dual-Use): Delivers immediate value on Earth by deploying the same offline-first, self-guided diagnostic capabilities to extreme, isolated environments. This includes Antarctic winter-over research stations (like Concordia and Amundsen-Scott) facing satellite blackouts, commercial maritime vessels at sea, and remote rural or indigenous clinics lacking on-site medical specialists.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Frontend & Visualization: Modern JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, Tailwind CSS for high-contrast accessibility compliance (NASA-STD-3001 Vol 2), and Chart.js for real-time telemetry sparklines and multi-parametric trend projections.
  • Core Computational Engine: WebAssembly (WASM) for local, client-side execution of deterministic diagnostic algorithms and lightweight computer vision inference without cloud dependencies.
  • Local Data Architecture: Client-side IndexedDB / SQLite-WASM implementing HL7 FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) and openEHR JSON schemas for encrypted, store-and-forward asynchronous synchronization with Mission Control.
  • Hardware Telemetry References: Ingestion models calibrated to flight-proven specifications: the Canadian Space Agency (CSA) Bio-Monitor / Astroskin smart garment, handheld semiconductor ultrasound (Butterfly iQ / POCUS), and Timepix active dosimeters.

5. How is your project creative?

  • The ECLSS-to-Physiology Cross-Coupling: Most medical apps treat the human body as an isolated system. AURA-MED’s creativity lies in directly interfacing spacecraft Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS) with human biology, recognizing that habitat conditions (such as mild hypercapnia or background radiation) multiply microgravity-induced bodily degradation.
  • AI "Centaur" Just-in-Time Training (JITT): Instead of static instruction manuals, the software uses real-time computer vision guidance overlays during diagnostic procedures (e.g., directing an astronaut’s hand angle during an ultrasound and auto-segmenting anatomical landmarks).
  • Interactive 3D Digital Twin HUD: Translates complex multi-omic, behavioral, and telemetry datasets into an intuitive 3D anatomical body map, reducing cognitive translation time for fatigued astronauts.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Cognitive Load & Environmental Stress: Accounted for mild executive fatigue caused by elevated cabin (CO2) (3.0-5.0 mmHg) and chronic sleep debt (<6hrs/night), designing clean, high-contrast, distraction-free interfaces that minimize required clicks during emergencies.
    • Universal Career Space Permissible Exposure Limit (SPEL) of 600 mSv (REID< 3%).
    • Acute Solar Particle Event (SPE) limit of 250 mSv per event.
    • Skeletal permissible outcome limit maintaining post-mission bone mineral density T-score (> -2.0).
  • Spacecraft Compute & Storage Constraints: Addressed microcomputer limits by implementing a Hierarchical Data Buffering architecture: continuous vitals are held in a rolling 10-minute high-resolution cache, and only downsampled trends or event-triggered anomalies are permanently stored.
  • AI Safety & Deterministic Verification: Mitigated AI hallucination risks by routing all machine learning recommendations through deterministic, flight-proven NASA clinical rule filters, ensuring the crew retains final manual master override authority.

projectDetails.summary:
ARES-1 Outpost Trainer is an interactive, browser-based life-support trade-off simulator created for cadets ages 7–12, directly answering the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge. Players take command as Flight Director for humanity’s first permanent Moon or Mars outpost, keeping a crew of 4 alive across 10 sols by balancing a scarce power grid between Life Support, Radiation Mass Shielding, Hydroponics, and Thermal Control.

Rather than relying on abstract facts or fictional numbers, our simulator turns authentic spaceflight engineering into gameplay where no choice is free: saving power on heating risks freezing the greenhouse, while underpowering scrubbers triggers toxic CO₂ accumulation. Every mechanic is grounded in real NASA open data—including live Coronal Mass Ejection tracking via the NASA DONKI API, astronaut radiation biology from the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR), closed-loop water recovery from NASA Marshall ECLSS, and surface extremes from Artemis and Mars Perseverance MEDA. 100% web-based with zero installs required.
projectDetails.details:
ARES-1 Outpost Trainer — Deep Space Habitat Simulator

1. What Does It Do & How Does It Work?

ARES-1 Outpost Trainer is an interactive, browser-based life-support trade-off simulator designed for young explorers (ages 7–12) answering the Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Players step into the shoes of Flight Director for humanity’s first permanent outpost on the Moon (Shackleton Crater) or Mars (Jezero Crater).

Each sol (mission day), the player manages a limited power grid across four interconnected subsystems:

  • Life Support: Drives oxygen generation and catalytic CO₂ scrubbers.
  • Radiation Mass Shielding: Powers the interior storm shelter to absorb cosmic rays and solar particles.
  • Hydroponics Bay: Cultivates fresh greens under LED lighting, generating food, supplementary O₂, and crew morale.
  • Thermal Control: Heats the habitat against freezing -173°C lunar nights and -60°C Martian chill.

Before committing a turn, players see a live "Causal Impact Preview" that reveals the consequences of their power choices. Over 10 sols, they must navigate 8 randomized crisis events (Coronal Mass Ejections, dust storms, water recycler biofilm, and thermal radiator leaks).

2. Benefits & Intended Impact

Most educational space content for children stays abstract (posters or passive trivia) without conveying the core reality of spaceflight: no choice is free. ARES-1 bridges this gap by turning genuine engineering constraints into playful mechanics:

  • Kids learn systems thinking—saving power on heating freezes crops, while starving life support builds toxic CO₂.
  • It demystifies real aerospace trade-offs in plain, kid-friendly English.
  • Being 100% web-based with zero installs or accounts, it is instantly accessible to classrooms, STEM clubs, and families worldwide on mobile, tablet, or desktop.

3. Tools, Coding Languages & Tech Stack

  • Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, and Vite 6 for high-performance client-side execution.
  • Styling & Design System: Tailwind CSS v4 (@tailwindcss/vite) with custom space-age animations.
  • UI Icons: Lucide React.
  • Procedural Sound Engine: Native Web Audio API (AudioContext) generating real-time radio chirps, warning alarms, and victory fanfares without external audio files.
  • Testing: Vitest test suite with 15 automated unit and balance simulation tests ensuring rigorous, fair gameplay math.
  • Deployment: Hosted continuously on Netlify and GitHub Pages via GitHub Actions CI/CD.

4. Creativity & Innovation

  • 100% Inline Procedural SVG Graphics: The habitat visualizer is crafted entirely in code—featuring dynamic solar panel dust accumulation that players can manually brush off via EVA, responsive radiation shield bubbles, greenhouse harvest animations, and an interactive rover soil scanner.
  • RoboCapcom Mentor: An inline SVG robot advisor that analyzes the player's telemetry in real time and provides tactical advice without spoiling solutions.
  • Post-Mission Debrief & Sparklines: When the mission concludes, players receive a flight evaluation with SVG telemetry sparklines, failure-chain post-mortems, and earned rank badges.

5. Real NASA Open Data & Science Grounding

Rather than inventing fictional parameters, our simulation connects directly to verified NASA open datasets:

  • NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database): Connects to api.nasa.gov/DONKI to query live Coronal Mass Ejections and solar flares, dynamically scaling in-game radiation risk based on current real-world solar conditions.
  • NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR): Incorporates findings from study OSD-100 (astronaut cellular DNA damage from deep space radiation) and OSD-37 (GeneLab microgravity plant photosynthesis efficiency).
  • NASA Marshall Space Flight Center ECLSS: Models real 98% closed-loop water recovery and Sabatier reactor CO₂ catalytic scrubbing.
  • NASA Artemis & Mars Perseverance MEDA: Grounds lunar South Pole thermal swings (+120°C in sunlight to -173°C in shadow) and Jezero Crater atmospheric dust opacity.

projectDetails.name: TerraTrace AI	NISAR-Powered Earth Surface Change Intelligence
projectDetails.summary:
TerraTrace AI is an AI-powered geospatial intelligence platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the challenge "Dancing with the SARs." It uses real NASA-ISRO NISAR L-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) observations to identify and investigate changes in Earth's surface over time.

Using Bengaluru, Karnataka, as our initial study area, TerraTrace AI analyses two NISAR observations acquired on October 29 and November 10, 2026. It processes HH and HV polarization measurements, compares temporal radar backscatter, identifies candidate surface-change regions, and visualizes the results through interactive maps, geospatial overlays, and statistical analysis.

Powered by a LangGraph-based AI agent, the platform connects specialized analysis tools and generates evidence-grounded explanations while preserving scientific uncertainty and data provenance.

Our vision is to make complex satellite radar observations accessible for monitoring urban landscapes, vegetation, water bodies, and other environmental changes, helping researchers and communities make better-informed decisions for a changing planet.
projectDetails.details:
TerraTrace AI: NISAR-Powered Earth Surface Change Intelligence

1. Project Overview

TerraTrace AI is an AI-powered geospatial intelligence platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under the challenge "Dancing with the SARs." The platform leverages NASA-ISRO NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) observations to analyse, identify, and visualize changes occurring on Earth's surface over time.

The project focuses on transforming complex satellite radar measurements into accessible geospatial information through temporal analysis, automated change detection, interactive visualization, and agentic AI orchestration.

2. System Architecture and Methodology

TerraTrace AI follows a modular processing architecture consisting of several interconnected components.

NISAR Data Acquisition and Validation: The platform works with real NISAR L-band Level-2 GCOV observations. It validates product metadata, acquisition dates, polarization availability, spatial coverage, coordinate reference systems, and data integrity before processing.

SAR Data Processing: HDF5-based NISAR products are inspected to extract available HH and HV polarization measurements. The processing pipeline performs data-quality checks, backscatter preparation, geospatial extraction, and spatial alignment to support temporal comparison.

Temporal Backscatter Analysis: Radar backscatter measurements from different acquisition dates are compared to identify variations in surface response. The system generates polarization-specific difference layers and statistical summaries.

Change Detection and Geospatial Analysis: Statistical screening techniques identify candidate radar-change regions. The resulting outputs include change masks, GeoJSON polygons, spatial statistics, and estimated candidate-change areas.

Agentic AI Orchestration: A LangGraph-based agent coordinates specialized analysis tools through task classification, tool selection, execution tracking, and evidence integration. This enables structured analysis workflows and traceable processing.

Interactive Visualization: A React-based dashboard with Leaflet mapping capabilities presents satellite observations, HH/HV comparisons, temporal difference maps, candidate regions, and geospatial statistics.

Evidence-Based Reporting: The platform organizes processing metadata, analytical outputs, geospatial evidence, and scientific limitations into understandable results and reporting workflows.

3. Bengaluru Case Study

Bengaluru, Karnataka, serves as the initial study area for demonstrating the platform's capabilities. The implementation uses two real NISAR L-band GCOV observations acquired on 29 October 2026 and 10 November 2026.

The observations contain HH and HV polarization measurements, which are extracted and analysed on a common 10-metre geospatial grid using the EPSG:32643 coordinate reference system.

The temporal analysis has generated polarization-specific difference maps, candidate change masks, spatial regions, and statistical summaries. The current results identify 5,741 HH candidate pixels and 3,762 HV candidate pixels, corresponding to estimated candidate areas of 57.41 hectares and 37.62 hectares, respectively.

These results represent candidate radar-backscatter anomalies and require independent supporting evidence before being attributed to specific environmental or human activities.

4. Technology Stack

The platform integrates technologies across artificial intelligence, backend development, geospatial processing, and interactive visualization.

  • Programming Languages: Python and JavaScript.
  • Backend: FastAPI.
  • Frontend: React.js and Vite.
  • Agentic AI: LangGraph.
  • AI/ML: PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers, BLIP, and PEFT.
  • Geospatial Processing: HDF5, h5py, Rasterio, GeoPandas, NumPy, and GDAL-compatible tools.
  • Visualization: Leaflet, Matplotlib, and interactive geospatial overlays.
  • Data Format: HDF5, GeoTIFF, and GeoJSON.
  • Primary Data Source: NASA-ISRO NISAR observations.

5. Innovation and Technical Contributions

TerraTrace AI integrates NISAR radar processing, temporal backscatter analysis, geospatial change detection, and agentic AI within a unified application.

Its modular architecture connects specialized analytical tools through an auditable agent workflow. Rather than presenting radar imagery as isolated visual outputs, the platform links observations, polarization measurements, temporal differences, candidate regions, and supporting metadata.

The combination of scientific processing and interactive geospatial visualization makes complex radar observations more understandable and accessible to users with different levels of remote-sensing expertise.

6. Benefits and Intended Impact

TerraTrace AI aims to support more accessible and informed monitoring of Earth's changing surface. Its potential applications include investigating urban surface changes, vegetation variations, water-body dynamics, and flood-related surface changes.

The platform is intended to benefit researchers, environmental analysts, urban planners, resource managers, and decision-makers by providing interactive spatial evidence and temporal comparisons.

By integrating NISAR observations with complementary optical, environmental, and geospatial datasets, the system can be extended to support broader environmental assessment and future disaster-monitoring applications.

7. Scientific Reliability and Responsible Interpretation

Data integrity, geospatial compatibility, reproducibility, and uncertainty are central considerations in the development of TerraTrace AI.

The platform preserves source observation metadata and distinguishes measured radar variations from algorithm-generated candidate changes and possible environmental interpretations. It does not treat backscatter anomalies as confirmed flooding, construction, deforestation, or urban expansion without independent corroboration.

This approach promotes transparent and scientifically responsible interpretation of satellite observations.

8. Future Development

Future development will focus on supporting additional NISAR observations, multiple study areas, longer temporal sequences, complementary Earth-observation datasets, and improved independent validation.

The long-term vision is to evolve TerraTrace AI into a scalable, agentic Earth-observation intelligence platform that transforms satellite radar data into accessible, evidence-grounded insights for understanding and monitoring a continuously changing planet.

projectDetails.name: Curious Cosmo: Chasing the Light Horizon
projectDetails.summary: Curious Cosmo: Chasing the Light Horizon is an interactive, browser-based astronaut survival simulator and mission trainer that guides aspiring flight directors from the Lunar South Pole to Mars and out to Voyager 1's 1 Light-Day milestone. Powered by live NASA Open APIs and real aerospace physics models, players manage life-support trade-offs, complete hands-on engineering tasks, customize their spacesuit with earned NASA mission patches, and transmit a visual-audio Morse code beacon across interstellar space.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works

Curious Cosmo: Chasing the Light Horizon is an interactive, browser-based astronaut survival simulator and mission trainer built for aspiring flight directors. Guided by Cadet Sunny and Hoot the Space Owl, players progress through a 3-chapter deep-space journey—from the Lunar South Pole to Mars and out to Voyager 1's 1 Light-Day milestone—solving real aerospace life-support trade-offs and hands-on engineering mini-games:

- Chapter 1 (Lunar Base at Shackleton Crater): Syncs live solar flare alerts from NASA's DONKI API. Players balance oxygen reserves against radiation shielding and pump water-ice walls to watch live dosimeter readings drop in real time via the exponential radiation attenuation formula (D = D0 * e^(-μx)).

- Chapter 2 (Mars Outpost at Jezero Crater): Simulates a 14-minute one-way communication delay and connects daily resistive exercise (modeled on NASA OSDR microgravity research) to astronaut EVA stamina during a Martian dust-storm solar array cleanup.

- Chapter 3 (Interstellar Relay at Voyager 1): Tracks Voyager 1's real-time approach toward its historic 1 Light-Day (24-hour signal delay / 16.09 billion miles) milestone. Players calculate Plutonium-238 Radioisotope Thermoelectric Generator (RTG) decay (P(t) = P0 * e^(-λt)) and shed non-essential instrument loads to keep the Golden Record transmitter online.

- Spacesuit Locker, V-G-R Beacon & Certificate Export: Players unlock official-style mission patches (NASA Artemis, Mars Perseverance, and Voyager Golden Record), customize Sunny's suit colorway, transmit "V - G - R" in synthesized audio-visual Morse code across one light-day, and download a dynamically generated PDF Mission Certificate.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Deep-space exploration involves complex physics and physiological challenges that can feel abstract in textbooks. By turning real NASA open data and aerospace engineering equations into interactive cause-and-effect gameplay, Curious Cosmo makes space science accessible, memorable, and engaging for young learners and space enthusiasts—inspiring the next generation of mission planners and flight directors.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

- Languages & Core Web Standards: HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+) for lightweight, zero-install browser performance.

- Graphics & Audio APIs: HTML5 Canvas API (for dynamic spacesuit and circular mission patch compositing) and Web Audio API (for real-time Morse code synthesis and interactive sound effects).

- Libraries & Deployment: jsPDF for automated client-side PDF certificate generation, hosted statically via GitHub Pages.

Creativity & Key Design Factors Considered

- Resilient Live-Data Architecture: Fetches live NASA DONKI solar flare classifications and NASA OSDR (Study OSD-48) metadata on launch while seamlessly falling back to curated NASA telemetry if offline or rate-limited, ensuring uninterrupted gameplay anywhere.

- Accessible Physics Visualization: Translates exponential radiation shielding and RTG half-life decay into intuitive interactive sliders, pumps, and live telemetry readouts rather than static equations.

- Zero-Barrier Access: Designed as a pure client-side web application so students, educators, and judges can launch and play immediately on any device without installations or logins.

projectDetails.details:
How Dancing with the SARs project works

Project objective: To demonstrate how the NASA–ISRO NISAR satellite uses L-band and S-band radar to monitor changes on Earth's surface.

* Display results: Show maps, graphs and radar visualisations.

* Save results: Store observations for future comparison.

* Simulation: Radar modelling and calculations.

* Data processing: SAR image analysis.

* Database: Store observations and results.

An interactive platform that helps users understand how NISAR satellite technology monitors floods, vegetation and ground movement.

projectDetails.name: NASA-FLAME
projectDetails.summary:
NASA-FLAME is a full-stack, AI-powered microgravity combustion research platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It focuses on understanding how flames behave in space, where the absence of normal gravity changes combustion patterns, flame shapes, heat distribution, and fuel behaviour.
On Earth, gravity causes hot gases to rise through natural convection, creating familiar flame shapes. In microgravity, this effect is significantly reduced, causing flames to behave differently and sometimes form nearly spherical structures. Understanding these differences is important for improving spacecraft fire safety and designing safer space missions.
Our solution combines a web-based research platform, backend APIs, scientific datasets, AI-powered analysis, and flame simulation capabilities. Users can explore combustion parameters, examine flame behaviour, compare experimental and simulated results, and understand how different conditions influence combustion in microgravity.
The platform uses a modern Next.js frontend and FastAPI backend, supported by a structured database and AI/ML components. It also references NASA combustion research, including ACME, FLEX, and other microgravity experiments.
Our goal: Make complex microgravity combustion research easier to explore, analyse, and understand while supporting safer future space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
NASA-FLAME: Fire Beyond Gravity

NASA-FLAME is an AI-powered microgravity combustion research platform designed to help users explore and understand how flames behave in space. On Earth, gravity drives natural convection, causing hot gases to rise and flames to take their familiar shape. In microgravity, this effect is significantly reduced, resulting in unusual flame shapes, heat distribution, and combustion behaviour. Understanding these differences is essential for improving fire safety aboard spacecraft and supporting future space exploration.

Our platform brings together scientific research, data analysis, and simulation capabilities in one interactive web application. Users can explore combustion parameters, examine flame behaviour under different conditions, compare experimental and simulated results, and understand how environmental factors influence microgravity combustion. AI-powered analysis helps interpret patterns and provides insights into combustion behaviour.

The project aims to make complex scientific information more accessible, support combustion research, and contribute to safer spacecraft design and fire prevention strategies.

We developed the platform using Next.js, React, TypeScript, Python, FastAPI, and a structured database, alongside AI/ML components and scientific data-processing tools. We also referenced NASA research and microgravity combustion investigations, including ACME and FLEX.

The creative aspect of NASA-FLAME is its integration of research, interactive visualisation, AI-driven insights, and simulation into a unified platform rather than presenting scientific information as static reports.

During development, our team considered scientific accuracy, data provenance, usability, accessibility, performance, scalability, and the practical challenges of analysing combustion in microgravity.

Our intended impact is to make microgravity combustion research easier to understand and explore while contributing to the broader goal of safer human spaceflight.

We developed ECHOES OF SPACE, an interactive digital archive that showcases the forgotten explorers of space, including historical spacecraft, rovers, landers, and scientific instruments.

This project is important because it preserves humanity's space exploration heritage, promotes scientific awareness, and inspires students and future generations to explore space science and technology.

projectDetails.name: Project DuoDa
projectDetails.summary: The game drops you right into space exploration and real world experience of how space missions work. We built a browser-based game that tackles what it's actually like to design a deep-space mission and deal with the fallout when things go sideways. Instead of basic survival tropes, you're wrestling with real aerospace trade-offs—like balancing a strict $3.0B budget and 10,000 kg mass limit between heavy hull armor or high-end science gear. If you skimp on armor, you're dealing with a brutal crash landing and intense repair work; if you over-insulate, you sacrifice crucial science instruments. Once you're on the surface, you're exploring -179°C methane lakes and cryovolcanic vents while managing finite data storage. And if you get stuck, our Socratic AI flight advisor won't just hand you the answers—it breaks down the physics and engineering realities so you have to make the hard calls yourself. It turns complex systems engineering into an engaging, high-stakes story that shows just how much sacrifice goes into true space exploration.
projectDetails.details: KHAGOL is a browser based space exploration and engineering game platform that makes learning about space more fun and interactive. It utilises real aerospace concepts to provide certain experiences like designing spacecraft, simulating space missions, exploring Mars with rovers, and surviving on Titan. Instead of just reading about space science, it helps users experiment with spacecraft designs, explore orbital mechanics, manage power systems and also understand how real space missions work. Our game runs directly in a web browser, so no installation is needed. Our aim is to make space engineering easier to understand and accessible to students, future engineers and possibly anyone who is curious about space. We built KHAGOL using Python, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS along with tools like Three.js for 3D models, E Charts for live data, GSAP for animations, and FastAPI for backend services. The thing that makes KHAGOL special is the way it combines real science with the excitement of a game. Users will get to design spacecraft, control Mars rovers, and explore distant worlds while learning how actual space missions work. While building it, we were focused on keeping the science realistic, while keeping the game easy to use and smooth across different devices.

It bridges the gap between complex astrodynamics and accessible STEM education.  The application works across four integrated modules:  Orbital Architect & 3D Spacecraft CAD: An interactive 3D workbench where players design spacecraft by mounting real-world components (optical imagers, Ka/X-band transceivers, ion thrusters, reaction wheels, solar arrays, and RTGs). Every design decision triggers authoritative aerospace margin calculations following AIAA S-120 standards (mass budgets, power balance, depth-of-discharge, link margins, and delta-v requirements). Authoritative Flight Simulator & Mission Operations: Propagates 365-day mission profiles across Earth, Lunar, Mars, Jovian, and Outer Solar System orbits, simulating solar eclipse cycles, telemetry downlink passes, battery degradation, thermal gradients, and anomaly mitigation. Mars Exploration Dual-Suite: A dual-mode simulation featuring a 50 kg orbital microsatellite designer and a Jezero Crater surface rover exploration game with battery energy economics, radio light-time delays, scientific rock drilling, and orbital relay coordination. Titan EVA Survival Game: A tactical atmospheric surface exploration game simulating cryo-methane lakes, radioisotope power dissipation, suit oxygen consumption, and scientific sample return. What benefits does it have? Active, Inquiry-Based STEM Learning: Replaces passive textbook formulas with real-time feedback—showing students exactly how mass margins affect launch costs or how orbital inclination impacts communication coverage. Zero-Install Accessibility: Runs directly in any modern web browser on laptops, desktops, and mobile devices with no specialized software or GPU requirements. Firewatch is a satellite-based fire monitoring and geospatial analysis system developed to address the challenge of harmonizing active fire hotspot observations from MODIS and VIIRS satellite instruments. It brings together observations from MODIS, NOAA-20 VIIRS and NOAA-21 VIIRS into a unified analytical platform, enabling consistent exploration and comparison of fire activity across South Asia. FIREWATCH

Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots

NASA Space Apps Challenge – Project Details

1. PROJECT OVERVIEW

FireWatch is a satellite-based fire monitoring and geospatial analysis platform designed to bring together fire hotspot observations from multiple satellite sources into one interactive dashboard.

It combines observations from NASA MODIS, NOAA-20 VIIRS and NOAA-21 VIIRS, allowing users to explore, compare and understand fire activity across South Asia through maps, visual analytics and geographic summaries.

2. PROBLEM STATEMENT

Fire observations are collected by different satellite instruments, and their datasets are often available separately. This makes it challenging to compare satellite observations, understand the geographical distribution of hotspots, analyze fire intensity and interpret large datasets efficiently.

FireWatch addresses this challenge by organizing multiple satellite observations into a common analytical platform.

3. HOW FIREWATCH WORKS

Step 1: Satellite Data Collection

FireWatch uses satellite fire observation datasets obtained from NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System).

The three datasets used are:

  • MODIS C6.1 – South Asia
  • VIIRS NOAA-20 – South Asia
  • VIIRS NOAA-21 – South Asia

These datasets contain information such as latitude, longitude, observation date and time, brightness temperature, Fire Radiative Power (FRP) and detection confidence.

Step 2: Data Processing

The datasets are loaded and processed using Python and Pandas. Important columns and formats are standardized, satellite sources are identified, and observations are combined into a common dataset for further analysis.

Step 3: Geospatial and Statistical Analysis

The processed observations are analyzed based on geographic location, observation time, fire intensity, detection confidence and hotspot density.

Step 4: Interactive Dashboard

The results are displayed through an interactive dashboard where users can filter observations and explore maps, charts, comparisons and regional summaries.

Note: The current prototype uses downloaded NASA FIRMS CSV snapshots. Automatic near-real-time data integration is planned for a future version.

4. CORE FEATURES

A. Geospatial Hotspot Mapping

Displays detected hotspot locations on an interactive map to help users understand their geographic distribution and identify areas with concentrated fire observations.

B. Fire Activity Timeline

Displays daily observation trends to explore changes in detected fire activity over the selected observation period.

C. Multi-Satellite Comparison

Compares observations from MODIS, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 in one analytical environment. Users can examine satellite-wise observation counts and FRP statistics.

D. Fire Radiative Power (FRP) Analysis

Examines Fire Radiative Power values to understand the intensity characteristics of observed fires. The dashboard displays average, minimum and maximum FRP and intensity distributions.

The project uses the following FRP categories:

  • Low: Below 20 MW
  • Moderate: 20–50 MW
  • High: Above 50 MW

E. Detection Confidence Analysis

Displays confidence information associated with satellite fire detections, helping users inspect the confidence characteristics of the observations.

F. Geographic Density Analysis

Groups observations into geographic grid cells and highlights areas with higher, moderate and lower hotspot concentrations. These are observation-density indicators, not predictions of future fires.

G. Multi-Satellite Grid Analysis

Uses rounded geographic coordinates to identify grid cells containing observations from multiple satellite sources. This provides a common spatial framework for examining overlapping satellite observations.

H. Country-Wise Activity Analysis

Provides regional summaries for countries across South Asia, including hotspot observations and FRP statistics. The current country grouping uses approximate geographic coordinate boundaries.

I. Fire Detection Records

Displays individual satellite observation records, including observation time, satellite source, latitude, longitude, brightness, FRP and confidence.

5. TECHNOLOGY STACK

  • Python: Main programming language used for application logic and data processing.
  • Pandas: Used to load, clean, standardize and combine satellite datasets.
  • NumPy: Used for numerical and array operations.
  • Streamlit: Used to develop the interactive web dashboard.
  • Folium: Used for interactive geographic mapping and hotspot visualization.
  • Matplotlib: Used to create charts and statistical visualizations.
  • Requests: Used for HTTP requests and potential future data integration.
  • NASA FIRMS: Source of satellite fire observation datasets.
  • Visual Studio Code: Development environment used to build the project.

6. WHAT MAKES FIREWATCH CREATIVE?

FireWatch goes beyond displaying individual fire locations. It brings multiple satellite datasets into one analytical environment and provides different ways to investigate the observations.

Its creative contributions include:

  1. Unified Satellite Analysis: Combines MODIS, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 observations into one platform.
  2. Spatial Intelligence: Uses geographic grid analysis to examine hotspot concentrations.
  3. Comparative Visualization: Provides satellite-wise statistics and FRP comparisons.

ORBITAL CREW — Space Crewmates 3D

I built a complete 3D mission-simulator game in a single 774 KB HTML file. You command a four-person NASA crew aboard the Orion MPCV · Gateway Relay during one eight-minute launch window, with thirteen procedures spread across a three-deck, ten-room spacecraft. There is no mission-select screen: everything is live simultaneously, and your AI crewmates choose their own work like people on a real shift.

The challenge's core demand was interaction, so the procedures are five genuinely different hands-on consoles — a colour-matching wiring loom, pressure manifolds you trim into green bands, a launch keypad, Simon-style gyro memory, and a sweeping antenna alignment — each feeding a live progress bar and countdown.

Everything is procedural: the ship, props, astronauts and all sound are generated at runtime with Three.js and the Web Audio API. The only assets are public-domain NASA photographs, embedded as base64 — zero network calls at runtime.

It matters because it turns passive "click-to-progress" busywork into the actual motor-and-judgement skills of ops work, and proves a rich, offline-capable 3D experience can ship as one file.

projectDetails.name: ZENITH
projectDetails.summary:
ZENITH – Integrated Astronaut Health Monitoring and Risk Intelligence System

ZENITH is an intelligent astronaut health-monitoring and risk-awareness platform designed to support human well-being during space missions. It brings together physiological, psychological, and environmental indicators by leveraging NASA datasets and APIs alongside simulated mission data, providing a unified view of astronaut health and mission conditions.

The platform monitors key health and wellness parameters, maintains historical records, analyzes changing trends, and generates timely alerts when potential risks or abnormal conditions are identified. Its voice-enabled alert system further enhances accessibility by communicating critical notifications and emerging concerns.

By connecting health indicators with mission-related environmental factors, ZENITH addresses the challenge of fragmented health monitoring in demanding spaceflight environments. The prototype establishes a foundation for more proactive astronaut healthcare, with AI-driven predictive health analytics and future risk forecasting envisioned as subsequent capabilities.

Ultimately, ZENITH aims to transform complex mission-health data into meaningful, accessible intelligence, helping support safer, more informed, and sustainable human space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – ZENITH

ZENITH is an integrated astronaut health-monitoring and risk-intelligence platform developed to enhance health awareness, support early risk identification, and promote astronaut well-being during space missions.

How It Works:
ZENITH consolidates physiological, psychological, and space-environmental indicators into a unified interactive dashboard. It monitors parameters such as heart rate, blood oxygen saturation, body temperature, blood pressure, respiratory rate, sleep duration, activity levels, fatigue, stress, and mood. It also incorporates mission-environment indicators, including solar flares, proton flux, and geomagnetic activity, to provide broader mission context. NASA's Spaceflight Standard Measures serve as a reference framework for organizing health-monitoring categories. The current prototype uses simulated dashboard readings and NASA-related references rather than live astronaut medical records.

The platform maintains historical health logs, allowing users to examine previous readings and identify changes over time. Its voice-enabled alert functionality communicates important notifications and potential health risks, making critical information more accessible. AI-driven predictive analytics for future health-risk forecasting are envisioned as a subsequent development phase.

Benefits and Intended Impact:
ZENITH aims to move beyond isolated health measurements towards a more comprehensive understanding of astronaut well-being. By combining health indicators, historical trends, and environmental context, it establishes a foundation for earlier risk awareness, informed health assessments, and improved mission preparedness. Its long-term vision is to support preventive healthcare and contribute to safer, more sustainable human space exploration.

Technology and Implementation:
The project uses React and JavaScript for its interactive frontend, HTML and CSS for interface development, and Fast API and Node.js for backend functionality. JSON-based data structures support data organization and exchange. NASA-related datasets and references inform the monitoring framework, while simulated data enables prototype functionality and demonstration.

Creativity and Innovation:
The distinguishing aspect of ZENITH is its integrated approach to astronaut health intelligence. Rather than treating physical health, mental wellness, historical health patterns, and environmental exposure as independent elements, it brings them together within a single monitoring ecosystem. The combination of historical health logging, voice-enabled risk notifications, and mission-environment awareness provides a foundation for evolving towards AI-assisted predictive healthcare.

Design Considerations:
The team considered the unique physiological and psychological demands of spaceflight, the effects of microgravity, the importance of continuous health observation, accessibility of critical alerts, historical data continuity, and the need for a scalable system that can accommodate additional health indicators and predictive capabilities in the future.

projectDetails.name: IgnisAI
projectDetails.summary:
IGNIS AI — Intelligent Gravity-Adaptive Fire Analysis System is an interactive space-combustion platform built around one interesting question: What happens to fire when gravity changes?
The homepage brings together NASA space research, real experiment images and videos, interesting facts about flames, and an animated flame visualization. The Flame Lab takes this experience further, allowing users to explore how fire behaves under different conditions, including Earth, microgravity, lunar and Martian gravity. It also covers cool flames, droplet combustion, solid-material burning, and fire extinguishment.
Users can interact with the 3D environment by rotating, zooming, selecting different flame regions, and changing environmental settings. They can also explore different scenarios, adjust the timeline, and compare flame behaviour. Each visualization comes with simple explanations to make scientific concepts easier to understand.
The platform also provides access to NASA research records and media, with links to their original sources. This helps users distinguish actual NASA research from our own visual representations.
An important note: The 3D flame visualization is an illustrative model designed for learning and exploration. It is not a scientific simulation, an exact recreation of NASA experiments, or a source of actual temperature measurements. Any hypothetical values or generated outputs are clearly presented as illustrative rather than real experimental data.
projectDetails.details:
The main goal of IGNIS AI is to make space-combustion research easier and more interesting to understand. Fire behaves differently when gravity changes, affecting its shape, movement, and burning process. Instead of learning everything through text, users can explore these differences through interactive 3D visualizations and access real NASA research for further learning.

The platform aims to make science more engaging and encourage people to explore how gravity, oxygen, pressure, airflow, and fuel influence fire. It also makes clear which information comes from NASA experiments and which comes from our own illustrative models.

We built the application using Next.js 15, React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei, GLSL shaders, CSS, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion, Lucide icons, and Recharts. We also use Next.js server routes to retrieve NASA media and research records. An optional Python FastAPI backend provides additional research, risk-analysis, and PDF-report features.

What makes IGNIS AI different is the way it combines NASA research, an interactive space-laboratory interface, and an animated 3D flame experience. Rather than simply displaying information, it allows users to explore and experiment with different scenarios.

While developing the platform, we focused on making it user-friendly, responsive, accessible, and easy to navigate. We also considered scientific accuracy, proper source credits, performance, and transparency. Our 3D visualization is illustrative, not a scientifically validated fire simulation, and we clearly separate actual NASA findings from hypothetical model outputs.

projectDetails.name: ASTRA – Autonomous Spaceflight Health Monitoring & Intelligence System
projectDetails.summary: ASTRA is an AI-powered astronaut health monitoring platform designed to support crew health during long-duration space missions. It brings together physiological indicators, sleep patterns, physical activity, wellness assessments and mission-related health information into a unified dashboard. Using machine learning, ASTRA identifies unusual health patterns and generates explainable alerts, while its AI assistant helps astronauts understand their health trends and access relevant medical information. Designed with offline-first capabilities, the system aims to support continuous health awareness and informed decision-making even when communication with Earth is limited.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRA – Autonomous Spaceflight Health Monitoring & Intelligence System

Problem Statement

Long-duration space missions expose astronauts to several health risks, including cardiovascular changes, bone and muscle loss, immune-system alterations, radiation exposure, sleep disruption and psychological stress. Limited medical resources and communication delays make continuous health monitoring and early identification of abnormalities essential.

Our Solution

ASTRA is a web-based health intelligence platform designed to help astronauts monitor, understand and manage their health during space missions.

The platform combines health-data visualisation, machine-learning-based anomaly detection and an AI-powered health assistant to transform health measurements into meaningful insights.

Key Features

  1. Astronaut Health Dashboard: Displays physiological indicators, health trends, sleep patterns and physical activity.
  2. AI/ML Anomaly Detection: Analyses health measurements and identifies unusual patterns relative to individual baselines.
  3. Intelligent Health Assistant: Provides context-aware explanations of health trends and relevant health information.
  4. Emergency Alert System: Generates alerts when monitored readings meet predefined risk criteria.
  5. Mental Wellness Monitoring: Supports periodic assessments of stress, mood, sleep and fatigue.
  6. Mission Control Dashboard: Enables authorised personnel to review crew health information, trends and alerts.
  7. Offline-First Monitoring: Supports local health-data processing and storage when internet connectivity is unavailable, with synchronisation when connectivity returns.

Technology Stack

Frontend: React.js and Tailwind CSS.

Backend: Python and FastAPI.

Database: PostgreSQL.

Machine Learning: Scikit-learn, Pandas and NumPy.

Data Visualisation: Recharts.

Communication: WebSockets.

AI Assistant: Large Language Model with Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).

Data Sources

The system uses simulated astronaut health readings alongside relevant publicly available NASA research resources and physiological datasets. Simulated data is clearly distinguished from actual research data.

Expected Impact

ASTRA aims to improve astronaut health awareness, support early identification of unusual health patterns, reduce dependence on continuous Earth-based assistance and provide a foundation for intelligent health monitoring during future Moon and Mars missions.

The proposed system is a research and hackathon prototype, not a clinically validated diagnostic or treatment system.

projectDetails.name: CropSense: NASA Earth Data for Farmer Crop Rotation Decisions
projectDetails.summary:
CropSense is a mobile and web app that helps Indian farmers choose what to sow using NASA Earth data and their own soil evidence. Farmers map a field on satellite imagery, add Soil Health Card values and simple field observations, then get explained crop suitability and three-season rotation plans—not opaque yield promises.

It addresses the challenge of turning Earth observations into practical farm decisions. CropSense pulls climate and moisture from NASA POWER, greenness from MODIS NDVI, mapped soil from SoilGrids, and climate outlook from CMIP6, then combines those with local soil tests. Advice is multilingual, transparent about sources, and framed for discussion with a Krishi Vigyan Kendra.

It matters because many smallholders face uncertain rain, limited irrigation, and conflicting advice. CropSense puts satellite intelligence and farmer knowledge in one place so crop choices better match soil, water, and season—reducing risk while keeping farmers in control.
projectDetails.details:
CropSense turns a farmer’s mapped field into practical crop-rotation guidance using NASA and open Earth data—so smallholders get field-specific advice instead of generic calendars.

What it does / how it works

A farmer signs in, maps a field boundary, and optionally adds soil-test details. CropSense then pulls live Earth observations for that location—NASA POWER (moisture, rainfall, temperature extremes), MODIS NDVI (crop greenness), SoilGrids (texture/pH), and Open-Meteo climate outlooks—and combines them with local crop rules to recommend a three-crop rotation plan with clear “why” explanations. It works as a mobile app (Expo) for use in the field and a desktop web app for planning and review.

Benefits

- Field-specific advice instead of one-size-fits-all crop lists

- Uses free public satellite/climate data—no expensive sensors required

- Helps improve soil health, reduce water stress, and diversify planting risk

- Simple, multilingual interface designed for real farm workflows

- Transparent sources so farmers can trust where the numbers come from

Intended impact

Help Indian (and similar) smallholder farmers make better rotation decisions that protect soil, conserve water, and improve resilience to climate stress—while making NASA Earth science usable at the village level.

Tools, languages, hardware, software

-Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript

-Mobile:React Native, Expo

Web: React, Vite, React Router, Leaflet / react-leaflet

- Data / APIs: NASA POWER, MODIS (ORNL DAAC), ISRIC SoilGrids, Open-Meteo

- Backend / auth:** Supabase Auth + Postgres (`account_farm_records`)

- Other:** Turf.js (field geometry), TanStack Query, Lucide icons

- Hardware:Standard smartphones and laptops/desktops (no custom hardware)

- Hosting: AntiDeploy (`https://cropsense.antideploy.app`)

How it’s creative

CropSense doesn’t stop at showing satellite maps—it translates NASA POWER, MODIS, and SoilGrids into a farmer-facing rotation plan with plain-language reasons. It bridges Earth observation and agriculture by fusing multiple open datasets into one decision workflow, with both phone and desktop experiences so advice is useful in the field and for longer planning sessions.

Factors the team considered

- Farmer trust (show data sources; decision support, not yield guarantees)

- Offline/poor-connectivity realities and simple Farmer ID onboarding

- Language accessibility (e.g. English/Hindi)

- Accuracy vs. usability (global grids vs. local soil tests—farmer input can override mapped soil)

- Water stress and climate risk, not only yield

- Privacy and secure account storage for farm records

- Cross-platform access: phone for mapping, web for deeper review

projectDetails.name: Project ExoLogic
projectDetails.summary:
ExoLogic: OUTPOST is an interactive space-outpost survival simulator developed for NASA's Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. It places players in command of a lunar or Martian settlement, where they must lead a crew through a 15-day mission while balancing essential resources such as water, oxygen, food and power.

Players make strategic decisions, manage crew health and morale, select specialist roles, operate outpost systems, research upgrades and respond to unexpected mission events. Each decision influences the survival of the crew and the success of the mission.

By transforming the challenges of space exploration into an engaging simulation, OUTPOST aims to help students understand the importance of resource management, engineering, teamwork and critical thinking when sustaining human life beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
What does the project do and how does it work?

OUTPOST is a turn based survival and resource-management simulator in which players take responsibility for maintaining a human outpost on either the Moon or Mars. The mission runs over multiple days, with players monitoring essential resources, managing crew conditions and deciding how to allocate limited supplies and energy.

Players can perform operations such as water recycling, food production, solar power generation, system maintenance, medical treatment, crew rest, surface exploration and system diagnostics. Different crew roles provide specialized abilities, while research upgrades improve the outpost's capabilities. Random mission events introduce unexpected challenges that require players to adapt their strategy.

What benefits does it provide?

The project introduces students to the practical difficulties of sustaining human settlements beyond Earth. It encourages resource awareness, strategic planning, problem-solving and understanding the consequences of engineering decisions.

What is its intended impact?

Our aim is to make space exploration more accessible and engaging for students. Rather than simply reading about the challenges astronauts face, players experience how interconnected systems, limited resources and unexpected events influence mission survival.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed using React, JavaScript, HTML and CSS, with Vite as the development environment and Three.js for the interactive 3D celestial visuals. The interface features Moon and Mars destination selection, animated planetary visuals and a mission management dashboard.

What makes the project creative?

OUTPOST combines an immersive space-themed interface with decision-driven survival gameplay. It brings together resource management, crew specialization, research, random events and mission progression in one interactive experience. The combination is designed to make the complex realities of operating a space outpost understandable through play.

projectDetails.name: Project EXOSteller
projectDetails.summary:
I developed the SPHEREx Sky Viewer & Exoplanet Atlas, a full-stack astrophysics suite that turns raw SPHEREx data into an interactive search for moving objects.

What I developed: The Sky Viewer features a custom all-sky map that queries the Caltech/IPCA IRSA archive via SIA2/TAP protocols. It downloads real FITS images, aligns them using WCS coordinates, and subtracts the median background to remove fixed stars. Users can then "blink" through the frames to spot moving objects—exoplanets, brown dwarfs, and asteroids. A "Visualize 3D System" button launches the Exoplanet Atlas, a WebGL engine built from scratch with custom GLSL shaders that renders 8,151 TESS planets, procedural atmospheres, tidal deformation, and a general relativistic black hole.

How it addresses the challenge: It provides the exact tool needed to find moving objects in the SPHEREx archive—the core goal of the "Planet X" challenge—while also giving users a 3D way to visualize their findings.

Why it is important: NASA generates petabytes of data, but the public cannot easily visualize it. This tool makes the search for distant worlds intuitive, interactive, and accessible to everyone. It bridges the gap between raw spectral data and a visual universe, empowering both researchers and the public to explore the cosmos.
projectDetails.details:
What it does:
The SPHEREx Sky Viewer & Exoplanet Atlas is a full-stack astrophysics suite. The Sky Viewer lets you search the entire sky (via an interactive map or coordinates) to find moving objects—exoplanets, brown dwarfs, and asteroids—in the SPHEREx archive. The Exoplanet Atlas is a 3D engine that visualizes 8,151 TESS planets, their atmospheres, and even a general relativistic black hole.

How it works:
The Sky Viewer queries the Caltech/IPAC IRSA archive (SIA2/TAP protocols), downloads real FITS images, aligns them using WCS coordinates, and subtracts the median background to remove fixed stars. Users "blink" through the frames to spot moving objects. The Atlas renders these planets in 3D using custom GLSL shaders for procedural atmospheres, tidal deformation, and gravitational lensing.

Benefits and Impact:
NASA generates petabytes of data, but the public can't easily visualize it. This tool makes the search for distant worlds intuitive and interactive. It turns raw spectral data into a visual universe, making astronomy accessible to everyone.

Tools Used:

  • Frontend: Vanilla HTML, CSS, JavaScript.
  • 3D Engine: Three.js with custom GLSL shaders.
  • Backend: Python 3 (standard library) for the CORS proxy and async TAP queries.
  • Data: Caltech/IPAC IRSA, NASA Exoplanet Archive, TESS catalog, DESI Legacy Surveys.

Creativity:
The integration is the creative part. Most tools show either 2D graphs or 3D models. This tool connects the raw data pipeline (custom FITS parsing, WCS alignment) to a 3D visualization engine. The custom FITS binary parser in JavaScript is rarely done in browser-based tools.

Factors Considered:

  • CORS Restrictions: Built a Python proxy with a manual CSV fallback.
  • Offline Capability: The Atlas runs entirely offline, ensuring a reliable demo.
  • Scalability: Designed to handle the full 8,151 TESS catalog and extend to the entire SPHEREx dataset.

projectDetails.details:
Overview

AFTERLIGHT: FORGOTTEN WORLDS is a proposed story-driven exploration game developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 challenge, “Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars.”

The project explores how historical space hardware can become a way to teach young audiences about planetary exploration, engineering, and scientific discovery.

Problem

Space missions leave behind landers, instruments, descent stages, rovers, and other equipment. These objects represent important engineering achievements and scientific history, but their stories can be difficult for young audiences to experience through static information alone.

Proposed solution

The project proposes an immersive exploration experience in which players investigate lunar and Martian environments, discover historic mission equipment, learn about its original purpose, and connect discoveries through a fictional mystery.

The intended full experience includes planetary navigation, distinct exploration regions, astronaut movement, interactive historical information, an evidence journal, environmental puzzles, and consequential story choices.

Current implementation

The current prototype provides a lunar exploration environment where players can move around and view three objects. It is an early proof of concept, and the full level system, detailed interactive information panels, and complete story progression are not yet verified as implemented.

Intended impact

The project aims to make space history more engaging for young learners by connecting real mission hardware to the science it enabled and the challenges engineers faced.

Tools

Astrocade was used to create the game prototype. AI assistance was used for concept development, narrative planning, and presentation preparation. The specific contributions of each tool are disclosed in the AI-use section.

projectDetails.summary:
**SPHEREx Explorer** is an interactive web platform developed to explore and analyse NASA's SPHEREx infrared observations. It allows users to locate celestial objects using Right Ascension and Declination coordinates, access available observations, and view infrared images through an interactive interface.

The platform offers several key capabilities, including 102-channel spectral analysis, individual spectrum visualization, multi-epoch observation comparison, and difference spectrum graphs. It also supports WCS-based image alignment and differencing, along with variance-weighted image stacking.

One of its standout features is **moving-object detection, isolation, and tracking**. When a potential moving object is detected, the system compares observations from different epochs, aligns the images, identifies differences, removes the surrounding background, and isolates the object's signal. It then visualizes the object across multiple observations and calculates its angular displacement and apparent motion.

Additionally, the platform incorporates catalogue information from Gaia DR3, AllWISE, and CSA NEOSSat wherever available. It also offers time-lapse animations to visualize how the same region of the sky changes across different observation periods.

By bringing these features together, SPHEREx Explorer makes complex infrared astronomical data easier to explore, analyse, and interpret, helping users investigate and discover changes in the universe.
projectDetails.details:
# What It Does and How It Works

SPHEREx Explorer is a full-stack, browser-based astronomical exploration and analysis platform designed to process, analyse and visualize NASA's available SPHEREx Level-2 Multi-Extension FITS (MEF) observations. It connects to the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) to retrieve observations based on celestial coordinates. Users can enter Right Ascension and Declination or select from five predefined targets: WISE 0855-0714, Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi Ba/Bb, RW Aurigae and R Draconis.

The backend processes the FITS data using zodiacal-light subtraction when the relevant extension is available, quality-bitmask filtering, background estimation, source centroiding and World Coordinate System (WCS) reprojection. The platform provides the following capabilities:

- **102-Channel Spectral Analysis:** Provides a 102-channel infrared spectral representation across the nominal 0.75 to 5.00 micrometre wavelength range, covering detectors D1 to D6. The current prototype combines available FITS-derived measurements with model-assisted spectral interpolation. Its graph interface supports individual spectra, multi-epoch spectral comparisons and difference spectra, where later flux is compared with earlier flux.

- **Multi-Epoch Time-Lapse:** Generates animated GIFs from available observations of the same sky region. It supports Fixed Sky mode, which aligns observations to fixed celestial coordinates, and Follow Object mode, which centres observations on the object's measured position. It selects observations from a common detector and attempts to maintain similar wavelengths, while reporting compatibility warnings when needed.

- **Difference Imaging:** Aligns observations using WCS, estimates and matches image resolution, corrects background levels and calculates the later-minus-earlier difference image. It also produces significance maps and identifies potential residual candidates, including brightening sources, fading sources and positive-negative moving-object dipoles.

- **Variance-Weighted Image Stacking:** Combines compatible observations from the same detector using inverse-variance weighting. It also measures background noise and estimates the improvement in signal-to-noise ratio.

- **Moving-Object Isolation and Tracking:** Allows a potential moving object to be investigated across two observation epochs. The system subtracts the estimated background, aligns the images and applies a spatial isolation mask to emphasize the object's signal while suppressing the surrounding sky. It generates isolated images for both epochs and calculates angular displacement, time baseline and apparent motion in arcseconds per year.

- **Photometry and Catalogue Cross-Matching:** Allows users to select an image position and retrieve celestial coordinates, centroid measurements, surface brightness in MJy/sr, derived point-source flux in microjanskys, signal-to-noise ratio and quality information. It decodes the 14 defined quality-bitmask categories. Catalogue integration includes proper-motion-adjusted Gaia DR3 positions, AllWISE sources and CSA NEOSSat observation information where available.

# Tools, Coding Languages and Software

**Backend**

- Python 3.12

- FastAPI and Uvicorn

**Scientific and Image Processing Libraries**

- Astropy for FITS handling, celestial coordinates, time calculations and WCS operations.

- Photutils for source detection and centroiding.

- NumPy and SciPy for numerical processing.

- Reproject for image alignment.

- Matplotlib and Pillow for image and animation generation.

**Frontend**

- React and TypeScript for the web application and interactive interface.

- Plotly.js for spectral graph visualization.

- Tailwind CSS, if used in the final frontend implementation.

**Astronomical Data Sources**

- NASA/IPAC IRSA for SPHEREx observations and AllWISE data.

- Gaia DR3 for stellar astrometry and catalogue cross-matching.

- Canadian Astronomy Data Centre (CADC) for CSA NEOSSat observation information.

The application does not require custom spacecraft hardware. It is designed to run as a software platform through a web browser.

# Benefits and Intended Impact

Astronomical observation data is often stored in specialized FITS formats that require scientific programming knowledge and dedicated software to process and interpret. SPHEREx Explorer aims to simplify this process by bringing observation retrieval, image visualization, spectral analysis and multi-epoch comparison into one accessible platform.

It can support students, astronomy enthusiasts and researchers in exploring infrared observations, studying brown dwarfs, investigating variable sources and examining high-proper-motion objects. Its combination of image differencing, moving-object isolation, spectral comparisons and time-lapse visualization provides multiple ways to investigate changes in the observed sky.

The intended impact is to make complex infrared astronomical data easier to explore and encourage wider engagement with publicly available space science observations.

# How the Project Is Creative

The creative aspect of SPHEREx Explorer is its combination of several scientific analysis methods in one interactive platform.

SPHEREx uses a Linear Variable Filter (LVF), which maps wavelength to position across its detector images. Full spectral coverage at a particular sky position is assembled from observations taken at different pointings over time. Our project explores how these observations can be brought together for spectral visualization and comparison.

Another distinctive feature is the moving-object analysis workflow. By combining WCS-based image differencing, residual candidate identification, background subtraction and spatial isolation, the platform helps users distinguish potential moving sources from changes in the surrounding sky. The isolated source can then be examined across observation dates and its apparent angular motion calculated.

The six-month time-lapse concept adds another dimension by turning separate astronomical observations into an animation, allowing users to visually investigate how the same region changes over time.

# Factors Our Team Considered

- **Survey Cadence and Observation Availability:** SPHEREx observations are not necessarily available at uniform intervals for every sky location. We considered variations in observation dates, detector coverage and wavelength sampling when grouping observations into epochs and generating comparisons. The application reports when adequate multi-epoch or compatible observation coverage is unavailable.

- **Data Quality and Edge Cases:** FITS data may contain missing pixels, flagged detector regions, non-finite values and unusually high pixel readings. We incorporated quality-bitmask filtering, background statistics, isolated-spike rejection and handling of invalid pixels to make image processing more robust.

- **Wavelength and Detector Compatibility:** Different detectors cover different wavelength ranges. We considered detector identity and wavelength compatibility when selecting observations for image stacking, difference imaging and time-lapse generation. Compatibility warnings help avoid misleading comparisons.

- **Image Alignment and Scientific Consistency:** Observations taken at different pointings may have different image orientations and pixel coordinates. WCS reprojection, background correction and image-resolution matching are used to bring compatible images onto a common reference grid.

- **Network Requests and Performance:** Retrieving large FITS observations can take time and create repeated network requests. We incorporated local caching, selective exposure sampling and retry logic to reduce redundant downloads and improve processing efficiency.

Our overall approach is to make the platform scientifically informative while keeping the user experience simple and accessible.

projectDetails.name: Flame-intelligence
projectDetails.summary: FLAME INTELLIGENCE uses NASA research data to explore spacecraft fire safety and combustion behavior through mission analysis, evidence tracking, interactive 3D visualizations, and scientific insights.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does your project do, and how does it work?

FLAME INTELLIGENCE is a web-based platform designed to help people understand how fire behaves in spacecraft and microgravity environments. On Earth, gravity affects how flames move, but in space, combustion behaves differently.

Our platform brings NASA research information into one place using NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) and Technical Reports Server (NTRS). Users can explore space-fire investigations, research findings, available data, and interactive 3D visualizations. It also includes analytics, reports, and an AI-assisted mission analysis workflow.

2. What benefits does it have?

The main benefit is that it makes complex spacecraft fire research easier to access and understand.

- Brings different NASA research resources into one platform.

- Helps users explore experiments and scientific findings.

- Provides interactive 3D visualizations to understand combustion concepts.

- Organizes research information and evidence in one place.

- Supports students, researchers, and space enthusiasts in learning about fire safety in space.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to support better understanding of spacecraft fire behaviour and contribute to space-fire safety research.

We want to make NASA research more accessible, help people identify important findings, and encourage further research into how flames behave in microgravity.

In the future, the platform could be expanded with more verified NASA datasets, improved AI analysis, and additional research capabilities. It is a research and learning platform, not a certified spacecraft safety system.

4. What tools did you use?

We used a combination of modern web development, data processing, visualization, and AI technologies.

- Frontend: React 19, Vite 8, Tailwind CSS

- Backend: Python, FastAPI

- Database: SQLite, SQLAlchemy

- AI integration: Google Gemini API

- 3D visualization: Three.js and React Three Fiber

- NASA resources: NASA PSI, NASA NTRS, and NASA media resources

- Development tools: VS Code, Git and GitHub

5. How is your project creative?

Our creativity comes from combining NASA scientific research with interactive technology.

Instead of presenting research as ordinary documents or static information, we created a platform where users can explore investigations, understand findings, compare available evidence, and visualize spacecraft combustion concepts in an interactive 3D environment.

We also focus on showing the source and reliability of information so users can distinguish verified research from illustrative or unverified data.

6. What factors did your team consider?

While developing FLAME INTELLIGENCE, our team considered several important factors:

- Scientific accuracy: Research information should be based on NASA sources wherever possible.

- Microgravity behaviour: Fire behaves differently in space compared with Earth.

- Data reliability: We distinguish NASA-backed information from unverified local records.

- User experience: The platform should be easy to navigate and understand.

- Technology: We selected tools that support interactive visualization, data processing, and AI integration.

- Future scalability: The platform should allow additional NASA datasets and features to be integrated.

- Safety: Our platform is intended for research and education, not real-time spacecraft fire control or safety certification.

The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”
