projectDetails.summary:
IrriSense is an intelligent, data-driven irrigation and water management system designed to optimize agricultural efficiency and combat water scarcity. By integrating NASA Earth observation data (such as soil moisture indices, evapotranspiration rates, and precipitation forecasts) with IoT ground sensors, IrriSense dynamically calculates precise watering schedules for crops.
​The platform addresses the global challenge of sustainable agriculture by minimizing water waste, preventing over-irrigation, and maximizing crop yield under changing climate conditions. It is crucial because traditional irrigation methods account for massive global water loss; by automating water delivery based on real-time satellite insights and local soil analytics, IrriSense empowers farmers to make climate-smart decisions, conserve precious water resources, and secure food production for the future.
projectDetails.details:
IrriSense is an intelligent, data-driven irrigation and water management system developed to optimize agricultural efficiency and combat global water scarcity. By bridging macro-level NASA Earth observation data with localized environmental tracking, the platform empowers farmers to transition from traditional guesswork to precision, climate-smart agriculture.

​At its core, IrriSense works by aggregating real-time meteorological and environmental variables—including satellite-derived soil moisture indices, evapotranspiration rates, rainfall forecasts, and local humidity levels—and cross-referencing them with specific crop water requirements. Our backend engine processes these datasets dynamically to calculate exact, tailored watering schedules. Through an intuitive, dashboard-driven web interface, farmers receive actionable insights and automated irrigation metrics that take the complexity out of daily water management.

​The primary benefit of IrriSense is substantial water and resource conservation. Traditional farming methods often result in severe water loss due to over-irrigation or poorly timed watering cycles. By delivering water only when and where crops genuinely need it, the system reduces freshwater waste, lowers operational energy costs, and prevents soil degradation caused by waterlogging. Furthermore, relying on continuous, live environmental forecasting equips farmers with greater climate resilience, allowing them to adapt swiftly to erratic weather patterns and prolonged dry spells. Ultimately, the intended impact of IrriSense is to protect vital freshwater reserves while maximizing crop yields and securing long-term food production stability, particularly in drought-prone and water-stressed agricultural regions.

​From a technical standpoint, IrriSense was built using a full-stack web architecture designed for reliability and accessibility. We developed the frontend interface and backend data-processing engine using Node.js alongside modern web development frameworks, utilizing VS Code and terminal workflows for coding and debugging. Collaborative version control and codebase management were handled via Git and GitHub, while live external weather and Earth observation APIs provide the real-time environmental telemetry powering our dashboard analytics. The application is structured for streamlined cloud deployment to ensure smooth, uninterrupted access for end users.

​What makes IrriSense particularly creative is how it translates complex space agency telemetry into everyday agricultural utility. Rather than leaving satellite observations confined to academic or macro-environmental research, our platform operationalizes NASA Earth data into a practical, user-friendly tool that any farmer can immediately act upon.

​Throughout development, our team carefully weighed several critical factors to ensure real-world viability. First, we prioritized data precision, designing our logic to account for varying crop types and dynamic weather shifts rather than relying on static timers. Second, we focused heavily on accessibility and user experience, ensuring the dashboard presents clear, easily digestible metrics rather than overwhelming users with raw scientific data. Finally, we factored in system scalability and stability, choosing a modular, cloud-ready tech stack capable of expanding to support diverse geographical regions, additional soil parameters, and future IoT hardware integrations without disrupting core functionality.

projectDetails.name: Project Aurora
projectDetails.summary:
AURORA: The Last Ascent is a cooperative Roblox game for 1-4 players that teaches the trade-offs of real mission design. A crew crash-lands on a fictional, Mars-like planet and has one goal: reach orbit.

Each player takes a role (Commander, Pilot, Mechanic or Science Officer). Together they scavenge resources, repair power, communications and propulsion, and make propellant through a multi-step process modelled on real in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) chemistry. In the Mission Planner, they choose payload, propellant load and target orbit. The planner shows live pass/marginal/fail checks for mass, thrust-to-weight, power and delta-v. Then the Pilot flies the rocket to orbit using a custom flight simulation (gravity, a NASA-based Mars atmosphere model, drag and the rocket equation), not Roblox’s built-in physics.

The debrief shows exactly how much delta-v gravity, drag and steering cost, and explains why the mission succeeded or failed. A built-in Codex and short quizzes teach rocket science, ISRU, power and teamwork, and simplified values are clearly labelled. Players learn that every kilogram, watt and decision matters.
projectDetails.details:
What it does
AURORA: The Last Ascent is a cooperative Roblox game for 1-4 players that turns end-to-end mission design into gameplay. A crew crash-lands on a fictional, Mars-like planet. Each player takes a role: Commander, Pilot, Field Mechanic or Science Officer. Together they restore power and oxygen, scan and collect resources, avoid or study unexplained anomalies, and repair propulsion, communications and power. They make propellant through a multi-step process based on real in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) chemistry: ice, water, electrolysis, then methane and oxygen. Nothing is instant.

In the Mission Planner, the team chooses the target orbit, payload (instruments, samples, spares) and propellant load. Live pass/marginal/fail checks cover mass, thrust-to-weight, delta-v, power and oxygen, with a one-line reason and a suggested fix. After a Go/No-Go vote, the Pilot flies the ascent live. The debrief scores the mission and shows how much delta-v gravity, drag and steering cost.

How it works
Roblox’s built-in physics can’t model orbital flight, so the rocket is driven by a custom double-precision flight simulation written in Luau. It uses Mars-analogue gravity, a NASA-based Mars atmosphere model, Mach-dependent drag and engine mass flow. It is checked against the rocket equation, Kepler orbits and energy conservation. The server owns all game state. Clients only send requests, which keeps four-player sessions in sync.

Benefits and intended impact
Players learn by making trade-offs, not by reading. Adding cargo visibly shrinks delta-v, and dust storms cut solar power. Short “Why?” pop-ups, a Codex and a quiz explain each concept at the moment it matters. Verified NASA figures are separated from simplified game values, which carry a gear icon. We want players to leave understanding why mission design is hard, and why teamwork and margins matter.

Tools

  • Roblox Studio and Luau
  • Rojo for syncing code files
  • AI coding assistants (Google Antigravity and Claude) for development
  • NASA public data and studies: Mars Fact Sheet, Glenn Mars atmosphere model, MOXIE results, Mars Ascent Vehicle studies
  • Standard laptops, no special hardware

Creativity
The game is built around survival, but the real lesson is the engineering trade-offs. Aliens are anomalies to study or avoid, so the focus stays on science, not combat. The debrief explains failures using the player’s own flight data.

Factors we considered

  • A 48-hour scope: one complete, playable mission
  • Accuracy versus fun: assisted flight controls for new players
  • Honesty: simplifications are labelled
  • Teamwork: each repair and the launch need several roles
  • Accessibility: solo play, with automation covering absent roles

projectDetails.name: Moon Cadet
projectDetails.summary:
Moon Cadet is a browser-based, first-person 3D simulation where the player works as a lunar outpost engineer. We built four hands-on missions:
1. Powering a habitat with solar arrays, batteries and a converter
2. Setting up life support with water loops, electrolysis, CO₂ scrubbing and a Sabatier reactor 
3. Running a hydroponic greenhouse
4. Responding to a radiation emergency by driving a rover to seal the shelter within ten minutes

The game addresses the challenge by turning real Moon-base engineering into something people can practise instead of just read about. Players see how power, air, water, food and radiation safety depend on one another, and they learn to troubleshoot under pressure.

It matters because a lasting human presence on the Moon needs engineers who think in whole systems. Moon Cadet makes that thinking accessible, engaging and free, and it can inspire students who may one day help build the next Moon base.
projectDetails.details:
Moon Cadet is a first-person 3D simulation that runs in the browser. The player walks around a lunar site, picks up equipment, connects cables, pipes and ducts, and operates consoles, using the keyboard and mouse. There are four missions:

Power generation: Survey sites, then install solar panels, batteries, a converter and a distribution unit.

Life support: Set up water purification, electrolysis, a CO₂ scrubber, a Sabatier reactor and fans.

Farm maintenance: Refill water, dose nutrients, inspect plants, check the LEDs, harvest and replant.

Radiation emergency: Find the breach with a detector, suit up, drive the rover for regolith and seal the shelter within a 10-minute timer.

The game has different playable components like picking up and placing objects, connecting equipment, etc. It helps the player understand life requirements on the moon.

Benefits of Moon Cadet:

It is free and needs no installation or account.

Players learn by doing, with instant feedback, instead of reading about it.

It shows how power, air, water, food and shelter depend on each other.

We want to make space engineering approachable for students and curious players. We want them to see the Moon as a place that needs systems thinkers, and to feel inspired to pursue STEM and space careers.

Tools and technology used:

Languages and rendering: JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3 and Three.js (r128, WebGL).

Browser features: The Web Audio API for sound, the Pointer Lock API for mouse look, and localStorage for saved records.

Fonts: Rajdhani and IBM Plex Mono from Google Fonts.

Hardware: A computer with a keyboard and mouse.

How our project is creative:

The player is the engineer who does the work, not a viewer watching a diagram.

Each mission plays differently: wiring, plumbing, farming and rover driving under time pressure.

The cockpit-style HUD gives a convincing mission-control feel.

Factors we considered:

Realism: One-sixth gravity is shown when the player jumps, a closed water and oxygen loop, a safe nutrient range and a crew radiation dose limit (50 mSv).

Learning: Guided task lists, hints and on-screen messages when something is wrong; intended to make learning easy for the player.

Accessibility: A drag-to-look fallback if the mouse can’t be captured, and reduced-motion support.

Limits: It works best on desktop, not touch screens.

projectDetails.name: Project Mission Architect (Green Minds)
projectDetails.summary: Mission Architect is a multiplayer 3D space mission design game for one to four players. Teams choose a destination such as Earth, the Moon, Mars or Venus, pick a rocket, and build a spacecraft in a live 3D builder. They then launch it in a 3D countdown and handle emergencies year by year. A score out of 100 and a leaderboard rank each mission. Players define a mission objective, choose instruments, a launcher and an orbit, and manage budget, mass, power, communications, data and lifetime on live gauges. Each player takes a role (Mission Lead, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead or Comms & Ops), so teams must discuss trade-offs. A launch simulation and scoring system reward good engineering. Real NASA solar-flare data from DONKI drives the emergencies, and the Astronomy Picture of the Day and Planetary Fact Sheet add real context. Real missions fail when one decision quietly breaks another part of the design. This game lets students and the public see those trade-offs first-hand, practise teamwork, and learn how space missions are planned, using real NASA data.
projectDetails.details: Mission Architect is a multiplayer 3D space mission design game where one to four players act as a mission team. After logging in with a team code, each player takes a role (Mission Lead, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead or Comms & Ops) and controls only that role's settings, so the team must discuss trade-offs. Players choose a destination such as Earth, the Moon, Mars or Venus, either from a card or by clicking a planet in an interactive 3D solar system, then pick a rocket, instruments and spacecraft settings while a 3D model rebuilds live and dial gauges track mass, power, data, lifetime and cost. A 3D launch with countdown, Max-Q and stage separation leads into a year-by-year mission where emergencies appear, some built from real NASA DONKI solar-flare data, and the result is a score out of 100 with achievements and a leaderboard. The game helps students and the public see how one decision affects every part of a mission and why teamwork matters, using real NASA data from DONKI, the Astronomy Picture of the Day and the Planetary Fact Sheet. It was built with Python, Flask, Flask-SocketIO, SQLite, JavaScript, Three.js, Web Audio, HTML and CSS, with Claude (Anthropic) assisting on the code, which is labelled throughout. We kept the engineering numbers simplified for gameplay, added fallbacks so the game keeps running if a data service fails, protected passwords and keys, and used no NASA branding or AI-generated media.

projectDetails.name: SpaceRelics
projectDetails.summary:
NASA’s Space-Time Capsule: The Hardware We Left Behind

Since the 1960s, NASA spacecraft have explored the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Some have stopped working, some still send data, and others are continuing their journeys through deep space. This project tells the stories of these machines: what they were built to do, what they discovered, and what their journeys can teach us about exploring safely and thoughtfully
projectDetails.details: Our project is a youth-friendly guide to NASA hardware left across the solar system. It features Moon landers and experiments, Mars rovers, and deep-space probes. Each story explains where the machine went, what it was designed to do, what it helped scientists discover, and whether it still works. The guide shows that “left behind” equipment has many different stories. Some machines completed their missions after making important discoveries. Others stopped working, while a few still send data from far away. Simple profiles, diagrams, and a solar-system map help young readers see how engineering choices—such as power, communication, and durability—shape what scientists can learn. Our goal is to spark curiosity about space science and engineering. We’ll use clear, age-appropriate language and consider accuracy, accessibility, and the effects of leaving equipment on other worlds.

Project Description:

LUNAR COMMAND is an interactive Moon Base Survival Simulator that explores the challenges of sustaining human life on the lunar south pole.

The project simulates a 30-day lunar mission involving a crew of four astronauts. Users must manage essential resources such as oxygen, water, food, electrical power, radiation shielding and greenhouse systems to ensure the crew's survival.

The simulation includes emergency scenarios, resource management, crew health monitoring, mission analytics and survival scoring. Users make critical decisions in response to changing mission conditions and unexpected events.

The platform also provides lunar environmental information and NASA scientific references to help users understand the challenges of establishing a sustainable human presence on the Moon.

  • Explore resource management and survival strategies.

  • Simulate emergency response and decision-making.

projectDetails.name: Project HackEarth
projectDetails.summary:
EarthTune – The Earth Information Jukebox is an interactive web application developed by HackEarth to transform Earth science information into an engaging audio-visual learning experience.

Our project aims to make understanding our planet easier, more interactive and accessible to people of different ages and backgrounds. EarthTune combines web technologies, environmental information, sound generation and educational explanations to help users explore the different systems of Earth.

The application allows users to explore topics such as ocean currents, night-time lights, atmospheric particles and forests. Its Earth Sound experience uses sound patterns to represent Earth-related concepts, helping users understand scientific information through audio. The Earth Guide provides simple educational explanations with voice narration, while the NASA Earth Events section retrieves natural-event information using NASA's EONET API.

Inspired by advances in Earth AI, satellite observations and environmental data science, HackEarth envisions EarthTune as a platform that connects scientific discoveries with interactive technology. Our goal is to encourage environmental awareness, curiosity and learning by presenting complex Earth science concepts in a simple and engaging way.

Through EarthTune, we want people not only to observe our planet but also to experience and understand it through sound, information and exploration.
projectDetails.details:
EarthTune is a web-based educational prototype designed to make Earth science more accessible through interactive exploration and sound. The application is built using HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Node.js with Express.

Its main features include an Earth topic explorer, a sound experience using the Web Audio API, an educational guide with browser-based speech narration, and a natural events section connected to NASA's EONET API.

Users can explore topics such as ocean currents, night-time lights, atmospheric particles and forests. The application converts illustrative data patterns into sound, helping users experience scientific concepts in a different way. The Earth Guide provides educational explanations, while the NASA events section retrieves available natural-event information.

We developed this prototype to encourage curiosity about Earth science and demonstrate how sound, web technologies and accessible explanations can support environmental learning. The project can be expanded with additional NASA datasets, geospatial visualizations and AI-powered analysis.

This describes the working prototype honestly. It does not claim that the current Earth Guide is a generative AI model or that the illustrative sounds are direct recordings from Earth.

**AETHERRAXIS – Beyond Earth. Beyond Limits.**

AETHERRAXIS is an immersive space exploration and simulation game where players become engineers, astronauts, and mission commanders. Design and build your own rockets, satellites, and planetary rovers using customizable components and realistic engineering principles. Launch missions into space, manage spacecraft systems, monitor live telemetry, and deploy satellites into orbit. Explore the Moon and Mars through challenging missions, transport custom-built rovers, perform safe landings, and navigate alien landscapes while completing scientific objectives. Manage fuel, battery power, speed, and other resources as you overcome unexpected challenges. Experience different planetary environments, gravity conditions, and terrain while making decisions that affect mission success. Players can also compete or collaborate through multiplayer missions, share achievements, and compare engineering performance. Every mission produces a performance report based on actual gameplay events. With creativity, strategy, science, and adventure combined, AETHERRAXIS challenges players to build, explore, experiment, and push the boundaries of space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
AETHERRAXIS – Beyond Earth. Beyond Limits.

AETHERRAXIS is an interactive space exploration and simulation game that allows players to experience the challenges of designing spacecraft, launching missions, and exploring other worlds. Players can build and customize rockets, satellites, and planetary rovers, manage fuel and other resources, perform launches, and complete exploration missions on the Moon and Mars. The game aims to connect engineering, science, creativity, and entertainment through interactive gameplay.

The project benefits users by introducing concepts such as rocket engineering, orbital mechanics, planetary environments, physics, resource management, and problem-solving in an engaging way. Its intended impact is to encourage curiosity about space science, inspire future scientists and engineers, and make space exploration concepts more accessible to students and gaming enthusiasts.

The project is being developed using Google AI Studio and Gemini, with the existing application's technology and codebase being extended. The planned technical architecture includes JavaScript or TypeScript, interactive 3D graphics, physics simulations, data visualization, and multiplayer technologies, depending on the capabilities of the existing application.

The creative aspect of AETHERRAXIS is its combination of spacecraft construction, realistic mission management, lunar and Martian rover exploration, and multiplayer challenges in one experience. Players are not simply observers; they make engineering decisions that influence mission outcomes.

Important factors considered include scientific accuracy, realistic resource limitations, different planetary conditions, user-friendly controls, accessibility, performance, educational value, and meaningful mission success and failure reports.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

Mars Trail Sentinel is an interactive Mars exploration and mission-planning platform developed by Team HACKTECH. It helps visualize Martian terrain, identify potential hazards, and support safer planning of astronaut and rover exploration routes.

The platform focuses on the Lower Mount Sharp region of Gale Crater, including the Boxwork Ridge area. It brings together terrain visualization, geological context, and mission-planning concepts in an interactive mapping experience. By helping users understand slopes, surface features, obstacles, and scientifically interesting locations, Mars Trail Sentinel demonstrates how planetary data can support informed exploration decisions.

Our goal is to make complex Mars surface information easier to explore and understand while highlighting the importance of astronaut safety, scientific discovery, and responsible route planning for future human missions to Mars.
projectDetails.details:
Mars Trail Sentinel is an interactive web-based Mars exploration and mission-planning application created by Team HACKTECH. The project focuses on the Lower Mount Sharp region of Gale Crater, particularly the Boxwork Ridge area, to demonstrate how planetary mapping and terrain information can support future Mars surface exploration.

The application provides an interactive map-based interface for exploring Martian surface features and understanding the challenges involved in planning rover and astronaut traverses. It is designed around the idea of combining different types of planetary information, including terrain, geological features, imagery, and potential hazards, into one accessible exploration environment.

The project aims to help users identify areas of scientific interest, understand terrain-related risks, and visualize possible exploration routes. Its intended impact is to make Mars exploration information easier to interpret and demonstrate how data-driven planning can contribute to safer and more effective future missions.

The project uses web technologies including React, TypeScript, Vite, and MapLibre for the application interface and mapping experience. Browser-based storage technologies such as IndexedDB support local data handling and offline-oriented functionality. Supabase is included in the project architecture for backend services.

The creative aspect of Mars Trail Sentinel is its focus on connecting planetary exploration with practical mission-planning needs. Instead of treating Mars imagery as isolated pictures, the project presents an exploration-oriented interface that encourages users to consider terrain, scientific value, and astronaut safety together.

The team considered usability, accessibility of planetary information, terrain awareness, mission-planning challenges, and the importance of reliable data when designing the project.

Far from home, the first astronauts to set foot on Mars will want the best map possible, with information on the details of their routes and destinations, updates on current conditions, and the data needed to complete their mission quickly and safely. Your challenge is to create a layered, integrated view of a location or route on the Martian surface that pulls together data from multiple NASA science missions and could help a human explorer plan and carry out a successful Marswalk while conducting new and exciting science along the way.

projectDetails.name: FlameLens: AI-Powered Fire Safety Intelligence for Human Space Exploration
projectDetails.summary:
Fire behaves fundamentally differently in microgravity than it does on Earth. In spacecraft, the absence of natural buoyancy changes flame propagation, smoke movement, oxygen transport, and fire suppression behaviour. These differences create serious safety challenges for astronauts and future lunar and Martian missions.

FlameLens is an interactive, research-driven decision-support platform that transforms fragmented microgravity combustion research into accessible fire-safety intelligence.

The platform brings together a curated catalogue of 22 space-combustion experiment records, interactive multi-criteria fire-risk rankings, side-by-side experimental comparisons, and an AI-powered assistant that generates research-grounded explanations. It also includes an interactive flame-behaviour simulator, spacecraft fire-safety guidance, and an educational learning module.

By combining scientific research, explainable analytical methods, interactive visualizations, and AI-assisted insights, FlameLens helps researchers, spacecraft engineers, mission planners, and students better understand combustion risks in space.

Our goal is to make decades of space-combustion research more accessible and useful for developing safer spacecraft and future human exploration missions.
projectDetails.details:
Problem Statement

Fire is one of the most critical hazards in human spaceflight. Unlike Earth, spacecraft operate in microgravity environments where natural buoyancy-driven convection is significantly reduced or absent.

As a result:

  • Flames can develop spherical, diffusion-dominated structures rather than familiar upward flames.
  • Smoke and combustion products do not naturally rise and may follow spacecraft ventilation pathways.
  • Low-speed airflow can influence flame propagation in unexpected ways.
  • Certain combustion processes, including low-temperature cool-flame reactions, may continue beyond visible flame extinction.
  • Future lunar and Martian habitats introduce additional challenges involving atmospheric pressure, oxygen concentration, and material flammability.

Although NASA and other space agencies have conducted extensive combustion experiments, their findings are distributed across research archives, technical reports, and scientific publications.

There is a need for an accessible platform that organizes these findings and helps users interpret their implications for spacecraft fire safety.

Our Solution: FlameLens

FlameLens is a unified research and decision-support platform designed to make microgravity combustion knowledge accessible, interactive, and actionable.

It combines structured experimental information, transparent risk-ranking methodologies, comparative analytics, and AI-assisted research explanations within a single application.

Core Features

1. Unified Microgravity Experiment Catalogue

A searchable catalogue containing 22 curated combustion experiment records. Users can explore experiments based on space agency, research platform, fuel type, gravity environment, and experimental conditions.

The catalogue includes detailed experiment information, findings, fire-risk implications, source references, and CSV/JSON export functionality.

2. Interactive Fire-Risk Ranking Engine

An explainable multi-criteria scoring system that assigns configurable 0–100 heuristic scores to experimental records.

The default weighting considers:

  • Fire-risk severity: 40%
  • Exploration relevance: 30%
  • Evidence strength: 15%
  • Suppression insight value: 15%

Users can adjust the weighting parameters and observe how experiment rankings change through interactive visualizations.

3. Multi-Experiment Comparison Engine

Allows users to compare two to four experiments simultaneously, examining differences in oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, fuel materials, and other experimental conditions.

Interactive charts and comparative summaries help users understand the potential engineering implications of different combustion environments.

4. AI-Powered Fire-Safety Assistant

An AI-assisted research interface that uses the curated experiment records as its evidence context.

It supports different audiences, including astronauts, engineers, and students, with English and Hindi responses. The assistant is designed to reference relevant experiment identifiers, communicate uncertainty, and encourage verification against original research.

A deterministic rule-based fallback is available when the external AI service is unavailable.

5. Interactive Flame Dynamics Simulator

A physics-education simulator that demonstrates how flame morphology changes across Earth gravity, lunar gravity, Martian gravity, and microgravity.

Users can explore the effects of gravity and airflow on combustion behaviour through interactive visualizations.

6. Spacecraft Fire-Safety Guide

A structured educational resource covering combustion physics, ignition, materials, atmospheric conditions, detection, suppression, and emergency-response considerations.

7. Interactive Learning Module

An eight-question knowledge assessment that explains answers and connects users with relevant experiment records. Users can also generate a personalized completion certificate.

8. Space Agency Research Profiles

Provides information about international space research programmes, relevant experimental platforms, ISS modules, and historical milestones in spacecraft combustion research.

Technology Stack

  • Frontend: Next.js 14 and React
  • Programming Language: TypeScript
  • Styling: Tailwind CSS
  • Data Visualization: Recharts
  • Interactive Graphics: HTML5 Canvas and Three.js
  • AI Integration: Anthropic Claude API
  • Backend: Next.js API Routes
  • Deployment: Netlify
  • Offline Support: Progressive Web Application capabilities

Methodology

FlameLens organizes experimental information into a standardized structure covering fuel materials, oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, gravity conditions, experimental findings, and safety implications.

These records are used by the experiment discovery interface, the configurable heuristic ranking engine, the comparison module, and the AI-assisted explanation system.

The ranking methodology is transparent and configurable rather than presented as a scientifically validated prediction model. Similarly, the AI assistant is a research-support tool and not a replacement for qualified spacecraft safety engineering.

Expected Impact

FlameLens aims to:

  • Improve access to fragmented microgravity combustion research.
  • Support comparative analysis of spacecraft fire experiments.
  • Help researchers identify potentially important fire-risk conditions.
  • Make space-combustion research easier to understand through interactive visualizations.
  • Support educational awareness of fire safety in human space exploration.
  • Contribute to research-informed discussions around safer lunar, Martian, and orbital habitats.

Future Scope

Future development could include deeper integration with NASA Physical Sciences Informatics datasets, automated scientific literature extraction, expanded experimental coverage, validation of the heuristic ranking methodology against domain-expert assessments, and more advanced physics-based simulations.

FlameLens is an independent research and decision-support prototype. It is not a certified spacecraft fire-safety system and is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA or any international space agency.

challengeDetails.title: Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data
challengeDetails.excerpt: For decades, NASA has studied how flames and fire behave in microgravity, gathering a trove of experimental data along the way. That knowledge matters more than ever as humans gear up to return to the Moon and press on to Mars, yet the volume of results makes them hard to find, compare, and understand. Your challenge is to create an interactive, super intelligence (SI) powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets those findings to deliver fire safety insights for human space exploration.

challengeDetails.title: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
challengeDetails.excerpt: Space-themed STEM content often oversimplifies the engineering trade-offs that define a real mission or presents them at a level too complex to hold a young learner's attention. Few tools make those trade-offs both tangible and fun. Your challenge is to design and build an interactive game or app that lets students run a lunar or Martian outpost, balancing competing demands like life support, radiation shielding, power, and food production, so they experience firsthand the decisions that determine whether a mission fails or succeeds.

challengeDetails.title: Planet X and SPHEREx
challengeDetails.excerpt: Since 2025, NASA’s SPHEREx mission has been mapping the entire sky every six months in 102 bands of near-infrared light, returning images of more than a billion objects. Comets, asteroids, stars, brown dwarfs, and even new planets reveal themselves by shifting position between images, but no one person can sift through all that data alone. Your challenge is to create a public-facing web tool to display images of the sky from SPHEREx mission, making it easy for anyone to quickly see how they change over time.

projectDetails.name: PROJECT PAWSTRO
projectDetails.summary:
Pawstro is a zero-dependency tablet and first-person Helmet Visor HUD web application developed by Team Hibernation Wale Bhalu for the NASA Space Apps 2026 Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge.

What We Developed:
Pawstro provides suited Mars astronauts with a hyper-local (10 by 10 km) tactical navigation console for Jezero Crater. It integrates five toggleable NASA layers including HiRISE/CTX optical imagery, MOLA/HRSC elevation contours, CRISM spectral minerals, steep no-go hazard zones, and THEMIS thermal data, alongside real-time Perseverance MEDA weather and Curiosity RAD radiation telemetry.

How It Addresses the Challenge:
Using an 8-directional A-Star pathfinding engine on a 2D Digital Elevation Model (DEM) cost grid, Pawstro calculates safe walking routes from the habitat to science targets. Routes dynamically adapt to spacesuit limits (maximum slope, distance, and oxygen budget) and optimization modes (Safest, Fastest, Most Science). A real-time 0 to 100 Safety Score, GO/NO-GO badge, Return-to-Base timer, and immersive Visor HUD featuring real Perseverance rover panoramas keep crew safety first.

Why It Matters:
Astronauts on Mars cannot rely on cloud-dependent global maps or fragmented GIS datasets. Pawstro unifies multi-instrument NASA data into a resilient, offline-capable survival tool that turns complex orbital telemetry into actionable, life-saving surface navigation.
projectDetails.details:
PAWSTRO: Tactical Mars EVA Mission Planner and First Person Helmet Visor HUD Challenge: NASA International Space Apps Challenge 2026 | Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map Team: Hibernation Wale Bhalu Mission Crew: Abhinav, Aditi, Harsha, Nikhil Target Site: Jezero Crater Western Delta, Mars (18.4447 N, 77.4508 E, Sol 142)

  1. EXECUTIVE OVERVIEW

When astronauts transition from orbital observation to surface exploration on Mars, global planetary maps are insufficient for day to day survival. Standing on the basin floor of Jezero Crater inside a pressurized spacesuit, an explorer requires immediate, localized intelligence to navigate steep scarps, manage consumable life support reserves, and locate high priority astrobiological samples before nightfall.

Developed by Team Hibernation Wale Bhalu, Pawstro is a localized (10 by 10 kilometer), zero dependency Extravehicular Activity (EVA) mission planning console and first person Helmet Visor Heads Up Display (HUD). Instead of requiring astronauts and flight controllers to cross reference multiple separate geographic information systems, Pawstro unifies NASA optical satellite imagery, topographic elevation contours, orbital spectral mineralogy, surface thermal inertia, radiation dose rates, and local Martian weather into a single, offline capable spacecraft interface. The platform pairs an 8 directional A Star pathfinding engine with an interactive mission communicator, CAPCOM Paw, ensuring that every surface traverse remains strictly within human physiological and hardware safety limits.

  1. SYSTEM FUNCTIONALITY AND TECHNICAL WORKFLOW

Pawstro operates as a dual mode tactical system engineered for the two primary phases of a Martian surface excursion: Pre EVA Tactical Planning (Tablet Console View) and Active Surface Traverse (First Person Helmet Visor HUD Mode).

A. Deep Space Mission Onboarding Upon initialization, operators enter an obsidian black Deep Space Landing Console (#030308) featuring an animated meteor field, live landing site coordinates (18.4447 N, 77.4508 E), the crew manifest plaque, and the floating polar bear astronaut mascot. Operators can transition directly into the main planning console or initiate the 30 second Automated Judge Demo, which loads optimal suit parameters, calculates a complete multi target traverse, and opens science target dossiers in a single action.

B. Five Layer NASA GIS Stack and Split Screen Comparison Engine Within the central viewport, Martian Orange (#ff6a3d) is reserved exclusively for the Jezero Crater map to maximize visual contrast against the surrounding dark avionics panels. Pawstro aligns five toggleable scientific datasets within a unified 700 by 460 orbital coordinate grid:

  1. Photo (Optical): High contrast shaded relief displaying the Neretva Vallis ancient river channel, the Western Delta fan, shaded impact craters (Belva Crater, Kodiak Butte, Santa Cruz), and aeolian regolith ripples across the volcanic Maaz formation floor.
  2. Terrain Height (Topography): Five elevation contour intervals ranging from the 2540 meter basin floor to the 2380 meter delta rim, modeled on MOLA and HRSC Digital Elevation Models.
  3. Minerals (Spectral): MRO CRISM spectral overlays identifying magnesium carbonate lakeshore margin units and iron/magnesium smectite clay and olivine deposits where ancient water interacted with bedrock.
  4. Steep and No Go Zones: Hatched crimson hazard polygons marking cliff scarps exceeding 18 degrees and dense boulder fields that compromise spacesuit stability.
  5. Heat (Thermal): THEMIS thermal inertia anomaly layers that assist crew members in distinguishing consolidated bedrock from unconsolidated dust traps.

Operators can blend overlapping layers using a continuous Opacity Slider (20% to 100%) or engage the Interactive Split Screen Layer Comparison tool. Using a dynamic SVG clipping mask and a cursor tracked vertical divider, users can swipe across Jezero Crater to compare raw optical imagery directly against spectral mineral deposits and topographic hazards. Full viewport controls (Zoom In, Zoom Out, Habitat Center, True North Reset, drag panning, and real time cursor Latitude/Longitude tracking) provide complete spatial awareness.

C. Slope Aware A Star Pathfinding Engine and Reactive Suit Limits At the core of Pawstro is a custom 8 directional A Star pathfinding algorithm operating over a 70 by 46 Digital Elevation Model (DEM) and slope cost grid at a 10 meter cell resolution. Planners can compute routes from Habitat Base (Octavia E. Butler Landing Site) to individual locations (Target A: Wildcat Ridge at 0.8 km; Target B: Kodiak Butte at 1.5 km; Target C: Neretva Delta Fan at 2.3 km) or sequence all targets into an integrated tour. The routing engine supports three optimization modes:

  1. Safest Mode: Applies an exponential cost penalty to terrain incline, directing the astronaut around steep ridges and boulder fields through flat basin corridors.
  2. Fastest Mode: Computes the shortest Euclidean path that remains below the spacesuit's maximum allowable slope threshold.
  3. Most Science Mode: Weights the traversal cost function to route the astronaut through high concentration CRISM carbonate and clay spectral zones, maximizing geological sampling opportunities.

The pathfinding engine is directly coupled to three interactive Spacesuit Limit Sliders: Maximum Slope (5 to 35 degrees), Maximum Distance (1 to 8 km), and Oxygen Reserve (1 to 10 hours). Reducing the Maximum Slope slider dynamically expands the red no go hazard zones on the map and forces the A Star algorithm to compute a wider detour around steep scarps in under 10 milliseconds, simultaneously updating the Elevation Profile Chart, Total Distance, Estimated Walking Time, and Steepest Incline metrics.

D. Real Time Safety Evaluation, Return to Base Timer, and Emergency Abort In alignment with NASA human rating priorities, Pawstro dedicates its lower avionics bay to continuous life support and environmental monitoring:

  1. Route Safety Score (0 to 100) and GO / NO GO Indicator: Continuously evaluates the active route's steepest incline, total distance, and estimated duration against the astronaut's suit limits, alongside Perseverance MEDA weather baselines (minus 12 degrees Celsius, 6 m/s wind speed) and Curiosity RAD surface radiation figures (0.6 uSv/h). If any suit threshold is exceeded, the safety score drops below operational minimums, the status badge transitions from emerald GO to crimson NO GO, and the console outputs the specific parameter violation.
  2. Head Back By Countdown Timer: Combining the current Martian Sol clock (11:05), available oxygen reserve, return walking duration, and local sunset time (17:12), Pawstro calculates the exact turn back deadline required to return to the habitat before nightfall.
  3. Emergency Return to Base (RTB): In the event of a suit anomaly or environmental hazard, engaging the Return to Base control aborts the active science tour, computes a direct low slope A Star escape path back to Habitat Base, and highlights the trajectory in high visibility coral.

E. First Person Helmet Visor HUD with Real Perseverance Rover Panoramas When transitioning from pre mission planning to surface execution, selecting HUD Mode switches Pawstro into a fullscreen, first person Helmet Visor Display. Framed by curved visor glass vignettes and instrumentation brackets, the HUD integrates actual NASA/JPL Caltech Perseverance Rover surface photographs of Jezero Crater for each waypoint (Sol 3 Octavia E. Butler Landing Hazcam panorama, Sol 466 Wildcat Ridge sulfate beds, Sol 63 Kodiak Butte delta foreset strata, and Sol 420 Western Delta scarp). Stepping through waypoints via the Next Waypoint control cross fades the visor background to the corresponding Martian surface photograph while updating the top cardinal compass tape, center target reticle, Slope Ahead warning module, oxygen progress bar, and synchronized Live Visor Mini Map. To guarantee operational resilience in offline environments, an integrated procedural HTML5 Canvas generator synthesizes a 1280 by 720 Martian surface panorama whenever external network connectivity is unavailable.

  1. OPERATIONAL BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT
  2. Cognitive Offloading During High Workload EVA Operations: Suited astronauts operate under physical exertion and restricted visibility. By synthesizing five separate orbital and surface datasets into a single 0 to 100 Safety Score and a clear GO / NO GO indicator, Pawstro reduces cognitive load during time critical surface decisions.
  3. Offline Mission Resilience: Surface exploration tools cannot depend on continuous high bandwidth connectivity. Pawstro packages its entire pathfinding engine, DEM cost grid, SVG cartography, persistent field notes, JSON route exporter, and printable PDF mission briefing generator into a single self contained bundle under 350 KB that executes 100% offline.
  4. Bridging Orbital Remote Sensing and Surface Execution: Pawstro demonstrates a scalable methodology for fusing orbital reconnaissance (HiRISE, MOLA, CRISM, THEMIS) with surface telemetry (Perseverance MEDA, Mastcam Z, Curiosity RAD). This architecture is directly applicable to future lunar Artemis surface traverses, human Mars expeditions, and terrestrial analog field campaigns.
  5. TOOLS, LANGUAGES, AND SOFTWARE ARCHITECTURE

Pawstro was engineered for high performance, cross platform portability, and zero dependency reliability:

  1. Core Technologies: Vanilla HTML5, CSS3 (Custom Properties, CSS Grid, Glassmorphic Backdrop Filters, Keyframe Animations, Print Media Queries), and ES6+ JavaScript.
  2. Cartography and Rendering Engines: Inline Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) utilizing dynamic clip paths, custom hazard hatching, and multi stop radial lighting gradients, paired with HTML5 2D Canvas for real time elevation profile plotting and procedural offline panorama generation.
  3. Algorithms and Local Persistence: Custom 8 directional A Star grid search algorithm over a 70 by 46 DEM and slope matrix; browser LocalStorage API for persistent astronaut field notes and sample collection tracking; Blob and ObjectURL APIs for structured JSON telemetry export.
  4. NASA Datasets Integrated: Mars 2020 HiRISE and CTX orthomosaics (USGS Astrogeology), MOLA and HRSC elevation models, MRO CRISM spectral mineral mappings (Mars Trek), Perseverance Mastcam Z and Hazcam surface imagery, Perseverance MEDA weather logs, and Curiosity RAD radiation baselines.
  5. Automated Verification Suite: Node.js verification environment executing a 14 suite, 132 assertion automated End to End (E2E) test script (test_e2e_full.js) that validates JavaScript compilation, A Star path geometry, slope limit enforcement, and HUD state synchronization.
  6. CREATIVE DESIGN AND HUMAN FACTORS
  7. Intuitive Telemetry Companion (CAPCOM Paw): To make complex planetary data accessible to both mission specialists and public audiences, our compact 96 pixel polar bear astronaut mascot serves as a context aware mission communicator in the corner of the viewport. Selecting science goals, logging rock samples, or breaching suit safety limits triggers immediate, human readable voice bubble updates alongside formal numerical telemetry.
  8. Multi Scale Geological Inspection: Within each Science Target Dossier modal, operators can cycle through a three view Rover POV Carousel (Wide Mastcam Z Outcrop, 2.2x Geological Strata Zoom, and False Color Spectrometer Overlay) and jump directly into the fullscreen Helmet Visor HUD focused on that exact outcrop.
  9. Biomechanical and Environmental Realism: Our team accounted for the physical realities of Martian exploration. Because climbing loose regolith in a pressurized suit exponentially increases metabolic oxygen consumption, our cost grid applies non linear slope penalties. Furthermore, because Martian surface temperatures drop below minus 80 degrees Celsius after sunset, our Return to Base timer cross checks both consumable oxygen hours and the 17:12 local sunset deadline. Finally, because the Perseverance rover does not carry an active radiation detector, we integrated Curiosity RAD surface dose baselines and documented all sample and historical data sources transparently within our technical manual and SOURCES.txt.

projectDetails.name: HOMEWARD
projectDetails.summary: Homeward is a Martian map, built only from real data, that plans a walk on Mars and always gets the walker home. On Mars, help is about 11 light-minutes away, so a crew member walking out from the habitat must know at every step how long the walk home takes, and whether air, power, radiation dose and daylight will last. That data already exists across many NASA missions, but no map brings it together for one walk. Homeward fuses nine kinds of data from seven missions into one 3D map: MOLA and HRSC relief, HiRISE, CTX, THEMIS, geology, thermal inertia, weather, radiation and space weather. It plans a route that avoids slopes and rocks a suit cannot cross, keeps every budget with a walk-back reserve, and guides the walk with a live helmet display that includes radio line of sight to the habitat. Every number is measured, computed or cited. It is free and runs in any browser.
projectDetails.details:
What it does. Homeward turns NASA’s Mars data into one map a crew can trust for a Marswalk. It runs one loop: Explore, Brief, Plan, Walk, Home.

  • Explore: a Google-Earth style 3D globe with real 200 m relief everywhere (MOLA and Mars Express HRSC) and 1 m HiRISE terrain at Gale Crater.
    • Search 2,064 named places and tour 13 landing sites, from Mars 3 to Zhurong.
    • See Spirit’s and Opportunity’s drive paths and the Viking 1 and 2 landing-site mosaics from JPL Mars Trek.
    • Turn on overlays for geology, thermal inertia and dust.
    • Any spot shows its USGS rock unit and every published USGS geologic map that covers it.
    • HiRISE stereo terrain becomes a 2 m slope and rock grid; cells steeper than 20° or with more than 1 m of rock relief are blocked.
    • An A* search finds the fastest route, using Tobler’s hiking function scaled to the Apollo walk-back rate of 3.3 km/h.
    • A Dijkstra “walk-back field” gives the time home from every point, so the plan checks the way home at every step, not just at the turnaround.
    • Life support (8 h minus a 30 min reserve), daylight, dose and the 2 km radius are hard budgets; any breach blocks approval.
  • Walk: walk it yourself at the planner’s pace, follow the plan, or fly anywhere at 10 to 1,000 m/s. The helmet display shows time home, air, dose, daylight and radio line of sight to the habitat, computed over the real terrain and the planet’s curvature.
  • Rover view: street view from Curiosity’s and Perseverance’s own photos, each placed where its camera pointed, plus the newest raw images from Mars.
  • Suit assistant: answers by voice, only with numbers the app computes, and names its sources.

Worked example. On sol 182 the walk from the habitat to the rock where Curiosity found an ancient lake is 905 m and 17 minutes of walking. It uses 1 h 17 min of the 7 h 30 min life-support budget, keeps at least a 6 h 13 min walk-back margin, and costs 0.034 mSv. The verdict is GO.

Benefits and impact.

  • Crew safety: the time home is known at every step.
  • Mission planning: orbiter and rover data are fused into one view.
  • Education: anyone can walk Mars for free.

Tools.

  • Code: TypeScript, React 19 and Vite; CesiumJS for 3D; Web Workers for terrain decoding and planning; zod validation.
  • On-device voice: Kokoro-82M and Whisper.
  • Server and data: Vercel serverless functions, and a Python data pipeline (NumPy, rasterio).
  • Testing: 84 automated tests, checked against published values from Mars24, NASA and ESA light times, and JPL Horizons.
  • Hosting: free, on Vercel’s Hobby plan.

What is creative. It is the first map to plan a Mars walk with the way home guaranteed at every step. Rover street view is built from NASA’s raw photos and camera models. Every number on screen carries a badge (MEASURED, COMPUTED, STANDARD or ASSUMPTION) and a source.

Factors we considered. Astronaut safety first; honest data (no demo numbers, and weather always dated); offline use; zero cost; a strict security policy; and screens from a habitat display to a tablet or a helmet HUD.

projectDetails.name: FIREWATCH: One Fire Calendar from Two NASA Satellites
projectDetails.summary: FIREWATCH harmonizes NASA's MODIS and VIIRS active-fire hotspots into one consistent burning-activity calendar for India from 2003 to 2026. VIIRS (375 m) detects about 7.8 times more hotspots than MODIS (1 km), so joining the two records naively creates a fake jump in 2012 and makes long-term trends misleading. We fitted 12 monthly MODIS-to-VIIRS ratios on the 2012–2018 overlap, scaled the earlier MODIS record onto the VIIRS S-NPP scale, and spliced in NOAA-20 after S-NPP ended. On held-out years 2019–2025, our method cut the error from 31,107 to 4,288 hotspots per month (MAPE 88.1% to 15.9%, correlation 0.98). Our web app lets anyone draw an area or enter coordinates and see which months and years burned most, compare this month with the historical median, explore trend, hot-spot cluster and chronic-burning map layers, read an AI summary of the numbers, see NASA POWER weather context, and download CSVs. This gives farmers, officials and researchers a fair long-term view of fire activity, such as the Punjab–Haryana stubble-burning season.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

FIREWATCH turns two NASA satellite fire records into one comparable 23-year history for any area in India. Users draw a rectangle, circle or polygon on the map (or enter coordinates) and get: a burning-activity calendar (which months and years burned most, 2003–2026), trends, this month compared with the historical median (above the 90th percentile is flagged as unusual), spatial analysis layers (per-cell trend with Theil-Sen slope and Mann-Kendall test, Getis-Ord Gi* hot/cold-spot clusters, and chronic burning where fires recur in at least 80% of years), a hotspot map, CSV downloads, an AI-generated plain-language summary, and NASA POWER rainfall and temperature context.

Live app: https://firewatch-india.streamlit.app

Code: https://github.com/KRITHIKYADAV06/FIREWATCH

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data: 11.5 million NASA FIRMS hotspots for India (MODIS C6.1 Aqua 2003–2025, VIIRS S-NPP 2012–2026, VIIRS NOAA-20 2018–2026), vegetation fires only (type 0), nominal/high confidence, gridded to 0.1°.

2. Harmonization: VIIRS detects about 7.8x more hotspots than MODIS, so joining the records naively creates a fake jump in 2012. We fitted 12 monthly VIIRS/MODIS ratios on 2012–2018, scaled earlier MODIS onto the VIIRS S-NPP scale, and spliced in NOAA-20 after S-NPP ended on 2 Nov 2026.

3. Validation on held-out 2019–2025 (India monthly totals): MAE 4,288 vs 31,107 for the naive splice and 8,758 for a single pooled ratio; MAPE 15.9% vs 88.1%; Pearson r 0.98.

4. Experimental ML forecast: gradient boosting predicts next month's fires per cell; on 2025 it scored MAE 1.28 vs 1.36 (same-month median) and 1.52 (same month last year), with a top-10% hit rate of 63%.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Without harmonization, "more fires" can simply mean "a better sensor". FIREWATCH gives farmers, district officials, researchers and journalists a fair long-term picture, for example of the October–November stubble-burning season in Punjab and Haryana, so that policies and trends can be judged on real change.

TOOLS

Python, pandas, NumPy, PyArrow, SciPy, scikit-learn, Streamlit, Folium/Leaflet, Plotly, Google Gemini API, NASA POWER API, GitHub, Streamlit Community Cloud, pytest (automated tests).

CREATIVITY AND CONSIDERATIONS

Season-specific ratios instead of one factor; an honest held-out validation against two baselines; zero detections treated as "no FIRMS detections", not "no fire"; the AI summary may only use our computed numbers and is labelled AI-generated; accessible colour palettes. Limitations: accurate for regional totals, not single 0.1° cells; data through 31 July 2026; near-real-time integration is future work.

TEAM

S Krithik Yadav (lead, data science & ML), Parth Pillai (data engineering), Avin ke (backend), Alisha Maharana (geospatial), Anthony Fernandes (frontend), Adrita Sarkar (testing & documentation).

projectDetails.name: FIELDWISE
projectDetails.summary: FIELDWISE ("From orbit to every field") is an interactive, bilingual (English and Kannada) decision-support dashboard designed to help Bengaluru farmers plan sustainable crop rotations—specifically evaluating the Ragi (Kharif) to Horse Gram (Rabi) cycle. By integrating NASA Earth observation datasets (NASA POWER climate data, HLS/Landsat NDVI, and NASA Worldview) with local agronomic knowledge, FIELDWISE translates complex satellite metrics into an instant, actionable Crop Rotation Suitability Score. Farmers and agricultural officers can adjust real-time "What-If" climate sliders (rainfall and temperature shifts) alongside personal priorities like water saving, yield, risk tolerance, and soil health. The platform visualizes seasonal rainfall against crop water needs, root-zone soil moisture, heat stress risks, and optimal sowing windows, while allowing users to export downloadable CSV reports. FIELDWISE bridges the gap between raw space data and grassroots farming to build climate-resilient agriculture.
projectDetails.details:
FIELDWISE is a climate-and-soil decision-support web app that helps smallholder farmers in Bengaluru evaluate crop rotation strategies using real satellite and ground data — directly from NASA's POWER API and Earth observation systems.

What it does: FIELDWISE analyzes one optimal rotation — Ragi (Kharif, Jun–Oct) → Horse Gram (Rabi, Nov–Feb) — and scores its viability (0–100) based on four pillars: rainfall adequacy, heat stress, soil moisture, and sowing-window timing. Farmers get a plain-language verdict ("Good", "Caution", "Risky"), actionable strategies, and downloadable reports — in both English and Kannada.

How it works: The app runs a 4-tier data pipeline — it first pulls real NASA POWER daily climate data for Bengaluru (2026), then derives soil moisture from precipitation balance, estimates NDVI from temperature/moisture proxies, and falls back to historical averages only when live data is unavailable. A weighted scoring model combines all signals into one recommendation with confidence percentage.

Tools & Stack: Python 3.13, Streamlit, NASA POWER API (MERRA-2 reanalysis), Plotly for interactive charts, Pandas/NumPy for data processing. Frontend design inspired by AgriOrbit design system (cream-paper UI, dark orbit hero banner, Fraunces + Manrope fonts).

Impact: Bridges the "last mile" gap between satellite data and field decisions for farmers with no GIS expertise. Fully offline-capable with cached NASA data, supports regional language (Kannada), and runs on any browser — no app install needed.

Creative factor: We combined NASA's orbital data with ground-level agronomic knowledge to give farmers a single trust score they can act on immediately — moving from "orbit to every field."

projectDetails.summary:
TerraShift AI is a crop-rotation decision-support platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under the theme “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data”. It combines NASA climate data with farm information to help users explore crop choices and compare rotation plans.

Users can enter their farm location, area, soil properties and irrigation details. The platform uses a crop library and eight parameters from the NASA POWER Daily Point API, covering temperature, rainfall, humidity, root-zone wetness, solar radiation and wind speed.

Six modules are Farm Profile and Provenance, Crop Library and Overrides, Climate Explorer and Data Coverage, Rotation Simulator and Weights, Compare and Insights, and Methodology and AI Advisor. The scoring model evaluates Soil, Water, Climate and Diversity, with default weights of 30%, 30%, 25% and 15%. Users can adjust weights and compare scenarios on a 0 to 100 scale.

Built with React 19, TanStack Start, Base44, JavaScript, Recharts and TanStack AI, it supports English, Hindi and Kannada. It includes private workspaces and a public read-only demo.

TerraShift AI aims to make climate-informed crop-rotation planning clearer and more accessible. Its scores are illustrative heuristic outputs, not verified soil-health assessments or predictions of crop yield or income. It supports decisions, not replaces farmer knowledge or validation.
projectDetails.details:
TerraShift AI

What does the project do and how does it work?

TerraShift AI is a crop-rotation decision-support platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under the theme “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data”.

The platform combines NASA climate data with farm information to help users explore crop choices, simulate crop rotations and compare different farming scenarios. Users can enter their farm location, land area, soil properties and irrigation details. The platform retrieves climate information for the selected location through the NASA POWER Daily Point API.

It uses eight NASA POWER parameters: temperature, maximum and minimum temperature, corrected precipitation, relative humidity, root-zone wetness, solar radiation and wind speed. These parameters provide climate context for exploring crop suitability and rotation scenarios.

TerraShift AI has six main modules: Farm Profile and Provenance, Crop Library and Overrides, Climate Explorer and Data Coverage, Rotation Simulator and Weights, Compare and Insights, and Methodology and AI Advisor.

Its scoring model evaluates four dimensions: Soil, Water, Climate and Diversity. The default weights are 30%, 30%, 25% and 15%, respectively. Users can adjust these weights and compare results on a scale of 0 to 100.

What are the benefits?

TerraShift AI brings farm information and NASA climate data together in one platform. It helps users understand local climate conditions, explore different crop-rotation combinations and compare scenarios using consistent evaluation criteria.

Its adjustable weights allow users to explore how different priorities affect the results. The platform also provides climate data coverage information and explains its methodology, helping users understand where the information comes from and how the results are calculated.

The interface supports English, Hindi and Kannada to make the platform more accessible to users in India.

What is the intended impact?

The intended impact is to make climate-informed crop-rotation planning easier to explore and understand. TerraShift AI aims to encourage better-informed agricultural discussions by connecting Earth observation data with farm-level information.

It can serve as an exploratory decision-support tool for farmers, students, researchers and agricultural practitioners. It is designed to support local knowledge and decision-making, not replace farmers or agricultural experts.

The scores are illustrative heuristic outputs. They are not validated soil-health assessments or predictions of crop yield, income or future climate conditions. Local agricultural validation is necessary before using the results for real farm decisions.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed as a software-based web platform using:

  • Frontend: React 19 and TanStack Start.
  • Platform and backend: Base44 SDK, entities and server functions.
  • Data source: NASA POWER Daily Point API.
  • Programming language: JavaScript.
  • Scoring and calculations: Deterministic JavaScript-based scoring model.
  • Charts and visualisation: Recharts.
  • AI functionality: TanStack AI through the Base44 AI gateway.
  • Location support: OpenStreetMap Nominatim and manual coordinate input.
  • Languages: English, Hindi and Kannada.

The project does not require dedicated physical hardware. It is designed to be accessed through a web browser.

How is the project creative?

The creative aspect of TerraShift AI is its combination of NASA Earth observation data, farm-level information and an adjustable crop-rotation simulation in one platform.

Instead of presenting climate data only as charts, it connects climate context to crop-rotation scenarios. Users can change evaluation priorities, compare alternative plans and explore how different combinations affect their scores.

The platform also includes data provenance, coverage information and methodology explanations so users can understand the basis of the results rather than receiving an unexplained recommendation.

What factors did the team consider?

The project considered farm location, soil properties, irrigation availability, land area, climate conditions, crop characteristics and crop diversity. It also considered the importance of transparent data sources, missing data handling, adjustable scoring weights and accessibility for users speaking different languages.

Another important factor was the distinction between NASA-provided climate information and farmer-entered or crop-library information. Soil properties are supplied by the user or represented through crop-library assumptions, rather than being treated as direct measurements from NASA POWER.

TerraShift AI was designed as an exploratory tool with clearly communicated limitations. Its results require local agronomic knowledge and field-level validation before they can be used as practical farming recommendations.

projectDetails.name: ORBITX
projectDetails.summary:
ORBITX is an interactive space mission design and simulation platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It lets anyone experience what it takes to plan, build, and run a real space mission, all from the browser.

Pick a destination, whether the Moon, Mars, Venus, an asteroid, or Jupiter, then set your scientific objectives. From there, you design your own spacecraft by choosing propulsion systems, power sources, communication equipment, thermal protection, and science instruments. Every choice has consequences. You'll need to balance mass, fuel, power, communications, spacecraft health, and budget while guiding your mission through each stage and handling unexpected anomalies along the way.

To keep things grounded in reality, ORBITX integrates NASA/JPL Horizons data, giving you real planetary positions and velocities rather than made-up numbers.

We built ORBITX because space engineering often feels out of reach. By turning complex mission design into a hands on experience, it helps students understand real world engineering trade offs, sharpen their problem solving skills, and test different strategies. Best of all, they can learn from both successes and failures in a risk free virtual environment, just like real mission teams do.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does the project do and how does it work?

ORBITX is a web based space mission design and simulation platform that lets you experience an entire mission, from the first sketch to the final report.

You start by choosing a destination: the Moon, Mars, Venus, an asteroid, or Jupiter. Then you set your scientific objectives and build your spacecraft piece by piece, picking the structural frame, propulsion system, power source, communication antenna, thermal protection, battery, and science instruments.

Behind the scenes, ORBITX runs engineering calculations covering mass, propellant needs, delta-v, power generation, communication capacity, thermal conditions, radiation protection, and budget. If your design passes these checks, you launch it.

From there, you guide the mission through each stage, watch simulated telemetry, and deal with unexpected anomalies as they appear. At the end, you get a mission report and a performance score.

To keep things grounded in reality, ORBITX pulls planetary positions and velocities from NASA/JPL Horizons, linking the simulation to actual astronomical data.

2. What benefits does the project provide?

  • Interactive learning: Complex aerospace concepts become easier to grasp through hands-on experimentation.
  • Engineering awareness: Users see how changing one component ripples through the entire spacecraft.
  • Safe experimentation: Try different designs and learn from failed missions without any real-world risk.
  • Scientific understanding: Introduces planetary exploration, science instruments, orbital information, and mission objectives.
  • Decision-making skills: Users make engineering choices while working within limited resources and budgets.
  • Accessibility: It runs in the browser, so anyone can explore mission design without expensive labs or hardware.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our main goal is to make space mission engineering more accessible, engaging, and easy to understand, especially for students and space enthusiasts.

ORBITX bridges the gap between textbook aerospace theory and practical mission planning. When users see how spacecraft design, scientific objectives, resource management, and mission outcomes connect, they naturally think more critically, creatively, and analytically.

We hope the experience sparks curiosity and inspires more students to pursue aerospace engineering, space science, physics, and other STEM fields.

4. What technologies and tools did we use?

We built ORBITX with a modern web stack.

Frontend and interface

  • React.js for the interactive UI
  • TypeScript for type safe application logic
  • Tailwind CSS for styling and responsive layouts
  • Three.js and React Three Fiber for 3D space visualizations
  • Recharts for telemetry and performance charts
  • Framer Motion for interface animations

Backend and data

  • Node.js and Express.js for the server and API
  • MongoDB and Mongoose for storing mission data
  • NASA/JPL Horizons API for planetary ephemeris data

Development and testing

  • Visual Studio Code as our editor
  • Vite for development and builds
  • Vitest for testing simulation and engineering logic
  • Git and GitHub for version control and collaboration

ORBITX is fully software-based and needs no specialized hardware.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

ORBITX brings together space exploration, spacecraft engineering, interactive simulation, and game-based learning in one platform.

Instead of just reading about planets and spacecraft, users become mission designers, and every decision has consequences. A more powerful instrument adds mass and power demand. Electric propulsion saves propellant but needs far more electrical power. Distant planets bring tougher challenges with communication, radiation, and available solar energy.

We also added mission anomalies, multiple difficulty levels, performance scoring, achievements, and interactive 3D solar-system visualizations to keep things engaging.

Finally, integrating NASA/JPL Horizons data ties real planetary information into the learning experience, so the simulation feels authentic rather than purely fictional.

6. What factors did our team consider?

While building ORBITX, we thought carefully about what makes a mission both realistic and fun to learn from:

  • Scientific objectives: Instruments must support the chosen mission goals.
  • Mass and payload: The spacecraft must stay within the launch vehicle's capacity.
  • Propulsion and fuel: Propellant is estimated with the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation.
  • Power management: Electrical demand must be balanced against generation.
  • Communication: The antenna must be able to support the mission.
  • Thermal and radiation protection: Temperature swings and radiation levels vary by destination.
  • Budget: Component, launcher, and operating costs all count.
  • Mission reliability: Unexpected events and spacecraft health keep every flight unpredictable.
  • Data accuracy and transparency: We use NASA/JPL Horizons for ephemeris data and openly document the assumptions and limits of our educational models.
  • User experience: The interface is intuitive and visually engaging, even for beginners.

Conclusion

ORBITX turns the complexity of space mission planning into a hands-on experience. By combining real planetary data, simplified engineering models, spacecraft configuration, and mission simulation, it lets users design, experiment, make tough calls, and learn how real missions depend on carefully balanced systems.

projectDetails.name: Field Shift: South India's Crops in 2050
projectDetails.summary:
Field Shift is an interactive 3D map that shows how climate change will reshape what South India's farms can grow. It scores 131 districts across Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Kerala, Andhra Pradesh, Telangana and Goa for paddy, ragi and maize, comparing today's climate (2001–2020) with 2041–2060 under two emission scenarios, SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5.

The scores come from NASA's NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 downscaled climate projections, checked against NASA POWER observations (r = 0.94). MODIS greenness and land surface temperature show what each district's fields have done over the last 20 years. A timelapse slider and a before/after swipe let anyone watch the shift happen. Clicking a district gives a plain-language plan: the best crop now and in 2050, how many weeks sowing should move as the monsoon shifts, and how much extra water each crop would need.

Climate projections rarely reach the people deciding what to plant. Field Shift turns NASA data into one map that a farmer, extension officer or planner can read in a minute.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

Field Shift scores how well each of 131 South Indian districts suits paddy, ragi and maize, today (2001–2020) and in 2050 (2041–2060), under SSP2-4.5 and SSP5-8.5. Districts are drawn as 3D columns whose height and colour show suitability. A slider animates the change from today to 2050, a swipe view compares the two side by side, and a guided story walks through the key findings.

How it works

The score is a transparent rule: 100 × the lower of a temperature factor and a rainfall factor. Each factor is 1 inside the crop's optimal range (FAO ECOCROP) and falls to 0 at its limits. Climate is the mean of five NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 models (ACCESS-CM2, IPSL-CM6A-LR, MIROC6, MRI-ESM2-0, NorESM2-MM) over the June–October kharif season, averaged to districts. We also derive monsoon onset from daily rainfall. NASA POWER rainfall validates the model baseline (r = 0.94). MODIS NDVI and land surface temperature, masked to cropland with ESA WorldCover, provide each district's observed 20-year record.

Benefits and impact

Each district gets an adaptation plan: the best crop now and in 2050, whether to switch crops, how many weeks sowing should move, and the water gap per crop in mm. Headline findings: kharif rainfall rises about 10–15% and temperature about 1.0–1.4 °C by 2050. Paddy gains on the wet coast (Thiruvananthapuram 30 → 68). Maize opens up in the dry interior (Anantapur 36 → 95). Ragi loses suitability in up to 65 of 131 districts.

Tools

Python (numpy, shapely, netCDF4, requests) for the data pipeline. FastAPI for an optional API. Next.js 14, TypeScript, MapLibre GL, deck.gl and Tailwind for the frontend. Hosted on Vercel. Every number is precomputed into static files, so the site is fast and works without a backend.

Creativity

The NASA data is shown as a 3D landscape that rises and falls as you scrub through time. Every number in the app links back to its source dataset.

What we considered

Honesty about limits. The model covers rain-fed crops in the kharif season only, so irrigated districts and the north-east monsoon (important in Tamil Nadu) are under-represented. District averages hide local variation. Results are scenarios, not forecasts, and model spread is shown for every district.
