projectDetails.name: FireScope
projectDetails.summary:
FireScope

FireScope is a national-scale satellite fire intelligence platform that transforms millions of raw satellite observations into an interactive, analysis-ready view of fire activity across India.

- Integrated 9.95 million MODIS Terra/Aqua and Suomi-NPP VIIRS observations spanning 2012–2026.
- Built an interactive Google Maps and deck.gl visualization with independently switchable MODIS and VIIRS layers and multi-resolution hotspot mapping.
- Developed historical activity calendars, sensor-specific FRP analytics, and a cross-sensor candidate matching explorer.
- Implemented a FastAPI and DuckDB backend for efficient querying of large-scale historical datasets.
- Designed a modern, unified scientific intelligence dashboard.

How it addresses the challenge
FireScope harmonizes observations from different satellite sensors, enables geographical and temporal exploration, and identifies potential cross-sensor relationships using spatial and temporal criteria.

Why it matters
It makes large-scale satellite fire data easier to explore, compare and interpret, helping researchers and decision-makers better understand historical fire activity while preserving the scientific distinction between detected hotspots, candidate matches and confirmed fire events.
projectDetails.details:
FireScope is a satellite-based fire intelligence platform that processes 9.95 million MODIS Terra/Aqua and Suomi-NPP VIIRS observations (2012–2026) to help users explore historical fire activity across India.

How it works: It harmonizes satellite observations, displays hotspots through interactive Google Maps and deck.gl visualizations, and identifies potential cross-sensor relationships using spatial and temporal matching. Users can explore maps, historical activity, sensor-specific Fire Radiative Power (FRP), analytics and candidate matches through a unified dashboard.

Benefits and intended impact: It makes large-scale satellite data easier to access, visualize and compare, supporting researchers and decision-makers in understanding fire patterns and investigating possible sensor relationships.

Technology: React, TypeScript, Vite, Python, FastAPI, DuckDB, Parquet, SQLAlchemy, Google Maps JavaScript API and deck.gl. NASA satellite datasets provide the observation data; development used standard computing hardware.

Innovation and design considerations: The project combines multi-sensor analysis, footprint-aware matching and multi-resolution mapping. Our team prioritized scalability, data accuracy, sensor-specific characteristics, scientific transparency, usability and secure API-key management. Importantly, candidate matches are presented as possible associations, not confirmed physical fires.

projectDetails.name: Project LunaSolo
projectDetails.summary: LunaSolo - Earth System Trend Detection tracks how our planet changed from 2000 to 2024. I analysed 4 real signals from NASA, NOAA, and NSIDC: global temperature, CO2, Arctic sea ice, and sea level. Using Python, Pandas, and Linear Regression in Google Colab, I cleaned the data, found long-term trends, and forecasted to 2030. Temperature rose by 0.9°C and is predicted to reach 1.23°C by 2030. CO2 is predicted to reach 434.2 ppm. Arctic ice fell by 30% and sea level rose by 80mm. My project makes complex climate data simple and visual, so anyone can see that all 4 signals agree - Earth is warming fast. It helps students, citizens, and decision-makers understand why urgent action is needed.
projectDetails.details: LunaSolo is a data analysis dashboard that detects trends in Earth's system from 2000-2024. I collected open data from NASA GISS for temperature, NOAA for CO2 and sea level, and NSIDC for Arctic sea ice. I used Python, Pandas for cleaning, Matplotlib for graphs, and Linear Regression for forecasting to 2030 in Google Colab. The tool shows 4 clear trends in one place, instead of searching 4 different websites. Its benefit is simple, evidence-based climate education. Its impact is to help people trust real data, not rumours. My creative idea was "One Planet, Four Signals" - showing that all signals point to the same warming story. I considered data accuracy, simple visuals, and honest forecasting without exaggeration. All data, analysis, graphs, and forecasts were done by me using real data. AI was used only to help improve the wording of titles and the summary.

projectDetails.name: Project LunaTabula
projectDetails.summary:
We developed Lunar Site Navigator, an interactive decision-support web application designed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to help mission planners and researchers evaluate candidate lunar south-polar regions.
​What we built: A live, responsive web tool that integrates official NASA Artemis III candidate regions, 360° local terrain horizon profiles, and topocentric Sun/Earth ephemeris geometry.
​How it addresses the challenge: It translates complex ephemeris data into intuitive visualizations, letting users scrub UTC timelines, view Sun and Earth sky-paths against local crater rims, and instantly identify mission risks. Crucially, it strictly separates geometric visibility from terrain line-of-sight and enforces data verification badges (VERIFIED, PROVISIONAL, ILLUSTRATIVE) to prevent scientific overreach.
​Why it is important: Safe lunar exploration depends on continuous power and communication. Our tool provides transparent, reproducible mission intelligence required for sustainable Artemis exploration.
projectDetails.details: Lunar Site Navigator is an interactive decision-support web application built to help mission planners, researchers, and students evaluate candidate lunar south-polar landing sites for the Artemis era. Users select from NASA's nine official Artemis III candidate regions, scrub through UTC timelines, and explore interactive 360° azimuth-elevation horizon plots. The application compares real-time Sun and Earth sky trajectories against local digital elevation model (DEM) terrain silhouettes to determine solar illumination availability and direct-to-Earth line-of-sight.

projectDetails.name: EARTH_SONIC
projectDetails.summary:
**EARTHSONIC – Listen to What Earth Is Telling Us**

EARTHSONIC is a web-based prototype developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, inspired by the idea of making Earth science more accessible through sound.

The project converts visual features of NASA Earth visualizations into audio, allowing users to explore images in a different way. As a scanline moves across an image, the system translates brightness, colour and position into changes in sound, pitch and stereo movement.

Users can explore NASA visualizations, select images, play or pause the audio, adjust playback speed and control volume. The goal is to provide a more engaging and accessible way to experience information about our planet, especially for people who may have difficulty interpreting visual content.

EARTHSONIC is an early prototype that demonstrates how sound can create a new connection between people and Earth's visual data. It is a step towards making scientific information more interactive and inclusive.
projectDetails.details:
EARTHSONIC is a web-based prototype developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Its main idea is to make Earth science more accessible by converting visual information into sound.

The project allows users to explore NASA Earth visualizations and listen to how different visual features are translated into audio. As a scanline moves across a selected image, the system analyses its pixels and maps their brightness, colour and horizontal position to sound characteristics such as pitch, tone, intensity and stereo movement. Users can play, pause, restart and control the speed and volume of the audio.

The main benefit of EARTHSONIC is that it offers a different way to experience scientific visualizations, particularly for people who are blind or have low vision. It can also help other users explore Earth imagery in a more interactive and engaging way.

Our intended impact is to encourage inclusive access to Earth science and demonstrate how sound can complement visual scientific information. We hope this concept can inspire further development of accessible tools for exploring our planet.

We developed the prototype using React and JavaScript for the frontend, Node.js and Express for the backend, and HTML and CSS for the interface. We used NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) resources to access Earth-related visualizations. The audio generation is handled through browser-based audio technologies, without requiring additional hardware.

The creative aspect of EARTHSONIC is its approach of turning visual patterns into an audio experience. Instead of only looking at an image, users can listen to its changing visual characteristics through a moving scanline.

During development, our team considered accessibility, ease of use, cost, browser compatibility and the accuracy of the information presented. We also considered the difference between sonifying image properties and representing actual scientific measurements. The current prototype focuses on image-based sonification and is an initial step towards a more complete accessible Earth science experience.

projectDetails.name: OrbitCare: A Core Health monitoring, forecasting and prediction system.
projectDetails.summary:
Long-duration spaceflight exposes astronauts to critical health risks like bone density loss and kidney stones, which are often diagnosed only after they become mission-threatening emergencies. Currently, tracking these interconnected issues requires time-consuming procedures that strain the crew's schedule.
Our solution is OrbitCare, an advanced predictive health monitoring software designed for maximum efficiency. OrbitCare transforms qualitative daily self-assessments—completed in under 60 seconds on a tablet—into quantitative, forecasted risk scores.

By analyzing the critical biological loops between bone loss, calcium excretion, spinal elongation, and reproductive health, our XGBoost machine learning engine calculates personalized risk profiles across three timelines: Current, Tomorrow, and Near Future. The software doesn’t just display data; its explainable AI identifies the root causes of elevated risks and instantly generates actionable countermeasures, such as automated hydration protocols or targeted resistive exercises.

Because real astronaut medical records are restricted, we validated our architecture using synthetic analog datasets built on robust clinical parameters. OrbitCare empowers astronauts to manage their health proactively and autonomously, mitigating serious medical events before they happen.
projectDetails.details:
How OrbitCare Works

OrbitCare operates as a highly efficient, closed-loop predictive health system. Astronauts interact with a minimalist UI to complete a daily 60-second digital assessment covering 38 critical biomarkers and subjective health indicators (e.g., hydration levels, pain scales, reproductive cycle data).

Behind the interface, an XGBoost Multi-Output Regressor processes these inputs. Instead of waiting for a threshold alert, the model maps the non-linear biological relationships and outputs a personalized Risk Percentage (0–100%) across three time horizons: Now, Tomorrow, and Near Future (3-months).
If a high risk is detected, our Explainable AI (Root Cause Analysis engine) extracts feature importances to tell the astronaut why the score is high (e.g., "85% Kidney Stone Risk due to high calcium excretion combined with low hydration"), and instantly triggers an actionable medical countermeasure.

Project Benefits

  • Extreme Time Efficiency: Replaces hours of cumbersome medical tracking with a sub-minute daily questionnaire.
  • Proactive vs. Reactive: Identifies the statistical trajectory of a kidney stone or spinal elongation pain days or weeks before it becomes physically debilitating.
  • Explainable AI Transparency: Doctors and astronauts require transparency. The system does not act as a "black box"; it justifies every high-risk score with concrete biological drivers.
  • Automated Countermeasures: Immediately translates predictive analytics into actionable steps, such as initiating targeted resistive exercises or adjusting fluid intake protocols.

Intended Impact

The primary impact of OrbitCare is enabling crew autonomy. As NASA looks toward Mars and deep-space Artemis missions, communication delays of up to 20 minutes make real-time telemedicine with Earth-bound flight surgeons impossible. OrbitCare empowers astronauts to independently monitor, forecast, and correct their own physiological degradation in microgravity, preventing mission-critical medical emergencies.
Tools, Languages, and Technologies

  • Machine Learning & Data Processing: Python, XGBoost, Scikit-learn (MultiOutputRegressor), Pandas, NumPy.
  • Development Environments: VS Code, Google Colab / Jupyter Notebooks, Python virtual environments.
  • Deployment & Backend: Flask/FastAPI (for the prediction endpoints) and Joblib for model serialization.
  • Frontend UI: HTML/CSS/JavaScript with responsive, space-friendly dark mode vectors and dynamic status charting.

Creativity and Innovation

Our core innovation is modeling the Calcium-Hormone Loop rather than treating health conditions in silos. Bone loss, kidney stones, and women's reproductive health are deeply intertwined in microgravity. Disruptions in menstrual cycles impact estrogen, which accelerates bone density loss, which dumps calcium into the urinary tract, which heavily spikes the risk of kidney stones.

By utilizing a Multi-Output Regression architecture, our AI maps these hidden, non-linear relationships across interconnected bodily systems simultaneously—something traditional linear monitoring software cannot do.

Key Factors Considered

  1. Astronaut Time Constraints: We heavily prioritized UI minimalism. Complex image-classification (CNN) workflows for daily scans were deemed too time-intensive for the crew. We pivoted to high-impact biomarker questionnaires that yield similar predictive value with zero setup time.
  2. Data Privacy Restrictions: Because real NASA Lifetime Surveillance of Astronaut Health (LSAH) data is restricted by HIPAA, we engineered a robust Python-based synthetic data generator. This allowed us to train and validate our XGBoost architecture using mathematically sound, clinical analog data without violating privacy laws.
  3. The "Black Box" Problem: We recognized that medical professionals will not trust a blind percentage. We intentionally engineered the system to extract and display Feature Importance, ensuring the AI is always clinically explainable.

Earth JS Jukebox Sonification is an advanced, multi-tier web application developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge by Team Meta Beats.

The platform bridges complex earth-science telemetry with human perception by translating official NASA satellite observation data into real-time, polyphonic acoustic soundscapes and hardware-accelerated 3D WebGL visualizations.

Core Project Pillars
3-Tier Architecture: Built on a clean, scalable stack featuring a responsive Frontend HUD (Three.js 3D Earth & Moon orbit), a Node.js/Express Backend REST API, and a Memory Archive housing certified NASA JSON datasets.

5-Channel Web Audio DSP Synthesizer: Dynamically maps satellite metrics (precipitation, ocean heat anomalies, and ice mass loss) into live harmonic leads, sub-bass drones, weather ambience, and anomaly sirens.

NASA-Certified Historical Datasets:

Disc 01 (Rain): 12-month South Asian monsoon cycle via GPM IMERG & MERRA-2.

Disc 02 (Ocean): 10-year Indian Ocean thermal swell & sea-level rise via MODIS Aqua & Sentinel-6.

Disc 03 (Glacier): 25-year polar ice sheet mass loss (-3,420 Gt total loss) via GRACE, GRACE-FO & ICESat-2.

Interactive & Export Tools: Includes a 15-key harmonic synth keyboard, a 16-step telemetry drum sequencer, touch-interactive globe shockwaves, and an automated jsPDF scientific report generator.
projectDetails.details:
🌍 EARTH JS JUKEBOX SONIFICATION // COMPLETE PROJECT BREAKDOWN

NASA Space Apps Challenge Hackathon Project

Team Name: Meta Beats

Lead System Architect & Main Developer: Shivam Raj

🚀 Executive Summary

Earth JS Jukebox Sonification is an advanced, multi-tier web application that bridges complex Earth-science telemetry with human perception. By transforming official NASA satellite observation records into real-time polyphonic acoustic soundscapes and immersive hardware-accelerated 3D WebGL visualizations, the application allows users and judges to "listen" to climate evolution across precipitation, ocean thermal swell, and polar ice sheet mass loss.

🏛️ 3-Tier System Architecture

The project is structured around a clean, modular 3-tier architecture designed for low-latency browser performance and scalable server routing:

Tier

Component

Description

Tier 1

Frontend Engine (1-frontend/)

Interactive HUD UI, Three.js 3D Earth & Orbiting Moon stage, 5-channel Web Audio DSP synthesizer, 15-key harmonic keyboard, and jsPDF report generator.

Tier 2

Backend API (2-backend/)

Lightweight Node.js and Express server routing /data/:track REST endpoints to serve normalized satellite time-series data.

Tier 3

Memory Archive (3-memory/)

NASA-certified historical JSON time-series datasets (rain.json, ocean.json, glacier.json) containing multi-epoch scientific metrics and physical mechanisms.

📀 The 3 NASA Scientific Discs & Datasets

🌧️ Disc 01: Atmospheric Rain & Monsoon (2025)

  • Source: NASA GPM IMERG v07B & NASA POWER MERRA-2 Reanalysis.
  • Scope: 1-year monthly cycle (Jan–Dec 2025) tracking South Asian monsoon thermodynamic progression.
  • Acoustic Mapping: Crystal pluck arpeggio combined with procedural monsoon white-noise static.

🌊 Disc 02: Indian Ocean Thermal Swell (2016–2025)

  • Source: NASA MODIS Aqua SST, Jason-3 & Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich Altimetry.
  • Scope: 10 landmark years tracking regional sea-level rise (+79mm to +112mm) and marine heatwave anomalies.
  • Acoustic Mapping: Deep FM pad chords with ocean filter sweeps and wave modulation.

🧊 Disc 03: Antarctic & Polar Ice Loss (2001–2025)

  • Source: NASA GRACE, GRACE-FO Satellite Gravimetry & ICESat-2 Laser Altimetry.
  • Scope: 25 consecutive years tracking cumulative polar ice sheet mass balance down to -3,420 Gigatonnes.
  • Acoustic Mapping: Sub-bass cryo drone coupled with glacier fracture transients and anomaly sirens.

⚙️ Key Technical Features

  1. 3D Planetary WebGL Stage: Hardware-accelerated Three.js rendering featuring a rotating Earth, plasma atmosphere halo, low-earth orbit satellite ring, and a fully orbital 3D Lunar Moon.
  2. 5-Channel Web Audio DSP Synthesizer: Real-time mixing rack with independent control over Harmonic Lead Synth, Deep Sub-Bass Drone, Procedural Weather FX, 808 Kick Percussion, and Anomaly Sirens, backed by a 60FPS FFT spectrum analyzer and oscilloscope.
  3. Smart Voice-Sync Pipeline: Asynchronous browser SpeechSynthesis integration with completion callbacks to ensure scientific narration never cuts off prematurely during playback.
  4. Automated PDF Scientific Dossier Generator: Built-in jsPDF export tool enabling judges to download a comprehensive report complete with physical mechanisms, sonification formulas, and date-by-date telemetry archives.

projectDetails.name: AstroQuest moon and mars survival game for child astronaut
projectDetails.summary:
Moon to Mars is a free, browser-based game where kids aged 7 to 12 run a Moon or Mars outpost for 10 days. Players manage Air, Power and Shield, plus food and crew health, and every action has a cost, so saving power today can cost oxygen tomorrow.
 Space education for kids is often too simple to show real trade-offs, or too complex to hold their attention. Astro Quest turns those trade-offs into play. A daily space weather forecast built from NASA DONKI solar storm data decides how dangerous each day is. Radiation, temperature and power figures come from NASA sources such as Curiosity RAD, LRO Diviner and Opportunity rover data. Every real value shows its source and a LIVE or ARCHIVED badge, and estimates are labeled.
 Young learners rarely see the decisions behind space missions, only the outcomes. Astro Quest lets them feel those choices, and each day ends with a "What happened and why?" card that explains the result. It needs no download or account.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works: Astro Quest: Moon to Mars is a free, browser-based game where kids aged 7 to 12 run a Moon or Mars outpost for 10 days. Players manage Air, Power and Shield, plus food and crew health. Every action has a cost, so saving power today can cost oxygen tomorrow. Each day, a space weather forecast built from NASA DONKI solar storm data (live when available, otherwise archived) decides how dangerous the day is. A "What happened and why?" card then explains the result and names the NASA source.

Benefits: Kids learn real engineering trade-offs through play, not just facts. It needs no download or account, so it works in classrooms and at home. Teachers also get a lesson guide and discussion questions.

Intended impact: We want a child to finish a game understanding one real constraint of deep space survival. We hope it builds problem-solving and decision-making skills and sparks interest in space science.

Tools used: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with unit tests, hosted as a static website. Data came from NASA DONKI, LRO Diviner, Curiosity RAD, the Chang'E-4 lander, Opportunity rover figures and NASA life support figures. We also used AI tools (Antigravity IDE and Claude) to help write code, draft text and cross-check figures. Our team reviewed and tested the results.

Creativity: Players can replay real storms (October 2003 and May 2024), so every game plays out differently. Moon and Mars video backgrounds react to the storm level, Mars adds a real communication delay, and an astronaut guide named Nova explains each choice in plain language. Failure is shown as learning, not punishment.

Factors we considered: age-appropriate language, honest LIVE or ARCHIVED labels, a source tag on every real value, no free choices, and keeping the game to three main resources so young players aren't overwhelmed.

projectDetails.name: CounterSAR: Is it unusual,or just the season?
projectDetails.summary:
CounterSAR: Is it unusual, or just the season?

A change detected by a satellite doesn't always mean something is wrong. Sometimes, it's just nature doing what it normally does. But how do we tell the difference?

That's the question that led us to build CounterSAR.

Focusing on Kuttanad, Kerala, where monsoon rainfall, paddy cultivation and changing soil moisture naturally influence the landscape, we wanted to address a common challenge in SAR-based monitoring: distinguishing normal seasonal changes from events that genuinely deserve attention.
CounterSAR takes a context-aware approach by comparing observed SAR backscatter with expected seasonal behaviour and considering environmental conditions before identifying unusual changes. Rather than treating every deviation as a potential disaster, it aims to understand whether a change is expected, can be explained by its surroundings, or needs further investigation.
With anomaly scoring, uncertainty awareness and an interactive dashboard featuring time-based comparisons, our goal is to make satellite data easier to interpret and more useful for real-world monitoring.
Because not every change tells a story of disaster. Sometimes, understanding the season is just as important as detecting the change.
projectDetails.details:
CounterSAR started with a simple question: how do we know if a change spotted by a satellite is something unusual, or just nature following its seasonal patterns?

Our project focuses on Kuttanad, Kerala, where monsoon rainfall, paddy cultivation and changing water levels naturally affect the landscape and its SAR signals.

We developed CounterSAR to compare observed satellite radar changes with expected seasonal behaviour while considering environmental conditions. This helps distinguish normal changes from unusual patterns that may need further investigation.

Using Sentinel-1 data, environmental context, Python and geospatial tools, we built an interactive dashboard with a time-based comparison feature to explore changes over time.

What makes CounterSAR meaningful is that it doesn't treat every change as a possible disaster. Instead, it tries to understand the reason behind it.

Our goal is to make satellite observations more meaningful and help people see not just what has changed, but why.

projectDetails.name: Project Mission controllers
projectDetails.summary:
Lunar Outpost: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive, browser-based educational game that challenges players to manage a lunar outpost over three simulated days. Players balance four essential resources—power, oxygen, water, and food—while protecting the crew’s health and morale.
Each day introduces a mission challenge, such as a power shortage, a clogged water-recycling filter, or an oxygen-generator warning. Players choose how to respond and see the consequences of their decisions. A final mission debrief explains how their choices affected resources and crew well-being, encouraging them to replay and explore different strategies.
Our project addresses the challenge of making space exploration understandable and engaging for beginners. By turning resource-management problems into simple choices with visible outcomes, it introduces systems thinking, problem-solving, and decision-making under constraints. Built with React, TypeScript, and Vite, the game offers an accessible introduction to lunar mission planning. It is a simplified educational simulation, not a professional astronaut-training tool.
projectDetails.details:
Project title

Lunar Outpost: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

1. What does our project do?

Our project is an interactive, browser-based educational game that introduces beginners to the challenges of managing a lunar outpost. The player takes the role of a junior mission controller responsible for keeping three astronauts safe over three simulated days.

Players manage four essential resources: power, oxygen, water, and food. Their decisions also affect the crew’s health and morale. Each day presents a different problem, requiring players to balance immediate needs against possible future consequences.

The aim is not simply to win the game, but to understand why a particular strategy succeeds or fails. The project is a simplified educational simulation, not a professional astronaut-training or survival-planning tool.

2. How does it work?

The game follows a simple cycle: observe the situation, make a decision, see the consequences, and adjust the strategy.

Start the mission: The player enters the lunar outpost dashboard and reviews the available resources and crew condition.

Receive a challenge: Each simulated day introduces an event, such as a power shortage, a clogged water-recycling filter, or an oxygen-generator warning.

Choose a response: The player selects one of three possible actions. Each action has a benefit and a cost.

Review the consequences: The game updates resource levels and crew status, showing how the decision affected the mission.

Continue or finish: After three days—or an earlier mission failure—the player receives a final result and a debrief explaining the outcomes.

Replay: The player can restart and explore a different strategy.

For example, in our game model, prioritizing oxygen production during a power shortage may protect oxygen levels but reduce the power available for water recycling. This illustrates how solving one problem can create pressure elsewhere.

The three days are simulated 24-hour mission periods, not three natural lunar day–night cycles.

3. What are the benefits of our project?

The project is designed to support learning in several ways:

Resource management: Players practise allocating limited supplies rather than using them without considering future needs.

Decision-making: Players compare alternatives and choose between competing priorities.

Systems thinking: Players explore how power, life-support equipment, supplies, and crew well-being interact within the game.

Cause-and-effect learning: Immediate feedback connects each choice to a visible result.

Reflection: The mission debrief explains why the final outcome occurred.

Experimentation: Replay allows players to test different approaches without real-world risk.

These are intended educational benefits. We would need user testing to measure how much the game improves understanding.

4. What is the intended impact?

Our intended impact is to make space-mission concepts more approachable for students and first-time learners.

We want players to move beyond the idea that space exploration is only about rockets and launches. Our game focuses on the planning, maintenance, teamwork, and careful use of resources needed after a crew reaches its destination.

The project could be used as a short interactive activity in classrooms, science clubs, or hackathon demonstrations. By making the experience understandable and replayable, we hope to encourage curiosity about aerospace engineering and STEM subjects.

A successful learning outcome would be a player being able to explain one resource trade-off after playing—for example, why protecting oxygen production might affect another system.

5. What tools did we use?

Our main AI-assisted development tool is Claude Code.

We use Claude to help translate our game idea into code, develop interface components, implement decision logic, explain errors, and refine the experience through prompts. Our team defines the challenge, selects the gameplay requirements, reviews the generated code, and tests the results.

6. How is our project creative?

The creativity lies in turning a resource-management lesson into a short mission with meaningful consequences.

Instead of asking players to memorize facts or answer a quiz, the game asks them to act. Players become responsible for the crew, make choices under constraints, and discover the effect of their decisions.

Our creative elements include:

An interconnected resource system rather than four unrelated meters.

A three-day story that gives the experience a clear beginning, escalation, and ending.

Trade-offs instead of an obvious “correct” answer for every situation.

Crew health and morale alongside equipment and supplies.

A decision-based debrief that turns the final score into an explanation.

Replay that lets the same mission produce different outcomes.

We do not claim that resource-management games are a new invention. Our contribution is combining that format with a beginner-friendly lunar mission and an emphasis on explaining decisions.

Short submission summary

Lunar Outpost: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a browser-based educational game that introduces beginners to lunar mission resource management. Players guide three astronauts through three simulated days, balancing power, oxygen, water, and food while protecting crew health and morale.

Daily challenges—including power shortages, water-recycling problems, and oxygen-generator warnings—require players to choose between competing priorities. Resource meters and consequence messages show the effects of each decision, while a final debrief explains the mission outcome.

Our project creatively replaces passive learning with interactive decision-making. Its intended impact is to encourage interest in space exploration and introduce resource management, problem-solving, and systems thinking.

We use Claude Code for AI-assisted development, supported by React, TypeScript, Vite, and CSS. Our team defines the gameplay, reviews the code, and tests the experience. Key design considerations include beginner usability, meaningful trade-offs, reliable demonstration, manageable scope, and responsible scientific communication. The result is a simplified educational simulation, not a professional astronaut-training tool.

Using a 3D lunar globe, four candidate landing sites, Sun and Earth elevation timelines, mission indicators, and date-slip analysis, MOONIX transforms complex lunar geometry into an accessible visual experience.

Users can select a landing site, examine its supported astronomical data, compare locations, and investigate how changing a planned landing date changes the displayed conditions.

Built using React, Three.js, D3.js, Python, SpiceyPy, NAIF SPICE and JPL DE440s, MOONIX aims to support preliminary lunar landing-site exploration and mission-planning education.

It addresses the Lunar Landing Site Navigator challenge by bringing location, time, illumination and Earth-visibility exploration into one interactive application.
projectDetails.details:
MOONIX — Lunar Landing Site Navigator

The Problem

Lunar landing-site planning involves understanding how environmental and astronomical conditions change with location and time.

Two important factors are solar illumination and geometric visibility of Earth. Their apparent positions relative to the local lunar horizon change over time and can influence preliminary landing-site and mission-schedule analysis.

When a planned landing date changes, mission planners need to investigate whether the conditions at a candidate location also change.

However, interpreting astronomical geometry across multiple locations and dates can be difficult without an accessible visualization tool.

Our Solution

MOONIX is an interactive lunar mission-planning platform designed to make these conditions easier to explore.

It combines a three-dimensional lunar globe, candidate landing-site selection, astronomical elevation timelines and date-based scenario exploration in one interface.

Key Features

1. Interactive 3D Lunar Globe

A three-dimensional visualization of the Moon with markers for the supported candidate landing locations.

2. Four Candidate Landing Sites

Users can explore:

  • Shackleton Rim
  • Malapert Massif
  • Nobile Rim
  • Apollo 11

3. Sun Elevation Analysis

Visualizes the apparent elevation of the Sun relative to the local lunar horizon, helping users investigate geometric sunlight availability.

4. Earth Elevation Analysis

Visualizes the apparent elevation of Earth relative to the local horizon, helping users investigate geometric Earth visibility.

5. Mission Dashboard

Provides elevation timelines, countdown information, illumination indicators and other available mission-planning metrics.

6. Date-Slip Analysis

Allows users to investigate how changing a planned landing date affects the displayed astronomical conditions within the supported data coverage.

7. Preliminary Viability Indicator

Provides a configurable screening indicator to help compare selected conditions. It is not a probability of mission success or a certified landing-safety assessment.

How It Works

MOONIX uses a scientific computation pipeline and a browser-based visualization interface.

The pipeline uses NAIF SPICE infrastructure, planetary ephemeris data and lunar reference-frame information to calculate celestial geometry for supported lunar observers.

Python and SpiceyPy are used in the computation pipeline. Precomputed ephemeris datasets are then made available to the React frontend.

The frontend presents the information through an interactive 3D Moon, D3-based elevation timelines and mission-planning controls.

The general workflow is:

Scientific Data → SPICE Computation → Local Lunar Geometry → Precomputed Datasets → Interactive Dashboard.

Scientific Data Coverage

The current project includes precomputed hourly ephemeris datasets for four candidate locations.

The documented coverage is January 1 through June 30, 2027.

Selected comparisons against JPL Horizons are documented in the project's validation materials.

The application distinguishes scientific ephemeris data from approximate or simulated outputs where applicable.

Technology Stack

Frontend:

  • React
  • TypeScript
  • Vite
  • Tailwind CSS
  • Three.js
  • D3.js

Scientific computation:

  • Python
  • SpiceyPy
  • NAIF SPICE
  • DE440s
  • Lunar reference-frame kernels
  • JPL Horizons for selected comparisons

Deployment:

  • GitHub
  • Vercel

Benefits and Expected Impact

MOONIX aims to:

  • Make lunar astronomical geometry easier to understand.
  • Help users explore solar illumination and Earth visibility.
  • Enable comparison of candidate landing locations.
  • Support preliminary landing-date investigation.
  • Make scientific information more accessible through interactive visualization.
  • Provide an educational tool for understanding lunar exploration challenges.

Current Limitations

MOONIX is a prototype for preliminary exploration and visualization, not an operational landing-safety system.

Its current ephemeris archive has a limited date range.

Geometric Earth visibility does not establish that a radio communication link will work. Actual communication analysis requires additional RF link-budget and system modelling.

Solar elevation does not establish actual power-system performance.

Detailed terrain obstruction should only be considered where validated terrain elevation and horizon calculations are implemented and available.

The configurable viability indicator is a preliminary screening metric, not a probability of mission success.

Future Development

Future improvements include:

  • Expanded ephemeris coverage.
  • Additional candidate landing sites.
  • Validated high-resolution lunar terrain integration.
  • Terrain-aware horizon obstruction calculations.
  • More detailed communication-link analysis.
  • Solar power-system modelling.
  • Improved uncertainty and data-provenance visualization.

projectDetails.details: Marswalk Planner is a browser-based tool for planning a spacewalk on Mars, set at the boxwork ridges Curiosity studied on Mount Sharp, Gale crater. It has three modes: Plan: The map covers a 1.28 × 0.88 km area at 8 m per grid cell, with up to seven data layers you can switch on and fade: optical, topography with contours, slope hazard, thermal inertia, mineralogy, rock cover and radiation dose. A route finder links the science stops so the walk takes the least time. Its walking-speed model accounts for slope, Mars gravity, loose sand, rocks and the weight being carried. Slopes of 25° or more and dense boulder fields are off-limits. Safety check: A GO / NO-GO status requires at least 25% of suit air and power left on return. It adds up the radiation dose along the route (more where the sky is open, less beside cliffs), flags returns after 4:30 PM local solar time, and a solar storm alert grounds the walk and highlights nearby shelter. Inspect: Tap any point to see its terrain type, slope, thermal inertia, minerals, rock cover, open sky and dose rate, plus a 3D first-person view toward the next stop, so the crew knows what to expect before they go. Visor HUD: Plays the walk through the helmet visor, with a compass strip, markers for each stop, elapsed time, air left, radiation dose, and warnings for steep ground, loose sand, cliffs and low supplies. Benefits: It combines datasets that are normally viewed separately into one local, safety-first view sized for a single walk, which global tools like Mars Trek aren’t designed for. It works for planning inside the habitat, on a tablet in the field, or as a helmet display. Tools: HTML5 Canvas and plain JavaScript (A* route finding, terrain shading, sky-view radiation model, 3D first-person terrain rendering). It runs in any browser with nothing to install. Current limitation: the demo terrain is generated by code to match the setting. Each layer is built to take real NASA maps of the area (HiRISE, THEMIS, CRISM) through a single replace-with-real-data point in the code.

projectDetails.name: Project Moonshot mappers
projectDetails.summary:
Moonshot Mapper is a single-page web app built for the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge “Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars.” It helps teams find places on Earth that resemble candidate lunar and Martian base sites, so technology and crews can be tested there.

You choose a target: the Moon’s south pole (Shackleton rim), Mars Jezero, or Mars Arcadia Planitia. The app compares it with 12 Earth candidates, including Atacama, Haughton Crater, Death Valley, Deccan Traps, Ladakh and Iceland. Each site gets a 0–100 similarity score for mean temperature, terrain relief, albedo and aridity. Four sliders set the weights, which feed a weighted total. The results appear as a ranked table and colored map markers. Selecting a site shows each variable’s value, source and uncertainty note.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

Moonshot Mapper is a single-page web app that ranks Earth locations by how closely they resemble candidate Moon and Mars base sites. You pick a target (the Moon's south pole Shackleton rim, Mars Jezero crater, or Mars Arcadia Planitia), adjust sliders for how much each variable matters, and read the ranking. A table and colored markers on a Leaflet map update live. Each site is scored 0 to 100 on four variables: mean temperature, terrain relief, albedo, and aridity. The similarity formula is 100 × (1 − |Earth − target| / range), and the total is a weighted average using your slider weights. Users can also inspect the values, sources, and uncertainty behind each variable.

Benefits

Gives teams a quick, transparent way to compare analog test sites.

Shows how each score is built, so results can be questioned and tuned.

Needs no install or backend, and works on mobile.

Swapping in real data requires changing only one JSON file.

Intended impact

The goal is to help researchers and mission planners choose Earth test sites for Moon and Mars base technology with less guesswork. Few places on Earth resemble these targets, so a good choice saves effort. The app is meant as a screening tool that narrows candidates before deeper study.

Tools and technology

HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript, with Leaflet for the map. All data sits in one JSON block, and everything runs in the browser, so no special hardware or server is required. The current values are placeholders, to be replaced with NASA, USGS, and ESA data.

Creativity

It turns a hard planetary-science question into an interactive "what matters most to you?" tool. Because the weights are adjustable, different teams can explore different priorities instead of getting one fixed answer. Putting the whole model in a single editable data file also makes it easy to extend.

Factors the team considered

Transparency: a simple scoring formula that anyone can follow.

Comparability: ranges are measured across all candidate sites plus the target, so each variable sits on the same scale.

Honest limits: Earth can't reproduce gravity (9.81 vs. Mars 3.71 and Moon 1.62 m/s²), radiation, or vacuum. The app has a Limitations panel beside the results.

Scope: geology, mineralogy, ice, regolith, and illumination are not yet scored.

Data quality: the sample output (best match for Shackleton: Mauna Kea) uses placeholder data and equal weights.

Next steps: add the missing variables, expand beyond 12 candidate sites, show uncertainty ranges, and validate with domain experts.

projectDetails.name: Project Narrative Nova 2.0
projectDetails.summary:
The 60s and 70s saw mankind leave amazing machines on the Moon, Mars, and even outer space! Although this information is preserved in NASA's archives, young enthusiasts are exposed to only current missions. In order to breathe life into these forgotten machines, we designed an interactive and narrative experience named "Abandoned, but not Forgotten."

With the help of NSSDCA data from actual missions, we crafted a "Digital Archeology" archive in the form of a cinematic experience. It allows us to explore the surface of 3D celestial bodies to discover stories of such machines as Apollo Lunar Module, Mars Rovers, and even deep-space probes. By using live comms feeds and synthesized audio, we turned cold telemetry into human empathy. The users will not only learn the facts but also understand the gravity of those final transmissions.
projectDetails.details:
Functionality: Our application is an interactive website archive that narrates the history of NASA's abandoned machinery left behind on the Moon, Mars, and outer space. The user interacts with this website by clicking on the glowing nodes on 3D representations of celestial bodies, which then leads to classified mission dossiers providing information about the true history and ultimate fate of machinery such as the Apollo Lunar Module, Opportunity Rover, and Pioneer 10.

Techniques: Developed using vanilla HTML, CSS, and JavaScript programming languages. Mathematical calculations are used to render the 3D planets through the Canvas API, making sure that they always load correctly. The interface includes a live telemetry readouts and an interactive 3D timeline.

Impact: Our intent is to help make the connection between complicated technical archives and young space fans. We achieve this by transforming the technical information into an emotionally compelling story.

Used Tools: HTML5, CSS3, Vanilla JavaScript (Canvas API, Web Audio API for synthesizing audio).


Creativity: Not only did we create a website; we created a virtual landmark. The design is fashioned in a way that makes it look like the terminal for a classified mission. The experience ends at "Last Transmissions," where users can listen to the last audio messages sent by Opportunity and InSight before losing contact.

Players take the role of astronauts and must manage essential resources such as oxygen, food, power, and safety while exploring the Martian environment, operating a rover, collecting supplies, and making important mission decisions. AstroSurvival aims to make space exploration more engaging while helping users understand the challenges of human survival, teamwork, and resource management on Mars.

projectDetails.name: New Horizons: Lunar Navigator - Moon Mission Planner
projectDetails.summary:
Lunar Navigator is a free, browser-based tool that helps mission planners, students and the public decide where and when to land on the Moon. Pick one of 17 landing sites or any point on the Moon and a date, and it shows in 3D where the Sun and Earth sit against the real horizon, built from NASA LRO elevation data. It reports hours of sunlight for solar power and hours of direct-to-Earth communication, and compares sites and dates side by side. That answers the challenge's core question: will this site have power and a link home on this date?

A Mission Designer adds the step before landing. Set the spacecraft's mass, engine and crew, drop a pin, and it finds every arrival opportunity, budgets fuel with the rocket equation, checks crew acceleration against NASA's Artemis limits and gives step-by-step burn guidance.

Sun and Earth positions agree with NASA JPL Horizons to within 0.034°, and 126 automated tests check the maths. At the lunar south pole the Sun stays within a few degrees of the horizon, so a small change in site or date can decide a mission. Lunar Navigator makes that trade-off visible in seconds.
projectDetails.details:
Lunar Navigator is an interactive web application developed by Newguys Studios for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge: Lunar Landing Site Navigator. It helps users investigate whether a chosen lunar location will have sunlight and a clear view of Earth during a mission. Near the lunar south pole, low solar elevation means that surrounding terrain can create prolonged shadows. The project combines NASA datasets, scientific calculations and interactive visualizations to help students, space enthusiasts and teams exploring preliminary mission concepts compare landing sites, dates and spacecraft requirements.

Languages and technologies: The application uses HTML to structure its pages, CSS for styling and responsive layouts, and JavaScript, including ES modules, for calculations, controls and interactions. Its three-dimensional views use WebGL, with three.js supporting the Mission Designer’s lunar and terrain views. Node.js supports automated testing and an optional local server. The published application runs in a browser, allowing users to explore it without installing dedicated desktop software.

Features and creative approach: Users can select from 17 preset landing sites, enter coordinates or choose a location on a three-dimensional Moon. The Surface and Space interface combines terrain exploration, a drivable rover, time playback, horizon panoramas and comparison tables. Its creative approach connects visual exploration directly with analytical results: users can examine a location, compare conditions over time, plan a mission there and return to the surface at a selected arrival time. This shared location-and-time workflow makes abstract relationships between terrain, illumination and orbital timing easier to understand. A resource calculator also connects environmental conditions with ideal energy availability and data-transfer capacity.

Mission planning and factors considered: The Mission Designer considers spacecraft wet and dry mass, thrust, specific impulse, fuel reserves, starting orbit, target location, search radius and mission duration. It estimates velocity-change requirements, candidate arrival opportunities and burn sequences for landings, orbit transfers and inclination changes. Surface planning considers latitude, longitude, UTC date and time, terrain elevation, horizon obstruction, Sun and Earth elevation, sunlight duration and overlapping visibility windows. Resource estimates consider solar-panel output, battery capacity, power demand, data volume and downlink rate. Crewed scenarios additionally consider felt acceleration, exposure duration, crew posture and compression-garment selection. Checks distinguish pass, warning, fail, not checked and not applicable.

Scientific foundation and validation: The project uses NASA LRO LOLA elevation, LROC lunar imagery, NASA Blue Marble Earth imagery and astronomical formulas from Jean Meeus. Terrain sampling is approximately 500 metres around preset sites and 1.9 kilometres elsewhere, with distant horizon profiles extending to 400 kilometres. Cached JPL Horizons DE441 positions provide an astronomical reference. Project documentation reports a maximum directional difference of 0.036° across 4,326 cached hourly directions, alongside automated checks covering astronomy, arrival searches, fuel calculations and other functions.

Limitations and purpose: Lunar Navigator supports preliminary planning and education. Its two-body orbital model does not solve complete powered descent or terrain-safe landing, and coarse terrain can miss small obstacles. Earth visibility alone does not establish a communications link, while resource estimates simplify operational power and thermal behavior. Presenting these limits helps users compare possibilities and identify where detailed engineering analysis is required.

projectDetails.name: TERRALIGN — Where Earth Meets Other Worlds
projectDetails.summary:
TERRALIGN is an interactive planetary analogue research platform designed to help explore how Earth's landscapes can serve as reference environments for lunar and Martian exploration. It combines an interactive 3D Earth globe, mission-specific analogue discovery, side-by-side 3D terrain comparison, solar-grazing illumination, and a six-axis Analog Reality Gap (ARG) assessment.

The platform brings together references from NASA LRO LOLA, NASA MGS MOLA, NASA SRTM, and USGS 3DEP elevation datasets to support terrain exploration and scientific context. Users can compare landscape characteristics, inspect elevation profiles, and explore model-assessed similarities and differences between terrestrial and planetary environments.

TERRALIGN presents analytical indicators as decision-support tools rather than scientific ground truth. Its goal is to make planetary analogue exploration more visual, accessible, and useful for research planning.
projectDetails.details:
TERRALIGN is a web-based planetary analogue research and decision-support platform that helps researchers explore how Earth's landscapes can serve as reference environments for lunar and Martian exploration.

Users can explore terrestrial analogue locations, switch between Earth, Moon, and Mars views, compare terrain through dual 3D WebGL viewports, inspect elevation profiles, and examine terrain similarities and differences using the Analog Reality Gap (ARG) assessment. Solar-grazing illumination helps visualize surface features under low-angle lighting. The platform also includes a mission-oriented discovery workflow, portfolio analysis, dataset uploads, and an AI Research Assistant.

The project uses scientific references from NASA LRO LOLA, NASA MGS MOLA, NASA SRTM, and USGS 3DEP. Data provenance and limitations are considered important: some planetary terrain representations use calibrated or static reference data, and ARG scores are model-assessed indicators rather than validated scientific measurements.

The application was developed using Next.js, React, TypeScript, Three.js, WebGL, Tailwind CSS, and Node.js. Its goal is to make planetary analogue exploration more visual, accessible, and useful for research planning while helping users understand uncertainty before applying Earth-based observations to other worlds.

projectDetails.name: MARS X MISSION
projectDetails.summary:
Mars X Mission is an AI-assisted Mars surface exploration planning system. We developed a single interface that brings NASA planetary data together to help a future Mars astronaut understand the terrain, identify science targets and plan a route. Users choose a region, such as Gale Crater, and layer NASA optical, elevation and thermal data, each shown with its source, date and units. They then mark science targets, build a route with stops and a return to base, and see distance, elevation change, slope and duration. Gemini then writes a mission briefing that explains the plan, its constraints and its data gaps.

The challenge asks for an interface that helps an astronaut understand terrain, find science targets and weigh mobility and environmental constraints. Our system addresses each of these in one workflow, instead of across separate datasets and tools.

It matters because it shifts the question from “where can I walk?” to “where should I explore, what can I learn, and what are the risks?” It also makes public NASA data more understandable and transparent by labeling data limits clearly. It is an educational simulation, not an actual NASA mission.
projectDetails.details:
Mars X Mission is an AI-assisted platform that helps a future Mars astronaut plan a surface expedition. Mars data is usually spread across separate optical, topographic, thermal, spectral and radiation datasets, so the project brings them together in one interface. The user picks a region and sets a base and an objective (our demo uses Gale Crater and Mount Sharp). The system then layers NASA imagery, elevation and thermal data on the map, showing each layer’s source, date, resolution and units. Next, the user marks science targets such as boxwork formations and observation waypoints, and builds a route with science stops that ends back at base. The system calculates distance, elevation change, slope and duration, and flags terrain warnings. Finally, Gemini writes a mission briefing that explains the route, the targets, the assumptions and the data gaps. Our demo, the Boxwork Discovery Expedition, investigates formations that may preserve evidence of ancient groundwater.

The main benefit is that everything sits in one workstation, so users no longer switch between tools to understand terrain, find targets and plan movement. It changes the question from “where can I walk?” to “where should I explore, what can I learn, and what are the risks?” It is also transparent. Every layer shows its source and date, and the system clearly labels data that isn’t available, such as the fact that thermal maps are not live temperatures and radiation data is historical. Future Mars astronauts, mission planners weighing targets against constraints, and educators and learners exploring real NASA data can all benefit from it.

The intended impact is to show how public NASA data can support thinking about future surface missions by making it easier to understand and more open to inspection. It is an educational planning prototype, not a validated safety system and not an actual NASA mission.

We built it with public NASA data and tools: NASA Mars Trek for map layers, tiles and API, ASU Mars Global Data for elevation and thermal data, and Curiosity rover observations for imagery and geology. The AI briefings use the Gemini API. The code is written in TypeScript, with shared typed data structures (MarsLocation, ScienceTarget and MissionAnalysis) that let the modules connect, and the team worked on GitHub with one feature branch per module. The backend has a scientific data service, a route analysis engine and an AI service, and the frontend has a Planetary Explorer map, Terrain and Science panels, a Route Planner and a Mission Dashboard. No special hardware is needed. It runs on ordinary devices.

The project is creative in how it frames the problem. Rather than being another map viewer, it is built around the astronaut’s decision-making, and it builds on the strengths of NASA Mars Trek by adding a unified, astronaut-focused interface on top. It pairs route planning with an AI briefing that explains its own assumptions and limits, and it uses a configurable educational route score (S = wd·D + ws·Sl + wr·R, combining distance, a slope penalty and a roughness penalty). It also treats scientific honesty as a feature, with unavailable data labeled rather than hidden.

As a team, we considered the limits of the data first: thermal data isn’t live and radiation data is historical, so both are shown with their source and date. We considered mobility constraints such as distance, steep areas and equipment, and terrain factors such as elevation, slope and roughness. We planned checks for map loading, layer switching, calculations, AI-failure handling and cross-device use. For feasibility, we used only public NASA data and tools and split the work into six parallel workstreams connected by one shared data contract. We scoped the prototype to real Mars imagery, an interactive map, optical, topographic and thermal data, science markers, route and distance calculations, and Gemini briefings. Future work includes elevation profiles, deeper slope analysis, CRISM mineral data, Curiosity radiation data, 3D terrain and route comparison. Throughout, we labeled it clearly as an educational simulation rather than a real mission.

projectDetails.name: Karnataka Farm Intelligence: FieldShift Orbit
projectDetails.summary:
Farmers make important decisions every season, but the information they need is often scattered across different sources. Soil conditions, weather patterns, crop requirements and seasonal information can be difficult to access and understand in one place.

Karnataka Farm Intelligence, built with FieldShift, aims to make agricultural information more accessible and location-specific. The platform brings together a farm-data backend and an interactive frontend, focusing on Karnataka's 31 districts. It provides district and taluk context, crop reference information, seasonal crop calendars and a foundation for integrating soil and satellite observations.

An important part of the project is transparency: instead of presenting incomplete information as fact, the platform identifies missing data and communicates uncertainty. With Kannada-language support as well, our goal is to make agricultural insights easier to understand and more useful to farmers, researchers and agricultural advisors.

Ultimately, we want to help people make better-informed farming decisions through accessible, locally relevant data.
projectDetails.details:
About the Project

Agriculture is not just about growing crops. Every farming season, farmers have to make important decisions about what to grow, when to sow, how to manage their soil and how to respond to changing weather conditions. But finding all the right information at the right time is not always easy.

Our project, Karnataka Farm Intelligence, aims to make this process simpler by bringing useful agricultural information together in one platform.

The platform focuses on Karnataka's 31 districts and is designed to help users explore crop information, seasonal crop calendars and location-specific agricultural data. It also aims to connect soil observations, weather information and satellite-based insights to provide a better understanding of farming conditions.

How Does It Work?

Users can explore agricultural information based on their location in Karnataka. The platform organises crop-related references and seasonal information so that users can understand what may be relevant to their region.

We are also building the foundation for integrating satellite observations and soil data. An important feature is that the platform highlights missing or incomplete information rather than displaying uncertain data as confirmed facts.

We have also included Kannada-language support with the aim of making the platform more accessible to local communities.

What Makes This Project Useful?

  • Location-specific information: Focuses on Karnataka's districts and available taluk-level information.
  • Crop awareness: Provides crop practices and seasonal calendar references.
  • Data-driven insights: Creates a foundation for combining soil, weather and satellite information.
  • Transparency: Identifies missing information and uncertainty instead of making unsupported predictions.
  • Local accessibility: Includes Kannada translation work to make the platform easier to understand.

Technology Used

We developed the platform using Python, FastAPI, React and JavaScript. We also worked with structured CSV and JSON datasets and explored NASA Earth observation resources for agricultural applications.

Our Vision

We don't want technology to make farming more complicated. We want it to make useful information easier to access and understand.

Our vision is to create a platform that helps connect agricultural knowledge with real farming conditions in Karnataka, supporting farmers, researchers and agricultural advisors in making better-informed decisions.

We believe that even a small improvement in the information available to a farmer can make a meaningful difference.

projectDetails.summary:

The platform generates three route options: **Safest, Shortest, and Balanced**, allowing users to compare routes based on distance, terrain elevation, and scientific considerations.

projectDetails.details:
Our project, Interactive 2-D Martian Survival Map, is an interactive 2D Martian terrain navigation platform designed to support safer and more efficient exploration of Mars.

The website generates three navigation options: Safest Route, Shortest Route, and Balanced Route. Each route is evaluated using distance, elevation variations, and terrain-related scientific considerations. An interactive elevation heat map helps visualize the Martian landscape and identify challenging terrain.

Users can select individual routes to view detailed explanations of why they were recommended, including distance calculations, terrain characteristics, and the scientific reasoning behind route selection. The map also features interactive geographical points that display images, latitude and longitude coordinates, and additional information about specific locations.

The project's primary objective is to address the difficulties of navigating unfamiliar Martian terrain by providing astronauts and mission planners with an accessible, data-driven decision-support system. Its creative approach combines interactive mapping, scientific terrain visualization, and comparative route analysis in one platform. By helping identify suitable exploration paths, the project aims to improve mission efficiency, reduce exposure to hazardous terrain, and support future human exploration of Mars.

projectDetails.summary: We developed an interactive space exploration game using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, based on India's important satellite missions. The game allows players to explore different planets and unlock new levels by completing challenges inspired by India's achievements in space technology. It addresses the challenge of making learning about space science and satellite missions more interesting and interactive rather than relying only on textbooks. projectDetails.details:
How It Works

Players begin their mission by answering questions focused on satellites launched by India (ISRO)—covering their objectives, technologies, and scientific achievements. Each correct answer powers the spacecraft to advance to the next level, traveling to a new planet in our solar system. Upon arriving at each new world, players unlock a fresh stage with questions centered on that specific planet’s characteristics, environment, and exploration history.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Traditional space education can feel static and overwhelming. By turning satellite knowledge and planetary science into a progressive, level-unlocking adventure, the game promotes active recall and sustained curiosity. Built as a lightweight web application, it requires no installation or high-end hardware—making STEM learning accessible to students and space enthusiasts on any device with a browser. Our goal is to inspire interest in aerospace and astronomy while highlighting how India's satellite milestones contribute to humanity's broader understanding of the solar system.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

Bullet Languages: HTML5 (along with CSS for styling and JavaScript for interactive level logic, if applicable)

Bullet Software & Deployment: Web browsers, source code editor, and cloud web deployment tools for hosting the live application

Bullet Hardware: Standard team laptops/PCs for development and cross-device browser testing

Creativity & Team Considerations

Rather than presenting a conventional trivia list, we designed the game as a cosmic voyage where mastering real-world satellite achievements serves as the gateway to exploring new planets. While building the app, our team prioritized accessibility (keeping the HTML build fast and lightweight for low-bandwidth connections), educational pacing (structuring levels so difficulty scales naturally from satellite basics to planetary science), and intuitive UI/UX so players of all ages can jump straight into playing.

projectDetails.summary: Meridian Seed is a 2D pixel-art story game, about 40 minutes long, where players run a mission they never planned. Two students accidentally launch the ark ship Meridian with 200 frozen embryos aboard, and the player must choose a destination and see the mission through. Across five chapters, players spend a limited Power budget on real exoplanet detection methods (transit, atmosphere spectroscopy and star checks) to scan three fictional planets modelled on worlds in the NASA Exoplanet Archive. They rebalance life support, cope with growing light-travel delay and survive a solar flare by splitting Power between shields, life support and comms. Choices lead to one of six endings, including a hidden one based on NASA's planetary protection principle. A codex labels every idea REAL or FICTION. It matters because it teaches mission trade-offs by making players live them.
projectDetails.details:
1. What it does and how it works

Players switch between Yuki (science) and Shan (ship systems). Oxygen and Power are shown on screen, while Trust between the characters and Earth's Confidence stay hidden. Every choice shifts these numbers, and together they decide which of six endings plays. The five chapters are:

Launch: the accidental launch.

Silence: fixing the air supply and calling Earth through a growing signal delay.

The Map: scanning three planets (transit, spectrum, star check), each costing Power.

The Storm: splitting Power between shields, life support and comms during a solar flare.

The Choice: deciding between going home, settling a planet or protecting an icy moon.

It also has a 10-minute demo mode, autosave, a skip button and chapter select.

2. Benefits

Players learn real concepts by needing them to make a choice. The game covers the transit method, the habitable zone, tidal locking, biosignatures, light-travel delay, closed-loop life support, solar particle events and radiation shielding. The 15-entry codex tags 11 ideas as REAL and 4 as FICTION, so players always know what is science and what is story.

3. Intended impact

We want to get players curious about exoplanets and space science, and to show that discovery comes with responsibility. The hidden ending shows that "we might not be alone" should lead to caution, not conquest. Players also practise making decisions with incomplete data, delayed information and no one to tell them what to do.

4. Tools used

ChatGPT Codex: built the entire game, including the voice pack.

Canva AI: character art.

NASA Exoplanet Archive: reference data for the three planets.

ChatGPT (confirm): your PDF says the dialogue script was written and organised with ChatGPT, so add it if that's right.

Mermaid (confirm): the PDF's choice-and-ending flowchart is written in Mermaid code.

If you used anything else (Google Docs, a text-to-speech tool, etc.), add it. The PDF doesn't name them.

5. Creativity

Hidden numbers: you feel Trust and Earth's Confidence through dialogue and the news ticker, not gauges.

LUMEN: a faceless ring of light that never lies but leaves things out.

Hidden ending: an optional deep scan finds Hush, an icy moon. The game never claims life, only "signs worth protecting".

Tone: funny early and sincere late, with six endings and pixel art in a gentle Ghibli-inspired mood.

6. Factors we considered

Scientific honesty: real science is separated from fiction (the Meridian Drive, LUMEN, the Seed and the planets), and signal delays are scaled down to fit the story.

Representation: both leads get equal agency, they're friends rather than a romance, and Shan's background shows through small details, not stereotypes.

Accessibility: captions on all voices, short dialogue lines for small screens and a skip button.

Pacing: the full game is about 40 minutes, and the demo mode lets judges see every chapter in 10.

Ethics: planetary protection, and not overclaiming alien life.

Originality: IMSA, the Pacific Concord and all characters are original and fictional. The Ghibli reference is a mood, not copied characters.

projectDetails.summary:
ASTRA-CARE | MICRO-G is an autonomous, edge-AI health-monitoring platform for astronauts on deep-space missions such as Artemis and Mars transit. We built an interactive software prototype, with a live demo (nasa1.html) and a six-module dashboard. It tracks heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, sleep, cumulative radiation dose and microgravity bone-mineral-density loss. It compares each astronaut’s readings against their own personal baseline and detects drift over time. It also correlates indicators, for example radiation spikes with sleep disruption, to separate sensor noise from real physiological change.

This addresses the challenge of helping astronauts monitor indicators, track changes and act on guidance without relying on Earth. With up to 20 minutes of one-way signal delay to Mars, real-time ground oversight isn’t possible. ASTRA-CARE runs entirely on local hardware and gives countermeasure recommendations, then escalates to flight surgeons when thresholds are crossed. It supports medical protocols and does not prescribe drugs. It also has terrestrial uses, including remote telemedicine, osteoporosis tracking and isolated-workforce monitoring.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works
ASTRA-CARE | MICRO-G is a five-layer health-intelligence pipeline designed to run locally on spacecraft hardware.

  1. Data acquisition: it takes in telemetry from wearables, radiation dosimeters and ultrasound units.
  2. Edge processing: onboard AI cleans and validates the readings, so the system keeps working during communication blackouts.
  3. Health intelligence: it analyses bone-density drift, cumulative radiation dose, fluid shift and cardiovascular strain against each astronaut's personal baseline.
  4. Recommendation engine: it generates countermeasures, verification prompts and escalation steps.
  5. Interface: a color-coded dashboard with six modules: Mission Overview, Health Monitoring, Microgravity Adaptation, AI Health Assistant, Health Analytics and Mission Reports.

A guided five-step workflow takes the astronaut from detecting a change to confirming the reading, comparing it to their baseline, getting guidance and escalating to a flight surgeon if needed. In our example scenario, a solar-particle spike that coincides with disrupted sleep triggers an automatic dosimeter check and a shelter recommendation, and flags the flight surgeon.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Crew can act on health changes immediately instead of waiting up to 20 minutes for a reply from Earth.
  • Monitoring is automatic, so astronauts don't have to log data by hand.
  • Early detection of bone loss (about 1–2% per month) and radiation accumulation supports mission safety and crew performance.
  • The same design can serve remote telemedicine, osteoporosis tracking and isolated-workforce monitoring on Earth.

Tools and technologies
We built an interactive web prototype (nasa1.html) that simulates live sensor streams and the countermeasure engine, plus a 13-slide presentation. [Add the languages, libraries and tools you actually used, e.g. HTML/CSS/JavaScript, any chart or 3D library, design tools.] The sensor inputs are simulated. The architecture is designed for real wearables, dosimeters and ultrasound hardware, but we did not build physical hardware.

Creativity
It combines radiation dosimetry and microgravity bone-loss tracking in one offline decision engine. It also correlates indicators with each other instead of reading each in isolation. The "Mars time-delay fail-safe" is the core design idea.

Factors we considered

  • Autonomy during signal blackouts.
  • Personalized baselines instead of population averages.
  • A clinical safety boundary: the system supports established protocols and does not prescribe medication.
  • Telling sensor noise apart from real physiological change.
  • A clear interface for high-stress environments.
  • Future dual use on Earth.

projectDetails.details:
LUNA-OPS is an interactive lunar colony-building and survival simulation that introduces young players to the challenges of establishing a sustainable human presence on the Moon.

The mission begins with a spacecraft landing and a crew of astronauts arriving on the lunar surface. Players must establish a functioning outpost and keep their astronauts safe throughout a 30-day mission.

The game features an interactive isometric lunar map where players can inspect terrain and construct six types of facilities: Moon Homes, Solar Panels, Greenhouses, Ice Drills, Storm Safe Rooms and Radio Dishes.

Players manage electricity, oxygen, water, food, building materials and astronaut health. Each mission day updates resource production and consumption, allowing players to understand the consequences of their decisions.

Additional features include animated astronauts, rover exploration, radio missions, educational messages, resource warnings, a solar storm forecast and a storm survival challenge. Players must plan ahead, balance limited resources and protect their crew.

The project is designed for children aged 7–12. Its goal is to make lunar exploration more accessible by turning complex scientific and engineering concepts into interactive learning experiences.

LUNA-OPS was developed using Phaser 3, JavaScript, HTML and CSS, with Visual Studio Code as the development environment. AI-assisted tools were used during development for coding support, debugging and the creation of certain audio and visual effects.

The project combines simulation, storytelling and educational gameplay to encourage curiosity about space exploration, engineering, sustainability and the future of human settlement beyond Earth.

projectDetails.details:
Mission Architect: Mars Odyssey is an interactive, open-world space exploration and Mars mission simulation game designed to make space science and aerospace engineering more engaging and accessible.

How Does It Work?

The game allows players to explore different space environments, select spacecraft, prepare missions, and experience various stages of space exploration. Players can perform launch operations, explore Earth and Mars orbits, inspect satellites, operate Mars rovers, and work towards establishing a Mars base. A mission progression system tracks achievements and completed objectives, while tutorials help beginners understand the controls and gameplay.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Our project transforms complex space-related concepts into an interactive learning experience. It helps players develop curiosity about space science, understand basic aerospace engineering concepts, and explore the challenges of interplanetary missions. Our intended impact is to encourage students and space enthusiasts to learn through exploration, experimentation, and problem-solving.

Tools and Technologies Used

We developed the project as a web-based game using:

  • HTML5: Game structure and interface.
  • CSS3: Styling, layouts, and visual design.
  • JavaScript: Game mechanics, interactions, mission progression, and functionality.
  • Visual Studio Code: Development environment.
  • AI-assisted development tools: Supporting code generation, debugging, and development.

What Makes It Creative?

Our main innovation is combining open-world exploration with mission-based gameplay and educational elements. Instead of presenting isolated missions, we aim to create one connected universe where players can travel between environments and experience space exploration as a continuous journey. The modular design also allows future missions, spacecraft, and locations to be added.

Factors Considered by Our Team

During development, we considered:

  • Scientific relevance and educational value.
  • Beginner-friendly controls and tutorials.
  • Engaging gameplay and realistic space environments.
  • Mission progression and player achievements.
  • Performance and browser compatibility.
  • Expandability for future space exploration missions.

Our ultimate goal is to make space exploration more interactive, educational, and inspiring while encouraging the next generation to think beyond Earth.
