### Project Summary – AstroVia: One Implant. Complete Health Insight.

**AstroVia** is an innovative, non-invasive smart health-monitoring patch designed to continuously monitor astronauts' health during long-duration space missions. The project aims to address the challenges of limited medical facilities, delayed health diagnosis, and the difficulty of monitoring multiple health parameters in space.

We propose a lightweight, flexible, skin-friendly wearable patch equipped with advanced biosensors, wireless communication, and AI-based health analysis. The system is designed to monitor vital parameters such as heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, glucose levels, liver function, bone health, and immune responses. Collected data would be transmitted wirelessly for real-time monitoring, early detection of abnormalities, and timely medical intervention.

Unlike conventional monitoring systems, AstroVia aims to integrate multiple health-monitoring capabilities into a single compact device without requiring needles or invasive procedures.

**The importance of AstroVia** lies in its potential to improve astronaut safety, reduce medical risks, and support longer space missions. Beyond space exploration, the technology could also contribute to remote healthcare and continuous patient monitoring on Earth.

AstroVia represents a proposed next-generation solution for safer, smarter, and healthier space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – AstroVia

Our project, AstroVia, is a smart health-monitoring patch designed to help astronauts stay healthy and safe during space missions. Astronauts face many health challenges in space, especially during long missions, where getting immediate medical help can be difficult. Our idea is to develop a simple, lightweight, and comfortable patch that can continuously monitor their health without using needles.

The patch is designed to be attached directly to the astronaut's arm. It uses multiple sensors to monitor important health indicators such as heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen levels, glucose levels, and other biomarkers related to liver, bone, and immune health. The collected information is sent wirelessly to a monitoring system, where AI can help analyze the data. If the system notices any unusual changes, it can alert the astronaut so that necessary action can be taken early.

The main benefit of AstroVia is that it aims to bring several health-monitoring functions together into one small device. Instead of depending on different medical instruments, astronauts could use a single patch to keep track of their health. This could save time, reduce discomfort, and make health monitoring easier during long space missions.

For the proposed development, we have considered technologies such as biosensors, microcontrollers, wireless communication, AI-based data analysis, and a digital health-monitoring dashboard. The exact hardware components, programming languages, and software tools will be finalized during prototype development.

What makes our project creative is the idea of combining multiple health-monitoring features into one non-invasive wearable patch specially designed for astronauts. While designing AstroVia, our team focused on important factors such as astronaut safety, comfort, accuracy, lightweight construction, low power consumption, and reliable performance in space.

Our goal is not only to support astronauts but also to explore how this technology could help people on Earth. In the future, a similar device could be useful for patients, elderly people, military personnel, and people living in remote areas where regular medical facilities are not easily available.

Currently, AstroVia is a proposed concept, and further research, prototype development, and testing are needed to confirm its performance.

Through AstroVia, our team hopes to make health monitoring simpler, smarter, and more accessible, helping astronauts stay healthier and making future space missions safer.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

Our website aims to make space science and exploration more interesting, informative and accessible through an interactive and visually engaging experience. It also highlights the importance of preserving human achievements in space and helps people understand that even the objects left behind tell valuable stories about humanity's journey beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
BEYOND EARTH – The Museum of Forgotten Spacecraft

Team: PIXEL COSMOS

Beyond Earth is a virtual space archaeology museum created to explore the stories of human-made equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars.

Space missions do not always bring every piece of equipment back to Earth. From lunar modules and scientific instruments to robotic rovers, these objects remain on other worlds as reminders of human exploration.

Our project brings these forgotten objects into one digital museum. It focuses on three examples from the Moon and three from Mars, explaining their purpose, the missions they belonged to, why they were left behind, and the discoveries associated with them.

Through our website, visitors can discover these objects, understand their historical importance, and explore the stories behind each mission in an engaging and accessible way.

We developed this project as a creative way to connect space exploration with storytelling and digital learning. Instead of presenting space equipment as ordinary mission hardware, we present each object as an important piece of space history.

Our aim is to make space archaeology interesting and understandable for everyone while encouraging curiosity about NASA missions and humanity’s journey beyond Earth.

Project Team: PIXEL COSMOS

projectDetails.details:
FieldShift is a browser-based decision-support tool for climate-aware crop planning. Users draw a field boundary on a map, then review available climate, soil, forecast, and market context. The app compares 27 crop profiles using transparent, rule-based scores and shows risks and data-confidence labels. Confidence describes how complete the available inputs are; it is not the probability of a successful harvest. Other tools help users explore climate trends, irrigation, soil health, pests, crop rotations, and illustrative gross-value scenarios.

NASA POWER daily climate data and long-term climatology provide the core NASA data. FieldShift also uses modelled ISRIC SoilGrids data and other available forecast and market sources. The interface brings these different inputs together so users can see the reasoning, sources, dates, assumptions, and limitations behind the guidance.

We built FieldShift with Python and FastAPI for the backend, JavaScript for the browser interface, SQLite for data storage, and Docker for deployment. The team considered data availability and age, the different spatial scales of the datasets, local water and soil conditions, crop risks, and market uncertainty. Its creative approach is to turn public Earth and agricultural data into an explainable field-planning workflow. The intended impact is to help farmers and planners explore options and ask better local questions as climate conditions change. FieldShift is a planning aid, not an agronomic guarantee, yield forecast, or financial advice.

projectDetails.summary:
### ASTRAMED — AI-Powered Astronaut Health Intelligence System

**ASTRAMED** is an AI-assisted astronaut health monitoring and decision-support platform designed to address the challenges of healthcare during long-duration space missions.

Astronauts face serious health risks from microgravity, radiation, isolation, and limited access to medical professionals. Communication delays with Earth make timely medical decisions even more challenging.

We developed an integrated software platform that combines **health monitoring, intelligent sensor failover, an AI medical copilot, human anatomy visualization, space fitness tracking, and offline medical support**.

ASTRAMED's key innovation is its **Evidence Continuity Engine**, designed to identify unreliable sensor readings, evaluate compatible backup devices, highlight missing medical information, and preserve health records during communication disruptions.

The platform also supports Earth-reference physiological data visualization, exercise tracking, and mission-specific health workflows.

**Our vision is to move beyond conventional health monitoring toward reliable, evidence-aware healthcare assistance**, helping astronauts make better-informed decisions even when communication with Earth is unavailable.

ASTRAMED aims to make future Moon, Mars, and deep-space missions safer, more autonomous, and medically resilient.

projectDetails.name: Project Root Cause
projectDetails.summary: NASA Earth Jukebox is an interactive, accessible web platform that transforms Earth Information Center satellite visualizations into real-time dynamic soundscapes. Developed to bridge the gap for blind and low-vision audiences, it uses computer vision to map visual elements—color spectrums, brightness, and pixel density—to musical parameters like pitch, rhythm, and spatial panning across curated scales. Featuring six authentic planetary datasets, a time-series frame scrubber, custom image sonification, and an interactive coordinate probe, the platform blends scientific rigor with artistic harmony. It includes working user authentication, live audio recording, high-contrast theming, and spoken audio descriptions to make Earth science universally accessible.
projectDetails.details:
NASA Earth Jukebox scans EIC satellite frames using computer vision on an HTML5 Canvas, translating visual data into real-time soundscapes via the Web Audio API. Color hues map to musical pitches across tuned scales, brightness controls dynamic filter cutoffs, and geographic coordinates drive spatial stereo panning.

Benefits & Impact:
It eliminates the visual-only barrier in STEM, empowering blind and low-vision audiences to experience Earth science while helping all users perceive subtle cyclical climate trends through multi-sensory immersion.

Tools & Technologies:
Built with vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5 Canvas, CSS3, Web Audio API, Web Speech API (TTS narration), LocalStorage, and Node.js—with zero third-party dependencies.

Creativity:
Replaces chaotic noise with harmonious ambient synthesis, features an interactive coordinate probe for instant point-by-point sonic inspection, tailors distinct synthesizer personas to physical datasets (e.g., icy chimes, deep ocean drones), and supports custom image sonification.

Factors Considered:
Accessibility-first architecture (ARIA-live announcements, high-contrast mode, keyboard navigation), scientific ground truth (MODIS, OCO-2, VIIRS data), complete offline autonomy via a single-file build, and user engagement through working authentication, saved soundscape playlists, and live audio recording.

projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Astro Health

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Astro Health is an AI-powered astronaut health monitoring platform designed to support astronaut safety during space missions. It focuses on monitoring important health parameters, analyzing health-related data, identifying unusual readings, and providing useful insights through a digital dashboard. The system aims to support early identification of potential health risks and help astronauts and medical teams make informed decisions.

2. What are the benefits?

  • Supports continuous astronaut health monitoring.
  • Helps identify unusual health conditions at an early stage.
  • Provides organized health information through a centralized dashboard.
  • Reduces dependence on delayed manual health assessments.
  • Supports better health awareness and medical decision-making during space missions.

3. What is the intended impact?

The main goal of AstroHealth is to improve astronaut health and safety in challenging space environments. It aims to contribute to safer long-duration space missions by supporting early health-risk identification and intelligent health analysis. In the future, the concept could also be adapted for remote healthcare and patient monitoring on Earth.

4. What tools and technologies were used?

The project uses a web-based platform and AI-oriented health monitoring concepts. The development technology stack includes the programming languages, frameworks, database, and software integrated into the AstroHealth application. The platform is accessible through:

https://astrohealth.ai.studio

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

AstroHealth combines space exploration and intelligent healthcare technology in one platform. Its creative approach focuses on applying AI-based health analysis and digital monitoring to the unique medical challenges astronauts face in space. It aims to make health information easier to understand and support faster responses to potential health concerns.

6. What factors did the team consider?

Our team considered astronaut safety, reliability of health information, ease of use, real-time monitoring requirements, data accuracy, accessibility, and the limitations of providing medical assistance in space. We also considered the challenges of microgravity and the importance of developing a solution that could be expanded for future space missions.

projectDetails.summary:
EVA Planner is a production-ready Mars mission planning tool that lets astronauts and flight controllers design safe, efficient extravehicular traverses using live NASA orbital data.

The app integrates seven NASA data sources — MOLA topography, CRISM mineralogy, HiRISE imagery, MAVEN atmosphere, REMS weather, RAD radiation, and time-aware predictions — to build a 2 km² safety grid at 10 m resolution. An A* router generates traverse paths with abort feasibility, comms continuity, and suit consumables tracking. Three mission profiles (geology traverse, mineral exposure, rapid survey) apply profile-specific safety thresholds. Multi-rover coordination adds relay placement optimization and deconfliction alerts. Crew operations include buddy-check protocols, metabolic cost modeling, and orbital comms windows.

It addresses the challenge by transforming raw NASA planetary data into an operational decision-making tool — bridging the gap between orbital science and surface operations. This matters because future Artemis and Mars missions will need exactly this: real-time, data-driven EVA planning that accounts for terrain hazards, radiation, dust, thermal stress, and suit limits simultaneously. The app runs in any browser, requires no WebGL, meets WCAG 2.1 AA, and falls back to seeded synthetic data when NASA APIs are unavailable — making it demo-ready and field-ready.
projectDetails.details:
EVA Planner — NASA Space Apps Challenge Submission Summary

What It Is

A Mars EVA (Extravehicular Activity) mission planner — a production-quality React/TypeScript app that helps mission teams plan safe, efficient rover/astronaut traverses on real Martian terrain using live NASA orbital data.

Core Capabilities

Domain

Features

Terrain & Safety

200×200 grid (2km²), 7 risk factors (slope, roughness, thermal, radiation, dust, obstacles, mineral), A* routing with abort paths

Real NASA Data

MOLA elevation, CRISM minerals, HiRISE imagery, MAVEN atmosphere, REMS weather, RAD radiation — all fetched live with caching

Multi-Rover Coordination

Up to 4 rovers, comms relay optimization, deconfliction alerts, shared waypoint library

Crew Operations

Buddy-check protocol, suit telemetry (O₂, CO₂, cooling, battery), metabolic rate tracking, orbital comms windows

Mission Profiles

Geology traverse, mineral exposure, rapid survey — each with tailored safety thresholds

Export & Logging

JSON mission runs, briefing packs, timeline with consumables

Tech Stack

  • React 18 + TypeScript + Vite (zero-config, fast HMR)
  • Vitest (unit + integration tests, coverage)
  • ESLint + Prettier + TypeScript strict (CI-gated)
  • Canvas 2D rendering (no WebGL deps, works everywhere)
  • WCAG 2.1 AA accessible charts & UI

Hackathon-Ready Checklist

Item

Status

✅ Live demo (Vite preview)

npm run dev

✅ All tests pass

npm run test:run

✅ Type-check clean

npm run typecheck

✅ Lint clean

npm run lint

✅ Build succeeds

npm run build

✅ Real NASA data integration

MOLA, CRISM, HiRISE, MAVEN, REMS, RAD

✅ Accessibility verified

Keyboard nav, screen readers, contrast

✅ No secrets in repo

All API endpoints public NASA services

✅ Rollback-safe

Feature-flag-ready architecture

Quick Start for Judges

bash

cd eva-planner
npm install
npm run dev # http://localhost:5173

Pick a zone → select profile → add stations → generate route → export briefing pack. The app auto-fetches real orbital data for the selected site (Jezero, Nili Fossae, Isidis).

Differentiators

  1. Real NASA data, not mocks — live WMS/WMTS + REST endpoints
  2. Safety-first routing — every path has abort feasibility, risk reasons, comms continuity
  3. Crew-centric — suit limits, buddy checks, metabolic cost drive feasibility
  4. Multi-rover from day one — relay placement, deconfliction, shared waypoints
  5. Production engineering — tests, CI, accessibility, error boundaries, observability hooks

Files to Highlight for Submission

  • src/core/routePlanner.ts — A* with multi-criteria safety
  • src/core/nasaTerrain.ts + nasaOrbital.ts — live data pipeline
  • src/core/safetyEngine.ts — risk classification
  • src/components/MapCanvas.tsx — canvas rendering, layer toggles
  • src/components/BriefingPack.tsx — printable mission summary
  • src/screens/RoutePlanner.tsx — main workflow

Risk I’m skipping: Full e2e Cypress tests (would add 30min setup, not critical for demo).
Risk you must know: NASA endpoints occasionally rate-limit; fallback synthetic data keeps app functional.

**Fhasal – Grow Smarter. Farm Better.**
projectDetails.details:
Fhasal – Smart Agriculture Platform

1. Project Introduction

Fhasal is a Smart Agriculture Platform developed to make agricultural field management easier, more organized, and accessible through technology. Agriculture plays an important role in society, but managing agricultural fields, maintaining field information, and accessing useful farming resources can be challenging. Fhasal aims to provide a centralized digital platform where users can manage their agricultural fields and access important features through a simple and user-friendly interface.

The platform is designed to improve the digital experience of farm management by bringing different field-related activities together in one application. It provides features such as user authentication, dashboard management, agricultural field management, interactive maps, notifications, and multilingual support.

2. Problem Statement

Managing agricultural field information manually can be time-consuming and difficult. Farmers and field managers may need to maintain information about different fields, their locations, areas, and soil types separately. Accessing and updating this information can become inconvenient when records are not organized in one place.

There is also a need for simple digital platforms that can be accessed by users with different language preferences. Fhasal aims to address these challenges by providing a centralized platform for managing agricultural field information.

3. Project Objectives

The main objectives of Fhasal are:

  • To develop a user-friendly smart agriculture web application.
  • To simplify agricultural field management.
  • To provide a centralized system for storing and accessing field information.
  • To allow users to add, view, update, and delete agricultural fields.
  • To provide interactive maps for visualizing field locations and boundaries.
  • To implement secure user authentication.
  • To provide multilingual support for better accessibility.
  • To create a foundation for future smart agriculture features.

4. Proposed System

The proposed system, Fhasal, is a web-based application that allows users to manage their agricultural field information through an organized digital platform.

Users can register and log in to access the application. After authentication, they can view their dashboard, manage their agricultural fields, explore individual field details, and access notifications. The application uses a frontend and backend architecture, with MongoDB as the database for storing application information.

The platform also provides interactive map functionality and supports seven languages to improve accessibility.

5. Main Modules and Features

5.1 User Authentication Module

This module manages user account access and authentication.

Features include:

  • User registration.
  • User login.
  • Password hashing.
  • JWT-based authentication.
  • Protected application pages.
  • Forgot-password and password-reset functionality.

5.2 Dashboard Module

The dashboard provides an overview of the user's agricultural fields and acts as the main navigation area of the application.

Features include:

  • Overview of registered fields.
  • Access to important application sections.
  • Navigation to field management and other modules.

5.3 Field Management Module

This module allows users to manage agricultural field information.

Features include:

  • Adding new agricultural fields.
  • Viewing registered fields.
  • Editing existing field information.
  • Deleting fields.
  • Maintaining details such as field name, field area, location, and soil type.

5.4 Field Details and Map Module

This module provides detailed information about individual agricultural fields.

Features include:

  • Viewing individual field information.
  • Displaying field geographical locations.
  • Visualizing field boundaries through interactive maps.
  • Using geographical tools for map-related operations.

5.5 Notification Module

The notification module provides a centralized place for viewing and managing application notifications.

Features include:

  • Displaying notifications.
  • Viewing notification details.
  • Managing notification status.
  • Accessing notifications through the application interface.

5.6 Multilingual Module

Fhasal supports seven languages to make the application accessible to users from different linguistic backgrounds.

Supported languages:

  1. English
  2. Hindi
  3. Kannada
  4. Marathi
  5. Telugu
  6. Tamil
  7. Bengali

5.7 Responsive User Interface

The application provides a user-friendly interface designed to work across different screen sizes, including desktops, laptops, and mobile devices.

6. Technologies Used

Frontend Technologies

React.js: Used to develop the interactive user interface and reusable components.

Vite: Used as the frontend development and build tool.

Tailwind CSS: Used for styling the application and creating responsive layouts.

React Router DOM: Used for navigation between different application pages.

Axios: Used to communicate with backend APIs.

Lucide React: Used to provide icons throughout the application.

Leaflet: Used to display interactive maps.

Turf.js: Used for geographical calculations and map-related operations.

Backend Technologies

Node.js: Provides the runtime environment for the backend application.

Express.js: Used to develop backend routes and REST API endpoints.

MongoDB: Used to store application data.

Mongoose: Used for database schemas, models, and database operations.

JWT: Used for token-based user authentication.

bcryptjs: Used to hash user passwords securely.

Development Tools

  • Visual Studio Code
  • Git
  • GitHub
  • MongoDB Atlas
  • Vercel

7. System Architecture

Fhasal follows a frontend-backend architecture consisting of three main layers.

Frontend Layer: Developed using React.js. It provides the user interface, forms, dashboard, field management pages, maps, and notifications.

Backend Layer: Developed using Node.js and Express.js. It handles API requests, authentication, application logic, and communication with the database.

Database Layer: Uses MongoDB with Mongoose to store and retrieve user and agricultural field information.

Application Workflow

  1. The user opens the Fhasal application.
  2. The user registers or logs in.
  3. The frontend sends requests to the backend through Axios.
  4. The backend validates requests and processes application logic.
  5. The backend communicates with MongoDB when data needs to be stored or retrieved.
  6. The backend returns a response to the frontend.
  7. The frontend displays the requested information to the user.

8. Database Description

Fhasal uses MongoDB as its database management system.

The application uses Mongoose to define database models and manage database operations.

The main data categories include:

User Information:

  • Name
  • Email address
  • Phone number
  • Password hash
  • User role
  • Password-reset information

Agricultural Field Information:

  • Field name
  • Field area
  • Area unit
  • Field location
  • Soil type
  • Geographical boundary information

The database structure supports storing and retrieving information required by the application modules.

9. Security Features

Fhasal includes authentication and security mechanisms to protect user accounts and application data.

These include:

  • Password hashing using bcryptjs.
  • JWT-based authentication.
  • Protected routes for authenticated users.
  • Backend authentication middleware.
  • Environment variables for sensitive configuration.
  • Password-reset token handling.

Sensitive credentials such as database connection strings and secret keys should be stored in environment variables and should not be uploaded to public repositories.

10. Functional Requirements

The application provides the following functional requirements:

  1. Users should be able to register and log in.
  2. Authenticated users should be able to access the dashboard.
  3. Users should be able to add agricultural field information.
  4. Users should be able to view their registered fields.
  5. Users should be able to edit field information.
  6. Users should be able to delete fields.
  7. Users should be able to view individual field details.
  8. Users should be able to access interactive maps.
  9. Users should be able to view and manage notifications.
  10. Users should be able to change the application language.

11. Non-Functional Requirements

  • Usability: The interface should be simple and easy to navigate.
  • Security: User authentication and password protection should be implemented.
  • Performance: The application should respond efficiently to user requests.
  • Maintainability: The code should be organized into reusable components and modules.
  • Scalability: The architecture should support adding more features in the future.
  • Accessibility: Multilingual support should help users with different language preferences.

12. Testing

The application can be evaluated through the following testing activities:

  • Registration and login testing.
  • Authentication and protected-route testing.
  • Field creation testing.
  • Field editing and deletion testing.
  • Field information retrieval testing.
  • Map display testing.
  • Notification interface testing.
  • Language switching testing.
  • Frontend and backend API communication testing.

Testing results should be recorded based on the actual tests performed on the application.

13. Future Scope

Fhasal can be improved further by introducing additional smart agriculture features, including:

  • Weather updates and forecasts.
  • Crop recommendations.
  • Soil health monitoring.
  • Smart irrigation management.
  • Crop disease detection.
  • Agricultural market price information.
  • Crop planning and farming activity tracking.
  • More agriculture-related services and tools.

These features can help develop Fhasal into a more comprehensive smart agriculture platform.

14. Advantages of the Project

  • Provides centralized agricultural field management.
  • Makes field information easier to maintain.
  • Allows users to update field details digitally.
  • Provides geographical visualization through interactive maps.
  • Offers a multilingual user experience.
  • Uses a modern frontend and backend architecture.
  • Provides a foundation for future agriculture-related digital services.

15. Conclusion

Fhasal is a Smart Agriculture Platform developed to simplify agricultural field management through technology. It combines user authentication, dashboard functionality, field management, interactive maps, notifications, and multilingual support in a single web application.

By providing a centralized system for managing agricultural field information, Fhasal aims to make everyday farm management more organized and accessible. The project also provides a foundation for future improvements, such as weather forecasting, crop recommendations, soil health monitoring, irrigation management, and crop disease detection.

Overall, Fhasal represents an effort to bring digital technology into agriculture and create a more convenient experience for managing agricultural information.

Fhasal – Grow Smarter. Farm Better.

projectDetails.name: TerraSpace Explorer: Earth Analog Discovery for Moon and Mars Missions
projectDetails.summary:
We built TerraSpace Explorer because we wanted a simple answer to a hard question: where on Earth can we practise for the Moon and Mars?

It’s a website with an interactive world map of 24 candidate sites. Each one is colour-coded by whether it looks more like the Moon, more like Mars, a bit of both, or is a newly discovered place that needs more study. You can filter by terrain, such as deserts, volcanic regions, impact craters, caves and polar areas. Click any site and you get its elevation, slope, temperature range, rainfall, and how closely it matches the Moon and Mars. The Atacama Desert in Chile, for example, scores 56.2% for the Moon and 74.2% for Mars. You can also adjust the scoring weights and compare sites side by side.

Behind it all is NASA data, including NASA POWER, ASTER GDEM, the Planetary Data System, Moon and Mars Trek and USGS Landsat.

This matters because testing rovers, habitats and astronaut routines on Earth is far cheaper and safer than testing them in space. We were also careful to be honest about the limits. A high score marks terrain worth studying, not proof that a place is equivalent, and the site shows which results are field-measured and which come from a catalog baseline.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works:

TerraSpace Explorer is an interactive website that helps people find places on Earth that resemble the Moon and Mars. The centrepiece is a world map of 24 candidate sites, colour-coded as Moon primary analog, Mars primary analog, dual Moon and Mars fit, or newly discovered and needing study. You can search or filter by terrain (polar, desert, volcanic, impact crater, caves and tubes, high-altitude) and click any site to open its profile. The profile shows elevation, slope, temperature range, precipitation, a geological description, data sources and Moon and Mars similarity scores. Other pages cover an overview dashboard, Moon and Mars comparisons, similarity analysis with adjustable scoring weights, a resource explorer and a NASA data sources page. When a site is inspected, the site fetches live NASA POWER, ASTER GDEM and USGS Landsat measurements.

Benefits and intended impact:

Researchers, students and mission planners can compare many sites in one place instead of searching scattered sources. Analog sites let teams test rovers, habitats, instruments and astronaut procedures on Earth, which is cheaper and safer than testing in space. We hope the platform supports early-stage site selection for future Moon bases and Mars missions, as well as training and education.

Tools and technology:

We built the interface with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with responsive navigation. The map uses Leaflet with OpenStreetMap and CARTO base tiles, and the site is hosted on Netlify. Data comes from NASA POWER, Earthdata (ASTER GDEM), the Planetary Data System, Moon and Mars Trek, GIBS, EONET, NASA Open APIs and USGS Landsat. No special hardware was needed.

What makes it creative:

Instead of a static list of analog sites, we built a scoring tool. Users can tune the weights, see Moon and Mars fit side by side, and spot newly discovered regions that are under-explored.

What we considered:

Scientific honesty was our main concern. The site states that high similarity marks candidate terrain for study, not validated equivalence. It also separates 8 field-measured sites from catalog-baseline entries, so users can judge how reliable each result is. We also made it easy to use on different screen sizes.

projectDetails.name: "VITALIS"
projectDetails.summary: Long space missions expose astronauts to five hazards: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields, and a hostile closed environment. These cause immune changes, bone and muscle loss, cardiovascular problems and behavioural health problems. Help is delayed, so astronauts must spot changes in themselves. The Space Apps challenge asks for a visual tool that gathers indicators and helps them judge and act on their own health.
projectDetails.details:
The idea in one line

An astronaut-first, offline-first self-check tool that compares each person to their own baseline, explains every result, and says what to do and when to call the ground. Guidance, never diagnosis.

What is measured

Hazard Indicators

  • Radiation: Dose against a mission budget, body temperature.
  • Isolation: Mood, sleep, workload.
  • Distance: Escalation guidance, offline mode, shareable report.
  • Gravity: Heart rate, blood pressure, exercise load, strength.
  • Closed Environment: Blood sugar, nutrition and hydration, temperature.

The brief names six indicators (blood pressure, heart rate, blood sugar, body temperature, sleep, mood). The plan added exercise load and radiation dose to carry the gravity and radiation hazards.

What I built

  1. ART style prompt to get the project outline: the plan i thought off revised through and rewritten using Act as / Request / Terms and then Prompted into Claude to build out the initial versions.
  2. v1 demo: clickable figure, Time Warp and scenarios (it felt like documentation).
  3. v2 app (current): green and white, human-centred flow: Home, a one-minute guided check-in, indicator detail with trend and actions, and a report for the flight surgeon.

Scenarios, data and plan

  • Scenarios: Skipped Gym, Isolation Slide, Radiation Event, Sugar Swing, Recovery Arc (stretch: EVA heat stress, cabin CO2).
  • Data: a browser simulator, shaped by public NASA bedrest and PhysioNet patterns, clearly labelled simulated.
  • Run plan: prep (10 to 13 Nov), then a 48-hour hackathon (14 to 15 Nov) with scope cut-lines and a feature freeze at hour 30. Never cut: the figure, the traffic lights, the Learn and Act panels, Time Warp, one working scenario.
  • Design: Streamlit for the front ends, FastAPI for the back ends, and SQLite through SQLModel. Both APIs read the same SQLite database.
  • Open questions: official deliverables, which indicators to go deepest on, clinician review, which datasets to cite, camera input.

I CANNOT call this A FINISHED project but its CREATIVE

There is still so much development to be done which isnt possible in a 48 Hours hackathon, a lot of refinement and error correction has to be done. Fitness tracker is fine and all. Why not something specific- something deeper catering to the need of the Astronauts in space, heck even those going to MARS its a worth while creative project in my opinion in terms of Space research.

Other Considerations

Originally i thought to make it like a game, then i realised you don't really need a game to keep such highly motivated astronauts engaged- So i made a health tracker. I thought also to add a mini doll like figure which monitors their activity but then it felt more underwhelming- It can be worked upon and refined later into the development cycle.

projectDetails.name: SKYNETICS
projectDetails.summary:
1. What we developed
Team Skynetics built Orbit Academy, a free, browser-based Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer for ages 8 to 14. Cadets play short 3-5 minute missions across five modules: Body in Space, Suit Up & Spacewalk, Mission Control Comms, Systems Check, and Launch, Orbit & Landing. A Moon Mission capstone, inspired by NASA's Artemis program, combines all five skills. Cadets earn XP and badges and rise from Cadet to Commander. It runs on any phone, tablet or laptop, works offline, needs no account, and opens each mission with credited NASA imagery.

2. How it addresses the challenge
The challenge asks for a trainer that lets juniors experience astronaut preparation. Each module is a hands-on simulation based on real training areas, such as pool-based spacewalk practice and daily crew exercise. Scoring rewards safety above speed, as in real spaceflight, and difficulty adapts to each cadet. Skill meters for safety, technical knowledge, teamwork and fitness show teachers what a student actually learned.

3. Why it is important
Children see launches, not the years of training behind them, and most space content is passive. Orbit Academy turns inspiration into practice, building problem-solving, teamwork and STEM interest early. Being offline-capable, account-free and ad-free, it reaches classrooms with limited bandwidth and keeps children's data on the device, helping widen the pipeline of future scientists, engineers and astronauts.
projectDetails.details:
Orbit Academy is a free, browser-based Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer for ages 8 to 14. Cadets play short missions based on real astronaut training, earn XP and badges, and rise from Cadet to Commander. The demo has three playable missions: Suit Up (put the spacesuit checklist in order), Systems Check (keep oxygen, power, water and temperature in range), and Orbit Sandbox (choose a launch speed and see whether you re-enter, orbit or escape).

Benefits: learners practise decisions instead of just watching videos, safety counts more than speed, and it needs no account, ads or install. Progress stays on the child’s device.

Impact: turn children’s curiosity about space into hands-on practice, build problem-solving and teamwork, and widen the pipeline of future STEM careers, including in classrooms with limited internet.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, the Canvas API, localStorage, and NASA Image and Video Library imagery. No special hardware is needed, and Claude helped produce the code and documents.

Creativity: real training turned into 3-5 minute games, a real gravity calculation in the orbit mission, and a rank ladder with badges.

Factors considered: age-appropriateness, offline access, privacy, scientific accuracy, accessibility and a small hackathon-sized scope. Adaptive difficulty and teacher dashboards are planned.

It includes a live crew dashboard and a simulated Earth-link toggle. It’s a decision-support concept only, using synthetic data, and not a medical device.
projectDetails.details:
Now I'll extract the text from the deck.

SmartVitals: S.M.A.R.T. Vitals is a student project from Dayananda Sagar University (team SmartVitals) that proposes offline health monitoring for astronauts on deep-space missions. Because radio delay makes real-time guidance from Earth impractical, the system runs on the spacecraft itself, analyzing vital signs locally and keeping records without any network connection.

The deck opens with the mission context. Communication delay prevents real-time medical advice from Earth, astronaut vitals fluctuate quickly with microgravity workload and sleep, and health records need to persist without external links. From this, the prototype sets four objectives: collect simulated vital-sign streams, analyze them locally for multi-vital anomalies, alert the crew with clear trends, and record events offline in SQLite.

The telemetry and workflow slide covers four monitored channels: SpO₂ (an oxygen saturation estimate), heart rate (a simulated BPM pulse), body temperature (core Celsius), and a stress index (a synthetic 0–100 workload score). These feed a four-step loop of Collect, Analyze, Alert, and Record.

The architecture slide describes the stack: a simulator producing NumPy vital arrays, a FastAPI backend for orchestration, an Isolation Forest model from scikit-learn for anomaly detection, a SQLite database for persistent history, and a Chart.js live dashboard. Anomaly detection is hybrid, combining the Isolation Forest with deterministic threshold rules. The deck is explicit that this flags statistical outliers in synthetic data and does not make clinical diagnoses.

The interface showcase shows a live crew dashboard for "Astronaut 01" with a status banner reading "Local AI Active • Earth Delayed," a sample SQLite event log of timestamped readings marked NOMINAL, and interactive controls for testing anomaly alerts, pausing the stream, and simulating Earth-link states.

The scope and roadmap slide separates what exists from what's planned. The current prototype uses synthetic data without physical sensors, runs inference and storage on-device, and includes a simulated Earth link toggle. Planned work includes benchmarking against public physiological datasets, personalizing anomaly thresholds per astronaut, and adding a buffer-and-replay system to sync queued telemetry after an outage. The deck closes with a safety principle: this is a decision-support concept only and does not replace qualified flight surgeons or mission protocols.

projectDetails.name: TERRA-VOICE
projectDetails.summary:
TERRA-VOICE — Earth Information Jukebox* is an interactive, multi-sensory web application and scientific gamified platform that translates real-time NASA Earth observations and NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) visual frames into dynamic, intuitive acoustic soundscapes. 

Addressing the challenge of making massive, abstract planetary datasets accessible to non-specialists, TERRA-VOICE couples a photorealistic 3D WebGL Earth globe and 2D GIS explorer with a mathematical sonification engine. When a user clicks or searches any coordinate globally, live environmental parameters—including air temperature, solar irradiance, precipitation, vegetation canopy density (NDVI), and soil moisture—are pulled dynamically from NASA APIs (NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, MODIS Terra, MERRA-2) and synthesized in real time into harmonious musical stems and an audible "Earth Pulse."

TERRA-VOICE is vital because it bridges the emotional and cognitive gap in climate communication. By transforming cold numerical spreadsheets into evocative melodies and rhythms, it democratizes planetary science, empowers visually impaired researchers through audio accessibility, and fosters deeper intuitive stewardship of our living planet.
projectDetails.details:
(1) What the Project Does & Technical Mechanics

TERRA-VOICE operates as an *Earth Information Jukebox*, allowing users to listen to the biospheric pulse of any location on Earth. Technically, it functions through a synchronized three-tier pipeline:

* *Visual Frame & Geospatial Architecture:* Built on Three.js (WebGL) and Leaflet GIS, the interface renders a photorealistic 3D Earth using NASA Blue Marble 2K true-color textures, specular ocean reflections, topographic normal relief bump maps, and dynamic atmospheric cloud transparency. Users can toggle seamlessly between multiple NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) visual modes—including NASA Blue Marble, VIIRS Night Lights (Black Marble), and MODIS Sea Surface Temperature (SST) heat anomaly maps.

* *Real-Time NASA Telemetry Integration:* Upon clicking any coordinate or searching a region, the platform connects to live satellite feeds:

* *NASA POWER API (v2.10.3):* Fetches 2-metre air temperature (T2M), all-sky surface shortwave solar irradiance (ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN), and 2m wind velocity (WS2M).

* *NASA GPM IMERG:* Streams real-time global precipitation rates (mm/hr).

* *NASA MODIS Terra:* Obtains Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) to assess terrestrial greenness and canopy density.

* *NASA MERRA-2 & SMAP L-Band:* Ingests surface wind vectors and root-zone soil moisture (m³/m³).

* *Mathematical Sonification Engine:* Using the native Web Audio API, raw planetary metrics are converted into acoustic parameters without pre-recorded audio loops:

* Temperature is normalized and quantized to a 9-note C4 Major Pentatonic Scale ($261.6\text{ Hz}$ to $784.0\text{ Hz}$), ensuring warming is audible as rising pitch without dissonance.

* Solar Irradiance controls a $24\text{ dB/oct}$ resonant biquad lowpass filter ($400\text{ Hz}$ to $2200\text{ Hz}$), giving sunlit areas acoustic brightness while night zones sound warm and muffled.

* Wind Speed & Rain govern tempo clocks ($75$ to $130\text{ BPM}$) and percussion velocity, accompanied by a dynamic "Earth Pulse" BPM indicator.

* *Six Planetary Channels & Multi-Modal AI:* Features 6 specialized ecosystem channels (Temperature Intelligence, Ocean Symphony, Forest Harmony, Polar Ice, Atmospheric Waves, and Earth in Transition), an interactive *1990–2026 Time-Travel Climate Slider, a **Dual-Region DJ Crossfader*, and computer vision AI modules that convert uploaded satellite photos and environmental video feeds into ambient sound profiles.

(2) Key Benefits*

* *Universal Accessibility:* Enables blind and visually impaired students, educators, and scientists to explore spatial and temporal climate trends through high-fidelity audio cues.

* *Intuitive Pattern Recognition:* The human ear detects micro-rhythms and harmonic shifts faster than visual inspection of complex multi-variable tables.

* *Zero-Friction Engagement:* Launches directly into Mission Control via a cinematic WebGL entrance with no sign-in or authentication barriers.

* *Low-Bandwidth Multi-Tier Resilience:* Built with automated fallbacks (serverless proxy $\to$ direct CORS client fetching $\to$ local geophysical baseline models) guaranteeing smooth 60 FPS operation even in low-connectivity classrooms.

(3) Intended Impact*

TERRA-VOICE is designed for *STEM classrooms, science museums, planetarium installations, and public climate advocacy*. By transforming passive satellite data into an interactive jukebox experience, it inspires students and the public to emotionally connect with Earth’s vital signs, turning climate anxiety into proactive scientific curiosity and planetary stewardship.

(4) Tools, Languages & Technologies Used*

* *Frontend & UI/UX:* HTML5, CSS3 Glassmorphism, Vanilla ES6 JavaScript Modules, Tailwind CSS, JetBrains Mono & Space Grotesk typography.

* *3D Graphics & Mapping:* Three.js (WebGL 3D Earth, custom shaders, specular and normal mapping), Leaflet GIS (2D mapping, administrative geo-boundaries).

* *Audio Engineering:* Web Audio API (polyphonic oscillators, BiquadFilterNode, ConvolverNode space reverb, GainNode envelope shaping, Canvas spectrum visualizer).

* *APIs & Data:* NASA POWER API, NASA GPM IMERG, NASA MODIS Terra, NASA EONET v3, OpenStreetMap Nominatim Geocoding.

* *Backend & Serverless Infrastructure:* Python 3.11 (Flask/HTTP multi-tier proxy), Vercel Serverless Edge Functions (vercel.json), Cloudflare Tunnel.

* *Deployment & Version Control:* Vercel Global Edge Network, Git, GitHub

projectDetails.name: BioHab: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
projectDetails.summary:
BioHab: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive, browser-playable educational simulation designed for students ages 7–12 to experience the real engineering and biological trade-offs of running a Lunar or Martian outpost over a 10-Sol mission.
Rather than oversimplifying space exploration, BioHab challenges young learners to balance three interconnected survival systems—Power, Bioregenerative Life Support (O2, water recycling, and food production), and Radiation Shielding—against real space hazards like lunar dust accumulation, deep shadows, and solar storms. Grounded in real NASA science from the Artemis program, ISS Veggie Plant Growth System, and ECLSS, every tactical choice shows transparent resource trade-offs (such as diverting recycled greywater into radiation-shielding walls or optimizing red/blue LED wavelengths for hydroponic crops) accompanied by bite-sized NASA science explanations and non-punitive failure diagnostics.
By combining systems engineering with closed-loop space biology in an accessible game format, BioHab turns complex mission constraints into intuitive, hands-on STEM discovery for the next generation of explorers.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works:

BioHab: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive, browser-based resource-management simulation built for the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge. Students command a lunar or Martian outpost across a 10-Sol mission, balancing three interconnected survival systems—Power (kW), Bioregenerative Life Support (O2, Water & Crops), and Radiation Shielding—against real space hazards like lunar dust buildup, deep shadows, and solar storms. Each Sol, players inspect interactive habitat modules (Solar Wing, Crew & Water Wall, Bio-Greenhouse, and ASTRO-BOT) and select two tactical engineering actions that preview exact resource trade-offs before execution.

Benefits & Intended Impact:

Traditional STEM materials often oversimplify mission engineering or overwhelm young learners with raw equations. BioHab turns complex closed-loop life-support trade-offs into tangible cause-and-effect decisions. Built-in NASA science explanations and non-punitive mission debriefs—including a 10-Sol Telemetry History chart—help students understand why engineering compromises happen in real spaceflight.

Tools, Languages & Software Used:

- Languages & Frameworks: React, TypeScript, HTML5, Tailwind CSS

- Visuals & Audio: Custom responsive inline SVGs and Web Audio API feedback

- Super Intelligence (SI) Acknowledgment: Built and debugged with the assistance of Google AI Studio (Gemini) for code generation, UI layout, and iterative troubleshooting.

- Hosting & Version Control: GitHub and Google AI Studio (.ai.studio)

Creativity & Design Factors Considered:

To keep learners engaged without sacrificing scientific accuracy, we designed an interactive cross-section habitat where every subsystem reacts visually to player decisions, paired with an ASTRO-BOT mission companion and clear resource-delta badges (+Power, -Bio-Life, +Shield) grounded in NASA Artemis, ISS Veggie, and ECLSS research.

Hosting & Version Control: GitHub https://github.com/TanushreeSapare/biohab-mission-trainer and Google AI Studio (.ai.studio)

projectDetails.name: Earth Jukebox
projectDetails.summary:
Summary:
Earth Jukebox is a browser-based studio that turns real NASA Earth data into music, so climate change can be heard as well as seen. Maps and charts leave out people who cannot rely on visuals, and slow change over decades is hard to feel on a line chart. Sound compresses time: users can hear 40 years of warming in about 20 seconds.

The app fetches live data from the NASA POWER API, computes anomalies against a 1991–2020 baseline, and maps them to pentatonic notes using the Web Audio API. Warmer years sound higher; larger jumps add more notes. Three modes are offered: Climate, Water Cycle, and Earth Symphony. A compare feature plays two places in the left and right ears on one shared pitch scale. For example, the Arctic is heard against Bengaluru.

A chart playhead and a NASA GIBS satellite map move in sync with the sound. Keyboard and screen-reader support, a written and spoken summary, a data table and .wav export make the data accessible to blind and low-vision users.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details:

What it does

Earth Jukebox lets anyone pick a place on a NASA satellite map and listen to its climate data. It offers three modes:

- Climate: a place's annual temperature anomaly since 1985, played in about 20 seconds. Higher note = warmer than average; a bigger jump = more notes; a tick marks each decade.

- Water Cycle: the last 60 days of rain, humidity and sunlight. Rain becomes droplets and patter, humidity sets the pad pitch, and sunlight sets brightness. Sea surface temperature is shown as a map layer.

- Earth Symphony: temperature, wind, rain, sun and humidity layered together. Temperature is the melody, wind the rhythm, rain the droplets, and sun the brightness.

Compare mode plays Location A in the left ear and Location B in the right, on one shared scale, so a faster-warming place literally sounds higher. A one-click demo compares the Arctic with Bengaluru over 40 years.

How it works

1. Fetch: data comes from the NASA POWER API (no key needed), as annual temperature since 1985 or daily data for the last 60 days.

2. Normalize: values become anomalies against the 1991–2020 average, on one shared scale so two places can be compared by ear.

3. Map to sound: values become pentatonic notes through the Web Audio API, proportional to the data, so the result stays musical rather than noisy.

4. Synchronize: a chart playhead and the map move with the sound.

Numbers come from NASA POWER. Imagery (true colour, land and sea surface temperature, precipitation, aerosols) comes from NASA GIBS.

Accessibility

Keyboard and screen-reader support; a written summary, data table and spoken summary; "Hear the scale" guide; speed control and scrubbing; no autoplay; .wav export of any soundscape.

Trust and honesty

The app is static HTML/CSS/JS with no server and no API key. Units, dates and sources are shown on screen. It never invents data, and it shows a clearly labelled cache if NASA services are down. It uses a Content Security Policy and Subresource Integrity. We state its limits: results are local, not a global climate signal; POWER data is gridded and a few days behind, not live sensors; GIBS map pixels are visual context, not the data being sonified. This is an independent educational prototype, not an official NASA product.

Tools used

HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Web Audio API, NASA POWER API, NASA GIBS. [Add any libraries you used, e.g. charting or map libraries.]

Why it is creative and why it matters

It turns decades of slow change into something you can feel in seconds, and it lets blind and low-vision users explore the same data as everyone else. The left-ear/right-ear comparison makes regional differences in warming immediately audible.

Next steps

Frame-by-frame playback over GIBS imagery, sonifying numeric ocean data, more datasets and regions, narrated tours, saved soundscapes, and co-design with blind and low-vision users.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project space exploration
projectDetails.summary:
The EVA (Extra-Vehicular Activity) Route Planner is designed to help astronauts explore the surface of Mars safely and efficiently. Focusing on the Jezero Delta region, it identifies suitable routes from the habitat to scientific locations and back.

Users can select three scientific objectives: clay-bearing rocks, carbonate outcrops and olivine-rich formations. The system uses the A* pathfinding algorithm to calculate efficient routes while avoiding steep and potentially dangerous terrain.

Safety is prioritised through adjustable slope limits and different environmental conditions, including dust storms and solar particle events. It also includes map layers displaying slope hazards and thermal differences between sand and rock.

Once a route is generated, the system displays the distance, estimated walking time, steepest slope, maximum distance from the habitat and approximate radiation exposure.

The project uses synthetically generated terrain and mineral data to demonstrate its functionality. However, its routing algorithm and safety calculations could be adapted to use actual NASA data.

Overall, the project demonstrates how computational algorithms and terrain analysis can support safer and more efficient human exploration of Mars.

projectDetails.name: MARS DEEP — Design. Launch. Explore.
projectDetails.summary:
MARS DEEP is an interactive 3D educational space mission simulation that takes players on a journey from Earth to Mars. Players experience the challenges of planning a robotic space mission, designing a spacecraft, managing engineering resources, completing mission calculations, launching a rocket, navigating through space, entering Mars orbit, and exploring the Martian surface using a rover.

The game combines simplified aerospace engineering concepts with interactive gameplay to make space exploration accessible to people of different ages and educational backgrounds. Players conduct simulated scientific experiments, investigate geological formations, study subsurface structures, monitor environmental conditions, collect samples, capture images, and transmit mission data back to Earth.

Inspired by NASA's Mars exploration missions and scientific instruments, MARS DEEP aims to transform complex space science concepts into an engaging learning experience.

DESIGN. LAUNCH. EXPLORE.
projectDetails.details:
MARS DEEP — Project Details

Project Overview

MARS DEEP is a 3D educational space mission design and Mars exploration simulation developed to make the process of planning and executing a robotic Mars mission interactive and accessible.

Instead of simply reading about space exploration, players become mission planners and participate in the different stages of a Mars expedition, from spacecraft configuration and rocket launch to planetary exploration and scientific data transmission.

How Does It Work?

The game follows a structured five-level campaign containing 23 mandatory engineering tasks.

Players begin by understanding their mission objectives and configuring a spacecraft using different components, power systems, propulsion equipment, communication systems and scientific instruments.

The engineering laboratory introduces simplified calculations involving spacecraft mass, electrical power, propulsion, orbital transfers and mission resources. Players must complete the required tasks to progress through the campaign.

After spacecraft preparation, players experience rocket launch, interplanetary travel, spacecraft manoeuvres and Mars orbital insertion.

Following landing, players deploy and control a rover to explore the Martian surface.

The exploration experience includes four scientific activity categories:

  1. Geological rock analysis.
  2. Subsurface investigation using radar.
  3. Martian environmental monitoring.
  4. Sample collection and scientific analysis.

Players can collect simulated scientific observations, capture rover photographs, and transmit mission information back to Earth.

Benefits and Educational Impact

MARS DEEP aims to make space science easier to understand through interactive learning.

It introduces players to:

  • Spacecraft design and engineering trade-offs.
  • Mass, power and resource management.
  • Rocket propulsion and launch procedures.
  • Interplanetary travel and orbital manoeuvres.
  • Mars landing and rover operations.
  • Planetary geology and scientific instruments.
  • Scientific observation and communication systems.

Beginner-friendly instructions help players who do not have a background in aerospace engineering, while mandatory engineering challenges provide additional learning opportunities.

Technology Used

  • Game Engine: Godot 4.7.2.
  • Programming Language: GDScript.
  • Development Environment: Google Antigravity.
  • Version Control: Git and GitHub.
  • 3D Environment: Native Godot 3D rendering and procedural modelling.
  • Data Storage: JSON-based mission and component configuration.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of MARS DEEP is the combination of mission planning, engineering problem-solving and hands-on planetary exploration in one continuous experience.

Players do not simply watch a Mars mission. They participate in its preparation, launch, navigation, landing, rover deployment and scientific operations.

The project also combines simplified engineering calculations with interactive visual feedback to demonstrate how scientific and engineering decisions influence mission outcomes.

Design Considerations

The project prioritizes accessibility, interactive learning, mission progression and performance.

Complex aerospace terminology is simplified wherever possible, and the game uses guidance indicators, mission objectives and visual feedback to help players understand their responsibilities.

Scientific readings generated within the simulation are educational approximations and are not presented as actual live measurements from Mars.

MARS DEEP is an independent educational project inspired by planetary exploration. It is not an official NASA product or an endorsed NASA mission.

projectDetails.name: LUNA-VIEW (Lunar Landing Site Intelligence & Mission Planning System)
projectDetails.summary:
LUNA-VIEW is an interactive lunar mission-planning platform designed to simplify the evaluation and comparison of potential landing sites near the Moon's south pole. Lunar missions face challenges due to extreme variations in sunlight availability and limited direct communication with Earth. Even small changes in landing location or date can significantly affect mission operations.

LUNA-VIEW brings essential mission-planning information into one intuitive application. Users can explore lunar landing locations, select mission dates, and visualize Sun and Earth positions relative to the lunar horizon.

Key features include interactive 3D lunar exploration, solar illumination analysis, Earth visibility and communication window tracking, dynamic mission timelines, and side-by-side landing site comparisons. It also aims to provide mission suitability assessments and AI-powered insights to help users evaluate alternative scenarios.

By transforming complex astronomical and geographical data into clear visualizations, LUNA-VIEW helps users understand how changes in landing locations and dates affect power generation and communication opportunities. It aims to support informed mission planning while making lunar exploration more accessible to researchers, educators, students, and the public.
projectDetails.details:
LUNA-VIEW

Lunar Landing Site Intelligence & Mission Planning System

Live Project: https://luna-view-frontend.vercel.app/

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/renuasmitha/Luna-View

Project Overview

LUNA-VIEW is an interactive web-based platform designed to simplify the evaluation and comparison of potential landing sites near the Moon's south pole. It addresses two major challenges in lunar mission planning: extreme and rapidly changing solar illumination conditions and limited direct-to-Earth communication opportunities.

The platform brings essential astronomical information into one intuitive interface, allowing users to explore potential lunar landing locations, select mission dates, visualize the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the local lunar horizon, and compare environmental conditions across different mission scenarios.

What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

LUNA-VIEW combines astronomical calculations, interactive visualizations, and mission comparison capabilities to help users understand changing lunar surface conditions.

Its key capabilities include:

1. Interactive Lunar Explorer

Allows users to explore potential lunar landing locations, examine candidate sites, and work with geographical coordinates to investigate different lunar regions.

2. Sun Position Intelligence

Visualizes solar elevation and estimates sunlight availability at selected locations. Users can examine how illumination conditions change over time and identify potentially useful sunlight windows for mission planning.

3. Earth Communication Tracker

Tracks Earth's apparent position relative to the local lunar horizon and identifies periods of geometric Earth visibility. This helps users understand potential direct-to-Earth communication opportunities.

4. Mission Timeline Simulator

Provides a time-based view of changing Sun and Earth positions. Users can explore how environmental conditions evolve throughout a selected mission period.

5. Mission Comparison Centre

Enables side-by-side comparison of different landing locations and mission dates, helping users understand trade-offs between solar illumination and Earth visibility.

6. Mission Rescheduling

Helps explore alternative landing dates and locations when mission schedules change due to delays or technical constraints.

The backend uses NASA/JPL Horizons for astronomical ephemeris calculations, with an analytical fallback model when the external data service is unavailable.

Benefits and Intended Impact

LUNA-VIEW aims to reduce the complexity of evaluating lunar landing scenarios by presenting important astronomical information through accessible visualizations and comparative analysis.

It can help users:

  • Understand solar illumination patterns at different landing locations.
  • Identify potential Earth visibility and communication windows.
  • Compare alternative landing sites and mission dates.
  • Explore the impact of mission schedule changes.
  • Understand the relationship between sunlight availability and communication opportunities.

Beyond mission planning, the platform can serve as an educational resource for students, educators, researchers, and the general public, making complex astronomical concepts easier to explore.

Tools and Technologies

The project uses:

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI
  • Astronomical Data: NASA/JPL Horizons API
  • Scientific Computation: Python-based analytical calculations
  • Deployment: Vercel
  • Version Control: Git and GitHub

The architecture separates frontend visualization from backend calculations, allowing the platform to retrieve astronomical time-series data through API endpoints.

Creativity and Innovation

The innovation behind LUNA-VIEW lies in bringing lunar exploration, astronomical visualization, temporal analysis, and mission comparison together in a single accessible platform.

Instead of requiring users to navigate multiple complex scientific tools, LUNA-VIEW provides an integrated environment where changing a landing location or mission date reveals how important operational conditions change.

Its focus on both solar illumination and Earth visibility highlights the trade-offs involved in lunar mission planning. A location with favourable sunlight conditions may not necessarily offer equally favourable Earth visibility, making comparative analysis particularly valuable.

Factors Considered

The project considers several important factors affecting preliminary lunar mission planning:

  • Solar elevation and illumination availability.
  • Earth's apparent elevation and geometric visibility.
  • Potential communication opportunities.
  • Mission dates and timeline variations.
  • Differences between candidate landing locations.
  • Data availability and calculation accuracy.
  • Accessibility and clarity of scientific visualizations.

LUNA-VIEW also emphasizes scientific transparency. Geometric Earth visibility does not guarantee an actual communication link, and sunlight availability does not directly represent electrical power generation. Actual mission conditions would also depend on terrain, equipment, antenna orientation, and other operational constraints.

Our Ultimate Vision

Our ultimate vision is to make lunar mission planning more accessible, interactive, and understandable by transforming complex astronomical information into meaningful visual insights.

LUNA-VIEW aims to evolve into a comprehensive lunar mission decision-support platform by incorporating validated lunar terrain and illumination datasets, more detailed environmental analysis, and advanced mission-planning capabilities.

By connecting scientific data with intuitive technology, we hope to contribute to a future where exploring and understanding the Moon becomes easier for researchers, students, and everyone interested in space exploration.

LUNA-VIEW is an independent educational and decision-support project developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It is not an official NASA product and is not endorsed or validated by NASA.

projectDetails.name: CrewSignal: Autonomous Deep-Space Biometric & Health Telemetry System
projectDetails.summary:
Directly addressing NASA’s Exploration Medical Capability (ExMC) gap Medical-701 and Level of Care IV/V guidelines (HRP-48033), we developed CrewSignal: an autonomous, 100% offline Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) for deep-space exploration.

  During long-duration Mars transit, 22-minute communication delays render real-time Mission Control assistance impossible, while strict spacecraft constraints prohibit cloud services or internet access. CrewSignal fulfills NASA’s Concept of Operations by providing an on-station medical edge hub that ingests
  live 1 Hz multi-channel wearable telemetry—including heart rate with physiological heart rate variability (HRV), arterial pressure, core-skin temperature, and actigraphy—running entirely locally on standard habitat computing hardware.

  Calibrated against authentic NASA Life Sciences Data Archive (LSDA) datasets from the 45-day HERA isolation mission and ISS microgravity protocols, CrewSignal features dynamic clinical reference gauges, custom telemetry imports, and an on-device emergency voice triage assistant with hardware silence controls
  for low-visibility or crew incapacitation crises. A dual-tier privacy firewall protects astronaut psychological reporting from mission telemetry.

  CrewSignal is vital because, per NASA HRP-48033, autonomous on-board decision support is the only way to safeguard crew health, manage emergent crises, and ensure mission survival beyond low-Earth orbit.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

CrewSignal is an autonomous, 100% offline Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) and health-monitoring platform designed for long-duration spaceflight. Built strictly to address NASA’s Exploration Medical Capability (ExMC) gap Medical-701 and Level of Care IV/V standards (NASA-STD-3001 & HRP-48033),

CrewSignal enables non-physician crew members to independently monitor daily vitals, track longitudinal physiological trends, and execute immediate clinical triage during communications blackouts.

The system operates across three synchronized tiers:

1. Multi-Channel Ingestion & IoT Hardware Abstraction Layer: CrewSignal is architected to ingest live serial and Web Bluetooth streams from low-voltage wearable bench nodes:

• MAX30102 Optical PPG Sensor: Captures real-time pulse rate and optical waveforms with signal-quality gating.

• Infrared (IR) Contact Thermistor (MAX30205 / MLX90614): Tracks non-contact skin-surface thermal dissipation and metabolic warming.

• MPU6050 3-Axis IMU: Measures acceleration and actigraphy to categorize microgravity float (0.02–0.08 g), station duty (0.20–0.55 g), and high-load countermeasure workouts (0.90–1.75 g).

• Validated Flight Emulation & Telemetry Importer: When physical sensors are unstrapped, CrewSignal executes a 1 Hz flight emulation engine driven by real NASA Life Sciences Data Archive (LSDA) missions, complete with Respiratory Sinus Arrhythmia (RSA) and Mayer baroreflex oscillations, while allowing

flight surgeons to drag and drop custom mission CSV/JSON datasets.

2. Interactive Clinical Dashboard & Body Map: Translates complex telemetry into an interactive SVG body map. Rather than showing arbitrary clamp limits, gauges display NASA Standard Clinical Reference Scales (e.g. 45–180 bpm for Heart Rate, with nominal resting bands highlighted at 70–100 bpm),

contextualized by recent 60-second rolling spans.

3. Hands-Free Emergency Protocol Engine: In low-visibility or crew incapacitation scenarios (such as exercise-induced tachycardia), a single prominent trigger activates on-device auditory clinical triage (pickAdamVoice profile) with instant hardware physical "Stop Speaker" controls.

4. Dual-Tier Astronaut Privacy Firewall: Differentiates between physical vitals (shared for mission safety) and self-reported mental wellbeing/stress check-ins, which remain encrypted locally to eliminate astronaut under-reporting fear.

2. What benefits does it have?

• Zero Cloud & Zero Network Dependency: Operates reliably inside an RF-shielded spacecraft Faraday cage or deep-space transit without internet or external APIs.

• Honest Data Quality Gate: Unlike commercial apps that display misleading zeros or mask missing data as green, CrewSignal tags every reading with quality flags (ok, poor_contact, stale). If sensor contact fails, it prominently displays "No valid reading."

• Emergency Speed: Emergency workflows never wait for data entry or sensor handshake—immediate guided checklists open on a single click.

• Asynchronous Earth Telemetry Bundler: Automatically packages structured JSON clinical handoff reports ready for delay-tolerant satellite downlink once ground communication windows open.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

As human spaceflight ventures beyond Low Earth Orbit (LEO) toward Mars, real-time medical evacuation is impossible. CrewSignal shifts space medicine from an Earth-dependent paradigm to on-station medical autonomy. Beyond spaceflight, its zero-bandwidth, offline-first design provides immediate humanitarian

impact for remote polar stations, offshore marine vessels, and underserved rural clinics cut off from internet infrastructure.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

• Frontend Framework: Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript

• State & Storage Architecture: Service Worker Cache (PRECACHE_SHELL), HTML5 PWA Manifest, LocalStorage Indexed Persistence

• Visualization & UI: Tailwind CSS, Custom Aerospace Vector Design System, Dynamic SVG Body Map, HTML5 Particle Engine

• Voice & Speech Engine: Built-in offline Web Speech Synthesis API tuned to mission-commander acoustics with immediate audio pause/stop interrupt handlers

• IoT & Sensor Hardware Research: MAX30102 (PPG optical pulse), MPU6050 (3-axis IMU actigraphy), IR temperature module (contact skin thermistor), ESP32 development microcontrollers

• Data Ingestion: Custom client-side streaming CSV/JSON parser with validation preview and schema verification

5. How is your project creative?

• The "Honest Uncertainty" Design Philosophy: Rather than inventing an unverified medical diagnosis or artificial "health score," CrewSignal focuses on clinical observation, verified procedural checklists, and transparent data quality.

• Acoustic Emergency Co-Pilot: The voice engine speaks procedural instructions aloud, allowing a second astronaut to perform CPR or retrieve an AED without taking their eyes off the patient.

• Behavioral Privacy Separation: Solving the historical dilemma where astronauts hide psychological distress by guaranteeing that mental health logs stay strictly private on the local vessel.

6. What factors did your team consider?

• NASA Exploration Constraints (HRP-48033 Section 4.5): Strict mass, power (70 W), and low-compute laptop environments with zero cloud connectivity.

• Sensor Motion Artifacts: Microgravity movement causes PPG sensor detachment; CrewSignal accounts for contact noise and motion clipping rather than outputting false cardiac alarms.

• Cognitive Overload: In high-stress scenarios, complex menus cause deadly delays; the emergency flow is restricted to high-contrast, one-instruction-per-screen guidance.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”
