projectDetails.name: ASTRA CARE
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRA CARE – AI-Powered Astronaut Healthcare and Monitoring Platform

ASTRA CARE is a smart healthcare and monitoring platform designed to support astronaut health and safety during space missions, especially long-duration and deep-space exploration. During space missions, astronauts face various health challenges, and communication delays with Earth can make medical assistance difficult. ASTRA CARE aims to bring essential healthcare features together in one centralized platform.

The project consists of six major modules:

1. Astronaut Health Monitoring: Displays important health indicators such as pulse rate, oxygen levels and body temperature.
2. Health Data and Historical Records: Organizes health information and previous records to track changes over time.
3. AI Predictive Health Analytics: Supports the analysis of health patterns and identification of potential health risks.
4. AI Medical Guidance: Provides a conversational interface for accessing medical information and guidance.
5. Medicine Inventory: Helps monitor available medicines and medical supplies.
6. Deep Space Mission Control: Provides a dedicated interface for mission-related information and control access.

The main objective of ASTRA CARE is to improve astronaut healthcare information management, support early identification of potential health concerns and make medical resources easier to access. The platform aims to contribute to safer and more independent future space exploration.

projectDetails.name: SKYTRACE
projectDetails.summary:
SkyTrace is A 3D Temporal Explorer for NASA SPHEREx Data is an interactive web platform designed to make complex astronomical observations easier and more engaging to explore.
We developed a 3D sky explorer that lets users navigate astronomical coordinates, access real NASA SPHEREx infrared measurements, and compare images depicting the same region of space at different times. Using scientific image-processing techniques, the platform creates difference maps, estimates the significance of observed changes, and marks potential astronomical change candidates for further investigation.
SkyTrace responds to the challenge of making NASA’s extensive infrared datasets easier to visualize, understand, and explore without requiring advanced astronomical software skills. It connects raw scientific data with a more intuitive and interactive analysis experience.
The project makes space science more accessible to students, researchers, and astronomy enthusiasts. It also creates opportunities for education, citizen science, and later investigations into moving or variable celestial objects. Any changes identified by SkyTrace are treated as candidates for scientific validation rather than confirmed discoveries.
projectDetails.details:
SkyTrace: Tracing Changes Throughout the Universe

SkyTrace is an interactive web-based platform that makes NASA’s SPHEREx infrared measurements easier to access, understand, and explore. It brings together 3D sky visualization, real astronomical data, scientific image processing, and time-based analysis in one application. The main goal is to help students, researchers, and astronomy enthusiasts examine the universe and investigate possible changes in celestial objects over time.

The platform includes an interactive 3D celestial sphere where users can browse different regions of the sky, zoom in on areas of interest, and select locations using Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec), the coordinate system commonly used in astronomy. Once a region is selected, SkyTrace connects to its backend and retrieves available SPHEREx infrared measurements from NASA/IPAC’s Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). These observations are provided in FITS (Flexible Image Transport System) format, which is widely used to store astronomical images and related scientific data.

SkyTrace processes the retrieved observations and allows users to compare images from the same region of the sky captured at different times. Before making a comparison, the system checks important factors such as wavelength compatibility and image quality. It then uses World Coordinate System (WCS) information to align the images, ensuring that corresponding pixels represent the same locations in the sky.

After alignment, the application calculates pixel-level differences and estimated significance values. This process creates difference maps and marks regions that may show interesting changes. These highlighted areas are treated as preliminary change candidates that need further investigation, not as confirmed astronomical discoveries.

SkyTrace takes on the challenge of making large and complex astronomy datasets easier to use. Although NASA provides a wide range of scientific data, exploring it often requires specialized software, knowledge of astronomical coordinates, and experience with scientific image processing. SkyTrace makes this simpler by combining data retrieval, visualization, and time-based analysis in one intuitive web interface. Instead of downloading and processing multiple files manually, users can browse the sky visually and examine observations through a more straightforward workflow.

The project provides several important benefits. It gives users easier access to real NASA astronomical data, supports astronomy education, and offers a convenient way to investigate regions of the sky that may have changed over time. Students can learn about infrared astronomy, celestial coordinates, scientific imaging, and the value of repeated observations. Astronomy enthusiasts can work with authentic space data, while researchers can use the platform to identify areas that may deserve more detailed study.

SkyTrace is built with TypeScript, JavaScript, and Python. The frontend uses React and Next.js to create a responsive and interactive web application. Three.js and React Three Fiber power the 3D celestial sphere, allowing users to move around the sky and select specific regions.

The backend uses Python and FastAPI to communicate with astronomical data services and perform scientific processing. Astropy handles FITS files, astronomical metadata, celestial coordinates, and WCS information. NumPy is used for numerical calculations and pixel-level image operations, while SciPy provides additional tools for scientific computing and image processing. The main data source is NASA/IPAC IRSA, which provides access to real SPHEREx observations. Microsoft Azure is also being considered for future cloud deployment.

What makes SkyTrace creative is the way it combines 3D sky exploration with time-based astronomical analysis. Instead of presenting observations only as files or static images, the platform lets users move through the sky, retrieve real infrared data, and compare observations from different periods. Its innovation comes from combining established astronomical methods with modern web-based visualization tools in one user-friendly environment. This makes scientific research more engaging without requiring users to handle every technical step themselves.

During development, the team focused on several key factors, including scientific reliability, data authenticity, observation compatibility, image quality, computing performance, usability, and scalability. Astronomical recordings can contain noise, instrumental artifacts, wavelength differences, and alignment errors, all of which may produce misleading changes in an image. To reduce these issues, SkyTrace uses compatibility tests, quality masking, WCS-based alignment, and difference-analysis methods.

Even with these safeguards, the change-candidate detection process still requires scientific validation. SkyTrace does not claim to confirm new astronomical discoveries. Separating the frontend visualization from the backend scientific processing also supports a clear architecture that can be improved and expanded over time.

The broader aim of SkyTrace is to reduce the distance between complex astronomical research data and general understanding. By making NASA’s infrared measurements easier to access, visualize, and compare, the project encourages scientific wonder, supports education, and opens space exploration to a wider audience. Future improvements could include support for additional space missions, more advanced analysis methods, improved tools for investigating candidates, and educational or citizen-science features.

SkyTrace shows how modern web development and scientific computing can work together to turn real NASA space data into an interactive experience. Through its combination of 3D navigation, authentic infrared observations, and time-based image comparison, the platform makes it easier for people to explore and understand a changing universe.

projectDetails.name: SAR-based flood detection project
projectDetails.summary:
Flooding can damage communities, agriculture, and infrastructure. Rapid identification of inundated areas is important for disaster response and planning. This project proposes a flood detection workflow using Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery from the Sentinel-1 satellite. Unlike optical satellites, Sentinel-1 collects useful observations during day and night and is less affected by cloud cover, making it valuable during severe weather.

The project will compare Sentinel-1 images acquired before and after a flood event over a selected study area. The imagery will be preprocessed through radiometric calibration, speckle filtering, and terrain correction. Changes in radar backscatter will then be analysed to identify locations where water has likely inundated previously dry land. A threshold-based classification method will create a preliminary flood extent map. Where reference data are available, the results will be compared with reference maps or optical imagery to assess reliability.

Expected outputs include processed SAR images, a flood extent map, and an estimate of the affected area. The project demonstrates how Earth observation and remote sensing can support flood monitoring and disaster management. It also highlights limitations such as radar shadow, urban surfaces, vegetation, and confusion with permanent water bodies. It can also help authorities prioritize emergency response and relief.
projectDetails.details: This project focuses on detecting and mapping flood-affected areas using Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellite imagery from the Sentinel-1 satellite. It works by comparing satellite images captured before and after a flood event to identify changes in water coverage and detect flooded regions. SAR technology uses microwave signals, allowing it to collect useful data during cloudy weather and at night. The satellite images are processed using techniques such as speckle filtering, backscatter analysis, and threshold-based classification to distinguish flooded areas from non-flooded regions. The project uses Python as the programming language, Google Earth Engine and Google Colab for satellite data processing, and libraries such as NumPy, Matplotlib, Rasterio, and Geemap for analysis and visualization. QGIS can also be used to view and analyse the generated flood maps. The major benefits of this project include faster flood detection, monitoring of affected agricultural and residential areas, and the use of freely available satellite data. Its intended impact is to support disaster management authorities, emergency response teams, and local communities by providing useful information for rescue operations and relief planning. The creative aspect of this project is the application of AI and remote sensing techniques to identify flooded areas using radar imagery instead of relying only on optical satellite images. Factors such as image quality, spatial resolution, terrain conditions, vegetation, permanent water bodies, urban structures, classification accuracy, and data availability are considered to improve the reliability of the results.

projectDetails.summary:
## Nova Care: Astronaut Health Monitoring Platform

Space missions can last for months or even years, making it important to keep track of astronauts' physical and mental well-being. With this in mind, we developed **Nova Care**, an astronaut health monitoring platform for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 challenge, **“Health Monitoring for Long-Duration Missions.”**

Nova Care brings important health information together in one place. It allows users to monitor health indicators, view historical records, complete behavioural health check-ins, and receive health-related alerts. We also integrated AI-assisted baseline creation, anomaly detection, and trend analysis to help identify unusual patterns and changes over time. The platform supports real-time telemetry updates, health reports, and CSV data exports. It also provides role-based demo access for astronauts, medical officers, pilots, and engineers.

Our goal is to explore how technology can make health monitoring more organized and accessible during long-duration missions, where continuous observation and timely awareness are especially important. Nova Care is our attempt to contribute towards safer and more informed space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Nova Care: Astronaut Health Monitoring Platform

Project Overview

Long-duration space missions create unique challenges for astronaut health. Astronauts may spend months or even years away from Earth, making continuous health observation and timely access to health information especially important. To address this challenge, our team developed Nova Care, a centralized astronaut health monitoring platform for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Nova Care brings together health monitoring, historical records, experimental AI-assisted analysis, behavioural health check-ins, alerts, and real-time telemetry in one platform. Our goal was to create a system that makes astronaut health information easier to access, understand, and monitor.

How Does Nova Care Work?

The platform provides a centralized dashboard where users can view astronaut health information and monitoring indicators. It also maintains historical health records, allowing changes to be observed over time.

One of the important components is our experimental AI service. It includes three implemented capabilities:

  • AI Baseline Creation: Establishes a baseline using available health data.
  • Anomaly Detection: Helps identify potentially unusual patterns in monitored data.
  • Trend Analysis: Examines historical records to estimate trends and changes over time.

Nova Care also includes behavioural health check-ins, allowing users to record and review behavioural health information. Health-related alerts help bring attention to relevant monitoring events.

For live monitoring, we integrated Socket.IO and WebSocket communication to receive and broadcast telemetry updates. Users can also access health reports and export available data in CSV format. The platform includes role-based demo access for astronauts, medical officers, pilots, and engineers.

Benefits and Intended Impact

We designed Nova Care around the idea that astronaut health information should be organized, accessible, and easier to monitor throughout a mission.

By bringing different monitoring capabilities together, the platform reduces the need to view separate information sources. Historical records provide context for understanding changes, while experimental AI-assisted analysis helps highlight patterns that may deserve attention.

Behavioural health check-ins also recognize that astronaut well-being involves more than physical indicators. Including both physical and behavioural health monitoring creates a broader view of astronaut well-being.

Our intended impact is to explore how integrated software systems can support health awareness, monitoring, and informed decision-making during long-duration space missions, particularly when astronauts are far from immediate medical support on Earth.

Technology and Tools Used

We developed Nova Care using a full-stack architecture:

Frontend

  • React
  • TypeScript
  • Vite

Backend

  • Node.js
  • Express.js
  • Socket.IO

AI Service

  • Python
  • FastAPI
  • NumPy
  • scikit-learn

Database

  • PostgreSQL
  • Neon Database

Deployment and Development

  • Render for deploying the frontend, backend, and AI service
  • Git and GitHub for version control and collaboration
  • Visual Studio Code for development

The frontend communicates with the backend, which handles application functionality and database interactions. The separate Python-based AI service handles the experimental baseline, anomaly detection, and trend analysis capabilities. Real-time telemetry updates are supported through Socket.IO.

What Makes Nova Care Creative?

Our approach combines multiple aspects of astronaut health monitoring in a single application instead of treating each capability as a separate tool.

We brought together historical health monitoring, AI-assisted pattern analysis, behavioural health check-ins, alerts, and live telemetry. We also considered the different people involved in a space mission by providing role-based demo access for astronauts, medical officers, pilots, and engineers.

Another important design decision was to keep the AI service separate from the main backend. This modular architecture makes the system easier to maintain and provides room for future improvements.

Factors Considered During Development

While developing Nova Care, we considered:

  • Long-duration mission conditions: The need to monitor health information over extended periods.
  • Physical and behavioural well-being: The importance of considering more than physical health indicators.
  • Accessibility of information: Keeping monitoring features organized in one dashboard.
  • Historical context: Making past records available to observe changes over time.
  • Real-time updates: Supporting live telemetry communication.
  • Different mission roles: Providing demo access for different users involved in astronaut health monitoring.
  • Modularity and scalability: Separating the frontend, backend, database, and AI service.
  • Responsible AI use: Treating AI outputs as experimental decision-support information rather than medical diagnoses.

Conclusion

Nova Care is our attempt to use software engineering, data processing, and machine learning concepts to address a real challenge in human space exploration. Through this project, we explored how different health monitoring capabilities can work together to support astronaut well-being during long-duration missions.

We hope Nova Care demonstrates how thoughtful technology integration can contribute to safer, more informed, and more sustainable space exploration.

projectDetails.name: Microgravity Combustion SI Dashboard
projectDetails.summary: We developed “Flame in Freefall,” an SI-powered web dashboard that makes NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion data easy to find, compare and interpret for fire safety in crewed exploration. Its built-in SI Research Guide lets users ask in plain language to rank studies for a Lunar Base, explain how electric fields mimic partial gravity (E-FIELD), or compare experiments side by side, and it summarizes each investigation’s findings. The dashboard ranks 25 PSI investigations by Fire Safety Relevance, Lunar and High-O₂ Relevance, and Partial-g and Modeling Value, and users can re-rank by habitat: ISS cabin, Lunar Base and rover (30% O₂ or more at 10.2 psi or less), Mars habitat, or spacesuit (up to 85% O₂ in ACME CFI-G). It also includes a 1g versus microgravity explainer, a 3D hardware and investigation network, a habitat flammability simulator with adjustable oxygen, pressure and airflow, a comparison table, and CSV, PDF and Word exports. It flags that PSI has no partial-gravity data yet and shows how existing results bound the Moon and Mars. It also links the research to Earth benefits, turning an overwhelming archive into clear answers that help make the next giant leap safer.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

Flame in Freefall is an interactive, AI-assisted web dashboard that makes NASA's microgravity combustion research easy to explore, compare and apply. It brings together 25 combustion and fire-safety investigations (PSI-10 to PSI-181) from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) archive. The data comes from experiments on the International Space Station, the Cygnus resupply spacecraft, the Space Shuttle and computational fluid dynamics models. The platform summarizes, ranks and simulates these findings so engineers, students and mission planners can see what they mean for crew safety on the Moon and Mars.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Enriched database. Each of the 25 studies is stored with technical metadata: burner and sample geometry, oxygen levels (13.5% to 85% O2), pressures (0.25 to 20 atm), ventilation speeds (0 to 65 cm/s), electric fields (0 to 10 kV) and diagnostic sensors. Studies are grouped into five research clusters: ACME Gaseous, Cool Flames, Solid Flammability, Soot and Smoke, and Fluid and Materials.

2. Ranking. Every study carries three 0-100 indicative scores: Fire Safety Relevance (crew-habitat fire safety), Lunar / High-O2 Applicability, and Partial-Gravity and Modeling Value. These scores were generated with AI assistance from each study's published PSI metadata. They are relative, comparison-oriented estimates meant to help users prioritize which studies to read first, not formally validated measurements. Users can rank by any score and filter by environment: ISS cabin, lunar base, pressurized rover, Mars habitat or spacesuit.

3. Physics visualizers. A split-screen view compares a buoyancy-dominated flame on Earth (1g) with a diffusion- and radiation-dominated spherical flame in microgravity, using live canvas models and annotated diagrams.

4. 3D hardware viewer. Rotatable Three.js models of four flight facilities: the ISS Combustion Integrated Rack, the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox, Cygnus (SAFFIRE) and the Space Shuttle (STDCE-1).

5. Knowledge graph. An interactive Vis.js network links the 25 studies through 25 engineering relationships, for example how the FLEX study (PSI-69) validates the OpenFOAM model (PSI-117).

6. Cabin fire hazard simulator. A parametric simulator, grounded in PSI-20, PSI-22, PSI-25, PSI-69 and PSI-159, lets users set oxygen (14% to 85%), airflow (0 to 45 cm/s) and cabin pressure (0.25 to 5.0 atm), or pick one of four mission presets, to see flame spread behavior and regime warnings.

7. AI Copilot (PSI Research Guide). The Copilot is powered by a large language model [Gemini API / Claude API]. Users ask questions in plain language, such as "Rank investigations for Lunar Base and Partial Gravity" or "Compare BASS-II and SAFFIRE-II". It answers from the platform's dataset and also operates the dashboard by filtering cards, re-ranking scores, switching 3D models and setting simulator sliders.

8. Comparison and export. Users can compare up to 4 studies side by side across 10 attributes, open a full telemetry dossier for any study with a link to its official NASA PSI record, and export PDF dossiers, Word briefs or CSV/Excel data.

KEY SCIENTIFIC INSIGHTS BUILT IN

- Turning off cabin ventilation does not put out fires in oxygen-enriched exploration atmospheres (26.5% to 34% O2), because burning polymers sustain themselves through radiative feedback (PSI-20).

- Gentle airflow (10 to 30 cm/s) in microgravity lets materials burn faster and at lower oxygen levels than on Earth (PSI-25, PSI-99).

- Electric fields can mimic lunar (0.16g) and Martian (0.38g) buoyancy, helping bound partial-gravity fire risk (PSI-22).

- Hot droplets that appear extinguished can burn as invisible cool flames (500 to 800 K) and reignite when disturbed (PSI-69, PSI-117).

- Smoke particles grow larger in microgravity and can evade older ionization alarms, so multi-wavelength optical sensors are needed (PSI-101, PSI-102).

- 85% oxygen tests bound spacesuit and airlock pre-breathe hazards (PSI-159).

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Decades of NASA data become searchable and comparable in one place, so users can find the findings that matter for a given mission environment in seconds instead of reading dozens of technical reports. The intended impact is better-informed decisions on spacecraft materials, ventilation, smoke detection and fire response for crewed Moon and Mars missions. It also gives students and the public an accessible way to learn from NASA's open science data, and it points to Earth spin-offs of the research.

WHERE OUR DATA CAME FROM

All scientific data and context come from NASA's official resources listed on the challenge page: the PSI Data Repository (Combustion Science), NASA Combustion Science, the NASA ScienceCasts video "The Power of Studying Combustion on the ISS", and "A Researcher's Guide to International Space Station Combustion Science" (2015). Historical context came from the Apollo 1, Apollo 13 and 1997 Mir fire reports, and the fire-safety technology spin-offs (Fireman's Air Tanks, Fire Detector, Fire Attire). Each study in the dashboard links back to its official NASA PSI record.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Backend: Python with FastAPI

- Frontend: HTML5 Canvas, SVG, Three.js (3D viewer), Vis.js (knowledge graph)

- Development: VS Code, Windows PowerShell and Windows Terminal

- Version control: GitHub

- Hosting: Render.com

- AI: Gemini and Claude

- Hardware: standard laptops, no special hardware

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Rather than a static archive, it is an operating console. A conversational Copilot controls a scored database, a physics visualizer, a 3D hardware viewer, a knowledge graph and a hazard simulator together. The three mission-specific scores and the habitat filters turn raw experiments into answers about which research applies to a lunar base, a Mars habitat or a spacesuit. The knowledge graph also shows how experiments validate and cross-calibrate each other, which is hard to see in a plain list.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Scientific grounding: studies, parameters and insights are tied to specific PSI investigations, and every study links back to its official NASA PSI record so users can verify the original data.

- Transparency about AI: the dataset enrichment, indicative scores and Copilot responses were produced with AI assistance. They are decision-support aids and should be checked against the official NASA records before any real engineering use.

- Mission relevance: scoring and filters reflect real exploration environments (ISS, lunar, Mars, spacesuit).

- Usability: keyboard search, one-click presets, and exports for Excel and Python users.

- Limitations: the scores and the hazard simulator are simplified, AI-assisted models. They are not official NASA safety standards and have not been independently validated.

USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE

This project was developed using AI tools throughout. Gemini and Claude helped generate and refine the code, structure the dataset from NASA PSI sources, write the indicative scores, and draft documentation. Development was done in VS Code, with GitHub for version control, Render.com for deployment, and Windows PowerShell and Windows Terminal for running and deploying the project. The in-app PSI Research Guide Copilot uses a large language model at runtime. The science content comes from NASA's official PSI Data Repository and the resources listed on the challenge page, and every study links back to its official PSI record. The team directed the concept, reviewed the outputs and integrated the platform.

projectDetails.name: mission control
projectDetails.summary:
Mission Control: Design a Space Mission is an interactive web game that teaches students how real space missions are planned. Players choose a mission (Earth Climate Satellite, Asteroid Scout or Mars Weather Probe). They then build a spacecraft in five guided steps: rocket, instruments, power, antenna and optional protection. Live meters show budget, mass and power as they choose.

When they launch, they pilot five stages: launch, travel, orbit, science and communication. Each stage is a hands-on timing challenge in a 3D scene with sound effects. The outcome comes mainly from the design: too little power slows the instruments, a weak antenna loses data, and a heat shield or backup computer cuts specific risks. Player timing adds only a small bonus (about ±8 points). The results screen gives a 0–100 score and explains what helped, what hurt and what to try next, so a failure teaches rather than punishes.

The game turns trade-offs between cost, weight, power and communication into something students can feel rather than memorize. That way of thinking is central to engineering, and the game needs no account or backend, so it is easy to use in classrooms.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works: Mission Control is a browser game where players plan and fly a space mission. They pick a mission (Earth, Asteroid or Mars), build a spacecraft in five guided steps (rocket, instruments, power, antenna, extras) while watching budget, mass and power meters, then fly five stages in 3D: launch, travel, orbit, science and communication. Simple rules turn design choices into results, such as weak power slowing instruments or a weak antenna losing data. A score from 0 to 100 explains what helped, what hurt and what to try next. Player timing adds only about ±8 points, so design decides most of the outcome.

Benefits: It teaches trade-offs by letting players feel them. It is beginner-friendly, encouraging after failure, free of accounts and installs, and works on desktop and mobile.

Intended impact: To make space engineering approachable and build engineering thinking: working within limits, weighing risk and improving a design. I haven’t tested it with students yet, so this is the goal, not a measured result.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Three.js for 3D and the Web Audio API for sound. It was built in a conversation with Claude, and the slides were made with pptxgenjs. Any modern browser is enough hardware.

Creativity: The game has a clear story (choose, build, launch, learn). Procedural 3D planets, a modeled rocket and probe, synthesized sound and a hands-on challenge at each stage give it a mission-control feel. Every part has a benefit and a cost, so there are several valid designs.

Factors considered: The lesson of trade-offs stays central. Rules are fair and always explained, every mission has a winning design and many partial ones, the language is friendly, and it works on phones and has a fallback if 3D isn’t available.

projectDetails.name: Project Survivors
projectDetails.summary:
SPACE TYCOONS: Survive, Save & Expand

Space Tycoons is a STEM simulation bridging aerospace engineering and financial literacy. It forces students to make critical survival decisions under strict economic constraints.

Players act as Mission Directors establishing a Lunar or Martian outpost. They must manage vital life-support systems (Oxygen, Food, Energy) that rapidly decay in hostile environments. Every infrastructure upgrade costs money, and prices inflate exponentially.

The core mechanic is the Emergency Reserve Fund. Players must maintain a locked capital reserve (20%-40% of funds). Overspending to maintain vitals and breaching this reserve triggers severe penalties, teaching the core philosophy: Survival is mandatory, spending is strategic, and savings determine the champion.

For authenticity, the app integrates live NASA APIs:

DONKI Space Weather: Triggers unpredictable energy crises via solar storm data.

NTRS/OSDR: Contextualizes space agriculture with real NASA data.

NASA Image Library: Injects authentic satellite telemetry into the UI.

Built as a zero-dependency HTML5 app, Space Tycoons features a CSS Grid "mission control" interface and an interactive AI companion. It delivers a high-stakes environment where students experience how real space exploration requires balancing human survival with limited funds.
projectDetails.details:
SPACE TYCOONS: Survive, Save & Expand

Space Tycoons is an interactive STEM simulation that bridges the critical gap between aerospace engineering and financial literacy. Unlike traditional educational games where players simply maximize technology to win, this project forces students to make critical engineering decisions under strict, realistic economic constraints.

Players act as Mission Directors tasked with establishing a Lunar or Martian outpost. They must constantly manage vital life-support systems—Oxygen, Food, and Energy—which rapidly decay due to the hostile environments. However, every infrastructure upgrade costs money, and prices inflate exponentially.

The defining mechanic of the simulation is the Emergency Reserve Fund. Players are subjected to a mandatory, locked capital reserve (20% to 40% of their starting funds, depending on the planet's difficulty). If a player overspends to maintain their vitals and breaches this reserve floor, they face severe penalties. This teaches the core philosophy of the game: Survival is mandatory, spending is strategic, and savings determine the champion.

To ensure deep authenticity, the application integrates live NASA APIs:

  • DONKI Space Weather: Triggers unpredictable energy crises via real-time Coronal Mass Ejection (solar storm) data.
  • NTRS/OSDR: Contextualizes space agriculture and hydroponics with real NASA open-source data.
  • NASA Image Library: Injects authentic, dynamic satellite telemetry of the Lunar and Martian surfaces directly into the UI.

Built as a highly accessible, zero-dependency HTML5 application, Space Tycoons features a high-performance "mission control" CSS Grid interface, an interactive AI companion (NOVA), and real-time visual analytics. It successfully delivers a high-stakes, consequence-driven learning environment where students experience firsthand how real space exploration requires balancing human survival with limited financial resources.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. projectDetails.name: MARS ATLAS
projectDetails.summary:
Mars Atlas is an interactive 3D Martian GIS and Extravehicular Activity (EVA) survival planner built for the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge. Using CesiumJS configured to the true IAU-2015 Martian ellipsoid (3,396.19 km equatorial radius) and a Python FastAPI scientific backend, it transforms fragmented NASA datasets into a unified mission control console.

Explorers can toggle five orbital layers: Viking true-color imagery, NASA MGS MOLA 32 ppd elevation (1.44 km/px with real 3D mesh terrain), Horn 3×3 slope-hazard maps, pole-to-pole THEMIS Night-IR thermal inertia (distinguishing solid bedrock from dust traps), and Mars Odyssey GRS + TES Dust Cover Index maps across 10 surface elements (H₂O, Fe, Si, S, Cl, K, Th, Al, Ca, DCI). A slope-penalized A* pathfinder routes astronauts and rovers safely around steep crater walls while computing live oxygen, battery, cooling water, radiation, walk-back limits, and Mars Sol Date / Local Mean Solar Time, validated against real Perseverance and Curiosity rover traverses.

By uniting hazard avoidance, resource mapping, and life-support telemetry in one tool, Mars Atlas helps keep future Martian explorers alive.

projectDetails.name: Tarukh (The Mars Explorer )
projectDetails.summary:
TARUKH is a browser-based 3D Mars exploration and mission-training game designed for children aged 7–12. Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge’s “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer,” it turns space science into practical activities where young explorers observe, experiment, solve problems and make decisions.

We developed a playable Martian environment containing an accessible outpost, six cultivation greenhouses, solar equipment, a rover garage and a driveable crew rover with working cockpit displays. Players can explore freely or follow the seven-mission Elysium Outpost story, preparing a habitat for its next crew. Activities include repairing electrical connections, cleaning solar panels, connecting water systems, calibrating sensors, comparing plant-growing conditions, planning rover journeys

TARUKH addresses the challenge by connecting each activity to a junior astronaut skill: observation, troubleshooting, resource planning, navigation, preparedness and reflection. Short instructions, visual feedback, optional science explanations and a mission journal help children understand why their choices matter. Guided missions support pause, saved progress and retries, allowing players to learn at their own pace.
projectDetails.details:
TARUKH is an interactive, browser-based Mars exploration and mission-training game designed for children aged 7–12. Our goal is to help young explorers understand what astronauts must observe, maintain and plan to live and work beyond Earth. The project combines a navigable 3D environment, practical science activities and a guided story grounded in NASA resources.

Players can choose Free Exploration or the seven-mission Elysium Outpost story. In the story, they help astronaut Kaelen Reeves prepare a Mars base for its next crew. They explore the habitat, greenhouses, solar equipment and garage, interact with nearby stations, and complete activities that affect their operating plan. Clear next-step instructions, optional science explanations and a mission journal connect individual tasks to the expedition’s wider objectives.

The activities cover several aspects of junior astronaut preparation:

- Energy: repair electrical connections, brush dust from solar panels and allocate power between essential systems.

- Life support: connect water-treatment systems, calibrate instruments and manage water recovery, oxygen generation and carbon dioxide removal as separate processes.

- Food production: compare plant trials and consider how light, water and electricity affect cultivation.

- Exploration: plan a rover journey, check battery reserves, restore a field sensor, collect samples and examine their visible characteristics.

- Preparedness: review a historical solar event, inspect shelter ventilation and power, and compare simulated shielding options.

- Integrated planning: submit an operating plan, respond to an equipment fault and revise decisions during a retryable overnight readiness exercise.

The environment makes these activities tangible. Players can walk through the outpost, enter cultivation greenhouses and drive a crew rover with a furnished cockpit. Its displays show simulated speed, battery and charging information, navigation and wheel diagnostics. A minimap and regional atlas support orientation, while contextual interactions connect the world’s equipment to the learning activities.

Scientific data is part of the experience. The terrain uses NASA Mars Global Surveyor’s Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter elevation data, with a region selected through Mars Trek. Distances are compressed and relief is exaggerated to make exploration practical. NASA research on life-support systems, plant cultivation and solar-panel dust informs the activities. The radiation phone fetches live NOAA near-Earth proton observations and provides simulated historical-event replays using NASA DONKI references. We distinguish these observations and historical records from the game’s authored Mars exposure and resource models.

The intended benefits include scientific curiosity, spatial awareness, problem-solving, data literacy and systems thinking. A child can discover that producing oxygen requires water and electricity, that growing crops competes for resources, and that a rover expedition needs enough energy for the return journey. The mission journal encourages players to explain their choices and reflect on what they learned. These are intended educational outcomes; classroom and child playtesting would be needed to measure learning gains.

Our development tools and technologies include:

- TypeScript and JavaScript for simulation, interactions and application logic.

- React for menus, mission interfaces, instruments and learning activities.

- Three.js and WebGL for 3D rendering, lighting, animation and cameras.

- HTML, CSS and Tailwind CSS for interface styling and responsive layouts.

- Blender and asset-processing scripts for model assembly and preparation, with GLB assets, Draco geometry compression and WebP textures.

- Vite, Git and GitHub for builds, version control and collaboration, with Vercel hosting the submitted game.

- Codex & Antigravity-assisted development, automated tests, TypeScript checks, production builds and browser checks for implementation and validation.

The project’s creativity comes from connecting scientific concepts within one explorable world. A solar-panel activity contributes to an energy plan; that plan influences life support, cultivation and rover preparation. The radiation phone brings space-weather information into a familiar interface, while the rover cockpit turns navigation and resource monitoring into part of the experience.

Our team considered age-appropriate instructions, keyboard and touch access, reduced-motion support, readable feedback, saved progress and opportunities to retry. We also considered device limitations through adjustable graphics, compressed assets, shared geometry and bounded terrain rendering. Scientific accuracy, transparent simulation assumptions and asset attribution were central considerations. TARUKH aims to make astronaut-style observation and decision-making approachable through an engaging learning experience.

projectDetails.name: Project Team Orbitronsss
projectDetails.summary:
**ORBITAL: Beyond the Impossible**

ORBITAL is an interactive 3D space mission simulator that turns anyone into a mission engineer. Players choose from five missions, from Earth observation to the Moon, Mars, the asteroid belt and Jupiter. They then design a spacecraft from 12 components, including chemical and ion engines, fuel tanks, solar panels, RTGs, antennas and science instruments, and pick one of three rockets with real payload limits.

Every decision follows real physics: the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, specific impulse, and sunlight that weakens with distance squared. During flight, players manage fuel, power and science data while responding to events like solar flares, micrometeorites, debris and communication failures. An in-game Mission Director explains each choice, so players learn by doing.

By building on NASA's open science and space-based data and technology (planetary orbits, ion propulsion, Voyager and Curiosity-style RTG power, and radiation and heliophysics data), ORBITAL makes complex mission trade-offs accessible, engaging and fun.

**Fail safely. Learn deeply. Try again.**
projectDetails.details:
The player picks one of five missions (Earth Observation, Lunar Landing, Mars Rover, Asteroid Survey, Jupiter Deep Space), then builds a spacecraft in a 3D workshop from 12 components: engines, fuel tanks, solar panels, batteries, antennas, science instruments, radiation shielding and landing legs. The 3D model changes as parts are added or removed, and the engineering numbers update at once: mass, cost, power, delta-v (from the rocket equation) and payload margin. The player then chooses a launch vehicle, and the game checks whether it can carry the craft. After a countdown and launch, the player flies the mission with pause and fast-forward controls and a live telemetry panel. Random emergencies appear (solar flares, debris, power loss, communication failure, fuel leaks). Each has three response options with real consequences that depend on the earlier design. A black-box timeline at the end explains what caused success or failure.

Benefits and intended impact: The game teaches how real missions are designed through play instead of a textbook. Players learn about trade-offs between mass, power and cost, why sunlight weakens with distance, why rockets have payload limits and why reserves matter. Short explanations appear as parts are chosen, and a Mission Director assistant answers questions like “Why is my power low?” The goal is to build interest in STEM and aerospace among students and curious players.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with the Three.js library (WebGL) for 3D graphics. All models, planets, particle effects and the interface are generated in code, so no paid assets or external services are needed. It runs on an ordinary PC in a standard browser, saves progress in local storage and is hosted with Git (GitHub Pages). Claude (by Anthropic) assisted with writing the code.

Creativity: It is a playable game rather than a quiz or dashboard. The same physics calculation (delta-v) drives both the design screen and the mission outcome. Emergencies depend on the player’s design, for example a ship with no shielding gets more solar flares.

Factors considered: Educational accuracy versus playability (physics is simplified and distances are scaled down), meaningful choices where nothing is free, accessibility with no install and plain-language explanations, and easy expansion because the parts, rockets and missions are simple data lists. It is a working vertical slice, and planned next steps include crew and life support, a what-if design lab, audio and planet textures.

projectDetails.details:
Orbit Guard – AI-Powered Space Waste Detection, Tracking and Collision Risk Monitoring System

1. Abstract

Orbit Guard is an AI-powered space monitoring system designed to detect, classify, track, and monitor space debris orbiting Earth. Space debris, also known as space junk, includes inactive satellites, abandoned rocket parts, broken spacecraft components, and small fragments. These objects create serious risks for operational satellites, space stations, astronauts, and future space missions.

Orbit Guard uses Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML), and orbital tracking technologies to identify and monitor space debris. It collects satellite orbital information from available datasets, analyzes object characteristics, and classifies different types of orbital objects.

The system also provides orbit visualization and collision-risk monitoring features to identify potentially dangerous close approaches between objects. An interactive web dashboard displays satellite locations, debris information, orbital paths, and warning notifications.

The main objective of Orbit Guard is to improve space safety, support satellite monitoring, and contribute to reducing the risks associated with increasing space pollution.

2. Introduction

Space technology plays an important role in modern life. Satellites are used for communication, navigation, weather forecasting, television broadcasting, and scientific research. However, the increasing number of satellite launches has resulted in growing space pollution.

Space debris consists of artificial objects orbiting Earth that are no longer useful. These objects include inactive satellites, abandoned rocket stages, and broken spacecraft components.

Even small debris fragments can damage operational satellites because objects in orbit travel at extremely high speeds. Collisions can also generate additional debris, increasing the problem.

Orbit Guard aims to address this challenge by developing an intelligent monitoring platform that combines AI, orbital data analysis, and interactive visualization to identify space debris and monitor potential collision risks.

3. Problem Statement

The increasing amount of space debris is becoming a major challenge for space organizations and satellite operators. Monitoring thousands of orbital objects and predicting their movements requires continuous tracking and complex calculations.

Traditional monitoring systems depend on specialized infrastructure and expert analysis. Therefore, an accessible and intelligent system is needed to identify orbital objects, track their movements, and estimate potential collision risks.

Orbit Guard proposes an AI-powered platform that simplifies space debris monitoring through automated classification, orbital visualization, and collision-risk alerts.

4. Objectives

  • To detect and classify space debris using AI and Machine Learning.
  • To collect and analyze satellite orbital information.
  • To track the positions and movements of orbital objects.
  • To visualize satellites and debris using a 3D Earth model.
  • To estimate potential collision risks.
  • To generate alerts for potentially dangerous close approaches.
  • To provide a user-friendly monitoring dashboard.
  • To support space safety and environmental sustainability.

5. Proposed System

The proposed Orbit Guard system combines Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, orbital mechanics, and web technologies.

First, the system collects orbital data from available satellite tracking sources. The collected information is processed using Python and stored in a database.

Next, a machine-learning model analyzes available object characteristics and classifies orbital objects into categories such as active satellites, inactive satellites, rocket bodies, and debris.

The orbital tracking module estimates object positions and displays their movements around Earth. A collision-risk analysis module compares predicted positions to identify potentially dangerous close approaches.

Finally, the system generates notifications and displays the results through an interactive dashboard.

6. Technologies Used

Technology

Purpose

Python

Main programming language

Machine Learning

Object classification

Scikit-learn

ML model development

OpenCV

Image processing

NumPy and Pandas

Data processing

Skyfield and SGP4

Flask / FastAPI

Backend development

HTML, CSS, JavaScript

Frontend development

Three.js

SQLite / MySQL

Database management

Streamlit

Interactive dashboard

7. Main Modules

Module 1: Data Collection

This module collects satellite and orbital information from available datasets and APIs. It stores object IDs, satellite names, orbital parameters, and other tracking details for further analysis.

Module 2: AI-Based Object Classification

This module uses Machine Learning to classify orbital objects into categories such as active satellites, inactive satellites, rocket bodies, and space debris. The model analyzes available object characteristics and historical datasets to identify different object types.

Module 3: Orbit Visualization

This module displays orbital objects using an interactive 3D Earth model. Users can view satellite positions, debris locations, orbital paths, and object information. Three.js can be used to create the visualization.

Module 4: Collision Risk Detection

This module analyzes the predicted positions of selected orbital objects to identify potentially dangerous close approaches. It estimates the separation distance and approach time and assigns Low, Medium, or High risk categories based on configured criteria.

A close approach does not automatically mean a collision. Reliable collision probability requires orbital uncertainty analysis.

Module 5: Alert and Notification

This module generates alerts when potentially dangerous close approaches are detected. Notifications include object IDs, estimated approach times, separation distances, and risk categories.

Module 6: Admin Dashboard

The dashboard displays total tracked objects, active satellites, identified debris, object classifications, orbital visualizations, and collision-risk alerts.

8. System Architecture

Orbital Data Sources

Satellite tracking datasets and APIs

Data Processing

Python, NumPy and Pandas

AI and Orbital Analysis

Classification, tracking and risk estimation

Collision Alerts

Orbit Guard Web Dashboard

9. Working Process

  1. Collect orbital data from available satellite tracking sources.
  2. Process and store the collected information.
  3. Use AI to classify different orbital objects.
  4. Calculate estimated satellite and debris positions.
  5. Display orbital movements through a 3D Earth model.
  6. Compare predicted positions to identify close approaches.
  7. Generate collision-risk alerts.
  8. Display object details and monitoring results on the dashboard.

10. Advantages

  • Provides centralized space debris monitoring.
  • Supports AI-based object classification.
  • Displays orbital movements in 3D.
  • Identifies potentially dangerous close approaches.
  • Generates automated monitoring alerts.
  • Reduces manual data analysis efforts.
  • Supports space research and satellite safety.
  • Can be expanded with additional datasets and features.

11. Applications

  • Space research organizations.
  • Satellite operating companies.
  • Aerospace engineering institutions.
  • Space traffic management.
  • Educational institutions.
  • Space sustainability research.
  • Satellite monitoring programs.

12. Future Enhancements

  • Integration with additional real-time orbital datasets.
  • Improved AI classification accuracy.
  • Advanced collision probability estimation.
  • Mobile application development.
  • Historical space debris analysis.
  • Automated monitoring reports.
  • Integration with space debris removal mission-planning simulations.

13. Expected Outcome

The expected outcome is an intelligent web-based application that identifies and classifies orbital objects, tracks their movements, visualizes satellite orbits, and estimates potential collision risks.

Users can explore a 3D Earth model, view tracked objects, monitor their orbital paths, and receive alerts about potentially dangerous close approaches.

14. Conclusion

Orbit Guard is an innovative project that combines Artificial Intelligence, Machine Learning, orbital mechanics, and data visualization to address the growing problem of space debris. It provides an intelligent platform for detecting orbital objects, monitoring their movements, and estimating potential collision risks. Through its interactive dashboard and automated alert system, the project supports better space awareness and safer satellite operations.

Orbit Guard aims to contribute to a cleaner, safer, and more sustainable space environment for future generations.

15. Reference Websites

  • CelesTrak  – Satellite orbital datasets.
  • Space-Track  – Space object tracking information.
  • NASA  – Space research and orbital debris information.
  • European Space Agency  – Space debris research.

Recommended hackathon demonstration: Show an orbital object being detected, classified by AI, displayed on a 3D Earth, and monitored for a potential close approach. This will demonstrate the complete working concept of OrbitGuard.

projectDetails.details:
ARES- Mars Mission Control & Interactive Surface Explorer

1. What does it do or how does it work?

ARES is an interactive, browser-based planetary exploration and mission operations platform designed to simulate Martian surface navigation, environmental analysis, and astronaut sortie planning. It integrates six core operational modules into a unified flight director interface:

  • Interactive 3D Mars Globe: Renders a photorealistic 3D Mars using Three.js and orbital textures, allowing users to rotate, zoom, inspect exact latitude/longitude surface coordinates, and focus on iconic landmarks.
  • Atmospheric Weather Station: Displays live environmental telemetry across active landing sites (Jezero Crater/Perseverance, Gale Crater/Curiosity, Elysium Planitia/InSight). Users can inspect diurnal thermal cycles, wind vector compass roses, UV radiation, and scrub through a 24-hour Sol timeline.
  • Multispectral Terrain & Hazard Analysis: Layers MOLA DEM elevation data, slope gradients, CRISM mineralogy (clays, carbonates, olivine), and thermal inertia to detect impact craters and steep escarpments with dynamic, user-adjustable hazard slope angle thresholds.
  • Astronaut Route Planner: Optimizes traverses between surface waypoints by comparing Fastest, Safest, and Science-Max routes, factoring in elevation cross-sections and an 8.5-hour solar daylight turnaround window before nightfall.
  • Science Explorer & Mission Journal: Catalogs detailed geological and astrobiological records alongside an astronaut EVA sortie logbook with local persistence and Markdown/JSON export.
  • Ares AI Companion: An unrestricted conversational AI powered by LLM integration and an offline Mars knowledge engine that explains complex astrophysics and surface survival in friendly, human terms.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Unified Planetary Interface: Consolidates fragmented GIS elevation data, meteorological tables, and rover navigation parameters into one intuitive web console.
  • Risk Mitigation for Human Exploration: Prevents rover rollovers and astronaut stranding by quantifying slope hazards, terrain roughness, and solar power time limits before departure.
  • Accessible STEM Education: Translates raw NASA telemetry into visual, interactive models that students and educators can explore without needing specialized GIS software.
  • Frictionless Deployment: Runs instantly via a one-click startup script (run.bat) without requiring complex configuration or environment setup.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The project bridges the gap between raw planetary scientific archives and actionable human mission planning. It empowers researchers, students, and space enthusiasts to visualize what living and operating on Mars requires. By democratizing access to high-resolution topography and atmospheric data, ARES aims to inspire the next generation of Artemis and Mars-generation scientists.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages: TypeScript, HTML5, CSS3, Modern JavaScript (ES Modules).
  • Frontend Framework: React Router 7, React 19, Tailwind CSS, Lucide & Tabler Icons.
  • 3D Visualization & Graphics: Three.js, WebGL shaders, HTML5 2D Canvas raster engine.
  • Backend & Server Engine: Nitro / H3 (Node.js runtime), Drizzle ORM, SQLite.
  • Artificial Intelligence: OpenRouter API (meta-llama/llama-3.3-70b-instruct), complemented by an isomorphic rule-based conversational synthesis engine.
  • NASA Data Sources & Basemaps: NASA Planetary Data System (PDS), Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA DEM), CRISM hyperspectral data, and environmental data from MEDA, REMS, and TWINS.
  • Tooling & Version Control: Git, GitHub, Vite bundler.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Gamified Yet Scientifically Rigorous: Combines actual NASA topographic datasets with mission-control interactivity—such as dynamic hazard angle sliders, turnaround time warnings, and elevation cross-section graphs.
  • Unrestricted, Human-Centric AI: Instead of a dry, keyword-restricted FAQ bot, the Ares AI Companion uses modern LLM reasoning to explain concepts through relatable everyday analogies (e.g., comparing Mars gravity to Earth, spacesuit depressurization physics, and farming potatoes in regolith).
  • Tactical Aerospace HUD Aesthetics: Built with an authentic mission-control theme featuring live Martian Local Mean Solar Time (LMST), Sol counters, pulsing telemetry beacons, and glassmorphic dashboards.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Martian Environmental Constraints: We accounted for extreme diurnal temperature drops (down to -85 °C overnight), thin atmospheric pressure (0.6% of Earth), dust optical thickness, and the critical limitation of relying on solar daylight (09:00 to 17:30 LMST) for safe EVAs.
  • Zero-Setup Accessibility: We engineered the platform entirely in full-stack TypeScript/Node.js, avoiding heavy Python/pip dependencies or C++ builds so anyone on a standard laptop can launch the system with one click.
  • Offline Resilience: Designed the application to remain functional even in offline environments or simulated communication blackouts, utilizing local fallback synthesis and cached scientific datasets.

projectDetails.name: Kepler
projectDetails.summary:
KEPLER (Lunar Landing & Horizon Decision Studio) is a terrain-aware mission planning platform designed to help astronauts and mission planners evaluate landing sites near the Moon’s South Pole.

We developed an interactive 3D lunar environment that combines NASA’s LOLA elevation data and SPICE ephemeris information to simulate surface illumination, terrain-obstructed sunlight, Earth visibility, communication windows, and solar power availability. Its Mission Control dashboard provides real-time mission metrics, while Horizon Replay allows users to compare landing sites and examine changing conditions over time. Science Explorer demonstrates how lunar terrain and curvature affect sunlight and communication line-of-sight.

KEPLER addresses a critical challenge in lunar exploration: a location that appears illuminated or suitable on a flat map may actually be shadowed or lose communication because of surrounding terrain and the Moon’s curvature. By making these constraints visible and measurable, KEPLER supports more informed landing-site selection, mission scheduling, and power planning. This is important for improving astronaut safety, operational reliability, and the success of future lunar missions.
projectDetails.details:
KEPLER (Lunar Landing & Horizon Decision Studio) is an interactive mission-planning platform designed to help evaluate potential landing sites near the Moon’s South Pole.

How it works:
KEPLER combines NASA’s LOLA elevation data with NAIF SPICE ephemeris information to create a terrain-aware lunar environment. Its Python backend calculates topocentric vectors and terrain horizon angles on demand, evaluating sunlight availability, terrain obstruction, and Earth communication line-of-sight. The scientific implementation is supported by 17 verified unit and scientific tests.

The platform includes:

  • Mission Control: Displays Sun and Earth elevation, terrain clearance, solar power availability, communication status, and mission operating states.
  • Horizon Replay: Compares landing sites and visualises changing illumination and communication conditions over time.
  • Science Explorer: Demonstrates how obstacle distance, terrain height, lunar curvature, and antenna mast height affect visibility.
  • Lunar Experience: Provides an interactive 3D view of the Moon and candidate landing regions.
  • Decision Support: Helps assess landing-site robustness, blackout periods, illumination windows, and battery requirements.

Tools and technologies:
The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Three.js. The backend uses Python and FastAPI. Scientific data sources include NASA LOLA elevation datasets and NAIF SPICE ephemeris kernels. The interface follows a minimalist, pitch-black (#000000) luxury design language, avoiding neon colours, unnecessary icons, and visual clutter.

Benefits, creativity, and intended impact:
KEPLER brings terrain, illumination, communication, and power analysis into one interactive decision-making environment. Unlike simplified visualisations that may overlook local terrain obstruction, it considers the lunar horizon and spherical curvature when evaluating visibility. This helps mission planners identify hidden risks, compare landing locations, and make better-informed operational decisions. By translating complex scientific calculations into accessible visual simulations, KEPLER aims to support safer, more reliable, and more efficient future lunar missions.

projectDetails.name: Mission X Spark
projectDetails.summary:
Mission X Spark is a free, mobile-first browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. Players run a Moon and Mars outpost for 10 days and manage three resources: power, oxygen and radiation safety. No download or account is needed.

It answers the challenge by turning real mission constraints into gameplay. Every decision has a cost. Boosting radiation shielding uses power that life support needs, and an extra experiment earns science points but strains oxygen. Solar storm events are based on real NASA space weather data (DONKI), so kids see how real solar activity affects survival. Events vary between playthroughs, and when a mission fails the game explains why, so kids learn from it.

It matters because most space content for kids shows the outcomes of missions, not the decisions behind them. Mission X Spark lets children experience the trade-offs that astronauts and mission planners handle, in plain language, with sources credited. They leave understanding that no choice in deep space is free.
projectDetails.details:
Mission X Spark is a mobile-first astronaut mission game for kids aged 7-12. Players act as junior astronauts running a Moon and Mars outpost over a 10-day mission. Each day they make decisions to balance three critical resources: power, oxygen, and radiation safety. We want to spark curiosity about space and science in young learners and show that space exploration depends on careful decisions as much as on rockets. By connecting gameplay to live NASA data, kids learn that space science is real, current, and something they could contribute to one day.

Tools and technologies

Deployment: Vercel (web hosting), with a custom domain at missionxspark.space https://mission-x-spark.vercel.app/

Front end: HTML, CSS, JavaScript [ e.g., React/Next.js, and any game or animation libraries]

Data: NASA space weather data ['DEMO_KEY', e.g., NASA DONKI, if that’s what you used]

Design: Mobile-first, responsive layout with a dark “space” theme [add design tools, e.g., Figma, Canva]

Hardware: Developed on [laptops/phones]; it runs on phones, tablets, and computers

It turns real, live NASA data into game events, so the game is never just a fixed script.

Balancing three competing resources creates real trade-offs: using more power may protect the crew, but it can drain oxygen.

Kids take on the role of mission commander rather than just answering quiz questions.

The Moon-to-Mars setting connects to NASA’s current exploration goals.

Age-appropriateness: Simple language, clear visuals, and a 10-day structure that is short enough to finish.

Accessibility: Mobile-first design, since many kids use phones or tablets, and no sign-up so there is no barrier to playing.

Scientific accuracy: Using real NASA data while simplifying concepts without making them wrong.

projectDetails.name: Project Technospace
projectDetails.summary:
We developed ASTRA-SENTINEL, an AI-powered crew health monitoring system for astronauts. Its "AstroHealth AI" dashboard streams live vitals (heart rate, SpO2, temperature, blood pressure) and fuses them into a single risk level (Normal, Warning or Critical), with a plain-language reason for every alert. An on-board AstroHealth agent answers questions like "What should I do?" and suggests clear next steps.

It addresses the challenge directly. Astronauts face silent body changes in microgravity, communication delays of up to 22 minutes each way to Mars, and disconnected sensors whose warnings get missed. ASTRA-SENTINEL links the signals together, detects unusual trends early, explains its reasoning, and works offline so crews are not dependent on Earth. It is built with React, TypeScript, a Python API, Claude AI and NASA open data (OSDR, DONKI, FIRMS) for baselines and risk context. Prototype telemetry is simulated.

This matters because on long missions, help is minutes away at best, so crews need continuous, explainable, autonomous health monitoring to catch problems before they become emergencies, making deep-space missions safer.
projectDetails.details:
STRA-SENTINEL is a live crew health monitor for space missions. Sensors stream vitals (heart rate, SpO2, temperature, blood pressure) into a processing layer. An AI analysis stage then assigns a risk level of Normal, Warning or Critical, which appears on a Mission Control dashboard. The user journey has four steps: *Sense* (vitals stream in), *Detect* (AI spots unusual trends), *Explain* (plain-language reasons) and *Act* (alert and action plan). An AstroHealth agent lets astronauts ask "What should I do?" and get a clear plan back.

*Benefits*

•⁠ ⁠*Early warning:* it catches trends before symptoms appear.

•⁠ ⁠*Explainable:* every alert shows its reason, so crews and doctors can trust it.

•⁠ ⁠*Autonomous:* on-board AI works offline when Earth is up to 22 minutes away one way.

•⁠ ⁠*Connected:* it fuses signals that would otherwise be isolated warnings.

•⁠ ⁠*Low barrier:* it needs no flight hardware to build and test.

*Intended impact*

We want healthier astronauts and safer missions. As crews travel farther, they need to detect and respond to health problems themselves, without waiting for Mission Control. The same approach could also support remote and extreme-environment healthcare on Earth (my inference, not in the deck).

*Tools, languages and software*

•⁠ ⁠*Frontend:* React and TypeScript

•⁠ ⁠*Backend:* a Python API

•⁠ ⁠*AI:* Claude AI, plus an on-device agent for offline use

•⁠ ⁠*Data:* NASA open APIs: OSDR (astronaut studies OSD-379 and OSD-137 for healthy baselines), DONKI (solar storm alerts for radiation and spacewalk risk), FIRMS (active-fire data to calibrate cabin fire detection) and the NASA Image & Video Library (mission imagery)

•⁠ ⁠*Hardware:* none yet. Telemetry is simulated, and the roadmap is to connect real wearables.

*What makes it creative*

•⁠ ⁠It combines health monitoring, space weather and fire detection in one risk picture.

•⁠ ⁠It uses NASA open data for calibration, so there is no hardware dependency.

•⁠ ⁠It pairs an explainable alert system with a conversational agent that gives action plans, not just numbers.

•⁠ ⁠It is designed to run offline for deep space.

*Factors the team considered*

•⁠ ⁠*Communication delay:* the system must work without Earth.

•⁠ ⁠*Trust:* the AI has to explain itself.

•⁠ ⁠*Integration:* alerts should be linked, not siloed.

•⁠ ⁠*Honesty about limits:* the prototype uses simulated data.

•⁠ ⁠*Validation:* next steps are testing accuracy against OSDR studies and reviewing alerts with flight surgeons.

•⁠ ⁠*Real-world readiness:* connecting actual wearables is the final step.

projectDetails.name: Lunar Ops
projectDetails.summary:
Lunar Ops is an interactive lunar outpost monitoring and survival simulation platform designed to explore the challenges of sustaining human operations on the Moon. It combines a mission-control-style dashboard, a ten-day survival simulation, and a NASA space-weather intelligence interface in one application.

Users can monitor life-support resources, crew status, equipment condition, and mission events while making decisions that affect the survival simulation. The NASA Data Intelligence module presents space-weather observations from NASA's DONKI services alongside archived event data, timelines, visualizations, and source references.

By connecting resource-management challenges with real NASA space-weather information, Lunar Ops makes lunar mission risks easier to explore and understand. It is an educational prototype that encourages awareness of crew safety, resource sustainability, and the importance of space-weather monitoring during future lunar exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Lunar Ops is built as a React-based web application with two connected but distinct experiences.

Mission monitoring: The dashboard provides dedicated views for life support, crew, systems, and mission logs. It presents resource levels, equipment condition, crew status, and mission information in a unified interface.

Survival simulation: A deterministic ten-day simulation lets users make operational decisions while managing illustrative oxygen, water, food, power, equipment condition, and crew safety. Decisions and events influence mission outcomes and the final score.

NASA Data Intelligence: The application retrieves space-weather event information from NASA's DONKI services, including CME, GST, SEP, and IPS categories. It provides event timelines, details, visualizations, source references, archived replay data, and offline access. NASA observations are presented separately from the fictional survival simulation; they do not automatically alter simulation resources.

The project uses JavaScript, React, Vite, Lucide React, Recharts, and Framer Motion. Its NASA data integration includes a server-side API layer with validation, error handling, caching, and provenance information.

Lunar Ops aims to make lunar outpost resource management and space-weather awareness accessible through an interactive educational prototype. All simulation values are illustrative and are not operational NASA mission data.

projectDetails.name: IGNIS-0G: The Six-Inch Microgravity Combustion Simulator
projectDetails.summary:
On Earth, NASA-STD-6001B certifies spacecraft materials using a six-inch vertical flame test governed by buoyancy-driven convection—where hot exhaust rises and pulls fresh oxygen into the flame. In microgravity (0g) and lunar gravity (0.16g), buoyancy vanishes, creating a critical fire-safety blind spot: flames collapse into oxygen-starved spheres sustained by subtle cabin ventilation, while low-temperature "cool flames" burn invisibly to the naked eye.

IGNIS-0G is an interactive microgravity combustion and spacecraft certification simulator grounded in 16 empirical flight datasets and 24 investigations from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository. Engineers and students can test materials across Earth, Lunar, and ISS cabin atmospheres (including Artemis 34% O2 / 56.5 kPa conditions), visualize real-time Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) U-curves, inspect invisible FLEX droplet cool flames via a simulated Thermal IR camera, audit flight certification margins, and query a NASA PSI citation copilot—complete with a hands-free 6-act Autopilot simulation.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES & HOW IT WORKS

IGNIS-0G bridges the gap between standard 1g terrestrial material screening and real low-gravity spacecraft fire behavior through six interactive telemetry modules:

1. Gravity & Buoyancy Morphing: Compares 1.00g Earth teardrop flames against 0.16g Lunar and 0.00g orbital spherical diffusion flames.

2. Cabin Atmosphere & U-Curve Oscilloscope: Models Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) and flame spread rates across varying O2 percentages, cabin pressures (kPa), and forced ventilation airflows (cm/s), including the Artemis Exploration Atmosphere (34% O2, 56.5 kPa).

3. Six-Inch Material Strip Burn Test: Benchmarks aerospace polymers and fabrics (Nomex, Kapton, Ultem, Silicone, Cotton) against NASA-STD-6001B pass/fail thresholds.

4. Lunar Certification Audit: Evaluates multi-zone bulkhead safety margins before clearing a cabin configuration for lunar flight.

5. Thermal IR Cool-Flame & Smoke Aerosol Detection: Toggles an infrared camera mode to expose low-temperature alkane cool flames (FLEX) invisible to standard optical sensors, paired with smoke particulate sizing (SAME).

6. NASA PSI Research Copilot & 6-Act Autopilot: Ranks citations across 24 NASA PSI flight investigations and provides a one-click "Run Simulation" virtual-cursor tour for rapid judge evaluation.

BENEFITS, IMPACT & CREATIVITY

- Replaces static PDF tables with a tactile, real-time mission telemetry deck so engineers, safety reviewers, and students can immediately see why materials passing Earth tests can fail in enriched-oxygen lunar cabins.

- Combines deterministic empirical physics equations with a zero-dependency retro-CRT GameBoy interface and hands-free virtual cursor demo.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES & ACCESSIBILITY / COST FACTORS

- Tech Stack: Zero-dependency Vanilla JavaScript (ES6 Modules), HTML5 Canvas 2D physics rendering, Web Audio API telemetry synthesis, and custom CSS3 styling.

- Cost & Accessibility: 100% browser-based with zero backend server costs, sub-second load times, offline-capable empirical JSON datasets, and keyboard/screen-friendly tactile controls.

- Live App: https://ignis-dusky.vercel.app/ | Source Code & Physics Whitepaper: https://github.com/Awwad-007/IGNIS

challengeDetails.title: Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data

projectDetails.name: LUNA-SCOPE
projectDetails.summary:
LUNA-SCOPE is a lunar landing-site analysis and decision-support prototype developed by Team TechTrivonix for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It helps mission planners compare potential lunar landing locations by evaluating sunlight availability, Earth visibility, and terrain characteristics.

The project uses NASA JPL Horizons to calculate the Sun's and Earth's azimuth and elevation, along with seven-day visibility estimates. It uses NASA LOLA (Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter) Digital Elevation Models to analyze lunar surface elevation and terrain slope.

The backend is developed using Python and FastAPI, while the interactive dashboard uses Streamlit and Plotly to display environmental indicators, terrain measurements, and landing-site comparisons.

A preliminary weighted scoring model combines sunlight, Earth visibility, terrain slope, and elevation variation to generate a suitability score for each location.

The goal is to provide a visual, data-driven tool that supports lunar landing-site evaluation and helps identify locations with potentially favourable environmental and terrain conditions.

Team Tech Trivonix : Prashant (Backend), Anant (Frontend), Praveen (AI/ML), and Sakshi (Research).
projectDetails.details:
LUNA-SCOPE is a project developed by our team, TECHTRIVONIX, for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our main idea is to make it easier to identify and compare suitable landing locations on the Moon.

The project provides an interactive dashboard where users can explore different lunar landing sites and understand important factors such as sunlight availability, Earth visibility, terrain slope and overall site suitability.

One of the main features we are developing is Terrain-Aware Horizon Analysis. Sometimes the Sun or Earth may be above the geometric horizon, but nearby mountains or crater rims can block the actual view. Our system aims to identify these obstructions and show which directions have a clearer view. It will also provide a 360-degree view of the surrounding terrain.

We are using Python, Streamlit and Plotly for the frontend and visualizations. Our planned backend uses FastAPI, NumPy and Rasterio. For data, we are working with NASA's LOLA lunar elevation data and JPL Horizons.

What makes LUNA-SCOPE different is that it combines terrain analysis and astronomical visibility in one platform instead of looking at these factors separately.

While developing the project, we considered terrain elevation, slope, sunlight conditions, Earth visibility, data accuracy and the challenges of working with lunar surface data.

Our aim is to help make lunar landing-site evaluation easier to understand and support better-informed decisions for future lunar exploration missions.
