projectDetails.name: NABD: Daily Health Check-ins for Astronauts Far From Earth
projectDetails.summary: NABD ("pulse" in Arabic) is a daily health check-in for astronauts on missions too far from Earth to call a doctor, built for the challenge "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions". In 4 minutes, a phone reads the astronaut's face, voice and reaction time, compares them with her own normal, and gives four readiness scores with one concrete step for today. It adds a body map grounded in NASA's human spaceflight risks, an AI doctor that works with the ship's medical kit and flags emergencies even offline, private women's health tracking, and family contact. Mission Control and the flight surgeon each see only what their role needs. It matters because small changes in sleep, mood and health build up quietly, and astronauts often don't report them; NABD catches them early. It is also useful anywhere help is far away.
projectDetails.details:
TRY IT: https://nabd-nasa-space-apps.vercel.app (best on a phone; on a laptop use Chrome → Inspect → device mode for the crew app. Mission Control and the flight surgeon are designed for laptops.)

Crew: tap Sara Haddad, PIN 1404 (also Adam 2201, Mei 3302, Lucas 4403). Mission Control: any email and password. Flight surgeon: after Mission Control, go to /surgeon. Family: /send. Code: https://github.com/malakanwarr/Nabd-NASA-Space-Apps

NABD (نبض, "pulse" in Arabic) is a daily health check-in for astronauts who are too far from Earth to call a doctor. Team MoonWalkerz · NASA Space Apps Cairo 2026 · Challenge: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions.

THE PROBLEM

On a Mars mission a message to Earth takes up to 20 minutes each way. The flight surgeon cannot see the crew every day, and NASA notes that astronauts can be reluctant to report when they are struggling. Small changes in sleep, mood, bone and heart build up quietly until they become a problem.

WHAT EXACTLY DOES IT DO?

NABD is one web app (installable on a phone, works offline) with four views, each built for one person's job:

- Crew member: a 4-minute morning check-in that reads her face (blink rate, eyelid openness, smiles), her voice (loudness, pitch range, pauses, pace) and her reactions (the Pollen catch game, based on NASA's vigilance test), plus six sleep questions. NABD compares every number with her own normal and returns four separate scores, never one diagnosis: cognitive readiness, physical readiness, sleep recovery and emotional wellbeing. Each is shown as Stable, Watch or Act, with the reason, a 7-day trend and one next step.

- Body map: a clickable astronaut with eight body systems (bones and muscles, mind and sleep, kidneys, heart, eyes, immune system, radiation, cycle). Each shows what it does, why space affects it and its NASA hazard, her own numbers and trend, what to do today, and when to get help.

- Act on it: "Adjust my workout" builds a plan from her muscle strength, energy and cycle, and a muscle "twin" does every move with her. Guided measurements (for example blood sugar) explain how to measure in space and what the result means.

- AI doctor that works without Earth: answers with her own data and the ship's medical kit, cites NASA research, never diagnoses, and shows an emergency banner with "Call the crew medical officer" for danger signs, checked before the AI is even called. She decides which answers go to her flight surgeon.

- No male default: private cycle tracking or period suppression that adjusts what counts as normal for each phase. Only she sees it.

- Habitat garden: sleep, water, exercise, vitamin D and mood become plants that grow or droop.

- Family: relatives hold one button to send a hug that makes her phone buzz, and see only her heartbeat and a simple mood. She has a "window home" with her family's avatars and messages.

- Mission Control (laptop): every crew member's status, readiness, last check-in and alerts, with filters and "add crew member". It never sees cycle data, face or voice details, or AI doctor chats.

- Flight surgeon (laptop): vitals, allergies and the AI doctor's notes with their send and arrival times, the cycle summary only with consent, and replies that show "reaches the ship in about 18 minutes".

HOW DOES IT WORK?

- On the phone, offline: Google MediaPipe Face Landmarker runs in the browser and turns about 10 frames a second into three numbers; the voice check (Meyda and pitchy) keeps four numbers from the first word to the last. Video and audio never leave the phone.

- Her own baseline: each score drops by how far each signal moves in the "tired" direction, weighted, with missing signals dropped and the rest reweighted. It reproduces all six days of our sample astronaut's history exactly (84, 82, 83, 74, 70, 66).

- AI doctor: Google Gemini with a summary of her data and a knowledge base built from NASA Human Research Program material; red flags are checked on the server first; safe fallback if the AI is unavailable.

- One React app and one Node/Express server with MongoDB, deployed on Vercel. The signed-in role (crew, Mission Control, flight surgeon, family) decides every page and every API answer.

WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?

- The astronaut notices slow changes she might not report, and gets a concrete step for today.

- Mission Control sees who needs attention at a glance; the flight surgeon gets useful notes despite the delay.

- Privacy by design: each role sees only what it should.

- Beyond Mars: anyone far from a doctor (polar stations, ships, remote communities) needs only a phone.

HOW WE TESTED IT

- Energy score matches all six sample days of our fictional astronaut.

- Fatigue experiment: we tested NABD on one team member, on Friday afternoon (her baseline) and again on Saturday morning after a 13-hour hackathon day and about 6 hours of sleep. Against her own normal, NABD labelled the second check-in "tired" (72 vs. 84): 6 of 8 signals moved in the tired direction, led by smiling (-80%) and voice pitch range (-62%).

- AI doctor safety tests: 10 scripted questions, each run twice; 10 of 10 passed both runs. Chest pain and low oxygen always gave the emergency answer first; it refused amoxicillin (penicillin allergy) and doses above the label; it linked symptoms to her own data and cited NASA correctly. The emergency word check, which works without the AI, was 20 of 20 correct with no false alarms. Offline mode gave 3 of 3 safe answers in 0.2 seconds.

- Face, voice and game check-in tested on iPhone over HTTPS.

Limits: a prototype, not a medical device; thresholds need clinical testing. Sara's history is fictional sample data, with vitals and sleep standing in for the wearables crews already wear; the check-in, game, AI doctor and hugs are live. Sign-in is simulated. The fatigue test is one person, one night and a different time of day: a first signal, not proof.

WHAT DO WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE?

Test with analog crews (HERA, Antarctic stations), run the AI doctor on the spacecraft with a local model, connect real wearables, and review every threshold with flight surgeons.

INTENDED IMPACT

Catch health changes days before they become a problem, when no doctor is in reach, and give the crew, Mission Control and the flight surgeon the right picture without overloading or exposing anyone. The same phone-only check-in can serve polar stations, ships and remote communities on Earth.

HOW IS IT CREATIVE?

- No wearables or lab needed: a 4-minute check-in on any phone reads fatigue from face, voice and a reaction game.

- Compared with HER normal, not a population average, and never one diagnosis: four scores, each with a reason and one step.

- An AI doctor designed for 20-minute delays: it uses only the ship's kit, cites NASA, and catches emergencies with a keyword check before the AI and even offline.

- No male default: the cycle adjusts what counts as normal, privately.

- Human touches that matter on long missions: a garden that grows with healthy habits, and family hugs that make her phone buzz.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Privacy: video and audio never leave the phone, and each role sees only what it should (Mission Control never sees cycle, face/voice details or AI chats; the surgeon sees the cycle only with consent).

- Safety: no diagnosis, label doses only, allergy checks, emergency escalation to the crew medical officer, and a tested offline fallback.

- Communication delay and no internet: works offline; surgeon replies show their arrival time.

- Under-reporting: a short, friendly daily routine instead of asking astronauts to report problems.

- Women's health and the fact that crews differ: personal baselines and cycle-aware norms.

- Honesty: we label sample data, simulated sign-in and the limits of our small tests.

TOOLS

React, Vite, React Router, vite-plugin-pwa, Recharts · Google MediaPipe Face Landmarker, Web Audio API, Meyda, pitchy · Node.js, Express, MongoDB Atlas, Mongoose, Vercel · Google Gemini API · JavaScript, HTML, CSS · Hardware: any phone with a camera and microphone, and a laptop. AI assistance: Claude and Claude Code (planning, design, code), Gemini (AI doctor), Manus (documents); all ideas and decisions are the team's.

projectDetails.name: Sonata
projectDetails.summary:
SONATA (Earth Information Jukebox) is a web app that turns NASA’s ECCO2 ocean model data into music, so people can hear the ocean instead of only looking at it. Each ocean metric is mapped to its own instrument, and users can toggle instruments on and off to hear how different measurements change across place and time.

It addresses the challenge by making complex Earth data approachable through sound. A scientific mode keeps the audio faithful to the data. A separate fun mode allows freer tuning and instruments, and lets users bring in their own musical taste. Users can choose a location and share what they hear as a short clip.

It matters because most ocean data is locked behind charts and maps. SONATA treats visually impaired users as a primary audience, with keyboard and screen reader access, a live data readout, audio cues, panning, and text equivalents, and it passes accessibility checks with zero violations. Sound makes ocean change easier to understand for everyone.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

SONATA turns NASA’s ECCO2 ocean model data into sound. Each ocean metric [confirm which, e.g. temperature, salinity, currents, sea surface height] is mapped to its own instrument, and users can toggle instruments on and off to hear how different measurements change across place and time. A scientific mode keeps the audio faithful to the data. A separate fun mode allows freer tuning and instrument choices, and lets users select or import music they like to shape the output. Users can pick a location, hear its ocean data, and share the result as a clip, card, or animation.

Benefits

  • Makes dense ocean data easier to grasp by ear, without needing to read charts or maps.
  • Works for curious people with no science background and for visually impaired users.
  • Lets people connect to ocean change in a personal way, through a place they know or music they like.
  • Gives everyone a shareable output, so the data spreads beyond the app.

Intended impact

We want more people to engage with NASA ocean data and understand what it says about a changing planet. Treating visually impaired users as a primary audience widens who can access this data at all. A clip someone can send to a friend turns a single visit into a conversation about the ocean and climate.

Tools and technology

  • Data: NASA’s ECCO2 ocean model
  • Development: mostly AI-assisted (vibe-coded), starting once the UI/UX design was ready
  • Hosting: sonata.manus.space

  • [Add framework, language, and audio engine, e.g. Web Audio API, if that is what you used]
  • [Add the design and video tools used by the UI/UX and motion graphics members]

Creativity

  • Sonification of a global ocean model, with one instrument per metric that users can mix like a band.
  • Two modes, so scientific accuracy and playful exploration each get what they need.
  • “Local” works at two levels: local to a place and local to a person’s own musical taste.
  • Accessibility is built into the core experience through keyboard and screen reader access, a live readout, audio cues, panning, and text equivalents.

Factors the team considered

  • Audience: a core experience for curious people first, with visually impaired users as a second priority but a primary group.
  • Scientific integrity: culture and personal taste must never distort the data-driven audio, which is why they live only in fun mode. We dropped the maqam idea for this reason and because judges may not be invested in Arabic music.
  • Team skills: we have no musician, so the design had to work without deep musical expertise.
  • Scope and time: we restarted the core engine from scratch to get a presentable demo on a clear dataset within the hackathon window.

Space Tales: Chronicles of the Cosmos

Space Tales is an interactive educational web application that brings the forgotten history of space exploration back to life. It explores 13 historic space missions and their equipment, including Apollo 11, Surveyor 1, Viking, and Voyager.

Through engaging first-person storytelling, audio narration, and educational visuals, users discover the journeys, achievements, and historical significance of spacecraft and scientific equipment left behind after their missions.

The platform combines four interactive experiences: Story Mode, an educational Mars Rover Game, a Space Quiz, and an Exploration Gallery featuring historical facts and AI-generated image prompts.

By combining storytelling, gamification, and authentic NASA mission information, Space Tales makes space history accessible and engaging, encourages scientific curiosity, and inspires young learners to explore space.

projectDetails.details:
Project Name

Space Tales: Chronicles of the Cosmos

Project Summary

Space Tales is an interactive, gamified educational web application designed to bring the forgotten history of space exploration back to life.

Throughout decades of space exploration, numerous robotic spacecraft, scientific instruments, and exploration vehicles have completed their missions and remained on the Moon, Mars, and beyond. Although these machines played important roles in advancing our understanding of space, their stories are often overlooked.

Space Tales transforms this forgotten space history into an engaging educational experience by combining storytelling, authentic NASA mission information, interactive games, quizzes, audio-visual content, and creative exploration.

Our mission is to make space history more accessible, exciting, and memorable, especially for young learners and future space explorers.

Detailed Description

1. What It Does

Space Tales takes users on an interactive journey through 13 historic space missions and their equipment, including missions such as Apollo 11, Surveyor 1, Viking, and Voyager.

Each featured mission introduces users to the spacecraft's journey, purpose, achievements, and historical significance through engaging first-person storytelling, educational information, and visual content inspired by real space exploration history.

Rather than presenting facts as ordinary textbook material, Space Tales turns each mission into a story waiting to be discovered.

2. How It Works

The platform combines four main interactive experiences:

A. Interactive Story Mode

Users can explore 13 historic space missions through engaging, child-friendly narratives written from the perspective of the spacecraft itself. Audio narration and visual elements help bring each mission's journey and scientific importance to life.

B. Interactive Rover Game

An educational mini-game where players guide a Mars rover across a grid, collect scientific samples, avoid obstacles, and manage battery power. The game includes score tracking and visual feedback, introducing basic concepts of planetary exploration through play.

C. Space Quiz

An interactive quiz that tests users' knowledge of space missions and equipment. Players answer questions based on the stories and educational content, earn stars, and track their scores while learning.

D. Exploration Gallery & AI Image Prompts

A visual gallery featuring mission cards, historical facts, and creative AI image prompts that help users imagine and visualize important moments in space exploration.

3. Benefits and Impact

Space Tales aims to transform overlooked space exploration history into an exciting educational opportunity.

By combining storytelling, interactive learning, and gamification, the platform:

- Makes complex space history easier for young learners to understand.

- Encourages curiosity about science, technology, and space exploration.

- Introduces users to real NASA missions and the equipment behind them.

- Promotes active learning through games, quizzes, and exploration.

- Helps preserve the stories and historical significance of space equipment left behind after missions.

Our goal is to remind people that even when a space mission ends, the discoveries, achievements, and stories behind it deserve to be remembered.

4. Tools and Technologies

The project was developed using:

- HTML5 – Web application structure.

- CSS3 – Styling, animations, and responsive space-themed design.

- JavaScript (ES6+) – Interactive features, games, and application functionality.

- Web Audio API – Audio-related functionality.

- LocalStorage – Saving user progress and scores.

The educational content is based on research from authoritative NASA resources, including NASA's National Space Science Data Center (NSSDC), NASA History Office, and NASA Image and Video Library (images.nasa.gov).

5. Artificial Intelligence (AI) Disclosure

Generative AI tools were used as supporting technologies throughout the development of Space Tales.

AI assisted our team in creative brainstorming, refining educational storytelling, developing visual concepts and image prompts, and supporting parts of the development process.

All AI-assisted content was reviewed and adapted by the team to maintain educational clarity and consistency with verified historical information from NASA sources.

AI served as a supporting tool in our creative and development workflow, while the project concept, decisions, integration, and final implementation were guided and reviewed by Team MYAHY.

projectDetails.name: Health_E
projectDetails.summary:
HEALTH_E is a browser-based educational prototype developed by Team METH for the Astronauts Health challenge. It brings together three experiences: a seven-stage interactive space-health narrative, a dashboard for manually entering selected health indicators, and a CSV analyzer that plots heart rate, SpO₂, body temperature, and cabin CO₂, with rule-based anomaly flags.
The project responds to the challenge by showing how mission-relevant health information could be presented in a visual interface for crew review. This matters because long-duration missions expose astronauts to health hazards, while distance from Earth can make clear communication especially important. HEALTH_E demonstrates a possible way to explore health topics and sample indicators together; it is not a validated medical tool. Its sample data and hard-coded rules should not be used to make care decisions.
projectDetails.details:
HEALTH_E is a browser-based educational prototype with three complementary modules. Its seven-stage narrative includes Explorer and Science modes and an interactive 3D scene to introduce spaceflight-health topics. The monitoring page lets users enter 11 selected indicators—such as heart rate, blood pressure, body-mass change, sleep and reaction time—and displays summary cards, charts and rule-triggered messages. Its built-in scenarios are synthetic examples. The analysis page accepts a user-selected CSV containing a time field and heart rate, SpO₂, body temperature and cabin CO₂; it plots the values and flags observations using programmed limits and a rolling statistical check. These pages do not share a medical record or connect to live sensors.

The prototype aims to make selected health topics and sample indicators easier to explore and review. Its creative approach is to pair an interactive educational narrative with separate, practical-looking monitoring and telemetry demonstrations. This may support awareness and discussion, but no usability study or health benefit has been measured.

The supplied project uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Three.js and GLTFLoader for 3D content and browser-side charts and CSV handling. No dedicated medical hardware or live sensor integration is documented. Design considerations included spaceflight hazards, clarity of information, and distinguishing synthetic examples and software flags from clinical findings. Thresholds and messages are not clinically validated, so they should not guide treatment or operational decisions.

projectDetails.summary:
STILL LISTENING
3D Sci-Fi Action & Adventure Game | 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge

We developed STILL LISTENING, a 3D sci-fi action-adventure game inspired by NASA’s 2026 Space Apps Challenge: Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA’s Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars.

Players battle alien creatures across extraterrestrial worlds to free abandoned NASA spacecraft and bring them back to life. Meticulously modeled after real NASA hardware, each liberated machine shares its history, original purpose, and scientific achievements—directly addressing the challenge by giving forgotten equipment a voice, identity, and emotional bond with players.

Immersive sound effects and dynamic voiceovers accompany every action. Players personalize their journey by naming and customizing both their avatar and spacecraft, while progressive difficulty levels welcome all ages and skill levels. Each stage features a distinct 3D celestial environment where gravity, climate, and terrain directly shape movement, mechanics, and mission challenges.

An integrated AI Agent powered by NASA’s database lets players explore verified space history, alongside in-game trivia unlocking bonus points and rewards. This matters because it turns passive history into hands-on learning—teaching real planetary physics, inspiring curiosity for space exploration, and ensuring these silent pioneers are never forgotten.

STILL LISTENING — Every machine has a story worth hearing.
projectDetails.details:
N1 Solution

STILL LISTENING is an interactive 3D browser game built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Its purpose is to make space history engaging and accessible by turning retired NASA hardware on the Moon and Mars—specifically Apollo 11 Eagle, Surveyor 3, Viking 1, Ingenuity, and Opportunity—into the central focus of a playable rescue mission rather than passive archival entries.

How does it Work:

Players start by setting up a profile (name, age, avatar, rover choice, and difficulty mode). They then drive across two distinct 3D environments—the Moon and Mars—to defend stranded NASA landers and rovers from enemy scavengers and reconnect them into a communication relay chain. Each environment alters gameplay mechanics: the Moon features low-gravity jumps and ground-based enemies, while Mars introduces dust storms, seismic shockwaves, and slope-tilt hazards. Rescuing each spacecraft unlocks a visual hologram card with verified NASA mission facts, synthesized audio/voice narration, a quick trivia check, and an interactive in-game Q&A archive (AURA) where players can explore each machine's history.

Benefits of the Game

  • Bite-Sized STEM Education: Presents real NASA landing coordinates, mission timelines, and discoveries through clean visual stat cards and trivia instead of dense text.
  • Story-Driven Engagement: Connects players emotionally to the real history of NASA's retired missions—culminating in Opportunity reactivating to restore the final signal.
  • Easy Access & Playability: Runs directly in a standard web browser with no installation required, offering three difficulty levels (Cadet, Ranger, Commander) and assisted laser targeting so players of different ages can play smoothly.

Our Goal

Our goal is to preserve the legacy of NASA’s abandoned lunar and Martian explorers through interactive storytelling—sparking curiosity about planetary science and inspiring players to learn more about the real missions that paved the way for future space exploration.

Tools and Technologies Used

  • Coding Languages & Web Technologies:
    • HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript (ES6+): Core game logic, UI overlays, state management, and interactive Q&A archive.
    • Three.js (WebGL): Real-time 3D terrain generation, lighting, particle dust effects, rover movement, and spacecraft models.
    • Web Audio API & Web Speech API: Browser-native synthesized sound effects (lasers, explosions, radio chimes) and voice narration.
    • NASA Science Mission Archives (science.nasa.gov): Verified mission timelines, landing coordinates, hardware specifications, and historical discoveries for Apollo 11, Surveyor 3, Viking 1, Ingenuity, and Opportunity.
    • Design: Used to brainstorm mission pacing, structure clear UI/UX layouts for the hologram data cards, and generate visual/audio clips for our 30-second demo video.
    • Implementation Guidance: Used to structure the Three.js scene setup, implement gravity and slope-tilt variables, and organize verified NASA facts into interactive in-game Q&A prompts.
    • Debugging Assistance: Used to resolve Three.js CDN loading fallbacks, refine laser-to-target collision detection, and fix browser audio/speech compatibility issues.

projectDetails.name: NABA'
projectDetails.summary:
Naba (نبأ, Arabic for “news”) is a newsroom for the Earth. It turns measurements from NISAR, the new NASA–ISRO L-band radar satellite, into short news stories on an interactive 3D globe. Each story gives a headline, a place, one measured number, a chart over time, possible causes, why it matters, and what to check next.
Radar sees through cloud and smoke, day and night, but its images are hard for non-specialists to read. Our Python pipeline, covered by 51 automated tests, streams only the small part of each NISAR product that covers a site, measures the change, and writes it as a plain-language story. Today Naba shows seven measured stories: a magnitude 7.7 earthquake in Panama, two wildfire burn scars in the USA, and wetland water changes at Lake Manzala (Egypt), the Okavango Delta (Botswana) and the Everglades (USA).
For the “Dancing with the SARs” challenge, Naba makes SAR data understandable to the public, journalists, teachers and local decision makers, starting with Egypt’s own Nile Delta.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

Naba turns NISAR radar measurements into news. Open the site and you see a dark 3D globe with coloured pins. Each pin is a story about a real place where NISAR measured a change. Click a pin and the globe flies there. A panel shows the headline, the measured number, a chart with one point per radar pass, what is happening, possible causes (as possibilities, never as proof), why it matters, and what to check next. A slider steps through the radar passes or months, and “Compare dates” puts radar images from two dates side by side.

Try it (main task)

1.    Open the website. Watch the 24-second narrated intro, or skip it.

2.    Take the guided tour. It shows an earthquake (Panama), a flood pulse (Okavango) and a wildfire (Big Sur) in under a minute.

3.    Click the red pin in California (“Radar maps a burn scar of about 31 km² in Big Sur”).

4.    Drag the slider from 16 August to 15 October and watch the burn scar appear pass by pass.

5.    Press “Compare dates” to see the radar false-colour image before and after the fire.

Direct link to one story: add /?story=plaskett-burn-scar to the site URL. Add /?demo=1 to autoplay the main path.

How it works

1.    Search. The Python pipeline (naba-data) queries NASA’s Common Metadata Repository for NISAR products over a site and period. Only metadata moves.

2.    Select. It keeps dual-polarisation (HH + HV) passes from one track, direction and frame, so every date is seen from the same angle and brightness can be compared.

3.    Stream. Each NISAR product is 4–6 GB. Naba uses HTTPS range requests to read only the HDF5 chunks over the site. For the two fires it read about 252 MB out of about 61 GB of products (0.4%). Every subset is cached as a GeoTIFF, so a re-run downloads nothing.

4.    Measure. Wetlands: each pixel is classed as open water (dark in HH and HV), flooded vegetation (bright HH, large HH−HV gap) or other, then composited per month. Fires: the HV signal of every pass is compared with the last pass before the fire; a drop of more than 3 dB is “likely burned” and 2–3 dB is “possibly burned”. Earthquakes: the unwrapped interferogram phase is converted to centimetres of ground motion along the satellite’s line of sight, keeping only pixels with coherence of 0.3 or more.

5.    Map. Class masks are turned into polygons with areas measured on the WGS84 ellipsoid, plus image frames for “Compare dates”.

6.    Tell. Each measurement is written as a story from fixed templates filled with the measured numbers. No language model writes the stories. Every number is traceable in provenance.json, which lists every granule, threshold, date and megabyte used.

The seven measured stories

Story

NISAR product and passes

Result

Earthquake, Azuero peninsula, Panama (M7.7, 9 Oct 2026)

GUNW interferogram, 2 Oct → 14 Oct 2026

Up to 1.16 m of line-of-sight motion; 11 fringes of 12 cm

Burn scar, Plaskett Fire, Big Sur, USA

GCOV, 6 passes, 16 Aug → 15 Oct 2026

31 km² likely + 15 km² possibly burned (reported fire size: 121 km²)

Burn scar, Everglades National Park, USA

GCOV, 6 passes, 20 Jul → 30 Sep 2026

19 km² likely + 30 km² possibly burned (reported: 97 km²)

Open water, Okavango Delta, Botswana

GCOV, 9 passes, Jun → Oct 2026

Open water fell from 48.0% to 14.3% of the area

Open water, Everglades, USA

GCOV, 10 passes, Jun → Oct 2026

Open water rose from 4.2% to 12.5%

Flooded vegetation, Everglades, USA

GCOV, 10 passes, Jun → Oct 2026

Rose from 4.4% to 8.4%

Flooded vegetation, Lake Manzala, Egypt

GCOV, 9 passes, Jun → Oct 2026

Rose slightly, from 2.4% to 2.6%

 

Tools and languages

•     Web app: TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL JS 5 (globe projection), Zustand, lucide-react icons.

•     Data pipeline: Python with earthaccess, h5py, fsspec/aiohttp, xarray, NumPy, SciPy, pandas, rasterio, pyproj, Shapely and Pillow. 51 automated tests (pytest) cover thresholds, burn tiers, polygon areas, story format and dataset merging; all pass.

•     Mixed reality (extra): Unity 6 with the Meta XR SDK, OpenXR and URP, for Meta Quest 3S. The same stories float on a globe in your room; tapping one unrolls it into a flat map with the radar layer.

Benefits and goals

•     Makes SAR readable by anyone: one headline, one number and a plain explanation, instead of a raw radar image.

•     Works when optical satellites cannot: through cloud, smoke and darkness.

•     Honest by design: every story lists causes as possibilities and says what to check next. Radar burn areas are shown next to the officially reported fire size.

•     Cheap to run: no backend, no API keys, and only the needed part of each product is read.

What works now, limits and next steps

Works now: the website with globe, story panel, charts, slider, Compare dates, narrated intro and guided tour, all seven stories measured from real NISAR data, the reproducible pipeline with its 51 passing tests, and the Quest version (built from the repo in Unity). All of it is in the public repo.

Limits: NISAR data is still PROVISIONAL. The wetland and burn classes are exploratory dB thresholds, not validated flood or burn-severity maps; wind on water, wet soil and look angle can move the numbers, so no story claims high confidence. Because only clear drops in the radar signal count as burned, the Big Sur scar we measure (31 km² likely burned) is well below the 121 km² reported fire. For the same reason, we call the Lake Manzala change (2.4% to 2.6%) small rather than treating it as a trend. Earthquake motion is along the line of sight only, from one pair. The globe shows simplified outlines, not full 20 m detail. The Quest version needs a headset and Unity to build.

Next: more sites through the same pipeline (more Egyptian sites first); validation against water gauges, official fire perimeters and GPS; a FastAPI + PostGIS service serving the same data (the frontend already supports it through one setting); and tiled rasters so the globe can zoom to full resolution.

Github repo Source Code: https://github.com/AhmedAshry7/naba

Use of AI

• Stories and numbers: no AI. Every story is filled in from fixed templates using the numbers the pipeline measures. No language model writes or changes them, and every value can be traced in provenance.json.

• Coding help: we used Claude as a coding assistant on parts of the web app and pipeline. The team reviewed every change, and the 51 tests check the results.

• Narration: the intro and tour voices are AI-generated with Microsoft neural text-to-speech (edge-tts), reading lines the team wrote.

projectDetails.name: Sols of Survival
projectDetails.summary: Welcome to Sols of Survival! For this NASA Space Apps challenge, we wanted more than a building game, so we made a survival adventure where every storm is real. Meet Nova, Cosmo, Rocket and Luna, four Space Kittens sent to run a tiny base on Mars. Their mission sounds simple: keep the crew alive for five Sols (a Sol is one day on Mars). But the Sun has other plans. Along the way, the crew faces events that really happened, like the giant sunspot of 2014, the 2017 solar storm that doubled radiation on Mars, the 2018 dust storm that silenced NASA's Opportunity rover, and the record-breaking storm of May 2024 measured by Curiosity. And this isn't just a story, it's you in charge. As the player, you pack the rocket, build the base and jump into hands-on missions like cleaning solar panels, melting ice for water and stacking bricks against radiation. Every choice helps one thing and costs another, just like it does for real mission planners. This is NASA space weather data like kids have never seen it before: not in charts or reports, but as a base they have to protect.
projectDetails.details:
Nah, We'd Win’s Project Solution

Sols of Survival is an educational survival game that teaches kids aged 7 to 12 what it really takes to keep a crew alive on Mars or the Moon, by turning real NASA space weather data into a story-driven base-building game. Players team up with a Space Kitten, build their own outpost, and use hands-on mini games to protect their crew from real solar storms, making space science both fun and easy to understand.

How Does Our Solution Work

In the game, four Space Kittens, Nova, Cosmo, Rocket and Luna, are sent to run a small base on Mars. The player picks one as their partner, packs a rocket with only 7 crates out of 11, and builds a base with Power Stations, Greenhouses, Water Stations, Radiation Shields and a Research Lab. Then they have to keep three bars above zero: Power, Life Support and Crew Health. Every Sol (one day on Mars), the base faces a space weather event that really happened, and the player spends 2 actions on hands-on missions before deciding how to face it.

  • A Calm Day (Mars, Sol 1):
    The crew lands on a quiet day, and the kitten shows the player around the base. But even calm days aren’t safe on Mars. NASA’s Curiosity rover measured about 0.67 millisieverts of radiation per day on the surface, so the crew’s health slowly drops every Sol. The player uses this day to build up their base before the storms arrive.
  • The Giant Sunspot (October 2014):
    Sunspot AR 2192, the biggest of its solar cycle, fires an X3.1 flare on 24 October 2014. It looks scary, but no cloud of particles comes toward the planet. Players who hide in the shelter lose a whole day of work for nothing, while players who did the Watch the Sun mission in the Research Lab already know the storm won’t follow. Through this, players learn that forecasting the Sun is hard and that good data changes everything.
  • The Storm That Reached the Ground (September 2017):
    On 10 September 2017, an X8.2 flare sends a particle storm across the solar system, and Curiosity measures radiation on the Martian surface at more than double anything it had seen before. In the gameplay, players protect the crew by choosing:
    Choice 1: Hide in the Radiation Shield bunker, which blocks most of the radiation but stops all work.
    Choice 2: Use a saved action to reinforce the walls.
    Choice 3: Keep working and take the risk.
    Players can also press Ask Earth, but Mars was on the far side of the Sun that day, so the reply takes 40 minutes and arrives after the storm hits. Through this, players learn why real crews on Mars have to make their own decisions.
  • The Dust Storm That Ended Opportunity (June 2018):
    A dust storm grows until it covers the whole planet, and sunlight drops so low that solar panels barely work. This is the same storm that silenced NASA’s Opportunity rover, which sent its last message on 10 June 2018. In the gameplay, players save their base by:
    Task 1: Rubbing the dust off the solar panels in the Dust Off the Panels mini game.
    Task 2: Connecting the right wires to charge the battery before the storm.
    Task 3: Deciding whether to power down the greenhouse or keep everything running.
    Through this, players discover that energy on Mars depends on the environment.
  • The Strongest Storm Ever Measured on Mars (May 2024):
    The final test. On 20 May 2024, a flare estimated at X12 sends the biggest burst of radiation Curiosity has ever recorded, 8,100 micrograys, which is about the same as 30 chest X-rays for an astronaut standing next to the rover. Everything the player built is tested at once: shields, shelter and stored power.
  • The Moon Base (Lunar Night and August 1972):
    Players can also choose the Moon’s south pole instead. There they face the lunar night, about 14 Earth days without sunlight, and the August 1972 solar storm that hit between the Apollo 16 and Apollo 17 missions. On the Moon, Earth answers in about a second, which shows kids how much distance changes everything.
  • Today’s Space Weather (Live NASA Data):
    In this mode, the game asks NASA’s DONKI database about the last 7 days of real solar activity and turns it into 3 Sols. If NASA can’t be reached, the game clearly switches to stored events and marks them OFFLINE, so stored data is never shown as live.

Every station also has 2 hands-on missions, and each one comes with a real science fact, from planting and harvesting crops (ISS astronauts first ate space-grown lettuce in 2015) to melting ice (Phoenix found ice on Mars in 2008), recycling water (the ISS recycles about 98% of its water) and stacking regolith bricks against radiation.

When the crew makes it through all five Sols, the kitten celebrates with a Certificate of Survival and a chart of everything that happened. If the crew doesn’t make it, there’s no “Game Over”. The kitten explains what went wrong and what to try next!

The game benefits

kids, students, teachers and families by:

  • Teaching how space weather, radiation and energy affect life on Mars and the Moon.
  • Showing that every engineering choice has a cost, using real events from NASA’s records.
  • Turning NASA’s open data into something kids can see, play and remember, instead of charts and reports.
  • Giving teachers a Family/Class mode with discussion questions and a printable debrief.

Our goal

To make NASA’s space weather data accessible and exciting for young kids, and to help them understand what real crews will face when they live on Mars and the Moon. Our game is a prototype, so bar sizes and station outputs are simplified to keep it playable, and the game says so on its “Real vs. Simplified” screen. We focused on solar storms, radiation and dust storms, and our game doesn’t yet cover other challenges like the long-term effects of space on the human body, which we’d like to add next using NASA’s space biology data.

Tools and Technologies Used

Coding Languages:

  • JavaScript, HTML and CSS → for the whole game, which runs in any browser with no account.
  • Web Audio API → for all the music and sound effects, made in code.

Data Sources:

  • NASA DONKI → for the real dates and strengths of our solar flares and particle storms, and for live space weather from the last 7 days.
  • NASA Open APIs → for the live DONKI connection, the Astronomy Picture of the Day on the title screen, and real Curiosity photos.
  • Curiosity RAD measurements and NASA mission news → for the real radiation numbers and the story behind each event.

Github Link:

https://github.com/2009abdr30-eng/Sols-Of-Survival

Use of AI:

Manus AI
How it was used: Used to structure the core game logic, state flow, and turn-by-turn resource trade-off mechanics. All scientific rules and numbers were verified by our team.
Claude (Anthropic)
How it was used: Used for writing and refactoring front-end HTML/CSS/JavaScript code and fixing gameplay bugs.
Google Flow (Google Labs)
How it was used: Used to generate initial 2D illustration drafts for our Space Kitten characters, isometric habitat buildings, station interiors, and event cards, which were then cropped, cleaned, and color-matched by the team.

projectDetails.name: X-Monitor
projectDetails.summary: AstroVitals OS (incorporating the Oslo Pulse Protocol v1.0) is an autonomous, 100% local-first hardware and software medical telemetry platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. During deep-space missions to the Moon and Mars, communication delays of up to 22 minutes one-way and periodic satellite blackouts prevent real-time reliance on Earth Flight Surgeons. AstroVitals OS empowers non-physician crews to monitor, interpret, and act on their vital signs autonomously.   Built with Next.js 16, TypeScript, and Zustand, the platform merges live Wi-Fi telemetry from a wearable ESP32 biometric node (MAX30102 optical Heart Rate, $\text{SpO}_2$, and Skin Temperature) with guided crew inputs for Blood Pressure, Blood Glucose, and Cabin $\text{CO}_2$. A Non-Terrestrial Network (NTN) layer encapsulates sensor streams into space-grade CCSDS frames and utilizes a Delay-Tolerant Networking (DTN) store-and-forward buffer so zero medical packets are lost during orbital blackouts.   Mapped directly to NASA’s 5 RIDGE Hazards, our adaptive risk engine dynamically recalibrates Green, Yellow, and Red thresholds across Spacecraft, Orbital Station, Rover, and Planetary Base modes—featuring an interactive 2D spacesuit scanner, microgravity measurement guides, a 10-second hypoxia cognitive reflex game, radiation dosimetry, and gamified XP countermeasure quests

projectDetails.name: Qamar Square
projectDetails.summary:
Qamar Square is an educational space game built for NASA Space Apps’ “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer” challenge. Players act as a Junior Astronaut running a lunar base through real life-support emergencies during the 14-day lunar night: power loss, extreme cold, a failing oxygen generator, and a clogged water recycler. Every choice maps to a real NASA engineering option, explained simply as what it does, why it helps, and what can go wrong, so playing means learning how astronauts and engineers actually make these trade-offs.

The team researched each subsystem against 56 NASA Technical Reports Server publications, peer-reviewed papers, and agency program pages, then ran a scientific-verification pass to correct early drafts and label every technology by its true maturity: flight-proven, ground-tested, or lab research only. Four AI tools supported the work: Claude Code and Codex built the game, ChatGPT checked research against submission guidelines, and Gemini AI Plus supported the demo, which the team recorded manually from real gameplay. The result turns dense engineering trade-offs into an interactive mission trainer that is scientifically accurate and genuinely fun to play.
projectDetails.details:
Qamar Square is a 2D browser-based educational lunar survival game designed for children aged 7–12, inspired by NASA’s Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge. Players take on the role of junior mission commanders, responsible for managing a lunar base and keeping its crew safe until sunrise.

The game consists of four connected challenges: Power & Food, Heat & Shelter, Oxygen, and Water & Waste. Players make decisions while managing limited resources, and each decision can affect the availability of resources in subsequent challenges. Through this experience, players learn how essential lunar-base systems work and how they depend on one another. The game also includes simplified scientific explanations and real examples from space exploration to connect gameplay with real science.

Benefits and Intended Impact: The project makes complex space-related concepts easier and more engaging for children. It encourages scientific curiosity, critical thinking, problem-solving, resource management, and responsible decision-making. Its main impact is to introduce young learners to the challenges of lunar exploration and demonstrate the importance of sustainability and interconnected life-support systems in future space missions.

Tools and Technologies: The project was developed using JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and SVG. We used Vite as the development and build tool, Node.js for the development environment, GitHub for version control and collaboration, and Vercel for deployment. The game runs in a web browser and does not require specialized hardware.

Creativity and Innovation: Qamar Square combines educational gaming with a realistic lunar-survival scenario. Rather than teaching each system independently, it connects power, temperature, oxygen, water, and waste management through decisions that have consequences throughout the mission. It transforms scientific concepts into interactive challenges while maintaining an age-appropriate experience.

Factors Considered: Our team considered the target age group, scientific accuracy, accessibility, interface simplicity, limited resources, and the consequences of player decisions. We also considered how to simplify complex scientific information without losing its essential meaning, and how to make the game accessible on different devices while keeping its educational purpose central to the experience.

projectDetails.name: Project NASA NUSC
projectDetails.summary:
NASA NUSC – Integrated Astronaut Health & Spacecraft Safety System

NASA NUSC is an integrated intelligent platform designed to enhance astronaut health and space mission safety through six interconnected systems:

- MIDCORE: Monitors astronauts' vital signs and detects health abnormalities.
- SPACE SHIELD: Monitors spacesuit and spacecraft conditions to identify potential malfunctions.
- RADIATION: Tracks radiation exposure and accumulated doses.
- GRAVITYFIT: Monitors the physical effects of microgravity on astronauts.
- CREW MIND: Supports mental well-being by tracking sleep, stress, and cognitive performance.
- LIFE SUPPORT: Monitors cabin air quality, oxygen, carbon dioxide, pressure, temperature, humidity, and water.

The platform also features an AI-powered assistant that allows astronauts to interact through voice or text, analyze system data, understand alerts, and receive protocol-based guidance.

Our mission is to move beyond monitoring toward intelligent, integrated space safety.
projectDetails.details: NASA NUSC Integrated Astronaut Health & Spacecraft Safety System 1. Project Overview NASA NUSC is an integrated intelligent platform designed to enhance astronaut health and ensure space mission safety, especially during long-duration space missions. The platform combines six specialized systems into one unified ecosystem, providing comprehensive monitoring of astronauts' health, spacesuit conditions, spacecraft systems, radiation exposure, physical and mental well-being, and cabin environmental conditions. It collects and analyzes data from multiple sources, detects abnormal indicators, generates alerts, and provides guidance to support astronauts and mission control teams in making informed decisions. 2. Problem Statement Astronauts face multiple interconnected risks during space missions, including: 1. Medical emergencies and unexpected health changes. 2. Spacesuit malfunctions and oxygen or pressure failures. 3. Spacecraft system malfunctions. 4. Exposure to harmful space radiation. 5. Microgravity effects on muscles, bones, cardiovascular health, and balance. 6. Psychological stress, sleep disturbances, and cognitive fatigue. 7. Environmental hazards involving air quality, water, and cabin conditions. These challenges are interconnected and cannot always be managed independently. Therefore, an integrated platform is needed to connect different monitoring systems and provide a comprehensive view of mission safety. 3. The Six Integrated Systems 1. MIDCORE – Astronaut Health Monitoring MIDCORE monitors astronauts' vital signs and tracks changes in their health conditions. Key functions: - Heart Rate Monitoring. - Blood Oxygen Saturation (SpO₂). - Body Temperature. - Respiratory Rate. - Blood Pressure. - Health Trend Analysis. - Abnormality Detection and Alerts. Its main objective is to identify unusual health indicators and support early awareness of potential medical concerns. 2. SPACE SHIELD – Spacesuit & Spacecraft Safety SPACE SHIELD monitors the operational condition of spacesuits and spacecraft systems. Key functions: - Spacesuit Pressure Monitoring. - Oxygen Level Monitoring. - Battery Status. - Temperature Monitoring. - Communication Status. - Spacecraft Telemetry Monitoring. - Potential Malfunction Detection. Its purpose is to identify potential equipment problems and provide alerts that support astronaut and mission safety. 3. RADIATION – Space Radiation Monitoring RADIATION tracks astronauts' exposure to space radiation and monitors accumulated radiation doses. Key functions: - Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCR) Monitoring. - Solar Particle Events (SPE) Monitoring. - Radiation Exposure Tracking. - Accumulated Radiation Dose Calculation. - Radiation Threshold Alerts. - Space Weather Data Integration. It helps astronauts and mission control teams understand radiation exposure and identify situations requiring attention. 4. GRAVITYFIT – Microgravity Adaptation GRAVITYFIT focuses on monitoring the physical effects of microgravity on astronauts during long-duration missions. Key functions: - Muscle Deterioration Monitoring. - Bone Health Tracking. - Cardiovascular Fitness Monitoring. - Balance and Coordination Tracking. - Exercise Monitoring. - Physical Adaptation Tracking. Its objective is to support astronauts in maintaining physical fitness and monitoring changes associated with prolonged exposure to microgravity. 5. CREW MIND – Mental & Cognitive Well-being CREW MIND focuses on astronauts' psychological and cognitive well-being. Key functions: - Sleep Monitoring. - Stress Level Tracking. - Mood Monitoring. - Fatigue Detection. - Circadian Rhythm Tracking. - Cognitive Performance Monitoring. - Mental Well-being Support. It aims to support psychological stability, concentration, and overall crew performance during space missions. 6. LIFE SUPPORT – Environmental Monitoring LIFE SUPPORT monitors environmental conditions inside the spacecraft to help maintain a safe and stable cabin environment. Key functions: - Oxygen (O₂) Monitoring. - Carbon Dioxide (CO₂) Monitoring. - Cabin Pressure Monitoring. - Temperature Monitoring. - Humidity Monitoring. - Air Quality Monitoring. - Water Quality Indicators. Its main objective is to monitor critical environmental parameters that directly affect astronauts' safety and comfort. 4. AI Assistant – Intelligent Interaction One of NASA NUSC's key features is its AI-powered assistant, which transforms the platform from a monitoring system into an interactive intelligent ecosystem. The AI Assistant allows astronauts to communicate through voice or text and access information across the six integrated systems. Key functions: - Natural Language Interaction: Communicating with astronauts through voice or text. - Health Analysis: Reviewing available health indicators and summarizing health information. - System Status Support: Providing information about spacesuit and spacecraft conditions. - Radiation Information: Explaining current exposure levels and accumulated doses. - Alert Summarization: Summarizing important warnings and system notifications. - Protocol-Based Guidance: Providing guidance based on established safety protocols. The AI Assistant helps astronauts understand complex system data through simple and accessible communication. It supports decision-making but does not replace medical professionals or certified spacecraft control systems. 5. How the Platform Works NASA NUSC follows an integrated workflow: Step 1 – Data Collection Collecting information from wearable devices, sensors, spacecraft telemetry, radiation dosimeters, and other available data sources. Step 2 – System Integration Distributing the collected data across the six specialized systems according to their functions. Step 3 – AI Analysis Analyzing available data, identifying abnormal indicators, recognizing potential risks, and generating understandable summaries. Step 4 – Smart Alerts Providing notifications when monitored parameters reach predefined warning thresholds or indicate potential problems. Step 5 – Guidance and Decision Support Delivering relevant information and protocol-based guidance to astronauts and mission control teams. 6. Target Users NASA NUSC is designed to support three main groups: - Astronauts: Monitoring personal health, equipment conditions, and environmental safety. - Mission Control Teams: Supervising astronaut conditions, spacecraft systems, and mission-related risks. - Space Mission Specialists: Supporting data analysis, risk assessment, and operational monitoring. 7. What Makes NASA NUSC Different? 1. System Integration: Combines six specialized monitoring systems within one unified platform. 2. Human-Centered Safety: Addresses astronaut health, equipment safety, and environmental conditions together. 3. AI-Powered Interaction: Provides an intelligent assistant that communicates through natural language. 4. Early Warning Support: Identifies abnormal indicators and generates relevant alerts. 5. Cross-System Analysis: Connects health, environmental, and operational information to provide a broader understanding of potential risks. 6. Unified Mission Awareness: Helps astronauts and mission control access multiple safety-related systems through one platform. 8. Future Vision Our vision is to develop NASA NUSC into a more advanced and fully integrated space safety platform capable of using real-time sensor data, improving risk analysis, strengthening communication between astronauts and mission control, and supporting safer and more sustainable long-duration space missions. 9. Project Mission NASA NUSC aims to move beyond traditional monitoring by connecting astronaut health, spacecraft safety, radiation protection, physical and mental well-being, and environmental monitoring in one intelligent ecosystem. Six Systems. One Mission. Beyond Monitoring. Towards Intelligent Space Safety. Protecting Astronauts. Supporting Missions. Exploring Beyond.

projectDetails.details:
3D solar system Explorer is an interactive, browser-based 3D visualization web application built using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js.

* Core Functionality: Users can explore a dynamic 3D model of the solar system by dragging to orbit, scrolling to zoom, and adjusting the orbital simulation speed (e.g., 1.0x).

* Interactive Inspection: Clicking on any planet, moon, or celestial body in 3D space—or selecting it via the navigation bar—opens an information panel displaying its classification (such as Terrestrial Planet), a brief description, and key planetary details.

* Architecture: Developed as a lightweight, single-file web app (index.html) designed for smooth, real-time 3D rendering directly in the browser without external backend dependencies.

[11:31 AM, 11/14/2026] Mazin Zabady: The 3D Solar System Explorer is an interactive, browser-based 3D visualization web application that simulates our solar system in real time. Users can freely navigate 3D space by dragging to orbit around celestial bodies, scrolling to zoom in and out, and dynamically adjusting the orbital simulation speed (e.g., 1.0x). Clicking on any planet, moon, or celestial body—or selecting it through the quick navigation bar—smoothly focuses the camera on that object and opens an educational side panel displaying its classification (such as Terrestrial Planet), core description, and planetary metrics.

Traditional 2D diagrams and textbooks often make it difficult for students and enthusiasts to grasp orbital mechanics, relative planetary positions, and spatial relationships in space. This project transforms astronomy education into an intuitive, hands-on experience. By making space exploration accessible directly through any standard web browser without requiring heavy installations or specialized hardware, it aims to inspire curiosity, enhance spatial understanding, and support STEM learning for students, educators, and space enthusiasts worldwide.

To develop this project, our team used HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript (ES6+), powered by the Three.js (WebGL) library for real-time 3D rendering, lighting, camera controls, and orbital animations, along with Google Fonts for clean UI typography. The entire application is built as a lightweight, self-contained single-file web app (index.html) hosted on OneApp for instant, zero-setup access across both desktop and mobile browsers without external backend dependencies.

What makes our project creative is the combination of scientific clarity with an engaging, game-like user interface. Key design factors our team considered include:

* Performance and Accessibility: Optimizing the codebase into a single lightweight file to ensure smooth frame rates and fast loading times on standard consumer devices.

* Intuitive User Experience (UX): Offering dual navigation so users can either explore freely in 3D space or jump directly between the 9 featured celestial bodies using a clean bottom navigation bar and live speed controller.

* Educational Clarity: Structuring the side information panel so complex astronomical details are presented in bite-sized, easy-to-read cards without cluttering the visual space.

projectDetails.name: TRUSTLINE
projectDetails.summary:
Space missions come with challenges that go far beyond reaching new destinations. Astronauts live in an environment where even small changes in their health can matter, and getting medical help from Earth is not always possible. That's why we developed TRUSTLINE.
TRUSTLINE is an AI-powered platform designed to help monitor astronaut health and make sense of the data collected during missions. It brings together health sensors, machine learning, medical documents, and specialized AI agents to analyze health signals, detect unusual patterns, and provide useful insights.
The platform also features a 3D human digital twin to visualize health data, an interactive dashboard, and a hybrid AI system that can continue supporting operations when communication with Earth is limited.
Our goal is simple: give astronauts and medical teams a clearer picture of what's happening, help them make better-informed decisions, and make health monitoring more reliable in one of the most challenging environments humans can explore.
projectDetails.details:
TRUSTLINE — Intelligent Astronaut Health Monitoring & Decision Support

TRUSTLINE is a research prototype designed to make astronaut health monitoring smarter, more connected, and more reliable during space missions. Our idea is to bring physiological data, medical knowledge, and AI-powered analysis together in one platform, helping astronauts and medical teams better understand changes in health conditions, especially when communication with Earth is limited.

How does it work?

TRUSTLINE collects and processes physiological signals such as heart rate, ECG, blood oxygen, skin temperature, respiration, EDA, and movement data. Its processing pipeline checks sensor quality before the data is used for further analysis.

The platform uses three specialized AI agents:

  • Sensor Quality Agent: Evaluates incoming signals and identifies missing, noisy, or potentially unreliable measurements.
  • Personal Health Agent: Analyzes health data in relation to an astronaut's personal baseline.
  • Risk Assessment Agent: Combines available evidence to identify potential concerns and support informed decisions.

A LangGraph Supervisor coordinates these agents. The system also includes machine learning for anomaly detection, medical document processing, and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), allowing relevant information to be retrieved from medical documents and presented with supporting evidence.

Benefits and intended impact

Our goal is to help astronauts and medical teams move beyond simply viewing sensor readings. TRUSTLINE aims to turn complex health data into clearer, evidence-supported insights. Its hybrid AI architecture is designed to support local processing and fallback capabilities when cloud services or communication with Earth become unavailable.

The platform also incorporates a 3D human digital twin concept to make physiological information easier to understand and connect different measurements to their corresponding body locations.

Technology and tools

We developed the AI and data-processing components primarily using Python, alongside FastAPI for backend services. Our technology stack includes:

  • AI and orchestration: LangGraph, LangChain, and specialized AI agents.
  • AI models and providers: Groq API, Hugging Face Inference API, and Ollama for local model execution.
  • Machine Learning: Scikit-learn and the WESAD dataset for physiological signal analysis and experimentation.
  • Medical intelligence: Groq Vision for document OCR and medical RAG pipelines.
  • Data and persistence: Structured data processing, SQLite-based storage, and evidence tracking.
  • Testing: Automated tests, regression testing, and simulated sensor scenarios.

Development and testing were carried out using an Apple Silicon Mac, with simulated physiological sensor data used to experiment with different conditions and system responses.

What makes TRUSTLINE creative?

What makes TRUSTLINE different is the way it combines multiple technologies into one health-monitoring workflow rather than relying on a single AI model. It connects signal-quality validation, personal health baselines, risk assessment, medical knowledge retrieval, and hybrid AI execution.

We also considered several important factors: limited communication with Earth, unreliable sensor readings, individual differences between astronauts, data privacy, uncertainty in AI-generated insights, and the importance of keeping simulated data separate from operational health information.

Ultimately, TRUSTLINE is built around one important idea: when astronauts are millions of kilometers away from Earth, understanding their health should never depend on a single data source, a single model, or a constant internet connection.

TRUSTLINE is a research prototype and is not clinically validated or approved for medical use.

projectDetails.name: Field Wise
projectDetails.summary:
We developed Field Shift, a bilingual Arabic/English agricultural decision-support website that helps farmers and agricultural advisors compare crop rotations in Egypt’s northern Nile Delta.
The prototype combines NASA rainfall, temperature, soil-moisture, terrain and Landsat observations with Sentinel-2 vegetation information and FAO/IIASA crop-suitability data. For a selected agricultural study cell, users can compare 13 crop-rotation options and adjust the importance of land suitability, modeled irrigation requirements and local agricultural practice. The dashboard presents ranked alternatives, component scores and historical environmental context, making the comparison transparent rather than providing an unexplained recommendation.
Field Shift addresses the challenge by turning Earth observation data into an accessible tool for water-aware agricultural planning. It helps users explore how different priorities affect their choices and discuss alternatives with local experts. The current pilot covers Sidi Salem and Qallin using historical, processed data. It supports informed decisions without claiming live measurements, guaranteed yields or proven water savings.
projectDetails.details:
What we developed and how it works

Field Shift is a bilingual Arabic/English agricultural decision-support website that helps farmers and agricultural advisors compare crop rotations in Egypt’s northern Nile Delta. Our prototype covers Sidi Salem and Qallin in Kafr El-Sheikh, using a grid of 560 approximately one-kilometre study cells, including 556 eligible agricultural cells.

Users select a study cell on the interactive map or enter a farm’s coordinates to match it to an eligible cell. The dashboard displays historical environmental indicators and compares 13 crop-rotation options involving wheat, sugar beet, potato, maize, rice, cotton, soybean and year-round alfalfa.

Each option receives three component scores: land suitability, modeled irrigation requirement and local agricultural practice. Users can adjust the importance of these criteria, and the system recalculates the ranking using a transparent weighted average. This lets users explore alternatives instead of accepting one unexplained recommendation.

Data and tools

We combined NASA POWER temperature data, GPM rainfall estimates, SMAP soil-moisture information, SRTM terrain data and NASA/USGS Landsat observations with ESA Sentinel-2 vegetation information and FAO/IIASA GAEZ agricultural data. NASA resources provide environmental context, while GAEZ supplies crop-specific suitability, modeled irrigation requirements and local-practice inputs.

The frontend uses HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Leaflet for interactive mapping. The backend uses Python, FastAPI, pandas and Pydantic for data handling, validation and scoring. We used pytest and HTTPX for automated testing, GitHub for version control and Vercel for hosting. The prototype is software-based and requires no specialised hardware or field sensors.

AI tools supported planning, coding and debugging after our team independently developed the original project idea.

Benefits, creativity and intended impact

Field Shift makes complex environmental and agricultural information easier to explore through maps, historical indicators and explainable comparisons. Its creative approach connects Earth observation data with an interactive, farmer-facing workflow where users control their decision priorities.

Arabic support makes the interface more accessible to local users. Farm checklists and JSON report export help users organise their planning and share comparisons with agricultural advisors.

Our intended impact is to support better-informed, water-aware agricultural decisions—not replace farmers’ experience or local agricultural expertise.

Factors considered and current limitations

We considered water requirements, land suitability, established agricultural practice, usability, language accessibility and data quality. We also accounted for differences in dataset resolution and the uncertainty of historical and modeled information.

The current version is limited to the pilot area. Study cells are not surveyed farm parcels, irrigation estimates are not measured consumption, and saved farms and tasks remain in the user’s browser. We do not claim guaranteed yields, higher profits or proven water savings. Future development would focus on broader coverage, updated data, additional agronomic and economic factors, and field validation with farmers and specialists.

projectDetails.name: Flame in freefall
projectDetails.summary:
Flame in Freefall – Project Summary

Flame in Freefall is a scientific and educational project that explores how flames behave under different gravitational conditions, especially in microgravity environments in space.

On Earth, flames usually move upward due to gravity-driven buoyancy and convection. However, in microgravity, these effects become weaker, causing flames to behave differently and sometimes form nearly spherical shapes.

Our project aims to develop an interactive web platform that helps users understand and compare combustion behavior on Earth and in space.

Main Features

- Scientific Simulation: Visualizes flame behavior under normal gravity and microgravity.
- AI Analysis: Uses artificial intelligence to analyze combustion data and identify patterns.
- Interactive Dashboard: Displays scientific data, graphs, and comparisons.
- NASA Open Data: Uses publicly available NASA research and experimental data.

Technologies Used

- Artificial Intelligence (AI)
- Data Analysis
- NASA Open Data
- Web Development
- Scientific Simulation

Project Impact

Flame in Freefall makes complex space science easier to understand through interactive simulations and data visualization. It also highlights the importance of studying combustion in space to improve scientific knowledge and support astronaut safety in future space missions.

Our Vision: To transform NASA's scientific research into an interactive learning experience that inspires curiosity and innovation.

projectDetails.name: AeroHealth OS - ( Nexora by Hindawy )
projectDetails.summary:
AeroHealth OS is an autonomous, client-side health monitoring and Clinical Decision Support (CDS) system engineered for astronauts on deep-space exploration missions, such as Mars Transit and Lunar Gateway. During deep-space transit, round-trip communication latencies with Earth range from 3 to 22 minutes, rendering real-time telemedicine and remote mission control interventions impossible during acute medical emergencies. 

To address this challenge, AeroHealth OS empowers non-physician crew members to autonomously detect, evaluate, and mitigate critical spaceflight hazards. The platform integrates an interactive anatomical body map, real-time procedural ECG waveform streaming with arrhythmia detection, diagnostic Frisén staging for Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), millisecond-accurate NASA PVT-B cognitive reaction testing, and behavioral gamification protocols to ensure physical countermeasure compliance. 

Grounded entirely in empirical datasets from the NASA Twins Study (OSDR-379) and MSL Curiosity cruise radiation telemetry, AeroHealth OS provides deterministic, color-coded triage protocols and clear step-by-step clinical countermeasures without requiring ground assistance.
projectDetails.details:
How it Works:

AeroHealth OS operates entirely client-side with zero external software dependencies, providing resilient offline performance in deep space. It ingests simulated physiological and environmental telemetry, running them through an autonomous triage state-machine:

1. Interactive Anatomical HUD: Astronauts click on key organs (Brain, Eyes, Heart, Lungs, Spine, Muscles) to inspect empirical biomarkers, etiology, and targeted mitigations.

2. Real-Time Cardiovascular Stream: Continuously plots procedural P-Q-R-S-T ECG waveforms on an HTML5 Canvas at 100ms intervals, with simulated arrhythmia anomaly injection.

3. SANS Staging: Diagnostic optical evaluation using clinical Frisén scale (Grades 0-4) mapped to retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) thickness and Lower Body Negative Pressure (LBNP) protocols.

4. Cognitive Readiness: A functional Psychomotor Vigilance Test (NASA PVT-B) measuring reaction latency to detect micro-sleep lapses (>380ms).

5. Behavioral Gamification: Daily mission quest hub awarding XP, ranks, and streak tracking for completing mandatory 2.5-hour resistance exercises.

Tools & Technology Stack:

- Frontend: Pure Vanilla HTML5, modern CSS3 Glassmorphism, and Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+).

- Rendering: HTML5 Canvas 2D API running at 60 FPS.

- Data Science Engine: Python 3.10, Matplotlib, and Pandas in Jupyter Notebook for empirical baseline validation.

- Interoperability: HL7 FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) telemetry export standard.

Benefits & Impact:

Provides autonomous self-reliance during critical communications blackouts, protects crew vision from microgravity cephalad fluid shifts, tracks cumulative cosmic radiation exposure against NASA career career limits (REID model), and standardizes medical telemetry for Earth-return synchronization.

projectDetails.name: Delta Sentry — 30 m Early Warning for the Nile Delta
projectDetails.summary:
Delta Sentry is an early-warning system for crop health in Egypt's Nile Delta. Egypt farms a thin strip of irrigated land, and district averages hide field-level failure: by the time a problem is visible from the road, it is already a loss.

We built a working web application that fuses 30-metre NASA HLS imagery with a fine-tuned Prithvi-EO-2.0 foundation model to forecast next month's vegetation, compares that forecast against what the satellite actually observed, and converts the disagreement into a ranked list of contiguous field patches. An inspector opens the site, sees 59 flagged blocks and the 12 worth visiting first, and prints a field order with coordinates and an observation checklist.

We audited 44 flagged patches against high-resolution imagery and published the result: 18 confirmed decline, 26 classified as harvest, cloud artefact or unclear. We report our error budget openly, including the baselines we do not beat.
projectDetails.details:
Delta Sentry turns a satellite forecast error into a work order.

THE PROBLEM

Egypt grows its food on a thin strip of irrigated land along the Nile. When a block of fields begins to fail, district-level averages do not move: a governorate mean stays flat while a hundred hectares go under, and by the time the loss is visible from the road it is already a compensation claim. Satellite monitoring of Egyptian agriculture is not new. What is missing is the step between a map and a decision. An agronomist cannot act on a raster of NDVI values, but they can act on a short list with a place, an area and a reason.

HOW IT WORKS

The pipeline runs in five steps.

1. We extract 30 m Harmonized Landsat-Sentinel imagery and 25 years of MODIS NDVI through NASA AppEEARS.

2. Every scene is cloud-masked with Fmask and reduced to monthly median composites.

3. A fine-tuned Prithvi-EO-2.0-300M model, with a frozen backbone and a custom U-Net decoder, predicts next month's NDVI from the previous four months of imagery.

4. The forecast is subtracted from what the satellite actually observed. Negative gaps are clustered into contiguous field patches.

5. Patches are ranked by area and exported as a printable field order with coordinates and an observation checklist.

An inspector opens one page and sees 59 flagged patches covering 175 feddan, and the 12 worth driving to first.

EVIDENCE, INCLUDING WHAT FAILS

We trained on 500 spatial-temporal samples spanning 2013 to 2023 and evaluated on held-out 2025 data. Seasonal climatology scores an RMSE of 0.1767, persistence 0.1858, and our model 0.1823. We beat persistence by 1.9 percent and we do not beat climatology. A 12-year same-month climatology is a genuinely strong baseline for a seasonal signal, and we say so on the site rather than in a footnote.

What we claim is narrower and testable: the model produces a spatial ranking that a climatology cannot, because a climatology is smooth across space by construction. A district average and a climatology are both blind to which field is failing. That is the gap this project fills.

We also audited 44 flagged patches one by one against high-resolution imagery. Eighteen, or 40.9 percent, showed a visible vegetation decline. Twelve were normal harvest or crop rotation, nine were cloud or sensor artefact, and five were unclear. We publish the 26 failures because a false-alarm rate is the number a ministry needs before it trusts a list.

Separately, a pixel-wise Seasonal Mann-Kendall test with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction on 25 years of MODIS found 78.6 percent of the area significantly greening, 21.4 percent with no significant trend, and 0.04 percent declining. The Delta is greening in aggregate, which is exactly why district averages hide the blocks that matter.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

The direct benefit is time. An inspector with a vehicle and a finite week gets a ranked shortlist instead of a district to drive around. The second benefit is early warning: the alert fires when reality departs from a model's expectation, which can happen before the decline is visible to the eye. The intended impact is a working interface between satellite data and a field visit, at a cost a governorate can carry, because the whole application is a static site and the model runs on a free hosting tier.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Python, PyTorch, TerraTorch, Xarray, Rasterio, NumPy and pymannkendall for the science. FastAPI on a Hugging Face Docker Space for live inference. A zero-dependency HTML, CSS and JavaScript front end with canvas rendering, no framework and no build step, so the entire application runs from a static host and loads without a server.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

The first creative decision was to build the product around the forecast error rather than the forecast. Most vegetation models are judged on how close they get to reality. We treat the distance from reality as the signal: a model that is confidently wrong is not a failure here, it is an alert. The second decision was to end the pipeline at a printable field order rather than a map, because the unit of action for an inspector is a visit, not a pixel. The third was to make the model runnable from the browser, so a judge or a ministry officer can press one button and watch inference happen rather than take our word for it.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Cloud cover over the Delta, which is why every scene is masked before compositing. The difference between seasonal senescence and genuine stress, which is why a flagged block is labelled bare soil when that is what the data shows instead of being called a stressed crop. The cost of a false alarm to a ministry with limited vehicles, which is why we audited our own alerts and published the failures. And the risk of presenting a prototype as a finished service, which is why every claim in the application is paired with its limit.

LIMITS

This is one pilot tile of about 12 square kilometres in Kafr El-Sheikh, not the Delta. An alert is an indicator for investigation, not a diagnosis of crop failure. Patch coordinates are mapped from the grid and are approximate, not surveyed GPS. In the December pilot month the district-wide NDVI drop is partly harvest and bare soil rather than stress. Re-basing the anomaly on same-month multi-year climatology, masking cells below NDVI 0.05, and adding Sentinel-1 SAR to separate harvest from failure are the next steps.
