projectDetails.name: SPHEREx sky time machine
projectDetails.summary: SPHEREx Sky Time Machine is a free website that turns NASA’s SPHEREx infrared survey into short videos of the sky. SPHEREx photographs the whole sky in 102 infrared colours every six months, but its data comes as hundreds of separate image files per spot, which NASA’s archive shows one at a time. Our pipeline finds every SPHEREx photo of a position, removes bad pixels and the glow of solar-system dust, lines the photos up on one grid, and stacks each six-month sky pass into a video frame. The website plays these frames like a flip-book, with a “what changed” view that makes moving or brightening objects stand out. Clicking a target shows its spectrum across all colours and how its brightness changed. Known stars from Gaia and WISE are drawn on top to check what is new. Tested on real data, it recovered all 14 sightings of two known fast-moving stars and confirmed a pulsating star’s change. A faint, slowly moving Planet X or a cold brown dwarf would look just like this. Our tool lets students, citizen scientists and researchers look for them, no code needed.
projectDetails.details:
What it does. SPHEREx Sky Time Machine plays NASA SPHEREx infrared photos of one spot in the sky as a short video, so anything that moves or changes brightness stands out. For any position, our Python pipeline asks NASA’s IRSA archive for every SPHEREx photo that covers it and downloads only the patch it needs. It removes bad pixels and the glow of solar-system dust, lines every photo up on one north-up grid, and averages each six-month sky pass into one video frame. The website offers a flip-book, a “what changed” view, a deep stack, single-colour views, and a spectrum and light curve for each target. Known stars from Gaia and WISE are drawn on top, moved to each photo’s date.

Benefits and impact. SPHEREx data comes as hundreds of separate files per spot, which today takes code and astronomy skills to use. Our tool lets students, teachers and citizen scientists simply look. Volunteers already found brown dwarfs by flipping through older WISE photos; we bring that method to NASA’s newest survey. A faint, slow-moving Planet X would look exactly like the movers we show.

Results (real data only). The pictures line up with Gaia stars to within 0.03″. The mover finder recovered all 14 sightings of two known fast-moving stars. WISE 0855’s brightness agrees with NASA WISE. The pulsating star R Draconis changes about 1.6×, while control stars stay steady. We claim no new objects.

Tools. Python (Astropy, astroquery, reproject, NumPy, SciPy), JavaScript with React and Vite, an optional Flask API, and GitHub Pages for hosting. We worked on our own laptops with no special hardware, and used Claude (AI) with full disclosure.

Creativity. One tool shows both motion over time and make-up across 102 colours, using the same photos.

What we considered. We considered honesty first. Every light curve gives a verdict: “steady”, “changes” or “inconclusive”. Unreliable data is flagged, not hidden, and we report our limits openly. We also wanted the tool free, with no login, shareable links and plain-language explanations.

projectDetails.name: AstroCare
projectDetails.summary: AstroCare is an educational astronaut-health monitoring Android prototype with a tested backend. The interface presents vital readings, measurement entry, guidance and safety information. The backend accepts heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, temperature and sleep records, preserves history, supports duplicate-safe synchronisation, and returns seven-day trends with rule-linked evidence. NASA Human Research Program hazard material provides space-health context for the guidance. The demonstration uses synthetic data, not real astronaut measurements. AstroCare aims to help a crew member notice and understand a change in routine health indicators; it does not diagnose, prescribe treatment or replace a flight surgeon.
projectDetails.details:
AstroCare addresses the challenge of gathering health indicators and making self-assessment understandable during a space mission. The intended workflow is to record a measurement or symptom, synchronise the record when a connection is available, and review the latest values, recent trends and evidence behind an indicator flag.

The team's actual Android screenshots show an English interface with Overview, Data, Trends and Settings navigation. Overview displays five vital indicators with units, timestamps and Demo labels. Data Entry lets a user choose a metric, enter a reading and optional note, then select Save & evaluate. Measurement guides explain the steps and label alert boundaries as illustrative. Safety information explicitly states that the app is decision support, not a medical diagnosis. Settings show sync and Wi-Fi-only controls. Screenshots demonstrate these UI states, not full end-to-end network or physical-sensor validation.

The reviewed implementation is a Node.js 22+/Express/MongoDB backend using Mongoose, Zod and JSON Schema validation, with shared contract version 1.0.0. It supports five measurement categories: heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation (SpO₂), temperature and sleep. A batch can also contain symptom check-ins and alert evidence. The API validates record structure and timestamps, enforces cross-field rules such as systolic pressure exceeding diastolic pressure, and returns item-level created, duplicate or rejected results.

Stable record identifiers and database unique indexes make ordinary retries duplicate-safe. History endpoints restore records using metric and time filters. An implemented proposed overview extension recomputes current status from the latest relevant evidence and returns derived alerts without saving them to uploaded alert history. Seven-day trend reports include daily points, baseline summaries, direction labels and insights. The production algorithm is deterministic Node code; it does not call a remote LLM or invoke Python in production. Versioned rules and measurement guides are available as immutable assets.

A reproducible local demonstration loaded 126 synthetic measurements and one symptom check-in. Repeating the seed inserted zero new records and skipped 127 existing fixtures. With the clock fixed to 13 November 2026 at 19:00 UTC, trends returned five metrics and one insight for 7–13 November, while overview returned a warning with two evidence-linked derived rules. The backend test suite was rerun successfully: 64 tests passed, zero failed and zero skipped; contract verification passed as well. This establishes tested software behavior, not clinical or flight suitability.

Current limits include a single demo astronaut, API-key-only access rather than production user authentication, synthetic fixtures, illustrative rules, and backend tests that do not establish Android-device/end-to-end integration. Sync batches are not all-or-nothing transactions. Future work includes secure individual accounts, tested client/sensor integration, clearer visualisation and expert review of health interpretation. Real human research data would require a specifically identified dataset and documented access, licence and processing before reuse.

projectDetails.name: Project Earth Print
projectDetails.summary: NUN is a scientific intelligence platform that combines satellite imagery, Earth observation data, and AI to monitor and analyze environmental changes in ancient Egyptian lake landscapes. By connecting modern scientific data with Ancient Egyptian heritage, NUN transforms complex environmental information into meaningful insights, interactive visualizations, and immersive storytelling.
projectDetails.details:
NUN: From Ancient Wisdom to Earth Observation Intelligence

1. What does your project do, and how does it work?

NUN is an Earth Observation Intelligence Platform that transforms satellite data into meaningful environmental insights through geospatial analysis, scientific indicators, and interactive storytelling.

Our first case study focuses on the Lake Chad Basin, one of the world's most environmentally significant and vulnerable freshwater systems.

NUN investigates three fundamental questions:
- Where is surface water changing?
- How rapidly are these changes occurring?
- Are the observed trends statistically significant?

The platform follows a scientific workflow that integrates satellite observations, processes environmental indicators, analyzes changes over time, and translates complex geospatial information into accessible visual insights.

Our proposed analytical pipeline includes:
1. Collecting Earth observation data from NASA and other relevant scientific sources.
2. Processing satellite reflectance data and applying water indices such as NDWI and MNDWI.
3. Identifying surface-water patterns and estimating water extent in square kilometers.
4. Aggregating observations across monthly and historical time periods.
5. Applying statistical methods, including the Mann–Kendall test and Sen's slope, to investigate long-term trends.
6. Presenting the findings through interactive visualizations and an engaging digital storytelling experience.

2. What benefits does your project have?

NUN provides several important benefits:

- Environmental Awareness: Makes long-term changes in water resources easier to understand.
- Data Accessibility: Converts complex satellite observations into understandable visual information.
- Scientific Decision Support: Provides a framework for identifying environmental trends and supporting further investigation.
- Historical Perspective: Connects present-day environmental observations with historical changes.
- Educational Value: Makes Earth observation and environmental science more engaging and accessible.
- Scalability: Establishes a methodology that can potentially be extended to other lakes, wetlands, and vulnerable ecosystems.

Instead of simply displaying satellite images, NUN aims to explain what those images reveal about environmental change.

3. What is the intended impact of your project?

Our intended impact is to make environmental change measurable, understandable, and actionable.

By investigating Lake Chad, NUN aims to support awareness of freshwater vulnerability, encourage evidence-based environmental research, and demonstrate how Earth observation technologies can contribute to understanding complex environmental challenges.

In the longer term, we envision NUN evolving into a scalable environmental intelligence platform that connects satellite data, scientific analysis, and human understanding.

Our ambition is to bridge the gap between scientific data and the people who need to understand it, including researchers, educators, environmental organizations, and decision-makers.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Our technical approach is built around Earth observation, geospatial analysis, statistical methods, and interactive web technologies.

Scientific Data Sources and Platforms:
- NASA Earthdata: Access to Earth observation datasets.
- NASA Giovanni: Environmental data exploration and visualization.
- NASA AppEEARS: Satellite data access and processing workflows.
- MODIS MOD09A1 Version 6.1: Surface reflectance data used as a primary source for the proposed water-index analysis.
- NASA IMERG and GLDAS: Supporting precipitation and land-surface context.
- NASA SWOT LakeSP: Potential complementary lake-observation data.

Scientific and Analytical Methods:
- NDWI and MNDWI water indices.
- Geospatial analysis and surface-water area estimation.
- Monthly and historical temporal aggregation.
- Mann–Kendall trend analysis.
- Sen's slope estimation.


Proposed Development Technologies:
- Python for data processing and scientific analysis.
- FastAPI for backend services.
- React for the interactive frontend.
- Geospatial visualization tools for presenting environmental information.

The project does not depend on specialized physical hardware; its core architecture is designed around satellite data and software-based analysis.

5. How is your project creative?

NUN introduces a distinctive approach by combining modern Earth observation science with the cultural and visual heritage of Ancient Egypt.

The name NUN is inspired by the primordial waters of Ancient Egyptian cosmology, creating a meaningful connection between the ancient understanding of water as the origin of life and modern scientific efforts to monitor freshwater systems.

Our creativity is reflected in three dimensions:

Scientific Innovation: Transforming satellite observations into measurable environmental indicators and long-term trend analysis.

Cultural Storytelling: Using Ancient Egyptian visual language and the symbolism of water to communicate environmental change through a meaningful narrative.

Digital Experience: Combining scientific intelligence, interactive data visualization, and immersive visual storytelling rather than presenting disconnected satellite images or static charts.

NUN is designed to make environmental science not only informative but also understandable, memorable, and engaging.

6. What factors did your team consider?

Our team considered several essential factors throughout the project:

- Scientific Accuracy: Selecting credible datasets and appropriate analytical methods.
- Data Quality: Considering cloud contamination, missing observations, spatial resolution, and temporal consistency.
- Environmental Complexity: Recognizing the influence of rainfall, evaporation, seasonal variation, and other environmental factors.
- Statistical Reliability: Distinguishing genuine long-term trends from short-term fluctuations.
- User Experience: Making complex scientific information accessible through clear visualizations and storytelling.
- Cultural Relevance: Building a visual identity inspired by Ancient Egyptian heritage without compromising scientific credibility.
- Scalability: Designing a methodology that can eventually be adapted to other freshwater ecosystems.
- Transparency: Distinguishing measured observations from interpretations and avoiding unsupported conclusions.
Our Vision
NUN represents a bridge between the wisdom of the past and the intelligence of modern Earth observation.

We believe that satellite data should do more than show us how our planet looks. It should help us understand how our planet changes, why those changes matter, and how knowledge can support a more sustainable future.

NUN — Reading Earth's Waters. Revealing the Stories Behind Change.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: AstroScout AI
projectDetails.summary:
AstroScout AI is a hybrid artificial intelligence system developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 9. It aims to find the most accurate geological environments on Earth that simulate Martian and Lunar terrains.
​The core idea goes beyond mere visual similarity by building a cloud-based engine that relies on three technical pillars:
​Data Engineering: Sanitizing and standardizing NASA maps into true-color, noise-free, nadir (satellite) views.
​Hybrid AI: Integrating three advanced computer vision models (ResNet-50, VGG-16, MobileNetV2) to deeply analyze terrain roughness and spatial patterns.
​Geochemical Reranking: Applying a mathematical algorithm that balances AI topographical similarity with chemical color signatures, ensuring the actual geological makeup (like iron or basalt) matches.
​The ultimate goal is to provide NASA with highly reliable data to pinpoint exact, safe simulation sites. These locations are crucial for training astronauts and testing rovers before space missions launch, significantly minimizing risks and ensuring mission success.
projectDetails.details:
The Problem:
Testing rovers and training astronauts for extraterrestrial missions requires highly accurate simulation sites on Earth. Relying on basic visual similarities often leads to selecting terrains with the wrong geochemical makeup or structural hazards.

Our Solution (AstroScout AI / GEO-MATCH):
We built a robust, cloud-deployed AI engine that doesn't just look at shapes, but analyzes the deep geological footprint of space terrains. Our solution is divided into three main pillars:
1. Data-Centric AI (Sanitization & Standardization): We prioritized clean data over complex generic models. We calibrated Mars/Moon inputs to true-color, nadir (satellite) views, and stripped text noise.
2. Hybrid Ensemble Architecture: We deployed a decentralized Cloud API on Hugging Face using three specific models: ResNet-50 (60% weight for topographical roughness), VGG-16 (20% for spatial patterns), and MobileNetV2 (20% for rapid feature extraction). We also integrated Gemini for intelligent data interpretation.
3. Mathematical Geochemical Reranking: To prevent "Texture Dominance", we developed a dual-evaluation algorithm. We extract the deep AI feature vector (Cosine Similarity) and penalize it using a mathematical color signature (Euclidean Distance of RGB mean/std) representing chemical makeup (e.g., Iron=Red, Basalt=Dark Gray).

Result:
A highly accurate matched Earth analog (like Jezero Crater to Atacama Desert), stored and retrieved instantly via a Supabase backend.

projectDetails.name: Mars Lifeline
projectDetails.summary: Mars Life Line is a browser game that puts young players in charge of a Martian outpost. Players choose a landing site, restore power and life support, grow food, and respond to a radiation warning. Each choice has a benefit and a cost: backup power helps immediately but leaves the solar panels dusty, while Emergency Mode saves power by pausing crop growth. PEBBLE, the station’s robot companion, helps players understand their next steps. NASA maps, radiation records, and life-support references connect the mission to real science. The game makes the engineering trade-offs of living on Mars interactive and easier to understand.
projectDetails.details:
Mars Life Line — Project Details

Mars Life Line is an interactive 3D educational survival game designed for children aged 7–12, developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer.

Our goal is to teach young explorers that surviving on Mars isn't simply about building a base—it's about making responsible engineering decisions when every resource matters.

The Experience

Players arrive at ARES-7, a fictional Martian research outpost damaged by a dust storm. Guided by PEBBLE, their robotic companion, they must restore the station and prepare it for the next crew.

The playable mission consists of seven connected scenes, combining first-person exploration, physical equipment interactions, an overhead station-management view, and a final mission evaluation.

Players restore solar power, repair water recycling, restart oxygen production, grow food, manage limited resources, and respond to a dangerous solar radiation event.

Meaningful Decisions and Learning Outcomes

Every major decision introduces a real engineering trade-off:

  • Solar Panels vs. Backup Power: Cleaning dusty panels takes time but restores long-term electricity generation. Activating backup power provides immediate energy but leaves the underlying problem unresolved. Players learn the difference between short-term fixes and sustainable solutions.
  • Life Support: Players must repair the water recycler before activating the oxygen generator, discovering how essential survival systems depend on one another.
  • Greenhouse Priorities: Survival, Balanced, and Farming modes distribute energy and water differently. Faster crop growth consumes more resources, teaching the importance of resource allocation.
  • Radiation Emergency: Players choose between Emergency Mode, which conserves electricity but pauses crop growth, and maintaining greenhouse production at greater energy cost. They must also protect equipment and reach a radiation shelter.
  • Consequences and Recovery: Power shortages interrupt machinery, neglected irrigation can destroy crops, and unsafe exposure can end the mission. PEBBLE explains the consequences so players can learn and try again.

The final mission report evaluates power, water, oxygen, food, and radiation safety, connecting the player's decisions to measurable outcomes.

How We Used NASA Data

NASA resources are incorporated into the experience in four distinct ways:

NASA/JPL Mars Trek: The landing interface uses a Viking global color mosaic and MOLA-based elevation information to introduce three Martian locations: Gale Crater, Jezero Crater, and Deuteronilus Mensae. Site-specific sunlight factors influence the game's solar generation.

NASA OSDR RadLab: Archived radiation measurements from Curiosity's RAD instrument, including the May 2024 solar event, provide real scientific context for the radiation lesson.

NASA DONKI: A documented May 2024 coronal mass ejection provides the historical reference for the fictional solar emergency.

NASA Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document (BVAD): Published crew oxygen and water requirements inform the educational explanations shown in the station's control interface.

Scientific transparency: NASA measurements, historical observations, and game simulation values are distinguished. The fictional outpost, simplified resource rates, shielding effects, and gameplay thresholds are educational approximations—not operational NASA measurements or validated astronaut safety limits.

Technology and Validation

The game was developed using TypeScript, React, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Drei, Rapier, Zustand, and Vite, with custom 3D assets created through a Kiln-based workflow.

The repository includes automated simulation and world-regression tests. These cover successful and risky mission paths, solar-power trade-offs, crop irrigation failures, resource depletion, and radiation exposure. A documented careful playthrough takes approximately 7.5 minutes.

Testing to date consists of development verification, automated checks, and documented walkthroughs; we do not claim a formal usability study with children.

PEBBLE provides built-in contextual guidance without requiring players to supply an API key. An optional Gemini-powered mode is available for local development testing.

Educational Impact

Mars Life Line transforms space science into decisions children can experience rather than simply read about. By connecting NASA research to interactive consequences, the game encourages systems thinking, scientific curiosity, resource awareness, and problem-solving.

Every watt. Every breath. Every choice.

AI Tools & Transparency

We used ChatGPT (OpenAI) for brainstorming, game design, planning, and educational content development; OpenAI Codex and Google Antigravity for AI-assisted coding, debugging, and implementation; Grok (xAI) for AI-generated visual assets; and Manus AI for producing our project demonstration video.

Our team directed the development process, reviewed the AI-assisted outputs, and made the final design and implementation decisions. NASA scientific data and references are distinguished from AI-generated creative content.

Source Code & Project Repository

The complete source code for Mars Life Line, including the 3D game implementation, mission simulation, NASA data integrations, and automated tests, is publicly available on GitHub.

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/baraa404/mars-life-line-game

The repository provides transparency into our development process, technical implementation, scientific references, and testing methodology.

projectDetails.name: Project Odyssey Cartography
projectDetails.summary: Odyssey is a browser-based survival map that turns real NASA data into a safe walking route across Gale Crater. Future crews will explore Mars on foot, but the elevation, imagery, mineral and geology data they need is scattered across separate tools. Odyssey merges the MSL Gale DEM, CTX orbital imagery, 21 CRISM mineral indices, USGS geology and Curiosity photos into one interactive 3D map. An A* route planner traces the safest walk between any two points under a strict 20-degree slope limit, reporting distance, walk time, climb and slope. A first-person EVA helmet visor previews the route, and a printable mission card summarizes it. The app runs fully offline in the browser - no login, no backend - so it works where Mars work happens.
projectDetails.details: Odyssey is a Vite + React + TypeScript web app that renders Gale Crater as an interactive 3D terrain (vendored Three.js r128) from a local 20 m DEM (238x238 cells, ~4.7 km patch in northwest Gale near 4.80S, 137.40E). Pick a start and destination; an A* search over the slope grid traces the safest walk under a 20-degree limit, with four planner modes (Balanced, Distance, Gentler, Safest) and full route stats: distance, walk time, max/mean slope, climb, descent, warnings. Safety screening estimates walk time, suit-hours with a 25% reserve and EVA radiation dose. A first-person helmet visor walks the route with a live HUD; a printable mission card summarizes the traverse. Benefits: one map instead of five scattered datasets, fully offline with no login or backend. Working now: all of the above; demo route 3.31 km, about 2 h 46 min, 13.9-degree max slope. Limits: 20 m screening DEM, synthetic demo waypoints (not rover telemetry), safety values are unverified demo assumptions. Planned: larger coverage, live orbital data, rover-scale obstacle detection, thermal modeling.

projectDetails.name: Astra
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRA is an autonomous, offline-first clinical decision support system designed to safeguard astronaut health during deep-space missions (such as Artemis and Mars transit) where up to 22 minutes of signal latency prevents real-time consultation with Earth-based flight surgeons. Built for non-medical crew members, the application transforms a 60-second daily check-in of wearable vitals, point-of-care blood biomarkers, and guided self-assessments into clear diagnostic predictions and countermeasure protocols.

To eliminate AI medical hallucinations in safety-critical environments, Astralis uses a two-tier hybrid architecture: a deterministic System 1 risk classifier (Laya AI, fine-tuned on 6,000 NASA-parameterized mission logs across 10 physiological attributes) calculates calibrated probabilities for 10 spaceflight conditions—including Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), Space Anemia, Decompression Sickness, and Renal Stone Risk—while a System 2 generative advisor translates active alerts into plain-English explanations and step-by-step NASA countermeasure checklists. Featuring an interactive anatomical dashboard, guided measurement tooltips, and one-click mission presets in a responsive Flutter interface, Astralis empowers astronauts to self-triage silent microgravity hazards before they escalate into mission-threatening emergencies.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

1. What Does It Do & How Does It Work?

1. Guided 60-Second Assessment & Education Layer:

  • Astronauts input 10 essential physiological, environmental, and psychological attributes organized across three rapid stages:
    • Stage 1 — Essential Vitals (Cardiovascular & Thermal): Resting Heart Rate (heart_rate in bpm), Systolic Blood Pressure (systolic_bp in mmHg), Diastolic Blood Pressure (diastolic_bp in mmHg), Blood Oxygen Saturation (spo2 in %), and Core Body Temperature (body_temp in °C).
    • Stage 2 — Blood & Habitat (Biomarkers & Exposure): Fasting Blood Glucose (blood_glucose(fasting) in mg/dL), Daily Radiation Dose (radiation_dose_daily in mSv/day), and Cabin $CO_2$ Partial Pressure (cabin_co2 in mmHg).
    • Stage 3 — Mental & Sleep (Neuro-Vestibular, Sleep & Readiness): Total Sleep Duration (sleep_hours in hours over the last 24h) and Mood & Cognitive Stress Score (mood_stress_score on a 1–10 scale).
  • Because astronauts are not all medical specialists, every metric features built-in "How & Why" measurement guides explaining proper collection technique in microgravity and why orbital baselines differ from Earth norms.

2. Tier 1 — Deterministic Diagnostic Engine (Random Forest Classifier):

  • Raw numerical inputs are serialized into a 10-feature state vectorand evaluated locally in milliseconds by a custom-trained Random Forest Classifier (scikit-learn).
  • Rather than guessing with generative text, Tier 1 uses ensemble decision-tree bagging to output calibrated probability scores (predict_proba) across 10 physiological states: Healthy, Cardiovascular Deconditioning, Immune/Viral Reactivation, Fatigue/Circadian Disorder, Hypoxia/$CO_2$ Anomaly, Space Anemia, Acute Radiation Stress, Renal Stone Risk, Decompression Sickness, and SANS (Neuro-Ocular Syndrome).

3. Tier 2 — Grounded Countermeasure Advisor & Gamified Bio-Sync:

  • Only conditions crossing the calibrated probability threshold ($P \ge 0.50$) are passed to the Tier 2 advisor (FastAPI backend with AI/local LLM integration).
  • The advisor translates the structured medical flags into plain-English physiological explanations and a 3-step operational protocol (immediate hydration/nutrition intervention, exercise/habitat countermeasure adjustment, and follow-up verification timing), clearly distinguishing between Level 1 Crew Self-Care and Level 2 Flight Surgeon Escalation, while rewarding crew adherence through a gamified Bio-Sync streak and task system.

2. Benefits & Expected Impact

  • Deep-Space Autonomy: Operates completely offline during communication blackouts or high-latency lunar and Martian missions.
  • Zero Medical Hallucinations & Explainable Triage: Strictly separates deterministic tree-based risk classification (System 1 Random Forest) from natural-language guidance (System 2), ensuring clinical reliability and transparent feature importance.
  • Cognitive Offloading & Gamified Engagement: Replaces spreadsheet telemetry and alarm fatigue with color-coded visual triage ribbons, interactive diagnostic wizards, and daily health streaks, allowing fatigued astronauts to grasp their health status in seconds.
  • Terrestrial Spin-Off Value: Directly adaptable to isolated, resource-constrained environments on Earth, including polar research stations, submarines, offshore rigs, and rural telemedicine clinics.

3. Space Agency Data & Resources Used

Because real astronaut medical telemetry is protected under medical privacy regulations, we grounded our diagnostic architecture, feature thresholds, and synthetic dataset generation in official space agency literature and hardware frameworks:

  • NASA Human Research Program (HRP) Evidence Books & Exploration Medical Capability (ExMC): Used to define our 10 target conditions, establish physiological perturbation rules across the "RIDGE" hazards (Radiation, Isolation, Distance, Gravity, Environment), and calibrate two-tier clinical alert thresholds.
  • NASA Crew Health and Performance Integrated Data Architecture (CHP-IDA): Inspired our unified aggregation of disparate habit logs, habitat environmental sensors (cabin_co2, radiation_dose_daily), wearable vitals, and metabolic markersinto a single clinical decision support interface.
  • ISS Point-of-Care & Environmental Monitoring Standards: Selected point-of-care metabolic (blood_glucose(fasting)) and spacecraft life-support/dosimetry indicators (cabin_co2, radiation_dose_daily)that match operational monitoring hardware flown aboard the International Space Station.

4. Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Frontend: Flutter & Dart (responsive dark-mode web/desktop terminal featuring custom starfield canvas painter, 3-stage assessment wizard, mission presets, gamified streak/task tracker, and interactive diagnostic dashboard).
  • Machine Learning (System 1): Python and scikit-learn (Random Forest Classifier trained and validated on our 10-attribute physiological & habitat dataset, serialized via joblib/pickle for ultra-fast local CPU inference).
  • Backend & System 2 Advisor: FastAPI (Python), REST API integration with Gemini API and local offline LLM fallback (Ollama / Gemma / Llama).
  • Data Engineering: Python (numpy, pandas) synthetic physiological dataset generator producing 6,000 training logs (60 simulated crew profiles) and 2,000 unseen test logs (20 separate crew profiles) across the 10 core telemetry featureswith zero subject leakage.
  • Design & Presentation: Stitch AI, Figma, and Manus / Gamma AI.

5. Honest Limitations & Next Steps

  • Current Limitation: The Random Forest classification model is trained and validated on parameterized synthetic telemetry rather than de-identified clinical flight records.
  • Next Step 1 (Hardware & Sensor Ingestion): Integrate Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) APIs for automated wearable syncing, spacecraft ECLSS telemetry streaming (for cabin_co2 and radiation_dose_daily), and webcam-based remote photoplethysmography (rPPG) for contactless heart_rate estimation.
  • Next Step 2 (Analog Validation): Validate the software workflow, gamified task adherence, and calibration accuracy in terrestrial space-analog missions (such as NASA HERA or the Mars Desert Research Station).

projectDetails.name: On Fire
projectDetails.summary:
On Fire is a web application that turns 25 years of NASA satellite fire detections into one consistent burning-activity calendar for the Middle East & North Africa and North America. NASA's MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) sensors count fire very differently, so their records cannot be compared directly. We harmonize them: instead of raw hotspots we count "burning units" (a ~10 km square with fire on one day) and convert MODIS to the VIIRS scale with a model fitted per country and season. On years held out from fitting, this cut the disagreement between the two sensors from 144.1% to 30.3%.

Users pick any country, draw any area or type latitude/longitude, choose any date range, and see which months and years burn most, how this month compares with the historical median, and download the calendar (CSV, PNG) and every hotspot detected (CSV). For fires burning now, On Fire shows where they are heading, which towns they could reach and when, how big they are compared with past fires at the same place, and exports a CAP alert file for authorities. An AI fire-risk model, tested against what really burned, adds early warning.

It helps fire services, civil protection, scientists and land managers see what is normal for a place and act early when a season is not.
projectDetails.details: WHAT IT DOES 1. A harmonized burning-activity calendar for every country and both regions: 25 years month by month (amount or "compared to normal"), the fire season (the fewest months holding 75% of a year's fire), the worst month, the trend since 2001, the busiest years and months, and this month against the median of the same month. Hovering a month shows its burning units, its % of normal and the raw hotspots each sensor detected. 2. Any area of interest: draw a box on the map or type its latitude/longitude corners. The area gets its own 25-year calendar, extended to the latest satellite day, and "this month so far vs the same dates in 2012-2025" (median, middle half, rank). A box outside the covered countries is refused with a clear message instead of a false "no fire". 3. Any date range (Nov 2000 to yesterday): total burning, % of normal, busiest month, hotspots detected, a monthly chart, and downloads: monthly summary (CSV), every hotspot in the range (CSV, MODIS + VIIRS), calendar (CSV, PNG). 4. Live fires from five satellites (refreshed every 20 minutes, gas flares removed) on one map for both regions. 5. One fire: projected spread for +3/+6/+12/+24 h from the wind forecast, the first town it could reach and when, smoke, air quality, people nearby, emissions, its size compared with every fire within 50 km since 2012, and a CAP 1.2 alert file for authorities. Alerts are decision support labelled as estimates; the app never issues evacuation orders. 6. AI fire risk per ~50 km cell with the reasons behind each cell, and Truth vs Prediction, which replays past fires (Dixie, Kabylie, Manavgat 2021 and three chosen by rule) against the frozen model's earlier risk map, including its misses. HOW IT WORKS 1. Collect NASA FIRMS detections: MODIS Collection 6.1 (Nov 2000 - Dec 2025) and VIIRS S-NPP 375 m (Jan 2012 - Dec 2025) yearly country archives; 2026 and live data from the FIRMS API. 2. Clean both sensors the same way: vegetation fires only, a common confidence filter, static heat sources (gas flares, industry) removed. 3. Count the same thing: fire cell-days = distinct (0.1 degree cell, day) pairs with fire. This removes most of the pixel-size difference. 4. Calibrate MODIS to VIIRS on the 2012-2025 overlap per country and season (power law + small-fire background), chosen on inner validation years and scored only on held-out years 2014, 2017, 2020, 2023. 5. One record: VIIRS from 2012, calibrated MODIS before, with an uncertainty band; then calendar statistics (mean, median, anomalies, fire season). EVIDENCE - Disagreement between MODIS-derived and VIIRS monthly country totals on held-out years: 144.1% before, 30.3% after. At the 2012 sensor switch the harmonized series is off by a factor of 1.25 against MODIS alone; a naive switch is off by 6.5. - Gas flares: in Qatar 93.7% of VIIRS detections are static industrial sources; our detector agrees with NASA's static-source flag with 96.2% precision and 97.0% recall. - Risk model (LightGBM, trained to 2018, tuned 2019-2020, frozen, scored 2021-2025): 59.2% of 8,728 large fires began inside the model's top 10% of risk vs 47.8% for the fire map alone (assumes a perfect 7-day weather forecast). TRY IT (main task) On Windows, install Node.js and Python 3.11+, download the GitHub repository and double-click setup.bat. Click "Area", type North 37.2, South 35.5, West 3, East 9 (northern Algeria): you get "fires peak in August", the 25-year calendar, this month vs the median, and CSV downloads. TOOLS JavaScript, Python, HTML/CSS. React, Vite, MapLibre GL JS, Recharts, Node.js/Express, FastAPI/Uvicorn, DuckDB, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-learn, LightGBM, Shapely, PyArrow. A standard Windows PC. WORKING NOW / LIMITS / FUTURE Working: everything above runs locally with setup.bat. Limits: prototype on the user's PC (no public hosting yet); values before 2012 are estimates (typically 0.58x-1.51x for a country-month); satellites miss fires under cloud; spread is a rule-of-thumb estimate; the risk model ranks places and cannot say where a fire starts; coverage is two regions. Future: extend to every region, add NOAA-20/21 VIIRS to the long record, public hosting for agencies.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response. projectDetails.name: Project OnFire🔥
projectDetails.summary:
OnFire brings two different satellite perspectives together to make active fire data easier to explore and understand. Using NASA's MODIS and VIIRS observations, the platform allows users to examine hotspot distribution and changes in fire activity across Punjab, India, during October–November 2025.

By presenting both datasets in one interactive environment, OnFire helps users explore where observations overlap, where they differ, and how satellite resolution and observation characteristics affect the picture of fire activity.

Instead of treating each satellite dataset separately, OnFire offers a clearer, more accessible way to investigate their complementary observations. The goal is to support better understanding of satellite-based fire monitoring data and make it easier to explore patterns that may otherwise be difficult to see.
projectDetails.details:
OnFire is a web-based platform that brings NASA MODIS and VIIRS active fire hotspot observations into one interactive environment. It helps users explore fire activity, compare observations from two satellite instruments with different spatial resolutions, and understand their differences.

The project focuses on Punjab, India, using NASA FIRMS data collected between October 20 and November 30, 2025. Our workflow includes data acquisition, cleaning, geographic filtering, validation, database storage, and interactive visualization through a web interface.

Users can explore hotspot locations, examine observations over time, and compare MODIS and VIIRS data through the platform's available visualization features.

OnFire aims to make satellite fire data more accessible and understandable, supporting researchers, environmental analysts, and other users interested in monitoring agricultural burning and fire activity.

The backend was developed using C# and ASP.NET Core, with a database and data importer pipeline. The frontend uses web technologies for interactive visualization. The project also uses Python for data processing and analysis. The exact frameworks and libraries are documented in the project source code.

Our approach focuses on combining different satellite perspectives in one platform while considering data quality, spatial resolution differences, observation timing, and the limitations of hotspot detection.

projectDetails.name: MISSION OBBY
projectDetails.summary:
Mission Oppy is a pixel-art story game developed by Team Oppy (Marwan Magdy and Anas Hassany) for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing "Abandoned but not Forgotten." Players travel to Mars to retrace the mission of NASA's Opportunity rover and find her where she fell silent during the 2018 planet-wide dust storm. Designed for 90 sols, Opportunity operated for more than 14 years.

Players complete three interactive tasks inspired by real discoveries: identifying hematite at Eagle Crater, reconstructing rock layers at Endurance Crater, and restoring rover photographs at Victoria Crater. A final drive leads them to Oppy.

The game integrates NASA data directly into gameplay, using authentic Photojournal images, mission facts, and key locations from Opportunity's exploration. Each task reveals real NASA imagery with its title, date, and image ID, while the in-game Resources page links to the original sources.

By turning a real mission into an accessible interactive experience, Mission Oppy makes planetary science engaging for younger audiences and celebrates the rover and the people behind her.

projectDetails.name: NOVA: BEYOND THE UNKNOWN
projectDetails.summary:
NOVA EXPLORER — EXECUTIVE PROJECT SUMMARY

NOVA Explorer is an immersive 3D space exploration and survival game designed to bridge the gap between interactive entertainment and scientific education.

The project places players in the role of space explorers, allowing them to navigate planetary environments, undertake exploration missions, investigate unknown locations, collect resources, and document scientific discoveries.

Through its combination of 3D environments, 2D navigation interfaces, mission-based gameplay, and planetary exploration, NOVA Explorer transforms complex space-related concepts into an engaging and interactive experience.

Beyond entertainment, the project aims to stimulate scientific curiosity, encourage exploration, and make knowledge about the solar system more accessible. Its future development envisions expanded planetary environments, advanced exploration systems, richer scientific content, and more interactive learning opportunities.

NOVA Explorer is more than a game; it is a journey that connects exploration, technology, and learning beyond Earth.

Explore Beyond. Survive the Unknown. Build Your Universe.
projectDetails.details:
NOVA EXPLORER — PROJECT DETAILS

1. Project Introduction

NOVA Explorer is an interactive 3D space exploration and survival game that combines immersive gameplay, planetary exploration, and educational experiences. The project is designed to provide players with the opportunity to explore the solar system, investigate unfamiliar environments, complete exploration missions, and discover scientific information through an engaging virtual experience.

The game places the player in the role of an astronaut whose mission is to explore different celestial destinations, investigate unknown phenomena, and uncover the mysteries of space.

2. Project Objectives

The primary objectives of NOVA Explorer are to:

* Promote interest in space science and planetary exploration.

* Transform scientific concepts into interactive experiences.

* Provide an engaging environment for exploration and discovery.

* Encourage problem-solving through mission-based challenges.

* Combine entertainment with educational value.

* Create opportunities for future integration of scientific datasets and advanced interactive technologies.

3. Game Concept and Gameplay

Players experience the game as space explorers navigating different planetary environments. Each exploration journey introduces opportunities to investigate locations, interact with objects, complete objectives, and record discoveries.

The core gameplay experience is built around:

* Exploring planetary landscapes.

* Navigating between space destinations.

* Completing structured exploration missions.

* Investigating geological formations and unknown objects.

* Collecting resources and scientific samples.

* Tracking mission objectives and exploration progress.

* Unlocking further exploration opportunities.

4. Solar System Exploration

A central element of NOVA Explorer is its solar system exploration concept.

The planned destinations include:

* Moon: Lunar landscapes, craters, and exploration locations.

* Mars: Rocky deserts, canyons, and research environments.

* Mercury: Extreme temperatures and heavily cratered terrain.

* Venus: Volcanic landscapes and challenging atmospheric conditions.

* Europa: Frozen surfaces and icy geological formations.

* Titan: Atmospheric haze and methane-lake environments.

* Triton: Frozen plains and icy geological structures.

* Pluto: Icy mountains, plains, and distant exploration locations.

Each destination is intended to provide a distinctive visual identity and exploration experience.

5. 2D and 3D Experience

NOVA Explorer combines two complementary visual approaches:

3D Environment:

* Immersive planetary landscapes.

* Astronaut exploration.

* Spacecraft and environmental objects.

* Interactive locations and exploration scenes.

2D Interface:

* Solar system navigation.

* Mission objectives and progress.

* Player status information.

* Exploration and discovery panels.

* Menus and game controls.

This combination supports both immersive gameplay and clear access to important information.

6. Mission and Exploration System

The mission system provides structure and purpose to the player’s journey.

Missions are designed to involve activities such as:

* Exploring specific planetary regions.

* Scanning geological formations.

* Collecting scientific samples.

* Investigating abandoned research locations.

* Discovering hidden structures.

* Completing exploration objectives.

Mission progress can be presented through objective indicators and progress information, helping players understand their current tasks and achievements.

7. Data Collection and Scientific Discovery

An important aspect of NOVA Explorer is the use of exploration-related information to support the player’s experience.

The intended system can organize:

* Collected resources.

* Scanned objects.

* Discovered locations.

* Mission completion records.

* Exploration progress.

* Scientific observations.

This information helps players monitor their achievements and build a record of their exploration activities.

The project also provides an opportunity for future integration of verified scientific information about planets and celestial bodies.

8. Survival and Interactive Systems

The broader game concept includes survival and exploration mechanics intended to make planetary journeys more challenging and realistic.

These systems include:

* Oxygen management.

* Health monitoring.

* Environmental hazards.

* Resource collection.

* Equipment management.

* Environmental interaction.

Their implementation and availability should be verified in the current playable build.

9. Technology and Development Approach

The project is designed as a 3D interactive game supported by visual interfaces and modular gameplay systems.

Its development priorities include:

* Realistic planetary environments.

* Interactive 3D objects and characters.

* Responsive user interfaces.

* Mission and progression management.

* Efficient asset and scene management.

* Performance optimization.

* Opportunities for future scientific data integration.

The exact technology stack and implemented architecture should be documented according to the current source code.

10. Target Audience

NOVA Explorer is intended for:

* Students interested in astronomy and space science.

* Young learners and science enthusiasts.

* Players who enjoy exploration and adventure games.

* Educational institutions interested in interactive learning experiences.

11. Future Development

Future development opportunities include:

* Expanding planetary environments and exploration areas.

* Introducing more advanced mission scenarios.

* Enhancing spacecraft and planetary travel.

* Developing deeper survival and resource systems.

* Expanding scientific databases and discovery records.

* Integrating verified real-world planetary datasets.

* Improving graphics, sound design, and immersive interactions.

* Introducing additional educational activities.

12. Project Vision

NOVA Explorer aims to create a meaningful connection between interactive gaming and scientific exploration.

By transforming the experience of discovering space into an engaging virtual journey, the project seeks to inspire curiosity, encourage scientific thinking, and make planetary exploration more accessible.

NOVA EXPLORER — Explore Beyond. Survive the Unknown. Build Your Universe.

projectDetails.name: AstroPou
projectDetails.summary:
Space missions expose astronauts to unique physical and psychological challenges, including physiological changes, radiation exposure, reduced physical activity, and isolation from Earth.

AstroPou is an AI-assisted mobile health monitoring companion designed to support astronauts throughout their missions. It combines health tracking, daily check-ins, mood assessments, and interactive visualizations to help astronauts explore their health indicators and understand changes over time.

Through Ophiuchus, a constellation-inspired health visualization, users can explore health metrics, trends, and target ranges. AI-assisted insights help explain health information, while personalized reminders and alerts encourage proactive health awareness. The application also supports sharing health information with flight surgeons and introduces AstroPou, a friendly virtual companion that makes daily check-ins more engaging and promotes a sense of connection with Earth.

By bringing physical health monitoring and emotional engagement together, AstroPou aims to make astronaut well-being more accessible, proactive, and human-centered.

Far from Earth, Never Far from Home.
projectDetails.details:
Space exploration pushes human capabilities beyond familiar limits. But behind every mission, there is an astronaut facing physical demands, environmental challenges, and the psychological effects of isolation and confinement.

As missions become longer and humans travel farther from Earth, supporting astronauts requires more than monitoring vital signs. It also requires making health information understandable, encouraging healthy routines, and preserving a sense of connection and emotional support.

This is where AstroPou comes in.

Developed by Team OrbitCode, AstroPou is an AI-assisted mobile health monitoring companion designed to bring physical health awareness and emotional engagement together in one experience.

Inspired by the virtual pets many of us grew up with, AstroPou introduces a friendly digital companion alongside interactive health monitoring, AI-assisted insights, health trends, reminders, and communication with Earth.

Our goal is to make astronaut well-being more accessible, engaging, and human-centered throughout space missions.

Because every astronaut deserves to feel supported, no matter how far from home they travel.

Featuring a cinematic rocket launch background, the screen introduces the message: "Space Is Tough. You Don't Have to Face It Alone." This reflects one of the key challenges astronauts face during space missions: maintaining their physical and emotional well-being while living and working far from Earth.

Rather than starting with technical health metrics or data dashboards, we chose to introduce AstroPou through an emotional message that highlights the importance of support, connection, and companionship.

The supporting text, "Stay healthy, feel connected, and never feel alone," summarizes the application's three guiding ideas: health awareness, human connection, and emotional well-being.

A prominent "Meet Your Companion" call-to-action invites users to begin their journey and discover AstroPou, the virtual companion at the heart of the experience.

This introductory experience establishes the project's identity and communicates that AstroPou is more than a health monitoring application: it is designed to make astronaut well-being a more personal, engaging, and human-centered experience.

The screen features AstroPou against a view of Earth from space, creating a visual connection between the astronaut's environment and the home they are far away from.

A friendly welcome message — "Hey, space buddy! Ready to make this journey amazing together?" — introduces the companion as a supportive presence throughout the user's journey.

We chose a virtual pet-inspired character to make the application feel more personal and approachable. Rather than presenting astronauts with another conventional health monitoring interface, AstroPou introduces a familiar, friendly interaction that encourages engagement with daily well-being activities.

The Explore button invites users to continue into the application and discover its features.

This screen establishes the emotional identity of AstroPou: a digital companion designed to make health monitoring feel more human, engaging, and connected to Earth, even during missions far from home.

The Astronaut Health Dashboard is the central screen of AstroPou, designed to give astronauts an accessible overview of their daily health information within the context of their space mission.

At the top, a personalized greeting introduces the astronaut's daily health status. The center of the interface features an astronaut visualization surrounded by three key monitoring indicators: Radiation, Cardiovascular Health, and Physical Activity.

Rather than displaying these indicators in a conventional list, we visually connect each one to a corresponding area of the astronaut's body through interactive hotspots. This astronaut-centered approach makes health information easier to explore and creates a more intuitive connection between the data and the human body.

AstroPou, the virtual companion, appears alongside the astronaut and provides contextual, encouraging messages. This adds a human-centered layer to the monitoring experience, making routine health awareness feel more personal and engaging.

At the bottom, a mission status card displays the mission day, mission context, and an overall status indicator, connecting the astronaut's health overview to the wider mission environment.

By combining health indicators, interactive exploration, companion messages, and mission context in one interface, the dashboard aims to make astronaut health monitoring more understandable, engaging, and accessible.

The displayed percentages and status values in the interface are illustrative UI values and should not be interpreted as validated clinical measurements.

We designed this experience to transform health monitoring into something more visual and intuitive. Instead of presenting health indicators as a conventional list of numbers, Ophiuchus represents them as stars connected within a constellation. Each star corresponds to a health metric, creating a unified visual overview of different aspects of an astronaut's well-being.

The visualization includes indicators such as heart rate, blood pressure, mood assessment, body temperature, and sleep duration. Users can explore individual indicators and view more detailed information about the selected metric.

For example, the Sleep Duration view presents a seven-day trajectory alongside the average duration, recent trend, and target range. This allows users to explore changes over time rather than relying on a single reading.

The interface also uses visual status indicators to make information easier to interpret and highlights the selected metric within the constellation.

Ophiuchus brings together space-inspired design and health data visualization in a distinctive experience. Its purpose is to make complex health information more accessible, encourage awareness of changing patterns, and help astronauts better understand their well-being throughout a mission.

We designed this feature around the understanding that astronaut well-being involves more than tracking health measurements. Astronauts also need encouragement, healthy daily routines, timely awareness of changes, and a sense of connection with the people they leave behind.

The screen organizes communication into four categories:

  • Daily Motivation: Encouraging messages from AstroPou that reinforce positive health habits and keep astronauts engaged with their well-being.
  • Health Reminders: Practical reminders, such as staying hydrated, that encourage healthy daily routines during missions.
  • Messages from Earth: A dedicated communication category for supportive messages from loved ones, helping maintain an emotional connection with home.
  • Health Alerts: Notifications that draw attention to changes in health patterns, such as variations in sleep, and encourage astronauts to review their recent information and consider appropriate next steps.

Each category has a distinct visual style, using different colors, icons, and contextual companion expressions to help users recognize the type of message quickly.

By bringing these interactions together in one place, AstroPou extends health monitoring beyond data visualization. It creates a more supportive experience that combines daily health awareness, emotional encouragement, and connection with Earth.

The alerts are intended to support awareness and follow-up, not to provide medical diagnoses.

AstroPou is built on the belief that astronaut well-being goes beyond monitoring vital signs. It is about understanding health patterns, encouraging healthy routines, supporting emotional well-being, and maintaining a connection with Earth.

By combining AI-assisted health insights, interactive health visualization through Ophiuchus, personalized reminders, and a friendly virtual companion, AstroPou aims to make astronaut health monitoring more accessible, engaging, and human-centered.

Our vision is to help astronauts feel supported throughout their missions, while giving health monitoring a more personal meaning.

Because even when exploration takes us farther from Earth, the human need for care, connection, and companionship remains.

AstroPou – Far from Earth, Never Far from Home.

projectDetails.name: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
projectDetails.summary:
Project name: OrbitNexus

OrbitNexus is a health-monitoring software prototype designed to help astronauts understand changes in their health during space missions. It brings physiological readings, activity recognition, stress estimation, and anomaly detection into a single dashboard, helping users review their health indicators and identify changes that may need attention.

Our approach combines machine learning with insights from NASA’s Human Research Program and exploration of NASA’s Open Science Data Repository. Public physiological and activity datasets support prototype development, while NASA resources provide context about the challenges of maintaining health in space.

OrbitNexus addresses the challenge by making health information easier to interpret and supporting informed self-assessment. This matters during long missions, when communication with Earth can be delayed and crews need greater independence. The prototype supports health awareness rather than providing a clinical diagnosis. Future development will focus on validation, reliable wearable integration, and clear guidance for crew follow-up.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview

OrbitNexus is a health-monitoring software prototype designed to help astronauts understand changes in their health during space missions. It brings physiological readings and machine-learning outputs into a single dashboard, helping users review their condition and identify changes that may require attention.

The project addresses a central question: when an astronaut’s readings change, how can the crew understand those changes and decide what to check next?

How It Works

The prototype receives physiological and activity inputs through its telemetry pipeline. A simulator supports demonstrations when physical sensors are unavailable. Specialized machine-learning components process different types of information:

* Activity recognition provides context about the user’s movement.

* Pulse-signal analysis estimates heart rate.

* Stress estimation explores patterns in physiological signals.

* Anomaly detection flags unusual combinations of readings for further review.

The dashboard presents these outputs together so users can interpret them in context. A conversational assistant, connected through Groq, provides an additional way to explore health information. This cloud-connected component requires internet access and is separate from the locally executed analysis components.

Scientific Foundation and Data

NASA Human Research Program resources informed our understanding of spaceflight hazards and the need for crew health monitoring. Public datasets, including BIDMC, PAMAP2, and WESAD, support the development of physiological-signal processing, activity recognition, and stress-estimation components.

NASA OSDR data also informed our exploration of spaceflight biology. Biological research data and wearable measurements serve different purposes in the project. They are not combined as if they were measurements from the same person, and gene-expression results are not treated as a real-time diagnosis of an astronaut.

Tools and Development

The prototype uses Python and a Flask backend with a browser-based dashboard and API endpoints. Its machine-learning components include Random Forest, ExtraTrees, XGBoost, and Isolation Forest. The project also explores incremental learning with an SGDClassifier to investigate how models could adapt as new observations become available.

Software testing focuses on API behavior, data flow, and integration between components. These checks establish software functionality, not clinical accuracy.

Creativity and Intended Impact

OrbitNexus combines activity context, physiological signals, and anomaly detection in one interface. Its creative contribution is connecting different indicators into a health-monitoring workflow that helps the user understand what has changed, rather than viewing each reading in isolation.

The intended impact is to support crew health awareness and informed self-assessment during long missions. Similar approaches could eventually support people in remote environments on Earth, subject to further validation.

Design Considerations and Limitations

We considered readability, individual differences, sensor quality, false alarms, connectivity limitations, and the distinction between simulated and measured data. Earth-based datasets do not establish performance in microgravity, and stress estimates are not mental-health diagnoses.

OrbitNexus is a research prototype, not a clinically validated medical device or a replacement for flight surgeons. Further work includes independent model evaluation, testing with representative mission data, verified wearable integration, privacy safeguards, and expert review of any health guidance.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

challengeDetails.title: Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data

Your challenge is to create a decision‑support tool that uses NASA Earth observations along with local soil information, crop characteristics, and farmer priorities to help farmers explore rotation strategies that could strengthen soil health and adapt their farms to changing conditions.

projectDetails.name: Project OrbitShadow
projectDetails.summary:
ORBITSHADOW is an integrated astronaut health-monitoring platform designed to support crew members during long-duration space missions. It addresses the challenge of monitoring health changes that may develop gradually in space due to microgravity, isolation, and prolonged missions.
The platform brings together vital signs, camera-based monitoring, laboratory results, medical scans, and health records into one centralized profile. It helps track changes over time, compare health indicators with each astronaut’s personal baseline, and flag unusual trends that may require medical attention.
Beyond monitoring, ORBITSHADOW supports routine follow-ups and provides evidence-based preventive recommendations informed by previous spaceflight research and ground-based studies. By turning scattered medical information into a clearer picture of each astronaut’s health, it aims to support earlier intervention, better medical decisions, and safer long-duration missions.
projectDetails.details:
### What Does It Do and How Does It Work?

ORBITSHADOW is an integrated astronaut health-monitoring platform that brings vital signs, camera-based monitoring, laboratory results, medical scans, and previous health records into one centralized health profile.

It uses camera-based monitoring to estimate selected vital signs without requiring continuous wearable devices. These measurements can be combined with other medical data to track health changes over time.

The platform is designed to compare new measurements with each astronaut's personal baseline, identify unusual trends, and generate early warnings when changes may require medical attention. It also supports scheduled follow-ups and research-based preventive recommendations.

### What Benefits Does It Have?

- Brings different medical records and measurements together in one platform.

- Supports non-contact monitoring of selected vital signs.

- Helps identify unusual health trends earlier.

- Encourages regular follow-up, even when no symptoms are present.

- Provides preventive recommendations informed by previous spaceflight and ground-based research.

- Helps astronauts and medical teams make better-informed health decisions.

### What Is the Intended Impact?

ORBITSHADOW aims to shift astronaut healthcare from a reactive approach toward continuous and preventive health management.

By connecting health information and tracking changes over time, it can help medical teams recognize potential concerns earlier, reduce gaps between assessments, and support safer long-duration space missions.

### What Tools, Programming Languages, and Technologies Were Used?

Our prototype was developed using a combination of web development, computer vision, and signal-processing technologies:

- **Frontend:** React, TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML5, and CSS3.

- **Backend:** Python, FastAPI, and WebSockets.

- **Computer Vision:** OpenCV and MediaPipe Tasks Vision.

- **Vital-Sign Estimation:** Open rPPG and research-based models such as PhysNet, EfficientPhys, and FacePhys.

- **Signal Processing and Data Analysis:** NumPy, SciPy, and HeartPy.

- **Development and Deployment:** Vite, Docker, GitHub Codespaces, and Vercel.

These technologies support the prototype's camera-based monitoring, data processing, and interactive health dashboard.

### How Is the Project Creative?

The main innovation of ORBITSHADOW is not simply measuring vital signs, but connecting different types of medical information to build a broader picture of an astronaut's health.

It combines non-contact monitoring, personal health baselines, early warnings, routine follow-ups, and research-based prevention in one platform.

It also looks beyond the astronaut's current measurements by using previous spaceflight and ground-based research to support preventive decisions.

### What Factors Did Our Team Consider?

Our team considered the major health challenges of long-duration space missions, including:

- Microgravity and its effects on bones and muscles.

- Cardiovascular and immune system changes.

- Isolation, sleep disruption, and behavioral health.

- Limited opportunities for immediate medical assessment.

- The need for frequent monitoring without relying entirely on wearable devices.

- Measurement accuracy, data integration, and individual differences between astronauts.

- Data privacy and the importance of reliable medical evidence.

We also considered the limitations of camera-based measurements and the need for medical validation. ORBITSHADOW is designed to support medical teams, not replace professional medical judgment.

projectDetails.name: Orbit-X
projectDetails.summary:
ORBIT-X is an interactive 3D web platform that transforms complex space science data into an immersive space exploration and mission design experience.

Our team developed a platform where users can explore ten celestial bodies, investigate planetary internal structures, travel back approximately 3.5 billion years to discover ancient Mars, assess potential landing sites, and simulate gravitational differences across different worlds.

ORBIT-X combines React, TypeScript, and Three.js to deliver interactive 3D experiences, alongside Google's Gemini API, which powers Commander X, an AI-driven mission assistant.

One of our most innovative features is the 4-Way Pyramid Hologram, which transforms four synchronized mobile screen views into a holographic-style planetary visualization.

By combining scientific information, artificial intelligence, interactive simulations, and immersive visualization, ORBIT-X makes space science more accessible and engaging. Our mission is to inspire curiosity, encourage scientific thinking, and help students experience space exploration beyond traditional learning methods.
projectDetails.details:
ORBIT-X – Project Details

1. What Does ORBIT-X Do and How Does It Work?

ORBIT-X is an interactive 3D web platform designed to transform complex space science concepts into an immersive space exploration and mission design experience.

The platform allows users to explore ten celestial bodies through interactive 3D models, investigate planetary structures, travel through the geological history of Mars, evaluate potential landing locations, and simulate gravitational differences across celestial bodies.

Users can interact with several integrated modules:

  • Explode Core: Explore the internal structures of celestial bodies, including their crust, mantle, and core.
  • Cosmic Time Machine: Travel approximately 3.5 billion years into Mars' past to discover its ancient environment and evidence of flowing water.
  • Mission Viability Assessment: Investigate potential landing locations using coordinates and environmental factors such as radiation and terrain conditions.
  • Gravity Simulator: Compare gravitational forces and calculate theoretical jumping heights on different celestial bodies.
  • Commander X: Interact with an AI-powered mission assistant that explains scientific concepts and guides users through the platform.
  • 4-Way Pyramid Hologram: Experience a synchronized four-view display that creates a floating 3D holographic-style visualization of celestial bodies when viewed through a transparent pyramid.

2. What Are Its Benefits?

ORBIT-X makes space science more accessible by converting complex scientific information into interactive visual experiences.

Its main benefits include:

  • Making planetary science easier to understand through 3D exploration.
  • Encouraging hands-on learning instead of passive reading.
  • Helping students understand planetary environments and mission-planning challenges.
  • Demonstrating how gravity and environmental conditions differ across celestial bodies.
  • Introducing users to the role of scientific data and AI in modern space exploration.
  • Combining education, experimentation, and interactive technology in one platform.

3. What Is the Expected Impact?

Our goal is to make space exploration more understandable, engaging, and accessible, especially for students and beginners interested in astronomy, physics, and space technology.

ORBIT-X encourages curiosity, critical thinking, scientific investigation, and problem-solving.

By connecting real scientific concepts with interactive simulations, the platform aims to inspire the next generation of space enthusiasts, researchers, and engineers.

It also demonstrates how digital technologies can transform complex NASA-related scientific information into meaningful educational experiences.

4. What Tools, Programming Languages, Hardware, and Software Were Used?

ORBIT-X was developed as an interactive web-based platform using modern web technologies, real-time 3D visualization, and artificial intelligence integration.

Technology Stack:

  • Frontend Framework: React – Used to build the interactive user interface and platform components.
  • Programming Language: TypeScript – Used to develop structured, maintainable, and type-safe application logic.
  • 3D Visualization: Three.js – Used to create and render interactive 3D celestial bodies and immersive planetary exploration experiences.
  • Artificial Intelligence: Google Gemini API – Integrated to power Commander X, the AI-powered mission assistant that helps users understand scientific concepts and navigate the platform.
  • Scientific References: NASA and NASA JPL resources – Used as references for planetary science and space-related information.
  • Development Environment: Web-based development environment for building, testing, and improving the platform.
  • Hardware: Computers for development and compatible mobile devices for testing the responsive interface and 4-way pyramid holographic display.

These technologies work together to deliver an interactive experience that combines scientific exploration, 3D visualization, and AI-powered assistance.

5. What Makes ORBIT-X Creative and Innovative?

The creativity of ORBIT-X comes from combining several different space exploration experiences into one interactive platform.

Instead of presenting planets through ordinary images and text, ORBIT-X allows users to explore their structures, investigate their history, simulate physical conditions, and participate in mission-planning activities.

One of its most distinctive innovations is the 4-Way Pyramid Hologram, which transforms a mobile screen into four synchronized views to create a holographic-style planetary visualization using a transparent pyramid.

Another innovative aspect is the integration of Commander X, which combines AI-assisted guidance with interactive scientific exploration.

The platform brings together education, visualization, simulation, and experimentation in a unified experience.

6. What Factors Did Our Team Consider?

During the development of ORBIT-X, our team considered several important factors:

  • Scientific Accuracy: Using reliable scientific references and maintaining consistency with established planetary science information.
  • Educational Accessibility: Making complex scientific concepts understandable for students and beginners.
  • User Experience: Creating an intuitive and interactive interface that encourages exploration.
  • Performance: Considering the computational requirements of 3D visualization and interactive simulations.
  • Innovation: Developing distinctive experiences that go beyond traditional educational websites.
  • Practicality: Designing features that users can access through standard web browsers and compatible mobile devices.
  • Scalability: Building a concept that can be expanded with additional celestial bodies, scientific datasets, and mission-planning capabilities.

Conclusion

ORBIT-X is more than a platform for viewing planets. It is an interactive gateway to understanding the science, challenges, and possibilities of space exploration.

By combining 3D visualization, scientific information, artificial intelligence, physical simulations, and an innovative holographic experience, ORBIT-X transforms learning about space into an engaging journey of discovery.

ORBIT-X – Your Mission. Your Universe. Your Discovery.
