projectDetails.name: Mars Crew
projectDetails.summary:
Mars Crew is a free browser game for children aged 7 to 12, in Arabic and English. One to four players run a small base on Mars, in Gale Crater, where NASA's Curiosity rover measures radiation. Each player has one job: the Engineer keeps the power on, the Farmer grows food and fresh air, the Doctor protects the crew from radiation, and Mission Control on Earth watches the Sun. Robots fill any empty job.

There is never enough power, so every choice costs something and the players have to talk it through. The solar storms in the game really happened: they come from NASA's DONKI records with their real dates, and the radio delay between Earth and Mars is worked out for the real date, so a warning from Earth can arrive up to 20 minutes late. Dusty, a friendly robot who speaks in a recorded Egyptian Arabic voice and in English, guides the crew. Every job is a short mini-game that teaches one real fact, and a Science Lab, a Mars Academy, a Mars Explorer with real craters and real rover landings, and two missions based on real NASA events turn NASA's data into things children can try for themselves.
projectDetails.details:
The problem

Children aged 7 to 12 love space, but what they meet is usually facts and posters. They see how missions end, not the decisions that make them work. On Mars every decision has a cost: the air is thin, dust storms cover the solar panels, solar storms bring radiation, and a message from Earth can take up to about 22 minutes to arrive. The challenge asked for a game where children run a Martian or lunar outpost and feel these trade-offs for themselves, using real NASA data instead of invented numbers.

Our solution

Mars Crew turns each part of a real mission into a job for one player, so the trade-offs become real conversations between children. Whatever power one player gets, another player loses. A mission lasts about 15 minutes, every day ends with a short report that links each choice to its result, and losing is safe: the crew can replay the same morning with a new plan.

Every objective of the challenge, in the game

  • Run a Martian outpost: a base in Gale Crater with a greenhouse, labs, a radiation shelter, a sleep room and solar panels outside. A mission lasts 5, 6 or 7 days.
  • Power budgeting: every morning the crew shares a few power bolts between the air machine, plant lights, the storm walls and the radio, and must keep 3 for the night heaters. Dust on the panels lowers tomorrow's power.
  • Life support: Air + Food runs down every day. Suit air runs out outside, so players must go back in to refill. An air leak drains the base until someone patches it.
  • Food production: the Farmer plants, waters and harvests. Plants need light and water and pay back days later, so today's choice decides next week's food and air.
  • Radiation shielding: real solar flares trigger storms. The crew runs to a shelter whose walls hold water; radiation shortens each health bar for the rest of the mission and never heals.
  • Communication delay: Mission Control sees flares first, but warnings reach Mars only after the real light-travel delay for that date (19.8 minutes in February 2026). Earth sees a Mars camera that is minutes old.
  • Real trade-offs: 8 crew dilemmas, a shared power plan, and choices whose results show up days later. Turning the radio off saves power but blocks storm warnings.
  • Real NASA data: 165 real flares from NASA DONKI with their dates and IDs, real photos of the Sun on each flare day from NASA's SDO, Mars terrain from NASA MOLA, a globe from the Viking mosaic, real craters and real landing sites.
  • Ages 7 to 12: short sentences, a robot guide, mini-games instead of menus, "Help me choose" for younger players, and a visible arrow to the next job.
  • Teamwork: 1 to 4 players with split screen. If a teammate goes down, someone has 28 seconds to reach them. Every night the whole crew must meet in the sleep room.
  • Learning that sticks: mini-games that each teach one fact, 11 hands-on experiments, 12 Academy levels with a science question each, and 24 science cards with their sources.
  • Accessible to everyone: full Arabic and English, free, no install, no account, and it still works from saved data when there is no internet.

How does our solution work

1. Meet Dusty, the crew's robot guide

When the game opens, Dusty leaves his corner, grows as he flies to the middle of the screen, and welcomes the player in his own voice, then laughs, winks and returns to his corner. He stays with the crew on every screen: he explains things in short sentences, points to the next job, reacts to what happens with 15 expressions, and has a "Tell me more" button for extra detail.

2. Choose your crew

Each player picks one job and types a name and a suit colour. The four astronauts are drawn in code, with four views and ten expressions each, and their faces and poses follow what is really happening to them.

3. Build the mission (Mission Blueprint)

Before launch, the crew can choose a landing site (Gale, Jezero or Elysium) and up to three instruments inspired by real NASA ones (MEDA weather, RAD radiation, MOXIE oxygen), inside a small budget. The choices change the starting battery, shelter or Air + Food. The game says clearly that these budgets and bonuses are game rules, not spacecraft specifications.

4. A day on Mars

  1. Choose. Every second day the crew votes on a dilemma. Both options cost something.
  2. Share the power. Give power bolts to four machines and keep 3 for the night.
  3. Work. Each player has a sticky-note job list: jobs come in order, and emergencies such as a leak or a hurt teammate jump to the top. Every job is a mini-game.
  4. Survive. Suit air, nightfall, space rocks, dust devils, air leaks and solar storms.
  5. Sleep and learn. At night the whole crew must gather in the sleep room. The night report shows the day's numbers, a real fact about sleep in space, and a new science card.

5. A real solar storm, and a delayed warning

Each mission uses a window of real days from one of four saved periods of NASA DONKI flare records (165 flares, 2016 to 2026). On the hardest level, the Sun is the real February 2026 Sun, with an X8.1 flare on 1 February. Mission Control sees the flare first, but the warning reaches Mars only after the real radio delay for that date. The crew runs to the shelter. After the storm, a "This really happened!" card shows the real Sun on that day, photographed by NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory, with a ring on the flare and its DONKI record.

6. Every job is a mini-game

Each mini-game teaches one idea: wipe the dust off a panel (dust blocks sunlight), find the flare on the Sun and see its class (flares are graded A, B, C, M, X), drill through sand and rock to ice (water on Mars is underground), press repair steps in order (crews follow procedures), keep the dish pointed at Earth, patch a leak before the air escapes, breathe slowly to rest, and more: 15 jobs in total.

7. Mars Academy (solo levels)

One player learns one job at a time: 12 levels, 3 for each job. Each level opens with a hands-on experiment, gives one short job with a goal list, and ends with a science question. Players earn up to 3 stars and become an Expert when they finish a job's path. Example: "Storm warning!" is built on a real X1.5 flare from 3 February 2026.

8. Science Lab

The Science Lab on the main menu holds 11 hands-on experiments: dust on a solar panel, power at night, a water wall against radiation, the health bar, plants and light, ice under the ground, the radio delay, a twin rover on Earth, space rocks, dust storms and the space suit. Each one opens with Dusty's explanation, which he can read aloud in his recorded voice, and a slider or button to try it. Example: in "Power comes from the Sun", the child moves the dust slider and watches the power bolts drop as the panel gets dusty. The lab also holds the sticker album of 24 science cards, each with its fact and its source, and real NASA photos of Mars.

9. Mars Explorer: real places, real craters, real landings

A rotating globe made from the NASA/USGS Viking colour mosaic shows 8 real landing places and 11 named features (10 craters and the Hellas basin). Clicking a crater flies down to a close-up map made from NASA MOLA elevation data, with verified facts, a NASA image with its credit, and Dusty's explanation. From a landing place, children can help one of 9 real spacecraft land the way it really did: parachute, legs, airbags or sky crane. For example, they help Perseverance land in Jezero Crater.

10. Real NASA Event Missions

The Mission Archive holds two short missions based on real events: "The Radiation Surge" (Curiosity's RAD instrument measured its largest radiation surge since landing, on 20 May 2024) and "The Darkened Sky" (the 2018 planet-encircling dust storm tracked by MRO's Mars Climate Sounder). Each has NASA images, an evidence briefing and source links. The debrief keeps "What NASA observed" separate from "What happened in your simulation", so children see the difference between real measurements and the game.

11. Winning and losing

A win is a party with confetti and the whole crew dancing. After a loss, Dusty gives a tip and the crew can go back to the morning of the same day and try a new plan. Between days the crew builds one thing for the base, such as an extra solar panel or a water tank, and it appears on the map.

Dusty's voice and the voice-over

  • Real recorded voice: Dusty speaks Egyptian Arabic with 140 recorded lines, and English with 34 lines. Every clip is a local file; nothing is generated while you play, and no online speech service is used.
  • Lips that follow the voice: the game reads the loudness of each recording every 20 milliseconds, so Dusty's mouth opens on the real syllables and closes in the pauses, in both languages.
  • Always readable: every line is also shown as text in Dusty's speech bubble. The 164 lines that have no recording yet show their text only, and the game never plays a wrong clip in their place.
  • Voice controls: voice on or off, replay, stop and volume, on every screen.
  • The pitch video: Dusty narrates the 30-second video with his real recorded lines, from "Whoever's closest, get there now!" to "Every step helps the crew." Each subtitle shows a small talking Dusty and his name; Arabic lines show the Arabic words with the English translation underneath.

What is real, and what is a game rule

  • Real: every flare's class, date and DONKI ID; the radio delay for the mission date (from JPL planet positions: 11.3 minutes on Perseverance's landing day, NASA's press kit says about 11.4); every science card fact and quiz answer, with its source; crater names, terrain and landing sites.
  • Game rules: a day lasts about 2 minutes and 1 minute of delay is 1 second or less; radiation and health are points out of 100, not millisieverts, and whether a flare reaches Mars is a dice roll by its class; power, Air + Food and water are simple numbers, not engineering values.

Benefits

  • For children: they learn by deciding, not by memorising. Failing is safe, and each report explains what to try next.
  • For teachers and parents: a 15-minute mission, Class mode with discussion questions at big moments, free, nothing to install.
  • For the Arab world: full Arabic, with Dusty speaking Egyptian Arabic, so children can learn space science in their own language.
  • For trust in science: every real number has a source, and the game always says what is a game rule.

Our goal, and our limits

Our goal is to turn NASA's open data into decisions children can make with their friends, so that they understand why a Mars mission is hard, not only that it is. Our limits today: the game has not been playtested with children yet; it is made for PC (keyboard, mouse and gamepad), not phones; 164 of Dusty's lines are still waiting for recordings; and the live NASA flare feed uses NASA's public demo key, which has a low hourly limit, so the game falls back to NOAA and then to its saved NASA records.

Tools and technologies used

  • Game: HTML5 Canvas and plain JavaScript, no game engine and no framework. All game art, sound effects and music are made in code.
  • Data: NASA DONKI flare records, NASA SDO images (through Helioviewer.org), NASA MOLA elevation, the NASA/USGS Viking colour mosaic, the IAU planetary names gazetteer, JPL planet positions, NASA OSDR studies.
  • Testing: Node.js: 89 automated checks (both languages, every source, every mini-game can be finished, survival rules, robot teammates, every file the game loads) and autopilot missions that check that strategy matters.
  • Video: our own tools record the real game in a headless browser and edit the video in code, with music made in code.
  • Hosting: GitHub and Vercel, as a static website. Source code: https://github.com/mohamed-saied-1/mars-crew

Use of Super Intelligence (SI) tools

We used SI tools to help us build the project, while we were brainstorming for creative ideas about the challenge:

  • Coding help: SI coding assistant (Claude) helped us as a helper in test and fix code, check our NASA data against its sources
  • Subtitles: an offline speech-recognition model (Whisper) helped us find the exact words and timing in Dusty's Arabic recordings for the video subtitles.
  • Dusty's Arabic voice is a human recording. The game's art is drawn in code, and the NASA images are real photos shown with their credits. No SI-generated image is presented as NASA data, and no NASA logo or branding is used.

projectDetails.name: Project WUNDERBAO
projectDetails.summary:
FLARE (Fire & Life-Safety Analysis and Risk Explorer) is an interactive platform for exploring combustion and fire safety in microgravity. It combines an adjustable D² Law analytical simulator with a 3D chamber, live visual readouts, and controls for gravity, oxygen, pressure, airflow, and fuel. Users can explore 16 NASA combustion investigations, compare research cases with model scenarios, and learn through a kid-friendly flame sandbox and AI science assistant.

FLARE addresses the challenge by making it easier to investigate how reduced buoyancy changes flame shape and how cabin conditions affect combustion. This is important because understanding fire behavior supports safer spacecraft design, fire detection, and crew protection on long-duration missions. Simulation results are analytical model estimates, not raw spacecraft measurements or full CFD predictions.
projectDetails.details:
FLARE (Fire & Life-Safety Analysis and Risk Explorer) is an interactive web platform for exploring how combustion changes in microgravity and why spacecraft fire safety matters. In the scientific workspace, users adjust fuel, sample size, gravity, oxygen concentration, pressure, and airflow. A simplified D² Law analytical model estimates combustion behavior and displays results in an interactive 3D chamber with diagnostic layers and telemetry. Users can also explore 16 curated NASA combustion investigations and compare research cases with model scenarios.

FLARE makes complex space-combustion concepts easier to investigate for students, educators, researchers, and the public. Its intended impact is to build understanding of how cabin conditions affect fire behavior and crew safety, while clearly distinguishing model estimates from measured data. The separate FLARE Kids experience introduces the same ideas through an interactive flame sandbox, guided learning worlds, and Sparky, a child-friendly science assistant.

We developed FLARE with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion, Three.js, and React Three Fiber. NASA Physical Sciences Informatics and NASA Technical Reports Server records inform the research experience; Gemini can power the AI assistant, which also has a demo mode.

Our creative approach combines a research instrument, NASA investigation explorer, scenario comparison tools, and a kid-friendly learning space in one platform. We considered scientific transparency, source attribution, accessibility, reduced motion, responsive layouts, and safe explanations for young learners. FLARE is an educational analytical tool, not a full CFD solver or a source of raw spacecraft telemetry.

projectDetails.name: SkyShift-X
projectDetails.summary:
The sky looks still—until you press play. 
SkyShift X turns SPHEREx archive images into interactive sky movies, making the changing infrared universe accessible to everyone. Users enter sky coordinates, choose a field of view, and explore observations across dates and wavelengths. Images are aligned on a shared sky-coordinate grid and played chronologically, helping reveal possible movement and brightness changes. Wavelength controls distinguish spectral differences from changes over time.

Two modes welcome different explorers:
Beginner Mode offers simple controls and guided explanations for people with little astronomy knowledge. Research Mode provides deeper access to comparison tools, measurements, quality flags, and observation metadata to investigate candidate changes.

An integrated narrator with captions explains the images and evidence behind highlighted changes. Interactive 3D storytelling introduces SPHEREx and its mission without requiring prior astronomy knowledge.

Our solution addresses the challenge by transforming separate scientific observations into an intuitive visual experience. SkyShift X helps people watch, explore, and understand—connecting NASA’s open data with public curiosity, classroom learning, and deeper scientific investigation.
projectDetails.details:
The sky looks still—until you press play. 🛰️

SkyShift X turns real SPHEREx archive observations into interactive sky movies, bringing beginners and researchers into the same exploration—with different levels of detail.

Explore a place in the sky

The Sky Navigator offers coordinate entry, name search, and featured targets. Visitors can select a field of view and explore cases including Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis.

Or they can point coordinates on the map and the engine will search it easily

Watch observations become a movie

The viewer plays aligned infrared observations chronologically, with dates, wavelength information, adjustable speed, frame stepping, zoom, and a thumbnail timeline. Users can watch every observation or alternate between the first and last dates to make movement easier to notice.

These movies contain separate observations taken across time—not continuous spacecraft video.

Two modes, one set of observations

  • Beginner Mode provides a simple viewing experience and a “Can you find it?” interaction. Visitors can investigate independently or choose “Just show me” to reveal the measured change.
  • Research Mode adds wavelength and date controls, blink and comparison views, difference images, stacking tools, catalog overlays, spectra, quality flags, and detailed measurements with uncertainties.

A narrator tells the story behind the images

Narrated explanations with synchronized captions connect the observation sequence to its findings. They explain where we are looking, highlight measured changes, and summarize what the evidence supports and what remains uncertain. The interpretation comes from measurements and structured explanation templates; the voice presents that story.

Understand the mission through interactive exploration

The Universe Explorer provides educational experiences about SPHEREx when click MEET SphereX, the solar system, and the search for hypothetical distant worlds. These illustrations are distinguished from real observations, with a 2D fallback when 3D graphics are unavailable.

Know the telescope more

We understood that SPHEREx’s mission extends beyond Planet X:

it maps the infrared sky to study galaxies, cosmic history, and interstellar ice. Our interactive 3D explorer translates that broader mission into an accessible learning experience, connecting scientific context with real sky observations.

Why it matters

SkyShift X makes scientific images easier to access, compare, and understand. Beginners receive context, while researchers and experienced enthusiasts can inspect the supporting evidence.

The published demo includes clearly labeled saved movies built from real IRSA observations. Live retrieval and refreshing require the scientific backend. Throughout the experience, candidate changes are presented as findings to investigate—not automatic claims of discovery.

projectDetails.name: Project programming with farmers
projectDetails.summary:
YANBOO – Smart Agriculture Platform

YANBOO is a smart agricultural platform designed to help farmers overcome farming and marketing challenges and reduce crop waste.

The project introduces an integrated mobile application that supports farmers throughout the agricultural process, from choosing suitable crops and planting times to harvesting and selling their products.

YANBOO aims to use NASA satellite data, such as NASA POWER and NASA Earthdata, combined with weather information, to help farmers monitor climate conditions and make better agricultural decisions.

The platform also offers an agricultural marketplace where farmers can buy and sell crops and farming supplies, rent agricultural equipment, and find workers.

YANBOO aims to connect space technology with real agricultural needs, improve farmers' access to markets, reduce food waste, and support sustainable agriculture.

Our goal is to turn space data into practical solutions that make a difference on Earth.

projectDetails.name: Project Tenacity
projectDetails.summary:
Project Tenacity is a browser tool for planning a walk on Mars before taking it. It borrows the way NASA's rover drivers work at JPL (sketch a drive, simulate it, validate it against rules) and gives the same loop to astronauts on foot at Gale Crater. It is built for astronauts and mission operations personnel, not for the general public.

The crew lays out a walk on real orbital imagery, or lets the tool find the easiest path over the terrain. Tenacity then simulates the walk step by step: time on every slope, oxygen, cooling water and battery, and how long it would take to get back to the refuge at any moment. Fifteen flight rules give one clear answer, GO or NO-GO, name the rule that decides, and show where on the map it bites.

More than 25 layers of NASA data (terrain, slope, shadow, minerals, subsurface water, rock chemistry, solar-storm forecasts and Curiosity's own photos of each stop) feed the same rules, so the map and the plan cannot disagree. A 3D flyover shows the ground before the crew walks it. Every number is labelled as measured, a NASA value, derived or assumed.
projectDetails.details:
WHO IT IS FOR

Tenacity is a professional tool, not a public outreach site. It is built for two kinds of user: astronauts, who plan the walk and then follow it, and mission operations personnel (flight controllers, EVA officers and planners), who have to clear it before the crew leaves. We chose completeness over simplicity, on purpose: a tool for trained users should keep every rule, number and source in view, not hide detail to look simpler. That is why the interface is dense, speaks in flight rules and NASA alert conventions, and shows its numbers and their sources instead of hiding them. A guided tour is built in so that judges and newcomers can find their way around.

WHAT IT DOES

Tenacity answers one question for a crew about to leave the airlock: is this walk safe, by how much, and what decides it?

1. Sketch. Load a ready-made walk, or click the map to add stations anywhere. Each leg can follow ground a rover has already driven, go in a straight line, or take the easiest path the terrain engine finds. Keep-out zones can be marked; paths go around them.

2. Simulate. The walk is simulated before it happens: pace and effort on every slope, oxygen, carbon dioxide, cooling water and battery, and the walk-home time from every point.

3. Validate. Fifteen flight rules are checked along the whole walk. Examples: the refuge must always be within 60 minutes at emergency pace, because that is how long a suit's backup supply lasts; ground steeper than 20 degrees may not be crossed in any direction; a solar eruption forecast to reach Mars blocks the walk. A rule whose data are missing or too old is shown as "not evaluated", never as a pass.

4. Understand. Click any point to read every layer there. Ask why a path was chosen: ground that cannot be crossed is shown in red, slow ground in yellow, and the straight line the path finder rejected is drawn. Fly along the route in 3D over real terrain and imagery, with Curiosity's own photograph of each station. Recordings of each of these steps in motion (sketching a walk, playback, the 3D flyover and the guided tour) are in the project repository: https://github.com/yara-hue24/Project-Tenacity#in-motion

WHAT INSPIRED THE DESIGN

The design is modelled on RSVP (Robot Sequencing and Visualization Platform), the tool suite NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory has used to plan surface operations on its Mars rovers and landers since 1997. Rover planners sketch a drive on the terrain, build it into a command sequence, simulate it, and check it before it is sent to Mars. Tenacity maps each part of that suite to a walk: the Activity list and sketching on the map follow MobSketch; the sequence table and console follow RoSE, the sequence editor; the walk simulation follows SSim, the surface simulation; and the terrain views, clocks and playback follow HyperDrive. Alert colours and layout rules follow NASA-STD-3001 and the crew-interface work at Johnson Space Center.

Source: https://www-robotics.jpl.nasa.gov/what-we-do/applications/user-interfaces/

HOW IT IS BUILT

A static web page: HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript modules, with Leaflet for the 2D map and our own WebGL code for the 3D view. There is no server and no build step. The terrain engine runs in the browser in a web worker on a 5-million-cell elevation grid: slope, cast shadow for the time of day, line of sight to the refuge, a walk-home time field and least-time path finding. Data files are built from NASA's public services by Python scripts in the repository, so every file can be regenerated. Plans, notes and the history of changes are stored in the browser. 113 automated tests cover the simulation, the Mars clock, the terrain engine and the 3D maths.

WHY IT IS CREATIVE

  • It treats a spacewalk the way mission operations treats a rover drive: a sequence that is simulated and checked against rules before anyone moves.
  • The layers are not pictures beside a planner. The same slope, shadow, sight-line and space-weather data drawn on the map are what the rules read.
  • It is honest about what is known. Every constant carries a tag (MEASURED, NASA VALUE, DERIVED, ASSUMED) and its source.
  • The interface follows NASA's display standard for alert colours and is built like a professional workstation: resizable docks, a guided tour, search, and a large mode for gloved hands.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Crew safety first: the limit that usually decides a walk is not oxygen but how far you can be from shelter if the suit fails. Mobility in a suit: slope limits, slow ground, loose ground. The environment: daylight for the season, cast shadow, radiation and solar storms. Working in pairs, with a pressurised rover as a refuge that can be re-parked. What the crew will see on arrival: rover photographs at the stations and a 3D view of the ground.

LIMITS WE STATE OPENLY

Walking speed and effort on Mars in a suit have never been measured; the model is extrapolated from Earth and Moon data. The elevation model is good for relative height, not absolute. Position error is not modelled. This is a first prototype for planning and training, not a certified flight product. The README lists every known limit.

INTENDED IMPACT

Rover planners simulate every drive before it happens. We want crews on foot to have the same habit and the same kind of tool.

USE OF AI

The team chose the challenge, set the concept, the requirements and the design direction, and reviewed and tested the result. Research was done in two ways: by hand (the team found and read primary NASA and JPL sources itself) and with AI tools (Perplexity, an AI search assistant, to locate and cross-check sources, and Claude, an AI coding assistant by Anthropic, for further background research). Most of the code and the data-building scripts were written with Claude under the team's direction. No AI-generated images, audio or video are part of the project: every picture is a screenshot or recording of the working tool.

Source code: https://github.com/yara-hue24/Project-Tenacity - Project paper (PDF): https://yara-hue24.github.io/Project-Tenacity/docs/Tenacity-project-description.pdf

projectDetails.name: Luminar Horizon
projectDetails.summary:
Luminar Horizon is an interactive 3D browser game that turns space mission design into a hands-on engineering challenge. Players build a fictional wildfire-monitoring CubeSat, select its instruments, orbit, launch service, and ground stations, then operate it across three simulated days.

Every decision has consequences: a better camera can demand more power, fill storage faster, and overwhelm communications. Success depends on delivering useful observations to the ground on time—not simply collecting data. An explanatory mission report helps players identify bottlenecks, redesign their spacecraft, and compare results.

The project addresses the challenge by connecting spacecraft design, launch, orbital operations, and scientific outcomes in one playable experience. Real NASA FIRMS fire detections provide clearly labeled geographical context. Designed for students and curious learners, Luminar Horizon makes mission trade-offs visible and encourages learning through experimentation.
projectDetails.details:
Luminar Horizon, developed by ZagQ, lets players experience the complete design–operate–evaluate cycle of an educational space mission.

Its first scenario, Earth Guardian, challenges players to design a CubeSat for wildfire observation. In an interactive 3D hangar, players configure the spacecraft’s structure, payload, solar arrays, battery, communications, storage, and pointing system. They also choose an orbit, launch service, and ground stations. Engineering checks reveal whether the design meets its budget, mass, power, and launch constraints.

Players then simulate three mission days around a 3D Earth. The simulation connects orbital position and sunlight with battery charge, observation opportunities, storage, ground-station visibility, and data transmission. Scientific observations earn credit only when they meet the mission’s requirements and reach the ground before their deadline.

The mission report explains the outcome, allowing players to investigate failures and compare redesigned missions. Preset designs demonstrate different engineering approaches and bottlenecks. Browser saves and export/import features support continued experimentation.

Our creative approach is to make the entire journey of scientific data part of the game: from collecting an observation to storing it onboard and delivering it to its users. This demonstrates why a powerful instrument alone cannot guarantee a successful mission.

An optional NASA FIRMS overlay displays a dated sample of real NOAA-20 VIIRS fire detections. These observations are clearly separated from fictional mission targets and scoring. The published version uses a bundled dataset rather than a live feed.

We built the project using TypeScript, React, Next.js, Three.js, HTML/CSS, Blender, and Python, with Vitest and Playwright supporting verification. Development included AI assistance through Codex and Claude, directed and reviewed by the project team.

Design priorities included understandable feedback, reproducible results, browser performance, fullscreen visualization, keyboard and touch alternatives, and light and dark themes. Hardware specifications and simulation assumptions are intentionally simplified for education. The intended impact is to help learners understand how connected engineering decisions shape mission success.

Your challenge is to create a layered, integrated view of a location or route on the Martian surface that pulls together data from multiple NASA science missions and could help a human explorer plan and carry out a successful Marswalk while conducting new and exciting science along the way.

projectDetails.name: TRACORA
projectDetails.summary: TRACORA is an interactive digital space museum and exploration map created by team ZENTHRA for the NASA Space Apps Challenge ("Abandoned but not Forgotten"). Our project bridges the gap between historical space engineering and young minds by bringing NASA's retired rovers, landers, and scientific instruments back to life. Through an immersive, story-driven web platform featuring the Moon and Mars, we transform dense technical archives into engaging first-person narratives. TRACORA inspires school-age space enthusiasts to explore the rich history of off-world artifacts and connects humanity's past achievements with future space pioneers.
projectDetails.details: TRACORA is a web-based interactive experience designed to make space exploration history accessible and engaging for school-age learners. Developed using HTML, Tailwind CSS, and JavaScript, the platform features a dual-planet interactive map (Moon and Mars) and a digital museum gallery. It uses first-person storytelling to present real historical mission data of abandoned hardware (such as Apollo modules and Mars rovers). Team ZENTHRA focused on intuitive navigation, rich visual design, and educational impact to spark curiosity in the next generation.

challengeDetails.excerpt: Since the 1960s, NASA has left hardware across the solar system–on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space. From rovers and instruments that completed their science missions to probes still traveling away from Earth this hardware varies widely in both its purpose and current level of functionality. Your challenge is to tell the story of some or all of this equipment that introduces school-age space enthusiasts to the hardware and the science it made possible.

projectDetails.name: Zero Flare : CIR - 1
projectDetails.summary: ZERO FLARE — FLAME EVIDENCE LAB turns NASA's underused microgravity-combustion archive into a live, evidence-grounded research environment for the Artemis generation. We ingested 24 NASA PSI combustion investigations — recovering 22 experimental tables (2,009 rows, SHA-256-verified against the acquisition manifest), 63 verified equations, and honest model cards — and built an AI research copilot, CIR-1, that answers every factual claim through 26 deterministic tools with visible provenance, never inventing data. Researchers explore investigations, run a comparability gate that refuses invalid cross-study claims, screen lunar/ISS/Mars habitats with a transparent facility-risk engine, walk a 3D equipment lab built from public NASA descriptions (plus official NASA ISS & Perseverance 3D assets), and export reproducible evidence packets. Missing data stays missing; negative results stay visible.
projectDetails.details:
ZeroFlare Evidence Lab - Start your Mission

1-Home page

This interface is the main dashboard of the ZERO FLARE platform. It provides access to NASA microgravity fire research, experimental datasets, investigations, scenarios, comparisons, 3D tools, and scientific resources. The homepage also highlights key research statistics, available environments such as ISS and Earth reference conditions, and provides direct access to the CIR-1 AI copilot for research assistance.

2-Mission

This interface presents the main research environments used in ZERO FLARE, including the International Space Station, lunar habitat, Mars habitat, and spacecraft cabin. Users can select an environment to explore how gravity, oxygen level, and atmospheric conditions affect fire behavior and combustion research.

This interface evaluates whether the selected environment stays within the limits of available microgravity combustion data. It compares oxygen level, pressure, and material-family test ranges, then highlights where the selected conditions are supported by experiments and where they fall outside the tested envelope.

This interface guides users to start from the available evidence. It provides direct access to investigations, comparisons, and scenarios, while clearly showing the limits of the platform, including unsupported predictions, missing media, and areas without validated experimental data.

This interface visualizes the evidence coverage across NASA combustion investigations. It shows which research dimensions—such as gravity, oxygen, pressure, material, hardware, outcomes, and measurement context—are observed, reported, condition-specific, or missing from the current dataset.

This interface presents curated NASA research videos and experimental media related to microgravity combustion. It allows users to explore visual evidence from real space-based fire experiments, including flame behavior, droplet combustion, and laboratory testing aboard the International Space Station.

 

This interface summarizes key findings from the available microgravity combustion evidence and ranks important scientific results with their supporting datasets and limitations. It also provides access to authentic NASA imagery related to combustion experiments, allowing users to connect research conclusions with real experimental media.

 

 3- investigations

This interface provides access to the available combustion investigations and their detailed research workspaces. Users can click any experiment in the investigation list to open it and explore its objectives, data, equipment, media, equations, graphs, metadata, related investigations, and research keywords.

This interface provides a visual analysis of the selected experiment’s dataset. It presents column statistics, data distributions, scatter plots, and condition-based comparisons, helping users quickly identify patterns, relationships, and important characteristics within the experimental measurements.

This interface displays authentic NASA images related to the selected combustion investigation. It allows users to explore real experimental hardware, laboratory setups, researchers, and spaceflight equipment, providing visual context for the scientific data and investigation results.

This interface provides the verified scientific equations related to the selected investigation. It organizes gas laws, pressure calculations, mixture properties, stoichiometry, and flammability equations, with references and direct links to use them inside the Scenarios workspace.

This interface presents a visual evidence graph showing the selected investigation and its related experiments, equipment, and research connections. Users can click any connected investigation node to open that experiment and return directly to its Overview page for further exploration.

 4- scenario

This interface supports fire-safety scenario analysis across the full lifecycle, from prevention and detection to prediction and suppression. Users can configure the environment, compare compartment risk levels, review facility screening results, and save scenario settings for further analysis.

 

This interface combines the CIR-1 Fire Safety Assistant with verified equations, prevention evidence, and scientific calculators. Users can ask questions about the selected facility, explore supporting NASA evidence, calculate atmospheric and flammability conditions, and review research gaps before making scenario-based decisions.

5- compare
This interface compares experimental conditions across multiple investigations. It visualizes observed ranges, such as oxygen concentration, and helps users identify where different studies overlap, differ, or may not be directly comparable before making cross-investigation conclusions.
 6- 3D lab

This interface provides an interactive 3D laboratory for exploring spacecraft combustion hardware and experimental apparatus. Users can browse hardware records, view reconstructed equipment models, inspect components, access related NASA media, and explore animated experiment demonstrations.

This interface provides a detailed 3D view of the selected combustion apparatus, including labeled components, related experiment information, and authentic NASA images. It also includes an animated experiment demonstration that shows the main stages of the procedure, allowing users to better understand how the hardware and experiment operate.

7-Data and Resources

This interface documents the data sources used across ZERO FLARE. It shows the recovered experimental tables, row and column counts, duplicate records, parse issues, file sizes, investigation IDs, and verification hashes, providing a transparent view of the project’s data provenance and integrity.

8- Chatbot

These interfaces show the CIR-1 Research Copilot in both compact and expanded views. The assistant is available across the platform to help users ask questions about experiments, datasets, equations, models, and NASA combustion evidence, while keeping the conversation connected to the current research context.

This interface shows CIR-1 responding to a research question about a specific investigation. The copilot retrieves experiment information such as the investigation title, research area, project type, objectives, and supporting references, allowing users to explore NASA combustion studies directly through natural-language questions.

Benefits

  •  Provides a centralized platform for exploring NASA microgravity combustion research, experimental datasets, scientific equations, and supporting media.
  • Makes complex fire-science information easier to understand through interactive dashboards, visualizations, comparison tools, and 3D representations.
  • Helps researchers explore individual NASA investigations in detail, including objectives, datasets, equipment, media, equations, graphs, and documented gaps.
  •  Allows users to compare multiple experiments and identify similarities, differences, overlapping conditions, and limitations before making cross-study conclusions.
  • Supports evidence-based analysis by connecting results to verified datasets, NASA records, scientific equations, and provenance information.
  • Uses the CIR-1 AI Research Copilot to answer natural-language questions about investigations, datasets, equations, models, and research evidence.
  • Reduces the time required to manually search through multiple research records and datasets.
  •  Helps users identify missing data, unsupported assumptions, and areas where additional experiments may be required.
  •  Supports scenario-based analysis for different environments such as the International Space Station, lunar habitats, Mars habitats, spacecraft cabins, and Earth-reference conditions.
  • Provides fire-safety scenario support across prevention, detection, prediction, and suppression stages.
  • Includes scientific calculators and verified equations that can be used directly inside research scenarios.
  • Provides interactive data analysis, including descriptive statistics, distributions, relationships, grouped comparisons, and correlation analysis.
  •  Supports the exploration of authentic NASA research media to provide visual context for combustion experiments and experimental hardware.
  • Provides interactive 3D models of combustion hardware and experimental apparatus to improve understanding of complex equipment.
  • Maintains transparency by clearly displaying data provenance, source references, duplicate records, parse issues, and evidence limitations.
  • Preserves missing information instead of automatically replacing it with artificial values.
  • Helps students, researchers, and engineers understand microgravity combustion research in a more accessible and interactive way.
  • Provides a single research environment that combines data analysis, scientific evidence, visualization, AI assistance, and engineering tools.
  • Supports faster and more informed research decisions by bringing multiple sources of evidence into one platform.
  • Can be extended in the future with additional datasets, experiments, scientific models, and AI capabilities.
  • Provides a web-based interface that can be accessed without requiring users to install specialized scientific software.
  • Encourages traceable and reproducible research by linking calculations and results back to their original sources.
  • Helps distinguish between experimentally observed results, reported information, condition-dependent evidence, and missing evidence.
  • Reduces the risk of presenting unsupported scientific conclusions by clearly identifying the tested limits of available data.
  • Creates an educational environment that can also support demonstrations, research presentations, and academic projects.

Development Tools

  • Next.js – Main full-stack web framework used to build the ZERO FLARE platform and server-side API routes.
  • React – Used to build reusable and interactive user-interface components.
  • TypeScript – Provides strong typing, safer development, and improved maintainability.
  • Node.js – Server-side JavaScript runtime used by the application and development environment.
  • npm – Used to install and manage project dependencies and development packages.
  • Google Gemini API – Powers the CIR-1 AI Research Copilot and natural-language interaction.
  • Google GenAI SDK (@google/genai) – Provides official server-side access to Gemini, structured responses, and native function calling.
  • Zod – Used for validating API requests, responses, tool arguments, and structured application data.
  • REST API Architecture – Used to connect the frontend, AI agent, scientific tools, and application services.
  • Next.js API Routes – Used to provide secure server-side endpoints such as the CIR-1 copilot API.
  • CSV Data Processing – Used to store and process the cleaned experimental datasets supplied by the research team.
  • JSON – Used for structured configuration, API responses, reports, tool outputs, and metadata.
  • Custom Data Query Layer – Used to filter, group, analyze, and calculate statistics from the experimental datasets.
  • Statistical Analysis Tools – Used for descriptive statistics, grouping, median calculations, correlations, and experimental-data exploration.
  • Scientific Equation Registry – Used to manage and execute verified scientific formulas throughout the platform.
  • BM25 Information Retrieval – Used to search and rank research evidence and knowledge-base documents.
  • Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) – Used to provide the AI assistant with relevant research evidence and source context.
  • Native AI Function Calling – Allows Gemini to select and execute validated ZERO FLARE research tools.
  • Structured AI Responses – Used to provide predictable and validated outputs from the AI assistant.
  • HTML5 – Provides the structural foundation of the web interface.
  • CSS / Responsive Styling – Used to create the visual design, space-themed interface, and responsive layouts.
  • JavaScript – Supports interactive browser behavior and application logic.
  • Interactive Data Visualization – Used to display charts, distributions, comparisons, and experimental relationships.
  • 3D Visualization Technologies – Used to display interactive combustion hardware and apparatus models.
  • NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) Data – Provides the main experimental research evidence used by the platform.
  • NASA Images and Video Library – Provides authentic NASA imagery and research media.
  • Git – Used for version control and tracking changes across development phases.
  • GitHub – Can be used for private source-code storage, collaboration, backup, and deployment integration.
  • Visual Studio Code / Coding Agents – Used for development, debugging, code inspection, and implementation support.
  • Codex / AI Coding Assistance – Used to support structured implementation, testing, debugging, and code review during development.
  • Automated Testing – Used to verify equations, dataset queries, API contracts, request isolation, provider integration, and user-interface behavior.
  • TypeScript Type Checking – Used to identify type errors before deployment.
  • Production Build Testing – Used to verify that the application can successfully compile and run in production mode.
  • Environment Variables (.env.local) – Used to securely configure private server-side settings such as AI API credentials.
  • Vercel – Intended as the deployment platform for the production Next.js application.
  • Porkbun – Used for management of the custom project domain and DNS configuration.
  • Custom Domain (zero-flare.study) – Intended as the final public address of the ZERO FLARE platform.
  • HTTPS / SSL – Used to provide secure communication between users and the deployed web application.
  • Browser-Based Speech Synthesis – Used to provide optional voice output for the CIR-1 Research Copilot.
  • Responsive Web Design – Allows the platform to adapt to different screen sizes and presentation environments.
  • Hash-Based Data Integrity Verification – Used to confirm that imported research files remain unchanged and traceable.
  • Provenance Tracking – Used to preserve the relationship between displayed results, experimental datasets, and original research sources.
  • Server-Side Secret Management – Prevents private AI API credentials from being exposed in the browser or public application code.

projectDetails.name: ZeroG Pulse
projectDetails.summary: ZeroG Pulse is a health self-assessment tool for astronauts on long missions, where a message to the flight surgeon takes minutes each way and can be lost in a blackout. The crew measures a vital sign (blood pressure, heart rate, glucose, temperature, SpO2, sleep, mood, stress or radiation dose). One Rust engine judges it against ranges for the environment it was taken in, tags the NASA Human Research Program hazards behind it, and places it on a four-step ladder: Monitor, Self-care, Consult ground, Urgent. A clickable body view shows status as colour, icon and word. Guidance offers only actions the onboard kit allows. When ground is needed, the app drafts an SBAR report and sends it over a delayed link, and keeps working offline. If the rich interface fails, a plain safe-mode console shows the same status from the same event log, so no two screens can disagree. Every range states whether it is adapted from NASA numbers or our own placeholder, and all crew readings are simulated. On the way to Mars, the crew has to judge their own health; ZeroG Pulse gives them a clear answer and a next step.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

ZeroG Pulse helps astronauts answer two questions without waiting for Earth: is this number a problem, and what do I do now? Deep-space crews face the five hazards NASA's Human Research Program names: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment. Near Mars a message to the flight surgeon takes minutes each way, so the crew must measure, judge and act on their own.

How it works

1. A body view opens on the crew's status. Today's checks flag what is due, for example a stale blood pressure reading.

2. A guided card explains how to measure in space and why it matters there. The astronaut enters the value; every reading carries its environment, device and confidence.

3. One deterministic Rust engine assesses it: a low-confidence reading never raises an alarm, and an out-of-range one is placed on a four-step ladder (Monitor, Self-care, Consult ground, Urgent). Two trusted out-of-range readings in a row escalate to Consult ground.

4. "Why?" explains the range, what is expected in flight and the source behind it, with a tag saying whether the range is adapted from NASA numbers or a placeholder.

5. Guidance offers only actions the onboard kit allows. When ground is needed, the app drafts an SBAR report (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) and sends it over a delayed link; the reply comes back after the same delay, and the outbox waits through blackouts.

6. If the rich interface is lost, a plain safe-mode console shows the same status and accepts readings, because every screen derives its view from the same append-only event log.

7. An activity-only crew score (streaks, XP) rewards doing checks without ever showing health values.

Benefits and impact

For the crew: a clear status and next step without medical training. For flight surgeons: structured SBAR reports, sent only when the ladder says ground is needed. For the mission: one engine, so the rich app, safe mode and ground can never disagree, and the tool keeps working when the screen or the link fails. On Earth, the same pattern fits remote clinics, ships and polar stations where a doctor is hours away.

Tools and languages

Rust (core engine, compiled to WebAssembly with wasm-bindgen), TypeScript with React and Vite (crew and ground web app, inline SVG body view), egui (safe-mode console, native and WebAssembly), axum (Ground Station API, JSONL storage), Tauri (desktop app), an Android WebView shell, GitHub Actions and Cloudflare Pages for CI and deployment.

What makes it creative

Status is computed once, in one engine, and every face renders what it says, so a reading entered in safe mode appears in the crew app and the reverse. The delayed ground loop is built in, not bolted on. The hazard lens ties every indicator to the NASA hazard that drives it.

What we considered

Honesty: all crew readings are simulated, never called NASA data, and every range shows its source status. No NASA document we found gives numeric in-flight vital-sign ranges, so we say so per indicator: sleep and radiation dose are adapted from NASA numbers; the rest are our own placeholders with NASA context. Safety: no diagnoses and no medication doses; ZeroG Pulse is not a medical device. Accessibility: status is always colour plus icon plus word. Resilience: the crew app and safe mode work fully offline.

Team: Tarek Darwish, Mostafa Emad El Din, Amr Yasser, Sama Waheed, Mohamed Naser.

projectDetails.name: Project ZeroG_Pulse
projectDetails.summary:
ZeroG Pulse is an autonomous deep-space telemedicine HUD and multi-organ digital twin designed to solve medical triage during deep-space communication blackouts (such as the 14m 28s light-delay on Mars transit). 

Developed by undergraduate computer science students at the Egyptian Chinese University (Team GTX Infinity-1), ZeroG Pulse features:
1. Real-time biometrical and environmental telemetry tracking aligned with NASA-STD-3001 and ECLSS thresholds.
2. A 5-organ holographic digital twin (CNS, Cardiovascular, Pulmonary, Hematopoietic, and Musculoskeletal systems) mapping cabin anomalies to organ-level stress in real time.
3. A 30-Minute Clinical Deterioration Predictor with actionable mitigation checklists.
4. Bilingual (English and Arabic) Web Speech API integration with multi-tier LLM failover (Groq, Gemini, OpenRouter, Hugging Face).

By operating locally first with deterministic rules, ZeroG Pulse ensures astronauts can diagnose, assess, and treat critical emergencies immediately without waiting for Earth's reply. Live application: zerog-pulse.vercel.app
projectDetails.details:
ZeroG Pulse is an autonomous deep-space telemedicine HUD and 5-organ digital twin designed to solve medical triage during deep-space communication blackouts (such as the 14m 28s light-delay on Mars transit).

What it does:

- Tracks live biometrical and environmental telemetry aligned with NASA-STD-3001 and ECLSS thresholds.

- Simulates a 5-organ holographic matrix (CNS, Cardiovascular, Pulmonary, Hematopoietic, and Musculoskeletal systems) mapping cabin anomalies to organ-level stress in real time.

- Features a 30-Minute Clinical Deterioration Predictor with actionable mitigation checklists.

- Integrates bilingual (English/Arabic) Web Speech API control and multi-tier LLM failover (Groq, Gemini, OpenRouter, Hugging Face).

Impact: Empowers crews to diagnose, assess, and treat critical emergencies immediately without waiting for Earth's reply, bridging the gap for deep-space missions and terrestrial remote telemedicine. Live application: zerog-pulse.vercel.app

projectDetails.name: Astro Health
projectDetails.summary: Developed an advanced, professional astronaut vital signs dashboard powered by authentic medical data. This project addresses the critical challenge of continuous in-flight health monitoring by rigorously analyzing an astronaut's medical status in real-time, detecting abnormal physiological indicators, and issuing immediate early-warning alerts accompanied by actionable treatment recommendations. The importance of this project lies in the extreme environments of space, where astronauts are constantly exposed to silent health risks and physiological shifts that they may be unaware of—such as cardiovascular strain, fluid shifts, or radiation effects—which could otherwise become life-threatening. By bridging real-time telemetry with predictive medical insights, this dashboard ensures proactive astronaut safety, minimizes mission risks, and acts as an essential lifeline beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

Our project is an advanced, real-time astronaut vital signs health dashboard designed to monitor physiological parameters based on authentic medical data. It works by collecting and simulating real-time telemetry data (such as heart rate, oxygen saturation, and body temperature), processing it through a Node.js backend, and visualizing it dynamically on the frontend. The interface incorporates Three.js to deliver an immersive 3D space-themed environment, alongside HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for a responsive, clean, and intuitive user dashboard. If any vital sign crosses safe thresholds, the system instantly triggers automated early-warning alerts and provides step-by-step actionable treatment recommendations.

2. What benefits and intended impact does it have?

Astronauts in deep space or on the ISS are constantly exposed to hidden physiological stressors, silent health risks, and sudden medical anomalies that they might not notice immediately. The primary impact of this project is saving lives by shifting from reactive healthcare to proactive, real-time prevention. It acts as an autonomous medical lifeline, reducing mission risks and ensuring crew safety.

3. What tools, coding languages, and technologies were used?

  • Frontend: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and Three.js for 3D visualizations.
  • Backend: Node.js for managing server-side logic, real-time data flow, and alert thresholds.
  • Data Source: Authentic medical parameters tailored for aerospace physiological monitoring.

4. How is your project creative and what factors did we consider?

The project stands out through its creative integration of Three.js to create a futuristic 3D interface that makes monitoring engaging and intuitive in a space-like setting. Key factors considered during development include data accuracy, low-latency alert mechanisms, UI/UX clarity under high-stress scenarios, and the specific physiological challenges astronauts face (such as fluid shifts and cardiovascular strain).The link of the live web : https://astro.zerog.qd.je/

projectDetails.name: Zij: one fire record from MODIS and VIIRS
projectDetails.summary:
NASA has recorded Earth's active fires since 2000, but with two instruments that cannot be compared directly: MODIS (1 km pixels) and VIIRS (375 m, since 2012). Over Egypt's Nile Delta, VIIRS reports 11 to 20 times more fire pixels than MODIS, so the joined record shows burning jump tenfold in 2012. The fires didn't change; the satellite did. As MODIS retires, the years before 2012 risk becoming unusable.

Zij turns both records into one burning-activity calendar, from November 2000 to today. A model fitted per area on the years both sensors flew converts the MODIS years into VIIRS units. Tested on years it never saw, its season error falls from 77% to 14% (25% when predicting later years), and to 7% in the Nile Delta (10% for later years). Every converted value carries its margin of error.

Draw any area in Egypt, Portugal or Argentina, pick a day or a date range, and Zij tells you in plain words whether this season is normal, with every fire on NASA imagery. Every number can be downloaded and reproduced from NASA FIRMS data.
projectDetails.details:
The problem

NASA's active-fire record is split between MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012). VIIRS sees far more small fires: over the Nile Delta in September to November, Suomi NPP reports 11 to 20 times as many fire pixels as Aqua in most years, and 42 times as many in 2018. Joined as they are, the records show burning explode in 2012. A fixed multiplier cannot fix it, because the gap changes with fire size and from year to year. With MODIS retiring, fire managers risk losing the years before 2012.

How it works

  1. Keep real fires. Vegetation fires only; gas flares, industry and weak detections are removed. 6.28 million detections are kept.
  2. One grid. A 0.1 degree cell with at least one fire on a day counts once, so one coarse MODIS pixel and many fine VIIRS pixels weigh the same.
  3. Each satellite. Terra, Aqua, Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 are counted separately and averaged within each sensor, so a new satellite never creates a jump. A week inside a satellite outage is "no data", never zero.
  4. Learn the bridge. On 2012 to 2020, when both sensors flew, a model per area learns how MODIS relates to VIIRS: by month, by fire size, and in quiet years.
  5. One record. 2000 to 2011 are converted to VIIRS units, and every converted value carries its error band. Where an area has too little data, Zij says so instead of guessing.

Does it work?

We tested every model on years it never saw: leaving each year out in turn, and predicting 2021 to 2025 from a fit that stops in 2020. Season error is 76.5% for raw MODIS, 24.1% with one fixed multiplier, and 14.2% with Zij (25.2% on the later years). In the Nile Delta it is 6.9%. A clean rebuild from the raw FIRMS files reproduces every published number (REBUILD.md in the repository).

What you can do with it

  • Choose one of 10 preset areas, or draw any box or polygon in Egypt, mainland Portugal or Argentina. A drawn area is fitted live in your browser.
  • Read the verdict in plain words: is this month or season normal here, and how does it rank among 26 years.
  • See the fire calendar (years by months), the typical year and its critical period, the busiest months and years, and unusual seasons.
  • Pick any day and see that day's fires from MODIS and VIIRS on NASA satellite imagery, with how that week and month compare with normal.
  • Download the hotspots and the harmonized record as CSV, the calendar as an image, or a one-page season brief.

What the record shows

Only a record that crosses 2012 in one unit can show this. In the Nile Delta, burning seen from space did not fall after Egypt's 2004 burning ban: it rose 97% by 2005 to 2011 (the record cannot say what the ban itself did). Since 2018 it has been about half its earlier level (53% lower), with 2023 the one exception. The 2026 season is preliminary data.

Who it is for

Early-warning and emergency teams, like the CONAE team behind this challenge, who need to know whether a fire season is unusual while they wait for imagery; environmental agencies checking whether a policy changed burning; scientists, journalists and land managers who need trends that cross the 2012 break.

What makes it different

FIRMS shows the two records side by side. Zij joins them, states how sure it is, refuses to convert where the data is too thin, and is small enough to calibrate a user's own area in the browser.

Roro's Fire Diary: the game

zij.watch/diary is a short game that shows how Zij works, in five levels on the real record of the Nile Delta, with Roro the hoopoe and two satellites: Spot, Sort, Count, Translate and Compare. Its numbers come from Zij's own data files, and each level has a one-sentence note for grown-ups.

Limits

The unit counts places and days with fire, not burned area or the size of one fire. Satellites see only what burns as they pass; clouds and smoke hide fires. The record covers three countries today. The newest weeks are near-real-time data, and FIRMS revises them.

Tools

Python, DuckDB, pandas, NumPy, Next.js, TypeScript, React, MapLibre GL JS, Apache ECharts, Terra Draw, Radix UI. Hosted on Vercel; code under Apache-2.0 at github.com/zij-watch/zij.

Team

Five people, one part each: a lead developer (data pipeline, model and app), a designer (interface, map and film), a researcher (validation against FIRMS and the literature), a tester (areas, devices and the demo), and a coordinator (documentation and submission).

Prepared before the event

Research, method decisions and the design system were prepared before the event, and the public FIRMS files were downloaded in advance. The README lists exactly what.

AI tools. Manus AI was used throughout the project, alongside Claude, for code, data work and writing; the game Roro's Fire Diary was built entirely with Manus, its drawings drawn in code (SVG). Claude and Claude Code (Anthropic) wrote and reviewed code for the data pipeline, the model fitting and the web app, and helped draft the documentation. No AI image, video or voice generators were used: the voice-over is a team member's own voice, and every number comes from code run on NASA FIRMS data.

projectDetails.name: Lost Signals
projectDetails.summary:
Our project brings the stories of forgotten space hardware to life through an immersive, interactive museum. Rovers, landers, and instruments left beyond Earth represent remarkable achievements, yet their purpose and scientific contributions can be unfamiliar to young audiences.

Visitors explore destinations, discover mission histories, and learn what each piece of equipment helped humanity understand. Cinematic visuals, sound, and storytelling create an emotional connection, while accessible explanations connect that experience to real science. A recurring “Unknown Signal” challenge invites visitors to identify missions through clues, encouraging friendly competition and continued exploration.

By making these stories engaging and approachable, the project aims to inspire curiosity and preserve the legacy of space exploration. It addresses **“Abandoned but Not Forgotten”** by introducing school-age learners to the hardware left behind and the discoveries that make it worth remembering.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Forgotten Explorers is a bilingual (Arabic and English) interactive educational web experience that brings the stories of forgotten space exploration hardware to life.

The project focuses on spacecraft and robotic explorers that were left behind on other worlds, particularly Opportunity and Spirit on Mars and Lunokhod 1 on the Moon.

Visitors begin with a cinematic space introduction before entering an interactive 2D Solar System. They can explore destinations, select available spacecraft, and discover their mission histories through interactive storytelling.

Each spacecraft has a dedicated mission console containing its launch date, last communication, actual versus planned mission lifespan, distance traveled, scientific discoveries, and a first-person diary explaining its journey.

Visitors can also explore interactive spacecraft blueprints to understand how different components work, use a dust and power simulator to understand how environmental conditions affect solar-powered missions, and discover lessons that can improve future space exploration.

The experience also includes recorded Arabic narration, English subtitles, NASA imagery, a mission quiz, a historical timeline called Time Machine, and downloadable achievement certificates.

2. What benefits does the project have?

The project makes space science more accessible, engaging, and understandable, especially for school-age learners.

Instead of presenting scientific information through traditional articles, it combines visual exploration, interactive simulations, storytelling, and audio explanations.

Its bilingual support helps reach a wider audience, while the combination of narration and subtitles provides different ways to consume educational content.

It also helps visitors understand real engineering challenges, such as power limitations, environmental conditions, communication failures, and spacecraft design.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our main goal is to inspire curiosity about space exploration and preserve the scientific legacy of missions that are often overlooked.

We want younger generations to understand that a spacecraft does not lose its importance when its mission ends. Even equipment that has stopped operating can represent significant scientific discoveries and engineering achievements.

By transforming these forgotten missions into interactive stories, we hope to encourage students to explore science, technology, engineering, and space research.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

We developed the project as a browser-based single-page application using:

  • HTML5 and CSS3: For the application structure, layouts, and visual presentation.
  • JavaScript and JSX: For application logic, interactions, animations, and dynamic content.
  • React 18: For building reusable UI components and managing interactive application states.
  • Babel Standalone: For transforming JSX directly in the browser without a traditional build process.
  • Tailwind CSS: For responsive styling and interface design.
  • HTML5 Canvas 2D: For rendering the interactive Solar System and animated visual elements.
  • Web Audio API: For cinematic sound effects, ambient audio, and audio mixing.
  • NASA Image and Video Library API: For retrieving real space exploration photographs and media.
  • Python and NumPy: For supporting the audio processing workflow and project utilities.
  • FFmpeg and FFprobe: For cleaning, mastering, and validating recorded narration.
  • Node.js and Playwright: For automated testing and checking application functionality.

We also developed Python utilities for local hosting and preparing the application for static deployment.

The project does not require specialized hardware. It runs through a standard modern web browser.

5. How is the project creative?

The project's main creative idea is to tell the story of space exploration from the perspective of the machines themselves.

Instead of simply showing photographs and technical specifications, we use first-person storytelling to help visitors imagine the experiences of spacecraft that explored distant worlds and eventually went silent.

We also combine several creative elements:

  • A cinematic introduction that transitions into an interactive Solar System.
  • Planetary environments and spacecraft illustrations.
  • First-person mission diaries with original Arabic voice recordings.
  • Interactive spacecraft blueprints that explain engineering components.
  • A dust and power simulator that demonstrates real mission challenges.
  • A Time Machine that allows visitors to explore missions through history.
  • An educational quiz that tests visitors' understanding and rewards successful completion with a downloadable certificate.

This combination of scientific information, interactive technology, sound design, and storytelling transforms a traditional educational topic into an exploratory digital experience.

6. What factors did the team consider?

During development, we considered several important factors:

  • Scientific accuracy: Using real mission information and NASA resources to represent spacecraft histories and discoveries accurately.
  • Educational accessibility: Presenting complex scientific concepts in simple, understandable language.
  • Bilingual experience: Supporting both Arabic and English to reach different audiences.
  • User engagement: Using interactive exploration, simulations, and quizzes instead of passive reading.
  • Audio accessibility: Providing recorded narration and synchronized English captions.
  • Visual experience: Creating an immersive space atmosphere without requiring specialized hardware.
  • Technical reliability: Supporting local media fallbacks, browser audio restrictions, and different navigation interactions.
  • Future scalability: Designing the experience so that additional missions and destinations can be introduced over time.

Ultimately, Forgotten Explorers aims to turn forgotten space hardware into meaningful educational stories and remind people that even when the signal disappears, the discoveries remain.

projectDetails.name: Project التربيزه العاليه
projectDetails.summary:
Road to Mars is a co-op space survival and flight simulator for up to 6 players, made by team El Tarabeza El Aaleya. The crew shares a room code and works together to get a ship from a NASA launch pad to Mars. There is no impostor.

Prepare: Pick a rocket, a science payload, and the amounts of food, oxygen and fuel. Heavier loads mean a slower trip and faster fuel burn.

Survive: On the 2D ship, tasks like farming, water recycling, fuel production and repairs keep resources from running out.
Fly: Any player can pilot in 3D, dodging and shooting real NASA asteroids for fuel and science points.
Decide: The crew can land on the Moon for extra food, or dump cargo or vote to eject a player (who stays on as a 0 kg ghost) when the ship is too heavy.
Finish: At 100% progress the crew wins and gets an engineering report, then Free-Play unlocks. The game never ends suddenly.
projectDetails.details:
What it does
Road to Mars is a co-op space survival and flight simulator for up to 6 players. The crew shares a room code and works together to take a spacecraft from a NASA launch pad to Mars. It borrows the feel of Among Us, with a 2D ship, tasks and emergency meetings, but there is no impostor. The whole crew works against the ship’s failing systems instead of each other.

Before launch, the crew chooses a rocket (Electron, Falcon 9 or SLS Block 1B), a science payload, and the amounts of food, oxygen and fuel. A live readout shows total mass, Δv, thrust-to-weight and travel time, so every kilogram has a visible cost. During the mission, players do tasks inside a 10-room ship: farming, water recycling, turning CO₂ into fuel, and repairs. Any player can switch to a 3D cockpit and fly through real NASA asteroids such as Bennu and Itokawa, shooting them for fuel and science points. The crew can also land on the Moon for extra food, or dump cargo or vote to eject a player when the ship is too heavy. At 100% progress the crew wins and receives an engineering report, then Free-Play unlocks.

Benefits and impact
The game teaches mission planning in a hands-on way. Players learn that mass, fuel, food and oxygen are linked, that life support is a closed loop, and that deep-space trips depend on teamwork and trade-offs. It is meant to make space engineering approachable and social for students and general audiences.

Tools
Built with Nodejs and Typescript using NASA asteroid data as the basis for the in-game asteroids.

Creativity
We combined three things: a social task-based ship, a 6-axis flight simulator, and an engineering weight-and-fuel model. We also added local humor (Romy cheese as in-game food) and a forgiving design with emergency guide arrows and a Free-Play mode, so the game never ends suddenly.

Factors we considered
Teaching real engineering trade-offs while keeping the game fun, cooperation instead of competition, fair pacing for first-time players, and keeping the 2D and 3D parts connected so tasks and flying affect each other.

Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.
