projectDetails.name: BioOrbit: Autonomous AI Space-Medical Telemetry & Psychological Platform
projectDetails.summary: BioOrbit is a bilingual (English/Arabic RTL), offline-first mobile and clinical telemetry platform developed by Team Gat Keda for deep-space missions where 20-to-40-minute communication delays make live Earth medical help impossible. Built with dual role portals—Astronaut (Astro) and Space Doctor (Doctor)—our Flutter prototype logs real-time cardiovascular, glycemic, and thermoregulation vitals (Heart Rate, Blood Pressure, Blood Sugar, and Body Temperature), tracks sleep duration and fatigue, and executes Computer Vision AI facial biometric scans (EAR, MAR, facial symmetry, and head pose) alongside automated ECG waveform interpretation. Aligned with NASA Human Research Program (HRP) hazards and NASA-STD-3001 standards, BioOrbit empowers crews to detect visual fatigue, psychological stress, and physiological risks early and apply immediate countermeasures autonomously onboard.
projectDetails.details:
## 1. The Deep-Space Medical Autonomy Challenge
During long-duration lunar (Artemis) and Mars missions, astronauts face severe physiological and psychological hazards: microgravity-induced bone and muscle atrophy, cosmic radiation, cardiovascular deconditioning, and extreme isolation. With round-trip signal delays reaching up to 40 minutes on Mars expeditions, astronauts cannot rely on real-time consultations with Earth's Ground Control during medical or behavioral emergencies. They require a 100% autonomous, onboard clinical ecosystem.

## 2. What BioOrbit Does (Our Solution)
Developed by **Team Gat Keda (جت كده)**, **BioOrbit** is a dual-role, bilingual (English / Arabic RTL) medical telemetry and AI diagnostic ecosystem connecting crew members and onboard medical officers:
* **Astronaut (Astro) Portal (Cyan Theme #00E5FF):** A daily tablet/mobile companion for rapid vital sign entry (Heart Rate, Blood Pressure, Blood Sugar, Body Temperature), sleep and fatigue logging, AI facial stress and eyelid-droop fatigue scanning, ECG waveform explanation, and 3D anatomical risk visualization across Muscle, Nerve, and Bone layers.
* **Space Doctor (Doctor) Portal (Emerald Theme #00E676):** A clinical command interface that aggregates 7-record weekly crew telemetry averages, flags early physiological or psychological anomalies up to 48 hours ahead, and dispatches direct treatment countermeasures to the crew.
* **Official Project Demo:** https://drive.google.com/file/d/1pMBM1K-yDFyKCQp7_g-1_mKLNGi59HCW/view?usp=sharing
* **Official Source Code Repository:** https://github.com/MoaazSakr/BioOrbit

## 3. How BioOrbit Works Step-by-Step (Verified Prototype Workflow)
### Step A: Role-Based Orbital Access Portal & Instant Bilingual (EN / AR RTL) Support
Upon launching BioOrbit, crew members receive an orbital session authentication banner (`Welcome back to orbit, moaaz sakr 3 (Astronaut)`), select their mission role—**Astronaut (Astro)** or **Space Doctor (Doctor)**—and switch effortlessly between English and full Right-to-Left Arabic (`عربي` / `English`).

### Step B: Real-Time Biomedical, Thermoregulation, Sleep & Fatigue Telemetry
1. **Vitals & Orbit Tab:** The astronaut logs daily **Heart Rate (75 BPM)**, **Systolic/Diastolic Blood Pressure (120 / 80 mmHg)**, **Blood Sugar Level (95 mg/dL)**, and **Body Temperature (36.8 °C)** using fine-tune steppers or quick-select presets (`36.5`, `36.8`, `37.0`, `37.5`). BioOrbit evaluates each reading against NASA-STD-3001 spaceflight baselines and displays real-time clinical status (`Nominal / Stable`).
2. **Psych & Sleep Tab:** The astronaut records **Actual Sleep Duration (0–12 hrs, e.g., 8.0 h)** and **Physical & Mental Fatigue (1–10 scale, e.g., 3 / 10)**, then taps **Sync Health Record to Backend** to store the telemetry record and update the 3D Muscle, Nerve, and Bone load model.

### Step C: Dynamic Computer Vision AI Facial Biometrics & ECG Waveform Engine
In the **Face AI** tab, the astronaut captures a selfie using the front camera or gallery. Our AI pipeline (achieving **~94.8% landmark detection accuracy**) dynamically computes geometric drowsiness, stress, and cranial alignment metrics, proven across two live test cases in our prototype:
* **1. AI Facial Measurements (Image To AI) — Two Verified Live Scenarios:**
* **Live Test Case A (Rested Crew Member):** `EAR: 0.33` | `MAR: 0.15` | `Facial Symmetry: 96.5%` | `Head Pose: 3.8°` -> Diagnosis: **Alert & Balanced** (*"Facial biometrics are balanced; eye aperture and facial muscle symmetry indicate good alertness and no orbital strain."*).
* **Live Test Case B (Fatigued Crew Member in Video Demo):** `EAR: 0.26` | `MAR: 0.18` | `Facial Symmetry: 96.2%` | `Head Pose: 0.7°` -> Diagnosis: **Mild Visual Fatigue** (*"Facial measurements show mild eyelid droop linked to fatigue; a rest period is advised."*).
* **2. ECG Waveform, Hemodynamics & Crew Clearance Summary (Metrics To AI):** Cross-references cardiovascular and metabolic telemetry to generate a clinical rhythm report:
* **ECG Waveform Analysis:** *"Normal Sinus Rhythm; P-waves are uniform, ventricular QRS complex is sharp and narrow, and QT interval is completely stable."*
* **Hemodynamics & Metabolism:** *"Vascular perfusion, glycemic energy, and core thermoregulation are well-balanced for mission operations."*
* **Crew & Doctor Summary:** *"Cardiac rhythm and vital indicators are reassuring—astronaut is cleared for full orbital duties."*

### Step D: 7-Record Weekly Telemetry Averages & Doctor-Astro Medical Link
In the **Reports** tab, BioOrbit automatically calculates **7-Record Weekly Telemetry Averages** (`المتوسطات الحيوية الأسبوعية - 7 سجلات`: Avg Heart Rate, Avg Sleep Hours, Total Weekly Exercise, Peak Fatigue, and Mental Status). Through the integrated **Doctor-Astro Medical Link (`قناة الاتصال الطبي`)**, the Space Doctor dispatches direct clinical countermeasures (such as *"Add 20 mins to ARED resistance training today"*) straight to the astronaut's device.

## 4. Benefits, Impact & Honest Prototype Roadmap
* **Deep-Space Autonomy:** Protects crew health during Artemis lunar operations, Gateway station stays, and future Mars expeditions without waiting for Earth communication links.
* **Terrestrial Healthcare Impact:** Directly adaptable for isolated environments on Earth with limited medical staff or internet connectivity, including rural desert clinics in Egypt/MENA, submarines, polar research stations, and offshore energy platforms.
* **Working Prototype vs. Current Limits & Next Steps:** Our live Flutter prototype currently supports bilingual (EN/AR RTL) role authentication, 4-metric vital & sleep telemetry logging, backend synchronization, dynamic AI facial biometric calculation (detecting both alertness and mild visual fatigue), ECG clinical interpretation, and doctor-astronaut messaging. Currently, vitals use interactive UI steppers/presets and cloud image relay (`ibb.co`) during testing. Next, we are embedding our interactive 3D Muscle/Nerve/Bone mesh directly into the main Vitals view, adding **Crew Emergency QR Medical Badges**, connecting Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) smart garments (CSA Astroskin), and packaging our AI weights into on-device TensorFlow Lite for 100% air-gapped spacecraft execution.

## 5. Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used
* **Source Code Repository:** https://github.com/MoaazSakr/BioOrbit
* **Mobile Frontend:** Flutter SDK & Dart (Responsive Dark Space-Medical UI: `#070B19`, `#00E5FF`, `#00E676`, `#8C52FF` with full English LTR & Arabic RTL support).
* **Backend & Database:** RESTful API Backend, JSON Telemetry Store, Role-Based Authentication, and ImgBB API (prototype image staging).
* **AI & Biometrics Pipeline:** Computer Vision Facial Landmark Geometry (MediaPipe / OpenCV EAR, MAR, Bilateral Symmetry, and Head Pose algorithms) + Large Language Model (LLM) Clinical Diagnostic Engine calibrated to NASA-STD-3001 thresholds.
* **UI/UX & Media Production:** Figma (Interface Prototyping) and FFmpeg/Premiere (30-second subtitled Demo Video & animated GIFs).

## 6. Team Gat Keda (جت كده) Crew Members & Roles
* **Moaaz Sakr:** Team Leader & Flutter Developer
* **Ahmed Ghoniem:** AI & Biometrics Developer
* **Mohamaed Alroba:** Backend & Sync Developer
* **Fady Samir:** Backend & Telemetry Developer
* **Mohamed Elarby:** UI/UX Product Designer
* **Saeed Emad:** Video Editing & Media Specialist

projectDetails.name: Project ضحايا عين شمس
projectDetails.summary:
Mars Explorer is an interactive 3D platform designed to make exploring Mars safer and more accessible. It combines Martian terrain visualization, hazard identification, and intelligent route planning to help users understand the planet's surface and identify suitable exploration paths.

We developed a concept that integrates 3D modeling, scientific data visualization, and AI-powered analysis. Using Blender, Three.js, and Python, the platform aims to transform NASA's planetary datasets into an interactive exploration experience.

By utilizing NASA's MOLA elevation data and Mars orbital imagery, Mars Explorer helps address the challenge of navigating unfamiliar Martian terrain. It is important because it demonstrates how scientific data and modern technology can support future robotic and human exploration missions.
projectDetails.details: Project Details – Mars Explorer Mars Explorer is an interactive 3D platform designed to make Martian exploration safer and more informative. It transforms scientific data about Mars into an immersive environment where users can explore the planet's surface, understand its terrain, identify potential hazards, and discover suitable exploration routes. The platform works by processing NASA's planetary datasets and converting elevation and surface information into 3D terrain visualizations. Users can explore different regions, examine elevation changes, identify steep slopes and potentially dangerous areas, and use intelligent route-planning concepts to find safer paths between exploration points. Benefits and Intended Impact: Mars Explorer makes complex scientific information easier to understand through interactive visualization. It can support educational activities, scientific exploration, and future mission-planning research by helping users understand the challenges of navigating Martian terrain. Tools and Technologies: - Blender: 3D modeling and terrain visualization. - Three.js: Interactive 3D web environment. - Python: Data processing and analysis. - NASA MOLA elevation data and Mars orbital imagery: Scientific data sources. - AI and machine learning: Potential hazard analysis and intelligent route recommendations. Creativity and Innovation: The project's main creative aspect is combining scientific datasets with interactive 3D exploration rather than presenting information through traditional maps or static dashboards. It aims to turn Mars exploration into an engaging and informative experience. Key Considerations: We considered terrain accuracy, navigation safety, scientific reliability, usability, and accessibility. Our goal is to ensure that visual elements and recommendations are grounded in real scientific data rather than fictional representations.

projectDetails.name: ATHAR
projectDetails.summary:
**Athar – Discovering Humanity's Footprints in Space**

Athar is an interactive 3D educational experience designed to introduce children aged 9–12 to the history of human exploration beyond Earth. Through an immersive space journey, young explorers can travel between planets, land on their surfaces, and discover the scientific equipment and spacecraft left behind by NASA missions.

By clicking on each piece of equipment, children can explore its story, understand its purpose, and learn about the discoveries it helped make possible. The experience combines 3D exploration, storytelling, and interactive mini-games to make learning engaging and enjoyable.

Athar addresses the challenge by transforming NASA's space exploration history into an accessible, child-friendly experience. It is important because it helps young generations understand humanity's achievements in space, appreciate the scientific value of these missions, and develop curiosity about science, technology, and the universe.
projectDetails.details:
Athar – Project Details

Athar is an interactive 3D educational platform that transforms the history of NASA's space exploration into an exciting adventure for children aged 9–12 (4th–6th grade).

How It Works:
Users begin their journey in an interactive 3D space environment where they can explore planets and choose their destinations. After selecting a planet, they experience an animated landing sequence and explore its surface. They can discover historical NASA spacecraft, rovers, and scientific instruments left behind, interact with each object, and listen to or read its story, including its mission, purpose, and scientific achievements. Interactive mini-games and mission-completion certificates make learning more engaging.

Benefits and Intended Impact:
Athar makes complex space science easier for children to understand through exploration rather than traditional reading.

It encourages curiosity, scientific thinking, and interest in astronomy, technology, and space exploration. Our goal is to help children appreciate the scientific legacy of NASA missions and understand how these discoveries contribute to our knowledge of the universe.

Tools and Technologies:

  • HTML → for structuring the website content and layout.
  • CSS → for styling and designing the user interface.
  • JavaScript → for interactive features, 3D graphics, and animations.
  • NASA Public Mission Resources → for providing reliable educational content about space exploration and NASA missions.

Creativity and Innovation:
Instead of presenting information through static articles, Athar turns learning into a space adventure. Children become junior space explorers, travel between planets, discover real mission hardware, and learn through interactive storytelling and challenges.

Team Considerations:
We focused on our target audience's age, using simple language, colorful visuals, intuitive controls, short educational stories, and engaging activities. We also considered educational accuracy, accessibility, and creating an enjoyable experience that balances entertainment with meaningful scientific learning.

projectDetails.name: Odyssey
projectDetails.summary: ODYSSEY is a web app that helps teams rehearse Moon and Mars missions on Earth. You describe a mission in plain English. An AI agent splits it into experiments, sets measurable requirements, and ranks 39 curated Earth analog sites for each experiment using open NASA data (LRO LOLA and Diviner, MOLA, NASA POWER, MODIS). Each site is compared with the lunar south pole or Jezero crater on 31 conditions, and the app shows exactly where Earth stops being a good stand-in. Gaps are never hidden: each is labelled as a dataset to connect, a field measurement to make, or physics Earth cannot provide, such as gravity or vacuum, with a proposed chamber test instead. It ends with a multi-site field campaign and a report. Analog sites are usually picked by reputation. ODYSSEY makes that choice traceable, per experiment, with every number tied to a source or a stated assumption.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

ODYSSEY turns a Moon or Mars mission brief into a field-testing plan on Earth. A user types a mission in plain English, for example "a seven-day lunar expedition with geological sampling, rover navigation, equipment deployment, thermal survival and dust mitigation".

How it works

1. Define. An AI agent maps the brief to experiments and quotes the words that justify each one. Each experiment gets measurable requirements, such as maximum slope or temperature range, each labelled as stated in the brief or as an assumption.

2. Discover. 39 curated Earth analog sites are checked against hard limits, then ranked separately for every experiment on terrain, temperature, geology, access and evidence. A global screen of 81,575 land cells found 80 more candidate regions. A "planetary twin" view puts each site beside the target (the lunar south pole or Jezero crater on Mars) on 31 conditions. Values are compared only when the quantity and scale match, so air temperature is never compared with surface temperature.

3. Validate. "Challenge this match" shows how a high similarity score drops once hard limits and missing evidence are checked; in the demo, 92 becomes 76. Every gap is named: a dataset not yet connected, a field measurement needed (with the standard test), or physics Earth cannot provide, such as gravity, vacuum or the lunar night. Sources the agent finds online stay unverified until the quoted value is found word for word in the full document.

4. Rehearse. For conditions no site offers, it proposes controlled tests, such as a thermal-vacuum chamber or gravity offload, in numbered steps labelled as proposals, not results. An optimiser then builds a multi-site campaign three ways: best science, least travel, fewest facilities. A report exports as Markdown or JSON.

Benefits and impact

Analog sites are often chosen by reputation. ODYSSEY makes the choice traceable and specific to each experiment: which site suits which test, why, and what must still be tested elsewhere. This can save mission teams field time and money and avoid false confidence in an analog. Students and the public can also see why a desert is or is not a good stand-in for the Moon or Mars.

What makes it creative

- It ranks sites per experiment, not per planet.

- It treats Earth's shortfalls as results, not failures, and offers a next step for each.

- It explains its reasoning visually:

- a similarity score broken into its weighted parts;

- Earth and the target side by side;

- log-scale pressure and gravity comparisons;

- sun-angle and crater-shadow diagrams for polar light;

- dust-flight arcs under each planet's gravity;

- relationships between measured conditions across sites.

- While the agent runs, Moon or Mars and Earth are scanned together in 3D. When the first sites are ranked, the view hands off to the best one.

Tools and technologies

- Code: TypeScript, React 19, Three.js and Vite for the interface; Node.js 22 with SQLite and live server-sent events for the backend.

- Data pipelines: Python (rasterio, STAC, H3).

- AI: DeepSeek V4.1 Flash through the OpenCode API for the agent. Every number comes from tested code, and the app also runs fully without the AI.

- Deployment and tests: Docker and Azure Container Apps; 71 automated tests.

- Data: NASA (LRO LOLA and Diviner, MGS MOLA, NASA POWER, MODIS, GIBS, NSSDC), ESA Copernicus (DEM, Sentinel-2, WorldCover), CSA RADARSAT-1 and Macrostrat.

What we considered

- Scientific honesty: missing data is never counted as a match, and fabricated precision is never shown.

- Traceable claims: every value links to its source, resolution and date.

- Clarity for non-experts: plain language and visual explanations.

- Accessibility: works on phones, supports reduced motion, and an open-source code base (Apache-2.0) others can extend.

Limits

This is a prototype:

- 39 curated sites and two targets.

- Reanalysis climate at about 50 km resolution and 40 m terrain.

- Several requirement thresholds are assumptions, and they're labelled as such.

- Simulation outputs are first-order models, not facility results.

Links: live app https://odyssey.qd.je · code https://github.com/MahmoudAdelbghany/ODYSSEY

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: AETHRION // MARS
projectDetails.summary:
AETHRION // MARS – Mars Mission Control & Astronaut Navigation System

AETHRION // MARS is an interactive planetary exploration and mission-planning platform designed to help future astronauts explore the Martian surface safely and efficiently. It integrates scientific datasets from NASA missions and instruments, including HiRISE, MOLA, InSight and MEDA, into a unified exploration environment.

The platform combines high-resolution orbital imagery, elevation and slope mapping, environmental information, geological hazard detection and A* multi-objective route optimisation. Astronauts can explore Mars in an interactive 3D planetary environment, identify scientific sampling targets, assess terrain risks, simulate surface traverses and generate mission dossiers.

By bringing multiple sources of planetary science data together, AETHRION // MARS addresses the challenge of making complex Martian information accessible and actionable for human exploration. It is important because future Mars missions will require informed decisions about navigation, astronaut safety, resource limitations and scientific discovery. Our goal is to help transform planetary data into practical mission intelligence for the next generation of explorers.
projectDetails.details:
PROJECT SPECIFICATION – AETHRION // MARS

1. What does your project do?

AETHRION // MARS is an interactive system, which can be used to aid in planning future human exploration missions on Mars. By integrating various forms of scientific and geographical information related to Mars, AETHRION can be used to provide insight into the terrain whilst identifying any hazards, highlighting valuable scientific sites and help plan surface exploration missions.

The system includes a simulated walking mission across Mars at Jezero Crater, which is a scientifically valuable area of Mars.

The system allows the user to explore Mars with an immersive 3D experience. Once in mission control they will be able to explore the Martian terrain, see different geographical layers and gain knowledge of the environment of Mars. They will have access to:

Multiple NASA science data and mission information such as HiRISE images, MOLA topography, InSight observations, MEDA weather data and other geological data so that the system can give a more complete picture of the environment Mars.

Multi-objective optimisation of routes. This means that the system can compare different routes to explore based on the terrain, slope, hazards and scientific value. This will allow users to find the fastest route, safest route and scientifically valuable route.

Visualisations to identify hazards in the terrain, geological targets, astronaut telemetry data, simulated Marswalking missions and a dossier to hold information and results from the mission.

2. What are the benefits of your project?

This system is very beneficial as it gives multiple forms of planetary information in one place. It can often be hard to understand how different environmental factors affect each other when planning an exploration mission with separate maps, data and scientific tools. AETHRION aims to make it easier to view the relevant information in one place.

Benefits include:

Increased situational awareness of the terrain, topography, slope and geological data.

Route planning based on different priorities will help show how distance, terrain and scientific objectives can be affected.

Hazards can be identified by seeing steep slopes, cliffs, boulders and other challenging terrain.

Geological targets and sampling sites can be identified to help prioritize the most scientifically valuable areas.

The mission dossier will help organize important information and results from the simulated mission.

The interactive visual environment will help to make complex planetary science information easier to understand.

Overall this shows how planetary science data can be turned into useful information.

3. What impact do you hope to make?

Long term AETHRION will help to make human exploration of Mars safer, more informed and scientifically valuable.

In the future astronauts will be exploring a completely different environment to Earth. This means they will be exploring a planet with a very thin atmosphere, very cold temperatures, challenging terrain and little chance of immediate help from Earth. All of their exploration decisions will need to take into account scientific objectives, resources available, environmental conditions and safety.

AETHRION helps to address this issue by showing how different planetary data sources can be integrated.

This will help bridge the gap between gathering planetary science data and how it can be used in real life situations. The science information will help the user understand how it relates to an actual exploration mission.

Whilst this is just a prototype and simulation, it shows how this concept can be developed by using higher resolution data, more detailed terrain analysis, accurate environmental models and more mission planning tools.

Ultimately we hope to help change how future explorers understand, plan and navigate the Martian surface.

4. What tools, languages, hardware and software have you used?

AETHRION // MARS is a browser based interactive web application. It uses front-end web development, interactive visualisations, planetary science data and route planning concepts.

Mainly using:

HTML – To create the structure of the web application.

CSS – To create styles, responsive design, layout and animations.

JavaScript – To create interactive elements, interactive interface, data and application.

GitHub – For version control.

GitHub Pages – To host the project as a website.

NASA planetary science data – To provide science data for the terrain, topography, images and environmental data.

Pathfinding – Used as the basis for multi-objective route planning.

Visualisations – Web based.

This doesn’t need any specific hardware to run, as it simply uses a modern web browser.

5. How is your project creative and innovative?

AETHRION is creative as it combines planetary exploration, science visualisation and mission planning.

Many planetary visualisation tools can often just present maps or individual science data. AETHRION provides a mission based experience, making the user feel like they are an astronaut exploring Mars in the future. The user can plan an exploration mission by choosing where to land, viewing environmental conditions, identifying hazards, finding scientific targets, planning a Marswalk and seeing the results from their mission.

The system also has multiple route planning priorities. The shortest route may not always be the best for an astronaut to take. Sometimes a longer route may have better terrain or provide access to scientifically valuable geological features. The system provides fastest, safest and scientifically valuable routes to show how the mission planning needs to balance multiple objectives.

The immersive planetary explorer also makes this project more engaging. The user can explore Mars in a more engaging way by moving away from traditional dashboards and providing an interactive visualisation. They can explore landmarks and also enter a dedicated mission control environment.

Overall this system is much more than a basic educational website as it combines an interactive planetary experience with integrated science data, terrain intelligence and route planning. It is a prototype for an integrated planetary mission planning environment.

6. What considerations have we made?

We made consideration of the following factors:

1. Safety for the astronauts – We considered hazards such as steep slopes, cliffs, unstable terrain and challenging geographical features.

2. Accuracy – We used existing NASA planetary science missions and instruments. We considered using multiple data types such as images, topography and environmental data to provide more informative exploration.

3. Multiple objectives for the mission – We considered that exploration isn’t just about getting there as fast as possible. We wanted to show that it’s important to balance route efficiency, terrain, scientific opportunities and getting back safely.

4. Environmental conditions – Mars has extreme temperatures, low pressure, dust and more. We considered this when creating the mission control and astronaut telemetry.

5. Engagement – We created an engaging interface with a cinematic introduction to Mars, interactive exploration tools and organized mission planning.

6. Accessible – We created a web based system so users and evaluators can easily explore the capabilities without having to install any specialist software.

7. Scalable – We created a concept that can be expanded upon with more NASA data, more detailed terrain, improved routing and more mission planning tools.

7. Conclusion

AETHRION // MARS is our attempt to overcome one of the main challenges of future human space exploration. Turning the vast amounts of science information gathered about Mars into useful intelligence to help astronauts on the surface.

By combining planetary exploration, NASA science data, terrain analysis, route planning, hazard awareness and mission reporting we hope to show how technology can help make future Mars exploration more informed, efficient and scientifically valuable.

Our vision is simple, explore the terrain, understand the environment, navigate the unknown and help humanity prepare for their next giant leap!

projectDetails.details:
AFTERLIGHT — The Machines That Stayed Behind

AFTERLIGHT is an immersive digital archive that explores the machines, scientific instruments and human-made objects left behind during humanity's exploration of the Moon and other celestial bodies.

Instead of presenting space history through conventional articles or static galleries, AFTERLIGHT transforms it into an interactive experience. Users can explore a reconstructed lunar environment, discover individual mission artifacts, examine 3D models, view historical NASA photographs, access technical information and follow the stories behind each object. The project begins with the Apollo 12 landing site at Statio Cognitum, featuring the Lunar Module's descent stage, ALSEP scientific equipment and the Surveyor 3 spacecraft.

The project's primary benefit is making space exploration history more engaging, accessible and understandable. It connects physical artifacts with the missions, scientific discoveries and human effort that gave them purpose. By placing these objects within their historical and geographical context, AFTERLIGHT encourages users to appreciate the scientific and historical significance of humanity's presence beyond Earth.

The intended impact is to preserve and communicate an often-overlooked part of space exploration history. These objects are more than abandoned equipment; they are physical records of human ambition, engineering and scientific discovery. AFTERLIGHT aims to make their stories accessible to students, educators, space enthusiasts and the wider public.

The project is developed using HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript with ES modules, Vite as the development and build environment, and Three.js for interactive 3D environments and artifact visualization. Anime.js is used for interface and visual motion. Its content incorporates NASA archival photographs, scientific documentation, terrain data, technical references and 3D models. The project is designed as a browser-based experience, with attention to performance, responsive interaction and accessibility.

AFTERLIGHT's creativity lies in its approach to storytelling. Rather than simply showing users what was left behind, it invites them to enter the environment, explore the artifacts and understand their stories through spatial interaction. The experience combines scientific information, archival material, environmental reconstruction and cinematic visual design.

Throughout development, we considered scientific accuracy, historical context, the distinction between documented information and visual reconstruction, usability, performance and accessibility. We also aimed to ensure that the experience remains immersive without compromising the credibility of the underlying science.

AFTERLIGHT is an attempt to bring the history of humanity's journey beyond Earth closer to people — by exploring not only where we went, but what we left behind.

projectDetails.name: LUNA-VISTA: An Intelligent Lunar Landing Site Selection and Mission Planning System
projectDetails.summary:
LUNA-VISTA is an interactive, science-based web application designed to assist mission planners, researchers, educators, and the public in identifying and comparing suitable landing locations near the Moon's south pole. The system combines astronomical calculations, lunar terrain analysis, and 3D visualization to simplify the evaluation of potential lunar landing sites.

The application allows users to select different candidate landing locations and mission dates to analyze the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the local lunar horizon. Using NASA/JPL SPICE data and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) terrain datasets, it calculates solar elevation, sunlight availability, Earth visibility, and potential direct-to-Earth communication windows. It also estimates solar energy generation based on illumination conditions and solar panel parameters.

An intelligent site comparison and recommendation module evaluates candidate locations using sunlight availability, communication visibility, and terrain suitability. The results are presented through interactive 3D lunar visualizations, graphs, comparative dashboards, and mission reports.

The main goal of LUNA-VISTA is to provide a user-friendly scientific decision-support platform that makes complex lunar environmental data easier to understand, helping users evaluate landing sites and mission dates for safer and more efficient future lunar exploration.
projectDetails.details:
LUNA-VISTA: Intelligent Lunar Landing Site Selection and Mission Planning System

LUNA-VISTA is a proposed lunar exploration planning system designed to help identify and compare suitable landing sites near the Moon's South Pole. It focuses on three important factors: sunlight availability, Earth visibility for communication, and local terrain conditions.

The system allows users to select candidate landing sites and dates. It then aims to analyze the positions of the Sun and Earth, examine terrain obstructions, estimate sunlight duration and communication windows, and compare different landing locations. Based on these factors, it provides an explainable ranking of candidate sites using configurable criteria.

The project is designed around scientific datasets, including NASA/JPL SPICE kernels for planetary positions and orientations, LOLA elevation models for lunar terrain analysis, and LROC imagery for surface visualization.

The main benefits of LUNA-VISTA are improved mission-planning support, easier comparison of landing locations, better understanding of lighting and communication constraints, and more accessible visualization of complex lunar environment information. Its intended impact is to support safer and more informed planning for future lunar exploration missions.

The creative aspect of this project is its combination of solar analysis, Earth visibility assessment, terrain evaluation, and site comparison in one integrated and user-friendly concept. It also emphasizes transparency by showing the criteria behind its recommendations.

This submission presents a concept demonstration. The sample site scores and comparison values shown in the presentation are illustrative mock data, not actual measured lunar results or official NASA rankings. The proposed system would require implementation and scientific validation using the relevant datasets.

projectDetails.name: Project Aithra Sentinel
projectDetails.summary:
We developed Monsoon & Landslide Sentinel, an open-source, interactive geospatial web application designed to detect and forecast monsoon-triggered floods and landslides in real time.
Our solution directly addresses the Dancing with the SARs challenge by overcoming a major limitation of traditional optical satellites: cloud cover. During severe monsoon storms, dense clouds obscure optical imagery precisely when disasters unfold. By utilizing cloud-penetrating NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) L-band data, our application monitors centimeter-scale ground deformation, soil saturation spikes, and surface water expansion beneath thick forest canopies and storm clouds. We fuse NISAR before-and-after change detection with NASA SRTM terrain slope data and NASA GPM IMERG rainfall measurements to explain the physical triggers behind slope instability.
This tool is vital because rapid, accurate early warnings save lives and infrastructure. By translating complex spaceborne radar datasets into intuitive, color-coded hazard maps and time-lapse visualizations, Monsoon & Landslide Sentinel empowers emergency responders and vulnerable communities to act before catastrophic slides or flash floods strike.
projectDetails.details:
OVERVIEW AND HOW IT WORKS

Monsoon & Landslide Sentinel is an early-warning geospatial system designed to detect and forecast monsoon-triggered floods and landslides in real time. Traditional optical satellites cannot see through dense storm clouds precisely when severe monsoons strike. Our solution solves this blind spot using NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) data.

Our Python-based risk engine processes sequential, cloud-penetrating NISAR L-band radar passes to detect subtle, centimeter-scale ground deformation, soil saturation spikes, and expanding surface water beneath thick forest canopies. To explain the physical mechanics behind slope failure, our model fuses these radar changes with terrain slope angles from the NASA SRTM Digital Elevation Model and 24-hour precipitation triggers from NASA GPM IMERG. The system calculates a weighted Slope Instability Index and categorizes terrain into High, Moderate, or Low hazard zones.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

Our primary goal is to turn complex orbital radar datasets into clear, actionable alerts for local disaster management authorities, civil engineers, and vulnerable hillside communities. By identifying steep, water-saturated slopes before catastrophic failure occurs, Monsoon & Landslide Sentinel provides crucial lead time for targeted evacuations, road closures, and infrastructure protection—saving lives during peak monsoon seasons.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, AND DATA SOURCES

- Programming & Modeling: Python (numpy, rasterio, geopandas) for computing the Slope Instability Index and processing geospatial layers.

- Satellite & Ancillary Datasets: NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR L-band and S-band products), NASA SRTM (30m Digital Elevation Model), and NASA GPM IMERG precipitation data.

- Presentation & Documentation: GitHub for open-source code hosting and a 7-slide architectural pitch deck.

CREATIVITY AND KEY DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS

Instead of treating radar imagery as a static visual overlay, we creatively combined dual-frequency radar physics with physical slope-stability mechanics (ground displacement, terrain gradient, soil moisture, and rainfall). When designing the project, our team prioritized:

- All-Weather Cloud Penetration: Ensuring uninterrupted monitoring during heavy monsoon storms when optical satellites fail.

- Canopy Penetration: Leveraging NISAR's 24 cm L-band wavelength to measure bare-earth movement beneath dense tropical vegetation.

- Open-Source Scalability: Structuring the risk model with lightweight, reproducible code so emergency teams in any hilly or flood-prone region worldwide can adapt it quickly.

Planet Pulse is a concept for an interactive sonification experience that turns NASA Earth science data into synchronized sound. Users choose a data layer (temperature, oceans, atmosphere, ice or vegetation), watch a NASA visualization, and hear the data as audio. Temperature anomalies map to pitch, ocean measurements to flowing rhythm, ice changes to evolving texture, and vegetation to pulse and density. A legend ties each sound to its scientific meaning.

It addresses the challenge of making Earth data creative and accessible by letting people hear patterns, not just read charts. The flagship demo is a 60-second “Temperature Symphony” built on a historical NASA temperature dataset such as GISTEMP. Its core rule is that every sound must trace back to a real data value, so the result stays scientifically grounded.

It matters because it adds an audio route into science for people who can’t easily use visual charts. It also helps students explore abstract patterns, and it gives the public a memorable way to connect with climate and Earth change.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

Planet Pulse is a web experience that turns NASA Earth science data into sound. The user picks a data layer and presses play. A line chart draws year by year while a tone rises and falls with the values. Each year’s value is normalized and mapped to a pitch between 220 Hz and 880 Hz (two octaves). A legend explains the mapping, and reference buttons let users hear the lowest and highest pitches first. The current prototype has two working layers: global temperature anomalies and Arctic sea ice. The planned flagship demo is a 60-second “Temperature Symphony.” Oceans, atmosphere and vegetation are designed but not built yet.

Benefits

  • It gives people who can’t easily read visual charts an audio way into the data.
  • It makes abstract trends easier to explore and discuss in classrooms.
  • It helps listeners notice rises, dips and rhythms over time.
  • Every sound traces back to a real data value, so it stays explainable.

Intended impact

Our aim is for people to explain what a sound represents and trace it back to the data. We want to make climate and Earth data more inclusive, memorable and engaging for students, educators and the public. Sonification adds to visual data and doesn’t replace it.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single web page
  • Web Audio API (oscillators and filters) to generate the sound
  • HTML Canvas for the animated chart
  • NASA GISTEMP (temperature) and NSIDC (sea ice) as the data sources
  • Claude (Anthropic’s AI assistant) helped build the prototype. Add your team’s own tools here, plus any design software you used for the slide deck.
  • No special hardware: any device with a browser and speakers or headphones

What makes it creative

It is “not music inspired by Earth, but music mapped from Earth’s data.” Each layer has its own sound character, and the sea ice mapping is deliberately flipped so that losing ice raises the pitch. The Earth Data DJ console idea makes exploring feel playful while the science stays visible.

Factors we considered

  • Scientific honesty: the mappings are transparent and labeled as proposed. The prototype’s values are approximate, interpolated from published trends, so the official data series must replace them before any scientific claim.
  • Accessibility: a keyboard-friendly timeline slider and a visual display alongside the audio.
  • Listening comfort: a moderate pitch range, soft tones and a gentle start and stop.
  • Scope: start with one dataset and one mapping, then expand to more Earth systems.
  • Validation: user testing for clarity, accessibility and scientific interpretation.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: After the Landing – A Space Heritage Explorer
projectDetails.summary:
After the Landing is a website that explores the objects and equipment humans have left behind on the Moon and Mars during space missions. We usually focus on the discoveries made by astronauts, landers and rovers, but we rarely think about what happens to the equipment after a mission ends.

Through this project, we bring together information about these objects from different NASA missions, including Apollo, Mars Pathfinder, Spirit, Opportunity, Perseverance and InSight. The website allows visitors to explore these missions, learn about the objects left behind and understand their history through images and information.

Our aim is to make space exploration more interesting and help people discover a side of space missions that is often overlooked. These objects may no longer be active, but they still represent important achievements in human exploration and scientific history.
projectDetails.details:
AFTER THE LANDING — Space Heritage Explorer

After the Landing, created by ANKH, is an interactive, cinematic educational archive that explores the human-made objects, scientific instruments and historical traces left behind on the Moon and Mars by space exploration missions.

While space missions are often remembered for their launches, landings and discoveries, the hardware and equipment left behind tell another important story. Our project brings this overlooked aspect of space exploration to life through an immersive digital experience.

What does the project do and how does it work?

The platform provides an interactive archive of 18 mission-related objects from lunar and Martian exploration. Users can explore dedicated Moon and Mars sections, discover individual mission objects, learn about their original purposes, understand their scientific contributions and examine their historical significance.

Each object has a dedicated information page containing its mission context, purpose, status, facts and legacy. The platform also features an interactive mission timeline, archive filters, educational content and animated planetary environments.

It distinguishes between deliberately impacted spacecraft, discarded landing hardware, scientific equipment and still-operational rovers, helping users understand the different categories of human-made objects on other worlds.

What benefits does it have?

  • Makes space exploration history more accessible and engaging.
  • Educates users about the scientific instruments and technologies used in lunar and Martian missions.
  • Preserves awareness of historical human activity beyond Earth.
  • Helps students and space enthusiasts understand the long-term legacy of space exploration.
  • Presents scientific and historical information through an easy-to-navigate visual archive.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to create awareness of humanity’s growing footprint beyond Earth and encourage people to look beyond the achievements of landing on another world.

Every object left behind represents engineering, scientific discovery and a moment in human exploration. By documenting these objects, we hope to encourage curiosity about planetary exploration, space heritage and the importance of preserving the history of our activities on other celestial bodies.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed as a lightweight, responsive web application using:

  • HTML5 – Structure and content.
  • CSS3 – Responsive layouts, visual design, animations and transitions.
  • JavaScript – Interactive features, navigation, archive filtering and dynamic content.
  • NASA Images API – Research and retrieval of representative space mission imagery.
  • Solar System Scope textures – Planetary surface textures for immersive visual environments.
  • GitHub Pages – Public hosting and deployment.

All 18 project photographs are stored locally within the project. The website does not require a backend, database, npm installation or external JavaScript libraries.

How is the project creative and innovative?

Instead of presenting space mission information as a conventional list of facts, After the Landing transforms it into a cinematic digital heritage experience.

The platform combines animated planetary environments, editorial storytelling, interactive mission-object dossiers, a colour-coded timeline and a searchable archive. Its Moon and Mars sections have distinct visual identities and educational content.

A key feature is its classification of deployed scientific equipment, discarded landing components, deliberately impacted hardware and active mission vehicles. This provides a clearer and more scientifically responsible understanding of what remains on these worlds.

What factors did we consider?

We considered scientific accuracy, historical context, accessibility, responsive design, performance and educational value throughout development.

Particular attention was given to distinguishing active mission hardware from abandoned or discarded objects, correctly representing mission events and providing appropriate image-source credits.

The website supports desktop and mobile devices, keyboard navigation and reduced-motion preferences. Local image storage also helps maintain availability without relying on external image servers.

After the Landing is more than an archive of objects. It is a digital record of humanity’s journey beyond Earth and the stories we leave behind.

projectDetails.details:
Project Details – LUNAR LEGACY

LUNAR LEGACY is a digital space archaeology museum concept designed to explore the stories of human-made equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars. It addresses the challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten” by turning space mission records into an engaging and accessible learning experience.

How It Works

The project organizes information about abandoned spacecraft, rovers, landers, and scientific instruments into a digital archive. Each artifact is presented with its mission background, original purpose, major achievements, and historical significance.

The planned platform includes:

  • Artifact Archive: Explore and discover forgotten space equipment.
  • Artifact Stories: Learn why each object was sent, what it accomplished, and what happened to it.
  • Mission Timeline: Understand important events in space exploration.
  • Exploration Atlas: Discover where selected artifacts were left behind.
  • Evidence Room: Access NASA references and supporting information.

Benefits and Intended Impact

LUNAR LEGACY makes space exploration history easier and more interesting to understand, especially for students and young space enthusiasts. It highlights the scientific contributions of equipment that is often overlooked after a mission ends.

The project aims to encourage curiosity, support informal space education, and inspire interest in future planetary exploration.

Technology Used

The web application was developed using React.js, Vite, JavaScript, CSS, React Router, and structured JSON data. GitHub was used for version control and project development. AI tools assisted with brainstorming, coding support, debugging, and content refinement.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative idea is to approach space exploration from a different perspective. Instead of focusing only on astronauts and successful missions, LUNAR LEGACY tells the stories of the machines that remained behind. It presents them as historical artifacts with their own scientific legacies.

Factors Considered

The project considers factual accuracy, educational value, accessibility, ease of navigation, and responsible use of AI-generated content. NASA mission resources are used as the foundation for research, and AI-generated visuals, where used, are not presented as authentic NASA photographs.

Current Development Status and Limitations

LUNAR LEGACY was developed as a web-based prototype. However, during final testing, technical issues with deployment and page routing caused some website pages to display blank screens or remain inaccessible. As a result, the website is not currently fully functional. The project concept, research, design, planned features, and development approach are presented in the submitted presentation. Further debugging and deployment are part of the ongoing development process.

One Explorer. One Legacy.

Reading Earth's Changing Surface Through Radar

FLAGWA is an interactive radar remote-sensing platform designed to help people explore and understand changes across Earth's surface using Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data, with a particular focus on NASA–ISRO NISAR mission observations.

Our flagship study area is Kuttanad, Alappuzha, Kerala, India — a unique wetland landscape where agriculture, waterways, soil conditions and managed water levels are closely interconnected. projectDetails.details:
FLAGWA — Global Surface Change Explorer

Reading Earth's Changing Surface Through Radar

1. What is FLAGWA?

FLAGWA is an interactive geospatial platform that explores Earth's changing surface using Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellite observations, with a particular focus on NASA–ISRO's NISAR mission.

Our goal is to make complex radar remote-sensing data more accessible, understandable and useful for students, researchers and environmental practitioners.

We selected Kuttanad, Alappuzha, Kerala, India, as our flagship study area. Known as the Rice Bowl of Kerala, Kuttanad is a unique wetland ecosystem where agriculture, waterways, soil conditions and managed water levels constantly interact. Understanding these changes is important for environmental monitoring and sustainable landscape management.

2. How does it work?

FLAGWA brings satellite data exploration, geospatial processing, visualisation and environmental context into a unified platform.

The workflow consists of:

  • Data Discovery: Accessing and exploring relevant SAR observations and satellite datasets, including NISAR products.
  • Radar Exploration: Visualising radar observations and comparing acquisitions to investigate changes over time.
  • Radar Lab: Providing analytical workflows to process and investigate radar observations.
  • Earthscore: Presenting interpreted environmental and surface-change information in an accessible format.
  • Groundwire: Connecting satellite observations with geographical and environmental context to support further investigation.

Users can explore locations, examine radar observations, compare datasets and investigate potential surface changes through an interactive interface.

3. Our scientific approach

SAR technology is particularly valuable because it uses microwave signals and can collect observations regardless of daylight and through many cloud conditions.

FLAGWA explores how changes in radar backscatter may reflect differences in surface conditions, including open water, flooded vegetation, wet soil and agricultural activity.

Our Kuttanad case study investigates changes between two L-band NISAR GCOV observations from 29 October 2026 and 10 November 2026.

An important part of our approach is scientific responsibility. A change in radar backscatter does not automatically confirm flooding, identify flood depth or establish its cause. Results must be interpreted with additional information such as rainfall, water levels, agricultural cycles, hydrological conditions and independent observations.

FLAGWA is designed to support this investigation rather than present every detected change as a confirmed environmental event.

4. Benefits and intended impact

  • Environmental understanding: Helps users investigate changes in wetlands, agricultural landscapes and other surface environments.
  • Research accessibility: Makes radar data exploration more approachable for students and researchers.
  • Disaster and water research: Provides a platform for investigating potential water-related surface changes.
  • Education: Encourages practical learning in SAR remote sensing, GIS and Earth observation.
  • Evidence-based investigation: Promotes combining satellite observations with environmental context and independent validation.

Our long-term vision is to support environmental research, educational institutions and organisations working towards better understanding of Earth's changing landscapes.

5. Technology and tools used

Frontend

  • React 19
  • TypeScript
  • Vite
  • React Router
  • TanStack Query
  • Zustand
  • MapLibre GL
  • GeoTIFF.js
  • Recharts

Backend and data processing

  • Python
  • FastAPI
  • PostgreSQL with PostGIS
  • Redis and Celery
  • NASA Earthdata and ASF data access workflows
  • Raster and geospatial processing workflows

Visualisation and infrastructure

  • Interactive geospatial maps
  • Satellite raster visualisation
  • Cloud-compatible object storage architecture
  • REST APIs
  • Git and GitHub for version control and collaboration

6. What makes FLAGWA creative?

FLAGWA is not intended to be just another satellite imagery viewer. Its central idea is to create a journey from radar observations to environmental understanding.

Instead of showing users complicated satellite data without context, FLAGWA organises the experience around exploration, analysis and interpretation.

Its modular experiences Explorer, Radar Lab, Earthscore and Groundwire help connect technical radar observations with real-world environmental questions.

Our Kuttanad-first approach also gives the project a meaningful geographical identity: starting with a real wetland landscape and developing a workflow that can eventually be adapted to other regions.

7. Team and future vision

FLAGWA is developed by Anson Joseph (Team Lead) and Sharun Tomy, from Mar Thoma College, Thiruvalla, affiliated with Mahatma Gandhi University, Kerala.

We envision FLAGWA growing into an accessible Earth observation and environmental research platform that connects universities, remote-sensing researchers, environmental practitioners and communities.

Our mission is simple: make the invisible changes in Earth's surface easier to explore, investigate and understand.

projectDetails.name: SkyLab:  A Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
projectDetails.summary: SkyLab: A Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a free browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. Players lead a crew of four on a Moon or Mars outpost for 20 sols, spending limited crew hours on air, power, food and radiation shielding. Every system depends on the others, so one weak choice can cause a chain of problems. Night, dust storms, fires, air leaks and solar flares force safe decisions, and each sol ends with a real space fact and a short quiz. Sunlight and radiation levels come from real measurements, which makes Mars harder on power and the Moon harder on radiation. The game addresses the challenge by turning outpost life-support trade-offs into something students can play and learn from. It matters because understanding a space mission as a set of connected systems builds planning and problem-solving skills.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works. The player commands a crew of four on a Moon or Mars outpost and must keep them alive for 20 sols (days). Each sol they have limited crew hours to spend on an air plant, solar panels, a greenhouse and a radiation wall. A forecast shows what will happen next sol, so players plan, test and adjust. A four-act story adds damage that carries over, so a broken system keeps hurting until the crew repairs it. Random emergencies such as fires, leaks, CO2 build-up, solar flares and dust storms teach the safe response, and each sol ends with a real space fact. A live outpost view shows the crew reacting to low oxygen, power or food. After each mission, players take a short quiz, earn XP and ranks, and can meet bonus goals.

Extra training modules deepen the learning: Mission Control (triage, timed decisions and a replay of the Apollo 13 emergency), ISS Spacewalk, Repair Mission, Moonwalk, Suit Up, Space Station Tour, Solar System Explorer and Pack the Cargo, where a weight limit forces trade-offs about what to launch.

Real data. The game uses real values for Mars and Earth sunlight (586.2 and 1361.0 W/m²), day lengths, and measured radiation on the Moon (1369 µSv/day), on Mars (624 µSv/day) and on the space station (731 µSv/day). These make Mars harder on power and the Moon harder on radiation. All other numbers are simplified game units, and the lunar day is compressed to fit 20 sols.

Benefits and intended impact. Students learn that habitats are connected systems, that every choice has a cost, and that staying calm and following a checklist saves lives. A Science and Teachers panel gives learning goals and discussion questions. The game is free, needs no account and runs offline.

Tools and technology. HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, the canvas for animated scenes and games, and the Web Audio API for sound effects generated in the browser. Progress is saved in the browser’s local storage. There are no external libraries and no network calls. It can be played on any devices be it smartphones, laptops or desktops.

Creativity. SkyLab turns life support into a story with consequences instead of a quiz. Damage carries over between sols, emergencies shuffle their answers so players must read carefully, and failing is treated as practice, like astronaut simulators. The game blends a survival simulation with real data, real mission events and hands-on training activities.

Factors we considered. Age-appropriate language and short text for ages 7 to 12, accuracy (simplified science, honest about what is simplified), accessibility (large buttons, keyboard and touch controls, a sound toggle, reduced-motion support), safety (no accounts or personal data) and classroom use (offline, quick sessions, and a reset button for shared devices).

projectDetails.name: TerraSonus
projectDetails.summary:
What if the Earth could tell us its story, not through charts, numbers or satellite images, but through music?

Every rise in temperature, shift in wind, change in vegetation and pulse of wildfire tells us something about our planet. TerraSonus - The Earth Information Jukebox, built by Team ASGARD, lets you hear that story.

TerraSonus is an interactive web application that transforms climate and environmental data into structured musical patterns. Through a 3D globe, six guided exploration tracks and an interactive Climate Time Machine covering 1980-2026, users can explore how Earth's conditions have changed over time through both sight and sound.

At its core, TerraSonus features a sound engine that maps environmental variables to distinct audio patterns. Its Visual Sonifier takes this further by transforming image pixel information into sound, creating another way to experience visual environmental data.

Accessibility is built into the experience through speech narration, keyboard controls and a dedicated Blind Access mode, allowing more people to explore and interact with environmental information.

Inspired by NASA's Earth-observation work and the possibilities of open environmental data, TerraSonus explores a new way to make complex planetary changes more engaging, accessible and understandable.

Earth's story deserves to be experienced, not just observed. Sometimes, the most powerful way to understand a changing world is to listen.
projectDetails.details:
TerraSonus – The Earth Information Jukebox is an interactive web app that turns climate-related data into structured music. A 3D Earth globe, five regional hotspots, six guided exploration tracks and a Time Machine covering 1980–2026 let users explore how our planet is changing through both sight and sound.

The sonification engine maps environmental variables such as temperature, CO₂, wind, vegetation (NDVI) and wildfire activity to distinct audio patterns, using musical mapping techniques and a pentatonic scale. The Visual Sonifier goes a step further by converting image pixel information into sound, so users can experience visual data by listening to it.

TerraSonus supports inclusive exploration with speech narration, keyboard controls, ARIA support, Blind Access mode and an in-app Sound Guide. We want to make Earth science more accessible, interactive and engaging, especially for people who run into barriers with visual information.

The project was inspired by NASA’s Earth-observation work and open environmental data, and it explores new ways of presenting planetary information. The current app uses embedded climate reference values, and we plan to integrate live NASA data in future development.

We built it with React, Vite, JavaScript, Three.js, Tone.js, the Web Audio API, Tailwind CSS and the Web Speech API, and deployed it on Cloudflare Pages.

The creativity of TerraSonus lies in turning environmental information into a musical experience. By bringing together data, sound, visualization and accessibility, we hope to offer a new way to understand and connect with our changing planet. While building it, we kept accessibility, musical clarity, meaningful data representation, user experience, technical feasibility and future scalability in mind

projectDetails.name: ExoMatch
projectDetails.summary: ExoMatch is a web application that makes NASA’s exoplanet data easier to explore and understand. Users can search confirmed planets, compare their properties, view discovery trends, and receive recommendations for similar worlds. The system uses K-Means clustering and similarity calculations based on planetary characteristics such as radius, mass, temperature, and orbital period. Built with Python and Streamlit, ExoMatch combines machine learning with interactive charts to turn complex astronomical records into an accessible learning experience. It helps students, educators, and space enthusiasts investigate patterns in known exoplanets while clearly distinguishing scientific measurements, illustrative images, and recommendations from evidence of habitability or life.
projectDetails.details: ExoMatch is an interactive web application that helps users explore, compare, and discover similarities among confirmed exoplanets using NASA Exoplanet Archive data. It uses K-Means clustering and Euclidean distance to recommend planets based on characteristics such as radius, mass, orbital period, and temperature. Built with Python, Streamlit, Pandas, NumPy, Scikit-learn, and Plotly, it provides searchable planetary information and interactive visualizations. The project makes astronomical data accessible to students, educators, and space enthusiasts. Its design considers missing values, feature scaling, usability, and scientific limitations. Recommendations highlight similarities between known planets without claiming to discover new worlds, confirm habitability, or identify extraterrestrial life.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: AstroQuest – Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
projectDetails.summary:
AstroQuest is an interactive educational application designed to help students understand how astronauts manage resources and survive during space missions. It allows users to experience a virtual Moon or Mars mission while taking on the role of an astronaut.

Users learn to manage essential resources such as oxygen, food, water and electricity while maintaining astronaut health and safety. They also face different mission challenges that require them to make decisions and understand the results of their choices. The application aims to include interactive mission levels, resource management activities and mission-success outcomes.

AstroQuest makes space exploration more interesting and easier to understand through learning and interactive experiences. It encourages curiosity about space, develops decision-making and problem-solving skills, and introduces students to the challenges of real space missions.
projectDetails.details:
AstroQuest – Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

What does the project do, and how does it work?

AstroQuest is an interactive educational game that allows players to experience the challenges of a space mission. Players take on the role of a junior astronaut and manage important resources such as oxygen, water, food, and electricity. During the mission, they face different challenges, including water shortages, power shortages, dust storms, and returning safely to base. Players must select suitable actions to manage resources and complete their mission successfully.

What benefits does the project have?

AstroQuest makes learning about space exploration more interesting and interactive. It helps students understand the importance of resource management, decision-making, and problem-solving during space missions. It also introduces young learners to some of the challenges astronauts may face.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Our aim is to encourage students and young learners to become interested in space science and exploration. We want to make space-related learning more accessible, enjoyable, and understandable through a simple interactive experience.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

We developed the project using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. We used a text editor (Notepad) to write the code and a web browser to test the game. We used Netlify to host the project online so that people can access and play it through a public link. No special hardware was required.

How is your project creative?

The creative part of AstroQuest is that it turns space-mission challenges into an interactive learning game. Instead of only reading about astronauts, players make decisions, manage resources, and experience how their choices affect the mission. The different challenges make the experience engaging and educational.

What factors did your team consider?

Our team considered simplicity, educational value, user-friendliness, and accessibility. We wanted to make the game easy to understand and play, especially for students and beginners. We also considered the importance of resource management and decision-making in space exploration while designing the mission challenges.

projectDetails.name: Earth Information Jukebox: Hear the Arctic Ice Disappear
projectDetails.summary:
Earth Information Jukebox: Hear the Arctic Ice Disappear turns NASA satellite-based Arctic sea ice data into sound. We developed an interactive web page where each year is one musical note: a low note means a lot of sea ice, and a high note means less. When you press Play, you hear the pitch climb across more than 45 years of data while a chart marker and live caption show the year and ice extent in million km².

This addresses the challenge by making Earth observation data something people can listen to and explore, not just read in charts. Sound also makes the data more accessible to people who have difficulty with visual graphs.

It matters because Arctic sea ice is a key indicator of climate change, and hearing the decline in under a minute makes it easy to understand and remember. We used the NSIDC Sea Ice Index (derived from NASA satellite observations), Python for data processing, and JavaScript with the Web Audio API for the page, hosted on GitHub Pages. The design can grow to include more Earth datasets as new tracks.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works
Earth Information Jukebox turns Arctic sea ice data into sound. I used the NSIDC Sea Ice Index (based on NASA satellite observations) and kept the September extent for each year from 1979 onward, which is the yearly minimum. Each value is mapped to a pitch: more ice gives a low note (220 Hz), and less ice gives a high note (880 Hz). When a user presses Play, each year is played as one note while a chart marker moves along the data and a live caption shows the year and ice extent in million km². The pitch climbs as the ice shrinks.

Benefits and intended impact

  • It makes a long climate record understandable in under a minute.
  • It gives people who cannot easily read charts another way to explore Earth data.
  • It helps students and the public connect with NASA data emotionally, not just numerically.
  • It works in any browser with one button, with no installation or technical knowledge.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NSIDC Sea Ice Index, monthly extent by year (Northern Hemisphere)
  • Python (Pandas, NumPy, SciPy) in Google Colab to clean the data and test the sound
  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript with the Web Audio API for the interactive page
  • GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting the code and live demo
  • Google Colab for running the data processing
  • An AI assistant (Claude) helped me plan the project, write and debug code, and draft documentation. I ran, tested and deployed the project myself.

Creativity
Instead of another chart, I treated data as music. The “jukebox” idea means each Earth dataset can become a track, and Arctic ice is the first song. Using the ear to notice a trend is a different way to experience satellite data.

Factors I considered

  • Clarity: low means more ice and high means less ice, so the direction is easy to understand.
  • Accuracy: pitch shows relative change, so the caption always displays the real value. The data source and units are credited.
  • Accessibility: sound adds a non-visual way to explore the data.
  • Simplicity: one dataset and one button, built to be reliable.
  • Limitations: this is a prototype with one track, September values only, and extent rather than ice thickness. Future work includes more tracks (Antarctic ice, sea surface temperature), NASA satellite imagery, and user controls.

Our project is an interactive digital museum that brings these forgotten machines back to life through storytelling.
Using photographs, interactive maps, mission timelines and educational games, we help people discover the stories behind NASA's abandoned equipment.
We also highlight their achievements, scientific discoveries and contributions to space exploration.
Our goal is not just to remember old machines, but to celebrate the incredible journeys and discoveries they made possible.
Because every machine has a mission, every mission has a story, and every story inspires a new discovery.

projectDetails.name: AstroPrep
projectDetails.summary:
AstroPrep is a browser game that teaches students the trade-offs of running a lunar or Martian outpost. Players manage three core resources (power, oxygen, and radiation shielding) plus crew health over a 20-day mission, with only three crew hours per day. Every action has a real cost: expanding solar arrays uses up shielding material, making oxygen drains power, and building shielding costs power and crew effort. There is no free, safe choice.
Each day, a forecast warns of incoming space weather, based on real solar events from NASA's DONKI database, such as the 2003 Halloween storms and the 2017 X9.3 flare. Players must prepare shielding in advance, just as mission planners do. Events are randomized, so every playthrough differs, and when a mission fails the game explains why.
The event data is a curated static snapshot, clearly labeled in the app as not live, with NASA DONKI and NOAA cited as sources.
projectDetails.details:
What it does: AstroPrep is a browser game where students run a Moon or Mars outpost for 20 days. With only 3 crew hours a day, players balance power, oxygen, and radiation shielding. Every action has a cost, so there is no free "safe" choice. Random crew events and upgrades keep each run different, and when a mission fails, the game shows what hurt the crew most.
NASA data: On start, the game requests the last 30 days of solar flares from NASA's DONKI database. Moderate (M) and strong (X) flares become nightly events, and a 3-day forecast lets players raise shielding before a hit, as real mission planners do. If NASA can't be reached, it uses a saved snapshot of real past events (like the 2003 Halloween storms) and labels it SNAPSHOT. Static data is never shown as live.
Benefits and impact: It makes real engineering trade-offs fun for young learners without overwhelming them, using only three core resources. Players learn that power, oxygen, and shielding depend on each other, and that space weather is a real mission risk.
Tools: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with SVG graphics, NASA DONKI API, GitHub Pages for hosting. No installs needed, so it runs on any device with a browser.
Creativity: Science points buy upgrades, balance streaks raise the score, and the outpost reacts to your choices (shield glow, dimming lights, screen shake on big flares).
Factors considered: Clear data labelling, three resources to avoid overload, learning from failure without punishment, and honest labelling of simplifications. Hazard levels and damage numbers are game simplifications, not real radiation doses.

To play the game:https://joe-ui7878.github.io/NASA-Space-Apps-Challenge-2026/
