projectDetails.name: Project Astrosearch
projectDetails.summary: Project Astrosearch answers the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge with two public web apps that help anyone see how the infrared sky changes over time. NASA's SPHEREx maps the whole sky in 102 infrared colours every six months, but its archive is hard for newcomers to use. COSMOS lets users search a sky position, discover real SPHEREx observation dates from NASA/IPAC IRSA, load real image cutouts for two periods and compare them with a blink comparator, split-screen wipe and date timeline. Sky Blink & Spectral Explorer is a clearly labelled simulation that teaches people to spot objects that shift position between epochs, the way comets, asteroids and brown dwarfs do, and to read a 102-band infrared spectrum. Together they make SPHEREx data easier for students, teachers and citizen scientists to explore.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES
Project Astrosearch answers the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge with two linked web apps that let anyone see how the infrared sky changes over time.
- COSMOS (https://cosmos-ahq.pages.dev) searches the official SPHEREx archive, lists real observation dates for a sky position, loads real image cutouts for two periods and compares them with a blink comparator, split-screen wipe and date timeline.
- Sky Blink & Spectral Explorer (https://nasa-citizen-science.netlify.app) is a labelled practice simulator with four epoch modes (blink, wipe, RGB motion map, 4-epoch timeline), a 102-band spectrum explorer (0.75-5.0 micrometres) and a citizen discovery log.

HOW IT WORKS
Users enter RA/Dec or pick a named object, choose a SPHEREx data release, discover the available dates, then compare two periods. COSMOS lists only dates returned by the archive and links each record to the original SPHEREx FITS product. Sky Blink uses simulated data so beginners can practise spotting moving sources and reading spectra first.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT
SPHEREx has imaged more than a billion objects, far too many for one person to sift. Our tools let students, teachers and citizen scientists see change over time in the browser, without special software or knowledge of FITS files.

CREATIVITY
We brought the blink comparator, the technique that revealed Pluto in 1930, to the browser and added a wipe, a timeline, an RGB motion map and a discovery log that turns practice into a game.

HONEST LIMITS
COSMOS images are for visual comparison only. It does not automatically detect asteroids, comets or Planet X. Sky Blink is an educational simulation, not live mission data. Both are independent student projects, not affiliated with NASA.

TOOLS
Browser-based web apps hosted on Cloudflare Pages and Netlify. Data comes from NASA/IPAC IRSA.

Gemi ai was used to create the video,netlify was used to to build, deploy, and host the website

ASTROCARE AI – Intelligent Astronaut Health Monitoring System

ASTROCARE AI is a futuristic, AI-powered astronaut health monitoring platform designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. It features an interactive humanoid astronaut interface that allows users to explore different body systems, monitor health indicators, and understand potential health risks.

The software tracks important indicators such as heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose, sleep duration, mood, and physical activity. It analyses health measurements and historical trends to identify unusual changes, provides risk alerts, and offers personalised health improvement recommendations. It also includes mental wellness monitoring, spaceflight hazard awareness, interactive health analytics, and daily wellness challenges.

ASTROCARE AI addresses the challenges of spaceflight by helping astronauts independently assess their physical and mental health, recognise potential problems early, and take appropriate preventive actions. It aims to reduce dependence on immediate medical assistance from Earth and support better health management during missions to the Moon and Mars.

By combining intelligent health analysis, interactive visualisation, and astronaut-centred design, ASTROCARE AI aims to make long-duration human space exploration safer and healthier.
projectDetails.details:
ASTROCARE AI – Intelligent Astronaut Health Monitoring and Decision Support System

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

ASTROCARE AI is an intelligent astronaut health monitoring platform designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions, including future lunar and Mars explorations.

The application features a futuristic interactive humanoid astronaut that acts as a visual health interface. Astronauts can select different body regions, such as the brain, heart, lungs, bones, muscles, and skin, to explore relevant health information, monitor indicators, and understand potential health risks.

The system collects health information through manual inputs and can be extended to support wearable sensors and medical devices. It monitors important indicators, including heart rate, blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose, sleep duration, mood, hydration, and physical activity.

The collected information is analysed using health assessment rules and historical trends to identify unusual changes. The application displays health insights, risk alerts, and appropriate preventive recommendations. It also includes mental wellness monitoring, health analytics, and daily wellness activities.

2. What benefits does the project provide?

ASTROCARE AI offers several important benefits:

  • Early health risk identification: Helps astronauts recognise unusual changes in health indicators before they potentially develop into serious problems.
  • Independent health monitoring: Enables astronauts to assess their health without always requiring immediate assistance from Earth.
  • Physical health management: Supports monitoring of cardiovascular health, bone loss, muscle weakness, temperature, and nutrition.
  • Mental wellness support: Helps astronauts track mood, stress, sleep quality, and psychological wellbeing.
  • Clear health visualisation: Uses an interactive humanoid interface, colour-coded indicators, and dynamic charts to make health information easier to understand.
  • Preventive health guidance: Provides educational recommendations and prompts for appropriate health assessments and follow-up.
  • Continuous health tracking: Maintains historical measurements to help identify long-term changes during missions.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our primary goal is to contribute to safer and healthier human space exploration.

During long-duration missions, astronauts face five major human spaceflight hazards: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity fields, and hostile closed environments. These hazards can affect different body systems and create physical and psychological challenges.

ASTROCARE AI aims to help astronauts recognise these changes, monitor their health independently, and take appropriate preventive actions.

The project could support future missions to the Moon, Mars, and other deep-space destinations where immediate medical assistance from Earth may be limited or delayed.

Ultimately, we aim to improve astronaut health awareness, support timely medical decision-making, and contribute to the safety and sustainability of future human space exploration.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software were used?

Our proposed development technology includes:

Frontend development:

  • React.js – Building the interactive user interface.
  • Vite – Application development environment.
  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript – Application structure, styling, and functionality.
  • Tailwind CSS – Responsive interface design.
  • Framer Motion – Animations and interactive transitions.

Humanoid visualisation:

  • Three.js – Creating interactive 3D astronaut visual

projectDetails.name: Project ASTROXX
projectDetails.summary:
TerraShield AI is an AI-assisted environmental monitoring dashboard for Kerala. It brings three NASA-based data streams into one visual interface: rainfall (FloodSense, from GPM precipitation data), land-surface temperature (from MODIS), and ocean health (OceanGuard). Users can explore monthly time series, spot unusual rainfall months, view a rainfall-based flood-risk indicator, and run trend tests that report slope and statistical significance. Ocean observations are classified as normal, moderate-change or high-change. A CSV upload feature lets users analyse their own environmental datasets in the same way.

The project addresses the challenge by turning raw, scattered environmental data into signals people can read quickly, using charts, anomaly markers, trend statistics and simple indicators. In the demo, rainfall showed no statistically significant trend (p = 0.073), while temperature showed a significant decreasing trend (p = 0.0011).

This matters because Kerala is vulnerable to floods and climate variability, and clearer historical patterns help people understand and communicate environmental change. TerraShield is an exploratory analysis tool, not an official warning service, so its risk indicators should be checked against authoritative local alerts.
projectDetails.details:
TerraShield AI is a single dashboard that combines three environmental signals for Kerala:

  • FloodSense (rainfall): Shows 141 months of NASA GPM precipitation data as a time series. It highlights unusual rainfall months (2 in the demo) and shows a rainfall-based flood-risk indicator (latest alert: Low, 0.241 mm/hr).
  • Temperature: Plots NASA MODIS land-surface temperature (min 23.11 °C, max 29.68 °C, average 26.43 °C) and runs a linear trend test.
  • OceanGuard (ocean health): Classifies monthly ocean observations as normal, moderate-change or high-change (7 / 2 / 1 in the demo).

For each trend, the dashboard reports the slope, the p-value and whether the result is statistically significant at the 0.05 threshold. Users can also upload their own CSV of environmental observations and explore it with the same charts and summaries.

Benefits

  • Puts rainfall, temperature and ocean data in one place instead of several separate sources.
  • Makes patterns easier to see and explain, using seasonal peaks, anomaly markers and plain-language indicators.
  • Reports whether a trend is statistically significant, so users don’t over-read noise. In the demo, rainfall showed no significant trend (p = 0.073), while temperature showed a significant decreasing trend (p = 0.0011).
  • The CSV upload makes it reusable with other datasets.

Intended impact

TerraShield AI aims to make historical environmental data easier for students, researchers and local communities to understand and communicate. It is meant to support awareness of flood risk and climate variability in Kerala, a region exposed to heavy monsoon rainfall and a long coastline. It is not an official emergency-warning system, and its risk indicators should be checked against authoritative local alerts.

Tools and technologies

  • Data: NASA GPM (rainfall) and NASA MODIS (land-surface temperature)
  • Analysis: Linear trend testing (slope and p-value), anomaly detection, threshold-based classification
  • [Add: programming languages, frameworks, charting libraries, hosting, and any AI/ML tools you used]
  • Hardware: [Add if relevant, e.g. standard laptops, no special hardware]

Creativity

  • It combines land, rainfall and ocean signals in one interface, rather than a single-purpose tool.
  • It pairs visuals with statistical tests, so it shows both what changed and whether the change is meaningful.
  • The modular branding (FloodSense, OceanGuard) gives each signal its own identity within one platform.
  • It is honest about its limits, with a clear note that it is exploratory and not a safety service.

Factors the team considered

  • Data reliability: Using established NASA sources and labelling them clearly.
  • Statistical honesty: Reporting p-values and stating when no significant trend is found.
  • Responsible use: Making clear that risk indicators are exploratory, to avoid false confidence in safety decisions.
  • Usability: Simple indicators and charts for non-experts.
  • Flexibility: CSV upload, so the tool isn’t limited to one dataset.
  • [Add if applicable: scalability, data limitations, ethical concerns, or future plans such as real-time data or more regions.]

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Moon Base Keeper : Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
projectDetails.summary:
Ask most kids what astronauts do and they’ll say “walk on the Moon.” Ask what keeps those astronauts alive and you’ll get a blank stare. Moon Base Keeper changes that.

In this free browser game, kids aged 7 to 12 run a lunar outpost near the Moon’s south pole for seven days. They build solar panels, air makers and radiation shields, give jobs to a crew of four, and make a call every day. Every choice costs something: shields use power, power makes air, and a solar flare won’t wait until you’re ready.

That flare isn’t made up. Each day’s space weather is based on NASA’s DONKI solar flare data, so the danger on screen comes from real solar activity. There’s nothing to download and no account to create. Just click, build, and find out that in space, nothing is free.
projectDetails.details:
Moon Base Keeper puts a kid in charge of a lunar outpost near the Moon’s south pole for seven days. Each day they check the space weather, build solar panels, air makers and shields, give their four astronauts jobs, and make one big call. Nothing is free: shields use power, power makes air, and a solar flare won’t wait until you’re ready. The flare warning is based on NASA’s DONKI space weather data, so the danger comes from real solar activity.

  • Why it helps: one mission (about 5 to 8 minutes) teaches that a space base is a balancing act. It’s free, runs in any browser, and needs no download or account, so a class can start from a link.
  • Impact we hope for: kids leave knowing that no one gets a free choice in space, and that astronauts are people solving hard problems, which might make them ask, “How would I solve that?”
  • What we used: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, hosted on Netlify with code on GitHub. We wrote it in the Antigravity editor with AI assistance (including Claude) and made the artwork ourselves. Data comes from NASA DONKI, plus facts inspired by NASA’s Open Science Data Repository.
  • What’s creative: the lesson is the game. Every choice has a visible cost, there’s no safe option, and real flare data drives the risk. Each astronaut has a job explained in kid-friendly words, and the game labels what’s real, simplified or fictional.
  • What we considered: ages 7 to 12 get overwhelmed, so we kept the main stats to three and unlocked extra buildings later. We used plain language, favoured accuracy over flashy looks, and made it easy to reach. The numbers are simplified, the 7-day plan is illustrative, and the crew are fictional.

projectDetails.name: Earth Jukebox – Hear Earth's Changing Systems
projectDetails.summary:
Earth Jukebox is an interactive Earth science platform that transforms real environmental data into sound, offering an alternative way to explore and understand our planet. By combining scientific data sonification with interactive visualizations, the project makes complex environmental measurements more engaging and accessible.

Users can select any geographical location and explore atmospheric parameters such as temperature, rainfall, wind speed and surface temperature using NASA POWER data. Through the Web Audio API, these measurements are translated into distinct sound patterns. The platform further integrates NASA MODIS NDVI imagery for vegetation monitoring, NOAA satellite data for ocean temperature and chlorophyll-a, and historical climate comparisons to explore environmental changes across different years.

By connecting data, visualization and sound, Earth Jukebox aims to transform the way people experience Earth science, encouraging environmental awareness, scientific curiosity and inclusive exploration of our changing planet.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Earth Jukebox

1. Project Overview

Earth Jukebox is an interactive Earth-science platform that transforms real environmental measurements into sound. It combines data sonification, interactive maps and scientific visualizations to provide an alternative way of exploring Earth's changing environmental systems.

Users can select geographical locations, retrieve environmental data and experience the measurements through both visual and auditory representations.

2. How It Works

The platform retrieves daily environmental measurements from NASA POWER, including:

  • Air temperature at 2 metres (T2M).
  • Precipitation (PRECTOTCORR).
  • Wind speed at 10 metres (WS10M).
  • Earth skin temperature (TS).

The retrieved measurements are validated and mapped to audio parameters using the Web Audio API.

Each variable has a distinct sound representation. Temperature controls musical pitch, rainfall controls the frequency of short sound pulses, wind influences noise brightness and loudness, and surface temperature produces a slow, wave-like tone.

Users can also listen to a sequence representing the last 30 days of measurements and explore how environmental conditions change over time.

3. Additional Features

Beyond atmospheric data, Earth Jukebox incorporates three additional exploration modules:

Vegetation Monitoring: NASA MODIS NDVI imagery, accessed through NASA GIBS, allows users to explore vegetation greenness across different years.

Ocean Monitoring: NOAA CoastWatch satellite products provide sea-surface temperature and chlorophyll-a measurements where data is available.

Historical Climate Comparison: Users can compare monthly temperature, precipitation and wind patterns between two selected years through interactive charts and audio sequences.

4. Technologies Used

The application is developed using HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript. Its primary technologies and resources include:

  • NASA POWER API – Environmental measurements.
  • NASA GIBS and MODIS – Vegetation imagery.
  • NOAA CoastWatch ERDDAP – Ocean measurements.
  • Leaflet.js and OpenStreetMap – Interactive maps.
  • Web Audio API – Real-time sound generation.
  • HTML Canvas – Data visualization.
  • Browser Geolocation API – Location selection.

The platform runs directly in a web browser without requiring additional software installation.

5. Innovation and Impact

The central innovation of Earth Jukebox is its use of sound as an additional medium for communicating scientific data. Instead of relying exclusively on conventional charts, maps and numerical readings, it translates environmental measurements into distinct auditory patterns.

This approach has potential applications in environmental education, public science communication and accessible exploration of Earth science.

By connecting real environmental data with sound and interactive visualization, Earth Jukebox aims to make complex planetary information more engaging, understandable and accessible.

projectDetails.name: Project Bifrost- AstroHealth Monitor
projectDetails.summary: AstroHealth Monitor is an interactive, multi-domain astronaut health and biomedical telemetry dashboard built for the "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions" challenge. Long-duration spaceflight exposes crews to microgravity, radiation, isolation, and closed-loop environments—triggering cardiovascular deconditioning, bone mineral loss, immune suppression, and behavioral fatigue simultaneously.   Modeled on published NASA Human Research Program (HRP) evidence reports, NASA-STD-3001 standards, and NCRP Report 132 radiation limits, AstroHealth Monitor consolidates 18 physiological, psychological, and radiation biomarkers across 5 health domains into a unified interface. It tracks longitudinal drift against pre-flight baselines, flags anomalies with automated clinical alerts, and pairs warnings directly with actionable NASA HRP countermeasure protocols (ARED resistance, CEVIS cardio, light therapy, and a 14-item weekly self-assessment). By turning fragmented telemetry into clear, self-guided actions, it empowers deep-space crews to maintain peak health autonomously when Earth communication delays increase.
projectDetails.details:
AstroHealth Monitor is an interactive biomedical telemetry and self-monitoring web app for long-duration spaceflight, modeled on NASA Human Research Program (HRP) evidence reports, NASA-STD-3001 standards, and NCRP Report 132 radiation limits. Demonstrated via a mid-mission Artemis Gateway-1 scenario (Day 142/240), it tracks 18 physiological, behavioral, and radiation indicators across 5 health domains (Cardiovascular, Bone & Muscle, Immune, Behavioral Health, and Radiation).

Across six synchronized modules—Mission Overview, Health Domains, Clinical Alerts, Daily Action Center, Self-Assessment (14-item Likert check-in), and Radiation Monitor—the app tracks longitudinal drift against pre-flight baselines, computes an Overall Health Index (71/100), flags anomalies, and pairs warnings directly with actionable HRP countermeasure protocols (ARED resistance, CEVIS cardio, 10,000-lux light therapy, and supplements).

Benefits, Impact & Tech Stack By turning fragmented telemetry into closed-loop countermeasures, AstroHealth Monitor supports deep-space crew autonomy during Earth communication delays and reduces flight-surgeon cognitive load—while offering direct spin-off value for remote telemedicine and ICU monitoring. Built with React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Recharts in a low-fatigue dark glassmorphism UI, it runs offline-ready without backend dependencies

projectDetails.name: ASTRA—Astronaut Health Intelligence and Monitoring System
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRA—Astronaut Health Intelligence and Monitoring System—is a research prototype developed by Team BLUE to bring astronaut health observations into one connected review workflow. It combines simulated vital signs, personal baselines, and cabin conditions in a mission-control dashboard.

BioMonitor streams physiological measurements, RiskWatch detects deviations from individual baselines, and SpaceHealth provides environmental context. ASTRA Copilot retrieves recorded evidence with source citations, while MissionCare supports human review, reports, shift handovers, and a historical timeline.

ASTRA addresses the challenge by helping users see what changed, understand the supporting evidence, and preserve observations for follow-up. This matters because isolated readings can miss the broader picture: a changing pulse becomes more informative when viewed alongside a personal baseline, recent activity, and cabin conditions.

Our working prototype demonstrates this connected workflow using explicitly simulated data and NASA-STD-3001 background references. It is not medically validated and performs no automated treatment. Our goal is clearer, traceable evidence for human-supervised astronaut health decisions.
projectDetails.details:
Project overview

ASTRA—Astronaut Health Intelligence and Monitoring System—is a software research prototype developed by Team BLUE: Rohith B and Sneha Prakasan. It brings physiological observations, personal baselines, environmental context, and human review into one connected workflow.

Our goal is to demonstrate how astronaut health information could become easier to interpret, trace, and communicate during space missions. ASTRA currently uses explicitly simulated measurements; it is not medically validated or connected to real astronaut sensors.

How it works

ASTRA connects five functional modules:

  • BioMonitor streams simulated heart rate, heart-rate variability, oxygen saturation, blood pressure, sleep duration, and hydration indicators.
  • RiskWatch compares measurements with individual baselines and applies statistical, temporal, and multivariate rules to identify deviations. Its scores are experimental engineering indicators, not clinical predictions.
  • SpaceHealth adds mission-scoped cabin conditions, recorded exercise activity, sleep context, and simulated radiation measurements.
  • ASTRA Copilot uses deterministic retrieval and response rules to explain recorded observations, identify supporting sources, and distinguish current measurements from historical alerts. It does not require an external language model to operate.
  • MissionCare supports human acknowledgement and review of alerts, evidence-preserving reports, PDF exports, shift handovers, and a combined historical timeline.

In our demonstration, a controlled anomaly changes simulated vital signs. RiskWatch detects the resulting deviation, Copilot retrieves the supporting evidence, and a reviewer records an observation and changes the alert’s review status.

Benefits and intended impact

Individual measurements can be difficult to interpret without context. ASTRA places observations alongside a person’s baseline, measurement timestamps, mission conditions, and previous events.

The intended benefit is a clearer review process: users can see what changed, inspect why an alert appeared, identify missing or stale information, and preserve evidence for follow-up. Reports and handovers help maintain continuity between reviewers.

We envision this approach supporting future research into crew health awareness and mission health workflows. Actual operational use would require sensor integration, authenticated access, further reliability testing, and formal clinical and operational validation.

Technology and resources

The backend uses Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, SQLAlchemy, and Alembic. The frontend uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Recharts. REST APIs and WebSockets connect the interface to the backend. SQLite provides the verified local database; Docker and PostgreSQL configurations are prepared, but their runtime has not been verified.

The prototype runs on a conventional computer without dedicated hardware. Its simulator generates physiological and cabin measurements and supports controlled anomaly scenarios.

NASA-STD-3001 Volumes 1 and 2 are background references. We did not ingest original NASA astronaut measurement datasets or use these documents to establish clinically validated thresholds.

Creativity and design considerations

ASTRA’s creative contribution is the connection between personal baselines, mission context, explainable deviations, source provenance, and human review. Rather than presenting an isolated alert, it carries supporting observations through explanation, review, reporting, and handover.

We considered:

  • Individual differences: comparisons use stored personal baselines.
  • Data integrity: astronaut and mission records remain correctly associated; duplicate telemetry is rejected.
  • Scientific honesty: synthetic data is labeled, and missing or stale measurements remain visible.
  • Traceability: alert evidence and generated report snapshots are preserved as new measurements arrive.
  • Human authority: ASTRA performs no automated treatment or flight-readiness decision.
  • Reliability: the current software passes 77 backend tests, 28 frontend tests, and the production frontend build. These results verify software behavior, not medical effectiveness.
  • Access limitations: the verified deployment is a trusted local demonstration; authentication and role-based access remain future work.

SI-assisted development

OpenAI Codex assisted with software implementation, testing, documentation, narration scripting, and video-editing code. The demonstration uses recorded interactions with the working prototype, alongside SI-assisted titles and captions. Its narration was generated using ElevenLabs. Simulated measurements are produced by the prototype’s software generator and are not observations of real astronauts.

ASTRA is an independent research prototype and does not claim NASA endorsement, medical certification, or spaceflight qualification.

projectDetails.name: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
projectDetails.summary: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a web-based learning experience that lets kids aged 8-14 train like an astronaut. Players complete five missions: Launch, Orbit, Spacewalk, Mars Landing and Return. Each mission has a short briefing built from real NASA imagery, a timed decision-based simulation where choices change the outcome, and a debrief that awards badges. Players rise from Cadet to Commander, and a crew mode lets 2-4 players share roles such as Commander, Engineer, Medic and Navigator. The project addresses the challenge by turning space training into something students can practise, not just watch. It matters because few students can reach space camps or simulators, and our trainer is designed to be inclusive, with read-aloud support, colour-blind-safe design and low-bandwidth use.
projectDetails.details:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a web-based trainer for kids aged 8-14. Players complete five missions: Launch, Orbit, Spacewalk, Mars Landing and Return. Each mission has three steps. Learn is a 60-second briefing built from real NASA imagery. Simulate is a timed decision scenario where the player's choices change the outcome. Debrief shows what worked, lets the player retry, and awards a mission badge. Badges raise the player's rank from Cadet to Pilot, Specialist and Commander.

Benefits and impact: Students practise the decisions astronauts make instead of only watching videos. Crew mode lets 2-4 players share roles (Commander, Engineer, Medic, Navigator) to build teamwork. It is designed to be inclusive, with read-aloud support, colour-blind-safe design and low-bandwidth use, so students without access to space camps or simulators can still take part.

projectDetails.name: Martian
projectDetails.summary: MARTIAN is an interactive Mars exploration guide and project concept created by Team Callistro for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. The platform aims to make Martian science more accessible by combining planetary maps, geological information, and surface images to help users investigate regions such as Olympus Mons, Jezero Crater, and Valles Marineris. It centers around authoritative scientific resources, including NASA JPL Mars Trek, USGS–NASA Planetary Geologic Mapping, and Mars Perseverance Raw Images. Emphasizing a critical understanding of data by distinguishing observations from assumptions, the project outlines a planned technology stack featuring Python, Streamlit, Pandas, and interactive visualization tools.
projectDetails.details:
MARTIAN is an interactive Mars exploration guide and project concept created by Team Callistro for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It works by connecting planetary maps, geological information, and surface images to help users investigate the Red Planet, allowing them to explore features like Olympus Mons, Jezero Crater, and Valles Marineris through an interactive concept interface.

​The project benefits users by making complex Martian science easier to understand, enabling them to compare different regions and comprehend the challenges of future space exploration. It equips users to explore Mars with curiosity while examining topography, volcanic geology, and past water activity.

​The intended impact of MARTIAN is to make Mars exploration information clearer, more engaging, and easier for the public to investigate. Furthermore, it encourages a grounded mindset by helping users distinguish direct observations from assumptions and emphasizing an accessible approach to planetary data.

​To develop and scale the interactive experience, the team planned a technology stack that includes Python, Streamlit, Pandas, and various mapping or visualization tools. The platform also leverages authoritative external resources like NASA JPL Mars Trek, USGS–NASA Planetary Geologic Mapping, and Mars Perseverance Raw Images.

​Creatively, the project bridges raw planetary data and public accessibility by uniting maps, geological data, and rover photos into a cohesive guide. In developing this, the team carefully considered the importance of connecting authoritative sources, explaining what each resource shows, and explicitly noting that the interface is an illustrative concept rather than a certified landing-site or astronaut-safety assessment.

projectDetails.name: Project VITALORBIT
projectDetails.summary: VITALORBIT is an advanced health monitoring web platform designed to track and safeguard the well-being of astronauts during space missions. In the demanding environment of space exploration, real-time physiological tracking is critical. Our solution provides a centralized dashboard that monitors vital health parameters such as heart rate, oxygen levels, body temperature, and stress indicators. By leveraging real-time data visualization and automated alert mechanisms, VITALORBIT enables ground control and crew members to proactively detect health anomalies, mitigate risks, and ensure rapid medical response. Built with a user-friendly interface, this project bridges the gap between complex biomedical telemetry and actionable insights, supporting astronaut safety and mission success for future space explorations.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview:

Our project, VITALORBIT , is a web-based application designed to address human health and wellness challenges during spaceflight. It provides an intuitive interface focusing on monitoring, understanding, and mitigating the physiological and psychological hazards faced by astronauts during long-duration space missions.

How It Works & Benefits:

The platform aggregates information and guidelines related to the primary hazards of human spaceflight (such as space radiation, isolation, and physiological adaptation). It offers structured insights to help users understand these risks and explore preventive health measures, promoting better crew safety and wellbeing.

Tools & Technologies Used:

The project was developed using modern web technologies including HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, hosted via GitHub Pages. Advanced AI (Super Intelligence) tools were utilized to assist in writing, structuring, and optimizing the frontend code, layout, and textual content to ensure a clean, responsive user experience.

Impact & Design Considerations:

The intended impact is to provide an accessible educational and monitoring tool that bridges complex space health data with user-friendly design. Our team prioritized accessibility, responsiveness, and clear data visualization to make space health concepts easy to navigate for both experts and the general public.

What it does

Mission Control Clicker is a browser game about space missions. You tap to collect science data, spend it on instruments like cameras, radar and rovers, and use the data to launch missions to the Moon, Bennu, Mars and Europa. As you progress, you unlock short lessons with pictures about why each place is hard to explore, such as radiation, weak sunlight and long signal delays. Random space events give bonus data.

Tools

HTML, CSS and JavaScript in one web page, with canvas for the planet view and Web Audio for sound. We used Claude, an AI assistant, to help write the code and text. [Add what your team did, like checking facts against NASA pages.]

Creativity

What we considered

projectDetails.name: Project Chaotic Cosmos
projectDetails.summary:
ASTROVITALS is a software-based astronaut health-monitoring prototype developed by our team, Chaotic Cosmos, for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. With the guidance and encouragement of Jiya CS, we worked together to turn our idea into an interactive PictoBlox project.

Our prototype focuses on six important health parameters: heart rate, blood oxygen, body temperature, blood pressure, hydration and sleep hours. Users enter an astronaut's name and manually provide the readings. The system checks them against programmed reference ranges and displays an overall status: NORMAL or CHECK REQUIRED. An astronaut character guides the user through the process.

We wanted to explore how technology could make health monitoring simpler and more organised for astronauts. Although our current version uses manually entered readings rather than live sensors, it represents our first step towards a more advanced system. This project has been a journey of teamwork, learning, problem-solving and turning curiosity into something we could actually build.
projectDetails.details:
What did we develop?

We developed ASTROVITALS, an interactive astronaut health-monitoring prototype using PictoBlox. Our aim was to create a simple system that brings important health readings together in one place.

How does it work?

The user starts the programme and enters the astronaut's name. An astronaut character welcomes the user and guides them to the dashboard. The user then enters six health readings: heart rate, blood oxygen, body temperature, blood pressure, hydration and sleep hours.

Using conditional statements, the programme compares the entered values with its programmed reference ranges. It then displays an overall system status: NORMAL or CHECK REQUIRED. A scan counter also keeps track of monitoring sessions.

Benefits and intended impact

We wanted to make health monitoring easier to understand and organise. By bringing six parameters into one interface, ASTROVITALS demonstrates how a simple software system can help identify readings that fall outside selected reference ranges.

We hope our idea encourages further exploration of technology for astronaut health and well-being.

Tools and technology

We used PictoBlox and its block-based programming environment. Our project uses variables, conditional statements, user inputs, broadcasts, sprites and backdrops to create an interactive experience.

The current version is a software prototype. It does not use physical sensors or collect live medical readings.

Creativity and team contribution

We brought together different ideas and worked towards creating one common project. From planning the interface and deciding what parameters to include to developing the programming logic and testing the prototype, each stage taught us something new.

We faced challenges along the way, especially while bringing our ideas together and making the different parts work as one system. Jiya CS supported us with guidance, suggestions and encouragement throughout this journey. Her support helped us approach the challenge with more confidence and keep improving our work.

Potential considerations

We understand that manually entered readings may not always be accurate. Health reference ranges can also differ depending on the individual and mission conditions. A real-world system would need reliable sensors, secure data handling, expert-reviewed medical standards and professional oversight.

Future scope

In the future, ASTROVITALS could be developed further by integrating actual sensors, collecting readings automatically, securely storing health information and displaying changes over time. These are ideas for future development, not features of our current prototype.

projectDetails.name: FieldShift AI: Farm-Level Digital Twins & Climate Adaptation Powered by NASA Earth Data
projectDetails.summary:
FieldShift AI is an open-source agricultural decision-support platform that transforms NASA Earth observations into actionable, farm-level climate adaptation decisions. While satellite datasets provide invaluable planetary insights, smallholder farmers often struggle to translate raw gridded data into daily field operations. 

FieldShift AI solves this by constructing a farm-level predictive Digital Twin for every registered field. It synthesizes NASA GPM IMERG precipitation, NASA POWER agroclimatology, NASA SMAP L4 rootzone soil moisture, Landsat/Sentinel vegetation indices, and NASADEM terrain hydrology with local soil lab tests. 

This intelligence powers:
1) 5-factor weighted crop suitability scoring across regional and global crops,
2) A dynamic multi-year crop rotation optimizer (Soil Health, Water Efficiency, and Balanced pathways),
3) A predictive "What-If" stress simulator,
4) A multilingual AI Farm Assistant featuring voice speech-to-text, audio read-aloud, and site-specific crop diagnostics, and
5) Transparent carbon credit readiness (Verra VM0042 / CDM AMS-III.AU) for smallholder aggregation.
projectDetails.details:
Project Functionality

FieldShift AI is designed as a modular, local-first agricultural intelligence platform that bridges spaceborne observations and ground-level farming realities:

1. Farm Digital Twin & Interactive Boundary Mapping

Farmers draw field boundaries using an interactive MapLibre GL interface with geodesic WGS84 area calculation. The system builds a live virtual replica synthesizing satellite environmental feeds, soil test calibrations, terrain drainage, and active crop cycles.

2. NASA Earth Observation Pipeline

- Precipitation Telemetry: NASA GPM IMERG v07 gridded daily and 30-day cumulative rainfall.

- Agroclimatology: NASA POWER temperature (T2M), relative humidity, and surface solar irradiance.

- Soil Moisture: NASA SMAP L4 Enhanced Global surface and rootzone moisture dynamics.

- Crop Vigor & Stress: Landsat 8/9 OLI-2 and Sentinel-2 MSI NDVI and NDMI vegetation indices.

- Hydrology & Drainage: NASADEM 30m elevation models calculate slope degrees, flow accumulation, and Topographic Wetness Index (TWI) waterlogging risks.

3. Soil Intelligence with Physical Lab Calibration

Integrates ISRIC SoilGrids 250m baseline soil profiles (pH, organic carbon, texture, bulk density) calibrated against physical Krishi Bhavan lab test intake. A strict scientific safeguard suppresses synthetic NPK dosage recommendations until certified physical soil tests are entered.

4. Multi-Year Crop Rotation Optimizer

An algorithmic rotation engine designs three alternative multi-year crop rotation trajectories:

- Strategy A (Soil Health Focus): Maximizes leguminous nitrogen fixation (+45 kg N/ha) and biological soil organic matter replenishment.

- Strategy B (Water Efficiency Focus): Minimizes irrigation requirements based on historical NASA GPM rainfall cycles.

- Strategy C (Balanced Strategy): Harmonizes market cash flow, labor feasibility, and pest-cycle interruption.

5. Multilingual AI Farm Assistant with Voice STT/TTS & Deep Diagnostics

A conversational farm advisor grounded in Kerala Agricultural University (KAU) and ICAR research:

- Voice Recognition (STT): Web Speech API supporting English, Malayalam (മലയാളം), Hindi (हिन्दी), Tamil (தமிழ்), and Spanish (Español).

- Text-to-Speech (TTS): Audio playback of agronomic advisories for smallholders.

- Multi-Session Topic Controls: Organize queries into separate, persistent topics.

- Site-Specific Crop Diagnostics: When asked about a specific crop (e.g. "I want to plant cashews"), it evaluates the crop's physiological tolerances against the farm's live telemetry (soil pH, humidity, rainfall during flowering, valley drainage), explains why it is or isn't ideal, highlights pest/disease risks (e.g. Blossom Blight, Tea Mosquito Bug), and recommends better-adapted alternatives.

6. What-If Stress Simulator

Allows farmers to stress-test their digital twin against simulated perturbations (-30% drought, +50% flood, monsoon delay, irrigation failure) to project yield impacts and risk scores before committing resources.

7. Carbon Credit Readiness & FPO Aggregation

Transparently models eligibility for Verra VCS (VM0042) and UNFCCC CDM (AMS-III.AU) carbon projects with conservative yield ranges and collective Farmer Producer Organization (FPO) pooling guidance.

Intended Impact

Over 500 million smallholder farmers globally produce a third of the world's food while bearing the brunt of extreme weather anomalies. Most satellite agriculture tools are designed for large industrial monocultures. FieldShift AI brings space agency data down to 1–3 acre family farms, enabling farmers to:

- Avoid crop failure by matching crop biology to microclimates.

- Transition away from monoculture through scientifically optimized crop rotations.

- Protect soil health and reduce excessive chemical fertilizer use.

- Access verified carbon credit aggregation without falling prey to greenwashing intermediaries.

Technology Stack

- Frontend: Next.js 16 (App Router, Turbopack), TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Lucide Icons, MapLibre GL JS, Recharts, Web Speech API (STT/TTS).

- Backend: Python 3.11, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy ORM, Pydantic v2, Uvicorn.

- Database: SQLite (default, zero setup) with PostgreSQL / PostGIS migration readiness.

- Geospatial & Math: PyProj, GeoJSON, NumPy.

- Deployment: Local-first architecture, mobile-first responsive UI with offline resilience.

Creativity and Innovation

FieldShift AI moves beyond static satellite viewers and generic LLM chatbots. Its primary innovations include:

1. Deterministic Grounding: The AI Assistant executes live database and telemetry tools rather than hallucinating agronomic advice.

2. Dialect & Voice Accessibility: Smallholders can speak and listen in their native regional languages (e.g., Malayalam, Hindi, Tamil).

3. The What-If Simulator: Bridges historical satellite data with future risk projection, allowing farmers to simulate climate shocks before they occur.

4. Transparent Carbon Economics: Refuses to over-promise carbon yields, explicitly deducting aggregator fees and highlighting smallholder pooling needs.

Factors Considered & Scientific Safeguards

- Spatial Resolution & Uncertainty: Clear labeling of satellite resolution (e.g., 0.1° GPM vs 30m Landsat vs 250m SoilGrids).

- Anti-Hallucination Guardrails: Synthetic fertilizer recommendations are locked until physical soil tests are recorded.

- Multi-Tenant Privacy: Strict authorization ensures farmers' field data remains private (HTTP 403 prevention).

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

On long missions, astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting these changes in themselves. Your challenge is to build a health monitoring software that gathers health indicators and enables astronauts to evaluate and act on the status of their health.

projectDetails.name: Project Cosmic Cadets
projectDetails.summary:
AstroQuest is an interactive web-based space exploration and engineering simulation developed by Team Cosmic Cadets. The project allows users to experience the challenges of establishing and maintaining a sustainable human outpost on the Moon or Mars.

The simulator challenges players to manage four essential resources: life support, radiation shielding, electrical power, and food supply. Players can perform engineering actions, respond to random mission emergencies, monitor system conditions, and make decisions to keep a crew of four astronauts safe throughout a 10-day mission. It also includes different difficulty levels, a mission log, scoring system, and a final mission report.

AstroQuest demonstrates the importance of resource management, engineering decisions, and problem-solving in space exploration. By turning complex space-habitat challenges into an interactive learning experience, the project helps users understand the difficulties of sustaining human life beyond Earth and encourages interest in space science and engineering.
projectDetails.details:
AstroQuest is an interactive, browser-based space exploration simulator designed to demonstrate the engineering challenges of establishing a sustainable human outpost on the Moon or Mars.

The project works as a 10-day mission simulation in which players manage four essential resources: life support, radiation shielding, electrical power and food supply. Players can perform engineering operations such as repairing life-support systems, reinforcing radiation shielding, restoring solar panels and maintaining greenhouse facilities. Random emergency events, including solar particle events, equipment faults and greenhouse problems, challenge players to make decisions and manage limited resources. The simulator also provides three difficulty levels, a mission log, a scoring system and a final mission report.

We developed the project using HTML for structure, CSS for visual design and JavaScript for interactive gameplay, resource calculations, random events and mission progression. It runs directly in a web browser without requiring installation.

The creative aspect of AstroQuest is its combination of space science, engineering concepts and game-based learning. Instead of simply reading about space habitats, users actively experience resource-management decisions and their consequences.

The intended impact is to improve awareness of the challenges of long-duration human space missions, encourage interest in STEM education and introduce users to the importance of sustainable systems for future exploration beyond Earth.

The project uses simplified educational simulations and does not represent actual NASA mission data.

projectDetails.name: Echoes in the Dust
projectDetails.summary: Echoes in the Dust is a poetic visual exploration of human space history, focusing on the spacecraft, landers, and rovers left behind on celestial bodies like the Moon and Mars. It highlights iconic artifacts—such as Apollo lunar module descent stages, bootprints in the lunar regolith, Viking frames, and the Spirit and Opportunity rovers resting in Martian dust. Preserved in windless vacuums and eternal sunlight, these inactive machines are framed not as abandoned debris or failures, but as silent sentinels and permanent monuments of human ambition. Ultimately, the project portrays these historic relics as enduring anchors of our past that quietly await the return of human footsteps.
projectDetails.details: Echoes in the Dust is a narrative multimedia project that chronicles the history of human space exploration by focusing on the physical artifacts, lunar modules, and robotic rovers left behind on celestial bodies like the Moon and Mars. Functionally, it guides viewers across interplanetary landscapes—highlighting Apollo descent stages, Viking frames, and the Spirit and Opportunity rovers—showcasing how these inactive spacecraft remain preserved in pristine, windless, and vacuum environments. The project offers significant benefits by reframing what is often viewed as space debris into enduring cultural and scientific monuments, making space history emotionally resonant and inspiring curiosity for future missions. Its intended impact is to evoke awe and bridge past milestones with future possibilities, serving as permanent anchors that await the return of human footsteps. To develop this project, a team typically utilizes 3D visualization software, video and audio editing suites (like VN), and multimedia scripting frameworks. The project achieves its creativity through poetic narration that personifies silent explorers, artfully contrasting the eternal stillness of extraterrestrial environments with the warm ambition of human engineering. In doing so, the creators carefully considered scientific accuracy regarding planetary atmospheres, balanced an emotional tone of reverence and hope, and maintained rhythmic pacing between the visuals and voiceover.

projectDetails.name: Cosmico
projectDetails.summary:
Cosmico is an interactive 3D space-tracking web app 

It helps spot faint, distant objects like Planet X by stripping away the observer's own motion through space—accounting for six layers of movement from Earth’s rotation all the way up to the Cosmic Microwave Background. Users can inspect multi-epoch infrared sky data using blink-comparator and image-subtraction tools, filter out stellar noise with a Lomb-Scargle periodogram, and jump straight to five real astronomical benchmark targets like Barnard’s Star and WISE 0855.
projectDetails.details: Cosmico is a browser-based 3D space-tracking tool built for the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge. Spotting faint objects in the outer solar system is hard because the observer is constantly moving through space and background stars flicker. Cosmico strips that noise away in three steps: 6-Layer Motion Subtraction: Models and removes observer movement across six reference frames—from Earth’s rotation and orbit up to Milky Way rotation and the Cosmic Microwave Background—using NASA ephemeris data and IAU coordinate transforms. Multi-Epoch Sky Viewer: Lets users compare sky scans over time using blink-comparator and image-subtraction tools to spot tiny shifts in position. Signal Filtering: Uses a Lomb-Scargle periodogram to separate real moving objects from flickering variable stars, tested against five benchmark targets (WISE 0855, Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis). Benefits & Intended Impact Cleaner Survey Data: Cuts down false positives when searching wide-field infrared surveys for distant objects like Planet X. Zero Setup: Runs completely in the browser with direct URL coordinate sharing, making quick visual checks accessible to students, citizen scientists, and researchers without heavy local software. Tools & Tech Stack Code & Hosting: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6+), hosted on GitHub Pages. 3D & Math: Three.js / WebGL for 3D visualization, custom matrix math for coordinate transforms, and a JavaScript Lomb-Scargle periodogram. Data: NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris data and SIMBAD/VizieR astrometric catalog targets.

projectDetails.name: Beyond The Mission - The Story of Legacy
projectDetails.summary:
For my project I created an interactive story about the NASA equipment that remains on the Moon and Mars including the old Apollo landers, silent rovers and retired probes.
When a mission is completed any remaining hardware is often seen as space junk or forgotten about in technical documents. By going through old mission logs, maps and images of the surface I was able to create a story to show where they are now and what they have been through.
While it may be easy to forget these rovers and landers are the very first items humans have placed on other worlds. As there are new missions going back to the Moon and Mars it is important to keep their stories alive to preserve our space history. This shows how space exploration is an amazing human adventure.

projectDetails.name: Project CosmicPulse X
projectDetails.summary:
We developed a full-stack Space Mission Design Game that enables individuals or teams of four to design, manage, and simulate complete space missions. Featuring a live 3D spacecraft builder, real-time resource dashboards, a global leaderboard, and an interactive arcade-style flight phase, our solution transforms abstract aerospace concepts into an engaging, hands-on experience.

Our project directly addresses the challenge by forcing players to navigate integrated engineering trade-offs. Powered by a custom physics evaluation engine, participants must balance strict constraints—including budget, mass, power generation, and data rates—across various instruments, power systems, and orbital configurations. Players instantly see the consequences of their decisions; for example, upgrading a scientific payload increases potential discoveries but immediately drains power and adds critical spacecraft mass.

This project is important because it bridges the gap between theoretical classroom learning and practical systems engineering. By providing immediate, visual feedback on how individual choices shape overall mission success, our game empowers the next generation of engineers to collaboratively solve complex problems and master the delicate balance required for real-world space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Our Mission

Our Space Mission Design Game is an educational simulator where players design a spacecraft, balance critical resources (power, mass, budget, communications, and time), and pilot their creation in an arcade-style flight mission. As players select components, a 3D model of the spacecraft builds dynamically alongside a live resource dashboard. The game supports both solo play and team mode (with up to 4 roles). Once a mission concludes, players receive a post-mission analysis detailing why their design succeeded or failed, earn XP, unlock badges, and compete on a global leaderboard. To ensure fairness, a backend anti-cheat system recalculates the maximum possible score for each design code and automatically rejects mathematically impossible submissions.

Benefits and intended impact

The project was built to solve a core educational problem: the complex trade-offs of mission design are incredibly difficult to learn from textbooks alone. The primary benefit of our game is that it provides a hands-on environment where abstract constraints become immediate and visible. The intended impact is to empower students and space enthusiasts to intuitively understand aerospace engineering, enabling them to see a real-time 3D model of their work, make integrated decisions, and clearly grasp the specific engineering trade-offs required for a mission to succeed.

Tools, coding languages, hardware, or software used

We developed a decoupled, full-stack web application using the following technologies:

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, and vanilla JavaScript for the UI; Three.js for the interactive 3D spacecraft builder; and the HTML Canvas API for the arcade flight and mini-games.
  • Backend API: Python with FastAPI and SQLite to manage the REST API, player database, XP progression, and global leaderboard.
  • Physics Evaluator: A zero-dependency Java 17+ microservice that serves as an authoritative physics engine and anti-cheat validator.
  • Deployment & Testing: Docker and Docker Compose for streamlined containerization, and pytest for backend testing.
    README.md

How the project is creative

Our project creatively bridges the gap between rigorous systems engineering and highly engaging gameplay. Instead of relying purely on spreadsheets or static menus, we integrated a live 3D visualizer, interactive mini-games, and an arcade flight phase to make the consequences of engineering decisions visceral. Furthermore, our architectural approach is highly creative: we decoupled the game logic into a frontend UI while building a standalone Java evaluator service strictly to calculate the mathematical limits of a design, ensuring a tamper-proof global leaderboard.

Factors the team considered

  • Educational Accessibility: We deliberately simplified the physics model for educational purposes to ensure the concepts remain approachable for students.
  • Fairness and Security: We prioritized competitive integrity by implementing a robust anti-cheat system that rejects invalid scores and validates player names to prevent injection attacks.
  • Diverse Play Styles: We considered different skill levels by adding a non-ranked Sandbox mode for constraint-free experimentation, alongside a Team mode to foster collaboration.
  • Future Scalability: We acknowledged current limitations (such as the lack of authenticated user accounts) and laid the architectural groundwork for future expansions, including network-based cooperative multiplayer and expanded mission scenarios

projectDetails.name: Project CosmicSix - EarthTrend-Lite Earth-System-Trend-Detective
projectDetails.summary:
Team CosmicSix developed EarthTrend Lite, an interactive web dashboard engineered for environmental and climate trend analytics.

Addressing the challenge of making complex Earth system data accessible and actionable, the application translates multi-year temperature and rainfall metrics into intuitive visual analytics. It features automated trend detection and anomaly spotting algorithms that immediately identify extreme weather shifts and long-term climate patterns across geographic regions. To empower open community research, the platform also enables users to upload and evaluate their own environmental datasets through client-side CSV processing—requiring zero backend setup, servers, or API keys.

This project is important because accelerating climate resilience requires democratizing data literacy. By turning raw environmental observations into clear, localized trends, EarthTrend Lite equips students, researchers, and citizens with the tools to detect critical planetary changes and make informed decisions.
projectDetails.details:
### What Does It Do & How Does It Work?

EarthTrend Lite is an interactive environmental analytics web dashboard designed to investigate Earth system trends. The platform processes multi-year climate observations (temperature and rainfall) across different global regions. When a user selects a region and year, the application's statistical engine dynamically evaluates monthly records, aggregates annual averages, and runs automated anomaly detection algorithms to flag abnormal climate deviations and shifts. In addition, users can upload their own environmental CSV datasets, which the application validates and visualizes entirely within the client's browser.

### What Benefits Does It Have?

- **Zero Configuration & Privacy:** Operates 100% in the browser with no backend servers, database setup, or API keys required.

- **Accessibility:** Converts raw, intimidating numerical climate tables into intuitive charts and summary metrics that anyone can interpret.

- **Custom Dataset Compatibility:** Empowers local community researchers and students to test and visualize their own local weather and climate records instantly.

### Intended Impact

Our goal is to democratize climate data literacy. By lowering the barrier between complex planetary observations and everyday citizens, EarthTrend Lite enables schools, grassroots climate researchers, and community planners to detect localized trends, assess climate variability, and advocate for informed environmental policies.

### Tools, Languages, Hardware & Software Used

- **Frontend Framework:** React 18

- **Build Tool:** Vite

- **Languages:** JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, CSS3

- **Development Environment:** Visual Studio Code / Node.js

- **Version Control & Hosting:** Git & GitHub

### Creativity & Innovation

Rather than relying on resource-intensive cloud backends or complex Python notebooks that require programming expertise, we packaged sophisticated trend and anomaly detection into a lightweight, responsive, single-page application. The dark scientific interface mimics research-grade observatories while remaining as easy to use as a consumer web app.

### Factors Our Team Considered

- **Performance & Bandwidth:** Ensuring the application remains fast and lightweight for users in regions with limited internet connectivity.

- **Data Validation & Robustness:** Handling inconsistent CSV formats gracefully with real-time error handling.

- **Data Privacy:** Ensuring user-uploaded climate data never leaves the user’s local machine.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: AstroHealth Command – An Intelligent Astronaut Health & Life-Support Monitoring System
projectDetails.summary:
AstroHealth Command – An Intelligent Astronaut Health & Life-Support Monitoring System

AstroHealth Command, developed by Team Crew.Life, is a proposed real-time health and life-support monitoring software designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. The system brings important health indicators, including heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen level (SpO₂), body temperature, blood sugar, sleep duration, and mood, into a single dashboard. It also monitors relevant spacecraft environmental and suit conditions, such as carbon dioxide levels, pressure, and radiation.

The software helps astronauts track their health, identify unusual changes, view trends, and receive clear alerts and guidance when readings require attention. It addresses the challenge by making health self-assessment easier and supporting early awareness of potential medical risks in isolated space environments.

AstroHealth Command is important because timely health monitoring can help astronauts make informed decisions, seek medical support when needed, and maintain their well-being during missions far from Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – AstroHealth Command

Team: Crew.Life

AstroHealth Command is a proposed astronaut health and life-support monitoring system designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. It aims to bring important health indicators and environmental information into one easy-to-understand dashboard.

What does it do and how does it work?

The proposed system monitors health indicators such as heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen level (SpO₂), body temperature, blood sugar, sleep duration and mood. It also considers environmental and life-support conditions such as carbon dioxide levels, pressure and radiation. The system is designed to display readings, track changes over time, identify unusual patterns and provide alerts or guidance when attention may be required.

What are its benefits?

It can help astronauts understand their health status, recognise changes earlier, maintain regular health check-ins and communicate concerns to medical support teams.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to support astronaut well-being and safer long-duration missions, especially when immediate medical assistance from Earth may not be available.

What makes the project creative?

The project combines personal health monitoring, spacecraft environmental awareness and understandable guidance in one proposed platform. It focuses on making complex health information easier for astronauts to review independently.

What factors did the team consider?

We considered the five major hazards of human spaceflight: radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, gravity fields and hostile closed environments. We also considered accessibility, simple visualisation, timely alerts, data reliability and the need for expert-validated medical guidance.

Tools and technologies

The current project showcase uses HTML and CSS, with a PowerPoint presentation and PDF demonstration. We have not yet developed a working monitoring application, live sensor integration or hardware prototype. No real astronaut health data is used; any sample readings are simulated.

projectDetails.name: Mannova
projectDetails.summary:
Mannova is an online software application designed to help farmers in Kerala choose rotations that will maintain healthy soils and cope with changes in weather. The farmer selects their farm from the interactive map (or one of seven Kerala agriculture zones), provides soil, irrigation and current crop information, and indicates priority – water savings, soil health, revenues or reduced climate risks.

Mannova analyzes 25 years of NASA POWER climate data from the selected location and assesses approximately 2,000 three-season rotations for droughts, water logging during rainy periods, heat stress and high evaporative demand. The farmer's current rotation is compared with three top replacements with rationales for each of them provided along with NASA climate data, benefits, data gaps, and local verifications needed. NASA GIBS satellite imagery layers (MODIS vegetation indices, SMAP soil moisture, GPM rainfall, land surface temperature) are provided for the area surrounding the farm.

In Kerala, precipitation is unpredictable, and many farms remain uncultivated or stuck with rice after rice. Mannova translates NASA climate data into practical solutions for the farmers.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

Mannova is a decision-support web app that helps Kerala farmers explore crop rotations that improve soil health and stand up to a changing climate. A farmer picks their field on a map (or one of 7 Kerala farming zones: Kuttanad, Palakkad, Onattukara, Kole lands, midland laterite, Wayanad and the northern coast), describes soil, drainage, salinity, irrigation and what they grow now, and sets their priorities: saving water, soil health, income or avoiding climate risk.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Mannova fetches 25 years (2001–2025) of NASA POWER data for the exact point: temperature, bias-corrected rainfall, humidity and root-zone soil wetness.

2. It builds a climate profile: monthly averages, 1-in-5 dry years, 1-in-10 wet years, trends, and the last decade compared with the first. It estimates evapotranspiration (FAO-56 Hargreaves) to find water-deficit months.

3. A scoring engine tests about 2,000 three-season rotations of 14 Kerala crops for water saving, soil health (legumes, green manure, cover and deep-rooting crops, crop-family diversity, bare months), income and climate safety (drought, waterlogging, heat, salinity), weighted by the farmer's priorities.

4. It compares the current rotation with the 3 best alternatives. Each option shows a 12-month field calendar (bare months and vulnerable seasons), why it was suggested, the NASA evidence, benefits, information gaps, what to check locally, and a score range for drier/hotter and wetter years.

5. NASA GIBS satellite layers show vegetation health (MODIS NDVI), soil moisture (SMAP), rainfall (GPM IMERG), land surface heat and true colour around the field. What-if sliders test less rain or more warming.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

For a Kuttanad paddy field, NASA data shows 6.5% less rain in the last decade and +0.57 °C in maximum temperatures. Replacing Rice–Rice–Fallow with Rice–Sunhemp–Sesame raises the soil health score from 24 to 73 and cuts irrigation by about 490 mm a year, while adding nitrogen-fixing green manure and breaking pest cycles. Mannova is designed to support, not replace, farmers and Krishi Bhavan officers: every result is explained and its limits are stated.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

It is built for Kerala: crop names in Malayalam, region presets for distinct farming zones, salinity and flooding risks specific to Kuttanad. It is transparent: rule-based scores with plain-language reasons, instead of a black box. It is honest about uncertainty, showing score ranges and information gaps.

TOOLS

Next.js, React, TypeScript, Recharts, Leaflet with OpenStreetMap, deployed on Vercel. NASA POWER API and NASA GIBS WMS.

Source code: https://github.com/BazilMathew/Mannova

Team: Bazil Mathew P Sajan, Aron Koshy, Blesji K Abraham, Ashwel Rinu Oommen

projectDetails.name: MoonSafe – Lunar Landing Site Safety Analysis
projectDetails.summary:
MoonSafe is a web-based lunar landing site suitability analysis platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The project aims to support early-stage assessment of potential landing regions near the Moon's south pole using NASA-derived terrain data.

MoonSafe compares two candidate regions, Shackleton Rim and Malapert Massif, using elevation and slope measurements obtained from lunar terrain datasets. The platform features an interactive dashboard, lunar surface imagery, terrain comparison, landing site safety scoring, and a mission recommendation system.

The application is developed using React, JavaScript, Python, Flask, and Rasterio. Its local backend processes lunar GeoTIFF datasets, while the deployed version uses precomputed terrain statistics to provide accessible online analysis.

MoonSafe makes complex lunar terrain information easier to visualize and compare. It demonstrates how space science data and web technologies can support exploratory mission planning. Future improvements could include solar illumination analysis, communication visibility, and more advanced hazard detection.

MoonSafe is an educational prototype, and its safety scores are not intended for operational landing decisions.
projectDetails.details:
MoonSafe – Lunar Landing Site Safety Analysis

Project Overview

MoonSafe is a web-based lunar landing site suitability analysis platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It helps users compare potential landing regions near the Moon's south pole using NASA-derived terrain data.

How MoonSafe Works

MoonSafe compares two candidate regions: Shackleton Rim and Malapert Massif.

The system uses lunar terrain datasets to examine elevation and slope characteristics. Python and Rasterio are used to process GeoTIFF terrain files and calculate statistics.

The application presents the results through an interactive dashboard with the following features:

  1. Terrain Analysis: Displays elevation and slope measurements for both regions.
  2. Lunar Map: Displays lunar imagery and allows users to select candidate landing regions.
  3. Safety Analysis: Calculates comparative terrain suitability scores.
  4. Mission Recommendation: Identifies a preferred candidate based on the implemented scoring method.
  5. Data Visualization: Makes complex terrain measurements easier to understand.

Technologies Used

  • Frontend: React, JavaScript, Vite, HTML and CSS
  • Backend: Python and Flask
  • Geospatial Processing: Rasterio and NumPy
  • Datasets: NASA-derived lunar elevation and slope GeoTIFF files
  • Deployment: Vercel and Render
  • Version Control: Git and GitHub

Creativity and Innovation

MoonSafe combines scientific terrain measurements with an accessible web interface. Instead of requiring users to examine large geospatial datasets manually, it presents comparative terrain statistics, safety scores, and recommendations in one dashboard.

The online version uses precomputed terrain statistics, enabling users to explore the results without downloading large raster files.

Benefits and Intended Impact

MoonSafe helps students, researchers, and space enthusiasts explore how lunar terrain affects potential landing site selection.

The project demonstrates how publicly available space science data can be transformed into an interactive educational decision-support tool.

Factors Considered

The current prototype considers elevation, slope, and terrain-based suitability. It does not yet include all factors required for real mission planning, such as solar illumination, Earth communication visibility, spacecraft constraints, and detailed landing hazards.

Future Scope

Future improvements include illumination analysis, communication visibility assessment, additional candidate landing regions, and more advanced hazard detection.

Project Links

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/alphonsasooter/MoonSafe

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”
