projectDetails.name: Project Earthlings 2.0
projectDetails.summary:
**Project Summary – Be An Earth System Trend Detective!**

Our project focuses on identifying and understanding significant trends and changes in Earth's interconnected systems using scientific data and observations. We developed a data-driven approach to explore patterns in environmental parameters such as temperature, rainfall, atmospheric conditions, land changes, and other climate-related indicators. By analysing Earth observation data from NASA and other reliable sources, the project aims to identify long-term trends, understand environmental changes, and highlight possible relationships between different Earth systems. It addresses the challenge by transforming complex scientific datasets into meaningful insights that help people better understand our changing planet. This project is important because recognizing environmental trends at an early stage supports climate awareness, informed decision-making, disaster preparedness, and sustainable development. Ultimately, it demonstrates how Earth observation data can help us become better informed about our planet's past, present, and future.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

Project Title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Our project aims to identify, analyse and understand long-term changes in Earth's systems using NASA satellite observations and Earth science datasets. It helps users investigate environmental trends such as temperature changes, rainfall patterns, soil moisture variations, vegetation changes and other climate-related indicators.

The system works by collecting Earth observation data from NASA sources, selecting a particular environmental variable and geographical region, and analysing the data over a specific period. It uses graphs, maps and statistical techniques to identify increasing or decreasing trends and present the findings in an easy-to-understand format.

2. What are the benefits of the project?

  • Helps people understand environmental and climate change.
  • Identifies long-term trends in important Earth system variables.
  • Makes complex NASA datasets easier to understand.
  • Supports environmental awareness and scientific learning.
  • Provides useful information for researchers, students and decision-makers.
  • Encourages data-driven environmental monitoring.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The main objective is to improve awareness of changes happening across Earth's systems and encourage people to use scientific data to understand environmental challenges. The project aims to make NASA Earth observation data more accessible and meaningful to students, communities and researchers.

In the long term, it can support climate awareness, environmental monitoring, sustainable planning and informed decision-making.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware or software were used?

The proposed project uses or can be developed using the following technologies:

  • Data sources: NASA Earthdata, NASA GES DISC and satellite observation datasets.
  • Data analysis: Python.
  • Libraries: Pandas, NumPy, Matplotlib and SciPy.
  • Data visualisation: Graphs, charts and geographical maps.
  • Statistical methods: Linear regression and Mann-Kendall trend analysis.
  • Development environment: Jupyter Notebook or Google Colab.
  • Hardware: A standard computer or laptop with internet access.

5. How is the project creative?

The creative aspect of our project is transforming large and complex Earth observation datasets into simple visual stories. Instead of presenting only raw scientific measurements, the project allows users to explore environmental changes through graphs, maps and trend summaries.

It combines Earth science, data analysis and visualisation to make users act like Earth System Trend Detectives, discovering patterns and understanding the changes happening around our planet.

6. What factors did our team consider?

Our team considered the following factors while developing the project:

  • Accuracy and reliability of NASA Earth observation data.
  • Selection of appropriate environmental variables.
  • Geographical coverage and time periods.
  • Seasonal variations and long-term environmental changes.
  • Missing data, uncertainty and statistical significance.

projectDetails.name: Project Èclipse
projectDetails.summary:
Artemis IV: Gateway to the Moon is a browser-based, interactive aerospace simulation developed by Team Éclipse for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Built with HTML5 Canvas 2D, Three.js WebGL, and the Web Audio API, it lets anyone experience the pivotal fourth mission of NASA’s Artemis program with zero installation required.

Players command every critical flight phase: launching the super-heavy SLS Block 1B rocket through Max-Q and stage separation, plotting a 3D gravitational slingshot to deliver the international I-Hab module to the Lunar Gateway in Near-Rectilinear Halo Orbit, piloting the Human Landing System down to Shackleton Crater at the lunar South Pole, and threading Earth’s narrow 2.0° atmospheric corridor for a 25,000 mph skip-entry return. To mirror real mission stakes, Orion’s propellant reserve carries over across phases, forcing players to balance orbital maneuvers against fuel needed to come home.

By pairing hands-on Newtonian physics with live telemetry, an offline CAPCOM AI flight controller, and an unlockable engineering archive, the project transforms complex orbital mechanics and deep-space exploration into an intuitive, accessible educational tool that inspires the next generation of explorers.
projectDetails.details:
Artemis IV: Gateway to the Moon is an interactive, browser-based educational game designed by Team Éclipse to introduce kids and young learners to the real science behind NASA’s return to the Moon. Built with HTML5 Canvas 2D, Three.js WebGL, and the Web Audio API, it runs instantly in any web browser with zero downloads or setup.

Instead of reading dense textbooks, kids step into the commander's seat across four hands-on space missions: launching the mega-rocket SLS Block 1B, slinging past Earth in 3D to dock with the Lunar Gateway, landing on the Moon’s South Pole in low gravity, and piloting Orion safely home through a fiery skip-reentry. Along the way, an interactive CAPCOM AI buddy answers space questions, live "Real NASA Science" popups explain physics as it happens, and beating the mission unlocks an illustrated comic finale and visual NASA space archive.

"Until We Meet Again, Moon" is a creative storytelling project inspired by NASA's three Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicles used during the Apollo 15, 16 and 17 missions.

projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Until We Meet Again, Moon

Until We Meet Again, Moon is a historical-fiction storytelling project inspired by NASA's Apollo 15, 16 and 17 Lunar Roving Vehicles.

The project presents the history of the three lunar rovers through an imaginative conversation. Each rover shares its mission, experiences, achievements and technical challenges, helping readers understand lunar exploration through storytelling.

The project aims to make space history more interesting and accessible, encourage curiosity about space exploration, and help readers appreciate the technology behind the Apollo missions.

We developed the project through historical research using NASA sources and creative writing. We used Google Docs for writing and organizing the story and Canva for designing and presenting the project. No programming languages or physical hardware were required.

The creative aspect is giving personalities and voices to real historical machines while keeping their experiences and achievements based on historical facts.

During development, we considered historical accuracy, creativity, storytelling structure, readability and reader engagement.

# Guía Lunar – Lunar Landing Site Exploration

Guía Lunar is a web-based lunar exploration and decision-support platform designed to help users investigate potential landing locations near the Moon’s south pole. As future lunar missions aim to explore this region, understanding terrain conditions, sunlight availability, and Earth visibility becomes increasingly important for mission planning.

The platform brings relevant lunar information together in an interactive, easy-to-understand dashboard. It focuses on three candidate locations: Shackleton Rim, De Gerlache Rim 2, and Malapert Massif. Using NASA’s Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) terrain datasets, the project explores elevation and surface slope information to help users understand the physical characteristics of selected regions.

Guía Lunar also incorporates NASA/JPL Horizons API integration for investigating the changing positions and visibility of the Sun and Earth over time. This information is intended to support the exploration of illumination opportunities and communication-related conditions at different locations.

Built using React and Vite, the platform aims to make scientific data more accessible through a clear and user-friendly interface. It is a prototype that demonstrates how publicly available space data can be combined to support preliminary site comparison and exploration.

projectDetails.name: LastPing
projectDetails.summary:
What happens when a spacecraft sends its final signal? Does its story end there?

LastPing was built around one powerful idea: a mission may end, but its legacy should never be forgotten.

LastPing is an immersive, interactive space exploration platform that transforms NASA's historic spacecraft, rovers, and instruments into unforgettable stories for the next generation of explorers.
We Combined the potential of Interactive Web Development with Creative 3D blender Visuals , Engaging Story Telling and Animation

Instead of simply reading about space missions, students can step into their stories through an interactive website featuring 3D models, cinematic walkthrough animations, and engaging mission narratives. Our Blender-created visual storytelling brings distant worlds and humanity's technological achievements closer than ever.

From the silent remains of lunar missions to the rovers that explored Mars and the probes journeying into deep space, LastPing connects each piece of hardware to the scientific discoveries it made possible.

By blending science, storytelling, and immersive technology, we address NASA's challenge of making space exploration accessible, exciting, and meaningful for school-age enthusiasts.

Because the final signal of a spacecraft shouldn't be the final chapter of its story.
projectDetails.details:
LastPing started with a simple thought: what happens to the spacecraft and rovers after their missions end? We often hear about their launches and discoveries, but rarely about what happens to them afterward. Some remain on the Moon or Mars, while others continue their journeys through deep space. Each of these machines has a fascinating story, and we wanted to find a creative way to share those stories with younger generations.

We developed LastPing as an interactive website that allows users to explore NASA's space hardware through 3D models, animations, and storytelling. Instead of presenting information through long paragraphs or static images, we wanted students to feel like they were actually exploring these distant worlds. Users can navigate through the experience, discover different spacecraft and rovers, and learn about their missions, scientific contributions, and current status.

One of the areas we focused on was creating the 3D experience. Each model was created separately rather than using the same generic designs for different spacecraft. We paid attention to the unique appearance and characteristics of the equipment so that students could visually recognize and understand what made each mission different. We also developed walkthrough animations and a cinematic video using Blender to make the experience more engaging and give users a better sense of the environments these machines explored.

Another important part of our work was researching the information behind every mission. We didn't want to create something that looked impressive but provided inaccurate scientific information. Each piece of mission-related information was individually researched and validated using NASA resources and other reliable scientific references. We focused on details such as when missions were launched, why they were sent, what they discovered, and whether the equipment is still operational. This helped us balance creative storytelling with educational accuracy.

For development, we used web technologies such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to create the interactive experience, along with Blender for 3D modelling and animations. We brought these elements together into a browser-based platform that users can explore without needing expensive hardware or specialized software.

What makes LastPing different from a typical space information website is the way we present the content. We wanted to give each spacecraft its own identity and story rather than treating it as just another object in a database. A rover that stopped working years ago might seem like an abandoned machine, but when students understand the challenges it faced and the discoveries it made, they begin to see how important its journey really was.

While developing the project, we considered several factors, especially the age of our intended audience. School students may not always be interested in reading technical mission reports, so we focused on visual learning, simple explanations, smooth interactions, and storytelling that creates curiosity. At the same time, we wanted to preserve the scientific value of the information rather than oversimplifying it.

Our main goal is to make NASA's history of space exploration more accessible and interesting to young learners. We hope LastPing can be used not only by individual space enthusiasts but also by teachers and students as an additional way to learn about space missions.

We believe that learning becomes much more memorable when people can connect with what they are exploring. Through LastPing, we want students to understand that even spacecraft that no longer function have contributed something valuable to science.

For us, LastPing is about more than showing where NASA's equipment ended up. It's about helping students understand why those machines were sent there in the first place, what humanity learned from them, and how those discoveries continue to influence space exploration today.

The machines may have stopped communicating, but their stories are still worth telling.

projectDetails.name: Field Shift Compass: Climate Twins for Adapting Farms
projectDetails.summary: Field Shift Compass is a decision-support web app that helps farmers adapt to a shifting climate. Using 26 years (2000-2025) of NASA POWER data for Nagpur district, Vidarbha, it answers three questions: What changed here? Who already farms my future? What should I do this season? The Shift Detector measures trends in monsoon onset, dry spells, heat days and rainfall. The Climate Twin matches the farm's projected 2040 climate to the current climate of one of 36 Indian districts (for Nagpur, Raipur is the closest match), so farmers can learn from places already living that climate. The Shift Advisor then gives ranked, rule-based advice such as sowing-date and variety changes, each with its evidence, data source and a confidence score. Advice is delivered through a chat with voice playback and a printable Season Plan, and an agronomist console adds human review. The project turns NASA climate data into farm-level adaptation decisions. The pipeline is region-agnostic and ready for SMAP, MODIS/HLS and NISAR layers in a pilot.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

Field Shift Compass turns NASA climate data into farm-level adaptation advice for Nagpur district (Vidarbha, kharif paddy). It has three layers: a Shift Detector (what changed), a Climate Twin Matcher (who already farms my future) and a Shift Advisor (what to do this season). Advice is delivered via a chat with voice playback, a printable Season Plan for farmers without smartphones, and an Agronomist Console where experts approve or correct advice.

HOW IT WORKS

- NASA POWER daily data (2000-2025) gives trends in monsoon onset, sowing-window start, dry spells, heat days, monsoon rainfall and rain days, each with a trend line, R2 and strength label.

- The Climate Twin builds the farm's projected 2040 climate from observed climatology plus approximate scenario deltas (+1.1 C, annual rain x1.08, monsoon rain x1.05, onset +6 days; SSP2-4.5) informed by NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 projections, then nearest-neighbour matches it against 36 districts' current NASA POWER climatology. For Nagpur the closest match is Raipur (87% relative similarity), then Rewa and Lucknow.

- The Shift Advisor uses transparent, deterministic rules. Each card shows evidence, its dataset, and a confidence score (trend strength x record length). No black-box model makes decisions.

FINDINGS (Nagpur, 2000-2025)

Monsoon onset is about 2.3 days per decade later; monsoon rainfall is +143 mm per decade (R2 = 0.29); rain days +8.2 per decade; the longest dry spell is flat and heat days are declining. Weak trends are shown as weak.

VALIDITY

Onset follows a simplified IMD hydrologic definition. A back-test replays the sowing rule over 26 seasons and flags 8 risky years; this is a consistency check, and independent comparison against rainfall-deficit or yield records is the next step.

CREATIVITY AND IMPACT

The Climate Twin ("learn from a place already living your future"), evidence-first advice built for the farmer trust gap, and the agronomist feedback loop. Relevant to climate-resilient agriculture and food security; the pipeline is region-agnostic.

TOOLS

Python, FastAPI, pandas, NumPy, SciPy, vanilla JavaScript with SVG charts, Leaflet, hosted on Render. Code: https://github.com/zeus10-11/field-shift-compass

LIMITATIONS

POWER data is district-level point data, not field-level. Future deltas are approximate ensemble-style values; a pilot would process actual NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 files per grid cell and add SMAP, MODIS/HLS, GPM IMERG and NISAR layers.

SI DISCLOSURE

SI tools were used for code generation/refactoring, UI code, documentation drafts and the pitch deck. SI was not used to fabricate data: every number is computed from cached NASA POWER data by deterministic modules. No SI-generated images, audio or NASA branding appear.

The platform features Planet Explorer, Space Science Lab, Lunar Outpost Construction, and Emergency Missions. It introduces two learning modes—Explorer and Commander—with adaptive difficulty to support different learning levels. Players learn about planets, space science, astronaut life, and space exploration while managing essential resources such as life support, power, and radiation protection.

ASTROQUEST addresses the challenge of making space education more interactive and practical rather than relying only on traditional learning methods. It is important because it encourages curiosity, scientific thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and interest in STEM subjects while inspiring the next generation of space explorers.
projectDetails.details: ASTROQUEST -THE SPACE ACADEMY ASTROQUEST – The Space Academy is an interactive space science learning platform designed to make learning about space exciting, educational, and accessible for children aged 12 and above, as well as anyone interested in space exploration. How It Works: ASTROQUEST transforms space education into an engaging game-based learning experience. It offers two learning experiences: Explorer Mode and Commander Mode. In Explorer Mode, users can explore planets, discover interesting space facts, and learn about the solar system through Planet Explorer and Space Science Lab. In Commander Mode, users take on astronaut-inspired challenges, construct a lunar outpost, manage resources, and complete emergency missions. Users must make decisions and solve problems while maintaining these essential resources. An adaptive difficulty system provides challenges suitable for different learning levels. projectDetails.name: Finding Mars on Earth
projectDetails.summary:
Finding Mars on Earth compares four Earth locations to Mars to show which best match its conditions. Mars is cold, extremely dry, covered in volcanic rock and salty dust, and has ice underground. No place on Earth matches all of this, so we scored four well-known analog sites on five Mars traits: cold, dryness, geology, ground ice, and special terrain features.
The Antarctic Dry Valleys ranked first (21/25) for extreme cold, dryness, and ground ice. Haughton Crater in the Canadian Arctic followed closely (20/25), offering a real impact crater in a polar desert. Iceland (16/25) and the Atacama Desert (15/25) scored lower overall but each excels at one job: Iceland for basalt rock and lava-tube caves, and the Atacama for ultra-dry, salty, high-UV soil.
The key finding is that no single site is a perfect Mars, so mission teams should match sites to what they are testing. The report includes a ranking chart, a satellite map of the four sites, and a guide to which site suits which test. Scores are based on published descriptions rather than raw satellite data, and future work would compute them from NASA datasets.
projectDetails.details:
What it does: Finding Mars on Earth is a comparison report that identifies which places on Earth are the best practice grounds for Mars missions. Mars is cold, extremely dry, covered in volcanic rock and salty dust, and has ice underground. No Earth site matches all of that, so we scored four well-known analog sites on five Mars traits: cold, dryness, geology, ground ice, and special terrain features. Each trait is scored 1 to 5 and the totals (out of 25) are ranked.
Results: The Antarctic Dry Valleys ranked first (21/25), followed by Haughton Crater in the Canadian Arctic (20/25), Iceland (16/25), and the Atacama Desert (15/25). Each site is also the best match for one specific job: ice drilling and cold-weather gear (Dry Valleys), crater exploration (Haughton), lava-tube and volcanic testing (Iceland), and life-detection instruments in dry, salty soil (Atacama).
Benefits and impact: The report gives mission planners and students a simple, transparent way to see why each site is a good or poor Mars analog, and which site suits which test. The takeaway is that no single site is a perfect Mars, so sites should be matched to what is being tested.
Tools: We used published scientific descriptions of each site and NASA satellite imagery for the map. An AI assistant (Claude) helped organize and draft the report, and Google Drive was used for sharing.
Creativity and factors considered: We chose four sites from different environment types (polar desert, impact crater, volcanic terrain, and hot desert) and built a clear scoring method anyone can check and adjust. We also considered what Earth cannot copy, such as Mars's low gravity and thin air, and we state limitations openly: scores are based on published descriptions, not computed from raw satellite data. Future work would calculate the same traits from NASA Earth and Mars datasets and add an interactive map and Moon targets.

projectDetails.name: VitalOrbit
projectDetails.summary:
VitalOrbit is a web-based crew health monitor for long-duration space missions, demonstrated with a fictional Expedition Meridian-7 crew. Astronauts log daily check-ins covering vital signs, sleep, body mass, radiation dose, exercise, reaction time, mood, stress, isolation and symptoms. VitalOrbit compares these with each person’s own baseline and rates six areas — cardiovascular and fluid shift, immune, bone and muscle, behavioral health, sleep and circadian rhythm, and radiation — as Nominal, Watch or Action needed, then offers clear protocols and emergency procedures.

This lets astronauts evaluate and act on their own health status, supported by trend charts, a health diary, a simulated ECG, two-tap crew and medical alerts that sync live across devices, and server-enforced privacy: crew see only their own data, while the Commander has read-only oversight.

This matters because on long missions, astronauts must spot health changes in themselves while far from Earth. Early, clear and actionable feedback on radiation, bone, immune and behavioral changes supports faster decisions and crew safety.

VitalOrbit is an unofficial educational demo: all data is simulated and thresholds are illustrative, not clinically validated.
projectDetails.details:
VitalOrbit is a web app that helps astronauts on long missions watch their own health and decide what to do about it. It is demonstrated with a fictional crew on Expedition Meridian-7: Commander, Crew Medical Officer, Pilot, Flight Engineer and Mission Specialist.

Collecting data. Each crew member logs a daily check-in covering:

heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂ and temperature

sleep, body mass, exercise and radiation dose

mood, stress, isolation and symptoms

reaction time, taken from a built-in reaction test

Evaluating health. Rule-based logic compares each entry with that person’s own earlier readings, because “normal” differs between people. It rates six areas as Nominal, Watch or Action needed:

cardiovascular and fluid shift

immune and infection

bone and muscle

behavioral health and cognition

sleep and circadian rhythm

radiation exposure

Acting on it. Every concern links to a protocol with concrete steps. The app also provides:

trend charts and a personal diary

emergency procedures for fire, depressurization, toxic atmosphere, radiation storm and medical emergency

a two-tap alert to the whole crew or to the Crew Medical Officer

Mission features.

crew readiness overview and vehicle-system status

a radiation-storm simulation

individual and team objectives

optional side missions that the Commander creates and crew accept

a simulated ECG at the latest heart rate

a cabin sound monitor that reacts to the microphone or an audio file

How the hosted version works. A Node.js server stores the data, enforces who can see what, and pushes alerts live to every signed-in device.

Crew members receive only their own health data.

The Commander can open anyone’s data, read-only.

Everyone sees only crew readiness counts.

A whole-crew alert shows a banner and sounds a siren on every device in that room. A medical alert is visible only to the sender, the Commander and the Crew Medical Officer, and has no siren.

In the public demo, each visitor gets a private demo crew with a room code that others can use to join.

What benefits does it have?

Self-monitoring when Earth is far away. Astronauts get clear, personal feedback even when contact with ground support is delayed.

Early warning. Comparing each person with their own trend can catch slow changes, such as sleep loss, rising dose or falling mood, before they become acute.

Clear next steps. Every status leads to an action, not just a number.

Privacy with oversight. Leadership sees readiness without crew members seeing each other’s health data.

Reliable emergencies. Two-tap confirmation prevents accidental alarms, and alerts reach the right people at once, with a visual banner and a screen-reader announcement as well as sound.

Open to everyone. Anyone can try it in a browser, with no install and no account.

What is the intended impact?

The project aims to show how a crew on missions to the Moon and Mars could be better aware of, and quicker to act on, their own health. It focuses on radiation, isolation, altered gravity, immune changes and behavioral health. It also works as a teaching and showcase tool that lets students and the public see how spaceflight affects the body. It is an unofficial educational demo, not a medical device.

What tools, languages, hardware or software did you use?

Languages: HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript, with no front-end framework. The server is Node.js.

Front end:

SVG for trend charts.

Canvas for the ECG, audio visualizer, particles and meteors.

Web Audio API for synthesized sounds and audio analysis.

Web Animations API and CSS transitions for animation.

Back end: Express for the JSON API, and Server-Sent Events for live updates.

Security: scrypt-hashed passcodes, signed HttpOnly session cookies, a Content-Security-Policy, rate limiting and server-side input checks.

Deployment and testing: Docker, a README with hosting steps, and Playwright browser tests.

AI assistance: Claude, an AI assistant from Anthropic, helped write and test the code. Adjust this line to your event’s disclosure rules.

Hardware: None is required. It runs in any modern browser, and a microphone is optional for the sound monitor.

How is your project creative?

Personal baselines: Each astronaut is compared with themselves rather than a population average.

Sound design: Clicks, typing and tab changes sound like a mechanical keyboard, with a chime for success. A siren is reserved for whole-crew emergencies, so routine use never causes alarm fatigue.

Mission-control motion: Animation is precise and never bouncy. The nav indicator glides between tabs, charts draw themselves on, new readings appear as new points, and dropdowns fade, slide and stagger their items with an animated checkmark.

Atmosphere: Interactive particles react to the pointer, clicks and scrolling and recover quickly. Meteors cross the screen, and the particles pulse with audio level.

Live ECG and sound monitor: A synthetic ECG draws in and sweeps at the latest heart rate, and the cabin sound monitor responds to real microphone or file input.

Demo design: Private demo rooms with shareable codes let a showcase audience try it without disturbing each other.

Original identity: It has its own name, terminology, logo and design language.

What factors did your team consider?

Honesty and safety: Simulated readings are labeled as simulated, thresholds are called illustrative and not clinically validated, and an on-screen notice says it is an unofficial demo.

Privacy: Health data is the most sensitive, so the server enforces access instead of just hiding things in the interface. The Commander’s access is read-only, and emergency banners no longer reveal the sender’s health status.

Emergency reliability: Confirmation before sending, live delivery to every device, and non-sound backups for each alert: a banner, a screen-reader announcement and a vibration cue on phones.

Accessibility: Keyboard navigation, skip link, labeled charts, screen-reader support, and dropdowns that follow the standard listbox pattern. Reduced-motion users get effects off by default, and sound, effects and theme can each be switched off.

Cognitive load: A minimal, high-contrast interface, because crew are often tired and stressed.

Independence: No agency logos, flags, branding or mission identifiers. A separate file lists the replaced names.

Safe public hosting: Isolated demo rooms, caps on how many exist, per-network limits, and no personal data collected.

Performance: The particle count scales to the screen, effects pause when the tab is hidden, and the blur effect behind menus is light enough for most devices.

projectDetails.name: Cosmo Pulse
projectDetails.summary:
CosmoPulse: Project Summary

On long missions to the Moon and Mars, astronauts will be far from real-time medical support, with delayed communication to Earth. CosmoPulse is a health monitoring platform that tracks an astronaut’s condition continuously and alerts both the crew and the ground medical team before small changes become serious problems.

It displays live vitals, including heart rate, blood oxygen, body temperature, sleep, and stress, and watches for spaceflight-specific risks such as bone and muscle loss, radiation exposure, fluid shift, and elevated CO₂. Each astronaut is compared against their own baseline, with green, yellow, or red alerts and trend graphs across mission days.

Cosmo Pulse works offline and syncs when a connection returns. Because medical data is sensitive, it uses encrypted storage, role-based access, and an access log.

Our prototype uses simulated data, with thresholds informed by NASA’s Twins Study and the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR).

Technologies: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Chart.js, Python (Flask), AES encryption.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works
CosmoPulse is a health monitoring dashboard for astronauts on long Moon and Mars missions. It tracks heart rate, blood oxygen (SpO₂), body temperature, sleep, and stress in real time, and watches for spaceflight-specific risks such as bone and muscle loss, radiation exposure, fluid shift, and elevated CO₂. Instead of relying only on population averages, it compares each astronaut with their own baseline and raises green, yellow, or red alerts with suggested actions, such as rest or exercise. Trend graphs show how health changes across mission days, and a daily risk score gives the crew a quick overview. The prototype runs on simulated data.

Benefits
Astronauts on deep-space missions can face communication delays of up to about 22 minutes each way between Earth and Mars, and onboard medical support is limited. CosmoPulse supports earlier detection of health problems, helps astronauts manage their own health, and gives the ground medical team a clear picture of the crew’s condition. It works offline and syncs when a connection returns.

Intended impact
We want crews to spot and act on health changes before they become emergencies, and to keep sensitive medical data private on missions far from Earth. The same approach could support remote clinics and other isolated environments on Earth.

Tools and technologies
HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Chart.js, and Python (Flask), with AES encryption for stored data. We also used AI-assisted development tools to speed up building the prototype. Thresholds are informed by published spaceflight research, including NASA’s Twins Study and the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR). No special hardware is required, and the design could later connect to wearable sensors.

Creativity
Most health trackers show averages. CosmoPulse personalizes alerts to each astronaut’s own baseline and combines health monitoring with security: encrypted storage, role-based access for astronauts, flight surgeons, and administrators, and an access log. Medical privacy is often forgotten in space health tools, and we made it a core feature. Its offline-first design also matches the real conditions of deep space.

Factors our team considered

  • Communication delays and unreliable connectivity, so we built offline mode with later sync
  • Privacy and safety of medical data, so we added encryption, access roles, and logging
  • Astronaut autonomy, so alerts include clear, simple recommendations
  • Realism and honesty, so we use research-informed thresholds and state clearly that the data is simulated
  • Usability under stress, so the interface uses simple color-coded status and a short daily risk score
  • Feasibility within the hackathon timeline, so we focused on a working prototype with the most important features

Space Mission is an interactive web-based space exploration project that allows users to experience a simulated rocket journey from Earth to different destinations in our solar system, including the Moon, Mars, and Jupiter.

Users can select a destination, launch a rocket, follow its journey through space, and experience a destination-side camera view upon arrival. The project aims to make space exploration more engaging and accessible through an interactive experience.

By combining rocket movement, destination selection, and changing camera perspectives, Space Mission encourages curiosity about astronomy and planetary exploration. It addresses the challenge of making space science more understandable and interesting, especially for people who may not have access to advanced space simulation tools.

Our goal is to inspire users to explore beyond Earth, learn about our solar system, and develop a greater interest in space science and future exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Space Mission – Interactive Solar System Exploration

Project Overview

Space Mission is an interactive space exploration experience that allows users to simulate a rocket journey from Earth to different destinations in our solar system, including the Moon, Mars, and Jupiter.

Users can select their destination, launch a rocket from Earth, and follow its journey through space. The experience uses changing camera perspectives, beginning with a third-person rocket view and gradually transitioning toward a closer first-person perspective. Upon reaching the destination, users can experience a camera view from the selected planetary environment.

How It Works

The project starts with a realistic Earth-based rocket launch. After selecting a destination, the rocket begins its journey through space. The camera follows the spacecraft during flight, providing a sense of movement and distance. Once the mission reaches its destination, the experience transitions to a pre-installed destination camera view.

Benefits and Intended Impact

  • Makes space exploration more interactive and engaging.
  • Helps users develop an interest in astronomy and planetary exploration.
  • Provides an accessible introduction to space missions and the solar system.
  • Encourages curiosity about different celestial destinations.
  • Creates an enjoyable educational experience through simulation.

Tools and Technologies

The project was developed as a web-based interactive experience using JavaScript, HTML, CSS, and web development tools. Vite was used as the development server and build tool, while Netlify was used to deploy and host the project online.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of Space Mission is its focus on experiencing a complete space journey rather than simply viewing planets. The combination of rocket launching, destination selection, camera transitions, and destination-side views creates an immersive exploration experience.

Factors Considered During Development

We considered visual realism, camera movement, destination selection, the feeling of distance during space travel, user experience, and accessibility through a web browser. Our goal was to make space exploration enjoyable and understandable for a wider audience.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

Earth System Trend Detective (Team JUPYTER, NASA Space Apps) is an interactive platform that automatically detects statistically significant environmental trends in noisy NASA data.
Problem: Temperature, water, and vegetation change together, often in opposite directions across regions, and finding real signals in huge datasets is manual and hard.

Data: MODIS, Landsat, and MERRA-2, ingested as NetCDF/HDF and aggregated in the cloud.
Tech: React or Streamlit frontend, Leaflet/Mapbox maps, Python backend (Pandas, Xarray, SciPy/Statsmodels), serverless cloud.
Impact: Makes spatial trend analysis accessible to researchers and policymakers, can add future satellite or sensor data, and turns trends into visual stories for the public.

projectDetails.name: Project JWALA
projectDetails.summary:
FireSync is a data harmonization framework that combines wildfire observations from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellites into a single, consistent long\-term record. These satellites detect fires differently due to variations in resolution, sensitivity, and measurement techniques, which can create misleading trends when their datasets are merged directly.

Our project addresses this challenge by correcting differences in fire measurements, spatial resolution, detection limits, and observation timing. By integrating remote sensing physics with statistical modeling, FireSync enables reliable comparisons between historical and current fire observations.

The project is important because it helps researchers, environmental agencies, and policymakers better understand wildfire trends, improve carbon emission estimates, and support climate change studies. Ultimately, FireSync ensures continuity in global wildfire monitoring as satellite technologies evolve, providing more trustworthy data for scientific research and decision\-making.
projectDetails.details:
FireSync is a project that creates a consistent wildfire dataset by harmonizing observations from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellites. Since these sensors detect fires differently due to differences in resolution, sensitivity, and observation methods, directly combining their data can produce misleading trends.

Our framework corrects these differences by adjusting fire measurements, matching spatial resolution, accounting for detection limits, and aligning observation times. This allows fire records from different satellite generations to be compared reliably.

The project can help scientists, climate researchers, and disaster-management agencies better track wildfire trends, estimate carbon emissions, and study the impacts of climate change.

We used Python, geospatial data analysis tools, satellite fire datasets, and Bayesian statistical modeling techniques. The creativity of FireSync lies in combining satellite physics with advanced statistical methods rather than relying only on simple data fitting.

When developing the project, our team considered sensor differences, fire detection accuracy, atmospheric effects, uncertainty, ecosystem variability, and the need for a continuous long-term wildfire record.

projectDetails.details:
Mission Control: Beyond Earth

Mission Control: Beyond Earth is an interactive educational space mission design and simulation game developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.

What does the project do?

The project transforms the complex process of space mission planning into an engaging, interactive experience. Players take the role of a Space Mission Director and make important decisions involved in designing, planning and managing a space mission.

Players can explore different mission destinations, customize spacecraft, select scientific instruments and launch vehicles, and manage essential engineering resources such as mass, power, fuel, communication and budget.

How does it address the challenge?

Designing a space mission involves balancing multiple engineering requirements. Students often find these concepts difficult to understand through theoretical learning alone.

Our game provides an interactive environment where players can experiment with engineering decisions and understand how different choices influence mission performance, resource availability and overall mission success.

Intended impact

The project aims to make aerospace engineering and space exploration more accessible to students. It encourages scientific curiosity, critical thinking, problem-solving and engineering decision-making through interactive learning.

Technology and development

The application was developed using Google AI Studio as part of our development workflow. Its development specifications include interactive web technologies, spacecraft engineering calculations, mission simulation and resource management. The implementation focuses on connecting player decisions with mission outcomes.

Creativity and innovation

The key innovation is combining space mission planning, engineering trade-offs and game-based learning in one interactive experience. Instead of simply learning about spacecraft systems, players experience the challenges of making decisions as a mission director.

Our vision is to turn complex aerospace engineering concepts into an accessible and engaging learning experience for the next generation of space explorers.

projectDetails.name: Project Leo Space
projectDetails.summary:
Team Leo Space built 'Still Out There', a virtual museum where visitors walk up to five 3D space artifacts and hear each one tell its story. The project addresses NASA Space Apps’ *Abandoned but not Forgotten* challenge by connecting equipment on the Moon, Mars, and in interstellar space to the discoveries it made possible.

Visitors can simulate bouncing a laser pulse off the Apollo 11 reflector to estimate the Moon’s distance, examine the mineral grains that helped Opportunity find evidence of past water on Mars, and listen to Voyager 1’s plasma-wave data as audio. The exhibits draw on NASA mission records, archival images, and 3D models. Narration and captions support exploration on computers and phones.

The museum helps young learners see how scientists use measurements to make discoveries and why a mission’s data can remain valuable for decades.
projectDetails.details:
What we built

Still Out There is a browser-based, first-person museum developed by Team Leo Space for NASA Space Apps’ Abandoned but not Forgotten challenge. Visitors explore five exhibits: the Apollo 11 retroreflector, Apollo 17 lunar rover, Opportunity rover, InSight lander, and Voyager 1. Walking up to an artifact starts its narrated story and timed captions. Visitors can replay the audio, read the full story, or use the exhibit directory to jump straight to an artifact. Approaching the exit starts a game-style credit roll with project references and team credits.

How it teaches

Each artifact tells its story in the first person and explains what it did and what scientists learned from it. Visitors can simulate a lunar laser-ranging experiment, inspect an image of the mineral grains Opportunity found on Mars, and listen to Voyager 1’s plasma-wave measurements as audio. These activities help young learners connect a piece of hardware to a measurement and understand how that measurement supported a scientific discovery.

How we built it

We used HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Three.js and WebGL for first-person movement and 3D rendering. We reconstructed the two Apollo exhibits from archival photographs and adapted NASA’s 3D models for Opportunity, InSight, and Voyager. We generated the narration using Kokoro Heart and paired the audio with timed captions. We used Vite to build the site, GitHub for version control, and Vercel for hosting.

What we considered

We designed the museum for keyboard and mouse on computers and touchscreen controls on phones. An opening guide explains how to move and look around. We optimized the models for browser loading and provided a CSS-based gallery for devices without WebGL. Full transcripts give visitors a way to follow each story at their own pace. We also credited the mission records, images, models, and recordings so visitors can explore the original sources.

Our intended impact is to help school-age learners understand how space science works and why the evidence a mission collects can keep teaching us long after the mission ends.

projectDetails.name: Project Field-Shift: NASA Farm Advisor
projectDetails.summary:
What we have developed:
We developed Field Shift: NASA Farm Advisor, an interactive web platform and decision-support system that translates NASA Earth Observation satellite telemetry into actionable, climate-resilient crop rotation and soil management strategies for farmers, agronomists, and agricultural extension workers worldwide.

How does it address the challenge:
Traditional farming often relies on static calendars and single-crop monoculture, leaving fields vulnerable to droughts, nutrient depletion, and climate volatility. To solve this, Field Shift converts raw NASA satellite data into straightforward agronomic guidance and models how crop sequences perform under local climate stress before seeds are sown. Additionally, a built-in climatological fallback model ensures rural advisory operations never stall when satellite connectivity drops

Why is it important:
To counter the topsoil loss and micronutrient depletion caused by monoculture, Field Shift deploys regenerative crop rotations that preserve soil health, sequester organic carbon, and disrupt pest cycles. Because agriculture drives ~70% of global freshwater withdrawals, the platform also aligns crop water demand with satellite-observed precipitation and root-zone moisture to mitigate aquifer depletion and crop failure. Finally, by forecasting nitrogen fixation gains and input cost reductions, Field Shift shields smallholders from volatile fertilizer markets and climate risks, securing long-term farm viability.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

Field Shift: NASA Farm Advisor is an interactive, space-enabled precision agriculture advisory platform designed to help smallholders, commercial growers, and agricultural researchers transition away from soil-depleting monoculture practices toward climate-resilient, regenerative crop rotations.

The application functions across four interconnected operational modules:

  1. Satellite Earth Observation & Telemetry Ingestion:
    • Ingests solar irradiance, daily surface temperature (T2M), and precipitation data in real-time from the NASA POWER API (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources, NASA Langley Research Center).
    • Incorporates a NASA SMAP-inspired (Soil Moisture Active Passive) root-zone hydrologic model that estimates volumetric soil moisture percentage and soil water deficit based on local 30-day precipitation history, regional soil texture (e.g., Loam, Clay Loam, Sandy Loam, Silt Loam), and evaporation demand.
    • Includes an offline climatology engine fallback to maintain zero downtime even in low-connectivity rural environments.
    • Evaluates agronomic scenarios (e.g., Continuous Monoculture, Soil Regeneration Rotation with legumes/cover crops, and Water & Thermal Resilient Rotations).
    • Dynamically weights options using customized farmer operational priority sliders for Water Conservation, Soil Health Preservation, and Target Profitability.
    • Penalizes water-intensive crop configurations when SMAP telemetry detects acute drought or severe soil moisture depletion.
    • Quantifies 3-to-5 year agronomic impacts, including projected net farm margin changes, synthetic fertilizer expenditure reductions through biological nitrogen fixation, total water savings (m3/ha), and soil organic matter/carbon sequestration gains.
    • Packages field coordinates, soil types, live satellite metrics, risk alerts, and crop recommendation schedules into downloadable PDF Field Advisory Reports ready for farm audits, extension agents, or bank credit assessments.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Actionable Climate Adaptation: Translates complex orbital Earth observation datasets into plain-language recommendations and clear risk alerts (e.g., heat stress warnings, drought index status).
  • Cost & Input Reductions: Suggests nitrogen-fixing legume and cover crop pairings (such as Winter Rye, Soybeans, Chickpeas) that reduce chemical fertilizer inputs by up to 20–35% and optimize irrigation schedules.
  • Long-Term Yield Stability: Replaces short-sighted monoculture with diverse rotation sequences that rebuild soil organic matter, minimize topsoil erosion, break pest cycles, and prevent root-zone degradation.
  • Global Access with Hyperlocal Usability: Automatically detects regional currencies (e.g., USD $, INR ₹, EUR €, GBP £, BRL R$, AUD A$, CAD C$) and offers native multi-language translation (including native scripts for major Indian and international languages) so non-English-speaking farmers can immediately use it.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Empowering Smallholder Farmers: Democratizes access to NASA Earth observation data—data typically restricted to enterprise agribusiness software or academic GIS suites—making it freely usable through intuitive, visual controls.
  • Food & Water Security: Mitigates the impact of shifting rainfall regimes and extreme weather events by guiding farmers toward drought-resilient crops before planting season begins.
  • Advancing UN Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs): Direct alignment with SDG 2 (Zero Hunger), SDG 6 (Clean Water & Sanitation), SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption & Production), and SDG 13 (Climate Action).

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Programming Languages: Python 3 (primary backend logic and analytics engine), JavaScript/TypeScript (Next.js architecture references).
    • NASA POWER API (Langley Research Center) for historical and daily agroclimatology telemetry.
    • NASA SMAP (Soil Moisture Active Passive) principles for soil hydration and root-zone water retention modeling.
  • Data Processing & Utilities: Pandas, NumPy, Requests, Regex.
  • UI/UX & Styling: Custom Glassmorphism CSS design system with dynamic high-resolution agricultural wallpapers and responsive card layouts.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Bridging the "Raw Data to Farmgate" Gap: Rather than overwhelming growers with raw raster files or NetCDF scientific arrays, the tool translates NASA parameters into practical farming actions (e.g., "High thermal stress detected—switch to Sorghum/Chickpeas rotation to conserve 28% water").
  • Multi-Factor Trade-off Slider System: Recognizes that sustainability must balance economics; growers can drag priority sliders between short-term cash flow and multi-year soil regeneration to see customized score cards in real-time.
  • Frictionless Onboarding: Provides one-click global presets (e.g., Iowa Corn Belt, Punjab Basin, Po Valley, Mato Grosso, New South Wales) alongside interactive GPS pin placement, instant currency localization, and Google Translate engine integration for native languages.
  • Resilient Architecture: Features built-in climatological fallbacks so the tool remains operational even during satellite API latency or field connectivity drops.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  1. Connectivity & Latency in Rural Contexts: Rural agricultural areas often have limited internet bandwidth. The platform utilizes lightweight API payloads, efficient caching, and an offline climatology model.
  2. Soil Diversity: Soil texture drastically dictates water retention. We accounted for differing retention coefficients across Loam, Clay Loam, Silt Loam, and Sandy Loam.
  3. Economic Feasibility for Farmers: A green recommendation is useless if it causes bankruptcy. The evaluation model pairs environmental scores with market liquidity profiles and realistic payback periods.
  4. Accessibility & Inclusivity: Implemented native language translation options, high-contrast visual indicators, auto-currency conversion, and clean PDF exports for farmers who prefer printed physical sheets.

projectDetails.name: Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars
projectDetails.summary: This project transforms technical telemetry and archival records of discarded NASA equipment on the Moon and Mars into an engaging, 20-slide interactive planetary storybook. Rather than viewing lunar descent stages, rovers, and landers as "space junk," our presentation gives 9 iconic spacecraft first-person voices—allowing learners of all ages to explore their exact coordinates, mission lifespans, and cosmic heritage.
projectDetails.details: The Challenge Over six decades of space exploration, more than 225 tons of human hardware across 80+ sites have been left behind on the Moon and Mars. To the general public and younger students, these remnants are often dismissed as "space debris" or buried in dense scientific catalogs, obscuring their historic value and lessons for planetary sustainability. Our Solution: An Interactive Planetary Storybook We designed Abandoned but not Forgotten as a visual, narrative-driven presentation structured into three chapters: Chapter 1 — Silent Sentinels of the Moon: First-person chronicles from Apollo 11 Eagle, Apollo 15 Moon Buggy, Surveyor 3, and Apollo 17 Challenger, alongside a six-decade timeline of lunar exploration. Chapter 2 — Pioneers of the Red Planet: Personal stories and longevity comparisons from Viking 1, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, and the Ingenuity Helicopter. Chapter 3 — Planetary Stewardship: Explores how NASA heritage guidelines, off-world material science, and future resource recycling protect cosmic history while enabling sustainable Artemis-era exploration. How We Built It We curated verified landing coordinates, mission durations, and archival imagery from NASA open repositories and synthesized them into a clean, dual-deck presentation system—featuring a concise 7-slide Project Demo for judges and a 20-slide Full Presentation for classroom and public storytelling.

projectDetails.name: ASTRAHEALTH: Camera-Assisted Astronaut Health Monitoring
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRAHEALTH is a health monitoring and decision support tool for astronauts on long duration missions. Due to the hazardous nature of deep space exploration astronauts are exposed to high health risks due to radiation, micro gravity and isolation. On Earth astronauts do not have real-time medical support.

ASTRAHEALTH provides real-time, non-contact health monitoring using computer vision and local personalised health data. ASTRA VISION can be applied to cameras on board the spacecraft or cabin. ASTRA VISION uses rPPG and facial and body landmarks to provide real-time non-invasive estimation of heart rate, respiratory rate, eye blinks to indicate fatigue and physical activity. ASTRAHEALTH compares real-time health data from the camera, wearables or wellness application to the personalised baselines. It has been designed with an Earth Communication Delay Mode so that all health data is processed locally to protect astronauts’ health data. Health data will be stored and reports will be made on priority for flight surgeons once communication is regained. This enables autonomous proactive health care for astronauts on future Lunar and Mars missions.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRAHEALTH is an intelligent, mobile-first health monitoring platform designed to help astronauts monitor their physical and mental health during long-duration space missions. Space environments expose astronauts to several health risks, including radiation, microgravity, isolation, sleep disturbances and cardiovascular changes. Since immediate medical assistance from Earth may not always be available, our aim is to make health monitoring easier, more accessible and proactive.

The platform allows astronauts to register their health information, record vital measurements, monitor sleep and wellness, and compare their current health indicators with their personal pre-mission baseline. It helps identify unusual changes over time and provides understandable health insights and recommendations so astronauts can take appropriate preventive action.

One of our main innovations is ASTRA VISION, a camera-based contactless health monitoring feature. Instead of depending entirely on manual measurements, it explores how cameras inside spacecraft, or dedicated cameras installed in crew areas, could support health monitoring through computer vision. By analyzing facial landmarks and specific regions such as the forehead, cheeks and eyes, the system explores experimental heart-rate estimation using remote photoplethysmography (rPPG), along with fatigue-related indicators. It also includes visual tracking of chest and shoulder movements for experimental breathing-rate estimation and posture analysis. This could make routine health observations less dependent on manual input. Our current prototype demonstrates camera access, facial landmark detection, tracking regions and camera quality assessment, while integration with actual spacecraft camera infrastructure is a future deployment possibility.

ASTRAHEALTH also considers the challenges of communication delays during deep-space missions. Its offline-first approach is designed to preserve health records when connectivity is unavailable and prepare medical summaries that can be shared with medical teams when communication becomes possible. Other features include space hazard monitoring, mental wellness assessments, health trend visualization, preventive health recommendations and medical report generation.

We developed the application using modern web technologies, including Next.js, JavaScript/TypeScript, HTML, CSS and browser-based computer vision technologies. We also use Firebase for authentication and are developing persistent health data management and offline capabilities using appropriate backend and browser storage technologies.

What makes ASTRAHEALTH creative is that it brings personal health monitoring, camera-assisted observations, baseline intelligence and space mission awareness together in one platform. Rather than simply displaying health numbers, our goal is to help astronauts understand changes in their health and know when further attention may be needed.

While developing the project, we considered the unique conditions of space missions, including microgravity, limited medical resources, communication delays, data privacy, ease of use and the reliability of measurements. We also recognize that camera-based estimates are experimental and cannot replace dedicated medical instruments or professional medical assessment.

Our ultimate goal is to support safer and healthier human exploration beyond Earth, especially during future long-duration lunar and Mars missions.

projectDetails.details:
Mission Mars: Junior Astronaut Base Trainer - NASA SPACE eX

Mission Mars: Junior Astronaut Base Trainer is an interactive space survival game developed using PictoBlox. It allows students to experience the challenges of managing a Mars base for 10 days.

How it works: Players control a Mars base and monitor four essential systems: Oxygen, Power, Food, and Shield. All systems start at 100% and decrease daily. Players receive three actions per day, with each action increasing one selected resource by 20%. Random events such as Dust Storms, Solar Flares, and Machine Breakdowns create unexpected challenges. Players must manage their resources carefully to survive all 10 days. If any system reaches zero or below, the mission fails.

Benefits and Impact: The game makes space science more interesting and accessible to young learners. It encourages critical thinking, problem-solving, resource management, planning, and decision-making while introducing the challenges of astronaut survival on Mars.

Tools and Technologies: We used PictoBlox and its block-based programming environment, including variables, loops, conditional statements, random number generation, broadcasts, and interactive sprites and buttons. No external hardware was required.

Creativity: Our project transforms Mars survival challenges into an interactive game with cartoon astronauts, a space-themed interface, resource indicators, and unpredictable events.

Factors Considered: We considered age-appropriate learning, simple game controls, limited resources, unexpected situations, balanced gameplay, and an engaging experience for young students.

projectDetails.summary:
LIFESIGNAL – AI-Powered Search for the Ingredients of Life

LIFESIGNAL is an AI-powered astronomical research project designed to explore the chemical ingredients necessary for life beyond Earth. Using NASA's SPHEREx mission data, our project aims to investigate infrared observations and identify potential signatures of life-related molecules, including water and other important chemical compounds.

We have developed an initial Python-based data collection system that retrieves SPHEREx observations and saves the collected information in CSV format. Our planned platform will integrate astronomical data processing, spectral analysis, visualization, and AI-based pattern recognition.

LIFESIGNAL addresses the challenge of exploring whether environments beyond Earth contain the essential chemical ingredients associated with life. This project is important because understanding the distribution of these ingredients can help scientists identify promising regions for future astrobiological research and bring us closer to answering one of humanity's biggest questions: Are we alone in the universe?
projectDetails.details:

Our project focuses on analysing astronomical data from NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) mission. The project aims to explore and understand the universe by studying the spectral information collected from celestial objects.

The system works by processing and analysing SPHEREx datasets to identify meaningful patterns and extract useful astronomical information. It can help researchers understand galaxies, stars, cosmic structures, and the distribution of matter across the universe.

Benefits: The project makes astronomical data easier to explore, understand, and interpret. It supports scientific research and helps transform large volumes of observational data into meaningful insights.

Intended Impact: The project aims to contribute to our understanding of the universe and demonstrate how data analysis and computational techniques can support space science.

Creativity and Innovation: The project combines space science, data analysis, and technology to make complex astronomical information more accessible and useful.

Development Considerations: Data accuracy, dataset reliability, processing efficiency, scientific relevance, and the clarity of the results were important factors considered during development.

AURORA – Lunar Outpost Survival Simulator

AURORA is an interactive browser-based survival management game that explores the challenges of sustaining a four-person human outpost on the Moon.

The player assumes the role of Mission Commander and oversees four fictional astronauts: Alex Morgan, Ethan Carter, Maya Quinn White, and Noah Williams. The objective is to sustain the crew throughout a 30-day lunar mission by managing limited resources, maintaining infrastructure, responding to emergencies, and making strategic decisions.

The game is designed around interconnected resource-management systems, including oxygen, water, food, electricity, battery reserves, crew health, and equipment maintenance. Its simulation incorporates simplified resource production, consumption, storage, recycling, and maintenance mechanics.

AURORA features a top-down drone-style perspective for monitoring the lunar base and selecting facilities, alongside a first person-style room inspection perspective. The interface includes astronaut profiles, base facilities, resource indicators, mission progression, and environmental storytelling.

The gameplay concept includes greenhouse food production, water recycling, oxygen generation, solar energy, battery storage, equipment failures, water leaks, filter damage, crew assignments, and emergency response. Players must balance immediate survival requirements against long-term mission sustainability.

The project aims to make space exploration and resource sustainability more accessible through interactive learning. Instead of simply explaining the difficulties of lunar habitation, AURORA lets players explore the consequences of their decisions in a simulated environment.

The current implementation is an educational game prototype using simplified game parameters. It is not an engineering-grade life-support simulator. Further development focuses on improving simulation accuracy, emergency forecasting, scientific data integration, and gameplay testing.

projectDetails.name: ORBITAL SPACE MISSION GAME
projectDetails.summary:
ORBITAL is a single-file, client-side Space Mission Design Simulator built with HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript, with no backend or libraries. It teaches spacecraft engineering by making users balance mass, power, data, and cost before launch.

Players pick one of four missions (Earth Watch, Lunar Scout, Mars Pathfinder, Deep Space Survey), a difficulty (Cadet, Pilot, Commander), and solo or 2-4 person crews with defined roles. They then assemble a spacecraft from four instruments, three buses, three power systems, and three communication systems, and choose an orbit, a launcher (400, 900, or 1,800 kg), and a 2-, 5-, or 8-year lifetime.

A central calc() function recalculates the whole design on every change, updating mass (including a 35 kg structural allowance), power demand, science value, data rate, and cost on a live dashboard with progress bars. Four checks (payload, power, downlink, budget) run against limits that tighten with difficulty (budget: $220M Cadet, $180M Pilot, $145M Commander) and show green passes or amber warnings that explain each failure.

Launching runs a scoring model combining mission bonus, instrument science, orbit bonus, lifetime, and failure penalties into a 0-100 score. Outcomes range from Outstanding Engineering to Mission Failure, with an event log, anomalies, and an engineering lesson. Results export as a downloadable .txt mission report. The responsive, space-themed interface works on desktop and mobile.
projectDetails.details:
ORBITAL – Space Mission Design Simulator

Category: Web Development | Space Technology | Interactive Simulation
Technologies: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript

Project Overview

ORBITAL is an interactive, web-based educational simulation that introduces users to spacecraft engineering and space mission planning. Users take the role of a mission planner: they design a spacecraft, select scientific instruments, configure power and communication systems, choose an orbital trajectory, and pick a launch vehicle.

How It Works

Users customize mission objectives, spacecraft platforms, instruments, power systems, communication technologies, launch vehicles, and mission duration. From these selections, the simulator automatically calculates:

  • Total spacecraft mass
  • Power demand
  • Scientific data generation
  • Science potential
  • Estimated project cost

Real-time validation then checks whether the configuration meets four essential constraints: payload capacity, power availability, communication capacity, and mission budget.

Key Features

  • Four mission scenarios: Earth observation, lunar exploration, Mars atmosphere study, and deep-space exploration.
  • Difficulty levels that adjust engineering and budget constraints.
  • Team mode with defined roles: Mission Planner, Spacecraft Engineer, Science Lead, and Flight Director.
  • Mission simulation that produces a performance score, mission outcome, engineering feedback, and a simulated flight event log.
  • Downloadable mission report summarizing the configuration and results.

Benefits and Intended Impact

ORBITAL makes complex mission engineering easier to understand through hands-on experimentation rather than theory alone. Users see how engineering decisions affect one another and learn to balance scientific goals, technical capability, and financial limits. It builds analytical thinking, problem-solving, decision-making, and resource optimization.

The platform is aimed at students, technology enthusiasts, and beginners interested in space science and aerospace engineering. It raises awareness of spacecraft systems and mission planning, and shows how software can communicate complex scientific ideas.

Interactivity, dynamic calculations, engineering validation, mission scoring, event generation, report downloading

ORBITAL turns spacecraft engineering into an interactive mission-control experience. Instead of only presenting information, it lets users make engineering decisions and see the consequences immediately. projectDetails.name: Echoes of Exploration: The Forgotten Machines of the Moon and Mars
projectDetails.summary:
Echoes of Exploration is an interactive educational experience that brings the stories of NASA's forgotten space exploration hardware back to life. From Apollo lunar module descent stages and scientific instruments left on the Moon to historic Mars rovers and landers, the project explores the machines that helped humanity discover new worlds.

Through engaging storytelling, interactive exploration, mission histories, and visual experiences, users can discover why these machines were sent into space, how they operated, what scientific discoveries they enabled, and what happened to them after their missions ended.

Designed especially for school-age students and curious space enthusiasts, the project transforms complex space mission information into an accessible and engaging digital journey. By connecting forgotten hardware with its scientific achievements, Echoes of Exploration celebrates the engineering, curiosity, and human ambition behind decades of space exploration while inspiring the next generation of explorers.
projectDetails.details:
Echoes of Exploration: The Forgotten Machines of the Moon and Mars

1. What does the project do?

Echoes of Exploration is an educational digital experience designed to introduce students and space enthusiasts to the forgotten machines left behind during NASA's exploration of the Moon and Mars. It brings attention to spacecraft, rovers, landers, descent stages and scientific instruments that completed important missions but often remain overlooked in popular space stories.

The project aims to transform mission histories into engaging stories that explain what each piece of equipment was designed to do, how it operated, why it was left behind and what scientific discoveries it helped make possible.

2. How does it work?

The proposed experience organizes space artifacts by destination, including the Moon and Mars. Users can explore individual artifacts and discover their associated missions, purposes, scientific contributions and operational histories.

The experience focuses on:

  • Exploring historical lunar and Martian equipment.
  • Discovering the missions behind each artifact.
  • Understanding the engineering and technology used.
  • Learning about scientific discoveries enabled by these machines.
  • Following the history of space exploration through engaging narratives and timelines.

3. Benefits and intended impact

The project makes space science more accessible to school-age students and casual learners. Instead of presenting complicated technical information, it connects scientific facts with interesting stories that encourage curiosity and exploration.

Its intended impact is to:

  • Inspire young students to learn about astronomy, engineering and space science.
  • Preserve awareness of important historical space missions.
  • Explain the relationship between space technology and scientific discoveries.
  • Encourage interest in STEM education.
  • Celebrate the achievements of robotic explorers and the people behind them.

4. Technology and tools

The project is designed as a web-based educational experience.

The proposed technology stack includes:

  • HTML for structuring the experience.
  • CSS for responsive layouts and visual design.
  • JavaScript for interactive exploration and navigation.
  • NASA mission information and relevant scientific datasets as educational content.
  • Web-based visualization techniques for presenting mission histories and artifacts.

A PowerPoint presentation has also been prepared to communicate the concept, its proposed features and its educational value.

5. Creativity and innovation

The creative aspect of Echoes of Exploration is its storytelling approach. Rather than treating abandoned equipment as obsolete objects, the project presents each artifact as a silent explorer with a remarkable history.

For example, the Apollo Lunar Module descent stage represents the engineering that made human lunar landings possible, while the Sojourner rover represents an important milestone in robotic exploration of Mars.

The experience connects these machines to the scientific knowledge they helped humanity gain. This transforms historical mission information into an engaging digital learning journey.

6. Factors considered

The project considers scientific accuracy, educational value, accessibility and ease of understanding. Information should be presented using reliable NASA sources, simple language and engaging visual elements.

Special attention is given to distinguishing between active, inactive and completed missions so that users understand the actual status of each artifact.

Ultimately, Echoes of Exploration aims to remind the next generation that even when a space mission ends, its scientific legacy continues.

projectDetails.summary:
Crew Self-Check is a health monitoring app that helps astronauts on long-duration missions spot health changes in themselves and act on them without waiting for Earth. Each day the astronaut logs mood, stress, sleep, exercise, resting heart rate, and symptoms. The software compares these against their personal baseline and rates five areas as Nominal, Watch, or Alert: heart and circulation, bones and muscle, immune system, mind and mood, and radiation and air quality. These areas map to the challenge’s hazards: radiation, isolation, altered gravity, and a closed environment.

For every area, the app explains why it flagged a change and gives a concrete next step, such as adding resistive exercise, booking a behavioral health call, or moving to the storm shelter. It also projects radiation dose to mission end and generates a report the astronaut can send to the flight surgeon.

This matters because on missions to Mars, communication delays of up to 20 minutes each way make real-time medical support impossible. Catching small trends early, such as slow bone loss, creeping stress, or rising heart rate, prevents serious problems and keeps crews mission-ready.

(Word count: about 175)
