projectDetails.details:
Crew Self-Check: Project Details

What it does and how it works

Crew Self-Check is a web app that helps an astronaut monitor their own health on a long mission. Each day the astronaut completes a short check-in: mood, stress, sleep, exercise minutes, resting heart rate from a wearable, contact outside the crew, and any symptoms.

The software compares the last few days with that astronaut's own baseline. It rates five areas as Nominal, Watch or Alert:

  • Heart and circulation: resting heart rate, palpitations and dizziness, linked to fluid shifts in microgravity.
  • Bones and muscle: exercise levels, back pain and a rough estimate of monthly bone loss.
  • Immune system: sleep, rashes and cold-type symptoms.
  • Mind and mood: mood, stress, irritability and isolation.
  • Radiation and air: career radiation dose projected to mission end, cabin CO₂ and headaches.

Each card shows a 30-day trend, the reason for its rating and a concrete next step. A "what to do today" list is sorted by severity. The app also writes a report the astronaut can copy and send to the flight surgeon. Demo buttons simulate three weeks of strain, a solar storm and a CO₂ fault.

Benefits

  • Catches slow changes early, such as creeping stress, falling exercise or rising heart rate.
  • Works when Earth can't answer quickly. Mars communication delays can reach about 20 minutes each way.
  • Compares against each person's own normal, which reduces false alarms. For example, exercise doesn't trigger a heart-rate alert.
  • Gives plain-language guidance and shows the reason for every rating, so astronauts can trust and check it.
  • Gives the flight surgeon a ready summary instead of a raw data dump.

Intended impact

The goal is to make astronauts active partners in their own medical care, which will matter more as missions go to the Moon and Mars. Healthier crews are safer and keep missions on track. The same approach could help people in remote or isolated settings on Earth, such as polar stations, submarines and rural clinics.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no frameworks. The app is one self-contained file.
  • Design: responsive layout with light and dark themes, keyboard focus styles, and status shown by text labels as well as color.
  • Fonts: Barlow and Barlow Semi Condensed from Google Fonts.
  • Development: built with Claude, Anthropic's AI assistant, and published as a hosted web page. The demo deck was made with Claude's slide tool.
  • Hardware: none. The prototype runs in any modern browser, and all readings are simulated.

Creativity

  • The astronaut is the primary user, not mission control. Most health dashboards are built for ground teams.
  • It links each space hazard to a body system and an action, not just a chart.
  • It looks ahead by projecting radiation dose to mission end, so the astronaut sees a limit coming before reaching it.
  • It treats mental health and sleep as seriously as heart rate.
  • It includes an escalation path for when ground can't reply in time.

Factors we considered

  • Delay and autonomy: advice has to work without real-time ground support.
  • Personalization: each astronaut has a different baseline, so alerts show change from their own normal.
  • Alert fatigue: a three-level system with context, such as exercise, keeps alerts meaningful.
  • Privacy: health data is sensitive, so we plan a private-by-default mode where the astronaut chooses what to share.
  • Honesty about limits: the data is simulated, thresholds are illustrative and bone-loss figures are estimates. It is decision support, not a medical device.
  • Future work: real wearable input, offline AI guidance that learns each baseline, voice check-ins, and validation with clinicians and NASA standards.

projectDetails.name: AstroPalate: Sensory-Compensated Astronaut Health & Nutrition Software
projectDetails.summary:
AstroPalate is a sensory-compensated health and nutrition monitoring platform designed to prevent microgravity-induced malnutrition and spaceflight anorexia during long-duration space missions.

In microgravity, upward fluid shifts cause chronic nasal congestion ("space sniffles"), suppressing olfaction—which drives nearly 80% of flavor perception. Combined with repetitive menus, this leads astronauts to consume 20–30% fewer calories than required, accelerating bone demineralization, muscle atrophy, and immune decline. Unlike passive calorie loggers, AstroPalate links a 10-second daily crew check-in (tracking sinus congestion, fatigue, hydration, circadian disruption, and radiation exposure) with Food Technology interventions. Its sensory engine recommends trigeminal stimulants (capsaicin, ginger, piperine) and umami-rich space rations to restore appetite without excess sodium, while prioritizing bone-protective micronutrients (Vitamin D3, calcium, potassium) and tracking shelf-life vitamin degradation (Vitamins B1, C, and K).

Powered by open NASA datasets—including Spaceflight Standard Measures, NASA OSDR/GeneLab, and the Human Research Program Evidence Book—AstroPalate requires zero extra hardware mass and transforms daily astronaut rations into precision preventive medicine for low-Earth orbit, lunar habitats, and Mars transit.
projectDetails.details:
AstroPalate is a sensory-compensated astronaut health and nutrition monitoring software designed to prevent microgravity-induced malnutrition and spaceflight anorexia during long-duration space missions. In microgravity, upward cephalic fluid shifts cause chronic nasal congestion ("space sniffles"), suppressing olfaction—which drives nearly 80% of human flavor perception. Combined with repetitive menus, astronauts often consume 20–30% fewer calories than required, accelerating bone demineralization, muscle atrophy, and immune decline.

AstroPalate replaces passive calorie logging with an active, four-stage Food Technology workflow:

  1. 10-Second Daily Cabin Check-In: Crew members log subjective symptoms (sinus congestion, taste fatigue, nausea, and stress on a 1–5 scale) alongside biometric telemetry (heart rate, sleep quality, hydration, and radiation exposure).
  2. Sensory-Compensation Engine: When nasal congestion is elevated, the software recommends space rations enriched with trigeminal stimulants (capsaicin, ginger, piperine, menthol) and umami compounds (glutamates, nucleotides) that stimulate oral nerve receptors directly—restoring appetite without adding excess sodium (which accelerates bone calcium loss in space).
  3. Micronutrient Bioavailability Matcher: Aligns meal selection with physiological deficits, prioritizing Vitamin D3, Calcium, Potassium, and Omega-3s to counter ~1–1.5% monthly microgravity bone loss, while scheduling tyrosine-rich daytime foods and melatonin-tart evening snacks to stabilize 90-minute orbital circadian cycles.
  4. Radiation Shelf-Life Guard & Flight Surgeon Sync: Tracks spacecraft ration inventory and prioritizes thermostabilized or rehydratable pouches before cosmic radiation degrades sensitive vitamins (Vitamins B1, C, and K), while exporting lightweight daily telemetry summaries for ground flight surgeons.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Prevents Spaceflight Anorexia: Projected to boost daily caloric compliance by up to +22%, protecting astronaut muscle mass, bone density, and cognitive performance on ISS, Lunar Gateway, and Mars transit missions.
  • Reduces Spacecraft Ration Waste: Cuts nutrient-degraded food waste by up to 35% through shelf-life prioritization.
  • Zero Additional Launch Mass: Runs natively on existing crew tablets and wearable telemetry feeds without adding hardware payload weight.
  • Earth Healthcare Spin-Off: Directly adaptable for chemotherapy patients, elderly care, and post-viral anosmia patients experiencing severe taste/smell loss.

Creativity & Key Factors Considered Most astronaut health tools (such as NASA's Food Intake Tracker and ESA's EveryWear) passively record macros or rely on delayed Earth-based dietitian reviews. AstroPalate is creative because it applies Food Technology and sensory biology to solve an aerospace medical bottleneck autonomously—making it essential for deep-space missions where Earth communication delays reach up to 20 minutes. Our team specifically accounted for sodium-induced hypercalciuria, radiation-driven vitamin decay kinetics, zero-gravity crumb/liquid packaging constraints, and low-friction usability for busy crew schedules.

Tools, Datasets & Software Used

  • Scientific & Data Benchmarks: NASA Spaceflight Standard Measures, NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR / GeneLab), NASA Human Research Program (HRP) Evidence Book, and NASA Space Food Systems Laboratory thermal-processing stability data.
  • Design, Prototyping & Documentation: Google Workspace (Docs, Slides, Drive), Canva / Adobe Express for crew tablet UI wireframes, and rule-based nutritional decision modeling.

projectDetails.name: EarthWaltz
projectDetails.summary:
Earth’s surface is in a constant waltz of environmental change, yet passive optical satellites are frequently blinded by monsoon storms, dense forest canopies, and darkness. To address the NASA Space Apps Challenge “Dancing with the SARs”, we developed EarthWaltz, an interactive, open-source global radar observatory that leverages active microwave Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data from the NASA-ISRO (NISAR) mission and partner constellations (ALOS-2, SAOCOM-1A, Sentinel-1, and RADARSAT-1).

EarthWaltz features a hardware-accelerated dual-map split curtain that allows users to peel back cloud-obscured optical satellite imagery and reveal calibrated 24 cm L-band and 9.3 cm S-band radar backscatter underneath. Users can explore six critical global biomes—from monsoon flood inundation across below-sea-level Kerala polders and hidden Amazon river surges to Himalayan glacial velocity, seismic fault slip in Turkey, and peatland wildfire risks in Sumatra. The platform integrates physical scattering telemetry, live NASA ASF/CMR STAC queries, and an innovative Web Audio sonification engine that translates radar backscatter rhythms into audible sound.

EarthWaltz is vital because it transforms abstract microwave physics into intuitive, multi-sensory insights, empowering disaster responders, resource managers, educators, and citizens with critical all-weather, day-or-night planetary situational awareness.
projectDetails.details:
EarthWaltz: Global SAR Observatory

Challenge: Dancing with the SARs (2026 NASA International Space Apps Challenge)
Repository: https://github.com/Nekhal-james/EarthWaltz
Live Application: Built with Next.js 15, MapLibre GL JS, and Vercel Multi-Service Architecture EarthWaltz: Global SAR Observatory, https://earthwaltz.vercel.app

1. What does it do or how does it work?

The Core Concept

Optical satellites rely on sunlight and clear skies, meaning persistent monsoon storm clouds, dense tropical canopy, blizzard whiteouts, and nighttime conditions blind conventional cameras when critical disasters strike. EarthWaltz is an interactive, dual-mode web observatory that uses Active Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data from the joint NASA-ISRO SAR (NISAR) mission (dual-frequency 24 cm L-band and 9.3 cm S-band) alongside partner constellations (ALOS-2 PALSAR-2, SAOCOM-1A, Sentinel-1, and RADARSAT-1) to penetrate clouds and track planetary surface change in real time.

How It Works Under the Hood

  1. Hardware-Accelerated Dual-Map Split Curtain:
    • Two synchronized WebGL MapLibre GL JS map instances (radarMap and opticalMap) run concurrently with zero-latency bidirectional camera locking (jumpTo synchronized across pitch, bearing, zoom, and pan).
    • An interactive spatial curtain dynamically clips the top optical layer using GPU-accelerated CSS clipPath: inset(0 calc(100% - pos) 0 0) at 120 FPS.
    • Users can drag the curtain or click the Optical Split View toggle to directly compare what passive optical satellites see (often heavy cloud cover or smoke) against what active microwave radar reveals underneath.
    • HH Polarization (Water & Inundation): Identifies specular reflection on flat open water (σ0<−17.5 dB σ0 < -17.5 dB σ0<−17.5 dB, dark cobalt) versus corner-reflector "double-bounce" where standing water meets upright crops and building walls (σ0>−6.8 dB σ0 > -6.8 dB σ0>−6.8 dB, intense signal amber).
    • HV Polarization (Canopy & Biomass): Maps volume scattering across dense vegetation (σ0>−12.0 dB σ0 > -12.0 dB σ0>−12.0 dB, lush emerald) versus cross-polarized loss from clearcuts, logging roads, and fire scars (σ0<−17.5 dB σ0 < -17.5 dB σ0<−17.5 dB, vermilion).
    • InSAR Phase (Δϕ): Visualizes repeat-pass interferometric rainbow fringe cycles along active seismic fault lines, showing centimeter-scale surface deformation.
    • Coherence (γ): Highlights structural phase stability in urban areas (γ>0.72 > 0.72γ>0.72, crisp white) versus temporal decorrelation in turbulent water and windblown foliage (γ<0.30 < 0.30γ < 0.30, deep violet).
    • An in-browser algorithmic audio synthesizer built with the Web Audio API translates calibrated backscatter values and coherence stability into audible frequencies (60 Hz to 1.2 kHz60 Hz to 1.2 kHz60 Hz to 1.2 kHz), enabling users to literally hear the seasonal pulse and tidal rhythms of Earth's surface.
    • Direct integration with NASA Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) DAAC Vertex search and NASA Earthdata CMR STAC 1.0 APIs, backed by a microservice architecture for verified mission granules.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Unlocks Data Hidden from Optical Satellites: Proves the life-saving necessity of SAR by visually demonstrating how radar cuts through monsoon storm clouds, wildfire smoke, and darkness to reveal submerged communities and shifting ice.
  • Demystifies Complex Radar Physics: Traditional SAR data is locked behind specialized software (SNAP, ISCE3, Gamma) and raw polarimetric matrices. EarthWaltz translates complex decibels, wavelengths, and phase fringes into plain-English scattering mechanisms and intuitive visual heatmaps.
  • Multi-Sensory Accessibility: In addition to high-contrast cartographic visualizations, the built-in sonification engine provides an acoustic interface for blind, visually impaired, or auditory learners.
  • Zero-Install, High-Performance Web Access: Requires no specialized GIS software or plugins—anyone with a web browser on mobile or desktop can explore 30m global radar observations with sub-100ms response times.
  • Dual Exploration Modes: Features a guided Story Mode (overview narratives for the public and educators) and an analytical Instrument Workbench (with cursor telemetry HUD, swath opacity, multi-band toggles, and live STAC query tools for researchers).

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  1. Disaster Response & Humanitarian Relief:
    • Empowering civil defense teams during tropical monsoons (such as in Kerala, India) to identify submerged roads and isolated settlements beneath total cloud cover hours before floodwaters recede.
    • Giving environmental agencies and indigenous guardians near-real-time visibility into illicit deforestation frontiers and road networks hidden beneath the dense Amazon canopy.
    • Providing early-warning alerts for subterranean peatland moisture depletion in Sumatra to prevent catastrophic wildfires before ignition.
    • Tracking surface strain and fault slip across earthquake zones (e.g., the East Anatolian Fault in Turkey) and monitoring glacial retreat and moraine dam stability in the Himalayas to mitigate Glacial Lake Outburst Floods (GLOFs).
    • Inspiring students, educators, and science communicators ahead of the official NISAR mission rollout by making active microwave remote sensing as engaging and accessible as browsing an online atlas.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

To develop EarthWaltz, we engineered a full-stack, hardware-accelerated web architecture using TypeScript, Next.js 15 (App Router), and React 19, structured into a Vercel Multi-Service Architecture with serverless Node.js API routes and an internal Python 3 microservice connected via runtime service bindings. The core mapping engine is powered by dual synchronized MapLibre GL JS and Deck.gl WebGL instances that deliver a seamless 120 FPS spatial split curtain via GPU-accelerated CSS clipping. Our user interface implements a Swiss Cartographic design system using Tailwind CSS, pairing Google Fonts’ Bricolage Grotesque with Atkinson Hyperlegible for high-contrast numeric readability, while the browser's native Web Audio API synthesizes live radar backscatter values into audible parametric frequencies.

For scientific data processing, our offline pipeline was built with Python 3, Rasterio, NumPy, SciPy, Pillow, and h5py to ingest and calibrate raw NISAR HDF5 data products (JPL D-102274 RevF) and compute physical backscatter anomalies against AWS Terrarium 30m Global DEM tiles and Esri World Imagery. The application interfaces directly with official Earth observation APIs—querying live SAR granule footprints via the NASA Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) DAAC Vertex API, searching STAC 1.0 catalogs through NASA Earthdata CMR, and overlaying true-color meteorological imagery from NASA EOSDIS GIBS WMTS—with end-to-end performance monitored using @vercel/analytics.

5. How is your project creative?

  • The "Earth’s Waltz" Metaphor: Rather than presenting SAR data as dry technical charts, we frame planetary surface change as an ongoing terrestrial choreography—the seasonal surge of floodwaters, the glacial crawl of mountain ice, the respiratory moisture cycle of agricultural soils, and the rhythmic fault slip of tectonic plates.
  • The Interactive Dual-Map Spatial Curtain: Instead of static before-and-after side-by-side screenshots, users actively drag a live curtain that peels back the cloud-covered optical satellite view to reveal the active microwave radar data beneath.
  • Algorithmic Radar Sonification: Converting decibel backscatter (σ0\sigma^0σ0) and phase stability into pitch, resonance, and harmonic rhythm allows users to experience satellite observations musically.
  • Selective Anomaly Overlay Design: Rather than draping an opaque, low-resolution raster across the entire screen, our pipeline selectively highlights physical anomalies (water double-bounce, deforestation scars, phase fringes) while allowing natural high-resolution terrain to show through underneath.
  • Swiss Cartographic Aesthetic: Designed with inspiration from Swiss topographic map standards—using Alabaster Vellum backgrounds (#F6F5F0), International Cobalt accents (#0047AB), disciplined survey rule lines, and accessible typography.

6. What factors did our team consider?

  1. Physical Accuracy & Scientific Provenance:
    • All microwave scattering thresholds were calibrated against empirical SAR literature: specular open water at < −17.5 dB < -17.5dB < −17.5 dB, double-bounce flooded vegetation at > −6.8dB > -6.8dB > −6.8dB, and volume scattering at > −12.0dB > -12.0dB > −12.0dB. Every study area links to real NASA DAAC granule IDs and WKT orbital swath footprints.
    • We selected 6 representative global study areas across 5 continents:
      • Kerala, India (Hometown Anchor): Monsoon flooding across Kuttanad's below-sea-level paddy polders.
      • Amazon Basin, Brazil: Hidden flood pulses and deforestation beneath the canopy.
      • Himalayas (Khumbu Glacier & Everest Massif): Glacial velocity and GLOF hazards.
      • Kahramanmaraş, Turkey: Coseismic fault rupture from the 2023 earthquakes.
      • Punjab, India: Agricultural soil moisture and intensive crop rotations through dust.
      • Sumatra, Indonesia: Subterranean tropical peatland moisture loss and fire warning.
    • Ensured the interface remains clean and uncluttered. The optical comparison split panel is off by default so users first see an unobstructed radar observatory, with on-demand controls to compare optical imagery and toggle cloud simulations.
    • Designed a multi-service Vercel architecture with decoupled Node.js and lightweight Python microservices (< 50 KB bundle), ensuring rapid global CDN delivery and smooth 60+ FPS map interaction.
    • Provided complete open-source transparency on GitHub under the MIT license, adhering to NASA Space Apps Challenge Super Intelligence (SI) attribution requirements with dedicated metadata tags and documentation.

challengeDetails.title: Dancing with the SARs
challengeDetails.excerpt: Earth's surface is an endless dance of natural processes and human activities, but these changes are often difficult to visualize, understand, and communicate. From wetland loss to forest wildfires, earthquakes, farming activities, glacier movement, and more, Earth is in a constant waltz of surface changes. Your challenge is to build an interactive application that uses radar remote sensing data from the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission to track and visualize one or more types of surface change at locations around the world.

projectDetails.name: MISSION X – Interactive Space Mission Design Game.
projectDetails.summary:
MISSION X – Interactive Space Mission Design Game

MISSION X is an educational, interactive space mission design game inspired by NASA's space exploration missions. It allows users to experience the process of planning a space mission by choosing destinations such as Earth, the Moon, and Mars. Players can design spacecraft, select scientific instruments, choose orbits and launch vehicles, and manage important resources such as mass, power, budget, and communication.

The project addresses the space mission design challenge by transforming complex mission-planning concepts into an engaging and accessible simulation. Players receive mission performance scores, engineering feedback, and a final mission report based on their design decisions.

MISSION X is important because it helps students understand the challenges of real-world space exploration, develop problem-solving and critical-thinking skills, and explore basic aerospace engineering concepts through interactive learning.
projectDetails.details: MISSION X is an interactive educational game that introduces users to the basic concepts of space mission planning. Users can choose a destination such as Earth, the Moon, or Mars and customise a spacecraft by selecting components and scientific instruments. They can also choose an orbit and launch vehicle. The game calculates spacecraft mass, power requirements, estimated budget, and science data capacity based on the selected equipment. It then runs a simplified mission simulation and provides a performance score, engineering feedback, and a mission report. The main benefit is that students can explore engineering trade-offs in an engaging, beginner-friendly way. For example, adding instruments can improve scientific data collection but also increases mass, power demand, and cost. The prototype was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with AI assistance. Its creative approach is to turn space mission planning into an interactive learning experience. The current calculations use simplified educational values and are not intended to represent real spacecraft specifications or flight predictions.

projectDetails.details:
EARTHPULSE – NASA Earth System Trend Analyzer

Project Description

EARTHPULSE is an interactive climate data analysis and visualization platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The project aims to improve the accessibility and understanding of historical climate information by transforming NASA datasets into meaningful visualizations and statistical insights. Its geographical focus is Kerala, India, with an emphasis on exploring regional temperature and precipitation patterns.

Functionality and Working

EARTHPULSE retrieves historical monthly climate data through the NASA POWER API. The primary parameters analyzed are T2M (temperature at 2 metres above the surface) and PRECTOTCORR (corrected precipitation).

The retrieved data is processed using Python-based data processing techniques and presented through an interactive Streamlit dashboard. Users can explore historical temperature variations, analyze monthly and yearly precipitation patterns, examine climate trends and compare supported geographical locations.

The platform incorporates statistical methods, including the Theil-Sen Estimator, Mann-Kendall Test and Kendall's Tau, to estimate trend magnitude, evaluate monotonic trend significance and understand the direction and strength of climate relationships.

Benefits and Intended Impact

EARTHPULSE simplifies the exploration of scientific climate datasets by presenting complex information through accessible visualizations and statistical analysis. It aims to support climate education, environmental awareness and exploratory research by helping users understand historical regional climate patterns.

The project also demonstrates the practical application of open NASA data in developing accessible environmental analysis tools.

Technology and Implementation

The application was developed using Python as its core programming language. Streamlit provides the interactive web interface, Pandas and NumPy support data processing and numerical computation, SciPy supports statistical analysis, and Plotly is used to generate interactive visualizations. NASA POWER API serves as the primary climate data source.

The project follows a modular software architecture that separates frontend components, backend data services, data processing and statistical analysis. No specialized hardware is required.

Creativity and Innovation

The primary innovation of EARTHPULSE lies in integrating NASA climate data retrieval, statistical trend detection and interactive visualization into a unified platform. Rather than requiring users to interpret raw scientific datasets independently, the application presents processed climate information in a more accessible and understandable format.

This approach provides an interactive way to investigate regional climate behaviour using publicly available Earth science data.

Development Considerations

During development, the team considered data reliability, scientific accuracy, usability, performance, accessibility and future scalability. Particular attention was given to selecting appropriate statistical techniques and interpreting results within the context of the selected location, observation period and available data.

Team Collaboration

EARTHPULSE was developed collaboratively by two team members.

Devu – Project Development and Integration: Primarily responsible for project implementation, frontend development, dashboard integration, project coordination, testing and debugging.

Sharon Binu George – Backend Development and Data Analysis: Primarily responsible for backend data services, NASA POWER API integration, climate data processing, statistical trend analysis and backend integration support.

Both members actively collaborated throughout the development, integration, testing and improvement processes.

Future Scope

Future development may include expanding geographical coverage, integrating additional Earth system variables, improving regional climate comparisons, introducing advanced analytical capabilities and enhancing geographical visualizations.

Conclusion

EARTHPULSE demonstrates how NASA climate data and modern software technologies can be combined to make historical climate information more accessible and understandable. By connecting data retrieval, scientific analysis and interactive visualization, the project aims to encourage greater awareness of regional climate patterns and support further exploration of Earth's changing environmental systems.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: LUNA NAV 2.0
projectDetails.summary:
LUNA NAV is an interactive lunar exploration and mission-planning platform developed to support the exploration of potential landing regions near the Moon’s south pole. It brings NASA lunar imagery, topographic data and preliminary mission-planning tools together in one accessible workspace.
Using imagery from NASA Moon Trek and elevation and slope datasets from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA), users can explore the lunar surface, select candidate locations, examine available terrain information and compare potential landing sites. The platform also includes distance and traverse calculations, preliminary solar and Earth visibility estimates, an interactive candidate comparison system, a research assistant and downloadable reports.
LUNA NAV addresses the challenge of making complex lunar data easier to explore and interpret by connecting scientific information with practical mission-planning tools. Its evidence-based approach distinguishes retrieved measurements from calculated estimates and unavailable data, helping users understand both the possibilities and limitations of their analysis.
The project aims to make lunar exploration more accessible and support informed, transparent planning for future lunar missions.
projectDetails.details:
LUNA NAV is an interactive lunar exploration and preliminary mission-planning platform focused on potential landing regions near the Moon’s south pole. It brings lunar imagery, topographic information, and mission-planning tools together in one workspace.

Users can explore the lunar surface through an interactive map, select candidate landing coordinates, examine available elevation and slope information, and compare potential sites. The platform also includes traverse-distance calculations, preliminary solar and Earth visibility estimates, candidate comparison tools, a research assistant, and downloadable reports and datasets. It uses NASA lunar imagery and data sources, including NASA Moon Trek and the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA).

The project aims to make complex lunar data easier to access, understand, and compare. It can help students, researchers, and space enthusiasts explore the challenges of lunar south-pole missions and investigate potential landing regions. Its intended impact is to encourage accessible, transparent, and data-informed lunar exploration.

LUNA NAV was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with web-mapping tools and NASA data services. The application is designed to run in a web browser without specialised hardware. Its local data storage and export features support convenient exploration and comparison.

The creative aspect of LUNA NAV is the integration of scientific lunar information with practical mission-planning features in a single interactive platform. During development, we considered usability, mobile accessibility, data availability, coordinate accuracy, terrain safety factors, transparency, and the limitations of remote scientific datasets. We distinguish retrieved measurements from calculated estimates and unavailable information so users can understand the reliability of the results.

LUNA NAV is a preliminary exploration and planning tool, not a certified lunar landing safety system.

projectDetails.name: Project Odyssey 01
projectDetails.summary: this would be an space game trying to help the people to experience what goes on in the operations of an actual nasa space program
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

NASA Mission Control: Gateway Alpha is an interactive 2D space systems engineering and station walk-around simulation game. Instead of navigating sterile spreadsheets, players take on the role of an astronaut and flight director living aboard an orbital research station (Gateway Alpha).

  • Embodied Exploration: Players walk through a 5-room space station using 8-directional movement (WASD / Arrow keys) with character step-bobbing and proximity-based interaction prompts ([E] ACCESS CONSOLE).
  • Interactive Mission Decks:
    1. 🚀 Command Bridge & Flight Desk (0, -60): Accesses the Mission Design Studio, where players configure spacecraft bus structures, instruments, propulsion, orbits, and launch vehicles while managing real-time SWaP-C (Size, Weight, Power, and Cost) trade-offs.
    2. 🧪 Botanical & Exobiology Lab (-600, 0): Features apothecary specimen benches to analyze extraterrestrial crystals and catalog research science points.
    3. 📻 Capcom & Telecoms Deck (600, 0): Downlinks telemetry to NASA’s Deep Space Network (DSN) Goldstone station, triggering authentic Quindar radio beeps and flight status updates.
    4. ⚡ Boiler & Power Bay (0, 420): Manages the station's energy balance, solar array tracking angles, and reserve battery states-of-charge.
    5. 🌌 Cupola Observation Bay (0, -380): Features a velvet bench overlooking a panoramic view of Earth and space, with smooth camera zooming to observe celestial horizons.
  • Flight Operations & Mission Progression: Players design and execute multi-tier missions (Artemis I, Artemis II, and Mars Odyssey) featuring automated T-minus 10s countdowns, orbital insertion, and deep-space hazard navigation.
  • Grand Victory Ceremony: Successfully managing all station operations and mission tiers unlocks an official NASA Grand Commendation Certificate granting the player the rank of Master Flight Director with S-Rank Gold Astronaut Wings.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Bridges Theory and Practice: Aerospace engineering trade-offs often remain abstract in textbooks. This project demonstrates how a single design change—such as adding a high-resolution spectrometer—has ripple effects across mass, power demand, launch vehicle sizing, and mission budget.
  • Dual-Tier Accessibility:
    • Beginners & Students: Enjoy an approachable, cozy walk-around game where they can explore, tend plants, and launch rockets.
    • Aspiring Engineers: Can experiment with authentic mathematical constraints (payload mass margins, power balances, and orbital parameters).
  • Immediate, Frictionless Access: Available both as a native desktop game in Godot Engine 4 and as a zero-install HTML5 web simulation that runs on any PC, Mac, or tablet browser.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Inspiring STEM / STEAM Careers: Sparks interest in space exploration, aerospace engineering, astrophysics, and computer science among students of all backgrounds.
  • Teaching Systems-Thinking: Instills the core engineering principle that there is rarely a single "perfect" solution; real mission design requires balance, compromise, and collaboration.
  • Team Collaboration: Enables cooperative problem-solving where up to 4 participants can specialize in roles such as Flight Director, Systems Lead, Capcom Operator, and Science Specialist.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Game Engine: Godot Engine 4.7.2 (Node hierarchy, 2D physics layers, Area2D collision triggers, dynamic Camera2D lerp smoothing, and CanvasLayer HUD).
  • Primary Code: GDScript (Godot 4's high-performance, object-oriented language utilizing custom classes, signal-slot architecture, and typed variables).
  • Web Engine: HTML5 Canvas, CSS3, and JavaScript (ES6+) for the zero-dependency browser simulation.
  • Graphics & Art: SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) for crisp, resolution-independent pixel art (the chibi astronaut, wooden CRT consoles, spacecraft, and celestial bodies).
  • Procedural Sound Synthesis: Custom in-engine 16-bit sound synthesizer in both GDScript (AudioStreamWAV) and JavaScript (Web Audio API), generating authentic 2525 Hz / 2475 Hz NASA Quindar radio beeps, thruster pulses, and chimes directly in memory with zero external sound files.
  • Target Hardware: Standard cross-platform consumer laptops and desktops (no high-end GPU required).

5. How is your project creative?

  • The "Stardew Valley in Space" Aesthetic:
    • Rather than relying on cold, intimidating neon-cyan sci-fi interfaces, the project reimagines the station as a warm, cozy orbital sanctuary. It features staggered oak timber floors, crimson Persian rugs with gold tassels, brass wall lanterns, terracotta potted ferns, and an antique vacuum-tube radio cabinet.
    • This aesthetic reduces cognitive fatigue and makes space systems engineering feel welcoming, tactile, and human.
  • Embodied Interaction:
    • Instead of navigating static spreadsheets, the player physically walks their astronaut to dedicated stations, grounding technical engineering decisions in an interactive living space.
  • 100% Code-Generated Procedural Worlds:
    • Starfields, twinkling brightness animations, floorboard seams, and sound waves are generated procedurally at runtime, keeping the entire project footprint under 100 KB with instant load times.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  1. Engineering Fidelity vs. Educational Flow (SWaP-C Constraints):
    • Mass Margin (MLV≥Mdry+MpropM_{LV} \ge M_{dry} + M_{prop}MLV​≥Mdry​+Mprop​): Enforcing strict launch vehicle lift capacities.
    • Power Balance (Pgen≥Pbus+PpayloadP_{gen} \ge P_{bus} + P_{payload}Pgen​≥Pbus​+Ppayload​): Modeling solar panel generation against instrument power consumption.
    • Budget & Comms Caps: Balancing scientific return against project cost and Deep Space Network downlink bandwidth.
  2. User Experience (UX) & Ergonomics:
    • Dynamic interaction pills ([E] ACCESS DESK), color-coded telemetry badges (green for nominal, amber for warning), and camera damping to ensure fluid gameplay.
  3. Cross-Platform Deployability:
    • Ensuring the project works as both a clean, single-click Windows .exe export and a zero-install web application.
  4. Human Factors in Spaceflight:
    • Incorporating restorative environments (like the Cupola viewing bay and warm hearth lighting) to reflect the real-world psychological needs of astronauts during long-duration space expeditions.

projectDetails.summary: PROJECT ORECX is a concept for an interactive simulator that helps users explore lunar south-pole landing sites as conditions change over time. projectDetails.details:
PROJECT ORECX is a concept for an interactive lunar mission simulator focused on south-pole landing sites. Users choose candidate locations and mission dates, then play or scrub through time to see how sunlight, shadows, and Earth’s position change. A “Horizon Window” presents the Sun and Earth from the lander’s perspective, making potential solar charging periods and direct communication windows easier to understand. Users can compare sites, explore notional battery impacts, and create a report explaining mission trade-offs.

The project could help mission planners, educators, and the public explore complex conditions through a visual, hands-on experience. Its intended impact is to make site comparisons easier to understand and communicate, while supporting informed decisions. The creative element is combining a lander-level horizon view with a time-based simulator and mission challenge in one workspace.

The proposed prototype uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Three.js for a 3D Moon view, Python for calculations, and Chart.js for timelines. The plan calls for sample sites and clearly labeled illustrative data first, followed by lunar terrain and NASA SPICE data, verified visibility calculations, and validation. The team considered changing illumination, terrain obstruction, time and coordinate handling, battery assumptions, communication visibility, usability, and the need to distinguish geometric visibility from terrain-blocked line of sight.

projectDetails.name: The Earth Information jukebox
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, Earth Information Jukebox, is an interactive platform that transforms NASA's Earth science data into meaningful sounds and music through a process called sonification. It allows users to explore different aspects of our planet, such as climate change, temperature, ocean conditions, rainfall, and environmental changes, not only through visualizations but also through sound.
The platform aims to convert scientific data into different musical patterns, tones, and rhythms, helping users experience Earth's changing conditions in a new and engaging way. By combining science, technology, and music, we aim to make complex Earth information easier to understand and explore.
This project addresses the challenge by providing an alternative way to experience and interpret Earth science data through hearing as well as seeing. It is especially valuable for people with visual impairments and for students and the general public who may find traditional scientific graphs and visualizations difficult to understand.
We believe this project is important because understanding our planet should be accessible to everyone. By turning Earth's data into sound, we hope to make science more inclusive, interactive, educational, and enjoyable while encouraging greater awareness of our planet and its environmental changes.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details: Earth Information Jukebox
What It Does & How It Works
Earth Information Jukebox is an interactive web platform that transforms NASA’s open Earth science datasets into meaningful sounds and music through data sonification. Users select environmental datasets, such as global temperature anomalies, ocean conditions, rainfall patterns, and long-term climate change, and the application maps numerical data points to musical parameters including pitch, rhythm, tempo, and harmonic tones. By pairing real-time audio synthesis with synchronized visual charts, users can literally hear planetary trends unfold alongside traditional visualizations.
Benefits & Intended Impact
Traditional scientific graphs rely almost exclusively on sight, creating barriers for blind and low-vision learners as well as students or general audiences who find complex charts intimidating. By translating data into intuitive auditory patterns, Earth Information Jukebox makes climate and environmental science accessible, multisensory, and emotionally engaging. Our intended impact is to democratize Earth science education, foster inclusive STEM learning, and inspire deeper public awareness of how our planet is changing.
Tools, Languages & Software Used
Frontend & Web Technologies: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6+)
Audio Synthesis & Sonification: Web Audio API (for real-time frequency, tone, and rhythm generation mapped directly from data arrays)
Data Sources: NASA Open Earth Science & Climate Datasets (temperature, precipitation, ocean, and atmospheric metrics)
Deployment & Hosting: Netlify (Continuous Deployment & Global Edge CDN)
Creativity & Design Considerations
Rather than treating data purely as numbers on a screen, we approached climate metrics as a musical composition—designing distinct sonic signatures so rising temperatures sound like ascending pitches and shifting rainfall patterns play out as evolving rhythms. Throughout development, our team prioritized accessibility (Universal Design for Learning), perceptual clarity (ensuring sound mappings remain pleasant and distinguishable rather than noisy), and cross-device responsiveness so anyone with a web browser can explore Earth’s soundtrack effortlessly.

projectDetails.summary: Wildfire: Global Inferno is an interactive global wildfire simulation that combines geographical visualisation, environmental modelling and strategy-based gameplay. Developed as a browser-based platform, it features a detailed 2D world map where users can observe wildfire propagation across countries. Factors such as wind, temperature, humidity and vegetation influence fire behaviour, while live statistics track affected nations, simulated casualties and environmental impact. The project addresses the challenge by making complex wildfire dynamics easier to explore and understand through interactive simulation. It aims to raise awareness about wildfire behaviour, environmental vulnerability and the importance of disaster preparedness. By turning environmental science into an engaging experience, we hope to encourage curiosity, learning and greater awareness of the risks wildfires pose to our planet.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details — WILDFIRE: GLOBAL INFERNO

What does it do and how does it work?

Wildfire: Global Inferno is an interactive, browser-based global wildfire simulation that combines geographical visualisation, environmental modelling and strategy-based gameplay. It uses a detailed 2D world map with country boundaries to demonstrate how wildfires can spread across different geographical regions.

The simulation considers environmental factors such as temperature, humidity, wind direction, rainfall and vegetation to influence fire propagation. Users can evolve their wildfire through upgrades, while countries respond with countermeasures. A live dashboard tracks affected and unaffected countries, simulated casualties and overall wildfire progression.

What benefits does it have?

The project transforms complex environmental concepts into an accessible and engaging experience. It helps users understand how environmental conditions influence wildfire behaviour, how geographical differences affect vulnerability, and why controlling wildfires can become increasingly challenging.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to encourage environmental awareness and improve public understanding of wildfire dynamics and disaster preparedness. By making wildfire behaviour interactive, we hope to inspire curiosity about Earth science, environmental protection and the importance of effective disaster management.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed as a browser-based application using HTML, CSS and vanilla JavaScript. JavaScript handles the simulation logic, environmental variables, country statistics and interactive gameplay, while HTML and CSS provide the interface and visual presentation. Geographical data is used to represent country boundaries and create the global map. Development and testing were carried out using Visual Studio Code and a local browser environment.

How is the project creative?

Instead of presenting wildfire information through static maps and statistics, we created an interactive global simulation that allows users to explore wildfire propagation and its potential consequences. The combination of a geographical world map, evolving fire mechanics, country-level statistics and simulated global casualties creates an engaging approach to environmental education.

What factors did our team consider?

We considered geographical accuracy, environmental variability, simulation performance, accessibility and ease of use. We also focused on distinguishing simulated outcomes from real-world observations, ensuring that estimated casualties and wildfire progression are understood as illustrative rather than scientifically validated predictions.

Our vision: One World. One Fire. Countless Consequences.

projectDetails.name: Abandoned but Not Forgotten: Ingenuity – The Little Helicopter That Changed Mars
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, **Abandoned but Not Forgotten: Ingenuity – The Little Helicopter That Changed Mars**, is an educational storytelling project about NASA’s Ingenuity Mars Helicopter.

We developed an engaging story that introduces Ingenuity, explains why NASA sent it to Mars, describes its historic first powered flight on another planet, and highlights its achievements during 72 flights. The story also explains how Ingenuity supported the Perseverance rover and how its flying mission came to an end.

This project addresses the challenge by bringing attention to important NASA equipment that remains on other worlds after its mission. It helps students and space enthusiasts understand the purpose, discoveries, challenges, and legacy of these machines through simple and interesting storytelling.

Ingenuity may no longer fly, but its achievements have opened new possibilities for future aerial exploration of Mars.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, Abandoned but Not Forgotten: Ingenuity – The Little Helicopter That Changed Mars, is an educational storytelling project about NASA’s Ingenuity Mars Helicopter.

How it works:
The project presents Ingenuity’s mission as an engaging story. It explains why the helicopter was sent to Mars, how it achieved the first powered and controlled flight on another planet, its 72 flights, its role in supporting the Perseverance rover, and how its flying mission ended.

Benefits:
It makes space exploration easier to understand, especially for students and beginners. It helps readers learn about NASA technology, scientific achievements, and the challenges of exploring Mars.

Intended impact:
The project aims to create awareness about NASA equipment left on other worlds and show that even after a mission ends, its discoveries and achievements can support future exploration.

Tools and resources:
The story was prepared using information from NASA resources, with AI assistance in organizing and presenting the information. This version is a written storytelling project and does not require custom hardware or a programming language.

Creativity:
The project uses a short, engaging narrative to tell the story of a small helicopter that achieved something historic on another planet.

Factors considered:
We considered scientific accuracy, information from NASA sources, simple language, educational value, and an engaging storytelling style. We also avoided presenting fictional events as real mission facts.

projectDetails.name: AstraTerra — Earth Analogs for the Moon and Mars
projectDetails.summary: AstraTerra is an interactive atlas that uses open elevation and surface-temperature data to help people find and evaluate Earth analogs for lunar and Martian exploration. In Terraform, choose a planetary region to rank 18 Earth sites by terrain relief, steepness and roughness. Each match shows its evidence and source, and a draggable divider compares the Earth and destination maps. In Explore, complete a Mars or lunar mission by comparing gravity, recording temperature evidence and testing suit protection or inspecting a candidate site. In Research, inspect individual terrain cells, switch map layers and export results. In the bundled catalog, Antarctica’s McMurdo Dry Valleys ranked first for Shackleton, with its strongest component in terrain roughness. The rankings can guide field-test shortlists. Differences in scale, gravity, atmosphere, temperature and radiation still matter when planning a mission.
projectDetails.details:
The challenge

Mission teams need Earth locations to test instruments, rover routes, sampling and field operations before deploying them on the Moon or Mars. Different analog sites help test different conditions: lava fields for broken volcanic terrain or polar valleys for isolated, uneven environments.

NASA’s challenge asks participants to use open data to identify these relationships and present them through maps, visualizations or tools. Team Red Shift built AstraTerra, combining destination mapping, ranked Earth analogs, a 3D mission lab and a research workspace.

What we built

AstraTerra compares 18 Earth terrain windows with six Moon and Mars regions. Lunar regions include Shackleton, Marius Hills and Mare Tranquillitatis. Mars regions include Jezero’s western delta and two Gale Crater areas.

The Earth catalog covers polar terrain, deserts, volcanic fields, impact craters and lava-cave-associated sites, including McMurdo Dry Valleys, Yungay, Death Valley, Meteor Crater, Nördlinger Ries, Lake Salda, Timanfaya, Kīlauea Iki and Lava Beds.

The app scores mapped surface windows, not underground caves. It supports three user levels: visitors can discover Earth matches, students can complete controlled missions, and reviewers can inspect measurements and export analyses. Recommendations include terrain sources and, where available, field research links.

Terraform · Map the surface and find Earth analogs

  1. Open Terraform, select Mars or Moon, and choose a destination such as South Pole: Shackleton.
  2. Explore Elevation, Slope and Roughness layers. Click the map to inspect individual terrain cells.
  3. Review ranked Earth candidates and select a site to see its overall and individual scores. Open Terrain source and Field research source for supporting information.
  4. Drag the divider between Earth and planetary maps to compare elevation, slope or roughness. Keyboard controls are also supported.
  5. Open Advanced maps, weights and export to adjust the importance of terrain features for different field exercises.

This workflow makes recommendations transparent. A site may score well in slope but poorly in roughness or elevation variability, helping users choose suitable field exercises.

How the ranking works

Digital elevation models represent surface heights as grids. AstraTerra processes selected terrain windows and calculates three main measurement groups:

  • Relief and elevation variability: Measures the height difference and distribution of elevations within a window.
  • Steepness: The Horn method estimates slope using neighboring elevation values. Scores consider average slope and the 90th percentile.
  • Roughness: The Riley Terrain Ruggedness Index measures elevation differences between neighboring cells.

Each component receives a score from 0–100. The overall index uses weighted averages: approximately 29% relief and elevation variability, 36% slope and 36% roughness after excluding temperature and rescaling.

Temperature remains visible where data exists but is excluded from ranking because Earth and planetary observations represent different measurement conditions. Users can adjust weights and examine their effects.

The final score is an exploratory terrain comparison, not a prediction of landing success or operational safety.

Findings and applications

Shackleton, lunar south pole

  • Top-ranked Earth site: McMurdo Dry Valleys
  • Overall similarity: 56.82/100
  • Roughness score: 69.15/100
  • Key finding: Offers a candidate for uneven-terrain route planning tests.

Gale Crater, Murray Buttes

  • Top-ranked Earth site: Mauna Kea
  • Overall similarity: 84.23/100
  • Roughness score: 90.97/100
  • Slope score: 83.46/100
  • Key finding: Supports traverse comparisons.

Mare Tranquillitatis

  • Top-ranked Earth site: Lava Beds, California
  • Overall similarity: 54.08/100
  • Slope score: 86.34/100
  • Key finding: Offers a starting point for volcanic terrain studies.

Jezero western delta

  • Top-ranked Earth site: Nördlinger Ries
  • Overall similarity: 35.25/100
  • Key finding: High slope similarity but lower overall similarity highlights differences in relief and ruggedness.

These results use the default catalog and weights. McMurdo and Mauna Kea are established analog sites. AstraTerra adds an inspectable comparison method for screening terrain windows. Field measurements and mission-specific engineering checks are still required before selecting operational test sites.

Explore · Complete a comparative mission

Atacama to Mars: Open Explore, select the Mars mission and enter the 3D Comparative Science Lab. Repeat the same object drop from 12 meters on Earth and Mars. The modeled fall takes 1.56 seconds on Earth and 2.54 seconds on Mars.

The model assumes release from rest and ignores air resistance, allowing users to observe how gravity affects fall time and impact speed.

Next, open Atmospheric Pressure & Survival. Test Mars without an EVA suit and then with a pressurized suit. The simulation displays ambient pressure, oxygen partial pressure and a separate internal suit environment under stated life-support assumptions.

In Temperature Exposure, log evidence for both worlds. Earth displays satellite surface-temperature observations where available, while Mars shows a planetary reference and identifies missing local observations. Select Complete Mission to open the debrief.

McMurdo to Shackleton: Repeat the gravity experiment on Earth and the Moon, log thermal evidence and inspect a Shackleton candidate. Lunar elevation, slope and roughness help identify access and traverse considerations. Diviner provides polar thermal observations within its seasonal and local-time context.

Permanent-base assessment also requires evidence about illumination, communications, subsurface resources, radiation and ground-bearing conditions. The debrief keeps these gaps visible.

Research · Inspect evidence and export analysis

Open Research and select an Earth site and planetary destination. Explore available elevation, slope, roughness, temperature or similarity layers. Click terrain cells to inspect numerical values and units, and adjust heatmap opacity to view the underlying terrain.

Use comparison controls to examine terrain profiles and weights. Save Analysis downloads a JSON record, while Export Scientific Report provides the report.

Research allows reviewers to inspect steep areas, source resolution and individual measurements. Terraform compares regional summary statistics, while Research's similarity heatmap compares corresponding positions within selected terrain windows. These windows may cover different physical areas and do not share geographic coordinates.

Data sources and evidence limits

  • Earth: NASADEM and Copernicus GLO-30 provide elevation data. Copernicus also supplies supplementary terrain windows, including McMurdo and the 12 added Terraform sites. Terra and Aqua MODIS provide land surface temperature composites, with possible cloud and coverage gaps.
  • Moon: LRO LOLA provides elevation, while Diviner Polar Cumulative Products provide polar surface-temperature observations. These datasets use separate grids.
  • Mars: MGS MOLA provides regional topography, including coarse Jezero terrain. The USGS/NASA Gale merged elevation model supplies localized Gale terrain. Published planetary temperature references support the educational mission but do not provide local mapped measurements.

Terrain resolution affects recorded relief, slope and roughness. Regional datasets show broad features, while rover navigation and landing preparation may require finer imagery and field verification. Geology, dust, ice and radiation also require separate evidence.

Future improvements include comparing windows at similar physical extents and resolutions, testing different locations and weights, and adding compatible measurements.

Software and implementation

  • React, TypeScript and React Router: Build the interface and connect the three workspaces.
  • Leaflet: Provides interactive geographic maps. Browser Canvas renders terrain layers and comparison controls.
  • Three.js and React Three Fiber: Power the 3D mission scenes.
  • Node.js, GeoTIFF.js and Proj4js: Support raster processing, coordinate conversion and terrain metric preparation.
  • Vite: Builds the application. GSAP and Lenis support animations and scrolling, while Lucide provides icons.
  • GitHub and Render: Support source handoff and static-site deployment. The browser loads bundled JSON and calculates rankings locally. Analysis exports are downloaded locally, without requiring a database or specialized hardware.
  • Testing: Node tests and Chrome checks verify calculations and key workflows, including source links, map comparisons and Mars mission completion.
  • AI assistance: OpenAI Codex supported code review, implementation, debugging, testing and documentation. Source measurements are credited to their providers, with additional team AI usage covered in the separate SI disclosure.

Intended impact

AstraTerra makes planetary data accessible to the public and provides educators with a practical way to teach controlled experiments, map reading and evidence quality.

Exploration teams can use its catalog to identify potential analog sites, plan field exercises and understand the limitations of each comparison. From mapping and ranking to mission debriefs and exported analyses, the platform keeps the investigation transparent and traceable.

projectDetails.name: ASTROHEALTH
projectDetails.summary:
Space missions are very challenging because astronauts have to work in an environment that is completely different from Earth. projectDetails.details:
ASTROHEALTH

A Smart Health Monitoring Application for Astronauts

1. Abstract

Space missions are very challenging because astronauts have to work in an environment that is completely different from Earth. During their missions, they may experience several physical and mental health problems due to microgravity, radiation exposure, isolation, changes in sleep patterns and other environmental conditions.

At present, monitoring the health of astronauts is an important part of space missions. However, continuous health monitoring and early identification of health problems can be improved with the help of smart technology.

This project proposes AstroHealth, a smart health monitoring application designed to monitor the physical and mental health of astronauts during space missions. The application aims to collect health-related information such as heart rate, blood oxygen level, body temperature, sleep patterns and activity levels through wearable devices and sensors.

The collected information will be displayed in a simple dashboard so that astronauts can monitor their health conditions. The application can also identify unusual changes in health parameters and generate alerts when necessary. It will provide basic health suggestions and help astronauts maintain their health throughout the mission.

2. Introduction

Space exploration has become an important part of scientific and technological development. Astronauts spend several days or even months in space, where their bodies experience conditions that are very different from those on Earth.

One of the major challenges faced by astronauts is maintaining their health in microgravity. Microgravity can affect muscle strength, bone density, blood circulation and balance. Apart from physical changes, astronauts may also experience stress, sleep disturbances and psychological difficulties due to isolation and limited communication.

Regular health monitoring is therefore necessary to ensure the safety and performance of astronauts.

Our proposed project, AstroHealth, focuses on developing a digital application that helps astronauts monitor their health in a convenient way. Instead of depending only on periodic medical assessments, the application aims to provide continuous access to important health information and alert users when unusual changes are detected.

3. Problem Statement

Astronauts work in an environment where immediate access to medical facilities and healthcare professionals is limited.

Some health-related problems may develop gradually and may not be noticed immediately. Changes in heart rate, oxygen saturation, sleep quality and physical activity can provide important information about an astronaut's health.

The main problem addressed by this project is the need for an accessible and integrated health monitoring system that can help astronauts identify possible health issues at an early stage.

4. Objectives

The main objectives of the AstroHealth application are:

1. To monitor important health parameters of astronauts.

2. To provide real-time or near-real-time health information through a digital dashboard.

3. To identify unusual changes in health conditions.

4. To generate alerts when health parameters move outside predefined safe limits.

5. To monitor sleep patterns and physical activity.

6. To provide basic health recommendations.

7. To maintain health records throughout the space mission.

8. To support communication of relevant health information to mission medical teams.

5. Proposed System

AstroHealth is proposed as a mobile and tablet-based health monitoring application that can work with wearable sensors.

The system collects health information from connected devices and processes the collected data. The information is then displayed through an easy-to-understand dashboard.

The application will have different sections for physical health, sleep monitoring, activity tracking, mental well-being and emergency alerts.

If any health parameter shows an unusual change, the application will notify the astronaut and can make the relevant information available to the authorised medical team.

The application is intended to support health monitoring and decision-making rather than replace professional medical diagnosis.

6. Main Features

6.1 Real-Time Health Monitoring

The application will monitor important health parameters such as:

- Heart rate

- Blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂)

- Body temperature

- Blood pressure (if supported by the connected device)

- Physical activity levels

6.2 Sleep Monitoring

Astronauts may experience changes in their sleep cycles because of unusual lighting conditions, mission schedules and the space environment.

This feature will track sleep duration and patterns and provide a summary of sleep quality.

6.3 Physical Activity Monitoring

This section will track daily physical activity and exercise routines. Since microgravity can contribute to muscle and bone loss, monitoring exercise activity is important for astronauts.

6.4 Mental Health and Stress Monitoring

Long-duration missions can affect the psychological well-being of astronauts.

The application can include a daily mood check-in, stress-level questionnaire and basic relaxation suggestions.

6.5 Smart Alerts

The application will generate notifications when monitored health parameters show unusual readings.

For example, if the astronaut's heart rate or oxygen saturation moves outside their personalised safe range, the application can generate an alert.

6.6 Health History and Reports

The application will maintain health records over time. Astronauts and authorised medical professionals can use these records to understand changes in health conditions throughout the mission.

6.7 Emergency Support

In case of a possible medical emergency, the application will provide an emergency alert interface that allows the astronaut to access relevant health information and notify the mission medical team.

7. Working Principle

The proposed application works through the following steps:

1. Data Collection: Wearable sensors collect health-related information from the astronaut.

2. Data Transfer: The collected information is transferred to the application through a connected device.

3. Data Processing: The application analyses the collected readings and compares them with personalised reference limits.

4. Health Dashboard: The processed information is displayed in a simple graphical format.

5. Alert Generation: If unusual readings are detected, the application generates an alert.

6. Health Recommendations: The application provides relevant basic suggestions based on the available information.

7. Data Storage: Health records are stored securely for future monitoring and analysis.

8. Technologies Proposed

The following technologies can be considered for developing the application:

- Frontend: Flutter or React Native for developing the mobile application.

- Backend: Python for processing and analysing health data.

- Database: Firebase or a suitable secure database for storing health records.

- Sensors: Wearable health monitoring devices.

- Data Analysis: Basic machine learning or rule-based algorithms for identifying unusual health patterns.

- UI/UX Design: Figma for designing the application interface.

These technologies are proposed options and can be modified depending on the available resources and project requirements.

9. Expected Outcomes

The expected outcome of this project is a user-friendly health monitoring application that helps astronauts keep track of their health during space missions.

The application is expected to:

- Provide a single platform for viewing important health information.

- Help identify unusual changes in health parameters.

- Improve awareness of physical and mental well-being.

- Maintain health records throughout the mission.

- Support astronauts and medical teams in monitoring health conditions.

10. Future Scope

The application can be improved in several ways in the future.

Advanced machine learning models can be introduced to identify possible health risks by analysing long-term health data. Integration with more wearable sensors can improve the amount of information collected.

The application can also be developed to work with limited or delayed internet connectivity, which is particularly important during space missions.

In the future, the system could be extended to include personalised health monitoring, advanced medical assistance and integration with spacecraft health management systems.

11. Conclusion

AstroHealth is a proposed smart health monitoring application designed to address one of the important challenges of human space exploration: maintaining astronaut health.

By combining wearable sensors, data analysis and a simple application interface, the project aims to make health monitoring easier and more accessible during space missions.

The main idea behind this project is that astronauts should be able to understand their health conditions without depending entirely on periodic medical assessments.

Although the proposed application is still a concept and requires further development and validation, it has the potential to become a useful supporting tool for astronaut health management in future space missions.

projectDetails.name: Project Renaissance architect
projectDetails.summary:
Imagine a future where humanity travels the stars, powered not by massive, volatile reactors, but by clean, compact, and self-sustaining energy. Our project introduces a novel theoretical architecture for Lattice Confinement Fusion (LCF) designed to make this ambitious vision a reality.
By utilizing Deuterium-Helium-3 (D-He3) fuel within a specialized erbium deuteride crystal lattice, we propose a system that bypasses the heavy, dangerous neutron radiation of traditional fusion. Instead, this aneutronic reaction relies on a nano-engineered structure that allows high-energy protons to escape smoothly and safely.
The true elegance of our approach lies in its closed-loop design. We trigger the fusion using an ultra-compact Wakefield accelerator. As the reaction ignites, a precise magnetic field funnels the escaping protons directly into a Traveling Wave Energy Direct Converter (TWEDC). This allows us to convert kinetic energy straight into electricity with a groundbreaking 90% efficiency—completely eliminating the need for bulky thermal turbines. A portion of this clean power is then fed back to sustain the accelerator.
This architecture isn't just about pushing the boundaries of quantum physics; it's about providing a safe, lightweight, and limitless power source to carry humanity deeper into the cosmos
projectDetails.details:
Our Advanced Lattice Confinement Fusion (LCF) architecture is a closed-loop power generation system that harnesses the energy of Deuterium-Helium-3 (D-He3) fusion. Operating within a specialized erbium deuteride or nano-engineered fluorite crystal lattice, the system utilizes the lattice structure to provide dense electron screening, lowering the Coulomb barrier for fusion. A compact Wakefield or particle accelerator is used as the triggering mechanism to initiate the reaction. At a theoretical target of 9 \times 10^{14} reactions per second, the fusion process releases high-energy alpha particles and protons. Because the lattice is uniquely engineered to allow these particles to fly out with minimal obstruction, a directional magnetic field can funnel the rapidly escaping protons (14.7 MeV, traveling at 17.65\% the speed of light) directly into a Traveling Wave Energy Direct Converter (TWEDC). The TWEDC captures this kinetic energy and converts it into electricity with up to 90\% efficiency, immediately feeding a portion back to power the accelerator trigger to sustain the closed loop.

Core Benefits Unprecedented Efficiency: By utilizing the TWEDC to directly convert the kinetic energy of charged particles into electricity, the architecture completely bypasses the highly inefficient thermal cycles (heating water to turn a turbine) that limit traditional power plants. Aneutronic Safety: The use of D-He3 fuel produces a primarily aneutronic reaction. By avoiding the heavy neutron radiation of standard D-T fusion, the system drastically reduces radiation hazards and prevents rapid structural degradation of the reactor components (though secondary mitigation is planned for minor D-D side reactions). Mass and Volume Reduction: The combination of a Wakefield accelerator and direct energy conversion eliminates the need for massive thermal machinery and heavy radiation shielding, resulting in an exceptionally compact footprint

Intended Impact This theoretical framework is designed to solve the critical mass and energy bottlenecks of deep-space exploration. By providing a lightweight, ultra-efficient, and self-sustaining power source, this LCF architecture aims to enable long-term lunar and Martian outposts, power advanced spacecraft propulsion systems, and provide reliable life-support energy without the massive payload penalties of traditional fuel or fission reactors. Beyond aerospace, successfully scaling this closed-loop system could pave the way for decentralized, ultra-clean, and hyper-compact power generation for remote locations on Earth.

projectDetails.name: LunaNav
projectDetails.summary:
LUNA NAV (Lunar Navigation, Illumination & Communication Analysis) helps people explore potential landing locations near the Moon’s south pole. Choose a site, date, and observation window to view the Sun and Earth relative to the local horizon. Live mode retrieves celestial positions from NASA/JPL Horizons; sample mode provides clearly labelled illustrative data.

The dashboard displays sky directions, elevation timelines, estimated sunlight and Earth line-of-sight periods, and side-by-side comparisons of up to three site-date plans. A schematic lunar explorer and plain-language user guide make the results easier to understand.

LUNA NAV is a screening and educational tool. It does not calculate terrain obstruction, surface power generation, landing safety, or a verified communications link budget.
projectDetails.details:
LUNA NAV — Lunar Navigation, Illumination & Communication Analysis

LUNA NAV is a web application for exploring potential landing locations near the Moon’s south pole. It helps users compare how the Sun and Earth appear from different places and at different times.

Choose a reference location or enter coordinates, set a local date and time, and select an evaluation window. In live mode, a Next.js API route requests Sun and Earth positions from NASA/JPL Horizons using the selected lunar location as the observer. The app displays the results in a sky view and elevation timeline, and lets users compare up to three site-date plans. A clearly labelled sample mode is available to demonstrate the interface when live data is unavailable.

The project is intended to make lunar illumination and Earth line of sight easier to explore for mission planners, students, educators, and the public. Side-by-side comparisons help users see trade-offs between scenarios without hiding the measurements behind a single ranking.

We used Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, SVG, and Three.js. Site information is stored in JSON, and the app uses Next.js API routes for server-side data requests. We did not use a database or specialized hardware.

Our approach combines a 2D sky view, timelines, a 3D lunar explorer, and scenario comparison in one tool. We considered clarity for non-specialists, local-time and UTC handling, transparent separation of live and illustrative data, and the limits of the available science. The current app does not calculate LOLA terrain obstruction, power generation, landing safety, or a verified communications link budget; its visibility results are geometric estimates.
