projectDetails.name: Echoes in the Dust: NASA’s Forgotten Explorers.
projectDetails.summary:
Echoes in the Dust is an interactive educational web application designed to introduce school-age students to the retired NASA rovers, landers, and instruments resting across the Moon, Mars, and deep space. Built using HTML, Tailwind CSS, and JavaScript, the platform transforms technical mission archives into an engaging, story-driven digital museum.

To address the challenge, the web app lets young explorers switch between interactive hubs for the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space to uncover the stories of iconic hardware—including the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicles, the Opportunity and Spirit rovers, the InSight lander, and the Ingenuity helicopter. Rather than reading dry specifications, students explore first-person "field journals" written from each machine's perspective, inspect their current status, and unlock interactive science cards explaining key discoveries (such as finding ancient water evidence on Mars or measuring moonquakes).

By framing discarded hardware as historic monuments of human curiosity rather than forgotten scrap, Silent Pioneers makes planetary science accessible and inspires the next generation of STEM explorers.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do or how does it work?
Echoes in the Dust: NASA’s Forgotten Explorers is an interactive, story-driven educational web application that transforms NASA’s retired and dormant hardware across the Moon, Mars, and deep space into an immersive digital museum for school-age students. Instead of presenting young learners with dense technical tables, the platform lets users step into the role of a planetary mission specialist tracking six iconic pieces of space hardware: the Opportunity rover, the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter, the InSight lander, the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle (Moon Buggy), the Apollo 11 Laser Ranging Retroreflector, and Voyager 1.

Users navigate the experience through three core interactive modules:

  1. Orbital Surface Scanner & Dynamic Sector Themes: Users can filter missions across Mars, the Moon, and Deep Space. Switching sectors dynamically shifts the UI color palette and alters the physics of an HTML5 Canvas background particle engine to simulate Martian dust, lunar regolith, or deep-space starfields. Clicking or hovering over radar blips locks onto the exact landing coordinates of each spacecraft.
    • Echo Log: Delivers a first-person diary entry via an animated typewriter readout, shares the spacecraft’s real final transmission, and explains why the hardware was left behind or how it continues to function.
    • The Science Unlocked: Breaks down three major scientific discoveries per mission alongside kid-friendly engineering facts.
    • Clear Dust & Earn Badge: Features a touch- and mouse-enabled HTML5 Canvas mini-game where students physically scrub accumulated planetary dust off a virtual solar array to reveal a "Mission Specialist" quiz question. Answering correctly unlocks custom mission badges accompanied by synthesized telemetry sound effects.

What benefits does it have? What is the intended impact of the project? 
For school-age space enthusiasts, official mission archives can feel intimidating and overly technical. Furthermore, public discussions often label retired spacecraft as "space junk." Echoes in the Dust reframes these machines as heroic pioneers and time capsules of human ingenuity. By combining first-person storytelling with tactile interactivity, the project promotes STEM literacy, improves retention of planetary science concepts (such as Martian geology, seismic activity, and Earth-Moon laser ranging), and inspires students to see engineering as a human story of curiosity and perseverance. Because it runs entirely in a standard web browser with zero installations or logins, teachers and students can use it immediately on any classroom tablet, Chromebook, or desktop.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?
Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+).
  • Styling & UI: Tailwind CSS for responsive layout design, custom CSS keyframe animations for radar sweeps and glassmorphism panels, and inline SVG graphics.
  • Interactive Graphics: HTML5 Canvas API for both the real-time cosmic dust background simulation and the interactive solar-panel scrubbing canvas (globalCompositeOperation = 'destination-out').
  • Audio Synthesis: Web Audio API to procedurally generate sci-fi UI clicks, radar pings, and badge-unlock chimes directly in the browser without requiring external audio files.
  • Development & Hosting: Developed on Windows 11 and hosted publicly as a fast, single-file static web application.

How is your project creative? What factors did your team consider?
Creativity & Factors Considered

  • Empathy-Driven Gamification: Rather than just telling students that Martian dust storms ended Opportunity and InSight's missions, the solar-panel scrubbing mechanic lets students experience that environmental challenge firsthand.
  • Accessibility & Zero-Friction Deployment: Knowing that school networks often block heavy downloads or external media assets, the entire application was engineered as a self-contained, lightweight architecture using procedural audio and vector graphics.
  • Age-Appropriate Balance: Every mission profile balances emotional storytelling ("last words" and first-person logs) with accurate NASA science and real operational statuses—clearly distinguishing between dormant hardware (Opportunity, InSight), passive instruments still used today (Apollo 11 Retroreflector), and active deep-space probes (Voyager 1).

For the README.md and the code refer this link:

https://github.com/xxalfyxd/echoesinthedust.git

projectDetails.name: Project RITCE
projectDetails.summary:
We developed "The Brave Little Explorer with the Atomic Heart," an illustrated, narrative-driven storybook that brings the historic 1976 NASA Viking 1 mission to life for young learners.

To address the challenge of making complex space exploration accessible and engaging, we translated real planetary science, engineering milestones, and NASA mission data into an emotionally resonant, chapter-by-chapter adventure. Through relatable analogies—such as "bunny suits" for planetary protection, an "atomic heart" for radioisotope power, and a "robot chef" for soil biology experiments—our story breaks down intricate aerospace concepts like orbital mapping, atmospheric entry, and telemetry into intuitive, memorable lessons without losing scientific accuracy.

This project is important because inspiring the next generation of explorers begins with sparking curiosity early. By humanizing robotic spaceflight and highlighting both the triumphs and human vulnerability behind deep-space missions, our story bridges the gap between technical STEM history and creative storytelling, empowering young readers to see themselves as future scientists, engineers, and pioneers of the next frontier.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, "The Brave Little Explorer with the Atomic Heart", is an educational storytelling project based on NASA's Viking 1 mission to Mars.

The story follows a little robot named Vicky, representing the Viking 1 lander, and her companion Orby, representing the Viking orbiter. It describes their journey from Earth to Mars, the landing process, and the exploration of the Martian surface. It also explains how Viking 1 captured photographs, collected soil samples and conducted experiments to investigate the possibility of life on Mars.

The main aim of this project is to make space science easy, interesting and enjoyable, especially for children and students.

Benefits: This project helps students understand Mars exploration, develops scientific curiosity and creates awareness about space technology.

Intended Impact: To inspire young learners to explore astronomy, science and future space missions.

Tools Used: Canva, Google Gemini, ChatGPT and Heyzine were used for designing, content development, creative writing and improving the presentation of the project.

Creativity and Innovation: The project presents a real NASA space mission through an imaginative robot adventure. Using storytelling, fictional characters and simple language makes complex scientific information easier to understand and remember.

Factors Considered: We considered scientific accuracy, creativity, educational value, simplicity of language and accessibility for young learners while developing this project.

projectDetails.summary:
Project Summary – Field Shift: Adaptive Crop Rotation Tool

We developed Field Shift, an adaptive crop rotation decision-support tool that helps farmers make better farming decisions using NASA Earth observation data and local soil information. The project integrates NASA datasets, including SMAP, GPM IMERG, ECOSTRESS, Landsat, and MODIS, to analyse soil moisture, rainfall, temperature, and crop health. It compares three farming strategies: traditional monocropping, legume cover sequencing, and drought-tolerant millet mixtures, helping farmers identify suitable crop rotation plans based on local conditions.

The tool addresses climate-related agricultural challenges such as water scarcity, extreme heat, soil degradation, and unpredictable rainfall. It provides practical recommendations that balance water conservation, soil health, and crop productivity.

This project is important because it promotes sustainable agriculture, reduces irrigation requirements, improves soil moisture retention, and supports farmers in adapting to climate change. By transforming NASA satellite data into actionable farming insights, Field Shift aims to build more resilient farms and secure future food production.
projectDetails.details:
How it works: It analyses soil moisture, rainfall, temperature, and crop health using NASA datasets such as SMAP, GPM IMERG, ECOSTRESS, Landsat, MODIS, and NASA POWER. It compares three farming strategies: traditional monocropping, legume cover sequencing, and drought-tolerant millet mixtures.

Benefits and intended impact:

Reduces irrigation water requirements.

Improves soil health and moisture retention.

Helps farmers adapt to drought and extreme heat.

Promotes sustainable farming and food security.

projectDetails.name: Terraspace
projectDetails.summary:
Our project identifies and maps terrestrial analog sites on Earth that closely replicate the geological, environmental, and extreme surface conditions of permanent Moon base locations and Mars landing zones. By analyzing remote sensing data, terrain elevation, and climate metrics, we developed a framework to pinpoint Earth-based testing grounds that mirror lunar craters, regolith compositions, and Martian deserts.
This solution directly addresses the challenge of preparing for deep-space exploration without incurring the extreme costs and risks of off-world trial runs. Having verified analog locations allows scientists and engineers to rigorously test rovers, life-support habitats, and astronaut exploration protocols in realistic conditions before launch. Ultimately, this research is vital for reducing mission failure risks, accelerating space technology readiness, and ensuring crew safety as humanity prepares for sustained planetary settlement
projectDetails.details: Our project identifies Earth-based analog sites that closely replicate the terrain and environmental conditions of potential permanent bases on the Moon and Mars. projectDetails.name: Burning activty calender
projectDetails.summary:
Burning Activity Calendar is a single-page web app that turns satellite active-fire detections into a year-by-week calendar for any area you choose.
The problem it addresses: MODIS and VIIRS can't be compared directly. VIIRS has a finer pixel and finds more small fires, so raw counts jump when VIIRS begins. 
Harmonization: For your area, it takes the ratio of VIIRS to MODIS detections over the fully overlapping years .The ratio is recomputed per area.
projectDetails.details:
What it does: A web app that turns satellite fire detections into one consistent year-by-week calendar for any area. MODIS (2000 onward) and VIIRS (2012 onward) can’t be compared directly, because VIIRS finds more small fires. The user picks an area. The app compares the two sensors over the years both cover (2013 onward) and rescales earlier MODIS counts to match VIIRS. The calendar can be coloured by how unusual each week is, and it also lists the busiest weeks of a normal year and the most unusual weeks on record.

Benefits:

  • Responders can see when fire seasons normally peak.
  • Land managers can tell whether a season is unusual.
  • Scientists get a record in which all years are comparable.
  • It needs no account or server, and it keeps data on the user’s device.

Impact: People who work with fire can tell real changes from changes of sensor. That supports earlier preparation, better use of resources and tracking of long-term shifts. It is free and light, so small agencies and students can use it.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript with the canvas, NASA FIRMS CSV files, Node.js with pptxgenjs for the slides, and Claude as an AI assistant. Any laptop or phone with a browser is enough.

Creativity: It shows when fires happen, not just where. It colours weeks by unusualness, recalculates the sensor ratio for each area, and shows raw against harmonized totals. It is a single file that anyone can host.

Factors considered: Sensor differences, overlap years, local variation, data quality, skewed counts, mobile use and privacy. Limits: the demo data is synthetic, one ratio per area ignores seasonal and land-cover differences, and the method hasn’t been validated against real FIRMS data.

projectDetails.name: Project SOL III
projectDetails.summary:
Monsoon Detective is a NASA Space Apps Challenge project by Team SOL III that aims to investigate how monsoon rainfall patterns are changing in Kerala, beginning with Idukki district. The project uses NASA's GPM IMERG Final Monthly V07 satellite rainfall data to study rainfall trends from 2002 onward, focusing on June–September monsoon rainfall.

The project follows four main stages: collecting NASA satellite data, preparing and checking the data, analysing rainfall trends, and presenting the findings through charts, maps, and an interactive Streamlit dashboard. Statistical methods such as linear trend analysis, the Mann-Kendall test, and Sen's slope are used to identify the direction, magnitude, and significance of rainfall changes. Trends are considered meaningful only when they pass the significance test (p less than 0.05).

Users will be able to select a district and explore rainfall trends, their significance, and uncertainty. Initially focused on Idukki, the project aims to expand across Kerala, validate findings using India Meteorological Department data, and eventually support extreme-rainfall alerts and a Malayalam-language interface. The project promotes open data, transparent analysis, and evidence-based understanding of monsoon changes.
projectDetails.details:
# **Project Details – Monsoon Detective**

### **1. What does your project do and how does it work?**

Monsoon Detective investigates changes in monsoon rainfall patterns in Kerala, initially focusing on Idukki. It uses NASA GPM IMERG satellite data, processes rainfall records, and applies statistical methods to identify trends. The findings are presented through charts, maps, and an interactive Streamlit dashboard.

### **2. What are the benefits of your project?**

The project helps people understand changing rainfall patterns, identify significant rainfall trends, and access complex satellite data in a simple visual format. It can provide useful insights for farmers, researchers, and disaster-management authorities.

### **3. What is the intended impact of the project?**

The project aims to improve awareness of changing monsoon patterns and support better agricultural planning, water-resource management, and disaster preparedness. In the future, it hopes to expand its analysis to all districts of Kerala.

### **4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?**

The project uses NASA GPM IMERG data collected through NASA Earthdata. Python is used for data processing and analysis, while Streamlit is used to develop the interactive dashboard. Charts and maps help visualise the results.

### **5. How is your project creative or innovative?**

It transforms complex satellite rainfall data into simple, interactive visual information. Instead of just displaying rainfall measurements, it identifies trends and checks their statistical significance, helping users explore rainfall changes more effectively.

### **6. What factors did your team consider?**

Our team considered data reliability, geographical accuracy, statistical significance, accessibility, and scalability. We also considered the challenges of analysing rainfall in Idukki's mountainous terrain and the importance of validating satellite findings with IMD ground-based rainfall records.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: BUILDSCAPES: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
projectDetails.summary:
**Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer** is an interactive 3D educational experience designed to introduce young learners to the challenges of human space exploration. Players take on the role of astronauts, undertaking simulated missions on the Moon and Mars, exploring environments, completing objectives, and managing essential resources such as water, oxygen, food, and power.

The project combines immersive first-person exploration, mission progression, habitat management, educational quizzes, and NOVA, an in-game mission guide character, to make space science engaging and accessible. Its missions are inspired by the lunar South Pole and Jezero Crater, helping learners understand the scientific and operational challenges of exploring other worlds.

By combining interactive gameplay with educational content and links to real scientific resources, the project aims to inspire curiosity, develop critical thinking, and encourage an interest in STEM among young learners.
projectDetails.details:
Source Code Repository:
https://github.com/thomasjoseph18/Junior-Astronaut-Mission-Trainer

Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a browser-based educational 3D game developed to introduce children to the challenges of human space exploration through interactive missions on the Moon and Mars.

Players explore simulated extraterrestrial environments, complete mission objectives, operate rovers, manage habitat resources, and make decisions involving water, food, oxygen, power, and radiation protection. The experience includes first-person exploration, mission progression, a journal, achievements, educational question-and-answer activities, multiple-choice quizzes, mission debriefs, and NOVA, an in-game mission guide character.

The lunar mission is inspired by the lunar South Pole and Shackleton Rim, while the Mars mission is inspired by Jezero Crater. These locations provide educational context for understanding planetary exploration. The project also provides links to scientific learning resources from NASA and Caltech.

The terrain is procedurally generated rather than rendered from downloaded NASA elevation datasets. NASA scientific resources are used as references and educational material, not as direct terrain inputs.

The project was developed using web technologies, including TypeScript, React, and 3D graphics technology. It combines interactive simulation, visual storytelling, and educational gameplay to make complex space exploration concepts easier for young learners to understand.

Its intended impact is to promote curiosity, scientific thinking, problem-solving, and interest in STEM through an accessible and engaging space exploration experience.

projectDetails.name: Project Solo Mission
projectDetails.summary:
Mission Architect is a game where you build a real space mission yourself. Pick a target, whether that’s a Mars rover, a lunar south pole prospector, or an orbiter around Europa, then assemble the spacecraft piece by piece: the rocket, the power source, the antenna, the instruments, and the ground stations that keep you in touch. Everything has to fit a budget.

Then comes the nervous part: a flight readiness review, a launch, and a debrief that shows where your design shone and where it fell short.

Real NASA planet data shapes the results. Sunlight is faint at Mars and nearly gone at Europa, so a power choice that works in one place can fail in another.

Space engineering can feel locked away behind expertise. This lets anyone feel what it’s like to balance trade-offs, make tough calls, and send something out into the solar system.
projectDetails.details: Mission Architect is a browser game where you design a real space mission yourself. Pick a destination (a Mars rover, a lunar south pole prospector, or a Europa orbiter), then build the spacecraft step by step, from the rocket and power system to the antenna and instruments, all within a budget. A readiness review checks your design against physics-based rules, using real NASA planet data, and then you watch the launch and see your score. You can play solo, against friends, or co-op, with each player taking a role like engineer or scientist. It’s built with TypeScript, React, and Vite, hosted on Vercel, with planets drawn on canvas and music synthesized in the browser. Our goal is to help students feel what it’s like to make hard trade-offs and work as a team to send something into space.

projectDetails.name: SPACE TIME CAPSULE: Humanity's Footprints Beyond Earth
projectDetails.summary: SPACE TIME CAPSULE is an interactive 3D digital museum and educational storytelling platform that chronicles the equipment NASA left across the Moon, Mars, and deep space. From the Apollo 11 Lunar Laser Retroreflector (which still reflects laser pulses today after 55 years) to the retired Ingenuity helicopter, this application combines a scientifically grounded 3D solar system with authentic NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) records, verified landing coordinates, and student-focused explainers ("What Did This Machine Teach Humanity?"), bridging historical space archaeology with next-generation STEM learning.
projectDetails.details:
Since the 1960s, NASA has deployed advanced robotic probes, lunar landers, rovers, and scientific instruments across our solar system. When missions end or hardware is left behind, these machines do not vanish—they become archaeological time capsules that continue to inform science.

The Problem

School-age space enthusiasts and the general public usually hear about active, ongoing missions. The silent sentinels—such as the Surveyor landers, Viking stations, Apollo descent stages, lunar rovers, and deep-space emissaries—are frequently forgotten or misunderstood as "space junk." Furthermore, educational materials often lack scientific rigor, featuring cartoonish planets or fabricated landing coordinates.

The Solution: Space Time Capsule

Space Time Capsule solves this through three core pillars:

1. Scientific Integrity: Every landing coordinate is verified against NASA LROC and HiRISE high-resolution orbital imagery (e.g. Apollo 11 at `0.67416° N, 23.47314° E`; Curiosity at `4.5895° S, 137.4417° E`).

2. Accurate 3D Celestial Visualization: Using Three.js and React Three Fiber, the application visualizes all 8 major planets with authentic axial tilts (Uranus rolling on its side at 97.8°, Venus spinning in retrograde), real rotation periods, and disclosed orbital scaling, accompanied by a 2D accessible fallback view.

3. Engaging Educational Storytelling: Every hardware record features a special section—"WHAT DID THIS MACHINE TEACH HUMANITY?"—translating complex geophysics into accessible, wonder-inspiring insights for school students.

projectDetails.name: Project Space Conqueror
projectDetails.summary:
I developed Space Conqueror, an interactive 3D lunar mission navigator engineered to evaluate Artemis candidate landing sites at the Moon’s South Pole.

Addressing the challenge of extreme polar topography and permanently shadowed terrain, I synthesized authentic NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LOLA) elevation datasets into a real-time WebGL mission cockpit. Working with Google Antigravity as an engineering partner, I built the platform using React, TypeScript, and Three.js to simulate low-angle solar illumination, dynamic slope hazard heatmaps, and traversability. High-fidelity Artemis lander and rover assemblies were modeled with aerospace precision in CATIA V5 and SolidWorks, textured with photorealistic lunar regolith materials in Blender, and integrated with ground-contact physics.

This tool is critical because Artemis missions require finding landing corridors that balance continuous solar energy, Earth line-of-sight communications, and safe slope gradients. Space Conqueror bridges raw planetary science and accessible simulation, empowering engineers and planners to de-risk surface operations before touchdown.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do or how does it work?

I built Space Conqueror as an interactive, browser-based 3D mission cockpit designed to evaluate and navigate Artemis landing zones across the Moon’s South Pole.

The application works by taking raw planetary data from NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO)—specifically the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) 240-meter-per-pixel digital elevation models—and converting that data into true-to-scale 3D terrain meshes. Across six key Artemis candidate landing sites (Shackleton Rim, Malapert Massif, Connecting Ridge, Mons Mouton, Nobile, and Haworth), the cockpit simulates:

  1. Low-Angle Polar Lighting: Because the Sun sits barely above the lunar horizon at the poles, mountains cast long, pitch-black shadows across crater floors. Space Conqueror dynamically calculates solar angles to show shifting shadow boundaries in real time.
  2. Slope Hazard Heatmaps: The system computes analytical surface gradients across every meter of the terrain, dynamically painting slopes green (<10∘<10^\circ<10∘), yellow (10∘–15∘10^\circ–15^\circ10∘–15∘), or red (>15∘>15^\circ>15∘) so landing planners can immediately spot rollover hazards.
  3. Interactive Surface Operations: Users can zoom from orbit down to ground level to inspect a CAD-engineered Artemis Lander touching down on real lunar dirt, deploy a cargo ramp, and drive a compliant-wheeled Lunar Rover across the crater rims using real-time terrain raycasting and suspension physics.

What benefits does it have?

  • Zero-Install, Universal Access: Planetary scientists and mission planners typically rely on heavy desktop GIS software (ArcGIS, QGIS, or custom SPICE toolsets) that require high-end workstations and extensive training. Space Conqueror runs entirely in a web browser at 60 FPS on any laptop or phone.
  • Unified Multi-Hazard Visibility: Instead of switching between disconnected 2D maps for elevation, lighting, and communications, Space Conqueror combines solar exposure, slope gradients, and direct-to-Earth visibility into one cohesive visual environment.
  • Ground-Level Operational Testing: You don’t just look at a contour map—you can physically drive a rover across the terrain to test egress routes, identify blind spots behind boulder ridges, and plan traversable corridors before metal touches regolith.

What is the intended impact of the project?

Returning astronauts to the Moon is the most complex spaceflight challenge of this decade. The primary goal of Space Conqueror is to de-risk surface operations at the South Pole. By transforming raw scientific rasters into an intuitive, interactive tool, it helps mission planners, university researchers, and aerospace engineers quickly vet landing sites for solar power stability and terrain navigability.

Beyond engineering, it bridges the gap between deep planetary science and the public. Anyone in the world can open the link, explore the South Pole candidate sites, and understand why landing at the lunar pole is so uniquely challenging and exciting.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Google Antigravity: My autonomous AI engineering partner throughout the challenge. Antigravity helped architect the end-to-end full-stack system, synthesize the Three.js rendering pipelines, automate data transformations, and verify mathematical accuracy.
  • Aerospace CAD (CATIA V5 & SolidWorks): Parametrically designed the mechanical assemblies for the Artemis Lunar Lander (descent frame, ascent stage, engine bell, quad landing gear) and the Lunar Rover (compliant wire-mesh wheels, rocker-bogie chassis, sensor mast) to real aerospace engineering standards.
  • Blender (Python 3D Pipeline): Textured the vehicles with physically based rendering (PBR) regolith materials, modeled realistic lunar optical properties, and baked optimized GLTF/GLB models for low-latency web streaming.
  • NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) & LOLA: Provided authentic polar elevation rasters (ldem_75s_240m) that form the physical bedrock of the topography.
  • Frontend Cockpit: Built with React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and Three.js / WebGL for in-browser real-time lighting, shadow maps, and ground-contact physics.
  • Scientific Backend: Python & FastAPI, integrating orbital mechanics and ephemeris validation against JPL standards.
  • Deployment & Version Control: Git, GitHub, and Vercel serverless edge hosting.

How is your project creative?

Traditional space mission planning relies on static 2D heatmaps and contour charts. Space Conqueror’s creativity lies in merging aerospace CAD precision with real-time video game mechanics and authentic planetary science.

Instead of reading a report stating that a slope is 16 degrees or that sunlight is lost at 14:00 UTC, the user is immersed directly on the surface: you can watch the Sun dip below the jagged crater rim, cast a 12-kilometer shadow over your solar panels, and test whether your rover can climb out of a permanently shadowed crater trap. It turns dry numbers into a tangible human experience.

What factors did your team consider?

  1. The South Pole’s Extreme Illumination Geometry: The Sun hovers at only 1.5∘1.5^\circ1.5∘ above the horizon. We had to calculate exact solar vectors because a slight dip in terrain can plunge equipment into cryogenic temperatures (40 K40\text{ K}40 K) and complete power loss.
  2. Lander Tip-Over & Rover Rollover Thresholds: Artemis landers cannot safely land on slopes exceeding 12∘–15∘12^\circ–15^\circ12∘–15∘. We prioritized immediate visual gradient detection so unviable zones are immediately flagged.
  3. Direct Line-of-Sight Communications: Lunar mountains easily block direct microwave links back to Earth. We factored in horizon clearance so landing corridors maintain reliable comms links.
  4. Web Optimization & Low-Latency Streaming: Large lunar DEM rasters and complex CAD assemblies can easily freeze a web browser. We implemented dynamic geometric level-of-detail (LOD), binary GLB compression, and asynchronous shader initialization to ensure butter-smooth 60 FPS performance on standard consumer hardware.

projectDetails.details:
NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 – Kanjirappally Local Event Title of the proposal: Creating MICROSPACE: A space biology–inspired digital health platform for early detection and prevention of diabetic microvascular and tissue complications.

Mission: Discovering how the human body adapts to space to develop smarter strategies for protecting human health on Earth and beyond.

Proposed Team

1. Dr Jobin K Thomas Paika, Director, DIA Heals Pvt Ltd, Kottayam, Kerala

2. Dr Sweety Jobin, Senior Scientist, DIA Heals Pvt Ltd, Kottayam, Kerala

3. Dr Goutam Chandra, Senior Scientist, Inter University Center for Biomedical Research & Super Specialty Hospital, Kottayam, Kerala

4. Dr Anoop Raj JR, Associate Professor, Department of Food Technology, Amal Jyothi College of Engineering, Kanjirapally, Kottayam, Kerala

5. Mathew Roy, Food and Nutrition specialist, DIA Heals Pvt Ltd, Kottayam, Kerala

6. Christina Maria Roy, Clinical Nutrion & Dietetics Student

summary of the proposal :Long-duration spaceflight exposes astronauts to a unique combination of physiological stressors, including microgravity, ionizing radiation, physical unloading, circadian disruption and environmental confinement. These stressors can adversely affect cardiovascular function, vascular regulation, skeletal muscle, bone metabolism, mitochondrial bioenergetics and tissue repair. Interestingly, several of these physiological changes have parallels in chronic diabetes mellitus, particularly in individuals who develop progressive microvascular complications, peripheral neuropathy, muscle dysfunction, impaired angiogenesis and non-healing diabetic foot ulcers. MICROSPACE proposes an innovative Space-to-Earth translational health platform that integrates publicly available NASA space biology data, physiological health indicators and clinical parameters associated with diabetic complications. The platform will use data-driven analytical approaches to identify overlapping biological pathways and develop a prototype system for monitoring tissue health, detecting early warning signals and supporting personalised preventive interventions. The project will establish two interconnected applications: (i) an astronaut health-monitoring framework for identifying physiological changes associated with prolonged space missions and (ii) a terrestrial clinical application for identifying individuals at increased risk of diabetic microvascular and tissue complications. By combining space biology, clinical research, artificial intelligence, mitochondrial pharmacology and integrative healthcare, MICROSPACE aims to transform discoveries from human space exploration into innovative approaches for preventing chronic diabetic complications on Earth.

Scientific rationale :The human body undergoes substantial physiological adaptations during prolonged spaceflight. Reduced mechanical loading, altered gravity, radiation exposure and other spaceflight-associated stressors can affect multiple organ systems. People living with long-standing diabetes also experience progressive alterations in several interconnected physiological systems. Chronic hyperglycaemia, oxidative stress, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation and impaired mitochondrial function contribute to vascular and neural injury, defective tissue repair and progressive organ dysfunction. We propose that selected biological pathways involved in spaceflight-associated physiological deterioration may provide useful insights into the mechanisms underlying diabetic complications.

The major areas of potential convergence include: a. Microvascular dysfunction and impaired tissue perfusion :Spaceflight-associated cardiovascular and vascular adaptations may provide insights into the regulation of tissue perfusion, vascular function and oxygen delivery. In diabetes, endothelial dysfunction and microvascular injury compromise tissue oxygenation and nutrient delivery, contributing to peripheral tissue damage and delayed wound healing. b. Mitochondrial dysfunction and cellular energy depletion: Mitochondrial bioenergetics and oxidative stress are important determinants of cellular adaptation to environmental stress. Mitochondrial dysfunction and excessive reactive oxygen species generation are also implicated in diabetic vascular injury, neuropathy and impaired tissue regeneration. c. Musculoskeletal deterioration: Spaceflight-associated unloading promotes muscle atrophy and alterations in bone remodelling. Chronic diabetes is associated with impaired muscle function, sarcopenia and abnormalities in bone quality and metabolism. d. Impaired angiogenesis and tissue regeneration: Changes in vascular signalling and tissue repair during spaceflight provide an opportunity to investigate mechanisms

projectDetails.name: FireX
projectDetails.summary: We built FireX for the NASA Space Apps Challenge—an interactive 3D map that brings together and cleans up years of active fire data across India from 2022 to 2026. The main headache with satellite data is that different sensors catch fires differently. To fix that, FireX cross-calibrates NASA's MODIS (1km) and VIIRS (375m) feeds using pixel-area math so everything lines up on the same page. The app lets you explore a sleek 3D globe where you can zoom smoothly from a national overview right down to individual states and districts, scrub through a seasonal time-lapse player, and check out detailed stats. It’s built to actually be useful: it gives local communities a heads-up on seasonal burning cycles, helps researchers dig into exact burn sizes and thermal power, and gives forest departments and emergency crews the clear insights they need to dispatch help where it's needed most. Ultimately, it’s about turning heavy, complicated NASA space telemetry into something clean, fast, and genuinely impactful.
projectDetails.details:
When we started building FireX for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we wanted to tackle a real headache with satellite data: different sensors see the world differently. To fix that, we built an interactive 3D geospatial dashboard that harmonizes NASA's MODIS (1km) and VIIRS (375m) fire feeds across India from 2022 to 2026, bringing everything onto a single, reliable scale using pixel-area normalization.

We wanted the app to feel like a modern mission-control tool. Users get a sleek 3D globe where they can smoothly zoom from a national view (L1) down to individual states (L2) and districts (L3), scrub through a seasonal time-lapse player, and click districts to check out burn areas (km2) and sensor breakdowns. On the tech side, we put it together using react-globe.gl, Three.js, custom Geo JSON mapping, and a Python-powered data pipeline.

Beyond the code, we really focused on making it useful. FireX gives local communities early visibility into regional burning cycles, helps researchers analyze precise thermal data, and gives forest departments and emergency responders clear insights to track fire intensity and allocate resources where they're needed most. It's all about turning heavy satellite telemetry into something fast, clean, and genuinely helpful.

projectDetails.summary:
OUTPOST ZERO is a browser-based space survival game where players take charge of a small astronaut outpost. Their task is to manage limited power and keep important systems running while looking after the crew. As the mission progresses, players must think carefully about how they use their resources and deal with the challenges of living on the Moon. projectDetails.details:
Play the game here: https://aleetaminnu.github.io/junior-astronaut-outpost-zero/

Github repository: https://github.com/Aleetaminnu/junior-astronaut-outpost-zero

​

The game begins with the player taking charge of an outpost on the Moon. The mission is divided into days, and the player has a limited amount of power to work with. They must keep track of important resources such as air, food and radiation shielding, while also making sure that the crew remains healthy.

You need to scroll down the how to play page to find 'Start mission' button.

*Some cool features:* Tapping the buildings on the small overview map also takes you there. You can move to a tapped location during gameplay even if it is not a building.


The Mission Control screen displays the current stage, day and resource levels. This helps players understand the condition of their outpost before deciding what to do next. The player can interact with the outpost and advance the mission using the END DAY button.

Space weather is also included in the game. The page checks NASA's DONKI database for space-weather information when it is available. If the data cannot be reached, the game can use saved events instead. This helps introduce players to the effects that space weather can have on space missions.

The resource values have been simplified for gameplay. They are not meant to be exact measurements of a real Moon mission, but they help demonstrate why power, life support and radiation protection are important.

We wanted the game to be simple enough for young players to understand while still giving them a small idea of the challenges astronauts and mission planners face.

projectDetails.name: Silent Explorers
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, "Silent Explorers: The Untold Stories of Forgotten Machines on the Moon and Mars," focuses on the spacecraft, rovers, and scientific equipment sent by NASA to explore the Moon and Mars. Although many of these machines have completed their missions or stopped functioning, they remain on these planets as reminders of human achievements in space exploration.
The project highlights important missions such as Surveyor 3, Apollo lunar missions, Spirit, and Opportunity. It explains their scientific contributions, discoveries about the lunar surface, and evidence of ancient water on Mars.
The main aim of this project is to understand the importance of these forgotten machines and appreciate their contributions to space science. Even though their missions have ended, their discoveries continue to inspire future generations of space explorers.
Main Message:
"Every forgotten machine carries a story of human curiosity, courage, and discovery. Their missions may have ended, but their contributions will never be forgotten."
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works
Our project is an educational storytelling experience designed to bring NASA’s retired lunar and Martian spacecraft back to life for school-age learners. Instead of presenting technical mission logs as dry facts, we turn historical missions—including Surveyor 3, Apollo lunar missions, Spirit, and Opportunity—into engaging, easy-to-follow stories. Each section introduces the spacecraft, explains what it discovered about the lunar surface or ancient water on Mars, and shows where it rests today as a monument to human exploration.
Benefits & Intended Impact
Many students know about active rovers like Perseverance, but few realize how much our current space knowledge relies on earlier, retired hardware. Our goal is to spark curiosity in young learners by showing that "abandoned" spacecraft are not forgotten failures—they are scientific pioneers. By connecting their discoveries to modern space exploration, the project inspires students to see space history as an ongoing human story they can be part of.
Tools & Resources Used
• NASA Open Data & Media: We used official NASA mission archives, historical summaries, and public-domain imagery (properly credited to NASA/JPL-Caltech) to ensure scientific accuracy.

• Creation & Design Tools: We created and formatted the final presentation using Google Slides
• AI Assistance: We used Google Gemini as a brainstorming and writing assistant to help organize the narrative structure and simplify complex planetary science concepts for a younger audience.

Creativity & Key Factors Considered
To make the project creative and accessible without relying on complex code, we focused on strong visual storytelling and age-appropriate language. When designing the narrative, we considered how to balance real scientific milestones—such as Opportunity's evidence of past water on Mars—with relatable themes of resilience, discovery, and legacy so students stay engaged from start to finish.

Project Summary: GeoWave Jukebox

What we developed

We developed **GeoWave Jukebox**, an interactive, user-friendly platform inspired by a classic jukebox that translates complex NASA Earth observation data into intuitive, bite-sized visual and audio-driven "tracks." Users can select different ecological, climatological, and geophysical themes to explore real-time or historical Earth science variables.

How it addresses the challenge

projectDetails.details:
Project Details: GeoWave Jukebox

What It Does & How It Works

GeoWave Jukebox is an interactive web platform modeled after a classic jukebox that turns complex NASA Earth observation data into accessible, bite-sized multimedia "tracks." Instead of forcing users to navigate technical satellite portals, the interface allows users to browse curated environmental themes—such as climate trends, ocean dynamics, and atmospheric changes—and simply press "play." Each selected track translates raw scientific measurements into intuitive visuals, audio cues (sonification), and concise, easy-to-read explanations of what is happening on our planet.

Benefits

Zero Technical Barrier: Anyone can explore NASA data without needing prior training in data science, coding, or geographic information systems (GIS).

Multi-Sensory Engagement: Combining visual storytelling with audio elements helps users perceive patterns, shifts, and anomalies in Earth data much faster than reading static spreadsheets or dense scientific reports.

Bite-Sized Learning: Curated "tracks" break overwhelming global datasets into focused, digestible stories ideal for quick exploration or classroom lessons.

Intended Impact

Our goal is to democratize NASA’s open Earth science data and bridge the gap between scientific research and public understanding. By making planetary data feel as approachable as playing a song, GeoWave Jukebox aims to boost science and climate literacy among students, educators, and everyday citizens—empowering communities to make informed, environmentally conscious decisions.

Tools, Software & Technologies Used

Web Platform & Hosting: Google Sites (used to structure, host, and embed the interactive full-page web experience).

Frontend & Embedded Interactivity: HTML, CSS, JavaScript `[add any other tools you used, e.g., Python, Canva, Figma, audio/sonification tools, or specific NASA portals like NASA Worldview / Earthdata]`.

Data Sources: Open-access NASA Earth science datasets and satellite observations.

How Our Project Is Creative

Rather than building another traditional scientific dashboard filled with intimidating charts, we reimagined Earth data through the familiar, nostalgic metaphor of a jukebox. Framing satellite datasets as "tracks" that users can queue up and experience turns passive data consumption into an engaging, curiosity-driven discovery experience—blending art, sound, and science.

Key Factors Our Team Considered

Accessibility & User Experience (UX): We prioritized a clean, clutter-free layout so users of all ages and technical backgrounds can intuitively navigate the platform on their first visit.

Scientific Accuracy vs. Simplicity: We carefully balanced simplifying complex Earth science concepts while staying faithful to NASA’s underlying data and scientific insights.

projectDetails.name: ARES AGRI
projectDetails.summary:
ARES AGRI is an interactive web-based project exploring the agronomic and engineering systems required to establish sustainable agriculture on Mars. It translates complex aerospace and botanical concepts into an immersive, data-rich platform documenting how to transform toxic Martian regolith into fertile biomass.

The project highlights six core environmental hurdles—such as perchlorate toxicity, extreme cold, and cosmic radiation—alongside technical paradigms like high-pressure aeroponics, bio-remediated regolith, and microalgae photobioreactors. Key features include real-time mission telemetry simulating the Jezero Crater, a curated Martian crop catalog, and an interactive Greenhouse Simulator where users adjust environmental parameters to test colony survival.

Designed as a comprehensive technical showcase, ARES AGRI bridges front-end development with advanced scientific research to visualize self-sustaining off-world life support systems.
projectDetails.details:
ARES AGRI is an interactive, data-driven web application that serves as a conceptual blueprint for establishing a self-sustaining biosphere on Mars. Built as an educational and technical project, it explores the intersection of aerospace engineering, astrobotany, and web development to visualize how humans could survive on a barren planet.

Here is a detailed breakdown of the project, how its mechanics function, and its practical utility:

1. Project Details (What It Is)

The website acts as a comprehensive digital dashboard for a hypothetical Martian farming colony (Ares-Biodome-04 in Jezero Crater). It translates dense scientific concepts into an accessible, visually engaging platform. The project systematically addresses the reality of off-world survival by breaking it down into:

  • The 6 Lethal Hurdles: Explaining the dangers of perchlorate-toxic soil, extreme cold, cosmic radiation, partial gravity, solar dimming, and the lack of nitrogen.
  • Agricultural Paradigms: Detailing three distinct solutions—High-Pressure Aeroponics, Bio-Remediated Regolith (treating Martian dirt with microbes), and Microalgae Photobioreactors.
  • Crop Database: A curated list of space-optimized crops like potatoes, leafy greens, and soybeans.

2. How It Works (Functional Mechanics)

From a technical and user-experience perspective, the project utilizes front-end web development (HTML, CSS, and likely JavaScript) to create an immersive, app-like environment:

  • Simulated Telemetry & UI: The header acts as a mission control interface, displaying real-time-style data like Martian Coordinated Time (MTC), current Sol days, and baseline environmental stats (temperature, pressure, solar flux). This creates immediate immersion.
  • Structured Information Flow: The layout uses anchor navigation to smoothly guide the user through the problem (Mars' harsh environment) to the solution (farming technologies) and finally to the application (the simulator).
  • Interactive Greenhouse Simulator: This is the core functional feature of the project. It uses front-end logic to allow users to act as a "Habitat Commander." By adjusting input variables like atmospheric pressure, temperature, CO2\text{CO}_2CO2​ levels, and LED photonics, users trigger calculations that output the resulting crop yield, oxygen generation, and overall colony survival rate.
  • Responsive Design: The layout is compartmentalized into data cards, side-by-side comparisons (Earth vs. Mars), and interactive modules, making heavy data easy to digest.

3. How It Is Useful (Value Proposition)

This project holds significant value across multiple domains:

  • Exceptional Portfolio Piece: For a developer or designer, it acts as a powerful resume builder. It demonstrates the ability to handle complex UI/UX design, build interactive logic (the simulator), and present dense data cleanly. It shows you can build more than just basic websites—you can build data-driven educational tools.
  • STEM Education & Science Communication: It bridges the gap between dense astrophysics papers and public curiosity. High school and college students studying biology, physics, or space exploration can use this to understand the practical challenges of colonizing Mars without reading a 50-page academic journal.
  • Interactive Conceptualization: By allowing users to tweak environmental variables in the simulator, it teaches the concept of "closed-loop systems" through cause and effect. It visually proves why relying entirely on Martian soil is dangerous and why systems like aeroponics are necessary.

TECHWO – Selene Cadet: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

Selene Cadet is an interactive web-based lunar astronaut mission simulator developed by TECHWO. Inspired by NASA's challenge, "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer," it allows students to experience simulated Moon exploration missions. Players take the role of astronaut cadets and complete three missions: Shackleton Rim Survey, Tranquillity Relay & Rover Link, and Malapert Outpost Prep. They explore lunar terrain, collect scientific data, complete mission objectives, and manage oxygen, power, and spacesuit resources. The simulator also introduces emergency response, navigation, and lunar base preparation. Through mission-based gameplay, it encourages scientific curiosity, critical thinking, problem-solving, decision-making, and resource management. Its goal is to make lunar exploration and space science more engaging and accessible to young learners.
projectDetails.details:
TECHWO – Selene Cadet: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

TECHWO has developed Selene Cadet, an interactive web-based lunar astronaut mission training simulator inspired by NASA's challenge, "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer." The project gives students an opportunity to experience the challenges of exploring and working on the Moon through simulated missions.

Users take the role of astronaut cadets and complete three lunar training missions: Shackleton Rim Survey, Tranquillity Relay & Rover Link, and Malapert Outpost Prep. During missions, they explore lunar terrain, navigate different surface zones, collect scientific information, and complete objectives using simulated scientific instruments such as simulated scientific instruments and activities, includingthermal probes, spectrometers, and regolith drills.

The simulator also introduces important survival challenges. Users must monitor oxygen, power, and spacesuit levels, use resources carefully, recharge at suitable locations, and respond to emergencies using available equipment. A mission dashboard displays the cadet's rank, training score, mission progress, and field guide notes.

The main goal is to make space science more engaging and accessible while developing students' problem-solving, critical-thinking, decision-making, teamwork, and resource-management skills. The project encourages curiosity about lunar exploration and inspires young learners to explore STEM fields.

Our project combines an interactive mission-based experience with scientific learning. We considered usability, beginner-friendly navigation, mission objectives, resource limitations, realistic lunar exploration challenges, and an engaging dark space-themed interface while designing the simulator.

Development tools: Google AI Studio was used for AI-assisted app development, and OpenAI ChatGPT was used for brainstorming, planning, writing, and development guidance. The project is designed as a browser-based application that can be accessed through a public web link.

AI tools assisted in the development process, while the project brings together our team's ideas to create an educational lunar exploration experience.

projectDetails.name: Project TENET blue
projectDetails.summary:
Imagine standing on the Moon, where a few degrees of sunlight can determine the success of an entire mission, and losing sight of Earth could mean losing communication with home. This is the challenge our project aims to solve.

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive lunar mission-planning application designed to help astronauts, scientists, and mission planners identify and compare suitable landing locations, particularly near the Moon's south pole. By combining lunar location data, date and time selection, and scientific calculations, our tool visualizes the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the lunar horizon.

Users can explore potential landing sites through interactive maps and 3D visualizations, evaluate solar elevation and sunlight availability for power generation, and identify direct-to-Earth communication windows. Our platform also enables side-by-side comparisons of different locations and landing dates, supported by clear timelines and visual indicators.

What makes our idea exciting is its ability to transform complex space science into an intuitive and engaging experience. We aim to bridge the gap between advanced scientific data and accessible technology, helping people understand the challenges of lunar exploration while supporting smarter, more informed mission planning.

Our vision: Making every landing decision smarter, every mission better prepared, and humanity's next giant leap towards the Moon a little closer.
projectDetails.details:
• What does it do or how does it work?
    TENET is an advanced web-based mission control and topographical navigation system designed for lunar exploration, focusing on lunar south polar landing sites (such as Shackleton Crater, Malapert Massif, and Nobile Rim). It operates via an interactive 3D WebGL Moon globe powered by Three.js, integrated with live NASA Lunar Mapping WMTS global mosaic tiles (LRO WAC) and LOLA (Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter) topography data. It dynamically computes selenocentric ephemeris, 29.5-day synodic solar cycles, Sun and Earth elevations, orbital mechanics, and local 360° horizon terrain occlusion masks to evaluate direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication and solar illumination windows.
    • Languages & UI: HTML5, CSS3, Tailwind CSS, JavaScript (ES6+).
    • 3D Graphics & Rendering: Three.js (r128) WebGL rendering engine.
    • Data Sources & Ephemeris: NASA Lunar Mapping WMTS REST endpoints (LRO_WAC_Mosaic_Global_303ppd_v02), LOLA DEM 5m/azimuthal horizon profiles, and JPL Horizons-based selenocentric mechanics.

projectDetails.name: The space relics
projectDetails.summary: SPACE RELICS – The Forgotten Footprints of Humanity is an interactive digital museum developed to explore abandoned and inactive equipment left behind by human missions on the Moon and Mars. Through 3D planetary interfaces, interactive location markers, and mission stories, users can discover the history and scientific contributions of these objects. It addresses the challenge by preserving their stories and raising awareness of humanity’s space exploration legacy. This project is important because it connects past discoveries with future generations and highlights the lasting impact of space exploration.
projectDetails.details: SPACE RELICS – The Forgotten Footprints of Humanity 1. What does the project do and how does it work? SPACE RELICS is an interactive digital museum designed to explore and preserve the history of human-made equipment left on the Moon and Mars. It focuses on objects such as landers, rovers, scientific instruments and other mission-related hardware that remain on planetary surfaces after their missions. The platform brings together information about these objects, their missions, locations, scientific achievements and historical significance in one accessible digital experience. Users can choose between the Moon and Mars through an interactive 3D planetary interface. They can rotate and zoom the planetary view, select highlighted markers representing different space relics, and access individual stories explaining the purpose of each object, its mission achievements and its legacy. A searchable catalogue and relevant source links provide additional information and opportunities for exploration. The project follows a simple exploration process: choose a planetary world, select an object marker, and explore its story. 2. What are the benefits of the project? SPACE RELICS provides several educational and informational benefits: - Preservation of space exploration history: Documents and highlights the stories of human-made equipment remaining on the Moon and Mars. - Improved accessibility to space information: Brings mission details, object locations and historical information together in one platform. - Interactive learning: Makes planetary exploration more engaging through 3D visualisation, selectable markers and individual object stories. - Public awareness: Helps students and the general public understand the importance of equipment used in space exploration. - Reliable information discovery: Provides source links that allow users to explore original mission and agency information. - Educational opportunities: Creates possibilities for future learning features such as timelines, quizzes and expanded object catalogues. 3. What is the intended impact of the project? The primary aim of SPACE RELICS is to make the overlooked physical legacy of human space exploration visible and meaningful to the public. Space missions are often remembered for their major discoveries, successful landings and scientific achievements. However, the equipment that made these achievements possible is frequently forgotten after missions end. Our project aims to change this perspective by presenting these objects as important evidence of human curiosity, engineering and scientific discovery. The intended impact includes: - Encouraging curiosity about planetary exploration. - Promoting awareness of the history and legacy of space missions. - Supporting space science education for students and the general public. - Making information about lunar and Martian objects easier to discover. - Encouraging responsible storytelling by distinguishing active scientific assets, inactive hardware and mission-ended objects rather than categorising everything as waste. Ultimately, SPACE RELICS aims to connect people with the history of humanity's exploration beyond Earth. 4. What tools, coding languages, hardware or software were used? The project is designed as a browser-based digital museum. Its core development requirements include: - Web technologies: HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the website structure, interface design and interactive functionality. - 3D visualisation: Interactive 3D planetary views for exploring the Moon and Mars, with rotation, zooming and selectable markers. - Data organisation: A searchable catalogue containing selected lunar and Martian objects and their mission information. - Information resources: NASA and other relevant space-agency mission information and source references. - Software environment: Web browsers and web development tools for developing and testing the experience. The project is software-focused and does not require dedicated physical hardware for its intended public-facing experience. Note: The specific 3D library, development environment and software tools should be added according to the actual technologies used by the team. 5. How is the project creative and innovative? The creativity of SPACE RELICS lies in presenting space exploration history through the concept of an interactive digital museum rather than a conventional information-based website. Instead of simply displaying a list of abandoned or inactive equipment, the project transforms planetary objects into individual stories that visitors can discover through an interactive 3D environment. Its creative features include: - Interactive planetary exploration: Users can explore the Moon and Mars through a rotatable and zoomable 3D interface. - Marker-based discovery: Glowing markers allow users to select specific objects directly from the planetary view. - Story-based presentation: Each object has an individual story explaining its mission, purpose, achievements and legacy. - Combined information experience: The platform integrates planetary visualisation, a searchable catalogue and mission source links. - A different perspective on space relics: It presents remaining equipment as historical and scientific evidence of human exploration rather than simply forgotten objects. This combination of visual exploration, storytelling and educational information makes the project an engaging way to experience the legacy of space missions. 6. What factors did the team consider? During the development and planning of SPACE RELICS, the team considered several important factors: 1. Information accuracy: Object details, locations, mission histories and current status should be verified using reliable NASA and other primary mission sources. 2. User accessibility: The interface should be understandable and easy to navigate for students and members of the public. 3. Educational value: Information should explain the purpose and significance of each object in a clear and engaging way. 4. Visual experience: The 3D planetary interface should make object discovery intuitive and interesting. 5. Historical preservation: The project should communicate the importance of equipment that remains on other planetary surfaces. 6. Responsible classification: Active scientific assets, inactive hardware and mission-ended objects should be distinguished appropriately. 7. Future scalability: The platform should support additional objects, planetary information, timelines, quizzes and accessibility improvements. 8. Source transparency: Users should be able to access original mission information through relevant references and source links. Conclusion SPACE RELICS – The Forgotten Footprints of Humanity is an interactive digital museum that connects planetary exploration with education, historical preservation and public engagement. By combining 3D planetary visualisation, object-based storytelling and searchable mission information, the project gives visibility to the equipment that remains on the Moon and Mars. Our central belief is that these objects are not merely forgotten hardware; they are evidence of human curiosity, engineering, exploration and discovery. Through SPACE RELICS, we aim to preserve their stories and inspire future generations to explore the history of humanity beyond Earth.

projectDetails.name: Project THE ODD ONES
projectDetails.summary:
Project Summary – ASTRA-MED: Autonomous Space Health Monitoring System

ASTRA-MED is an offline-first, AI-assisted health monitoring system designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. We developed a proposed software dashboard that collects and organizes health information from wearable sensors, manual medical measurements, and scheduled health assessments. It analyses health trends by comparing individual readings with pre-flight baselines and incorporates NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) research, including gene-expression findings, to understand potential spaceflight-related health risks.

The system addresses the challenge of identifying health changes in astronauts who operate in isolated environments with limited access to immediate medical assistance. It uses a colour-coded alert system (green, amber, and red) to indicate health status and provides appropriate guidance for follow-up and medical review.

ASTRA-MED is important because it can improve crew health awareness, support early identification of potential health concerns, and promote greater medical autonomy during space missions. Its approach could also benefit remote and rural communities on Earth through accessible health monitoring.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRA-MED is an offline-first, AI-assisted visual health monitoring dashboard and diagnostic guide designed specifically for non-physician astronauts on long-duration deep space missions (such as the Moon or Mars).

It operates through a structured 5-stage decision-support pipeline:

Collect: Gathers multi-modal health data through automated wearable syncing (heart rate, SpO2, body temperature, sleep) alongside guided manual logs for blood glucose, blood pressure, crew mood/fatigue check-ins, exercise adherence, and portable ultrasound imagery.

* Compare: Compares real-time physiological readings against each astronaut's personal pre-flight baseline.

* Analyse: Uses a local edge-computing analytics model to evaluate trends across cardiovascular, sleep, temperature, musculoskeletal, and immune health indicators, cross-referencing them with NASA spaceflight research norms.

* Alert: Categorises crew health status into three intuitive tiers:

* Green (Nominal): Routine reminders for hydration, exercise, and scheduled check-ups.

* Amber (Watch): Step-by-step instructions for targeted follow-up exams (e.g., ocular or spinal ultrasound).

* Red (Critical): Immediate emergency stabilisation protocols and a compressed data packet prepared for Earth flight surgeons.

* Respond: Provides clear, actionable guidance and countermeasures for the crew while preserving human clinical review.

2. What benefits does it have?

* Zero-Connectivity Autonomy: Because it runs offline-first using local edge computing, astronauts can evaluate symptoms and execute medical protocols without waiting for delayed communications with Earth.

* Accessible for Non-Physicians: Translates complex biometric trends into plain-language explanations, visual sensor-placement overlays, and step-by-step countermeasures so any crew member can act confidently.

* Early Anomaly Detection: Spots subtle physiological deviations against personal baselines before they escalate into mission-threatening medical emergencies.

* Unified Health View: Consolidates scattered wearable telemetry, self-reports, and clinical test results into a single, easy-to-read interface.

* Deep Space Mission Readiness: Directly supports crew safety, self-reliance, and sustained health on extended missions like NASA’s Artemis lunar programme and future Mars expeditions.

* Terrestrial Healthcare Access: The offline diagnostic assistant and guided self-exam workflows are directly transferable to remote, rural, and underserved communities on Earth that lack immediate access to doctors, as well as at-home monitoring for chronic health conditions.

* NASA Open Data & Research: Grounded the system's baseline modelling and risk categories using the NASA Open Science Data Repository (OSDR)—specifically the "Spaceflight Modulates Gene Expression in Astronauts" dataset (Dataset ID: 10.25966/qsf7-cr81), which analysed 234 stress-response genes across 6 astronauts pre- and post-flight—alongside NASA Human Research Program (HRP) evidence reports.

* Software & Architecture Concept: Designed as an offline-first visual web/mobile application powered by a local edge-computing analytics engine, a simulated 180-day longitudinal telemetry feed, and an offline natural-language symptom checker trained on space medicine protocols.

* Hardware Integration (Proposed): Engineered to interface with approved biometric wearables (heart rate, temperature, sleep trackers), manual clinical instruments (blood pressure and glucose monitors), and portable diagnostic ultrasound probes.

(Note: Be sure to explicitly list the specific programming languages, UI design tools like Figma, or frontend frameworks you used to build your actual prototype slides/mockup!)

* Responsible Use of Research Data: Rather than falsely treating pre-/post-flight genomic research data as a live sensor feed, the system creatively integrates NASA's gene-expression findings as background biological context to define "normal spaceflight adaptation" versus "clinical risk".

* Action-Oriented Guidance Over Raw Data: Instead of overwhelming astronauts with raw medical charts, it pairs every alert with interactive exam overlays (showing exact sensor/probe placement) and "how/why/what" protocol cards.

* Mission-Phase Adaptation: Features a Smart Check-Up Scheduler that dynamically adjusts monitoring frequency depending on whether the crew is in launch, deep-space transit, or surface EVA.

* Spaceflight Environmental Hazards: Accounted for the four primary deep-space stressors—space radiation (immune dysregulation and cellular damage), altered gravity (bone density loss, muscle atrophy, cardiovascular deconditioning), isolation/confinement (circadian disruption and cognitive fatigue), and communication latency with Earth.

* Human-in-the-Loop Clinical Safety: Explicitly designed the software to support human decision-making and clinical review rather than replacing medical professionals with automated diagnoses.

* Crew Cognitive Load: Prioritised a clean, dark-mode visual hierarchy with simple Green/Amber/Red status indicators so fatigued astronauts can interpret health trends quickly under stress.

projectDetails.details:
Orbital Foundry — 3D Space Rocket Design & Launch Simulator

Short Overview:
Orbital Foundry is an interactive, browser-based 3D aerospace engineering and spaceflight game where players design custom multi-stage rockets, customize their paint and liveries, test their designs on a launchpad, and fly missions to orbit and distant planets.

1. What does it do and how does it work?

Orbital Foundry combines a 3D vehicle assembly workshop with a real-time flight physics simulator:

  • Step-by-Step Rocket Building: Players assemble rockets from 14 modular 3D parts across six categories—Nose Cones & Crew Capsules, Body & Avionics Rings, Fuel Tanks, Engines, Jettisonable Side Boosters, and Aerodynamic Wings/Fins. Parts can be added from the builder dock or clicked directly in the 3D viewport to highlight, reorder, or remove with a 100% cost refund.
  • Customization & Pre-Flight Engineering: Players name their spacecraft, pick primary/accent colors, and apply procedural hull liveries (stripes, roll checkers, hazard bands, thermal gold foil). Live engineering diagnostics automatically calculate dry/wet mass, total thrust (kN), Thrust-to-Weight Ratio (TWR), stability score, burn time, and pre-launch warnings.
  • Launchpad, Countdown & Flight Simulation: Moving to Launch Complex 39A initiates a T-5 countdown during which umbilical gantry swing arms retract and cryogenic vapor vents. At ignition, players control throttle (0–100%), steer pitch (A/D or touch controls), jettison spent side boosters (Space), switch between four camera angles (Follow, Wide, Nozzle, Orbit), and engage time-warp (1x–10x) in space.
  • Realistic Failure Testing & Space Exploration: Improperly built rockets fail realistically—underpowered builds (TWR < 1.0) stall on the pad, and finless rockets tumble in the atmosphere—triggering a failure debrief explaining how to improve the design. Successful launches ascend through a shifting sky-to-space atmosphere past Earth's curved horizon to reach the Orbital Relay Station, The Moon, Mars, and Jupiter, earning money and fuel rewards across 6 missions.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Learn Aerospace Principles Through Play: Introduces real concepts—Thrust-to-Weight Ratio, aerodynamic drag, center-of-pressure stability, fuel-to-mass ratios, and multi-stage booster separation—in a hands-on, forgiving environment.
  • Zero Installation & Instant Accessibility: Runs directly in any modern web browser on desktop or laptop without downloads, accounts, or heavy game-engine installers.
  • Beginner-Friendly & Never Soft-Locked: Includes starter rocket presets (Scout Mk-I, Selene Explorer, Ares Heavy), optional beginner SAS flight-stabilization assist, full refunds when iterating on parts, and safety-net Space Grants so players can experiment freely.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The goal of Orbital Foundry is to spark curiosity in aerospace engineering, physics, and space exploration—especially for students and beginners who might find traditional orbital simulators intimidating. By turning trial-and-error failure into clear, actionable engineering feedback ("why did my rocket tip over?" or "why was it too heavy to lift off?"), the project encourages iterative problem-solving and STEM literacy in an engaging 3D format.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Languages: TypeScript, HTML5, CSS3, and GLSL (custom vertex/fragment shaders).
  • Frameworks & Libraries: React 19, Three.js (WebGL 3D rendering, PBR materials, RoomEnvironment IBL, OrbitControls, LatheGeometry, ExtrudeGeometry, InstancedMesh, and Points particle systems), Tailwind CSS v4, and Lucide React icons.
  • Build & Runtime Tooling: Vite 8, Node.js, and npm.
  • Procedural Audio & Graphics: HTML5 2D Canvas API (for procedural hull paneling, concrete launchpad textures, smoke sprites, and planetary maps) and the browser Web Audio API (for real-time synthesized engine roar, countdown tones, staging clunks, and alert chimes).
  • Storage: Browser localStorage for saving rocket designs, funds, fuel reserves, and mission progress.

5. How is your project creative?

  • 100% Procedural Assets (Zero External Media Files): Every 3D rocket component, planetary surface (Earth clouds, Moon craters, Mars canyons, Jupiter bands & Great Red Spot), hull livery texture, custom GLSL Mach-diamond exhaust plume, Fresnel atmospheric glow, and sound effect is generated mathematically in code.
  • Constructive Failure-Driven Design Loop: Rather than blocking players from launching flawed rockets, Orbital Foundry lets them test flawed builds on the pad, witness the physical consequence (pad stall, atmospheric tumble, or mid-flight fuel depletion), and receive a tailored engineering tip to fix and relaunch.
  • Clean, Unobstructed Cockpit HUD: Collapsible bottom docks keep the central 3D viewport completely clear so players can inspect their rocket craftsmanship and planetary vistas without visual clutter.

6. What factors did our team consider?

  • Usability for Beginners vs. Engineering Depth: Balanced authentic physics variables (TWR, mass depletion, drag, stability) with intuitive controls, starter presets, and an optional SAS flight assist toggle so both newcomers and space-sim fans enjoy playing.
  • Performance Across Hardware & Software WebGL: Implemented automatic software-WebGL detection, zero-garbage-collection math loops, pooled particle buffers, and avoidance of heavy CSS backdrop-filter blurs over the canvas so frame rates stay smooth across laptops and low-GPU environments.
  • Economic Balance & Replayability: Tuned part prices, 100% part-removal refunds, fuel reserves, and progressive mission payouts so players feel rewarded for scaling up from small suborbital hops to heavy planetary missions.
  • Visual Clarity & Accessibility: Paired high-contrast dark obsidian interfaces with tabular monospace telemetry, clear text diagnostics (never relying on color alone), and both keyboard (W/A/S/D, Space) and on-screen button/slider controls.
