projectDetails.details:
Abandoned but not Forgotten is a responsive educational website about NASA spacecraft and scientific equipment left on the Moon and Mars. Visitors can search and filter seven artifact records, open mission histories and discoveries, explore an interactive timeline, and select markers on schematic lunar and Martian maps.

The project makes mission history easier to explore by connecting each artifact with its purpose, scientific contributions, current status, and reported location. It highlights the scientific legacy of past missions, the historical value of their landing sites, and the need to consider preservation and debris when planning future exploration.

We built the site with HTML5, CSS3, and vanilla JavaScript. It runs in a browser without a backend, database, or framework. Mission information is drawn from NASA-published catalogs and mission records, with imagery from NASA’s Image and Video Library.

Our creative approach treats artifacts as clues to stories that continue after a mission ends. We considered scientific accuracy, mobile usability, and clear sourcing. The maps are explicitly schematic: marker positions are illustrative and do not claim precise coordinates or use live telemetry.

projectDetails.name: SAR-HydroTwin: Physics-Informed NISAR & Edge-IoT Flood Digital Twin
projectDetails.summary:
SAR-HydroTwin is an interactive, physics-informed geospatial digital twin built for the Dancing with the SARs challenge. Optical Earth-observation satellites are blinded by thick monsoon cloud cover precisely when flash floods and landslides strike mountainous regions like Kerala’s Western Ghats. While Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) from missions like NASA-ISRO NISAR penetrates clouds to detect standing water and soil moisture shifts, satellites experience multi-day revisit gaps.

SAR-HydroTwin bridges this gap by combining dual-polarization L-band/C-band SAR backscatter physics ($\sigma^0$ dB specular reflection drop and cross-polarization volume-scattering ratios) with Digital Elevation Model (DEM) slope masking to eliminate mountain radar-shadow false positives. We fuse these orbital inundation masks with real-time ground telemetry from simulated ESP32 ultrasonic river-level nodes via a hybrid machine-learning fusion engine. Users can interactively explore before-and-after SAR backscatter maps, inspect polarization drivers, and simulate real-time flash-flood alerts across the Meenachil and Pamba river basins.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works

SAR-HydroTwin is an interactive web-based radar remote sensing and early-warning platform designed to track monsoon surface-water inundation, soil moisture saturation, and terrain instability in cloud-covered regions.

  1. Physics-Driven SAR Backscatter Engine: Smooth standing floodwater acts as a specular reflector, bouncing radar pulses away from the satellite and causing a sharp drop in co-polarized backscatter intensity ($\sigma^0_{HH}$ / $\sigma^0_{VV}$ in dB). Simultaneously, saturated soils and flooded vegetation alter cross-polarized ($\sigma^0_{HV}$ / $\sigma^0_{VH}$) volume scattering. Our Python processing pipeline applies adaptive Otsu thresholding and log-ratio change detection across multi-temporal SAR scenes to isolate inundation and soil-moisture anomalies.
  2. Topographic Radar-Shadow Correction (DEM Masking): In steep terrains like the Western Ghats (Kanjirappally/Kottayam region), radar layover and mountain shadows mimic low-backscatter water signatures. We integrate NASA SRTM Digital Elevation Model (DEM) slope derivatives to mask out slopes $>15^\circ$, drastically reducing false-positive flood classifications.
  3. Orbital-to-Ground AI Sensor Fusion: Because orbital SAR passes occur on multi-day cycles, our hybrid Gradient-Boosted / Physics-Informed fusion model combines baseline SAR inundation maps with high-frequency ground river-gauge telemetry (modeled on ESP32 + JSN-SR04T ultrasonic sensor nodes) to interpolate basin-wide flood spread and forecast 6-hour flash-flood risk during satellite revisit gaps.
  4. Interactive Storytelling & Visualization: The web interface features a synchronized Before/After SAR swipe comparator, polarization toggle (HH vs. HV vs. RGB Composite), physical driver annotations, and live basin telemetry gauges.

Tools, Languages & Technologies Used

  • Core Processing & AI: Python 3.11, NumPy, SciPy, Scikit-Image (Otsu thresholding & morphological filtering), Scikit-Learn (spatio-temporal risk fusion), Rasterio / GeoPandas.
  • Interactive Frontend: Streamlit / React + Leaflet (Folium) with custom HTML/CSS before-and-after SAR imagery sliders and Plotly telemetry charts.
  • Edge Telemetry Architecture: Simulated MQTT/JSON telemetry streams modeled after ESP32 microcontrollers and JSN-SR04T waterproof ultrasonic level sensors.

Uniqueness, Creativity & Key Design Factors

Rather than treating SAR imagery as static pictures or relying on generic AI wrappers, SAR-HydroTwin embeds radar wave-surface interaction physics directly into its classification pipeline. By pairing local lived experience in Kerala’s monsoon-prone Western Ghats foothills with NASA-ISRO NISAR’s L-band vegetation-penetrating capabilities, our system demonstrates how orbital radar and low-cost ground sensors work together to protect vulnerable communities.

projectDetails.name: PYRO-0G: Flame in Freefall
projectDetails.summary: PYRO-0G is an interactive fire-safety cockpit that makes NASA microgravity combustion research useful for mission planning. It turns records from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) Combustion Science repository into a searchable dataset and lets users compare how materials burn across oxygen levels, pressure, airflow, and gravity. A simulator explores crew environments including the ISS, Orion, lunar bases, and pressurized rovers; a transparent Flame Hazard Index ranks conditions; and a “Will it burn?” checker and experiment matrix link results to source evidence. Each record includes a NASA source and evidence quote. Twenty of the 25 records currently pass independent verification checks; the rest are flagged, and missing source values are shown as data gaps rather than guessed. PYRO-0G helps researchers and mission planners explore evidence for safer spacecraft materials while making NASA experiments easier to inspect and reuse.
projectDetails.details:
PYRO-0G combines a data pipeline with an interactive web app. We compiled publicly available NASA PSI Combustion Science investigations, including BASS, BASS-II, Saffire I–III, SAME/SAME-R, FLEX, DAFT, and DAFT-2, along with related NASA Technical Reports Server sources.

Python scripts extract structured fields from source text, including fuel or material, oxygen, pressure, airflow, gravity, outcome, and an evidence quote. Claims are checked through an independent verification ladder and human review. Twenty of the 25 records currently pass independent verification; the remaining records are visibly flagged. When a source does not report a measurement, the app shows a data gap instead of estimating a value.

The Simulator Workbench lets users explore crew-environment presets, choose a material, adjust atmospheric conditions, and compare the same sample at 1g and 0g. The Flame Hazard Index uses a visible formula: HI = 100 × (0.35·S + 0.25·O + 0.20·E + 0.20·C). The experiment matrix, hazard cards, and “Will it burn?” checker help users explore the dataset. An evidence inspector links each record to its NASA source and quote, and users can export the data as CSV.

The project is intended to help researchers and mission planners investigate fire safety for spacecraft, stations, lunar bases, and pressurized rovers. It also makes decades of microgravity combustion research easier for the public to explore. We built the pipeline in Python and the static app with JavaScript, Canvas, and SVG; the app is hosted on Vercel.

projectDetails.name: Forgotten in Space: Exploring NASA’s Abandoned Space Technologies and Their Scientific Legacy
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, “Forgotten in Space: Exploring NASA’s Abandoned Space Technologies and Their Scientific Legacy,” is an educational website that explores NASA hardware left across the solar system since the 1960s. We developed an interactive platform where visitors can discover different spacecraft, rovers, landers, and other technologies, learn where they were sent, understand their original purposes, and explore what happened to them after their missions ended.

The website addresses NASA’s challenge by bringing together the stories of space equipment that was intentionally left behind, became inactive, or completed its mission. It highlights the scientific discoveries and technological achievements made possible by these missions, while distinguishing retired equipment from spacecraft that are still operating.

This project is important because these technologies are more than forgotten objects: they represent decades of exploration, innovation, and scientific progress. By sharing their stories in an engaging and accessible way, we hope to inspire curiosity about space exploration and help people appreciate the lasting impact of NASA’s missions.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details: Forgotten in Space

Our project, “Forgotten in Space,” is a website about NASA's old spacecraft, rovers, landers, and other equipment that have been left behind in space or on other planets. We wanted to explore what happened to these technologies after their missions ended and what they helped us discover.

What does it do and how does it work?

Our website allows visitors to explore different NASA missions and the equipment used in them. They can learn when and where each spacecraft or rover was sent, what its purpose was, what discoveries it made, and why its mission ended. We also include pictures and useful information to make everything easier to understand.

What are its benefits?

It helps students and other visitors learn about space exploration in an interesting way. It also brings information about different NASA missions together in one place, so people don't have to search through many websites to learn about them.

What is the intended impact?

We want people to understand that even though some space missions have ended, the discoveries they made are still important. We also hope our project encourages students to become more interested in space, science, and technology.

What tools and technologies did we use?

We used Python and Flask to build the website, HTML to create the pages, CSS to design them, and JavaScript to add interactive features. We used SQLite to store information about the missions and NASA's Image and Video Library API to find space-related pictures. We also used Visual Studio Code to write our code and GitHub to manage our project.

How is the project creative?

Instead of focusing only on famous and currently active space missions, we chose to look at the equipment that was left behind after missions ended. We thought it would be interesting to show what happened to these machines and how they helped NASA learn more about the solar system.

What factors did our team consider?

We focused on making the website easy to use and understand. We also considered the accuracy of the information, the quality of the pictures, and how to organize the content so visitors could find what they were looking for. Another important point was explaining the difference between equipment that was abandoned, equipment that stopped working, and missions that simply came to an end.

Through this project, we want to show that even the machines left behind in space have stories worth learning about.

projectDetails.name: Outpost 14
projectDetails.summary: OUTPOST 14: Lunar Frontier is a 3D, browser-based Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer for students aged 10–16. The player commands a research outpost near the lunar South Pole for a 14-cycle mission. They walk an astronaut around the base, inspect nine facilities, and balance four connected systems: life support, radiation shielding, electrical power and food production. Three hands-on missions turn science into action: cleaning dust off the solar array, repairing the water recycler and getting the crew into the radiation shelter during a solar event. Every decision changes the simulation, and the student immediately sees why. For example, cleaning the array raises generation from 195 to 281 kWh per cycle. Crew needs and recycling rates are based on NASA reference values. This matters because future Artemis-era crews must think in systems, and OUTPOST 14 lets students practice that thinking through play. It runs offline in any modern browser.
projectDetails.details:
What it does / how it works: OUTPOST 14 puts the student in charge of a lunar research base. They move the astronaut with WASD, interact with E and open the map with M. They visit nine facilities: the crew habitat, solar arrays, battery storage, water recovery, oxygen generation, greenhouse, radiation shelter, communications and the rover bay. Each mission cycle can bring one of 12 crisis events, such as dust storms, solar particle events and equipment failures. The student responds by repairing, rerouting power or rationing resources. A single tested TypeScript simulation engine calculates every outcome. The 3D world, the HUD and the mission report are just views of that engine, so what the student sees always matches the science. Walking around never advances time, so students can explore without pressure. At the end, a forensic mission report replays the decisions and compares runs.

Benefits: Students learn by consequence instead of by memorizing. Student Mode explains things in plain language. Engineer Mode shows the underlying numbers and formulas. A rule-based Mission Advisor answers five help questions (“Why is power low?”, “Where is the damaged system?”, etc.). A Space Academy has eight short science topics, and each links to NASA learning resources.

Intended impact: To help classrooms and young learners build systems thinking, meaning how power, water, oxygen, food and radiation protection depend on each other. These are the skills future lunar crews will need. Teachers can use the built-in three-minute demo mode, which plays the same way every time.

Tools and languages:

  • TypeScript, React 19 and Three.js (WebGL) for the 3D world, with LOW/MEDIUM/HIGH graphics settings and a 2.5D fallback for weaker devices
  • esbuild, which builds a single offline HTML file of about 1.1 MB, plus Vite for development
  • Node’s test runner with tsx for 67 unit tests, and Playwright for automated browser play-throughs
  • No special hardware: it runs in any modern browser

Creativity: Instead of a quiz, it is an explorable 3D base where the science is the game mechanic. Dust really lowers power output, and shielding really lowers exposure. The low 8° sun and long shadows are inspired by NASA’s South Pole illumination visualizations. The mission report replays the student’s own decisions like a flight-data recorder.

Factors we considered:

  • Age-appropriate language and two difficulty modes
  • Scientific validity, with NASA reference values and a disclaimer that the models are simplified
  • Accessibility and low-end hardware, through graphics presets, a 2D fallback and offline use
  • Saving and loading progress
  • No real people or minors in any visuals

Use of AI: AI tools were used to help write the code, the documentation and the presentation text. All NASA data values were checked against the cited sources.

Farmo is a free, multilingual web app designed to empower smallholder farmers with AI tools to prevent crop loss. It features voice assistance in local languages, AI disease diagnosis from photos, an irrigation planner, and a climate simulator using NASA satellite data to predict yields.
Built with React, Tailwind CSS, Supabase, and Deno, it makes precision agriculture accessible and free, aiming to improve food security and farmer income without requiring accounts or technical expertise.

**HABITAT ZERO – Design. Survive. Investigate.**

HABITAT ZERO is a browser-based space exploration and survival game designed to introduce players to the challenges of establishing a sustainable human habitat beyond Earth. Players take on the role of junior astronauts, making decisions, managing resources, designing habitats, and completing missions to survive in an unfamiliar space environment.

The project combines interactive storytelling and gameplay with real-world space science, incorporating NASA data and resources to make the experience more informative and engaging. Instead of simply reading about space exploration, players learn by making decisions and experiencing the consequences of their actions.

HABITAT ZERO addresses the challenge of making space science more accessible and engaging, particularly for younger audiences. It highlights the importance of resource management, scientific thinking, problem-solving, and sustainable habitat design—skills that are essential for humanity's future exploration of space.
projectDetails.details:
HABITAT ZERO – Design. Survive. Investigate.

HABITAT ZERO is an interactive, browser-based space habitat simulation game designed to introduce students and young learners to the challenges of establishing and maintaining human settlements on the Moon and Mars.

Players take on the role of a space habitat engineer and mission commander. They select a mission, choose a landing location, design a habitat and manage essential systems such as power generation, oxygen supply, water recycling, food production and crew health. As the mission progresses, players must balance limited resources, respond to unexpected emergencies and make decisions that affect the survival of the crew.

The game demonstrates how interconnected life-support systems work. For example, a power failure can interrupt oxygen generation and carbon dioxide removal, creating further risks for the crew. Players must understand these connections, identify problems and make informed decisions to keep their habitat operational.

One of the project's key features is its Mission Investigation and Replay System. Instead of simply showing a failure, the game helps players investigate the sequence of events that caused it, understand the consequences of their decisions and replay the same scenario using a different strategy. This encourages experimentation, critical thinking and learning from mistakes.

The project draws inspiration from NASA's planetary exploration research and publicly available space-science resources, including information related to lunar terrain, planetary environments and space weather. Scientific concepts are adapted into simplified educational simulations so that complex engineering challenges are understandable to younger audiences. The game is an educational model, not a real-world spacecraft or habitat control system.

The intended impact is to make space exploration and habitat engineering more accessible and engaging. It encourages students to explore STEM subjects, develop problem-solving skills and understand the scientific and engineering challenges involved in long-duration human space missions.

The project was developed as a web-based application using Google AI Studio and modern web development technologies, with a focus on interactive gameplay, simulation logic, user interface design and browser-based accessibility. It is deployed publicly so that users can access and experience the game through a web browser.

What makes HABITAT ZERO creative is its combination of game-based learning, resource-management simulation and failure investigation. Rather than presenting space science through only text or quizzes, it allows players to experience the consequences of engineering decisions. The design considers scientific plausibility, educational value, age accessibility, gameplay engagement, resource interdependence and the importance of distinguishing real scientific information from simplified game scenarios.

Ultimately, HABITAT ZERO aims to turn the challenge of surviving beyond Earth into an interactive learning experience where every decision matters.

projectDetails.name: Earth Echo
projectDetails.summary: EarthEcho: The Earth Information Jukebox is a browser-based project that makes NASA Earth imagery more accessible by turning visual patterns into sound. It is designed to help people explore information about our planet through both sight and hearing. The prototype scans an Earth image using a visible cursor and converts image features into musical tones. As the scan progresses, users can hear changes in the generated sounds and follow the visual movement on the screen. Playback controls allow users to start, pause, and explore the experience at their own pace. Plain-language explanations describe how image features are connected to the sounds, helping users understand the process rather than treating it as a mysterious effect. EarthEcho focuses on transparency, accessibility, and interactive learning. By combining imagery, sound, and clear explanations, the project offers another way to engage with Earth observation data and encourages curiosity about environmental patterns and the changing planet.
projectDetails.details: EarthEcho is a browser-based prototype that transforms visual patterns in Earth imagery into interactive sound. Designed for The Earth Information Jukebox challenge, it aims to help users explore NASA Earth Information Center visualizations through hearing as well as sight. The project combines a visible scanning cursor, generated tones, playback controls, and plainlanguage explanations. Its central principle is transparency: users should understand which image feature produces each sound and what that sound cannot establish. The prototype code has been generated and packaged. Its browser performance, audio synchronization, and accessibility have not yet been independently tested. A verified NASA visualization still needs to replace the synthetic teaching image before the final NASA-based demonstration. 1. Problem and intended users EarthEcho explores how sound can provide an additional way to investigate an Earth visualization. Rather than simply adding background music, it connects audio directly to identifiable image features. The intended users include: Students exploring Earth imagery. Teachers developing interactive demonstrations. Visitors to science exhibitions and public displays. People interested in alternative ways to explore visual information. The intended benefit is greater engagement and understanding of the selected visualization. These benefits remain project goals until evaluated with users. The project does not claim that its accessibility or educational effectiveness has already been validated. 2. Proposed solution EarthEcho provides a guided exploration sequence: 1. Choose an image and inspect its source information. 2. Hear calibration sounds explaining the mapping. 3. Play a le-to-right scan of the image. 4. Follow the cursor while listening to the corresponding tones. 5. Pause, adjust speed, or inspect an individual column. 6. Read the mapping explanation and scientific limitations. For the initial NASA-based version, the scope is deliberately limited to one verified visualization and one consistent sound mapping. 3. How the sonification worksThe prototype divides the displayed image into 96 columns and eight horizontal bands. Image feature Audio representation Horizontal position Playback order, from le to right Vertical band Pitch, with higher image bands producing higher notes Mean displayed RGB brightness Tone strength Selected column The region inspected or played Scan duration The speed of exploration For each analysis cell, the application calculates: Here, is the number of pixels in the cell, and the red, green, and blue channel values range from 0 to 255. The result is a normalized summary of displayed RGB brightness. Each horizontal band uses a fixed pitch. The application converts the brightness summary into tone amplitude, with an additional user-controlled master volume. This is a designed translation of image features—not a reconstruction of physical sound or an environmental measurement. 4. Main prototype features The generated application code includes: Feature Purpose Local image import Load a PNG, JPEG, or WebP image Synthetic teaching pattern Demonstrate the system without misrepresenting it as NASA data Calibration sounds Explain brightness and pitch before playback Scanning cursor Connect the audio to the current image location Playback controls Play, pause, and restart exploration Adjustable scan duration Let users explore at different speeds Volume control Support user-controlled listening levels Column inspection Examine a selected part of the image Source metadata fields Record the title, source, credit, and observation period Image-description field Provide a written description of the selected visualization Feature export Download the calculated grid and entered metadata Built-in feature tests Check defined image-processing behaviors These are features present in the generated source code, not independently verified performance results. 5. Technical implementationThe proposed implementation uses a small, static web application. Component Role HTML Page structure and controls CSS Layout and visual styling Component Role JavaScript Interaction, processing, and playback logic Canvas Image display and pixel analysis Web Audio API Tone generation and audio scheduling JSON Metadata and feature-grid export The processing sequence is: Imported image ↓ Documented image preparation ↓ Displayed RGB feature extraction ↓ 96-column × 8-band feature grid ↓ Playback position ↓ Generated tones + visible cursor ↓ User exploration and explanation The generated version does not require an application backend, user accounts, or a live NASA data feed. 6. NASA data and visualization contribution NASAʼs contribution should be the Earth visualization that users explore. EarthEcho adds the interactive audio layer; it does not create new Earth observations. Before the final demonstration, the team must select and document a verified NASA Earth Information Center resource, including: Exact visualization title. Original source page. Observation period. Required credit and attribution. Any cropping, resizing, or other preparation. A description of the image and its relevant limitations. No NASA image is currently bundled with the generated prototype. The starter pattern is synthetic and must remain clearly labeled as such. The final demo should visibly connect the selected NASA resource, the user experience, and the resulting project, as requested by the supplied guide. [36]7. Creativity and distinguishing approach EarthEchoʼs proposed creative emphasis is not simply turning an image into music. It is making that translation inspectable. The design combines: Calibration before exploration. A visible connection between scan position and sound. User-controlled pacing. Individual-column inspection. Source attribution alongside the experience. Clear separation between visual features and scientific quantities. The project does not claim to have invented sonification. Its focus is an understandable, reproducible interaction built around a NASA visualization. 8. Scientific validity and limitations The project distinguishes three separate claims: Level Appropriate claim Source The image comes from the cited visualization Processing The algorithm calculates a documented displayed-image feature Interpretation The sound offers a way to explore that image’s visual patterns Important limitations include: Displayed RGB brightness is not calibrated radiance. Color palettes and contrast settings affect the output. Labels, legends, and borders can introduce unwanted sounds. Resizing and image compression can change feature values. Averaging can reduce the influence of small bright features. Different image renderings cannot automatically support scientific comparisons. Audio patterns do not establish population, electricity consumption, environmental risk, or causation. Accordingly, EarthEcho makes no “100% accuracy,” prediction, or scientific-diagnostic claim. 9. Testing and evaluation planImage-processing tests The generated application includes tests for: 1. A black image producing zero brightness values. 2. A white image producing maximum brightness values. 3. A uniform gray image producing the expected normalized value. 4. A bright patch appearing in the correct analysis cell. 5. Repeated processing producing identical output. The tests must be executed and their actual results recorded. Playback and interaction tests The next evaluation stage should check: Cursor-to-audio synchronization. Play, pause, restart, and column selection. Audio levels and clipping. Behavior across the browsers and devices used for the demo. Keyboard-only operation. Error handling for unsupported or missing images. User evaluation Participants should attempt to: Identify which of two regions produces the stronger tone. Associate higher and lower pitches with the correct image bands. Pause and inspect a selected column. Explain what tone strength represents. Identify what the audio cannot establish. These tasks would provide evidence about mapping comprehension rather than relying on general claims that the experience is intuitive. 10. Expected impact and development statusEarthEchoʼs intended outcome is a small educational experience that encourages curiosity while keeping its mapping and limitations visible. Potential settings include classroom demonstrations, science exhibitions, and public Earth-information displays. Project element Current status Project concept and technical specification Created Browser application source package Generated Project element Current status Project PDF and seven-slide presentation Created Verified NASA asset integration Pending Browser execution and performance verification Pending Audio synchronization measurements Pending User and accessibility evaluation Pending Public deployment Not completed The immediate milestone is one verified NASA visualization, one tested playback experience, and a demonstration supported by actual results. 11. Submission presentation The supplied guide evaluates projects under Impact, Creativity, Validity, Relevance, and Presentation. It requires either a video of no more than 30 seconds or a slide deck of no more than seven slides, including title and introduction slides. The demo must be externally hosted and publicly accessible; slides and submission materials must be in English, with English subtitles required for non-English video narration. [36] The final submission must include the actual team name and members, selected challenge, working project demonstration, user experience, and NASAʼs contribution. Until the missing source, testing, identity, and public-link details are completed, EarthEcho should be presented as a prototype under development rather than a fully validated solution.

projectDetails.name: Project Wrath
projectDetails.summary: Using ambient Wi-Fi signals for device-free environmental sensing relies on extracting Channel State Information (CSI) from the Physical (PHY) layer of the Orthogonal Frequency-Division Multiplexing (OFDM) protocol. While legacy systems rely on the Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI)—a coarse, scalar metric—CSI provides fine-grained amplitude and phase data across multiple frequency subcarriers. This allows the Wi-Fi network itself to act as a contactless multipath radar.
projectDetails.details: FireWatch AI is a contactless, device-free environmental monitoring and autonomous fire suppression system. Instead of relying on traditional point-based smoke or heat detectors, it repurposes ambient Wi-Fi signals into a spatial radar network. It works by extracting Channel State Information (CSI) from standard Wi-Fi transmissions and feeding that data into a Machine Learning (Random Forest) model. The system actively monitors 8 core parameters bridging the RF and physical worlds: 1. 2.4 GHz Phase Shift: Acts as a proxy for ambient temperature rises (thermal refraction). 2. 2.4 GHz Amplitude Variance: Detects chaotic thermal convection currents unique to open flames. 3. 5 GHz Time of Flight (ToF): Tracks ambient moisture and humidity changes. 4. 60 GHz Attenuation Loss: Tracks oxygen depletion (oxygen naturally absorbs 60GHz signals; as a fire consumes O2, signal strength anomalously increases). 5. Temperature Forecast: Derived environmental output. 6. Moisture Level: Derived environmental output. 7. Oxygen Concentration: Derived environmental output. 8. Combustion Probability Matrix: The final ML output dictating the likelihood of smoldering vs. active fire. When the ML model detects a high-probability permutation of these variables, it autonomously triggers physical relays to activate zone-specific fire suppression systems. What benefits does it have? Volumetric Coverage: Traditional smoke detectors only monitor the exact point on the ceiling where they are installed. Wi-Fi RF signals bounce around the entire room, providing true volumetric monitoring of the whole space. Immunity to Physical Blindness: Dust, dirt, and spider webs can block optical smoke detectors, rendering them useless. RF signals are unaffected by visual obstructions. Predictive, Not Reactive: By monitoring the combination of dropping oxygen and rising moisture (steam) before active convection starts, the system can detect smoldering fires long before thick smoke is produced. What is the intended impact? The intended impact is to drastically reduce fire response times in high-value, hazardous, or complex environments—such as server farms, lithium-ion battery storage facilities, chemical warehouses, and smart factories. By catching the earliest chemical and thermal shifts in the air, FireWatch AI aims to save lives, minimize property damage, and prevent the catastrophic failure of critical infrastructure.

projectDetails.name: Abandoned Legacy
projectDetails.summary:
Abandoned Legacy is an interactive educational web platform developed for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, addressing the challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars.”

The platform transforms the history of inactive lunar and Martian exploration equipment into an engaging multimedia experience. It features first-person storytelling based on historical mission records, a real-time chronometer tracking the time since selected missions' final communications, an interactive mission explorer, technical instrument dossiers, a historical timeline, and a scientific discoveries matrix. Browser-based audio synthesis and speech narration bring these silent explorers to life.
By presenting their engineering achievements and scientific contributions in an accessible format, Abandoned Legacy challenges the perception of these machines as forgotten space debris. It highlights how their discoveries continue to contribute to our understanding of the Moon and Mars, making planetary exploration history more engaging and accessible to students, educators, and the public.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details — Abandoned Legacy

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Abandoned Legacy is an interactive educational web platform that preserves the scientific and historical legacy of inactive lunar and Martian exploration equipment. It transforms historical NASA mission records, engineering achievements, and scientific discoveries into an accessible multimedia storytelling experience.

The platform consists of several interactive sections:

  • Mission Explorer: Allows visitors to search and filter seven mission profiles by destination, including the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space. Each profile provides operational lifespan comparisons, landing locations, and technical information.
  • Chronometer of Silence: Displays live elapsed-time counters showing how long it has been since the final recorded communications of five selected missions: Apollo ALSEP, Viking 1, Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner, Spirit, and Opportunity.
  • Voices from the Silence: Presents first-person narratives based on historical mission records, allowing visitors to explore each spacecraft's journey, discoveries, and final moments. Users can listen through browser-based speech synthesis or explore reconstructed telemetry-style displays.
  • Mission Timeline: Presents important milestones in planetary exploration chronologically, connecting historical missions with the broader history of space exploration.
  • Scientific Discoveries Matrix: Highlights important findings from these missions and explains their continuing relevance to planetary science.
  • Technical Dossiers: Provides detailed information about scientific instruments, their functions, technical specifications, and mission records.

The website also features synthesized radio carrier tones generated directly in the browser, creating an immersive experience inspired by deep-space communication.

2. What benefits does it provide?

Abandoned Legacy makes complex planetary exploration history easier to understand and explore. Instead of presenting spacecraft merely as inactive hardware, it highlights their engineering achievements and scientific contributions.

Students and educators can learn about real scientific instruments such as Alpha Particle X-Ray Spectrometers (APXS), Mössbauer Spectrometers, and seismic experiments. Comparisons between planned and actual mission lifespans also demonstrate engineering endurance and the challenges of operating robotic equipment in extreme environments.

The platform combines scientific information with storytelling, making historical mission archives more engaging and accessible to the general public.

3. What is the intended impact?

The project's primary goal is to change how people perceive decommissioned planetary exploration equipment. These machines may have stopped transmitting, but their discoveries continue to contribute to our understanding of other worlds.

By connecting historical missions with modern exploration, Abandoned Legacy encourages curiosity about planetary science, space engineering, and scientific research. It also aims to serve as an educational resource for students, teachers, and space enthusiasts.

4. What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed as a responsive, client-side Single Page Application using:

  • React 19: Building the interactive user interface.
  • TypeScript: Structuring the application with static typing.
  • Vite: Development and build environment.
  • Tailwind CSS v4: Responsive styling and visual design.
  • Lucide React: Interface icons.
  • Web Audio API: Generating radio carrier tones and audio effects directly in the browser.
  • Web Speech API: Providing browser-native text-to-speech narration.
  • Google AI Studio: Assisting with code development, debugging, and AI-generated visual illustrations.
  • Google Cloud Run: Hosting the deployed application.

The application uses static mission data and does not require a backend, database, external API connection, or runtime AI model to function.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

The central creative idea is to give silent exploration machines a voice. The first-person storytelling approach transforms technical mission histories into narratives that visitors can connect with emotionally.

The Chronometer of Silence turns the passage of time since a spacecraft's final communication into an interactive experience. Synthesized radio carrier tones and telemetry-style displays further recreate the atmosphere of deep-space communication.

The combination of historical records, interactive technical information, scientific discoveries, and storytelling creates a different way to experience planetary exploration history.

6. What factors did the team consider?

During development, we considered scientific accuracy, accessibility, usability, technical feasibility, and transparency.

Historical information and scientific findings were cross-referenced with publicly available resources from NASA JPL, NASA NSSDCA, the Lunar and Planetary Institute, and the NASA Planetary Data System.

We also prioritized a responsive interface that works across desktop, tablet, and mobile devices without requiring installation, user accounts, or external API access.

AI-generated illustrations are used as visual representations rather than authentic NASA archival photographs. AI assistance was also used during development and in structuring the storytelling content, while the deployed application itself does not use runtime AI.

Overall, Abandoned Legacy aims to preserve the stories of planetary exploration pioneers and make their scientific legacy accessible to future generations.

projectDetails.name: Project Yggdrasil:The World Tree
projectDetails.summary:
We developed Earth System Trend Detective, an interactive 3D web-based climate investigation platform built with Three.js, Globe.gl, Leaflet.js, Chart.js, and Satellite.js. Starting from a real-time orbital command center tracking NASA Earth observation satellites, users dive through volumetric clouds into high-resolution satellite imagery across a four-tier hierarchy—spanning over 90 countries down to detailed local case studies in Kottayam and Kanjirappally, Kerala (India).

The project directly addresses the "Be an Earth System Trend Detective!" challenge by transforming 20 years (2006–2025) of environmental metrics from NASA MODIS, GPM, GLDAS, Landsat, and ECOSTRESS datasets into an accessible analytical tool. Using an interactive timeline and on-the-fly statistical analysis—including linear regression slopes and Pearson correlation coefficients—users can evaluate significant links between rising surface temperatures, evapotranspiration, soil moisture, vegetation health (NDVI), and extreme monsoon cloudbursts such as the 2018 Kerala floods.

This work is important because turning complex satellite data into clear, localized evidence empowers communities, researchers, and policymakers to recognize climate shifts early and strengthen regional resilience.
projectDetails.details:
What Does It Do & How Does It Work?

Earth System Trend Detective is an interactive, 3D space-to-ground climate investigation platform built to turn users into Earth system detectives analyzing 20 years (2006–2025) of environmental change.

  • Phase 1 — Orbital Command Center: Users begin in space around a 3D Earth with J2000.0 celestial ephemeris lighting, a dense starfield, and real-time SGP4 orbital propagation tracking 8 NASA/Earth-observation platforms (Terra, Aqua, GPM Core, SMAP, Landsat 9, Suomi NPP, ICESat-2, and ISS/ECOSTRESS) using NORAD Two-Line Elements (TLEs). Users can inspect live satellite telemetry (sub-point coordinates, altitude, velocity) or click any country on the globe.
  • Cinematic Cloud-Dive Transition: Selecting a study area triggers a procedural Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) volumetric cloud fly-through, seamlessly transitioning from orbital altitude down to high-resolution hybrid satellite imagery.
  • Phase 2 & 3 — Four-Tier Climate & Statistical Investigation: Using a synchronized Leaflet satellite map (with a toggleable 3D perspective tilt) and a glassmorphic analytics dashboard, users explore a Country → State/Province → District → Town hierarchy spanning 90+ countries worldwide, alongside a deep-dive case study into Kottayam and Kanjirappally, Kerala (India). An interactive 20-year bar timeline, sparkline cards, dual-mode charts (Temperature vs. Soil Moisture and Rainfall vs. NDVI), and an on-the-fly statistical engine calculate linear regression slopes and Pearson correlation coefficients (
    )across indicators derived from MODIS, GPM, GLDAS, SMAP, Landsat 8/9, ECOSTRESS, and GRACE-FO datasets.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Making Satellite Science Intuitive: Bridges the gap between complex orbital telemetry and everyday understanding by showing which NASA satellites observe the planet and what their long-term measurements reveal on the ground.
  • Actionable Local Context: Connects macro-scale climate shifts (such as regional warming and altered evapotranspiration) to hyper-local impacts—like extreme monsoon cloudbursts, the 2018 Kerala floods, soil moisture depletion, and urban heat islands.
  • Zero-Barrier Accessibility: Engineered as a portable, zero-install web application that runs directly in any modern browser, making it immediately usable by students, educators, citizen scientists, researchers, and local resilience planners.
  • Intended Impact: Empower communities and decision-makers—especially in climate-vulnerable regions like the Western Ghats—to recognize statistically significant environmental trends early and plan better flood mitigation, watershed management, and agricultural adaptation.

Tools, Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Languages & Core Web Tech: HTML5, CSS3, Vanilla JavaScript (single-file architecture), HTML5 Canvas (procedural FBM cloud rendering).
  • 3D, Mapping & Data Visualization Libraries: Three.js (0.160.0), Globe.gl (2.30.0), Leaflet.js (1.9.4) with Esri World Imagery and Google Hybrid tiles, Chart.js (4.4.1), and Tailwind CSS.
  • Astrodynamics & Scientific Computing: Satellite.js (5.0.0) for SGP4 orbital propagation, J2000.0 ephemeris calculations, NORAD TLEs, and custom JavaScript linear regression / Pearson correlation functions.
  • NASA Data Sources & Missions Referenced: MODIS (Terra/Aqua), GPM IMERG, GLDAS, SMAP, Landsat 8/9, ECOSTRESS, VIIRS (Suomi NPP), ICESat-2, and GRACE-FO.
  • Development Environment & AI: Git, GitHub Pages for live deployment, standard consumer laptops/modern web browsers, and Generative AI (Gemini) used transparently as a pair-programming assistant for ephemeris math, volumetric cloud shaders/rendering, and visualization scaffolding.

How Is the Project Creative?

Rather than presenting climate data in static 2D tables or isolated graphs, our team designed a unified "mission control to street-level" narrative. Starting at live orbital mechanics, diving physically through sunlit procedural cloud decks, and landing on a tiltable 3D satellite map creates an emotional and spatial connection between global Earth observation and local lived reality. Combining real-time satellite tracking with a 4-level geographic drill-down and live statistical trend proof transforms passive data viewing into active scientific detective work.

Key Factors Our Team Considered

  1. Accessibility & Portability: We intentionally built a lightweight, dependency-free single-file web architecture using pinned CDNs so anyone with a browser can launch it without servers, API keys, or local installations.
  2. Scientific Rigor Over Raw Visuals: We paired visual timelines with live linear regression slopes and Pearson correlation coefficients so users can distinguish normal year-to-year weather variability from statistically significant multi-decade climate shifts.
  3. Global Breadth + Local Depth: While supporting 90+ countries so users anywhere in the world can investigate their own region, we curated granular district- and town-level profiles for Kerala to demonstrate how regional climate forcing translates into localized flood and drought hazards.
  4. Usability & Interaction Polish: We carefully handled pointer-event layering over the 3D globe, added searchable breadcrumbs across all four geographic tiers, and ensured smooth transitions between orbital and surface views.
  5. Open Science & Transparency: In accordance with NASA Space Apps guidelines, we clearly documented all satellite mission inspirations and transparently disclosed AI-assisted development components.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Mission Pulse AI
projectDetails.summary: Mission Pulse AI helps astronauts interpret their own health readings and decide what to check next during a mission. In a simulated Artemis II case, the app compares three nights of sleep with the crew member’s personal baseline and flags a missing reading for follow-up. The crew can test a maintenance change, see when it conflicts with a fixed briefing, and choose a slot that gives them eight hours of scheduled rest instead of six. Mission Pulse also records follow-up measurements beside the originals and exports a handover for crew or flight surgeon review. The prototype uses published NASA mission records and clearly labeled synthetic crew data.
projectDetails.details:
Astronauts on long missions need to assess changes in their own health and balance follow-up with fixed work. Mission Pulse groups health check-ins, personal baselines and the mission schedule in one browser app. It tracks sleep, pulse, blood oxygen, blood pressure, glucose, temperature and breathing rate. Each flagged value shows the comparison rule and relevant measurement context. The app marks missing readings explicitly and records a recheck beside the original reading.

In the Artemis II rehearsal, the app rejects a maintenance slot that overlaps the 09:00 briefing. Moving the work to 07:00–09:00 increases the scheduled rest window from six to eight hours. The crew can export a local handover draft with the evidence, the proposed change and NASA sources. The ISS rehearsal shows a simulated pulse of 106 bpm after exercise alongside a 64 bpm resting recheck. The Apollo 17 rehearsal illustrates missing baseline data and multiple vital-sign flags.

NASA’s Artemis II agenda informs the sleep-window scenario. NASA’s ISS sleep brief and Apollo records provide historical context. Crew measurements, decisions and schedules used in the drills are synthetic. Guidance focuses on checking data quality, repeating readings and preparing a review. It is intended for simulation and review.

I built the dashboard in React and TypeScript with Vite and hosted the public demo on Lovable. The public app stores rehearsal data in the browser and answers supported typed questions from its current records. I used OpenAI Codex to assist with planning, writing and reviewing code, testing, synthetic data and submission materials. Lovable assisted with the import and deployment. The optional local prototype uses OpenJarvis for model-backed replies and actions, and Faster Whisper for transcription.

projectDetails.name: Project 3-Minute Decision
projectDetails.summary:
On Mars, a three-minute choice can shape a whole mission. Our app turns this idea into an interactive game where players act as a Mars rover support team. When the rover reports a problem and Earth cannot reply straight away, players have three minutes to study the clues and decide what to do. They can protect the rover, carefully approach a science target, or gather more information first. Each choice leads to different consequences for rover safety, scientific discoveries, time, and power.
We used NASA research about Mars communication delays, rover hazard checks, and science instruments to make the situation feel realistic. The app addresses the challenge by showing why a team may need to think independently when Earth is far away. This matters because space exploration depends on making careful decisions with incomplete information. We hope the game makes players curious about Mars while giving them a chance to practice making thoughtful choices.
projectDetails.details:
What does your project do, and how does it work?

Our app is an interactive Mars rover decision game with six emergencies. For each one, players have three minutes to read the rover’s alert and clues, such as the slope, wheel slip, and safer route. They choose one of three actions and see how it affects the rover’s safety, energy, and science reserves. Players can also write a short mission note to explain their reasoning. At the end, they can review their results and download a report.

What benefits does your project have?

The game makes a real space-exploration challenge easier to understand and fun to try. It helps players practise reading evidence, thinking under pressure, weighing risks, and explaining their choices. Because different choices have different consequences, players can see that protecting the rover, saving energy, and collecting science may require trade-offs.

What is the intended impact of your project?

We hope our app helps people understand why rover teams may need to make decisions without waiting for an immediate reply from Earth. We also want to spark curiosity about Mars exploration and show how important careful thinking is when information is incomplete.

What tools, coding language, hardware, or software did you use?

We built the app as a web application using Python and Streamlit, and hosted it on Streamlit Cloud. It can be opened in a web browser on a regular computer or device. No special hardware or account is needed to play.

How was your project creative?

I think our idea is creative because communication delay is easy to overlook. People might think a rover can simply ask Earth what to do, but messages between Earth and Mars take time. We turned that hidden challenge into a game with a countdown, clues, and choices that lead to different outcomes. Instead of giving players one obvious answer, we let them weigh what matters most for the mission.

What factors did your team consider?

We considered the communication delay, the limited information available, and the need to balance rover safety, energy, and science goals. We wanted the clues and choices to be clear, the consequences to help players learn, and the six emergencies to keep the game interesting. We also made it clear that the game’s telemetry and outcomes are fictional and inspired by NASA research, so they are not mistaken for real NASA mission data.

projectDetails.name: Mission Architect: Interactive Space Mission Design Game
projectDetails.summary: Mission Architect is an interactive space mission design game that allows players to experience the challenges of planning and carrying out a space mission. Players choose a destination, design and build their spacecraft, and make important decisions throughout the mission to ensure its success. The game combines space exploration, strategic thinking, problem-solving, and teamwork in an engaging, browser-based experience. It aims to make space science more accessible and enjoyable while helping players understand the complexity of spacecraft design, mission planning, and exploration. By turning these concepts into an interactive simulation, Mission Architect encourages creativity, critical thinking, and a deeper interest in space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

Mission Architect lets players experience a full space mission lifecycle: choose a destination, design a spacecraft, launch it, fly it and get a scored debrief.

HOW IT WORKS

  1. Crew: 1–4 players split four roles. Director (budget and testing), Engineer (structure, power, battery, shielding, fuel), Scientist (instruments) and Flight Ops (rocket, orbit, antenna, ground stations). Each role must report "GO" before launch, like a real launch poll.
  2. Mission: six destinations of rising difficulty, each with realistic constraints. Mars gets 43% of Earth's sunlight, Jupiter about 1/27, so players must choose between huge solar arrays and nuclear power. Europa needs heavy radiation shielding. Far targets need stronger comms to send data home.
  3. Build: live gauges show budget, mass vs. rocket capacity, power, data downlink, fuel and lifetime. A 3D model of the spacecraft updates as parts are added, and a science forecast shows how well the design meets the mission goal.
  4. Flight: an animated 3D launch with booster separation, fairing separation, solar array deployment, a transfer orbit and orbit insertion. Random events (solar storms, debris strikes, computer glitches, budget cuts) go to the matching crew role to decide. Testing level affects the chance of part failures.
  5. Debrief: a score out of 1000 across mission success, science return, efficiency and decisions, with plain-language feedback explaining what went wrong and how to fix it.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Students rarely get to experiment with a whole mission. Mission Architect makes engineering trade-offs visible and memorable: failing, seeing why, and flying again is the core learning loop. Team roles build collaboration and communication. It runs free in any browser on phones, tablets and laptops, so any classroom can use it.

CREATIVITY

A GO/NO-GO launch poll, a flight director voice, mission twists (random constraints like budget cuts or a grounded rocket), agency ranks, a Hall of Fame leaderboard, collectible badges and a mission patch keep it replay-able.

TOOLS

HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single web page. Three.js for 3D graphics, with procedurally generated planet textures. Web Audio API for the rocket engine sound, music and effects. Kokoro text-to-speech for the flight director voice. Lucide icons and Google Fonts. Built with help from Claude (Anthropic).

projectDetails.name: C.R.O.P - Climate and Resource Optimization for Plants
projectDetails.summary:
C.R.O.P. is a decision-support platform that helps farmers in hot, saline, water-limited regions choose which crop to grow next. It is built around a one-acre vegetable farm in Al Ain, UAE, where more than 80% of food is imported and where roughly 10,000 Abu Dhabi farms have been abandoned, largely because of soil and water salinity.

The platform draws on three sources. NASA POWER provides daily temperature, humidity, solar radiation and wind, used to calculate evapotranspiration and heat-stress days for each crop. Landsat adds vegetation indicators. Low-cost ESP32 nodes measure soil moisture, soil temperature, electrical conductivity (salinity) and pH, and an experimental electrode module records plant bioelectric signals. Where a sensor reading exists, it replaces the regional salinity estimate.

RotationIQ, the decision layer, first excludes crops whose salinity or water limits the field exceeds. It then scores the remaining options on water fit, salinity margin, heat risk and compatibility with the previous crop. Scoring is deterministic, and each result lists its inputs as measured, estimated or simulated. A scenario such as a +2°C season shows how the ranking shifts and why.

Hardware for one acre is budgeted at about AED 1,930, with running costs of AED 500-1,050 a year. The system breaks even if it avoids about AED 1,400 of water and input waste per acre each year. Next steps are calibration in local soil, validation against laboratory tests and a working-farm pilot.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

C.R.O.P. (Climate and Resource Optimization for Plants) is a web-based decision-support platform that helps a farmer decide which crop to plant next and how to manage the crop already in the ground. It combines NASA climate and satellite data, a regional salinity estimate and measurements from low-cost sensors in the field. It ranks crop-rotation options and gives day-to-day management advice, each with an explanation. It was developed around a one-acre vegetable farm in Al Ain, UAE, where summer heat, saline soil and limited water make crop decisions difficult.

Three layers feed every result. The first uses NASA POWER, which provides daily temperature, humidity, solar radiation and wind. From these the platform calculates reference evapotranspiration (FAO-56 Penman-Monteith method). Multiplying that by a crop coefficient gives each crop’s water demand, and maximum temperatures identify heat-stress periods. NASA GIBS imagery (MODIS/Terra NDVI and true colour) adds regional vegetation context on the field map.

The second layer is a set of ESP32 monitoring nodes. Each carries a capacitive soil-moisture sensor and a DS18B20 soil-temperature probe. The farm also has an air temperature and humidity sensor (DHT22), a soil electrical conductivity (EC) sensor for salinity, and a pH kit that measures a prepared soil-water sample. An experimental electrode module records plant bioelectric signals. When a measured EC value exists, it replaces the regional salinity estimate, so the recommendation reflects the actual field. The demonstration readings in the current build are simulated and labelled as such.

The third layer is RotationIQ, the decision engine. First, hard constraints remove any crop whose salinity tolerance or water requirement the field cannot meet. Then the remaining crops are scored on water fit, salinity margin, heat risk and compatibility with the previous crop. The scoring is deterministic and rule-based, so the same inputs always give the same ranking. Each result lists its inputs and labels them as measured, estimated or simulated. A scenario control lets the user raise the season’s temperature, for example by +2°C, and watch water demand and the ranking change.

Combined advice for the growing crop

C.R.O.P. compares what NASA data says the crop needs with what the sensors show is happening in the soil, and turns the gap into advice with numbers. Every advice card names its evidence, its confidence, and the check the farmer should make.

Watering. For tomato in mid-winter, NASA POWER temperatures give a reference evapotranspiration of about 3.8 mm/day. With a mid-season crop coefficient of 1.15, the crop uses about 4.4 mm/day. One millimetre over an acre is 4.05 m³, so that is about 17.7 m³ per acre per day. Drip irrigation at 90% efficiency makes the gross requirement about 19.6 m³ per acre per day. If the farmer applied 30 m³ and the moisture sensor stayed above its saturation threshold for 9 hours, the card reads: “Applied 30 m³ against about 20 m³ needed, 53% more than the crop uses. Reduce to about 20 m³ per acre per day.” Over a month that excess is roughly 300 m³ per acre. The reverse case is flagged too: 12 m³ applied against 19.6 m³ needed, with moisture dropping below the crop’s stress threshold before the next irrigation, is reported as 39% short.

Timing. When recent NASA daily maximum temperatures exceed 40°C, the platform suggests moving irrigation to early morning or evening to reduce evaporation.

Salinity. Using the FAO-29 relationship, tomato tolerates a soil salinity (ECe) of 2.5 dS/m before yield falls, then loses about 9.9% of yield per additional dS/m. At a measured 4.0 dS/m, expected relative yield is 85%, a loss of about 15%. With irrigation water at 2.0 dS/m, keeping tomato at 90% of potential yield needs about 8% (drip) to 13% (conventional irrigation) extra water for leaching, which on a 19.6 m³ day is 1.6 to 2.5 m³. The card gives these figures and recommends a leaching irrigation where drainage allows.

Heat. Tomato fruit set suffers above about 35°C. NASA POWER (2015-2024) shows Al Ain’s average daily maximum is below 35°C only from December to February, so the platform warns when a planting window falls outside it.

Nutrient risk indicators. The sensors measure pH and EC, not nutrient content, so the platform reports risk rather than a measured deficiency. When pH rises above about 8.0, iron, zinc and phosphorus become less available, and the card warns of the risk and recommends a laboratory test. Calcium-uptake risk, which causes problems such as blossom-end rot in tomatoes and peppers, is flagged when irregular moisture (for example, swings of more than 15 percentage points in a day), high salinity and temperatures above 35°C occur together. Confirming any nutrient deficiency needs a laboratory soil test, and the card says so.

Sensor reliability. Readings that are stuck, out of range or jumping abruptly are marked suspect and left out of the calculations, so one faulty probe cannot trigger false advice.

The figures above are a worked example with illustrative farm readings and an ET0 estimated from Al Ain temperatures. All thresholds are documented assumptions that are designed to be tuned during the pilot.

Benefits and intended impact

Farmers in arid regions often choose crops from habit or local advice, without a way to test how heat, salinity and water supply will affect the next season. C.R.O.P. turns that choice into a comparison that can be inspected, and it supports the daily decisions that follow.

The UAE imports more than 80% of its food, and about 10,000 farms in Abu Dhabi have been abandoned, largely because of soil and water salinity. No record exists of how many farms are affected. Field-level salinity monitoring addresses the same pressures and builds that missing record, one farm at a time. Better rotation and irrigation decisions can reduce wasted water, avoid planting salt-sensitive crops on saline soil, give earlier warning of salinity build-up, and keep productive land in use.

Economic impact and payback

The one-acre hardware budget is about AED 1,930, including a 15% contingency (line items total AED 1,679, plus AED 252). Running costs are AED 500-1,050 a year for hosting, calibration and replacements. Over two years the full cost is about AED 2,900-4,000 per acre. For the system to repay that in two years, it needs to avoid roughly AED 1,500-2,000 per acre per year of water, input and crop-loss costs. If the hardware lasts three years, the threshold falls to about AED 1,400 per acre per year.

A two-year payback is a target to test in a pilot, since no savings have been measured yet. Three sources of avoided cost would count toward it: irrigation water and pumping that over-watering wastes (the 300 m³ per month in the example above), fertiliser and inputs applied without need, and crop losses avoided through earlier warnings of salinity, heat and moisture stress. A single avoided crop failure on a vegetable plot can be a large part of that threshold. The platform includes a break-even calculator that takes the farmer’s own water price, irrigation volume and input costs, so the result reflects the farm instead of a generic estimate.

The pilot would measure payback directly. Over one growing cycle on a working farm, it would compare irrigation volume, input purchases and crop outcome between a monitored plot and an unmonitored control plot, with the farmer logging harvest and costs in the platform.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

Hardware: ESP32 microcontrollers, capacitive soil-moisture sensors, DS18B20 soil-temperature probes, a DHT22 air sensor, an EC sensor, an analogue pH kit, and an electrode setup with signal-conditioning electronics for the experimental bioelectric module. Sensor readings use ADC1 pins, since the ESP32’s second ADC cannot be used while Wi-Fi is active. The nodes send readings to the platform over HTTP with an API key. The demonstration readings in the current build are simulated and are labelled as such. The wiring and firmware sketch are documented with the project.

Software: The web application is built with Next.js 16 (App Router) and React 19 in TypeScript, styled with Tailwind CSS 4 and shadcn/ui components, with Recharts for charts and MapLibre GL for the field map. Data is stored through the Prisma ORM, in SQLite during development and in PostgreSQL (Neon) for the hosted version. The runtime and package manager is Bun. The FAO-56 Penman-Monteith ET0, crop water demand, FAO-29 salinity response and RotationIQ ranking are written as plain TypeScript functions rather than external libraries, and are covered by 22 unit tests, including a check against FAO-56 Example 18. NASA POWER data is stored in the database, so the calculations keep working when the NASA service is unavailable.

Datasets and what each is used for:

  • NASA POWER (daily, community AG, about 0.5° grid, retrieved for the Al Ain field location, 2015 to 2026, cached in the database): temperature, humidity, solar radiation and wind for the ET0 and crop water-demand calculation, heat-stress days and temperature scenarios.
  • NASA GIBS, MODIS/Terra NDVI (8-day) and true-colour imagery, shown as live map layers: regional vegetation context for the field’s surroundings.
  • FAO-56 (crop coefficients and ET0 method) and FAO-29 (crop salinity tolerance): the crop database of 12 crops. Each value is marked confirmed or needing verification.
  • Esri World Imagery and OpenStreetMap: base maps for the field location.
  • Our own ESP32 sensors: soil moisture, soil temperature, EC, pH, air temperature and humidity, and the experimental plant signal. A measured EC value replaces the regional salinity estimate when it exists.

Planned or contextual, not yet connected in the current build:

  • Landsat 8/9 NDVI at field level, which would show how vigorously the previous crop grew and whether the field is uniform.
  • UAE Federal Geographic Information Centre (FGIC) soil layers (soil salinity polygons and soil classes). The current build shows placeholder polygons, because no official dataset was programmatically accessible, and labels them as estimated.
  • NASA GPM IMERG, ECOSTRESS and SMAP, and the ADAFSA irrigation guidance: rainfall history, land-surface temperature, regional soil moisture and crop references, intended as cross-checks and regional context rather than primary field inputs.

AI use: general-purpose AI assistants (ChatGPT, Gemini and Base44) were used to help write and debug code, draft documentation and generate plain-language explanations. They do not generate the rankings, the advice or the sensor interpretation, which are rule-based.

Creativity

The project’s originality lies in combining three kinds of evidence in one loop: satellite and climate observations, measurements from the soil, and an experimental plant-level signal. Most agricultural tools use only one of these. Comparing NASA-derived crop water demand with measured soil moisture is what turns raw data into advice with quantities, for example “about 30 m³ applied against about 20 m³ needed per acre today”. A measured soil reading also takes priority over a regional estimate, so the platform improves as sensors are added.

Two design choices set it apart. The first is explainability: the farmer receives hard limits, per-criterion scores, advice cards and the inputs behind them, with a clear label for data that is measured, estimated or simulated. The second is affordability. Building the monitoring nodes from individually priced components keeps the one-acre budget near AED 2,000. A scenario control for future temperature turns the platform from a record of current conditions into a planning tool.

Questions we also considered

Who uses it, and how would a farmer use it day to day? The intended user is a smallholder or farm manager with a phone. In the morning they open the dashboard and see one status (OK, Watch or Alert), today’s water need in m³ per acre, and any advice cards. Once per season they open RotationIQ to plan the next crop. They never need to read raw data unless they want to.

How accurate is it, and how will we know? Accuracy depends on calibration, so the plan measures it. Moisture readings are compared with gravimetric samples, and EC and pH with laboratory results, reporting error and bias. The advice rules are checked against irrigation records and an agronomist’s judgement, and the pilot compares monitored and control plots. The calculations themselves are unit-tested, including against a published FAO-56 worked example. Until the field validation is done, every output is labelled preliminary, and the demonstration readings are marked as simulated.

What happens when data is missing? The platform falls back to the next-best source and says so. If the NASA service is unavailable, it uses the NASA POWER data stored in its database. If a sensor is missing, it uses the regional estimate and labels it as estimated. The node firmware is designed to keep readings on the device while the network is down and upload them later.

What does C.R.O.P. not do? It does not predict yield, diagnose plant disease or pests, or measure soil nutrients. It gives risk indicators and recommends a laboratory test for nutrients. Its advice supports a decision that stays with the farmer.

How is it different from existing tools? To our knowledge, most agricultural monitoring tools report conditions from one source. C.R.O.P. links NASA data, soil sensors and rotation ranking in one explainable workflow, built from open data and parts costing about AED 2,000 per acre. A commercial comparison has not yet been done and would be part of the pilot.

Who owns the data? The farmer. Readings are stored per farm, can be exported, and are not shared without the farmer’s consent.

How does it scale, and how is it sustained? The monitoring nodes are modular, and the shared EC and pH equipment is reused across a field, so cost per acre falls as area grows. The running costs (AED 500-1,050 per year) cover hosting, calibration and replacements. The software and hardware designs are documented so a farm cooperative, a university or an extension service can run it.

Is it safe and sustainable? The sensors are low-voltage and the plant electrodes are non-invasive. Nodes can sleep between readings to save energy, can run on solar, and use individually replaceable parts to limit electronic waste. Less over-irrigation also means less pumped groundwater and less fertiliser runoff.

Can it work elsewhere? NASA POWER covers the globe. The crop table, thresholds and regional soil source are configurable, so another region needs a local soil source and a validated crop list, not new software.

Why Al Ain? It combines extreme heat, saline soil and real working farms, UAE University is nearby for laboratory validation, and UAE agencies publish soil and salinity maps. If the platform is useful here, the conditions are demanding enough to suggest it can work in milder regions.

Factors the team considered

Sensor quality. Low-cost capacitive moisture and EC sensors need calibration in the actual soil, and the EC sensor needs checking against a laboratory reference before its readings drive decisions. A probe’s EC reading is not the same as laboratory saturated-paste ECe, so the platform applies a calibrated conversion. The pH kit measures a prepared soil-water sample and cannot be buried in the field.

Demonstration data. The readings shown in the current build are simulated and clearly labelled. The NASA POWER series is real data for the field location. Real sensor readings will replace the simulated ones once the nodes are calibrated and deployed.

What the sensors cannot measure. Moisture, temperature, EC and pH cannot tell the farmer how much calcium or other nutrients the soil holds. Nutrient advice is therefore limited to risk indicators, each with a recommendation to confirm by laboratory test.

Bioelectric signals. Plant electrical signals are small and noisy, so this module is treated as experimental. It needs an instrumentation amplifier and filtering, and its output is kept separate from the ranking and the advice until it can be validated.

Data resolution and access. NASA POWER is a grid of about 0.5° (tens of kilometres) and the GIBS MODIS imagery is coarse (hundreds of metres to a kilometre), so both describe the surroundings rather than one row of crops. Field sensors fill that gap. Landsat (30 m), GPM (about 10 km), ECOSTRESS and SMAP are planned as cross-checks and regional context, not as primary field-level inputs. The regional soil layer is currently a labelled placeholder because no official dataset was programmatically accessible, and it is replaced by a field measurement wherever one exists.

Transparency. Scoring weights, crop coefficients and advice thresholds are documented assumptions rather than fitted values, each crop value is marked confirmed or needing verification, and each result states its uncertainty. Randomness and language models are kept out of the ranking and the advice so the output can be checked.

Practical deployment. The budget assumes existing farm Wi-Fi and mains power, and adds about AED 540 for solar if the field is off-grid. Sensor nodes are replaceable individually.

Validation plan. The next steps are calibrating sensors in Al Ain soil, comparing EC and moisture readings with laboratory measurements, testing the advice rules against irrigation records, testing the bioelectric module under controlled stimuli, connecting field-level Landsat and the official FGIC soil layers, and running a pilot with a control plot to measure water use, input costs and crop outcomes.
