projectDetails.name: Project ajman american private school
projectDetails.summary: Mission Control lets anyone design, launch and operate a real space mission. Players balance mass, power, money, data and fuel, pass a NASA-style Go/No-Go poll, survive solar storms and get a scored engineering debrief. Pixel, a robot co-pilot, makes it easy for beginners, while real orbital mechanics and link budgets run underneath.
projectDetails.details:
The problem. Space engineering is exciting, but its core lesson is hard to feel from a textbook: every decision is a trade-off. Bigger instruments need more power, more power needs bigger solar panels, panels add mass, mass needs a bigger rocket, and the rocket costs money you don't have.

What we built. Mission Control is a complete, playable mission design game in a single web page. Players choose one of five missions (Earth, Moon, Mars, asteroids, deep space), build a spacecraft from 23 components, pick an orbit and a rocket, then launch. Seven live gauges show whether the design works, and the mission simulation runs on the player's actual numbers. A weak radio really loses data, a thin power margin really causes brownouts, and too little fuel really leaves the spacecraft in the wrong orbit.

Easy and fun. Pixel, a robot co-pilot, gives step-by-step quests. One-click "Fix it" buttons solve problems and explain what changed. Players earn stars, XP, ranks, badges and Space Credits to spend on research upgrades and paint jobs. Their agency's funding grows as they fly better missions, so skill unlocks bigger budgets.

Real engineering. Under the friendly surface, every number comes from a published method:

  • vis-viva orbital mechanics and Hohmann transfers
  • the rocket equation
  • SMAD solar power sizing with eclipse geometry
  • full decibel link budgets to NASA's Deep Space Network
  • TRL-based mass growth
  • a 5×5 risk matrix

A "∑ math" button on every gauge shows the equations with the player's own numbers. The results match real missions: a 1,847 m/s burn to reach geostationary orbit, and a 259-day cruise to Mars.

What makes it different. It works for a 16-year-old on their first try, and it holds up when an engineer checks the math. It is transparent about what is simplified, with a Methods page that lists every equation and source.

How it works (tech)

Plain JavaScript, HTML and CSS in one self-contained file, with Three.js for 3D, Canvas for orbit diagrams, ground tracks and charts, and the Web Audio API for sound. Progress is saved with localStorage. There is no install and no build step: open index.html and play.

Challenges we ran into

  • Making real physics produce good gameplay. We tuned the reference designs so each mission is winnable, while weaker designs fail for real engineering reasons.
  • Explaining decibel link budgets and power sizing to beginners without hiding them. The answer was two layers: plain-language gauges on top and ∑ math panels underneath.

What's next

  • Online multiplayer across devices with Supabase Realtime.
  • A shared global leaderboard.
  • Landers and rovers as new mission types.

projectDetails.name: Project amazing.astronauts
projectDetails.summary:
Outpost Commander is an interactive, browser-based simulation and mission training game designed specifically for children ages 7–12 to explore space exploration and resource management. Developed as a web application using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript, the project addresses the "Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge by teaching young players real aerospace engineering trade-offs.

Players must balance critical habitat resources—Power, Life Support, and Radiation Shielding—while navigating dynamic environmental hazards like solar flares and multi-sol lunar night cycles. This project is important because it makes complex space science concepts engaging, accessible, and intuitive for kids, inspiring the next generation of space explorers through interactive play and zero-install browser accessibility.
projectDetails.details:
• What does it do and how does it work?
    Outpost Commander is a web-based simulation game where players manage a lunar or Martian habitat. Players make strategic resource management decisions across turns (Sols), balancing Power generation, Life Support stability, and Electromagnetic Shield integrity against environmental challenges like solar flares and dark lunar phases.
  • What benefits does it have & what is the intended impact?
    The game educates children ages 7–12 on aerospace engineering trade-offs, systems thinking, and space science. Its intended impact is to spark early curiosity in STEM fields and space exploration through gamified learning.
  • What tools, languages, and software did you use?
    The project was built using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript (ES6+) for frontend game logic and dynamic SVG UI rendering, Web Audio API for interactive synthesized sound effects, and hosted via GitHub Pages.
  • How is your project creative?
    Unlike static quizzes or passive videos, Outpost Commander combines live animated habitat visuals, real NASA scientific grounding (such as ECLSS life support and solar weather constraints), and an interactive day/night hazard cycle that forces kids to plan ahead.
  • What factors did your team consider?
    We focused heavily on user experience (UX) for young children—ensuring high-contrast visual cues, intuitive touch/click controls, zero required downloads, and bite-sized educational pop-ups explaining real NASA missions.

projectDetails.name: Project ANS Galaxy guardians
projectDetails.summary:
MARS: Beyond the Mission

MARS: Beyond the Mission is an educational space exploration and survival game developed by Team Galaxy Guardians for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. The game follows six astronauts on an ambitious mission to Mars. After their spacecraft crashes on the planet, they must work together to survive, repair their equipment, and find a way to continue their mission.

Players explore eight different destinations, complete 24 missions, investigate the Martian environment, collect resources, grow food, and upgrade their technology. They also repair an abandoned rover and receive guidance from a mini robot to help them navigate the challenges of Mars.

The game combines science, technology, engineering, exploration, and problem-solving in an interactive experience. Its main goal is to help players understand the challenges of exploring Mars and discover how scientific research and teamwork could contribute to building a sustainable human settlement on the Red Planet.
projectDetails.details:
What does the project do and how does it work?

Our project is a space exploration and survival game where six astronauts travel to Mars, but their spacecraft crashes during the mission. Players must help them survive, explore different locations, collect resources, and complete 24 missions across eight destinations. They also need to repair equipment, fix a rover, and work with a small robot assistant.

What benefits does it have?

The game helps players learn more about Mars and space exploration in a fun and interactive way. It also encourages teamwork, problem-solving, creativity, and critical thinking.

What is the intended impact?

We hope our project inspires people to become more interested in space and understand the challenges astronauts might face when exploring Mars. We also want to show how important science and technology are for future space missions.

What tools or software did we use?

We used Base44, an AI-powered platform, to build our game, design its interface, and create its interactive features.

How is our project creative?

We combined a story, survival challenges, and space exploration to create a game where players learn by playing instead of just reading information. Each mission gives players something new to discover and solve.

What factors did our team consider?

We considered several real challenges of living on Mars, including extreme temperatures, radiation, lack of oxygen, limited water, food supplies, and astronaut safety. We also thought about how people could grow food, manage resources, and eventually build a sustainable settlement on Mars.

projectDetails.summary: Lunar Frontier is an immersive, first person perspective simulation, that launches players into the boots of an astronaut on a high-stakes lunar mission. Experience a full day of lunar survival: maintain life support, manage critical base operations and conduct scientific breakthroughs. Lunar Frontier transforms the meticulous details of space exploration into a gripping educational adventure that reveals what it truly takes to be an astronaut.
projectDetails.details:
Lunar Frontier is an immersive, first person perspective simulation that launches players into the boots of an astronaut on a high-stakes lunar mission. Players awaken in the lunar base with a set of mini-missions to accomplish, simultaneously managing their life support and assessing risks. Mirroring real space missions, the tasks follow strict sequences with tangible consequences and an element of unpredictability, challenging the player to act swiftly and decisively.

Designed to be authentic and engrossing, Lunar Frontier features intuitive mechanics that younger players can grasp, paired with layered, critical challenges that keep teens and adults engaged. It aims to inspire awe in the players, revealing space exploration and protocols in unprecedented detail.

By researching multiple extraterrestrial missions for the mechanics of the game, the factors that an astronaut has to weigh in order to live in a lunar habitat are translated into practical gameplay, though it retains the grit of real missions.

The game is modeled and coded in Godot.

projectDetails.summary:
ASM Space Pioneers: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive space-learning project created by four Grade 5 students from Al Salam Charter School, Abu Dhabi, for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Inspired by the theme The Next Frontier, our project explores an important question: How can future astronauts prepare for the challenges of living and working on Mars?

We developed two connected educational tools: Mission Mars, an interactive game created using Scratch, and ASM Space Pioneers Buddy, an AI-powered learning chatbot.

Through six exciting missions, players experience Mars landing, mineral exploration, habitat repair, dust storms, scientific investigation, and a final knowledge challenge. They must make decisions, manage simulated survival resources, and solve problems.

Our chatbot complements the game by explaining Mars science, life-support systems, and engineering decisions using NASA educational resources.

Our goal is to transform complex space exploration concepts into accessible, engaging learning experiences that inspire curiosity, critical thinking, creativity, and future careers in STEM.

We believe tomorrow's space explorers can begin their journey in today's classrooms.

projectDetails.name: ASTERIA: Astronomical SPHEREx Time-series Extraction & Rapid Image Analysis
projectDetails.summary: ASTERIA is an interactive astronomical dashboard designed to make NASA’s SPHEREx all-sky survey data accessible, comparable, and understandable for researchers, educators, and space enthusiasts. Since 2025, SPHEREx has been mapping the entire sky every six months across 102 near-infrared bands, capturing over a billion objects. ASTERIA solves a major challenge: exploring massive infrared image sequences and spotting subtle cosmic changes over time is difficult for non-experts and often requires switching between multiple fragmented tools. By bringing SPHEREx observation metadata, multi-catalog overlays (Gaia DR3 and SIMBAD), an interactive time-series timeline, and an integrated AI research assistant into one unified interface, ASTERIA empowers users to inspect sky regions, compare observations across dates, and uncover moving objects, brightness variations, and chemical signatures.
projectDetails.details:
ASTERIA is a research dashboard built to transform complex infrared all-sky survey data into intuitive visual exploration. Traditionally, exploring multi-epoch astronomical observations requires cross-referencing separate catalogs, downloading heavy FITS files, and writing custom scripts. ASTERIA unifies search, sky plotting, catalog comparison, and AI-guided analysis in a single view.


How it works:
Users search for a celestial target or survey field (such as the COSMOS Deep Field) or input specific coordinates (RA/Dec). ASTERIA plots SPHEREx observation markers alongside Gaia DR3 sources (stars, galaxy candidates, quasar candidates) and SIMBAD catalog records on an interactive sky map. Users can scrub through observation dates via a built-in playback timeline, click individual sources to inspect classifier probabilities, magnitudes, and parallax distances, and view detected chemical signatures (such as Hydrogen, Helium, and Carbon) alongside an integrated AI Research Chat.


Key Benefits & Impact:

  • Reduces tool-switching: Combines target search, multi-catalog comparison, observation metadata, and research discussion in one workspace.
  • Empowers students & educators: Makes sky coordinates, source classifications, and multi-epoch observations approachable through hands-on visual investigation.
  • Supports initial research: Helps astronomy enthusiasts and researchers inspect nearby sources, identify data limitations/missing measurements, and generate hypotheses quickly.
  • Plain-language insights: Translates complex astronomical records into clear explanations via an integrated AI research assistant.

Tools & Technologies:

  • Frontend & Visualization: HTML/CSS, Tailwind CSS, React / Next.js with interactive sky plotting (MapLibre / Deck.gl / Three.js)
  • Backend & Processing: Python (FastAPI, NumPy, Astropy, OpenCV) and JavaScript for data retrieval, alignment, and difference detection
  • Data Visualization: Matplotlib and custom interactive sky plot overlays
  • AI & Development Assistants: ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Claude, GitHub Copilot

Creative Elements:

  • Unified Multi-Catalog Sky Plot: Visually distinguishes SPHEREx observations, Gaia DR3 stars, galaxies, quasars, and SIMBAD objects on a single interactive coordinate grid.
  • Interactive Observation Timeline: Lets users step or play through SPHEREx observation epochs to track changes over time.
  • Context-Aware Research Chat: Keeps the selected sky field and source telemetry in view while users ask follow-up questions about terminology, demographics, or spectral correlations.
  • Transparent Data Reporting: Clearly flags unavailable parallax distances or catalog timeouts so users understand measurement boundaries.

projectDetails.name: Project ASTRA: Mission Control
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRA is a free 3D browser game for the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge. Players aged 9 to 14 run a crewed outpost on the Moon, then on Mars, and keep their crew alive by balancing power, air, water, food and radiation shielding.

Six short missions each teach one trade-off by making players live with it: solar power stops at night, making oxygen uses up water, grow lights compete with life support for stored power, and solar storms force a choice between sheltering and getting work done. Players build modules, drive rovers, make decisions where every option has a cost, and walk through their habitat in first person, where every console shows live mission numbers. Missions can be won or lost, and each debrief explains the real science. Solar storms are modelled on real events from NASA's DONKI database, and the Science library charts radiation measured at the Moon, on Mars and on the ISS (NASA OSDR RadLab).

Why it matters: the first crews on the Moon and Mars will face exactly these choices. ASTRA lets students practise this systems thinking, where every choice affects something else, free in any browser, including school Chromebooks and tablets.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

ASTRA is a free 3D browser game that puts students aged 9 to 14 in charge of a crewed outpost, first on the Moon and then on Mars. A campaign of six 10 to 20 minute missions (First Light, Ice Hunters, Green Thumb, Solar Storm, Red Planet, Mars Colony), plus Free Play, each builds around one idea that players learn by living with the consequences:

- Power: solar arrays only work in daylight; batteries carry the outpost through the night, and a forecast says when the battery will run out.

- Life support: each crew member needs 0.84 kg of oxygen, 3 L of water and 3 meals a day (NASA life support figures). On the Moon oxygen is made from water, so the rover mines ice in a crater that never sees the Sun; on Mars it is made from carbon dioxide, like NASA's MOXIE.

- Food: greenhouse grow lights compete with life support for stored power at night.

- Radiation: solar storms come with warnings; players choose a storm shelter, regolith shielding or both, and track each crew member's dose against a limit.

- Trade-offs: every module has a "catch", decision cards arrive mid-mission where every option costs something, and some choices come back later.

CAPCOM, a friendly voice at Mission Control, explains causes and warns before trouble. Every supply shows how long it will last, and time pauses for emergencies so players can think. Missions can be won or lost; each debrief shows a chart of what happened, the real science behind it, a NASA source and a quiz question.

Players can also step inside: a two-storey habitat with 14 rooms, furnished from real analogs (NASA's CHAPEA Mars Dune Alpha, HI-SEAS, the Mars Desert Research Station and the ISS), and a colony of 12 buildings around it. Its consoles show the simulation's live numbers, and some are the game's own controls: switch off the oxygen plant at its console and the HUD and the forecast change with it. Players can suit up, cycle the airlock and walk outside to repair modules, and drive two rovers: a crew rover that brings home ice and regolith, and a robotic science rover that maps buried ice with radar.

REAL NASA DATA

Every solar storm is modelled on a real solar particle event from NASA's DONKI database, and CAPCOM names it (for example the X5.8 flare of 11 May 2024). The Science library's "Real NASA data" tab charts the May 2024 storms as measured at the Moon (CRaTER on the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter), on Mars (RAD on Curiosity) and on the ISS (DOSTEL), from NASA OSDR RadLab; cites six NASA OSDR studies behind crew health and the greenhouse; points to a real candidate Mars base site in NASA Mars Trek; and covers the Canadian Space Agency's food-production projects. A "Check the real Sun now" button asks DONKI for the last 30 days, live.

BENEFITS

- Students practise systems thinking: everything is connected, and a choice in one place shows up somewhere else later.

- Failing is safe and teaches: the debrief explains what happened and suggests what to try next.

- Teachers get a built-in page with learning goals, NGSS links and discussion questions, and can unlock any mission to teach one topic in a 10 to 20 minute lesson.

- It is free, needs no account or install, collects no personal data and works offline once loaded.

INTENDED IMPACT

Any classroom with a browser, including school Chromebooks and tablets, can use real NASA data to teach how a crew survives away from Earth: energy budgets, life support, food and radiation. We want students to leave understanding the trade-offs that real Moon and Mars crews will face, and wanting to learn more about space science and engineering.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE

TypeScript, React 19, Three.js (WebGL), Zustand, Vite and Vitest, hosted on GitHub Pages; sound is synthesised with the Web Audio API. Every 3D model, texture, sky and sound is generated by code while the game runs, with no downloaded models, images or sound files. 176 automated tests, including scripted wins and losses for every mission. Graphics adapt to the device so the game stays smooth on slower computers. No special hardware: it was built on a laptop and runs on laptops, Chromebooks and tablets.

Source code: https://github.com/HamzaAli0911/astra-mission-trainer

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

A live 3D outpost that students run from above and walk through on foot, with consoles that are real controls; real storms that CAPCOM names; and science shown honestly: there is no sound outside on the Moon, radiation and carbon dioxide are invisible (instruments show them, not coloured fog), and the sped-up clock always says how fast time is running.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Age: one new idea per mission, plain language and rounded real numbers.

- Accuracy: numbers come from NASA and Canadian Space Agency sources cited in the game, and what we simplified is written down (docs/SCIENCE.md in the repository).

- Classrooms: short sessions, a teacher page, offline play and low-end school hardware.

- Accessibility: the Lexend typeface, high contrast, larger text, reduced motion, read-aloud, and keyboard and touch controls.

- Privacy: no accounts, no tracking and no personal data.

USE OF AI (SUPER INTELLIGENCE)

We used Anthropic's Claude (Claude Code) as an AI coding assistant. It wrote most of the code, tests, documentation and in-game text from our ideas and instructions; we chose what to build, played and tested every version, and decided what to keep. The game's 3D visuals and sounds are made by that code while it runs; no AI image, video or audio generator models were used for the game. The 28-second demo video is real gameplay recorded from the game and edited with Claude, and its music and sound effects were synthesised by code written with Claude; it is marked "SI-generated video and audio" on screen and in its file metadata. Every commit in the repository carries a "Co-Authored-By: Claude" line.

projectDetails.name: Offline Astro-Twin: Autonomous Crew Health & Air-Gapped Flight Surgeon Copilot
projectDetails.summary: Offline Astro-Twin is an air-gapped astronaut health monitoring system and local Flight Surgeon Copilot built for long-duration ISS, Lunar, and Mars missions where communication delays or solar blackouts cut off real-time ground support. Grounded in Canadian Space Agency (CSA) Radi-N2 radiation measurements and NASA Human Research Program (HRP) bone-loss benchmarks, it empowers non-physician crew members to detect physiological risks early through an interactive biometric body twin, plain-English self-exam protocols, actionable countermeasure simulations, and cited offline medical guidance.
projectDetails.details:
Long-duration spaceflight exposes astronauts to space radiation, microgravity bone/muscle unloading, isolation, and closed-loop cabin hazards—leading to Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), bone mineral density (BMD) loss, cardiovascular deconditioning, and behavioral fatigue. When missions push to the Moon (~2.6s round-trip) or Mars (up to ~44-minute round-trip light-time delay), astronauts carry primary responsibility for monitoring and acting on their own health.

Offline Astro-Twin delivers a complete, zero-internet onboard health workstation:

Interactive Biometric Body Twin: Visualizes Cardiovascular, Skeletal/Bone, Brain/Eyes (SANS & Behavioral), and Immune/Radiation systems with color-blind-safe status indicators (Green, Amber, Red, No Data) and strict per-metric data provenance chips (Real, Extrapolated, Synthetic, or Unverified Manual Entry).

Actionable Countermeasure & Self-Exam Guidance: Replaces passive disclaimers with plain-English self-exam instructions (e.g., Amsler visual grid, dosimeter checks), concrete NASA-documented preventive actions ("What You Can Do Now"), escalation triggers, and a "5 Core Questions" quick reference per body system.

7-Day Countermeasure Trajectory Simulator & Trend Tracking: Tracks 14-day mission telemetry in local SQLite with sensor-plausibility validation and projects 7-day outcomes across countermeasure protocols (ARED resistance loading, water-wall shelter concept, fluid-loading/thigh cuffs, circadian light scheduling) benchmarked against NASA HRP's 1.0–1.5%/month bone-loss band.

Air-Gapped Local RAG Flight Surgeon Copilot: Uses ChromaDB vector retrieval over curated NASA HRP, NASA OSDR, and CSA Radi-N2 knowledge files with local Ollama LLM inference and a deterministic offline extractive fallback—answering crew questions with exact source citations even in total comms blackouts.

Latency-Aware Ground Handover & Crew Check-In: Queues and exports timestamped Markdown situation reports tailored to ISS, Lunar, or Mars round-trip delay windows, paired with a daily protocol checklist and crew readiness tracker.

Built in Python using Streamlit, Plotly, Pandas, SQLite, ChromaDB, and Ollama (llama3.2 / nomic-embed-text with an offline stdlib embedding fallback), verified by an automated unittest suite

Github Repo: https://github.com/haurz/Nasa-Health-Monitoring-System-

projectDetails.name: Moon Base Ready: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
projectDetails.summary:
We built a browser game that trains young astronauts, aged 7–12, to run a Moon outpost near the lunar south pole. Players follow six chapters, from a flyby test and robot scouts to landing, building and surviving at the outpost. Every choice costs something: power spent on science is power not saved for the dark, and sheltering from a solar storm keeps the crew safe but stops that day's work.

In the Survival chapter, players pick one of NASA's candidate south-pole landing regions, then manage energy, air and radiation dose through five short challenges. Solar storms come from real archived NASA DONKI records (May 2024 and December 2019), clearly labelled as archived, not live. A decision log shows what each choice gave and cost, finds the player's turning point, and lets them test a "what if" with the same storms. Facts come with their NASA sources and two reading levels.

It matters because tomorrow's explorers learn best by making real trade-offs, not by memorising numbers.

projectDetails.name: IGNIS-0G: Microgravity Combustion & Spacecraft Fire Safety Intelligence
projectDetails.summary: IGNIS-0G is an interactive microgravity combustion and spacecraft fire safety intelligence platform grounded in 17 verified NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) flight experiments (Saffire, FLEX, BASS, ACME, SoFIE, and BRE). Designed to bridge decades of orbital combustion research with next-generation Artemis lunar and Mars mission safety, the platform integrates four core engineering modules: a real-time 60FPS Navier-Stokes and diffusion flame simulator across planetary gravities (1.0g Earth, 0.38g Mars, 0.16g Moon, and 0.0g ISS); a NASA-STD-6001B material flammability and toxicity risk matrix; multi-axis telemetry correlation visualizations; and a zero-hallucination Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Flight Safety Analyst supporting both offline TF-IDF search and multi-provider LLMs. IGNIS-0G empowers aerospace engineers and mission planners to evaluate cabin fire hazards and suppression trade-offs before flight.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works

IGNIS-0G is an interactive microgravity combustion and spacecraft fire safety intelligence platform grounded in 17 verified NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) flight experiments (Saffire, FLEX, BASS, ACME, SoFIE, and BRE). It translates raw orbital fire data into four integrated engineering tools:

1. Real-Time 60FPS Combustion & Aerodynamics Simulator: Approximates Navier-Stokes flow fields, buoyancy forces (Grashof and Froude numbers), and diffusion flame kinetics across four planetary gravity regimes (1.0g Earth, 0.38g Mars, 0.16g Moon, and 0.0g ISS), featuring interactive forced-ventilation airflow (0–20 cm/s), oxygen concentration (15%–36% O2), and cool-flame chemical reaction modes.

2. NASA-STD-6001B Material Flammability Risk Matrix: Evaluates spacecraft cabin materials (Nomex, PMMA acrylic, Kapton wiring, Polyurethane foam, Cellulose, and Kevlar) across mission atmospheres (ISS Nominal, Artemis EVA 34% O2, Orion Launch, and Mars Habitat), comparing flame spread rates, toxic CO offgassing, and Water Mist vs. CO2 suppression trade-offs.

3. Multi-Axis Telemetry Correlation Graphs: Visualizes non-linear relationships between oxygen fraction, forced ventilation velocity, flame temperature, and toxic emissions across NASA flight datasets.

4. Zero-Hallucination RAG Flight Safety Analyst: A hybrid Retrieval-Augmented Generation assistant combining deterministic offline TF-IDF cosine-similarity search with optional multi-provider LLM synthesis (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, OpenRouter), strictly anchored to verified NASA PSI record citations.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Fire in microgravity behaves counter-intuitively—forming spherical diffusion flames, invisible low-temperature cool flames, and accelerating rapidly in elevated-oxygen exploration cabins like Artemis (34% O2). IGNIS-0G gives spacecraft engineers, safety officers, and mission planners an immediate, accessible pre-flight decision-support environment to test ventilation thresholds, select NASA-STD-6001B compliant materials, and query historical flight evidence without needing supercomputing clusters.

Tools, Languages & Architecture

- Frontend & Physics Engine: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, HTML5 Canvas (60FPS particle/vector field solver), and Recharts.

- AI & Data Retrieval: Custom client-side TF-IDF vector retrieval engine with strict citation grounding over structured NASA PSI flight records.

- Open-Source Repository: https://github.com/Eyad-Yahia/ignis-0g

- Live Deployment: https://darling-longma-a7d1e1.netlify.app

Creativity & Engineering Considerations

To ensure maximum reliability and zero hallucination in safety-critical engineering queries, IGNIS-0G operates 100% client-side with an offline-first TF-IDF retrieval engine that works even without external API keys, while storing any optional user-supplied LLM keys strictly in volatile session memory (RAM) rather than persistent storage.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: AUA DUO AEROFLAME ANALYTICS
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, FLAME IN FREEFALL, is an advanced research platform that uses super intelligent AI and Large Language Model (LLM) tools to explore how fire behaves in microgravity. It helps users access, understand, summarise and compare scientific research related to space combustion and spacecraft fire safety. The platform includes AEROFLAME, a scientific research dashboard, and IGNIS, an AI powered assistant that helps users explore complex research and scientific information. It also features an interactive space simulation where users can explore microgravity and learn about fire safety through realistic scientific scenarios.

Our goal is to combine AI, scientific research and interactive technology to create a platform that supports researchers, engineers and professors in understanding combustion in space and contributes to making future space missions safer.
projectDetails.details:
FLAME IN FREEFALL is an AI powered scientific research platform focused on understanding combustion and fire safety in microgravity. The project explores how flames behave differently in space compared to Earth and how this research can contribute to safer spacecraft and future human space exploration.

The platform combines scientific research, artificial intelligence, interactive simulations, and data exploration in one environment. Its main research system, AEROFLAME, helps users explore, organize, understand, summarize, and compare microgravity combustion research. It also includes IGNIS, an AI powered assistant designed to help users understand scientific concepts and navigate research information. The Simulation Experience provides an interactive space environment where users can explore microgravity concepts and observe how different conditions influence flame behaviour.

The project aims to make complex scientific research more accessible, organized, and easier to understand while supporting further exploration of spacecraft fire safety. It is designed for researchers, aerospace engineers, professors, and university students.

The platform was developed using AI assisted development tools, large language models, and modern web technologies. These tools supported the development of the interface, AI assistant, research features, and interactive experiences. The project combines scientific accuracy with an innovative digital experience to connect research, technology, and space exploration.

projectDetails.name: Project Banat Zayed
projectDetails.summary: What if we could make Earth’s hidden changes visible and turn satellite data into a powerful tool for understanding our planet? Dancing with the SARs is an interactive web application inspired by NASA’s NISAR mission, designed to make Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) technology easier to explore, understand, and use. Through an interactive global map, users can select locations around the world, investigate different types of surface changes, including ground movement, forest and vegetation changes, wetlands, flooding, and glacier movement, and search NASA’s Earthdata catalog for available NISAR observations. The application also introduces important radar concepts, such as backscatter, interferometric coherence, and surface displacement, helping users understand how satellites can reveal information about Earth’s surface during both day and night and through clouds. Our project transforms complex satellite science into an accessible, engaging experience that encourages curiosity, exploration, and scientific thinking. By connecting NASA’s powerful Earth observation technology with real-world environmental questions, Dancing with the SARs aims to inspire the next generation of innovators to understand our changing planet and use space-based science to help build a more sustainable future.
projectDetails.details: Dancing with the SARs is an interactive web application inspired by NASA’s NISAR mission, designed to help people explore how Earth’s surface changes over time using Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) technology. The application works as an interactive Earth observation explorer where users can select any location on a global map, choose a research theme, such as ground movement, forest and vegetation changes, wetlands and flooding, or glaciers and ice, and search NASA’s Earthdata catalog for available NISAR observations within a selected date range. It also includes an educational section explaining radar concepts such as backscatter, interferometric coherence, and surface displacement, helping users understand how radar signals reveal information about our planet. The main benefits are making complex satellite science easier to understand, encouraging independent investigation, and helping users discover satellite observations relevant to environmental changes and natural processes. Our intended impact is to encourage students, researchers, and the public to become more interested in Earth observation and use scientific information to better understand environmental challenges. To develop the project, we used HTML to structure the application, CSS to create its visual design, and JavaScript to build its interactive features and functions. We also used Leaflet to create the interactive global map, NASA GIBS for the satellite-based map background, and NASA’s Common Metadata Repository (CMR) API to search for NISAR collection and observation metadata. No additional hardware was required. What makes our project creative is the idea of turning radar observations into a journey of exploration, where users can choose their own location and research question instead of simply reading information about satellites. The dancing theme represents the continuous movement and transformation of Earth’s surface. Our team considered accessibility, user experience, scientific accuracy, global coverage, different environmental applications, and the importance of clearly explaining what the available satellite data can and cannot show. We also designed the interface with a modern NASA-inspired appearance using dark navy, turquoise, and gold details to make scientific exploration engaging and easy to navigate.

projectDetails.name: Asclepius: an explainable health expert system for astronauts
projectDetails.summary: Asclepius is an explainable health expert system for astronauts on long missions, where the flight surgeon can be minutes away or out of contact behind the Moon. Every day the crew fills in a short morning and evening check-in: vitals, sleep, symptoms, mood, reaction time. The app also reads cabin CO2 and radiation dose. It compares each value with the astronaut's own six-month pre-flight baseline, not with population averages, and runs transparent IF-THEN rules built from NASA's medical knowledge, covering all 100 conditions of NASA's Integrated Medical Model plus 15 more from HRP evidence. The result is a hypothesis with a confidence level, an urgency color (green, yellow, orange, red), a "Why?" chain that names the rule and its NASA source, the steps to take now and the next measurement to make. On red it prepares a compact flight-surgeon packet and queues it while there is no link. Astronaut health records are not public, so instead of training an AI on data we do not have, we built clear rules and tested them on real data, including real Inspiration4 crew lab results from NASA OSDR.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

Asclepius helps astronauts assess their own health when the flight surgeon is far away: up to 20 minutes of delay on the way to Mars, or no link at all behind the Moon. The crew fills in a short morning and evening check-in (vitals, sleep, sleepiness, symptoms, mood, reaction time, workload, food and fluid). The app adds mission context: cabin CO2, radiation dose, communication delay. It returns hypotheses with a confidence level, an urgency level (GREEN, YELLOW, ORANGE, RED), a "Why?" chain that names each rule and its NASA source, concrete steps to take now, and the next best measurement when data is missing. On RED it builds a compact flight-surgeon packet; with a long delay or no link it puts onboard steps first and queues the packet until the link returns.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Facts: the latest values are compared with the astronaut's own six-month pre-flight passport (personal baseline and range), plus streaks, 7-day counts and clinical scores (NEWS2, qSOFA).

2. Rules: 86 encoded IF-THEN rules (220+ documented in the knowledge base) fire by forward chaining; several rules for one hypothesis combine as certainty factors.

3. Safety guard: "expected adaptation to spaceflight" never hides a red flag in the same body system.

4. Missing data is never treated as normal: rules without inputs stay pending and ask for the next measurement.

5. Expected in-flight shifts from NASA evidence (for example lower blood pressure) are taken into account, so normal adaptation is not flagged as illness.

KNOWLEDGE BASE

Built from the challenge resources: NASA HRP hazards and risks (every risk is a body system), all 100 conditions of NASA's Integrated Medical Model plus 15 from HRP evidence, NASA-STD-3001 and OCHMO technical briefs for limits (CO2, radiation, sleep, behavioral health, bone, workload), Human Research Roadmap evidence reports, NASA Standard Measures for the pre-flight schedule, and the CSA radiation monitoring article. 115 conditions, 102 actions, 131 references; every rule cites its source.

DATA

No public time series of astronaut vital signs exist, so each fictional crew member's six-month pre-flight passport is built from real donors: real Inspiration4 astronaut labs and microbiome data (NASA OSDR OSD-569, OSD-575, OSD-572), NHANES exams, LifeSnaps wearable streams, MMASH hormones, PTB-XL ECGs, PhysioNet tilt tests; NASA DONKI and NOAA solar events and MSL RAD dose rates for radiation. Every value carries a provenance label (real-astronaut, real-ground, real-population, synthetic-calibrated, authored).

VALIDATION ON REAL DATA

- Healthy volunteers (LifeSnaps, 23 people, 1,276 days): 92% GREEN, 0 RED.

- Real astronaut lab draws (Inspiration4, 28 draws): 4 trigger the glucose rules, flagged for flight-surgeon review.

- Emergency patients, triage vitals only (MIMIC-IV-ED demo): 27% of urgent patients escalated from vitals alone.

- Orthostatic criteria on healthy controls (PhysioNet tilt): 0 false positives.

- Radiation biodosimetry from blood gene expression (NASA OSDR OSD-410): exposure detected in 84% of samples.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Crews get explainable, source-backed guidance when Earth cannot answer in time; flight surgeons get a short, structured packet instead of raw data. Because every decision is a readable rule with a citation, the system can be reviewed, corrected and certified, which a black-box model cannot offer for medical use.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

Instead of training AI on astronaut data that is not public, we turned NASA's own medical knowledge into transparent rules, the approach NASA itself pioneered with the CLIPS expert-system tool. Each astronaut is compared with their own six-month baseline, and the app adapts to communication delay and loss of signal.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

Python (FastAPI, Pydantic, pandas, PyYAML, pytest; 166 automated tests), TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Recharts. Deployed on a Linux server with nginx and systemd. Live demo: https://asclepius.phronesisco.tech

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

Safety (decision support for self-assessment, not a diagnosis; no drug doses, medication always defers to the onboard checklist), honest handling of missing data, communication delay, privacy (a user's own crew data stays in their browser; nothing is stored on the server), no real astronaut is identified (the demo mission Hygieia I and its crew are fictional), readability (Atkinson Hyperlegible font; urgency shown by color, shape and text), and clear labelling of every synthetic value.

challengeDetails.title: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
challengeDetails.excerpt: Long-duration missions expose astronauts to space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment, which can bring immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events, and behavioral health problems. projectDetails.name: Project Challenger Seekers
projectDetails.summary: Curiosity is humanity's utmost feature that we must express. Through science, we best feel the thrill of knowledge and community. Team Challenger Seekers addresses this specific challenge to show that what we know and have is not the limit to what there is. Reading through the available Earth analogs for Mars and the Moon sparked a need to discover new characteristics that can help and provide use to NASA and other space agencies. In this project, we made it our ultimate goal to help our minds by learning in this experience and, more importantly, contribute to society's achievements and progression. Engaging with one another in actions and will has gotten us so far throughout histroy and can only continue to do so. We researched possible analog locations on Earth and analyized data from NASA and other credible sources to ensure a valid and smooth project. We covered deserts, polar regions, volcanic & arid terrains as well as caves. We followed exact scientific method sequences that not only remove worry for scientists but also provide new insights and discoveries that can be effective in their missions. All of our observations have been presented with the best methods one could understand: visuals, interactive maps, and graphs to further confirm the math and thought processes are as accurate as possible. As two seniors in high school with an intermediate level of experience in this field, we are grateful and ready to take on this challenge and be judged.
projectDetails.details:
Hello! This is Team Challenger Seekers speaking. We want to note that there was use of AI during this project. What we personally did was research databases and compile all the information and resources to use; we then worked together, read through the websites, and gathered details. During this process, we used the help of ChatGPT to further validate our findings & also used Claude for help with interactive features and overall checking. We hope our work benefits scientists & engineers, and we hope you enjoy the reading journey, as we enjoyed the experience of this challenge!!

We considered some data limitations and the fact that not all conditions must be satisfied for an analog to be valid; as long as one is true and is genuinely useful for astronauts, then it would still be suitable in the study. Alongside that, we incorporated every minor and major detail worthy of note, such as impact on human biology, EVA engineering components, operational cost, and lithology. We used the above to determine a credible grading system for the characteristics of each new analog with rescept mars and the Moon. We considered the new math that we'd be learning and included statistical measures and formulas to further show accuracy in graphs and in formats like log, etc that would help the scale at which information is presented.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: ClimaLens UAE
projectDetails.summary:
ClimaLens UAE is an interactive web platform built with Python, Flask and NASA POWER meteorological data derived from the MERRA-2 reanalysis. It helps users investigate long-term environmental trends across selected locations in the United Arab Emirates, including Al Ruwais, Abu Dhabi, Dubai, Al Ain and Liwa Oasis. The displayed analysis covers 1984–2025.

Climate records contain seasonal cycles, year-to-year fluctuations and extreme observations that can make long-term changes difficult to identify. ClimaLens addresses this by grouping monthly observations into All-Year, Summer and Winter (DJF) baselines and analysing trends using two complementary statistical methods: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) linear regression and the non-parametric Mann–Kendall test.

The platform presents trend direction, estimated change per decade, confidence intervals and statistical evidence through interactive visualisations. Its Plain Language / Detailed views make findings accessible to general users while retaining statistical information for deeper investigation.

By combining regional comparisons, statistical analysis and transparent data limitations, ClimaLens UAE connects NASA Earth science data with potential applications in cooling demand, heat exposure, energy planning and environmental resilience.
projectDetails.details:
1. What It Does & How It Works

ClimaLens UAE is an interactive climate investigation platform developed to help users explore long-term environmental trends across the United Arab Emirates using NASA POWER climate data.

Climate datasets contain seasonal cycles, year-to-year fluctuations and occasional extreme observations. These variations can make it difficult to distinguish long-term changes from short-term variability. ClimaLens addresses this challenge by allowing users to investigate different locations, environmental variables and seasonal periods through interactive visualisations and statistical analysis.

The platform follows three main stages:

1. Seasonal Aggregation

Users can investigate All-Year, Summer and Winter (DJF) conditions. Monthly observations are grouped into the selected seasonal baseline, allowing trends to be examined across different parts of the year rather than relying on a single annual average.

2. Statistical Trend Analysis

Each selected dataset is analysed using two complementary methods:

  • Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Linear Regression estimates the direction and magnitude of the trend, including its rate of change per decade, 95% confidence interval and associated p-value.
  • The non-parametric Mann–Kendall test evaluates whether the observations show a consistent increasing or decreasing trend over time.

ClimaLens identifies trends supported by both tests at the 0.05 significance level. These results indicate statistical evidence of a trend, not proof of its cause. The analysis also communicates limitations such as potential year-to-year autocorrelation.

3. Regional Comparison and Interpretation

Users can compare locations, examine different climate variables and explore a regional ranking of estimated trend rates. A Plain Language / Detailed interface presents findings at two levels: accessible explanations for general users and statistical information for users interested in the underlying evidence.

2. Key Discoveries & Intended Impact

ClimaLens uses regional analysis to explore how different environmental variables behave across the UAE.

Widespread Temperature Increases

The analysed locations show statistically significant upward trends in mean air temperature under the platform's dual-test criterion. In the displayed analysis, Al Ruwais has an estimated increase of approximately +0.389 °C per decade, while Dubai shows approximately +0.369 °C per decade.

These findings highlight the importance of examining regional temperature trends when discussing long-term cooling demand, heat exposure and infrastructure resilience.

Seasonal Humidity Patterns

The platform allows users to investigate relative humidity across different seasons, including winter conditions along the UAE coast. This provides a basis for exploring environmental patterns relevant to coastal infrastructure and atmospheric conditions.

Rainfall Variability

Precipitation analysis demonstrates the importance of distinguishing individual rainfall fluctuations from sustained long-term trends. Where statistical evidence is insufficient, ClimaLens communicates that a significant trend has not been established rather than presenting fluctuations as a confirmed climate signal.

From Data to Decisions

Beyond presenting statistical results, ClimaLens provides operational interpretations that connect environmental findings to potential planning considerations, including cooling infrastructure, heat exposure and water-resource management.

These interpretations are intended to support further investigation and informed discussion, not replace detailed engineering assessments or local measurements.

3. Tools, Data & Technologies Used

NASA Earth Science Data

ClimaLens uses NASA POWER climate data derived from the MERRA-2 meteorological reanalysis. The analysed variables include:

  • Mean Air Temperature (T2M)
  • Maximum Air Temperature (T2M_MAX)
  • Relative Humidity (RH2M)
  • Corrected Precipitation (PRECTOTCORR)
  • All-Sky Surface Shortwave Downward Irradiance (ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN)

Backend and Statistical Analysis

  • Python — application logic and data processing.
  • Flask — web application backend.
  • Pandas and NumPy — data processing and numerical calculations.
  • SciPy — linear regression and statistical calculations.
  • pymannkendall — Mann–Kendall trend analysis.

Frontend and Visualisation

  • HTML5 and Tailwind CSS — interface and styling.
  • JavaScript — interactive controls.
  • Plotly.js — interactive charts, trend lines and confidence intervals.
  • Geographic visualisation — regional exploration of UAE locations.

4. Creativity & Scientific Integrity

ClimaLens UAE combines regional climate investigation, statistical analysis and accessible communication in one interactive platform.

Its main distinction is the connection between scientific evidence and practical interpretation. Rather than simply displaying environmental charts, the application helps users investigate the direction and magnitude of trends, examine statistical evidence and understand the limitations behind the results.

The Plain Language / Detailed interface makes the platform accessible to users with different levels of scientific knowledge, while its regional comparison tools encourage exploration beyond a single location.

Scientific transparency is central to the project. NASA POWER provides gridded environmental estimates rather than direct measurements from individual ground stations. Nearby locations may therefore share underlying grid cells, and the results should not be interpreted as precise site-level measurements.

ClimaLens is designed as an exploratory tool for understanding regional environmental patterns and communicating scientific evidence responsibly.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: The Invisible Flood: Tonle Sap Seen by NISAR
projectDetails.summary:
Every rainy season the Mekong River pushes water backwards into Tonle Sap, Cambodia's great lake. The lake grows about five times in size and floods the surrounding forest, which becomes the nursery for one of the world's largest inland fisheries. That flooded forest is shrinking and the yearly flood is weakening, yet it is hard to see from space: clouds block cameras, and the water hides under the trees.
We built an open-source interactive story map from 11 NISAR L-band radar images (19 June – 29 October 2026, mostly one every 12 days). NISAR's long waves pass through the canopy and bounce off the water and tree trunks (a "double bounce"), revealing flooded forest that cameras miss. On 30 August the flooded forest stood out from the surrounding trees by 2.3 dB in NISAR but only 0.8 dB in Sentinel-1. The HH channel captured the change, while HV barely moved.
What we found (40 × 40 km on the north shore, near Siem Reap):
* Flooded forest grew about 8× by 30 August (39 → 311 km²).
* Open water grew 72% by 17 October (611 → 1,050 km²).
* The hidden flood under the trees peaked 5–7 weeks before the open-water flood.
Users can play through the season, compare dates and click any spot to see its history. Repeated each year with free NISAR data, these maps could flag weak-flood years for fisheries managers, forest protection teams and disaster agencies.
projectDetails.details:
What it does
The Invisible Flood is an interactive web story map that shows how Cambodia’s Tonle Sap lake floods its forest each rainy season, including the part of the flood hidden under the trees and under monsoon clouds. It turns 11 NISAR radar images into maps, an animation and charts that anyone can explore.

How it works

  1. We downloaded NISAR Level-2 GCOV products (track 083 ascending, frame 008, 20 m, HH + HV) from NASA’s ASF DAAC with the earthaccess library, reading only our 40 × 40 km window from each ~3 GB file.
  2. We averaged pixels to 100 m cells in linear power to reduce radar speckle, then converted to decibels.
  3. Each cell was classified on every date: open water (HH below −15 dB) and flooded forest (tree cells, from ESA WorldCover, with HH at or above −5 dB, plus a strict −3 dB version).
  4. We built a time series of areas, a time-colour composite, and a “time under water” map.
  5. We compared NISAR with Sentinel-1 radar and cloud-covered Sentinel-2 photos from the same week.

Key results
• Flooded forest grew about 8× from 19 June to 30 August (39 → 311 km²).
• Open water grew 72% from 19 June to 17 October (611 → 1,050 km²).
• The flood under the trees peaked 5–7 weeks before the open-water flood.
• The HH–HV gap over forest rose from 4.9 to 7.7 dB as water arrived: the double-bounce signature.
• 84% of the forest in the study area (452 of 540 km²) flooded at least once.

Benefits and intended impact
Tonle Sap’s flooded forest is the nursery for about 600,000 tonnes of fish a year, and it has shrunk by about 31% since 1993. Our maps show where and for how long the forest was actually under water, even under cloud. Fisheries managers can estimate nursery habitat, conservation teams can protect the forest that really floods, and disaster agencies can track water reaching rice fields. Repeated every year with free NISAR data, the method can flag weak-flood years early.

Tools and technologies
Python (earthaccess, h5py, NumPy, SciPy, pyproj, matplotlib, odc-stac, pystac-client); MapLibre GL and Chart.js for the web map; Microsoft Planetary Computer for Sentinel and WorldCover data; GitHub and Vercel for hosting. Code is open source (MIT): https://github.com/afk-2/tonle-sap-invisible-flood

What makes it creative
It tells a story with radar: the flood is invisible to cameras, so we show what NISAR alone can see. A slider, a play-through of the season and click-to-inspect let non-experts explore real radar measurements.

What we considered
We state our limits openly: one season of data only (NISAR data here start in June 2026), an instrument gap from 26 July to 17 August, provisional calibration for most dates, thresholds taken from published values rather than field checks, and 2021 land-cover labels. We report both forest thresholds so the trend can be judged independently of the exact km².

Our hypothesis for the pattern: the Mekong's monsoon rise reverses the Tonle Sap River and refills the lake. The water first spreads under the forest canopy, giving a bright double bounce. As it keeps rising, it covers low trees and shrubs completely, and they switch from bright to dark like open water. That is why flooded forest falls after late August while open water keeps growing into October.

node.excerpt: We are Comic Drift, a team of students passionate about space exploration, technology, and innovation. For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we developed Root Cause, an interactive game where young players investigate emergencies at a Martian outpost...

projectDetails.name: Root-Cause
projectDetails.summary:
Something is wrong at the Mars base, and it is your job to find out what it is. Root Cause is a browser game for kids aged 7–12. Players are flight controllers at Suhail Base in Gale Crater, Mars. Each case starts with an alarm. Looking at the readings is free, but every test costs crew hours. To win, players must think like scientists: predict, test, rule things out and fix the real cause.

The six cases cover power, food, life support and radiation shielding, and show how the systems depend on each other. A weak battery leads to the heater being cut, the greenhouse freezing, and the lettuce stopping growing. Asking Mission Control costs crew hours too, because messages take 4 to 24 minutes each way between Earth and Mars. The game uses real NASA data from InSight, Curiosity and DONKI, every case ends with the true NASA story it is based on, and it runs in any browser in English, Arabic, French and Spanish.
projectDetails.details:
HOW A CASE WORKS

1. Alarm. Something is wrong. Press the master alarm to start.

2. Quick decision. A trade-off with no free option. For example: switch the lab off to save battery (and lose a sol of science), or keep it running (and risk the greenhouse heater being cut tonight).

3. Look at the readings. Free charts of the outpost's systems, with a dotted "normal day" line to compare against.

4. Run tests. Each test costs crew hours. Before it runs, the player predicts the result.

5. Ask Mission Control if stuck. It costs 2 crew hours, because messages take 4 to 24 minutes each way between Earth and Mars.

6. Call the root cause. A wrong call costs 2 hours.

7. Build the chain. Put the cause-and-effect steps in order. One card is fake, and a wrong card costs an hour.

8. Fix it. Some fixes only treat the symptom. Only fixing the cause closes the case.

9. Real mission. Each case ends with the true NASA story it is based on, with a link.

Stars are awarded for fixing the problem, using few tests, and predicting every test correctly. The root cause is picked at random from 2–3 possibilities each time, so replaying a case can lead to a different answer.

THE SIX CASES

1. Dim Day (tutorial), power: dust slowly covered InSight's solar panels (2018–2022).

2. Cold Lettuce, food and power: a dust storm put InSight into safe mode (January 2022).

3. Stuffy Air, life support (CO₂): Apollo 13's CO₂ filter fix (1970).

4. Oxygen Alarm, life support (oxygen): the ISS ammonia false alarm (January 2015).

5. Slow Leak, life support (air pressure): the ISS slow air leak hunt (2020).

6. Storm Incoming, radiation shielding: the solar storm that hit Mars (May 20, 2024).

HOW IT FITS THE CHALLENGE

- Life support, radiation shielding, power and food: each has at least one case, and cases show how the systems depend on each other. A weak battery leads to the heater being cut, the greenhouse freezing, and the lettuce stopping growing.

- Communication delay: Ask Mission Control costs crew hours because of the real Earth–Mars message delay.

- No free choices: tests, wrong calls, wrong chain cards, wrong fixes and asking for help all cost crew hours. Every quick decision has a downside on purpose, because real mission planners never get a free choice.

- Replayability: random root causes, plus stars to improve on.

- Plain language: short sentences. Words like sol, ppm, kPa and ohms are explained next to the chart where they appear.

- Low barrier: runs in any browser, with no download or sign-up needed.

- Four languages: English, Arabic, French and Spanish.

NASA DATA USED

All of this is also listed in the game under "NASA data used" on the title screen.

- InSight lander solar power: about 5,000 Wh per sol after landing (2018), cut by dust to about 500 by spring 2022. Used in Dim Day's "InSight's solar power" reading.

- Curiosity rover REMS weather station: Gale Crater, sol 4189 (May 19, 2024): low −68 °C, high −5 °C, 861 Pa. Sol 4190 (May 20, 2024): low −69 °C, high −3 °C, 860 Pa. Used in the "Air outside" reading in every case.

- DONKI space weather database: CME 2024-05-20T05:36:00-CME-001, from Sun region 13664, about 2,678 km/s. Used in Storm Incoming's space weather alert from Mission Control.

- Curiosity rover RAD radiation detector: 8,100 micrograys on May 20, 2024 (about 30 chest X-rays), against about 180–225 on a normal sol. Used in Storm Incoming's "Radiation dose" reading.

- Earth–Mars message delay: 4 to 24 minutes each way. Used for Ask Mission Control.

- Real mission stories: Apollo 13, InSight and the ISS, in the "Real mission" box at the end of each case.

This is archived data stored in the game, not a live feed. The outpost's own readings (battery, greenhouse, CO₂ and so on) come from a simple simulation (js/sim.js), so each case behaves in a consistent, realistic way.

PLAYTESTING

21 people played the game and filled in a feedback form. 62% were in our target age of 7–12, and 67% rated the game 4 or 5 out of 5 for being easy to play. 5 of the 7 who played in another language rated the translation 4 or 5 out of 5, and nobody rated it below 3. Two of the three written suggestions asked for clearer instructions, and one asked for more levels. We listened and made significant changes to help with the gameplay: we addressed these complaints by adding a tutorial and instructions.

HOW IT'S BUILT

Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no frameworks, libraries or build step. Sounds are generated in code with the Web Audio API.

- index.html: screens and layout

- css/style.css: mission-control look and visuals

- js/cases.js: the six cases (readings, tests, causes, fixes, costs)

- js/sim.js: 48-hour outpost simulation and chart data

- js/game.js: game logic

- js/graph.js: chart drawing

- js/sound.js: sound effects

- js/lang/*.js: all game text in English, Arabic, French and Spanish

## Use of SI

We used Claude (Anthropic) explicitily for:

- **Translations:** the Arabic, French and Spanish versions of all game text. The game says this on the title screen.

- **One bug fix:** a logic error in the chart drawing (`js/graph.js`) which we could not fix by ourselves..

- **Review and testing:** Claude reviewed the game against the challenge brief, found bugs, tested every case in every language, Our team built these changes ourselves.

projectDetails.name: Project SPHEREx Time Machine
projectDetails.summary:
SPHEREx Time Machine is an interactive website where users can view and visualize astronomical discoveries accessible to everyone using data directly from NASA’s mission. Our website allows users to enter their coordinates or pick ones on a map and view the stars, comets and galaxies at that time period, which can be picked from our options. By displaying observations in an interactive, video-like viewer, users can easily identify moving objects, changes in brightness, and other astronomical phenomena, including asteroids, comets, stars, and brown dwarfs.
 
Our website’s aim is to transform SPHEREx’s expansive collection of astronomical data captured through out the years of research into one cohesive, engaging website. Through infra-red scans and time-band image comparisons, the tool empowers both astronomy enthusiasts and researchers to investigate the universe, recognize unusual patterns, and contribute to new scientific discoveries. Our goal is to make exploring the changing universe simple,
interactive, and accessible to everyone.
projectDetails.details: SPHEREx Time Machine is a website that allows users to interact and see stars, comets and asteroids by inputting desired coordinates and viewing infra-red images of these astronomical species. The screen of these infra-red photos can be played to view the movement of these asteroids, comets and stars, over 8 periods of time, showing the movement. The main benefit of this website is that users don’t need to browse through thousands of years of data and can view all of this data easily on one singular website. The intended impact is to enable non-professional users to understand and connect to any astronomical interests they may have without having any prior knowledge to space. To develop our project, we have used Base44 via inputting various prompts and adding new prompts to change or alter certain features based off feedback to allow users to have the best possible experience. Our project is creative through adding extra features other than solely viewing the stars and seeing what each object is on the infa-red camera, whilst also describing how each object will be in real-life. Our team considered various factors, such as clear steps defined and bigger fonts to adapt our products to all of our user needs.

projectDetails.name: Project Cosmic Rangers UAE
projectDetails.summary:
Space Explorer UAE is an immersive Roblox-based educational game designed to train young explorers on the fundamentals of space exploration. The project simulates a complete interplanetary mission, taking players through the entire process of launching a rocket, navigating deep space, searching for Mars, and successfully landing on the Martian surface.

This project addresses the challenge of making aerospace education accessible, engaging, and interactive for youth. Traditional learning methods can often feel abstract, but by gamifying complex space missions, players actively learn physics, orbital mechanics, and problem-solving through hands-on gameplay.

This is important because inspiring the next generation of scientists, engineers, and astronauts is vital for the future of space exploration—especially in the UAE, which has rapidly growing ambitions in the space sector. By turning a Roblox experience into an interactive training simulator, we are sparking early curiosity in STEM fields and giving young minds a tangible taste of real-world space missions.
projectDetails.details:
• What it does and how it works: The game functions as a step-by-step space training simulator. Players begin at a launch control center inspired by UAE space facilities, where they complete pre-launch checklists and ignite the rocket. Once in orbit, they use navigation controls to pilot the spacecraft through space hazards toward Mars. Finally, players switch to a lander view, managing their descent velocity and thrusters to achieve a safe touchdown on the Red Planet.
  • Benefits and intended impact: The primary benefit is experiential learning—players learn by doing rather than just reading. The intended impact is to build confidence and interest in STEM subjects among children and teenagers, inspiring them to pursue future careers in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics.
  • Tools, coding languages, hardware, and software used: The project was developed using Roblox Studio, utilizing Luau (Roblox's version of Lua) for scripting spacecraft physics, UI elements, and interactive game loops. 3D modeling software like Blender was used to design custom spacecraft, launch pads, and Martian terrain. Development was done on standard PC hardware.
  • Creativity: The project is creative because it bridges the gap between mainstream gaming and aerospace education. Instead of a standard quiz or video, players experience the high stakes and mechanics of a real Mars mission inside a familiar, highly engaging virtual world.
  • Team considerations: Our team focused heavily on user experience (UX) to ensure the controls are intuitive for younger players while maintaining scientific realism. We also considered performance optimization so the game runs smoothly across different devices, and we integrated cultural elements reflecting the UAE’s inspiring space milestones to give players a sense of national pride and purpose.

projectDetails.name: Red Dust Outpost
projectDetails.summary:
I developed Red Dust Outpost, an interactive Mars survival game for the NASA Space Apps Junior Astronaut Program. Players act as Junior Commanders keeping four astronauts alive for 12 sols until resupply arrives.
To make complex space logistics accessible to kids, we replaced complicated math with a simple daily loop across five gauges: oxygen, power, water, food, and shielding. Every choice—like splitting water for air or charging solar panels—reflects real aerospace science, including ISS electrolysis, dust storms, and Earth communication delays.
This teaches young learners critical thinking and real-world space exploration constraints through intuitive, engaging play.
projectDetails.details: Red Dust Outpost — Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a turn-based Mars survival strategy game built on Base44 (using modern web technologies like React, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS) for the NASA Space Apps Challenge that challenges players to keep four astronauts alive for 12 Martian sols until a resupply ship arrives. Designed so children as young as seven can play independently after one round without heavy math or spreadsheets, the game follows a simple four-step daily loop where players read a Mission Control briefing, spend a single crew action to manage interconnected resources (like splitting water into oxygen, charging batteries, or patching radiation shielding), watch how planetary events shift their telemetry gauges, and read one-line explanations for every change. Its creative strength lies in translating real NASA and ISS constraints—such as water electrolysis, dust storms blocking solar panels, solar flare radiation, and 5-to-20-minute Earth communication delays—into accessible, high-stakes trade-offs inside an authentic mission-control interface. When designing the project, we carefully balanced scientific accuracy with low cognitive load and constructive failure logs, aiming to build systems-thinking skills, resilience, and early excitement for space exploration among young learners.
