projectDetails.name: Project Darkstar
projectDetails.summary:
Darkstar is an AI-powered Martian survival and navigation platform developed for NASA Space Apps 2026's *Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map* challenge. It combines real NASA mission data, interactive planetary exploration, terrain-aware navigation and artificial intelligence to help astronauts plan scientific expeditions across Mars.

Darkstar features an interactive map of Mars with surface imagery, 3D terrain visualization, topography and geological information. Using NASA elevation datasets and the A* pathfinding algorithm, it calculates routes based on distance, terrain gradients and estimated energy consumption.

Its Marswalk planning system allows astronauts to establish habitats, select scientific objectives, plan return journeys and estimate mission duration, oxygen consumption, power requirements and emergency reserves. Environmental information highlights potential hazards, including radiation, temperature extremes and dust.

An AI survival assistant powered by Groq interprets mission information and retrieves verified NASA research to provide evidence-backed guidance with scientific citations.

Darkstar addresses the challenge by transforming scattered scientific datasets into an accessible, integrated exploration tool. Its purpose is to support informed decisions in unfamiliar, hazardous environments, including situations where visibility is limited and reliable planning becomes essential.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details — Darkstar

Darkstar is an AI-powered Martian exploration, navigation and survival-planning platform developed for the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge, Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map. Our objective was to transform scientific data collected by NASA missions into a practical, interactive system that could help astronauts explore Mars, conduct scientific investigations and make informed decisions in a hazardous environment.

How Darkstar Works

Darkstar combines planetary mapping, terrain analysis, route optimization, mission planning and artificial intelligence into one integrated application.

1. Interactive Martian Exploration

Darkstar provides an interactive map of Mars using NASA and USGS scientific datasets. Users can explore the planet through multiple visualization modes, including surface imagery, topography, geological mapping and three-dimensional terrain.

The platform uses imagery from the Viking missions and Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter's Context Camera (CTX), alongside elevation measurements from the Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA). A higher-resolution CTX digital elevation model provides more detailed terrain analysis within a selected region of Jezero Crater.

Users can navigate to prominent Martian landmarks, inspect coordinates and elevation, and explore areas of scientific interest.

2. Intelligent Terrain Navigation

Unlike conventional navigation systems, Mars has no established road network. Astronauts and exploration vehicles must navigate uneven, potentially hazardous terrain while managing limited resources.

Darkstar addresses this using the A* pathfinding algorithm, combined with numerical terrain analysis. Its navigation engine considers geographic distance, elevation changes, terrain gradients and configurable mobility constraints.

For rover exploration, Darkstar can compare the shortest-distance route against a route optimized for estimated energy consumption. This allows users to investigate trade-offs between direct travel and avoiding energy-intensive terrain.

The system also identifies unsupported terrain and communicates the limitations of available elevation data rather than assuming every route is traversable.

3. Astronaut Marswalk and Survival Planning

Darkstar includes a Marswalk planning system designed around extravehicular activities (EVAs).

Users can establish a habitat location, select a scientific destination and calculate an outbound and return journey. The mission planner estimates travel duration, elevation changes, oxygen requirements, electrical power consumption and emergency reserves.

Astronaut mobility parameters and resource budgets can be adjusted to explore different mission scenarios.

These calculations use hypothetical engineering assumptions and are intended as planning demonstrations rather than validated astronaut life-support predictions.

4. Environmental Awareness

Mars presents significant environmental challenges, including extreme temperatures, low atmospheric pressure, radiation exposure and airborne dust.

Darkstar incorporates historical scientific information from NASA missions and planetary data archives, including environmental observations and radiation research associated with Curiosity.

The application presents relevant hazards, scientific sources, geographic coverage and uncertainty. Historical observations are explicitly distinguished from real-time environmental conditions.

5. NASA-Grounded AI Survival Assistant

Darkstar integrates an AI assistant using Groq-hosted openai/gpt-oss-120b, with support for alternative language-model providers.

Rather than depending entirely on a language model's existing knowledge, Darkstar uses retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to supply relevant information from authoritative NASA and USGS scientific resources.

The assistant can explain Martian environmental hazards, discuss survival challenges, interpret scientific information and analyze available mission-planning context.

Users can attach their Explorer data, allowing the AI to reference actual route statistics, terrain information, resource estimates and environmental context. Scientific references are provided through clickable citations.

Technologies and Development Tools

Darkstar was developed using a modular software architecture:

  • Next.js, React and TypeScript: Interactive frontend, planetary maps, visualization and mission-planning interfaces.
  • Python and FastAPI: Backend APIs, terrain processing, route calculations and AI integration.
  • NumPy and rasterio: Processing numerical elevation datasets, terrain grids and geospatial information.
  • A pathfinding:* Terrain-aware route generation and optimization.
  • Groq API and GPT-OSS: AI inference and scientific question answering.
  • NASA/PDS and USGS datasets: Scientific imagery, elevation, geological mapping and environmental information.
  • Git and GitHub: Version control, project management and development collaboration.

The project was designed to work on conventional computers without requiring specialized aerospace hardware.

Creativity and Innovation

Darkstar's main innovation is the integration of multiple traditionally separate capabilities into a single exploration platform.

Instead of simply displaying a Martian map, Darkstar connects terrain information with navigation decisions, resource estimates, scientific objectives and AI-assisted explanations.

One important design consideration was the difference between the shortest route and the most resource-efficient route. A longer path around difficult terrain may consume less energy than a direct route across steep slopes.

Another consideration was exploration under limited visibility. Darkstar's underlying terrain-based navigation approach provides a foundation for planning journeys without relying exclusively on visible surface landmarks, although operational navigation would require additional positioning and hazard-detection systems.

We also prioritized scientific transparency. Darkstar identifies data sources, communicates geographic coverage and distinguishes measured observations from hypothetical calculations and uncertain information.

Intended Impact

Darkstar aims to demonstrate how planetary science, software engineering and artificial intelligence can work together to support future human exploration.

By making NASA data easier to explore and interpret, the platform can help users understand the practical challenges of operating on Mars, including terrain selection, mission logistics, environmental risks and scientific decision-making.

Although Darkstar is currently a research and educational prototype rather than a flight-qualified navigation system, its architecture demonstrates a possible foundation for more advanced planetary mission-planning tools.

Our guiding idea is that even when visibility is lost, scientific knowledge and intelligent navigation can continue to guide exploration.

projectDetails.name: DeepSpace Vitals
projectDetails.summary:
DeepSpace Vitals is an astronaut health-monitoring and mission-support platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It demonstrates how astronaut health information and mission operations can be organised in one accessible platform.

The prototype includes separate Mission Control and Astronaut dashboards, simulated vital-sign telemetry, health indicators, trend visualisations, alerts, crew assignments, mission briefings and communication-status indicators.

The project explores how software could support astronaut health monitoring during future space missions. All displayed health readings are simulated and are not real astronaut medical data.
projectDetails.details:
DeepSpace Vitals was developed to explore how astronauts and Mission Control could monitor health information during space missions.

The platform has two roles:

  • Mission Control (Admin): Mission and crew management, astronaut overview, alerts and briefings.
  • Astronaut: A personal dashboard with mission information, health indicators and updates.

The prototype demonstrates simulated vital-sign readings, health trends and communication statuses such as LIVE, DELAYED and NO LINK.

The project was developed using Base44, Figma, Miro, Canva and ChatGPT.

Important limitation: All health readings and telemetry are simulated. The prototype is not connected to real astronaut medical systems and is not intended for medical diagnosis.

projectDetails.summary:
AFTERLIFE is an interactive educational webpage that explores the stories of spacecraft, rovers and scientific equipment that have been left behind after their missions. It takes visitors on a journey across three destinations: the Moon, Mars and Deep Space.

Through interactive profiles, short mission stories, interesting discoveries and a final quiz, the project introduces visitors to lesser-known space explorers. It explains what happened to them after their missions ended.

The project aims to make space exploration more accessible and engaging, particularly for younger audiences, while highlighting how past missions continue to contribute to our understanding of the universe.
projectDetails.details:
AFTERLIFE is an interactive educational webpage that takes visitors on a journey through the Moon, Mars and Deep Space, introducing them to spacecraft, rovers and scientific equipment whose missions have ended or whose signals have gone silent.

The webpage is organized into different destinations, each featuring interactive elements that reveal the stories, discoveries and final journeys of lesser-known space explorers. It also includes interesting facts and a final quiz to help visitors test what they have learned.

I aim to make space exploration more engaging and accessible, particularly for younger audiences. Rather than focusing only on famous astronauts and major missions, AFTERLIFE highlights the machines that explored beyond Earth and the discoveries they left behind. Through this project, I hope to encourage curiosity, appreciation for scientific progress, and a deeper interest in space exploration.

The creative aspect of my project lies in its storytelling approach. Instead of presenting information as a collection of facts, I have turned completed space missions into stories that visitors can explore at their own pace through interactive elements and visual content.

While developing the project, I considered the intended audience, ease of navigation, accuracy of scientific information, and the amount of content displayed on each page. I aimed to keep the information concise and understandable without losing the significance of each mission.

projectDetails.name: Outpost Odyssey
projectDetails.summary: Outpost Odyssey puts kids aged 7 to 12 in charge of a deep-space habitat on the Moon or Mars, turning real NASA mission logistics into a hands-on survival game. Most space materials for young learners stick to flat facts or feel way too technical, leaving kids out of the actual tough calls astronauts have to make every day. In our game, nothing is free. If a solar storm hits, players might have to pull power away from oxygen scrubbers or greenhouse crops just to keep their radiation shields running. We built the simulation around real NASA open datasets—tracking actual space weather spikes and harsh surface conditions—so every dilemma reflects genuine engineering constraints rather than made-up rules. By letting players test strategies, fail safely, and see how a small choice early on snowballs days later, Outpost Odyssey helps kids build real systems-thinking skills while learning what it truly takes to survive off-world.
projectDetails.details:
Outpost Odyssey is a lunar-based survival and mission-control simulator. Across a multi-sol mission timeline, players manage core habitat systems: Power, Life Support (Oxygen & Food), and Radiation Shielding.

Each turn presents players with realistic operational scenarios and environmental events, such as incoming solar flares, micrometeorite showers, or equipment maintenance needs. Instead of offering a "safe" or zero-cost answer, every decision forces a tangible trade-off. For example, running a high-energy scientific experiment yields mission points but drains battery reserves needed for overnight heating and hydroponic food production. Similarly, locking down the habitat to block radiation keeps crew health stable while temporarily halting external communications and solar array efficiency, allowing players to learn directly from scenarios.

projectDetails.name: Cosmic Besties
projectDetails.summary: Cosmic Besties is an interactive, Duolingo-style space academy built specifically for middle schoolers (ages 13–14) that brings NASA’s retired and deep-space missions to life. Since the 1960s, NASA has sent extraordinary rovers, landers, and probes across the Moon, Mars, and the outer solar system, yet most school websites present their history as dry textbook notes. As a 13-year-old who loves space, I designed this app so 20 iconic spacecraft across four sectors (Early Pioneers, Red Planet Mars, Outer Giants & Ice Worlds, and Comet Chasers & Cosmic Hunters) speak in the first person to share where they are, what they discovered, and how they sent their final signals. Players explore 6-branch Interactive Mission Mind Maps to earn Space Coins, play an adaptive Arcade with a smart hint system that gives helpful clues instead of discouraging wrong answers, sketch their own astronaut avatar in the HTML5 Canvas Cadet Art Studio (saved seamlessly in browser localStorage with zero login barriers), and unbox collectible Mystery Capsules. Every mission also features a direct "Explore on Official NASA.gov" button alongside a dedicated Resources Corner powered by real NASA Science (science.nasa.gov), NASA Image Library (images.nasa.gov), and NSSDCA (nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov) archives, all built and published as a live web app using Google AI Studio.
projectDetails.details:
Cosmic Besties is an interactive, Duolingo-style space academy built specifically for middle school students that brings NASA’s retired and deep-space missions to life. Instead of reading passive textbook articles, students explore 20 iconic NASA missions grouped into four cosmic sectors (Early Pioneers, Red Planet Mars, Outer Giants & Ice Worlds, and Comet Chasers & Cosmic Hunters). Every spacecraft speaks in a warm, first-person voice to share where it is, what it discovered, and what happened to its final signal. Clicking any mission opens a 6-branch Interactive Mission Mind Map (Origin & Engineering, Cosmic Journey, Deep Discoveries, Survival & Drama, Final Signal & Fate, and Mission Legacy) that rewards curiosity with Space Coins. Students can then test their knowledge in an adaptive Arcade (featuring an infinite trivia quiz, a signal memory-match game, and a launch-order sorting game), draw their own astronaut avatar in the Cadet Art Studio, and spend their earned coins on collectible Mystery Capsules. Every mission also includes a direct "Explore on Official NASA.gov" button alongside a dedicated Resources Corner linking straight to NASA’s official archives.

Benefits & Intended Impact Most space education websites present historic spacecraft as dry lists of dates and technical specs, which quickly loses the attention of middle schoolers. By combining emotional storytelling, game-based rewards, and zero-login instant access, Forgotten Giants of Space makes real space history feel personal, exciting, and approachable. My goal is to help students my age connect emotionally with NASA's robotic explorers, build curiosity about STEM and planetary science, and learn how to verify space facts using real NASA public archives.

Creativity & Design Factors Considered: As a teen building for teens, I focused heavily on what actually keeps kids engaged without feeling like homework:

  • First-Person Storytelling & Hint-Based Learning: Giving spacecraft their own voices makes them feel like real heroes, while the Arcade's smart hint system gives players a helpful 1-sentence character clue and a second chance instead of discouraging them when they miss a question.
  • Creative Self-Expression & Collection: Adding an interactive drawing pad for custom avatars and Mystery Capsule card packs gives students creative ownership and a fun reason to keep exploring all 20 missions.
  • Privacy & Frictionless Access: Because the app is designed for students, I avoided logins, passwords, or personal data collection by saving all progress, Space Coins, and custom drawings locally in the browser.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

  • Development & Live Hosting: Built and deployed as a public web app using Google AI Studio (Build Mode).
  • Frontend & Web Technologies: HTML5, CSS3, TypeScript / JavaScript, HTML5 Canvas API (for the Cadet Art Studio drawing pad), and Browser localStorage (for instant, no-login progress and coin saving).
  • NASA Open Data & Archives: NASA Science Missions (science.nasa.gov), NASA Image & Video Library API (images-api.nasa.gov), NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov), and the NASA Open Data Portal (data.nasa.gov).

projectDetails.name: Project EXPLONAUT+
projectDetails.summary: EXPLONAUT+ is a Mars surface mission-planning and decision-support platform that helps users choose where to go, which science activities to complete, and how much time to keep for the journey home. It combines NASA’s MRO HiRISE terrain and imagery with Perseverance’s archived locations in Jezero Crater, bringing observations from two missions into one interactive planning view. Users set their time budget, walking speed, slope limits, activity priorities, and reserve. The platform compares routes, activity combinations, and visiting orders to select the highest-scoring plan that fits those assumptions. Its disruption laboratory lets users simulate slower walking, extra fieldwork, or a blocked route, then see which objectives remain achievable. In a 105-minute scenario, a two-stop plan requires 95.2 minutes; a slowdown and fieldwork delay increase this to 120.2. Replanning selects one stop requiring 69.5 minutes, including reserve. Route comparisons, timelines, shareable scenarios, and downloadable mission briefs make each decision understandable and reproducible. EXPLONAUT+ turns NASA observations into visible trade-offs between scientific ambition and return constraints. Independent calculation checks support the software; activities and disruptions are scenario assumptions, and operational astronaut safety remains unvalidated.
projectDetails.details:
A Marswalk has a one-time budget. Every additional journey or activity leaves less time for another objective or the return to base. EXPLONAUT+ helps users choose an itinerary, test changing assumptions, and understand why the plan needs to change.

WHAT WE DEVELOPED:

EXPLONAUT+ is a working Mars surface mission-planning and decision-support platform covering approximately 2.07 × 2.07 kilometres of Jezero Crater. It combines MRO HiRISE elevation and orbital imagery with Perseverance’s archived locations, connecting observations from two NASA missions in one interactive planning view.

Users explore relief, slope and imagery layers, choose science activities, and set their time budget, walking speed, slope cutoff, activity priorities and reserve. The platform compares enabled stop combinations and visiting orders, selecting the highest-scoring itinerary that fits those assumptions.

WHEN A PLAN STOPS FITTING:

In a 105-minute scenario, the planner selects stops A and C. Travel, activities and a 20-minute reserve require 95.2 minutes. A 20% walking slowdown and 15-minute fieldwork delay increase that requirement to 120.2 minutes.

Replanning selects stop A alone, requiring 69.5 minutes, including reserve. The user can see the consequence directly: one objective is dropped, and the revised excursion fits the specified disruption.

The disruption laboratory also allows users to mark synthetic exclusions on the map. The application recalculates routes around those cells and reassesses which activities remain achievable. These are planning scenarios, not detected hazards or live emergency navigation.

HOW IT WORKS:

An eight-neighbour Dijkstra search calculates shortest three-dimensional grid paths between the base and candidate stops. It excludes missing terrain, slopes above the selected cutoff, and user-blocked cells, while preventing diagonal shortcuts through blocked corners.

Required time includes the complete round trip, activity durations, and reserve. Disruption mode applies the reduced walking speed and one extra fieldwork allowance. The planner selects the highest scenario activity score within the budget, using shorter nominal duration to break ties.

Route comparisons, a modeled timeline and a time-versus-activity-points frontier expose the alternatives. Shareable scenario links preserve the inputs and exclusions. Downloadable mission briefs record sources, assumptions, and results. Activity points express planning priorities, not measured scientific value.

NASA DATA AND SCIENCE CONTEXT:

MRO HiRISE digital terrain model DTEEC_045994_1985_046060_1985_U01, version 1, supplies elevation. Its associated georeferenced orthoimage supplies the imagery layer. Mars 2020 PLACES records provide Perseverance’s historical positions.

Elevation at approximately 1.01-metre source spacing is aggregated into a 128 × 128 planning grid with approximately 16.15-metre cells. Native-resolution slope maxima control exclusions, and cells require at least 95% valid elevation coverage. Rover coordinates are transformed into the terrain projection and snapped to planning cells, with placement offsets disclosed.

Stop A represents Perseverance’s sol-116 viewpoint for imaging the layered Artuby outcrop from 615 metres away. The marker identifies the viewpoint, not the outcrop. Its proposed activity is remote imaging to examine visible layering. Stops B and C are archived traverse positions used for proposed surface documentation and comparative imaging.

Activities, durations, priorities, and reuse of the landing position as a habitat remain scenario assumptions.

CREATIVE CONTRIBUTION AND INTENDED BENEFIT:

EXPLONAUT+ connects terrain routing with activity selection under one return budget. NASA observations affect the route, route distance affects available fieldwork time, and changed assumptions affect the objectives selected.

The distinctive interaction is an inspectable decision: users can see what no longer fits, what the revised plan sacrifices, and how much time remains. This supports students, educators and researchers exploring simplified mission-planning scenarios. Educational and operational benefits have not yet been measured.

VERIFICATION:

Automated tests cover known-grid distances, missing terrain, blocked corners, independent route-segment summation and budget arithmetic. Additional checks cover synthetic exclusions, an impassable barrier, disruption feasibility, and a reserve exceeding the available budget.

A separate Python shortest-path implementation reproduced the default JavaScript route within 1e-6 metres. A recorded independent GDAL slope comparison covers 4,186,116 native interior pixels, with a maximum difference below 0.000008 degrees. These results support calculation consistency, not physical measurement precision or astronaut performance.

The evidence page provides verification records, source references, and provenance hashes. The downloadable source package includes the application and reproduction instructions.

TOOLS AND DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS:

HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Canvas power the browser application. Python, NumPy, Pillow and GDAL support terrain processing and verification. Node.js runs software tests. OpenAI Artifact Tool supports the presentation, and ReportLab produces the PDF. No specialist hardware or user registration is required.

The design prioritises source traceability, understandable comparisons and clear separation between observations, calculations and assumptions. ChatGPT/OpenAI Codex assistance is acknowledged in the project materials.

LIMITATIONS:

The model assumes constant walking speed and symmetric travel. Its coarse grid cannot resolve every obstacle or narrow passage, and historical observations do not establish current Mars conditions. Validated suit physiology, oxygen use, fatigue, energy, weather, radiation, communications, and loose-ground mechanics remain outside the model.

User testing and external astronaut-mobility validation remain outstanding. EXPLONAUT+ is a research and education prototype and does not certify operational astronaut safety.

projectDetails.name: Trendsleuth - Earth System Trend Detective
projectDetails.summary:
TrendSleuth is an advanced Earth science investigation platform engineered for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The project directly
addresses the core hackathon mandate: enabling both students and professional scientists to explore multi-decadal satellite observations (1990–2025),
visualize regional environmental change, and test whether observed trajectories constitute statistically significant climatic trends rather than random
historical fluctuations.
Built on Next.js 16 and styled with modern responsive components, TrendSleuth pioneers a Dual-Persona Architecture. In ■ Student Mode, complex
climate science is translated into intuitive investigative clues, interactive 3D WebGL globe navigation, colorful Ed Hawkins barcode warming stripes, and
plain-English agricultural advisories. In ■ Expert Mode, the platform unlocks an uncompromising scientific laboratory executing full non-parametric
statistical engines: the Mann-Kendall Rank Trend Test (S, Z, p-value), the Hamed-Rao Variance Correction for serial autocorrelation, and the
Theil-Sen Robust Median Estimator with exact 95% confidence intervals.
By ingesting 432 consecutive monthly observations per variable across six core Earth system indicators (Surface Temperature, Precipitation, Solar
Insolation, Root-Zone Soil Moisture, Wind Speed, and Relative Humidity) from NASA POWER, MERRA-2, and GLDAS, TrendSleuth bridges the gap
between raw Earth observation telemetry and actionable climate intelligence.
projectDetails.details:
PROJECT DETAILS & DUAL-MODE ARCHITECTURE

A central requirement of the NASA Space Apps Challenge was designing for diverse user personas — high school and college students alongside research scientists and experienced analysts. TrendSleuth solves this through a unified dynamic reactive state that instantly adapts visual depth, tone, terminology, and mathematical transparency without sacrificing scientific rigor.

Empirical Real-World Regional Case Studies:

• Arctic Polar Thaw (Svalbard, Norway): Demonstrates Arctic Amplification with accelerated warming of +1.18 °C/decade, strongly significant (p < 0.001) with drying root-zone moisture anomalies.

• Sonoran Desert Heat Strain (Phoenix, USA): Persistent escalating summer heat (+0.54 °C/decade) coupled with decreasing relative humidity, driving extreme HVAC grid cooling surges.

• Tropical Monsoon Coast (Kochi, India): Elevated coastal thermal baseline (+0.24 °C/decade) accompanied by high interannual precipitation volatility during June–September monsoon periods.

• Amazon Rainforest Hydrology (Manaus, Brazil): Multi-decadal soil moisture depletion and extended dry spells, highlighting vulnerability to basin-wide drought cycles.

• Arabian Gulf Thermal Surge (Dubai & Abu Dhabi, UAE): Hyper-arid thermal acceleration (+0.35 °C/decade) with stable, minimal precipitation (< 0.2 mm/day) and intense solar insolation.

MATHEMATICAL & CLIMATOLOGICAL FRAMEWORK

Earth science observations violate classical assumptions of ordinary least squares (OLS) regression: environmental records exhibit significant seasonality, skewness, outliers, and serial autocorrelation. TrendSleuth implements a mathematically sound, peer-reviewed non-parametric statistical suite:

1. Deseasonalization (Monthly Anomaly Transform):

To eliminate the annual solar cycle without losing temporal resolution, monthly climatological baselines are computed: µ_m = (1/N) ∑ x_{y,m}. The deseasonalized anomaly time series is evaluated as: x'_{y,m} = x_{y,m} - µ_m.

2. Mann-Kendall Non-Parametric Rank Trend Test:

Evaluates monotonic upward or downward trend without assuming normality. The test statistic ‘S’ is defined as:

S = ∑_{k=1}^{n-1} ∑_{j=k+1}^n sgn(x_j - x_k)

where sgn(θ) = +1 if θ > 0, 0 if θ = 0, -1 if θ < 0.

Variance with tie correction for tied observation groups t_i:

Var(S) = (1/18) [ n(n - 1)(2n + 5) - ∑_{i=1}^m t_i(t_i - 1)(2t_i + 5) ]

3. Hamed-Rao Modified Variance for Serial Autocorrelation:

Positive serial autocorrelation (memory between consecutive months) inflates false-positive trend significance. TrendSleuth corrects the variance using the empirical lag-k autocorrelation factor η (Hamed & Rao, 1998):

η = 1 + [ 2 / (n(n - 1)(n - 2)) ] ∑_{k=1}^{n-1} (n - k)(n - k - 1)(n - k - 2) r_k^*

Var*(S) = Var(S) × η

The standardized test statistic Z_{MK} is computed and evaluated against standard normal two-sided critical values (p < 0.05).

4. Theil-Sen Robust Median Slope Estimator:

The true rate of change (velocity per year/decade) is computed as the median of all pairwise coordinate slopes:

β = median( (x_j - x_k) / (j - k) ) ∀ 1 ≤ k < j ≤ n

Theil-Sen provides a 29% breakdown point, remaining immune to catastrophic weather outliers, volcanic spikes, or sensor glitches.

5. Exact 95% Non-Parametric Confidence Intervals:

Confidence limits are derived from the ranked pairwise slope distribution using the standard normal critical value C_α = Z_{1-α/2} √(Var*(S)), yielding rigorous lower and upper velocity boundaries: [Sen_lo, Sen_hi].

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: MISSION HORIZON
projectDetails.summary:
We developed NASA: Mission Horizon, an educational, browser-based space exploration game that places players in the role of newly recruited NASA mission specialists in 2045. Players undertake ten missions involving spacecraft launches, orbital mechanics, Solar System exploration, Mars, exoplanet detection, spectroscopy, planetary habitability, stellar activity, and spacecraft emergencies. The website also includes interactive science tools, hints, achievements, and mission logs to create an engaging learning experience.
Our project addresses the NASA Space Apps Challenge by transforming complex space-science concepts and astronomical information into interactive investigations. Rather than simply reading scientific facts, players observe data, form hypotheses, conduct experiments, and make decisions based on evidence. For example, they identify potential exoplanets using light curves and investigate atmospheric gases through spectroscopy, exploring methods used in real astronomical research
Mission Horizon is important because space science can often seem complicated and inaccessible, particularly to students. Our game aims to make astronomy easier to understand, more engaging, and accessible to a wider audience. It encourages curiosity, critical thinking, problem-solving, and scientific reasoning while inspiring young people to explore astronomy and STEM. Most importantly, it helps players understand not just what scientists discover, but how scientific discoveries are made.
projectDetails.details:

NASA: Mission Horizon is a browser-based space exploration game where players take on the role of NASA mission specialists and complete ten missions involving space exploration, exoplanet detection, spectroscopy, and planetary habitability through interactive challenges and scientific investigations.

What benefits does it have?
It makes complex astronomy concepts easier to understand while developing curiosity, critical thinking, problem-solving, and scientific reasoning.

What is the intended impact?
Our goal is to inspire students and space enthusiasts to explore astronomy, develop an interest in STEM, and understand how real scientific discoveries are made.

What tools did you use?
We used Base44 to build the website and Claude to assist with developing, refining, and improving the project.

How is your project creative?
Mission Horizon creatively combines space exploration, storytelling, interactive simulations, and real scientific investigation into one immersive learning experience, allowing players to learn astronomy by acting as scientists rather than simply memorising facts.

projectDetails.name: AstroFlame
projectDetails.summary:
Fire behaves strangely in space. With no buoyancy there's no flame to watch dance upward, just a dim, round glow that lingers and hides. Most people have never seen it, so we built a place where you can. Drag the gravity slider from freefall to Earth and the flame changes shape in front of you; turn up the oxygen and it gets hotter, dirtier and faster.

Everything behind that is real. We went through NASA's combustion research and pulled out 24 experiments, from decades of ISS work to a candle that burned for 45 minutes on Mir, each one with its facility, its years and a link to the actual source. Nothing is made up. On top of that, a what-if simulator lets you try cabin setups and suppression tactics, and an AI co-pilot answers your questions by quoting those experiments back at you, with the IDs, so you can check its work.

One thing stuck with us: NASA's own results show the standard fire test for spacecraft materials is too optimistic, and some flames keep burning long after the visible fire goes out. That felt worth making impossible to ignore.
projectDetails.details:
Flame in Freefall pulls together a bunch of NASA studies on how fire behaves without gravity into one interactive setup. It lets users dig through experiments and materials while looking at mission scenarios that might come up later on longer trips. The timeline part shows how some of those discoveries built on each other over time.

There is a chamber that compares flames on Earth to what happens in microgravity and that helps make the differences clearer. An AI assistant pulls answers from the research collection when people ask questions about it. I think the whole thing tries to make the science less distant and maybe spark more interest in space work but fire safety challenges still feel pretty big for moon or mars missions.

The mix of 3D visuals with the research database and AI is what stands out instead of keeping everything in separate reports. They used React and Three js along with some other tools to build it and tried to keep things accurate and easy to use during development. It seems like an independent prototype so it is not meant to replace any official systems.

projectDetails.name: Galactic Aerospace Simulation & Design.XP
projectDetails.summary:
GASD.XP (Galactic Aerospace Simulation and Design) is an interactive space mission design and simulation game where players will be able to see how difficult the process of designing a space mission may be. We came up with the idea of the game with three missions: a Mars Rover Mission, a Moon Landing Mission and an Asteroid Mining Probe Mission.

The player will be able to customize their spacecraft, choose scientific instruments, pick launch vehicles and manage various resources, which include budget, mass, power, fuel and communications. The decisions will affect the performance of the mission, making players analyze the process and see the engineering challenges behind the missions. 

GASD.XP provides the solution to the challenge by turning the space mission planning into an interactive process. It is significant because it helps make the concepts of aerospace science more accessible, inspires scientific interest, helps develop critical thinking and decision-making skills of the players.
projectDetails.details:
Our Project Solution

GASD.XP (Galactic Aerospace Simulation & Design.XP) is an interactive educational platform that introduces students to space exploration, astronomy and aerospace engineering through games and simulations.

When we think about space exploration, we often picture rockets launching or astronauts travelling to other planets. However, there is much more involved in planning a space mission. Engineers have to consider spacecraft mass, fuel, power supply, communication systems, scientific instruments, mission objectives and available budgets. Even a small change in one of these factors can affect the entire mission.

We wanted to make these concepts easier for students to understand, especially those who have never had the opportunity to experiment with spacecraft design. This led us to develop GASD.XP, where players can explore space, plan missions, make engineering decisions and see how their choices affect the results.

Instead of learning everything through written explanations, players get to interact with the concepts themselves. The platform brings together mission simulations, interactive space environments, mini-games, quizzes, weekly challenges, leaderboards and achievements, along with a Space Academy and Help Centre.

How Does Our Solution Work?

GASD.XP brings different space-related activities together in one platform. Each section introduces players to a different aspect of space science and exploration.

1. Space Mission Design and Simulation

The mission design system is one of the main features of GASD.XP. Players take on the role of aerospace engineers and plan missions by choosing spacecraft components, scientific instruments and launch systems.

However, they cannot simply select every available component. Each choice comes with certain requirements and limitations.

Players have to consider several factors during mission planning.

Mass and Payload Capacity: The spacecraft must remain within the payload capacity of its launch vehicle. If its mass exceeds the permitted limit, the launch can fail.

Power Management: Scientific instruments require electricity to operate. Players must make sure their total power requirements do not exceed the available supply.

Mission Budget: Each mission has a limited number of credits. Players have to decide which components are necessary and how much they can spend.

Launch Vehicles: Different launch vehicles are suited to different missions. Choosing an appropriate vehicle is important for reaching the intended destination.

Scientific Instruments: Players select instruments based on what they want to investigate. Each instrument has its own mass and power requirements.

Communication Systems: Collecting scientific information is only part of a mission. Spacecraft must also be able to transmit their findings back to Earth.

Mission Objectives: The purpose of each mission influences the spacecraft design and the components required.

These requirements make mission planning more than just selecting components. Players have to think about how their choices work together and make changes when their design does not meet the mission requirements.

2. Multiple Space Missions

GASD.XP includes different missions to introduce players to various types of space exploration.

Mars Rover Mission

Players experience the challenges of operating a rover on Mars. They navigate the Martian surface, manage available energy, locate scientific investigation points, analyse discoveries and transmit collected information.

This mission introduces rover operations, scientific exploration, energy management and communication limitations.

Moon Landing Mission

Players explore the requirements involved in planning a lunar landing mission. They learn about spacecraft design, launch systems and the challenges associated with reaching and exploring the Moon.

Asteroid Mining Probe

Inspired by real asteroid exploration missions such as NASA's OSIRIS-REx, this mission introduces players to asteroid exploration and spacecraft operations in a distant environment.

Each mission offers a different experience and allows players to explore how mission requirements change depending on the destination and objectives.

3. Interactive Space Environments and Orbital Activities

We also wanted players to explore space beyond the individual missions.

GASD.XP includes interactive space environments and orbital activities that introduce concepts such as orbital motion, celestial objects and planetary environments. Players can explore how objects move in space and become more familiar with astronomical concepts through visual interaction.

This gives students an opportunity to understand topics that can sometimes be difficult to imagine through textbooks alone.

4. Space Mini-Games

The platform includes several space-themed mini-games involving exploration, navigation, observation, coordination and logical reasoning.

These activities provide another way to interact with space-related concepts and allow players to practise their knowledge without having to complete a full mission simulation every time.

5. Interactive Quizzes

Quizzes test players' understanding of astronomy, space science and aerospace-related topics. They can use them to check what they have learned through the different activities and practise recalling information instead of simply reading educational material.

6. Weekly Challenges

Weekly challenges introduce additional objectives for players to complete. They add variety to the platform and give players new reasons to explore different activities and improve their performance.

7. Leaderboards and Competitive Learning

GASD.XP includes a leaderboard where players can compare their scores and achievements. This adds a competitive element to the learning experience and encourages them to participate in different activities and challenge themselves.

8. Awards and Achievements

The awards and achievements section recognises players' progress across the platform. Players can work towards unlocking achievements by exploring different features and completing activities, giving them additional goals beyond finishing individual missions.

9. Space Academy and Help Centre

We included a Space Academy to support players who want to learn more about space related topics.

The Help Centre provides guidance on using the platform, understanding its features and learning the game controls. These sections are particularly useful for beginners who may be unfamiliar with aerospace engineering or the different activities available.

10. Player Profiles and Accessibility

GASD.XP includes optional login and registration functionality. Players can explore the platform without being required to create an account, while those who choose to register can access profile-related features.

We also considered how students would use the platform on different devices. Computer users can navigate the games using keyboard controls, including arrow keys, while mobile and tablet users can use virtual touch controls. The interface is designed to adjust to different screen sizes.

We wanted the platform to be straightforward to navigate so players could spend more time exploring and less time figuring out how to use it.

The Benefits of Our Project

GASD.XP offers students a way to explore aerospace engineering and space science through practical activities rather than relying entirely on theoretical explanations.

It makes STEM learning more engaging by introducing scientific concepts through games, simulations and interactive environments. It also develops problem-solving skills because players have to find solutions while working within limitations involving mass, power, budgets and mission requirements.

Students get an introduction to the decisions involved in designing and managing spacecraft. They can experiment with different choices, understand how engineering decisions influence mission outcomes and develop an interest in scientific exploration.

The platform also supports independent learning, allowing players to explore different sections at their own pace. Quizzes, leaderboards, weekly challenges and achievements provide additional motivation to participate and improve.

What Makes Our Project Creative?

What makes GASD.XP different is the way it brings several aspects of space education together in one platform.

We did not want to create just another space themed quiz or a game where players simply travel between planets. We wanted them to understand some of the thinking that takes place behind actual space missions.

For example, a player designing a spacecraft might want to include several scientific instruments. However, adding more instruments also affects the spacecraft's mass and power requirements. The player then has to decide which instruments are worth including while staying within the mission's limitations.

Similarly, the mission budget means that players cannot always choose every component they want. They have to prioritise what is necessary for their objectives.

These interactions allow players to experience how different engineering requirements are connected rather than learning about each one separately.

We also combined these simulations with retro pixel-inspired visuals, interactive space environments, mini-games, quizzes and competitive features. Players can move between different activities depending on what they want to explore.

Our aim was to make the platform feel like an interactive space exploration experience while still having a clear educational purpose.

Factors Our Team Considered During Development:

While developing GASD.XP, our team had to consider both the scientific content and the experience of the people using the platform.

One of our main considerations was scientific relevance. We wanted the missions to introduce concepts connected to real space exploration rather than making them entirely fictional. This influenced our inclusion of spacecraft mass, payload capacity, power requirements, mission budgets, launch vehicle suitability, scientific instruments and communication systems.

We also considered how these factors would affect one another. For instance, adding an instrument changes the spacecraft's mass and power requirements, which may affect whether the mission design is suitable.

Another challenge was deciding how to present these concepts to younger students. We wanted the simulations to introduce meaningful engineering decisions without becoming too complicated for beginners.

We also thought about the variety of activities needed to keep the platform interesting, the clarity of game instructions, keyboard and touch controls, navigation and compatibility across different devices.

Balancing educational value, technical requirements and ease of use was an important part of developing GASD.XP.

Our Goal and Intended Impact:

Our main goal is to make space science and aerospace engineering more accessible to younger students.

Not everyone gets the opportunity to experiment with spacecraft design or understand how a space mission is planned. Through GASD.XP, we want to give students a way to explore these ideas, even if they have little or no previous knowledge of aerospace engineering.

We hope the platform encourages students to ask questions, test different possibilities and think about the science behind space exploration.

In the longer term, we want GASD.XP to encourage more students to explore STEM subjects, increase awareness of aerospace engineering, make difficult scientific concepts easier to understand and introduce students to careers in astronomy, engineering and scientific research.

Ultimately, we want students to see space exploration as more than something they watch from Earth. We want them to understand the decisions behind it and experience some of the challenges involved in making a mission possible.

Tools and Technologies Used

Development Platform

Base44 was used as our AI-assisted website development platform to build the GASD.XP website and develop its features.

AI-Assisted Development

AI-assisted tools supported parts of the website development process, including website structuring, feature development and refinement.

Web Development Technologies

HTML was used for structuring web content.

CSS was used for styling, visual presentation and responsive layouts.

JavaScript was used for interactive functionality and game-related logic.

Design Approach

The platform uses a retro pixel-inspired visual design with space-themed interfaces, interactive game elements, animations and responsive layouts for different screen sizes.

Galactic Mission is an interactive space exploration game designed for children aged 7–12. We developed a virtual Moon Base where players take on the role of astronauts and complete different missions and activities.

It is important because it makes learning about space more engaging, encourages problem-solving and teamwork, and helps younger children become more interested in science and space exploration
projectDetails.details:
Galactic Mission is an interactive space exploration game designed for children aged 7–12. Players become astronauts and explore a virtual Moon Base while completing missions and learning about space.

The game works through different sections. In Moon Adventure, players move their astronaut, collect energy crystals and complete levels. In Mission Control, they make decisions that affect their mission. They can also explore different Moon Base locations, learn space facts in Space School, complete astronaut training activities, and look after their crew. The game also includes a Character Studio and Star Shop where players can customise their astronauts.

The main benefit of Galactic Mission is that it makes learning about space fun and interactive. It encourages problem-solving, decision-making, teamwork and curiosity about science. Our goal is to help younger children understand some of the challenges astronauts face and become more interested in space exploration.

We developed the game using HTML, CSS and JavaScript. We used GitHub to store our code and publish the game online, and Canva to create our presentation. We also used ChatGPT to assist with coding, improving features, debugging and organising information.

What makes our project creative is that it combines learning with gameplay. Instead of only reading about astronauts, children can experience a simplified version of a space mission themselves. While developing it, we considered the target age group, making the controls simple, the activities educational, and the design colourful and engaging.

I built an interactive planner for the Moon south pole challenge. You compare candidate landing sites and dates by sunlight and Earth contact, and a sky view shows where the Sun and Earth sit on the horizon.

I checked the ephemeris against the lunar phases for this month. The Sun and Earth positions come out right, though I haven’t opened the page in a browser, so the layout and charts are unchecked. The site coordinates are approximate and the Moon is modeled as smooth, so use it for comparing sites and dates rather than mission design.

projectDetails.name: ARES ATLAS: Martian Surface Exploration & EVA Mission Planner
projectDetails.summary: ARES ATLAS is an interactive mission-planning map for future astronauts walking on Mars, like Google Maps for Mars. We processed a real NASA HiRISE elevation model of part of Jezero Crater and combined it with Perseverance’s actual traverse from NASA’s PLACES data. Users explore the terrain in 2D and 3D, view slope and elevation layers, and generate walking routes using a pathfinding algorithm. They can compare a shorter route with a slope-aware route, and an animated astronaut (EVA-01) walks the chosen route. It addresses the challenge by layering data from several NASA missions into one view that helps plan a Marswalk. It matters because crews will need practical, understandable tools to plan safe and scientifically useful surface excursions.
projectDetails.details:
What it does: ARES ATLAS lets a user explore a real part of Jezero Crater (about 6.6 × 14.4 km), select destinations, and generate Marswalk routes between them. It shows elevation and slope-hazard layers, Perseverance’s historical traverse, a mission dashboard (distance, elevation gain and loss, maximum and average slope, estimated walking time, terrain exposure), and an animated astronaut that walks the route. It also has a NASA weather reference panel and a data-sources panel that marks each source as integrated, partial, reference-only or simulated.

How it works: We parsed the 380 MB HiRISE DTM (DTEEC_045994_1985_046060_1985_U01, a PDS3 float32 raster, 14,266 × 6,673 pixels at about 1 m) and checked its projection against its label. We resampled it to a 16 m browser-friendly grid and computed slopes from it. We projected Perseverance PLACES positions into the same coordinate system and checked them against the terrain elevations (median offset about 4 m). Routes are computed with A* over the terrain grid. The Shorter route minimizes distance. The Safer route adds penalties for steep slopes and for cells near gaps in the data. Both avoid no-data areas.

Benefits: It gives a quick, understandable way to compare route options using real terrain, and it clearly separates real, derived and simulated information.

Goal: A prototype showing how NASA data from several missions can be combined into one planning tool for human explorers.

Limitations: Coverage is one HiRISE terrain model, not the whole crater. The Mars Trek imagery previews were not georeferenced, so the surface is shaded from the elevation data, not satellite imagery. The “safer” route is slope-aware only and does not model dust, radiation, loose soil, ice or weather. The 12 demo destinations, the ice layer, the 2.5 km/h walking speed and the 320 kcal/h energy figure are simulated or assumed and are labeled as such in the app.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Three.js for 3D, HTML canvas for the 2D map, Python (NumPy, pandas, SciPy, Pillow) for data processing, Netlify for hosting.

Use of AI tools: The project concept and requirements were defined by our team, and we used AI tools to help refine and develop it. Claude (Anthropic) helped write the application code and the data-processing script, and helped draft this description and our presentation slides. We also used AI tools to help research and understand the NASA data resources. All NASA data was processed and checked using the files we downloaded from NASA.

challengeDetails.title: Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map
challengeDetails.excerpt: NASA has explored Mars robotically for decades, studying its extreme environment, mapping its surface, and collecting many types of data. Far from home, the first astronauts to set foot on Mars will want the best map possible, with information on the details of their routes and destinations, updates on current conditions, and the data needed to complete their mission quickly and safely. projectDetails.name: Graveyard of Unforgotten Triumphs
projectDetails.summary:
Voices of the Void — The Moon’s Backyard Party

An imaginative and educational digital comic storybook designed to bring historic Apollo hardware and lunar scientific equipment to life. It uses a dual-format structure combining Story Pages (comic illustrations, speech bubbles, and humor) with Mission and Science Pages (explaining real history and scientific discoveries). Hardware is transformed into memorable personalities like the "Apollo Brothers" and "Moon Buggies," highlighting key moments from Apollo 11 through 17. It was designed using Microsoft PowerPoint, researched via NASA resources, and published as an interactive digital flipbook using Heyzine. 

It makes dense aerospace history approachable by pairing creative storytelling with accurate, NASA-backed documentation. It distinguishes fictional dialogue from documented history, teaching technical distinctions (such as why laser retroreflectors remained on the Moon while the solar wind foil was brought back). It turns traditional textbook facts into a relatable narrative, allowing learners to explore space science at their own pace without feeling overwhelmed. 

It shifts the public perception of items left on the lunar surface, reframing them from "space junk" into vital testaments of human achievement. By showing that science can be learned through storytelling, humour, and creativity, it sparks curiosity in astronomy, engineering, and STEM fields for younger generations.
projectDetails.details:
Voices of the Void: The Moon’s Backyard Party

NASA Space Apps Challenge – Project Description

Project Overview

What happens to spacecraft, rovers and scientific instruments after their missions end? While astronauts return to Earth, some remarkable pieces of human exploration remain behind on the Moon. These objects are far more than forgotten machinery; they are lasting reminders of humanity’s curiosity, courage and achievements in space.

Voices of the Void: The Moon’s Backyard Party is an imaginative educational digital comic storybook that brings historic Apollo hardware to life. By giving these silent explorers unique personalities, voices and a sense of humour, the project transforms real space history into an entertaining story. It invites readers to imagine what these objects might say if they could talk about their experiences on the Moon.

What Does the Project Do?

The storybook introduces readers to different pieces of Apollo hardware and scientific equipment, turning them into memorable characters. The Apollo Lunar Module descent stages become the “Apollo Brothers”, the Lunar Roving Vehicles become the “Moon Buggies”, and scientific instruments such as seismometers and laser-ranging retroreflectors join the conversation.

Through funny dialogues, character interactions and illustrated comic scenes, readers discover the fascinating stories behind these objects and the important roles they played in lunar exploration.

The story explores memorable moments from Apollo missions, including the first crewed Moon landing during Apollo 11, Alan Shepard’s famous golf shots during Apollo 14, the discovery of the Genesis Rock during Apollo 15, the geological investigations of Apollo 16 and the orange volcanic-glass beads discovered during Apollo 17.

How Does It Work?

The project follows a comic page and science page format, connecting imagination with real scientific information.

1. The Story Pages

Readers meet the Apollo hardware as characters through comic illustrations, speech bubbles, conversations and humour. Each character has a personality inspired by its real history and purpose. These fictional conversations make the subject enjoyable and encourage readers to explore further.

2. The Mission and Science Pages

The following pages explain the actual science behind the characters. They describe what each object was designed to do, which mission carried it, how astronauts used it and what scientists discovered.

For example, the Apollo 14 section uses Alan Shepard’s famous golf shots as part of the story, while the accompanying science page explains the mission’s exploration of the Fra Mauro region. Similarly, the Lunar Rover characters introduce readers to the vehicles used during Apollo 15, 16 and 17, while the fact pages explain their design and contribution to lunar exploration.

The storybook also explores the work of seismometers and laser-ranging retroreflectors. It highlights an important scientific distinction: the laser retroreflectors remain on the Moon, while the Solar Wind Composition Experiment's foil was brought back to Earth for laboratory analysis.

The fictional conversations are designed to entertain, while the accompanying fact pages distinguish imagination from documented mission history. Scientific information is supported by NASA mission reports and educational resources.

What Benefits Does It Have?

The project makes space science more accessible and engaging, especially for younger readers who may find traditional scientific information difficult or less interesting.

Its benefits include:

  • Makes science enjoyable: Comic illustrations, humour and characters make complex scientific topics easier to approach.
  • Connects imagination with facts: Readers enjoy fictional conversations while learning the real history and purpose of Apollo hardware.
  • Encourages curiosity: Interesting discoveries inspire readers to ask questions and explore astronomy, engineering and space science.
  • Preserves space history: It highlights the importance of objects that remain on the Moon and the scientific knowledge they have contributed.
  • Supports independent learning: The digital storybook allows readers to explore the content at their own pace.
  • Combines creativity and research: It demonstrates how storytelling can be used to communicate real scientific knowledge in a memorable way.

What Do I Hope to Achieve?

My aim is to change the way people look at the objects left behind on the Moon. Rather than seeing them as forgotten machines or abandoned equipment, I want readers to recognise them as important reminders of human exploration and scientific achievement.

I hope to inspire younger generations to become curious about space, ask questions and discover the science behind historic missions. I also want to show that learning about science does not always have to involve complicated explanations or textbooks. It can begin with an interesting story, a funny character or a surprising discovery.

The central message of my project is:

“A mission may end, but its discoveries and legacy continue.”

Tools and Technology Used

The project was developed using digital presentation, research and publishing tools:

  • Microsoft PowerPoint: Used to design the comic pages, arrange illustrations, create speech bubbles, develop character scenes and present the scientific information.
  • Canva and Pictory.ai

         Used to create short demo video

  • NASA websites and educational resources: Used to research Apollo missions, lunar hardware, scientific instruments and discoveries, and to support the factual content.
  • PDF export: Used to prepare the completed storybook for digital publishing.
  • Heyzine: Used to publish the PDF as an online, page-turning digital flipbook that readers can access through a shared link.

The project does not require custom coding or additional hardware. Its strength lies in the creative combination of storytelling, humour, comic illustrations and real NASA science. By turning historic Apollo equipment into memorable characters while keeping the scientific information factual, the project offers a fresh and engaging way to learn about space exploration.

It shows that creativity can make even complex scientific history exciting, understandable and inspiring.

projectDetails.name: Project Heart and Space Health
projectDetails.summary:
I developed SpaceHealth, an astronaut health monitoring dashboard designed to help astronauts track their physical and mental health during long-duration space missions. The system focuses on six main areas: cardiovascular health, sleep, radiation exposure, bone health, mental wellness, and overall health trends. It brings important health information together in one dashboard using visual graphs, daily reports, and warning notifications.

SpaceHealth addresses the challenge by helping astronauts recognize changes in their health and monitor their condition while living in space. It compares health measurements with each astronaut’s personal baseline to identify unusual changes over time. It also provides suggested next steps, such as repeating a measurement or contacting the medical team when necessary. This is especially important because astronauts experience challenges such as microgravity, radiation exposure, isolation, and limited access to medical assistance. By organizing health information in one accessible place, SpaceHealth can support better health awareness, early identification of potential problems, and communication with medical professionals. The goal is to make long-duration space missions safer by helping astronauts take a more active role in monitoring their health.
projectDetails.details: SpaceHealth is a health-monitoring software system designed to help astronauts track their physical and mental health during space missions. It works by collecting information from wearable sensors, medical devices, and daily astronaut check-ins. The software organizes this information and displays it on a digital dashboard using graphs, health indicators, and reports. It monitors six main areas: heart health, sleep, radiation exposure, bone health, mental wellness, and overall health trends. The system compares new measurements with each astronaut’s usual health levels to identify unusual changes. If a potential problem is detected, it displays a warning and suggests next steps, such as repeating a measurement or contacting the medical team. The software can store information onboard the spacecraft so astronauts can access their health records even when communication with Earth is limited. Its purpose is to help astronauts understand their health, recognize potential problems early, and make long-duration space missions safer.

challengeDetails.title: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions

projectDetails.name: What We Left Behind
projectDetails.summary:
What We Left Behind is a website designed to give young space enthusiasts an accessible and engaging overview of unique pieces of NASA hardware left behind across the Solar System, and sometimes beyond.

The website features an interactive map highlighting the current locations of each piece of equipment. Visitors can click on individual symbols to explore dedicated pages about each machine. Told from the machine’s own first-person perspective, each page explores its history, what makes it extraordinary, and what it has taught humanity about space and exploration.

Each page also includes an expandable educational section that explains the science and technology behind key components in simple, easy-to-understand terms. These include technologies such as SEIS, LLRR, and RTGs, helping visitors understand not only what these machines have accomplished, but also how they work.
projectDetails.details:
Project Description: What We Left Behind

What does the project do, and how does it work?

What We Left Behind is an educational website designed to introduce young space enthusiasts to the fascinating pieces of NASA hardware that have been left behind across the Solar System and beyond. The website features an interactive map that displays the current locations of these objects. Visitors can click on individual symbols to access dedicated pages about each piece of equipment. Each page tells the story from the machine's own first-person perspective, exploring its history, purpose, achievements, and contributions to space exploration. It also includes expandable educational sections that explain the science and technology behind important components, such as SEIS, LLRR, and RTGs, in simple, accessible language.

What benefits does the project have?

The project makes complex scientific information more accessible and enjoyable for younger audiences. It encourages curiosity about space, develops scientific awareness, and helps visitors understand the technology behind some of humanity's greatest achievements in space exploration. The interactive format also makes learning more engaging than simply reading information from a textbook or article.

What is the intended impact of the project?

The main goal is to inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, and space enthusiasts by highlighting the often-overlooked technology that has made space exploration possible. We hope to help young people develop a deeper appreciation for scientific innovation and understand how even machines that are no longer active continue to contribute to humanity's knowledge of the universe. Ultimately, the project aims to make space science more approachable and encourage people to explore beyond Earth.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

The project was developed as a website using mobile-friendly website builders such as Bolt.new. The organization and paraphrasing of information were assisted by large language models (LLMs), including ChatGPT and Gemini. The solar system diagram, space background and interactive machine symbols were also generated using Gemini.

Note: I wasn't able to add watermarks to these as I'm currently out of Bolt credits to make further edits to the site. Thank you for understanding.)

How is your project creative?

Our project takes a creative approach to science communication by telling the stories of space hardware from the machines' own first-person perspectives. The interactive map adds an element of exploration, letting users discover these objects across the Solar System. Combining storytelling, interactive technology, and scientific education makes the learning experience both distinctive and memorable.

What factors did your team consider?

Our team considered our target audience, accessibility, scientific accuracy, educational value, and overall user experience. Since the website is aimed at young space enthusiasts, we wanted to explain complex scientific concepts in language that is easy to understand without sacrificing important information. We also considered how to make the website visually appealing and simple to navigate, ensuring that visitors could easily find and explore different pieces of hardware. Finally, we focused on presenting reliable information, creating an engaging storytelling experience, and highlighting the historical and scientific significance of each object.

projectDetails.name: Horizon
projectDetails.summary:
Horizon is an immersive educational space exploration game that combines realistic space science, engineering, and interactive gameplay. Players can choose between Spacecraft Mission and Astronaut Mission, designing rockets, spacecraft, and planet-specific rovers using customisable components. In Spacecraft Mission, players build rockets, plan journeys, navigate space hazards, and explore celestial destinations. In Astronaut Mission, players launch from Earth, manually perform rocket separation, control crew capsules, dodge asteroids and comets, and land on planets or moons.

Players explore hyper-realistic celestial bodies featuring detailed terrain, craters, atmospheres, weather, and environmental conditions. They can drive rovers, sprint as astronauts, explore planetary surfaces, plant mission-specific flags, and conduct diverse scientific experiments.

The game includes quests, achievements, badges, experience points, levels, coin rewards, planetary unlocking, global rankings, and multiplayer missions. Dynamic solar system exploration, realistic physics, interactive landing simulations, and scientifically inspired challenges make every mission engaging.

The ultimate vision is to transform space exploration into an interactive learning adventure, inspiring players to understand the universe while experiencing the challenges of becoming real space explorers.
projectDetails.details:
Space Mission Design Game

Project Description

Space Mission Design Game is an interactive educational space exploration game that combines space science, engineering, and gaming. It allows players to experience the challenges of space exploration by designing spacecraft, planning missions, exploring celestial bodies, and conducting scientific experiments.

What Does the Project Do and How Does It Work?

The game offers two primary modes: Spacecraft Mission and Astronaut Mission. In Spacecraft Mission, players design rockets, customise spacecraft components, plan journeys, navigate obstacles, and explore planets and moons. In Astronaut Mission, players experience launching from Earth, manually separating rockets, navigating crew capsules, dodging space hazards, landing on celestial bodies, and exploring their surfaces.

Players can construct specialised rovers, conduct scientific experiments, plant mission-specific flags, complete quests, and unlock new destinations. AI-powered mission and landing assistants provide guidance throughout gameplay. Progression systems include achievements, badges, experience points, levels, and rewards.

What Are Its Benefits?

  • Makes complex space science accessible through interactive learning.
  • Encourages problem-solving, creativity, and engineering thinking.
  • Introduces planetary science, spacecraft design, and mission planning.
  • Demonstrates challenges associated with real space exploration.
  • Encourages curiosity about astronomy and scientific discovery.

Intended Impact

The project's primary impact is to inspire students and young learners to explore STEM subjects, understand space exploration, and develop an interest in science and engineering. It aims to transform passive learning into an engaging experience where players learn through experimentation, decisions, and exploration.

Tools, Technologies, and Software

The project is developed as a digital game using programming, interactive graphics, and 3D simulation technologies. Its development involves game logic, spacecraft and rover modelling, animation, physics, user-interface design, and AI-assisted guidance.

Note: Specific programming languages, frameworks, engines, and software should be listed according to the technologies actually used in development.

What Makes the Project Creative?

The game combines mission planning, spacecraft construction, astronaut gameplay, planetary exploration, scientific experiments, and AI assistance into one interactive experience. Its unique approach allows players to experience both the engineering and exploration aspects of space missions rather than simply learning about them through textbooks.

Hyper-realistic celestial environments, planet-specific rover engineering, interactive rocket separation, space navigation challenges, and progression-based exploration make the experience distinctive.

Factors Considered During Development

  • Scientific accuracy and educational value.
  • Realistic planetary environments and terrain.
  • Different gravitational and atmospheric conditions.
  • Appropriate spacecraft and rover capabilities.
  • Accessible and engaging gameplay.
  • Performance across different devices.
  • Fair challenges and meaningful progression.
  • User interface clarity and usability.
  • Integration of AI guidance and interactive learning.
  • Balancing realism with enjoyable gameplay.

The project ultimately aims to make space exploration more engaging, educational, and accessible while inspiring the next generation of scientists, engineers, and explorers.
