AstroPulse is a real-time spacecraft telemetry and health monitoring web application developed with C#, .NET 10, and Blazor Server, containerized via Docker and deployed on the cloud.

The project addresses the challenge of managing complex aerospace data by providing a dynamic telemetry engine that tracks vital spacecraft metrics, operational statuses, and system alerts through an interactive web interface.

It is important because it bridges the gap between raw backend telemetry and immediate situational awareness, enabling developers and operators to monitor system health, test fault-tolerance scenarios, and visualize simulated deep-space mission data efficiently.
projectDetails.details:
Core Overview & Mission

  • What it is: A real-time web application built to monitor spacecraft health and telemetry on the fly.
  • Core Function: Bridges the gap between raw backend numbers and clear, human-friendly visuals, giving operators and astronauts a fast way to track life-support systems, catch radiation spikes early, and monitor crew health.
  • Emergency Testing: Features built-in simulation controls to test how the system reacts to sudden emergencies like solar particle events or gravity shifts.
  • Mission Impact: Boosts safety and resilience during long deep-space trips, acting as a reliable testing ground for student teams and mission planners to practice emergency drills.

Architecture & Technical Stack

  • Languages: C#, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
  • Frameworks & Runtimes: .NET 10.0, ASP.NET Core, and Blazor Server.
  • Development & Toolchain: Visual Studio, Git, and GitHub.
  • Deployment & Hosting: Docker containerization hosted live on Render.com.

Under the Hood: Telemetry & Design

  • Custom Engine: A deterministic TelemetryEngine refreshes and pushes simulated mission data every 500ms, tracking cabin pressure, habitat temperature, noise levels, radiation flux, and crew vitals.
  • Blazor Server Integration: Delivers fast, low-latency SignalR updates without needing external files or messy data feeds.
  • Holistic Tracking: Blends hard technical engineering with astronaut wellness, combining habitat telemetry with biological tracking (body maps and daily check-ins) into a single dashboard.

Engineering & UX Challenges

  • Performance & Responsiveness: Maintaining a stable, high-performance Blazor Server architecture under continuous, 500ms real-time data streams without memory bloat.
  • User Experience & Clarity: Designing straightforward color-coded threshold alerts (e.g., Caution states at baseline deviations and Critical warnings during sudden pressure drops or radiation spikes) to keep cognitive load low during high-stress scenarios.
  • Cloud Compatibility: Managing the containerization setup (.NET 10 Docker configuration) to ensure smooth, reliable cloud deployment.

Team Considerations & Hardware Scope

  • Framework Trade-off (Blazor Server vs. WebAssembly): The team deliberately chose Blazor Server to maintain heavy computational workloads and state management securely on the backend, ensuring low-latency client rendering without overloading browser memory during prolonged simulations.
  • Refresh Rate vs. Server Memory: We balanced our telemetry loop at a 500ms interval—frequent enough to provide dynamic, realistic life-support fluctuations, yet optimized to prevent excessive SignalR packet overhead.
  • Hardware Context: AstroPulse is structured as a pure software simulation designed for standard mission-control workstations, ruggedized laptops, or habitat tablets, serving as a reliable telemetry interface ready for future integration with physical IoT sensors.

projectDetails.name: Project Ninth
projectDetails.summary:
NINTH is a public astronomy website and blink comparator based on actual NASA SPHEREx observations of the M101 field. It lets people compare eight images from different times, switch between views, explore changes in wavelengths and spot objects that might have moved. 
The project addresses the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge by converting a professional search technique into a public-friendly tool. It also helps users understand how motion can reveal distant solar-system objects and also clarifies the limits of the data. 
It's important to note that NINTH does not announce a Planet Nine discovery. Instead, it shows people a transparent way to check out real observations and see how scientific evidence gets tested.
projectDetails.details:
NINTH loads eight SPHEREx Level 2 spectral images from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive. Users can select any two dates, blink between them, drag a comparison seam, view a difference map, and inspect the wavelength at any point in the image. They can also record field marks and export them as JSON for later review.

The project was built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, supported by Python scripts for querying archive data, processing FITS files, handling WCS information, reprojecting images, and generating comparison assets. It runs in a standard web browser and does not require special hardware.

The creative focus was making a technical astronomy workflow feel understandable and engaging without overstating the results. The team considered accessibility, clear instructions, scientific honesty, responsive design, visual storytelling, image noise, detector differences, wavelength variation, and traceable data sources. The intended impact is to help more people experience how astronomers investigate possible moving objects and why repeated observations are necessary before calling something a discovery.

projectDetails.name: Helios
projectDetails.summary:
Helios is an AI-powered astronaut health monitoring and support system designed to improve the physical and mental well-being of astronauts during long-duration space missions. At its core is an intelligent health-monitoring chip that collects and analyses astronaut health data, helping identify potential health concerns and providing personalised recommendations and possible solutions.
Helios also features an AI-powered robotic companion dog, Medibot, which acts as an additional support system. It assists astronauts by providing health-related guidance, encouraging physical activity, supporting mental well-being and helping locate essential supplies. By combining intelligent health monitoring with interactive robotic assistance, Helios aims to make space missions safer, healthier and more sustainable, while reducing the challenges astronauts face when living far from Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Helios is designed as an integrated astronaut healthcare ecosystem that combines intelligent health monitoring, AI-assisted analysis and robotic support.

How it works:

The central component is a health-monitoring chip that collects and displays astronaut health information. An AI-powered system analyses the collected data, identifies potential health concerns and provides personalised recommendations to help astronauts manage their well-being. This allows astronauts to monitor their health and receive guidance while operating in the isolated environment of space.

Medibot – Robotic Companion:

As a supporting feature, Helios includes Medibot, an AI-powered robotic dog that acts as an interactive health assistant. It helps astronauts follow exercise routines, provides daily wellness check-ins, offers companionship, helps locate essential medical supplies and communicates important health alerts.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

Helios aims to improve astronaut safety, support physical and mental well-being and make healthcare more accessible during long-duration space missions. By combining continuous health monitoring with interactive robotic assistance, the system could help astronauts respond to health concerns earlier and reduce their dependence on immediate assistance from Earth.

Innovation and Creativity:

The main innovation is bringing health-monitoring technology and robotic assistance together into one connected ecosystem. Rather than focusing only on detecting health concerns, Helios also focuses on providing astronauts with practical support and guidance.

Development Considerations:

The project considers the challenges of limited medical assistance, isolation, communication delays, restricted resources and the demanding conditions of space environments. Its proposed design focuses on accessibility, reliability, astronaut safety and adaptability for future space exploration.

projectDetails.name: Project LUNA-SAFE
projectDetails.summary:
LUNA-SAFE is a browser-based simulation prototype designed to support astronaut health monitoring and lunar mission safety.

The project began with an idea to protect future lunar habitats using sensors that could monitor temperature, vibration, structural tilt, and cabin pressure. It then expanded to focus on astronaut health, including heart rate, blood oxygen levels, activity, and health alerts.

As a physiotherapy student, I also introduced a Physical Therapy & Rehabilitation section to support astronaut health before, during, and after space missions. This feature records reported pain, fatigue, exercise activity, and recovery trends.

The prototype demonstrates how astronauts can request medical or rehabilitation reviews and how Mission Control can acknowledge and document those requests. A supporting Site Planner explores lunar terrain using NASA-derived data.

LUNA-SAFE currently uses simulated health readings. Our future goal is to connect a wearable monitoring device and validated sensors to the software, creating a more integrated system for astronaut health and safety.
projectDetails.details:
How LUNA-SAFE Works

LUNA-SAFE is an interactive web application developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It brings astronaut health monitoring, rehabilitation tracking, lunar habitat safety, and site exploration into one interface.

1. Astronaut Health

This section simulates astronaut health readings, including heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), and activity. It displays alerts when selected values reach demonstration warning thresholds. The health history feature records simulated readings and displays trends over time. Body temperature can also be recorded manually.

2. Medical Assistance and Mission Control

An astronaut can request medical assistance through the application. Mission Control can acknowledge and document the request. The software also demonstrates oxygen-related review requests initiated by an astronaut or Mission Control. These are requests for qualified review, not automatic changes to oxygen delivery or life-support equipment.

3. Physical Therapy & Rehabilitation

This section was inspired by the project developer's physiotherapy background. It includes three mission phases: pre-flight, in-flight, and post-flight.

Users can record discomfort, fatigue, perceived exertion, exercise type, and session duration. The application displays symptom flags, records rehabilitation check-ins, and tracks reported fatigue over time. Users can request a rehabilitation team review, which Mission Control can acknowledge and document.

4. Base Safety

The Base Safety section demonstrates how future sensors could monitor a lunar habitat's temperature, vibration, structural tilt, and pressure conditions. It displays simulated alerts to help explain how environmental monitoring could support crew safety.

5. Site Planner

The Site Planner explores potential lunar habitat locations near Shackleton Rim. The project uses NASA-derived lunar terrain and illumination resources to investigate slope conditions and possible site candidates. These results are exploratory and do not certify any location as safe for construction.

6. Future Wearable Device

A future version could connect a wearable device containing suitable heart rate, oxygen saturation, temperature, and motion sensors. The device would send readings to the software, where they could be recorded, visualized, and reviewed. Hardware accuracy, communication reliability, clinical thresholds, and safety would require further testing and validation.

Technology and Impact

The current prototype runs locally in a web browser and uses simulated health and safety data. Some records can be saved locally and exported as CSV files.

LUNA-SAFE aims to demonstrate how a connected monitoring interface could help astronauts and mission teams recognize changes, document concerns, and coordinate appropriate reviews.

The prototype is not a certified medical device, does not diagnose health conditions, and does not control physical life-support systems.

Project Title: Space Mission Design Game

Space Mission Design Game is an interactive educational website developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It allows users to experience the exciting process of planning and designing a space mission through a fun, game-like environment. Players can choose their mission objectives, select spacecraft components, manage their available resources, explore planets, and complete different space challenges.

The project combines space science, creativity, problem-solving, and basic mission-planning concepts to make learning more engaging. It addresses the challenge by transforming complex space exploration ideas into an interactive experience that students and beginners can easily understand and enjoy.

This project is important because it encourages curiosity about space, develops critical-thinking and decision-making skills, and inspires young learners to explore science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). Our goal is to make space exploration educational, accessible, and enjoyable for everyone.
projectDetails.details:
Detailed Project Description – Interactive Space Mission Design Game

Our project, Interactive Space Mission Design Game, is an educational space exploration game created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It allows players to experience how real space missions are planned, designed and carried out.

How does it work?
Players begin by choosing their destination: the Moon, Mars, an asteroid or Earth orbit. They then select a mission objective, such as exploration, photography or scientific research. Next, they design their spacecraft by choosing its weight category and selecting equipment and instruments while balancing weight, power and budget.

Once the spacecraft is ready, players launch their mission. During the journey, they must navigate through space, avoid incoming meteors and collect fuel. They also monitor important factors such as fuel, lives, score and distance. The final challenge involves safely landing the spacecraft within the designated lunar landing zone.

Benefits and Intended Impact
The game makes space science easier and more enjoyable to understand. It develops decision-making, logical thinking, creativity and problem-solving skills. It also introduces players to real-world concepts such as spacecraft design, resource management and scientific instruments.

Our intended impact is to inspire students and young learners to become curious about space exploration and develop an interest in STEM education.

Tools and Technologies
- HTML: Website structure.
- CSS: Visual design, styling and layout.
- JavaScript: Interactive gameplay, controls and game mechanics.
- GitHub:Code storage and project sharing.
- Web Browser:Running and testing the game.
- Prezi:Presenting and explaining the project.

Creativity and Innovation
The creative part of our project is that it combines spacecraft engineering with an interactive arcade-style game. Instead of simply reading about space missions, players become mission designers and pilots. Every decision, from selecting spacecraft equipment to managing fuel during flight, affects their mission experience.

Factors Considered
We considered educational value, user-friendliness, gameplay experience, realistic mission-planning concepts, resource limitations and accessibility. Our goal was to create something that is both entertaining and educational, allowing beginners to explore the challenges of space missions in an engaging way.

projectDetails.name: Rovers in the red dust,Project MAS Explorers
projectDetails.summary:
Rovers in the Red Dust brings the historic journey of NASA's twin Mars Exploration Rovers, Spirit and Opportunity, to life through an engaging, first-person narrative. Told from the perspective of the rovers in "Echoes Across the Red Desert," our project transforms complex space exploration data into an accessible story of discovery, resilience, and companionship on Mars.

Alongside the narrative, the presentation breaks down the rovers' engineering ("What Are Rovers Made From?"), key scientific findings about past water activity on Mars ("What Did They Teach Us?"), mission milestones, and data visualizations comparingmission expectations against real-world achievements. Finally, our project highlights the critical importance of planetary protection and responsible space exploration ("Why We Must Protect Other Worlds"). By blending storytelling with verified NASA mission data, Rovers in the Red Dust inspires audiences to appreciate Mars exploration and safeguard extraterrestrial environments for future generations.
projectDetails.details:
About Our Project

Rovers in the Red Dust was created for the "Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars" challenge. Our project introduces school-age students to NASA's twin Mars Exploration Rovers-Spirit and Opportunity-by combining an engaging first-person story with clear explanations of the hardware they were made from and the science they made possible.

How It Works & Why It Is Creative

Instead of presenting dry facts, we tell the rovers' mission from their own point of view in "Echoes Across the Red Desert," alongside visual breakdowns of:

• Rover Hardware: Lightweight aluminum frames, aerogel insulation to survive -96°C nights, solar arrays with lithium-ion batteries, a six-wheel rocker-bogie suspension, panoramic cameras, and the Rock Abrasion Tool (RAT).

• Scientific Discoveries & Stats: Although planned for only 90 Martian days (sols), Spirit lasted 2,208 sols (driving 7.73 km) and Opportunity lasted 5,111 sols (driving 45.16 km), uncovering mineral veins and hematite "blueberries" that proved liquid water once flowed on Mars.

• Our Message: Though these rovers now rest silent on Mars, they are abandoned, never forgotten-reminding us that we are responsible for making these extraordinary machines and remembering what they achieved.

Benefits, Impact & Tools Used

• Intended Impact: Helps young space enthusiasts easily understand how real space hardware works and inspires curiosity about planetary exploration.

• Tools & Resources Used: Built using Canva for visual design and storytelling, grounded in official NASA/JPL-Caltech Mars Exploration Rover mission records and imagery.

Our Story: Echoes Across the Red Desert

The Awakening

It was January 4th, 2004, when I landed on the dusty red planet I had been sent to explore. I rested on my lander platform, absorbing the Sun's energy through my solar panels. Once I had gathered enough energy. I rolled off my landing platform, ready to explore the rolling red hills and observe the distant skies. Red hills and rusty soll stretched as far as my cameras could see. I spent the day roaming the desolate desert, observing the strange rocks and distant hills. Everything was unfamiliar, yet there was so much to discover. The landscape was quiet, almost as though the entire planet was waiting for me to uncover its secrets. At first, I thought I was entirely alone on this unfamiliar world. But I soon discovered that I wasn't the first visitor to Mars. High above me, circling the planet, was an older spacecraft. His name was Mars Global Surveyor.

He had arrived in 1997, long before my journey began. He was one of the earliest explorers to study Mars from orbit, spending years mapping its surface and observing its many features. I imagined him as a quiet, wise old guardian, watching over the planet from the skies. A few years later, another spacecraft joined him. His name was Mars Odyssey. and he had arrived in 2001. He would soon become an important part of my journey, helping me study my surroundings and relaying my messages. discoveries and observations to the humans back on Earth. For a while, both orbiters continued their journeys above me. I was a newcomer, with an entire world waiting to be explored, while they had already spent years studying it. Eventually, in November 2006, Mars Global Surveyor fell silent. His transmissions stopped, but I like to imagine him continuing his quiet journey around Mars, an old observer who had witnessed so much of the Red Planet's history.

A Memorable Discovery

Mars certainly had many secrets. The rocks scattered across the landscape contained fascinating minerals, and I spent much of my time photographing and examining them. One particular rock caught my attention. It was considerably larger than the others, and something about it made me curious. I brushed away the layer of dust covering its surface, hoping to get a better look. Its exterior was still a familiar dusty reddish-brown. I wasn't ready to give up, though. I had a feeling there was something more beneath that rusty exterior. After several minutes of examining and brushing away the dust, I noticed a change in colour. Beneath the reddish surface was something much darker. I carefully examined its exposed interior, revealing fresh, dark-grey rock. almost the colour of the night sky. What fascinated me even more were the tiny veins of lighter-coloured minerals running through it. They were clues left behind by ancient water, evidence that this seemingly lifeless world had once been very different.

To think that this dry, dusty planet had once held rivers and lakes was remarkable. Mars had a history far richer than its barren landscape suggested, and I was only beginning to uncover it. I spent the following days examining the rocks scattered across the landscape, noticing the differences in their colours, textures and mineral compositions. Each one seemed to hold another piece of Mars's ancient history. I carefully recorded my observations and sent my discoveries to Mars Odyssey, the spacecraft orbiting above me, which relayed my findings back to the humans on Earth. One day, while preparing to send another message to Odyssey about a recent discovery, something unexpected happened. Instead of receiving a confirmation from the orbiter, I picked up a different transmission. It was a message from another rover. Another rover? Here on Mars?

A Friend Across the Red Desert

It was quite strange. I had never imagined there was another rover exploring Mars alongside me. The message contained details of an interesting discovery: millions of tiny. BB-sized mineral spheres scattered across the Martian soil. They had been nicknamed "blueberries" because of their round shape. These little spheres were made largely of hematite, a mineral that can form in the presence of water. They were remarkable clues, suggesting that liquid water had once flowed through or soaked the Martian ground. I found it fascinating that, somewhere on this enormous planet, another explorer was uncovering secrets of its own. Perhaps I wasn't quite as alone as I had first thought. I continued exploring my side of the planet, and messages from the other rover gradually became a familiar part of my days. I had learned her name was Opportunity. Through her transmissions. I discovered more about her adventures and the fascinating things she encountered on her side of Mars.

Eventually, I decided to send her a message of my own. I shared some of my recent discoveries and waited for a reply. And waited. An entire day passed, but nothing came back. There was no response, no familiar transmission, only silence. The following day, when I contacted Mars Odyssey again. I received an explanation. It seemed that messages weren't always delivered Immediately. Sometimes transmissions could be delayed, depending on the spacecraft's position and orbit. I asked Odyssey if there was another way I could reach Opportunity, but unfortunately, she had already passed beyond the area where Odyssey could relay my message to her. She was continuing her journey along the other side of Mars. I returned to my explorations, hoping that one day our paths, or at least our transmissions, would cross again.

I was exploring a nearby crater when I received an unexpected message through Mars Odyssey. It was from Opportunity! She had sent some of her latest exploration data, along with a rather curious question: Was I really exploring the other side of Mars? Over the following days, our messages became more frequent. We exchanged discoveries, observations and little details about our surroundings. Sometimes we even spoke about the night sky above us and the harsh Martian winters. I told her about the freezing temperatures on my side of the planet, how the cold could affect my instruments and make exploration increasingly difficult. She explained that winters on her side were no gentler. I told her about the freezing temperatures on my side of the planet, how the cold could affect my instruments and make exploration increasingly difficult. She explained that winters on her side were no gentler.

Our transmissions gradually became a familiar part of my days. We continued exchanging messages, sharing discoveries from opposite sides of our enormous red world. Then, one day. I received some interesting news from Mars Odyssey. A new spacecraft had arrived in orbit around Mars. Its name was Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, or MRO. He was quite different from Odyssey. Efficient, observant and equipped with an incredibly powerful camera, he was designed to study Mars in extraordinary detail and send valuable information back to Earth. It seemed Mars had welcomed another explorer.

A Little Machine, A Lasting Legacy

The days passed, and our explorations continued. I wandered across my side of Mars while Opportunity explored hers. We sent our discoveries and observations back to Earth, each of us uncovering another little piece of this planet's history. Then, one day, everything changed. I was exploring near a crater when my wheels sank into a patch of soft sand. I tried reversing, but instead of freeing myself. I sank deeper and tilted at an awkward angle. I tried moving forward, then backward, desperately searching for firmer ground But nothing worked. I wasn't going to give up. I had so much more to discoverl I still wanted to explore the distant hills, examine unfamiliar rocks and perhaps, one day, meet Opportunity.

However, my attempts were consuming too much energy. I had to stop moving and conserve what little power remained. My tilted position left my solar panels unable to gather enough sunlight. I sent what I hoped would be one last message through Odyssey. I wanted to tell Opportunity that I was in trouble, that I was still trying, that I hadn't given up. But my energy was fading. The landscape grew darker. My Instruments fell silent, and my transmissions came to an end... Opportunity waited for another message from her twin. An entire day passed. but nothing arrived. Concerned, she contacted Mars Odyssey and asked if he had heard from Spirit. He hadn't received anything since the previous evening.

Eventually, she learned what had happened. Her twin had become trapped in soft Martian soil, tilted at an angle that prevented his solar panels from receiving sufficient sunlight. Despite his efforts to escape, his energy had eventually run out. Spirit had been my companion throughout our journey across Mars. His messages had made the long days of exploration interesting, and I had grown accustomed to sharing my discoveries with him. Now, the familiar transmissions were gone. I continued exploring the red deserts, climbing over hills and examining rocks and minerals. I still sent my daily observations to Odyssey and MRO. just as I had always done. But something was missing. The silence was palpable, and the loneliness that I had once known during my earliest days on Mars returned. Days turned into months, and months into years.

Then, one day. MRO sent me a warning. A dust storm was forming nearby. It appeared distant and not particularly threatening, so I continued my work. I was examining a stone when I noticed a sudden change in the atmosphere. A cold breeze swept across the landscape, followed by enormous clouds of red dust. The storm arrived almost all at once. Sand swirled around me in powerful gusts, obscuring everything my cameras could see. I decided to remain still until it passed, but the winds continued. Eventually, I attempted to move forward, hoping to escape its path. Yet wherever I went, the dust seemed to follow. The days passed. The sunlight disappeared behind the enormous clouds. and my solar panels struggled to gather enough energy. I could no longer send my usual messages to Odyssey or MRO.

I had survived countless Martian winters, crossed vast stretches of desert and uncovered secrets buried beneath the red soll. But this storm was different. My energy continued to fade. My movements grew slower, and the familiar landscape disappeared behind an endless haze of red.I had once wondered what it would be like to explore Mars without my twin. Now, I understood. And then, darkness came. Silence followed.

Note on Historical Accuracy: This story is a fictionalised retelling of the Mars rovers' journeys, narrated from their perspectives. Their personalities, emotions, thoughts and conversations have been imagined. and certain events have been dramatised for storytelling purposes. However, the major historical events, scientific discoveries and mission details are based on real events and NASA records.

Note: All images in our presentation were sourced from NASA/JPL-Caltech (and Cornell University for PIA05591)

projectDetails.name: Project Mhis pathfinders
projectDetails.summary:
MHIS PATHFINDER is an intelligent Global Flood Intelligence Database designed to collect, organize, and analyze satellite-based flood information from around the world. The platform aims to transform complex environmental data into accessible information that helps users understand how floods develop, evolve, and affect different regions over time.

Using NASA satellite observations, particularly data associated with the NISAR mission, the application provides a searchable archive of flood events, tracks changes in affected areas, and allows users to compare historical flood patterns. It also introduces the concept of “Flood DNA” profiles, which highlight the unique characteristics of individual flood events.

Our goal is to make flood information easier to explore, compare, and understand while supporting environmental research and improving awareness of the impact of flooding on communities and infrastructure.
projectDetails.details:
MHIS PATHFINDER is a web-based environmental intelligence application featuring:

* Global Flood Database: A searchable collection of flood events from different regions.
* Flood Evolution Tracking: Examines how flood-affected areas change over time.
* Flood DNA: Creates distinctive profiles for individual flood events based on their characteristics.
* NASA Data Library: Organizes satellite observations and related datasets.
* Historical Comparison: Allows users to compare flood events and identify environmental patterns.
* Environmental Impact: Helps explore the effects of flooding on communities and infrastructure.

3. NASA Data

Yes, our project is designed around NASA satellite observations, particularly the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission.

projectDetails.name: Project Mission Architect
projectDetails.summary:
Mission Architect is a browser-based simulator where players design and launch a real-style NASA space telescope mission, from first idea to orbit.

What it is: Players choose science objectives (one to three, across three levels), then select wavelengths, instruments and optics, an orbit, a launch vehicle, and a budget across the four mission segments: launch, space, ground and user. A 3D spacecraft updates as they build it, then flies to its orbit with live telemetry. A final report scores the design and compares it to real missions such as Hubble, Webb, Chandra and Fermi.

How it addresses the challenge: It makes a whole space mission understandable through interactive 3D visualisation. It covers the mission concept, trajectory, timeline and spacecraft layout. Its steps follow NASA's Concept Maturity Levels and Mission Design Lab studies, with GMAT-style orbit readouts and a Mission Viz-style flight.

Why it matters: Mission design involves trade-offs between science goals, engineering limits and cost. Players learn that every choice affects the others, and that a mission succeeds only if all four segments work together. It needs no special software and runs on phones and computers.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

Mission Architect is a browser game that teaches how a space mission is designed. The player picks one to three science objectives across three levels, such as exoplanet atmospheres, black holes or the first galaxies. They then follow six steps modelled on NASA's Concept Maturity Levels and Mission Design Lab studies:

  1. Choose the science objectives.
  2. Choose wavelengths. Options that don't fit the objectives are disabled.
  3. Choose instruments and optics. A 3D spacecraft updates as they build it.
  4. Compare four orbits, with a GMAT-style readout of period, signal delay and launcher performance.
  5. Pick a launch vehicle that can carry the spacecraft's mass to that orbit.
  6. Split a budget across the space, ground and user segments.

The game then runs a countdown and flies the spacecraft in 3D with live telemetry. It ends with a score out of 100 and an explanation of each choice. The report also compares the design to real missions (Hubble, Webb, Chandra, Fermi, Swift, TESS) and shows a mission timeline. Underfunding any of the four segments (launch, space, ground, user) makes the mission fail.

Benefits and intended impact

Players learn that mission design is a series of trade-offs, and that a mission needs all four segments to work. It runs in a browser on phones and computers, with no installation. It is meant for students and beginners, and it points them to the NASA resources it draws on.

Tools

I built it as a single HTML file in JavaScript and CSS, using Three.js for the 3D view and the Web Audio API for sound effects. The deck was made with Claude's Slides tool. I checked the game logic with Node scripts and captured the interface screenshots with Playwright. I did not use any special hardware.

Creativity

Instead of a quiz, the game lets players build a spacecraft and watch it fly. Every NASA resource in the challenge became a game mechanic, such as the CML progress bar and the GMAT-style orbit readout. Choices have realistic consequences: infrared telescopes do best at L2, X-ray telescopes do best in a highly elliptical orbit, and a rocket that is too small fails at launch.

Factors considered

Accuracy vs. simplicity: The numbers are simplified, inspired by real missions, and the game says so.

Accessibility: It works on phones, laptops and ipads it doesnt need to install.

Clear feedback: The game gives a reason for every score and failure.

Scope: It covers space telescopes only, not other mission types.

projectDetails.name: Mission:Lifeline
projectDetails.summary:
Mars Outpost is an interactive educational simulation game developed by Team Mission:Lifeline for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The game introduces players to the challenges of managing and sustaining a human settlement on Mars.

Developed using Godot 4.7 and GDScript, the game allows players to explore a Martian base, interact with essential facilities, and manage five critical resources: oxygen, water, food, energy, and radiation shielding.

Players encounter realistic space-related challenges, including dust storms, resource shortages, and radiation emergencies. Each decision involves trade-offs, teaching players how limited resources affect astronaut safety, scientific research, and mission success.

Our project addresses the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by transforming complex space engineering concepts into an accessible and engaging learning experience. It encourages strategic thinking, problem-solving, and an understanding of the difficulties involved in sustaining human life beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Mars Outpost is a 10-minute, top-down educational game developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge's Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. Players control an astronaut managing a Martian research base while balancing five essential resources: oxygen, water, food, energy, and shielding.

Throughout five mission stages, players encounter challenges such as water shortages, dust storms, and radiation warnings. Every important decision has benefits and consequences, encouraging players to consider competing engineering priorities.

Developed using Godot 4.7 and GDScript, the game features interactive buildings, resource management, Mission Control guidance, and a final mission assessment based on crew safety, scientific progress, and return readiness.

Our goal is to make space exploration engineering understandable, interactive, and engaging for younger learners.

Echoes of Space is an educational web application that makes learning about space fun and interactive. We created a game where students can explore NASA equipment left on the Moon and Mars, including Apollo 11, Opportunity, Ingenuity, and InSight.

Users can discover the stories behind each mission, answer quizzes, complete challenges, and earn an explorer certificate.

Our project addresses NASA’s challenge by helping people learn about forgotten spacecraft and their important discoveries in a simple and enjoyable way.

This project is important because it encourages young students to explore space, learn about science, and understand how past NASA missions have helped us discover more about our universe.
projectDetails.details:
What does our project do?
Echoes of Space is an interactive website that teaches students about NASA spacecraft left on the Moon and Mars. Users can explore four space missions, read their stories, answer quizzes, complete challenges, and earn a certificate.

What are the benefits?
Our project makes learning about space fun and easy. It helps students understand NASA's discoveries and encourages them to become interested in science and space exploration.

What tools did we use?

  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript to create the website.
  • PowerPoint to present our project.
  • NASA resources to research space missions.
  • AI-generated images to make the project more visually interesting.

How is our project creative?
Instead of just reading information, students can become space explorers through interactive stories, games, and quizzes.

What factors did we consider?
We wanted our website to be simple, educational, fun, and easy for students to use. We also made sure the information was based on real NASA missions.

Our goal is to keep the stories of forgotten spacecraft alive and inspire future generations to explore space.

projectDetails.name: ASTRO - astornaut health monitoring sotware
projectDetails.summary:
Astronauts face many health challenges in space, including radiation, muscle loss, stress, and sleep problems.

Astro is a smart website designed to help astronauts monitor their health using information from connected medical devices and sensors.

It also demonstrates health alerts, wellbeing check-ins, and communication with Earth.

Astro aims to make space exploration safer and healthier for future astronauts.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRO — Astronaut Health Monitoring System

NASA Space Apps Challenge | Presentation Speech

Imagine being millions of kilometres away from Earth.

You're travelling through space, surrounded by darkness and stars, when suddenly, you begin to feel unwell.

There's no hospital nearby, no doctor you can immediately visit, and contacting Earth could take more than 20 minutes, depending on how far away you are.

So, how can astronauts monitor their health when help is millions of kilometres away?

Hello everyone!

Today, I'm excited to introduce my project, Astro — Astronaut Health Monitoring System.

Space exploration is one of humanity's greatest achievements, but living in space creates serious challenges for the human body.

Without Earth's gravity, astronauts can experience muscle weakness, bone density loss, changes in blood circulation, and problems with vision and balance.

They are also exposed to space radiation, disrupted sleep schedules, and psychological stress caused by isolation.

These challenges become even more serious during long-duration missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond.

That's where Astro comes in.

Astro is a connected health-monitoring platform designed to help astronauts understand their physical and mental wellbeing while travelling through space.

But here's the important question: How does Astro actually work?

Astro is designed to connect with different monitoring devices, including wearable health bands, medical instruments, radiation dosimeters, and spacecraft environmental sensors.

These devices can collect information about cardiovascular health, oxygen levels, radiation exposure, and conditions inside the spacecraft.

Astro brings this information together into one easy-to-understand dashboard.

Instead of displaying complicated medical numbers without explanation, Astro helps astronauts understand what the readings mean and whether something may need attention.

For example, imagine an astronaut's wearable device detects an unusual cardiovascular reading.

Astro could examine the reading alongside the astronaut's recent activity, identify a potentially concerning change, and display a warning recommending further assessment.

The platform also includes a wellbeing questionnaire where astronauts can record their mood, stress, energy, sleep, and physical discomfort.

Astro can also help monitor exercise routines, radiation exposure, and cabin conditions such as carbon dioxide and oxygen levels.

And because communication with Earth isn't always immediate, Astro is designed to support onboard health awareness while preparing reports for ground control.

For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, I developed an interactive website that demonstrates how these features could work together.

My prototype includes simulated health measurements, a device-connection demonstration, health-risk monitoring, mission selection, wellbeing check-ins, and a ground communications interface.

Although the current prototype uses simulated data, the long-term vision is to connect Astro with real, validated medical and spacecraft monitoring equipment.

What makes Astro important is that it doesn't just show health information. It aims to help astronauts understand that information and take appropriate action.

I believe that the future of space exploration isn't only about travelling farther, discovering new planets, or building advanced spacecraft.

It's also about protecting the people who make those discoveries possible.

Because when humanity travels beyond Earth, we must make sure astronaut health travels with us.

Astro — Monitoring Health. Supporting Astronauts. Advancing Human Space Exploration.

projectDetails.name: Project NASASIANSS
projectDetails.summary: Collective Brain is an AI-powered astronaut health management system that monitors the entire crew as one connected ecosystem rather than focusing on individuals. It analyses astronauts' physical health, mental wellbeing, sleep patterns, workload and environmental conditions to detect potential problems early and recommend personalised solutions. The system includes features such as tracking muscle and bone loss, monitoring heart health and vision changes, detecting stress and isolation, improving sleep schedules, tracking immune health and managing radiation exposure. projectDetails.details:
Collective Brain is an AI-powered astronaut health intelligence system designed to monitor the wellbeing of an entire crew rather than focusing on individual astronauts separately.

During space missions, astronauts face challenges such as muscle and bone loss, radiation exposure, vision changes, sleep disruption, stress and immune-system changes. These problems can affect not only individuals but also the performance and stability of the entire crew.

Our solution connects different aspects of astronaut health and analyses how they influence one another. It aims to identify patterns, detect potential risks and predict how individual health conditions could affect the crew as a whole. For example, if several astronauts experience stress, exhaustion or isolation at the same time, Collective Brain can identify a possible decline in crew stability and highlight risks to communication and mission efficiency.

The system includes eight specialised features: Muscle Trading Network, Heartbeat Balancer, Crowdsourced Eyes, Mood Gravity, Sleep Orchestra, Immune Shield, Radiation Budget System and Bone Credits System. Each feature focuses on a different astronaut health challenge while contributing information to the overall crew-health picture.

What makes our project unique is its crew-based intelligence approach. Instead of simply displaying separate health measurements, it considers the connections between astronauts and aims to recommend actions such as personalised exercise, workload adjustments, improved sleep schedules and radiation-aware task distribution.

The intended impact is to support healthier astronauts, stronger teamwork, earlier risk identification and safer, more efficient long-duration space missions. In the future, Collective Brain could be developed further with more advanced predictions, improved health-data integration and personalised recommendations.

projectDetails.name: Project Nasweats 2.0
projectDetails.summary:
EarthSignal – Environmental Change Across the Arabian Peninsula (2000–2025)

EarthSignal is an interactive research platform investigating how atmospheric and land-surface conditions across the Arabian Peninsula have changed between 2000 and 2025, and how they correlate with each other. Our team processed four NASA MERRA-2 data collections, each providing 312 months of data from January 2000 to December 2025, and used the data to analyse nine environmental variables across five regions. We developed an interactive website featuring maps, time-series graphs, regional comparisons and statistical analysis. Our findings show that temperatures increased by 0.239°C per decade, with the strongest warming in the Northwest (+0.369°C). Root-zone and topsoil wetness also increased. Wind speed was positively associated with dust concentration (r = 0.382), while precipitation was positively associated with soil wetness (r = 0.556–0.658). However, overall dust concentrations showed no statistically significant long-term trend. EarthSignal combines interactive visualisations with linear regression, Mann–Kendall tests, Sen's slope and correlation analysis to identify environmental trends and assess their significance. Our aim is to make complex NASA data easier to explore and understand, helping users see where environmental changes are happening, how significant they are and how different conditions relate to one another.
projectDetails.details:
🌍 EarthSignal is an interactive platform that explores how environmental conditions across the Arabian Peninsula have changed between 2000 and 2025, particularly in relation to dust activity.

🔬 Our project uses NASA's MERRA-2 data to investigate nine environmental variables, including temperature, humidity, wind speed, precipitation, soil wetness and dust concentration. We collected and processed data files for 312 months from four NASA datasets using Python. We divided the Arabian Peninsula into five regions so that we could compare how environmental conditions have changed in different areas.

💻 We then developed a website where users can explore these changes through maps, graphs, regional comparisons and statistical results. To make sure our findings were meaningful, we used methods such as linear regression, Mann–Kendall tests and correlation analysis to identify trends and examine relationships between variables.

📊 One of our key findings was that temperatures across the study area increased by approximately 0.239°C per decade. We also found that wind speed was positively associated with dust concentration, although dust levels did not show a statistically significant overall long-term trend.

🌱 What makes EarthSignal different is that it does not look at environmental variables separately. It brings together atmospheric and land-surface conditions to help users explore how they relate to one another. Throughout the project, we considered regional differences, seasonal changes, data quality and the statistical significance of our results.

We hope EarthSignal makes NASA's environmental data easier to understand and allows more people to explore the changes taking place across the Arabian Peninsula, rather than simply reading about them.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project NoteBlock
projectDetails.summary: Our project turns NASA nighttime-light imagery and satellite data into synchronized sound and moving map scans. The project includes two visual sonifications: a global 2012–2023 change map, where purple and orange guide pitch and volume, and India-centered annual night-light frames, where pixel brightness and coverage shape the notes. A data-based approach compares quality-screened VIIRS radiance from 2012 and 2023 across selected city regions, mapping spatial changes into chords. The challenge asked us to make the Earth science accessible and we believe that with providing both approaches we have made it engaging and accessible. Our interactive player lets audiences switch between places and years, watch each scan, and understand how the sound is made. By offering an auditory way to explore patterns in Earth-at-night observations, we make NASA data more approachable. It also distinguishes image-based interpretation from numerical radiance comparison. This project is important as it is going to help communities and young adults get a basic idea on sonification, with different major cities and understand how we can map different colors, intensity, radiance changes to sounds.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, NoteBlock, is an interactive way to explore Earth’s nighttime lights through maps and sound. People can choose the global map, an India map from a particular year, or a city map, then watch a synchronized scan while listening. Our website also explains how each map is translated into sound.

We developed two visual approaches and one data-based approach. For the global map, we classify its purple and orange colors and scan across it in sections: purple raises the pitch, orange lowers it, and the amount of classified color affects the volume.

For India, we analyze brightness in NASA’s yearly map images and turn a grid of those brightness patterns into chords. This approach sonifies the image’s brightness; it does not distinguish the map’s “more light” and “less light” colors.

For the city maps, the notebook compares quality-screened VIIRS radiance from 2012 and 2023. The direction and size of the change, along with its position on the grid, shape the sound.

We hope the project makes NASA night-light information more engaging and offers another way to notice patterns across places and years. Its creative element is the set of clear, repeatable rules that connect what people see on the map to what they hear. The player presents those rules alongside each video so listeners can understand the sonification, rather than hearing an unexplained soundtrack.

We used Python notebooks in Google Colab to process the imagery and data, with tools including NumPy, h5py, tifffile, Matplotlib, and FFmpeg. The interactive website uses HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The project runs on a standard computer and requires no specialized hardware.

Our team considered scientific accuracy, clarity, sound and scan synchronization, and making the interface easy to navigate. We also distinguish image-based sonification from numerical radiance comparison: neither method by itself explains why night lights changed.

projectDetails.name: Project O(NO)
projectDetails.summary:
EarthWatch is a browser-based Earth observation explorer that turns NASA satellite imagery into an interactive 3D globe. Instead of a flat map or a static chart, users spin a live planet and toggle environmental layers—NDVI (vegetation greenness), surface pressure, soil moisture, CO₂ concentration, and sea level change—to see how land, atmosphere, and oceans shift over time. The app pulls public NASA GIBS imagery, drapes it on a Three.js globe, and lets people scrub dates, compare seasons, highlight vegetation “bloom,” extrude pressure into height, and sample any point for a plain-language reading—without downloading raw files or writing code.

This matters because Earth trends are usually locked in specialist tools, Jupyter notebooks, or Earth Engine scripts. EarthWatch makes the same public NASA products explorable in one page: no API key for the core globe, no install step, and a workflow that is visual first—menu → layer → timeline → sample—so students, interns, and researchers can spot vegetation pulses, dry soils, CO₂ patterns, pressure systems, and sea level signals quickly and share them as a living demo rather than a screenshot.
projectDetails.details:
EarthWatch is a front-end Earth visualization app focused on time-aware satellite layers on a globe. The system requests equirectangular PNG composites from NASA’s Global Imagery Browse Services (GIBS) WMS for a chosen date, loads them as textures in Three.js, and wraps them on spheres slightly larger than a Blue Marble base Earth.

Current layers include:

  • NDVI — MODIS Terra 8-day vegetation index, with month-to-month crossfade and an optional bloom shader for places greener than the prior month
  • Surface pressure — MERRA-2 monthly pressure, with a custom shader that can extrude lows and highs into 3D height
  • Soil moisture — satellite soil moisture browse imagery for wet vs dry land patterns
  • CO₂ concentration — atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration maps for spatial greenhouse-gas context
  • Sea level change — ocean height / sea level trend imagery to show coastal and basin-scale change

A left-side menu switches layers; a bottom dock controls playback, layer-specific tools (such as Bloom and Extrude), Spin, and a date scrubber. Hover raycasting samples pixels and classifies them into readable categories shown in the info card and legend for each active layer.

The benefit is accessibility with honest presentation: EarthWatch uses NASA’s published color imagery and clear legends rather than inventing exact geophysical numbers from RGB alone. The intended impact is a lightweight, shareable way to explore multiple Earth systems in one globe—for education, demos, and early analysis—with a clear path to add more GIBS layers by swapping the layer name and legend.

We built the project as a single-page app with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript modules, Three.js (WebGL globe, OrbitControls, shaders), and NASA GIBS WMS. Hosting is static; the GitHub repo is the source of truth for the current build.

The project is creative because it treats satellite “browse” imagery as a first-class interactive medium: not a dashboard of charts, but a planet you can spin, layer, and query by point across vegetation, soil, carbon, atmosphere, and sea level. We optimized for clarity over spectacle—solid UI panels, readable typography, and layer toggles that hide data until asked—so the globe stays the focus.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.details:
Project Overview: TerraCycle

Empowering Farmers Worldwide with NASA Earth Observations and AI-Driven Crop Rotation

1. Background & The Problem

Farmers around the globe face escalating challenges from shifting temperatures, erratic rainfall patterns, prolonged water shortages, extreme weather events, and declining soil health. Traditional farming calendars and monocropping (planting the exact same crop season after season) are no longer viable under modern climate pressures. While crop rotation is a proven method to protect fields, conserve water, and restore soil fertility, choosing the right rotation sequence is complex, highly localized, and difficult to calculate without agronomic expertise.

2. Solution Summary

TerraCycle is a global, AI-powered decision-support tool designed to bridge the gap between complex space-based science and daily farm management. By combining NASA Earth observations, global soil databases, FAO crop characteristics, and farmer-specific priorities, TerraCycle generates tailored, multi-season crop rotation plans in under 30 seconds. It requires no expensive hardware or ground sensors, making it accessible to farmers anywhere in the world using just a smartphone or low-bandwidth connection.

3. Core Features & User Workflow

  • 3-Tap Simple Interface:
    1. Location: The farmer drops a GPS pin (or selects a region) to instantly pull local climate and soil baselines.
    2. Crop Selection: The farmer selects their current and planned crops from a visual icon grid (e.g., corn, wheat, rice, soybeans, legumes).
    3. Priority Setting: The farmer specifies their primary goal—such as $\text{💧 Saving Water}$, $\text{🌱 Restoring Soil Health}$, $\text{💰 Maximizing Yield}$, or $\text{🔥 Surviving Extreme Heat}$.
  • Automated Data Integration: Behind the scenes, the app queries free public datasets—including NASA POWER (for temperature, radiation, and rainfall trends), NASA SMAP (for soil moisture and drought stress), and ISRIC SoilGrids (for soil texture, pH, and organic carbon).
  • The Decision-Support Engine: An AI-backed rules engine cross-references local environmental conditions with a built-in FAO Crop Characteristics Knowledge Base to match heavy feeder crops with nitrogen-fixing or drought-hardy rotation partners.
  • Actionable Output Dashboard: Generates a 3-season rotation timeline complete with impact metrics (e.g., water savings percentage, soil nitrogen boost) and a plain-language explanation of why the rotation protects their harvest.

4. Dataset Foundation

TerraCycle is built on robust open-access data sources categorized into four operational pillars:

  • Space & Satellite Observations: SMAP (soil moisture), GPM/IMERG (precipitation), Landsat & MODIS (vegetation indices/NDVI), ECOSTRESS (land surface temperature and evapotranspiration), and SRTM (elevation and slope).
  • Soil & Land Cover Data: ISRIC SoilGrids, USDA Web Soil Survey, and Cropland Data Layer (CDL).
  • Climate & Agroclimatology: NASA POWER agroclimatological normals, PRISM, and FAO GAEZ.
  • Agricultural Context: USDA Ag Data Commons and NASS QuickStats for agronomic baselines.

5. Impact & Vision

TerraCycle transforms raw satellite data into practical, field-level wisdom. By helping farmers diversify their fields sustainably, the tool enhances long-term climate resilience, reduces the need for synthetic fertilizers, conserves vital water resources, and secures food production worldwide.

projectDetails.summary:
إليك النسخة المحدثة والمختصرة لتكون جاهزة تماماً وضمن حدود أقل من 1500 حرف:

---

**GeoAgri Pro by OrbitX2026**

OrbitX2026 presents **GeoAgri Pro**, an AI-powered, mobile-first precision agriculture web platform that transforms NASA and ESA Earth observation data into real-time, actionable farm decisions.

### The Challenge

Global agriculture loses over **32%** of crop yields to hidden stresses—such as root-zone salinity, soil nitrogen depletion, and sudden weather shocks—weeks before visible damage appears.

### Core Technological Solutions

* **Multi-Source Data Fusion:** Fuses 10-meter Copernicus Sentinel-2 indices (NDVI, NDWI, SAVI, LST) with NASA SMAP soil telemetry, Open-Meteo forecasts, and 6-month NASA POWER climate models.
* **3D Geospatial Digital Twin:** Provides an interactive, immersive 3D digital representation of fields for precise monitoring.
* **Automated Sub-Zoning (A/B/C):** Automatically segments fields into operational management zones based on insights.
* **Crop Rotation Planner:** A specialized 5-season planner designed to restore soil health.
* **Gemini AI Agronomist:** An intelligent virtual agronomist executing voice commands and multimodal photo-based disease diagnoses.

GeoAgri Pro safeguards food security in climate-vulnerable, water-scarce regions. By bridging space agency data and farmers, it rescues threatened yields, prevents flood losses, and saves an estimated **47 m³ of irrigation water per feddan**.
projectDetails.details:
إليك النص الكامل بصياغة احترافية ومخصصة بالكامل لفريق OrbitX2026، مع الحفاظ على كافة التفاصيل التقنية والعلمية الدقيقة وجاهزيته للتقديم:

1. What does it do / How does it work?

Developed by Team OrbitX2026, GeoAgri Pro is a mobile-first, AI-powered precision agriculture and predictive decision support platform that turns complex space agency Earth observations into immediate, actionable field decisions for farmers, agronomists, and land managers.

How it works:

  1. Interactive 3D Digital Twin & High-Resolution Atlas: Using CesiumJS and Leaflet, Team OrbitX2026 engineered a 3D orbital globe and 20+ live analytical map layers, allowing farmers to digitize parcel boundaries, inspect elevation gradients, and visualize micro-zones at 10-meter spatial resolution.
    • NDVI & SAVI: Canopy vigor and biomass density with soil-brightness adjustments.
    • NDWI & NDMI: Leaf moisture content and root-zone water stress.
    • EVI & LST: Enhanced vegetation greenness and radiometric land surface temperature.
    • Soil Telemetry: Surface moisture (0–7 cm), deep root moisture (7–28 cm), electrical conductivity (salinity EC), and soil pH from SMAP and SoilGrids.
  2. Sub-Zone (A/B/C) Diagnostics: Rather than treating entire farms uniformly, the platform automatically segments parcels into distinct sub-zones, detecting early degradation in stressed sectors before problems spread.
    • 14-Day Microclimate Radar: Pairs real-time Open-Meteo telemetry with NASA POWER 6-month harmonic predictive models to forecast precipitation, frost, heat waves, and wind gusts.
    • 12-Crop MCDA Engine: Ranks optimal seasonal crops based on water availability, soil salinity tolerance, and localized market profitability.
    • 5-Season Crop Rotation Planner: Automatically balances cereal and legume cycles to eliminate nitrogen depletion (-68 kg N/feddan) and disrupt 75% of soil-borne pest cycles.
    • NPK Commercial Dosage Calculator: Translates elemental crop nutrient deficits into exact commercial fertilizer applications (Urea, Superphosphate, Potassium Sulfate) over a 4-week timeline.
  3. Agentic Voice & Vision AI Advisor (GeoAgri AI): Powered by Google Gemini multimodal intelligence, the advisor analyzes uploaded photos/videos of crop diseases, understands hands-free voice commands in both Arabic and English, and autonomously executes 13 in-platform actions (navigating layers, generating PDF agronomic audits, adjusting irrigation, and logging pest incidents).

2. What are its benefits?

  • Catches Invisible Stress Weeks in Advance: Detects root-zone salinity spikes and moisture deficits up to 14 days before visible foliar yellowing occurs, preventing irreversible yield decay.
  • Substantial Water Conservation: Saves an estimated 47 m³ of water per feddan per irrigation cycle by dynamically halting automated watering schedules when predictive rainfall probabilities exceed 80%.
  • Crop Loss Prevention from Extreme Weather: Provides a 24-hour advance warning protocol that mitigates up to 85% of flood-induced root drowning and delivers lodging-shield alerts against high-velocity dust storms (>33 km/h).
  • Restores Soil Health: Improves parcel soil health scores from 74% to 94% across 5 seasons by substituting continuous cereal monocultures with nitrogen-fixing cover crops.
  • Optimized Input Costs: Eliminates chemical fertilizer over-application through calibrated 4-week NPK calculations, reducing farm expenditure and preventing groundwater nitrate contamination.
  • Zero-Barrier Usability: Designed by Team OrbitX2026 with a smartphone-first responsive interface, complete bilingual support (Arabic & English), and voice control for farmers in the field.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Democratizing Space Data: Team OrbitX2026 bridges the critical technical divide between space agencies (NASA, ESA) and smallholder farmers by translating raw multi-spectral satellite rasters into clear, plain-language agronomic actions.
  • Strengthening Food Security in Climate-Vulnerable Regions: Tailored specifically for arid and semi-arid agricultural belts (such as Egypt and the MENA region) experiencing severe water scarcity, soil salinization, and climate volatility.
    • SDG 2 (Zero Hunger): Protecting crop yields against sudden climate shocks and pest outbreaks.
    • SDG 6 (Clean Water and Sanitation): Preventing agricultural runoff and optimizing every cubic meter of irrigation water.
    • SDG 12 (Responsible Consumption & Production): Minimizing excess chemical fertilizer and pesticide usage.
    • SDG 13 (Climate Action): Building farm-level resilience against intensifying drought and heatwaves.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did we use?

  • Programming Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript (ESNext), HTML5, CSS3, SQL.
  • Frontend Framework & Tooling: React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS v4, Lucide React icons, Recharts (for dynamic spectral index and weather time-series charts).
    • CesiumJS: Real-time 3D Earth digital twin with terrain elevation models and free-camera orbital navigation.
    • Leaflet: 2D interactive parcel atlas, multi-spectral tile layers, and polygon GIS vector digitization.
    • NASA POWER API: Daily solar radiation flux, surface meteorology, and thermal Growing Degree Days (GDD).
    • Copernicus Sentinel-2 & NASA SMAP: 10m multi-spectral bands, surface and root-zone soil moisture.
    • Open-Meteo API: Hyper-local 14-day forecasts, wind vector components, soil temperature, and leaf wetness duration.
    • ISRIC SoilGrids: Global soil physical and chemical properties (bulk density, clay content, CEC, pH).
    • Google Gemini API (@google/genai): Multimodal visual diagnosis, agricultural reasoning, and tool-calling agentic execution.
    • Web Speech API: In-browser speech-to-text transcription for voice commands.
    • Express.js & Node.js: Backend API handling session persistence, user profiles, and GIS processing.
    • Firebase: User authentication and cloud zone persistence.
    • GitHub & GitHub Pages: Version control, automated continuous deployment pipeline (gh-pages), and global web hosting.

5. How is our project creative and innovative?

  1. Agentic "Tool-Calling" Agronomist: Unlike static chatbots that only output text, GeoAgri AI is an active agent engineered by OrbitX2026. When a farmer speaks or asks a question, the AI autonomously commands the map, toggles NDVI layers, recalculates NPK balances, highlights high-risk sub-zones, and compiles downloadable PDF reports in real time.
  2. 3-Year Historical Anomaly Isolation: Soil salinity often mimics water drought in simple NDVI checks. GeoAgri Pro innovates by cross-referencing current 10m reflectance against 3-year multi-seasonal baselines combined with SMAP root-depth moisture, allowing the system to decisively isolate true soil salinization from standard seasonal water stress.
  3. Automated Micro-Zoning (A/B/C): Instead of assuming uniform field conditions, OrbitX2026's proprietary algorithm subdivides fields into intra-parcel management units, enabling Variable Rate Application (VRA) for targeted fertilizer and water delivery.
  4. Resilient Dual-Engine Architecture: If network connectivity drops or API quotas are exceeded in remote rural areas, the platform automatically falls back to an internal, deterministic client-side agro-scientific engine, guaranteeing continuous offline operation for the farmer.

6. What factors did Team OrbitX2026 take into consideration?

  • Smallholder Farmer Realities & Literacy: Many farmers do not read complex data tables or speak English. Team OrbitX2026 prioritized native Arabic RTL support, clear visual color-coded alert badges, voice-driven interaction, and automated photo diagnosis.
  • Extreme Arid Agronomy & Nile Basin Constraints: We specifically engineered our crop matrices around Mediterranean and Egyptian agricultural dynamics—factoring in high alkaline soil pH (7.5–8.2), canal irrigation quotas (2,500 m³/feddan water budgets), and localized salinity thresholds.
  • Local Economic Viability: Suitability scores do not solely look at botany; our Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) factors in expected revenue per feddan in Egyptian Pounds (EGP), local market demand, and input production costs.
  • Low-Bandwidth Mobile Optimization: Heavy 3D Cesium terrain and satellite tiles are lazy-loaded with adaptive HTTP/2 request concurrency throttling, ensuring smooth rendering even over spotty 3G/4G cellular connections in agricultural fields.

projectDetails.summary:
Summary – How ORBITAL Works
ORBITAL uses one engineering model to calculate all its numbers, based on real scientific principles. It uses the rocket equation to calculate velocity changes, orbital mechanics and Kepler's equation to determine spacecraft trajectories, and other models to calculate communication, temperature, solar power, and rocket performance. The spacecraft's movement is simulated using a realistic two-body orbital model with high precision. ORBITAL combines three types of elements:
Real: Physical constants and scientific principles.
Model: Simplified educational approximations used for simulations.
Fictional: The agency (OXD), crew, rockets, hardware, costs, and discoveries.
Overall, ORBITAL combines real physics, simplified models, and fictional elements to create an educational spaceflight simulation.

projectDetails.name: Project Parallax.UAE
projectDetails.summary:
We built "Abandoned but not Forgotten," an interactive web experience that tells the stories of 25 NASA machines left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Visitors tap markers on stylized maps to open a "file" on each machine: where it sits, what it achieved and how its mission ended. Extras include a comic of Opportunity's final months, charts showing how far machines outlived their plans, a live Voyager 1 countdown to one light-day from Earth, and a ten-question quiz.

It answers the challenge by turning discarded equipment into engaging storytelling for ages 9–15, with imagined voices clearly labeled and every fact linked to its source.

It matters because these machines are not junk. Apollo mirrors still measure the Moon's drift, and Opportunity's record stood for years. Silent hardware preserves history, inspires young explorers and reminds us to care for what we leave behind.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

"Abandoned but not Forgotten" is an interactive storytelling website about NASA's discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars. It argues that "abandoned" is the wrong word for most of these machines. Many still work, many still tell us something, and a few are still sending data. Visitors explore a Moon map and a Mars map and tap pins to open a record for each of 25 landers, rovers, orbiters and probes. Each record covers what the machine did, how it was left, its current status and its sources. They can filter the Moon by who left the equipment there (human or robot) and whether it is still in use. The site also covers deep-space explorers such as Voyager 1, Pioneer 10 and 11, Dawn and NEAR.

Benefits and intended impact

The site makes space heritage easy to understand for people with no background in it. It replaces the idea of "space junk" with the idea of an archive and a set of working instruments. Examples are the retroreflectors left on the Moon that scientists still use, and Voyager 1, which is still communicating from interstellar space. I want visitors to see these machines as part of a continuing story and to care about preserving them.

How it is creative

- A six-panel comic follows the Opportunity rover from landing to its last transmission. Imagined voices are labelled as such, so the story never passes for a real quote.

- A "built for less" chart compares how long each mission was designed to last with how long it actually survived.

- A distance "ladder" and a live countdown show how far away each machine is in light-time.

- The Moon and Mars are drawn in the browser on a canvas, and the Mars surface is generated from noise. There are no stock images.

- A ten-question quiz and a glossary turn reading into participation.

Tools and how it was built

The site is a single page of plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no frameworks or external libraries. I used Google Fonts for typography. I tested it in a headless Chromium browser with Playwright on desktop and phone sizes. I built it with AI assistance (Claude by Anthropic), and I directed the concept and reviewed the content and sources.

Factors we considered

Accuracy: facts were checked against NASA, JPL and NSSDC pages, and sources are listed on the site. Map positions are approximate.

Accessibility: the pins are keyboard-reachable buttons, the contrast is high, and the layout works on phones.

Honesty: anything imagined or poetic is labelled.
