challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: AegisμG — Microgravity Fire Safety Intelligence
projectDetails.summary:
**AegisμG — Microgravity Fire Safety Intelligence**, developed by Team SPECULATRON AI, is an interactive, evidence-driven research platform designed to advance understanding of fire behavior in microgravity and support future spacecraft fire-safety research.

Addressing NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026's *Flame in Freefall* challenge, AegisμG transforms NASA combustion research into accessible scientific insights through six integrated demonstrations: mission exploration, NASA evidence discovery, experimental data analysis, scientific comparison, explainable intelligence, and a digital twin sandbox.

Using NASA's BASS-II combustion report (NASA/TM-20210011385), our platform analyzes 20 PMMA combustion tests comprising 43 airflow segments, preserves missing measurements, and highlights important experimental exceptions.

Our SPECULATRON intelligence engine combines evidence-grounded retrieval, scientific comparison, research-gap identification, and DIWA provenance tracking to produce transparent, traceable insights. An educational oxygen-balance simulation illustrates hypothetical scenarios while clearly distinguishing simulations from NASA observations.

AegisμG helps researchers, engineers, students, and future mission planners explore complex combustion evidence, identify knowledge gaps, and prioritize further experiments toward safer human space exploration. It is an independent research prototype, not a validated fire-safety prediction system.
projectDetails.details:
AegisμG — Microgravity Fire Safety Intelligence

Team: SPECULATRON AI | NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

1. Project Overview

AegisμG is an interactive, evidence-driven scientific intelligence platform developed for the Flame in Freefall challenge. It helps researchers explore NASA microgravity combustion experiments, compare scientific measurements, identify knowledge gaps, and investigate fire-safety questions with transparent evidence and clearly defined limitations.

Fire behaves differently in microgravity because buoyancy-driven convection is greatly reduced. This creates important challenges for spacecraft and future lunar and Martian habitats. Although NASA has conducted valuable combustion experiments, their findings are distributed across technical reports, scientific archives, and datasets that can be difficult to compare.

AegisμG addresses this challenge by transforming NASA combustion evidence into an accessible, traceable research environment.

2. How Our Application Works

Our platform provides six integrated scientific demonstration stages:

Stage 1 — NASA Evidence Explorer

Users explore NASA combustion research, identify relevant investigations, inspect scientific sources, and distinguish verified measurements from metadata-only references.

Stage 2 — BASS-II Experimental Data Atlas

The application organizes 20 PMMA combustion tests and 43 airflow segments from NASA's BASS-II Summary Report (NASA/TM-20210011385, Table 5.1).

It preserves 39 numerical flame-spread observations and four untracked measurements without inventing missing values. Oxygen measurements unavailable at the individual airflow-segment level remain explicitly unreported.

Stage 3 — DIWA Scientific Provenance

Our DIWA framework connects research claims to their originating sources, experimental conditions, and measurements. It distinguishes NASA observations, derived calculations, interpretations, and hypothetical model outputs.

Stage 4 — Experiment Comparator

Researchers can compare combustion experiments while examining airflow velocity, oxygen conditions, material geometry, flame-spread rates, units, and missing uncertainty information.

For example, the BASS-II M3 experiment reports flame-spread rates of 0.029 mm/s and 0.024 mm/s at successive airflow conditions of 10 cm/s and 20 cm/s. This counterexample demonstrates why scientific interpretation must consider changing experimental conditions rather than assuming that higher airflow always produces faster flame spread.

Stage 5 — SPECULATRON Scientific Intelligence

Our intelligence engine uses evidence-grounded information retrieval, scientific relevance ranking, research-gap identification, and traceable explanations.

The offline question explorer uses deterministic BM25 retrieval and can operate without an external AI API key. When evidence is insufficient, the system explicitly declines unsupported conclusions instead of generating fabricated scientific results.

Stage 6 — Digital Twin Sandbox

The platform includes an educational simulation environment that separates calculations based on reported NASA measurements from a hypothetical zero-dimensional oxygen-balance model.

Users can explore assumptions and sensitivity scenarios. Hypothetical outputs are explicitly labeled as not NASA data, not validated, and not suitable for real-world fire-safety predictions or certification.

3. Innovation and Creativity

AegisμG goes beyond conventional scientific dashboards by integrating experimental evidence, explainable intelligence, scientific provenance, research-gap mapping, and educational modeling within one interactive platform.

Our principal innovations include:

  • Evidence-first scientific intelligence: Answers are grounded in identifiable sources rather than unsupported AI-generated claims.
  • DIWA provenance framework: Research claims can be traced back to their source documents and supporting measurements.
  • Scientific integrity safeguards: Missing measurements remain missing; incompatible experimental conditions are flagged.
  • Offline research capability: Core evidence exploration and deterministic question answering operate without paid AI services.
  • Research-gap identification: The platform distinguishes measured microgravity evidence from unsupported lunar and Martian gravity extrapolations.
  • Transparent simulation boundaries: Hypothetical model results are separated from NASA experimental observations.

These features make scientific uncertainty visible rather than hiding it behind apparently precise predictions.

4. Tools, Software, and Technologies

AegisμG was developed using the following technologies:

Frontend and visualization: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Recharts.

Backend and data processing: Node.js, Express, Zod, and PapaParse.

Scientific intelligence: Deterministic BM25 retrieval, evidence-grounded research workflows, and optional Google Gemini integration.

Development and collaboration: Google AI Studio, GitHub, Git, and AI-assisted software development using Google Gemini and ChatGPT.

Testing and quality assurance: Vitest, TypeScript checks, linting, scientific data validation, and documented source-integrity checks.

Research sources: NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS), NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI), and publicly available NASA fire-protection references.

The current prototype is software-based and does not require specialized physical hardware or combustion sensors.

5. Benefits and Intended Impact

AegisμG is intended to support scientists, engineers, students, educators, and future space mission researchers.

Its potential benefits include:

  • Making NASA combustion research easier to explore and understand.
  • Reducing errors caused by incompatible units, missing data, and unsupported assumptions.
  • Helping researchers identify meaningful experimental comparisons.
  • Improving scientific transparency and reproducibility.
  • Highlighting knowledge gaps that may guide future combustion experiments.
  • Supporting education and early-stage investigation of spacecraft fire-safety challenges.

Our long-term vision is to develop AegisμG into a more comprehensive research environment incorporating additional verified combustion datasets, uncertainty analysis, validated physical models, and interdisciplinary research collaboration.

6. Scientific Responsibility and Limitations

Scientific credibility is central to our design.

We recognize that experimental results from near-zero-gravity spacecraft environments cannot automatically be applied to lunar gravity (approximately 0.165 g) or Martian gravity (approximately 0.38 g).

Our current application does not provide validated predictions of spacecraft fire hazards, flame spread, smoke transport, or fire suppression effectiveness.

The educational oxygen-balance simulation is hypothetical and uncalibrated. It is not a substitute for experimental testing, validated computational fluid dynamics, or engineering certification.

AegisμG is an independent research prototype and is not endorsed or certified by NASA.

7. Conclusion

AegisμG demonstrates how open NASA research data, explainable scientific intelligence, and transparent computational tools can work together to improve access to complex microgravity combustion evidence.

By connecting research questions to verifiable observations, identifying uncertainty, and highlighting future research needs, Team SPECULATRON AI aims to contribute a practical foundation for more transparent and responsible fire-safety research supporting humanity's future in space.

projectDetails.summary:
Earth2Space

We are Team Starlings ACS from Al Azm Charter School, UAE, and our project, Earth2Space, is inspired by the UAE’s ambitious vision for space exploration, scientific research, and innovation.

We developed an interactive website that identifies and compares locations on Earth with environmental and geological characteristics similar to those found on the Moon and Mars. Our project addresses the challenge of finding suitable Earth locations where scientists can test equipment, study extreme environments, and prepare for future space missions.

Using NASA’s open scientific resources, our platform allows users to explore an interactive map and compare locations based on geology, terrain, aridity, temperature, and isolation.

Inspired by the UAE’s achievements, including the Hope Probe and its lunar exploration ambitions, our goal is to support future space research and explore the potential of UAE desert environments as planetary testing sites.

Earth2Space reflects our commitment to innovation and our pride in representing Al Azm Charter School and the UAE. We believe the next generation of space explorers begins in our classrooms today.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Earth2Space

We are Team Starlings ACS from Al Azm Charter School, UAE, and our project, Earth2Space, is inspired by the UAE’s vision to become a global leader in space exploration, technology, and innovation.

The UAE has already achieved important milestones in space exploration through the Emirates Mars Mission (Hope Probe) and its ambitious plans for future lunar exploration. Inspired by these achievements, we wanted to develop a project that reflects our country's determination to explore beyond Earth.

How Does Our Project Work?

We developed Earth2Space, an interactive website that identifies and compares locations on Earth with environmental and geological characteristics similar to those found on the Moon and Mars.

Using NASA's open scientific resources, our platform evaluates locations based on five factors: geology, terrain, aridity, temperature, and operational isolation.

Users can explore an interactive map, compare different locations, select mission scenarios, and download research reports. The current comparisons are preliminary scientific assessments, with plans to integrate more detailed satellite measurements.

Technology and Tools Used

We developed our website using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, along with interactive mapping and data visualization tools.

Our research was supported by scientific resources such as NASA Earthdata, Moon Trek, Mars Trek, and publicly available planetary observations.

Creativity and Innovation

What makes our project unique is how it connects the UAE's space ambitions with practical scientific research.

We believe the UAE's desert environments could offer valuable opportunities for future planetary research. Our project creates a foundation for investigating whether locations within the UAE could serve as testing grounds for equipment designed for Moon and Mars missions.

Rather than simply studying space, we wanted to create a tool that could help prepare for future exploration.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Earth2Space aims to help researchers identify promising locations for testing robotic equipment, studying challenging environments, and preparing future space missions.

Our goal is to contribute ideas that could support the UAE's growing space sector, encourage scientific collaboration, and inspire young people to explore careers in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics.

During development, we considered the scientific suitability of each location, the availability of reliable data, environmental differences between Earth and other planets, and the importance of making our platform accessible and easy to use.

Our Vision for the UAE

As students of Al Azm Charter School, we are proud to be part of a country that encourages young people to dream big and innovate.

Through Earth2Space, we want to demonstrate that the next generation of scientists, engineers, and space explorers can begin their journey in UAE classrooms.

Our ambition is to develop Earth2Space further by researching potential analog locations within the UAE and contributing to our nation's vision for a future driven by knowledge, innovation, and space exploration.

projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Stars of Al Azm: Junior Astronauts Mission Trainer

Our project, Stars of Al Azm – Junior Astronauts Mission Trainer, is an educational project designed to introduce young students to the exciting world of space exploration and astronaut training. The main idea is to create an interactive training experience that allows children to imagine becoming real astronauts and learn how astronauts prepare for space missions.

The project works by taking students through different astronaut training activities and mission challenges. These activities help students understand how astronauts live and work in space, how they prepare for missions, and what challenges they may face beyond Earth. Students can explore space-related information, learn about planets, stars, gravity, the solar system, and discover the importance of teamwork and problem-solving during space missions.

Benefits of the Project:

Our project has many educational benefits. It makes learning more enjoyable, interactive, and exciting instead of relying only on traditional classroom lessons. It encourages students to think creatively, ask questions, solve problems, work together, and develop an interest in science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). It also helps younger students build confidence and develop curiosity about the universe.

Intended Impact:

The main impact of our project is to inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, and astronauts. We want students to understand that space exploration is not just something they see in movies or books, but something they could become part of in the future. Our project supports the UAE’s vision and achievements in space exploration and encourages young people to contribute to the country’s future scientific developments.

Tools, Technology, and Software:

We plan to use creative digital design tools and educational technology to develop the astronaut training experience. Depending on the final prototype, this may include computers, tablets, interactive presentations, digital illustrations, and coding tools to create activities and simulations. The project can also include physical materials to represent astronaut equipment and mission challenges.

Creativity and Innovation:

What makes our project creative is that it transforms learning about space into an astronaut training adventure. Instead of simply reading facts about space, students get to imagine themselves as astronauts and experience different stages of a space mission. We combine education, imagination, science, and technology to create an exciting learning experience for children.

Factors Considered by Our Team:

Our team considered several important factors while developing the project:

  • Safety: Making sure all activities are safe for younger students.
  • Educational Value: Providing accurate and useful information about space.
  • Accessibility: Making the experience simple and suitable for different age groups.
  • Creativity: Designing activities that capture students’ attention.
  • Teamwork: Encouraging students to communicate and cooperate.
  • Innovation: Using technology and creative ideas to improve the learning experience.
  • Cost and Materials: Choosing practical materials and tools that are affordable and easy to use.

Overall, Stars of Al Azm – Junior Astronauts Mission Trainer aims to make space education more exciting, encourage students to dream big, and show them that today’s young learners could become tomorrow’s astronauts and space explorers.

projectDetails.name: Vanguard Atlas
projectDetails.summary:
Vanguard Atlas is an open-source planetary analog comparison tool that identifies where on Earth to test hardware and field procedures for permanent Moon and Mars base operations, and shows exactly where the analogy breaks down.

The challenge asks us to identify Earth locations that analog permanent Moon base sites and Mars. The core problem we solved is that no single Earth site replicates another world, and collapsing terrain, thermal, geological, and subsurface conditions into one "similarity score" hides the trade-offs mission planners most need to see. Vanguard Atlas instead scores each Earth analog against a real orbital target footprint one dimension at a time, never blended.

Using a reproducible Python pipeline, we scored eight terrestrial analogs against two targets, the Lunar South Pole and Jezero Crater, across four dimensions, producing 16 site-target pairs with per-dimension scores, explicit confidence badges, documented strengths, and specific breakdown limits. Terrain metrics come from 30 m Copernicus GLO-30 DEM tiles on Earth, 240 m LRO LOLA on the Moon, and 463 m MGS MOLA on Mars; thermal, geological, and subsurface baselines come from WorldClim, LRO Diviner, MGS TES, and published USGS/PDS catalogs.

The result is a zero-backend interactive web atlas where engineers can compare candidates per dimension, see exactly why a site matched or failed, and know what Earth cannot replicate vacuum, partial gravity, radiation, and 40 K polar cold traps.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do / how does it work?​

Vanguard Atlas is a static web application that compares terrestrial analog field sites against extraterrestrial target footprints across four independent physical dimensions — terrain, thermal, geology, and subsurface — and never blends them into a single similarity score.

A reproducible Python pipeline does the work. Target raster data is ingested directly from NASA Planetary Data System archives: LRO LOLA GDRDSM (240 m, lunar south polar slope map) and MGS MOLA MEGDR (463 m, Mars topography), both decoded by custom readers that convert raw binary PDS images into slope statistics. Earth terrain features are extracted from Copernicus DEM GLO-30 30 m tiles using a 5 km circular footprint per site. Thermal baselines come from WorldClim v2.1 on Earth, LRO Diviner on the Moon, and MGS TES / Mars 2020 MEDA on Mars. Geology and subsurface baselines draw on published USGS, CRISM, Diviner/Mini-RF, and cave/pit catalogs. Each Earth site is then scored against each target dimension by feature-wise similarity using configurable tolerances, passed through a confidence model that downgrades scores when data is catalog-based or resolution-mismatched, and exported as contract-valid JSON records.

The web app loads those records at runtime and renders them: interactive maps per target body, ranked tables sortable by any single dimension, multi-axis radar comparisons, and detailed site cards stating what a place is good for, where the analogy stops working, and what you could actually test there.

What benefits does it have?​

Terrestrial analog selection is currently guesswork. Engineers pick sites by reputation, and a single composite score hides the exact mismatch that matters — a site with perfect terrain can have completely wrong thermal or mineralogical behavior. Vanguard Atlas surfaces those trade-offs explicitly, so a team testing rover mobility on flat slopes is never misled by a site that fails thermally. Every result carries a confidence badge and named breakdown limits, which keeps methodological honesty visible in the interface rather than buried in an appendix.

What is the intended impact?​

Every major Moon and Mars mission plan includes analog field campaigns. We intend Vanguard Atlas to be the starting point for that selection: open, reproducible, and backed by documented NASA data with per-dataset licensing and access dates. Anyone can add a new target raster or candidate site and get a comparable, confidence-tagged result.

Creative tools, coding, hardware, or software used?​

Python (pandas, numpy, PyYAML, jsonschema, pytest) for ingestion, feature extraction, scoring, confidence, validation, and export. Vanilla JavaScript ES modules with MapLibre GL for the front end — no framework, no backend, no build step. GitHub Actions for automated deployment to GitHub Pages. No custom hardware; all data is open NASA/ESA/JAXA orbital and ground archives.

What factors did your team consider?​

We deliberately avoided a single composite score, because averaging erases exactly the trade-offs the challenge asks us to expose. We also prioritized honesty over polish: all 16 site-target pairs are currently tagged low confidence because the target profiles rely on catalog and proxy data that remains unverified, and we say so in the interface. Automated validation checks our scoring against published analog literature, including positive controls (Atacama, Death Valley, Haughton, McMurdo) and negative controls (Hawaiian shield volcanoes) to confirm the pipeline rejects false matches.

projectDetails.name: The Forgotten Space Museum
projectDetails.summary:
The Forgotten Space Museum is an interactive digital museum. It explores the stories of spacecraft, rovers and scientific equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars after their missions ended. The website transforms these forgotten pieces of space exploration history into a virtual exhibition, allowing visitors to discover their purposes, mission ,scientific contributions, challenges and lasting legacies.

Through dedicated exhibition halls, visitors can explore missions of such spacecrafts , learn about the technology used in space exploration, discover where these artifacts are located  now and understand the discoveries they helped make. The website also incorporates interactive elements, educational content and quizzes to make learning engaging and accessible.

Its main purpose is to preserve the history of space exploration and remind visitors that even when a mission ends, its scientific contributions continue to matter.
projectDetails.details:
The Forgotten Space Museum is a virtual museum designed to make the history of space exploration more interactive and accessible. It focuses on the scientific equipment and spacecraft that remain on the surfaces of the Moon and Mars after their missions have ended.

The website is organised into themed exhibition halls, including the Red Planet, the Moon, Inside the Machines and the Legacy Gallery. Visitors can explore individual artifacts such as the Opportunity and Spirit rovers, the Phoenix lander, Sojourner and Surveyor 3. Each exhibit presents information about the machine's original purpose, mission history, scientific discoveries, engineering and final status.

The project aims to turn historical and scientific information into an engaging learning experience. Its interactive museum format encourages visitors to explore at their own pace rather than simply reading a collection of facts. It also highlights the lasting importance of missions that helped scientists understand other worlds and develop future exploration technologies.

The project was developed using Base44 for website creation and AI-assisted development, with AI tools used to organise the museum structure and develop written content. Canva was used for designing.

During development, I considered ease of navigation, visual design and the needs of visitors who may have little prior knowledge of space exploration. The futuristic museum concept was chosen to make the subject feel immersive while keeping the information understandable and educational.

projectDetails.name: Project TALA JANA AND BROOJ TEAM
projectDetails.summary:
We developed AEGIS-1, an interactive game where players design, manage, and simulate a complete space mission from start to finish.

We address the challenge by letting players make real engineering decisions. They choose a destination, then design their spacecraft while balancing budget, mass, and power. They select a launch vehicle, power system, communications, orbit, and scientific instruments, and every choice has a trade-off. After that, they fly the mission, avoid asteroids, collect data, and handle problems like solar storms. Then they manage the spacecraft in orbit by distributing limited power between science, communications, and shielding.

At the end, they receive a mission report showing science return, budget efficiency, engineering, and survival, plus a what-if analysis.

This is important because it is easy to read about space missions, but hard to really understand them. Our game lets players learn by doing, feel the pressure of real trade-offs, and think like engineers
projectDetails.details:
We developed AEGIS-1, an interactive game where players design, manage, and simulate a complete space mission.

It works in five steps. First, players choose a destination like Europa, Mars, or an asteroid. Second, they design their spacecraft by choosing a launch vehicle, power system, communications, orbit, and up to three scientific instruments. Third, they fly the mission, avoid asteroids, collect fuel and data, and handle problems like solar storms. Fourth, they manage the spacecraft in orbit for 90 seconds by distributing 100% power between science, communications, and shielding. Fifth, they receive a mission report with science return, budget efficiency, engineering, and survival, plus a what-if analysis.

The benefit is that players learn by doing instead of just reading. They see immediately how one decision changes the whole mission.

Our intended impact is to make space engineering feel accessible and fun for students who never get to try a full mission. We want them to start thinking like engineers and feel confident about STEM.

We used HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with Canvas for the game, Web Audio for sound effects, and Google Slides and Google Drive for our demo.

Our project is creative because it combines a game, a simulation, and a decision-making tool in one place. It is not a quiz. The what-if analysis is what makes it different.

When we designed it, we considered budget, mass, power, communications, orbital constraints, scientific value, difficulty, and how to keep it fun but still educational for different levels.

It deals with the problem by turning the abstract systems engineering trade-offs into actual decisions. Every choice has its consequences: a very capable instrument will give you a lot of science return but at the cost of mass, power, cost and the data that you have to downlink. You have a built-in launch vehicle check, a live resource dashboard and you get random events (e.g. a micrometeoroid hit) to mirror the real world constraints. You get a post-flight report which scores eight categories and explains each of those in plain English, and links the design choices back to real NASA missions (Landsat, Hubble etc).
This is important because the current tools out there teach the space concepts in isolation. There's a gap between the individual topics and the actual decision making in a mission. Orbital Forge closes that gap. It's accessible to the novice via tooltips and 3 difficulty levels, it's collaborative for up to 4 people in a team with different engineering roles and it's all based on NASA's systems engineering approach (GMAT) and JPL's CML. You learn why a mission works or doesn't work rather than just whether it does or not.
projectDetails.details:
Orbital Forge is a browser-based space mission design game (all in one HTML/CSS/JS file). You build your entire mission in six stages: science objective, spacecraft bus, instruments, orbit, launch vehicle, and launch. There's a live dashboard that tracks your budget, mass, power, and data as you go, and at the end of the mission you get a post-flight report that scores your mission across eight categories, explaining each point in plain English and linking your design to real NASA missions.

The game really does make the systems engineering trade-offs tangible (better instruments = more science return but also more mass, more power, more cost, and more data that you've got to downlink). There are three difficulty levels, random events (e.g., micrometeoroid hits), and team play for up to 4 players, with each player having a different role.

Its impact is in closing the gap between learning about individual space concepts and then being able to make integrated mission decisions. It's accessible to the novice through embedded explanations, and failure is a learning opportunity. It's built on NASA's systems engineering approach (GMAT) and JPL's CML

projectDetails.name: CELESTRA
projectDetails.summary:
Celestra is an analogue planet search tool and 3D mission planner that identifies terrestrial testing sites for lunar and Martian technologies. It uses satellite data from NASA, ESA, CSA and JAXA sources to find similarities between 14 terrain and environmental factors at 20 lunar and Martian sites and 60 terrestrial locations.

Users can search for an analogue planet, view top matches and see how well their rover can drive, land and drill at different analogue sites. A machine learning algorithm predicts uncertainties. A similarity matrix indicates how well each terrestrial location can be used for testing and where variations in gravity, atmosphere and temperature may be an issue.

Celestra goes beyond finding places that look alike: it helps users understand which characteristics make an Earth site useful for a particular test and where differences in gravity and atmosphere limit what that test can reveal. This can avoid misleading results, reduce resource waste and create more reliable hardware for future lunar and Martian exploration.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars

Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: Terrasonic
projectDetails.summary:
TerraSonic: The Earth Information Jukebox is an interactive, accessibility-first audio-visual prototype that transforms NASA Earth science data into expressive musical soundscapes. Using historical global temperature datasets and satellite observations from NASA’s Earth Information Center (EIC), NASA GISS, and NASA Worldview, I mapped decades of warming trends (2000–2024) into dynamic changes in musical pitch and intensity through data sonification.

This directly addresses The Earth Information Jukebox challenge by converting complex, visual-only climate charts into intuitive sound patterns that anyone can immediately understand without needing technical training.

TerraSonic is important because vital climate data is often locked behind dense graphs that exclude blind and low-vision audiences. 

By turning environmental shifts into a multi-sensory listening experience, my project makes NASA’s Earth observations more inclusive, emotionally engaging, and accessible for classrooms, museums, and communities worldwide.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works
TerraSonic: The Earth Information Jukebox is an interactive audio-visual prototype that turns NASA Earth science datasets into expressive musical soundscapes. Using historical Global Land-Ocean Temperature Index measurements (2000–2024), TerraSonic maps numerical warming anomalies directly to musical pitch, tempo, and harmonic intensity through data sonification. Users listen to a chronological climate symphony paired with side-by-side satellite imagery, where lower, calmer tones represent cooler baselines and rising pitches signal accelerating global warmth.

Benefits & Intended Impact
Traditional climate data relies almost exclusively on dense graphs and visual maps, which can overwhelm everyday audiences and completely exclude blind and low-vision individuals. TerraSonic breaks down that visual barrier by making environmental trends immediately understandable through sound—requiring no technical or data-science background. Our intended impact is to empower classrooms, science museums, and global communities with an inclusive, multi-sensory tool that fosters deeper accessibility and emotional connection to how our planet is changing.

Tools & Software Used

  • TwoTone (twotone.io): Browser-based, no-code data sonification platform used to convert NASA CSV climate datasets into synthesized .mp3 musical tracks.
  • Canva Presentations: Used to design our interactive, high-contrast 7-slide prototype and integrate synced satellite imagery with audio playback.
  • NASA Open Data Portals: NASA Earth Information Center (earth.gov), NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis, and NASA Worldview.

Creativity & Key Design Factors
Rather than treating sound as background music, we treated musical pitch as a direct scientific measurement—turning climate data into a "playable" jukebox experience. During development, our team prioritized three core factors:

  1. Accessibility First: Designing high-contrast visuals alongside self-explanatory audio cues so blind and low-vision users can interpret trends independently.
  2. Intuitive Mapping: Selecting instruments and pitch scales where rising numbers naturally sound more urgent without needing complex explanations.
  3. Rapid Prototyping & Scalability: Building a lightweight, browser-accessible prototype that can easily scale to live NASA Earthdata APIs and multi-variable harmonies (such as sea-level rise and CO₂ levels) in the future.

projectDetails.name: TrendLens: From NASA Data to Defensible Discoveries
projectDetails.summary:
Environmental data can reveal how our planet is changing, but understanding those changes requires more than plotting a graph. 

TrendLens is an interactive, open-source scientific investigation platform that makes NASA Earth science data more accessible to students, educators, and citizen scientists.

Built for NASA's 'Be An Earth System Trend Detective!' challenge, TrendLens transforms complex temperature datasets into guided, reproducible investigations. Its primary demonstration analyzes 24 complete years (2002–2025) of NASA Giovanni MERRA-2 temperature data for a region near Abu Dhabi. Users can visualize historical patterns, calculate rates of change, examine uncertainty, and download the original evidence and methodology. A second investigation compares NASA POWER temperature data for Abu Dhabi and Oslo over consistent time periods.

What distinguishes TrendLens is its emphasis on scientific transparency. Instead of presenting every apparent trend as a proven conclusion, it explains statistical limitations, distinguishes descriptive trends from validated significance, and preserves data provenance.

Our goal is to make environmental analysis more understandable, reproducible, and scientifically responsible.
projectDetails.details:
TrendLens is an open-source Earth science investigation platform developed by Team Terravect for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It transforms NASA environmental datasets into accessible, interactive, and reproducible scientific investigations.

While NASA provides powerful tools for accessing Earth observation data, interpreting long-term environmental trends can still require specialized knowledge in data processing and statistics. TrendLens helps bridge this gap for students, educators, and citizen scientists.

Users can explore environmental temperature records, investigate historical patterns, compare geographical locations, and examine the evidence behind calculated trends.

Our primary investigation uses NASA Giovanni to analyze MERRA-2 monthly air-temperature data for a region near Abu Dhabi. From 24 complete years of measurements (2002–2025), TrendLens estimates a descriptive warming trend of approximately +0.356°C per decade.

A second investigation uses NASA POWER data to compare Abu Dhabi and Oslo across 25 shared years (2001–2025).

The platform provides interactive visualizations, annual temperature calculations, trend estimates, uncertainty information, data-coverage checks, and downloadable scientific investigation reports.

TrendLens goes beyond displaying environmental graphs by creating a guided, evidence-first investigation experience.

Its distinguishing capabilities include:

  • Scientific transparency: Clearly separates observed patterns and descriptive estimates from conclusions that require further statistical validation.
  • Reproducibility: Preserves original NASA data, provenance, processing methods, and SHA-256 checksums.
  • Consistent comparisons: Aligns time periods across locations and provides both absolute-temperature and relative-change visualizations.
  • Accessibility: Explains scientific findings in understandable language without requiring users to write code.

Rather than creating another climate model, TrendLens makes existing NASA scientific information easier to investigate critically.

TrendLens uses genuine NASA data, excludes incomplete years from annual analyses, performs documented unit conversions, and retains the source measurements.

Our trend estimates use ordinary least-squares regression. Because temporal autocorrelation has not been adequately accounted for, we do not claim validated statistical significance, causal attribution, or definitive climate-change detection.

These limitations are explicitly presented to users rather than hidden.

TrendLens was developed using Python, Streamlit, Pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Plotly, and NASA data services. It is hosted on Streamlit Community Cloud, with publicly available source code on GitHub under the MIT license.

Our objective is to make NASA Earth science data more accessible, understandable, and reproducible. TrendLens could support classroom investigations, citizen science, and exploratory environmental research by helping users evaluate evidence rather than simply interpret isolated graphs.

Live application: https://terravect-trendlens.streamlit.app/

Source code: https://github.com/laithmunir9/terravect-trendlens

projectDetails.name: Astraea: Space Mission Simulator
projectDetails.summary:
We developed ASTRAEA: Space Mission Simulator, an interactive, browser-based mission architecture and 3D orbital flight game. Players manage an end-to-end space mission across six connected phases—Concept Selection, 3D CAD Subsystem Assembly, Launch Vehicle Integration, 3D Orbital Flight Operations, Deep Space Network Science Downlink, and Post-Flight Engineering Review—across 12 solar-system destinations or custom missions.
It directly addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by turning abstract engineering trade-offs into live, playable decisions. Every choice across structure, power (solar vs. MMRTG), propulsion, thermal control, telecom, and scientific payloads dynamically updates inverse-square solar flux, eclipse battery depth-of-discharge, wet mass, and grant budgets—and players fly the exact spacecraft they built in 3D orbit.
This is important because students rarely get to experiment with a full mission lifecycle. By making real aerospace systems engineering accessible in any web browser with zero installation, ASTRAEA builds practical STEM intuition for how competing constraints shape mission success.
projectDetails.details:
We created ASTRAEA: Space Mission Simulator, an interactive, browser-based space mission design game built for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. It lets students and participants design, manage, launch, pilot, and evaluate a complete space mission from initial concept to post-flight review while navigating real-world engineering trade-offs.

What it does & how it works:
Players progress through a coupled six-phase mission lifecycle:

  1. Concept: Select from 12 solar-system mission profiles (including Low Earth Orbit Climate Surveillance, Lunar Shackleton Crater Ice Survey, Mars Sample Return, Europa Astrobiology, Titan Cryo-Explorer, 16 Psyche, Asteroid Kinetic Deflection, and a Solar Corona Grazing Probe) or build a custom target mission. Players evaluate required
    inverse-square solar flux, radiation exposure, one-way communication latency, and grant budgets.
  2. CAD Bay: Assemble a 3D spacecraft across 8 coupled subsystems (Structure, Power, Battery, Propulsion, ADCS, Telecom, Thermal, and Payload) with an exploded-assembly inspection slider. Every component or propellant change dynamically recalculates wet mass, Tsiolkovsky
    power balance, eclipse battery Depth-of-Discharge, and thermal equilibrium.
  3. Launch: Match total spacecraft wet mass and escape requirements to a launch vehicle at LC-39A (SmallSat, Medium Lift, Heavy Lift Tri-Core, or European Modular Heavy).
  4. Flight Ops: Pilot the exact spacecraft designed in the CAD Bay inside a live 3D WebGL orbital arena (WASD steering, boost, sensor scan pulse, Chase/Cockpit/Overview cameras, and 1x–25x time warp) while monitoring real-time EPS, propellant, and GNC telemetry graphs.
  5. Science: Trigger instrument sweeps into a solid-state flight recorder and downlink data to Earth through a simulated Deep Space Network complex (Goldstone DSS-14 70m) with realistic carrier link margins and light-time delays.
  6. Debrief: Receive a Post-Flight Engineering Review scoring science yield, systems margin, and cost stewardship, with tailored engineering recommendations.

Benefits:

  • Turns abstract aerospace concepts—mass fractions,
    budgets, inverse-square solar decay, eclipse battery sizing, and telecom latency—into immediate visual cause and effect.
  • Requires zero downloads, paid licenses, or specialized hardware, and runs directly in any web browser, including on school devices.
  • Connects every design decision end-to-end: the spacecraft configured in Phase 02 is the exact vehicle launched in Phase 03 and piloted in Phase 04.

Intended impact:
Our goal is to make end-to-end spacecraft systems engineering approachable and hands-on for high school and university STEM students, classrooms, and citizen scientists. By letting learners experiment with competing demands—payload capability vs. propellant mass, solar arrays vs. nuclear MMRTGs, and science yield vs. grant caps—ASTRAEA builds practical engineering intuition for how real space missions are planned and operated.

Tools, coding languages, hardware, and software used:

  • Languages & Core Stack: TypeScript, React, Tailwind CSS, HTML5/CSS3.
  • 3D Rendering & Audio: WebGL and Three.js for the interactive 3D spacecraft CAD assembly, exploded inspection, and 3D orbital flight simulator, plus the Web Audio API for procedural audio cues.
  • Build & Hosting: Node.js, Vite, and Google Cloud Run for public browser deployment.
  • Presentation & Pitch Export: pptxgenjs and qrcode. React for the interactive 7-slide pitch deck and .pptx export.
  • Hardware: Built and tested on standard consumer laptops, so the simulator runs smoothly without a dedicated GPU.

How it is creative:
Most existing tools either oversimplify space into arcade games with unlimited fuel and power, or hide mission design inside complex, expensive engineering spreadsheets. ASTRAEA unifies concurrent spacecraft CAD assembly, real-time physics margin telemetry, 3D orbital piloting, and Deep Space Network science operations into one continuous interactive game—complete with a Custom Mission Builder so educators and students can design missions to any world they imagine.

Factors considered:

  • Coupled Physics & Competing Demands: Balancing Tsiolkovsky
    against dry payload mass, launch vehicle capacity, and grant limits.
  • Space Environment Extremes: Modeling inverse-square solar irradiance (
    ) from ( near the Sun) to ( at Europa) and ( at Titan), alongside planetary umbra eclipses, radiation tiers, and Stefan-Boltzmann thermal limits.
  • Communications & Latency: Incorporating realistic one-way light-time delays (
    in LEO, at Mars, at Titan) and DSN carrier link margins.
  • Accessibility & Onboarding: Providing a built-in Reference Guide, live nominal/caution telemetry alerts, and a quick-launch 3D flight option alongside the full 6-phase engineering workflow.

projectDetails.name: Project The Apples
projectDetails.summary: I made Skyshift, a small website for exploring NASA SPHEREx observations of comet 3I/ATLAS. A timeline switches between images from the August and December 2025 observing campaigns. The page gives a short explanation of the comet and links to the NASA and IRSA sources.
projectDetails.details:
Skyshift — project submission

Team

The Apples — one-person team

Project links

Website: https://azanramees1-pixel.github.io/skyshift-spherex-time-explorer/

GitHub repository: https://github.com/azanramees1-pixel/skyshift-spherex-time-explorer

Project summary

I made Skyshift, a small website for exploring NASA SPHEREx observations of comet 3I/ATLAS. A timeline switches between images from the August and December 2025 observing campaigns. The page gives a short explanation of the comet and links to the NASA and IRSA sources.

The problem I wanted to help with

SPHEREx is collecting a lot of infrared sky data. If you are new to astronomy, it can be hard to know where to start or what you are looking at. I wanted to make one real example easier to explore.

What Skyshift does

Move the timeline to switch between the August and December campaign views. The text on the page changes with the image and explains what NASA reported about the comet. There is also a short explanation of its coma—the cloud of gas and dust around a comet—and links to the original sources.

Data and credits

I used NASA-published SPHEREx images of 3I/ATLAS. The images are credited to NASA/SPHEREx and NASA/JPL-Caltech. The underlying archive resources are provided by NASA/IPAC-IRSA.

  • NASA's 3I/ATLAS image gallery: https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/comets/3i-atlas/comet-3i-atlas-image-gallery/
  • NASA's December SPHEREx image and article: https://science.nasa.gov/photojournal/nasas-spherex-examines-comet-3i-atlass-coma/
  • IRSA's SPHEREx 3I/ATLAS data page: https://irsa.ipac.caltech.edu/data/SPHEREx/docs/comet3iatlas/index.html
  • SPHEREx Data Explorer: https://irsa.ipac.caltech.edu/applications/spherex/

Use of Super Intelligence (SI)

I used ChatGPT to help create and revise parts of the website code, layout, and explanatory text. The NASA images and science data are from the linked NASA/IRSA sources; they were not generated or modified using AI. The decorative comet scene is made with CSS. I did not use AI-generated images, video, or audio.

What the comparison shows

NASA reported that 3I/ATLAS brightened during the December 2025 SPHEREx campaign. Skyshift lets visitors switch between NASA's published August and December campaign images and read that explanation.

The two pictures were prepared separately, so they are not matched images for a precise pixel-by-pixel measurement. Skyshift is for exploring the observation story; it does not calculate brightness or announce a discovery.

What I would add next

I would like to let visitors choose more SPHEREx observations by date and wavelength. A more advanced version could use matched images from the IRSA archive and account for image alignment and data quality before measuring differences.

projectDetails.name: OUTPOST
projectDetails.summary: OUTPOST is an interactive game for young scientists aged 7 to 12 to immerse themselves in the world of space exploration. It features a plethora of educational tools, such as a breakdown of mineral compositions in Martian soil and real-world data sprinkled throughout each feature. Our website features data from various instruments, such as the Mars Climate Sounder, which provided important data on Martian temperatures at numerous geographical locations, compiled with interactive games and quizzes to provide an engaging and informative experience of the trade-offs real-world scientists and engineers must make.
projectDetails.details:
OUTPOST is an interactive online game that allows users to simulate what it’s like to command an outpost on Mars. By completing three missions involving real-world decision-making scenarios and exploring activities based on authentic NASA datasets, players can deepen their understanding of NASA’s Mars exploration Missions in a fun and accessible way. As they progress, players can gain experience points (XP) and unlock new ranks, going from a Space Cadet all the way to a Mission Commander.

Players progress through three missions, completing tasks and making decisions to manage their Martian outpost. They can also explore the Sky Lab and Rock Lab, where they interact with real NASA datasets through graphs, experiments, and quizzes, including the "Hot or Cold?" temperature challenges. Additionally, players can browse an interactive album featuring images of Mars, test their knowledge through various quizzes throughout the game, and explore the Sky Lab and Rock Lab to dive into information from NASA’s Reconnaissance Orbiter and Curiosity Rover.

OUTPOST balances its engagement and detail by dividing a substantial amount of NASA data into separate games and activities all available on the same website, whether that be through the multiple labs, quizzes, or decision-based games. This way, young learners can experience running a Martian outpost while still being able to digest real-life data through gamification and hands-on exploration. OUTPOST allows users to develop their data interpretation and critical thinking skills in a fun way, rather than simply reading about previous Martian missions. 

We created OUTPOST to make space exploration engaging and accessible to young learners from the comfort of their own home. We want players to be able to gain a practical understanding of why facts and figures about Mars are significant through managing their own outpost rather than consuming information in a way that’s hard to comprehend, let alone to remember or to utilise. Ultimately, we hope to spark curiosity about STEM and demonstrate how real-world engineering decisions made under pressure and constraints can shape the success of space exploration.

For web development, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript were used. To allow for shared collaboration on the project amongst our team’s frontend and backend developers, GitHub was used. The programming was done in VS Code, and the website was deployed through Vercel. To aid with programming and debugging, Claude Code was used, as well as ChatGPT.

projectDetails.name: MarsNav - Every Step on Mars, Mapped.
projectDetails.summary:
MarsNav, a layered, interactive 3D map that helps astronauts plan and carry out a safe, science-focused Marswalk. It integrates NASA satellite imagery and terrain data into switchable layers showing slopes, rocks, minerals, cliffs, radiation zones, temperature, and wind, so explorers can see a route and its destinations in full detail.
To address the challenge, MarsNav combines data from multiple NASA missions into one view and adds real-time-style mission awareness. Its Safety System tracks radiation, temperature, wind and dust, suit oxygen, power, and radio communication, and checks whether a mission meets its safety requirements. Walk Stops guide astronauts to scientifically valuable sites, each with research objectives and estimated exploration times. Crew and Rover modes and simulations let teams test scenarios in advance. Everything is compiled into a downloadable Mission Report.
This matters because the first humans on Mars will be far from help, and every decision must be informed. MarsNav helps them complete missions quickly, safely, and with maximum scientific return.
projectDetails.details:
• Scientific Realism vs. Usability Grounded slopes, temperatures (-14 Celsius sunlit rock vs. -62 Celsius canyon shadow), dust opacity, radiation, and 20% suit reserve thresholds in published NASA datasets while keeping explanations in plain, human-readable language.
  • Crew Safety Margins Enforced buddy-pair route spacing, UHF radio line of sight checks, and direct emergency return-time calculations from the farthest waypoint back to Base Camp.
  • Accessibility & Field Ergonomics: Designed a high contrast dark volcanic UI (#0B0D10 / #EE5A1C), Glove Mode enlarged controls, keyboard-accessible interactive elevation scrubbing, and voice input/output.
  • Provenance & Transparency: Explicitly separated real NASA public domain orbital/rover imagery (PIA26306, PIA19303, PIA21606, PIA21041–21043, PIA25075) from simulated EVA prediction models inside a dedicated Resources & Provenance registry.
  • Performance: Kept 3D terrain rendering, stipple canvas textures, and multilayer map compositing lightweight so the full 3D planner runs smoothly in a standard browser.

projectDetails.name: Astral Atlas
projectDetails.summary:
Mars remains largely unexplored, with large regions holding geological mysteries that could completely change our understanding of the planet's history. Although NASA has collected extensive data through satellites, rovers, and scientific instruments, much of this information is still spread across different datasets.
Astral Atlas aims to bridge this gap by using existing NASA observations into an interactive predictive mapping system designed to support future Martian exploration safely.
Focusing on Jezero Crater, Astral Atlas combines geological, mineralogical, topographic, and environmental data to find potentially significant features in areas with limited direct observations. By analysing relationships between existing measurements, the system aims to predict unexplored geological characteristics, highlight uncertainty, and identify locations with high scientific potential. 
Beyond mapping, Astral Atlas explores how terrain elevation, atmospheric conditions, and environmental hazards can inform astronaut route planning by predicting the safest and easiest route, helping balance accessibility with opportunities for scientific discovery. It includes a current map, as well as the predicted map based on pattern recognition to predict future hazards. 

Ultimately, Astral Atlas demonstrates how NASA’s existing knowledge could be used not only to understand where exploration has already taken place, but also to guide where humanity should explore next.
projectDetails.details: It works as an interactive map, where you initially choose your objective, the start points, the crew limits and what you want to include on the map. The interface then shows all the hazards, predicted science, the explored and non explored areas, as well as the route to guide the astronaut. It has many benefits as it allows the astronaut to have a safe route to the expected destination and has exact timestamps of when the astronaut will reach each checkpoint. It has a dedicated section for safety, which means that the safety of the astronaut is always considered in the route chosen. The map can then be updated with new data from other sections of the Mars’ surface. We used JavaScript, Python, Claude, HTML, CSS as our main tools and software to create the website. Our project is creative as it not only includes the route, but all potential factors that might influence their route, like mentioned before.

projectDetails.name: TerraTrace: An Earth System Trend Detective
projectDetails.summary:
TerraTrace is an interactive Earth-system investigation platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It helps anyone explore how the planet is changing, and test whether an apparent trend is real before drawing conclusions.

Using NASA Earth science datasets (POWER/MERRA-2, GPCP, GISTEMP and GLDAS), TerraTrace analyses temperature, rainfall and soil moisture from 2001 to 2024. Every trend is tested with the Mann–Kendall test, Sen’s slope with a 95% confidence interval, a correction for autocorrelation, false-discovery-rate control and a step-change check, to separate meaningful change from statistical noise.

What makes TerraTrace different is cross-dataset validation. Each trend is re-tested against a second NASA record, and the app reports agreement, disagreement and uncertainty rather than presenting every result as certain. For example, one NASA record shows the Central African Republic cooling significantly, while NASA’s station-based record shows warming. TerraTrace flags the conflict, traces the “cooling” to a sudden 2007 data jump, and keeps it out of its rankings.

Users explore any place on an interactive 3D globe, examine tested trends and unusual years, and export fact sheets and investigation reports with data and citations. It’s free, needs no login and works on a phone.

TerraTrace makes Earth-system science accessible while teaching people to question, test and understand environmental evidence.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

TerraTrace is a free, browser-based investigation platform that lets anyone pick any place on Earth and find out whether its climate is really changing. Users click a location on an interactive 3D globe, search a city, or choose a one-click example, then pick an indicator: air temperature, rainfall or root-zone soil moisture, 2001-2024. TerraTrace returns a tested trend for that place, says how confident we can be, checks it against a second NASA record, and lets the user export the evidence as a fact sheet, a nine-step investigation report, CSV data and ready-made APA, Harvard and BibTeX citations.

HOW IT WORKS

A Python pipeline collects and cleans NASA data on a 5-degree global grid. It made 6,162 requests to NASA POWER (MERRA-2) and processed 576 monthly files from NASA GES DISC (GPCP V3.3 rainfall and GLDAS-2.1 soil moisture), plus NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 temperature. It removes invalid fill values, never fills gaps by guessing, and converts monthly data to annual values to remove the seasonal cycle. Every place is then tested with the methods climate scientists use:

- Mann-Kendall trend test, with the Hamed-Rao correction for autocorrelation

- Sen's slope with a 95% confidence interval

- Benjamini-Hochberg false-discovery-rate control across the whole map

- A step-change test that catches "trends" that are really one sudden jump

- Detection of unusual years

The same statistics run in Python and in the browser, and the two agree on all 5,846 trend tests.

CROSS-DATASET VALIDATION

What makes TerraTrace different is that no trend is trusted on one record alone. Each trend is re-tested on a second NASA record: temperature against GISTEMP (stations), rainfall against MERRA-2, and soil moisture against GLDAS. The app then gives one of six verdicts, from "Independent Verification" to "Cross-Dataset Divergence". For example, MERRA-2 shows the Central African Republic cooling significantly, while NASA's station-based GISTEMP shows warming. TerraTrace flags the conflict, traces the "cooling" to a sudden drop around 2007, and keeps it out of its rankings. Where records share inputs, we say so, and we report weak results honestly: only 17 of 336 significant rainfall trends survive map-wide false-discovery control.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

NASA's Earth data is free, but turning it into a defensible claim normally takes coding, GIS software and statistics. TerraTrace removes that barrier. Students can turn a question into a cited, defensible answer. Teachers can set investigations on any place on Earth. Anyone with a phone can explore it, with no login. Above all, we want people to learn to question evidence before believing it. Most tools show you the data. TerraTrace teaches you to question it.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

- Front end: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules, no build step), globe.gl and three.js for the 3D globe, Chart.js for charts, GSAP for animation, and d3-geo with topojson and Natural Earth borders for country averages.

- Data pipeline: Python with NumPy, pandas, requests and netCDF4.

- Data: NASA POWER, NASA GES DISC (GPCP, GLDAS) and NASA GISS (GISTEMP), accessed with NASA Earthdata login.

- Hosting and code: Cloudflare Pages, and GitHub under the MIT licence.

- Hardware: standard laptops only; the app runs fully in the browser and works offline when run locally.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

TerraTrace treats climate data like a detective case: discover a trend, test it, call a second witness, investigate disagreements, and produce a citable finding. Other tools show a single dataset as fact. TerraTrace shows uncertainty openly, flags data artefacts, and turns every result into a step-by-step investigation that a non-specialist can follow.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Scientific integrity: we report confidence intervals, autocorrelation, multiple testing and how independent the datasets are, and never fill gaps or overstate results.

- Accessibility: plain-language explanations, a glossary of terms, a mobile-friendly design and no login.

- Transparency: every number links to its NASA source, with open code and documented methods.

- Limitations: a 5-degree grid and a 24-year record are stated clearly in the app and the documentation.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.summary: Project Summary - SpaceFolio SpaceFolio is an educational app created by The Lunar League to make learning about NASA's space missions fun and interesting. It has two sections: Moon and Mars, with four stories in each section. Readers can choose from three reading levels: 6-10, 11-15 and 16+. Our app addresses the challenge by explaining NASA's space equipment and discoveries through simple, interesting stories. Each story also includes a glossary to explain difficult words, fun facts, a quiz and a short written question to test what readers have learnt. SpaceFolio is important because it helps people understand how NASA's equipment works and why it was sent into space. It makes learning about space easier, more enjoyable and encourages young learners to explore science and discover more about the universe.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details - SpaceFolio

SpaceFolio is an educational app created by our team, The Lunar League. We made it to help people learn about NASA's space missions in a fun and interesting way.

The app has two sections: Moon and Mars, with four stories in each. Readers can choose their age group: 6-10, 11-15 or 16+. Every story has a glossary to explain difficult words, fun facts, a quiz and a short written question. This makes learning more interesting and helps readers check what they have understood.

We created this app because we wanted to make learning about space easier and more enjoyable, instead of just giving people long paragraphs of information. We hope it encourages more students to become interested in space and science.

We used Base44 to build our app. Our team focused on making it simple to use, suitable for different ages and full of interesting information. What makes SpaceFolio creative is that it combines storytelling, learning and quizzes in one place.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

projectDetails.name: AURA (Astronaut Utility Risk Assessment)
projectDetails.summary:
(we couldnt get a domain due to the site not working)
AURA is a software-based astronaut health-monitoring system designed to support astronaut safety during space missions. We developed a prototype made with a HTML-powered interface to collect, display and analyse health data. AURA evaluates readings against defined reference ranges and considers different environments, including Earth, space and the International Space Station, to help identify potential abnormalities. By presenting health information in an accessible format and highlighting readings that may require attention, AURA aims to support early detection of potential health concerns. This project addresses the challenges of monitoring human health in space, where environmental conditions can affect astronauts and access to immediate medical assistance may be limited. AURA is important because maintaining astronaut health is essential for successful space missions, and reliable monitoring technology can help make future space exploration safer.
projectDetails.details:
AURA (Astronaut Understanding, Response & Assessment) is a software-based astronaut health-monitoring system designed to support astronaut safety during space missions. It collects, displays and analyses health-related data to help identify potential abnormalities.

AURA evaluates readings against predefined reference ranges and considers different environments, including Earth, space and the International Space Station (ISS). This helps provide more relevant interpretations of health readings. Its interface presents information in an organised and accessible format, highlighting values that may require attention.

The project was developed using HTML to create its interactive interface, alongside software-based data processing and simulated readings for testing.

AURA offers several potential benefits, including:

  • Early recognition: Highlighting unusual readings that may indicate potential health concerns.
  • Environment-based assessment: Considering different environmental conditions when interpreting health data.
  • Accessible information: Presenting health readings in an organised and understandable format.
  • Astronaut safety: Supporting astronauts and mission teams in monitoring important health indicators.

The intended impact is to contribute to safer space exploration by making astronaut health information easier to monitor and understand, particularly during longer missions where immediate medical assistance may be limited.

projectDetails.name: Project Yassin
projectDetails.summary:
The Solar System Hall of Fame is an educational narrative guide created to introduce school-age students to the robotic explorers and scientific instruments NASA has left across the Moon, Mars, and deep space since the 1960s.
The guide addresses the challenge by organizing complex aerospace history into three clear, engaging geographic chapters—the Moon, Mars, and Interstellar Space—paired with a scannable quick-reference table. By using relatable comparisons, such as comparing a seismic sensor to a stethoscope or an SUV-sized rover to a mobile laboratory, the text translates technical engineering into accessible storytelling while clearly distinguishing between retired hardware and active missions.
This project is important because it bridges the gap between historic space milestones and ongoing scientific discovery. Showing young learners that space hardware continues to gather data decades after launch—or rests silently as a monument to human curiosity—sparks early interest in STEM fields and demonstrates how engineering turns bold questions into real planetary knowledge. Note: SI was used for the project in parts 1 , 2, and 3 of the storytelling.
projectDetails.details: Solar System Hall of Fame is an educational guide and slide deck that takes school-age students on a three-stop tour of NASA's hardware in the Moon, Mars, and Interstellar Space. It uses simple analogies, real NASA photos, status tags (Active, Grounded, or Retired), and a quick-reference table to show what each machine discovered and whether it still works today. This project turns complicated aerospace science into a fun and an easy-to-read stories for K-12 students. The goal of this project is to spark interest in STEM among school students by making rovers and space probes feel exciting and inspiring. I used official NASA Science mission portals and the NASA Image and Video Library, super intelligence (SI) to brainstorm kid-friendly analogies and organize the flow of my storytelling, and I used Microsoft Word to type the storytelling (in addition with the images and reference table), PowerPoint for the demo, and Google Drive for the public-view links. It is creative because it shows space missions just like a tour around the solar system by using real pictures from NASA, and visual status tiers to turn engineering facts into an entertaining story. I factored on using vocabulary that is suitable for any age in school to read and used correct visual layouts with photos and a comparison table for learners, and confirmed data from NASA for finished NASA accuracy.

projectDetails.name: ZAR3A
projectDetails.summary: ZAR3A (زرعة, "cultivation") is a bilingual English-Arabic, mobile-friendly web app that turns NASA Earth observations into crop-rotation decisions for UAE farms. It uses NASA POWER daily and 35-year monthly climate data for Al Ain, Abu Dhabi City, and Liwa Oasis, shows NASA GIBS satellite imagery, and gives a plain-language "what to do today" action. A rotation planner compares crop sequences on water demand, heat fit, salinity fit, crop-family diversity and legume use, weighted by the farmer’s own priorities and soil salinity. It addresses the challenge by joining NASA data, local soil input, crop references (FAO-56 and the UAE planting calendar) and farmer priorities, judged against long-term climate change, not just this season. It matters because UAE farmers face heat, water scarcity, and salinity, and free NASA data is hard to use on a farm. ZAR3A makes it actionable, shows every formula, and states its limits. It is a screening tool, not a forecast.
projectDetails.details:
ZAR3A (زرعة) helps UAE farmers choose crop rotations using NASA Earth observations. It runs entirely in the browser, with no account, server, or API key. It calls NASA POWER directly and keeps the last good result on the device as an offline fallback.

  • Today view: daily data gives heat, rain, and humidity in plain language, plus one suggested action.
  • Climate shift: 35 years of monthly data show how temperature and rainfall have changed at each location, and provide the monthly averages used for planning.
  • Satellite view: compares high-resolution farm imagery, daily NASA true-colour imagery and the NASA vegetation index.
  • Rotation planner: for each season, it takes the planting month (UAE calendar or the farmer’s choice) and scores water demand (reference evapotranspiration × FAO crop coefficient), heat fit, salinity fit (the farmer’s soil EC against crop thresholds), crop-family diversity and legume inclusion. The farmer’s priorities weight these into a ranking. Anything that can’t be scored is left out, and every formula is shown in the app.

The interface works in English and Arabic (right-to-left) and installs as a mobile web app.

Benefit: Farmers can see which rotation uses less water or tolerates heat and salinity better, and why. Advisers get a transparent starting point for conversations.

Intended impact: Better-informed crop and planting-month choices, lower irrigation demand, more diverse rotations, and wider everyday use of NASA data by people who aren’t data specialists. It supports an agronomist’s advice and doesn’t replace it.

Tools: NASA POWER (daily and monthly), NASA GIBS (VIIRS, MODIS NDVI), Esri World Imagery, FAO-56 and FAO salinity tables, and the UAE planting calendar. Software: React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, Leaflet, Vitest.

Creativity

  • A plain-language “what to do today” action.
  • Scoring that shows its formulas and leaves out what it can’t measure, instead of guessing.
  • Honest labelling of data limits: NASA’s satellite solar series lags about 71 days, so the app says so.
  • An interactive satellite comparison.
  • An English-Arabic identity rooted in the region it serves.

Factors we considered

  • NASA values describe a grid cell, not the inside of a greenhouse.
  • It is a rule-based screening tool, not a trained model, forecast, or yield prediction, and crop coefficients are general, not calibrated to a UAE cultivar.
  • Usability: large touch targets, plain wording, and testing with agronomists and growers planned.
  • Privacy: soil inputs stay in the browser.
  • Reliability: an offline fallback and automated tests for the scoring and data parsing.
  • The Arabic translations still need native-speaker review.

projectDetails.name: Astro Health Monitor
projectDetails.summary:
Developed by Team Aero Engineers, the "Space Radiation Defense" project provides an integrated, autonomous shielding framework to protect astronauts during deep-space lunar and Mars missions. Outside Earth's geomagnetic protection, crews face three key threats: Solar Particle Events (SPE), Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCR), and Van Allen Belts.

The system operates on a three-pillar defense strategy:

Detection: Utilizes active silicon detectors, TEPC monitors, and solar X-ray sensors to provide a 15–60 minute early warning lead time before storms arrive.


Mitigation:Employs a multi-layer graded-Z hull featuring low-Z, hydrogen-rich materials like High-Density Polyethylene (HDPE) and water to slow heavy ions without generating harmful secondary cascades.


Survival:Integrates a central core storm shelter that cuts acute solar dosage by over 50% using reconfigured, dual-use mission consumables like water jackets and supply racks with zero mass penalty.
projectDetails.details:
Developed by Team Aero Engineers, the "Space Radiation Defense" project is an autonomous deep-space shielding framework designed to protect astronauts from lethal radiation during lunar and Mars missions without adding heavy launch mass penalties.

The Project Challenge & Solution

Operating outside Earth's geomagnetic field exposes crews to severe radiation hazards, specifically Solar Particle Events (SPE), Galactic Cosmic Rays (GCR), and trapped radiation within the Van Allen Belts. To solve this, the project introduces a comprehensive, three-pillar defense architecture:

  • Pillar 01: Detection & Early Warning – Utilizes real-time active cabin dosimetry (silicon detectors and TEPC), passive crew tracking, and deep-space heliophysics sensors to provide a 15 to 60-minute early warning lead time before solar proton storms arrive.
  • Pillar 02: Mitigation & Shielding – Employs a multi-layer graded-Z hull architecture that integrates light-weight aluminum structural bumpers with hydrogen-rich materials like High-Density Polyethylene (HDPE) and water. These low-Z materials effectively slow down heavy ions and block radiation without generating dangerous secondary X-ray cascades. Surface options also incorporate local regolith and wearable AstroRad vests.
  • Pillar 03: Survival & Storm Shelter – Features a central core refuge inside the habitat that can be rapidly assembled within 60 minutes during a solar storm. This shelter achieves a zero mass penalty by utilizing dual-use mission consumables—such as water storage jackets, food rations, and supply racks—to surround and protect the crew, cutting acute solar storm dosage by over 50%.
