projectDetails.name: FLAMORA- Flame in Free fall
projectDetails.summary:
FLAMORA – Flame in Free Fall

Team: Agastya

FLAMORA transforms NASA's microgravity fire experiments into an interactive platform for exploring space combustion research.

We collected and organised 1,825 test records from 23 NASA investigations, including BASS, FLEX, Saffire and ACME. The platform features a Research Hub to explore NASA datasets, visualise real experimental measurements and compare investigations.

Its AI Research Assistant answers questions using cited NASA sources and supports multilingual interaction and voice input. The Mission Brief feature identifies experiments relevant to different space environments, including the ISS, Moon and Mars, while highlighting existing research gaps.

The Fire Simulation Lab allows users to explore how gravity, oxygen concentration, pressure and airflow affect flame behaviour. Simulated results are clearly distinguished from actual NASA measurements.

FLAMORA also offers Researcher Mode for detailed scientific exploration and Kids Mode, featuring simplified explanations, animations and guided learning.

Our goal is to make microgravity combustion research accessible, encourage scientific exploration and help identify knowledge gaps in fire safety for future space missions. Every result is distinguished as measured, derived or modelled to maintain scientific transparency.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do and how does it work?

FLAMORA is a web platform that makes NASA's microgravity fire research searchable, comparable and easy to understand. It works in four layers:

1. Data: We downloaded the open experiment records and test tables for 23 combustion investigations from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository, including BASS, BASS-II, FLEX, Saffire and ACME. We cleaned them into 1,825 test records and 17,944 test conditions. Every cleaned value keeps its original value, unit and source file row. Suspect values are flagged, not deleted.

2. Database: The data is stored in a PostgreSQL database (Supabase) with search, links between experiments, materials, findings and sources, and security rules so the public can only read research data.

3. Analysis:

- Comparison engine: checks whether investigations can really be compared.

- Evidence ranking: shows which NASA tests are closest to the conditions of the ISS, a Moon base, a lunar rover or a Mars base, with the scoring criteria visible.

- Mission Brief: turns this into a one-page cited report for a chosen habitat.

4. AI assistant: a chatbot that searches our NASA database first and then writes an answer from that evidence only. Every answer cites its sources, and the server rejects any source the AI invents. If the data doesn't contain an answer, the assistant says so.

Users can also explore real flight data in charts, where clicking a point shows its source. A Fire Simulation lab lets them change gravity, oxygen, pressure and airflow to see how a flame changes, with the results always labelled "Modelled".

What benefits does it have?

- Saves time: findings spread across many datasets and papers are in one place, in comparable units.

- Honest comparisons: it explains when two experiments can't be compared (for example, a gas burner vs a solid sample), instead of mixing them.

- Shows the gaps: for example, NASA's PSI data has no solid materials tested at Moon-base air (30%+ oxygen at low pressure), and no fire tests at Moon or Mars gravity.

- Open to everyone: a Researcher mode for scientists and engineers, a Kids mode for students, and four languages (English, Mandarin, French, Hindi), with voice input.

What is the intended impact?

Future Moon bases and rovers will likely use air with more oxygen at lower pressure, which can make fires spread more easily. FLAMORA helps engineers and mission planners see quickly what NASA has already tested near those conditions and what still needs testing. It also helps students and the public understand why fire safety in space is hard, using real NASA results rather than guesses. More broadly, it shows how AI can make scientific data easier to use without inventing facts.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

- Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, SQL, Python (data cleaning and checks).

- Frontend: Next.js, React, Tailwind CSS.

- Backend and database: Next.js API routes, Supabase (PostgreSQL) with full-text search and row-level security.

- AI in the app: Google Gemini API (main) and Groq API (backup), behind a provider-independent layer.

- AI tools used to build it: Claude and Claude Code (research support, data checking, coding), Manus (first dataset build, then checked and corrected by our team), Google Stitch (UI designs).

- Testing: Vitest (117 automated tests) and production build checks.

- Data sources: NASA PSI open data (CC0), NASA Glenn fact sheets, NASA Technical Reports Server papers.

- Hardware: our own laptops. No special hardware.

How is the project creative?

- Every number has a label: Measured, Derived, Modelled, Illustrative or Not evaluated. Users always know whether they're looking at a real NASA measurement or a model.

- The AI is limited on purpose: it can only cite sources in our database. A made-up source is rejected, and "the data doesn't say" counts as a valid answer.

- Mission Brief: turns scattered research into a practical one-page report for a real future habitat, including what has never been tested.

- One dataset, two experiences: scientists and children see the same real numbers, explained at different levels.

- Simulation next to measurement: the model's prediction sits beside the nearest real NASA test, so users can see where the model is trustworthy and where it is only an estimate.

What factors did your team consider?

- Scientific accuracy:

- no invented data;

- suspect values and unit problems flagged openly;

- historical accidents (Apollo 1, Apollo 13, Mir) never treated as experiments;

- Moon and Mars results always labelled as model estimates.

- Data quality: we found and fixed real problems in the raw data, including blank rows, typos such as "3400%" oxygen, mixed units and skipped columns, and we documented every fix.

- Accessibility:

- two reading levels;

- four languages, with the right fonts for Chinese and Hindi;

- voice input;

- keyboard navigation;

- mobile layouts.

- Privacy and security:

- API keys kept on the server;

- the public can only read research data;

- no personal data stored from the chat.

- Cost: free-tier AI and database services, so the project can stay online after the hackathon.

- Time: we built the most important features first, and clearly label anything unfinished as "Coming soon" instead of faking it.

challengeDetails.title: Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data
challengeDetails.excerpt: For decades, NASA has studied how flames and fire behave in microgravity, gathering a trove of experimental data along the way. That knowledge matters more than ever as humans gear up to return to the Moon and press on to Mars, yet the volume of results makes them hard to find, compare, and understand. Your challenge is to create an interactive, super intelligence (SI) powered dashboard that summarizes, ranks, and interprets those findings to deliver fire safety insights for human space exploration.

node.title: AgniCal (solo)
node.excerpt: Solo participant from Coimbatore. I work in data science and built AgniCal, a tool that tests whether NASA's satellite fire counts still track crop burning in India.

projectDetails.name: Project AgniCal (solo)
projectDetails.summary:
Every winter, smoke from crop burning in Punjab and Haryana reaches Delhi, and India tracks that burning using NASA's satellite fire counts. Those counts fell about 95 percent between 2016 and 2025. I wanted to know if the fires really disappeared, or if farmers simply started burning later in the day, after the satellites had already passed over.

I built AgniCal, a web app that puts NASA's MODIS and VIIRS fire records on one scale and tests every Indian state to see if its count can still be trusted. Out of 13 states with enough fires, only Punjab and Haryana show the problem. The count says burning fell 95 percent, but it fell by no more than about 83 percent. Anyone can check their own region.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works? AgniCal is a web app that checks whether NASA's satellite fire counts can still be trusted for crop burning in India. I put MODIS fire detections from Terra and Aqua, and VIIRS detections from Suomi NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21, for 2003 to 2025 onto one scale. For every state and season it asks one question: is the count still comparable with earlier years? These satellites pass at fixed hours, close to 1:30 pm, but Terra and Aqua have drifted in local time. Together they give several looks at the fire day. In Punjab, the later Aqua pass now sees about four times more fires per Suomi NPP fire than before. Across the border in Pakistan it sees about one times, so satellite drift is not the cause.

Benefits: Out of 13 states with enough fires, only Punjab and Haryana fail the test. A later pass also gives a floor: burning fell no more than about 83 percent, not the 95 percent the count shows. Anyone can check their own region by choosing a state or uploading NASA FIRMS files, right in the browser.

Intended impact: India uses this fire record to judge farm burning and its smoke. If the count quietly stops seeing late burning, policy can look more successful than it is. AgniCal tells people which seasons and regions are still safe to compare.

Tools: Python, pandas, scikit-learn, LightGBM, geopandas and Plotly. The site is a static web app hosted on GitHub Pages. Data: NASA FIRMS active fire archive. Code, under the MIT License: https://github.com/Prithika-97/agnical

How it was creative? Terra and Aqua are normally seen as a flaw in the record. I used their drift as a scanner, since each year they look at the same fires at a different hour. I also built a region checker that works on any place on Earth.

Factors I considered: Satellite drift could fake the whole result, so I ran every test twice: on Punjab and Haryana, and on calm states and Pakistan under the same satellites. I also reported the tests that failed, including one signal I threw out. The limit is that polar satellites can bound the burning hour but cannot measure it. Hourly satellites such as GK-2A and INSAT are the next step.

node.title: ARCNAVE
node.excerpt: We are a team building SPHEREx AI Sky Explorer, a web-based tool that uses NASA SPHEREx data and AI to help discover and investigate changes in the sky over time.

projectDetails.name: ARCNAVE: Watch the sky change. Find what moves.
projectDetails.summary: NASA's SPHEREx telescope photographs the entire sky every six months, but its pictures sit in a scientific archive that only experts know how to use. ARCNAVE opens that archive to everyone. Type any place in the sky, or a star's name, and ARCNAVE plays NASA's real SPHEREx pictures of that spot like a short video, so anything that moves or changes stands out, just as Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in 1930 by flipping between two photographs. Every moving star is circled, measured, and checked against ESA's Gaia map of the stars. We tested ARCNAVE on all five stars NASA chose for this challenge, and it caught every one: Barnard's Star, for example, moved 9.9 arcseconds in a year, where astronomers expect 10.2. ARCNAVE runs on any phone and needs no sign-in, so a student, a teacher or a curious stargazer can watch the real sky change, and perhaps spot the next moving world.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

  1. Pick a spot. Type a sky position (RA and Dec) or a name such as "Barnard's Star".
  2. Watch it change. NASA's real pictures of that spot play in date order, like a little video. You can also blink between two dates, or subtract one from the other to see only what changed.
  3. See what moved. Every moving star is circled in each picture, its speed is measured, and the result is compared with known star catalogues. Every result says how sure we are.

How it answers the challenge

  • Enter the RA and Dec of a patch of sky: type a position or a name, or click the map of the whole sky.
  • Show the pictures like a little video: play as a video, step by step, blink or swipe.
  • Make moving objects easy to spot: movers circled in every picture, with their path.
  • Test on the five named stars: all five measured and compared with known values.
  • Easy to update with new data releases: NASA's newest release (November 2026) appeared with no change to our code.

We also built every extra idea the challenge suggested: SPHEREx's 102 colours and the spectrum of any star, adding and subtracting pictures, choosing the field of view, Gaia and WISE star maps on top, links that open any spot, NASA's data-quality flags, and export to Python and Aladin.

NASA's five test stars

  • Barnard's Star, the fastest-moving star in our sky: moved 9.9" a year (expected 10.2").
  • Epsilon Indi B, a pair of brown dwarfs near the Sun: moved 4.3" a year (expected 4.7").
  • WISE 0855, the coldest brown dwarf known: moved 8.8" a year; agrees with NASA WISE.
  • RW Aurigae, a young star that dims: became about half as bright in a year.
  • R Draconis, a pulsating giant star: its brightness changed about three times over.

Why you can trust it

Before trusting ARCNAVE, we tried to fool it. We hid 19,880 fake planets in real SPHEREx pictures across 18 parts of the sky, picked before we started. A planet as far as 1,000 times Earth's distance from the Sun was found in all 18. Where it misses, we show the miss. Nothing is ever called a discovery.

Why it matters

  • Students and the public: real space data as a video, on a phone, with a 60-second "Find the asteroid" game and a 90-second story.
  • Citizen scientists: a free tool to look for nearby brown dwarfs and distant moving objects, with the usual checks done for them.
  • Scientists: real measurements with error bars, and a Python notebook to repeat them.
  • NASA: every new SPHEREx release is ready for the public on the day it comes out.

What's next

Re-measure every result on SPHEREx's newest release, and add a volunteer mode where many people check the same patch of sky together.

Built with

JavaScript in the browser, a small Node.js server with no add-ons, the Aladin Lite sky viewer, Python and Astropy for the notebook export, and Cloudflare hosting. ARCNAVE reads only the part of each picture it needs (about 4 MB instead of 65 MB), so it stays quick even on a phone.

projectDetails.name: ASTRAVEX INNOVATIONS
projectDetails.summary:
Be An Earth System Trend Detective!

Our project aims to create an interactive tool to identify, analyze, and visualize changes in Earth's environmental systems. It is part of the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, focusing on Earth Science and Software.

Environmental variables such as temperature, rainfall, vegetation, ocean conditions, and water levels change over time. Their trends can differ between regions: a variable may increase in one place and decrease in another. Understanding large environmental datasets can be challenging.

Our tool will explore NASA Giovanni, Hydrology Time Series, NASA AppEEARS, NOAA Climate Data Online, KNMI Climate Explorer, and the SWOT Mission. Users can select variables and time periods, examine historical measurements, and compare regions.

Graphs, charts, and interactive maps will display results. Trend-detection methods will identify increasing, decreasing, or stable patterns. Statistical analysis will help assess whether trends are significant rather than random variations.

The project will answer five questions: What is changing? Where? How much? How is it changing over time? Are the changes statistically significant?

The expected outcome is a dashboard that transforms scientific data into visual insights. It can help students, researchers, and environmental scientists understand patterns across our changing planet.

Our vision is to make Earth science data easier to explore and help everyone become an Earth System Trend Detective!
projectDetails.details: Project Details – Be An Earth System Trend Detective! Our project, Be An Earth System Trend Detective!, is an interactive platform designed to identify, analyze, and visualize environmental changes across the Earth. It helps users understand what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and whether those changes are statistically significant. How It Works: The platform uses Earth science datasets from NASA and other scientific organizations. Users can select environmental variables such as temperature, rainfall, vegetation, and water levels, choose geographical regions, and examine changes over different time periods. The system processes the selected data using time-series analysis and statistical trend detection methods. It identifies increasing, decreasing, and stable trends and presents the results through interactive graphs, charts, and geographical maps. Tools and Technologies: Our project draws on resources such as NASA Giovanni, NASA AppEEARS, Hydrology Time Series, NOAA Climate Data Online, KNMI Climate Explorer, and the SWOT Mission. Python and GIS-based tools are potential technologies for data processing and visualization. The final programming languages, software stack, and hardware will depend on the implementation. Benefits and Impact: The platform makes complex environmental datasets easier to understand. It can support students, researchers, and environmental scientists in studying climate patterns, comparing geographical regions, identifying environmental trends, and understanding changes in Earth's interconnected systems. It can also support environmental monitoring and scientific research. Creativity and Innovation: The creative aspect of our project is bringing multiple Earth science data resources, geographical visualization, and statistical analysis together in one platform. Instead of simply displaying environmental measurements, it acts as a trend detective by identifying patterns and explaining how environmental conditions change across different locations and time periods. Factors Considered: We considered data availability, accuracy, reliability, geographical differences, historical trends, missing measurements, statistical significance, and ease of use. We also considered the importance of presenting scientific results in a simple and understandable format. Our ultimate goal is to transform complex Earth science data into meaningful insights and help people better understand our changing planet.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project ASTRAVYNE
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRAVYNE — Spatial Intelligence for Climate-Resilient Agriculture

ASTRAVYNE is a Spatial Intelligence-powered agricultural decision-support platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under the theme "Resilient Crop Rotation Using NASA Data." Our mission is to transform NASA Earth observations into actionable insights that help farmers make sustainable, climate-resilient decisions.

Agriculture faces growing challenges from unpredictable rainfall, rising temperatures, soil degradation, and water scarcity. ASTRAVYNE addresses these issues by combining satellite observations, agricultural knowledge, and location-specific environmental information.

Our platform integrates NASA POWER, SMAP, GPM, Landsat, MODIS, and ECOSTRESS datasets to analyze rainfall, temperature, soil moisture, vegetation health, and environmental stress. Our initial prototype focuses on Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu.

At its core, ASTRAVYNE features a Spatial Intelligence Engine designed to assess crop suitability, generate potential crop rotation sequences, and evaluate alternatives based on water efficiency, soil health, climate resilience, and agricultural feasibility.

Through an interactive geographical interface, farmers can explore environmental conditions, compare crop rotations, and understand the reasoning behind recommendations.

ASTRAVYNE aims to bridge NASA Earth science and sustainable agriculture, helping farmers understand what to grow, where, when, and why.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRAVYNE — Project Details

ASTRAVYNE is a Spatial Intelligence-based agricultural decision-support platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It addresses the challenge of building climate-resilient crop rotation strategies using NASA Earth observation data.

Problem Statement:
Farmers face unpredictable rainfall, rising temperatures, soil degradation, and water scarcity. Conventional crop planning often lacks access to location-specific environmental intelligence, making it difficult to select sustainable crop rotations.

Our Solution:
ASTRAVYNE combines NASA satellite observations, agricultural knowledge, and farmer-specific information to analyze environmental conditions and recommend suitable crop rotation strategies.

Technology and Data Sources:
The platform integrates NASA POWER, SMAP, GPM, Landsat, MODIS, and ECOSTRESS datasets to study rainfall, temperature, soil moisture, vegetation health, and environmental stress.

Core Architecture:
Our Spatial Intelligence Engine is designed to perform environmental profiling, crop suitability analysis, rotation generation, historical climate stress testing, and multi-criteria evaluation. It compares crop rotations based on water efficiency, soil health, climate resilience, and agricultural feasibility.

Key Features:

  • Interactive geographical exploration and environmental visualization.
  • Location-specific crop suitability assessment.
  • Climate-resilient crop rotation recommendations.
  • Historical environmental analysis and risk evaluation.
  • Explainable recommendations supported by scientific evidence.

Prototype and Impact:
Our initial prototype focuses on Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, with an architecture designed for future geographical expansion.

ASTRAVYNE aims to bridge NASA Earth science and practical agriculture, enabling farmers to understand what to grow, when to grow it, and why certain crop rotations are more suitable for their land.

Our ultimate goal is to make satellite-powered agricultural intelligence accessible, explainable, and useful for sustainable farming.

projectDetails.name: Project AstraX Nova
projectDetails.summary:
Team ASTRA-X built ASTRA-X Space Academy, an interactive web app that turns NASA’s discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars into stories students can explore. It covers 24 real explorers, from the Surveyor landers and Apollo descent stages to Viking, Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity. Each one appears on 3D globes of the Moon and Mars at its real landing coordinates and tells its own story in first person: why it went, what it discovered, how its mission ended, and where it rests today.

To meet the storytelling challenge, the app uses NASA photographs, official NASA 3D models and NASA landing-site terrain. It includes 20 real-time 3D mission videos with narration, an Earthrise scroll journey, AR views, and games based on real missions. Quizzes, badges and fun facts help students learn while they play. Every fact links back to a NASA source, and simulations are clearly labelled.

This matters because more than a hundred pieces of NASA hardware lie silent on other worlds, and most people have never heard of them. Our ASTRA-X turns these “abandoned” machines into heritage sites students can visit and learn science from. The app runs offline on laptops and phones.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

ASTRA-X Space Academy is an interactive web app that tells the stories of 24 NASA explorers that were left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. It runs entirely in the web browser, on a laptop, PC or phone, and works offline from a single HTML file.

  • 3D Moon and Mars maps: NASA imagery of the Moon and Mars wrapped onto globes, with each explorer marked at its real landing site. Tap a marker to open the explorer’s story, told in first person: why it went, what it discovered, its final days and where it rests today. Each story links to its NASA source.
  • 20 real-time 3D mission videos: one for each Moon and Mars explorer, plus “Twelve Moonwalkers”. They use NASA’s official 3D models and NASA’s 3D landing-site terrain, with automatic narration and captions.
  • Earthrise Journey: a cinematic scroll story that recreates Apollo 11’s flight from Earth to the Moon in 3D.
  • Solar System and Deep Space: live 3D views with planets at their approximate real positions for today’s date, and probes like Pioneer, Dawn and Kepler.
  • AR Mission Lab: places a NASA Moon or Mars globe over the camera view.
  • Games: Land the Eagle and Opportunity’s Last Drive, with 49 non-repeating NASA fun facts, plus the “Who Am I?” quiz.
  • Learning extras: a rule-based AI mentor answering from the app’s fact library, XP, ranks, badges, a certificate, a 3D photo vault of real NASA images and a sources page.

Benefits

  • Free and offline: no installation and no internet needed, so it suits classrooms with weak connections.
  • Hard-to-find knowledge in one place: history and science that is usually scattered across NASA archives.
  • Accessible: narration, captions, a reduce-motion setting, a light theme, adjustable text size, keyboard controls and a simple-language mode.
  • Trustworthy: facts are labelled “Verified”, “Simplified” or “Simulated”, and the 3D videos are marked as recreations.

Intended impact

Most people don’t know that more than a hundred pieces of NASA hardware sit silently on other worlds. ASTRA-X turns these “abandoned” machines into heritage sites that students can visit, care about and learn from. The aim is to spark interest in space science and engineering, and in protecting space heritage, especially among school students who may never visit a museum or NASA centre.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and GLSL for the graphics-card shaders.
  • Graphics: WebGL, three.js (r147) with its glTF loader, the Draco 3D decoder, Canvas 2D and Google model-viewer for the AR Lab.
  • Browser features: Web Speech API for narration, getUserMedia for the AR camera, and local storage to save progress.
  • NASA data:
    • NASA Science 3D Resources: models of the Lunar Module, Astronaut, Viking, Opportunity, Ingenuity and InSight, plus landing-site terrains.
    • NASA SVS CGI Moon Kit: Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter colour and elevation maps.
    • NASA Image and Video Library, JPL Photojournal, NSSDCA, and the NASA Planetary Fact Sheet.
  • Development help: built with help from Claude (Anthropic’s AI assistant). Disclose this if your submission rules ask about AI use.
  • Hardware: any laptop, PC or phone. A webcam or phone camera is only needed for AR.

What makes it creative

  • Machines tell their own stories: each explorer narrates in first person.
  • Real NASA 3D content, not cartoons: real NASA models and terrain bring each mission back to life in 3D.
  • Real details: dust follows lunar gravity, Earth appears where it really sits in each landing site’s sky, and Mars frost, ice polygons, dust storms and blue sunsets match each site.
  • Learning through play: games, fun facts, quizzes and badges keep students exploring.

Factors the team considered

  • Accuracy: every fact traced to a NASA source, with simplifications clearly labelled.
  • Age-appropriate design: kid-friendly fonts, colourful navigation and clear language.
  • Performance: detail adjusts automatically so it stays smooth on phones and older laptops.
  • Offline use: works without internet, for classrooms with limited connectivity.
  • Accessibility: the options listed under Benefits.
  • Privacy: no account, no server and no tracking. Progress and camera video stay on the device.
  • Copyright and ethics: only public-domain NASA material, credited with its NASA IDs. No real astronaut likenesses are created. Imagined future scenes are labelled.

projectDetails.name: Astrobiotix Labs — SpaceOps 🚀
projectDetails.summary:
ARCADIA is an interactive Mars colonisation and survival game made by ASTROBIOTIX LABS – SpaceOps. It allows the user to see what astronauts may have to go through when trying to colonise Mars.

The game enables the user to navigate around Mars, manage resources such as oxygen, water, food and electricity, plan rover missions and learn the importance of creating a sustainable colony.

ARCADIA helps overcome this issue by allowing the user to gain a better understanding of how complex space exploration and survival can be by making it interactive. You can see how it all fits together and what decisions will be needed to keep the colony alive.

This is an important project as it helps encourage scientific curiosity, problem solving and shows the user the challenges that would occur when sending humans to Mars in the future.
projectDetails.details:
ARCADIA was created by our team ASTROBIOTIX LABS - SpaceOps as a colonisation and survival simulator designed to give insight into how humans may be able to live on Mars.

Our idea was to give people some insight into the challenges they may face when trying to create and maintain a human settlement on another planet. You get to explore the Martian environment, manage key resources (oxygen, water, food and power), and plan missions using rovers. Alongside this, we also show how important research, infrastructure and resource management is.

We believe ARCADIA can help to make space science more interesting. Providing an interactive learning experience, it will appeal to those interested in space, including students.

Our intention is to pique peoples interest in space, improve their problem solving skills and make them think about the challenges of sending humans to Mars in the future.

During our development we used C++ and OpenGL to create our Windows based prototype. We looked into creating a 3D web based simulator to create the interactive Martian environment. We used AI tools to help us during development.

What makes our project stand out is the combination of exploration, survival and colony management. We thought about key factors such as resource limitations, conditions, astronaut safety, sustainability and the challenges of being far away from Earth.

Ultimately, we want to improve our game to provide a more detailed and realistic simulation of Mars to help teach people about the future of human space exploration.

projectDetails.name: ASTROHEALTH – Astronaut Health Monitoring and Mission Support System
projectDetails.summary: ASTROHEALTH is a health monitoring and mission support platform designed to help monitor astronaut well-being during space missions. It brings together simulated astronaut health measurements, digital twin visualization, ECG monitoring, sleep and behavioral health indicators, radiation and space-weather information, and decision-support features in one dashboard. The system is designed to help identify unusual health patterns and present useful information to support mission monitoring. It also explores NASA space-weather and space biology research resources through dedicated data modules. The platform combines an interactive interface, data visualization, and explainable alerts to make complex health information easier to understand. It is a prototype: astronaut biometric readings are simulated and its alerts are not medically validated. ASTROHEALTH aims to support safer, more informed health monitoring during long-duration space missions.
projectDetails.details:
1. Project Overview

ASTROHEALTH is a web-based astronaut health monitoring and mission support system designed for long-duration space missions. It brings important astronaut health indicators and space-related information together in one interactive dashboard.

2. How It Works

The platform provides simulated astronaut profiles and health measurements, including heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), blood oxygen (SpO2), blood pressure, and ECG visualization. A digital twin interface helps users explore astronaut health status.

It also includes modules for sleep and behavioral health, cardiovascular monitoring, cranial health, musculoskeletal health, and radiation-related space-weather information. An anomaly monitoring feature highlights unusual patterns and provides decision-support information for mission monitoring.

NASA data modules are designed to explore space-weather information from NASA DONKI and space biology research resources from NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR).

3. Benefits and Intended Impact

ASTROHEALTH aims to make astronaut health information easier to understand and monitor. It brings multiple types of information into one interface, helps users explore possible health-related patterns, and supports awareness of potential issues during long-duration missions. It may also help students and researchers understand the challenges of astronaut health monitoring.

4. Technology Used

The project was developed using React, TypeScript, Vite, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It uses interactive charts, data visualization, and state management to present information. NASA data services are included for exploring DONKI space-weather events and OSDR research resources.

5. Creativity and Innovation

The main innovation is combining astronaut health visualization, digital twin concepts, space-weather information, research exploration, and explainable monitoring features in a single platform. The design focuses on making complex information accessible through an interactive dashboard.

6. Current Limitations

ASTROHEALTH is a prototype. The astronaut biometric readings are simulated and are not collected from real astronauts or medical devices. Its alerts are experimental decision-support features, not medically validated diagnoses or flight medical advice. NASA space-weather events are not direct measurements of an individual astronaut's radiation dose.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: EXOSKY
projectDetails.summary:
EXOSKY – Discover the Universe Through the Eyes of Other Worlds

EXOSKY is an interactive platform for space exploration aimed at making astronomy and planetary science fun, engaging, and educational. We have created a web application, which enables users to explore planets and exoplanets, examine 3D models of planets, create custom-made space mission with destinations, spacecraft, launch vehicle, satellites, rovers, and instruments.

Our platform offers exoplanet explorer with the NASA Exoplanet Archive database, planet comparison tool, creative constellation creator, and scientific data center with resources of NASA, ESA, and ISRO.

The EXOSKY platform solves the problem of making the process of comprehending complex astronomical data more intuitive with the help of interactive visualizations, real scientific data, and hands-on discovery.

It creates a connection between scientific information and public knowledge and makes space science exciting and educational
projectDetails.details:
EXOSKY – Explore the Universe Through Another World's Eyes

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

EXOSKY is an interactive web-based space exploration platform that makes astronomy and planetary science easier and more engaging to understand. It provides six main features: Mission Builder, Explore Exoplanets, Constellation Creator, Planet Comparison, Scientific Data Centre, and Settings.

Users can select planets such as Earth, Mars, Venus, and Mercury, explore interactive 3D planetary models, and learn about their characteristics. The Mission Builder allows users to create a space mission by choosing destinations, spacecraft, and mission equipment, followed by an interactive mission simulation. The Exoplanet Explorer allows users to browse planets beyond our Solar System, search and filter them, and retrieve confirmed-planet records from the NASA Exoplanet Archive. Users can also create and save custom constellations and compare planetary information.

2. What benefits does it have?

EXOSKY makes complex scientific information easier to understand through interactive visualizations and hands-on learning. It encourages users to explore space independently rather than only reading theoretical information. It brings together planetary exploration, mission planning, exoplanet information, creative activities, and scientific data resources in one platform.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to increase interest in astronomy, space science, and scientific research, especially among students and young learners. We aim to make space exploration more accessible, inspire curiosity about worlds beyond Earth, and encourage the next generation to learn more about science, technology, and space missions.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

We developed EXOSKY as a browser-based application using:

  • HTML5 – application structure.
  • CSS3 and Tailwind CSS – styling, layout, and responsive interface.
  • JavaScript (ES6) – application logic and interactivity.
  • React 18 – reusable components and interface state management.
  • Three.js and WebGL – interactive 3D planetary visualization.
  • GLTFLoader and GLB models – loading 3D planetary assets.
  • HTML Canvas API – interactive constellation creation.
  • NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP API – retrieving confirmed exoplanet records.
  • Web Audio API – optional ambient soundscape.
  • Babel Standalone – browser-side JSX transformation.
  • Lucide Icons – interface icons.
  • Browser Local Storage – saving user selections, settings, and constellation designs.

The project runs in a modern web browser and uses no dedicated hardware requirement beyond a compatible computer or device.

5. How is the project creative?

EXOSKY combines scientific exploration with creativity and interactive simulation. Instead of presenting astronomy as static information, it lets users interact with 3D planets, design their own constellations, compare planetary properties, and build a space mission step by step. The combination of scientific information, visual exploration, mission simulation, and creative activities makes the platform an engaging way to experience space science.

6. What factors did the team consider?

We considered accessibility, ease of use, educational value, scientific reliability, visual clarity, and interactive experience while developing the platform. We also considered browser compatibility, performance, responsive layouts, and the ability to preserve user-created work. Scientific data sources are identified in the Data Centre, and illustrative demo estimates are distinguished from measured planetary conditions so that users are not misled about exoplanet habitability.

EXOSKY's central idea is to transform space science from something people simply read about into something they can explore, understand, and experience interactively.

projectDetails.name: Selene Navigator
projectDetails.summary:
SELENE NAVIGATOR – Making Lunar Mission Planning More Accessible
SELENE NAVIGATOR is an interactive lunar mission planning platform designed to help young engineers, students, and small teams explore and understand the challenges of planning missions to the Moon.
Using publicly available NASA and international space-agency datasets, the platform brings key mission-planning considerations into one workspace. Users can explore the entire Moon in 3D, investigate potential landing sites, examine terrain and sunlight conditions, understand communication visibility, compare locations, and experiment with mission timelines and rover routes.
Lunar exploration involves complex decisions that require both scientific understanding and engineering considerations. SELENE NAVIGATOR aims to make these concepts easier to explore by providing an accessible starting point for developing early mission ideas.
It also encourages teams to connect different mission requirements, evaluate trade-offs, and understand how individual decisions can influence an overall mission plan.
Rather than replacing professional mission-planning systems, it encourages users to learn, experiment, evaluate possibilities, and think through the challenges of operating on the lunar surface.
Our vision is to make lunar mission planning more approachable and give the next generation of space explorers the opportunity to think and plan like engineers.
projectDetails.details: SeleneNavigator is an interactive web suite built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 that uses a 3D lunar globe, 2D descent simulator, and multi-criteria scoring to evaluate Artemis candidate landing zones at the lunar south pole. It streamlines mission planning by combining real-time solar and Earth communication tracking, dynamic priority sliders, and instant JSON, CSV, or PDF data exports into a single browser-based tool. By pinpointing sunlit crater ridges right next to water-ice-rich permanently shadowed regions, the project aims to accelerate sustainable lunar exploration and In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) while making real planetary science accessible to everyone. Built and hosted on GitHub Pages using standard web technologies, the platform integrates live NASA JPL Horizons ephemeris geometry alongside multi-mission datasets from NASA LRO, ISRO’s Chandrayaan-3, JAXA’s Kaguya, and KASA’s ShadowCam. Its creative edge comes from gamifying raw elevation rasters into a hands-on 2D landing simulator, matching lunar zones to real terrestrial analog testbeds across six space agencies, and packaging complex telemetry into a judge-ready guided walkthrough. Throughout development, our team carefully weighed solar illumination duty cycles, Direct-to-Earth radio visibility, terrain slope and boulder hazards, and cryogenic water-ice stability—while transparently accounting for scientific caveats like crater-wall shadowing and subsurface drilling needs.

projectDetails.name: Project AYARU - Echoes of Earth
projectDetails.summary:
Earth Jukebox is a web application that turns NASA Earth imagery into sound, so people can hear changes on our planet as well as see them. A playhead sweeps across a world map from west to east. Each latitude band becomes a voice, pixel brightness controls loudness, and position controls pitch and stereo panning. Users can choose records such as sea surface temperature, sea ice, carbon dioxide, vegetation and fires. A year slider gradually detunes the sound to show the planet changing over time. A hue mode maps color to timbre, so warm and cool regions sound different. Users can also load any Earth Information Center frame and hear it instantly.

The project addresses the challenge by pairing EIC visuals with sonification generated in real time in the browser. It is also accessible, with keyboard controls, drag-to-scrub listening and a live text description of what is being heard. This matters because Earth science is mostly shared through images, which excludes blind and low-vision people. Sound makes climate data more inclusive and memorable for everyone.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

Earth Jukebox is a web application that turns Earth imagery into sound, generated in real time in the browser. A playhead sweeps across a world map from west to east, like the planet turning under the sound. The map is split into 18 latitude bands, and each band is one voice. Pitch rises toward the north, brightness controls loudness, and longitude controls stereo position. A year slider (1980-2025) gradually detunes the voices, so the same record sounds more strained as the years pass. A hue mode maps color to timbre, so warm regions sound bright and cool regions sound mellow. Users can pick records such as sea surface temperature, sea ice, carbon dioxide, vegetation and fires, or load any Earth Information Center frame and hear it straight away. They can also record the mix. In a self-hosted version, the app can pull live imagery from NASA GIBS.

Benefits and intended impact

Earth science is mostly shared through images, which leaves out blind and low-vision people. Earth Jukebox gives them another way in, and it also helps anyone who learns well through sound. The intended impact is to make climate and Earth observation data inclusive, memorable and easy to explore, in classrooms, science outreach and public exhibits, without any installation.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single page, with no framework
  • Web Audio API for oscillators, filters, stereo panning and compression
  • Canvas for rendering the maps
  • MediaRecorder API for recording the audio
  • NASA GIBS imagery for the live-data version
  • [Add any AI tools, libraries or other software your team used. Space Apps asks teams to disclose AI use, so say how it was used.]

Creativity

The jukebox idea turns datasets into “records” you can pick and play, which makes data exploration feel like listening to music. Using the year slider to detune the sound lets people hear change over time, not just a snapshot. Mapping hue to timbre makes color audible too, and users can bring in their own frames.

Factors we considered

  • Accessibility: keyboard controls, drag-to-hear listening and a live text caption that screen readers announce.
  • Simplicity: it runs in any modern browser, with no accounts or downloads.
  • Pleasant sound: each record uses its own musical scale so the sound is easy to listen to, not harsh.
  • Honesty about data: the built-in maps are illustrative, and real NASA imagery is loaded through the live version or by uploading a frame. The sound reflects the brightness and color of the rendered image, not raw measurements.
  • Future work: real EIC datasets, spoken summaries and a distinct sound for coastlines.

projectDetails.name: IGNIS
projectDetails.summary:
IGNIS – Beyond the Hotspot is a satellite-based wildfire intelligence platform developed to harmonize NASA's MODIS and VIIRS fire observations into meaningful fire events.

Satellite instruments often detect overlapping thermal anomalies, creating duplicate or fragmented representations of the same fire activity. IGNIS addresses this challenge through geospatial and temporal matching, bipartite assignment, and fire-event harmonization. It processes satellite observations, identifies coincident detections, groups nearby events, and provides probabilistic classification into Forest Wildfire, Agricultural Burning, Industrial Heat, and Unknown categories.

The platform features an interactive 3D Earth built with CesiumJS, allowing users to explore fire observations, harmonized events, and historical datasets. Integrated with NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), IGNIS aims to transform individual satellite detections into more accessible and actionable fire intelligence.

By reducing duplicate observations and providing contextual information, IGNIS supports better understanding of global thermal activity and demonstrates how satellite data processing can contribute to wildfire monitoring and environmental awareness.
projectDetails.details:
IGNIS

IGNIS is a satellite-based wildfire intelligence platform designed to transform individual thermal anomaly observations into unified and meaningful fire events.

How it works:

The platform integrates NASA FIRMS data from MODIS and VIIRS satellite instruments through a Python FastAPI backend. Its harmonization engine uses geodesic distance calculations, temporal matching (2.5-hour threshold), and bipartite assignment (1.5 km matching distance) to identify observations that may represent the same fire activity.

The processed observations are organized into harmonized events and analyzed using a probabilistic classification engine that identifies potential Forest Wildfires, Agricultural Burning, Industrial Heat, or Unknown sources. Spatial clustering functionality supports grouping geographically related events.

Key Features:

  • Interactive 3D Earth visualization using CesiumJS.
  • NASA FIRMS satellite data integration.
  • MODIS–VIIRS observation harmonization.
  • Probabilistic fire-source classification.
  • Historical fire archive exploration.
  • Live data feed integration and fire-event analytics.
  • Global geographic exploration.

Technology Stack:

Frontend: React, JavaScript, Vite, CSS and CesiumJS.

Backend: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn and Pydantic.

Data Processing: Geospatial calculations, temporal matching, bipartite assignment and spatial clustering.

Database: DuckDB and PostgreSQL (Neon migration).

Deployment: Vercel and Render.

Innovation and Impact:

IGNIS goes beyond displaying individual satellite hotspots. Its primary innovation is attempting to reconcile observations from two different satellite instruments into unified fire events, reducing fragmented and potentially duplicated representations. It also recognizes that thermal anomalies do not automatically indicate wildfires, using probabilistic source classification rather than treating every detection as a confirmed forest fire.

The project aims to make satellite fire observations easier to explore, interpret and analyze, supporting environmental monitoring and better-informed fire intelligence.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

projectDetails.name: Project Bio-nauts
projectDetails.summary:
### BIO-NAUTS – Smart Health Monitoring for Astronauts

BIO-NAUTS is a smart wearable health monitoring system designed to monitor astronauts' health during space missions. It uses a Smart Sensor T-Shirt and a Smart Health Watch to collect important body information such as heart rate, blood oxygen level (SpO₂), body temperature, breathing, and physical activity.

The system uses different sensors, including optical, heart rate, temperature, and motion sensors. These sensors continuously collect health data and send it wirelessly to a central system. A processor analyses the collected data, while AI software checks the astronaut's health condition and identifies possible problems. If any unusual changes are detected, the system provides alerts and warnings.

The real-time health dashboard displays health measurements, health trends, and sensor status. This system helps detect health problems early, supports continuous health monitoring, and improves astronaut safety during space missions.

Main Goal: To provide smarter, faster, and more reliable health monitoring for astronauts in space.
projectDetails.details:
Bionauts – Smart Astronaut Health Monitoring System

Bionauts is a smart health monitoring system designed to monitor the health and physical condition of astronauts during space missions.

Our project focuses on monitoring important health parameters using different sensors such as ECG sensors, heart rate sensors, optical sensors, temperature sensors, respiration sensors, motion sensors, EMG sensors, and GSR sensors.

The system aims to collect and display health-related information to help identify unusual changes in an astronaut's physical condition. It can support early detection of potential health concerns and improve astronaut safety during space missions.

The main benefits of this project are continuous health monitoring, early identification of abnormal changes, and improved awareness of astronaut health.

We developed our project prototype using HTML to create a web-based interface that presents the project concept and its features.

Our main goal is to support astronaut health and contribute to safer future space exploration.

projectDetails.name: Project BlazeGuard
projectDetails.summary: FireWatch is a satellite-based fire hotspot monitoring system designed to help identify and monitor potential fire activity across India, with a special focus on Tamil Nadu. The platform uses NASA FIRMS satellite data to display hotspot observations on an interactive map. It provides hotspot counts, detection confidence levels, date-based filtering, regional filtering, searchable records, and downloadable CSV reports. Marker clustering helps users explore large numbers of hotspot observations more efficiently. FireWatch aims to make satellite hotspot information easier to understand and access, supporting environmental monitoring and early awareness of potential fire events. These observations require verification and do not represent confirmed fires.
projectDetails.details: FireWatch – Satellite-Based Fire Hotspot Monitoring System FireWatch is a web-based application designed to monitor satellite-detected fire hotspots using NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System) data. The application retrieves satellite hotspot observations and displays their locations on an interactive map. Users can explore observations across India and Tamil Nadu, filter them by date and detection confidence, search observation details, and view information such as latitude, longitude, acquisition date, time, and satellite source. The application also provides summary counts and allows users to download filtered observations as CSV reports. FireWatch helps users understand the geographical distribution of satellite-detected hotspots and makes fire-related information easier to explore. Its intended impact is to improve public awareness, support environmental monitoring, and help users identify areas that may need further investigation. The project was developed using Python, Flask, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. The interactive map uses Leaflet and MarkerCluster, while NASA FIRMS provides satellite hotspot data. The application was developed and tested using PyCharm. The creative aspect of FireWatch is its integration of NASA satellite observations with an easy-to-use web interface. Features such as interactive hotspot clustering, confidence-based filtering, regional selection, and downloadable reports make large amounts of satellite data easier to understand. Our team considered data accessibility, usability, map performance, geographical filtering, and the importance of presenting satellite observations responsibly. We also considered that a satellite hotspot detection does not necessarily represent a confirmed fire. FireWatch is designed as a monitoring and awareness tool, not as an automatic fire-confirmation or prediction system.

projectDetails.name: FIRELYTICS AI — Flame in Freefall
projectDetails.summary:
FIRELYTICS AI is an independent research workbench developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under the Flame in Freefall challenge. It brings NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion research and selected archived SAME-R analysis into one interactive platform for exploring spacecraft fire-safety evidence.

The platform deeply indexes 14 investigations from a wider repository scope of 24 studies and includes tools for comparing experiments, exploring hypothetical space-habitat conditions, and analysing six archived SAME-R experimental runs. Users can examine how oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, gravity and material conditions relate to combustion research.

FIRELYTICS addresses the challenge by making complex microgravity-combustion research easier to explore, compare and understand. It also highlights scientific assumptions, evidence gaps and the limitations of calculated results, helping researchers investigate fire-safety questions relevant to future crewed missions to the Moon and Mars.
projectDetails.details:
About FIRELYTICS AI

FIRELYTICS AI is an interactive scientific research platform developed to make NASA microgravity combustion research easier to explore and understand. It connects NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) investigation metadata with selected archived SAME-R analysis to support research into spacecraft fire safety.

How the Project Works

The application provides five main research workspaces:

  1. Mission & Habitat Simulator: Allows users to explore five hypothetical research profiles, including ISS, lunar and Martian environments. Users can adjust oxygen concentration, pressure, airflow, gravity and material inputs and examine the resulting screening calculations.
  2. Catalogue & Comparison Matrix: Organizes 14 deeply indexed NASA PSI investigations and allows users to compare experimental conditions, fuel phases, hardware and research parameters.
  3. SI Fire-Safety Synthesis: Organizes research around prevention, detection, suppression, partial-gravity conditions and potential applications on Earth.
  4. SAME-R Telemetry & Lineage Lab: Provides access to reconciled archived analysis from six selected PSI-101 Pyrell runs, including cycle classifications, validation checks and source-row references.
  5. All-in-One Executive View: Brings the major research workspaces together for a unified overview.

The application also includes scientific visualizations for oxygen-pressure conditions, partial-gravity screening, evidence ranking and SAME-R archive analysis.

Technology Used

The frontend is developed using Next.js, React and TypeScript. The backend uses Python and FastAPI, with Pydantic for request validation. A Next.js API proxy connects the browser to the backend. Scientific calculations, catalogue matching and reporting are handled by the backend, with results displayed through browser-native SVG and HTML/CSS visualizations.

The platform distinguishes NASA source metadata, archived analysis and code-generated screening outputs. Its ranking, evidence coverage and physics-proximity measures are presented separately rather than as fire-risk scores. Its partial-gravity and minimum-oxygen-concentration calculations are exploratory screening surrogates, not validated fire predictions.

Innovation and Intended Impact

The main strength of FIRELYTICS is bringing different combustion investigations into one traceable research environment. It helps users understand the available evidence, compare experimental conditions and identify gaps that require future research.

The project also explores potential research connections to smoke-versus-dust detection, fine-water-mist suppression and fire-resistant material screening.

By making scientific assumptions and limitations visible, FIRELYTICS aims to support better-informed fire-safety research for future human missions to the Moon and Mars.

Project Website: https://firelytics-ai.vercel.app/

Source Code: https://github.com/mantuchaurasiya092-source/firelytics-ai
Technical Documentation

For detailed information about the project's scientific methodology, system architecture, implementation, data processing, and technical design, refer to our technical documentation:

https://docs.google.com/document/d/1rkG3dfFZfJCMFG79XQFZlMp0PNZ-EdIl/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=116056661474776921869&rtpof=true&sd=true

FIRELYTICS AI is an independent educational and research prototype. It is not affiliated with, sponsored by or endorsed by NASA.

projectDetails.summary:
ASTRA-X, developed by team CASSINI-X, is an explainable, data-driven intelligence platform that solves a foundational challenge in space exploration: "Given a region of interest on Mars or the Moon, which locations on Earth possess comparable terrain characteristics?"

Historically, terrestrial analog sites for robotics testing and astronaut training were chosen ad hoc. ASTRA-X replaces subjective guesswork with rigorous quantitative science. Ingesting open orbital elevation rasters (NASA/USGS MOLA, LOLA, and SRTM), the platform standardizes spatial scale and extracts measurable morphometric features—including relative relief, slope gradients, and surface roughness. Candidates are ranked using a transparent weighted Euclidean similarity model alongside independent data-confidence scoring and traverse pathfinding.

ASTRA-X transforms planetary mission planning by providing verifiable, reproducible decision support, accelerating exploration readiness and operational rover qualification before hardware ever leaves Earth.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRA-X — Complete Project Dossier

Platform: ASTRA-X — Planetary Terrestrial Analog Discovery Platform
Team: CASSINI-X
Tagline: "Discover Earth. Understand Other Worlds. Prepare for Exploration."

Project Summary

ASTRA-X, developed by team CASSINI-X, is a data-driven web application that answers a crucial question in space exploration: "Given a selected region on Mars or the Moon, which locations on Earth have comparable terrain characteristics?" Historically, terrestrial analog sites for rover testing and astronaut training were chosen ad hoc. ASTRA-X replaces subjective guesswork with a quantitative, repeatable standard. It ingests open orbital elevation datasets from NASA and USGS, standardizes them onto a unified spatial grid, extracts measurable physical terrain features, and ranks Earth candidate locations using a transparent weighted-distance model with independent confidence scoring. Every match comes with a clear, feature-by-feature explanation so mission planners can inspect and verify why a site was selected.

How It Works

ASTRA-X operates through a transparent five-stage pipeline:

Stage 1 — Planetary Data Ingestion: The system ingests authentic open planetary elevation rasters — NASA/USGS MOLA for Mars (128 px/deg), LOLA for the Moon (118 m/px), and SRTM for Earth (30 m / 1 arc-sec). These are real satellite-derived digital elevation models, not simulated data.

Stage 2 — Spatial Standardization & Feature Extraction: Raw altimetry is resampled onto a uniform 500-meter grid to resolve planetary datum differences. Three physically grounded morphometric features are computed: (1) Relative Elevation — detrended residual relief removing planetary sea-level bias, (2) Horn Slope — two-dimensional finite-difference surface gradient in degrees, and (3) Surface Roughness — local standard deviation of elevation across a 5×5 kernel window.

Stage 3 — Similarity Engine & Spatial ML: Candidate Earth regions are evaluated using an inverted normalized weighted Euclidean distance in standardized feature space. Unsupervised machine learning provides additional insight through Silhouette-optimized K-Means clustering, DBSCAN spatial density grouping, and Isolation Forest anomaly detection to surface morphologically unique terrain.

Stage 4 — Tripartite Scoring: Three independent metrics are strictly separated across the entire system — Similarity Score (physical terrain match percentage), Confidence Score (data coverage fraction and resolution ratio), and Mission Suitability Score (preliminary landing slope hazard screening). These are never merged, ensuring data gaps cannot be confused with terrain safety.

Stage 5 — Decision Support & Reporting: The platform provides 8-connected A* rover pathfinding with slope hazard avoidance and elevation profile charts, plus automated publication-ready PDF scientific dossiers with full data provenance tables.

▼

Important Notes & Scientific Integrity

Scientific Honesty Protocol (Strictly Enforced)

  1. Zero Data Fabrication — Every number shown is computed from real open planetary datasets or clearly labeled as DEMO DATA in demo mode.
  2. Metric Separation — Similarity, Confidence, and Mission Suitability are three independent fields everywhere (database, API, UI, reports). They are never merged.
  3. No Safety Claims — The platform never states that a site is "safe for landing." Suitability output is labeled "preliminary screening for decision support only."
  4. No Identity Claims — Results say "comparable on the selected features," never "identical to Mars."
  5. Explicit Data Gaps — Missing raster cells are masked, not filled. Coverage fraction is displayed as a data quality indicator.

Open Data Sources & Attribution

  • Mars Elevation: NASA/USGS Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) — Mars Global Surveyor
  • Moon Elevation: NASA/USGS Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) — Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter
  • Earth Elevation: NASA Shuttle Radar Topography Mission (SRTM) GL1 — 30m resolution
  • Earth Visualization: NASA Visible Earth Blue Marble — cloud-free satellite composite
  • Moon Visualization: LRO WAC Mosaic — Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera
  • All datasets are publicly available through NASA PDS, USGS Astrogeology, and AWS Open Data Registry.

Benchmark Validation Results

The similarity model was validated against 3 established planetary analog benchmark pairs from peer-reviewed literature:

  • Devon Island (Haughton Crater) ↔ Jezero Crater Floor: Ranked #2 out of 4,147 candidates (95.68% similarity)
  • Lanzarote Volcanic Field ↔ Mare Tranquillitatis: Ranked #16 out of 4,147 candidates (93.49% similarity)
  • Mauna Kea & Kilauea ↔ Mare Tranquillitatis: Expected negative control, ranked #3,787 (10.56% similarity — correctly identified as non-analog)

Creativity & Innovation

  1. Cross-Planetary Altimetric Normalization — Solves the multi-body datum problem by comparing detrended local relief rather than absolute altitude, which would fail across planets with different radiuses and no shared sea level.
  2. Aerospace-Grade Interactive UX — Features a cinematic Three.js 3D scene with a photorealistic rotating Earth, orbiting Moon, multi-colored twinkling starfield, and SpaceX-inspired bold typography — all rendered in real-time WebGL.
  3. Explainability-First AI — Instead of opaque deep learning that cannot explain its predictions, every similarity score provides an exact mathematical decomposition showing which terrain feature contributed to the match and by how much.
  4. Integrated Mission Planning — Goes beyond mere similarity discovery to provide operational rover traverse optimization using A* pathfinding with slope gradient constraints, directly supporting real mission hardware qualification.

Intended Impact

  • De-risks Planetary Hardware: Enables roboticists to test rovers and instruments on Earth terrains that mathematically mirror Martian and lunar environments.
  • Optimizes Mission Budgets: Eliminates wasteful ad-hoc field site scouting, saving aerospace programs significant logistical costs.
  • Accelerates Astronaut Training: Identifies accessible, geologically relevant training grounds for Artemis lunar surface crews.
  • Democratizes Planetary Science: Bridges open NASA/USGS data archives into an accessible, explainable tool for students, researchers, and space agencies worldwide.

Live Deployment

  • Frontend (Vercel): Globally distributed via Edge CDN with automatic HTTPS
  • Backend API (Render): Python FastAPI service with continuous deployment from GitHub
  • Source Code (GitHub): github.com/Karthick-2307/CASSINI-X

Developed by Team CASSINI-X | All planetary datasets courtesy of NASA, USGS Astrogeology Science Center, and AWS Open Data Registry.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

CropPulse directly addresses the challenge by moving beyond static farming traditions, giving farmers actionable insights to conserve water, naturally restore soil organic matter, break pest cycles, and mitigate extreme weather risks.

projectDetails.details:
Project Overview: Climate-Smart Crop Rotation Decision Support Tool

To address the compounding pressures of climate change, water scarcity, and degrading soil health, this project proposes an intelligent, data-driven decision-support platform designed for farmers, agronomists, and agricultural extension officers. The tool integrates NASA Earth observations, local soil properties, crop agronomic profiles, and individual farmer priorities to recommend and simulate optimal, resilient crop rotation strategies.

1. What It Does & How It Works

The platform functions as a digital agronomist that bridges global satellite data with hyper-local field realities:

  • NASA Earth Observations Integration: Pulls historical and real-time satellite data—such as precipitation anomalies, evapotranspiration rates (using MODIS/ECOSTRESS), soil moisture estimates (SMAP), and land surface temperature—to assess microclimate stresses and drought risks.
  • Local Soil & Environmental Profiling: Combines satellite insights with local data sources (like regional soil databases and optional on-farm sensor inputs) to evaluate baseline soil organic carbon, pH, texture, and nutrient retention capacity.
  • Agronomic Matching & Multi-Objective Optimization: Evaluates hundreds of potential crop rotation sequences against the user's specific goals (e.g., maximizing profit, minimizing water usage, building soil organic matter, or breaking pest cycles).
  • Scenario Simulation: Allows farmers to run "what-if" simulations comparing their current rotation against recommended regenerative alternatives under different climate scenarios.

2. Key Benefits

  • Water Conservation: Identifies drought-tolerant crops and deep-rooting cover crops that improve water infiltration and retention in moisture-stressed regions.
  • Soil Health Regeneration: Prioritizes crop diversity and legume integration to naturally fix nitrogen, reduce synthetic fertilizer dependency, and curb erosion.
  • Risk Mitigation: Helps farmers anticipate extreme weather vulnerabilities and diversify income sources across multiple harvest seasons.
  • User-Friendly Accessibility: Translates complex satellite datasets into actionable, localized insights via a simple mobile and web interface.

3. Intended Impact

  • Short-Term: Empower farmers to make immediate, confident planting decisions for the upcoming season that conserve water and input costs.
  • Long-Term: Build regional climate resilience, restore degraded agricultural soils, secure food security, and enhance the economic viability of small- and medium-scale farming operations.

4. Technology Stack & Development Tools

  • Data Sources & APIs: NASA Earth Data (MODIS, SMAP, ECOSTRESS), OpenWeather API, and global soil databases (e.g., SoilGrids).
  • Backend & Processing: Python (Flask/FastAPI) for core logic, rasterio/GDAL for geospatial data processing, and NumPy/Pandas for statistical analysis and optimization algorithms.
  • Frontend: React.js / React Native for cross-platform web and mobile accessibility, paired with Leaflet.js or Mapbox for interactive farm mapping.
  • Cloud & Infrastructure: Cloud-hosted geospatial processing pipelines to handle satellite data extraction efficiently.

5. Creativity & Innovation

  • Translating Macro to Micro: Most satellite tools remain locked in research papers; this project translates macro-scale orbital data into hyper-local, field-level recommendations.
  • Holistic Prioritization: Instead of focusing solely on yield maximization, the optimization engine balances ecological health (soil carbon, water conservation) with economic feasibility.
  • Dynamic Adaptation: Rather than static rotation templates, the system dynamically updates recommendations based on shifting seasonal weather forecasts derived from satellite telemetry.

6. Key Design Considerations

  • Data Accessibility in Rural Areas: Designed with offline caching and low-bandwidth considerations so farmers with intermittent internet connectivity can still access core recommendations.
  • Actionable Simplicity: Ensured that complex scientific metrics (like evapotranspiration anomalies or soil moisture indices) are presented as intuitive, easy-to-understand color-coded indicators and direct advice.
  • Socio-Economic Realities: Factored in local market access, seed availability, and equipment constraints so that recommended rotations are practically implementable, not just theoretically ideal.

projectDetails.details:
Abandoned but Not Forgotten: Storytelling About NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars

Project Overview:

Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive educational website designed to help young learners explore the spacecraft, rovers, landers and scientific instruments left behind on the Moon and Mars. The website uses two fictional young explorers, Anaya and Kabir, who guide children through an exciting space exploration journey using storytelling and character narration.

How It Works:

The website provides four interactive chapters through which users can explore different space artifacts. Each artifact includes images and educational information explaining its purpose and contribution to space exploration. Users can navigate between chapters, listen to character introductions and storytelling narration, view artifact images in full size and enjoy background music.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

The project makes space science easier and more enjoyable for children. It transforms complex scientific information into simple, interactive learning content. It aims to develop curiosity, improve awareness of historical space missions and inspire young learners to explore science, technology and space research.

Technologies Used:

- HTML – Website structure and content.

- CSS – Visual design, animations and responsive interface.

- JavaScript – Interactive features and navigation.

- Speech Synthesis API – Character voice narration.

- HTML Audio – Background music.

- Local Image Storage – Character and space artifact images.

Creativity and Innovation:

The creative aspect of this project is its storytelling approach. Instead of presenting space artifacts as ordinary scientific information, the website introduces them through two young explorers, Anaya and Kabir. The combination of character narration, interactive chapters, visual exploration and background music creates an engaging learning experience for children.

Factors Considered:

- Child-friendly design and simple navigation.

- Easy-to-understand educational information.

- Accessibility through a web browser.

- Interactive and engaging learning experience.

- Accurate representation of historical space artifacts.

- Use of images and audio to improve understanding.

Overall Impact:

Our project aims to remind young generations that even when space missions end, the equipment they leave behind continues to tell important stories about human curiosity, scientific discovery and exploration. It encourages children to look beyond Earth and become the next generation of space explorers.
