projectDetails.name: Field-Shift
projectDetails.summary: Field-Shift is a decision-support tool designed to help farmers pick their crop rotation. It uses NASA Earth observation data to guide these choices. Farmers input details about their farm and the current crop rotation. Field-Shift then evaluates at three strategies, including the one they are already using. It compares them using NASA POWER climate data along with Earth observation data like soil moisture and vegetation indices. The results are ranked based on what matters to the farmer—things like profit, water use, soil health or climate risk. The demo shows a farm near Coimbatore in Tamil Nadu. The app runs completely on -fetched static data so it loads quickly and does not need a backend. All the text is stored in a translations file making it easy to add Tamil. Field-Shift turns satellite data into side-by-side recommendations for crop rotation. It helps farmers move away from decisions made by habit and, toward data-driven choices.
projectDetails.details:
FieldShift helps farmers compare crop rotation options for the place they farm. They enter the two crops they currently grow, add what they know about their soil and water, and choose what matters most to them, such as saving water or protecting soil. The app compares the current rotation with other options and explains what influenced each result.

FieldShift uses NASA POWER climate records, GPM rainfall estimates and, when available, SMAP soil moisture data. It also draws on SoilGrids, MODIS, elevation data and a global crop calendar. The app summarizes past climate patterns and shows how much the results vary. These records can help people discuss possible choices, but they cannot predict a harvest or replace local knowledge. Map layers provide a wider regional view, not measurements of an individual field.

We built FieldShift with JavaScript, React and Vite. It uses Leaflet and Google Maps/Places for maps and location search, and Recharts for climate charts. The app runs in a browser and is hosted on GitHub Pages.

Our goal is to make climate information easier to use in conversations between farmers and local advisors. Farmers can see why an option scored well or poorly and which details still need checking, such as crop calendars, soil tests, water access or local prices. FieldShift is an early decision-support tool, so its crop assumptions and scoring rules still need to be reviewed with farmers and agricultural experts.

projectDetails.name: TerraTrend - Earth System Trend Explorer
projectDetails.summary:
TerraTrend is an interactive Earth-system trend exploration platform developed by CODEVERSE'26 for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 - “Be an Earth System Trend Detective.”

Using historical environmental data from NASA POWER,TerraTrend enables users to explore changes at selected locations and across regional grid cells.It supports variables including near surface temperature,maximum and minimum temperature,precipitation,wind speed,relative humidity and surface solar irradiance.

The platform visualizes temporal patterns and geographic trends, estimates trend magnitude using Sen's slope, and evaluates monotonic trends using Mann-Kendall statistics. Regional analysis also incorporates Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate filtering to help interpret multiple grid-cell comparisons.

TerraTrend helps users investigate what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and whether statistical evidence supports the observed trend. It is designed as an exploratory tool for students, educators and researchers, not as an operational forecast or an official NASA product.
projectDetails.details:
Overview

TerraTrend is a NASA data-driven Earth-system trend exploration platform built to make historical environmental changes easier to investigate, visualize and interpret.

How it works

The application combines a Next.js frontend with a Python FastAPI backend. Users can select environmental variables and locations, explore historical time-series behaviour, and inspect regional grid-cell trends through interactive charts and geographic maps.

The platform supports seven environmental variables:

  • Temperature at 2 metres (T2M)
  • Maximum temperature (T2M_MAX)
  • Minimum temperature (T2M_MIN)
  • Corrected precipitation (PRECTOTCORR)
  • Wind speed at 10 metres (WS10M)
  • Surface solar downward irradiance (ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN)
  • Relative humidity at 2 metres (RH2M)

Historical data are accessed through the NASA POWER Monthly and Annual API. Meteorological variables primarily use NASA GMAO MERRA-2 data, while solar radiation products have their own NASA source lineage, including CERES and related radiation datasets.

Scientific analysis

The Python analysis engine uses:

  • Sen's slope estimation to quantify trend magnitude.
  • Mann-Kendall statistical testing to evaluate monotonic trends.
  • Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate control for regional multiple-grid-cell analysis.
  • Data cleaning and missing-value handling before statistical computation.

Results are presented through time-series charts, regional maps and statistical indicators.

Technology stack

Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript and Tailwind CSS.

Visualization: Recharts, Leaflet and React Leaflet.

Backend: Python, FastAPI and Pydantic.

Scientific computing: NumPy, pandas, SciPy and pyMannKendall.

Intended impact

TerraTrend aims to make Earth-system data exploration more accessible to students, educators, researchers and people interested in environmental change. It provides a common interface to investigate the direction, magnitude, geographic distribution and statistical evidence of historical environmental trends.

Limitations and scientific transparency

TerraTrend is an exploratory research and educational prototype. NASA POWER products have their own spatial resolutions, temporal coverage and uncertainties. Regional rectangular selections should not be interpreted as exact administrative boundaries, and estimated trends should not automatically be interpreted as causal relationships or forecasts.

Use of AI tools

AI-assisted tools, including ChatGPT, OpenAI Codex and Google Antigravity, were used during software development for coding assistance, debugging, documentation and technical review. The team reviewed and integrated the resulting work. Environmental observations and data values are sourced from NASA POWER; they are not AI-generated.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: TerraCycle
projectDetails.summary:
TerraCycle is an intelligent agricultural decision-support platform that combines NASA satellite observations, local soil information, historical climate patterns, and artificial intelligence to recommend sustainable crop-rotation strategies.

The platform analyses rainfall variability, soil moisture, temperature fluctuations, vegetation health, and seasonal environmental changes to identify agricultural vulnerabilities.

Farmers can select their agricultural land, enter existing crop sequences, provide soil information, and specify their priorities. The platform generates at least three crop-rotation strategies, including the farmer's existing rotation, and compares them based on soil health improvement, water conservation, climate resilience, erosion reduction, and economic suitability.

Using explainable machine learning and multi-objective optimization, TerraCycle provides evidence-based recommendations, risk assessments, and long-term agricultural planning insights.

The objective is to transform complex NASA Earth observation data into understandable and actionable agricultural intelligence while keeping farmers and agricultural experts in control of final decisions
projectDetails.details:
A. What exactly does the project do?

TerraCycle addresses the problem of selecting suitable crop rotations under changing environmental conditions.

It provides five major capabilities.

1. Satellite-Based Agricultural Intelligence

The system collects and processes NASA Earth observation datasets to understand environmental conditions surrounding agricultural fields.

It analyses:

  • Historical rainfall patterns.
  • Temperature variations.
  • Soil moisture anomalies.
  • Vegetation health.
  • Seasonal agricultural productivity patterns.
  • Periods of potential water stress.
  • Seasonal bare-field windows.

2. Soil Health Assessment

Farmers can enter their local soil-test information, including:

  • Soil pH.
  • Nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium.
  • Organic carbon.
  • Soil texture.
  • Water-holding capacity.
  • Electrical conductivity.

The platform combines these measurements with environmental observations to assess soil-related constraints.

It also estimates potential soil-health benefits from different rotation strategies using crop characteristics such as nitrogen fixation, root depth, biomass production, and residue retention.

Importantly, satellite data alone cannot directly establish soil nutrient concentrations or organic carbon levels. Laboratory measurements are used for these parameters.

3. Intelligent Crop Rotation Recommendation

The platform generates three or more rotation strategies:

Strategy

Crop Rotation Concept

Expected Benefits

Strategy 1

Existing farmer rotation

Baseline for comparison

Strategy 2

Cereal–legume rotation

Nitrogen fixation and crop diversification

Strategy 3

Main crop–legume cover crop rotation

Soil cover and organic matter contributions

Strategy 4

Drought-tolerant crop rotation

Potential reduction in water demand and improved climate resilience

Crop selections are filtered according to local growing seasons, soil characteristics, irrigation availability, and market suitability.

4. Climate Risk Assessment

The platform identifies agricultural vulnerabilities by analyzing historical environmental patterns.

Examples include:

  • Increasing temperature during critical crop-growth periods.
  • Declining seasonal soil moisture.
  • Irregular rainfall distribution.
  • Extended dry spells.
  • Abnormal vegetation stress.
  • Potential erosion vulnerability.

It highlights periods when the current crop rotation may become increasingly vulnerable.

5. Interactive Agricultural Simulator

Farmers can modify environmental conditions and explore different agricultural scenarios.

For example:

  • What happens if seasonal rainfall decreases by 20%?
  • What happens if average temperature increases by 2°C?
  • Which crop rotation is more suitable under water scarcity?
  • Which rotation provides better soil cover during dry periods?
  • Which strategy offers better long-term resilience?

The simulator recalculates strategy scores based on the modified assumptions. These are scenario explorations, not guaranteed climate forecasts.

B. How does the system work?

The proposed system follows a six-stage architecture.

Stage

Process

Function

1

Data Acquisition

Collect NASA satellite and local agricultural information

2

Data Processing

Clean, process, and harmonize geospatial datasets

3

Feature Extraction

Calculate rainfall anomalies, temperature stress, vegetation indices, and soil moisture indicators

4

AI/ML Analysis

Identify historical patterns and environmental vulnerabilities

5

Optimization Engine

Generate and rank suitable crop-rotation strategies

6

Visualization

Display recommendations, risk indicators, and scenario comparisons

Proposed system architecture:

NASA Earth Data + Local Soil Data + Farmer Inputs

↓

Geospatial Data Processing

↓

Environmental Feature Extraction

↓

Machine Learning and Climate Pattern Analysis

↓

Multi-Objective Crop Rotation Optimization

↓

Recommendation and Risk Assessment Engine

↓

Interactive Farmer Dashboard

C. What makes the project intelligent?

The main innovation is the Multi-Objective Crop Rotation Optimization Engine.

Instead of recommending crops based on a single parameter, the system evaluates multiple agricultural objectives simultaneously.

The optimization model evaluates:

Parameter

Evaluation

Soil Health

Nitrogen fixation, residue contribution, root characteristics

Water Conservation

Seasonal water requirements and irrigation availability

Climate Resilience

Temperature and rainfall suitability

Erosion Reduction

Soil cover duration and terrain-related vulnerability

Economic Suitability

Market demand, cultivation cost, and farmer preferences

Crop Diversification

Crop-family diversity and potential pest-cycle interruption

A weighted scoring algorithm is used:

\[ R=\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_iS_i \]

Where:

  • \(R\) = Overall rotation suitability score.
  • \(w_i\) = Weight assigned to each agricultural objective.
  • \(S_i\) = Normalized score for each objective.
  • \(n\) = Number of evaluation parameters.

The weights are adjustable according to farmer priorities.

For example, a farmer facing water shortages can assign greater importance to water conservation, while another farmer may prioritize soil improvement or economic returns.

Agronomic constraints, such as unsuitable soil conditions and growing-season incompatibility, are applied before ranking.

The system also explains why each recommendation received its score.

D. What hardware, software, or tools are used?

Component

Proposed Technology

Frontend

React.js / Next.js

Backend

Python / FastAPI

Machine Learning

Scikit-learn

Optimization

Python, NumPy, SciPy

Geospatial Processing

Rasterio, GeoPandas

Satellite Data Processing

Google Earth Engine

NASA Data Access

NASA Earthdata APIs

Climate Data

NASA POWER API

Database

PostgreSQL + PostGIS

Interactive Maps

Leaflet / Mapbox

Data Visualization

Plotly

Deployment

Vercel / Cloud Infrastructure

Hardware requirements:

The initial prototype requires no specialized agricultural hardware.

A laptop or desktop computer and internet connection are sufficient.

Optional integration with ground-based soil moisture sensors and weather stations can improve field-level validation.

projectDetails.name: ASTRA – Astronaut Smart Tracking, Risk Assessment & Assistance
projectDetails.summary:
**ASTRA – Astronaut Smart Tracking, Risk Assessment & Assistance** is an AI-assisted astronaut health monitoring and decision-support platform designed for long-duration space missions. It integrates health data from sensors, manual self-assessments, and historical records to help astronauts monitor key indicators such as heart rate, SpO₂, body temperature, sleep, physical activity, mood, and stress.

ASTRA analyzes changes against an individual's health baseline, highlights unusual trends, and presents understandable insights through an interactive dashboard. It also connects health indicators with the five hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity fields, and hostile environments. The platform provides alerts, preventive-care suggestions, and guidance on when to seek medical support.

By combining Embedded Systems, IoT, Python-based analytics, and AI-assisted assessment, ASTRA aims to make astronaut health monitoring more accessible, informative, and proactive. It supports crew self-awareness and informed decision-making when immediate medical assistance from Earth may be limited.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRA is an AI-assisted astronaut health monitoring and decision-support platform designed to support crew members during long-duration space missions. It addresses the challenges of monitoring physical and psychological health in an environment affected by space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity fields, and hostile closed environments.

How it works: ASTRA collects health information through sensor-based inputs, manual self-assessments, and historical health records. It monitors indicators such as heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), body temperature, physical activity, sleep duration, mood, and stress. The system analyzes measurements against an astronaut's personal health baseline, identifies unusual variations, visualizes trends, and generates understandable health insights, alerts, and preventive-care recommendations. Its interactive dashboard enables astronauts to review their health status and determine when medical support may be needed.

Benefits and intended impact: ASTRA promotes proactive health awareness, supports early identification of unusual health trends, organizes health information, and helps astronauts make informed decisions when immediate medical assistance from Earth may be limited. Its offline-first design direction also supports operation in communication-constrained environments.

Technology and tools: The software prototype uses React.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Python, FastAPI, SQLite, SQLAlchemy, NumPy, Pandas, and Scikit-learn. The proposed hardware integration uses an ESP32 microcontroller with MAX30102, MPU6050, and suitable temperature sensors. MQTT and REST APIs provide communication between the hardware and software. A simulated telemetry mode allows the application to be demonstrated without physical hardware.

Creativity and innovation: ASTRA combines embedded sensing, IoT, AI-assisted personal-baseline analysis, interactive health visualization, and spaceflight hazard awareness in one platform. Rather than displaying raw measurements alone, it aims to explain health changes and provide actionable guidance.

Engineering considerations: Our team considered sensor limitations, data reliability, personal health variations, privacy, offline operation, usability, and the need for explainable alerts. ASTRA is designed as a decision-support prototype and does not replace professional medical assessment or mission-specific medical protocols.

projectDetails.name: Astra-Mind
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRA-MIND is a prototype health monitoring platform for astronauts on long-duration space missions. It tracks five domains: cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, immune, behavioral and radiation. A FastAPI backend and SQLite database store every measurement with a data-provenance tag, and a live dashboard shows current values and trends.

It addresses the challenge in four ways:

It learns each astronaut’s personal baseline instead of relying on population thresholds.
It flags deviations and links alerts that appear across several domains at once.
It forecasts the next 24 hours with a stated uncertainty range.
It summarises overall status as a digital twin score.

It keeps working through communication outages. Data and alerts queue onboard, then sync to an Earth-side view once the link returns.

This matters because crews on deep-space missions will face delayed contact and limited medical support, so early, personalised, offline-capable monitoring could help catch problems sooner.

All data here is synthetic, and the scores show deviation from baseline, not diagnoses. They need medical review.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

ASTRA-MIND is a prototype that monitors an astronaut’s health on a long mission. It simulates ten signals across five domains: cardiovascular, musculoskeletal, immune, behavioral and radiation. A live dashboard shows current values, trends and alerts.

  1. Data: a generator produces hourly synthetic readings for each crew member, including slower periodic assessments such as blood markers.
  2. Storage: a FastAPI backend saves every raw measurement in SQLite with a provenance tag (SYNTHETIC) and a synced flag.
  3. Baseline: each person’s normal range is learned from their first 72 hours.
  4. Alerts: readings far from that baseline are flagged. When several domains deviate together, a combined cross-domain alert lists the supporting observations.
  5. Forecast: a 24-hour projection comes with a 90% uncertainty range.
  6. Digital twin: a score per domain and overall summarises current status.
  7. Offline mode: during a simulated communications outage, monitoring continues onboard and data queues locally. After reconnection the queue syncs to the Earth-side view.

Benefits

  • Alerts are personalised, so each astronaut is compared with their own normal instead of population thresholds.
  • Monitoring does not depend on a live link to Earth.
  • Alerts come with the observations behind them, so they are explainable.
  • Raw data is preserved and labelled by origin.

Intended impact

The aim is to help flight surgeons and crews notice health drift sooner on missions where medical support and communication are limited. It is a decision-support concept, not a diagnostic tool.

Tools and technology

  • Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML and CSS.
  • Backend: FastAPI with Uvicorn, and SQLite.
  • Frontend: a plain browser dashboard with hand-drawn SVG charts and no external libraries.
  • Statistics: median and MAD baselines, robust z-scores, and Holt damped-trend forecasting.
  • Testing: pytest, with 3 passing tests.
  • Hardware: only an ordinary computer. There are no real sensors, because all data is simulated.

What is creative about it

  • It joins three ideas in one lightweight tool: personal baselines, cross-domain alert linking, and a single digital twin status score.
  • The offline-first design treats a communications blackout as the normal case.
  • Every data point carries its provenance, so simulated and real data can never be confused.

Factors considered

  • Safety: scores are deviations from baseline, not disease probabilities, and nothing is presented as a diagnosis. Medical review is required.
  • Honesty about data: everything is clearly labelled synthetic.
  • Resource limits: it uses simple statistical methods that run anywhere, even without internet, instead of large models.
  • Demonstrability: injected events and a communications outage button let the system be shown end to end.
  • Known gaps: Isolation Forest, Chronos-2, a medical assistant with retrieval over NASA documents, and a React frontend are planned but not built.

projectDetails.name: LIGHTTIME
projectDetails.summary:
LIGHTTIME is a human-centred autonomous lunar mission simulator designed to explore the challenges of sustaining human life on the Moon. We developed an interactive 3D lunar mission environment where users manage a 30-day mission with a four-member crew. The simulator includes habitat resource monitoring, crew health and wellbeing indicators, rover exploration, sample collection, mission operations and emergency response scenarios.
By integrating NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LOLA) illumination dataset, LIGHTTIME also visualizes lunar polar illumination conditions, helping users understand how sunlight availability influences lunar mission planning.
The project addresses the challenge of planning sustainable human operations in the lunar environment by combining scientific lunar data, resource management and interactive mission simulation. It is important because future lunar exploration will require careful coordination of crew safety, limited resources, environmental conditions and autonomous decision-making. LIGHTTIME provides an engaging platform to explore these challenges.
projectDetails.details:
LIGHTTIME – Project Details

1. What does it do?

LIGHTTIME is a human-centred lunar mission simulator that allows users to manage a 30-day Moon mission with a four-member crew. It features a 3D lunar environment, resource monitoring, crew wellbeing tracking, rover exploration, sample collection and emergency response scenarios. It also visualizes NASA LOLA lunar illumination data.

2. What are its benefits?

It helps users understand lunar mission challenges, including resource management, crew safety, environmental conditions and exploration operations through interactive simulation.

3. What is its intended impact?

To promote awareness of sustainable human exploration beyond Earth and demonstrate the importance of combining technology, scientific data and human wellbeing in future space missions.

4. What technologies were used?

- TypeScript, JavaScript, React and CSS

- Three.js, React Three Fiber and Drei

- Framer Motion

- NASA LOLA scientific dataset and NASA 3D assets

- Visual Studio Code, GitHub and Vercel

5. How is it creative?

It combines 3D lunar visualization, mission management, crew wellbeing and scientific NASA data into one interactive experience, allowing users to explore mission decisions rather than simply read about them.

6. What factors did the team consider?

Crew safety, oxygen and water availability, power management, psychological wellbeing, lunar illumination, rover exploration, emergency handling and user experience.

projectDetails.name: GlobeLens
projectDetails.summary: Our website GlobeLens provides a way to look into changes within the environment. They can search up a factor they wish to look at, a location and when they want to look at how the data has changed. Using graphs, maps and statistics we have provided a way to easily visualise how temperature, rainfall and more have changed. This was created as environmental data can often be messy and difficult for people to understand. GlobeLens can be used by students, researchers, environmental analysts and the general public. We want to help give people knowledge on how the earth is changing and why it is important to monitor.
projectDetails.details:
GlobeLens is a web application that allows users to look into how the environment has changed in different parts of the world. We wanted to create this as environmental data whilst easy to find can be very difficult to understand. Most data is stored in large data sets or technical reports and so someone wanting to know how the rainfall in their city has changed over the years would struggle to find the answer. We wanted to solve this issue.

Users can easily navigate the website by selecting what environmental factor they want to look at (temperature, rainfall etc.), then select a location and time frame. The data will then be retrieved and displayed using:

Graphs: showing how the value has changed over time. Increasing, decreasing or staying the same. Maps: allowing users to select where they want to look at. Statistics: allowing users to get a quick overview of the data. Showing averages, maximum/minimum values and overall change during the time frame selected.

GlobeLens has been designed to be used by 4 different types of users. Students can use it to view real data rather than just reading about it in textbooks. Researchers can use it to get an initial overview of trends within a region. Environmental analysts can use it to monitor changes across different locations and time frames. And finally the general public can use it to satisfy their curiosity and learn more about what is going on around them. We wanted this to be simple for new users but still provide useful information.

For the frontend we used React, Vite, JavaScript and TailwindCSS. React allowed us to create reusable components, Vite allowed for quick builds and TailwindCSS allowed us to create a clean and responsive layout. For the backend we used Python and FastAPI. This will receive the request from the frontend, process the data and return the results. FastAPI was chosen as it is quick and easy to use when creating an API. Python is great for working with data and calculations.

We also used a few libraries. Chart.js for the graphs, Leaflet for the interactive maps and Axios for communication between the frontend and backend.

We had some issues whilst creating this project. Firstly making sure the scientific data was easy to understand. As environmental data can sometimes be quite large and confusing we made sure our layout was clean and the most important information was shown. Secondly making sure the frontend and backend were linked correctly so the correct data was shown when changing the factors, locations and time frames. We tested each section to ensure they are all reacting correctly.

We feel this project is important as raising awareness is the first step to taking action. By being able to see how temperature and rainfall have changed in their region makes this a real and personal topic for them. Helping them understand how important it is to monitor the environment.

Going forward we would like to add more environmental factors, the ability to compare 2 locations, download data and more in depth statistical tools for more advanced users.

Overall GlobeLens is our attempt to simplify environmental data. By providing graphs, maps and statistics we hope to help users look into how the earth is changing and raise awareness of our world.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

projectDetails.name: Lunaris - Lunar Landing Site Navigator
projectDetails.summary: Lunaris is a free web app that helps mission planners choose where and when to land near the Moon's south pole. There, the Sun skims only a degree or two above the horizon, so a ridge kilometres away can decide whether a lander gets solar power or can talk to Earth. Lunaris traces each site's real horizon from NASA's LOLA laser-altimeter terrain and combines it with JPL ephemerides. For any site and landing date it shows when the Sun is visible, how much power a solar panel would produce, when Earth is in view, and when a direct radio link through NASA's Deep Space Network is possible. Up to four site-and-date scenarios can be compared side by side: a plain-language summary, a 360° sky view, lit 3D terrain with live shadows, a timeline, and a full numbers table. Any comparison can be shared with one link. Lunaris turns heavy orbital and terrain geometry into answers anyone on a team can read in seconds, which matters as Artemis and other missions target the pole's few well-lit, Earth-facing spots.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunaris compares lunar landing sites and dates by what a lander can actually see from the surface: the Sun, for power, and Earth, for communication.

Pick up to four scenarios, each a site plus a landing date and mission length:

• curated sites: Artemis III candidate areas such as Connecting Ridge and Malapert Massif, the Chang'e-7 target, IM-2 Athena, and permanently shadowed craters;

• contrast sites: Apollo, Chandrayaan-3 and Chang'e-4;

• or any point dropped on a zoomable south-pole map.

For each one, Lunaris shows:

• Summary: sunlight, Earth in view and radio link to Earth as percentages, plus one plain sentence.

• Sky view: the real 360° skyline around the site, with the Sun's and Earth's paths and current positions, labelled when hidden by terrain.

• 3D terrain: the south pole lit by the real Sun direction at the chosen moment, with live shadows and site markers.

• Timeline: every window of sunlight, Earth visibility and radio link over the mission.

• All numbers:

◦ countdowns ("Sets in 3 days 4 hours");

◦ period totals and the longest night;

◦ average solar power and total energy for three panel orientations;

◦ a CSV download of every time step.

One time control drives every view, and Share copies a link that reopens the exact comparison.

HOW IT WORKS

• Sun and Earth positions: NASA JPL's DE440 ephemeris through Skyfield, in the Moon's mean-Earth frame (NAIF lunar frame kernels), so libration is included. Checked against JPL Horizons: the largest difference in 12 checks was 0.0038°.

• Terrain horizon: from NASA's LRO LOLA polar elevation model (LDEM_80S_80M, 80 m per pixel). For 720 directions around each site, we trace the true great circle out to 150 km and keep the highest elevation angle, including the Moon's curvature.

• Visibility: the visible share of the Sun's disk above the local horizon. Earth counts as in view when at least half its disk clears the terrain.

• Radio link: Earth must be in view from the site, and at least one Deep Space Network complex (Goldstone, Madrid or Canberra) must see the Moon at 10° or more.

• Power: 1361 W/m², scaled by Sun distance, visible disk share and panel angle, for a 1 m² panel at 30% efficiency. The panel can be upright and Sun-tracking, flat, or fixed facing north.

• Sanity checks:

◦ Shackleton's floor gets 0% sunlight.

◦ Connecting Ridge gets 100% in December 2026 and 38% in June 2027.

◦ Chang'e-4, on the far side, never sees Earth.

◦ Apollo 11 gets about 50% sunlight.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

At the pole, small differences decide a mission. In December 2026, Connecting Ridge is sunlit 100% of the time and could collect about 303 kWh from a 1 m² panel over a month, while Shackleton's floor next to it gets nothing. Moving a few kilometres, or landing a month later, changes everything.

Lunaris makes these trade-offs visible in seconds without specialist software. Engineers, students and the public can test "what if we land here, or later?" and share the answer. We hope it helps teams shortlist sites and dates early, and helps people understand why the lunar south pole is so hard and so valuable.

WHAT MAKES IT CREATIVE

It turns heavy geometry into views anyone can read: a skyline "from the lander's eyes", a lit 3D pole, and plain sentences instead of raw angles. It is built for comparison: several sites and dates side by side, synced to one clock and shareable as a link. An interactive 8-step tutorial teaches the app by doing.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

• Accuracy: checked against JPL Horizons and published heights.

• Honest limits: no boulders under 80 m, and no relay satellites or heat modelling. Sites outside the polar terrain model are flagged.

• Readability: plain words, a highly legible font, and keyboard access.

• Speed: horizons are precomputed for curated sites and cached; custom pins are computed on demand.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

• Backend: Python (FastAPI, Skyfield, NumPy), hosted on Render.

• Frontend: TypeScript, React, Vite, zustand and three.js (react-three-fiber), hosted on Vercel.

• Demo video: Playwright (capturing the live site) and Remotion.

• Open source (Apache-2.0): https://github.com/AryanKingSir/lunar-landing-site-navigator

projectDetails.name: ASTRO LIFE
projectDetails.summary:
Astro Life is an immersive, STEM-infused gaming simulation set in a lunar outpost. We developed a narrative-driven game following a 16-year-old resident named Dorothy, where players resolve time-sensitive crises like micro-meteorite leaks and life-support fluctuations while piloting lunar rovers for sample collection.

The project addresses the EdTech challenge of educational tools being either too superficial or overwhelmingly technical by striking a balance between real science and engaging gameplay. Players apply genuine scientific and engineering solutions—such as closed-loop recycling and radiation shielding—through a rewarding upgrade and survival cycle.

This project is important because it transforms complex aerospace concepts into an interactive, emotionally resonant experience. By gamifying critical thinking and practical problem-solving, it fosters a deeper, lasting connection to STEM for students.
projectDetails.details: Astro Life is an immersive, STEM-infused gaming simulation designed to make space science genuinely exciting and approachable for students. Set in a lunar outpost through the eyes of a 16-year-old resident named Dorothy, the game strikes a perfect balance—avoiding overly dry technical jargon while steering clear of superficial science that lacks real educational value. Players dive into hands-on problem-solving by managing life-support systems, upgrading base defenses against solar flares and moon dust, and piloting rovers across hazardous lunar craters to collect samples. By gamifying realistic aerospace challenges like power grid management and closed-loop recycling into a rewarding upgrade cycle, Astro Life turns complex survival mechanics into an engaging, emotionally resonant learning experience.

projectDetails.name: Echoes from the Dust: An Interactive 3D Museum of NASA’s Forgotten Machines
projectDetails.summary: Echoes from the Dust is an interactive 3D web museum designed to introduce school-age space enthusiasts to the historic spacecraft, rovers, and landers NASA has left across the Moon and Mars. By transforming planetary coordinates into a navigable celestial globe with first-person machine diaries, the platform turns distant space hardware into accessible stories of scientific discovery.
projectDetails.details: The Problem & Vision Since the 1960s, NASA has left dozens of pioneering machines on the Moon, Mars, and deep space. To many young students, these deactivated landers and rovers seem like distant relics or forgotten hardware. Echoes from the Dust reframes these machines as enduring pioneers that unlocked humanity’s understanding of the solar system. ​How It Works Built as a lightweight, browser-based 3D interactive museum, the application allows students to: ​Explore Celestial Worlds in 3D: Users can freely rotate, zoom, and switch between high-resolution 3D globes of Mars and The Moon, rendered with authentic NASA planetary surface maps. ​Inspect Real Landing Coordinates: Glowing interactive beacons mark the exact latitude and longitude where historic missions touched down—including the Opportunity Rover at Endeavour Crater, Viking 1 at Chryse Planitia, the Apollo 11 Descent Stage in the Sea of Tranquility, and the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle at Hadley Rille. ​Read First-Person Machine Logs: Clicking any beacon opens an exhibit card featuring a first-person narrative written from the perspective of the hardware itself, making space history emotionally engaging and easy for K–12 students to grasp. ​Discover the Science Legacy: Each exhibit translates complex instrumentation into clear takeaways—explaining how Opportunity found evidence of ancient Martian water through hematite "blueberries," how Apollo 11’s laser retroreflectors are still used today to measure the Moon's distance, and how early landers paved the way for human exploration. ​Technical Stack & NASA Open Data ​Frontend & 3D Graphics: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and Three.js (WebGL) for real-time 3D spherical rendering, raycasting pin selection, and orbital camera controls. ​NASA Data & Resources: Utilizes NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) and Mars surface imagery, along with authentic mission landing coordinates and historical mission logs. ​Impact By combining interactive 3D visualization with empathetic storytelling, Echoes from the Dust requires zero installation and works on any classroom computer or mobile browser—inspiring the next generation of engineers, scientists, and space explorers.

projectDetails.name: ORBIT-X
projectDetails.summary:
**ORBIT-X – Space Mission Design & Simulation**

ORBIT-X is an interactive 3D space mission design and simulation platform that makes aerospace engineering concepts accessible through an immersive, hands-on experience. It allows users to design and configure spacecraft by selecting structural components, propulsion systems, fuel, power systems, communication equipment, and scientific instruments while managing mass, power consumption, and mission budgets.

The platform guides users through spacecraft validation, launch preparation, rocket launch simulation, stage separation, orbital insertion, and mission operations. It features three progressive missions: Lunar Explorer, Earth Observer, and Mars Pathfinder. Real-time flight telemetry, mission objectives, performance analysis, and an AI-powered assistant help users understand engineering decisions and correct design mistakes.

ORBIT-X addresses the challenge of making complex space mission concepts easier to explore, understand, and simulate through an engaging, educational 3D environment.
projectDetails.details: ORBIT-X is an interactive, science-first space-mission design game. Players choose Lunar Explorer, Earth Observer, or Mars Pathfinder, then build a spacecraft from modular structure, propulsion, propellant, power, communications, and science-instrument components. Live engineering indicators show how mass, cost, power balance, payload fit, and delta-v change with each design decision. Players validate a launch vehicle, follow a 3D launch and telemetry timeline, manage mission anomalies, make operational decisions, and receive a scored debrief. A shared-screen hot-seat mode supports up to four team roles, while password-free judge routes let reviewers explore mission stages and selected failure scenarios. ORBIT-X was built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js, React Three Fiber, and Zustand, with optional Supabase cloud sync and a Gemini-powered flight advisor. NASA imagery, 3D assets, and published mission and planetary references ground selected visuals and model checks. The intended impact is to make spacecraft engineering trade-offs more understandable to students and educators through hands-on experimentation. The simulation is educational, not engineering-certified: ascent follows a reference telemetry spline, orbits are simplified, and radio links use a simplified link budget.

projectDetails.name: Project Energy1goal1
projectDetails.summary: The research investigates the application of NASA POWER satellite-based climate data for monitoring peanut crop development and predicting pod maturity in agricultural regions where ground-based weather stations are unavailable. The study compares satellite-derived climate information with observations from conventional meteorological stations across four peanut-producing fields in Georgia, USA. Different climatic parameters, including maximum, minimum and average temperatures, solar radiation, relative humidity, wind speed and surface pressure, were examined using statistical techniques such as correlation analysis, linear regression and Principal Component Analysis (PCA). The findings indicate that temperature and solar radiation data obtained from NASA POWER provide reliable estimates and demonstrate meaningful relationships with peanut pod maturity. However, wind speed and relative humidity show comparatively lower accuracy due to spatial resolution and measurement variations. Overall, the research establishes NASA POWER as a useful alternative for agricultural climate monitoring and crop management, particularly in locations without conventional meteorological infrastructure.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does the project do or how does it work?

This project utilizes NASA POWER satellite-based meteorological data to monitor climatic conditions and estimate peanut crop maturity in regions without conventional weather stations. It collects climatic parameters such as maximum and minimum temperatures, average temperature, solar radiation, relative humidity, wind speed and surface pressure. These data are compared with ground-based weather observations using statistical techniques, including correlation analysis, linear regression and Principal Component Analysis (PCA), to identify the climatic factors influencing peanut pod maturity.

2. What benefits does it have?

The project provides accessible and cost-effective climatic information without requiring weather stations near every agricultural field. It helps farmers understand crop development, improve harvesting decisions and adopt data-driven agricultural practices. The approach can also be extended to agricultural regions with limited meteorological infrastructure.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The main objective is to improve agricultural decision-making through satellite-based climate monitoring. It aims to reduce dependence on conventional weather monitoring systems, provide useful climatic information to farmers and encourage sustainable farming practices through scientific analysis and technology.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware or software were used?

NASA POWER was used to obtain satellite-based climatic data. Python and Jupyter Notebook were employed for data processing, correlation analysis and visualization. SAS JMP Pro 14 was used for statistical analysis and regression modelling, while R software (version 2023.06.2) with the factoextra package was used for Principal Component Analysis. Microsoft Excel 2013 was used to prepare graphs. Existing surface weather stations provided reference measurements, and peanut fields were used for crop maturity assessment. No new physical hardware device was developed.

5. How is your project creative?

The innovative aspect is the integration of freely available NASA satellite data with agricultural crop maturity assessment. Instead of depending entirely on physical weather stations, the research uses remote climate information and statistical modelling to understand crop development. Applying PCA to identify important climatic variables further strengthens the research approach.

6. What factors did your team consider?

The study considered temperature, solar radiation, relative humidity, wind speed, surface pressure, peanut pod maturity, geographical location, seasonal variations, data accuracy and satellite spatial resolution. Data from four peanut-producing locations in Georgia, USA, collected during 2018 and 2019, were evaluated to assess the reliability of NASA POWER information.

projectDetails.name: Echoes Beyond Earth
projectDetails.summary:
Echoes Beyond Earth is an interactive 3D educational experience that explores the legacy of NASA's spacecraft, landers, and scientific equipment left across the Solar System. From the Apollo Lunar Module and Lunar Roving Vehicles on the Moon to the Viking 1 Lander and Sojourner Rover on Mars, and Voyager 1 travelling through interstellar space, the platform brings these historic missions back into focus.

Users can explore destinations, discover individual artifacts, understand their scientific purpose, follow mission timelines, and experience engaging stories based on historical facts. Through immersive 3D visualizations, interactive exploration, and accessible storytelling, the project transforms complex space-history information into an engaging digital museum.

The project addresses the challenge by making NASA's scattered space heritage easier to discover, understand, and appreciate. It highlights not only what humanity sent into space, but also the discoveries, engineering achievements, and scientific legacy these machines represent. Echoes Beyond Earth aims to preserve the stories of these extraordinary missions and inspire the next generation of space explorers.
projectDetails.details:
Echoes Beyond Earth – Project Details

Echoes Beyond Earth is an interactive digital space museum developed to explore the legacy of NASA hardware that remains on celestial bodies or continues travelling through space. The project focuses on three exploration regions: the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space.

The experience features six historical space artifacts:

1. Apollo 11 Lunar Module Descent Stage – the component of the lunar module that delivered astronauts to the lunar surface and remains there.

2. Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicles – the vehicles used during Apollo 15, 16, and 17 to support lunar surface exploration.

3. Viking 1 Lander – the first successful US Mars lander, which conducted experiments and transmitted data from the Martian surface.

4. Sojourner Rover – the first successful Mars rover, deployed during the Mars Pathfinder mission in 1997.

5. Mars Pathfinder Lander – the robotic lander that delivered Sojourner and conducted experiments on Mars.

6. Voyager 1 – the spacecraft launched in 1977 that travelled beyond the heliosphere and entered interstellar space.

Users can explore these destinations, inspect individual artifacts, understand why each mission was launched, learn about scientific objectives and discoveries, and examine the operational status of the equipment. The planned interactive experience combines a 3D solar system environment, artifact exploration, mission timelines, educational storytelling, and knowledge quizzes.

The project's distinctive approach is to connect historical NASA missions through an immersive visual experience instead of presenting them as disconnected articles. It also distinguishes equipment left on planetary surfaces from spacecraft that are still travelling through space.

Google Antigravity is used as the AI-assisted development environment, with web technologies and interactive 3D components forming the development approach.

The project aims to make space exploration history accessible to students and the public, increase awareness of scientific and engineering achievements, and preserve the educational value of humanity's robotic and crewed missions.

projectDetails.summary: PROJECT ASTRA is an AI-powered space mission training and operations platform designed to make space exploration education more interactive and accessible. projectDetails.details:
PROJECT ASTRA is an AI-powered space mission training and operations platform designed to make space exploration education more accessible and interactive.

The platform combines three major components:

  1. Astronaut Training Centre: Provides interactive educational training scenarios related to astronaut operations, planetary exploration and simulated emergency situations.
  2. AI Mission Control: Provides a centralized dashboard to monitor simulated mission telemetry, including oxygen levels, temperature, battery status, power generation and mission events.
  3. Planetary Digital Twin: Provides an interactive digital representation of Moon and Mars environments, including research habitats, planetary terrain and life-support systems.

ASTRA AI acts as an educational assistant to help users understand space science, mission systems and simulated telemetry.

The platform is developed using modern web technologies, including TypeScript, JavaScript, React and Vite, along with supporting libraries and tools used in the implementation.

Our goal is to create an educational environment where students can explore astronaut operations, understand planetary habitats and learn about the engineering challenges of future human space exploration.

The prototype uses simulated data for demonstration purposes and is not connected to actual NASA spacecraft or planetary hardware.

projectDetails.name: ExoSomatic Health
projectDetails.summary: ExoSomatic Health is an autonomous, plain-English preventative health and telemetry digital twin designed for astronauts on deep-space Artemis and Mars missions. On long-duration spaceflights, crew members face severe physiological hazards including space radiation, microgravity deconditioning, circadian drift, and isolation stress. ExoSomatic Health addresses this by gathering key health indicators (blood pressure, heart rate, sleep duration, mood, and radiation flux) and translating raw telemetry into actionable, color-coded self-evaluation insights. Featuring an interactive human body-system map, 180-day mission telemetry trends, and a hazard simulation engine, ExoSomatic Health empowers astronauts to catch health anomalies early and take preventative countermeasures without requiring on-board medical expertise.
projectDetails.details:
What it does & how it works: ExoSomatic Health simulates a 180-day deep-space mission telemetry stream, monitoring core human physiological indicators against NASA Human Research Program (HRP) risk thresholds. It features: (1) An interactive body-system diagnostic tab (Cardiovascular, Musculoskeletal, Neurological/Sleep, Immune/Radiation); (2) Dynamic time-series vitals charts with green/amber/red anomaly alerts; (3) A spaceflight hazard simulator (Solar Flare radiation spike, sleep deprivation, microgravity deconditioning); and (4) Plain-English self-exam guides and countermeasures.

Tools & Languages: Built purely in Python using Streamlit for a responsive mission-control UI, Plotly for interactive telemetry charts, and Pandas/NumPy for telemetry data modeling.

Note to Judges: If the Streamlit live app is in sleep mode, please click "Yes, get this app back up!" to wake it instantly, or review the complete source code and architecture on GitHub: [https://github.com/vermaansh0609-rgb/exosomatic-health/tree/main]

projectDetails.summary:
ASTRO CARE is a web-based prototype designed to display important health information for astronauts during space missions.

Astronauts may face health challenges in space due to the space environment and microgravity. Our project aims to make health information easier to view and understand through a simple dashboard.

The website displays sample heart rate, oxygen level and body temperature readings. It also includes health graphs, warning messages, an astronaut profile and space-related information.

We developed this project using HTML, CSS and JavaScript. We also used Chat GPT and other digital platforms for ideas, guidance and development support.

Currently, the health readings are simulated sample data and are not collected from real astronauts or medical sensors.

Our Future Goal: We aim to improve ASTRO CARE by connecting real health sensors, adding secure data storage and developing more advanced monitoring features.

Our Mission: To explore how technology can help astronauts view and understand their health information during space missions.

1. Project Summary

ASTRO CARE is a web-based prototype designed to display important health information for astronauts during space missions.

Astronauts may face health challenges because of microgravity and the space environment. Our project aims to make health information easier to view and understand through a simple dashboard.

Our website displays sample heart rate, oxygen level and body temperature readings. It also includes graphs, warning messages, an astronaut profile and space-related information.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: AFTERLIGHT
projectDetails.summary:
AFTERLIGHT is an interactive educational web experience celebrating humanity’s robotic pioneers and lunar monuments resting across the cosmos. Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, the project explores nine historic NASA missions across the Moon, Mars, Saturn, and the interstellar void. Rather than treating deactivated spacecraft as discarded debris, AFTERLIGHT reframes them as permanent archaeological time capsules of human curiosity.

Designed specifically for students aged 9–14, the platform pairs an interactive 3D WebGL solar system with rich documentary chapters, animated timelines, and accessible science explainers. Learners explore how Spirit’s jammed wheel accidentally unearthed ancient Martian hot springs, how Apollo 11’s Moon mirror still bounces Earth lasers today, and why Cassini made a fiery sacrifice into Saturn to safeguard alien ocean worlds.

Powered by 54 authentic NASA archival photographs, interactive Three.js 3D models, and real-time synthesized ambient audio, AFTERLIGHT proves that while missions eventually end, their stories and scientific discoveries illuminate our universe forever.
projectDetails.details:
A. What AFTERLIGHT Is

AFTERLIGHT is an interactive, cinematic educational web application that chronicles humanity’s mechanical outposts across the solar system. Spanning nine historic NASA missions across the Moon, Mars, Saturn, and the interstellar void, AFTERLIGHT reframes space hardware left behind—from Apollo 11’s descent stage at Tranquility Base to the Opportunity rover on the rim of Endeavour Crater—not as discarded space junk, but as permanent scientific time capsules and cultural monuments of human exploration.

B. The Educational Opportunity & Problem Addressed

When space missions conclude, public attention quickly fades once headlines stop reporting daily operations. Many students and young learners believe that when a spacecraft’s battery expires, its journey and scientific usefulness end permanently. In reality:

  1. Physical Artifacts Remain: The hardware rests on extraterrestrial surfaces as archaeological records of human ingenuity.
  2. Enduring Science: Data gathered by past missions—and even active hardware like Apollo 11's Laser Ranging Retroreflector—continues to drive active research, satellite navigation, and future astronaut landing plans.
  3. Planetary Protection: Sacrifices like Cassini's plunge into Saturn’s clouds demonstrate humanity’s moral obligation to preserve pristine alien environments (such as the ocean moons Enceladus and Titan).

AFTERLIGHT bridges the gap between dry academic mission archives and young students' imaginations, turning complex planetary astrophysics into an inspiring, story-driven journey.

C. How the Website Works

AFTERLIGHT is architected as a high-performance single-page web application (SPA) built with React 19, TypeScript, and Vite. The application runs client-side with zero paid API dependencies, zero external backend requirements, and instantaneous hash-based navigation:

  • Client-Side Data Architecture: All telemetry, scientific discoveries, chronological timelines, and metadata for the 9 missions are stored in typed local datasets (src/data/missionsData.ts).
  • Authentic Asset Loading: 54 high-resolution NASA archival photographs (6 per mission) are stored locally and mapped via an automated image manifest (image-manifest.json), eliminating external rate limits, broken third-party links, or paid content delivery networks.
  • Synthesized Ambient Audio: A real-time procedural sound generator powered by the browser's native Web Audio API synthesizes a cinematic deep-space drone (55 Hz sub-bass, 110.5 Hz harmonic, 164.8 Hz resonant shimmer) with zero external audio assets.

D. Major Implemented Features

  1. Interactive 3D WebGL Solar System (SolarSystem3D.tsx):
    • Built with Three.js, rendering an interactive 3D solar system featuring an animated glowing Sun with multi-layer coronal halos, Earth-Moon system, Mars with polar ice caps, Saturn with tilted 3D double-sided rings, and an interstellar escape trajectory.
    • Distinct 3D Spacecraft Probe models with dual solar panel arrays, communication dish antennas, and planetary survey lasers.
    • Interactive orbit controls (360° rotate, smooth scroll zoom, pan), hover raycasting with floating HUD tooltips, click-to-fly camera animations, and quick-focus jump buttons.
    • A clean 2D vector fallback view with real-time switching between 3D Cosmos and 2D Schematic modes, complete with responsive Hardware Dossier preview cards.
    • Dedicated documentary experiences for: Apollo 11, Surveyor 3, Viking 1, Mars Pathfinder, Spirit (MER-A), Opportunity (MER-B), Phoenix, Voyager 1, and Cassini-Huygens.
    • Technical breakdowns of equipment mass, power sources (RTG nuclear vs. solar arrays), primary tools (rock grinders, spectrometers, robotic claws), and exact final hardware fates.
    • Chronological event feeds with phase tags (Launch, Cruise, Landing, Discoveries, Conclusion) and interactive expanded event details.
    • Categorized discoveries explaining what the robot found, why it shocked scientists at the time, and why it matters today, filterable by dynamic tags (Ancient Water, Moon Rocks, Alien Volcanoes, Weather, etc.).
    • Full-screen photo lightbox with keyboard navigation (ArrowLeft, ArrowRight, Escape), original NASA Center credits, capture dates, NASA image IDs, and links to the original NASA archive entries.
    • Interactive split-slider and side-by-side toggles comparing early exploration limitations with modern missions (e.g., Apollo 11's 2-hour walk vs. the Artemis Lunar Base; Sojourner microrover vs. Perseverance).

E. How Visitors Interact with the Experience

  • Explore Freely: Visitors rotate the 3D Solar System, click on glowing spacecraft beacons, and immediately see mission dossiers update on the fly.
  • Journey by Destination: Filter missions across three planetary theaters: The Moon, Mars Surface, and Saturn & Deep Space.
  • Examine Historic Hardware: Inspect authentic NASA photographs of actual hardware resting on lunar soil and Martian sand.
  • Deep-Dive into Mission Chapters: Read step-by-step stories of bouncing airbag landings, stuck wheels uncovering hot springs, and message-in-a-bottle golden records.

F. Intended Audience

Specifically tailored for learners aged 9 to 14 (middle school / upper elementary grades), as well as educators and family science enthusiasts. Scientific vocabulary is intentionally translated into clear, relatable stories and analogies without compromising factual accuracy.

G. Educational Benefits

  • Demystifies Space Exploration: Explains complex concepts (laser retroreflection, hydrothermal vents, atmospheric sublimation, rocker-bogie suspension) using everyday metaphors.
  • Encourages Engineering Problem-Solving: Shows students that mission anomalies often yield historic breakthroughs (e.g., Spirit’s broken wheel dragging backward and uncovering volcanic hot springs; Surveyor 3’s camera retrieved by Apollo 12).
  • Instills Planetary Ethics: Explains planetary protection and why scientists sacrificed Cassini in Saturn’s atmosphere to safeguard potential life in Enceladus' underground oceans.

H. Intended Impact

AFTERLIGHT transforms passive history into active curiosity. By highlighting the enduring legacy of NASA's hardware, it connects past achievements to upcoming exploration—such as NASA's Artemis Moon landings, the Mars Sample Return campaign, and the Dragonfly drone to Titan—inspiring the next generation of engineers, astronomers, and explorers.

I. Creative Approach & Storytelling

Instead of presenting a clinical database or generic dashboard, AFTERLIGHT adopts a Hybrid Cinematic Museum Editorial design:

  • Deep-space black and navy color palettes accented by celestial gold and cyan.
  • Editorial typography featuring Cinzel for monumental headlines, Plus Jakarta Sans for readable prose, and Space Grotesk / JetBrains Mono for telemetry data.
  • Narrative framing that treats each spacecraft like a brave pioneer with its own personality and enduring legacy.

J. Technology Stack & Development Tools

  • Core Framework: React 19 (react 19.3.1, react-dom 19.3.1)
  • Language: TypeScript (typescript 5.7+ / 7.0.2 compiler)
  • 3D Graphics Engine: Three.js (three 0.187.0) with OrbitControls & WebGL
  • Bundler & Dev Server: Vite (vite 8.3.8) with @vitejs/plugin-react (Oxc engine)
  • Linter: Oxlint (oxlint 1.90.0)
  • Audio: HTML5 Web Audio API (procedural harmonic synthesizer)
  • Styling: Pure CSS Custom Properties (CSS variables, modern grid, responsive flexbox)
  • Image Pipeline: Node.js script querying the official NASA Image and Video Library API (https://images-api.nasa.gov/)
  • Hosting Target: Vercel (static edge deployment ready)

K. Design & Accessibility Considerations

  • Responsive Layout: Fluid layouts adapting across smartphones, tablets, laptops, and ultra-wide desktop monitors.
  • Keyboard Navigation: Lightbox supports Escape to close, ArrowLeft for previous image, and ArrowRight for next image.
  • Reduced Motion & Control: Sound starts muted by default; 3D auto-spin can be paused with a single click; 2D schematic fallback is always accessible.
  • Readability: High contrast ratios (WCAG AA compliant) with crisp off-white text over deep void backgrounds.

L. Scientific Accuracy & Source Attribution

  • Every photograph is authentic NASA documentary imagery with complete provenance: capture date, originating NASA center (JSC, KSC, JPL, MSFC, HQ), and public NASA image ID.
  • Hardware statuses distinguish between Intentionally Abandoned (Apollo 11), Visited Time Capsule (Surveyor 3), Decommissioned Equipment (Viking 1, Pathfinder, Opportunity, Phoenix), Failed Equipment (Spirit), Controlled Planetary Protection Disposal (Cassini), and Operational Spacecraft (Voyager 1).
  • No facts, discoveries, or technical capabilities have been fabricated.

projectDetails.name: EVAsuit ; Astronaut health monitoring system
projectDetails.summary:
Astronauts on long missions have to watch their own health. Nobody on Earth can help them quickly, and they may not know what a bad reading means.

EVA-SUIT is a small wearable kit and a website that helps with that. We built it with an ESP32 board and sensors. They track heartbeat, muscle movement, breathing, brain activity, and the temperature and humidity inside the helmet. The readings go live to a 3D astronaut on the screen, built from NASA’s own model. The astronaut can click on any body part to see how it is doing.
When something looks wrong, the screen flashes red. We compare each reading to the limits NASA’s Human Research Program gives for spaceflight. Then the app gives a short checklist and walks the person through it, one step at a time. There is also an AI chat that knows their recent readings, so they can ask what is going on in plain words.
projectDetails.details:
EVA-SUIT is a wearable health monitor for astronauts, with a live website at gravitydefiers.pages.dev. The sensors sit in the suit and helmet, and an ESP32 board reads them and sends the data to the site over Bluetooth. Everything you see is real data, with nothing faked. The site shows a 3D astronaut built from NASA’s own model. You can click the helmet, chest, arms or legs, and a live screen opens for that part. You can also pull the suit apart in an “explode” view to look at each piece on its own.

The app tracks heart rate, ECG, breathing sound, muscle activity, motion, and the temperature and humidity inside the helmet. Electrodes read brain activity. An AI compares each reading with NASA’s limits and with the person’s own recent history. If something looks wrong, the screen flashes red, and an emergency checklist walks the astronaut through what to do, one step at a time. A chat assistant also sees the live readings, so the astronaut can just ask what is going on in plain words. One health score, based on NASA’s Standard Measures, shows how they are doing at a glance, and a button exports a medical report for the flight surgeons.

This matters because on a trip to the Moon or Mars, help from Earth is slow. The astronaut becomes the first doctor. EVA-SUIT helps them catch problems early and know what to do next, which fits NASA’s own worry about distance from Earth.

For the build, we used an ESP32, an MPU6050 for motion, an INMP441 microphone for breathing, a DHT11 for temperature and humidity, a heartbeat sensor, and ECG electrodes. The website uses Three.js for the 3D model, plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, Web Bluetooth for the connection, and an LLM API for the chat and analysis. We think the creative part is putting real hardware, a 3D body you can click, and an AI guide in one place. The screens also change with the mission phase, such as docked, transit, spacewalk, launch and landing.

We kept in mind that astronauts are busy and stressed, so the screens are simple and the checklists are short. We also tied everything back to NASA’s research on spaceflight hazards and risks, like heart changes, poor sleep, immune changes and mental strain.
