projectDetails.name: Grus Health AI
projectDetails.summary: Astronaut Health Monitor is a proactive AI that watches five simulated data streams for each astronaut (suit vitals, urine chemistry, habitat air, radiation, and face-camera fatigue signals). It detects 20 health and safety conditions, from hypoxia and cabin CO2 buildup to dehydration and solar particle events. Using an explainable machine-learning ensemble, hard safety rules, sensor-fault checks and trend-based early warning, it raises graded alerts with the likely cause, the readings behind it, and a recommended action. On 420 unseen simulated test rows it reached 86.7% accuracy and missed none of the 400 problem cases. All data is simulated and AI-assisted, and thresholds are placeholders, so this is a research prototype, not a medical device.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRONAUT HEALTH MONITOR
A proactive AI that detects health and safety problems early, explains them, and recommends what to do

THE PROBLEM

On missions to the Moon and Mars, crews will be days or months from medical help, and messages to Earth will be delayed. Problems that are easy to fix when caught early, such as rising cabin CO2, dehydration, a failing suit scrubber or a solar particle event, can become dangerous when noticed late. Many risks do not show up in a single sensor. Tiredness, for example, appears as a mix of slower blinking, more yawning, falling heart rate variability and rising CO2. Crews need a system that watches many signals at once, notices trends before limits are crossed, and tells them clearly what it sees and why.

OUR SOLUTION

Astronaut Health Monitor is a proactive monitoring AI built around classical machine learning. It reads five streams of simulated data for each astronaut, predicts which of 20 health or safety conditions is developing, and raises graded alerts (watch, caution, warning, critical). Each alert includes the most likely condition, a confidence level, the readings that drove the decision, and a recommended action. The system is designed to speak up early: it tracks how the probability of “normal” falls over time and can flag a developing problem before any hard limit is crossed.

WHAT MAKES IT DIFFERENT

Most monitors compare one sensor to one limit. This system combines signals: it reads breathing, CO2 and facial signs together to separate fatigue from CO2 exposure, and urine chemistry together with heart rate to separate dehydration from heat stress. It is proactive, using trends and a falling normal-probability to alert before a limit is crossed. It is layered for safety, with hard rules, model predictions, anomaly checks and sensor-fault checks working together. And it is transparent: every alert says what it sees, why, and what to do.

FIVE DATA STREAMS

All data in this project is simulated. No real astronaut data was used.

  • Suit, per astronaut: heart rate, blood oxygen (SpO2), breathing rate, heart rate variability, skin temperature, activity level, suit oxygen and suit CO2.
  • Urine, per astronaut, every simulated two hours: pH, oxalate, volume and specific gravity, which indicate hydration and kidney stone risk.
  • Habitat, shared: CO2, oxygen, pressure, temperature and humidity.
  • Radiation: dose rate, cumulative dose, a solar particle event flag and the shielding zone the astronaut is in.
  • Face camera, per astronaut: eye aspect ratio, blink rate, yawn rate, head tilt and a drowsiness flag, used to detect fatigue, stress and motion sickness.

THE 20 CONDITIONS

Cardiovascular: resting tachycardia, cardiovascular deconditioning, irregular rhythm. Respiratory and air: hypoxia, hypercapnia (cabin CO2 buildup), suit scrubber failure, cabin pressure loss. Thermal and fluids: heat stress, cold stress, dehydration, kidney stone risk. Brain and behaviour: acute fatigue, chronic sleep deprivation, psychological stress, space motion sickness. Radiation: solar particle event exposure, approaching the cumulative dose limit, poor shielding. Physical: overexertion and sedentary deconditioning. A healthy “nominal” class lets the system recognise normal readings at every activity level.

HOW IT WORKS

  1. Data. We generated about 150 examples per condition with AI assistance, then cleaned and validated them, removing malformed rows, impossible values and duplicates. This gave about 3,200 rows. Each example is a snapshot of one astronaut that includes short-term trends, such as how fast heart rate or SpO2 is changing.
  2. Context-aware features. A heart rate of 140 is normal during exercise and alarming at rest, so the model works with deviations from what is expected for the astronaut’s current activity. We also derive scores for hydration stress, kidney stone risk, fatigue, stress, respiratory load, heat load, and effective radiation dose given the shielding zone.
  3. Ensemble model. Four models vote: gradient boosting, random forest, extra trees and logistic regression. Probabilities are calibrated so that confidence values are more meaningful.
  4. Safety layer. Hard rules for critical limits, such as very low SpO2, high CO2, low pressure or a solar event in an exposed zone, fire immediately and do not depend on the model. Life-critical thresholds should never rest on a learned model alone.
  5. Reliability checks. The system flags sensor problems (impossible values and flat-lined sensors) and uses an anomaly detector to warn when a reading matches none of the known conditions.
  6. Alert logic. Alerts require the same prediction on consecutive readings, which prevents flickering. An early-warning flag appears when the probability of “normal” keeps falling.
  7. Explanations. Every alert lists the readings that deviate most from normal, plus a recommended action.

We chose classical machine learning deliberately. It trains in under a minute on a laptop, runs on modest hardware without a GPU (important for spacecraft computers), and is easier to inspect and explain than a large language model.

TESTING AND RESULTS

We tested the system in two ways. Cross-validation, where entire blocks of similar rows are held out, gave about 98.8% accuracy. This number is optimistic, because all the data comes from one generation process. The more meaningful test used a separate set of 420 unseen simulated rows (20 per condition), generated independently. On it the system reached 86.7% accuracy and classified none of the 400 problem rows as healthy. In a safety setting, missing a real problem is the worst failure, so this is the figure we care about most.

The test also showed weaknesses. Most errors came from conditions that look alike, such as cardiovascular deconditioning versus sedentary deconditioning. Healthy readings at higher activity were sometimes flagged as problems (9 of 20 healthy test rows in our first test). We plan to add more healthy examples and to measure how much the persistence rule reduces these false alarms. We report these results as they are, because they show where the system needs to improve.

WHAT WE TRIED FIRST

We first tried fine-tuning a Qwen language model with LoRA on 2,400 examples. Training failed with a GPU out-of-memory error on the free hardware available to us, so it produced no usable model. We kept the attempt in our Drive folder, labelled as an experiment, and switched to the classical approach, which turned out to be faster, lighter and more explainable.

CURRENT STATUS

Working and verified: the trained model, the alert engine (rules, sensor-fault checks, anomaly detection, persistence and early warning), and the evaluation on unseen data. The public demo page replays recorded outputs of the trained model on unseen simulated scenarios, showing how status and alerts evolve as problems develop. Prototype code for a live API, a data simulator and the dashboard is in the repository, but a fully connected live deployment is still future work, and we describe it that way.

LIMITATIONS AND RESPONSIBLE USE

This is a research prototype, not a medical device. All data is simulated and was generated with AI assistance, so the accuracy numbers show how the system behaves on our simulated scenarios, not how it would perform on real astronauts. Thresholds and recommended actions are placeholders that must be replaced with values from NASA standards and reviewed by flight surgeons. A real system would also need a personal baseline for each astronaut, because normal heart rate and HRV differ between people. The system is meant to support human decisions, never replace them, so every alert shows its reasons and leaves the decision to the crew and medical team.

AI USE DISCLOSURE

We used AI tools (Google Gemini and Anthropic’s Claude) to help generate synthetic training examples and to write and debug code. Our team defined the problem and the 20 conditions, chose the approach, ran the experiments, evaluated the results and made the design decisions.

NEXT STEPS

  • Validate against public NASA datasets, such as those in the NASA Open Science Data Repository, and real physiological recordings.
  • Replace placeholder thresholds with clinician-reviewed limits.
  • Learn a personal baseline per astronaut and add longer-term trend models.
  • Connect real sensors and live camera analysis, processed on the device to protect privacy.
  • Reduce false alarms and separate look-alike conditions with richer signals, such as heart rate variability over time.
  • Deploy the live backend and dashboard.

WHY IT MATTERS

Autonomy will be essential for deep-space missions. A monitoring system that is explainable, runs on modest hardware and is honest about its uncertainty could help crews catch problems early and decide what to do when Earth cannot answer in time.

projectDetails.name: CombustionLens: Source-Linked Fire Safety Evidence for Space Missions
projectDetails.summary: CombustionLens is a source-linked research workspace that helps researchers explore NASA microgravity combustion findings and see where they do and don't apply to future missions. Its evidence explorer links four NASA campaign summaries (BASS, FLEX, Saffire VI, SoFIE-GEL) to their original sources, ranks them with a disclosed, explainable method, and keeps published observations separate from our interpretations. A mission-applicability check compares gravity, fuel class, oxygen, pressure, ventilation and geometry for orbital, lunar and Mars-transit contexts, marking each as aligned, mismatched or unknown, so missing evidence is visible and unknown conditions are never treated as safe. Users can export source-linked research briefs. A research backend retrieves and reranks passages from NASA Technical Reports Server reports with page-level citations and numerical checks. It is a research prototype, not a flight-qualified fire-safety tool, and it does not predict fire risk.
projectDetails.details:
The Problem
NASA has decades of microgravity combustion results, but a correct finding can still be wrong for a given spacecraft. Gravity, fuel geometry, atmosphere and ventilation can all make a result non-transferable. Finding a result is not enough. Researchers need to know whether it applies to their mission.

What It Does

  • Evidence Explorer: four curated NASA campaign summaries with searchable findings, explainable ranking by mission priority (for example detection and extinction), and three mission contexts. It runs without a backend or API key.
  • Mission Applicability: six physical boundary checks that give aligned, mismatch or unknown results, plus exportable research questions. For lunar surface contexts it shows an explicit partial-gravity evidence gap instead of inventing a threshold.
  • Research Backend: dense retrieval over NASA reports, cross-encoder reranking, page-level citations and numerical-claim checks. Without a generative model it returns labeled source excerpts.
  • Verified Comparator: only independently verified experiment records are eligible. None are verified yet, so the comparator shows an empty state on purpose.
  • Exports: Markdown research briefs that carry citations, limitations and mission context.

Data and Evidence
We collected 6 NASA Technical Reports Server reports (549 pages) and kept their rights determinations and SHA-256 hashes. Three reports with explicit public-use permission are indexed as 457 passages. We also staged 31 BASS test-condition rows and 8 Saffire measurements, which await independent review.

Tools and Technology
React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS and Recharts on the frontend. Python, FastAPI, ChromaDB, sentence-transformers, DuckDB and PyMuPDF on the backend.

Validation
68 backend tests and 20 frontend tests passed, and the production build succeeded. A small retrieval benchmark scored 8/8 development and 7/8 held-out gate classifications. These are not scientific answer-accuracy measurements.

Design Choices and Creativity
Ranking scores are not probabilities. Unknown conditions are never labeled safe. Public access alone is not treated as permission to index a report. When no evidence matches a search, the app shows an empty state instead of an invented conclusion.

Impact and Next Steps
CombustionLens makes the boundaries of microgravity fire-safety evidence auditable for Moon and Mars mission planning. Next steps are independent review of run-level records, broader evaluation and a validated public deployment. No NASA endorsement is claimed.

projectDetails.name: HyperFlood - The Hyper Local Flood Early Warning System
projectDetails.summary:
HyperFlood is a web-based Hyper Local flood early warning system developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge “Be an Earth System Trend Detective!” It investigates how Earth-system variables such as precipitation and temperature have changed over time using NASA data, and connects these historical trends with present-day environmental conditions.

Users can select any location on the map to explore NASA historical trends alongside elevation and terrain, soil wetness and runoff potential, rivers and drainage, and recent rainfall. By connecting changes across multiple parts of the Earth system, HyperFlood transforms complex environmental data into simple, explainable insights that help people understand how changing conditions may contribute to local flood vulnerability.
projectDetails.details:
HyperFlood is a web-based flood intelligence platform that combines NASA satellite data, geographical information and weather forecasts to assess local flood vulnerability. It analyses historical rainfall, soil moisture, elevation, nearby waterways and forecast precipitation using NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, MERRA-2, Copernicus DEM, OpenStreetMap and Open-Meteo. Developed using HTML, CSS and JavaScript, it is hosted on GitHub Pages.

Its innovative Past–Present–Future approach combines historical trends, current geographical conditions and future rainfall to identify potential flood threats. HyperFlood aims to improve flood awareness, identify vulnerable areas and support disaster preparedness. The project considers terrain, soil conditions, rainfall patterns, data accuracy and satellite limitations, demonstrating how NASA Earth observation resources can support accessible, location-specific flood intelligence.

Data Sources and Their Purpose:

  • NASA POWER: Historical rainfall and temperature trends to understand long-term environmental patterns.
  • NASA GPM IMERG: Satellite-based precipitation estimates to analyse rainfall intensity and distribution.
  • NASA MERRA-2: Historical atmospheric and soil moisture data to assess environmental and ground wetness conditions.
  • Copernicus DEM GLO-90: Elevation and terrain data to identify low-lying areas and drainage patterns.
  • OpenStreetMap / Overpass API: River, stream and canal locations to assess proximity to waterways.
  • Open-Meteo: Weather forecasts and future precipitation to evaluate potential rainfall-related flood threats.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project Innovasai
projectDetails.summary:
The Quiet Ones is a short story told by Sai Rakshan, a 10-year-old who inherits his grandpa's old radio station. One night it picks up voices from NASA's retired machines, and he starts writing them down as postcards. Each machine tells him why it was sent, what it found out, and where it is now.
The story covers Opportunity, Spirit, Viking 1, Sojourner, Ingenuity, the Apollo landing sites, Surveyor 3, Voyager and Pioneer 10. Instead of listing facts, it lets kids hear them from another kid. For example, Opportunity was built to last 90 days and kept going for almost 15 years. Its little hematite "blueberries" showed that Mars once had water, which is why Perseverance is now looking for signs of ancient life.
Most space stories are about what's launching next. We wanted to show that finished missions still matter, because every old machine left a question behind that newer missions like Perseverance and Artemis are still answering. The machines' voices are made up, but every date, distance and discovery is real.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

The Quiet Ones is a short story told by Sai Rakshan, a 10-year-old who inherits his grandpa's old radio station. Every so often the radio picks up a "postcard" from a retired NASA machine. Each postcard answers the same three questions: Why was I sent? What did I find out? Where am I now?

The story covers ten sets of hardware on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space: Opportunity, Spirit, Viking 1, Sojourner, Ingenuity, the Apollo 11 landing site, the Apollo rovers, Surveyor 3, Voyager 1 and 2, and Pioneer 10. Instead of reading a list of facts, kids hear them from another kid who is just as surprised by them as they are. By the end, Sai works out that none of the machines are really gone, because newer missions like Perseverance and Artemis are still answering the questions the old ones left behind.

Benefits

•       Kids learn real mission facts without it feeling like homework.

•       It's short, about three pages, so it's easy to read in one sitting or read aloud in class.

•       It connects old missions to new ones, so students see space exploration as one long story.

•       A "what's real and what's made up" section at the end helps kids tell facts from imagination.

Intended impact

We want kids to feel a bit attached to these machines, the way you feel about a toy that's been through a lot. Most children only hear about missions that are launching now. We hope this story shows them that a mission doesn't end when the signal stops, and that it makes them curious enough to go look up Perseverance, Artemis and the Voyagers on their own. Teachers could also use it as a reading activity that happens to teach some science.

Tools and software

•       Claude, an AI assistant, helped us brainstorm the idea, outline it and write early drafts. We then rewrote the story in a child's voice and simplified the language.

•       Microsoft Word for the final story and these project documents.

•       Facts are based on NASA's published mission histories.

No coding or special hardware was needed for this version. An interactive web version (HTML, CSS and JavaScript) with a clickable map of the Moon and Mars is an idea for a next step.

What makes it creative

•       The narrator is a child, so the science sounds like something a friend would tell you, not a textbook.

•       The postcard idea gives every machine its own little voice and the same simple structure, which makes them easy to remember.

•       The story turns real details into emotional moments. Spirit got stuck in sand and kept working anyway. Opportunity was built for 90 days and lasted almost 15 years. Ingenuity was planned for about five flights and flew 72.

•       It's honest about what's imagined. The voices are made up, but the facts are real, and the story says so.

What we considered

•       Age: we aimed at ages 9 to 14, with short sentences and simple words.

•       Accuracy: we corrected small details that often get repeated wrongly. For example, Opportunity's famous "my battery is low and it's getting dark" line was a reporter's way of explaining the data, and the story says that. Spirit got stuck in 2009, not 2010.

•       Facts that change: Voyager's distance grows every day, so the story says "almost a whole day" for its signal time instead of an exact number.

•       Tone: the machines are curious and a little funny, not dramatic or sad, so kids come away inspired.

•       Credit: any NASA pictures added later should follow NASA's media usage guidelines.

projectDetails.summary:
# Project Summary – EARTHLAB

EARTHLAB – Earth Information Jukebox is an interactive educational website designed to explore our changing planet through science, technology, visualization and sound. The project focuses on important environmental parameters such as global temperature, atmospheric carbon dioxide (CO₂) and Arctic ice changes.

It aims to transform Earth science data into meaningful visual experiences using interactive dashboards, 3D Earth models and dynamic sonification. Users can explore environmental information and understand how our planet changes over time.

The website is designed to make complex scientific information easier to understand, especially for students and educators. By combining scientific data with engaging visual and audio experiences, EARTHLAB encourages environmental awareness and helps people connect with our planet.

**"Explore Earth. Understand Change. Hear Our Planet."

projectDetails.name: ASTRA-MED: Autonomous Astronaut Health Monitoring & Triage System
projectDetails.summary:
When astronauts travel to the Moon or Mars, round-trip communication delays with Earth can reach up to 44 minutes. Crews cannot wait on flight surgeons for routine checkups or sudden medical emergencies, yet most astronauts are not physicians.

ASTRA-MED is an interactive, onboard health monitoring and triage web application built for deep-space crews. Astronauts can switch between LEO/ISS, Lunar, and Mars mission modes, click directly on a human body map to inspect five major physiological systems, and view color-coded vitals with plain-language instructions on how and why to take each measurement in microgravity. Grounded in NASA research baselines, ASTRA-MED turns raw health readings into immediate, step-by-step countermeasures and flight-surgeon telemetry packets.
projectDetails.details:
### Why We Built ASTRA-MED

Long-duration missions expose astronauts to NASA's Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity fields, and hostile closed environments. Because deep-space signal delays make real-time consultations impossible, astronauts need a fast, self-guided medical console that explains what is happening in their bodies and what to do next.

### How It Works

- **Mission Environment & Latency Switcher:** Crew members switch between LEO/ISS (~0.5 s latency, microgravity), Lunar (~2.6 s round-trip latency, 0.16g), and Mars (4–22 min one-way latency, 0g/0.38g) modes so triage workflows reflect real communication constraints.

- **Interactive Diagnostic Body Map:** Clicking any of the five body regions—Neurological, Cardiovascular, Immune/Metabolic, Musculoskeletal, or Radiation/Environment—opens live vital signs, explains how spaceflight affects that system, and displays immediate countermeasure steps.

- **Color-Coded Triage & Zero-G Measurement Guides:** Every indicator uses clear Green (Nominal), Amber (Watch), or Red (Critical) status badges. Built-in "How & Why to Measure in Zero-G" panels walk non-physician astronauts through taking accurate readings in space and understanding why each exam matters.

- **Anomaly Simulation & Flight Surgeon Telemetry Packets:** Built-in scenario presets (such as a Mars Solar Particle Event radiation spike) trigger immediate crew stabilization alerts—such as EVA abort and storm-shelter protocols—while packaging a structured telemetry report for Earth flight surgeons.

- **Mission Health Readiness & Daily Routine:** A live 0–100 readiness score, check-in streak badge, and interactive daily checklist (morning vitals, 2-hour ARED resistive exercise, sleep quality log, and circadian light reset) encourage consistent preventive care.

### Impact Beyond Space

The same self-triage workflow designed for Mars transit vehicles translates directly to remote environments on Earth—including polar research stations, submarines, and rural telemedicine clinics—where specialist doctors are not immediately available.

### Tools & Source Code

- **Built With:** HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6+), and interactive SVG anatomical graphics

- **Live App:** https://joffinranjith.github.io/Astra-Med/

- **GitHub Repository:** https://github.com/joffinranjith/Astra-Med

projectDetails.name: Project KARASTRA
projectDetails.summary:
KARASTRA is a planetary analogue intelligence concept designed to identify and evaluate Earth environments that can help people prepare for their future human missions to the Moon and Mars. The project shows a comparative analysis of terrain, surface temperature, geological characteristics, dryness, water or ice potential, and environmental conditions.
This project focuses on three terrestrial analogue regions: the Atacama Desert in Chile, the McMurdo Dry Valleys in Antarctica, and volcanic basaltic landscapes in Hawaii. These environments offer different conditions relevant to planetary exploration, from Mars-like chillness to lunar-like volcanic terrain. KARASTRA aims to develop a data-driven ranking framework and interactive map to help researchers identify promising analogue locations, understand their limitations, and plan more effective robotic and human exploration missions. By connecting Earth observations with planetary datasets, KARASTRA supports safer, better-informed and more scientifically grounded exploration beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
KARASTRA is a planetary analogue intelligence project that explores how environments on Earth can help prepare humanity for permanent lunar settlements and future Mars exploration. It addresses the challenge by proposing a data-driven framework to identify, compare and evaluate terrestrial locations that share environmental and geological characteristics with the Moon and Mars.

The project focuses on three potential analogue environments: the Atacama Desert in Chile, the McMurdo Dry Valleys in Antarctica and the volcanic basaltic landscapes of Hawaii. Each representing a different condition relevant to planetary exploration, including extreme aridity, low temperatures, volcanic geology and surface terrain.

KARASTRA uses publicly available Earth-observation and planetary datasets from NASA, CSA, ESA and JAXA. Resources include NASA Earthdata, NASA Worldview, the Planetary Data System, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter observations and Diviner temperature measurements, alongside RADARSAT and Copernicus datasets. The proposed workflow compares parameters such as terrain, surface temperature, geological characteristics, dryness, dust and potential water or ice indicators. These factors can be incorporated into a weighted ranking framework to evaluate the relevance of each Earth analog to specific lunar or Martian environments.

The project's intended benefit is to make planetary site research more accessible, systematic and evidence-based. Rather than relying only on visual similarities, KARASTRA aims to connect measurable Earth observations with actual planetary data. Its intended impact is to support researchers, students and future mission planners in understanding environmental challenges, testing exploration concepts and making better-informed decisions about robotic and human missions.

The initial project was developed as a research and presentation concept using publicly available scientific resources and a structured comparative methodology. The proposed technical implementation can use Python for data processing and analysis, libraries such as NumPy, Pandas, Rasterio and GeoPandas for geospatial workflows, and tools such as QGIS for spatial visualisation. An interactive web map could be developed using Folium or Leaflet. The project is designed around open datasets and accessible software rather than requiring specialised hardware.

KARASTRA's creativity lies in connecting multiple space agencies' datasets into one comparative Earth-to-planetary research approach. It considers not only similarities but also limitations: Earth's atmosphere, gravity, weather, biological activity and radiation environment differ significantly from those of the Moon and Mars. By accounting for these differences, KARASTRA aims to move beyond simply finding places that look extraterrestrial and toward understanding which environments are genuinely useful for preparing for exploration beyond Earth.

projectDetails.name: Crew Health Companion
projectDetails.summary:
Summary: Crew Health Companion is a prototype app that helps astronauts check their own health during long missions. A crew member takes guided measurements, such as heart rate and sleep, and sees a color-coded status with a plain-language explanation and the next step. A red reading opens an immediate-action screen that puts the crew procedure first, and prepares an escalation message for the flight surgeon. The app links each body region to the NASA hazard that threatens it.
How it addresses the challenge: The challenge asks for software that lets astronauts assess their own health and act on what they find. The app gives guided checks, clear status, and clear escalation, and it does not diagnose or prescribe.
Why it matters: Long missions limit how quickly crews can reach ground medical help. Early detection and clear escalation can help the crew and the flight surgeon act sooner.
projectDetails.details:
What it does: It lets a crew member check heart rate and sleep through guided steps. It shows each reading as green, amber, red, or grey, with the rule used, a plain-language explanation, and the next step. It also keeps a trend chart, a weekly handoff summary for the flight surgeon, and an escalation log.

How it works: A body map links each region to its function and to the NASA hazard that threatens it. Each reading is scored against provisional ranges. Emergency signs stop the normal flow and show the crew procedure. A red reading prepares an escalation message. Three amber days in a row create a routine escalation. Missing or invalid data is shown in grey and is not scored.

Benefits: It helps a crew spot changes early, explains what each reading means, and makes escalation clear. It is designed to work offline, with no server.

What we hope to achieve: A validated tool that adds more indicators, such as blood pressure, blood glucose, and a vision check, with thresholds confirmed by flight surgeons and clinical guidelines.

Limits of this prototype: Readings are simulated. Only heart rate and sleep are scored. Thresholds are provisional. The app has not been tested with astronauts or flight surgeons.

Tools and languages: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in one file, with no frameworks. Hosted on GitHub. The demo deck is a PDF on Google Drive, with the Inter typeface.

projectDetails.name: KIRA Earth — Earth System Trend Detective
projectDetails.summary: KIRA Earth helps people investigate what is changing in Earth's climate, where it is changing, how much, and whether the evidence is statistically significant. Its interactive globe lets users select a place, rank eight NASA POWER climate variables, explore trends through charts, seasonal fingerprints and climate spirals, and cross-check model records against NASA MODIS satellite measurements. Regional maps and a two-region calculator reveal how neighboring or distant places differ, while before-and-after satellite imagery makes environmental change visible. Each result keeps its source, measurement period and uncertainty accessible. Built for students, planners and curious explorers, KIRA Earth turns complex Earth science records into an understandable, repeatable investigation rather than a single unexplained climate headline.
projectDetails.details:
KIRA EARTH — EARTH SYSTEM TREND DETECTIVE

THE PROBLEM

Earth's connected systems change in different directions across regions. A long list of variables and a visually striking map are not enough: people need to know what changed, where, by how much, and how strong the evidence is.

WHAT WE BUILT

KIRA Earth is an interactive globe and 2D map that turns NASA records into a repeatable investigation. Search by place name or coordinates, select a location, then request its evidence. Change Studio ranks eight NASA POWER variables: mean, maximum and minimum air temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind speed, surface pressure and root-zone soil wetness. It also includes an SPI drought index. Seasonal fingerprints, charts, climate spirals and stripes reveal how the record changes through time.

The spatial trend map tests native grid cells within a selected extent. A regional calculator compares two sampled regions, reports trends and uncertainty, and tests whether adding a lagged source-region signal improves predictions over a target-only baseline. It withholds response estimates when validation fails. This is statistical association, not proof that one region causes climatic impacts in another.

Independent satellite evidence includes MODIS vegetation, day/night land-surface temperature, evapotranspiration and productivity records accessed through Microsoft Planetary Computer. Quality flags, coverage and limitations accompany the analysis. Air temperature and satellite surface temperature are different measurements and are identified separately. Before-and-after imagery swipes show visible change, including the Aral Sea; land-cover and surface-water layers add context.

THE SCIENCE AND TRUST

We use Theil–Sen slopes, Mann–Kendall tests, record-length and lag-1 autocorrelation screens, and Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate control across variable, seasonal or spatial test families. Slopes are reported in native units per decade with intervals and standardized change. A permutation visualization is marked inapplicable when its independence assumptions fail. Missing or unavailable provider values are not replaced with invented data. Sources, dates, units, coverage and uncertainty remain accessible.

A current-weather panel adds WeatherNext 2 and ECMWF ensemble context through Open-Meteo. Weather forecasts are distinct from observed long-term trends and are not climate projections. Optional local analog intelligence uses Laya to compare historical patterns; the lightweight public deployment excludes neural checkpoints and uses the documented fallback. It does not claim to run Laya in the cloud.

IMPACT AND CREATIVITY

Students, journalists, planners and curious explorers can move from a location to an understandable evidence trail. Our distinctive combination is automatic variable screening, comparable standardized trends, seasonal animation, significance screening, satellite cross-checks and two-region comparison in one progressive interface. A guided tour follows a concrete Cairo investigation rather than leaving users with an unexplained map.

IMPLEMENTATION AND VALIDATION

React, TypeScript, CesiumJS, Recharts and Vite power the interface. Python FastAPI, NumPy, pandas, SciPy, xarray and ecCodes support the backend. A Docker container serves the frontend and API on Render Free. The production build and 126 automated tests passed. We verified Cairo Studio, the WeatherNext 2 forecast and Cairo–Nairobi Compare on the public deployment; the team also confirmed the globe and Cairo load on a phone. Free hosting can cold-start, and regional values are weighted grid samples rather than full-area or station averages. Scientific limitations and open improvements are documented in the repository.

AI / SI DISCLOSURE

Code, documentation and presentation were developed with assistance from Anthropic Claude Code and OpenAI Codex. Scientific statistics are calculated from provider records, not generated as fictional measurements. The 30-second demo edits a recording of the real application; its captions and end card use HyperFrames. The narration is AI-generated locally with Kokoro-82M (af_heart), not a cloned voice. That disclosure appears on screen, is spoken in the outro, and is included in metadata. Optional in-app generated explanations are labelled. NASA is identified as a data source; no NASA branding was generated for this project. Full details: https://github.com/saggamer/kira-earth/blob/main/AI_USE.md

PUBLIC LINKS

Live application: https://kira-earth.onrender.com

Source code and methods: https://github.com/saggamer/kira-earth

30-second demo with English subtitles: https://github.com/saggamer/kira-earth/releases/tag/hackathon-demo-v1

Deployment verification: https://github.com/saggamer/kira-earth/blob/main/deploy/VERIFICATION.md

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project Kyberverein
projectDetails.summary:
Astro-Care: Keeping Astronauts Healthy Beyond Earth is a health monitoring software solution developed by Team Kyberverein for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under the theme Next Frontiers. It addresses the healthcare challenges faced by astronauts during long-duration space missions, where communication delays, limited medical assistance, and harsh space environments make real-time healthcare difficult.

Astronauts face several health risks, including radiation exposure, bone and muscle loss, immune system changes, cardiovascular problems, and mental health challenges caused by isolation and confinement. Existing healthcare tools are often fragmented, making it difficult to identify early warning signs.

Our solution, Astro-Health, is an autonomous, offline-first health monitoring application that collects, tracks, analyzes, and alerts astronauts about potential health risks. It integrates wearable devices, daily health check-ins, exercise records, and environmental data to establish individual health baselines and detect unusual changes.

Its key features include daily health check-ins, wearable integration, bone and muscle monitoring, mental wellness assessment, radiation exposure tracking, and smart alerts with personalized recommendations and medical guidance.

projectDetails.name: Galactic Field Guide
projectDetails.summary: Galactic Field Guide: Relics of the Moon & Mars is an interactive field guide that turns seven real spacecraft left behind on the Moon and Mars into a kid-friendly explorer's journal. Each relic — the Apollo 15 Moon buggy, Surveyor 3, Intrepid, Eagle, Perseverance, Ingenuity, and the Three Forks sample depot — gets its own chapter organized as Start (what it is), End (why it stayed), and Your Turn (games). The site pairs storybook framing with real NASA data: a 3D Lab lets kids rotate and click simplified models of every craft; a topographic Radar Map plots each relic at its real landing coordinates; quizzes, matching games, and a Rocket Balancer build understanding through play. A friendly XP-and-badge system rewards exploration, and every fact is sourced from NASA, LROC, and the Apollo Lunar Surface Journal.
projectDetails.details:
Galactic Field Guide: Relics of the Moon & Mars is an interactive, kid-friendly web field guide to seven robotic machines humanity has left on the Moon and Mars. Instead of presenting space history as a static article, the project turns it into an explorable "field trip": visitors open craft files, follow mission stories, zoom around an interactive lunar map, inspect machines in a 3D viewer, and test what they've learned through built-in games and quizzes. The experience opens with a short cinematic intro and then lets learners choose their own path through the guide.

How it works: The site is a single-page web app built with HTML5, CSS3, and vanilla JavaScript. Content is organized into sections — Home, Craft Files, Map, 3D Lab, and Credits — with a persistent navigation bar and progress indicators. The interactive map is drawn with SVG so pins, craters, and labels stay sharp at any zoom level and remain keyboard-accessible. The 3D Lab uses an in-browser canvas/WebGL viewer to let users rotate and inspect models without installing anything. A quiz/game layer gives immediate feedback, and a cinematic intro sets the tone before the guide begins. The layout is responsive, supports dark mode, and respects reduced-motion preferences.

Benefits: The guide makes space history approachable for young learners by combining short, readable stories with visual and hands-on interaction. It supports different learning styles — reading, exploring, watching, and testing knowledge — and gives teachers a low-friction classroom resource that runs in any modern browser. Because it is static and lightweight, it avoids logins, installs, and data collection. The 3D and map interactions help learners understand scale, location, and engineering context that are hard to convey in plain text.

Real-world testing and validation: The guide was tested in person with a group of 12 middle school students in a classroom setting. Students were given the site with no instructions beyond "explore it," and were observed and then asked for their reactions afterward. The response was overwhelmingly positive — every student who participated said the guide was great. Students specifically responded well to the 3D viewer, the interactive map, and the quiz/game layer, and several said they would use it again or show it to someone else. The session also surfaced small usability notes that were addressed in a follow-up revision, which is exactly what the test was for: real kids, on real school hardware, using the guide the way it was always intended to be used.

Intended impact: The goal is to spark curiosity about STEM, space exploration, and engineering heritage, and to help learners see these machines as real artifacts with stories, not just names in a textbook. The project is designed for classrooms, museums, libraries, after-school programs, and independent exploration at home. The positive response from the middle school test group confirmed that the guide lands the way it was designed to — as something genuinely engaging rather than something students feel obligated to read — and supports expanding it to other age groups and classroom settings.

Tools, languages, and software: HTML5, CSS3 (custom properties, Grid/Flexbox, responsive design, dark mode, reduced-motion support), and vanilla JavaScript. SVG is used for the interactive map; Canvas/WebGL is used for the 3D model viewer. Google Fonts provides typography. The project was developed in a code editor, tested in modern desktop and mobile browsers, and validated in a live classroom pilot with 12 middle school students. No special hardware is required — it runs on ordinary laptops, tablets, and phones.

What makes it creative: The project borrows the metaphor of a naturalist's field guide and applies it to space hardware. The cinematic opening, starfield theme, collectible-style map pins, craft "dossiers," and 3D inspection lab turn a reference site into an adventure. The tone is intentionally warm and kid-friendly rather than technical, and the visual design uses a space-themed palette with playful accents instead of a dry museum aesthetic.

Factors the team considered: Age-appropriate language and readability; accessibility, including keyboard focus, contrast, and reduced-motion support; responsive layouts for school devices; performance on low-end hardware; privacy, with no tracking or accounts; maintainability of a static site; and clear navigation so learners do not get lost. The team also balanced visual richness against load time, chose lightweight web technologies over heavy frameworks to keep the guide fast and easy to host, and used feedback from the 12-student middle school classroom pilot to make concrete improvements before finalizing the project.

projectDetails.name: SPHEREx Sky Explorer
projectDetails.summary:
SPHEREx Sky Explorer is an astronomy-based project that aims to make space survey data easier to explore and understand. We developed a prototype that processes astronomical images, detects possible light sources, and displays their locations through visualisation and a source catalogue.
Our prototype currently uses preliminary WISE survey data for testing. Using Python-based image processing and source detection techniques, it identified 38 possible sources in the test image. The results can be explored through a Streamlit web application, which displays the processed image, detected sources, and catalogue.
This project aims to make astronomical data exploration more accessible to students, researchers, and space enthusiasts. It provides a foundation for future integration of SPHEREx observations and more advanced analysis of the universe.
projectDetails.details: Project Details – SPHEREx Sky Explorer SPHEREx Sky Explorer is an astronomy-based project designed to make space survey images easier to explore and understand. It processes astronomical images, identifies possible light sources, and displays their locations in a visual format. The system also generates a source catalogue containing information such as source position, brightness, and other measured properties. Our current prototype uses a preliminary WISE astronomical image as test data. Using image processing and source detection techniques, we successfully identified 38 possible sources in the test image. The results are displayed through an interactive web application, where users can view the processed image, explore detected sources, and download the source catalogue. Integration with SPHEREx data is planned as the next development stage. We developed the project using Python, Google Colab, Streamlit, NumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib, and astronomical image-processing tools. FITS image data was used for processing and analysis. The application provides a simple and user-friendly way to explore astronomical observations. The creative aspect of our project is the combination of astronomical image processing, automated source detection, visualisation, and catalogue generation in one platform. Our team considered data reliability, processing time, ease of use, accessibility, and the possibility of future expansion. The intended impact is to support students, astronomy enthusiasts, and researchers in exploring space survey data more easily. In the future, we aim to integrate SPHEREx observations and develop more advanced tools for comparing astronomical sources and studying changes in the sky.

ASTRA is an interactive scientific exploration platform that brings multiple Earth, space, and planetary science workflows together in one console. It is designed to help users explore scientific concepts, investigate environmental patterns, interact with analytical tools, and navigate different mission-oriented workbenches through a unified interface.

  • AstroTrainer (CH03): Astronomy learning and exploration.
  • Flame Lab (CH08): Interactive flame-related exploration.
  • MissionForge (CH13): Mission-oriented tools and workflows.

ASTRA brings these different experiences together through a single dashboard, allowing users to navigate between scientific workbenches without needing separate applications.

The project was developed using JavaScript, Node.js, Hono, HTML, CSS, and browser-based technologies. Its architecture combines a web frontend with a backend server to provide an interactive application experience.

The project focuses on making scientific exploration more accessible through a unified interface, interactive workflows, and a collection of tools spanning Earth science, remote sensing, fire investigation, and planetary exploration.

ASTRA aims to demonstrate how multiple scientific workflows can be organized into one accessible and extensible platform.

projectDetails.name: Project MareZero
projectDetails.summary:
The 3D Hemispherical Sky-Dome View puts a virtual glass dome over the lunar lander, so you can see the whole 360-degree sky in one interactive picture. The flat base shows compass direction (azimuth, 0 to 360 degrees). The curved walls show elevation, from the horizon up to the zenith at 90 degrees. Along the bottom edge, a dark, jagged outline marks the mountains and crater rims around the landing site. It’s built from LOLA topography data, so it shows exactly what terrain blocks the view.

On top of that skyline, the dome traces the Sun’s path around the horizon over the 29.5-day lunar cycle. It also shows Earth’s small oval wobble in the sky, which comes from lunar libration. When the Sun slips behind the skyline, the view flags a solar power shadow. When Earth does, it flags a direct-to-Earth communication blackout.

Mission planners can drag a time slider or switch landing sites and watch the line-of-sight rays move as they do it. That lets them compare operating windows in seconds.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works Lunar Landing Site Navigator calculates where the Sun and Earth sit in the sky at a lunar landing site on any chosen date and turns complex ephemeris math into two plain-language answers: Can it make power? and Can it phone home?

Users pick a site (Apollo, Artemis/CLPS candidates, Chang'e-4, or custom coordinates) and a date. Using the astronomy-engine library, the app rotates Moon-to-Sun and Moon-to-Earth vectors into the Moon's body-fixed frame (including lunar libration) and compares them against the local horizon silhouette. Results are displayed across four views:

  • 2D Horizon Panorama: A flat skyline view with exaggerated vertical elevation so sub-7° polar grazing angles are easy to read.
  • 3D Hemispherical Sky-Dome: An interactive 3D dome tracing the Sun’s 29.5-day path and Earth’s libration wobble against local terrain obstacles.
  • 30-Day Timeline & Side-by-Side Comparator: Compares up to three site/date combinations at once and simulates 7-, 14-, or 21-day launch slips.
  • Technical Toggle: Reveals raw azimuths, elevations, solar flux, and exact bisected sunset/Earth set times (to within ~1 minute) for mission planners.

Benefits & Intended Impact Tools like JPL Horizons, Moon Trek, and Quick Map are built for deep analysis, not fast comparison. Our tool lets users evaluate schedule slips or backup sites in seconds without learning coordinate frames. It serves three audiences at once: the public gets clear mission verdicts, educators get an intuitive visual showing why south-pole lighting and Earth visibility are so extreme, and mission planners get a rapid screening aid before moving to heavy GIS tools.

Tools, Languages & Software

  • Frontend & 3D: TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Three.js, deployed on Vercel.
  • Astrodynamics & Validation: astronomy-engine (IAU rotation model) and Vitest. We validated our math against live NASA JPL Horizons API queries across 12 test cases (Shackleton, Malapert, and Apollo 11 on 1 Jan, 3 Jul, and 15 Nov 2026), matching Horizons to within 0.02°.
  • Development Workflow: We used AI coding assistants (Claude and OpenAI Codex) to help write and review code, while our team defined the architecture, caught and fixed an early Sun-vector frame offset via JPL Horizons testing, and verified all outputs.

How It Is Creative

  • Experience-to-Instrument Flow: A scroll-driven 3D launch-to-landing story transitions directly into the working Sky-Dome at the selected site.
  • Built for Polar Geometry: Exaggerated horizon rendering makes tiny polar elevation angles legible at a glance.
  • Launch-Slip Simulator: Directly solves the real-world challenge of hardware delays by showing how a 1- to 3-week slip changes mission viability.

Factors Our Team Considered

  • Accuracy First: Our initial build had a Sun-position frame error; we caught it by testing against independent calculations and JPL Horizons, fixed the body-fixed transformation, and added multi-date regression tests.
  • Honest Data Labeling: Bundled terrain profiles are explicitly labeled as approximate (with custom horizon upload support), and the app reports explicit "Always Up" or "Never Up" states instead of fake countdowns.
  • Accessibility & Attribution: Built with plain language by default, technical metrics on demand, keyboard navigation, and reduced-motion support. Ephemeris methods rely on astronomy-engine and NASA JPL Horizons.

projectDetails.name: Project MID STRANGERS
projectDetails.summary:
COSMOCONSTRUCT is a browser-based, interactive space mission design and simulation game developed by MID STRANGERS for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

The game allows 1–4 players to collaboratively design, build, manage and simulate a complete space mission, with the flagship scenario being an Earth-to-Mars science mission.
How the game works
1. Mission planning: Select a destination and define scientific objectives.
2. Spacecraft construction: Choose spacecraft components and scientific instruments.
3. Launch planning: Select a suitable launch vehicle and orbit.
4. Resource management: Balance budget, mass, power, data, communications and mission lifetime.
5. Mission simulation: Launch the spacecraft and handle unexpected technical problems.
6. Mission evaluation: Receive a performance score, understand failures and improve the design.
What makes it special?
The game demonstrates how engineering decisions affect one another.

For example, adding an advanced scientific instrument might increase scientific value, but it also increases spacecraft mass, power consumption, cost and data generation.

Players must make strategic decisions rather than simply selecting the most powerful components.
Multiplayer roles

projectDetails.details:
COSMOCONSTRUCT is a browser-based, interactive space mission design and simulation game developed by MID STRANGERS for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

The game allows 1–4 players to collaboratively design, build, manage and simulate a complete space mission, with the flagship scenario being an Earth-to-Mars science mission.

How the game works

  1. Mission planning: Select a destination and define scientific objectives.
  2. Spacecraft construction: Choose spacecraft components and scientific instruments.
  3. Launch planning: Select a suitable launch vehicle and orbit.
  4. Resource management: Balance budget, mass, power, data, communications and mission lifetime.
  5. Mission simulation: Launch the spacecraft and handle unexpected technical problems.
  6. Mission evaluation: Receive a performance score, understand failures and improve the design.

What makes it special?

The game demonstrates how engineering decisions affect one another.

For example, adding an advanced scientific instrument might increase scientific value, but it also increases spacecraft mass, power consumption, cost and data generation.

Players must make strategic decisions rather than simply selecting the most powerful components.

Multiplayer roles

  • Mission Planner
  • Spacecraft Engineer
  • Science and Payload Lead
  • Operations and Resources Lead

HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with browser-based simulation and visualizations.

projectDetails.details:
Outpost Twin is a playable digital twin of a four-person Moon or Mars outpost. You manage power, air, water, food and cabin heat one hour at a time, and you can copy the live mission and run it forward to test a plan before committing. Each mission replays a real stretch of space weather: when a solar particle event from NASA’s DONKI archive arrives, you choose to shelter (almost no dose, but no outdoor work and a cramped crew) or carry on (people outside take the full dose). Doses add up toward NASA’s 600 mSv career limit. Passing it grounds a person and slowly costs health, and a big dose in one storm makes someone ill.

The aim is to show that radiation is a budget, not a single event. In my scripted tests over a busy 365-day year, a crew that always carries on lost everyone, while a crew that sheltered from strong storms and watched its dose survived.

Two modes run the same rules: Assisted (plain words, hints, fewer controls) and Standard (every control). Everything is labelled “Real world” with a source link or “Game rule” when it is my estimate. Storm timing, surface dose rates and the limits are real. Storm doses and penalties are game estimates, because the archive gives no dose.

Built with JavaScript modules, Vite and three.js. It includes a self-test that runs 560 scripted missions and checks the numbers stay sane. I’m a solo participant: I designed, playtested and balanced the game, and used an AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic) to help write the code.

projectDetails.name: VITALS
projectDetails.summary: VITALS is offline-first health-monitoring software built for astronauts on long-duration missions, where help from Earth can be minutes to tens of minutes away. A hand-built ESP32 sensor box reads heart rate and SpO₂ from a MAX30102 pulse oximeter, a real or simulated ECG, and cabin temperature, humidity, and air quality, sent over USB, Bluetooth, or Wi-Fi to a crew dashboard that marks every vital green, yellow, or red against medically grounded ranges and the crew member’s own baseline. Seven subject-focused chatbots answer first-aid and space-health questions from a knowledge library sourced from NASA and partner-agency research; genuine emergencies are always handled by built-in first-aid logic, never an AI model, and each chatbot reads its answers aloud in its own voice. A 3D training simulator puts the crew through seven scenarios — dehydration, CO₂ buildup, sleep loss, a radiation storm, a spacewalk repair — where choices carry consequences into later missions. Every page, 3D model, voice line, and knowledge article is cached for full offline use: a signed-in crew member stays signed in with no connection, and every reading, profile edit, and status update syncs to the database the moment the link returns — even after the mission ends.
projectDetails.details:
What it does: VITALS has four parts: a sensor box placed in the crew’s module; a readings dashboard that classifies heart rate, SpO2, ECG, room temperature, and humidity against safe ranges and the crew member’s own baseline; a set of seven chatbots (one per health topic — fluid shift, bone and muscle, hygiene, isolation, medicine, environment, and a general health assistant) that answer questions and give first-aid steps; and a 3D training simulator with seven voice-acted mission scenarios.

The hardware: A hand-built sensor box, centered on an ESP32 microcontroller. It reads heart rate and blood oxygen from a MAX30102 pulse oximeter, a real ECG trace from an AD8232 sensor, cabin temperature and humidity from a DHT11 sensor, and air quality from an MQ-135 gas sensor. Two OLED screens on the box show live readings to the crew and the cabin conditions. It sends one JSON reading a second over USB serial, and can also be reached wirelessly over Bluetooth or a local Wi-Fi link, so the website works the same way whichever one is used.

How it works: The sensor box streams live readings over USB serial, Bluetooth, or a local Wi-Fi WebSocket link. The web app runs as an installable, offline-first progressive web app: a service worker caches every page, 3D model, and audio file after one online visit, so the whole site — chatbots, simulator, and readings — keeps working with no connection at all, for the length of a mission, once you’ve signed in at least once. Chatbot answers come first from a curated library of space-health facts drawn from NASA and partner-agency sources; for emergencies, the system always uses built-in first-aid rules rather than any AI model, so critical advice never depends on a generative model’s judgment. When online, an optional cloud language model (Cloudflare Workers AI) and, locally, an on-device model (Ollama) rephrase library answers into a more natural conversation, with every reply checked against the source facts before it’s shown, so the assistant can’t invent treatment advice. Each chatbot has its own voice and reads its answers aloud on request. Readings, crew profile edits, and baseline changes made offline are queued on the device and uploaded automatically, in batches, the moment the connection returns — which could be after the whole mission, since a signed-in crew member’s session is kept through long offline stretches rather than expiring and locking them out.

How to use it: A crew member signs up or signs in once — this step needs an internet connection, as does signing out later — and fills in their crew card: name, role, crew ID, and personal baselines like resting heart rate and sleep. On the Live Monitor page they pair their sensor over USB, Bluetooth, or Wi-Fi, or use the built-in Demo mode to try VITALS with no hardware at all. From there, readings update live on the dashboard and each health module page (Bone & Muscle, Fluid Shift, Environment, Hygiene, Isolation, Medicine), each one marked green, yellow, or red. Anyone can type a symptom or question to the relevant chatbot and turn on “Read aloud” to hear the answer spoken back. The Simulator lets the crew train through any of the seven scenarios in any order, with their choices affecting later quests and a final scored debrief. Commanders and flight surgeons get a crew-wide status board on the account page. Once signed in, everything else — chatbots, simulator, readings, the account page — keeps working offline for as long as needed.

Benefits and impact: Long-duration missions put much of the responsibility for spotting health changes on the astronauts themselves, with no doctor on board and communication delays that make real-time guidance from Earth impractical. VITALS gives the crew an always-available first read on their own condition and a trained way to practice handling emergencies before they happen for real, without needing a live connection to function.

Tools and technologies: React, TypeScript, and three.js for the web app and 3D scenes; an ESP32 (Arduino framework) sensor box with a MAX30102 pulse oximeter, AD8232 ECG front end, DHT11 and MQ-135 environmental sensors, and OLED displays, connected over USB, Bluetooth, or Wi-Fi; Supabase (Postgres with row-level security) for accounts and cross-device sync; Cloudflare Workers AI and a locally run Ollama model for the online/offline chatbot brains; browser-native text-to-speech for live chatbot voices; Kokoro-generated recorded voice lines for the simulator’s crew and mission control.

AI tool use: Claude (Anthropic) was used throughout development to write and review code, draft the chatbot knowledge library and prompts, help design the UI, and help draft the documentation and presentation text, under the team’s direction; the team reviewed and edited all content, including the safety logic and the final slides. The VITALS chatbots run on Google’s open Gemma models: Gemma 4 (26B) through Cloudflare Workers AI when online, and Gemma 3 270M locally through Ollama when offline; they support decisions only and never diagnose. The simulator’s spoken voice lines were generated with Kokoro, an open-source AI text-to-speech model, run locally and recorded as audio files. No images or video in the final project are SI-generated: the presentation uses screenshots of our website and our own photos, the website uses real photography and NASA 3D Resources models, and no SI-generated content uses NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers.

projectDetails.name: NILAVE – Lunar Landing Site Navigator
projectDetails.summary:
NILAVE – Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a proposed visual decision-support concept designed to simplify lunar south pole landing-site planning. The project presents an approach for comparing candidate landing locations and mission dates by examining the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the local lunar horizon.
NILAVE aims to help users understand how sunlight availability can influence solar power generation and how Earth visibility can affect direct-to-Earth communication opportunities. The proposed workflow includes selecting a landing site, choosing a mission date and time, and comparing Sun and Earth visibility through a simple visual interface.The concept identifies NASA's LRO/LOLA and LROC datasets, along with JPL Horizons, as potential data sources for future integration. NILAVE is important because it aims to make complex lunar mission-planning information easier to understand and support more informed comparisons of potential landing sites.
projectDetails.details:
NILAVE – Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a proposed visual decision-support concept designed to make lunar south pole landing-site planning easier to understand.

The concept focuses on two important mission-planning factors: sunlight availability for solar power generation and Earth visibility for direct-to-Earth communication. Users would select a candidate landing site and mission date/time, then compare the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the local lunar horizon. Objects above the horizon may be visible, while objects below it may be obstructed by the local terrain.

The project aims to help mission planners compare different landing locations and dates more clearly. It can also support education and public understanding of the challenges involved in lunar exploration.

For future development, we identified NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO/LOLA) for lunar topography, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) for lunar imagery, and NASA/JPL Horizons for celestial position data. These are proposed data sources for integration.

Our creative approach is to bring two critical mission questions—solar power potential and communication visibility—into one simple visual comparison concept. We considered terrain elevation, local horizon obstruction, sunlight, Earth visibility, mission date/time, and ease of use.

Tools and technologies: The current submission was prepared as a PowerPoint-based concept presentation and interface mock-up. No programming language, hardware, live calculations, or real-time data integration has been used in this submission. These are planned for future development.

Intended impact: NILAVE aims to make complex lunar visibility information easier to interpret and support more informed comparisons of potential lunar landing sites. Working calculations, NASA data integration, and an interactive web application are planned next steps.

projectDetails.name: PRITHVI: The Sound of Earth
projectDetails.summary:
PRITHVI is an interactive web experience developed for NASA Space Apps 2026's Earth Information Jukebox challenge. It uses NASA's Earth Information Center Climate Spiral (SVS #5190) and NASA GISTEMP v4 surface-temperature anomaly data as its primary case study.
The project connects scientific visualizations with deterministic, browser-generated sound. Selected temperature measurements and their changes over time are mapped to audio parameters such as pitch and rhythm, allowing users to explore Earth's changing systems through both sight and sound.
By combining interactive Earth visualization, scientific data exploration and real-time sonification, PRITHVI aims to make Earth science more engaging and accessible. It also explains the data sources, measurement units, baseline and sound-mapping methodology behind the experience.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview

PRITHVI: The Sound of Earth is an interactive scientific experience developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 — The Earth Information Jukebox.

The project explores how Earth science visualizations can be paired with sound to create another way of understanding changes in our planet.

GitHub : https://github.com/vishanth14/Prithvi-The-Sound-of-Earth.git

How It Works

PRITHVI uses the NASA Earth Information Center Climate Spiral (NASA SVS #5190) and the underlying NASA GISTEMP v4 temperature-anomaly dataset as its primary case study.

Scientific observations are processed and validated before being passed through a documented sonification system. Temperature magnitude influences pitch, changes over time influence rhythm, and measurement variation influences the sound's timbre. The browser generates audio dynamically using Tone.js and the Web Audio API rather than relying on prerecorded music.

Users can explore the 3D Earth, inspect scientific visualizations, navigate the data timeline, listen to generated sound and understand how the measurements are translated into audio.

Technology

The application is developed using React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, GSAP, D3.js, PapaParse, Zod, Zustand, Tone.js and the Web Audio API.

Creativity and Impact

PRITHVI combines interactive planetary visualization, scientific storytelling and data-driven sonification in one experience. It aims to make complex Earth observations more engaging for students, educators and the general public, while offering an additional auditory perspective on scientific data.

The project distinguishes original scientific measurements from their normalized and sonified representations, with attention to source attribution, sampling limitations and accessibility.

projectDetails.details:
Our project, CosmoEarth AI – Explore Beyond Boundaries, is an AI-powered platform designed to bring Earth and space exploration together in one user-friendly dashboard. The main aim of our project is to help people understand our planet, explore the universe, and learn about environmental and astronomical changes through simple explanations and visual information.

What does the project do and how does it work?

Our project has two major exploration sections: Earth Exploration and Space Exploration.

The Earth Exploration section focuses on forests, climate and weather, glaciers, oceans, and natural disasters. Users can search for locations, explore satellite-image previews, and learn how satellite observations can help identify environmental changes. For example, comparing satellite images from different dates can help us understand changes in forest cover or glacier boundaries.

The Space Exploration section allows users to learn about stars, galaxies, comets, meteors, asteroids, and changes in the night sky. Our project is inspired by NASA's SPHEREx mission, which studies the universe using infrared observations across 102 spectral bands.

Another important feature is Mr. Booth, our friendly AI chatbot represented by a funny white ghost. It is designed to explain complicated Earth and space topics in simple, understandable language. Users can ask questions and learn scientific concepts through easy explanations.

The dashboard also includes Detected Changes, which describes how Earth images and space observations can be compared and verified, and Reports & History, which is planned to maintain observation details and analysis reports.

What are the benefits of the project?

  • Brings Earth and space exploration topics together in one platform.
  • Makes scientific information easier for students and beginners to understand.
  • Helps users learn about environmental changes such as deforestation and glacier melting.
  • Introduces users to astronomical objects and space research.
  • Provides a simple chatbot interface for learning and asking questions.
  • Encourages awareness about our planet and the universe.

What is the intended impact?

Our intended impact is to create awareness about Earth's environmental changes and increase interest in space science. We want to make scientific knowledge more accessible to students, learners, and the general public. In the future, the platform can support environmental education, scientific learning, and better understanding of observations from Earth and space.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, and software were used?

We developed the current dashboard prototype using:

  • HTML: To create the structure and sections of the website.
  • CSS: To design the interface, colours, layouts, animations, and responsive appearance.
  • JavaScript: To add navigation, search, filtering, and interactive chatbot demonstration features.
  • Web browser: To run and test the dashboard.
  • Computer or laptop: Used for development and testing.

The current prototype uses illustrative images and sample educational chatbot responses. Future development can integrate NASA open datasets, verified satellite feeds, official weather and disaster-warning APIs, and a connected AI language model to provide live information and more advanced analysis.

How is the project creative and innovative?

The creative aspect of CosmoEarth AI is that it combines two different areas of exploration—Earth science and space science—in one platform. Instead of making users visit multiple websites to learn about these subjects, our dashboard provides a common place to explore both. We also created Mr. Booth, a friendly ghost-themed chatbot, to make scientific learning more interactive and enjoyable. The change-detection concept adds another innovative feature by showing how observations from different dates can be compared to understand changes.

What factors did our team consider?

Our team considered user-friendliness, accessibility, educational value, accuracy of information, reliability of data sources, and responsive design. We also considered the importance of using verified scientific information rather than presenting unconfirmed observations as facts. We designed the dashboard to be useful for beginners while keeping the possibility of adding advanced scientific features in the future.

Overall, CosmoEarth AI aims to make Earth and space science more accessible, interesting, and understandable. Our vision is to help people explore our planet, discover the universe, and understand the changes happening around us through intelligent technology.

projectDetails.summary:
The "Junior Astronaut" project is an interactive lunar outpost simulator developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, designed with a target audience of children ages 7–12. The game immerses players in managing a lunar South Pole base at Shackleton Crater, where they must carefully balance core operational resources such as power, life support oxygen, and hydroponic food.

To maximize educational value, the application enforces strict engineering trade-offs where every decision involves a genuine cost, such as balancing active water-wall and electromagnetic shielding against available battery power. Furthermore, the simulator grounds its mechanics in authentic space science by incorporating real-world data and references from NASA's DONKI space weather alerts, RadLab BLEO radiation baselines, and OSDR biological repositories.
projectDetails.details: Avengers Assemble is a browser-based 3D space survival game for kids ages 7–12 where players run a 7-Sol outpost on the Moon or Mars, balancing power, oxygen, hydroponic food, radiation shielding, and Earth radio delays under strict "no free lunch" trade-offs while driving a 3D rover and sheltering from solar flares. Requiring zero downloads on laptops or phones, it benefits young learners by turning intimidating aerospace science into hands-on play, aiming to spark STEM curiosity and public understanding of deep-space survival. Built with Python, Streamlit, Three.js, HTML5/CSS/JavaScript, and Web Audio API, it is grounded in real NASA DONKI space weather feeds, NASA OSDR (OSD-137, OSD-767, OSD-895), RadLab, and the CSA Food Production Toolkit. The project creatively blends unlockable Avengers commanders—each with unique 3D shields, rover driving, and fun emotes—with real Moon and Mars physics, while prioritizing age-friendly clarity, cross-device controls, replayability, and clear data attribution.
