United by a shared vision of innovation, technology, and problem-solving, our team aims to transform ideas into meaningful solutions that address real-world challenges.

Our challenge, “Be an Earth System Trend Detective!”, focuses on understanding the dynamic and interconnected environmental systems of our planet. Earth is constantly changing, and identifying these changes across different regions and periods is essential to understanding environmental patterns and trends.

Our goal is to explore and develop an innovative, data-driven tool that can select relevant Earth science variables obtained from NASA missions and Earth science models, visualize their changes over time, and analyze the patterns they reveal. The solution aims to help users identify what is changing, where the changes are occurring, how much change is taking place, and whether those changes are scientifically significant.

Through data analysis, visualization, research, and collaborative problem-solving, NEXORA INNOVATIONS strives to make complex Earth science information easier to understand and interpret. We believe that combining scientific knowledge with technological innovation can open new possibilities for understanding our planet.

Think. Innovate. Collaborate. Create Impact.
projectDetails.details:
Project Title: EarthTrend – An Intelligent Earth System Trend Analysis and Visualization Platform

EarthTrend is an innovative, data-driven platform designed to help users understand and investigate changes occurring across Earth's interconnected environmental systems. The project focuses on identifying, analyzing, and visualizing trends in Earth science data collected through NASA satellite missions and Earth science models.

The platform aims to allow users to select relevant environmental variables, explore historical data, and visualize how these variables change over time and across different geographical regions. Through interactive graphs, trend comparisons, and data visualization, users can identify increasing or decreasing patterns, understand the magnitude of changes, and recognize potentially significant environmental trends.

The primary objective is to simplify complex Earth science datasets and make environmental trend analysis more accessible, understandable, and useful. The platform will help users investigate questions such as what is changing, where the changes are happening, how rapidly they are occurring, and whether the observed changes are scientifically significant.

The project emphasizes creativity through the integration of scientific data, interactive visualization, and analytical approaches into a unified platform. It aims to support students, researchers, environmental enthusiasts, and other users in exploring Earth's changing systems and gaining meaningful insights from scientific observations.

Through this initiative, NEXORA INNOVATIONS aims to transform complex environmental data into understandable information and encourage data-driven awareness of our planet's changing environment.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

GeoPulse – NEXTRONZ

Smart Disaster Monitoring and Early-Warning System

GeoPulse is an innovative disaster monitoring and early-warning prototype developed by Team NEXTRONZ, inspired by the geographical challenges of Wayanad, Kerala. We developed an integrated system using ESP32 technology, multiple environmental sensors, an ESP32-S3 camera, IoT connectivity and GSM communication.

The system monitors temperature, humidity, rainfall, soil moisture, gas levels, vibration, movement and ground orientation using sensors connected to an ESP32 DevKit V1. An ESP32-S3-CAM provides live video streaming, allowing users to observe the monitored surroundings remotely. Sensor readings are displayed on a 2.8-inch TFT screen and a mobile-friendly Wi-Fi dashboard featuring real-time values, graphical analysis, historical data and warning messages.

A SIM800L GSM module provides emergency SMS notifications and automatic phone calls to configured contacts. Audible warnings are also provided for selected rain and soil-moisture conditions.

GeoPulse addresses the challenge by combining environmental monitoring, visual observation and multiple alert methods in one affordable prototype. It is important because timely awareness of changing environmental conditions can support better preparedness and faster responses. Our vision is to make disaster monitoring more accessible, understandable and useful for communities in vulnerable regions.
projectDetails.details:
GeoPulse – NEXTRONZ

Smart Disaster Monitoring and Early-Warning System

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

GeoPulse is an intelligent disaster monitoring and early-warning prototype inspired by the geographical and environmental challenges of Wayanad, Kerala. It is designed to monitor environmental changes and identify conditions that may indicate potential landslide and earthquake-related risks.

The system uses an ESP32 DevKit V1 connected to multiple sensors, including an MPU6050 accelerometer and gyroscope, vibration sensor, soil moisture sensor, rain sensor, MQ-2 gas sensor, DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor, and PIR motion sensor. These sensors continuously collect environmental and movement-related data. The ESP32 processes the readings and identifies abnormal conditions using programmed threshold values.

An ESP32-S3-CAM provides live video streaming through Wi-Fi, allowing users to observe the surrounding environment using a mobile phone. A 2.8-inch ILI9341 TFT display shows sensor readings and system status.

A dedicated Wi-Fi dashboard provides real-time sensor values, graphical representations, historical readings and warning messages. The SIM800L GSM module enables emergency SMS notifications and automatic phone calls to two configured mobile numbers. It can also support incoming calls and SMS with suitable programming. A buzzer provides audible warnings for selected rain and soil-moisture conditions.

2. What benefits does it provide?

GeoPulse combines several monitoring technologies into one system. It helps users observe environmental changes, monitor rainfall and soil conditions, detect unusual vibrations and movement, and view the surroundings through a live camera stream.

The dashboard makes sensor information easier to understand through graphs and warning messages. GSM communication provides another way to receive alerts when internet connectivity is unavailable, provided cellular coverage is available.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact of GeoPulse is to improve environmental awareness and support disaster preparedness, particularly in geographically vulnerable regions.

By combining sensor monitoring, live visual observation and multiple communication methods, the project aims to help communities and monitoring teams identify potentially concerning environmental changes earlier and respond more effectively.

It also demonstrates how affordable electronics and connected technologies can contribute to community-focused disaster preparedness.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware and software were used?

Hardware components:

- ESP32 DevKit V1 microcontroller
- ESP32-S3-CAM camera module
- MPU6050 accelerometer and gyroscope
- Vibration sensor
- Soil moisture sensor
- Rain sensor
- MQ-2 gas sensor
- DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor
- PIR motion sensor
- SIM800L GSM module
- 2.8-inch ILI9341 SPI TFT display
- Buzzer
- Power supply and connecting wires

Programming languages:

- C/C++ for ESP32 firmware
- HTML for the web dashboard
- CSS for dashboard design
- JavaScript for live dashboard updates and graphical visualization
- JavaScript with Node.js for the dashboard server

Software and development tools:

- Arduino IDE / ArduinoDroid
- ESP32 board support package
- Arduino libraries for sensor communication and display control
- Node.js
- Android mobile browser
- Blynk platform for IoT integration

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

The creativity of GeoPulse lies in integrating multiple monitoring features into a single affordable prototype. Instead of depending on only one sensor or one communication method, it combines environmental sensing, ground movement monitoring, live camera streaming, a visual TFT interface, a web-based dashboard and GSM-based communication.

The combination of graphical sensor histories, live camera observation and SMS and phone-call alerts provides different ways to understand and communicate environmental conditions.

The project also focuses on making technical information accessible through a mobile-friendly dashboard, allowing users to monitor multiple sensor readings from one place.

6. What factors did our team consider?

Our team considered the following factors during development:

1. Affordability: Selecting accessible and relatively low-cost electronic components.
2. Environmental relevance: Monitoring rainfall, soil moisture, vibration and other environmental conditions relevant to disaster preparedness.
3. Real-time monitoring: Displaying updated sensor information and camera footage.
4. Communication reliability: Combining Wi-Fi and GSM communication to provide alternative alert channels.
5. User accessibility: Designing a dashboard with understandable readings, graphs and warning messages.
6. Power requirements: Considering suitable power supplies for the ESP32, camera and GSM module.
7. Modularity: Designing the system so that sensors and features can be tested and improved separately.
8. Safety and reliability: Considering sensor calibration, false alerts, connectivity failures and the limitations of a prototype.
9. Future development: Allowing additional sensors, improved data analysis and more advanced warning features to be integrated.
GeoPulse – NEXTRONZ demonstrates how embedded systems, environmental sensors, IoT technology, live camera streaming and cellular communication can be combined to support disaster preparedness. Our vision is to develop an affordable, accessible and expandable monitoring system that helps people understand environmental changes and become better prepared for potential natural hazards.

projectDetails.name: Project Nexus crew
projectDetails.summary: Outpost Command is a game where students design and run a Moon or Mars outpost. Before launch, players split limited rocket weight between solar panels, batteries, radiation shielding, a greenhouse and spare parts. Then they keep three astronauts alive for 14 days through lunar nights, dust storms and solar flares, choosing each day how to spend crew time and power. Every choice costs something, so missions can fail, and a debrief explains exactly why. Players can replay real events, such as Opportunity’s 2018 dust storm, Chandrayaan-3’s lunar night and the 1972 solar storm, and rewind to try a different decision. It makes real engineering trade-offs tangible and fun without overwhelming young learners, using a tutorial, a simple Junior view and 18 languages. NASA data and videos power the learning, and teachers can run it in class with no accounts.
projectDetails.details:
What it does
Outpost Command lets students experience the decisions behind a real mission. First, in “Design your outpost”, players split 10 units of launch weight across five systems: solar panels, batteries, radiation shielding, a greenhouse and spare parts. These limits are physical: battery size sets how much power can be stored, shielding sets the most radiation protection crew work can reach, and spare parts decide how far repairs can restore life support. Then they run the outpost for 14 days with three astronauts, choosing two crew jobs a day and whether to spend power on grow lights and the science lab. Core events (cargo landers, solar storms, leaks, the lunar night, Mars dust storms, illness) and 11 random extra events, such as mold, water ice and a dust devil, force trade-offs where every option costs something. After each day, colored chips show what changed. At the end, a debrief names the main cause of success or failure, explains how the launch design mattered, and shows the real NASA science and NASA videos behind it.

How it addresses the challenge
It covers life support, radiation shielding, power and food production, and lets missions fail or succeed on the player’s decisions. It avoids oversimplifying through real figures (Moon and Mars radiation levels, Mars sunlight at about 43% of Earth’s, lunar night, ISS water recycling). It avoids overwhelming young learners with a 4-step tutorial, a Junior view with six simple bars (Commander mode shows every number), a daily tip from the Cosmo companion, and a “what if?” rewind to any decision day.

What makes it creative
Mission History lets players replay real events: NASA’s Opportunity rover and the 2018 dust storm, India’s Chandrayaan-3 and the lunar night, and the 1972 solar storm between Apollo 16 and 17. They try to survive what history could not, then read what really happened. The storm in a mission can come from the strongest real solar flare in NASA’s DONKI space-weather database. Players earn stars, badges, levels and a companion wardrobe, with no streak pressure.

Benefits and intended impact
Students learn that engineering is about trade-offs, and teachers get tools to prove it. A before-and-after learning check uses different questions on the same ideas and explains every answer. Teacher mode creates class codes, so a whole class plays the same scenario, and a dashboard shows average scores, common causes of failure and learning gain. It needs no accounts and stores no student data on a server. Crew mode lets three students share one phone. The game supports 18 languages with a searchable language screen, color-blind friendly bars, adjustable text size, a reduced-motion option and a kid-safe mode.

Tools
React Native, Expo and TypeScript, with react-native-svg for the planets, Supabase for optional sync and AI functions, Jest and tsx for automated tests, and Netlify and GitHub for the web version and code. NASA resources used: the NASA Image and Video Library, Astronomy Picture of the Day and DONKI APIs. The simulation is a deterministic, tested engine, so every result can be explained. It runs on phones and in a web browser; no special hardware is needed.

Use of Super Intelligence
Code, tests, data tables, text and translations were created with help from Claude (Anthropic) and reviewed by the team. The sound effects are generated by a script, and the visuals are drawn in code. The game contains no NASA logos or mission identifiers.

Factors considered and limits
We simplified the numbers into a 0 to 100 scale and shortened the lunar night in one replay, so it is a teaching tool, not a mission planner. The translations are machine-assisted and need native-speaker review. The project has not yet been tested with students, and the next step is a classroom trial to measure learning gain.

projectDetails.name: Project NexussAI
projectDetails.summary: AstroHealth is a crew-facing health monitoring platform for long-duration spaceflight. It continuously fuses measured physiology with crew self-assessment, treating disagreement between sensor data and crew reports as a finding rather than noise. The system uses a Random Forest strain classifier, Isolation Forest anomaly detection, rule-based threshold monitoring, and trend analysis to produce explainable health assessments. It provides decision support including ranked contributing signals, concrete next actions, and EVA clearance gating. A what-if harness lets operators perturb physiological parameters and observe detector responses. All data is synthetic and physiologically grounded, with provenance documented. The platform includes 37 automated tests, a live web dashboard, and a published model card disclosing limitations including 84.1% leave-one-archetype-out accuracy. AstroHealth addresses the critical need for crew health monitoring when no clinic is available during deep space missions.
projectDetails.details:
AstroHealth is a crew-facing health monitoring platform for long-duration spaceflight. It addresses the challenge of monitoring astronaut health when no medical clinic is available during missions.

What it does:

- Continuously monitors 16 physiological features across 7-day rolling windows

- Classifies strain level (low/moderate/high) using a Random Forest model

- Detects unknown patterns using Isolation Forest anomaly detection

- Surfaces disagreement between crew self-reports and sensor measurements

- Provides EVA clearance gating based on health status

- Offers a what-if harness to simulate parameter changes

How it works:

- Deterministic synthetic signal generator creates physiologically grounded crew data

- Feature extraction produces 16 features from 7-day windows

- Random Forest classifier predicts strain level with 89.9% accuracy (5-fold)

- Isolation Forest detects novel patterns not seen in training

- Rule, trend, and baseline detectors flag threshold breaches and drift

- Self-assessment data is fused into the composite score

- Disagreement between subjective and objective measures is surfaced

Benefits:

- Early detection of crew health deterioration

- Explainable predictions with ranked contributing signals

- Decision support for EVA clearance

- Honest limitations disclosure

Tools used: Python, FastAPI, scikit-learn, NumPy, Chart.js, Vercel

Creativity: The platform treats disagreement between crew reports and sensors as a finding rather than noise, which is a novel approach to space health monitoring.

projectDetails.name: TerraLuna(Earth Analog Finder)
projectDetails.summary: TerraLuna(Earth Analog Finder) is an interactive web map that ranks places on Earth by how well they resemble a chosen Moon or Mars site. Pick a target, such as the Shackleton Crater rim or Jezero Crater, and the tool scores 22 Earth sites on slope, roughness, temperature extremes, aridity and volcanic geology using open NASA data. Every score is explainable: users can change factor weights, compare sites side by side, and see for each site where the analogy breaks down. An AI model writes plain-language explanations from the data only. It matters because mission teams need analog sites to test equipment and methods before flying, and many analogs are poorly characterized.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

TerraLuna(Earth Analog Finder) helps mission planners and the public discover which Earth locations best rehearse a Moon or Mars site. Users choose a target (Shackleton Crater rim, Malapert Massif, Jezero Crater or Gale Crater), then see a ranked list and map of 22 Earth candidate sites, including lesser-known ones such as the Danakil Depression, Salar de Uyuni, Dasht-e Lut, Tibesti, Pinacate and Svalbard, not only famous analogs.

HOW IT WORKS

Each site is described by five factors normalized to 0-1: slope, roughness, temperature extremes, aridity and volcanic/basaltic geology. Per-factor similarity is 1 minus the absolute difference; the overall score is a weighted average, so users can re-weight factors with sliders and the ranking updates instantly. Earth values come from NASA POWER climate data and a global elevation dataset. Moon slope and roughness are measured from the LRO LOLA south-polar DEM using the same 5x5 grid method as the Earth sites, so values are comparable. A FastAPI backend serves the data and an AI explanation endpoint; the AI only receives the numbers in our dataset and falls back to a template if unavailable.

WHERE ANALOGIES BREAK DOWN

Each site shows its own limits, and every explanation notes that Earth cannot reproduce reduced gravity, vacuum or thin atmosphere, or radiation. Values that are estimates, not measurements, are labelled "est." in the app.

BENEFITS AND GOALS

A transparent, adjustable way to compare analog candidates, to find overlooked sites, and to explain why a site is or is not a good analog. We hope it becomes a starting point for a global, systematic analog search.

TOOLS

Python, FastAPI, NumPy, rasterio, pyproj, matplotlib; JavaScript, Leaflet, Chart.js; Google Gemini API; hosted on Render. Code: https://github.com/Drish23-sys/Nasa_challenge

LIMITATIONS

Curated set of 22 sites, not a global search. Earth temperature is annual air-temperature range while Moon/Mars use surface temperature (a proxy). Moon temperature ranges, geology tags and Mars slope/roughness are team estimates and are labelled as such.

challengeDetails.excerpt: Space-themed STEM content often oversimplifies the engineering trade-offs that define a real mission or presents them at a level too complex to hold a young learner's attention. Your challenge is to design and build an interactive game or app that lets students run a lunar or Martian outpost, balancing competing demands like life support, radiation shielding, power, and food production, so they experience firsthand the decisions that determine whether a mission fails or succeeds.

projectDetails.name: ASTRAVITA
projectDetails.summary:
NOVA SHIELD

See the Hidden. Predict the Risk. Protect the Crew.

NOVA SHIELD is an AI-assisted environmental and astronaut health monitoring system proposed for long-duration space missions.

It combines three integrated modules:

- AEROMAP – Environmental Intelligence: Monitors CO₂, temperature, humidity, and airflow across spacecraft zones, identifying unusual environmental changes.
- ASTRA-SYNC – Health Impact Intelligence: Connects environmental trends with relevant health information, including sleep, fatigue, concentration, and well-being.
- ZENVITA – Wearable Health Integration: Optionally displays wearable measurements such as heart rate, HRV, SpO₂, sleep, and activity.

The system aims to detect developing environmental conditions, identify possible contributing factors, estimate future trends, and help astronauts and authorised Mission Control personnel review relevant health information.

Its dashboard includes spacecraft zone mapping, predictive warnings, historical charts, health indicators, an action-review checklist, and post-action verification.

NOVA SHIELD is a proposed decision-support prototype, not a medical device or replacement for existing spacecraft safety systems. All demonstration readings are simulated. Safety-critical decisions remain with authorised humans.

Challenge: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
Event: NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026
projectDetails.details:
Project: ASTRAVITA

App: Nova Shield

Team: OrbitFit

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 — Challenge: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions

Live App: https://mmabyadh-cmd.github.io/novashield/

GitHub: https://github.com/mmabyadh-cmd/novashield

WHAT DOES IT DO / HOW DOES IT WORK?

ASTRAVITA — Nova Shield is an AI-powered environmental + health intelligence system for long-duration space missions. It is ONE app, not three separate apps.

It answers 6 questions in seconds for every alert: WHERE? WHAT? WHY? WHAT NEXT? WHAT TO DO? DID IT IMPROVE?

It has 3 equal core modules + 3 supporting stations, all in one dashboard:

1. AEROMAP — Environment (6 zones, all equal)

Monitors zone-level CO2, temperature, humidity, airflow, pressure, VOC, particulates, noise and light for: Sleeping Compartment, Lab, Exercise, Galley / Kitchen, Control, Medical. In microgravity, natural convection is reduced, so a cabin average hides local pockets. AEROMAP shows each zone separately.

Live Demo: Sleeping Compartment YELLOW — CO2 850 ppm, Airflow 0.12 m/s Down 30%, Temp 23.1°C. After the crew checks the vent + filter and clicks Mark as Done, it verifies: CO2 610 ppm GREEN, Recovery 68 to 82. Full audit trail: 08:00 Alert → 08:05 Acknowledged → 08:20 Inspection → 08:40 Verified.

2. ASTRA-SYNC — Health Impact

Connects environment timing with health timing. It does NOT claim the environment causes a body change. It shows association only. Example: CREW-001 Commander — Sleep 5.8h, Recovery 68, HRV Down 18%, HR 72, SpO2 97% on the same nights CO2 was high. The other 5 crew stayed GREEN, Recovery 83-88.

3. ZENVITA — Full Wearable Body Data (Opt-in, No Delivery)

Complete wearable app inside Nova Shield.

- Dashboard: Health Score, Recovery, Sleep, HRV, SpO2, HR, Steps, Calories, Water, Mood for CREW-001 to CREW-006 (crew selector)

- Sleep Lab: Last night 5.8 h, Deep 14%, REM 18%, Onset 28 min, Wakes 3, Quality 62%, 7-day trend 7.5 • 5.8 h falling

- Recovery & Strain: Recovery, Strain 72, Readiness Low, Resting HR 68

- Activity & Exercise: Steps 4200, Active 28 min, Treadmill 20 min, Resistance 15 min, Add Workout

- Nutrition & Hydration: Calories 2100/2600, Water 1.8L/2.5L, Add Meal, Add 250ml Water, Macros

- Mind & Well-being: Mood / Energy / Focus / Stress check-in 1-5 + Save, Breathing 4-7-8 timer, Journal

- History: 7-day table for Sleep, HRV, Recovery, HR, SpO2

- Privacy: Opt-in only, no audio/video, Data stays local, Share trends with Crew Medical only

4. Space Smart Kitchen Station

Galley + Nutrition Hub, onboard inventory only, no delivery, no ordering from Earth. No bread in space — crumbs float. Tortillas only.

Inventory — Real NASA / ISS Food Types:

Main (Thermostabilized pouches): Shrimp Cocktail 12, Beef Stroganoff 10, Chicken Teriyaki 11, Spaghetti with Meat Sauce 9, Grilled Chicken 8.

Breakfast (Freeze-Dried): Scrambled Eggs 14, Oatmeal with Raisins 12, Granola 10.

Sides (Freeze-Dried / Thermostabilized): Macaroni & Cheese 12, Mashed Potatoes 13, Rice Pilaf 10, Corn 9, Green Beans 9.

Bread + Spread: Tortillas 18, Peanut Butter 6, Cheese Spread 7.

Snacks (Natural Form / Freeze-Dried): Trail Mix 15, Almonds 10, Dried Apricots 4 LOW STOCK, Freeze-Dried Strawberries 9.

Desserts: Brownies 8, Freeze-Dried Ice Cream 7.

Drinks (Freeze-Dried): Coffee 20, Orange Juice 14, Tea 16.

Condiments: Ketchup, Hot Sauce, Salt & Pepper 12.

Water: Water Pouches 40 — for rehydration + drinking.

Search + filter, expiry dates, low-stock warnings. Example: Dried Apricots 4 = LOW STOCK warning.

Today's Menu for each crew: Breakfast 450 kcal, Lunch 750 kcal, Dinner 500 kcal, Snack 190 kcal. Total 1890 kcal / day.

Example Day: Breakfast — Scrambled Eggs + Tortilla + Coffee 450 kcal. Lunch — Shrimp Cocktail + Rice Pilaf 750 kcal. Dinner — Beef Stroganoff + Mashed Potatoes 500 kcal. Snack — Trail Mix 190 kcal.

Choose a Meal from Space Kitchen: Astronaut chooses a meal from what is already onboard. No ordering. Choosing takes 1 portion from stock, logs it in ZENVITA Nutrition, and updates Food Status + Survival live.

Food Status + Survival: Food Left 592,800 kcal, Water Left 920L. Calculation: 592,800 ÷ (6 crew × 2,600 kcal/day) = 38 days of food. 920L ÷ (6 × 2.5L/day) = 61 days water. Food runs out first. So the crew can live 38 days. What-If Simulator: change crew size or ration (Normal / Ration / Emergency) to see new survival days.

Recipe Builder: Pick 3 ingredients → Suggest recipe (e.g. Tortilla + Peanut Butter + Freeze-Dried Strawberries = Space PB & Berry Wrap 450 kcal) + Cook Log → Syncs to ZENVITA Nutrition.

Food Safety: Fridge 3.5°C GREEN, Freezer -18°C GREEN, Hygiene checklist. Waste: Food waste 0.2 kg, Recycling 92%, Water recycling 92%. Equipment: Rehydration Station, Food Warmer, Dispenser — all GREEN.

5. Exercise Station: Treadmill, Cycle Ergometer, Resistance device, weekly plan, equipment status, syncs to ZENVITA.

6. Sleep Station: Sleep environment (CO2, Temp, Noise, Light), sleep schedule for all 6 crew, sleep hygiene checklist.

5 AI MODELS — VISIBLE IN ALL MODES:

Model 1 Pattern: 82% — Rising CO2 pattern detected

Model 2 Prediction: YELLOW again in 90 min (Range 75-110 min) if not fixed

Model 3 Cause: Reduced ventilation 82% / Filter load 11% / Other 7%

Model 4 Health: Sleep Down 28%, HRV Down 18%

The same 4 models appear in Dashboard, Astronaut, Mission Control, Crew, Health, Body, ZENVITA and Kitchen modes. Never hidden.

WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?

- Early warning: Predicts risk 90 minutes before the threshold, not after.

- Zone-level truth: Finds hidden local CO2 pockets that cabin averages hide.

- Faster decisions: WHERE / WHAT / WHY / NEXT / ACTION / IMPROVED in one screen.

- One app: Environment + Health + Body + Kitchen + Exercise + Sleep together, no switching apps.

- Verified action: Mark as Done proves improvement with before/after numbers, not just an alert that disappears.

- Equal coverage: 6 zones equal, 6 astronauts equal, 3 health areas (Sleep / Physical / Mental) equal.

- Human in control: AI suggests, human approves. AI never auto-acts on safety actions.

- Private and resilient: Opt-in, no audio/video, offline-first, works with communication delay to Earth.

WHAT IS THE INTENDED IMPACT?

To make long-duration missions safer when Earth cannot help instantly. To protect sleep, recovery and daily performance, not just to sound alarms. To support independent health monitoring for Lunar Gateway, Moon, and Mars missions, where delays range from minutes to tens of minutes, and the crew must decide alone.

On Earth, the same logic helps submarines, isolated research stations, hospitals and remote workplaces where air + health + food + sleep are connected.

Vision: See the Hidden. Predict the Risk. Protect the Crew.

WHAT TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES, HARDWARE, OR SOFTWARE DID YOU USE?

- Languages: HTML (single-file web app, index.html)

- Fonts / Design: Inter — one font for all text, spacious layout, high-contrast cards for readability

- Platform: GitHub Pages (public, no login) — Live: https://mmabyadh-cmd.github.io/novashield/

- Code: GitHub repo GitHub.com/mmabyadh-cmd/novashield (MIT, public)

- Data: Simulated environmental sensor data + simulated wearable data, modelled on NASA ECLSS concepts and NASA-STD-3001 human factors guidance. No real astronaut data used.

- AI Logic: Rule-based logic + pattern detection + trend analysis + confidence scoring (prototype logic, clearly labelled with % confidence and ranges, not a black box)

- Conceptual hardware foundation: Existing spacecraft sensors (CO2, temp, humidity, airflow, pressure) + commercial wearable sensors (HR, HRV, SpO2, sleep, steps) + galley equipment (rehydration station, warmer, fridge/freezer). No new hardware required for the prototype.

- Presentation: 7-slide Google Slides demo (ASTRAVITA / Nova Shield / Team OrbitFit)

HOW IS YOUR PROJECT CREATIVE?

Most systems monitor spacecraft OR astronauts separately, and only alert after a threshold. ASTRAVITA is creative because it does 5 things together:

1. Zone-level + Prediction: It finds WHERE the problem is and WHEN it will return, not just that a threshold was crossed.

2. Environment + Body + Kitchen + Sleep in one loop: Air → Sleep → Recovery → Food → Exercise → Air. A poor sleep night, a low recovery score, a low-stock food item and a high-CO2 zone are shown together, not in separate tools.

3. Verified loop: Alert → Action → Mark as Done → Before/After proof. Judges and crew can see improvement, not just warnings.

4. Transparent AI: Every AI claim shows its confidence and range, and health claims are labelled association only.

5. Honest, human-centred design: Privacy-first, opt-in, offline-first, equal importance to every zone, crew member and health area. SpO2 does NOT measure CO2 — we state this clearly and never merge the two.

WHAT FACTORS DID YOUR TEAM CONSIDER?

Team OrbitFit considered:

- Astronaut safety first: Early warning, verified actions, human approval, never auto-action on safety.

- Scientific honesty: Simulated data clearly labelled, decision-support only, not a medical device, association not causation, SpO2 ≠ CO2, confidence + ranges shown.

- Privacy: Opt-in wearable sharing, no audio/video, share trends with Crew Medical only, local/offline data.

- Communication delay: Offline-first, crew can decide without Earth.

- Usability: One app, one font, spacious layout, big numbers, 6 questions answered in seconds, works on mobile + desktop, no login.

- Compatibility: Works with existing sensors / wearables / galley equipment, no new hardware needed.

- Equality: 6 zones equal, 6 astronauts equal, Sleep / Physical / Mental equal, AEROMAP / ASTRA-SYNC / ZENVITA equal.

- Practical limits: Prototype uses simulated data; future work needs real telemetry, real wearable validation, personal baselines, radiation / noise / lighting, and specialist medical validation before any real use.

- Food and daily life: Nutrition, hydration, waste, food safety and exercise are part of health, not extras — so Smart Kitchen, Exercise and Sleep Stations are included, with no delivery feature.

ZenVita AI App is a companion model originally built for a separate hackathon challenge on nutrition and lifestyle. It was first generated with Bolt AI, then I personally edited, corrected, and adapted the code, data, and logic for use inside ASTRAVITA

In ASTRAVITA, ZenVita is not a separate app. It is one integrated module inside Nova Shield — for body data, sleep, food, and mind — rebuilt for astronauts, with an onboard-only Space Kitchen and real NASA/ISS food.

ZenVita AI Nutrition & Lifestyle Ecosystem

challengeDetails.title: Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions
challengeDetails.excerpt: Long-duration missions expose astronauts to space radiation, isolation and confinement, altered gravity, and a hostile closed environment, which can bring immune changes, bone loss, cardiovascular events, and behavioral health problems. On long missions, astronauts carry much of the responsibility for spotting these changes in themselves. Your challenge is to build a health monitoring software that gathers health indicators and enables astronauts to evaluate and act on the status of their health.

projectDetails.name: Project ORBITRON NEON
projectDetails.summary:
Project Summary: A.R.I.S. (Advanced Responsive Integrated Suit Intelligence)

What we created:

A.R.I.S. is an autonomous astronaut health monitoring system and intelligent smart spacesuit. This system uses multi-modal biosensors to monitor cardiovascular, musculoskeletal and behavioural data. The system also has anomaly detection algorithms operating in real time, self-assessment tools and active emergency protocols.

How we solved the problem:

When exploring deep space, there will be a lag in communication between the astronaut and Earth. With A.R.I.S. the crew can monitor their health in real time with automatic risk detection and protocols for medical interventions.

Why it is important:

By allowing the astronaut to have an autonomous health triage system with continuous biosensors it can ensure they are still able to carry out vital operations whilst also keeping them safe and ensuring mission success.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does our Project Do? & How Does It Work?

This project is an interactive Jarvis Inspired Smart Spacesuit and Astronaut Health Monitoring System. The project acts as an intelligent interface with real time data from the suit, life support and the command system.

How it works:

Live Health and Suit Monitoring: This project takes live vital signs from the astronaut such as heart rate, oxygen saturation, body temperature and stress/fatigue levels. It also takes live data from the suit including oxygen tank level, suit pressure, CO₂ scrubber, battery life and radiation.

3D Interactive Visual: The main screen of this system has a 3D animated version of the smart spacesuit. It will show you interactive visuals depending on what the data is showing and what parts you interact with (Helmet HUD, Life Support Pack, Heating System).

AI Voice Assistant: This project uses English as the universal language which means it acts like an AI assistant. You can ask questions about your suit and run diagnostics with simple voice commands.

Automatic Emergency Response: If any of the data goes outside of the safety range, the project will automatically display and play an emergency alarm. It will isolate the issue, calculate remaining EVA time and send the most important data to the main ship.

2. What benefits does it provide?

Zero Latency Understanding: This project takes all data from dozens of sensors and puts them all together, reducing the astronauts cognitive workload.

Voice Commands: The astronauts can use voice commands to see what their vitals are, control heating and log issues whilst their hands are busy.

Early Detection: This project will automatically detect if any data goes out of range. This means any issues can be picked up early such as O2 leakage or increased heart rates.

Send Data To Mission Specialists: This project will automatically send all of the data to the mission specialists.

Expandable: since it uses generative AI, it can easily add modules, missions and diagnostics.

3. What impact will your project have?

With humans going further into space, we are now doing longer missions to the moon, mars and deep space. Communication with earth can take several minutes to over 20 minutes each way meaning we will not be able to have real time control from the ground.

This project will give astronauts an autonomous intelligence inside their suit that acts like a personal mission specialist. With real time health data, 3D visuals and voice AI it will:

Save lives in critical situations during EVA.

Increase mission time by not letting the astronauts get fatigued or have issues with life support.

Create inspiration for aerospace engineering by showing how the latest generative AI and web technology can create cutting edge human machine interfaces. This can also be used in high risk environments on earth such as deep sea divers, firefighters and hazardous material response.

4. What tools, languages and hardware did we use?

Our team created a unique multi AI solution using the latest LLM coding tools and generative video tools.

Google AI Studio: Was used to create the base of the application, logic, prompts and simulation.

Claude Code: Was used to improve the base, improve the UI and add the interactive 3D animation.

Google Gemini: Was used to come up with ideas for the project, create a structure for prompts to create visuals and code, debug and create code.

ChatGPT Image Generator: Was used to create detailed concept art, futuristic suit designs and base images.

Google AI Vids: Was used to create movement from the suit concepts and prompts.

Ezgif Video to JPG: Was used to create a series of high quality JPG images from the videos.

HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript / TypeScript & React: Was used to create the UI, live vitals, frame sequence animations and styling for the HUD.

5. How is our project creative?

Frame Sequence 3D Animation: Rather than using resource heavy 3D modelling software we used our creativity to create a new way to create 3D animation. We used ChatGPT to create visuals, Google AI Vids to animate, Ezgif to create frame sequences and Claude Code to make them interactive. This creates rich cinematic 3D visuals.

Multiple AIs: We gave each AI its own role. Gemini was the creative director and prompt designer. Google AI Studio was the main engine. Chat GPT and Google AI Vids was the visual effects team and Claude Code was the main programmer.

JARVIS Style: Most dashboards are just massive spreadsheets of data. This project converts the complex data into a simple Sci-Fi style HUD with voice. This makes it easy to understand any important information.

6. What did you consider?

Human Factors: In an emergency the astronaut won’t have time to read lots of text. We made sure all of the data was shown using high contrast visuals, colours to indicate issues and short voice alerts.

Performance: Using high quality 3D visuals can cause crashes in regular browsers. We converted the animations into frame sequences with Ezgif to make sure we had smooth transitions on regular laptops.

Realistic: When creating the data we considered realistic factors when astronauts would be in space. For example increased exercise will increase heart rates and O2 usage whilst increasing CO₂.

No Internet: Deep space suits will not have internet. We made sure the suit would work with no internet by creating local state and instant alerts.

Visual Consistency: We made sure the AI generated visuals would match the color scheme, font and design of the HUD. This makes the 3D suit look like it would fit in with the rest of the dashboard.

So, these are all the specifications and properties of our project A.R.I.S (Health monitoring software for astronauts in space missions).

Work done by : Harshavardhan.B.S , Praneeth.V , Chinnam Ronan Abhishikth , Abhijith V Abhilash.

projectDetails.name: Project Param Intelligence
projectDetails.summary:
When human explorers take their first steps on Mars, they will face an unforgiving vacuum with zero GPS, treacherous terrain drops, and an Earth radio delay of up to 22 minutes. Ground control cannot rescue them in real time.

To solve this life-critical challenge, we developed Mars Sentinel—an autonomous Interplanetary Survival Guide and surface EVA navigation workstation for human Marswalks around Jezero Crater.

Mars Sentinel directly solves the challenge by synthesizing multi-mission NASA data into an integrated, tactical heads-up display. It layers sub-meter MRO HiRISE and CTX orbital imagery with a 20-meter digital elevation model, real-time Perseverance MEDA atmospheric telemetry, and MSL Curiosity RAD radiation tracking. Its safety-first routing engine enforces non-negotiable rules—blocking slopes over 25° and maintaining a 40-meter hazard buffer—while plotting safe traverses to actual Perseverance rock-core caches within an 8-hour life-support ceiling.

Mars Sentinel is vital because it bridges the gap between robotic orbiters and human survival. It gives future crews the local autonomy needed to protect life-support consumables, navigate extreme topography, and conduct transformative science safely on an alien world.
projectDetails.details:
Mars Sentinel

An Interplanetary Survival Guide for Humanity’s First Marswalks

Live App: mars-sentinel.vercel.app

Base: Octavia E. Butler Landing, Jezero Crater

The Problem: Survival on an Unforgiving World

Mars is not just remote; it is lethal. With an atmospheric pressure under 1% of Earth's, nighttime temperatures dropping to −79 °C, zero GPS satellites, unshielded radiation, and up to a 22-minute communication delay to Earth, a basic map is not enough. Astronauts need an Interplanetary Survival Guide.

Mars Sentinel turns decades of robotic NASA data into an autonomous, real-time survival guide for surface spacewalks (EVAs). It translates complex orbital scans into four simple rules of survival: know your terrain, respect your life-support limits, monitor your radiation dose, and always guarantee a safe path back to base.

1. What does it do and how does it work?

Mars Sentinel gives astronauts an autonomous navigation co-pilot across a 12 km × 12 km operational grid (20-meter cells) in Jezero Crater:

  • High-Resolution Terrain Engine: Pre-processes USGS/NASA elevation data (JEZ_ctx_B_soc_008_DTM) into lightweight 32-bit binary arrays (elevation.f32, slope.f32) so hazard calculations happen instantly in the browser without lag.
    1. Strict 25° Slope Cutoff: Spacesuits easily lose traction on steep regolith. The system blocks paths through slopes steeper than 25°.
    2. 40-Meter Hazard Buffer: Enforces a mandatory 40-meter standoff distance from cliff edges, loose scree, and unverified ground.
  • Sub-Meter Visuals: Fuses NASA Mars Trek imagery from MRO HiRISE (25 cm/pixel) and CTX (6 m/pixel) so astronauts can clearly identify surface boulders and landmarks.
  • Multi-Scale Views: Seamlessly transitions from the 2D tactical navigation grid to an interactive 3D Mars globe (/globe.html) rendered with real MOLA elevation data.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Protects Spacesuit Consumables: An astronaut's life depends on their Primary Life Support System (PLSS). Mars Sentinel calculates exact uphill climbs and descents (+107 m / −107 m) and total outside time against a strict 8-hour EVA ceiling and 5 km walk-back limit.
  • Safety Explora Sector Scoring: Evaluates all 8 compass directions from the base to show which sectors have the most safe, flat ground (highlighting 9.8 km² of safe ground to the West) and the clearest paths to sample sites.
  • Guides Mission Science: Plots safe routes directly to verified Perseverance rock-core targets (Skinner Ridge, Wildcat Ridge, Observation Mountain, Cheyava Falls), allocating 20 minutes of collection time per stop within the safe return window.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Tools like NASA Mars Trek provide great bird’s-eye views for scientists on Earth, but an astronaut standing on the surface needs immediate answers to stay alive: Is that ridge safe to cross? Will I make it back before dark? What is my radiation dose?

Mars Sentinel bridges the gap between robotic orbiters and human spacewalks. By packaging elevation, weather, and radiation data into an easy-to-read heads-up display, it gives future crews the autonomy they need to explore alien worlds safely without waiting on Earth-based mission control.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did We use?

  • Front-End: Modern vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, and CSS3. Designed with high-contrast tactical palettes (cyan, amber, red) for clear visibility through helmet visors under harsh sun glare.
  • Mapping Engine: Leaflet.js customized with non-Earth planetary coordinates and Mars Trek tile streaming.
  • 3D Planetary Engine: Hand-coded in raw WebGL2 (globe.js)—rendering real MOLA vertex displacement at 60 FPS without the overhead of heavy third-party 3D libraries.
  • Data Processing & Testing: Python (GDAL, NumPy) to convert USGS elevation rasters into raw binary grids; Node.js test suite (tests/mars.test.js) to verify that the pathfinding math never breaches safety limits.
  • Hosting: Deployed on Vercel for fast edge delivery worldwide.
  • AI TOOLS: Antigravity- Claude, Gemini and GPT Models

5. How is Our project creative?

  • Combines 4 NASA Missions in One View: Unifies telemetry and observations from MRO (imagery and slope models), MGS (MOLA global elevation), MSL Curiosity (RAD radiation baseline: 0.64 mSv/day), and Mars 2020 Perseverance (live MEDA weather and sample sites).
  • "Shortest vs. Safest" Route Comparison: An interactive card shows the exact trade-off between routes. For example, taking the safer path only adds 5 minutes of walking time, but triples clearance from steep drop-offs from 50 meters to 131 meters.
  • Built-in Survival Guide: Integrates an interactive Survival Guide panel directly into the workflow, providing sector hazard ratings, ground rules, and consumable depletion warnings.

6. What factors did Our team consider?

  • Spacesuit Ergonomics: Pressurized EVA gloves eliminate fine-motor touch controls, and helmets restrict peripheral vision. We used large controls, high-contrast monospace text, and clear color warnings.
  • Operating Without GPS: With no satellite constellation on Mars, routes are anchored to visible HiRISE terrain landmarks so astronauts can visually cross-check their path.
  • Martian Diurnal Freezing Risk: Jezero Crater temperatures plummet to −79.3 °C at night, and daylight ends at 17:13 (late autumn). The system factors in remaining sunlight so crews are never caught outside after dark.
  • Zero-Trust Safety Principle: Any unmapped pixel or grid edge is mathematically treated as a hazard. In space exploration, assuming missing data is "safe" is how accidents happen.

Source Code: https://github.com/Sai-Krishnan0001/mars-sentinel

projectDetails.name: ANVIS
projectDetails.summary:
We built Anvis, a web tool that lets anyone watch a patch of the infrared sky change over time using NASA’s SPHEREx data. Users enter a position (RA and Dec) or click one of the five challenge targets. Anvis finds every SPHEREx image of that spot in NASA’s IRSA archive, downloads small cutouts, removes the zodiacal-light background, aligns the frames to one north-up grid and plays them as a flip-book.

To help spot movers, it offers Blink and Difference modes, stacked images for each survey visit, Gaia DR3 and WISE overlays moved to each frame’s date, a light curve, plain-word quality flags and a shareable link. New data releases are added by changing one setting.

This matters because SPHEREx has imaged over a billion objects, too many to check by hand, and most known comets and brown dwarfs were found by people comparing images over time. Anvis removes the coding barrier, so students and volunteers can make that comparison in a browser.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works
Anvis is a web tool for watching a patch of the infrared sky change over time. You enter RA and Dec, or click one of the five challenge targets. The Python backend finds every SPHEREx image of that spot in NASA’s IRSA archive and downloads only a small cutout of each. It subtracts the zodiacal-light background, reads the wavelength and quality flags, and lines all the frames up on one north-up grid. The browser then plays them as a flip-book. A user can also switch to Blink or Difference mode, stack the frames of each survey visit into one cleaner image, overlay Gaia DR3 and WISE sources, plot a light curve, and share the exact view as a link.

Benefits and intended impact
Moving and changing objects are hard to find because the data is huge and the raw files are hard to use. Anvis lets students, volunteers and researchers do that comparison in a browser, with no coding. We hope it helps more people spot candidate movers such as brown dwarfs, asteroids, comets and variable stars.

Tools used

  • Python, Flask and Gunicorn for the backend
  • Astropy and NumPy for FITS files, sky coordinates and resampling
  • Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with HTML5 Canvas for the interface
  • NASA IRSA (SPHEREx images, WISE catalogues) and MAST (Gaia DR3)
  • Docker and a Procfile for deployment
  • pytest, with 118 offline tests that don’t need the internet, plus browser tests for the interface
  • Claude for development and debugging, and Gemini for research
  • No special hardware, only normal computers

What is creative

  • Stacked images for each survey visit, weighted by their noise
  • Difference images shown in units of noise, so constant stars cancel and a mover leaves a yellow and blue pair
  • Gaia and WISE positions moved to each frame’s date, so a source with a WISE match but no Gaia match is flagged as a brown-dwarf candidate
  • A light curve, plus quality flags shown in plain words

What we considered

  • Honest science: wavelength changes across each detector, so we show it on every frame, and we label saturated stars as relative measurements.
  • Being kind to NASA’s servers: limited parallel requests, retries with waiting time, caching, and small downloads.
  • Easy updates: a new SPHEREx release is added by changing one setting.
  • Clear credit: the page says it is an independent tool and not an official NASA site.

projectDetails.name: ASTROVITAL
projectDetails.summary:
ASTROVITAL is a passive, body-centric health-monitoring cockpit for astronauts on long-duration missions, built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. Spaceflight degrades the body silently, system by system, including bone density, muscle mass, vision (SANS from fluid shifts), and cardiovascular health. Crews are too busy to track dozens of metrics, and population-wide thresholds miss what is abnormal for an individual.

ASTROVITAL is fully passive: suit-integrated and spacecraft sensors feed all data automatically, so no manual entry is needed. Its centerpiece is a real-time 3D human body built with Three.js, where astronauts rotate, zoom, and click any region or organ to see live status. A keyboard-accessible region list mirrors it for use without WebGL.
Trust is built through personalized baselines, with each indicator scored against the astronaut's own 30-day mean ± 1 SD. Three-tier alerts (Baseline, Caution, Warning) use anti-desensitization limits to prevent alert fatigue. DoctorBot offers plain-language suggested actions, never diagnoses, with a Contact Flight Surgeon option on every warning, and the astronaut keeps final authority.

Data sources are labeled, and indicators needing new hardware carry a NEW badge. The design meets Section 508 standards, with text alongside color, full keyboard navigation, and glove-friendly 48px touch targets. Built with Three.js, Express, and vanilla ES modules, it uses simulated client-side data with 30 days of history.
projectDetails.details:
ASTROVITAL is a passive, body-centric health-monitoring cockpit for astronauts on long-duration missions, built for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge.

On long flights the human body degrades system by system — bone density, muscle mass, vision (SANS from fluid shifts), cardiovascular and more — slowly and silently. Crews are too busy to watch dozens of numbers, and generic population thresholds miss what’s abnormal for one individual. ASTROVITAL closes that gap.

The approach is fully passive: every value arrives automatically from suit-integrated and spacecraft sensors — the astronaut never enters health data by hand. The dashboard works perfectly with zero manual input; they can optionally ask questions, log symptoms, or explore any body part.

The centerpiece is a real-time 3D human body (Three.js). Rotate, zoom, and click any region — down to individual organs — to see that part’s live status. The 3D model is the primary navigation, not decoration, and it’s mirrored by a keyboard-accessible region list that works even without WebGL.

What makes it trustworthy:

Personalized baselines — each indicator is scored against the astronaut’s own 30-day mean ± 1 SD, shown as a band on every chart, not population averages.

Three-tier alerts (Baseline → Caution → Warning) with anti-desensitization limits to prevent alert fatigue, so a warning still means something.

DoctorBot gives plain-language, step-by-step suggested actions — never a diagnosis; every warning has a Contact Flight Surgeon path, and the astronaut keeps final authority.

Hardware-aware — each data source is labeled, and indicators needing new hardware (microneedle patch, wearable ultrasound, neck-ring impedance) carry a NEW badge.

Section 508 accessible — text alongside every color, full keyboard navigation, glove-friendly 48px touch targets, ARIA roles.

Tech: Three.js (WebGL) + a minimal Express server, vanilla ES-module front end, no database — all sensor data is simulated client-side with 30 days of history.

Live demo: https://dhakshesh7575-lang.github.io/ · Source: ASTROVITAL-Dhakshesh

projectDetails.name: Project Quantum_maniac
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, “Abandoned but Not Forgotten: Storytelling About NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars,” is an educational research and presentation project that explores the equipment left behind during NASA's space missions. We developed a visual presentation explaining the history, purpose, and scientific importance of objects such as Apollo lunar equipment, rovers, scientific instruments, Mars landers, and landing components.

The project addresses the challenge of understanding what happens to space equipment after missions are completed. It highlights that these objects are not simply discarded waste but can serve as valuable scientific evidence and historical records. This project is important because it creates awareness about space exploration, technological achievements, environmental responsibility, and the importance of preserving human history beyond Earth. It also encourages students to develop an interest in astronomy, science, and future space research.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview:

Our project, Abandoned but Not Forgotten, explores the equipment and technology left behind by NASA astronauts and robotic missions on the Moon and Mars. It explains why certain equipment is no longer used, how it was left behind, and how these objects continue to contribute to scientific research and space exploration.

How It Works:

The project uses storytelling, research, images, and presentations to explain the history and purpose of abandoned space equipment. It highlights examples such as Apollo lunar equipment, lunar rovers, scientific instruments, Mars landers, and the parachute and backshell used during the Perseverance rover's landing.

Benefits:

  • Creates awareness about the history of space exploration.
  • Explains the scientific importance of equipment left on other planets and the Moon.
  • Helps students understand NASA missions and space technology.
  • Encourages curiosity about science, engineering, and astronomy.
  • Highlights the importance of preserving historical achievements in space.

Intended Impact:

The main aim is to make people understand that equipment left behind during space missions is not simply waste. Many of these objects have historical, scientific, and educational value. The project encourages interest in future space missions and responsible exploration of other celestial bodies.

Tools and Software Used:

  • Microsoft PowerPoint – to create the project presentation.
  • Internet research – to collect information and reference materials.
  • NASA and NASA/JPL websites – to obtain reliable scientific information and mission details.
  • Images and diagrams – to explain the equipment and space missions visually.

This is a research and presentation-based project; no physical hardware or programming languages were required.

Creativity and Innovation:

The creative aspect of this project is presenting space exploration from a different perspective. Instead of focusing only on successful missions and discoveries, it tells the stories of the objects left behind. It connects science, technology, history, and storytelling to make the topic interesting and easier to understand.

Factors Considered by the Team:

  • Accuracy and reliability of scientific information.
  • Historical importance of the equipment.
  • Scientific purpose and usefulness of abandoned objects.
  • Environmental impact of human activities on the Moon and Mars.
  • Clarity of explanations and visual presentation.
  • Educational value and relevance to future space exploration.

projectDetails.details:
Mission: Beyond is a NASA-inspired educational space adventure game developed by Manya, Monica and Shayantra. As a team, we wanted to bring together our understanding of science and our imagination to create something that was not just informative but genuinely engaging. We spent time thinking about how space exploration could be turned into an experience where players could investigate real challenges, make decisions and learn through their own discoveries. Our aim was to combine scientific knowledge with creative gameplay and build something that could spark curiosity in others.

Our challenge, “Build a Junior Astronaut Mission,” inspired us to create a game that gives young learners a taste of what it takes to explore space. Mission: Beyond takes players across 10 space destinations, including the Moon, Mars, Jupiter and Deep Space. Each destination presents a challenge inspired by real space research, such as lunar dust, radiation, asteroids and space debris.

Players customise their astronauts, explore a star map and complete missions by answering questions. Each destination has five levels, with 10 questions per level. We have also included special power-ups, animated space environments, background music and voice instructions to make the experience more interactive.

Our aim is to help young aspiring astronauts develop scientific curiosity, logical thinking and problem-solving skills. By facing different challenges, players get an idea of the decisions and difficulties involved in real space exploration.


Inspired by genuine NASA research, Mission: Beyond turns scientific concepts into an exciting learning experience. We hope it encourages young minds to ask questions, explore science and dream about future discoveries.


We believe every great discovery begins with curiosity. Through Mission: Beyond, we hope to inspire the next generation to explore, learn and imagine what is possible beyond Earth.

projectDetails.name: Project RAKS_CODIFIERS
projectDetails.summary:
We developed Mission Tara-1, a browser-based Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer in which the player sits in the Flight Director’s chair and leads a full crewed Moon mission. It has five parts: launching from a real site after a GO / NO-GO poll, travelling 384,000 km to the Moon, landing at the Sea of Tranquility, keeping a four-person south pole base alive for seven days in 3D, and flying the crew home to splashdown.

It addresses the challenge by training young players the way real astronauts train: through hands-on simulation. Every part uses real physics and real NASA data, offers three difficulty levels for different ages, scores each decision, and ends with lessons from real missions such as Apollo 11 and Chandrayaan-3.

It is important because it shows students that spaceflight depends on teamwork, checking and careful decisions, and it makes science and maths exciting. The game is free, runs in any browser with no install or log-in, and works on ordinary school computers, so any classroom can use it.
projectDetails.details:
Our project is a simple Junior Astronaut Trainer which involves many tasks that the 'Junior Astronaut ' has to complete . Our project lets you sit in The Flight Director's chair to check the rocket,count it down,fly it to orbit,cross 384,000km of space,land on the Moon, keep a moon base alive , and fly the crew home again .Every number comes from real rockets and real missions. What does it do or how does it work?
Mission Tara-1 is a browser game that puts the player in the Flight Director’s chair for a full crewed Moon mission, in five parts:

  1. Launch: pick a real launch site (Sriharikota, Kennedy, Kourou or Baikonur), run a GO / NO-GO poll across six stations to catch hidden problems, then fly the rocket to orbit by hand.
  2. Travel: burn out of Earth orbit, cross 384,000 km in a 3-day cruise with obstacles, and brake into Moon orbit.
  3. Landing: pilot the lander down to the Sea of Tranquility, handling a 1202 program alarm, a boulder field and low fuel, as Apollo 11 did.
  4. Moon base (3D): keep a 4-person base near the south pole alive for 7 days by managing air, water, food, power, radiation, a solar storm and the radio delay to Earth.
  5. Return: burn for home, correct course, re-enter and splash down.

Each part runs on a physics simulation, scores the player, and ends with lessons from real missions. A built-in assistant called TARA answers questions about the game and spaceflight.

What benefits does it have?

  • Players learn by doing: for example, a launch site nearer the equator gets more free speed from Earth’s spin, and fuel saved at launch carries into the trip to the Moon.
  • Three difficulty levels (Cadet, Pilot, Commander) let beginners and confident players both enjoy it.
  • Failure teaches: every crash or abort explains what went wrong and what real engineers did about it.
  • It is one file that opens in any browser, with no install and no log-in needed.

What is the intended impact?
We want young students to see that spaceflight is about teamwork, checking, and careful decisions, not only the rocket. We hope it builds curiosity about science and maths, shows Indian missions like Chandrayaan-3 alongside Apollo and Artemis, and gives teachers a free tool that works on ordinary school computers.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
  • Graphics: HTML Canvas for the 2D parts, and three.js (WebGL) with bloom effects for the 3D Moon base.
  • Maps: D3 (d3-geo, d3-array) and TopoJSON with a world map for the rotating globe.
  • Sound: Web Audio API for synthesised effects, and the browser’s speech voice for mission control.
  • Storage: the browser’s local storage for scores and optional crew accounts.
  • Data: NASA sources such as DONKI solar flare records, the life support baseline values, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter and LCROSS findings, and Apollo mission records.
  • AI: Claude, an AI assistant made by Anthropic, was used for touch-ups at the end of the game.
  • Hardware: no special hardware, only a computer or tablet with a modern browser.

How is your project creative?

  • It covers the whole journey in one connected story, so choices early on affect later parts.
  • All the art and sound is generated in code: Earth, the Moon, stars, smoke, rocket roar and radio beeps, with no image or audio files.
  • It turns real moments into gameplay, such as the Apollo 11 alarm and the 1.3-second radio delay.
  • The Moon base mission turns real NASA numbers into a survival challenge.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Accuracy: every real number is listed with its source, and simplified “game values” are labelled as such. Recorded data is never shown as live.
  • Age and skill: simple language, guidance arrows on Easy, and short sessions (a 7-day base mission fits in about 8 minutes).
  • Access: works by keyboard and touch, includes screen reader labels and a reduced motion option, and keeps working if sound is blocked.
  • Privacy: accounts are optional, stay on the device, and passwords are salted and hashed.
  • Honesty(SI):We state our use of SI for our project during the hackathon but we used SI only for touch-ups at the end of the game

projectDetails.name: DUSTBOUND
projectDetails.summary: Space exploration leaves machines, experiments and stories behind, and complex archives can overwhelm young learners. DUSTBOUND turns these into a guided journey. Dusty introduces four Mars rovers (Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity and Perseverance), and Selene explains the six Apollo landings and the hardware left on the Moon. Learners can also play six mission games and a "Which rover are you?" quiz. All missions, dates and discoveries link to NASA sources. The site is built with HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript and hosted on Netlify.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works
DUSTBOUND is an interactive website that tells the stories of NASA machines left behind on Mars and the Moon. A visitor chooses a planetary journey. On Mars, the guide Dusty introduces the Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity and Perseverance rovers, and on the Moon, the guide Selene explains the six Apollo landings and the equipment left on the surface. Each chapter pairs a short story with a “NASA Record” box that gives the real facts and a link to the source. Visitors can then play six mission games and take a “Which rover are you?” quiz, earning Star Points and achievements.

Benefits and intended impact
Space archives are often too technical for young learners. DUSTBOUND turns them into a short, friendly story, so students aged 10 to 18 and their teachers can learn real space history without a science background. We want to support STEM accessibility, spark youth curiosity and give retired space hardware the recognition it deserves.

Tools and technologies
HTML5 for structure, CSS3 for design, JavaScript for interactivity and games, and Netlify for hosting, so anyone can open it with a link. All content comes from NASA resources: NASA Science (Mars missions, Ingenuity and the Moon), the NASA Apollo Program pages, the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter mission, and NASA’s imagery with credits.

How it is creative
Instead of a fact list, two imagined narrators, Dusty and Selene, speak for the machines themselves. Learning is built around play, and visitors can read in silence or turn the narration on.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: every fact is checked against NASA sources and credited.
  • Honesty: illustrations are labeled as illustrations, and findings are described carefully (for example, “evidence of habitability, not proof of life”).
  • Accessibility: narration controls, a silent-reading option and image descriptions.
  • Fit with the challenge: we focus on retired and left-behind hardware, and present the active rovers as the next chapter.
  • Audience: short story chunks and games that suit students.

projectDetails.name: Project Raks_HAM
projectDetails.summary:
Abandoned, But Not Forgotten is a first-person 3D story game that runs in a web browser, made for school-age space enthusiasts. A fictional comet is heading for Earth, and the knowledge needed to stop it lies in six real machines NASA left on the Moon and Mars: Surveyor 3, the Apollo 12 science station, the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity.

In each chapter the player scans the machine, reads fact cards that name their NASA sources, operates it in a short simulation, and then chooses whether to take a piece or leave the site untouched. Along the way players learn each mission's objectives, what it achieved, and how it shaped the missions that followed. What the player learns decides the ending. A map shows 21 real objects left on other worlds.

The challenge asks for a story that teaches what this equipment is and why it matters. Our game shows that abandoned hardware still holds knowledge, and asks players to weigh science against preserving history.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

Abandoned, But Not Forgotten is a first-person 3D story game that runs in a web browser. A fictional comet, KAIROS, is heading for Earth. In the prologue Commander Mitra fails, again, to push it aside in simulation. So she and her robot partner Evvi visit six real machines NASA left on the Moon and Mars: Surveyor 3 and the Apollo 12 landing site, the Apollo 12 science station, the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Opportunity, InSight and Ingenuity.

Each chapter follows the same steps. The player walks to the machine, scans its parts to open fact cards, watches a reconstruction of what happened there, tries something hands-on (re-enacting how Apollo 12 cut the camera from Surveyor 3, driving a rover, flying a helicopter, reading a seismometer trace), and then makes one choice: take a piece for the mission, or leave the historic site untouched. Each chapter earns a data card, and the cards decide how the Finale goes. If a chapter is skipped, the mission has to guess at that part.

READ MODE

The same six missions can be read instead of played. Read mode is a stamp book: each mission is a short deck of seven cards (a picture, the question the mission was sent to answer, one number to remember, what it achieved, a closer look at its parts, three things to learn, and a question). Answering the question earns that mission's stamp. It is built from the same sourced fact cards as the game, so the two cannot disagree. It is there for anyone who prefers to read, for classrooms, and for devices that cannot run the 3D game.

THE ARTIFACT MAP

A map shows 21 real objects NASA left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space, each with what it is, why it was sent, what it found and a link to the NASA page.

BENEFITS

Players learn why each mission was sent, what it achieved and how it helped the missions that followed. Every fact card names the NASA page or report it came from. The game is free, runs in a browser with nothing to install, works with keyboard and mouse or touch, and has settings for text size, sound, graphics level and whether dialogue moves on by itself.

INTENDED IMPACT

We want school-age space enthusiasts to see abandoned hardware as knowledge that is still useful, and to think about a real question: when is it right to disturb a historic site for science? The game lets the player decide, records the choice, and keeps a count of sites left undisturbed.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

TypeScript, React, Three.js with React Three Fiber and drei, Zustand, Vite, Vitest and Playwright for testing, and Cloudflare Workers for hosting. The Opportunity, InSight, Ingenuity, Apollo Lunar Module and astronaut models and the Moon, Mars and Earth maps are NASA media. Surveyor 3, the Lunar Roving Vehicle and the science station are rebuilt by hand from NASA descriptions. Evvi's body is a free (CC0) robot model by Quaternius. The text is set in IBM Plex. Music and sound effects are generated in the browser. No special hardware was used.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

The story turns the challenge's subject into the solution: the old machines are what save Earth. The Apollo 12 crew really did walk to Surveyor 3 and cut parts off it, and the game asks the player to face the same decision. Reconstructions are drawn as cyan projections, so the player can always tell a rebuilt moment from the real machine in front of them.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED

Accuracy: the game states what is real and what is fiction, and labels every simulation and reconstruction.

Audience: plain language and short lines for young players.

Access: a read mode, touch controls, adjustable text and a low-graphics setting.

Respect for the sites: the choice to leave things untouched is always available and always recorded.

projectDetails.name: Project RAKS_INTERSTELLAR REAPERS
projectDetails.summary: Interstellar Reapers is a browser-based space mission game built in a single HTML file with Three.js. You start in the Mission Designer, choosing the rocket, power, antenna, and instruments across six stages while balancing mass, power, and budget. Then you pilot your rocket in 3D from Earth to the Moon, Mars, the asteroid belt, or Jupiter. You steer with the mouse, use cruise drive and brakes, avoid debris, and slow down to enter orbit. Your hull condition and piloting speed affect the science data you send home and your final score. A separate Asteroid Fact File mission lets you fly through an asteroid field collecting 10 facts, each with NASA images and source links.
projectDetails.details:
Interstellar Reapers is a browser-based space game where players design a spacecraft, launch it across the Solar System, and explore a 3D asteroid belt. Players choose a destination, rocket, power system, antenna, and science instruments while managing mass, power, budget, and science data. They then fly through space, collect 10 NASA-powered Fact Files, protect their shield, and earn a science score.

The project makes space science fun and easy to understand. It teaches players about solar power, antennas, spacecraft design, asteroids, and the importance of returning scientific data to Earth. Its goal is to inspire interest in space exploration and STEM learning through interactive gameplay.

It was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and runs in a web browser on a normal computer or laptop. The project is creative because it combines mission planning, 3D exploration, NASA imagery, and educational facts in one game. The team focused on making it engaging, easy to control, visually immersive, and educational.

challengeDetails.title: Space Mission Design Game
challengeDetails.excerpt: Designing a space mission requires careful consideration of competing demands, including mission objectives, spacecraft design, scientific instruments, launch vehicles, budgets, power, mass, communications, and orbital constraints. Your challenge is to create an interactive game that allows participants to design, manage, and simulate a complete space mission while making engineering decisions, managing limited resources, and evaluating how each choice shapes the success of their mission.

projectDetails.details:
Project Details: APOGEE

What it does & how it works: APOGEE is a browser-based aerospace simulator where players pick a launchpad on a 3D Earth, snap together a modular spacecraft from 27 parts, and pilot it from Earth to the Moon and onto the exoplanet GL-1500 using a real-time 120 Hz physics engine.

Benefits: It helps students actually see and test how rocket physics works—like weight, thrust, drag, and weather—right in a browser without needing to download anything.

Intended impact: We want to get other students excited about space exploration, coding, and engineering by letting them build and test their own rockets.

Tools & languages: We coded the whole project using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with HTML5 Canvas for graphics, Web Audio for sound effects, and a browser so it runs on normal school laptops and tablets.

Creativity: Instead of using pre-made images or sound files, we programmed every rocket part, flame, explosion, and engine sound directly in code.

Key factors considered: We made sure the physics felt realistic without being too hard to play, kept the frame rate smooth, and built a step-by-step live tutorial so anyone can learn how to fly.

projectDetails.name: RAKS_THE_RED_DEVILS
projectDetails.summary: Earth trends explorer is an interactive, multi-page web platform designed to bridge the gap between raw satellite telemetry and public understanding. By guiding users through dedicated, story-driven modules—covering global sea level rise, long-term planetary trends, and localized environmental shifts—our app transforms decades of Earth observation data into intuitive visual narratives.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

Earth Trend Detective is an interactive website that uses NASA data to explore Earth's climate, weather, natural disasters, and satellite imagery. It combines NASA APIs to make environmental information easy to understand and explore.

2. What benefits does it have?

It raises environmental awareness, helps users understand climate change and natural disasters, and makes scientific data accessible for students, researchers, and the public.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our goal is to educate people about Earth's changing environment, encourage climate awareness, and inspire communities to take action to protect our planet.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript
  • NASA POWER API
  • NASA EONET API
  • NASA EPIC API
  • Three.js / WebGL for 3D visualization, where applicable
  • Visual Studio Code and Netlify
  • Computer and internet connection

5. How is your project creative?

It transforms complex NASA data into an interactive experience using visualizations, satellite imagery, climate insights, and 3D Earth exploration. It makes learning about our planet engaging and accessible.

6. What factors did your team consider?

We focused on data accuracy, user-friendly design, accessibility, performance, educational value, and the project's potential to create environmental awareness.

Our mission is simple: Make Earth data understandable, inspire curiosity, and encourage people to protect our planet.
