challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: SPHEREx Tools, an open-source library to access IRSA data seamlessly
projectDetails.summary:
SPHEREx Explorer is a project designed to make NASA's SPHEREx data easier to access and explore. It consists of a proof-of-concept web application for searching, visualising, and comparing astronomical observations, alongside Python tools intended to simplify programmatic access to the archive. By combining these capabilities, the project aims to make SPHEREx data more accessible to students, researchers, and developers, while providing a foundation for building further applications using real astronomical observations.

IRSA can be the victim of a DDoS attack, during which operations may temporarily suspend and requests may fail.
projectDetails.details:
Overview:

The SPHEREx Explorer is a web application used to easily visualise and explore the data provided by NASA's SPHEREx space telescope.

SPHEREx provides data from scanning the whole sky across 102 near-infrared wavelengths. This can be used to understand our universe better. However, it can be complex to understand and explore different data products due to needing to use astronomical archives, specific file types and science software.

This project has created an interactive tool which allows users to input coordinates in Right Ascension and Declination. A radius can then be entered to search for observations within that area. It can download and display FITS images for users to analyse such as IMAGE, FLAGS, VARIANCE and ZODI.

Features such as sky navigation and observation comparison have been included in this prototype. Observations can be compared together by aligning them using their World Coordinate System. A difference map can be created to compare two observations. This shows any unusual pixels that can be investigated further. These aren’t actual discoveries but are just candidates.

The aim of this project was to increase the ease of exploring SPHEREx data. By using this application users can carry out some of the tasks required to explore the data rather than having to do it manually. This could encourage students, teachers, developers and researchers to explore the data as it is much easier to understand.

The project was mainly created using Python. Streamlit was used to create the interactive web application. Astroquery was used to interact with the IRSA archive. Astropy was used to work with astronomical coordinates, FITS files and World Coordinate System. Other packages used were NumPy and Pandas to process data, Matplotlib to visualise data, Requests to obtain data products and SciPy to align and process images. The application was deployed using Streamlit Community Cloud.

The creativity behind this project is that the search, FITS analysis, sky navigation and observation comparison was all put into one easy to use application. We wanted to ensure users were actually interacting with real data from the mission rather than just creating another visualisation.

Factors such as ease of use, public data, large astronomical files, accurate coordinates and accurate comparisons were all considered.

Alongside the web application, we have developed a reusable Python library for accessing SPHEREx data. It aims to simplify common tasks involved in searching the archive and retrieving astronomical data products, allowing other developers to integrate SPHEREx data into their own applications. This library and the web application provide two different ways to explore and work with the mission's public data.

Use of SI tools: ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot were used during development to assist with coding, debugging, troubleshooting, and editing written documentation. The team reviewed and tested the resulting code and made project decisions and implementation changes themselves.

projectDetails.name: Project Space-Traveller
projectDetails.summary:
Space Traveller is a free browser game for students aged 8–12 that turns real mission trade-offs into hands-on play. Players choose one of the eight planets and pack their spacecraft with a limited number of modules: solar panels, nuclear power, an air maker, a water maker, a greenhouse, a radiation shield or supplies. They then pilot it along a 3D space path to their destination, where space rocks can damage their cargo. After landing, they walk their astronaut around the outpost to explore, repair or rest, and keep the crew’s air, water, food and health going for 10 days.

The game addresses the challenge by making students live with the results of their engineering choices. Solar power fails at Neptune, dust storms block it on Mars, and the crew needs a shield against radiation storms on Mercury. A clear report card explains why a mission succeeded or failed and adds a fact from a real NASA mission.

This matters because space engineering is about balancing limited power, mass and life support. Space Traveller lets students fail safely and learn why, which builds the problem-solving skills future explorers need.
projectDetails.details:
Project details: Space Traveller

What it does and how it works

Space Traveller is a free browser game for students aged 10–14. Each mission has five steps:

  1. Choose a planet. Players pick one of the eight planets. Each has real differences in sunlight, radiation, cold and water. Earth is a training level.
  2. Pack the ship. Players choose 4–5 modules: solar panels, nuclear power, an air maker, a water maker, a greenhouse, a radiation shield or a supply crate. The space is limited, so every choice is a trade-off. A mission check warns about problems, but players can still launch and learn from mistakes.
  3. Launch and fly. After a countdown, liftoff and stage separation, players steer the ship along a curving 3D space path with the arrow keys, or with on-screen buttons on phones. They collect science and dodge space rocks that damage their cargo. Banners show when they cross other planets’ orbits, and a minimap shows the curves ahead.
  4. Run the outpost. Players walk their astronaut around the base with W A S D. Each day they choose to explore for science, fix a broken module or rest the crew. They must keep air, water, food and health up for 10 days, while handling dust storms, radiation storms, breakdowns and cold snaps.
  5. Read the report card. It shows stars and badges, explains why the mission succeeded or failed, and shares a real fact from a NASA mission. Players earn SpaceCoins to spend on ship upgrades in the Hangar.

Benefits

  • It turns abstract engineering trade-offs into choices students can see and feel. Solar panels fail at Neptune, dust storms cut solar power on Mars, and skipping the shield on Mercury hurts the crew.
  • Students learn by failing safely and seeing exactly why things went wrong.
  • It’s simple to play: four bars, three daily jobs and one mission takes about 5–10 minutes. That fits a classroom lesson.
  • It’s free, needs no account, collects no personal data, works offline and runs on computers, tablets and phones.

Intended impact

We want young students to understand that space missions depend on balancing power, mass, life support and safety. We hope it builds problem-solving skills and curiosity about science, technology, engineering and maths (STEM) careers. Teachers can use it to start class discussions, such as “Why does Neptune need nuclear power?” Every planet’s facts come from real NASA missions, including MOXIE, MESSENGER, Juno, Cassini, Voyager 2 and CHAPEA.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no game engine or frameworks.
  • Graphics: HTML5 Canvas. The planets, 3D space path, launch animation, outpost and astronaut are all drawn in code.
  • Installable app: a web app manifest and a service worker, so it can be installed and played offline.
  • Phone features: touch controls, landscape mode and vibration feedback (including on iPhone).
  • Hosting: GitHub and GitHub Pages.
  • Testing: Playwright for automatic play-testing on different screen sizes, and for balancing the difficulty of each planet.
  • Video: FFmpeg to make the demo video.
  • AI help: we used Claude, an AI assistant, to help write and test the code.
  • Hardware: laptops and phones for testing. No special hardware is needed to play.

Creativity and design

The game combines three kinds of play in one mission: planning (packing), action (piloting) and management (running the outpost). Each planet changes the rules, so players have to think differently each time. We kept the controls and screens simple so younger students can focus on the science and their decisions.

projectDetails.name: SPHEREx HUNTER
projectDetails.summary:
NASA’s SPHEREx space observatory maps over 1 billion celestial objects across 102 near-infrared bands every six months. Sifting through this petabyte-scale stream to uncover elusive near-Earth asteroids, ultra-cool brown dwarfs, and hypothetical outer solar system bodies like Planet X is a massive challenge for automated pipelines alone.

To solve this, Team RIP developed SPHEREx Hunter—a high-performance, web-based time-domain astronomical observatory. SPHEREx Hunter enables researchers and citizen scientists to enter any sky coordinates and stream sub-pixel WCS-aligned multi-epoch cutouts spanning 26 years (2MASS→WISE→ SPHEREx). It features a digital Clyde Tombaugh blink comparator, a mathematically rigorous ZOGY difference-imaging engine (𝐼2−𝐼1) that subtracts static stars into neutral gray while isolating moving dipoles, and an on-the-fly 102-band infrared spectroscopy analyzer (0.75−5.0𝜇m)  resolving atmospheric H2O,𝐶𝐻4 and CO2. By democratizing discovery through one-click shareable deep links, SPHEREx Hunter ensures no moving world in SPHEREx's survey goes unnoticed.
projectDetails.details:
SPHEREx Hunter: Project Details

1. WHAT DOES IT DO OR HOW DOES IT WORK?

SPHEREx Hunter is a web-based astronomical observatory and citizen-science discovery engine that enables anyone to search for moving asteroids, ultra-cool brown dwarfs, and hypothetical outer solar system bodies (like Planet X) in NASA SPHEREx survey data.

The platform operates through four integrated stages:

- Multi-Epoch Astrometric Alignment: When users input celestial coordinates (RA/Dec) or choose a benchmark target, the backend queries NASA IRSA, CDS Strasbourg, and ESA Gaia DR3. It reprojects historical FITS cutouts across 26 years (1999 2MASS, 2010/2020 unWISE, and 2025 SPHEREx) onto a common tangent plane using standard Gnomonic (TAN) WCS transformations, achieving sub-pixel registration across heterogeneous detector resolutions.

- Digital Clyde Tombaugh Blink Engine: A hardware-accelerated 60 FPS HTML5 Canvas rapidly alternates between multi-epoch frames at adjustable speeds (50 ms to 2 s). By leveraging the human brain's motion reflexes, millions of static background stars freeze while moving worlds visibly leap across the screen.

- ZOGY Difference Imaging: Implements the mathematically optimal Zackay, Ofek, & Gal-Yam (ZOGY 2016) algorithm. Background stars cleanly subtract to flat neutral gray, isolating moving objects and transients as high-contrast white-and-black dipole pairs (>650 SNR).

- 102-Band Infrared Spectroscopy: Measures and plots the full Spectral Energy Distribution (SED) across all six SPHEREx detector arrays (0.75 - 5.00 microns). Dynamic array co-addition boosts signal-to-noise ratio by >4x, overlaying diagnostic absorption markers for atmospheric water vapor (1.40 um), water ice (3.05 um), methane CH4 (3.30 um), and carbon dioxide CO2 (4.27 um).

2. WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?

- Zero-Installation Barrier: Runs entirely in modern web browsers on standard laptops, tablets, or phones without requiring IRAF, DS9, or Python environments.

- 26-Year Time Baseline: Comparing 1999 2MASS, 2010 WISE, and 2025 SPHEREx turns glacial 0.1"/yr motion into clear multi-pixel jumps.

- False-Positive Reduction: Pairs automated ESA Gaia DR3 star masking with human visual verification to eliminate false alarms from diffraction spikes and bad pixels.

- Instant Atmospheric Classification: The 102-band spectrophotometer immediately identifies whether a moving target is a normal star, an icy asteroid, or a freezing substellar Y-dwarf (T < 300 K).

3. WHAT IS THE INTENDED IMPACT OF THE PROJECT?

The project democratizes petabyte-scale infrared astronomy. With SPHEREx mapping over 1 billion objects every six months, automated pipelines produce too many candidates for professional teams to verify alone. SPHEREx Hunter turns this firehose into an open, collaborative citizen science mission to:

- Accelerate the discovery of cold brown dwarfs and rogue planetary-mass objects near our Solar System.

- Track near-Earth asteroids and Kuiper Belt objects for planetary defense and solar system architecture studies.

- Empirically search for or place strict observational limits on Planet X.

- Provide STEM educators and students worldwide with an accessible gateway to real space mission data.

4. WHAT TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES, HARDWARE, OR SOFTWARE DID YOU USE?

- Backend: Python 3.11+, FastAPI (asynchronous REST API with RFC 7807 error responses), Astropy (WCS coordinate transformations and FITS parsing), Astroquery (TAP queries), NumPy & SciPy (matrix subtraction, PSF convolution, array co-addition), Uvicorn.

- Frontend: Modern JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5 Canvas 2D API (sub-pixel rendering and affine transform matrix control), Tailwind CSS (responsive astronomical dark UI), CDS Strasbourg Aladin Lite v3 (HiPS all-sky context), Web Audio API (acoustic target acquisition cues).

- Hardware: Standard consumer laptops (Intel Core i5/i7, 8-16 GB RAM); designed to run efficiently without requiring GPU servers.

5. HOW IS YOUR PROJECT CREATIVE?

- Honoring Clyde Tombaugh: Digitizes the optical blink comparator used to discover Pluto in 1930, enhancing it with modern sub-pixel WCS alignment and multi-epoch animation.

- Dynamic Spectral Co-Addition: Users can interactively co-add spectral arrays via a slider to trade spectral resolution for signal depth (>4x SNR boost), turning complex spectrophotometry into an intuitive hands-on tool.

- Audio-Visual Sonification: Integrates subtle frequency cues via Web Audio API during epoch transitions and auto-detections, creating a multi-sensory discovery platform.

6. WHAT FACTORS DID YOUR TEAM CONSIDER?

- Astrometric Plate Scale Variations: Harmonized disparate survey resolutions (2MASS 2.0"/px, WISE 2.75"/px, SPHEREx 6.2"/px) using rigorous Gnomonic tangent projections to prevent false dipoles.

- Extreme Astronomical Dynamic Range: Implemented real-time arcsinh and zscale contrast stretching with 99.5% percentile clipping to make faint 250 K targets visible without saturating bright field stars.

- Usability for Beginners: Created curated benchmark targets (Barnard's Star, WISE 0855, Epsilon Indi B), an interactive Mission Codex explaining the science, and 1-click candidate flagging with shareable deep links.

- Performance & Bandwidth: Implemented client-side canvas caching and dynamic Level-of-Detail (LOD) streaming so users with standard internet connections experience zero lag.

projectDetails.name: Fire Parallax: A Sensor-Aware Burning Activity Calendar
projectDetails.summary:
Fire Parallax is an interactive, sensor-aware analysis platform that explores how MODIS and VIIRS satellite observations represent burning activity differently across Punjab and Haryana, India. Using NASA FIRMS active-fire data from October–November 2022, the project processes MODIS Aqua and VIIRS NOAA-20 detections and organizes them into a weekly activity calendar.

Users can explore sensor-specific activity, compare spatial co-detections, examine confidence categories, and investigate how results change with different spatial grid sizes and temporal matching windows. The platform makes sensor differences visible while explaining the limitations of interpreting satellite detections.

Fire Parallax addresses the challenge of harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS hotspots by providing a transparent, interactive way to compare observations without treating every detection as a unique fire or assuming that differences indicate missed fires.
projectDetails.details:
What does Fire Parallax do?

Fire Parallax is an interactive satellite-data analysis platform that compares MODIS and VIIRS active-fire observations over Punjab and Haryana, India. It helps users explore how two satellite sensor systems represent seasonal burning activity differently through weekly calendars, spatial comparisons, confidence categories, and sensitivity analysis.

How does it work?

The project uses NASA FIRMS active-fire observations from October–November 2022. We select MODIS Aqua and VIIRS NOAA-20 detections classified as presumed vegetation fires and preprocess the datasets through validation, coordinate projection, and regional filtering.

The observations are organized into spatial grid cells and UTC dates. When both sensors report at least one qualifying detection in the same state, grid cell, and date, we classify that cell-day as a co-detection. We also examine sensor-specific detections, confidence categories, temporal matching windows, and different grid resolutions (1 km, 2 km, and 5 km).

The results are presented through a seven-section interactive dashboard, allowing users to explore patterns and investigate where the two sensors agree or differ.

What are its benefits and intended impact?

Fire Parallax makes satellite active-fire observations easier to compare and interpret. It helps users understand how sensor characteristics, confidence classifications, spatial resolution, and temporal matching choices influence the patterns they observe.

The intended impact is to encourage more informed interpretation of satellite-based fire monitoring data and demonstrate why observations from different sensors should be compared carefully rather than treated as identical measurements.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed using Python, pandas, GeoPandas, Shapely, and pyproj for data processing and spatial analysis. Streamlit and Plotly were used to build the interactive dashboard and visualizations. Git and GitHub were used for version control and collaboration.

The project uses satellite observations from NASA FIRMS and administrative boundary data from geoBoundaries. OpenStreetMap and CARTO provide map basemap services. No specialized hardware was required.

What makes the project creative?

Instead of simply displaying hotspot counts, Fire Parallax investigates how the apparent picture of burning activity changes depending on the observing sensor and analytical choices. Its combination of weekly activity calendars, spatial co-detection analysis, confidence exploration, temporal tolerance, and grid-resolution sensitivity gives users multiple ways to investigate sensor disagreement.

It also makes methodological limitations visible, helping users distinguish satellite detections from confirmed physical fire events.

What factors did the team consider?

We considered differences in the MODIS and VIIRS confidence systems, sensor selection, geographic boundaries, UTC acquisition dates, spatial grid resolution, temporal matching tolerance, and grid-origin sensitivity.

We also considered the limitations of the study period and administrative boundary data. The analysis is a two-month, single-year case study, not a multi-year trend analysis.

Importantly, FIRMS detections are thermal observations. They do not independently establish unique physical fires, burned area, or confirmed agricultural burning. Our results are therefore presented as sensor-observation comparisons rather than verified fire-event measurements.

projectDetails.name: Space Mission Design Game by Rocket Raccoons
projectDetails.summary:
**Space Facts Game – Learn Space While You Play!**

Space Facts Game is an interactive educational rocket game developed by Team Rocket Raccoons using Scratch on PictoBlox for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

The game aims to make space exploration and mission-related learning fun and accessible for beginners. Players control a rocket travelling through space, collecting stars to increase their scores. For every 10 points earned, a new space fact is unlocked, rewarding players with interesting knowledge about our universe. For example, players discover fascinating facts such as a day on Venus being longer than a year on Venus.

Inspired by educational resources, quizzes and digital activities from the Canadian Space Agency, our project combines simple gameplay with interactive learning.

The project addresses the challenge by introducing students to space concepts through hands-on digital gaming. As a future enhancement, we plan to introduce rocket, fuel and budget choices to demonstrate the real-world trade-offs involved in designing space missions.

Our vision is simple: **Make space learning exciting, interactive and accessible to everyone!**
projectDetails.details:
Project Name: Space Facts Game

Team: Rocket Raccoons
Challenge: Space Mission Design Game
Team Members: Aadhinath S.V. Nair and Rithu Krishna S.V. Nair
Technology: Scratch on PictoBlox

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Space Facts Game is an interactive educational rocket game designed to make learning about space exciting and accessible to beginners. Players control a rocket travelling through space and collect stars to increase their scores. Every time they reach 10 points, they unlock a reward in the form of an interesting space fact. This creates a fun learning experience where gameplay and space education go hand in hand.

2. What benefits does it offer?

The game introduces children and beginners to fascinating space concepts without requiring prior knowledge of astronomy or space science. It encourages curiosity, active participation and learning through exploration rather than traditional methods of memorisation.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to make space education more engaging and accessible, especially for young learners. By combining gaming with scientific facts, we hope to inspire more students to explore space science, technology and future space missions.

4. What tools and technologies were used?

The game was developed using Scratch-based visual programming on PictoBlox. We also referred to educational resources, including space quizzes, digital games and e-books from the Canadian Space Agency.

5. How is the project creative?

The creative element is the combination of a simple rocket adventure with a reward-based educational system. Instead of simply presenting facts, the game encourages players to discover them by collecting stars and achieving scores. Every 10 points creates a new learning opportunity.

6. What factors did the team consider?

We focused on:

  • Accessibility: Making the game simple enough for beginners.
  • Engagement: Using rocket movement, star collection and scoring to maintain interest.
  • Learning: Presenting space facts as rewards.
  • Simplicity: Avoiding complex scientific terminology so children can enjoy learning.
  • Future development: Planning to introduce rocket selection, fuel and budget choices to demonstrate the real-world trade-offs involved in space mission design.

Our vision is to make space exploration concepts easier to understand through interactive learning and creativity.

projectDetails.name: EARTH-ECHO
projectDetails.summary:
EARTH ECHO  The Living Memory of Earth's Surface

EARTH ECHO is an interactive geospatial analysis platform developed to explore how Earth's surface changes across repeated observations from NASA–ISRO's NISAR satellite. It processes NISAR Level-2 Geocoded Polarimetric (GCOV) HDF5 data, identifies supported radar backscatter layers, and validates whether observations are scientifically compatible before comparison.

The platform converts calibrated radar backscatter measurements into decibel values, detects significant differences between acquisitions, and visualizes spatial patterns of change over time. Its project-defined Change Memory metric is designed to measure how frequently anomalous conditions recur across multiple observations, helping distinguish isolated variations from potentially persistent changes.

EARTH ECHO addresses the Dancing with the SARs challenge by turning repeated SAR observations into an interactive way to investigate Earth's changing surface. It is important because radar can observe the Earth independently of daylight and, within its operating capabilities, through cloud cover. By making temporal radar analysis more accessible while clearly communicating scientific limitations, EARTH ECHO aims to support better exploration of environmental change and its long-term patterns.
projectDetails.details:
What distinguishes EARTH ECHO from conventional satellite analysis platforms is its focused integration of NISAR-specific data compatibility validation, pixel-level backscatter change detection, and a project-defined Change Memory metric within a unified interactive workflow. Rather than simply identifying differences between two satellite observations, EARTH ECHO aims to investigate how frequently radar anomalies occur across repeated acquisitions, providing an additional temporal perspective on Earth's changing surface. Its compatibility-validation pipeline checks polarization, radiometric properties and spatial alignment before comparisons, helping reduce misleading results from incompatible datasets. While established platforms already offer SAR processing and multitemporal change detection, EARTH ECHO brings these capabilities together in an accessible NISAR-focused environment and introduces a framework for exploring anomaly frequency and recurrence. Its distinctive contribution lies in this integration and its proposed temporal-analysis approach, with further multi-date testing and benchmarking needed to establish its scientific advantages.

HOW TO ADD DATA?

Monitor environmental changes

Support forest and land monitoring

Support infrastructure monitoring

Help agricultural research

Improve research and decision-making

Understand persistent changes

Intended impact

  1. Environmental monitoring: Help researchers identify unusual surface changes that may require further investigation.
  2. Disaster research: Support the investigation of possible flood-related and other disaster-related surface changes through repeated radar observations.
  3. Agricultural research: Provide additional information for studying changing land and field conditions.
  4. Infrastructure and land monitoring: Help investigate unusual surface patterns around developed and natural areas.
  5. Long-term research: Introduce Change Memory to explore how frequently anomalies recur across multiple observations.
  6. Accessible scientific analysis: Make NISAR data easier to inspect, compare and interpret through an interactive platform.

Programming Languages:

  • Python

Development Tools and Software:

  • Visual Studio Code (VS Code) — application development and code editing.
  • Git and GitHub — version control, source-code management and public repository hosting.
  • Streamlit — interactive web application development and deployment.
  • Python scientific and data-processing libraries — numerical computation, geospatial data handling and visualization.

Data Formats and Scientific Technologies:

  • HDF5 — reading and processing NASA–ISRO NISAR Level-2 GCOV datasets.
  • NISAR SAR backscatter data — radar observations used for surface-change analysis.
  • Geospatial coordinate systems and raster-grid validation — ensuring compatibility between satellite observations.

Cloud and Deployment:

  • Streamlit Community Cloud — application deployment and public access.
  • GitHub — source-code hosting and integration with deployment.

Hardware:

  • A personal computer for software development, testing and processing satellite datasets.
  • No dedicated external hardware or physical sensors were used in the current software prototype.

EARTH ECHO is creative because it moves beyond conventional satellite-image visualization and introduces a time-oriented approach to understanding Earth's changing surface.

Its key innovation is the project-defined Change Memory metric, which explores how frequently radar anomalies recur across multiple satellite observations. Rather than treating every detected difference as an isolated event, the platform aims to investigate whether changes are temporary, recurring or potentially persistent.

Another creative aspect is the integration of several scientific processes into one interactive platform. EARTH ECHO combines NISAR HDF5 data extraction, radar-layer selection, spatial and radiometric compatibility validation, backscatter change detection, and temporal visualization into a unified workflow.

The project also emphasizes scientific reliability by checking whether datasets are compatible before comparing them and by distinguishing radar anomalies from confirmed environmental events.

Ultimately, EARTH ECHO introduces a different way of thinking about Earth observation: treating repeated radar measurements as pieces of a larger story about how our planet evolves over time.

During the development of EARTH ECHO, we considered several important factors:

  1. Scientific Accuracy: Ensuring that radar observations are interpreted correctly and that detected backscatter anomalies are not automatically classified as confirmed environmental events.
  2. Data Compatibility: Verifying polarization, radar frequency, radiometric quantity, coordinate reference systems, spatial grids and valid-data coverage before comparing NISAR observations.
  3. Temporal Analysis: Considering the importance of repeated satellite acquisitions to distinguish isolated changes from recurring patterns.
  4. Data Reliability: Using genuine NASA–ISRO NISAR Level-2 GCOV datasets rather than relying on fabricated or simulated observations for our real-data experiment.
  5. Usability and Accessibility: Designing an interactive interface that allows users to upload datasets, select radar layers, explore results and understand the processing workflow.
  6. Computational Efficiency: Considering the size of satellite HDF5 datasets and implementing a workflow that can process selected spatial subsets.
  7. Scalability and Future Development: Designing the platform to accommodate additional NISAR observations and support future multi-date Change Memory analysis.
  8. Practical Relevance: Considering how the resulting analysis could support environmental research, agricultural monitoring and investigation of disaster-related surface changes.

These factors helped guide our development towards a platform that prioritizes scientific transparency, meaningful analysis and future applicability.

projectDetails.name: Field Shift
projectDetails.summary:
FieldShift is a web-based agricultural decision-support platform that helps farmers make informed decisions about crop rotation, irrigation, and field management using real-time and historical satellite and weather data.

The platform integrates five years of NASA POWER rainfall and temperature records, NASA GIBS MODIS Terra NDVI satellite imagery, Meteomatics soil moisture and evapotranspiration data, and Open-Meteo terrain information. By combining these datasets, FieldShift identifies vegetation health, soil moisture conditions, erosion-prone areas, and potential climate risks. It translates complex Earth observation data into practical field recommendations, including crop rotation alternatives, irrigation guidance, and timely responses to drought, heat, frost, and runoff risks. Its interactive Pipori Field Advisor further helps farmers understand conditions and explore suitable actions.

FieldShift addresses the challenge by making NASA's Earth observation data accessible and actionable for everyday farming decisions. It aims to promote climate-resilient agriculture, improve resource efficiency, reduce crop losses, and support sustainable farming practices.
projectDetails.details: Built by Team RWS NOVA INNOVATORS for the NASA Space Apps Challenge ("Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data"), FieldShift is a practical web app that helps farmers adapt their crop rotations and daily farm decisions using real satellite and weather data. We built the PHP backend and CSS styling ourselves, used Claude and Gemini to put together the interactive JavaScript, API integrations, and the Pipori Field Advisor, and relied on VS Code for coding and testing everything along the way. The platform pulls together 5-year NASA POWER rainfall and temperature records, 8-day NASA GIBS MODIS Terra NDVI satellite vegetation layers, Meteomatics temperature, evapotranspiration, and -15 cm soil moisture readings, and Open-Meteo terrain slope data into one clear workspace. For a farmer, this means raw Earth observation data turns into straightforward, on-the-ground help: marking a plot on the map reveals erosion-prone slopes, NDVI layers show where crops are thriving or leaving bare soil, soil moisture and climate readings help time irrigation and save water, and 5-year weather trends highlight upcoming heat, drought, runoff, or frost windows. By pairing those signals with a farmer's current crop practice, irrigation setup, and main goal, FieldShift lays out clear field actions, side-by-side rotation options, and easy answers through Pipori Field Advisor.

projectDetails.name: FireMind — Microgravity Fire Safety Intelligence
projectDetails.summary:
For over 15 years, NASA has investigated microgravity combustion aboard the International Space Station through landmark experiments including BASS, FLEX, ACME, SoFIE, and FLARE. However, these critical findings remain buried in dense technical publications and fragmented telemetry archives, inaccessible to mission architects preparing for lunar (Artemis) and Martian human exploration.

FireMind is an interactive, Super Intelligence (SI)-powered decision-support dashboard that unifies, compares, and interprets decades of microgravity fire research. Featuring a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) research engine, multi-variable telemetry visualization, query-driven experiment ranking, and mission-specific risk matrices for ISS, Moon, Mars, and Deep Space, FireMind bridges the critical gap between raw zero-gravity physics and life-or-death spacecraft engineering decisions.
projectDetails.details:
What exactly does it do?

FireMind is an end-to-end scientific intelligence platform and autonomous flight safety architecture specifically engineered for spacecraft and extraterrestrial habitats:

1. Interactive Microgravity Flame Dynamics (PINN-Surrogate): Real-time in-browser fluid and molecular diffusion simulation allowing engineers to manipulate gravity levels (0g, 0.16g Moon, 0.38g Mars, 1g Earth), forced airflow velocities (0–25 cm/s), and oxygen concentrations (10–30%), dynamically visualizing spherical blue diffusion envelopes, cool flame zones, and Damköhler numbers.

2. LangGraph Autonomous Multi-Agent ECLSS Swarm: A distributed 4-agent cognitive safety architecture (Perception Agent, Physics Neural Surrogate PINN, Scientific RAG Agent, and Autonomous ECLSS Mitigation Controller) operating closed-loop life-support safety in under 12ms.

3. Research Discovery Engine (RAG): Natural language interrogation of NASA microgravity combustion literature powered by Gemini 3.5 Flash, providing evidence-based answers with verified citations to NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) and Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repositories.

4. Experimental Parameter Visualizer: Multi-variable interactive telemetry comparing flame spread rates, limiting oxygen indices, and mission safety radar across BASS, FLEX-2, ACME, SoFIE, and FLARE.

5. Mission Environmental Safety Matrix: Cross-gravity hazard synthesis evaluating ISS, Artemis Lunar Habitats (1/6g), and Martian Surface Missions (1/3g), exposing the deadly failure of terrestrial NASA-STD-6001 standards in low gravity.

6. AI Experiment Relevance Ranker: Dynamic relevance scoring evaluating operational safety criteria against historical flight data.

How does it work?

- Data Engineering: Curated multi-dimensional datasets representing published empirical findings from 5 NASA flight programs (BASS, FLEX, ACME, SoFIE, FLARE), including solid fuel flame spread, droplet extinction diameters, and gravity-scaled flammability boundaries.

- Artificial Intelligence Layer: Powered by Google Gemini utilizing Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG). The model is strictly prompted with NASA domain guardrails to prevent hallucinations, distinguish measured data from computational models, and mandate explicit citation.

- Frontend Architecture: Built using Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, TypeScript, and Tailwind CSS, featuring Recharts for interactive scientific telemetry visualization.

What benefits does it have?

- Astronaut Safety: Exposes counter-intuitive microgravity fire behavior—such as the "low-flow danger zone" (1–5 cm/s ventilation speeds) and invisible second-stage "cool flames" (300–500°C)—directly informing ventilation shutdown protocols and sensor designs.

- Artemis & Mars Readiness: Synthesizes partial-gravity flammability boundaries from FLARE, preventing engineers from dangerously interpolating 1g Earth or 0g ISS data for Moon (1/6g) and Mars (1/3g) surface bases.

- Accelerated Engineering Workflows: Slashes research cross-comparison time from days of manual literature retrieval down to seconds of interactive exploration.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

- Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3, Python

- Frameworks & Libraries: Next.js 16, React 19, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, React-Markdown, Lucide-React

- AI & Super Intelligence: Google Gemini API, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) Architecture, Physics-Informed Neural Surrogate (PINN)

- Version Control & Hosting: Git, GitHub, Vercel Serverless Platform

- Data Repositories: NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI), NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS)

projectDetails.name: TerraEcho AI
projectDetails.summary:
TerraEcho AI is a multisensory Earth observation and change intelligence platform designed to transform Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) satellite data into understandable, evidence-based insights. It addresses the Dancing with the SARs challenge by analysing radar observations from different dates to identify changes on Earth's surface, even when optical imagery is limited by cloud cover or darkness.

The platform combines TerraShift for SAR-based change detection, Earth Change Fingerprints for structured change representation, and Historical Change Memory for comparing current observations with past patterns. Its Spectral Verification Matrix organizes supporting and conflicting evidence, while Eco-Pulse converts selected radar features into audio to provide an alternative way to explore detected changes. An evidence-grounded AI interpretation module explains observed changes, possible causes, and uncertainty. The platform also provides interactive geospatial visualizations and investigation reports for technical experts and communities.

TerraEcho AI is important because detecting environmental and surface changes is only the first step. Understanding the evidence, comparing historical patterns, communicating uncertainty, and supporting informed human decisions can make satellite observations more useful for environmental monitoring and Earth science investigations.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

Answer:TerraEcho AI is a multisensory geospatial intelligence platform that transforms complex Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) observations (such as NASA-ISRO NISAR data) into structured, evidence-supported Earth-change intelligence.

How it works:

  • Detect (TerraShift): It processes SAR acquisitions to identify and segment surface changes (e.g., flooding, vegetation disturbance, or land deformation).
  • Fingerprint: It bundles each change into a structured Earth Change Fingerprint tracking spatial, radar ($\sigma^0$ decibels, polarization), temporal, and quality signatures.
  • Verify & Compare: It checks historical memory for seasonal recurrence and opens a Spectral Verification Matrix to show raw decibel shifts and Z-score anomalies against historical baselines.
  • Experience & Interpret: Users can explore data visually on an interactive map or sonify radar parameters into ambient soundscapes using Eco-Pulse (Web Audio API). An AI reasoning engine then ranks candidate explanations while explicitly surfacing uncertainty and missing data.
  • Act: It exports a structured Human-Reviewed Investigation Brief via a Dual-Audience Gateway (Expert GIS Mode vs. Community StoryMap Mode).

2. What benefits does it have?

Answer:

  • Lowers the SAR Complexity Barrier: Translates dense orbital radar physics into intuitive visual, numerical, and auditory formats for non-specialists.
  • Eliminates Black-Box AI Risk: Provides absolute scientific transparency through the Spectral Verification Matrix and explicit missing-evidence flags, ensuring users never confuse model guesses with confirmed physical causes.
  • Multi-Sensory Exploration: Introduces data sonification (Eco-Pulse), allowing analysts to perceive temporal variation and spatial texture through sound.
  • Dual-Audience Agility: Instantly bridges the gap between high-level GIS analysts (GeoJSON/STAC outputs) and local community stakeholders (plain-language StoryMaps).

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Answer: TerraEcho AI is designed as a rigorous decision-support and investigation tool for environmental analysts, researchers, and local planning groups. Its intended impacts are:

  • Accelerating Environmental Response: Helping stakeholders quickly prioritize which areas of surface change warrant urgent human investigation.
  • Improving Open-Science Transparency: Making NASA Earth observation data more accessible without sacrificing scientific credibility or overstating causal certainty.
  • Empowering Communities: Bridging the gap between orbital satellite missions and local communities by converting complex remote sensing insights into actionable, human-reviewed briefs.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

Answer:

  • Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS (Dark Mode Design System), Deck.gl & MapLibre GL JS (Geospatial Rendering), Native Web Audio API (Eco-Pulse Sonification).
  • Backend & Geospatial Processing: Python 3.11, FastAPI, Rasterio, GDAL, NumPy, Pandas, Scikit-learn, PostGIS.
  • Data Sources & Standards: NASA Earth data STAC APIs, Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (COGs), NISAR proxy data cubes, and Sentinel-1 L1 GRD/SLC products.

5. How is your project creative?

Answer: While 95% of hackathon teams submit standard map viewers with basic image split-sliders, TerraEcho AI introduces true multi-sensory and conceptual creativity:

  • The Earth Change Fingerprint: Moving away from binary raster masks to a multi-variable vector identity for every detected spatial anomaly.
  • Eco-Pulse Sonification: Translating radar backscatter intensity, spatial entropy, and coherence into real-time audio synthesis, letting users hear the structural stability of an ecosystem change.
  • Humble, Guardrailed AI: Designing an AI layer that actively searches for conflicting evidence and reports missing data rather than hallucinating definitive physical causes.

6. What factors did your team consider?

Answer:

  • Scientific Boundaries & Integrity: We strictly separated measured observations, derived features, and model interpretations, ensuring we never claimed arbitrary image pairs yield uncalibrated millimeter-level InSAR displacement.
  • Hackathon Feasibility & Demo Stability: Rather than risking a live, crash-prone backend pipeline, we structured our architecture around pre-cached Cloud Optimized GeoTIFFs (COGs) and structured JSON matrices to guarantee a 100% stable, lightning-fast demonstration.
  • Actionability vs. Caution: We designed the system as a decision-support platform that generates investigation briefs for human review, explicitly avoiding automated public emergency warnings or unsupported causal declarations.

projectDetails.name: TerraTwin: Multi-Scale Moon & Mars Planetary Analog Discovery Engine
projectDetails.summary:
Selecting future lunar bases and Mars landing sites requires testing equipment in terrestrial analogs; however, traditional site selection relies on visual approximations and overlooks physical differences. We developed TerraTwin, a multi-scale computational planetary analog discovery engine that moves beyond visual similarity by evaluating sites across 8 quantitative geophysical dimensions derived from open NASA, CSA, ESA, and JAXA datasets.

TerraTwin characterizes 8 flagship planetary targets (including Artemis III Shackleton Crater, Marius Hills lava tubes, and Mars Jezero Crater) against 10 global Earth analogs spanning 6 continents and subterranean volcanic cavities. To overcome single-site physical limits, TerraTwin introduces algorithmic Dual-Site Campaign Synthesis (combining sites to achieve >92% exploration coverage) alongside deterministic hardware protocols for Bekker wheel sinkage, rover mechanical gravity offloading, and optical solar attenuation. The system features a responsive Next.js mission workbench, live NASA CMR API querying, and an unsupervised 2D PCA latent space explorer.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

TerraTwin is a full-stack planetary analog characterization system combining an interactive web workbench with automated scientific data pipelines:

  • 8D Calibrated Vector Characterization: Every planetary target and Earth analog is mapped to an 8-dimensional normalized feature vector (v∈[0,100]8\mathbf{v} \in [0, 100]^8v∈[0,100]8) covering: Geology/Mineralogy, Topography/SAR Roughness, Thermal/Insolation, Cryogenic Volatiles/ISRU, Aeolian Dynamics, Astrobiology/Extremophiles, Subsurface Cavities, and Terramechanics/Mobility.
  • Hybrid Similarity Scoring Engine: Uses a calibrated Gaussian Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel combined with Cosine directional alignment (SFinal=0.55⋅SRBF+0.45⋅SCosine−δS_{\text{Final}} = 0.55 \cdot S_{\text{RBF}} + 0.45 \cdot S_{\text{Cosine}} - \deltaSFinal​=0.55⋅SRBF​+0.45⋅SCosine​−δ), preventing artificial score clustering and yielding a realistic 75%–96% match spread.
  • Unsupervised 2D Latent Space (PCA & K-Means): Projects multi-agency planetary dimensions into a 2D coordinate plane capturing 61.7% of total variance, automatically categorizing sites into 4 geophysical archetypes: Lacustrine/Sulfate Basins, Cryogenic Polar Traps, Basaltic Impact Rims, and Subterranean Lava Cavities.
  • Dual-Site Campaign Synthesis: Recognizes that no single Earth site replicates all conditions, automatically pairing complementary micro-sites (e.g., pairing lunar highland calcic anorthosite with high-Arctic permafrost polygons) to reach >92% exploration envelope fidelity.
  • Operational Hardware Protocols: Computes Bekker terramechanic wheel sinkage (z0z_0z0​) under lunar and Martian gravity, specifies rover counterweight offloading in Newtons, and calculates neutral-density optical attenuation filters for testing planetary cameras under terrestrial sunlight.
  • In-Browser Custom Outcrop Scanner: Enables field scientists to input custom GPS coordinates, slope, radar backscatter, and temperature to project uncharted field sites live into the PCA latent space.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Eliminates Visual Confirmation Bias: Replaces "looks like Mars" intuition with calibrated radar decibels (σ0\sigma^0σ0), Sentinel-2 SWIR mineral ratios, and thermal inertia (PPP).
  • Tactical Micro-Site Precision: Targets sub-kilometer zones (e.g., ejecta blankets and volcanic skylights) rather than over-generalized geographic regions.
  • Risk Mitigation & Cost Reduction: Helps flight teams verify robotics, mobility, and scientific instruments under mathematically modeled boundary conditions before mission deployment, preventing multimillion-dollar hardware failures.
  • Comprehensive Failure Analysis: Explicitly outlines both "Why This Analog Works" and "Where It Breaks Down & Constraints" for every location.

3. What is the intended impact?

TerraTwin directly assists mission planners, roboticists, and planetary scientists designing hardware and astronaut protocols for NASA's Artemis III lunar south pole expeditions, long-duration lunar base infrastructure, and future human Mars landing missions.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

  • Frontend Workbench: Next.js 14, React 18, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Lucide React icons, and dynamic SVG rendering for the 8-axis radar profiles and 2D PCA latent space.
    • nasa_earthdata_fetcher.py: Automated, zero-key HTTP client connecting to NASA's EOSDIS Common Metadata Repository (CMR) API.
    • sar_backscatter_calculator.py: Canadian Space Agency (CSA) Rayleigh roughness & LRO Mini-RF Circular Polarization Ratio (CPR) processor.
    • cli_analog_finder.py: Terminal-based analog discovery CLI with mission hardware weighting presets.
  • GIS & Mapping: Embedded Google Maps Satellite Viewport, NASA Moon Trek GIS, and NASA Mars Trek GIS integrations.

5. How is your project creative?

TerraTwin solves the fundamental challenge of planetary analog science: the single-site paradox. Instead of forcing a single Earth location to act as an impossible 100% twin, TerraTwin creatively synthesizes dual-site mission campaigns. Furthermore, it embeds real-time mathematical Bekker terramechanics and mechanical gravity compensation into the interface, transforming analog scouting into an active engineering test simulator.

6. What factors did your team consider?

Our team implemented solutions for all 11 Official NASA Space Apps Challenge Considerations:

  1. Beyond visual similarity: Integrated radar backscatter (σ0\sigma^0σ0), SWIR mineralogy, and thermal inertia.
  2. Multiple dimensions: Exact 1-to-1 parity with NASA’s 8 physical dimensions.
  3. Strengths & breakdowns: Dual cards for every site detailing operational limits.
  4. Geological processes: Dedicated process twins (e.g., cryoturbation, impact shock metamorphism, lava tube inflation).
  5. Beyond well-known sites: Uncovered uncharted gems (Rogaland anorthosite, Lonar basalt rim, Dallol acid delta, Umm Jirsan tube) alongside benchmarks.
  6. Whole Earth & subsurface: Explored 6 continents plus subterranean lava conduits.
  7. Multi-agency data: Synthesized data across NASA, CSA, ESA, and JAXA.
  8. Scale: Micro-scale resolution (<1 km2<1 \text{ km}^2<1 km2 grids) with tactical coordinates.
  9. Exploration connection: Bekker wheel sinkage, rover counterweights, and solar flux filters.
  10. Earth's physical limits: Quantified gravity offload percentages (Luna 83.5%, Mars 62.2%) and vacuum chamber requirements.
  11. Surprise factor: Interactive in-browser PCA latent space and dual-site synergy pairing.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: SiteLight - Lunar Landing Site Navigator
projectDetails.summary: SiteLight is a web application that helps people compare lunar south-pole study sites and mission dates. It brings NASA terrain data and Sun-Earth geometry into one clear, interactive workspace. Users can compare two scenarios, see sunlight and Earth-visibility windows, inspect the local horizon, and test alternative start times within the loaded data. Terrain screening and historical thermal,Apollo seismic records add context, while clearly labeled research models explore engineering assumptions. An evidence section connects results to their sources, and downloadable reports preserve the settings and limitations. Our goal is to make complex lunar planning information easier for educators, the public and early-stage mission teams to understand. The public demo uses prepared real-data records; additional on-demand scientific calculations require the separate backend. SiteLight supports exploration and comparison, not flight certification or a guarantee of landing safety.
projectDetails.details:
AppLink: https://sitelight.vercel.app/  Sourcecode: https://github.com/manojkalyan/siteLight

The problem

At the lunar south pole, nearby terrain can block the Sun or Earth. A small change in location or date can change lighting and direct-to-Earth visibility. Comparing these trade-offs across separate technical tools is difficult for non-specialists.

Our solution

SiteLight places two independent mission scenarios in one visual workspace. Users select study sites, UTC start times and duration, then compare sunlight, Earth visibility and simultaneous availability against shared requirements. The app explains which conditions fall short and keeps an alternative date as a preview until the user applies it.

How it works

A Python preparation pipeline processes NASA LOLA terrain and pinned JPL/NAIF SPICE kernels. It calculates local terrain horizons and sampled Sun/Earth directions. The browser evaluates available records against user requirements and displays timelines, horizon plots and comparison results. Source manifests retain acquisition details and SHA-256 identities. Missing coverage is reported rather than filled with invented measurements.

What is creative

The main contribution is an understandable, evidence-linked comparison workflow: compare sites, identify the limiting condition, preview a different start, and inspect the source behind the result. Historical Apollo impact waveforms and moonquake/scarp context connect visible terrain with subsurface science without pretending to predict a local seismic hazard.

Benefits and intended impact

Educators and the public can understand why lunar timing matters. Early-stage mission teams can communicate site/date trade-offs and revisit assumptions when schedules change. The intended impact is clearer decisions and better scientific communication; operational time savings and mission safety improvements have not been established by field trials.

Tools and implementation

The interface uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js and Vite. The scientific preparation/service uses Python, NumPy, rasterio, SPICE/spiceypy and FastAPI. Node tests and Playwright support software checks. GitHub hosts the source and Vercel hosts the public frontend. No specialized physical hardware is required to view the prototype.

Factors considered

We considered polar terrain obstruction, solar elevation, Earth visibility, overlapping windows, data coverage, sampling intervals, uncertainty, source traceability, performance, screen size and readable explanations. The cinematic terrain is illustrative; quantitative terrain analysis uses the separately identified DEM data.

Current scope

The public frontend runs prepared real-data assessments, comparisons, loaded January-March 2027 starts, historical context, exploratory models and exports. The separate scientific backend is not connected to the public deployment. New custom terrain points, dates outside bundled coverage, monthly record generation and recomputed terrain ensembles need that backend. Results are a research prototype, not NASA approval or flight-qualified advice.

projectDetails.name: Project SpaceXTN
projectDetails.summary:
Overview

Relics is an interactive web experience that tells the stories of the equipment NASA has left behind on the Moon and Mars. Instead of treating these objects as space junk, it presents each one as a character in humanity’s exploration story, with a purpose, an achievement, an ending and a lesson. Visitors choose a world, tap a relic on a map, and read what the object did, why it was left, what condition it is in, and what we learned from it.

The Problem

Most people know that astronauts walked on the Moon and that rovers have driven across Mars, but very few know what remains there today. Descent stages, lunar rovers, landers, instruments and even a helicopter still sit where their missions ended. Information about them is spread across technical archives, mission pages and image libraries that are difficult for students and the general public to navigate.
The topic is also becoming more relevant. NASA’s Artemis program is preparing to return people to the Moon, and commercial missions are following. That raises practical questions: how should historic landing sites be protected, and what can aged hardware teach us about building equipment that lasts? These questions deserve public attention, and storytelling is one of the best ways to create it.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

Relics is an interactive web experience that tells the stories of equipment NASA has left behind on the Moon and Mars. A visitor chooses a world, then explores a coordinate map where each pin marks a relic’s approximate landing location. A date-ordered list sits beside the map, so any story can be reached either way.

Selecting a relic opens a story card with four parts:

  • Current state: where the object is now and what condition it is in
  • Its story: what it was built to do and why it was left behind
  • What we learned: the lesson it offers future missions
  • NASA images: a link to NASA’s image library, so visitors can see real photographs

The prototype covers twelve relics. On the Moon these are the Apollo 11 descent stage, Surveyor 3 and the Apollo 12 visit, and the lunar rovers from Apollo 15, 16 and 17. On Mars they are the Viking 1 and 2 landers, Sojourner and Pathfinder, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight and the Ingenuity helicopter. A short quiz at the end reinforces what visitors learned.

What benefits does it have?

  • It turns scattered technical records into short, readable stories for students, teachers and the general public.
  • It needs no installation or account, loads quickly, and works on phones and computers.
  • It is accessible, with keyboard navigation, visible focus states, light and dark themes, and reduced-motion support.
  • The quiz and the consistent story format make it useful in classrooms.
  • New relics are easy to add, because every entry follows the same data structure.

What is the intended impact?

We want people to see these machines as part of a shared human journey rather than as space junk. As NASA’s Artemis program returns people to the Moon, we hope the project builds public awareness of why preserving historic landing sites matters, and of what aged hardware can teach us about building equipment that lasts in dust, vacuum and radiation. It also aims to inspire curiosity in younger audiences about planetary exploration.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

  • Languages: HTML, CSS and JavaScript
  • Format: a single self-contained web page with no external libraries
  • Data: a structured data set listing each relic’s name, site, coordinates, year, status, story and lesson
  • Hosting: a public web link, so no installation is needed
  • Presentation: a 7-slide demo deck
  • AI assistance: an AI assistant (Claude) helped draft the story text, summary and page code
  • Hardware: any ordinary computer or phone; the project needs nothing special
  • Reference sources: NASA Image and Video Library, NASA Moon Trek and Mars Trek, LROC (Arizona State University), HiRISE (University of Arizona), and NASA mission pages

How is the project creative?

  • Objects as characters: Each relic is written as a character with a purpose, an achievement, an ending and a lesson, not as a catalog entry.
  • Human-scale details: Opportunity was built for months and lasted nearly fifteen years. Apollo 12 astronauts walked to Surveyor 3 and brought parts home. These details make the history memorable.
  • Museum-placard design: The page uses calm typography and a structure like a museum placard, so the relics feel like heritage rather than debris.
  • Two worlds, one map style: The Moon and Mars share one interface, which invites visitors to compare how exploration differs between them.

What factors did we consider?

  • Accuracy: Mission facts and coordinates must be verified against NASA sources. All locations on the map are approximate.
  • Clear creative framing: Stories are plain retellings, and any creative narration should be labeled as interpretation, not NASA quotes.
  • Honest AI use: We disclose that an AI assistant helped with drafting and code, and that a human team reviews the content.
  • Licensing: NASA imagery is linked rather than copied, and any future use should credit NASA, ASU and the University of Arizona.
  • Accessibility and reach: The design supports many devices and abilities, and future versions could add narration and more languages.
  • Scope: We kept the first version focused on twelve well-documented relics, rather than a large catalog done poorly.
  • Heritage and ethics: The project respects the historic value of the sites and does not claim NASA endorsement.

Before submitting, check the facts and coordinates against NASA sources and edit any statement that doesn’t match what your team actually did.

projectDetails.name: Astronaut Health Monitor
projectDetails.summary: Astronaut Health Monitor is a one-minute daily health check-in for astronauts far from Earth. On a Mars mission a message takes up to 22 minutes each way, and during solar conjunction there is no contact for about two weeks, so the crew must judge their own health. The app records nine health indicators (blood pressure, heart rate, glucose, temperature, sleep, mood, oxygen, body mass, radiation), compares each reading with the astronaut's own normal from readings taken on Earth before launch, and answers one question: can this wait for Earth? If Earth's reply would come after the problem becomes dangerous, it says ACT ON BOARD NOW and gives a plain-language, drug-free checklist; otherwise it says ASK EARTH and builds a report for the flight surgeon. Results appear on a clickable 3D body. It works offline, with touch, as a desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux. All crew and readings are simulated; it does not diagnose.
projectDetails.details:
The problem we started with. We began by reading NASA's Human Research Program material on the Five Hazards of Human Spaceflight and on how crews are monitored today. One fact kept coming back: on a Mars mission a message takes up to 22 minutes each way, and during solar conjunction there is no contact for about two weeks. On the ISS a flight surgeon is minutes away. On Mars the crew has to decide alone. We asked what a health tool must do when Earth cannot answer in time.


Our first version, and what we did not like. Our first idea was a dashboard of health numbers, plus a concept video made from mock-ups. Looking at it honestly, a wall of numbers does not tell a tired astronaut what to do, and a number means nothing without knowing what is normal for that person. So we changed the question the app asks. It no longer says "here are your readings". It says "can this wait for Earth?".


Before launch versus after launch. A healthy heart rate of 58 is normal for one astronaut and a warning for another, so the comparison has to be personal. Before launch, on Earth, we record 10 days of readings per crew member (blood pressure, heart rate, glucose, temperature, sleep, mood, oxygen, body mass, radiation). That becomes their own baseline. After launch, every daily check-in is compared with that baseline, not with a population average. The decision rule then compares Earth's reply time (ISS about 20 minutes, Mars transit 64 minutes, conjunction no contact) with how long the problem can safely wait. If Earth would answer too late, the app says ACT ON BOARD NOW and gives a drug-free checklist; otherwise it says ASK EARTH and builds a Consult Packet for the flight surgeon that queues offline until contact returns.

What the research changed. The NASA Five Hazards (gravity, isolation, radiation, distance from Earth, closed environments) decided which hazards each of the nine indicators is linked to. Every safety rule sits on a condition card that cites its source, so nothing is a guess. The NASA flight-surgeon material and the NASA Technical Reports Server papers on Earth-independent medical care and the rHEALTH ONE ISS demonstration showed that crews are monitored with a doctor on the ground. That is why the app prepares a report for the flight surgeon instead of pretending to replace one. The Canadian Space Agency Bio-Monitor wearable shaped the check-in: wearable values arrive filled in and one tap on Measure fills the device readings.


Three explainable checks. (1) Safety rules written as data. (2) An "unusual day" detector (Mahalanobis distance with shrinkage, solved by Cholesky factorisation) that notices several readings that are each a little off. (3) A slow-drift detector (CUSUM) with a Theil-Sen forecast of when a reading will reach its limit. We checked the method on 300 simulated astronauts: every full fever was caught on day one and false "unusual day" alarms were 1.3 % per normal day. This tests the method only; it says nothing about clinical accuracy.


Making it usable in space. Crews may wear gloves or use a touch panel, so we designed for touch first: 56 px targets, an on-screen number pad, and status shown with colour, shape and word together. We applied UX principles (Fitts's law, Tesler's law, progressive disclosure) and cut the Recovery and Hazards pages when they showed too much at once. Results appear on a clickable 3D body with real organ models and a 2D line drawing. The first look was too playful for a medical tool, so we redesigned the type and colours to be calm and professional. It runs offline as a desktop app for Windows, macOS and Linux.

Then we worried that users would not know what to do. So we added a plain-language verdict at the top of every result, a "How it decides" page, an on-board assistant, and Demo mode, which plays a full voiced check-in with a cursor that clicks and types by itself. The assistant works offline and uses no AI model. It answers from the same cited condition cards, shows what each answer was built from, and refuses medicine doses and diagnoses in code. We chose this on purpose: a made-up answer in a medical setting is a risk we did not want to take. The Crew Medical Officer decides on any treatment.

What is simulated, and what is next. All crew and readings are simulated, and the app does not diagnose. Next we will set up a whole crew with roles and every member's Earth records, pair a real wearable before launch, add a crew tab with alerts to everyone, and send reports to Earth on a schedule set by the reply time.

Tools. TypeScript, React, Vite, Zustand, Dexie (IndexedDB), Recharts, three.js with React Three Fiber, Zod, Vitest (66 tests), Electron and electron-builder, GitHub Actions. Fonts Archivo and IBM Plex; Phosphor icons; Hairline engine for the 2D body; HyperFrames for the video.


Use of Super Intelligence. The idea, the problem framing and the product decisions are by Team Spades. Code and documentation were written with Claude (Anthropic) through Claude Code, directed and reviewed by the team. The narration in the 30-second video is AI-generated with Kokoro-82M text-to-speech, labelled on screen and in the file metadata. Demo mode narration uses the viewer's browser text-to-speech. The logo and icon were drawn as SVG code with AI assistance. All screenshots are real captures of the app, and the 3D organ models are by Sketchfab authors (CC-BY 4.0). No NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers are used.

projectDetails.summary: LAST LIGHT 2.0 is an interactive 3D Junior Astronaut Training experience designed to introduce students to the challenges of human space exploration through immersive missions and hands-on learning. The experience follows four major stages: astronaut training on Earth, space launch and orbital ascent, establishing a lunar outpost, and developing a Martian outpost. Players explore mission scenarios involving spacecraft operations, life-support systems, resource management, habitats, and survival beyond Earth. By combining interactive gameplay, realistic 3D environments, educational narration, and mission-based progression, LAST LIGHT 2.0 aims to make complex STEM and space-science concepts engaging and accessible to young learners.
projectDetails.details:
Project Description – LastLight (Astronaut’s Mission)

What does it do / How does it work?
LastLight is an interactive 3D browser-based space exploration and survival game. Players take on the role of an astronaut training for deep-space missions. They must manage critical resources (Oxygen, Stamina, Health, Hydration, Suit Battery, and Colony Power) while navigating different environments — from a training academy to a spacecraft, a lunar outpost, and a Martian colony. Players explore in first-person and third-person views, interact with objects, face environmental challenges like dust storms, and make decisions that affect the mission’s outcome.

What benefits does it have?

  • Makes space exploration and resource management engaging and fun for young learners
  • Teaches the importance of careful planning, resource conservation, and decision-making under pressure
  • Runs completely in the browser — no downloads or installations required
  • Accessible on both computers and mobile devices

What is the intended impact of the project?
The project aims to inspire the next generation of explorers, scientists, and engineers by giving them a hands-on, immersive experience of what it feels like to live and work in space. It encourages curiosity about space science, planetary exploration, and human survival beyond Earth.

Tools, coding languages, and software used:

  • HTML5 – structure of the game
  • CSS3 – styling and user interface
  • JavaScript – game logic and interactivity
  • Three.js – 3D graphics and rendering
  • GitHub – version control and source code hosting
  • Vercel – free and fast web hosting

How is your project creative?
Instead of a traditional 2D educational game, LastLight uses real-time 3D graphics to create an immersive astronaut experience. Players can freely explore different space environments, switch camera perspectives, and face realistic survival challenges. The combination of storytelling, resource management, and interactive 3D exploration makes learning about space feel like an adventure.

What factors did your team consider?

  • Making the game educational yet entertaining
  • Ensuring it works smoothly in a web browser without requiring powerful hardware
  • Designing simple and clear controls (WASD movement, mouse look, interactive keys)
  • Creating a meaningful progression from training → spacecraft → Moon → Mars
  • Keeping the entire project lightweight so it loads quickly and works on most devices

projectDetails.name: Tetra
projectDetails.summary: TERRA-X is a Planetary Analogue Intelligence System that identifies and analyzes Earth environments resembling the terrain and environmental conditions of the Moon and Mars using scientific datasets. It helps researchers explore potential analogue sites, compare planetary characteristics, and evaluate mission suitability through interactive maps, data visualization, and intelligent similarity analysis.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

AnalogFinder is an interactive web tool that searches the whole Earth for places that resemble the Moon and Mars. Instead of picking one site because it looks similar, we turn the question into a measurable one. We describe a target (Moon South Pole, Mars Jezero, or Mars Gale) as a numeric profile built from space-agency data. We describe each Earth candidate site with the same features from NASA Earth observations. We then compute a weighted similarity score across six dimensions: terrain, temperature, geology, ice and water, dust, and subsurface.

Users see the results on an interactive world map, with markers colored from low to high match. They can adjust weight sliders to reflect their mission priorities, and the map re-scores instantly. Selecting a site opens a report with a radar chart, an explanation of why it matches, where the analogy breaks down, and how the site could be used for exploration. A “Hidden Gems” mode excludes well-known analog sites so that overlooked locations surface.

Benefits

It gives mission planners a systematic, data-driven way to find and compare analog sites instead of relying on a few well-known locations.
Weighting lets different missions (rover mobility, resource extraction, habitat construction, instrument testing) find the analog that fits their needs.
Each site report states its limits clearly, which supports honest scientific use.

Intended impact

We want to widen the set of Earth sites considered for lunar and Mars preparation, make it easier to find lower-cost and more accessible testing locations, and help the public understand that no Earth site is a perfect analog, but many can be useful for specific purposes. The method is reproducible, so it can be extended to a global grid search and to more targets.

Tools, languages, and software

Data: NASA and open datasets including [SRTM / Copernicus DEM, MODIS, SMAP, MERRA-2, LRO LOLA, LRO Diviner, MGS MOLA, USGS Astrogeology: list only what you actually used]
Languages and libraries: [Python (pandas, NumPy) for feature normalization and scoring; JavaScript, Leaflet, and Chart.js for the map and charts]
Design: Google Stitch for UI design [and the tool you used to build the working app]
Hosting and documentation: [GitHub, deployment platform]

How the project is creative

It is a method, not a single-site answer. Anyone can rerun it with new data or new targets.
It looks beyond visual similarity by combining multiple datasets into one comparable score.
The “Hidden Gems” filter deliberately excludes famous sites to find unrecognized analogs, including sites in places like India [confirm against your final results].
Interactive weighting lets users define what “analogous” means for their own mission.
Every result includes a “where the analogy breaks down” section, so the tool shows its limits rather than hiding them.

Factors our team considered

Analogy is dimension-specific. A site can be an excellent terrain analog but a poor temperature analog, so we score each dimension separately.
Earth cannot reproduce reduced gravity (0.166 g on the Moon, 0.38 g on Mars), vacuum or a thin atmosphere, or the radiation environment. We state this in every site report.
Scale matters. A specific crater or valley can match better than a whole desert, so we scored individual sites rather than whole regions.
Data quality and resolution differ across datasets, so we normalized features before comparing them.
Usability for mission planners, including clear visuals, adjustable priorities, and a side-by-side comparison mode.
