projectDetails.name: AGROADAPT AI
projectDetails.summary: We built a crop-rotation decision-support tool that helps farmers choose rotations that protect soil, conserve water and withstand a changing climate. A farmer drops a pin on their field and sets priorities such as soil health, water conservation, profit, drought resilience and erosion control. The tool pulls live data at runtime: NASA POWER weather, GLDAS and SMAP soil moisture, IMERG rainfall, MODIS/VIIRS and Landsat vegetation indices, ECOSTRESS heat and water stress, and SRTM terrain. It combines these with USDA soil data, Cropland Data Layer rotation history and local climate records. From this it builds a field condition profile, scores candidate crops and multi-year rotations against a sourced crop knowledge base, and tests them under drier, hotter and late-frost scenarios. Each recommendation explains why, cites its data sources and fetch times, and shows a confidence score that drops when data are missing. Farmers worldwide face drought, heat and declining soils, and a poor rotation choice is costly. By turning NASA Earth observations into plain-language, field-specific guidance, the tool makes long-term resilience decisions easier and evidence-based.
projectDetails.details:
How It Works

AgroAdapt AI is an end-to-end agricultural decision-support platform that turns satellite telemetry and soil chemistry into actionable, multi-season planting schedules:

  1. Interactive Satellite Parcel Selection: Farmers drop a pin or search any farm location on an interactive hybrid satellite map, specifying parcel size, irrigation setup, and primary farming goals (profit maximization, water conservation, or soil regeneration).
  2. Automated Multi-Sensor Environmental Telemetry: Using the selected coordinates, the system queries live agroclimatology, soil moisture, rainfall reliability, vegetation vigor, land-surface thermal stress, and terrain slope datasets.
  3. Agronomic Scoring & 3-Season Sequence Engine: A multi-criteria matching model evaluates local water availability, thermal risk, and soil parameters (pH, organic carbon, NPK, texture) to compute a prominent Rotation Match Score alongside an optimized 3-season crop sequence (such as a cereal–legume–cereal rotation), 3 alternative rotation blocks, and a Top 5 individual crop leaderboard.
  4. Interactive Crop-Swapping & Financial Simulation: Farmers can swap individual crops within any season to see real-time recalculations of soil nitrogen balance, irrigation savings, pest-cycle interruption, and net profit across four global currencies ($ USD, ₹ INR, € EUR, and ¥ JPY).

Key Benefits

  • Natural Soil Fertility Restoration: Prioritizes nitrogen-fixing legumes in rotation cycles to replenish soil organic matter and reduce synthetic fertilizer dependency.
  • Water & Drought Resilience: Matches crop water requirements against historical rainfall reliability and root-zone moisture to minimize crop failure during dry spells.
  • Pest & Disease Cycle Interruption: Breaks host-specific pathogen and weed cycles by alternating crop families across consecutive seasons.
  • Financial Clarity Across Markets: Translates agronomic yield estimates into clear net return projections in multiple currencies, helping growers compare economic trade-offs before planting.
  • Zero-Barrier Accessibility: Eliminates scientific jargon by converting complex Earth-observation metrics into plain-language Farmer Q&A insights and visual scorecards.

Intended Impact

Continuous monocropping and unpredictable weather patterns degrade topsoil, deplete groundwater, and threaten smallholder livelihoods worldwide. AgroAdapt AI aims to democratize space-agency climate intelligence and precision agronomy—giving everyday farmers, agricultural extension workers, and rural cooperatives free, instant access to tools previously limited to large commercial agribusinesses. Over multiple harvest cycles, widespread adoption supports higher net farm incomes, lower chemical runoff, improved carbon sequestration, and long-term food security.

Tools, Languages & Technologies Used

  • Frontend & Application Logic: React (Hooks, Memoized Agronomic Scoring Engine), JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, and Tailwind CSS for responsive, mobile-friendly UI design.
  • Mapping & Geospatial APIs: Google Maps JavaScript API (Hybrid Satellite View, Geocoding, and Interactive Coordinate Pinning).
  • Earth Observation & Climate Data Sources:
    • NASA POWER API: Solar radiation, temperature extremes, humidity, and agroclimatology parameters.
    • NASA Earthdata / CMR Streams: GLDAS/NLDAS root-zone soil moisture, GPM IMERG precipitation reliability, MODIS/VIIRS/HLS vegetation indices (NDVI/EVI), ECOSTRESS thermal stress, and SRTM digital elevation/slope data.
    • SSURGO / Soil Lab Modeling: Soil texture, pH, organic matter, and NPK nutrient diagnostics.
  • Icons, Build & Deployment Stack: Lucide React iconography, Vite bundler, StackBlitz cloud IDE, GitHub version control, and Vercel / Netlify static hosting.
  • Hardware Requirements: Designed as a lightweight cloud web application requiring only a standard smartphone, tablet, or desktop browser with internet access—no specialized on-farm IoT sensors or high-end computing hardware needed.

What Makes the Project Creative

  • Multi-Season Systems Thinking Over Single-Crop Guessing: Most agricultural apps only recommend a single crop for the current season. AgroAdapt AI models 3-season agronomic synergy, scoring how one harvest prepares the soil and breaks pest cycles for the next.
  • Telemetry-to-Plain-Language Translation: Instead of overwhelming farmers with raw satellite bands or statistical charts, the platform frames complex datasets around intuitive, real-world questions (e.g., "Is my soil holding enough moisture?" or "Will heat stress hurt flowering?").
  • Live "What-If" Rotation Sandbox: Combining a bold, centerpiece Match Score with interactive crop-swapping cards turns complex agronomic modeling into an intuitive, tactile planning experience.

Factors Considered by the Team

  • Farmer Usability & Low Cognitive Load: Designed a streamlined, minimal-text interface with clear visual hierarchy, icon-driven navigation, and step-by-step guidance so users with varying levels of technical literacy can navigate effortlessly.
  • Data Reliability & Graceful Fallbacks: Accounted for intermittent rural connectivity and API rate limits by structuring resilient data pipelines that combine live satellite feeds with localized baseline models.
  • Global & Regional Adaptability: Incorporated multi-currency conversion (USD, INR, EUR, JPY), diverse soil profiles, and rainfed vs. irrigated farm configurations so the tool works equally well for a smallholder plot in India or a commercial farm abroad.
  • Environmental & Economic Balance: Weighted both immediate net profit and long-term ecological indicators (nitrogen balance, erosion control, and water conservation) so short-term yield gains do not come at the expense of soil degradation.

projectDetails.name: Field Shift - Rotation Scenario Explorer : Bridging NASA Data to Farm Decisions
projectDetails.summary:
Farmers worldwide face an escalating dilemma: shifting frost windows, intensifying heatwaves, and erratic rainfall make multi-generational intuition unreliable, trapping growers in defensive, high-water monocultures. Trying an unfamiliar crop rotation can restore soil health and save water, but gambling on the wrong crop risks total stand loss and financial ruin. Meanwhile, NASA captures petabytes of open Earth observations that could guide these decisions, but orbital data remains locked in complex scientific formats that never reach the field.

We built Field Shift, an open-source, client-side decision-support tool that bridges 35 years of NASA Earth observations directly to field-level seasonal management. By harmonizing 7 NASA missions and calibrating them against local weather stations, Field Shift allows producers to outline any field parcel, set their own priorities (conserving water, keeping soil covered, nitrogen fixation, cash flow), and test multi-year rotation scenarios in under 5 milliseconds. The tool provides transparent mathematical evidence and local agronomist checklists—comparing options without ever dictating what to plant.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does your project do, and how does it work?

Field Shift is an interactive, browser-based decision-support workspace designed to help agricultural producers and local extension officers navigate climate volatility through crop rotation.

Instead of treating crop selection as a static recommendation, Field Shift operates as an interactive flight simulator for the field:

  1. Interactive Field Selection: A user selects an agricultural basin or sketches their own field boundary anywhere on a satellite basemap.
  2. Multi-Mission Zonal Ingestion: The system instantly queries a precomputed 140 m raster atlas fusing 7 NASA Earth observation missions, displaying the parcel's 35-year climate history, soil moisture anomalies, vegetative greenness cycles, and terrain slope.
  3. The 12-Month Rotation Ring: The parcel's annual canopy dynamics are projected onto a circular 365-day wheel. Living crop cover is traced in colored arcs, while vulnerable bare-soil windows appear as empty gaps.
  4. 3-Vector Stress Calendar: The platform cross-references seasonal bare-ground periods (NDVI<0.25NDVI < 0.25NDVI<0.25) against historical high-intensity rainfall events (GPM IMERG), wind erosion months, and peak heat stress windows (NASA POWER).
  5. Deterministic Scenario Exploration: The farmer sets their own operational priorities using 8 adjustable weights and 3 hard feasibility constraints (irrigation water allocation caps, machinery availability, and guaranteed buyer access). In less than 5 milliseconds, the system evaluates alternative multi-year crop rotations, displaying ranked strategies alongside auditable point breakdowns and risks.

2. What benefits does it have, and what is the intended impact?

  • Risk-Free Exploration: Farmers can test alternative cropping sequences against historic droughts, shifting frost dates, and water cutbacks on screen before spending a dollar on seed or expending limited water rights.
  • Aquifer and Soil Conservation: Crop diversification breaks autotoxicity cycles, adds biological nitrogen, and eliminates critical post-harvest bare-fallow windows that drive topsoil erosion.
    • Arid Alluvial Basins (Nevada High Desert): Proved 118 mm/yr118\text{ mm/yr}118 mm/yr (~17%) irrigation savings (15M to 59M liters15\text{M to }59\text{M liters}15M to 59M liters per center pivot) by transitioning continuous alfalfa into winter triticale and sorghum-sudangrass.
    • Intensive Breadbasket Plains (Punjab): Proved ∼650 mm/yr\sim 650\text{ mm/yr}∼650 mm/yr irrigation reduction by replacing summer puddled rice with maize-wheat-moong rotations.
    • Tropical Canal Deltas (Cauvery Delta): Demonstrated canal water stabilization by replacing double-paddy with single Samba rice and residual moisture pulses.
  • Responsible Deployment: Every strategy card includes a mandatory "Verify with Local Agronomist" checklist covering herbicide carryover plant-back restrictions, soil salinity thresholds, and seed availability.

3. How is your project creative and unique?

  • Rejection of Black-Box AI: Commercial agricultural technology often relies on opaque neural networks that attempt to predict unvalidated yields, eroding farmer trust. Field Shift uses transparent, deterministic Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis (MCDA) backed by FAO-56 and USDA standards. Every score is fully auditable.
  • The "Rotation Ring" Abstraction: Multi-year crop sequences are complex. Visualizing them as an annual circular clock allows growers to immediately spot bare-soil gaps and water demand peaks at a glance.
  • 100% Client-Side Architecture: The entire scoring engine runs locally in compiled TypeScript within the user's browser. It requires zero server infrastructure, eliminates server latency (<5 ms<5\text{ ms}<5 ms response), protects farmer privacy, and works reliably in low-bandwidth rural settings.

4. What tools, coding languages, and software did you use?

  • Frontend & Visualization: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, MapLibre GL JS (satellite map rendering), Recharts (climate time-series), and Canvas API (custom Rotation Ring rendering).
  • Data Harmonization & Pipeline: Python 3.12, GDAL/Rasterio, Shapely, NumPy, Pandas, and Parquet.
  • Quality Assurance & Verification: Automated Pytest suite with 49 tests. This includes a strict parity testing engine (test_parity.py) that runs both the Python reference model and the browser’s TypeScript engine on identical fields, verifying that scores match to 3 decimal places and output text matches word-for-word.

projectDetails.name: CHRONO EARTH
projectDetails.summary: What can satellites reveal about a changing lagoon—and where does the evidence stop? CHRONO EARTH turns real Earth observations into a time journey through Chilika Lagoon, Odisha. Its Time Stone opens REWIND, where visitors explore 25 Sentinel-1 radar and 25 Landsat optical observations from 2015–2026; WITNESS, which presents a real NISAR radar pass from November 6, 2026; and EXPLORE, which compares actual dry-season and monsoon-season observations. Because the historical record is sparse and lacks independent, date-matched ground truth, CHRONO EARTH does not claim to forecast future conditions. Instead, it makes satellite evidence easier to explore and helps researchers, educators, and wetland managers ask better questions about seasonal change.
projectDetails.details:
CHRONO EARTH turns satellite observations of Chilika Lagoon into an interactive journey through time. The Time Stone opens three experiences: REWIND compares 25 Sentinel-1 radar and 25 Landsat optical observations from 2015–2026; WITNESS presents a real NISAR L-band observation from November 6, 2026; and EXPLORE compares actual dry-season and monsoon-season observations as historical what-if scenarios.

The project displays radar backscatter and Landsat NDVI, NDWI, and MNDWI as distinct measurements. It makes coverage, data quality, and uncertainty visible: candidate water indicators are unvalidated, NDVI is not a vegetation classification, and sparse observations without independent ground truth are not enough to forecast future conditions. The app does not claim measured community impacts.

Our creative approach uses the Time Stone to make a complex satellite archive easier to explore. We built the frontend with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, and the analysis pipeline with Python and geospatial libraries including Rasterio, Shapely, NumPy, and SciPy. We considered seasonal gaps, cloud and quality masks, spatial coverage, differences between radar and optical sensors, and the limits of validation. CHRONO EARTH is designed as a clear starting point for researchers, educators, and wetland managers to ask better questions about seasonal change.

projectDetails.name: BASELINE
projectDetails.summary:
We developed BASELINE, a web app that helps astronauts answer one question about their health readings: "Is this space, or is this me?"

In space, normal moves: resting core temperature rises about 1 °C over the first ~75 days (Stahn et al. 2017), so Earth limits and pre-launch values alone give wrong answers.

BASELINE compares each daily reading (core temperature, resting heart rate, sleep and mood) with what is normal for this astronaut on this mission day. It gives one of four plain statuses (Normal for you, Keep an eye on it, Tell your medical officer, No data), explains why, shows how sure it is, and drafts an SBAR note for the crew medical officer.

What makes it different: it combines a research-based expected change with the size learned from the astronaut's own data, instead of only following recent readings. When adaptation and a real problem look the same, it says "can't tell" rather than "normal". And we tested it openly: on a slow unexplained drift, a "last 14 days" baseline caught 0 of 9 problem days; BASELINE caught 9 of 9.

All data is simulated; it is a decision-support prototype, not a medical device.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

BASELINE is a web app that helps an astronaut on a long mission understand their own health readings: "Is this space, or is this me?" In space the body changes — resting core temperature rises about 1 °C over the first ~75 days (Stahn et al. 2017, 11 ISS astronauts) — so Earth limits miss changes that are large for one person, and comparing only with pre-launch values raises weeks of false alarms.

For four daily measures (core temperature, resting heart rate, sleep, mood), BASELINE asks five questions in order:

1. Is there a usable reading?

2. Is it different from her normal before launch?

3. Is it still different after the expected space change?

4. Has it lasted more than one day (2 of the last 3 days)?

5. Is it past a general Earth medical limit (shown for context)?

The answer is one of four plain statuses — Normal for you, Keep an eye on it, Tell your medical officer, No data — with a confidence level (High / Medium / Low, always with the reason) and a "Why this result?" explanation. When readings stay unusual, BASELINE drafts an SBAR note (Situation, Background, Assessment, Request) for the crew medical officer, which the astronaut reviews, edits, copies or downloads.

The app has four screens: Today (overall status, four measure cards, what needs attention, data quality, daily check-in), Over time (a chart of the whole mission), Note to doctor, and Science & sources. A 2-minute guided demo walks through the key moments.

BENEFITS

- Fewer false alarms on changes that are expected in space.

- Catches changes that are unusual for this person even when they stay below Earth limits.

- Missing data is never shown as normal; confidence drops when readings are missing.

- A ready, structured handoff for the crew medical officer instead of raw numbers.

INTENDED IMPACT

On long missions to the Moon and Mars, communication delays mean crews must interpret their own data on board. BASELINE is a decision-support prototype for that situation: it helps the crew notice what matters, explains why, and supports — never replaces — the crew medical officer.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE (WHAT IS DIFFERENT)

- It combines a research-based expected change with the size learned from the astronaut's own in-flight data, instead of only following recent readings. Example: the same 37.6 °C reading is "Keep an eye on it" on day 4 but "Normal for you" on day 90.

- A "can't tell" safeguard: when normal adaptation and a real problem look the same, it says so instead of calling the reading normal.

- We tested it against other methods and show the results, including weak spots. The same engine runs on 8 simulated astronauts who adapt more, less, faster or not at all, or drift slowly. On a slow unexplained drift, a "last 14 days" baseline caught 0 of 9 problem days and BASELINE caught 9 of 9. Our first version missed a slow drift in 15 of 20 simulated runs; after adding the safeguard it missed 0 of 20. Fast or strong adapters still get extra alerts, and the app shows this openly.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

React 19 and TypeScript, built with Vite; charts with Recharts; 132 automated tests with Vitest; hosted on Vercel; source code on GitHub (https://github.com/sridharan-71/baseline-space-health). It runs entirely in the browser — no backend, no database, no hardware. Daily check-ins are saved only in the browser. The scientific engine is kept separate from the user interface, and all research numbers live in one place in the code.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Scientific honesty: every rule is labelled Research, Clinical reference or Design assumption. Only core temperature has a research-based space model; heart rate, sleep and mood are compared with the astronaut's own history, and the app says so.

- No combined health score: each measure is judged on its own, so one warning can never be averaged away.

- Safety: BASELINE never diagnoses, never suggests medicine and never replaces the crew medical officer.

- Limits we state openly: all data is simulated (fictional astronaut Cmdr. Asha Rao); thresholds are prototype choices, not clinically validated; the temperature model comes from a small study.

- Clarity: plain-language statuses, icons and words as well as colour, and a layout that works on desktop and phone.

USE OF AI

Code, documentation and slide text were written with Anthropic's Claude (an AI assistant) under our team's direction. We chose the idea, scope, scientific sources and rules, and reviewed and tested the result. Screenshots are of our own app.

projectDetails.name: NISAR Earth Pulse
projectDetails.summary:
NISAR Earth Pulse is an interactive web map that turns radar data from the new NASA–ISRO NISAR satellite into surface-change maps that anyone can read. Floods, fires and other disasters often hit when clouds, smoke or darkness block optical satellites, so responders lose sight of the ground just when they need it most. NISAR’s L-band radar sees through cloud and rain, works day and night, and revisits every location every 12 days. Its data is free, but reading it usually takes specialist SAR software and training.

We built a Python pipeline that downloads NISAR Level-2 GCOV products from NASA’s ASF DAAC, calibrates and filters them, and detects change between passes. It then measures the changed area in km² and publishes the results to a lightweight browser app. Users can swipe between before and after images, switch between HH, HV and RGB radar views, and play a 12-day timeline with a chart of flooded area. Plain-language notes explain what the radar signal means. Disaster teams, farmers, insurers, city planners and students can all use NISAR’s view of a changing Earth without being radar experts.
projectDetails.details:
What it does
NISAR Earth Pulse is an interactive web map that shows how Earth’s surface changes over time, using radar data from the NASA–ISRO NISAR satellite. A user picks a study area and an event, such as a monsoon flood, and compares NISAR passes taken 12 days apart. The app shows what changed, how much area was affected in km², and why the radar signal looks the way it does.

How it works

  1. Data: We download NISAR L-band Level-2 GCOV (geocoded backscatter) products from NASA’s ASF DAAC.
  2. Processing: A Python pipeline converts the backscatter to decibels, applies a speckle filter and clips the data to the study area.
  3. Change detection: We compare before and after passes using the dB difference and a water threshold. Calm floodwater reflects the radar pulse away from the satellite, so flooded land turns dark in HH. Flooded trees and buildings cause double-bounce scattering, so they look brighter.
  4. Measurement: For each pass, we calculate the changed or flooded area in km² to build a time series.
  5. Web app: The results are exported as map layers and shown on a lightweight static HTML/JavaScript site that needs no server.

Features

  • A before/after swipe slider to compare any two dates
  • HH, HV and RGB polarization views to tell apart water, vegetation and urban areas
  • A 12-day timeline with playback and a chart of flooded area over time
  • Optional context layers: Sentinel-2 optical imagery, ESA WorldCover land cover and population density
  • A plain-language “What is happening here?” panel that explains the radar signal and likely causes
  • GeoTIFF download and shareable views

Benefits and impact
Optical satellites are blind under cloud, smoke and darkness, which is exactly when floods, fires and storms are at their worst. NISAR’s L-band radar works day and night, through cloud and rain, and partly through vegetation. Its data is free, but using it normally takes SAR expertise. Our app removes that barrier so these groups can use it:

  • Disaster response teams can see flooded areas on every pass, even under cloud.
  • Farmers and insurers can check crop-field flooding.
  • City planners can spot areas that flood every monsoon.
  • Students and the public can learn how radar sees Earth by exploring real NASA data.

Tools and technologies

  • Languages: Python for data processing; HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the web app
  • Environment: Google Colab
  • Python libraries: [e.g., NumPy, rasterio/GDAL, h5py, matplotlib]
  • Mapping: [e.g., Leaflet / MapLibre]
  • Data: NISAR GCOV (ASF DAAC), Sentinel-2, ESA WorldCover, [population dataset, e.g., WorldPop]
  • Hosting: [e.g., GitHub Pages]
  • Hardware: no special hardware; it runs entirely in the cloud and the browser

What makes it creative
Most SAR tools are built for specialists and show raw images. We turned radar physics into a visual story: you can swipe through time, switch polarizations to see different surface types, and read a plain-language explanation next to the map. Combining radar with optical, land-cover and population layers shows both what changed and who was affected.

What our team considered

  • Accessibility: a clear interface, simple language and a static site that loads quickly on low bandwidth
  • Scientific accuracy: we used analysis-ready GCOV products and checked water detection against Sentinel-2 on clear days
  • Scalability: the pipeline works for any study area and can rerun on each new NISAR pass
  • Limitations: speckle noise, wind-roughened water, and steep terrain that can create radar shadow
  • Future work: automatic updates on every new pass, InSAR ground motion for subsidence and landslides, and flood alerts for nearby communities

projectDetails.name: FIRETRACE – Satellite-Based Global Fire Intelligence Platform
projectDetails.summary:
FIRETRACE is a satellite-based fire intelligence platform designed to analyze, visualize, and understand wildfire activity across the globe using historical and near-real-time satellite observations. It integrates fire detection data from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS instruments, including Terra, Aqua, Suomi-NPP, and NOAA-20 satellites.

The platform processes millions of historical fire observations to identify spatial and temporal patterns, compare detections across satellite sensors, and explore changes in fire activity over time. It provides an interactive 3D globe, geographic fire visualization, sensor-based filtering, historical timelines, and analytical summaries to help users investigate fire hotspots and understand their distribution.

FIRETRACE also explores cross-sensor observation matching using spatial and temporal proximity, alongside historical analysis and fire radiative power comparisons. Its goal is to improve the interpretation and consistency of satellite-derived fire observations while communicating uncertainty and data-quality limitations.

By combining satellite datasets, geospatial visualization, and analytical techniques, FIRETRACE aims to transform complex fire observation data into an accessible intelligence platform that can support researchers, environmental analysts, disaster management teams, and policymakers in understanding wildfire patterns and strengthening fire-monitoring capabilities.
projectDetails.details:
FIRETRACE – Project Description

FIRETRACE is a satellite-based global fire intelligence platform that transforms large-scale satellite fire observations into meaningful, interactive information for understanding wildfire activity. It uses NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite datasets from Terra, Aqua, Suomi-NPP, and NOAA-20 to explore fire locations, historical trends, and differences between satellite observations.

What does it do and how does it work?

FIRETRACE collects and processes satellite fire observation datasets containing information such as latitude, longitude, acquisition date and time, fire radiative power (FRP), and sensor details. It standardizes and analyzes these observations to identify spatial and temporal patterns.

Users can explore fire observations through an interactive 3D globe, filter data by satellite sensor, examine historical fire activity, and view analytical summaries. The project also investigates cross-sensor matching using spatial and temporal proximity to understand when different satellites detect potentially related fire activity.

What are its benefits?

  • Makes large and complex satellite datasets easier to explore.
  • Provides a global view of fire observation patterns.
  • Helps compare observations from multiple satellite instruments.
  • Supports historical fire analysis and identification of potential hotspots.
  • Improves understanding of satellite detection differences and data limitations.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to make satellite-derived fire information more accessible and useful for researchers, environmental scientists, disaster management teams, and policymakers. FIRETRACE aims to support better wildfire monitoring, historical analysis, and evidence-based environmental decision-making. It is designed as an analytical support platform, not a replacement for official emergency alerts or ground-based verification.

What technologies did we use?

  • Programming languages: Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, SQL, HTML, and CSS.
  • Frontend: React, Vite, MapLibre GL, CesiumJS, and Recharts.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Pandas, NumPy, GeoPandas, and Scikit-learn.
  • Data sources: NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS satellite fire observation datasets.
  • Development tools: Visual Studio Code, Git, GitHub, and npm.

How is the project creative?

FIRETRACE combines satellite observation analysis with an interactive 3D Earth visualization. Instead of presenting fire data only through static maps or spreadsheets, it allows users to explore observations geographically and historically. Its multi-satellite approach also investigates how different sensors observe fire activity and where their detections may overlap.

What factors did our team consider?

Our team considered data accuracy, satellite sensor differences, geographical coverage, observation timestamps, processing performance, scalability, usability, and scientific reliability. We also considered uncertainty: nearby detections are treated as potential matches rather than confirmed individual fires. The platform is designed to preserve data quality and communicate the limitations of satellite observations while remaining expandable for future analytical capabilities.

projectDetails.summary:
**FIELD SHIFT – Grow Smarter, Farm Better**

FIELD SHIFT is a smart agriculture web application developed to help farmers make more informed farming decisions using geospatial technology and environmental data. The platform allows users to create a farmer profile, locate their farms, mark farm boundaries on an interactive map, and select crops based on agricultural categories.

It integrates NASA POWER API to retrieve environmental information, including temperature, rainfall, relative humidity, and wind speed. This information is processed and presented through interactive charts, environmental indicators, and a farming condition dashboard. The platform also aims to provide smart recommendations and voice-based agricultural assistance.

FIELD SHIFT addresses the challenge of making environmental information more accessible and understandable for farmers. By combining farm mapping and NASA Earth observation data in one platform, it helps users explore local environmental conditions and supports data-informed agricultural planning.

The project is important because it demonstrates how accessible digital technologies and Earth observation data can contribute to smarter, more informed, and sustainable agricultural practices.
projectDetails.details:
FIELD SHIFT – Smart Agriculture Platform

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

FIELD SHIFT is a smart agriculture web application designed to help farmers understand their farm information and environmental conditions through a single platform.

The application allows users to enter their farming details, identify their farm location, visualise farm boundaries on an interactive map, and select crops. It integrates NASA POWER environmental data to analyse important parameters such as temperature, precipitation, relative humidity, and wind speed.

The collected data is processed and presented through interactive dashboards, charts, farming condition indicators, and smart recommendations. A Voice Agri-Advisor feature is also designed to make agricultural information easier to access.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Provides a centralised platform for farm information.
  • Helps users visualise farm boundaries using interactive maps.
  • Displays environmental information obtained through NASA POWER.
  • Presents complex environmental data through understandable charts and indicators.
  • Supports better-informed agricultural planning.
  • Provides an accessible interface for users interested in smart farming.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The main objective of FIELD SHIFT is to encourage data-informed agriculture by making environmental information easier to understand and use.

It aims to improve farmers' awareness of environmental conditions, support agricultural planning, encourage the adoption of digital farming technologies, and contribute to more informed and sustainable farming practices.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

Programming Language:

  • Python

Framework:

  • Streamlit

Libraries and Technologies:

  • Folium – Interactive farm mapping.
  • Streamlit-Folium – Map integration.
  • Pandas – Data processing.
  • Requests – API communication.
  • Geopy – Location identification and geocoding.
  • NASA POWER API – Environmental data collection.

Development Environment:

  • Python IDE / Visual Studio Code.
  • Web browser for application testing.

The current prototype is software-based and does not require dedicated hardware.

5. How is the project creative?

FIELD SHIFT combines farm mapping, crop selection, environmental data analysis, and farming insights within a single web application.

Instead of presenting environmental information as raw numerical data, it transforms the information into visual dashboards and easy-to-understand indicators. Integrating NASA POWER data with interactive farm mapping creates a useful connection between geographical information and environmental observations.

The platform is designed with a simple interface to make smart agriculture concepts more accessible.

6. What factors did the team consider?

The project considered:

  • Ease of use and simple navigation.
  • Accessibility of agricultural information.
  • Reliability and availability of environmental data.
  • Integration of geographical and environmental information.
  • Clear visualisation of complex data.
  • Scalability and future hardware integration.
  • Practical usefulness for agricultural planning.

Conclusion:

FIELD SHIFT demonstrates how web technologies, geospatial tools, and NASA environmental data can be combined to support smarter and more informed agriculture. It aims to bridge the gap between environmental data and practical agricultural understanding.

projectDetails.name: Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Earth Data
projectDetails.summary: Climate variability and shifting monsoons threaten smallholder agricultural productivity across South Asia. In coastal and riverine farming regions, farmers struggle to decide what to plant across three annual seasons as rainfall arrives late, dry spells intensify, and soil salinity creeps inland. Field Shift translates raw NASA Earth observations (NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, SMAP L4, MODIS 250m NDVI, and MERRA-2) into ranked, explainable 3-season crop rotation strategies on a single screen. Combining machine-learning monsoon onset forecasting, multimodal Gemini 2.0 Flash plant disease diagnostics, Turf.js geodesic field area computation, and live 7-day weather alerts, Field Shift empowers farmers to adapt their agricultural calendars with confidence in their native languages (English, Bengali, and Tamil). Every recommendation shows the exact satellite data points, environmental penalties, and positive agronomic benefits behind its score. Built with Next.js 16 and open-source science.
projectDetails.details: What does it do or how does it work? Field Shift is an explainable decision-support platform for smallholder farmers facing shifting monsoon patterns, coastal soil salinity, and climate volatility. It ingests historical satellite climate feeds (NASA POWER, GPM IMERG, SMAP, MODIS, MERRA-2) to evaluate and rank thousands of 3-season crop rotation strategies for local fields. The platform features an offline-first rotation engine, a backtested machine-learning monsoon onset predictor, a multimodal Gemini 2.0 Flash plant disease diagnostic scanner (/disease), a Turf.js geodesic field area calculator (/locate), and 7-day micro-weather alerts. Every recommendation provides transparent SHAP-style factor contributions, penalty breakdowns, and SMS-ready advisory text. What benefits does it have and intended impact? 1. Reduces Climate Vulnerability: Shifts crop sowing calendars to synchronize with actual usable rainfall rather than outdated historical calendars. 2. Prevents Soil Degradation: Recommends nitrogen-fixing legumes and green manures to replenish organic matter and break pest/pathogen cycles. 3. Language & Digital Equity: Fully localized in English, Bengali (বাংলা), and Tamil (தமிழ்), with Web Speech voice priority controls and offline PWA capability to ensure zero barrier for rural smallholders. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use? - Framework & Web: Next.js 16.3.6 App Router, React 19, TypeScript 5, Tailwind CSS v4, View Transitions API. - AI & ML: Google Gemini 2.0 Flash Multimodal Vision API, Chrome 127+ On-Device Gemini Nano (window.ai), Scikit-learn conformal prediction for monsoon onset. - Geospatial & Climate: Turf.js GIS engine, Open-Meteo 7-day weather API, NASA POWER point APIs, GPM IMERG precipitation grids. - Testing & Deployment: Vitest (701 passing tests), GitHub, Vercel edge deployment. How is your project creative? Rather than treating agricultural advice as a black-box prediction, Field Shift makes every recommendation mathematically transparent. Farmers see the exact penalty points deducted for drought or salinity risks and positive bonuses awarded for early monsoon onset or soil recovery. Its multimodal Crop Doctor combines satellite planning with field-level plant pathology, enabling farmers to break pathogen cycles through crop rotation. Major System Upgrades & Decision-Support Features: 1. Adaptation Margin Stress-Testing: Quantifies safe late-monsoon onset buffer (+15 to +25 days) and soil salinity buffer (dS/m) before rotation turnaround failure or yield loss. 2. Sustainability ROI & Resource Scorecard: Real-time calculation of conserved groundwater (+1,950 m³/ha), diesel pumping fuel saved (~24 L / BDT 2,500/ha), biological nitrogen fixation (+42 kg N/ha via legume nodulation), and soil organic carbon sequestration (+0.35 t CO₂e/ha/yr). 3. Trilingual Audio Advisory (Text-to-Speech): Web Speech Synthesis audio readout in Tamil (தமிழ்), Bengali (বাংলা), and English for illiterate and low-vision smallholder farmers. 4. NASA GIBS Live Satellite Observation Viewer (/satellite): Real-time embedding of NASA Terra/Aqua MODIS 250m True Color, VIIRS 375m, and SMAP L4 root-zone soil moisture over regional fields.

projectDetails.name: NISAR EARTHWATCH
projectDetails.summary:
Dancing with the SARs – NISAR EarthWatch is an interactive web-based platform developed using NASA-ISRO's NISAR satellite mission. Its main objective is to make satellite radar observations accessible and understandable through an interactive 3D globe, before-and-after SAR image comparison, and multilingual voice assistance.

The platform uses NASA's L-band and ISRO's S-band radar technologies to monitor environmental changes in different regions. It focuses on four major locations: Brahmaputra for flood monitoring, Coimbatore for agricultural observation, Ridgecrest for earthquake-related ground movements, and Everglades for wetland ecosystem monitoring.

Its key features include smart location search, satellite orbital visualization, multi-temporal SAR comparison, backscatter analysis, and surface displacement monitoring. The multilingual voice assistant supports Tamil, Malayalam, Telugu, Hindi, and English, helping users understand complex satellite information through simple audio explanations.

This project aims to support farmers, researchers, disaster management teams, and local communities by transforming advanced satellite data into meaningful environmental insights. Our vision is to democratize space technology and make Earth observation accessible to everyone.
projectDetails.details:
Dancing with the SARs – NISAR EarthWatch is an interactive web-based platform designed to make satellite radar observations easier to understand and accessible to everyone. Our project is based on NASA and ISRO's NISAR mission, which uses L-band and S-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) technology to monitor changes on Earth's surface.

The platform features an interactive 3D Earth globe with smart location search, allowing users to explore important geographical regions. It focuses on four major monitoring locations: Brahmaputra for flood detection, Coimbatore for agricultural monitoring, Ridgecrest for earthquake-related ground movements, and Everglades for wetland ecosystem observation.

One of our major features is the Before-and-After SAR Image Comparison, which helps users identify environmental changes between different observation dates. It also includes backscatter difference analysis, coherence changes, and surface displacement monitoring to demonstrate how radar observations can reveal changes on Earth even under cloudy conditions or at night.

Another innovative feature is our multilingual voice assistant, supporting Tamil, Malayalam, Telugu, Hindi, and English. Users can navigate locations through voice commands and receive simplified audio explanations of complex satellite observations. This makes scientific information more accessible to local communities, farmers, researchers, and disaster management teams.

Our project's creativity lies in combining dual-band SAR technology, interactive 3D visualization, multi-temporal comparison, and multilingual voice intelligence into a single platform. We considered accessibility, usability, geographical diversity, environmental applications, and the importance of communicating scientific information in regional languages.

The project is developed as a web-based application and deployed on Netlify. Its intended impact is to bridge the gap between advanced space technology and everyday users by transforming satellite observations into understandable environmental insights. Our ultimate goal is to democratize Earth observation and support better environmental awareness, research, and disaster preparedness.

projectDetails.name: ASTRO MISSION
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRO MISSION is an Artificial Intelligence (AI) simulator for astronaut training for kids aged 7-12 to make real space science fun for them. It turns space exploration into an interactive survival game, in which players are responsible for a settlement on the Moon or Mars, the health of the astronauts, oxygen, water, food and energy, as well as for responding to emergency situations like solar radiation storms, equipment failures or resource shortages.

It combines NASA data sources (DONKI, OSDR, BVAD, Mars RAD, and lunar terrain datasets), machine learning models, and a NASA-focused AI Mission Commander. Children learn about the actual functioning of space missions through interactive gameplay, 3D visualization of planets, predictions on resources, classification of the terrain, and educational quizzes.

One key innovation is transparent data provenance of distinguishing NASA observations, engineering baselines, synthetic calibrated data, and ML predictions. ASTRO MISSION makes science understandable, fostering the next generation of astronauts, engineers and scientists.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRO MISSION: AI-Powered Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

1. Introduction

ASTRO MISSION is an interactive astronaut training and space survival simulator designed for children aged 7–12. The project transforms complex space science into an engaging, hands-on learning experience.

Players take responsibility for managing a human settlement on the Moon (Shackleton Crater) or Mars (Jezero Crater). They must make decisions about limited resources, astronaut health, life-support systems, and unexpected emergencies.

Unlike traditional educational platforms that focus primarily on memorizing scientific facts, ASTRO MISSION teaches through practical decision-making. Every action has consequences, helping children understand the challenges of real human space exploration.

2. How the Application Works

The application provides several interactive modules:

Mission Control

  • Monitor the status of the space settlement.
  • Track oxygen, water, food, and energy supplies.
  • Monitor astronaut health and environmental conditions.
  • Advance through mission sols and observe resource consumption.

Base Builder

  • Construct and manage seven infrastructure modules.
  • Build greenhouses, power plants, laboratories, medical bays, storage facilities, communication systems, and living quarters.
  • Understand how infrastructure affects survival.

Radiation Predictor

  • Estimate radiation exposure and risk levels.
  • Use NASA Mars Radiation Assessment Detector data for scientific calibration.
  • Present radiation risk information through an interactive interface.

Resource Predictor

  • Estimate oxygen, water, food, and power requirements.
  • Incorporate NASA BVAD engineering baselines.
  • Compare model predictions with baseline calculations.

Terrain Classifier

  • Explore lunar surface terrain.
  • Classify crater-related terrain categories.
  • Incorporate a CNN trained using NASA JPL LROCNet imagery.

AI Mission Commander

  • Ask questions about space exploration, astronaut safety, and mission operations.
  • Retrieve relevant information from NASA technical documents using TF-IDF-based Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG).
  • Provide educational explanations and NASA references.

Science Center

  • Explore NASA datasets and scientific resources.
  • Understand the origin of observations, engineering baselines, and predictions.
  • Learn how scientific data supports space exploration.

Space Academy and Quiz

  • Access seven educational lessons.
  • Complete interactive quizzes.
  • Learn about radiation, life-support systems, planetary environments, and astronaut survival.

3. Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning

ASTRO MISSION incorporates four AI/ML components:

  1. Radiation Risk Forecaster:
    Random Forest and Gradient Boosting models designed to estimate radiation exposure and risk levels.
  2. AI Mission Commander:
    A local TF-IDF-based RAG system that retrieves information from NASA knowledge documents and generates educational responses using templates.
  3. Resource Consumption Predictor:
    Four independent Random Forest regression models designed to estimate oxygen, water, food, and power requirements using NASA BVAD-calibrated scenarios.
  4. Lunar Terrain Classifier:
    A MobileNetV2 convolutional neural network trained using real NASA JPL LROCNet images, supported by morphological terrain classification.

The models were developed and evaluated during the project. However, some trained model artifacts are not currently loading in the production deployment, and the frontend uses fallback mechanisms for affected features.

4. NASA Data Integration

The project incorporates six NASA-related scientific data resources:

  • DONKI: Space weather events, solar flares, coronal mass ejections, and solar energetic particle events.
  • OSDR: Space biology and astronaut health research.
  • BVAD: Engineering baselines for human life-support requirements.
  • Mars RAD: Radiation measurements collected by the Curiosity rover.
  • LROCNet: Lunar surface imagery used for terrain classification.
  • RadLab: Radiation and dosimetry reference information.

These resources help connect gameplay mechanics with real scientific information.

5. Key Innovation: Transparent Data Provenance

One of the main innovations is the four-category data provenance system.

  • NASA_OBSERVATION: Information obtained from NASA observations and datasets.
  • NASA_ENGINEERING_BASELINE: Values derived from NASA engineering references.
  • SYNTHETIC_CALIBRATED: Synthetic training data calibrated using NASA scientific references.
  • ML_PREDICTION: Results generated by machine learning models.

This approach teaches children not only scientific concepts but also how to understand the origin and reliability of information.

6. Benefits and Intended Impact

For Children:

  • Develop critical thinking and decision-making skills.
  • Understand the relationship between life-support resources.
  • Learn about radiation and planetary environments.
  • Explore scientific concepts through interactive gameplay.
  • Develop an interest in STEM education.

For Educators:

  • Provide an interactive space science learning platform.
  • Introduce engineering concepts through practical scenarios.
  • Encourage problem-solving and systems thinking.
  • Support learning through quizzes and educational modules.

Intended Impact:

ASTRO MISSION aims to inspire the next generation of astronauts, engineers, scientists, and space researchers by making authentic space science accessible to younger learners.

It demonstrates that human space exploration requires scientific knowledge, engineering, resource management, teamwork, and responsible decision-making.

7. Technologies and Tools Used

Programming Languages:

  • Python 3.11
  • JavaScript ES6+
  • SQL

Frontend:

  • React 18
  • Vite
  • Tailwind CSS
  • Framer Motion
  • Three.js
  • Recharts

Backend:

  • Python FastAPI
  • SQLAlchemy
  • Pydantic
  • Uvicorn

AI and Machine Learning:

  • Scikit-learn
  • TensorFlow
  • NumPy
  • Pandas
  • TF-IDF Vectorization
  • Random Forest
  • Gradient Boosting
  • MobileNetV2 CNN

Database:

  • SQLite
  • PostgreSQL-compatible architecture

Deployment:

  • AWS CloudFront
  • AWS EC2
  • Caddy Reverse Proxy

Testing:

  • Playwright
  • Pytest
  • Automated ML testing

8. Creativity and Innovation

ASTRO MISSION combines interactive gaming, NASA scientific resources, machine learning, and educational storytelling into one platform.

Its major creative elements include:

  • Interactive Moon and Mars settlement management.
  • Three-dimensional planetary visualization using Three.js.
  • Realistic resource management and survival scenarios.
  • AI-powered NASA knowledge retrieval.
  • Machine learning-based scientific prediction components.
  • Transparent scientific data provenance.
  • Emergency scenarios involving radiation storms, oxygen leaks, water recycling failures, and power outages.

The platform encourages children to experience the complexity of space exploration rather than simply read about it.

9. Factors Considered During Development

Scientific Accuracy:
NASA scientific datasets and engineering references were considered when designing resource management and radiation-related calculations.

Age-Appropriate Design:
The interface uses visual indicators, accessible controls, interactive gameplay, and educational explanations suitable for children aged 7–12.

Accessibility:
The application is browser-based and responsive across mobile, tablet, and desktop devices.

Educational Value:
The project focuses on practical understanding, critical thinking, systems engineering, and scientific literacy.

Performance:
Frontend fallback mechanisms allow several educational and gameplay features to remain usable when backend services are unavailable.

10. Conclusion

ASTRO MISSION bridges the gap between classroom science and real-world space exploration.

By combining NASA data, interactive simulations, AI-assisted learning, and resource management challenges, the project creates an engaging environment where children can experience the responsibilities of managing a human settlement beyond Earth.

Our vision is to make the next generation curious about space, confident in science, and prepared to solve the engineering challenges of future lunar and Martian exploration.

projectDetails.name: COSMIC LEGACY
projectDetails.summary:
COSMIC LEGACY – Every Machine Has a Story. Every Discovery Leaves a Legacy.

COSMIC LEGACY is an interactive, browser-based 3D storytelling and learning platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Inspired by the challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars,”the project brings the history of space exploration equipment to life using information and resources from NASA's published mission records and official materials.

Through an immersive 3D solar system, users can explore 13 artifact entries across three categories: Moon and Mars. Each discovery presents mission histories, equipment details, scientific contributions, and historical facts based on NASA resources. The platform combines interactive 3D exploration, voice narration, quizzes, mini-games, and an AI-assisted mission information experience.

Built using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Three.js, COSMIC LEGACY transforms authentic space exploration information into an engaging and accessible digital learning experience.
projectDetails.details:
Here is a comprehensive breakdown of Cosmic Legacy by Team TechTitanz for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing each of your questions based on the presentation:

1. What does it do and how does it work?

Cosmic Legacy is a browser-based interactive 3D platform that tells the stories of NASA's discarded and inactive spacecraft, rovers, and equipment left behind on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space.

Users follow a five-step interactive workflow:

  1. Interactive 3D Solar System: Explore planetary models in a 3D environment.
  2. Artifact Selection: Browse 13 artifact entries categorized across three exploration zones (such as the Moon, Mars, and deep space).
  3. Mission Info & 3D Inspection: Inspect detailed spacecraft models with interactive camera controls. Users can toggle an Exploded View (using a separation slider and leader lines to inspect individual hardware parts like gold foil, plaques, and retroreflectors), switch to a First-Person perspective, check simulated or live Space Weather and Mission Ops telemetry, and query the built-in Mission AI assistant about mission histories and statuses.
  4. Narration & Quizzes: Listen to mission stories via an integrated voice narration engine and play interactive quizzes and mini-games.
  5. Points & Certificate: Track progress locally to earn points, badges, and a completion certificate.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Zero-Barrier Accessibility: Because it runs directly in a web browser without requiring specialized software or high-end installations, students anywhere can explore space artifacts easily.
  • Active Hands-On Learning: Instead of reading static text archives, learners visually dissect spacecraft components, test their knowledge through mini-games, and ask questions directly to Mission AI.
  • Multi-Sensory Engagement: Combining 3D visual exploration, text-to-speech audio narration, and gamified rewards accommodates different learning styles.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The project aims to transform the overlooked remnants of space missions from forgotten hardware into an unforgettable educational journey. Specifically, it intends to:

  • Democratize access to authentic NASA mission histories and landing coordinates for students worldwide.
  • Spark curiosity and encourage self-directed exploration of space engineering.
  • Inspire the next generation of space explorers by preserving the legacy of humanity's milestones beyond Earth.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

  • Languages: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript.
  • 3D Graphics & Rendering: Three.js for browser-based 3D rendering, planetary scenes, exploded-view assembly mechanics, and interactive camera controls.
  • Browser APIs & Engines: HTML5 Canvas for interactive mini-games, the Web Speech / browser text-to-speech engine for voice narration, and browser local storage for progress tracking.
  • Data Architecture: A structured spacecraft and mission database powering the 13 artifact profiles, telemetry displays, and Mission AI responses.
  • Hardware: Standard consumer computers/browsers capable of WebGL rendering (no specialized VR or external hardware required for end users).

5. How is your project creative?

  • Reframing "Space Junk" as Storytelling: Rather than focusing only on active launches, the project humanizes abandoned hardware—treating silent rovers, lunar modules, and probes as historical monuments with personal stories.
  • Interactive Engineering Dissection: Including an adjustable Exploded View with component-by-component percentages and leader lines blends museum-style storytelling with CAD-like engineering inspection.
  • Simulated Mission Context: Integrating a Mission Ops dashboard with live/simulated space weather (solar wind speed, geomagnetic Kp index) and an interactive Mission AI makes users feel like active flight controllers rather than passive readers.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Accessibility & Performance: Building a lightweight browser-based stack (vanilla JS + Three.js) ensures smooth performance on standard student laptops without downloads.
  • Educational Engagement & Retention: To prevent information overload, the team balanced technical mission data with audio narration, interactive quizzes, mini-games, and a certificate reward system.
  • Historical & Technical Accuracy: Structuring authentic NASA mission details—such as exact landing coordinates, mission end dates, component breakdowns, and realistic space weather telemetry—ensures the platform serves as a credible educational resource.
  • User Experience (UX) & Navigation: Designing clear camera transitions (from solar system overview to first-person surface view and exploded hardware view) keeps complex 3D navigation intuitive for first-time users.

projectDetails.name: Project TERRAVEX
projectDetails.summary:
TERRAVEX is an interactive planetary analog exploration platform designed to help researchers and space enthusiasts identify and study Earth locations that resemble the environmental and geological conditions of the Moon and Mars. Our project combines geographic visualization, NASA datasets, and comparative analysis to explore potential Earth analog sites for future planetary exploration research.

The platform features an interactive 3D global visualization that allows users to explore selected locations, view their geographical characteristics, and understand their relevance to lunar and Martian environments. Our initial study focuses on three locations: the Qaidam Basin in China, Tenoumer Impact Crater in Mauritania, and the Tanezrouft region in the Algerian Sahara.

By presenting scientific information, location-based comparisons, and accessible visual insights in one platform, TERRAVEX aims to support the identification of potential planetary analog environments. This can help scientists, students, and researchers better understand planetary geology, evaluate exploration environments, and prepare for future lunar and Martian missions using Earth-based research locations.
projectDetails.details:
TERRAVEX – Exploring Earth's Potential as a Gateway to Moon and Mars

1. Introduction

TERRAVEX is an interactive planetary analog exploration platform developed to identify and study Earth locations that share geological and environmental characteristics with the Moon and Mars. Our project uses geographical visualization, NASA resources, and comparative analysis to connect Earth's landscapes with future planetary exploration.

2. NASA Data and Location Comparison

Our project explores NASA scientific resources and planetary information to understand the similarities between Earth's geological environments and the surfaces of the Moon and Mars. By examining geographical features, terrain characteristics, impact structures, and environmental conditions, we aim to identify promising Earth locations for planetary analog research.

3. Our Selected Earth Locations

We selected three geographically distinct locations for our investigation:

Qaidam Basin, China: An arid, high-altitude basin with distinctive geological and environmental characteristics that make it valuable for studying planetary analog environments.

Tenoumer Impact Crater, Mauritania: A remarkable impact structure that provides an opportunity to study crater morphology and geological features relevant to understanding impact processes on planetary surfaces.

Tanezrouft Region, Algerian Sahara: An extremely arid desert landscape with distinctive terrain characteristics, offering opportunities to investigate dry environments and surface processes relevant to Mars analog research.

4. Why We Selected These Locations

Our selection focuses on geological diversity, environmental conditions, terrain characteristics, and their potential scientific relevance to lunar and Martian exploration. Studying different landscapes helps researchers understand how planetary environments can be investigated and compared using Earth-based locations.

5. Special Focus: Tanezrouft Region, Algeria

The Tanezrouft region is an important focus of our project because of its extensive arid landscape and remote desert environment. Its geographical and geological characteristics offer opportunities for studying Mars-like surface conditions and developing Earth-based research approaches.

Using accessible Earth locations for preliminary research can help optimize scientific field studies, support mission preparation, and potentially reduce the cost of conducting early-stage planetary exploration research.

6. TERRAVEX Interactive Platform

TERRAVEX presents our research through an interactive global visualization. Users can explore the Earth, locate our three selected sites, and access information about their geographical characteristics and scientific relevance.

The platform connects location discovery, planetary comparisons, and scientific information in one accessible interface, making Earth–Moon–Mars analog research easier to understand.

7. Scientific Impact and Future Scope

TERRAVEX aims to support planetary science education, geological research, and future space exploration planning. By exploring Earth's diverse environments, our project highlights how terrestrial landscapes can contribute to understanding the Moon and Mars.

Our future vision includes expanding the location database, integrating additional satellite and terrain datasets, improving comparative visualization, and developing more detailed scientific analysis to support future lunar and Martian exploration missions.

projectDetails.name: Echoes Across the Void
projectDetails.summary: Echoes Across the Void is an interactive, scroll-driven story website for school-age kids and curious teens. It tells the stories of ten NASA machines left on the Moon and Mars, from Surveyor 3 and the Apollo rovers to Viking, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight and the Ingenuity helicopter. Each machine gets a chapter with real mission facts, a count-up stat showing how far it outlived its plan, and a short imagined “last words” line, labeled as imagined. It answers the “Abandoned but not Forgotten” challenge by turning dusty mission archives into something young people want to read, and shows that these machines still matter: they proved what is possible and showed where to go next. The site opens on a single title and reveals the story as you scroll, ending with a “ping the void” interaction.
projectDetails.details: Echoes Across the Void is a single-page website that works like a short film. It opens on the title alone, and the story arrives as you scroll: a prologue, then ten chapters (3 on the Moon, 7 on Mars), then a finale where visitors “ping” the Moon or Mars and see how long a reply really takes. Each chapter has an animated signal scope, a count-up stat, a planned-versus-actual lifespan bar, three facts and a typewriter “last words” line. Mission dates, lifespans and facts come from NASA mission archives. The goal is to make space history approachable for kids with no science background, and to show that the machines left behind still matter. We built it with HTML, CSS, JavaScript and canvas (starfield and scroll effects), with original line-art icons drawn in code. We chose a dark, cinematic, poetic style with big modern type so it feels like a story, not a fact sheet. It is mobile-friendly and has a reduced-motion mode. We used Claude (Anthropic) to help write code, draft story copy and draw the icons, and the site footer says so.

projectDetails.name: Project Tesseracted
projectDetails.summary:
The Problem: When Noise Masquerades as Trend
Detecting genuine environmental trends is difficult due to seasonal cycles, extreme weather, sensor drift, and autocorrelation. Traditional statistical tests can mistake natural variations for long-term climate changes, producing false alarms.

The Solution: TrendScope
TrendScope is a climate analysis platform using NASA POWER monthly data (MERRA-2 and CERES) from 2001–2024. It applies four statistical methods:

Seasonal Adjustment: Removes recurring monthly patterns.
Yue-Pilon TFPW: Corrects autocorrelation while preserving genuine trends.
Theil-Sen Estimator: Calculates robust trends with 95% confidence intervals.
Benjamini-Hochberg FDR: Controls false discoveries across spatial grids.

The statistical engine achieves 100% numerical parity with pymannkendall 1.4.3.

Key Features & Discoveries
Planetary Radar: Analyses five climate variables across Svalbard, Manaus, Chennai, and Jaipur.
Indian Grid Analysis: Examines 16 spatial cells, finding 11 significant warming cells (up to +0.31°C/decade) and five neutral or cooling cells (down to -0.29°C/decade).
No-Trend Detection: Shows Chennai's temperature trend is insignificant (p=0.2755) after autocorrelation correction.
Time-to-Significance: Estimates the observation period needed to detect genuine trends
Open Science: Supports NASA data analysis, CSV/PNG exports, shareable links, and offline access.

TrendScope makes climate trend detection more reliable, transparent, and accessible.
projectDetails.details:
GITHUB LINK: https://github.com/harishcjcoder/TrendScope
What it does and how it works
TrendScope is a free web tool that helps students and the public find out whether a change in Earth’s climate is real or just random variation. The user picks a NASA variable (air temperature, rainfall, humidity, root-zone soil wetness, or surface sunlight) and a location by typing coordinates or choosing a preset. The tool fetches 24 years (2001–2024) of monthly NASA POWER data, removes the seasonal cycle, and draws the time series with a trend line and 95% confidence band. It then answers four questions: What is changing? Where? How much (per decade)? Is it statistically significant? The trend is estimated with the Theil-Sen slope and tested with Mann-Kendall, using trend-free pre-whitening to correct for autocorrelation. We show both the naive and corrected p-values. A Trend Radar ranks the variables for a place. A 4×4 Trend Map of India shows where a variable rises or falls, with false-discovery-rate (Benjamini-Hochberg) correction. Case Files give four ready examples, and a Reliability score and a time-to-significance estimate show how much to trust a result.

Benefits
Users don’t need statistics knowledge. Results come with plain-language explanations, definitions, and honest “not significant” verdicts. The interface offers Simple and Scientist modes, English, Tamil and Hindi, dark mode, and CSV, PNG and share-link exports.

Intended impact
We want to build data literacy and show that trends must be tested before they are believed. This makes NASA Earth data easier to use in classrooms and for anyone curious about their local climate.

Tools and technologies
HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the front end and the statistics engine; Node.js scripts to build cached case data; a Netlify serverless function as a fallback proxy; Netlify for hosting. Data comes from the NASA POWER API (MERRA-2 and CERES-based products). We validated our statistics against Python’s pymannkendall. [Add any AI coding or design tools your team used.]

Creativity
We combine the “detective” idea with scientific rigour. The tool corrects for autocorrelation, controls false discoveries across the map, flags short or weak records, and estimates how much longer a record would need to become significant. It can also show opposite trends within the same region, which the challenge highlights.

Factors we considered
Accuracy, since we validated the engine and excluded fill values. Honesty about uncertainty and the fact that correlation is not causation. Reliability, since cached examples work if the API is slow. Accessibility, with colour-blind-safe colours, keyboard use, and multiple languages. Limits: monthly resolution, linear trends only, and model-derived data.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: AGRI SMART
projectDetails.summary:
AgriSmart is an intelligent agriculture assistance system designed to help farmers make better farming decisions through smart technology. Our project integrates an underground soil monitoring hardware system with a web-based application to provide real-time agricultural information.

The hardware uses soil sensors to collect important soil parameters such as soil moisture and temperature. The collected sensor data is transmitted to our AgriSmart website, where farmers can monitor soil conditions through an interactive dashboard.

The platform also provides weather information, rainfall updates, soil health analysis, and AI-based crop recommendations according to soil and environmental conditions. It helps farmers identify suitable crops, understand their land conditions, and make informed agricultural decisions.

To make the system accessible to everyone, AgriSmart includes multilingual support for English, Tamil, Hindi, Telugu, and Malayalam, along with voice assistance for farmers who may have difficulty using text-based applications.

By combining IoT, AI, and multilingual technology, AgriSmart aims to reduce uncertainty in farming, improve resource management, and support smarter, more sustainable agriculture.
projectDetails.details:
AgriSmart – Smart Farming for a Sustainable Future

AgriSmart is a farmer-focused smart agriculture platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the challenge "Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data."

The main objective of AgriSmart is to help farmers make informed decisions about soil health, crop selection, and changing environmental conditions using agricultural technology, data analysis, and NASA Earth observation resources.

Our proposed system combines three major components:

1. Soil Monitoring: A proposed low-cost underground IoT monitoring system using soil sensors and an ESP32 controller to collect parameters such as soil moisture, temperature, pH, and NPK nutrient levels. Sensor integration with the live application is part of our planned hardware development.

2. NASA Earth Observation Data: AgriSmart is designed to incorporate NASA resources such as POWER for climate information, SMAP for soil moisture observations, and GPM for precipitation data. These datasets can help farmers understand changing weather and environmental conditions affecting their fields.

3. Intelligent Farmer Assistance: Our web application provides soil health information, temperature and rainfall updates, and AI-based crop recommendations using available agricultural and environmental information. It aims to help farmers identify suitable crops and make better-informed farming decisions.

AgriSmart also includes a farmer-friendly dashboard, voice assistance, and multilingual support for English, Tamil, Hindi, Telugu, and Malayalam, making agricultural information more accessible to farmers from different regions.

Technology Used:

- Frontend: HTML, CSS, JavaScript

- Web application: Netlify hosting

- Proposed hardware: ESP32, soil monitoring sensors, and solar power

- Data sources: NASA POWER, SMAP, and GPM resources

- AI: Data analysis and crop recommendation assistance

- Development tools: AI-assisted development tools and web technologies

Innovation and Impact:

Unlike conventional farming information platforms that may provide general recommendations, AgriSmart aims to combine soil conditions, NASA Earth observation data, and crop guidance in one accessible platform. Its farmer-first design considers affordability, regional languages, ease of use, changing climate conditions, and the needs of small-scale farmers.

The expected impact includes improved agricultural awareness, more informed crop selection, better soil management, reduced unnecessary fertilizer use, and increased climate awareness among farmers.

Our long-term vision is to make data-driven agricultural assistance affordable, accessible, and useful for farming communities, supporting sustainable agriculture and climate-resilient farming.

projectDetails.name: AstroBuddy
projectDetails.summary: AstroBuddy is a calm health-monitoring software prototype for astronauts on long missions. A wearable band and radiation badge would send readings automatically, so astronauts do not need to type anything. AstroBuddy brings blood pressure, heart rate, oxygen, glucose, sleep, stress, exercise and radiation into one dashboard. It stays quiet when readings are steady. When a reading moves outside an illustrative range, it explains the concern in plain language, suggests calm next steps, and shows how urgent cases could be flagged for medical review. It also includes an optional, private cycle-tracker demo for crew members who menstruate. The prototype uses simulated data and fictional crew. AstroBuddy matters because astronauts far from Earth carry much of the responsibility for spotting health changes themselves, and clear, calm guidance may help them act early without added stress.
projectDetails.details:
What it does: AstroBuddy is a decision-support dashboard concept for astronauts. It shows a status ring, a plain-language message, suggested next steps, trend lines, an event log, a calm-breathing guide, and demo-only alert buttons.

How it works: A simulated wearable stream updates readings every 1.5 seconds. Each reading is compared with illustrative ranges (steady, watch, review needed). When something changes, the dashboard explains it calmly and suggests steps. It builds on sensing that already exists, such as the CSA Bio-Monitor smart shirt.

Benefits and intended impact: Astronauts have little time and no hospital nearby, so automatic sensing and calm guidance could reduce workload and stress. These are intended benefits, not clinically tested results.

Tools: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, GitHub Pages, Canva (slides), Nunito font.

What is creative: calm by design, quiet when steady, a built-in breathing guide, and an optional cycle tracker for inclusive health tracking.

What we considered: crews cannot type in data, so readings arrive automatically. Guidance follows onboard procedures and does not give medicine doses. All data is simulated, ranges are illustrative, and a real system would need validated thresholds and clinical review. We used design thinking (Empathize, Define, Ideate, Prototype, Test with five simulated scenarios).

AI use: Claude, an AI assistant by Anthropic, helped with parts of the code and wording. The Solution_concept, direction and design decisions are ours.

challengeDetails.title: Space Mission Design Game
