projectDetails.name: Threadline
projectDetails.summary: Threadline is a browser game for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. You are Mission Director for a Moon orbiter: you choose three instruments, a launcher, a battery, a solar array, fuel and data storage, then fly through a solar storm with one in-flight decision. Coloured threads link every choice to the weight, power, cost, fuel, data and science it moves, and every outcome is traced back to the decision that caused it. Rewind keeps the same random seed, so you can change one decision and see exactly what it did. It matters because the trade-offs in mission design are usually invisible: here you can see and replay them. It is a game model, not a simulator, and every number is labelled NASA DATA, SIMPLIFIED PHYSICS or GAME MODEL.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

Threadline is a browser game for the "Space Mission Design Game" challenge. The player is Mission Director for a Moon-orbiting mission. In the Design Bay they pick three instruments, a launcher, a battery, a solar array, fuel and data storage, and coloured threads show which meters each choice moves: weight, power, cost, fuel, data and science. After launch, a solar storm hits on an orbit the player cannot predict. They get one in-flight decision; each answer shows its cost and its risk, and none is recommended. The outcome screen gives a tier, four scores and the top cause chains, each traced from a decision the player made, through a resource, to the result. Rewind keeps the seed, so the luck stays identical and only the decision changes; a diff shows the effect. Also built: a guided first run, four mission variants, share links, saved progress and a 90-second demo mode.

HOW IT WORKS

The whole simulation is one pure, deterministic function. The Design Bay preview runs the same loop as the flight, so the meters never disagree with the result. Luck comes only from the seed, which makes Rewind fair. While it simulates, the game keeps a log of causes, so each explanation is built from the player's own decisions. Balance was checked by sweeping thousands of designs for dominant strategies before the interface was built. Every number on screen carries a label: NASA DATA, SIMPLIFIED PHYSICS or GAME MODEL. The Moon's radius, gravitational parameter and Earth-Moon distance come from NASA's Moon Fact Sheet; everything else is invented for play and says so. A Truth Ledger records every real-world claim with its source, or marks it unverified, and automated tests check the ledger against the data file. The game's stages line up with the four mission segments named in the challenge resources: launch (launcher choice and launch), space (spacecraft and instruments), ground (downlink and Mission Control), user (science return and the outcome). That is a structural match only.

BENEFITS

A player can see, replay and test cause and effect in mission design instead of only reading about it. Rewind turns "what if I had chosen differently?" into a one-click experiment. Honest labels show which numbers are real and which are invented. It needs no account, no server and no install, and an offline package runs with no internet. It has high-contrast and text-size settings. It has been checked in Chromium only and no stranger has played it yet.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

To make the chain from decision to consequence in space mission design something a player can see and replay: you do not read about trade-offs, you feel them. Next: sourced numbers in place of the placeholders, more missions, and tests with real first-time players. Not built: team play, orbit options, objective definition, a sandbox, leaderboards, audio, live NASA data.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES, HARDWARE

TypeScript 6.0.3, Vite 8.3.4 (build), Phaser 3.90.0 (launch animation only), zustand 5.0.15 (state), Vitest 5.0.3 and happy-dom 21.0.4 (tests), ESLint 10.12.0 (lint), Python Playwright 1.63.0 with Chromium (browser audits and screenshots). Static site, hosted on GitHub Pages. No special hardware. SI: Claude (Anthropic) wrote most of the code, tests and documentation; see the Use of SI field and SI_DISCLOSURE.md in the repository. Source code (MIT licence): https://github.com/Zenith-Sagar/threadline

projectDetails.name: FirePulse: Spatially and Temporally Harmonized Active-Fire Intelligence Platform Subtitle / Tagline: Harmonizing NASA MODIS & VIIRS Hotspots on a 1km Equal-Area Grid for Consistent Global Wildfire Monitoring
projectDetails.summary:
Title: FirePulse — Spatially & Temporally Harmonized Active-Fire Intelligence Platform

What We Developed:
We developed FirePulse, an open-source geospatial platform that harmonizes active-fire and thermal anomaly observations from NASA’s MODIS (1,000m) and VIIRS (375m) satellite sensors into a unified, cross-calibrated intelligence system.

How It Addresses the Challenge:
Raw thermal hotspot counts cannot be directly compared across sensors due to vast differences in spatial resolution, equatorial crossing times, and swath geometries. Comparing them directly creates false burning trends—VIIRS detects 3 to 4 times more thermal pixels than MODIS for the exact same fire. FirePulse solves this by ingesting NASA FIRMS feeds, projecting observations onto a standardized 1km × 1km equal-area cylindrical grid (EPSG:6933), and aggregating co-located detections into daily "active cell-days." It classifies cross-sensor co-detections and contextualizes historical trends across four distinct observational eras (MODIS baseline, early overlap, JPSS constellation, and post-Suomi-NPP).

Why It Is Important:
Wildfire risk and climate assessments require reliable, long-term trends spanning 2000 to the present without sensor-transition artifacts. FirePulse delivers mathematically rigorous, de-duplicated wildfire metrics, interactive global time-lapse playback, and API exports—equipping fire managers, climate scientists, and disaster response teams with trustworthy active-fire intelligence.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details: FirePulse

1. What does it do or how does it work?

FirePulse is an automated, web-based Earth Observation intelligence platform designed to eliminate spatial and temporal disparities between NASA’s legacy MODIS (1,000m) and modern VIIRS (375m) active-fire observations.

The platform operates via a four-stage pipeline:

  1. Multi-Sensor Ingestion: Ingests near-real-time (NRT) and historical thermal anomaly feeds from NASA FIRMS (Terra, Aqua, Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21) via REST APIs and archive datasets.
  2. Equal-Area Geospatial Projection (EPSG:6933): Rather than relying on standard latitude/longitude grids which suffer severe area distortion towards the poles, FirePulse reprojects raw observation points onto a standardized 1km × 1km Equal-Area Cylindrical Grid.
  3. Temporal Harmonization & Co-Detection Logic: Satellite observations are binned into daily 24-hour UTC cycles ("active cell-days"). Co-located detections occurring within the same 1km cell on the same day are cross-calibrated into unified fire events, computing joint Fire Radiative Power (FRP) metrics (mean, max) and tagging whether an event was co-detected or sensor-exclusive.
  4. Interactive Analytics & Time Machine: Delivers a full analytical suite featuring interactive global maps, spatial filtering by Area of Interest (AOI), seasonal trend decomposition, sensor concordance matrices, and a lightweight 60 FPS "Time Machine" playback engine powered by dynamic 3-degree spatial binning.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Eliminates False Detection Artifacts: A single fire viewed by VIIRS often produces 3–4 adjacent 375m hotspot pixels, whereas MODIS observes it as a single 1km pixel. FirePulse standardizes both into unified 1km cell-days, preventing artificial 300%–400% wildfire increase claims.
  • Cross-Era Comparability: Bridges the historical 2000–present baseline so that pre-2012 MODIS-only records can be reliably analyzed alongside modern multi-satellite JPSS constellations.
  • High-Performance Responsiveness: Bypasses browser memory crashes by pre-aggregating 25,000+ global observations into regional geographic clusters, ensuring sub-100ms API queries and smooth animations.
  • Transparent Data Export: Provides researchers and agencies with one-click GeoJSON and CSV exports categorized by sensor dominance, co-detection confidence, and FRP.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • Climate Science & Carbon Accounting: Provides climate researchers and IPCC reporting bodies with statistically consistent 25-year active-fire time series, preventing erroneous trend conclusions caused by sensor transitions.
  • Wildfire Management & First Responders: Grants regional disaster management teams a single, cross-verified operating picture that highlights high-confidence co-detections while reducing false positives.
  • Environmental Policymaking: Equips policymakers and forestry departments with verified fire seasonality data and cross-country burning comparisons to evaluate the true effectiveness of fire bans and land-use policies.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Programming Languages: Python 3.12 (Backend & Ingestion Engine), TypeScript (Frontend).
  • Backend Architecture: Flask, SQLAlchemy ORM, SQLite with spatial indexing, NumPy, and Pandas for statistical transformations.
  • Frontend & Visualization: React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Leaflet & React-Leaflet (custom canvas layers), Recharts (interactive time-series & histograms), Lucide Icons.
  • Geospatial & Remote Sensing Standards: NASA FIRMS API, NASA LANCE feeds, EPSG:6933 (NSIDC EASE-Grid 2.0 Global Equal-Area Cylindrical projection), WGS-84 (EPSG:4326).
  • Deployment & Cloud Infrastructure: Vercel Serverless Architecture, Git/GitHub for version control, and pre-seeded spatial databases.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Equal-Area "Cell-Day" Metrology: Instead of simply buffering points with arbitrary circular radii (which creates overlap ambiguity and polar distortion), FirePulse establishes equal-area grid cells as standard units of burning activity.
  • Dynamic Multi-Cluster Playback: Traditional web maps freeze when animating tens of thousands of global points over years. FirePulse uses a creative server-side spatial-binning algorithm that preserves continental dispersion patterns (Australia, Amazon Basin, Sahel, boreal forests) while maintaining fluid frame rates.
  • Sensor Era Awareness: FirePulse actively prevents user error by embedding satellite mission timelines directly into analytical charts (e.g., highlighting the Suomi-NPP operational decommissioning on Nov 2, 2026), ensuring historical trend analyses are scientifically defensible.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Orbital Mechanics & Diurnal Cycles: Accounted for differing equatorial crossing times—morning overpasses (Terra ~10:30 AM), afternoon overpasses (Aqua & Suomi-NPP ~1:30 PM), and offset orbits (NOAA-20 at 12:45 PM)—which capture distinct phases of daily wildfire intensity.
  • Scan Geometry & Off-Nadir Distortion: Acknowledged MODIS "bow-tie" pixel growth (from 1km at nadir up to ~4.8km at swath edges) versus VIIRS onboard pixel trimming and aggregation.
  • Operational Reality & Serverless Boundaries: Designed the data storage and ingestion pipelines to operate reliably within serverless execution constraints, handling ephemeral environments, read-only file systems, and API rate limits without service disruption.

Agrisense AI – Smart Crop Rotation & Soil Health Decision Platform
Agrisense AI is an intelligent agriculture platform designed to help farmers make smarter and more sustainable farming decisions using Artificial Intelligence and NASA Earth observation data.
We are developing a farmer-friendly web application with the following features:
1. Smart Dashboard: Displays farm information, environmental conditions, and agricultural insights.
2.Soil Health Analysis: Helps farmers understand soil conditions, fertility, pH, and nutrient status.
3.Crop Explorer: Provides suitable crop recommendations based on soil, climate, and environmental conditions.
4.Crop Rotation Planner: Suggests sustainable crop rotation plans to improve soil health and productivity.
5. NASA Data Integration: Uses NASA POWER, GPM, and SMAP datasets for temperature, rainfall, and soil moisture analysis.
6.AI Plant Disease Detection: Identifies potential plant diseases from uploaded images and provides treatment suggestions.
7.AI Agriculture Chatbot: Offers friendly conversations and personalized agricultural guidance.
8.Farm Management: Allows farmers to manage farm details and access location-based information.
Technology Stack: React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Python FastAPI, MongoDB Atlas, TensorFlow, Gemini AI, and NASA Earth observation APIs.
Our Vision: To empower farmers with accessible AI-powered insights, improve soil health, support sustainable farming, and make agriculture smarter.
projectDetails.details:
AgriSense AI is an AI-powered agriculture platform that helps farmers make smarter and more sustainable farming decisions using NASA satellite data.

It includes a Smart Dashboard, Soil Health Analysis, Crop Explorer, Crop Rotation Planner, AI Plant Disease Detection, and an Agriculture Chatbot. It uses NASA POWER, GPM, and SMAP data to analyze temperature, rainfall, and soil moisture and provide location-based agricultural insights.

The platform helps farmers select suitable crops, improve soil health, manage water resources, identify plant diseases, and adopt sustainable farming practices.

We developed AgriSense AI using React.js, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Python, FastAPI, MongoDB Atlas, TensorFlow, Gemini AI, and NASA APIs.

Our goal is to combine space technology and artificial intelligence to make farming smarter, easier, and more sustainable.

projectDetails.name: SPACE WARS – Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
projectDetails.summary:
SPACE WARS is an interactive, NASA-inspired space adventure game designed for children aged 7–12. It transforms space science and astronaut training into a fun, colorful, and educational gaming experience. Players take on the role of junior astronauts and complete missions involving rocket launches, space exploration, planetary landings, space station survival, radiation safety, and communication.

The project integrates real NASA data, including information from NASA's DONKI service, to introduce players to actual space weather events such as coronal mass ejections, solar flares, and radiation-related alerts. These events help create science-based mission scenarios, allowing children to understand how real space conditions can affect astronauts and spacecraft.

By combining interactive gameplay, simple instructions, mission-based challenges, and real-world space science, SPACE WARS makes complex space concepts easier for young learners to understand. Our goal is to inspire curiosity about astronomy, science, and space exploration while helping children learn through playing.
projectDetails.details:
SPACE WARS

SPACE WARS is a browser-based educational space adventure game designed for children aged 7–12. It transforms astronaut training and space exploration into interactive missions where players learn by doing rather than simply reading information or answering repetitive quizzes.

How It Works

Players become junior astronauts and progress through space missions involving rocket launches, spacecraft navigation, planetary exploration, safe landings, space station construction, oxygen management, radiation protection, and communication with Earth. Each mission contains objectives, challenges, clues, and simple instructions. Players must complete the required tasks to unlock the next stage. If they fail, they can retry and improve their performance.

NASA Data Integration

The project connects with NASA data services, particularly NASA's DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information). Real space-weather information, including coronal mass ejections, solar flares, and radiation-related events, can be used to create science-based mission conditions. This helps children understand how actual space events can affect spacecraft and astronauts. Other NASA resources, such as OSDR, RadLab, and Mars Trek, support the project's broader educational direction. Real NASA information is distinguished from simulated gameplay scenarios.

Technologies Used

  • Frontend: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript
  • Backend: Node.js and JavaScript
  • API Integration: NASA Open APIs and DONKI
  • Deployment: Vercel
  • Development Tools: Visual Studio Code, Git, and GitHub
  • Data Handling: Server-side API routes to securely communicate with NASA services

Benefits and Intended Impact

SPACE WARS makes space science more accessible and enjoyable for young learners. It encourages problem-solving, logical thinking, curiosity, decision-making, and basic scientific understanding. Children learn about real space phenomena through interactive experiences instead of complex scientific explanations.

Creativity and Design Considerations

The game combines colorful visuals, animations, mission progression, interactive controls, simple language, and retry options to create a child-friendly experience. We considered the target age group, ease of navigation, learning objectives, gameplay difficulty, accessibility, and the accuracy of NASA-related information.

Our ultimate goal is to inspire the next generation of space explorers by making science education interactive, engaging, and connected to real-world space research.

projectDetails.name: Project Aspirants of SpaceX
projectDetails.summary:
We built "Abandoned, But Not Forgotten", a pixel-art storytelling website for school-age space fans. The guide is "Elias 2-24 b", a young planet who has never heard of human spacecraft. 

The journey has 17 discoveries across the Moon, Mars and deep space, plus an opening scene and two bonus lessons. Each stop has Elias's dialogue, a fact card and a scrapbook entry. 

Interactive elements include a moonquake seismograph, a laser-aiming game, driving games, a helicopter take-off and hover game, a lander, a flashlight search, ordering puzzles and a quiz. A Space Scrapbook fills up as Elias learns, and Elias can read the story aloud using the browser's built-in voice.

The challenge is to tell the story of NASA's left-behind hardware on the Moon and Mars to school-age space enthusiasts. 
our project answers 3 critical questions-

- What was left behind?
- Why it was left?
- Why it still matters?


Left-behind spacecraft can look like debris, but they are evidence of what humans learned, from measuring the Earth–Moon distance with a laser mirror to hearing moonquakes. As more missions head to the Moon and Mars, young people also need to understand why the historic sites must be protected from future explorers. By making that history interactive, we help students connect with real NASA missions, build curiosity about science and engineering, and think about what humanity chooses to leave behind next.
projectDetails.details:
We a created a free, browser-based, pixel-art storytelling adventure for school-age space fans. It tells the story of NASA’s discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars.

The user follows Elias 2-24 b, a baby planet who has never heard of human spacecraft. His scanner finds objects marked “ORIGIN: EARTH” on other worlds, and the user learns alongside him. The journey has 20 screens:

an opening scene,

17 discoveries across the Moon, Mars and deep space,

2 bonus lessons, “The Weight Problem” and “Protect the Footprint”.

It explores the following places and discoveries

Moon - Surveyor landers, Apollo descent stage, ALSEP seismometers, laser retroreflector, Lunar Roving Vehicles, personal objects (family photo, golf balls, flags)

Mars - Viking, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, Phoenix and InSight, Ingenuity, landing hardware, impact debris

Deep space - Pioneer 10 and 11, NEAR Shoemaker, Dawn, Kepler

Each stop includes Elias’s dialogue, a fact card, a scrapbook entry and usually a mini-game. The site also has a Space Scrapbook that fills up, a Back button, and optional spoken narration.

Technical design.

The whole site is in an index.html file. The story is stored as a list of scenes (title, dialogue, fact, scrapbook line, game), and a small engine plays them one by one.

Each game is a function that tells the engine when the player has won.

Games with movement use the HTML canvas. Others use ordinary page elements.

A skip button appears after 20 seconds so nobody gets stuck.

Narration uses the browser’s built-in text-to-speech, with a settings panel to change voice, pitch and speed.

Elias’s picture is built into the file, so the site needs no database, server code or accounts.

Benefits

Engaging for children. The story, humor and games make real mission history feel like play, not a database of facts.

It's Accessible, It’s free, needs no install, and runs on a laptop or phone.

A clear message is conveyed . It changes “space junk” into “history and science”, with each object shown as “once a scientist”.

Responsible exploration

Young users learn why historic sites on the Moon need protecting from future explorers.

Low-cost and easy to update.

One file makes it simple to host and to edit.

We hope to help students connect with real NASA missions and the science each one made possible.

Spark curiosity about science, engineering and space exploration.

Build awareness that exploration leaves footprints, and that people must choose responsibly what to leave behind.

Grow the project into a classroom resource, with more missions (such as later Mars missions and Chinese or Indian lunar missions), translations, a more child-like narrator voice and teacher worksheets.

Tools, languages and software used

Languages- HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript (no frameworks or libraries)

Graphics - HTML canvas for games, CSS for the Moon and Mars terrain, emoji for objects, the Press Start 2P pixel font (Google Fonts), and the Elias mascot art got using ai inspired from NASA's blog.

Audio-The browser’s Web Speech API for narration

Hosting -netlify


Our Project is creative in the following ways
1. A new point of view: We tell the story through Elias 2-24 b, a baby planet who knows nothing about humans. The user discovers the objects with him, so the learning feels like curiosity, not a lecture.

2. Changing “space junk” into history: The challenge could be read as a story about waste. We turned it around: “Every machine here was once a scientist.” The finale crosses out “SPACE JUNK”, then “LEFT-BEHIND OBJECTS”, and replaces them with “MISSION FOOTPRINTS”. The same idea carries through the slogan “Abandoned does not mean useless.”

3. Games that teach the science: Each game is tied to what the object actually did.

4. A retro pixel-art style with a personal touch: The pixel look suits school-age users and the “old hardware” theme. The Space Scrapbook gives children something to collect, and Elias can read the story aloud.

5. Humor and emotion together: Moon golf balls and “a really long parking break” for the rovers make children smile. Charles Duke’s family photo and the idea of protecting footprints add a more thoughtful moment.

Factors Considered

Audience: School-age children, so short lines, simple words, a friendly character and a non-graphic treatment of the astronaut waste items (“personal consumables”).

Preservation: Using NASA’s lunar heritage recommendations (contact, dust, exhaust, contamination) so the project also explains why these sites must be protected.

Chronology: Moving from the Moon to Mars to deep space, so the story shows how exploration advanced.

Accessibility: One free web page, no install or account, keyboard, mouse and touch controls, a skip button if a game is too hard, and an option to turn the voice off.

projectDetails.name: Project ASTRAVIGIL
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRAVIGIL is a research-based astronaut health monitoring prototype designed to explore biochemical health changes during space missions. Using NASA's OSD-575 Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP) dataset, we developed an interactive dashboard that visualizes 19 blood chemistry analytes across pre-flight and post-flight timepoints for four participants.

The prototype provides participant-level trends, group averages, and reference-range screening to help users explore changes in measurements such as glucose, creatinine, sodium and potassium. It aims to make astronaut biomedical research data easier to understand and explore, supporting future approaches to mission health monitoring.

ASTRAVIGIL demonstrates how space research datasets can be transformed into accessible, data-driven health visualization tools. It is a research prototype, not a live medical monitoring or diagnostic system.
projectDetails.details: ASTRAVIGIL is a mobile-first research prototype designed to help astronauts and mission teams explore health-related information relevant to long-duration spaceflight. It organizes information into cardiovascular, bone and muscle, radiation, and wellbeing modules, with a NASA research-study explorer. The current prototype references NASA OSDR study OSD-575, which contains pre-flight and post-flight blood-serum metabolic and immune/cardiovascular biomarker research from the Inspiration4 crew. It presents study context, sample timelines, assay information, and data provenance in an accessible interface. The project was developed as a lightweight web application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with a focus on mobile usability, clear navigation, and scientific transparency. It distinguishes published research metadata from live sensor measurements and does not claim to provide real-time astronaut monitoring, automated diagnosis, or validated medical alerts. ASTRAVIGIL aims to demonstrate how accessible research tools can support exploration of astronaut health evidence and inform future health-monitoring software.

projectDetails.name: ORCA
projectDetails.summary:
ORCA (Marine Ecosystem Reasoning with Collaborative Agents) is an AI-powered multi-agent platform designed to strengthen India's coastal security and marine ecosystem monitoring. It addresses the challenge of fragmented ocean data, delayed threat detection, and limited real-time coordination across marine monitoring systems.

ORCA integrates satellite imagery, sonar signals, AIS vessel tracking, and water-quality data through specialized AI agents working collaboratively. An Orchestrator Agent coordinates tasks, specialist agents analyze different data sources, and Debate & Verification agents cross-check findings to reduce false alarms. A Fusion Agent generates explainable intelligence reports with evidence and confidence scores.

The platform provides a unified dashboard, conversational AI through Ask ORCA, and operational modules for coastal alerts, fisherman support, and forecasting. By enabling early detection of oil spills, algal blooms, illegal fishing, and other marine threats, ORCA aims to protect marine biodiversity, improve coastal safety, safeguard fisherfolk livelihoods, and support India's Blue Economy and SDG 14.
projectDetails.details:
Lunar Landing Slide Navigator is a multi-agent AI system designed to support safer and more reliable lunar landings through intelligent terrain analysis, collaborative decision-making, and onboard reasoning.

The system addresses key challenges during lunar descent, including steep slopes, loose regolith, boulders, shadowed craters, fragmented sensor data, communication delays, and potential navigation-data spoofing.

It uses an Orchestrator Agent to break down landing objectives and coordinate specialized agents, including Terrain Vision, LiDAR Hazard, Slope and Regolith Stability, and Trajectory agents. These agents analyze available sensor data in parallel. Debate and Verification agents cross-check their findings, resolve conflicts, and flag suspicious inputs. Finally, a Fusion Agent generates an explainable landing recommendation with supporting evidence and confidence scores.

The platform includes a Navigator Console with a live hazard map, slope heatmap, sensor-health monitoring, and Ask Navigator conversational AI. Operational modules include a Hazard Map, Abort Advisor, and Trajectory Planner.

Its architecture combines multi-agent LLM orchestration, vision models, LiDAR and radar signal-processing machine learning, slope-stability estimators, and onboard edge inference. It also considers fixed fallback rules, signed telemetry, sensor-integrity checks, and public lunar elevation and imagery datasets.

The project's creative approach is to make multiple specialized AI agents reason collaboratively before recommending a landing decision. This aims to improve mission safety, protect valuable spacecraft and scientific payloads, support access to challenging lunar regions, and create a reusable framework for future lunar, Mars, and asteroid exploration.

projectDetails.name: Cosmic Fire
projectDetails.summary: Cosmic Fire is an AI-powered fire-safety explorer built from real NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) data. Fire behaves very differently in microgravity, and a crew can't simply walk away from one, so understanding how materials burn and how smoke behaves is critical for spacecraft safety. The data arrived as dozens of mixed files (PDFs, Excel, CSV, Word, PowerPoint, text), so I built a pipeline that sorts them by type: tables become interactive charts, and documents are split into searchable chunks. The dashboard compares solid-fuel burn tests (BASS-II), smoke tests (SAME-R), and spacecraft-scale fire tests (SAFFIRE-II). Anyone can ask the research reports questions in plain language and get cited answers from Google Gemini, and an "Explain" button turns computed statistics into fire-safety insights. It makes dense NASA research easier for students and the public to explore.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

Cosmic Fire lets a user explore microgravity combustion and smoke experiments from NASA PSI in two ways: (1) interactive charts built from experiment tables, and (2) a question box that answers from the investigations' own reports, with the source files shown.

HOW IT WORKS

- Text pipeline: PDFs, Word, PowerPoint and text files are converted to text, split into chunks, and tagged by investigation. A keyword (TF-IDF) search finds the most relevant chunks for a question, and Google Gemini writes a plain-language answer that cites its sources. It is instructed to answer only from the retrieved excerpts.

- Table pipeline: the experiment tables for BASS-II (solid fuel burning), SAME-R (smoke) and SAFFIRE-II (spacecraft-scale fires) are cleaned in pandas and plotted with Plotly. The "Explain what the data shows" button sends Python-computed summary statistics (not raw data) to Gemini, which is instructed not to do its own arithmetic or interpret columns it can't verify.

- Data used: NASA PSI investigations BASS-II, SAME-R, SAFFIRE-II and ACME (ACME as a document source).

TOOLS

Python, pandas, Plotly, scikit-learn, Streamlit, Google Gemini API, deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud.

USE OF AI

Code was written with assistance from Claude (Anthropic). Answers and chart explanations in the app are generated at runtime by Google Gemini from NASA PSI text and tables. No images, video or audio were AI-generated, and no NASA logos or branding are used.

LIMITATIONS

The charts use each investigation's summary experiment table, not the raw sensor data. Test counts per material are small, so findings are observations rather than proof. Retrieval is keyword-based and sometimes surfaces weak matches, which could be improved with embeddings.

IMPACT

Dense technical reports are hard for students and the public to read. This tool lets someone ask a question about spacecraft fire safety and see where the answer comes from, and it shows how to handle a messy mix of file types for any future dataset.

LINKS

Live website: https://cosmicfire.streamlit.app/

Code: https://github.com/Venky0608/Cosmic-Fire

projectDetails.name: P.U.L.S.E
projectDetails.summary: Beyond Low Earth Orbit, light-speed communication delays of 5 to 22 minutes eliminate real-time telemedicine with Mission Control, leaving astronauts without immediate clinical support during deep-space emergencies. To address NASA’s Exploration Medical Capability mandate for Artemis and Mars missions, Team ElectroPulse developed P.U.L.S.E. (Predictive Universal Life-support & Somatic Evaluator), an edge-native, zero-dependency autonomous medical intelligence platform. P.U.L.S.E. replaces cluttered telemetry with a cinematic, 3,697-structure 3D human somatic atlas driven by the Stanford OpenJarvis hands-free voice agent. When physiological anomalies or trauma are detected, the system smoothly glides the camera, peels anatomical layers to expose affected tissue, and locks a laser reticle onto the lesion. Crucially, P.U.L.S.E. eliminates synthetic hallucinations by anchoring every clinical intervention in five pure deterministic mathematical engines—solving intracranial pressure biophysics, Borbély circadian sleep fatigue, and microgravity pharmacokinetics in under 10 milliseconds. Calibrated directly on official NASA-STD-3001 flight standards, 17 Human Research Program risks, and 22 active countermeasure studies, P.U.L.S.E. operates completely offline in less than 50 MB of memory on radiation-hardened spacecraft avionics, delivering trusted, life-saving clinical autonomy when Earth is out of reach.
projectDetails.details:
P.U.L.S.E. is an edge-native autonomous medical intelligence system for deep-space missions where communication latency to Earth (5 to 22 minutes) eliminates real-time telemedicine. It replaces cluttered data screens with an interactive 3,697-structure 3D human somatic atlas and hands-free voice co-pilot powered by Stanford OpenJarvis. When an anomaly is detected, the system glides the camera, peels anatomical layers by ghosting bones to glass, dollies into the damaged tissue with a macro zoom, and locks a laser reticle onto the lesion while speaking concise clinical countermeasures aloud.

It operates 100% offline in less than 50 MB RAM on radiation-hardened flight avionics with zero cloud dependence. Crucially, it eliminates AI hallucinations by computing all triage through five deterministic mathematical engines solving fluid biophysics, circadian drift, and pharmacokinetics in under 10 milliseconds.

The intended impact is fulfilling NASA's Exploration Medical Capability Level 5 autonomy mandate for Artemis and Mars missions, with dual-use terrestrial applications in remote wilderness clinics, polar bases, submarines, and battlefield trauma care.

We developed the project using Python 3.10+ (FastAPI, NumPy, SciPy), TypeScript/JavaScript (React 18, Three.js, WebGL shaders), and SQLite for longitudinal medical memory, designed for embedded flight hardware.

Creatively, it translates cinematic holographic trauma interfaces into functional flight reality: in standby it is a clean floating emblem, and upon activation the surrounding UI completely vanishes, leaving the targeted 3D organ floating alone in deep space with precision laser crosshairs.

We accounted for light-speed delay, cephalad fluid shifts causing SANS optic edema, rapid bone demineralization, and secondary neutron radiation cascades, calibrating every countermeasure directly on official NASA-STD-3001 standards and 17 NASA Human Research Program risks

projectDetails.name: IGNITION.AI Pro: Microgravity Combustion & Fire Safety Engine
projectDetails.summary: IGNITION.AI Pro is an AI-powered microgravity combustion and fire safety engine built on NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) datasets (BASS, Saffire, FLEX, SAME, and SoFIE). Using Python, TF-IDF semantic ranking, and non-linear flame spread physics, it helps mission planners predict spacecraft fire risks across oxygen, pressure, and ventilation regimes while translating orbital combustion insights into safer materials, clean engines, and smart smoke detectors on Earth.
projectDetails.details: What it does & How it works: IGNITION.AI Pro bridges microgravity combustion theory and practical spacecraft fire safety through three integrated modules: 1. SI Semantic Experiment Ranker: Built with Python and scikit-learn (TF-IDF Vectorization & Cosine Similarity), it indexes flagship NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) datasets (BASS, Saffire, FLEX, SAME, and SoFIE) so mission engineers can query complex scenarios in natural language and retrieve ranked experiments with critical Limiting Oxygen Index (LOI) thresholds and governing equations. 2. Microgravity Flammability Regime Simulator: Models non-linear spacecraft flame spread across oxygen concentration (14%–40%), cabin pressure (45–101.3 kPa), ventilation velocity (0–40 cm/s), and concurrent vs. opposed airflow—mapping radiative quenching (<1.5 cm/s), peak diffusion spread (5–18 cm/s), and convective blow-off (>25 cm/s) zones. 3. Theory-to-Earth Engineering Matrix: Translates orbital combustion findings into actionable terrestrial safety innovations with one-click CSV export. Benefits, Creativity & Intended Impact: By uniting NLP search with microgravity fluid-combustion physics (Gr → 0, Damköhler and Richardson scaling), IGNITION.AI Pro helps mission designers evaluate polymer flammability for ISS operations and Artemis lunar habitats (34% O2, 56.5 kPa) while advancing aviation fire-resistant textiles, low-emission engines, and multi-wavelength smart smoke detectors on Earth. Tools, Languages & Software Used: Python, Streamlit, scikit-learn, NumPy, Pandas, Plotly, Google Docs, and Google Slides.

node.title: SONAR: SPHEREx Observations Narrated through Audio Rendering
node.excerpt: Our team has built a new shift-and-stack system through interactive sonification, which even blind people can use! We intend to use this with blinking and ML for the ultimate asteroid detector, combining AI with real human work.

projectDetails.name: Project SONAR: SPHEREx Observations Narrated through Audio Rendering
projectDetails.summary:
SONAR (SPHEREx Observations Narrated through Audio Rendering) is a web tool for finding moving asteroids in real SPHEREx images. Users blink through frames of one patch of sky and click the moving object in each. Then comes the original part: we turn shift-and-stack into sound. The frames are lined up along the object’s path, and how strongly the signal builds up becomes pitch and loudness, so a real asteroid can be heard. To our knowledge, using sonified shift-and-stack to verify asteroids is a new approach. An optional machine check then gives a second opinion, after the user has decided.

SPHEREx maps the whole sky repeatedly, so asteroids hide in its data as small changes over time. Blinking alone is hard: faint movers are easy to miss, mistakes are common, and blind or low-vision people are shut out. Hearing adds a second sense, so more people can check real NASA data.

Try it and join our testing: https://asteroid-research-study.vercel.app/#/
projectDetails.details:
What does it do, or how does it work?
SONAR loads real SPHEREx spectral images of one patch of sky taken hours apart. You blink between them and click the moving object in each frame. The tool then lines the frames up along that track (shift-and-stack) and plays a sound whose pitch and loudness rise when the signal adds up strongly. A rule-based check, and optionally a trained model, gives a second opinion only after you commit your verdict.

What benefits does it have?
It gives people a second sense for a task that is hard by eye alone. It supports blind and low-vision users, helps confirm faint movers, and uses real NASA data. The code is open source.

What is the intended impact?
To let students, citizen scientists and blind or low-vision people help check moving objects in SPHEREx data, and to give us a way to test whether looking, listening, or both works best.

What tools, languages or software did you use?
Python (NumPy, SciPy, Astropy) to process the SPHEREx FITS images, and JavaScript, HTML/CSS and the Web Audio API for the page. We used SPHEREx data from NASA-IPAC IRSA and JPL Horizons to check known asteroids such as 7 Iris. Claude (Anthropic) assisted with the code, and we note this in the repo.

How is your project creative?
Our main original idea is sonified shift-and-stack: instead of only looking at stacked images, people hear how strongly a track’s signal builds up, so faint asteroids that are hard to see can still be heard. It also makes the task usable by blind and low-vision people. Sound is used as a verification step, not decoration, and the human always decides before the machine gives its opinion.

What factors did your team consider?
SPHEREx frames change brightness by about 2x between exposures because each samples a different wavelength, so we re-measured our thresholds on SPHEREx data instead of reusing ground-based numbers. Within one 2-minute sequence, an asteroid barely moves, so we used frames hours apart. Results so far come from a small number of known asteroids, so we treat them as promising, not proven. We cite all sources, list our earlier asteroid-hunter work as prior work, and note that NASA does not endorse the project.

projectDetails.name: Crashfall
projectDetails.summary:
Crashfall is a top-down Mars outpost builder designed as a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. Players crash-land on the Martian surface and must rebuild a dead outpost by placing modules, waiting for construction to complete, and physically wiring power from solar panels to a central reactor. Rather than abstracting power into a menu, the game makes every connection tangible: cables stretch like rubber bands across the dust and snap back if released on empty ground, construction states hide modules and their sockets until built, solar panels continuously re-aim at the reactor, and placement rules forbid building too close to the reactor — forcing the same spatial and power trade-offs real mission planners face.

It addresses the challenge by letting students experience competing outpost demands — power generation, construction time, spatial constraints — rather than reading about them. Real NASA Mars data (sol length, solar irradiance at 586 W/m², gravity) drives the day cycle and panel output, grounding the fiction in fact.

It matters because it turns abstract mission-planning decisions into a felt, playable lesson — the kind of intuitive understanding that sparks the next generation of astronauts and engineers.
projectDetails.details:
What it does / How it works

Crashfall is a top-down, diegetic Mars outpost builder. The player crash-lands on the Martian surface and must rebuild a dead station by placing modules, waiting for them to construct, and physically wiring power from solar panels back to a central reactor.

The core loop is:

  1. Place a module on the station grid — but not too close to the reactor (rejected placement, no cost lost).
  2. Wait for construction — the module and its wire socket stay invisible and non-interactable until built.
  3. Wire the module to the reactor — grab a cable, drag it across the dust. The wire stretches infinitely like a rubber band; release on empty ground and it snaps back elastically to its origin; release on a valid plug and the connection holds.
  4. Power flows — solar panels continuously rotate to face the reactor, and real NASA Mars data scales their output to ~43% of Earth-equivalent.

Everything is felt rather than read: no menu bars, no abstract power numbers. The wiring is the game.

Benefits

  • Teaches systems thinking. Players learn that outpost survival is a trade-off between power, space, and time — not a checklist.
  • Accessible to students. No prior base-builder experience needed; the tutorial points at the action, not the screen edge.
  • Runs offline. Live NASA imagery is fetched when available, with bundled fallbacks so the trainer works in classrooms without internet.
  • Open source. Fully open code, so educators can fork it, reskin it for lunar scenarios, or extend the module set.

Intended impact

The official challenge asks students to experience the decisions that determine mission success — not memorize facts about them. Crashfall makes those decisions tactile: a rejected placement stings, a snapped-back wire costs a second, a solar panel that produces half what you expected forces you to re-plan. That felt understanding is what turns curiosity into the next generation of mission planners, engineers, and astronauts. We want a middle-schooler to play for ten minutes and walk away knowing why power routing matters on Mars.

Tools, languages, hardware, software

  • Engine: Godot 4.4 (MIT-licensed)
  • Language: GDScript
  • Systems built: CharacterBody2D player with plug/pickup mechanics, TileMapLayer station grid with per-tile collision, custom wire-drag system with elastic snap-back tweens, animation-driven sprite state machine, scene-switching cutscene → crash → gameplay flow with audio cues.
  • NASA data: NSSDC Mars Fact Sheet (sol length 88,775 s, solar irradiance 586 W/m², gravity 3.73 m/s²) drives gameplay constants; APOD API with bundled fallback for the crash cutscene backdrop.
  • Hardware: Developed on standard laptops; no specialized hardware required.
  • Version control: Git (public repository).

How the project is creative

Most base-builders abstract power into a HUD number. We made it physical. The wire is a rubber band you can stretch across the screen and let snap back. Construction hides the module and its socket until it's real. Solar panels turn to face the reactor in real time. The tutorial doesn't sit in a corner — it tracks the object you're acting on. Every mechanic is diegetic: the game shows its rules through motion, not text.

Factors the team considered

  • Feasibility over scope. We chose four deep mechanics (construction gating, physical wiring, solar aiming, placement constraints) over twenty shallow ones. Every mechanic ships in the demo.
  • Demo reliability. API calls are wrapped with bundled fallbacks — the demo never breaks on stage or in a classroom without Wi-Fi.
  • Educational framing. We tuned the tutorial to be predictive (points at the object you'll act on) rather than descriptive (walls of text), because student retention comes from doing, not reading.
  • Asset licensing. All third-party art, sound, and tilesets are used under their free/commercial licenses and credited in CREDITS.md, so the project is redistributable.
  • Extensibility. The module system is data-driven, so a classroom can add lunar modules, greenhouse mechanics, or radiation shielding without touching core code.
  • Accessibility. Simple controls, readable UI, no fail state that punishes exploration — students can experiment without fear.

projectDetails.name: Space Reclaim
projectDetails.summary:
Every space mission begins with a dream of discovery. But what happens when that mission ends?

Humanity has sent machines beyond Earth: rovers, landers, probes, and scientific instruments. They have explored worlds, collected data, and expanded our understanding of the universe. Yet many remain where their missions ended, while others continue travelling through space.

Beyond the Mission is an interactive visual storytelling experience that uncovers the stories of this hardware. Audiences discover where these machines are now, what they accomplished, and why their presence matters. The experience explores concerns surrounding orbital debris, collisions, and the responsibility of future exploration.

Not everything left behind is junk. Some objects are scientific and historical records; others can create risks for spacecraft and satellites. By showing this difference, our project encourages viewers to understand the impact of human activity in space.

The journey inspires young explorers everywhere. Our goal is to turn curiosity into awareness and inspire the next generation to imagine safer, more responsible ways to explore the universe.

Because a mission may end, but its footprint can last for generations.
projectDetails.details:
Space Reclaim is an interactive visual storytelling project designed to educate school-age audiences about the hardware humanity has left behind during space exploration. It takes viewers on a journey through the history and aftermath of space missions, exploring equipment left on the Moon, Mars, in Earth's orbit, and across deep space.

The project works through an interactive storyboard that combines striking visuals, short explanations, animations, and audience participation. Instead of presenting information through conventional slides, it encourages viewers to explore different scenarios, discover the stories behind individual spacecraft, and understand what happens when their missions come to an end.

Its primary benefit is making complex space-related topics accessible, engaging, and easier to understand. It distinguishes scientifically valuable mission remnants from harmful orbital debris while introducing concerns such as collisions, environmental impact, and responsible space exploration.

Our intended impact is to create awareness among younger generations and encourage them to think critically about humanity's growing presence in space.

The project uses presentation and visual design software to create its interactive storytelling experience. Its creative approach lies in combining education with a cinematic, story-driven format, transforming a scientific topic into an engaging journey of discovery.

Throughout development, we considered scientific accuracy, age-appropriate explanations, visual clarity, accessibility, and audience engagement.

projectDetails.name: Foresight: The Climate-Twinner
projectDetails.summary: Foresight is a climate-intelligence web application designed to help understand how regions around the world may experience changing climate conditions in the future. By combining historical meteorological data from NASA POWER with future climate projections from Open-Meteo, the platform identifies geographical locations whose present-day climates most closely resemble the projected future climate of a selected region. It uses climate indicators such as temperature, precipitation, seasonal variability and growing degree days to rank climate analogues and visualise them through an interactive global map. Foresight also integrates regional agricultural intelligence, including crop patterns, growing seasons, soil characteristics and irrigation context, to explore the potential implications of climate change for agriculture. By translating complex climate datasets into accessible geographical insights, Foresight aims to support climate adaptation research, agricultural planning and long-term decision-making. It is particularly important for understanding how communities and agricultural systems may need to adapt to a changing climate.
projectDetails.details:
Foresight is a web-based climate intelligence application developed to explore how climate change could transform the environmental conditions of different geographical regions. Users can search for locations worldwide, select a historical climate baseline and a future projection period (2021–2040 or 2041–2049), and analyse how the selected location's climate may change. The application combines historical meteorological data from NASA POWER with future climate projections from Open-Meteo's Climate API, using two HighResMIP climate models: MRI-AGCM3-2-S and EC-Earth3P-HR. Through a delta-based projection method, it applies projected changes in temperature and precipitation to the observed historical climate profile. It then compares the resulting climate profile against reference locations using eight indicators, including seasonal precipitation, growing degree days, frost-free days, hot-day frequency and rainfall variability. The closest climate analogues across 1,000 worldwide locations are ranked and displayed on an interactive global map.

A major feature of Foresight is its expanded global reference network. The latest version includes a systematically generated dataset of 1,000 geographically distributed land locations, designed around NASA POWER's underlying meteorological grid. Historical climate information is collected through a dedicated ingestion pipeline, processed into comparable climate indicators and stored in a precomputed database. This allows future analyses to compare locations against the stored reference network without repeatedly downloading large historical datasets. The application also provides geographical filtering, similarity visualisation, detailed climate comparisons, and CSV export capabilities. Where curated information is available, it presents regional agricultural context, including major crops, growing seasons, crop rotations, soil characteristics and irrigation practices.

The primary benefit of Foresight is that it translates complex climate projections into understandable geographical comparisons. Rather than presenting climate change only through temperature graphs or statistical summaries, it identifies places whose present-day climate resembles the potential future climate of a selected region. This can help researchers, agricultural planners and communities explore possible adaptation strategies, identify emerging climatic challenges and understand how agricultural practices may need to evolve. Its intended impact is to make climate intelligence more accessible and encourage data-informed approaches to climate adaptation, particularly in agriculture and regions vulnerable to changing rainfall and temperature patterns.

The application was developed using TypeScript, JavaScript, React and Next.js, with CSS for interface styling. MapLibre GL JS powers the interactive geographical visualisation, while Open-Meteo's Geocoding API enables worldwide location searches. NASA POWER's Daily API supplies historical meteorological data, and the Open-Meteo Climate API provides future climate projections. The project also uses Node.js, npm, JSON-based data storage, spatial indexing and custom data-processing scripts. Vercel is used for deployment. No specialised physical hardware was required, as Foresight is entirely software-based.

The creative aspect of Foresight lies in its use of the climate-analogue approach. Combining this concept with global spatial analysis and agricultural context creates a practical way to explore otherwise abstract future climate scenarios. During development, important considerations included scientific validity, geographical coverage, consistency between historical and projected datasets, spatial resolution, API limitations, computational efficiency, reliability, accessibility and transparency about uncertainty. The project also distinguishes climate similarity from actual agricultural suitability, recognising that local soil, elevation, water availability and other environmental factors influence real-world outcomes.

projectDetails.name: ORBITONE
projectDetails.summary: ORBITONE is an interactive multiplayer space mission design game that turns complex aerospace systems engineering into a collaborative, real-time team challenge. Aligned with the Space Mission Design Game challenge, up to four players step into distinct mission specialist roles—coordinating spacecraft architecture, propulsion, power, communications, orbit selection, and scientific payloads under strict mass, budget, and power limits. Grounded in real NASA open data, every engineering choice triggers cascading trade-offs across the spacecraft, teaching students and aspiring engineers why missions succeed or fail through hands-on experimentation rather than passive facts.
projectDetails.details:
ORBITONE

Every space mission is a team decision.

An interactive multiplayer space mission simulator that makes the engineering trade-offs behind space exploration accessible to everyone.

The Problem

A successful space mission is never designed around one decision. Every subsystem depends on the others.

A more powerful science instrument might collect better data, but it also adds mass, consumes more power and generates more data that must be transmitted back to Earth. A heavier spacecraft could exceed the launch vehicle’s capacity. A power-intensive payload could struggle during periods when the spacecraft is in Earth’s shadow.

These are the kinds of trade-offs that real mission engineers have to work through together.

But for most students, these decisions remain hidden behind equations, technical terminology and textbooks. They rarely get the opportunity to experience how changing one part of a spacecraft can affect the entire mission.

We wanted to change that.

What is ORBITONE?

ORBITONE is a multiplayer space mission design simulator where players work together as a mission control team to plan, build and test a spacecraft.

Instead of simply reading about aerospace engineering, players get to make the decisions themselves, see the consequences and work with their teammates to find solutions.

The experience is built around four stages:

1. Choose a Mission. Build a Team.

Players begin by selecting a mission scenario, with options including Earth Observation, Lunar Reconnaissance and Deep Space Science.

Each player takes responsibility for a different part of the mission:

* Mission Architect: Oversees the overall mission design and makes sure the different subsystems work together.

* Propulsion & Orbit Lead: Handles propulsion choices and orbital requirements.

* Power & Thermal Engineer: Manages energy requirements and thermal constraints.

* Science & Communications Lead: Balances scientific payload capabilities with data collection and communication requirements.

Every role has its own responsibilities, but no player can complete the mission alone.

2. Make the Trade-offs.

This is where the real challenge begins.

Players configure their spacecraft by making decisions about individual subsystems. Each decision updates the mission’s overall parameters in real time.

For example, choosing a higher-resolution science payload may improve scientific return, but it also increases spacecraft mass, power consumption and data requirements.

That decision could affect launch feasibility, battery capacity and communication requirements.

Players must discuss their choices, understand the compromises and find a configuration that works for the entire mission.

3. Run the Mission.

Once the team is satisfied with its design, it can run the mission simulation.

ORBITONE evaluates the spacecraft configuration and shows whether the mission can meet its launch and operational constraints.

Players can see how their design performs across factors such as orbital requirements, power margins and communications.

A mission that looks good on paper might not perform as expected once all the subsystems are considered together.

4. Learn From the Results.

Every mission ends with a post-mission analysis.

Rather than simply showing a success or failure screen, ORBITONE explains what happened and why.

Players can understand which decisions created problems, where they made effective compromises and how they could improve their design.

They can then return to the design stage, make changes and try again.

What Makes ORBITONE Different?

Learning through experience

Players discover aerospace concepts by making decisions and seeing their consequences. They do not need prior knowledge of aerospace engineering to get started.

Collaboration, not competition

Real spacecraft are designed by teams of specialists. ORBITONE reflects this by giving every player a distinct responsibility and making teamwork essential to mission success.

Complex engineering, made accessible

The interface presents technical relationships through intuitive visuals, live mission metrics and simple explanations. Even beginners can understand why a design works or fails.

Built for learning beyond the screen

ORBITONE is designed with schools, student clubs, STEM workshops and hackathons in mind. It gives educators a practical way to introduce aerospace, engineering, problem-solving and systems thinking through a shared experience.

Technology & Implementation

We built ORBITONE as a responsive, browser-based multiplayer application.

Application & Simulation

* Vite

* TypeScript

* Three.js

UI/UX & Testing

* Figma

* Chrome DevTools

* Playwright

NASA Data Integration

* NASA MCP integration

* NASA Open APIs

NASA’s open-data ecosystem provides a foundation for connecting the simulator with real space science and mission-related information.

Feasibility & What’s Next

Within the hackathon timeframe, we developed a playable, responsive multiplayer experience that brings mission planning, subsystem trade-offs and post-mission analysis into one platform.

There is still plenty of room to take ORBITONE further.

Our next priorities include:

* Richer orbital visualisation: More detailed orbital mechanics and spacecraft visualisations to help players understand how their designs behave in space.

* Live space-weather events: Integrating NASA DONKI data to introduce real-world space-weather events as mission challenges, with appropriate effects on spacecraft systems.

* Classroom sandbox: A dedicated mode where teachers can create scenarios, guide student teams and explore engineering concepts at their own pace.

* More mission scenarios: Expanding the simulator with additional destinations, spacecraft configurations and scientific objectives.

Our goal is to make ORBITONE a learning environment where students can experiment, collaborate and develop an appreciation for the engineering behind space exploration.

Because understanding space exploration should not stop at learning how missions work. Students should have the opportunity to experience what it takes to make one work.

projectDetails.summary:
ASTRAVITAL: Mission Medical Intelligence

ASTRAVITAL is an interactive prototype of a health-monitoring platform for astronauts on long-duration missions. Set in a simulated Mars expedition (MARS-01), it brings crew health information into one connected workspace so a flight surgeon or astronaut can understand it at a glance.

Problem: On deep-space missions, crews are far from Earth, communication is delayed and medical help is limited. Health signals are often tracked separately, making gradual changes hard to spot early.

Solution: The core is an interactive Astronaut Digital Twin, a living anatomical model. Users can explore 11 body systems through layers such as skeleton, muscular, cardiovascular, nervous system and a health-risk heatmap. Selecting a region opens indicators, trends, spaceflight risks, examination history, observations and guidance. Readings are compared with the astronaut's personal baseline; in the demo, a resting heart rate of 65.6 bpm against a 58.1 bpm baseline is flagged as a mild drift. A 13-module workspace also covers AI health intelligence, cognitive performance, mental wellbeing, environmental monitoring and preventive healthcare.

Responsible design: All data is simulated. The prototype makes no diagnoses, is not a medical device, is not endorsed by NASA and does not replace flight surgeons.

Built with AI: Created entirely with AI apps and websites and published on Framer.

Live prototype: https://astravital.framer.website/
projectDetails.details:
ASTRAVITAL: Mission Medical Intelligence

ASTRAVITAL is an interactive prototype of a health-monitoring platform for astronauts on long-duration space missions. It is set in a simulated Mars expedition (MARS-01), currently in the transit phase on Mission Day 147. It shows how a flight surgeon or crew member could view, track and understand astronaut health in one connected workspace. All data is simulated, and the site says clearly that it is not a medical device, is not endorsed by NASA and does not replace flight surgeons.

Mission workspace and navigation

The interface is a dashboard-style workspace. A top bar shows the active mission, the mission day and phase, an online status indicator and an Emergency Access button. A sidebar lists 13 modules:

  • Mission Command Center
  • Astronaut Digital Twin
  • Medical Body Scanner
  • Health Monitoring
  • AI Health Intelligence
  • Cognitive Performance
  • Mental Wellbeing
  • Environmental Monitoring
  • Mission Health Timeline
  • Preventive Healthcare
  • Medical Operations
  • Crew Health Network
  • Medical Knowledge Center
  • Settings

A status line reads “All systems operational”, and the footer tags the build as Local Prototype v1.0.

Astronaut Digital Twin (the core feature)

The main screen is a living digital twin of the astronaut Alex Morgan (AST-001). It shows an interactive anatomical map with a mission-elapsed-time clock. Users can:

  • Switch between layers: Anatomical, Skeleton, Muscular, Cardiovascular, Nervous system, Health-risk heatmap and Examination.
  • Rotate between front and back views, or reset the view.
  • Select any of 11 connected regions: brain, eyes, heart, lungs, blood vessels, musculoskeletal system, bones, kidneys, digestive system, skin and immune system.
  • Read the colour-coded legend, where each region is marked either routine or attention.
  • Start a Guided Demo that walks a first-time viewer through the twin.

Region intelligence panel

Selecting a region opens a detail panel with six tabs: Indicators, Trends, Spaceflight Risks, Examination History, Observations and Guidance. The Cardiovascular example shows a resting heart rate of 65.6 bpm, which is 7.5 bpm above the astronaut’s personal baseline of 58.1 bpm. A trend line runs from Day 118 to Day 147 and flags a mild resting heart-rate drift over the last 8 days. The wording is careful: it suggests reading the drift alongside sleep and recovery trends and states that no diagnosis is inferred. An “Open in Scanner” button links the region to the Medical Body Scanner.

Summary tiles

Four tiles give the astronaut’s status at a glance:

  • Systems monitored: 11
  • Overall status: Stable, with 2 observations for attention
  • Last examination: Day 140, a routine mission assessment
  • Next health review: Day 150, a cardiovascular follow-up with the flight surgeon

Design and tone

The look is a dark, mission-control style. The language is informational and cautious, with “Simulated data” and “Informational only. Not a diagnosis.” repeated on the key screens.

Built entirely with AI

ASTRAVITAL was created entirely with AI apps and websites. The concept, content, layout and design were produced using [list your tools here, e.g. ChatGPT, Claude, Framer AI], and the site is published on Framer. No traditional manual coding was needed. It shows how a complex, data-rich product concept can go from idea to a working interactive prototype using AI tools alone.

projectDetails.name: FLARE-X: AI Scientific Discovery Platform
projectDetails.summary:
FLARE-X is an AI-powered scientific discovery platform that analyses microgravity combustion research to find hidden patterns in how fire behaves in space. Instead of only displaying existing results, it harmonises experiment data, learns how conditions such as oxygen level and airflow relate to flame behaviour, and flags anomalies, meaning results that deviate from what similar experiments predict. It also maps research gaps in the tested parameter space and recommends the next experiments with the highest expected information gain.

We built a working prototype with an anomaly explorer, a gap map, an experiment recommender, and a natural-language “ask the data” tool. It currently runs on synthetic demo data and is designed to ingest NASA’s real combustion datasets.

This addresses the challenge by turning scattered data into actionable fire-safety insight. It matters because fire is a critical hazard on spacecraft and future Moon and Mars habitats, and experiment time is scarce. FLARE-X helps scientists get more from existing data and focus on the questions that matter most.
projectDetails.details: FLARE-X is an AI-powered discovery platform for microgravity combustion research. It follows four steps: ingest, learn, discover, recommend. Ingest: Combustion experiment data is harmonised into one schema (oxygen level, airflow, fuel or material, spread rate), with each record linked to its source. Learn: The platform estimates the flame behaviour expected under each set of conditions, based on similar experiments. Discover: Experiments that deviate strongly from that expectation are flagged as anomalies and ranked by novelty. Examples are flames that persist at oxygen levels where similar runs burn slowly, or flames that are unexpectedly suppressed. Recommend: A gap map shows which oxygen × airflow regions have little or no data. The recommender ranks the next experiments by sparse coverage, closeness to anomalies, and relevance to crewed-cabin atmospheres. The prototype has four views: an anomaly explorer, a research gap map, a recommended-experiments list, and an “ask the data” search. It currently runs on synthetic demo data that imitates microgravity flame-spread experiments. The analysis pipeline runs live in the browser and is built to accept NASA combustion datasets, such as those in the Physical Sciences Informatics repository. Benefits and intended impact Scientists get more from existing data and can find non-obvious patterns faster. Limited ISS and drop-tower time goes to the experiments most likely to answer open questions. Fire-safety engineers get a clearer picture of which conditions are well understood and which are not. This matters for spacecraft and future Moon and Mars habitats. Findings about flames without buoyancy can also improve combustion models on Earth. Tools and technologies The prototype is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with SVG charts and no external libraries. The anomaly detection (neighbour-based expectation with residual scoring), gap mapping and recommendation scoring are implemented in JavaScript. The demo deck was made with Claude. Planned for the full version: Python (pandas, scikit-learn, PyTorch), Isolation Forest or autoencoders for anomaly detection, SHAP for explainability, Bayesian optimisation for experiment suggestions, and an LLM layer for extracting data from papers and answering questions. No special hardware is required. Creativity Most research tools only display data. FLARE-X is built to generate hypotheses: it points to what looks unusual, shows what has never been tested, and suggests what to run next. Combining anomaly discovery, gap mapping and experiment recommendation in one loop is the core idea. Factors considered Scientific honesty: An anomaly is a hypothesis, not a finding. The platform reports confidence, links each result to its source, and is designed for expert review. Small datasets: Microgravity combustion data is limited, so models can be uncertain and should not be over-trusted. Data quality: Combining datasets with different formats and units can introduce errors, so provenance and spot checks are built in. Transparency: The prototype uses synthetic data, and we state this clearly so no demo result is mistaken for a real discovery. Usability: Researchers and safety engineers can explore the data without writing code.

projectDetails.name: AI WaterWise Kerala
projectDetails.summary: AI WaterWise Kerala is an AI-powered agricultural and environmental monitoring web application that uses NASA POWER rainfall and temperature data to analyse climate patterns across all 14 districts of Kerala. It identifies unusual climate conditions, assesses potential drought risks and provides farmer-oriented recommendations. Through an interactive Streamlit dashboard, users can explore district-level rainfall, temperature, climate anomalies and risk categories. The project aims to transform NASA's open climate data into accessible information that supports climate awareness, agricultural planning and sustainable water management.
projectDetails.details:
Problem Statement Agriculture and water management are affected by changes in rainfall and temperature. Understanding climate variations is important for farmers to make informed agricultural and water-management decisions. Proposed Solution AI WaterWise Kerala is a district-level environmental monitoring and agricultural decision-support web application developed using NASA POWER climate data. Objectives - Monitor rainfall and temperature across 14 districts of Kerala. - Analyse monthly rainfall and yearly average temperature. - Identify unusual climate conditions. - Assess potential drought risks. - Generate farmer-oriented recommendations. Methodology 1. Collect historical rainfall and temperature data from NASA POWER. 2. Process and organise data for all 14 Kerala districts. 3. Calculate monthly rainfall and yearly temperature summaries. 4. Calculate rainfall and temperature anomalies. 5. Classify climate conditions into Normal Condition and Unusual Condition. 6. Categorise drought risks into Normal, Watch and Severe Dry Conditions. 7. Generate recommendations and display the results through a Streamlit dashboard. Technologies Used - Python - Pandas and NumPy - Scikit-learn - Matplotlib - Streamlit - Google Colab - GitHub - NASA POWER Project Results The processed dataset contains 7,714 monthly records covering 14 Kerala districts. The condition classification produced 7,096 Normal Condition labels and 618 Unusual Condition labels. Expected Impact The application makes historical climate information easier to understand and supports agricultural awareness, climate monitoring and sustainable water-management decisions. Limitations and Future Scope The current prototype uses historical climate data and defined drought-risk thresholds. It is not an official weather forecasting or warning system. Future improvements include real-time weather updates, crop-specific recommendations and early-warning notifications. AI Assistance Acknowledgement ChatGPT was used for coding guidance, explanations, documentation and presentation preparation. AI and machine-learning techniques were incorporated into the climate-condition analysis.
