projectDetails.name: Field Shift: Earth Observation-Driven Resilient Crop Rotation Planner
projectDetails.summary:
Smallholder farmers in erratic monsoon regions face severe monocropping degradation, sudden rainfall deficits, and rising temperatures. Field Shift is an open-source, explainable decision support tool that transforms multi-sensor NASA Earth Observations and ground-truth soil testing into resilient 3-to-5 year crop rotation sequences. 

The platform synthesizes NASA POWER agroclimatology, SMAP surface soil moisture, GPM satellite precipitation, MODIS vegetation indices, and Landsat field-scale land surface data alongside ISRIC SoilGrids and local wet-chemistry soil assays. 

Rather than relying on ungrounded black-box AI, Field Shift enforces Stage 1 Hard Agronomic Constraints (temperature biological limits, planting windows, soil pH, and seasonal water budgets) followed by Stage 2 Transparent Linear Scoring across three distinct trade-off profiles: Balanced, Water-First, and Soil-First. An interactive "What-If" climate simulator tests farm resilience under −20% rainfall scenarios in real time, empowering smallholders and agricultural extension officers with portable, downloadable planting calendars.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Field Shift bridges satellite Earth Observations and localized smallholder agriculture through a transparent, 7-step decision workflow:

1.Field Registration & Boundary Confirmation:Smallholders verify their parcel boundary via an interactive Leaflet mapping interface with automated geodesic area calculation (pre-loaded with a 2.4-hectare benchmark farm).

2. Multi-Sensor Environmental Observation: Fetches daily and monthly solar irradiance, temperature extrema, and precipitation totals from the NASA POWER API, alongside satellite soil moisture (SMAP), precipitation estimates (GPM IMERG), and canopy vegetation trends (MODIS/Landsat).

3. Dual-Source Soil Intelligence:*Combines accredited laboratory wet-chemistry tests (pH, organic carbon %, N-P-K in kg/ha, texture, depth) with 250m ISRIC SoilGrids data, displaying explicit data-class badges ([Measured], [Observed], [Modeled], [Farmer-Entered]) and calculating calibration deltas.

4. Stage 1 (Hard Agronomic Constraints): A deterministic screening engine that screens out crops violating physiological temperature ranges, seasonal planting windows, soil pH/drainage thresholds, or water budgets.

5. Stage 2 (Explainable Multi-Year Scoring): Evaluates qualifying crops via a transparent weighted formula:

Suitability = Σ(w_i × s_i)

across Climate, Soil, Water, Season, and Rotation Fit, generating 3-to-5 year sequences across three profiles: Plan A (Balanced Resilience), Plan B (Water-First Optimization), and Plan C (Soil-First Regeneration).

6. Interactive "What-If" Climate Simulator:Allows farmers to stress-test their plan under −20% rainfall deficits, heat spikes (+1°C to +5°C), or delayed monsoons, instantly recalculating constraints to flag water-budget violations.

7. Actionable Decision & Export:Generates one-click standard .ICS planting calendars, comprehensive printable HTML/PDF agronomic audit reports, CSV telemetry datasets, and workspace JSON backups.

What benefits and intended impact does it have?

- Smallholder Climate Resilience:Protects smallholders from catastrophic single-crop failures caused by erratic monsoons and dry spells.

- Soil Health Regeneration: Breaks monoculture pest cycles and rebuilds depleted soil organic carbon through biological nitrogen fixation (cowpea, groundnut) and green manure cover crops (sunn hemp).

- Zero-Cost Accessibility:Built purely on free, publicly accessible NASA Earth Observations and open-source web technologies, requiring no expensive proprietary hardware or subscription fees.

- Farmer Agency & Extension Collaboration: Includes a "Human Override" audit log ensuring local agronomic knowledge (such as canal release dates and lime amendments) takes precedence over coarse satellite grids.

What tools, coding languages, and software were used?

- Frontend & Core Engine: Vanilla JavaScript (ES2024), Semantic HTML5, CSS3 Custom Properties (zero bloated framework dependencies for ultra-fast low-bandwidth loading on rural devices).

- Spatial Mapping: Leaflet.js with OpenStreetMap cartography and surveyor-grade polygon geodesic area calculations.

- Data Analytics & Visualization: Plotly.js for multi-trace dual-axis time-series visualization (rainfall bars, temperature curves, solar radiation).

- APIs & Data Feeds: NASA POWER Agroclimatology API, ISRIC SoilGrids REST API, Open-Meteo near-real-time weather feed.

- Storage & Offline Resilience: Client-side Web Storage (localStorage) and IndexedDB caching for offline field operation.

- Deployment & Hosting: Netlify Static Edge CDN.

4. How is the project creative and innovative?

- Explainability over Black-Box AI:While many modern agricultural apps use opaque generative AI that hallucinates crop recommendations, Field Shift enforces transparent, auditable agronomic rules where every score breakdown is visible and customizable via interactive sliders.

- Multi-Sensor Synthesis: Rather than relying on a single weather dataset, it synthesizes 5 NASA missions spanning optical, thermal, radar, and microwave wavelengths with ground-level laboratory chemistry.

- Uncertainty Safeguards: The platform strictly labels all simulated outputs as "Scenario Assumptions" rather than deterministic forecasts, adhering to the highest standards of scientific integrity.

projectDetails.name: Burn Budget — Design it. Launch it. Don’t run out of fuel.
projectDetails.summary:
Our project is an interactive space mission simulator designed to help students understand the engineering decisions involved in planning and executing space missions.

Players can choose between different exploration missions, design their spacecraft by selecting components and scientific instruments, and manage limited resources such as budget, mass, fuel and power. During the simulated flight, unexpected events require players to make decisions that influence mission performance and success.

The simulator combines mission planning, resource management and interactive decision-making in an engaging learning experience. It aims to make complex space engineering trade-offs easier to understand through experimentation and immediate feedback.
projectDetails.details:
Overview

MISSION CONTROL: Space Mission Simulator is a browser game where you play the mission director. You pick a destination (the Moon, an asteroid, or Mars), design a spacecraft within a budget, launch it, and find out in a debrief whether your design worked and why.

How it works

  1. Choose: Pick a mission. Each one has its own difficulty, budget, mass limit, sunlight level and science goals.
  2. Build: Select the engine, fuel tank, solar panels, antenna and science instruments. A live summary tracks money, mass, fuel needed versus carried, and power balance, with warnings before launch.
  3. Fly: Watch the animated countdown, launch, stage separation and cruise. Random events like faults and signal problems force quick decisions.
  4. Debrief: Get a score out of 100 and a rank from Cadet to Flight Director. The debrief covers mission success, science results, resource management and budget use, with plain-language advice on what went well and what to improve.

The core idea is trade-offs. Heavier craft need more fuel, efficient engines draw more power, and solar panels produce less power far from the Sun. Science objectives only count if you carried the right instrument, it survived, and its data was transmitted back to Earth.

Benefits and impact

The game teaches students and the public that space missions are about engineering decisions, not just launches. Players learn how mass, fuel, power, communications and cost affect each other, and that failure is a useful part of the process. It runs in any browser on desktop or mobile with no install or account, so it is easy to use in classrooms and at outreach events.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript in one self-contained file
  • HTML Canvas API for all graphics (rocket, spacecraft, planets, stars, animation), drawn in code
  • Web Audio API for sound effects, synthesized in the browser with no audio files
  • Google Fonts (Barlow, Barlow Condensed)
  • NASA Solar System Exploration (https://science.nasa.gov/solar-system/) as a reference for mission themes and science goals
  • Claude (Anthropic), a large language model, used to generate about half of the code. The team wrote the rest and reviewed, tested and modified all SI-generated code.

Team

A team of six. We handled the concept, game design, balancing, testing and writing, and wrote about half of the code ourselves.

Creativity

The game turns real engineering constraints into gameplay. Each destination changes the rules, so the design phase decides the outcome and no two missions feel the same. All visuals and sounds are generated by code, which keeps the game small and fast, and it uses no NASA logos or branding.

Factors we considered

  • Realistic trade-offs, simplified for gameplay (values are not real mission data)
  • Easy, Medium and Hard missions so beginners can start with the Moon
  • Scoring that penalizes both overspending and hoarding the budget
  • Clear, encouraging feedback, mobile support and no downloads
  • Transparent SI use: AI-assisted code is disclosed in the project’s metadata, code comments and on-page text

projectDetails.name: Project ARGAL
projectDetails.summary: ARGAL is an analogue finder that links places on the Moon and Mars to similar places on Earth. We built a curated database of sites: 10 lunar, 10 Martian and 15 Earth analogue locations, including Lake Salda in Turkey, the Atacama Desert in Chile and Hawaii’s lava tubes. Every site is described using the same six measures: surface temperature, atmospheric pressure, solar/UV flux, relief variance, regolith grain size and surface slope. A user picks a planetary site, such as Jezero Crater, and ARGAL compares it with the Earth sites, scores each match out of 100 and ranks them, with coordinates and a short geological description. Our top pairing is Jezero Crater and Lake Salda, at 89/100, because both involve ancient lake environments and carbonate deposits. This addresses the challenge by using open NASA data, including LRO, MGS and SRTM, to characterize Earth analogues in a consistent, comparable way. It matters because missions to the Moon and Mars are costly and hard to repeat, so teams must test rovers and habitats on Earth first. ARGAL gives them a clear starting shortlist, and it highlights fragile landscapes worth protecting. The similarity scores are platform-provided and no Earth site matches every condition, so ARGAL is a guide for choosing where to look closer, not a replacement for field testing.
projectDetails.details: ARGAL is an interactive web platform that helps people find places on Earth that resemble sites on the Moon and Mars. You explore the Moon, Mars or Earth on a 3D globe or a flat 2D map and pick a site, and a side panel shows its six physical characteristics: surface temperature, atmospheric pressure, solar/UV flux, relief, grain size and slope. ARGAL then compares that site with its catalogue of Earth locations and ranks them, combining terrain similarity (60%) with environmental similarity (40%), and lets you open any match for a detailed comparison that includes rover compatibility and field experiments. This saves researchers and students from piecing together scattered papers and maps, because every site is described the same way and comparison reports can be exported as Markdown. Our aim is to make planetary analogue exploration more accessible and visual, to point mission teams toward sensible places to test rovers and habitats before launch, and to highlight Earth landscapes, such as polar deserts, lava tubes and ancient lakebeds, that are worth studying and protecting. We built it with HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript, using JavaScript for the 3D globes, Leaflet for the 2D maps, and NASA Trek and Esri map services for imagery . It is creative because it lets you travel across the Moon and Mars like a globe and see the Earth “twin” of any site, instead of reading a table of numbers. While designing it, we kept in mind that no Earth site can fully reproduce the Moon or Mars, so we treat the scores as a guide for deciding where to look closer, not as a replacement for field testing.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. projectDetails.details:
SkyVale is an interactive astronomical exploration and research platform that makes real NASA SPHEREx infrared observations accessible to students, astronomy enthusiasts, and aspiring researchers. Our goal is to transform complex space telescope data into an engaging, understandable, and scientifically meaningful experience.

What does SkyVale do, and how does it work?

NASA's SPHEREx mission surveys the sky across 102 infrared spectral bands, collecting valuable information about astronomical objects. However, accessing and interpreting this data can require specialized scientific knowledge and software.

SkyVale bridges this gap through a guided, five-stage investigation process: Select, Discover, Explore, Analyze, and Report.

Users begin by searching for an astronomical object or selecting a suggested target. SkyVale retrieves relevant information from astronomical databases and NASA's infrared archives, including object coordinates, classifications, observations, and available measurements.

Users can then explore real FITS observations, adjust image visualizations, investigate infrared wavelengths, and interact with scientific graphs. Depending on the available data, SkyVale offers tools for studying stellar motion, brightness variability, and differences between observations. Findings are organized into a research notebook, with options to export scientific reports and data.

The platform also features educational discovery missions, AI-powered assistants, and multiplayer collaboration, allowing users to learn and investigate together.

What are the benefits and intended impact?

SkyVale makes astronomy more accessible by reducing the technical barriers between publicly available scientific data and the people who want to explore it.

Its key benefits include:

  • Accessibility: Beginners can investigate authentic astronomical observations without mastering complicated research software.
  • Scientific exploration: Interactive graphs, image controls, and analytical tools help users understand what the data reveals.
  • Education: Guided investigations encourage curiosity, critical thinking, and practical scientific reasoning.
  • Collaboration: Shared exploration tools allow students and teams to investigate astronomical objects together.
  • Research communication: Structured reports make discoveries easier to document, understand, and share.

Our intended impact is to encourage more young people to engage with astronomy and scientific research, transforming passive interest in space into active exploration using real observational evidence.

What technologies did we use?

SkyVale combines modern web development technologies with established astronomical research tools.

Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, and CSS provide the interactive website, investigation interface, visualizations, and educational features.

Backend: Python and FastAPI handle scientific computations, astronomical data processing, API integrations, and report generation.

Scientific tools: Astropy and related Python libraries support FITS processing, celestial coordinates, World Coordinate System (WCS) transformations, image analysis, and astronomical calculations.

Astronomical resources: NASA's SPHEREx observations are accessed through the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA). Additional integrations include Gaia DR3, SIMBAD, JPL Horizons, AllWISE, and 2MASS for astronomical reference information, positional data, and catalog comparisons.

Artificial intelligence: Groq-powered AI assistants help explain astronomical concepts and guide users through investigations.

Collaboration and development: WebSockets support real-time multiplayer functionality, while Git and GitHub are used for version control and team collaboration.

The platform is software-based and does not require specialized hardware beyond an internet-connected computer or compatible device.

What makes SkyVale creative?

SkyVale's innovation lies in combining real scientific research capabilities with the accessibility of an interactive exploration platform.

Rather than displaying astronomical images without context, SkyVale guides users through a complete investigation. Every stage introduces new information, from identifying an astronomical object to examining infrared observations, interpreting measurements, and producing a research report.

Its combination of NASA infrared data, interactive scientific visualizations, AI-assisted learning, guided investigations, and collaborative exploration creates an experience that is educational without sacrificing scientific purpose.

SkyVale is designed to make users feel like active investigators rather than passive viewers.

What factors did our team consider?

Throughout development, we prioritized scientific accuracy, accessibility, usability, performance, and educational value.

We considered the complexity of infrared astronomical data and designed the platform to explain scientific information progressively. We also focused on maintaining traceability to authentic observations, distinguishing measured information from catalog references, and ensuring that available analysis tools depend on the underlying data.

Because astronomical archives can involve large datasets and external service requests, we considered efficient data retrieval, caching, responsive interactions, and reliable scientific processing.

Finally, we wanted SkyVale to appeal to both beginners and more experienced users while supporting collaborative investigation.

Ultimately, SkyVale aims to make the universe more than something people simply observe. We want to give anyone the opportunity to investigate it, understand it, and make discoveries using real scientific data.

projectDetails.details:
ASTRAEON – The Stories of Spacecraft Beyond Their Missions

ASTRAEON is an interactive space exploration website developed for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, addressing the challenge “Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA’s Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars.” The project aims to bring the stories of spacecraft, landers, rovers, and scientific equipment left behind during space exploration to life.

What Does the Project Do and How Does It Work?

ASTRAEON transforms space exploration into an engaging and interactive learning experience. Users can explore a space-themed environment, navigate between celestial bodies, and discover spacecraft and equipment associated with past NASA missions. The website integrates mission information, scientific discoveries, historical timelines, and spacecraft locations into its exploration experience.

Through interactive exploration, users can learn about objects such as the Apollo Lunar Modules, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Viking landers, and other spacecraft. The website also incorporates spacecraft storytelling, where missions narrate their experiences through creative educational dialogue clearly distinguished from authentic NASA transmissions. Mission timelines and scientific information help users understand the purpose, achievements, and eventual fate of these spacecraft.

Benefits and Intended Impact

ASTRAEON makes complex space science more accessible and enjoyable, particularly for students and young space enthusiasts. It encourages curiosity, independent learning, and interest in astronomy, planetary science, and space technology.

The project highlights the scientific and historical value of spacecraft that are no longer operational, showing that even after their missions end, they continue to contribute to humanity’s understanding of the universe. ASTRAEON hopes to inspire future scientists, engineers, and explorers while preserving the stories of humanity’s achievements in space.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, and Software

The project is developed as a web-based interactive experience using:

  • HTML – for the structure and content of the website.
  • CSS – for the visual design, layout, animations, and responsiveness.
  • JavaScript – for interactive exploration, navigation, controls, and dynamic features.
  • NASA’s publicly available mission information and scientific resources – for accurate mission details and educational content.
  • GitHub – for source-code management and project hosting.
  • Claude AI – for assistance with coding, refining website features, and development.
  • Gamma AI – for assistance in preparing the project presentation.

The project primarily uses software and web technologies and does not require specialized hardware.

Creativity and Innovation

ASTRAEON combines scientific education with interactive exploration and storytelling. Instead of presenting spacecraft information as a conventional list or article, it allows users to discover mission stories through an immersive space environment.

Its creative features include interactive exploration, spacecraft-inspired narration, mission timelines, and the integration of scientific facts with engaging storytelling. This approach transforms abandoned or retired space equipment into meaningful educational experiences and gives users a new perspective on space exploration.

Factors Considered by the Team

During development, the team considered scientific accuracy, educational value, accessibility, user experience, and technical feasibility. NASA mission information and official resources were considered important for ensuring that the content remains reliable.

The team also focused on making the website understandable for school-age audiences, maintaining a clear and user-friendly interface, and preserving the distinction between factual scientific information and creative storytelling. The project was designed to be accessible through a web browser and suitable for further development and expansion.

ASTRAEON ultimately aims to demonstrate that the end of a spacecraft’s mission does not mean the end of its story. Every piece of equipment left in space represents a milestone in humanity’s journey of discovery.

projectDetails.name: Handover
projectDetails.summary:
What did we develop?
We developed HANDOVER, a browser-based space mission design and calibration game where you never fly your own spacecraft. As the Architect, you design a lunar orbiter (such as our baseline Astraquill configuration) under strict mass, power, and budget constraints, inspect uncertainty fog ranges, declare six engineering assumptions with confidence sliders (50%–99%), buy up to three verification tests, and write a strict 200-word Handover Document. Another player—via a shareable Base64 Handover Code—or a rule-based AI Operator then flies 12 operations turns seeing only that document against a hidden, deterministic Reality Engine.
How does it address the challenge?
HANDOVER turns systems engineering into interactive gameplay by uniting real aerospace trade-offs (rocket equation, solar/eclipse energy, thermal, radiation, and link budgets) with risk communication. A post-flight Mission Court traces anomalies through a causal blame graph and scores epistemic calibration alongside mission science.
Why is it important?
Real missions like Mars Climate Orbiter failed from overconfidence and ambiguous handovers. HANDOVER teaches players to quantify uncertainty and document limits clearly.
projectDetails.details:
HANDOVER: Build a spacecraft someone else can fly.

HANDOVER is a browser-based space mission design and calibration game. Most space games test whether a player can build a spacecraft. HANDOVER tests whether the player knows what they do not know, and whether they can pass that knowledge to someone else.

How it works. There are three ways to play:

  • Architect Mode: The player selects a target mission (Lunar Orbiter, with Mars Orbiter as an extended option) and assembles 9 spacecraft subsystems under a strict budget. They inspect “uncertainty fog” around each subsystem, declare 6 engineering assumptions with confidence sliders (50%–99%), and choose from 4 verification tests under a 3-turn schedule cap to narrow uncertainty. They then write a strict 200-word Handover Document with explicit units on every limit. The Lunar Orbiter scenario is modeled on a 100 km low lunar orbit with a 118-minute period, a 40-minute nominal eclipse, a 20% dry mass margin, and a 1361 W/m² solar constant.
  • Operator Mode: The Architect’s design is packed into a Base64 Handover Code (HO1:...). A teammate pastes the code and flies 12 operations turns while seeing only the 200-word document and up to 3 Q&A answers. They face the exact seeded “Reality Engine” truth, just as a real operations team inherits a spacecraft.
  • Ghost Partner Play: Solo players fly one of three prebuilt Ghost Architect packages—Artemis Minimalist (balanced, well-documented), Icarus Express (high risk, flawed handover with a unit-discipline trap), and Aegis Heavy (heavy thermal and power management)—or hand their own design to a deterministic AI Operator.

A deterministic Reality Engine with an optional “Murphy Mode” (which shifts the Architect’s lowest-confidence assumptions adversely) reveals how the design performs across 4 mission events (long eclipse season, solar particle flare, star tracker dropout, and DSN comms dropout). Brier Calibration Scoring (100 × (1 − Brier)) and an interactive Mission Court blame graph trace any anomaly back to an assumption, a skipped test, a documentation/units gap, or an operator mistake. The app also includes Aerospace Learn Cards, a local Heritage Log of flown parts, and a NASA Figures reference.

Benefits. Players practice stating assumptions honestly, matching confidence to evidence, deciding which verification tests are worth their budget and schedule cost, and writing concise, unambiguous handovers. Unclear handovers and overconfident assumptions have contributed to real mission failures—such as the Mars Climate Orbiter’s unit mismatch—and HANDOVER lets players experience that risk safely in about 5 minutes.

Intended impact. It makes systems engineering and flight operations thinking accessible to students, educators, and space enthusiasts while promoting a culture of transparency, unit discipline, and calibrated confidence across engineering teams.

Tools and technology. HANDOVER is a client-side web application with no backend required, built with React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Zustand, and Lucide Icons. It uses a deterministic Mulberry32 seeded random-number generator and truncated normal sampling so every run is reproducible and fair. Handover Codes are Base64-encoded for server-free sharing, and browser localStorage persists the Heritage Log on the player’s device. It incorporates NASA data and case studies including NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) orbital and eclipse parameters, NASA SORCE/TIM Total Solar Irradiance (1361 W/m²), Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (MRO) parameters, the Mars Climate Orbiter Mishap Investigation Board Phase I Report, the Apollo 13 Review Board Report, and the NASA Systems Engineering Handbook (NASA/SP-2016-6105).

Creativity. Rather than rewarding only hardware performance, HANDOVER scores epistemic calibration—penalizing overconfidence and rewarding honest uncertainty. The strict 200-word limit forces engineering prioritization, the unit-trap mechanic turns a historic NASA mishap into playable systems engineering, and the swap-play loop lets players experience the consequences of their own documentation firsthand.

Factors the team considered. Scientific realism, fairness through deterministic seeding, accessibility for non-experts via visual uncertainty fog and Learn Cards, a fast ~5-minute replayable loop, and seamless solo or team play with zero backend dependencies.

projectDetails.name: Project Astra XYZ
projectDetails.summary:
I work in preventive medicine, where a surveillance signal should tell us where to look next. I built Astra XYZ to bring that way of thinking to NASA Earth data. The tool lets users explore 33 years of air temperature, relative humidity, and surface soil wetness across five locations in Ghana using NASA POWER data.

Users can compare locations, switch between annual means and baseline anomalies, and see the direction, rate, and uncertainty of each trend. In Accra, mean air temperature rose by 0.17 °C per decade, with a nominal 95% confidence interval of 0.13 to 0.20 °C per decade. Accra was the only location where both adjusted temperature trend tests flagged a change.

For a public health team, that is a starting point for investigation. The next step is to compare these environmental signals with local weather, mosquito surveillance, and confirmed cases before setting any threshold for action.
projectDetails.details:
In preventive medicine, the first question a surveillance signal should answer is where should we look more closely? I built Astra XYZ to ask that question of NASA Earth data. The interactive tool lets users explore 33 years of air temperature, relative humidity, and surface soil wetness at five locations in Ghana using NASA POWER data from 1991 to 2023.

Users select a variable and location, then switch between annual values and departures from the 1991–2007 baseline. Sen’s slope estimates the change per decade, with a nominal 95% confidence interval. An annual Mann–Kendall test assesses the trend, and a Newey–West trend t-test checks how sensitive the result is to serial dependence. We adjusted for 15 comparisons and flagged a trend only when both tests met the significance criterion and the slopes agreed in direction. In Accra, air temperature rose by 0.17 °C per decade, with a nominal 95% confidence interval of 0.13 to 0.20 °C. It was the only location where both adjusted temperature tests flagged a trend.

The creative step was to treat environmental trends as leads for public health surveillance. A district team could use a flagged location to decide where to review local weather records, mosquito surveillance, and confirmed cases together. We considered seasonal variation, correlation between successive years, multiple comparisons, and the limits of interpreting five model grid locations. Disease forecasting would require local outcome data and validation before setting thresholds for action.

We used Python, NumPy, and SciPy for the analysis and HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the browser-based explorer. The project runs on a standard computer and includes the original NASA data, analysis code, and downloadable results so others can check and reproduce the findings.

projectDetails.name: Project A S T R I X
projectDetails.summary:
Space Survival: The 5-Day Mission is an interactive astronaut survival game developed using PictoBlox. Players take the role of an astronaut stranded in space after Earth's communication systems suddenly fail during their first mission. Their objective is to survive for five days until a rescue rocket arrives.

Players must carefully manage three essential resources: oxygen, food, and spacecraft power. Each resource decreases over time, and reaching zero in any one of them results in mission failure. With limited money, players must make strategic decisions to recharge resources and stay alive.

The project addresses the challenges of space exploration by introducing players to resource management, life-support systems, and emergency decision-making. It is important because it transforms complex survival challenges into an engaging and educational gaming experience, encouraging critical thinking and awareness of astronaut safety.
projectDetails.details:
Space Survival: The 5-Day Mission is an interactive astronaut survival game developed using PictoBlox. Players take on the role of a newly trained astronaut whose first space mission goes wrong when Earth's communication systems suddenly crash, leaving them stranded in space for five days until a rescue rocket arrives.

To survive, players must carefully manage three essential resources: oxygen, food, and spacecraft power. Each resource decreases over time, and if any one reaches zero, the mission fails. Players must strategically spend their limited money to recharge these resources and make critical decisions to stay alive until rescue.

The project's main benefit is its educational approach to introducing resource management, logical thinking, strategic decision-making, and the challenges of space exploration. It aims to raise awareness of the importance of life-support systems, limited supplies, and emergency preparedness in astronaut missions.

The game was developed using PictoBlox, incorporating interactive gameplay, resource-management mechanics, and survival conditions. Its creativity lies in transforming real-world space survival challenges into an engaging, time-based gaming experience.

During development, we considered resource limitations, survival conditions, gameplay simplicity, player engagement, and the importance of connecting the game to real-world space exploration challenges.

Our goal is to make players think like astronauts: every decision matters, and survival depends on how wisely resources are managed.

projectDetails.name: VYOMA – Astronaut Health Intelligence System
projectDetails.summary:
VYOMA – Astronaut Health Intelligence System is an intelligent health monitoring and self-management platform designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. It addresses health challenges associated with microgravity, radiation exposure, isolation, and changing space environments by integrating physiological, behavioral, and environmental health monitoring.

VYOMA enables astronauts to track vital signs, sleep patterns, stress levels, and environmental conditions through a unified dashboard. Its personalized health analysis engine compares current measurements against individual health baselines to identify unusual patterns and potential risks. An AI-powered health assistant helps astronauts understand health changes, interpret alerts, and access actionable, protocol-based guidance. The platform also emphasizes offline accessibility, ensuring essential health records and monitoring capabilities remain available during communication disruptions.

By combining personalized health insights, anomaly detection, and intelligent decision support, VYOMA aims to empower astronauts to take a more proactive role in managing their health and well-being throughout space missions.
projectDetails.details:
VYOMA – Space Health Intelligence System

Space missions can last for months or even years, and keeping astronauts healthy throughout these missions is a major challenge. VYOMA is our attempt to address this challenge through a digital platform that helps monitor astronaut health, identify unusual changes in vital signs and provide useful health insights in one place.

How VYOMA works

The platform is built around four main modules:

  1. Dashboard: Gives a quick overview of an astronaut's health, including recent readings, overall status and important alerts.
  2. VitalWatch: Keeps track of important health parameters such as heart rate, heart rate variability (HRV), blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), blood pressure, body temperature and respiratory rate. It also allows users to view historical readings and compare them with individual baselines.
  3. HealthSense AI: Examines changes in physiological readings and highlights values that differ from an astronaut's usual baseline. It also provides explanations and suggested checks to help users understand these changes.
  4. Alerts & Triage: Brings abnormal readings to the user's attention, displays their severity and allows alerts to be acknowledged and resolved.

NASA resources and how we used them

While developing VYOMA, we referred to NASA's Human Research Program resource, 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight. It helped us understand some of the major health challenges astronauts may face during space missions and guided our thinking while designing the platform.

We considered the five hazards in the following ways:

  • Radiation: Helped us recognize the importance of considering radiation exposure when thinking about astronaut health and environmental safety.
  • Isolation and confinement: Made us consider the psychological well-being of astronauts and the need for support during long missions.
  • Distance from Earth: Highlighted why reliable health monitoring is important when astronauts may not have immediate access to medical support from Earth.
  • Gravity fields: Helped us understand why physiological changes associated with spaceflight should be considered when monitoring vital signs.
  • Hostile and closed environments: Encouraged us to consider how environmental conditions inside a spacecraft could affect astronaut health.

We used this NASA resource as a reference while planning the project; it is not directly connected to the application's data system. The current prototype uses simulated astronaut telemetry for demonstration and testing. It does not use actual astronaut medical records or live NASA spacecraft data.

Technologies and tools used

We developed the backend using Python and FastAPI, with PostgreSQL to store astronaut profiles, vital readings and health alerts. SQLAlchemy handles database interactions, while Pydantic is used for data validation and API schemas. The frontend brings these components together through dashboards, charts and interactive monitoring screens.

We also used AI tools such as ChatGPT and Claude during development. They helped us with debugging, understanding technical concepts, improving code and refining the user interface. OpenAI's image-generation tools were used to create some of the illustrations included in the website. These images are clearly marked as AI-generated.

Expected impact

Through VYOMA, we aim to demonstrate how a single platform can make astronaut health information easier to monitor and understand. By bringing together vital readings, historical trends, explainable insights and alerts, the system could help medical teams identify unusual changes and review them more efficiently during long-duration missions.

VYOMA is currently a prototype developed for demonstration and research purposes. Its simulated readings, thresholds and automated insights have not been clinically validated. The platform is intended to support health monitoring concepts, not replace professional medical judgement.

projectDetails.name: Field Shift: Satellite-Driven Crop Rotation & Resilience Planner
projectDetails.summary:
Field Shift: Satellite-Driven Crop Rotation & Resilience Planner is a user-friendly web decision support system that provides information to farmers on how best to rotate crops on their farms to accommodate changes in climatic conditions year after year.

The online portal combines 10-year earth observation data from NASA including SMAP, root-zone soil moisture, GPM extreme precipitation and runoff, ECOSTRESS vegetation water stress and POWER agro-climatology data with local soil characteristics and crop properties. The users can weigh various factors such as water management, soil conservation, profit variability, and pest breaks to assess four years of customized rotation strategies relative to the current strategy. Users also have the option to substitute crops and stress test their chosen crop rotation strategy through the portal.

With the translation of earth observation satellite databases into simple language suggestions for the growers’ fields, Field Shift enables growers to preserve topsoils, conserve water, minimize the use of chemical fertilizers and build farm sustainability.
projectDetails.details:
🌱 Field Shift – Helping Farmers Make Smarter Decisions

Field Shift is a web app that helps farmers plan which crops to grow over the next four years. Nowadays, climate change is making farming more difficult because of changing rainfall, rising temperatures, and water shortages. Our idea is to help farmers prepare for these challenges and make better decisions.

The app uses the last 10 years of NASA satellite data (2016–2026), along with local soil details, to understand the farming conditions.

Farmers can enter information about their soil and choose what they want to focus on, such as saving water, improving soil health, earning a steady income, or reducing pest problems. Based on their choices, Field Shift suggests three different crop rotation plans: Water-Saver, Soil-Builder, and Balanced Resilience. It also compares these plans with the farmer's current farming method.

One useful feature is that farmers can check how their crop plans might perform during difficult weather conditions, like a 2°C rise in temperature or a 30% drop in summer rainfall. They can also change crops and see how it affects water usage, soil health, and profit. Once they are happy with the plan, they can download it as a PDF or CSV file.

🌍 Impact

Our main aim is to make farming information easier to understand and use. Instead of showing complicated satellite data, the app gives farmers simple alerts and clear crop recommendations.

In water-stressed conditions, our model shows the potential to reduce irrigation requirements by up to 46%. It also suggests growing legumes and cover crops, which can improve soil quality, prevent soil erosion, and reduce fertilizer expenses.

We considered different farming conditions while developing this idea, including farms in the U.S. High Plains and small farms in Kerala, India.

💻 Technologies Used

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript
  • Tailwind CSS
  • Chart.js
  • NASA SMAP, GPM, ECOSTRESS and POWER data
  • ISRIC SoilGrids

🎨 Design and User Experience

We wanted to make the app simple enough for farmers to use without needing technical knowledge. The main screen shows important information like water requirements, soil condition, and suggested crops instead of complicated scientific data.

Farmers are free to change the suggested crops according to their needs. Another important feature is that the app works offline, so it can still be used in areas where internet connectivity is poor.

Our Vision

We believe farming should be prepared for the future, not just the present. Through Field Shift, we want to help farmers save water, improve soil health, reduce farming risks, and make better crop decisions even as the climate changes.

projectDetails.name: Project AstroMark V
projectDetails.summary:
Mars: Last Line of Defence is a mobile-friendly, interactive mission trainer that lets young learners command a crewed Mars mission and experience the trade-offs behind real spaceflight. Players explore a 3D Mars with 51 proposed landing sites, choose a landing zone, then take command of the crew and manage life support, power, oxygen and hull integrity while crises unfold, such as a solar storm, a failing oxygen tank or a rover running low on power.

Each decision is explained afterwards, so students learn why NASA crews make the calls they do. This addresses the challenge by turning engineering trade-offs into tangible, fun choices instead of oversimplified facts.

The game is connected to real NASA data (DONKI solar storms and CMEs, OSDR, RadLab radiation doses, plus APOD and near-Earth object feeds) through a secure Netlify proxy, with an offline archive fallback. Players learn that radiation shielding, power and food production determine whether a mission fails or succeeds. Built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, it needs no install and runs in any browser.
projectDetails.details:
Mars: Last Line of Defence is a browser-based interactive mission trainer for young learners. Players explore a 3D Mars with 51 proposed human landing sites, choose a site, then take command of a crew and keep life support, power, oxygen and hull integrity running through emergencies such as solar storms, a failed oxygen tank or a rover short on power. After every decision the game explains what real NASA crews do and why, so students feel the engineering trade-offs instead of memorising facts.

Benefits: it makes radiation shielding, power budgeting and risk decisions tangible and fun, and it runs on any phone or computer with no install.

Impact: it helps students understand why Mars missions succeed or fail and builds interest in space science and engineering.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, three.js for the 3D globe, Netlify for hosting, and a Netlify serverless function that proxies NASA APIs so the key is not exposed. Live NASA data (DONKI solar storms, OSDR, RadLab, APOD, NEO, planetary K-index) is shown in the DATA tab, with an offline archive fallback.

Creativity: real mission scenarios and live space-weather data are combined into one playable story.

projectDetails.name: Project Vitals Deck
projectDetails.summary:
Vitals Deck is an offline health self-check for astronauts on long missions. Crew log a two-minute daily check-in covering vitals, sleep, mood, exercise, cabin CO₂ and radiation. The app then flags problems against fixed limits, personal baselines, trends and patterns, shows a clickable body map, and gives clear next steps.
Also even if they want to send a message to earth it would take 3-22 minutes to arrive and another 22 minutes to receive a response. that's why its offline
projectDetails.details:
Here are the details about your project, structured around the questions you asked:

  • What it does and how it works

    • It is an instrument-panel dashboard and crew health self-assessment tool designed for spaceflight environments (such as a low Earth orbit station, lunar transit, or Mars transit).
    • It allows crew members to log a daily check-in of vital physiological and psychological indicators (including resting heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, blood oxygen, glucose, sleep, mood, exercise minutes, cabin CO₂, and radiation dose).
    • It evaluates these entries against absolute safety limits, personal baselines established over the first 7 check-ins, multi-day trends, and known clinical symptom combinations to flag potential health risks.
    • It provides actionable self-care steps or flags when to contact the crew medical officer or flight surgeon, alongside a generated report summary that can be copied.
    • Empowers crew members to monitor health proactively in isolated environments without requiring live telemetry links.
    • Accounts for communication delays on deep space missions (such as Mars transit) by providing immediate, local triage guidance.
    • Tracks longitudinal trends rather than just isolated noise, catching multi-day drifts in sleep, exercise, or mood.
    • Mitigates prominent human spaceflight hazards identified by NASA's Human Research Program—such as cardiovascular deconditioning, behavioral strain, sleep disruption, and reduced musculoskeletal fitness.
    • Enhances crew autonomy and safety during long-duration exploration missions.
    • Built as a complete, offline-first web application using standard front-end web technologies (HTML, CSS, and JavaScript wrapped in a single file).
    • Leverages local storage to keep user readings securely and privately within the browser.
    • Designed to mirror manual data logging procedures used with actual spacecraft medical devices.
    • Translates complex aerospace medical frameworks and NASA Human Research Program risk lists into an intuitive, gamified instrument-panel aesthetic with interactive body maps and real-time visual status indicators.
    • Features adaptive feedback that tracks custom baselines and multi-symptom patterns (like headache paired with high cabin CO₂ or short sleep paired with low mood) rather than isolated thresholds.
    • Operational Realism: Factoring in communication light-speed delays for deep space exploration versus low Earth orbit.
    • Privacy & Reliability: Ensuring the app works entirely offline inside a browser without relying on external servers or cloud databases.
    • Psychological Safety: Rewarding consistency (streaks and logging) rather than penalizing bad health numbers, keeping the tool supportive and honest.

projectDetails.details:
ASTROGUARD 360 – Project Details

Project Overview

ASTROGUARD 360 is an AI-assisted astronaut health monitoring and early warning platform designed to explore ways of supporting crew health during long-duration human spaceflight missions.

Astronauts travelling to the Moon, Mars and other deep-space destinations may face physiological, psychological and environmental challenges. Monitoring individual health trends can help improve awareness of potential risks.

How It Works

The platform presents astronaut health measurements such as heart rate, blood pressure, blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), body temperature, sleep duration and mood.

It organizes health information into individual profiles and displays measurements, personal baselines, historical trends and alerts. The prototype uses simulated crew telemetry for demonstration purposes.

The anomaly-monitoring concept aims to identify unusual changes compared with individual baselines and provide understandable explanations. These alerts are intended to support awareness and are not medical diagnoses.

NASA's Five Human-Spaceflight Hazards

ASTROGUARD 360 connects astronaut health monitoring with NASA's five major human-spaceflight hazards:

  1. Space radiation.
  2. Isolation and confinement.
  3. Distance from Earth.
  4. Altered gravity fields.
  5. Hostile and closed environments.

The platform explains how these hazards can affect astronaut health and mission safety.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The project aims to improve awareness of astronaut health trends, support individual health monitoring and demonstrate how AI-assisted technologies could contribute to future space-health decision-support systems.

It is particularly relevant to long-duration missions where communication delays and limited access to medical support create additional challenges.

Technology and Development Tools

Google AI Studio Build Mode was used to assist in developing the ASTROGUARD 360 web application and its user interface. The application demonstrates astronaut health dashboards, simulated crew telemetry, health measurements, visualizations, alerts and space-health information.

ChatGPT was also used to support brainstorming, technical explanations, content preparation and development assistance.

Only technologies and services actually implemented in the final application should be listed as additional development tools. The prototype uses simulated health data for demonstration and does not claim to access real astronaut medical records.

Creativity and Innovation

The main idea behind ASTROGUARD 360 is to bring astronaut health measurements, individual baseline monitoring, understandable alerts and NASA's five human-spaceflight hazards together in one platform.

Instead of displaying health readings in isolation, the project focuses on understanding changes over time and presenting relevant health information in a clear dashboard.

Factors Considered

The team considered data reliability, individual health differences, scientific references, privacy, communication delays, system availability and the limitations of AI-generated information.

All synthetic demonstration data are identified as simulated. ASTROGUARD 360 is an educational prototype and decision-support concept, not a clinically validated medical device.

projectDetails.name: Outpost Explorers
projectDetails.summary:
Outpost Explorers is an interactive educational website developed by Team ASTRONAVIGATORS for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It is designed to help children and young learners explore the Moon, Mars, and the scientific and engineering challenges of living beyond Earth.

Our project combines four learning experiences: an introduction to future space outposts, a Mission Atlas featuring real space missions, an interactive space quiz, and a 3D Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer.

In the mission trainer, players select a Moon or Mars environment, choose their difficulty level, examine orbital clues, and undertake simulated astronaut duties. They must think about limited resources such as power, water, and food while exploring habitats, laboratories, greenhouses, and planetary surfaces.

The experience also introduces two cooperative astronaut roles, Engineer and Scientist, encouraging communication, teamwork, and shared problem-solving.

Outpost Explorers addresses the challenge by transforming complex space-exploration concepts into accessible, interactive learning experiences. Rather than only reading about astronaut survival, students can explore simplified scenarios, make decisions, and consider their consequences.

Our goal is to inspire curiosity, scientific thinking, and confidence in the next generation of space explorers.

The trainer is an educational simulation, not a real mission-planning system.
projectDetails.details:
## Outpost Explorers — Detailed Project Description

### The problem

Living on the Moon or Mars involves complex challenges. Astronauts must operate in environments without breathable air, protect themselves from radiation, manage limited resources, conduct scientific investigations, and maintain communication with Earth.

These concepts can be difficult for young learners to understand through descriptions and diagrams alone.

Our project aims to make the underlying scientific ideas more accessible through interactive exploration and decision-making.

### Our solution

Outpost Explorers is an educational website that brings together information about real space exploration and a playable 3D astronaut-training simulation.

The website contains four main components:

**1. Outpost Exploration**

Learners discover the essential systems required for a future Moon or Mars settlement, including crew habitats, laboratories, greenhouses, power systems, rovers, and communication equipment.

**2. Mission Atlas**

The Mission Atlas introduces real space missions conducted by organisations and space agencies around the world.

Users can select missions to learn about their purposes, explore mission summaries, and view available 3D demonstrations.

**3. Space Quiz**

An interactive quiz helps learners review their understanding of space exploration and the scientific concepts introduced throughout the website.

**4. 3D Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer**

The trainer is the central interactive component of Outpost Explorers.

Players begin by choosing either Beginner or Pro mode.

Beginner mode provides simpler instructions and more available supplies, making it suitable for new learners. Pro mode introduces more demanding resource conditions and detailed choices.

Players then select a Moon or Mars environment and begin their mission.

### How the mission works

**Stage 1: Orbital investigation**

Before reaching the surface, learners choose an orbital scan and consider evidence related to possible water, available sunlight, terrain, routes, and communication.

The trainer encourages players to distinguish between scientific clues and confirmed conclusions. For example, evidence suggesting water may be present does not prove that usable water exists.

**Stage 2: Surface operations**

After arriving at the outpost, players monitor their mission panel, examine current problems, and select duties for the Engineer and Scientist.

They consider the effects of their choices on simplified resources such as power, water, food, and other supplies.

**Stage 3: Exploration and investigation**

Players can explore the outpost's laboratory, farm, and crew home, use airlock controls, operate a rover, and collect nearby rock samples for study.

First-person and third-person camera options help users examine indoor environments and navigate outdoor areas.

**Stage 4: Collaborative exploration**

The Connect Crew feature allows two players to join a shared experience using an invitation link or code.

The Engineer and Scientist can coordinate their tasks using a built-in text chat, encouraging communication and cooperation.

### What makes the project different?

Outpost Explorers combines educational content, interactive 3D exploration, simulated resource-management decisions, scientific investigation, and cooperative gameplay.

Rather than treating space exploration as a collection of isolated facts, it introduces learners to the connections between technology, environmental conditions, scientific evidence, and teamwork.

### Educational benefits

Our project is designed to encourage:

- Scientific curiosity and evidence-based reasoning.

- Problem-solving and decision-making.

- Understanding of resource limitations and trade-offs.

- Awareness of Moon and Mars exploration.

- Communication and teamwork.

- Interest in STEM subjects.

Teachers, students, parents, and science enthusiasts can use the website as an introduction to the challenges of future space exploration.

### Our long-term vision

We hope to develop Outpost Explorers into a richer educational experience with additional mission scenarios, improved scientific data integration, more interactive equipment, and expanded learning activities.

Our larger goal is to make space science engaging, understandable, and accessible to young learners.

**Scientific limitation:** The astronaut trainer uses simplified educational scenarios and fictional resource values. It is not intended for real astronaut training, engineering operations, or actual mission planning.

projectDetails.name: AstroMission – Space Mission Design Game
projectDetails.summary: AstroMission is an interactive space mission design game that allows users to experience the challenges of planning a space exploration mission. Players can select a destination, choose spacecraft and scientific instruments, and manage important resources such as fuel, power, mass and budget. The game demonstrates how engineering decisions affect mission success. It aims to make space exploration and mission planning easier to understand through an engaging and educational simulation. By combining game-based learning with space science concepts, AstroMission encourages students to explore the technologies and decisions involved in real-world space missions.
projectDetails.details:
AstroMission is an interactive space mission design game. Players choose a destination (Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune or Pluto), a mission type (flyby, orbiter or lander), a spacecraft bus, launch vehicle, power system, propulsion and science instruments. Live meters show budget, launch mass, power, delta-v and flight time. When every check passes, the player launches and watches the transfer orbit, and each mission phase (launch, cruise, course correction, arrival, operations) succeeds or fails based on the design's margins.

How it works: the game uses NASA Planetary Fact Sheet values (mass, diameter, gravity, escape velocity, distance from the Sun, orbital period and velocity). From these it calculates Hohmann transfer delta-v and flight time, propellant mass with the rocket equation, and solar power with the inverse-square law using the 1361 W/m2 solar constant. Budget tiers and the power and instrument classes are modelled on NASA's Europa Clipper (about $5.2 billion, 9 science instruments) and Mars 2020 (about $2.4 billion, 110 W radioisotope power, 7 instruments).

Benefits and impact: students and teachers can feel why real missions need more fuel, power and money as targets get farther away, without needing equations. We hope to make mission planning approachable and inspire interest in space careers.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript (single page with canvas animation) and Google Fonts. The code, interface and visuals were generated with an SI tool (Claude, by Anthropic) from our own game concept and design brief, and are labelled as SI-generated in the game (canvas watermark, footer and page metadata).

Creativity: gravity-assist and electric-propulsion trade-offs, three real-budget tiers, and a success chance for every mission phase based on the player's margins.

Limitations: calculations are simplified (patched conics, Hohmann transfers). Instrument masses, power and costs are game-balanced estimates, not real instrument specifications.

projectDetails.name: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
projectDetails.summary:
The Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive, browser-based space exploration simulator designed to introduce elementary students to aerospace engineering, space science, and robotics through hands-on learning.

We developed a six-mission training platform that follows a Plan → Execute → Evaluate approach. Students can assemble and launch rockets, manage space station life-support systems, establish lunar bases, program Mars rovers, design Earth-observation satellites, and simulate asteroid deflection. The platform combines realistic physics calculations, interactive simulations, coding activities, and post-mission assessments to make complex scientific concepts accessible and engaging.

It addresses the challenge of making STEM education more practical, immersive, and inclusive by transforming theoretical concepts into interactive space missions. With COPPA-compliant zero-PII student accounts, educator dashboards, accessibility features, and NGSS-aligned learning outcomes, the platform provides a safe and inclusive learning environment.

Our goal is to inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers, and astronauts by making space exploration an engaging educational experience.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

The Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive, browser-based STEM learning platform designed for children aged 5–11. It transforms space science and aerospace engineering into an engaging, hands-on learning experience through six simulated space missions.

How It Works:

The platform follows a Plan → Execute → Evaluate learning cycle. Students begin by assembling rockets, selecting engines, fuel tanks, and payloads while observing real-time physics calculations such as mass, thrust, Delta-V, and thrust-to-weight ratio. They then execute simulated rocket launches featuring countdowns, engine effects, atmospheric transitions, and orbital velocity tracking.

Beyond rocket launches, students can manage space station life-support systems, design lunar bases, program Mars rovers using drag-and-drop commands, configure Earth-observation satellites, and simulate asteroid deflection. Each mission includes learning assessments, progress tracking, and achievement badges.

Technology and Tools Used:

  • Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS.
  • Backend: Node.js with a custom REST API.
  • Database: JSON-based data storage.
  • Physics: Newton's laws of motion, Tsiolkovsky's Delta-V equation, and atmospheric drag simulation.
  • Audio: Web Audio API and Web Speech API.
  • Security: COPPA validation middleware, input sanitization, and zero-PII data handling.
  • Testing: Node.js native test runner.

The application is developed as a browser-based software solution and does not require dedicated external hardware.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

The project makes complex scientific concepts easier to understand through interactive experimentation rather than traditional textbook learning. It encourages critical thinking, problem-solving, computational thinking, creativity, and engineering skills. Educators can monitor classroom progress, track mission completion, and evaluate student understanding through a dedicated command center.

Creativity and Innovation:

The project's uniqueness lies in combining six different areas of space exploration into one educational platform. Instead of simply learning about rockets, planets, and satellites, children actively participate in simulated missions and experience the consequences of their engineering decisions.

Factors Considered:

Our team considered age-appropriate learning, scientific accuracy, accessibility, child safety, data privacy, usability, and educational relevance. Features such as adjustable text sizes, high-contrast mode, colorblind-friendly patterns, keyboard navigation, and voice narration make the platform more inclusive. COPPA-compliant zero-PII architecture helps create a safer digital learning environment.

Ultimately, our vision is to make aerospace education accessible, interactive, and inspiring, encouraging young learners to explore STEM and become tomorrow's scientists, engineers, and astronauts.

projectDetails.details:
Detailed description

NISAR – AI-Powered Earth Observation App 🌍

Our project is an AI-powered Earth Observation App designed to help people explore and understand Earth's surface using satellite data from the NISAR mission, a joint project of NASA (USA) and ISRO (India).

NISAR stands for NASA–ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar. It uses advanced radar technology to observe Earth's surface during both day and night, even through clouds. It collects important information about changes in land, forests, glaciers, water and other natural features.

Our app is being developed using Emergent.sh, an AI-powered app-building platform. It aims to convert complex satellite information into simple maps and visual displays that everyone can understand.

Main Features of Our App

Interactive Earth Map: Allows users to explore different locations on Earth.

Satellite Data Display: Shows available NISAR satellite measurements.

Surface Change Detection: Helps users explore changes in Earth's surface over time.

Environmental Monitoring: Supports the study of forests, glaciers, land and water.

AI Explanation: Uses AI to explain satellite data in simple language.

Location-Based Exploration: Allows users to select an area and explore available satellite observations.

Purpose of the Project

The main purpose is to make advanced space technology useful and understandable to everyone. It can help students, researchers and scientists explore Earth's changes and learn more about environmental conditions.

Expected Impact

Better understanding of natural disasters.

Awareness about climate change.

Monitoring of forests and the environment.

Support for scientific learning and research.

Increased awareness about protecting our planet.

Our Vision: To transform complex satellite data into simple and meaningful information, helping everyone understand our changing Earth.

projectDetails.details:
GALAXY RUN – MISSION BEYOND EARTH

1. What does your project do or how does it work?

GALAXY RUN is an interactive space exploration and mission simulation game inspired by the Google Chrome Dinosaur game. Instead of a dinosaur, players control a futuristic spaceship travelling through space. Players must avoid obstacles such as asteroids, fireballs, meteor showers, and space debris. The game also includes spacecraft design, mission selection, fuel management, power management, scientific instruments, and communication systems. Players make engineering decisions to complete missions to the Moon, Mars, and asteroids successfully.

2. What benefits does your project have?

The project makes learning about space exploration and engineering more interesting and interactive. It helps students understand spacecraft design, resource management, scientific instruments, orbital challenges, and mission planning. It also develops problem-solving, critical-thinking, and decision-making skills through gameplay.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our main aim is to make complex space engineering concepts easier for students to understand through an enjoyable gaming experience. The project encourages curiosity about astronomy, space technology, and scientific exploration. It demonstrates how engineering decisions and limited resources influence the success of real-world space missions.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Programming Language: Python.
  • Game Development Library: Pygame.
  • Development Environment: Google AntiGravity.
  • Deployment Platform: Vercel (for the browser-compatible version).
  • Scientific References: Official NASA educational resources.
  • Hardware: A computer or laptop for development and gameplay.

5. How is your project creative?

The creativity of GALAXY RUN comes from combining an endless-runner arcade game with space mission simulation. Instead of simply avoiding obstacles, players must also manage spacecraft resources, select scientific equipment, and make important engineering decisions. The space-themed environment, animated obstacles, interactive missions, and real astronomical facts create an educational gaming experience.

6. What factors did your team consider?

Our team considered several important factors while designing the project:

  • Mission objectives: Different goals for Moon, Mars, and asteroid exploration.
  • Budget: Keeping spacecraft development within limited credits.
  • Mass: Ensuring the spacecraft does not exceed its mass limit.
  • Fuel: Maintaining sufficient fuel for the journey.
  • Power: Managing energy for spacecraft operations and scientific instruments.
  • Communication: Maintaining contact with the spacecraft.
  • Safety: Avoiding asteroids and other space hazards.
  • Scientific accuracy: Using educational information from official NASA resources.
  • User experience: Making the game attractive, simple, interactive, and enjoyable.

Overall, GALAXY RUN demonstrates how gaming can make space science and engineering education more engaging while helping students understand the importance of planning, resource management, and effective decision-making.

projectDetails.name: Project Terralens
projectDetails.summary:
TerraLens (PlanetIQ) is an open-source Earth observation and environmental analysis platform built with NASA Earth science datasets and geospatial visualization tools. Designed for students, researchers, and the general public, it helps users explore interactions across Earth's ocean, atmosphere, and land systems.
Core NASA Datasets:
 * Ocean (SWOT Mission): Tracks Sea Surface Height anomalies and ocean topography.
 * Atmosphere (GPM IMERG): Analyzes global precipitation and extreme weather trends.
 * Land (MODIS): Monitors vegetation dynamics, photosynthetic activity, and drought impacts.
Technology & Architecture:
 * Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL JS for mapping, and Recharts for data visualization.
 * Backend & Database: Python 3.11+, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy 2, and PostgreSQL 16 with PostGIS 3.4 for spatial data management.
 * AI & Deployment: Integrates the Google Gemini API for scientifically grounded data interpretation and deploys via Render Blueprints.
projectDetails.details: TerraLens (PlanetIQ) is an open-source, interactive Earth observation and environmental analysis platform powered by NASA Earth science datasets and geospatial visualization technologies. What It Does & How It Works TerraLens visualizes and analyzes interactions across Earth's interconnected ocean, atmosphere, and terrestrial systems. It ingests real NASA Earth observation data—specifically SWOT Mission ocean topography, GPM IMERG global precipitation (GPM_3IMERGM), and MODIS vegetation indices (MOD13C2)—into a spatial database. Users explore these datasets through interactive maps and charts while leveraging the Google Gemini API for scientifically grounded data interpretation. Benefits & Intended Impact * Accessibility: Translates complex satellite datasets into intuitive visual and AI-assisted insights. * Target Audience: Empowers high school students, university researchers, and the curious public to understand environmental changes, drought impacts, sea level dynamics, and extreme weather trends. * Open Science: Released under the MIT Open-Source License with transparent dataset documentation covering provenance, units, and scientific limitations. Tools, Languages & Software Used * Frontend: TypeScript, React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL JS (mapping), Recharts (charting), and Lucide Icons. * Backend & Database: Python 3.11+, FastAPI, Pydantic v2, SQLAlchemy 2, asyncpg, GeoAlchemy2, and PostgreSQL 16 with PostGIS 3.4. * AI & DevOps: Google Gemini API, GitHub Actions (CI), Docker/Render Blueprints (render.yaml), and uv/npm. Creativity & Key Design Considerations * Creative Integration: Combines multi-domain NASA satellite telemetry with interactive geospatial rendering and generative AI to bridge raw scientific data and public comprehension. * Scientific Integrity & Security: Enforces strict development rules against hardcoding sample data as real observations, documents dataset limitations explicitly, and uses strict .gitignore and environment templates to protect secrets.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Nova’s Mission Control
projectDetails.summary: Mission Control Academy is a kid-friendly game where players design, launch and run a NASA-style mission to Mars, the Moon or Earth. Every choice trades off money, weight, power, data, signal and lifetime. After launch, real NASA photos and space-weather data show what the mission discovered.
projectDetails.details:
The problem. Real space missions are a puzzle of competing limits: a better instrument adds mass, power, cost and data. Students rarely get to try a whole mission from idea to operation, so these trade-offs stay abstract.

Our solution. Mission Control Academy turns mission design into a simple, colorful game for ages 7 and up. A robot guide named Nova explains every step in short sentences. Players pick a destination (Earth, Moon or Mars), a spacecraft size (from CubeSat to large observatory), instruments, power and communications hardware, a rocket and an orbit.

What players see. Six live bars (money, weight, power, data, signal, lifetime) change with every choice. When something doesn’t fit, such as a rocket too small to reach Mars or a ship too heavy to launch, Nova explains why in plain words and offers a fix. Locked options show a “Why is this locked?” reason.

Learning loop. Players compare two alternative designs, verify a Pass/Fail checklist with reasons, then launch. The mission earns a score out of 100 (science value, requirements met, efficient resource use, surviving events, trade-space exploration) and a report that explains what worked, what failed and why, with tips to improve. [confirm: launch phase, events and report match the live game]

Real NASA connection. After a mission, players see real NASA photos of the world they studied in a research gallery. The game’s missions are modeled on real NASA missions: LRO (Moon), MAVEN and Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (Mars) and Terra and Landsat (Earth). Spacecraft sizes follow NASA’s CubeSat standards.

Play together. The design supports one to four players with NASA-inspired roles (Mission Designer, Spacecraft Engineer, Communications and Ground Officer, Science Lead). [confirm: online rooms working, or say “one-screen team play” and “online rooms in progress”]

Built for everyone. It works on phones and laptops, needs no login, has a sandbox mode, a high-contrast option and a lightweight 2D default. It is built with Next.js, deployed on Vercel, and was created with AI assistance (see section 4).

Impact. The game helps students understand that there is rarely one perfect design, only good trade-offs, which is the heart of real mission engineering.
