projectDetails.name: Mission Control - Space Game
projectDetails.summary:
MISSION CONTROL – Design. Launch. Fly.

Mission Control is an interactive, browser-based space mission design game developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It transforms complex space mission planning into an engaging learning experience where players take the role of mission planners and spacecraft operators.

Players choose scientific objectives and destinations, assemble spacecraft using different instruments and subsystems, and balance critical constraints such as mass, power, budget, data capacity, orbit and communications. They then select a launch vehicle and ground station before operating their mission through a 12-month simulation.

Featuring four mission scenarios, solo and up-to-four-player gameplay, specialised crew roles, interactive minigames, random mission crises and post-mission performance analysis, Mission Control encourages scientific curiosity, teamwork and systems thinking through play.

Design. Launch. Fly. Experience the challenges of space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
MISSION CONTROL is designed as a self-contained educational simulation that demonstrates how different spacecraft subsystems interact throughout a space mission.

How it works: Players begin by selecting one or two scientific objectives, choosing a destination, crew size and difficulty. They then enter the spacecraft design phase, where they select instruments and subsystems while balancing mass, available funds, power generation and consumption, and data capacity.

After spacecraft assembly, players select a launch vehicle, orbit and ground communication network. The spacecraft then enters a 12-month simulated mission featuring interactive activities such as science data collection, spectrum identification, communication and data transmission, power balancing, power routing and meteor defense. Random mission events, system damage and repair decisions introduce additional challenges.

Key benefits and intended impact:

  • Makes space mission planning concepts interactive and easier to understand.
  • Demonstrates systems thinking through connected engineering constraints.
  • Encourages strategic decision-making, experimentation and problem-solving.
  • Supports individual learning and collaborative gameplay for teams of up to four players.
  • Allows players to compare and share spacecraft configurations through design codes.

Technology used: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, HTML Canvas, Web Audio API and browser localStorage. The project is implemented as a self-contained browser application without requiring a backend or external JavaScript framework.

Creativity and design considerations: The project combines spacecraft design with interactive minigames, mission events, crew roles and post-mission analysis. It considers science objectives, spacecraft mass, power, budget, communication capacity, orbital choices, system reliability and mission risk.

The mission scenarios and engineering values are simplified for educational gameplay and are not intended to represent operational spacecraft specifications or real NASA mission predictions.

projectDetails.details:
What it does: Mission Architect is a game that teaches how real space missions are designed. Players act as mission engineers for four clients, from an Earth-watching satellite to a Mars orbiter. In the Design Lab they build a rocket from real materials (aluminium-lithium alloy, steel, titanium, carbon fibre) and a satellite with power, instruments and an antenna. They then choose an orbit and a ground station, launch, and watch the flight. The rocket equation appears live as the rocket climbs. A pre-launch check, a score with stars and an engineering review show why the mission worked or failed, along with the closest real NASA mission.

Benefits and impact: Players learn the real trade-offs between weight, power, cost and science. They see why farther destinations need bigger rockets, why Mars gets weak sunlight and why radio signals get slower with distance. Failing is safe, so players learn by fixing their design and flying again.

Tools: One self-contained HTML, CSS and JavaScript file, with WebGL and canvas graphics and Web Audio for all sound effects (no audio files). It runs offline in any browser and is also packaged as an Android app. No special hardware is needed. We used an AI coding assistant (Claude) during development. Planet textures use NASA imagery.

Creativity: The game turns real orbit, power and radio-link science into decisions a beginner can make. Each mission changes the problem: distance, sunlight or rocket size.

Factors we considered: The audience is both kids and adults, so the text is beginner-friendly. We simplified the physics for learning (circular orbits, ideal rocket equation) and say so in the game. The Launch button is always available, so players find out what goes wrong at the moment it happens. Source code: https://github.com/Jinan007/mission-architect

projectDetails.summary:
BrainForge is an educational and interactive Space Mission Design Game that allows users to create, plan, and manage their own space exploration missions. Players assume the role of mission architects responsible for designing spacecraft, selecting mission objectives, managing resources, and overcoming real-world challenges faced by space agencies.

The game uses NASA data and scientific principles to simulate mission planning, orbital mechanics, planetary exploration, resource management, and risk assessment. Players must make strategic decisions regarding fuel consumption, payload capacity, crew safety, mission duration, and scientific objectives to successfully complete missions.

BrainForge transforms complex aerospace concepts into an engaging gaming experience, inspiring students and space enthusiasts to learn STEM subjects through practical problem-solving. The project aims to promote curiosity about space exploration while helping users develop critical thinking, engineering design, and decision-making skills.
projectDetails.details:
What Does the Project Do?

BrainForge is a simulation-based educational game where players:

  • Design spacecraft and mission architecture.
  • Select destinations such as the Moon, Mars, asteroids, or deep-space targets.
  • Manage fuel, budget, crew, and scientific instruments.
  • Plan mission trajectories using real scientific concepts.
  • Respond to unexpected mission events and emergencies.
  • Complete exploration objectives to earn mission success ratings.

How Does It Work?

The platform presents users with mission scenarios requiring strategic decision-making.

Players:

  1. Choose a space destination.
  2. Build a spacecraft based on mission requirements.
  3. Select scientific payloads and instruments.
  4. Allocate resources and budget.
  5. Simulate launch and mission operations.
  6. Handle environmental and technical challenges.
  7. Analyze mission outcomes and scientific achievements.

Each decision impacts mission success, reinforcing engineering thinking and systems design principles.

Intended Impact

BrainForge aims to:

  • Increase interest in STEM education.
  • Teach real-world space mission planning concepts.
  • Encourage creativity and innovation.
  • Develop analytical and problem-solving skills.
  • Make NASA science accessible to students worldwide.

Benefits

  • Interactive learning experience.
  • Gamified STEM education.
  • Real-world engineering challenges.
  • Practical understanding of space exploration.
  • Encourages teamwork and strategic thinking.

Innovation

Unlike traditional educational tools, BrainForge combines:

  • Real NASA datasets.
  • Interactive gameplay.
  • Space mission engineering.
  • Scenario-based decision systems.
  • Educational storytelling.

This creates a learning experience that is both scientifically accurate and entertaining.

Abandoned, but Not Forgotten.

After the Mission is an interactive digital museum that takes visitors across the solar system to discover NASA’s spacecraft, rovers and landers. Through cinematic visuals, interactive 3D planets and spacecraft models, the website brings these explorers into the spotlight.

The journey begins with a question: What happens to the machines we send into space when their missions are over? Visitors travel from the Moon to Mars, then to Saturn and beyond, discovering the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Cassini and Voyager 1. Each destination reveals a chapter in humanity’s exploration.

Visitors can examine spacecraft models, learn how they were designed and explore their discoveries. Interactive timelines follow each mission from launch to its final chapter, with accessible explanations.

Not every explorer has the same ending. Some completed their missions, some became inactive, and others lost contact with Earth. Voyager 1, however, continues travelling through interstellar space. These stories show that a mission’s end does not mean the end of its importance.

Their journeys remind us that exploration is not only about reaching new worlds, but also about the knowledge we bring home.

Their missions ended, but their discoveries live on even now, too. They may have been left behind, but they should never be forgotten.
projectDetails.details:
After the Mission is an interactive digital museum that allows visitors to explore NASA spacecraft, rovers and landers that remain across the solar system after their missions. Through an interactive 3D solar system, visitors can select destinations such as the Moon, Mars and Saturn to discover the explorers associated with them. They can examine spacecraft models, explore their technology, learn about their scientific discoveries and follow their journeys through interactive timelines.

The project focuses on six explorers: the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Cassini and Voyager 1. Each has a dedicated section explaining its purpose, mission, achievements and current status. By combining scientific information with interactive exploration, we aim to make space history engaging and accessible, particularly for younger audiences.

The main benefit of the project is that it transforms traditional research into an immersive learning experience. Instead of simply reading facts, visitors can visually explore spacecraft and understand the engineering and science behind their missions. Our intended impact is to increase interest in space exploration, encourage scientific curiosity and highlight the lasting contributions of missions that are often overlooked.

For development, we use Lovable as our primary website-building platform, with technologies such as React, TypeScript, Three.js and React Three Fiber for the interactive experience. We also use NASA's publicly available images, scientific information and 3D resources wherever suitable, ensuring proper attribution and reliable information.

What makes our project creative is its storytelling approach. Rather than focusing only on successful launches and discoveries, we tell the stories of what happens AFTER a mission ends. We considered scientific accuracy, accessibility, visual quality, performance across devices and the availability of authentic NASA models. We also distinguish between completed missions, inactive spacecraft and explorers that are still travelling.

Ultimately, our goal is to remind visitors that although these machines may be left behind, their discoveries and contributions continue to shape humanity's understanding of the universe.

projectDetails.name: FlameGuard: Where Is the Fire Data for the Moon?
projectDetails.summary: FlameGuard is an interactive web dashboard that summarizes, ranks and interprets NASA's microgravity combustion research for fire safety on the Moon, Mars and in orbit. Its main finding: crews are expected to live at 30% oxygen or more, yet none of the 208 real per-test rows we read from NASA's PSI database (BASS-II and CFI) starts above 22.2%, and PSI holds no Moon- or Mars-gravity data. FlameGuard maps this blind spot, ranks investigations by readiness for Moon-base conditions, and adds a PSI Table Checker: a browser tool that audits any PSI experimental table for missing oxygen, pressure, airflow and outcome columns and flags duplicates and impossible values. It also offers a merged starter dataset and recommended columns so future prediction models can learn from PSI. Every number links to NASA, and the site states its limits.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

FlameGuard turns NASA's combustion records into answers a safety planner can use. It summarizes 17 investigations and incidents (Apollo 1, Mir, Saffire, BASS-II, CFI, FLEX-2, E-FIELD, SAME and more), ranks them for Moon-base relevance, and shows real data from five PSI experimental tables.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Blind-Spot Map: a gravity-by-oxygen grid shows where NASA has evidence and where it has none. Only squares backed by a NASA source are marked "found".

2. Data Lab: real PSI tables (BASS-II 129 burns, CFI 79 droplet tests, E-FIELD 142 flames on 13 test days, SAME, FLEX-2), cross-checked against NASA's own totals.

3. PSI Table Checker: drop in any PSI table CSV. In the browser it checks whether oxygen, pressure, airflow, outcome, fuel and gravity are columns, and flags duplicate rows, gas fractions that do not sum to 1, impossible oxygen values and odd dates. On NASA's real files it found missing pressure and outcome columns, 2 impossible final-oxygen values, and 8 duplicate rows.

4. For NASA: three recommendations from the gaps, a merged 221-row dataset and a recommended-columns file to download.

5. Ask the data: answers computed live from the tables, plus Google Gemini limited to our records.

IMPACT

Prediction models need data that is complete and machine-readable. We found that oxygen, pressure and airflow often sit in report text, not in table columns. The Checker and the recommended columns give NASA a reusable way to find and fix this.

TOOLS

React, Vite, Framer Motion, Recharts, plain CSS, a Vercel serverless function, Google Gemini. Code was written with SI help (see SI section).

HONEST LIMITS

Curated sample, not the full archive. Readiness scores and recommendations are our own, not NASA ratings. The map covers PSI only; partial-gravity studies may exist elsewhere. FLEX-2 comes from test ranges, not per-run results.

projectDetails.details:
EarthTrend 3D – Interactive Earth System Trend Explorer

Problem

Earth's climate and environmental systems are continuously changing. However, satellite observations and climate datasets are often difficult for the general public to explore, compare and interpret. Understanding regional environmental changes requires accessible visualization tools and reliable statistical analysis.

Our Solution

EarthTrend 3D is an interactive 3D Earth observation platform that combines NASA Earth science imagery, climate reanalysis data and statistical trend detection.

Users can rotate and zoom the Earth, select geographical locations and explore environmental variables through scientific visualization layers.

Key Features

  • Interactive 3D globe powered by CesiumJS.
  • Environmental layers for air temperature, land surface temperature, rainfall, wind, vegetation, humidity and aerosols.
  • Historical visualization using a date-based timeline.
  • Global geographical exploration with country, state and district boundaries wherever open datasets are available.
  • Location-based environmental analysis using NASA POWER.
  • Trend detection using Mann–Kendall statistical testing and Sen's slope.
  • Anomaly visualization and historical comparisons.
  • Transparent scientific overlays with dataset attribution, units and spatial-resolution information.
  • Responsive interface for desktop and mobile devices.

Technology

Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS.

Globe visualization: CesiumJS.

Charts: Recharts.

Data: NASA GIBS, NASA POWER, NASA AIRS, MODIS, GPM IMERG and MERRA-2.

Additional geographical and wind resources: Natural Earth, geoBoundaries and Open-Meteo.

Hosting: Netlify.

Impact

EarthTrend 3D makes Earth observation data easier to explore and understand. It helps users investigate environmental patterns, compare historical conditions and identify statistically supported trends across geographical regions.

The platform emphasizes scientific transparency by communicating dataset resolution, temporal coverage, missing observations and limitations instead of presenting false local precision.

Future Scope

Future improvements include expanding administrative boundary coverage, adding more Earth observation datasets, enhancing regional trend comparisons and introducing more advanced environmental analysis.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.details:
TERRA TRACE

An Intelligent Earth Observation and Environmental Investigation Platform

1. What Does TERRA TRACE Do?

TERRA TRACE is an interactive Earth observation and environmental intelligence platform designed to help users investigate, understand, and interpret changes occurring across Earth's interconnected environmental systems.

Environmental changes involving temperature, precipitation, atmospheric conditions, land surfaces, and water systems generate enormous amounts of scientific data. However, accessing and interpreting these datasets can be challenging for people without specialized scientific knowledge.

TERRA TRACE addresses this problem by bringing geographical exploration, environmental data visualization, historical trend investigation, regional comparisons, and AI-assisted scientific interpretation into one unified platform.

Its primary objective is to transform environmental data from isolated measurements into meaningful scientific investigations.

2. How Does It Work?

TERRA TRACE follows a structured investigation workflow:

Geographical Exploration: Users can explore geographical regions through an interactive map interface, allowing them to investigate environmental conditions across different locations.

Environmental Variable Exploration: Users can examine environmental indicators such as temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, and atmospheric conditions using available datasets.

Historical Investigation: The platform is designed to help users explore environmental observations across different periods, making it possible to investigate changes and identify potential long-term patterns.

Scientific Analysis: Statistical investigation capabilities are intended to help identify trends, variations, and relationships within environmental observations. These include analytical approaches such as regression and non-parametric trend testing.

Regional Comparison: Users can compare different geographical regions to investigate similarities and differences in environmental behaviour.

ATLAS AI: TERRA TRACE incorporates an intelligent scientific assistant called ATLAS. It is designed to help users understand scientific concepts, interpret investigation context, and navigate the platform.

Research Documentation: The platform aims to help users organize their investigation findings into structured scientific reports.

The overall workflow connects geographical selection, environmental observations, scientific investigation, and interpretation within one environment.

3. What Benefits Does It Have?

TERRA TRACE offers several important benefits:

  • Scientific Accessibility: Makes environmental investigation more approachable for students, educators, and the general public.
  • Environmental Awareness: Helps users explore real-world environmental changes rather than relying exclusively on general information.
  • Data-Driven Learning: Encourages evidence-based thinking and scientific reasoning.
  • Simplified Interpretation: ATLAS is designed to make complex scientific information easier to understand.
  • Regional Understanding: Enables investigation of geographical differences in environmental conditions.
  • Historical Perspective: Encourages users to examine how environmental conditions change over time.
  • Scientific Transparency: Emphasizes the importance of reliable data sources, analytical methods, and verifiable findings.

4. What Is the Intended Impact?

Our intended impact is to make Earth-system science more accessible and encourage people to become active investigators of our planet.

We want students to understand that environmental science is not simply about memorizing facts or observing charts. It involves asking questions, examining evidence, identifying patterns, and developing scientifically supported conclusions.

TERRA TRACE aims to support environmental education, scientific curiosity, climate awareness, and preliminary environmental research.

In the long term, we envision developing it into a comprehensive environmental intelligence platform capable of connecting multiple scientific data sources and helping people investigate complex environmental questions.

Our goal is to bridge the gap between the availability of Earth observation information and people's ability to understand and use it.

5. What Technologies and Tools Were Used?

TERRA TRACE was developed using modern web development technologies and AI-assisted development tools.

Programming Languages:

  • TypeScript
  • JavaScript
  • HTML5
  • CSS3

Frontend Technologies:

  • React
  • Vite
  • Tailwind CSS
  • Recharts

Geographical Visualization:

  • SVG-based geographical rendering.
  • Custom equirectangular map implementation.

Development Tools:

  • Bolt.new for AI-assisted application development.
  • Visual Studio Code for code editing and development.
  • Git and GitHub for version control and source code management.

Artificial Intelligence:

  • ATLAS, the platform's integrated scientific assistant.
  • Rule-based intelligence for built-in assistance and capability routing.
  • OpenAI API integration was explored for extending ATLAS.

Hardware:

The application was developed using a personal computer with a standard software development environment. No specialized physical sensors or scientific hardware were required for the current software implementation.

6. How Is the Project Creative and Innovative?

The creativity of TERRA TRACE lies in its investigation-oriented approach.

Instead of functioning as another environmental dashboard that simply displays statistics, it aims to connect multiple stages of scientific exploration within a single platform.

Its most distinctive component is ATLAS, an integrated scientific assistant designed to work alongside the investigation environment.

Another innovative aspect is the combination of geographical exploration, historical investigation, regional comparisons, and statistical analysis. This approach encourages users to explore environmental questions rather than passively consume information.

The platform also emphasizes the distinction between scientific observations and AI-generated explanations, reinforcing the importance of data reliability and scientific transparency.

We aim to make scientific investigation both engaging and meaningful without sacrificing its technical foundations.

7. What Factors Did Our Team Consider?

During development, we considered several important factors:

Scientific Accuracy: Environmental information must be based on reliable observations and appropriate analytical methods.

Data Reliability: Data sources, availability, and limitations must be clearly distinguishable. Generated or illustrative information must never be misrepresented as actual satellite observations.

Accessibility: The interface should be understandable to users with different levels of scientific and technical knowledge.

Usability: Complex scientific workflows should be presented through an organized and intuitive interface.

Scalability: The architecture should support additional environmental datasets, analytical capabilities, and scientific resources in the future.

Performance: Data processing and geographical visualization should remain efficient and responsive.

AI Transparency: AI should assist scientific understanding rather than replace scientific evidence or independently establish environmental conclusions.

Educational Value: The platform should encourage curiosity, critical thinking, and evidence-based investigation.

Conclusion

TERRA TRACE represents our vision of a more accessible and interactive approach to understanding Earth's changing systems.

By bringing environmental exploration, scientific investigation, and AI-assisted interpretation together, we aim to transform how people interact with Earth observation information.

We believe that understanding our planet should not be restricted to experts with access to specialized scientific tools. With the right technology and approach, anyone should have the opportunity to explore Earth's environmental changes and develop a deeper understanding of the world around them.

TERRA TRACE — Discover the patterns. Investigate the changes. Understand our planet.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Afterlight

AFTERLIGHT is an immersive, story driven digital museum that explores the forgotten remains of humanity's space exploration missions. Developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026's "Abandoned but not Forgotten" challenge, it brings abandoned spacecraft, rovers, landers and scientific instruments on the Moon, Mars and beyond back into the spotlight.

Through interactive archives, planetary tracking, historical timelines and cinematic storytelling, visitors can discover why these machines were sent into space, the missions they accomplished, the scientific discoveries they made and what eventually happened to them. Each artifact has a story that connects its engineering, mission and legacy.

By combining space exploration history with accessible educational experiences, AFTERLIGHT aims to make space science engaging for students and casual enthusiasts while preserving the remarkable contributions of the machines humanity left behind.
projectDetails.details:
AFTERLIGHT is an interactive digital museum that explores the equipment humanity has left behind on the Moon, Mars and beyond. Through immersive storytelling, interactive maps and timelines, visitors can discover why these machines were sent, what they achieved, the scientific discoveries they contributed to, and what happened to them.

Our goal is to make space history engaging and accessible, especially for students and space enthusiasts, while inspiring curiosity about science and exploration.

We developed the project using React, Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion and Lucide icons, using NASA resources for mission information.

What makes AFTERLIGHT creative is its storytelling approach: instead of presenting artifacts as a list of facts, we bring them to life as silent witnesses to humanity's space missions. We focused on scientific accuracy, simple explanations, accessibility and an engaging user experience.

projectDetails.name: TerraScope: Earth System Trend Detective
projectDetails.summary:
TerraScope: Earth System Trend Detective is an interactive data visualization platform designed to explore long-term changes in September Arctic sea ice extent from 1979 to 2026.

The project uses satellite-derived sea ice observations to investigate how Arctic sea ice has changed over time. It provides an interactive dashboard with historical trend visualization, year-by-year comparisons, statistical analysis, and access to the underlying dataset.

Using Python, statistical methods, and data visualization, TerraScope calculates the long-term trend and helps users understand the significance of Arctic sea ice decline. The project aims to make climate data easier to explore and interpret, helping students, researchers, and the public understand changes in Earth's cryosphere and their importance to the global climate system.
projectDetails.details:
1. Project Overview

TerraScope: Earth System Trend Detective is an interactive web-based platform that investigates long-term changes in September Arctic sea ice extent using satellite-derived observations.

The main objective is to make historical climate data accessible and understandable through interactive visualizations and statistical analysis.

2. How It Works

The project uses the September Arctic sea ice extent dataset from the National Snow and Ice Data Center (NSIDC).

The data is processed using Python to extract September observations, organize the historical records, and calculate trends.

The dashboard provides six main sections:

  • Overview: Displays key statistics and the overall historical trend.
  • Trend Explorer: Visualizes changes in Arctic sea ice extent over time.
  • Year Comparison: Allows users to compare sea ice extent across selected years.
  • Statistical Lab: Presents linear regression results, slope, R-squared, p-value, and decadal change.
  • Data Explorer: Provides searchable historical records and CSV downloads.
  • About: Explains the project, data source, and methodology.

3. Technologies Used

  • Python
  • Streamlit
  • Pandas
  • NumPy
  • Matplotlib
  • SciPy
  • Google Colab
  • GitHub
  • Streamlit Community Cloud

4. Benefits and Intended Impact

TerraScope transforms scientific observations into an accessible and interactive experience. It helps users identify long-term patterns, compare historical observations, and understand the statistical significance of changes in Arctic sea ice.

The project supports climate awareness and encourages data-driven exploration of Earth's changing environmental systems.

5. Creativity and Innovation

The project combines data analysis, statistical methods, and interactive visualization in one platform. Instead of presenting static charts, TerraScope allows users to explore the data, select years for comparison, examine statistical results, and download the underlying observations.

Its goal is to make climate science more understandable and engaging for a wider audience.

projectDetails.name: COSMOSIS
projectDetails.summary: COSMOSIS is an interactive 3D space exploration and flight academy that tells the story of NASA’s abandoned hardware, from lunar landers and rovers on the Moon to Mars rovers and deep-space probes like Voyager. Instead of reading about equipment that has been left behind, students fly to it, explore it in 3D, and learn what each machine was built to do, what science it made possible, and what condition it’s in today. projectDetails.details:
COSMOSIS is an interactive 3D “student space academy” that tells the stories of NASA’s left-behind hardware, built for school-age space enthusiasts. Learners fly through a 3D solar system and open the Command Deck, which holds 10 worlds, a 3D spacecraft hangar, 6 mission chronicles, and 4 physics labs.

How it works: Clicking a world zooms in on its story, live telemetry, and a gravity simulator (for example, your weight on Mars). The Mission Chronicles are narrated, choice-driven stories about real hardware: the Apollo 11 Eagle lunar module, the Opportunity rover, whose 90-day mission lasted 5,352 sols, and Voyager 1 with its Golden Record. Learners then try the science themselves with a lunar-lander simulator across the Moon, Mars, and Europa, and an orbital-mechanics lab based on Newton’s cannonball. XP, levels, and mission patches keep students engaged.

Benefits and impact: It turns “discarded” machines into stories of discovery and connects each one to the physics behind it. It is free, runs in the browser, and needs no install or login.

Creativity: Instead of a static timeline, learners play through the decisions behind each mission, such as the Apollo 1202 alarm.

Tools: HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Three.js for 3D, hosted on Vercel

Factors considered: Age-appropriate language, accuracy of mission facts, accessibility (keyboard controls, optional sound), and keeping it fun enough to learn from.

projectDetails.name: Project A.R.E.S by CodeArmy
projectDetails.summary:
Project A.R.E.S. 2.0 asks one question: can YOU keep four astronauts alive on Mars for 50 sols? 
Every kilogram you pack into your Starship is a kilogram you can never take back, so choose wisely, launch, build a habitat on the Red Planet, and survive whatever space throws at you. Real solar storms from NASA’s DONKI space weather database become live in-game hazards, while a Gemini-powered AI Flight Director writes fresh mission objectives, reviews your decisions and springs surprise problems on you, so no two missions are ever the same. 
Hands-on mini-games like Shard Collector, Shard Memory and Fragment Catcher build the skills junior astronauts need, and a two-player crew mode lets you invite a friend (they have to accept!) and run the mission together, live, with a shared pause. Wrapped in a retro terminal style with falling-code rain, it plays free in your browser and installs on Android, iOS, Windows, Mac and Chrome. 
Built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to teach real space science through play. Ready, Commander? Pack light, think fast, and bring everyone home.
projectDetails.details:
Overview

PROJECT A.R.E.S. 2.0 (Advanced Resource & Environment Simulator) is a single-file browser game that trains junior astronauts to plan, build and survive a 50-sol Mars mission, made for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. You pack a Starship, fit out its interior, land at Arcadia Planitia and keep a crew of four alive.

The game teaches one idea over and over: every resource is linked to another. Oxygen needs water, water needs power, power needs mass, and mass is limited. Good choices before launch decide how hard the surface is.

  • Who it is for: students and first-time space fans. A guided Cadet mode and a free-text Flight Director mode cover both levels.
  • Where it runs: any modern browser, from one HTML file. It can also be installed as an app.
  • Goal: survive 50 sols with oxygen, water and food above zero, and finish the mission objectives Mission Control sets.
  • Look and feel: a green retro terminal, with canvas-drawn cutscenes and mini-games.

Main attraction

The main attraction is the packing-to-survival loop: what you choose to launch with is what you live with on Mars. Everything else in the game supports that loop.

  1. The mass budget. You get 24,000 kg and 60 m³ of cargo space. Each item has a weight, a volume, power use and ports it needs.
  2. A real interior to build. You place modules on three decks (Habitat & Crew, Science & Greenhouse, Utility & EVA Yard) and connect the ports each one needs (power, water, oxygen, methane, light).
  3. Live consequences. Power, oxygen, water, food, radiation, morale and methane all update every sol, so a bad layout shows up as numbers falling.
  4. Real space weather. The game reads NASA's DONKI feed and uses a real solar event to time a hazard. If the feed is offline, it simulates one.
  5. An AI trainer. Gemini, or a local Ollama model as backup, writes mission objectives, judges typed fixes and speaks problem alerts.
  6. SHIP DRIVING. A separate big button starts a deep-space flight with planets to dock at, debris to dodge and ship faults that stop the ship until you fix them.
  7. Cinematics. A launch cutscene, a landing and an ending sequence, all drawn live.
  8. Co-op. Up to three friends can join the same mission over a peer-to-peer link.

Key to understanding it all

The whole game fits in one chain: mass limits what you carry, what you carry limits your power, and power limits your life support. Read the three tabs as three stages of that chain.

Glossary

Sol : One Martian day. The mission runs 50 sols; the clock ticks on its own

Manifest : The list of everything loaded onto the Starship

Ports : Connections (PWR, H2O, O2, CH4, LIGHT) a module needs before it

: produces or consumes anything

ISRU : Making resources on Mars (ice drill for water, electrolyzer for oxygen)

Methalox / CH4: Methane fuel reserve; fuel cells burn it for power

Battery buffer : Stored power that carries you through the night and dust storms

Shielding : Protection from radiation; falls during solar events

Morale Crew mood (0 to 100). Low morale triggers problems; some actions spend it :

EVA : Going outside. Needs an Airlock or Suit Locker; collects samples

Cadet mode : Easy mode: pick one of three fixes for each problem

Flight Director mode Hard mode: type your own fix and an AI or local judge scores it

Mini-game : Short arcade game that gives crew morale or supplies

Sol clock hold : The sol counter pauses while a mini-game or problem is open

Safety margin to remember: the Starship launches with only 10 sols of emergency O₂, water and food. Without bulk reserves or production systems, the crew runs out on Sol 11.

Step-by-step walkthrough

A full run takes you from the start screen to either MISSION COMPLETE or CREW EXTINGUISHED.

  1. Start screen. Choose START MISSION for solo play. The other buttons are MULTIPLAYER, AI SETUP (check Gemini or Ollama), DOWNLOAD APP and HOW TO PLAY. Read HOW TO PLAY the first time.
  2. Pick a training mode. CADET gives guided choices. FLIGHT DIRECTOR makes you type your own fixes. You can switch on the manifest screen.
  3. Tab 01, Manifest & Mass Budget. Watch payload mass and cargo volume left. Add power, life support, food, shielding, EVA and science items, then bulk reserves (oxygen, water, food, fuel cans, methane). Use the category filters to find things.
  4. Check the pre-flight notice. Remember the 10-sol emergency supply. You need reserves or ISRU production before you seal.
  5. Seal the manifest. Press SEAL MANIFEST. Mission Control then issues secondary objectives (the AI drafts them).
  6. Tab 02, Interior Configuration. Drag each item into a slot on its deck. Connect the ports it needs. Items you could not place are listed as unplaced. Items that need pressurized space, such as the CO₂ Scrubber, must go in the Habitat deck.
  7. Launch. Start the mission. The launch cutscene plays, then the landing at Arcadia Planitia.
  8. Tab 03, Surface Operations. The sol clock starts. Each sol the game recalculates power, oxygen, water, food, radiation and morale.
  9. React to problems. A problem box opens and the sol clock pauses. Solve it in Cadet or Flight Director style (see Problems and decisions).
  10. Keep the reserves up. Use ADD FUEL for the generator, the Morale Bank for boosts, and mini-games for morale.
  11. Collect science. With an airlock or suit locker, EVA collects up to 5 samples. A spectrometer analyses them. Three analyzed samples can reveal an anomaly, and RUN CONFIRMATION PROTOCOL then confirms life.
  12. Optional: SHIP DRIVING. Press the big button for a deep-space run. It advances 10 sols and costs supplies (see Ship Driving).
  13. Reach Sol 50. Survive past Sol 50 for MISSION COMPLETE and the ending cinematic. If oxygen, water or food hits zero in a way that kills the crew, the failure cutscene plays and the mission ends at that sol.

Mini-games and Ship Driving

There are three arcade mini-games and one big-button flight. All of them hold the sol clock while you play, and none can be opened during a problem.

Shard Collector : Mini-games row, Surface Ops. Collect falling shards.

Reward: crew morale. Cooldown: 3 sols.

Shard Memory : Mini-games row. Match shards from memory.

Reward: crew morale. Cooldown: 3 sols.

Fragment Catcher : Mini-games row. Catch fragments outside (EVA suit-up costs 4 kg O2;

a habitat window works with no airlock).

Reward: crew morale. Cooldown: 3 sols.

Ship Driving : Big button above the mini-games row. Fly a deep-space route.

Reward: loot crate, 10 sols pass. Cooldown: about 4 minutes of real time.

How SHIP DRIVING works

  1. Press the big ▶ MARS TRANSIT: SHIP DRIVING button.
  2. Steer with UP/DOWN or W/S, or drag on the screen. Stay inside the dashed route.
  3. Near a planet or moon, hold SPACE (or the HOLD TO DOCK button) for about 1.5 seconds to collect loot: oxygen, water, food or fuel. A cargo crate collects it.
  4. Dodge the debris. Each hit costs 1 hull point (3 in total) and a little oxygen; time off the route costs water and oxygen.
  5. Ship faults. Two or three times during the flight, the ship stops. A fault panel opens (coolant leak, hull puncture, CO₂ alarm, solar storm and others). In Cadet mode, choose one of three fixes. In Flight Director mode, type your fix. Each wrong answer costs 2 kg O₂, and running out of tries costs 1 hull point.
  6. Press CONTINUE FLIGHT (or Enter) and the ship flies on from where it stopped.
  7. At the sector exit you get a summary. The run advances 10 sols and uses about 35 L water, 20 food and about 1% of battery capacity. Open the cargo crate icon to store the loot.

SKIP TRANSIT ends the run with no stops made.

Problems and decisions

Every problem pauses the sol clock, opens a red problem box and is read aloud. There are six core problems, plus AI-written complications and anomalies that Mission Control can add during sols 4 to 26.

Payload overweight : Lander too heavy for descent.

Fixes: drop Hydroponics, burn methane, or offload rations.

CO2 scrubber saturation: CO2 rising, crew headaches.

Fixes: vent cabin (costs O2), max regen (costs power), or use the storm shelter.

Water recycler rupture : Clean water production offline.

Fixes: cannibalize the ISRU drill, ration water, or boil down (drains batteries).

Solar array dust blanket Output down 60% :

Fixes: EVA brush-off (needs airlock), battery buffer, or overdrive fission.

Crew morale diminished : Exhausted, arguing crew.

Fixes: Shard Memory night, comfort rations, or push on (worse).

Micrometeorite puncture: Hab pressure falling.

Fixes: seal the section, brick patch (needs printer), or EVA repair.

Modes

Cadet mode. You pick one of three fixes. Some are locked until you own the hardware they need, and each shows its cost. Every option trades one resource for another.

Flight Director mode. You type your own fix. Empty or off-topic messages are rejected. The AI judge (Gemini or Ollama) reads your answer and decides whether it is safe and plausible; if no AI is running, a local keyword judge accepts a fix that names the right actions. An improvised fix costs 10 morale. A weak answer can trigger a complication.

The rule to remember: there is no free fix. If a choice looks free, look again at what it spends.

Do's

  • Do pack bulk reserves of oxygen, water and food, or ISRU production, before you seal the manifest.
  • Do add a power source that survives a dust storm (Kilopower fission) and a battery buffer for the night.
  • Do put the CO₂ Scrubber and other pressure-bound items on the Habitat deck.
  • Do connect every port an item needs (power, water, oxygen, methane, light), or it produces nothing.
  • Do include an Airlock or Suit Locker, a spectrometer and comms if you want the science and communication objectives.
  • Do include a Medical Bay, exercise rig and hydroponics for morale on a long mission.
  • Do read the cost line on every fix before you click it.
  • Do use the Morale Bank and mini-games when morale is falling, but keep morale at least 5 above the cost of any boost.
  • Do check the cooldown on mini-games (3 sols) and SHIP DRIVING (about 4 minutes) before planning around them.
  • Do budget supplies for SHIP DRIVING: it advances 10 sols and uses water, food and power.
  • Do answer ship faults by naming the action and the system (for example, isolate the loop and switch to the backup).
  • Do save or keep the one HTML file, and use the same file on every device in multiplayer.

Don'ts

  • Don't seal the manifest with no reserves and no production. The crew runs out on Sol 11.
  • Don't rely on solar panels alone. A dust storm cuts their output to about 20%.
  • Don't forget that the fuel cell burns your methane reserve, and the generator only runs while it has fuel cans.
  • Don't overload the mass or volume budget; items you cannot afford simply do not fit.
  • Don't drop Hydroponics, the drill or other key hardware as a quick fix unless you have a plan to replace what it gave you.
  • Don't vent the cabin to clear CO₂ when oxygen is already low.
  • Don't start a mini-game or SHIP DRIVING while a problem is open; the game blocks it.
  • Don't start SHIP DRIVING when water or food is nearly gone; the run drains both and can leave you short.
  • Don't leave the dashed route or hit debris on purpose; both cost oxygen, water and hull.
  • Don't type empty, joke or off-topic answers to Flight Director problems; they are rejected.
  • Don't ignore low morale. It makes every problem harder.
  • Don't mix game files in multiplayer. A guest on a different version is refused by the host.

Multiplayer, tech notes and learning goals

Multiplayer. One player hosts and up to three guests join with a room code over a peer-to-peer link (PeerJS). Everyone sees the same mission. Guests send actions to the host, which runs the simulation. All players must use the same game file version, or the host refuses the join. SHIP DRIVING and the mini-games are started through the host's rules.

Tech notes.

  • One self-contained HTML file with inline CSS and JavaScript; it also works as an installable web app.
  • Graphics are canvas drawings in a green CRT style, with no external image assets for the mini-games.
  • Data sources: NASA DONKI (space weather) with a simulated fallback.
  • AI: Gemini or a local Ollama model, with the other one as backup. The game works with no AI, using local judging.

Learning goals. Players practise budgeting mass and volume, seeing resource dependencies, planning for risk, choosing between trade-offs and explaining an engineering fix in plain words.

Thank you for your patience.

projectDetails.details:
The Forgotten Explorers – Stories of the Machines Left Behind in Space

Our project is an educational digital storybook that explores the journeys of four important space explorers: the Lunar Roving Vehicle, Sojourner Rover, Ingenuity Mars Helicopter, and Pioneer 10 and 11.

The storybook presents the missions through creative storytelling, allowing each explorer to tell its own story. It explains why these machines were sent into space, their missions, important discoveries, challenges, and where they are now.

The main aim of this project is to create awareness about space exploration and help people understand the contributions of robotic explorers. It makes scientific information easier and more interesting to learn, especially for students and young readers.

Our project combines scientific information with storytelling in a chapter-based digital format. Its creative approach helps readers connect with the explorers and understand their importance in space exploration.

The project was prepared using digital document and presentation tools, along with AI-assisted tools for content organization and preparation.

projectDetails.name: Mission Control: Your Mission, Your Choices, Your Survival
projectDetails.summary:
Mission Control is an interactive educational space exploration game that challenges students to experience the decisions involved in establishing a sustainable human outpost beyond Earth. Players take on the role of a space scientist, choose between a lunar or Martian mission, manage essential resources such as oxygen, fuel, food, power and crew morale, and respond to unexpected mission challenges.

Through interactive scenarios, exploration activities and decision-based gameplay, players discover how the Moon and Mars differ and why careful planning is essential for astronaut survival. The lunar path focuses on exploring the lunar environment and investigating potential water ice resources, while the Mars path introduces the challenges of exploring the Red Planet and searching for signs of past or present life.

By transforming complex space exploration concepts into an engaging game, Mission Control makes space science more accessible to students and encourages scientific curiosity, critical thinking and responsible decision-making.
projectDetails.details:
How Mission Control Works

Mission Control is designed as a decision-based educational simulation that takes players through the different stages of a space exploration mission.

Players begin at Mission Control, where they prepare for launch, select equipment and choose their destination: the Moon or Mars.

The game then takes them through a shared space journey, where they encounter unexpected situations and must make decisions that influence their mission resources.

Two Exploration Paths

Moon Mission: Players explore the lunar environment, learn about its extreme conditions, investigate the lunar south pole and discover why water ice is important for future exploration.

Mars Mission: Players explore the Red Planet, learn about its thin atmosphere, cold environment and dust storms, and investigate evidence of ancient water and the scientific search for signs of past life.

Resource Management and Decision-Making

Throughout the mission, players manage five essential resources:

  • Fuel
  • Oxygen
  • Food
  • Power
  • Crew morale

Their choices affect resource availability, mission progress and the final outcome. Interactive challenges and educational facts help players understand the scientific reasoning behind each decision.

Technology Used

The project was developed using React.js, JavaScript, HTML and CSS, with Vite as the development and build tool. GitHub was used for version control and collaboration, and Vercel was used for deployment.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Mission Control turns space exploration concepts into an interactive learning experience. It encourages students to think critically, understand planetary environments, explore scientific challenges and appreciate the importance of sustainable resource management in future human space missions.

Its creative approach combines game-based learning, planetary exploration and decision-making to make space science more accessible and engaging for young learners.

projectDetails.name: Cosmic Six – AI-Powered Astronaut Health Monitoring System
projectDetails.summary:
Project Title: Cosmic Six – Astronaut Health Monitoring System

Cosmic Six is an AI-powered Astronaut Health Monitoring System designed to monitor and analyze astronauts’ health during space missions. We developed a full-stack web application using the MERN stack, integrated with a Python-based Machine Learning service. The system uses simulated health data to monitor important indicators such as heart rate, oxygen saturation (SpO₂), body temperature, blood pressure, and respiratory rate.
The platform provides a real-time health dashboard, visualizes health trends, detects abnormal readings, and generates alerts when health indicators cross predefined safety limits. Machine Learning is also used to identify unusual health patterns and support early anomaly detection.
This project addresses the challenge by providing a centralized system for continuous astronaut health monitoring and timely identification of potential health risks. It is important because astronauts work in extreme space environments where immediate access to medical assistance is limited. Early detection and clear health insights can help mission teams make informed decisions, improve astronaut safety, and support healthier space missions.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Cosmic Six: Astronaut Health Monitoring System

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Cosmic Six is an AI-powered Astronaut Health Monitoring System designed to monitor astronauts' health during space missions. It collects simulated health readings, including heart rate, oxygen saturation (SpO₂), body temperature, blood pressure, and respiratory rate. The system displays these readings through a centralized web dashboard with real-time updates and graphical visualizations.

The system uses predefined safety thresholds to identify abnormal health readings and automatically generates alerts. In addition, a Python-based Machine Learning model analyzes health data to identify unusual patterns and support early anomaly detection. Mission teams can view health trends, monitor astronaut status, review alerts, and access health records.

2. What benefits does it have?

- Enables continuous monitoring of important astronaut health indicators.

- Helps identify abnormal readings at an early stage.

- Provides clear visualizations of health trends.

- Generates timely alerts when readings cross predefined safety limits.

- Supports mission teams in understanding astronaut health conditions.

- Centralizes health information in one dashboard.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to improve astronaut health monitoring and support safer space missions. In space environments, astronauts face challenges such as microgravity, isolation, and limited access to immediate medical assistance. By providing continuous health insights and early anomaly detection, Cosmic Six aims to help mission teams recognize potential health concerns and make informed decisions.

4. What tools, programming languages, hardware, and software were used?

Frontend:

- React.js with TypeScript (TSX)

- HTML and CSS

- Tailwind CSS

- Recharts for data visualization

- Axios and Socket.IO Client

Backend:

- Node.js

- Express.js

- MongoDB

- Mongoose

- Socket.IO

Machine Learning:

- Python

- Scikit-learn

- NumPy and Pandas

- FastAPI

- Isolation Forest for anomaly detection

Development tools:

- Visual Studio Code

- Git and GitHub

- Postman

Hardware and data source:

- No specialized physical hardware is required for the prototype.

- Simulated astronaut health data is used for testing and demonstration.

5. How is the project creative?

The creativity of Cosmic Six lies in combining a real-time health monitoring dashboard, rule-based safety alerts, and Machine Learning-based anomaly detection in one platform. Instead of simply displaying health values, the system analyzes patterns and highlights unusual readings that may need attention. It also allows different simulated health scenarios to demonstrate how the system responds to changing astronaut conditions.

6. What factors did the team consider?

Our team considered astronaut safety, reliability, data accuracy, real-time monitoring, usability, scalability, and the limitations of space environments. We also considered the need to distinguish normal variations from potentially concerning readings, avoid unnecessary alerts, and make health information easy for mission teams to understand.

Since this prototype uses simulated data, its outputs are intended for demonstration and decision-support research, not medical diagnosis or replacement of professional medical assessment.

projectDetails.name: TIERRA
projectDetails.summary:
TIERRA is an interactive web map that finds and explains places on Earth that resemble the surface of Mars or the Moon. It goes beyond listing well-known analog sites by researching overlooked regions as well.

The platform centers on one satellite map of Earth. Small markers distinguish established analog sites from newly investigated candidates. Clicking a marker opens a simple panel with the site’s coordinates, local environment, the matching Mars or Moon region, side-by-side comparisons, and links to supporting research and NASA data.

The design is minimal and slightly vintage: dark, muted colors, small markers, and no clutter or heavy animation. It’s built with HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Leaflet.js, using satellite imagery, NASA datasets, and peer-reviewed research. The goal is to use visual exploration to identify and scientifically validate new terrestrial analogs.

Even shorter version: TIERRA is a satellite map of Earth that highlights known and newly proposed sites resembling Mars and the Moon. Each marker opens a data panel with coordinates, environmental details, planetary comparisons, and NASA and research references, all in a clean, minimal interface.
projectDetails.details:
TIERRA (Terrestrial Analog Explorer) is an interactive web map that presents places on Earth whose geology and environment resemble those of Mars and the Moon. It shows both identified analogs and newly proposed candidates. Each site appears as a marker on a satellite map of Earth, and clicking a marker opens a small window with the site’s details: coordinates, environmental characteristics, its Mars or Moon counterpart, and supporting research. Users can search by country or site name, filter by planetary target, classification, and analog characteristics, and add their own placemarks. A side panel summarizes the research inventory, which currently covers 42 sites.

The platform gathers scattered analog research into one visual, searchable tool. This helps students, researchers, and space enthusiasts compare terrestrial and planetary environments quickly. Its intended impact is to make comparative planetology more accessible, to encourage research on overlooked regions of Earth, and to support future mission planning, astronaut training, and technology testing in places that are cheaper and easier to reach than other worlds.

TIERRA was built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, using Leaflet.js for the interactive mapping and Esri satellite imagery as the base layer. Its content draws on NASA datasets and peer-reviewed planetary research, and it runs in any web browser with no special hardware.

The project is creative in treating the map as a research tool rather than a static list: it separates “found” from “possible” analogs, and it lets users contribute new locations. Its minimal, slightly vintage scientific-interface style keeps the focus on the data. The team considered scientific accuracy, clear and uncluttered design, ease of use, accessibility on a lightweight web stack, and the ability to grow as new analogs are discovered.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. projectDetails.name: Project CTRL_ALT_ELITE
projectDetails.summary: Lunar Mission Planner is an AI-powered lunar mission planning platform designed to make Moon exploration smarter and safer. It uses NASA's JPL Horizons and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LOLA) elevation data to analyze solar illumination, lunar terrain, energy conditions, and communication visibility at potential landing locations. Its interactive lunar map and mission analysis dashboard help users understand environmental conditions and assess mission feasibility. The integrated Super Intelligent System (SIS) provides AI-powered text and voice interaction, making complex scientific results easier to understand for both researchers and the public. By transforming NASA's open space data into accessible mission insights, Lunar Mission Planner aims to support safer rover operations and more informed lunar exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Lunar Mission Planner — See the Moon Before You Explore It

Lunar Mission Planner is an AI-powered platform designed to help researchers and mission planners assess potential lunar rover exploration areas before a mission begins. Lunar missions face challenges such as extreme and changing sunlight, hazardous terrain, craters, limited energy, and communication constraints. Our project brings relevant lunar data and mission insights together in one interactive platform.

What does it do and how does it work?

Users can enter a potential lunar landing location using its latitude and longitude, along with the mission date and time. The platform uses NASA's JPL Horizons system to obtain relevant Sun and Earth position information and elevation data from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA), aboard NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) to examine the surrounding lunar terrain.

It presents mission-related information through an interactive lunar map and analysis dashboard, helping users understand sunlight conditions, terrain characteristics, and communication visibility. The platform also considers energy-related factors relevant to rover planning. Its integrated Super Intelligent System (SIS) provides an AI-powered assistant that users can interact with through text and voice to better understand the results.

What are the benefits and intended impact?

The platform makes complex scientific information easier to access and interpret. It can help users identify potential environmental challenges, compare mission conditions, and make more informed planning decisions. Our intended impact is to support safer, more efficient, and better-informed lunar exploration, particularly for rover missions operating in challenging regions such as the lunar south pole.

What tools and technologies did we use?

Our software was developed using Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and Python. We integrated NASA's JPL Horizons data and LOLA lunar elevation data. For the conversational AI system, we used LiveKit Agents and Google's Gemini AI, with LiveKit supporting real-time text and voice interaction.

The project is a software platform; no custom hardware was required for its development.

How is the project creative?

Our main innovation is bringing lunar scientific data, interactive mission visualization, and a conversational AI assistant together in one planning platform. Instead of requiring users to interpret separate scientific datasets independently, SIS helps explain the information in an accessible way through both text and voice. This combines data-driven exploration planning with an intuitive human-AI interface.

What factors did our team consider?

We considered the changing illumination conditions on the Moon, surrounding elevation and terrain hazards, crater-related risks, rover energy requirements, communication visibility, and the influence of mission date and time. We also considered data availability, scientific accuracy, and the need to communicate uncertainty clearly. Lunar Mission Planner is intended as a decision-support tool to assist mission planning, not as a replacement for professional mission validation or safety certification.

**Project Summary – Cybernetic Chooms: Mission May Be Possible: Starbound**

*Mission May Be Possible: Starbound* is an interactive, browser-based space adventure developed by Team Cybernetic Chooms, consisting of Christy Abraham, Govind Krishna, and Kenan Thomas.

The project places players in the role of mission director of the Aurora spacecraft, responsible for preparing three astronauts to deliver a research beacon into orbit. The game features 12 decisions across four episodes, with three choices per decision that influence two hidden readiness scores: flight preparation and crew training. Based on these scores, players can unlock three possible endings: Mission Accomplished, Mission Lost, or Crew Lost.

Built using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Canvas 2D, the game includes animated characters, interactive dialogue, cinematic endings, achievement tracking, and saved game progress. It also supports offline play, responsive layouts, keyboard navigation, and reduced-motion accessibility settings.

The project demonstrates how storytelling, decision-making, programming, and visual design can combine to create an engaging and accessible interactive gaming experience.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Cybernetic Chooms: Mission May Be Possible: Starbound

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Our project, Mission May Be Possible: Starbound, is an interactive, choice-based space adventure that runs in a web browser. The player takes the role of the mission director of the Aurora spacecraft, responsible for preparing the rocket and its crew to deliver a research beacon into orbit. The game consists of four episodes and twelve decisions, each offering three choices with immediate narrative feedback. The decisions influence two hidden readiness scores: Flight Preparation and Crew Training. Depending on these scores, the player reaches one of three endings: Mission Accomplished, Mission Lost, or Crew Lost.

2. What are the benefits of the project?

The project provides an engaging way to explore decision-making, teamwork, preparation, and responsibility. It helps players understand how individual choices can influence the outcome of a complex mission. It also encourages critical thinking, planning, and awareness of the importance of safety and crew coordination.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our aim is to create an enjoyable and educational gaming experience that demonstrates the importance of careful planning, effective teamwork, training, and responsible decision-making. We want players to understand that successful missions depend on both technical preparation and human readiness.

4. What tools, programming languages, and software were used?

We developed the project using:

  • HTML: To structure the game interface.
  • CSS: To design the visual appearance and responsive layouts.
  • JavaScript: To manage game logic, decisions, scoring, navigation, and animations.
  • HTML Canvas 2D: To draw the rocket, launch complex, astronauts, Earth, and ending scenes.
  • localStorage: To save mission progress, discovered endings, and motion preferences.

The game works offline once the HTML file is available locally and requires no installation.

5. How is the project creative?

The project combines interactive storytelling with space exploration. It features animated astronauts, character dialogues, colour-coded speech bubbles, a detailed launch complex, visual effects, cinematic endings, and achievement tracking. Players experience different consequences based on their decisions, making each playthrough an engaging experience.

6. What factors did the team consider?

Our team considered:

  • Gameplay: Meaningful choices and balanced scoring.
  • Storytelling: An engaging space mission with multiple possible outcomes.
  • Visual design: Attractive backgrounds, animations, and clear dialogue.
  • Accessibility: Keyboard controls, visible focus indicators, descriptive canvas labels, and reduced-motion settings.
  • Usability: Saving progress, restarting missions, and navigating between screens.
  • Compatibility: Responsive layouts and offline functionality.
  • Reliability: Validating saved game data before loading.

Through this project, our team gained experience in connecting narrative choices to game logic, improving existing interfaces, creating animations, and developing accessible browser-based applications.

They must navigate a fully realized 3D environment, switching between three distinct roles (Engineer, Explorer, Medic) to complete 50 critical repair tasks across massive futuristic facilities. Players are forced to balance Oxygen and Base Power while surviving random catastrophic events like Martian dust storms and solar flares. Built entirely with Three.js and procedural generation, the game provides immediate, accessible fun while subtly teaching core STEM principles about life support, resource management, and the unforgiving nature of the Red Planet.
projectDetails.details: The game addresses the challenge by making the complex, invisible trade-offs of space survival tangible in a 3D space. Kids don't just read about life support; they have to physically run across a Martian landscape to choose whether to fix the oxygen scrubbers or repair the solar array while a dust storm rages outside. We used Three.js (WebGL), HTML5, and CSS3 for the game engine, UI, and state management. The logic dictates a base degradation rate, forcing the player to prioritize tasks and switch roles dynamically (1: Engineer, 2: Explorer, 3: Medic). The game features a dynamic third-person camera, custom Martian sky shaders, particle-based weather systems, and massive interactive structures with animated sliding doors. It is creative because it wraps hard science in a fast, replayable, and visually stunning arcade-style loop.

projectDetails.name: Mission Design Lab
projectDetails.summary:
Mission Design Lab is a browser game we built for the NASA Space Apps Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players plan their own space mission, then run it. They pick one of five destinations (Earth orbit, the Moon, Mars, asteroid Bennu or Jupiter’s moon Europa), build a spacecraft from about 30 parts within a budget and a launch-mass limit, survive random events like solar storms and power loss, and finally fly the arrival in real-time 3D.

It meets the challenge by making mission design the gameplay. Distances and sunlight levels come from NASA fact sheets, and the rocket equation and inverse-square law decide whether a design works. Players quickly learn why Mars is far, why Europa is dark, and why every kilogram counts. When a mission fails, the game explains why.

This matters because real missions are won through trade-offs in mass, power, fuel and budget, a side of exploration most people never see. Our game makes that thinking free, instant and playable in any browser, helping inspire the next generation of engineers and scientists.
projectDetails.details:
🚀 Mission Design Lab

Can you design a space mission that actually works?

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

🎯 The Idea in One Line

Most space games ask, "Can you shoot fast?" We asked, "Can you plan smart?"

In Mission Design Lab you build the spacecraft first, launch it, and then fly the final approach yourself. Whatever you chose on the build screen decides whether you survive.

🛠️ What It Does and How It Works

Four steps, from idea to landing.

Step

What the player does

What's happening underneath

1. Pick a mission

Choose from 5 destinations: Earth orbit, Moon, Mars, asteroid Bennu, or Jupiter's moon Europa

Each card shows real NASA numbers: sunlight, distance, signal delay

2. Build the spacecraft

Choose from about 30 parts (cameras, radar, solar panels, RTGs, engines, fuel tanks, shields) within a budget and a weight limit

Every part costs mass, power and money. You can't take everything

3. Survive the mission

Watch it run through 8 phases, from launch to completion. Solar storms, power drops and broken antennas strike at random

The game checks whether your design can handle them

4. Fly the approach

Steer a real-time 3D flight through gates and obstacles, or use autopilot at a cost to accuracy

The final score depends on science, efficiency, safety and budget

Two real physics rules run the whole game:

  • 🔥 The rocket equation: extra fuel adds weight, and weight needs more fuel. Each kilogram buys you less.
  • ☀️ The inverse-square law: the farther you are from the Sun, the weaker your solar panels and your signal. Europa gets about 1/27th of Earth's sunlight.

If a mission fails, the game tells you why, for example "Your Δv is too low, add more fuel." So players learn engineering from their failures.

🧠 What Factors Did We Consider?

We're students, so we kept asking ourselves, "Would this actually work, and would someone enjoy it?"

  • Scientific accuracy: We used real NASA fact sheets for distances and sunlight, and real physics formulas. We simplified costs and part stats on purpose so the game stays playable, and we say so openly.
  • Learning through play: Every trade-off teaches something. No lectures, just consequences.
  • Difficulty curve: Earth is the forgiving tutorial. Europa is brutal. The difficulty rises with real-world mission difficulty.
  • Making each mission different: Mars is about distance, Bennu is about precision, and Europa is about radiation and darkness. No two missions play the same.
  • Fairness: Failures always have a reason the player can understand and fix.
  • Accessibility: It works on desktop and touch screens, supports reduced-motion settings, and uses screen-reader labels.
  • Zero friction: Players don't need to install anything or create an account. They just open the website link in their browser and play.
  • Trustworthy data: We cite every NASA source and clearly separate real facts from gameplay simplifications.

🎯 Intended Impact

  • 🎓 Show how real missions are planned. Missions are won or lost on trade-offs among mass, power, fuel and budget, long before launch.
  • 🌍 Make NASA's challenges feel real. Players feel why Mars is far and why Europa is dark and dangerous.
  • 🙌 Open space engineering to everyone. It's free, instant, and needs no background knowledge.
  • 💡 Spark STEM curiosity. It connects classroom physics to real missions like OSIRIS-REx, Europa Clipper and the Mars rovers.

💻 What We Used

Category

Tools

Languages

HTML, CSS, vanilla JavaScript (no frameworks or libraries)

Graphics

HTML5 Canvas, a custom 3D engine we wrote for the flight section, SVG for spacecraft art

Sound

Web Audio API: every sound effect is generated by code, with no audio files

Browser features

localStorage (saves best scores), vibration on touch devices, reduced-motion support

Fonts

Google Fonts: B612 (designed for aircraft cockpits), B612 Mono, Chakra Petch

Hosting

Deployed as a static website, so it runs on any device with a modern browser

AI partner

Claude (Anthropic): we used it to design, build and refine the game

Data

NASA fact sheets, mission pages, JPL Small-Body Database (full source list included)

Hardware

Any laptop, desktop, tablet or phone with a modern browser (Chrome, Edge, Firefox or Safari) and a stable internet connection. Recommended: a laptop or desktop with 4 GB RAM or more, a screen of 1280×720 or larger, and a keyboard and mouse for the 3D flight section. Touch screens are supported too.

The game is a lightweight website: nothing to download, no setup, no account. Just open the link and play.

✨ What Makes It Creative?

  1. Engineering is the game. The "boss fight" is a power budget.
  2. Your build screen decides your flight. Fuel, shielding and navigation parts you picked earlier directly change how the approach goes.
  3. Everything is made by code. Planets, nebulae, spacecraft art and sound are generated rather than imported, which keeps it small, fast and fully ours.
  4. Mission-control atmosphere. Codenames (TERRA-01, SELENE-02, ARES-03, OSIRIS-04, EUROPA-05), live telemetry and a Deep Space Network ticker make players feel like part of the team.
  5. Failure teaches. Instead of "Game Over," you get a debrief on what went wrong and how to fix it.

📌 Final Note

Our costs and part stats are simplified for gameplay, but the physics and destination data are real. We built Mission Design Lab to show that space exploration isn't just about rockets, it's about making smart decisions.
