projectDetails.name: Forgotten Footprints
projectDetails.summary:
Forgotten Footprints is an interactive educational website that brings attention to the human-made machines left behind on the Moon and Mars after their missions. Through engaging stories, illustrations, timelines, and historical facts, the project explores three significant artifacts: the Apollo 11 Lunar Module descent stage, NASA's Sojourner rover, and the Mars Pathfinder lander.

Designed for school-age learners and curious space enthusiasts, the platform explains what these machines were built to do, how they contributed to space exploration, and why their scientific legacy still matters. By transforming technical mission history into an accessible storytelling experience, Forgotten Footprints aims to inspire curiosity about planetary exploration and the engineering achievements that made it possible.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview

Forgotten Footprints is a web-based educational storytelling platform developed in response to NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: "Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars."

The project focuses on the stories of three important pieces of space exploration hardware:

  • Apollo 11 Lunar Module Descent Stage: The descent stage that enabled the first crewed lunar landing and remained on the Moon after the astronauts departed.
  • Sojourner Rover: NASA's first Mars rover, which demonstrated the potential of robotic mobility and scientific investigation on another planet.
  • Mars Pathfinder Lander: The stationary lander that delivered Sojourner to Mars and acted as a communication relay between the rover and Earth.

How It Works

The website presents these artifacts through an interactive experience. Visitors can explore individual artifact cards to learn about their purpose, mission history, scientific contributions, and significance. A historical timeline connects the missions, while a dedicated educational section explains why these objects remain important to the history of space exploration.

Technology Used

The project was developed using:

  • HTML5 for the website structure.
  • CSS3 for styling, responsive layouts, and original visual illustrations.
  • JavaScript for interactive artifact information panels and navigation.
  • GitHub for source code management.
  • Vercel for public website deployment.

The website does not require a backend, database, user account, or external API.

Innovation and Educational Impact

Instead of presenting mission information as lengthy technical documentation, Forgotten Footprints uses simple storytelling and interactive visual elements to make space exploration history accessible to younger audiences and casual learners.

Its intended impact is to encourage curiosity about planetary science, robotics, engineering, and the scientific discoveries made possible by earlier NASA missions.

Use of Super Intelligence

ChatGPT was used as an AI-assisted development tool to help draft educational text and generate HTML, CSS, and JavaScript code. The website's artifact illustrations are original CSS-based visual representations created in code, not NASA photographs or official mission diagrams. No AI-generated photographs, audio, or videos are included.

NASA Resources and Attribution

The project references NASA's official Apollo 11, Mars Pathfinder, and Sojourner mission resources for historical and educational information. Relevant source links are provided on the website.

Forgotten Footprints is an independent educational project and is not an official NASA website or affiliated with NASA.

projectDetails.name: TerraTrace – An Interactive Earth System Trend Detection and Analysis Platform
projectDetails.summary:
Project Summary

TerraTrace is an interactive web-based platform designed to identify and analyze environmental changes on Earth using NASA Earth science data.

The platform focuses on important environmental variables such as temperature, rainfall and soil moisture. It collects historical data from NASA sources and displays the changes through interactive graphs, charts and maps.

Users can select a location, choose an environmental variable and compare its changes over different years. The system analyzes the collected data to identify increasing or decreasing trends and estimates the rate of change.

It also uses statistical methods to determine whether the observed trends are significant.

The main aim of TerraTrace is to make complex Earth science data easier to understand and help students, researchers and the public understand how our planet is changing.
projectDetails.details: Project Details Problem Statement Earth's environmental conditions are continuously changing. However, understanding these changes using large amounts of scientific data is difficult. People need a simple tool to identify environmental trends, compare different locations and understand the importance of these changes. Proposed Solution TerraTrace provides an interactive platform that analyzes NASA Earth science data and presents the results in simple visual formats. Main Objectives 1. To identify environmental changes over time. 2. To analyze temperature and rainfall patterns. 3. To compare environmental trends between different locations. 4. To visualize historical data using graphs and maps. 5. To calculate the rate of environmental change. 6. To identify statistically significant trends. 7. To make NASA Earth science data accessible to everyone. Study Area Kerala, India. Proposed locations: - Kochi - Thiruvananthapuram - Wayanad Environmental Variables - Temperature - Rainfall - Soil moisture Technologies Used - Python - Streamlit - Pandas - NumPy - Plotly - SciPy - NASA POWER API Expected Outcome The platform will provide an easy way to understand environmental trends, compare locations and identify important changes using NASA data.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project DINGAN
projectDetails.summary:
**EarthTrend AI – An Earth System Trend and Multi-Hazard Intelligence Platform**

EarthTrend AI is an intelligent data analytics platform designed to explore historical natural disasters and identify patterns in multi-hazard activity. The system integrates selected datasets from NOAA, USGS and IBTrACS to analyse floods, tornadoes, landslides and tropical cyclones. It uses data ingestion, preprocessing, geospatial visualisation, statistical trend analysis and anomaly detection to transform historical records into meaningful insights. Through an interactive dashboard featuring a rotating 3D Earth, multi-hazard maps, graphical visualisations and analytical reports, users can explore disaster distributions, examine historical trends and identify unusual activity. Developed as a proof of concept using limited historical datasets, EarthTrend AI demonstrates how data analytics and geospatial technologies can support better understanding of natural hazards, with future scope for expanded global coverage and advanced predictive capabilities.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – EarthTrend AI

EarthTrend AI is a prototype of an Earth System Trend and Multi-Hazard Intelligence Platform developed to analyse historical natural disaster data and identify meaningful patterns. The project integrates selected datasets from NOAA, USGS and IBTrACS, covering floods, tornadoes, landslides and tropical cyclones. It includes data ingestion, preprocessing, statistical trend analysis, anomaly detection, geospatial visualisation and an interactive Streamlit dashboard with a 3D rotating globe. The system helps users explore historical disaster records, understand geographic distributions and identify unusual patterns in disaster activity. However, EarthTrend AI is currently a partially developed proof of concept and not a complete or fully operational disaster monitoring and prediction system. It uses limited historical datasets and requires further development, including wider geographical coverage, additional data sources, improved analytical models and advanced predictive capabilities. The project demonstrates the potential of combining artificial intelligence, data analytics and geospatial technologies to support better understanding of natural hazards.

projectDetails.name: NØLA THE SPACE TRAINER
projectDetails.summary:
What did we develop? 
We developed NØLA – The Space Trainer, an interactive educational platform that combines a Space Survival Academy with an immersive 3D and 2D space-station simulation. It teaches young learners about oxygen management, food production, water conservation, energy systems and radiation protection through interactive lessons, quizzes and practical missions.

How does it address the challenge?  
NØLA addresses the challenge of making complex space science engaging and easy to understand. Instead of relying only on theoretical learning, students can apply their knowledge through space-station simulations, resource management, repair activities and missions. A customizable astronaut and NØLA, a friendly robot companion, make the experience more interactive and enjoyable.

Why is it important?
NØLA inspires curiosity about space, encourages critical thinking and develops problem-solving skills. It helps young learners understand the science behind human survival in space and motivates the next generation to explore science, technology and space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
NØLA – The Space Trainer is an interactive educational platform designed to introduce young learners aged 10–16 to the challenges of living and surviving in space. It combines a Space Survival Academy with immersive 2D and 3D space-station simulations, creating an engaging environment where students can learn scientific concepts and apply them through practical experiences.

The platform consists of two interconnected components: the Space Survival Academy and the Space Station Simulation. In the academy, learners explore essential space-survival systems through interactive lessons and quizzes covering oxygen management, food production through hydroponics, water conservation and recycling, energy generation, and radiation protection. Completing these learning modules unlocks corresponding systems and challenges in the simulation, connecting theoretical knowledge with practical application.

Inside the simulation, learners experience life aboard a space station, where they can explore different systems, manage limited resources, respond to environmental challenges, and understand the complexities of maintaining a sustainable space habitat. They can interact through a customizable astronaut character, accompanied by NØLA, a friendly robot assistant who guides them throughout their learning journey. This lesson-to-simulation progression encourages learners to understand a concept before applying it in a simulated environment.

The primary benefit of NØLA is making complex space-science concepts accessible and enjoyable for younger audiences. It promotes experiential learning, critical thinking, problem-solving, scientific curiosity, and an understanding of the engineering challenges involved in sustaining human life beyond Earth. Its intended impact is to encourage young learners to develop an interest in science, technology, engineering, and space exploration while building awareness of the challenges associated with future lunar and Martian missions.

NASA data and scientific resources are incorporated into NØLA's simulation to make the learning experience more realistic and scientifically grounded. These resources help represent space environments, planetary conditions, and survival challenges that astronauts may encounter during future missions. NØLA Bot acts as an interactive AI-powered guide, helping learners understand these concepts, navigate the platform, and receive explanations and guidance throughout their learning journey. Together, they connect real-world space science with an engaging, interactive learning experience.

The project is developed using React, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS for its web interface, with Firebase Authentication and Firestore for authentication and data management. Phaser 3 is used for the interactive 2D simulation, alongside the technologies supporting the 3D experience. The project is primarily software-based and does not require specialized hardware, making it accessible through compatible devices with a web browser. AI-assisted development tools are also used to support the development process, while NASA-related scientific information and datasets help connect the learning experience to real-world space science.

NØLA's creativity lies in its integration of education and simulation through a progressive learning approach. Rather than presenting lessons and gameplay as separate experiences, it allows learners to unlock and apply systems based on their understanding of the concepts. The project also considers age-appropriate content, accessibility, intuitive navigation, scientific accuracy, user engagement, and the balance between educational value and entertainment. The overall goal is to create an experience that makes learning about space exploration both meaningful and memorable.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Beyond the Mission
projectDetails.summary:
Beyond the Mission: The Machines We Left Behind is an interactive, cinematic storytelling website that explores the legacy of NASA's robotic and human space exploration missions. It focuses on the equipment and machines left behind on the Moon and Mars, revealing the stories behind hardware whose missions have ended but whose scientific and historical significance remains.

Through four immersive chapters—Deep Space, Moon, Mars, and Legacy—the project takes visitors on a visual journey using NASA imagery, animations, scroll-driven transitions, and concise storytelling. It highlights examples such as Apollo lunar equipment, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, ALSEP experiments, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, and InSight.

The project aims to make space exploration history more engaging and accessible, especially for students and the general public, while encouraging people to look beyond mission achievements and remember the machines that made those discoveries possible.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview

Beyond the Mission is a cinematic, interactive educational website created in response to the NASA Space Apps Challenge theme, "Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars."

The website presents the stories of space exploration hardware through four chapters: Deep Space, Moon, Mars, and Legacy. Visitors experience the project by scrolling through a sequence of visual sections, each introducing a different part of the journey.

How It Works

The experience begins with an animated view of Earth and introduces the idea of exploring beyond our planet. The Moon chapter explores Apollo-era equipment, including lunar module hardware, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, and the Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP).

The journey then moves to Mars, highlighting robotic explorers such as Sojourner, Spirit, and Opportunity, along with the InSight mission. The visual transitions help communicate the increasing distance from Earth. The final Legacy chapter reflects on how equipment can become inactive or remain behind while its discoveries continue to contribute to our understanding of space.

The website uses NASA imagery and mission information, with source references and image credits included to help visitors explore the original material.

Technology and Tools

  • Frontend: React and JavaScript
  • Development environment: Vite
  • Animation: GSAP and ScrollTrigger
  • Code development: Visual Studio Code and GitHub Copilot
  • Version control and source code: Git and GitHub
  • Deployment: Vercel
  • Visual assets and mission references: NASA's official websites and image library

Creative Approach

Instead of presenting mission information as a conventional list or dashboard, the project uses cinematic storytelling, large-scale imagery, animated transitions, and scroll-based interactions. The changing visual relationship between Earth, the Moon, and Mars reinforces the scale of space exploration.

The experience is designed to be accessible to students, space enthusiasts, and general audiences. Responsive layouts and reduced-motion support were considered during development.

Intended Impact

Beyond the Mission encourages visitors to appreciate the equipment and engineering behind space exploration, not just the missions' headline achievements. It aims to preserve the stories of these machines and make NASA's exploration history more engaging, understandable, and memorable.

projectDetails.name: Abandoned but not forgotten solar system
projectDetails.summary:
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive space story we built in PictoBlox. Players explore all eight planets, the Moon and deep space, guided by an astronaut called Astro. On each world they tap the robots NASA left behind, such as the Apollo 11 lander Eagle, the Opportunity rover, the Ingenuity helicopter, Cassini and Voyager 1. Each machine tells its own story in the first person, with narration and sound effects. It explains why it was sent, what it discovered and how its mission ended.

This answers the challenge by turning forgotten equipment into characters people can care about, instead of a list of mission facts. A short eight-question quiz checks what players learned and keeps score.

It matters because most students only hear about active missions. Stories like Opportunity’s, built to work for 90 days and lasting 14 years, show how good engineering leads to discovery and can inspire the next generation of explorers. The simple tap-and-listen design lets young learners use it without help.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive, narrated story game made in PictoBlox. The player starts at a menu with an astronaut guide, Astro, and can take a Solar System Tour, visit the Moon, go to Deep Space or take a quiz.

  • Planets: on the tour, the player taps any of the 8 planets. Each planet has its own scene, and Astro narrates its story with on-screen captions.
  • Robots: on each world the player taps a spacecraft or robot. Eleven of them speak in the first person, in their own voice. They include Eagle, the Lunar Rover, Opportunity, Ingenuity, Voyager 1 and 2, MESSENGER, Magellan, Skylab, Galileo and Cassini.
  • Quiz: an 8-question quiz covers all the planets, reads each question aloud and keeps score.

The project uses PictoBlox’s broadcast messages to switch scenes and a shared variable so only one voice speaks at a time.

Benefits and intended impact
The project turns dry mission data into stories that students remember. It teaches the history of NASA’s older missions, which are rarely taught, and shows how engineering leads to discovery. It needs no instructions, so young learners can use it alone, and the narration helps those who find reading difficult. We hope it inspires the next generation of explorers.

Tools and software

  • PictoBlox, which uses block coding, for all the game logic.
  • Python to generate the artwork as SVG images and to synthesize the sound effects, such as the launch, whoosh and quiz chimes.
  • The eSpeak NG text-to-speech engine for the narration voices.
  • FFmpeg to process the audio.
  • Claude, an AI assistant from Anthropic, helped us write the scripts. Please check the challenge’s rules on AI use and mention this if required.

We used no extra hardware.

Creativity
The challenge asks for stories, so we let the machines tell their own, which gives each one a personality. Eagle’s lower half is still at Tranquility Base, and Ingenuity flew far beyond its plan. Each robot has its own voice, and the whole solar system is one connected journey.

What we considered

  • Accuracy: facts come from NASA sources, and we checked them against NASA’s Resources tab.
  • Age: short sentences and big buttons suit school-age players.
  • Accessibility: captions match the narration word for word.
  • Honesty: the artwork and voices are computer-generated, not real NASA images or recordings, and we credit NASA for the facts.

projectDetails.name: Project Earth Trend Detective
projectDetails.summary: EarthTrend Explorer is a web app that lets anyone check whether the temperature or rainfall in an Indian state has really changed. We built it for the challenge Be An Earth System Detective.
projectDetails.details:
EarthTrend Explorer lets anyone check whether temperature or rainfall in an Indian state has really changed. The user picks one of 28 states, a variable (temperature or rainfall) and a range of years from 2003 to 2023. The app plots the yearly values with two trend lines and runs three tests: linear regression, the Kendall tau test and Sen's slope. It then gives a plain verdict: Increasing, Decreasing or No clear trend. A trend is reported only when regression and Kendall tau both give p < 0.05 and point in the same direction. A second page compares all 28 states at once using pre-calculated trends, showing which states changed most and how many results are significant.
Data from NASA
We used NASA POWER (T2M, air temperature at 2 m, in °C) and NASA Giovanni, which gave us the PRECTOTCORR variable (corrected precipitation, in mm/day). We turned them into yearly values for 28 states over 2003–2023, 1,176 yearly records in total.
Benefits
Students can learn to read real data and see what "statistically significant" means.
Journalists can fact-check claims such as "it's getting hotter here" for a specific state.
Local planners can see where change is real and where it is not.
No coding or data skills are needed, and the test results and units are shown, not just a chart.
Intended impact
We want more people to ask climate questions about their own region and answer them with evidence. Making NASA Earth data easy to check builds data literacy and helps tell real change from a few unusual years. Next steps are more NASA variables, district and city level, corrections for seasonality, regional languages and a mobile version.
Tools, languages and software
Python, pandas, NumPy, SciPy and Matplotlib for the analysis and charts, and Streamlit for the web app (we also made a Tkinter desktop version). Code is on GitHub. No special hardware was used, just ordinary laptops. We drafted code and slide content with AI assistance (Claude). No AI-generated images were used, and all screenshots come from our own app.
Creativity
It acts as a "detective": instead of only showing a chart, it gives a verdict a beginner can understand.
It says "no clear trend" when there isn't one, rather than forcing a story.
It requires two independent tests to agree, so one lucky result isn't enough.
Factors we considered
Honesty about limits: the p-values assume independent years, and the all-state page runs 56 tests (28 states × 2 variables), so about 3 are expected to look significant by chance. We treat results as leads to investigate, not proof of long-term climate change.
Clear units: every result is shown in °C or mm/day, and slopes are per year.
Data scope: the app's own notice says the values are not state-wide averages.
Beginner-friendliness: simple steps, plain wording and no jargon in the verdict.
Reliability: a fixed, repeatable rule for the verdict, so the same inputs always give the same answer.

projectDetails.name: Project EnvKo Trend
projectDetails.summary:
EnvKo Trend is an interactive climate analysis and forecasting web application developed as a solution to the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, “Be an Earth System Trend Detective!”

The project uses historical climate data from NASA POWER for Kochi, Kerala, covering January 2001 to October 2026. It analyzes five climate parameters: average, maximum and minimum temperature, monthly rainfall, and average humidity.

EnvKo Trend helps users explore historical climate patterns, identify long-term trends, and detect unusual variations through interactive graphs and visualizations. It also uses statistical models (SARIMA) to generate monthly temperature, rainfall, and humidity forecasts for 2027.

The application is developed using Python, Pandas, NumPy, Plotly, and Streamlit. Statistical analysis includes the Mann-Kendall test, Sen's slope, and STL decomposition. ChatGPT and Google Gemini were used as debugging assistance during development.

The main goal is to transform complex NASA climate data into simple, understandable insights and help people explore how the local climate is changing over time.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – EnvKo Trend

EnvKo Trend is an interactive climate analysis and forecasting web application developed as a solution to the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, “Be an Earth System Trend Detective!” The project focuses on Kochi, Kerala, and aims to make climate data easier for people to explore and understand.

What does it do and how does it work?

The application uses historical climate data from NASA POWER, covering January 2001 to October 2026. It analyzes five climate parameters: average temperature, maximum temperature, minimum temperature, monthly rainfall, and average humidity.

The data is collected through the NASA POWER API, cleaned, and converted from daily observations into monthly records. The application then:

  • Displays historical climate patterns through interactive graphs.
  • Identifies long-term climate trends.
  • Highlights unusual monthly variations using STL decomposition.
  • Generates monthly temperature, rainfall, and humidity forecasts for 2027 using SARIMA models.

What are its benefits?

  • Makes complex climate data easier to understand.
  • Helps users explore historical climate changes in Kochi.
  • Highlights unusual climate variations.
  • Provides a simple way to visualize possible future climate patterns.

What is the intended impact?

The main goal is to improve awareness and understanding of local climate patterns by transforming NASA's climate data into meaningful visual insights. It encourages people to explore environmental changes using real data.

What tools and technologies were used?

  • Programming language: Python
  • Data processing: Pandas, NumPy
  • Visualization: Plotly
  • Web application: Streamlit
  • Statistical analysis: Mann-Kendall Test, Sen's Slope, STL Decomposition
  • Forecasting: SARIMA
  • Development tools: VS Code, Jupyter Notebook
  • Version control: Git and GitHub
  • AI-assisted debugging: ChatGPT and Google Gemini

How is the project creative?

EnvKo Trend combines historical climate exploration, trend identification, unusual variation detection, and statistical forecasting in one interactive dashboard. Instead of presenting climate information as complicated tables, it converts the data into visual insights that are easier to explore.

What factors were considered?

The project considered data availability, historical coverage, location relevance, data quality, visualization clarity, forecasting accuracy, and the limitations of statistical predictions. NASA POWER provides gridded estimates rather than direct measurements at every local location, and the forecasts are statistical estimates, not exact weather predictions.

Overall, EnvKo Trend connects NASA's Earth data with local climate understanding, helping users explore what has changed, identify unusual patterns, and investigate what might happen next.

projectDetails.name: NovaHealth: Autonomous Astronaut Health & Diagnostic System
projectDetails.summary:
NovaHealth is an offline-first, web-based health monitoring and decision-support tool engineered for long-duration space missions. We developed an intuitive dashboard featuring an interactive anatomical body map, multi-modal telemetry inputs, dynamic historical trend charts, and an intelligent diagnostic engine.

The software directly addresses the NASA Space Apps challenge by translating NASA’s Human Research Program (HRP) guidelines into practical, crew-operated care. It maps critical health indicators—such as sleep hours, cardiovascular metrics, and metabolic markers—against the primary hazards of human spaceflight, using instant color-coded status alerts to flag deviations.

NovaHealth is vital for deep-space exploration, such as lunar bases and Mars transits, where communication delays with Earth make real-time ground support impossible. By empowering astronauts to autonomously assess their health, follow structured diagnostic workflows, and determine when crew medical officer intervention is required, NovaHealth ensures crew safety and operational resilience far from Earth.
projectDetails.details:
NovaHealth is an offline-first, web-based autonomous health monitoring and decision-support system designed specifically for astronauts on long-duration space missions.

How It Works & Key Features The application processes multi-modal health inputs—such as biometric telemetry, sleep hours, blood sugar, and radiation logs—through an intelligent diagnostic engine. It features an Interactive Anatomical Body Map divided into key sectors (Head/CNS, Cardiovascular, Metabolic/Abdomen, and Musculoskeletal). Astronauts can click on any body region to instantly inspect health indicators mapped against NASA's Human Research Program (HRP) hazards. Metrics are categorized using intuitive color-coding (Green for nominal, Yellow for moderate deviation, Red for critical attention) to allow for rapid self-assessment at a glance.

Benefits & Intended Impact NovaHealth provides total mission autonomy by operating entirely offline, making it impervious to the severe 20-minute communication blackout delays experienced during deep-space transit to Mars. By automating medical triage and providing clear guidance—explaining what an exam measures, why it is needed, and when it requires intervention—the tool significantly reduces astronaut cognitive load under high-stress conditions. Its intended impact is to safeguard human life and operational continuity as humanity pushes further into the cosmos through Artemis and future Mars missions.

Technical Stack

  • Frontend Framework: React with Vite for high-performance rendering
  • Styling & UI: Tailwind CSS (NASA Mission Control dark-mode aesthetic) and Lucide React iconography
  • Data Visualization: Recharts for dynamic, multi-week health telemetry trend charts
  • Development Architecture: Built and optimized using modern AI-assisted engineering tools for rapid prototyping and deployment

Innovation & Design Considerations NovaHealth transforms complex clinical data into an engaging, spatial user experience via an interactive visual body map rather than dense spreadsheets. In designing the solution, the team explicitly accounted for the five primary spaceflight hazards (space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity fields, and hostile closed environments), minimized click-depth to combat astronaut fatigue, and anchored the architecture in an offline-first design philosophy.

projectDetails.name: MISSION FORGE // Aerospace Command
projectDetails.summary: For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, our team developed MISSION FORGE, an interactive aerospace simulation game and systems architecture tool that bridges the gap between complex orbital mechanics and engaging gameplay. The challenge addresses how to effectively communicate the intricacies of spacecraft engineering, launch logistics, and long-term Earth and space science campaigns to the public and aspiring engineers. MISSION FORGE solves this by putting players in the role of a chief mission architect where they must balance rigorous engineering trade-offs—including mass budgets, power generation, data downlink bandwidth, and financial constraints. By simulating real-world orbital dynamics, scientific data accumulation, and mid-mission crisis management (such as solar flares and telemetry anomalies), our project transforms raw aerospace principles into an accessible, educational experience. It empowers users to explore space exploration design firsthand, fostering deeper STEM interest and spatial systems thinking.
projectDetails.details:
What it does & How it works:

  • Briefing & Setup Lobby: Enables solo or team players to select mission objectives (such as Climate Watch, Deep Space, or Moon Mapper), configure target orbits, and adjust difficulty parameters before starting.
  • Hangar Workbench: An intuitive systems-design hub where players manage four core mission pillars—Planner, Engineer, Science, and Comms—while monitoring real-time telemetry updates.
  • Simulation & Launch Engine: Features a cinematic launch sequence that transitions smoothly into a live, month-by-month telemetry loop, complete with orbital radar tracking and science data downlinks.
  • Crisis Management System: Introduces randomized mid-mission emergencies (like solar flares or gyro glitches) that force players to make high-stakes strategic choices under pressure.

Key Benefits & Intended Impact: Mission Forge transforms complex aerospace engineering concepts into an accessible, highly engaging experience. It acts as an educational sandbox that teaches players about satellite constraints, power management, and the nuanced decision-making behind real NASA missions.

Tech Stack & Tools: Built using modern HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript, and custom canvas-based UI animations to deliver high-performance, cross-platform execution directly in the browser with zero backend dependencies.

Creativity & Design Choices: Unlike traditional, static dashboards, Mission Forge combines rigorous engineering physics with fast-paced, gamified decision loops. It features an authentic, dark-themed command-center aesthetic, live black-box flight recorders, and an immersive scoring system that makes systems thinking genuinely fun.

projectDetails.details:
Project Details — Coastwatch

What does the project do and how does it work?

Coastwatch is an interactive coastal observation explorer designed to help users explore coastal surface changes around Alappuzha, Kerala, using NISAR (NASA-Aperture Radar) satellite observations.

The application provides a dashboard where users can explore available satellite observation dates, view HH and HV polarization information, inspect product metadata and coverage footprints, and browse corresponding satellite-image previews. Users can switch between observations, explore the map and export selected observation information as a JSON file.

Our approach focuses on making complex Earth observation information easier to explore and understand through an accessible, interactive interface.

What benefits does it provide?

Coastal regions such as Alappuzha are exposed to environmental processes including coastal erosion, flooding and sediment movement. Understanding these changes is important for coastal planning, environmental awareness and disaster preparedness.

Coastwatch aims to make satellite observation products more accessible to students, researchers and people interested in coastal environments. By presenting observation information through maps, visual previews and structured metadata, the platform provides a foundation for exploring coastal conditions over time.

What is the intended impact?

Our long-term vision is to support better understanding and monitoring of coastal environments through satellite-based Earth observation.

CoastWatch could eventually help researchers, students, environmental organizations and coastal communities explore changes in coastal landscapes and identify areas that may require further investigation.

Future development will focus on integrating actual georeferenced NISAR GCOV raster data, developing land-water classification techniques, extracting shoreline boundaries and validating coastal-change measurements.

What tools and technologies were used?

Our team developed the project using:

- *React.js* – Building the interactive frontend.

- *JavaScript* – Application logic and interactive functionality.

- *HTML and CSS* – Structuring and styling the interface.

- *Leaflet* – Interactive map visualisation.

- *Vite* – Development environment and application build tooling.

- *GitHub* – Source-code management and collaboration.

- *Vercel*– Hosting and deployment of the web application.

- *NASA–NISAR data products* – Satellite observation products used as the project's intended data source.

- *AI-assisted development tools* – Supporting software development, debugging and project planning.

What makes the project creative?

CoastWatch combines satellite observation information, interactive mapping and an accessible dashboard into a single exploration platform.

Rather than presenting satellite products as complicated technical files, the application aims to make them easier to navigate through observation selectors, polarisation information, map-based coverage visualisation and image previews.

The project also focuses on a specific coastal study area, Alappuzha, connecting advanced satellite Earth observation technology with a regional environmental challenge.

What factors did the team consider?

During development, we considered data accessibility, ease of use, geographical relevance, visual clarity, technical feasibility and scientific reliability.

We also considered the importance of distinguishing actual satellite observations from illustrative previews and product coverage from extracted shoreline boundaries.

At the current prototype stage, the existing browse images and coverage footprint support product exploration; the HDF5 GCOV datasets have not yet been independently processed or validated. Therefore, CoastWatch does not currently claim measured shoreline displacement or erosion rates.

Our next objective is to integrate the actual satellite datasets and develop a scientifically validated coastal-change analysis workflow.

projectDetails.summary:
Aeolis: A Mars Science Expedition is a story-driven 3D game set in Gale Crater. Players become field geologists investigating an orbiter’s clue that water may have altered Martian rocks. They choose a science objective and compatible telescope design, learning how mission goals shape engineering trade-offs. Planning is interactive.

Players traverse procedural terrain using astronaut movement, jumping, sprinting, and a fuel-limited jetpack. Changing daylight and dust storms shape the expedition. At three sites, they collect basalt, clay-bearing rock, and dune samples, then return to the lander to uplink results and complete the story.

The project connects launch, spacecraft and relay operations, surface exploration, and science analysis. Its journal introduces simplified concept development and verification stages. The game was built in Godot with GDScript.

Aeolis is inspired by NASA mission-design, GMAT, Mission Viz, and telescope-design resources. It does not use live NASA datasets or APIs, nor connect to GMAT or Mission Viz. Orbital displays and telemetry are simulated; the story is fictional. Procedural terrain and a built-in astronaut model keep the prototype playable without optional art assets.
projectDetails.details:
Aeolis: A Mars Science Expedition is a 3D game set in Gale Crater. Players are field geologists testing whether water altered Martian rocks. They plan observations by matching a science goal with a wavelength, instrument, and telescope design, then explore three sites, collect samples, and uplink results to Earth.

The game features procedural terrain, astronaut movement, a jetpack, changing daylight, dust storms, and a mission HUD. Its journal connects launch, spacecraft and relay operations, surface work, and science analysis. Each sample advances a story about Mars’s changing environment.

Aeolis makes mission planning and planetary science approachable through play. Instrument trade-offs, field evidence, communication, and science return become choices and actions. The design prioritizes clear controls, a manageable scope, and a link between player decisions and mission outcomes.

Built in Godot with GDScript, the prototype uses generated terrain and a simple astronaut model; it includes no external images or 3D models. NASA mission-design, GMAT, Mission Viz, and telescope concepts informed its design. It uses no live NASA datasets or APIs; orbital displays and telemetry are simulated.

projectDetails.summary: Our team Exon developed a project based on "Field Shift:Adapting Farms with NASA Data"; which will help farmer to save their crops from withering landslides, floods, droughts etc. and it will give plans for non-farmers on how to take care of specific crops and also provide good plans for crop rotation.
projectDetails.details:
Orbit Crop is a web application for farm planning and early warning. Orbit Crop helps farmers look at field conditions compare crop choices plan crop rotations and get ready for weather danger. A farmer can type in coordinates use GPS or search for a location and then draw a boundary around a field. Orbit Crop mixes that location with NASA climate information and other public data to give soil and moisture reports, estimates of which crops fit best advice on rotations and warnings about dangers such as heavy rain, flooding, heat, drought and strong wind.

The project brings types of information together into a useful workflow. NASA POWER supplies data on rainfall, temperature, sunlight and wetness. NASA GIBS offers a MODIS Terra NDVI map layer and NASA EONET adds reports of nearby natural events. Open‑Meteo gives forecasts, soil‑moisture estimates at depths and flood model data. SoilGrids and OpenLandMap supply modeled soil characteristics. Orbit Crop turns all of this input into comparisons of crops, seasonal planning views and recommended actions. It shows when a data source can not be reached.

Our aim is to make environmental information easier to reach and more helpful for farmers, especially where local monitoring toolsre scarce. Knowing about weather and moisture danger earlier can help farmers guard crops plan irrigation and choose planting and rotation plans that're better informed. Orbit Crop is a decision‑support tool: its data can be in grids or models and crop fit scores are estimates. Farmers should double‑check Orbit Crops advice with field checks, soil tests and local agricultural specialists.

We made Orbit Crop using Python and FastAPI on the end React and JavaScript on the front end and Tailwind CSS for a flexible interface. Leaflet and OpenStreetMap let users map fields without needing a paid map key. Orbit Crop is a Progressive Web App for phones and computers. To develop or use Orbit Crop you need a web‑ready computer or phone; you do not need farm sensors.

Orbit Crop’s creative idea is to link field mapping NASA Earth‑observation data, crop rotation plans and disaster readiness, in one worldwide tool. The team thought about how much data's available how far the coverage goes how trustworthy the sources are, how to use the tool on a phone how to keep saved alerts when offline and the limits of modeled data. Orbit Crop’s code and the recommendations it creates use SI assistance; the external data still gives credit to the providers.

Due to time restrictions, SI was used to help generate most things on this project except the concepts, ideas and about what features are to be added.

projectDetails.name: Earth is our laboratory for the Moon and Mars
projectDetails.summary:
Team EXOVAND developed the Mars & Moon Analog Globe, an interactive platform that explores locations on Earth with geological and environmental similarities to the Moon and Mars.

Our project addresses the challenge of identifying Earth locations that can serve as analog environments for future lunar bases and Martian exploration. The website features an interactive globe containing 10 selected analog sites across different parts of the world. Users can explore locations, search for sites, and discover their geological characteristics.

The platform also includes a Mission Lab with three tools: Similarity Meter, Compare Two Sites, and Location Filter. These features help users estimate similarities between locations and explore which environments may be useful for specific mission requirements.

Our accompanying PDF presentation explains the challenge, selected locations, comparisons, methodology, and conclusions. Similarity scores are project estimates rather than measured scientific values.

Our goal is to show how Earth can serve as a natural testing ground for understanding other worlds and preparing for future space exploration.

Team: EXOVAND
projectDetails.details: EXOVAND – Mars & Moon Analog Globe NASA International Space Apps Challenge 2026 Challenge: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars. Project Overview Team EXOVAND developed the Mars & Moon Analog Globe, an interactive platform that explores real locations on Earth with geological and environmental characteristics similar to selected regions of Mars and the Moon. Our project focuses on the idea that Earth can serve as a natural testing ground for planetary exploration. By identifying and characterizing analog environments, we can better understand the challenges future lunar and Martian missions may face. Problem Statement Before exploring other worlds, scientists and mission planners need to understand their terrain and environmental conditions. Testing equipment and methods in relevant Earth environments can help prepare for future missions. However, many potential analog locations are not easy to discover, explore or compare. Our platform brings selected Earth analog environments together in one accessible interactive experience. Our Solution We created an interactive globe featuring Mars and Moon analog locations around the world. Users can switch between Mars and Moon, rotate and zoom the globe, select location markers, and explore information about each site. The project includes five Mars analog entries and five Moon analog entries, with Devon Island represented for both worlds. Selected Analog Locations Mars: Lonar Crater (India), Lake Sandvatn (Iceland), Yana–Indigirka Lowland (Russia), Holuhraun Lava Field (Iceland), and McMurdo Dry Valleys (Antarctica). Moon: Mistastin Lake (Canada), Nördlinger Ries Crater (Germany), Sudbury Impact Structure (Canada), Pinacate Volcanic Field (Mexico), and Devon Island/Haughton Crater (Canada). These locations represent features such as impact craters, basaltic lava, volcanic terrain, polar deserts, polygonal ground and ice-rich environments. Main Website Features - Interactive 3D globe with selectable location markers. - Separate Mars and Moon exploration modes. - Search by location, country, mineral or geological feature. - Location information including temperature, pressure, minerals and geological characteristics. - Mission Lab for comparing and evaluating analog sites. Mission Lab The Mission Lab contains three main tools: 1. Similarity Meter: Estimates how closely an Earth location matches selected Mars or Moon conditions. 2. Compare Two Sites: Allows users to compare two analog locations side by side. 3. Location Filter: Recommends potential analog sites based on the selected world, mission activity and environmental conditions. Our presentation includes example estimates, such as Devon Island's 67% similarity to Mars and the comparison of McMurdo Dry Valleys and Holuhraun. These scores are project estimates, not measured scientific values. Data Sources and Research Our project draws on open resources and references from NASA Earthdata, NASA Worldview, NASA Planetary Data System, ESA, JAXA, CSA, Copernicus and ISRO, along with location-specific geological and climate references. Limitations No Earth environment can fully reproduce the Moon's vacuum or Mars's thin atmosphere, low gravity and radiation conditions. Our analog locations represent selected geological and environmental similarities rather than exact planetary equivalents. Expected Impact The Mars & Moon Analog Globe aims to make planetary analog research more accessible, help users understand the similarities and differences between Earth and other worlds, and demonstrate how Earth environments can support preparation for future space exploration. Team: EXOVAND Project tagline: Earth is our laboratory for the Moon and Mars.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

Abandoned but Not Forgotten: The Stories Behind NASA's Space Equipment

Our project, explores the stories of NASA's equipment left behind on the Moon, Mars and in deep space. Through educational storytelling, we highlight missions such as Apollo, Curiosity, InSight, Perseverance and Voyager, explaining the purpose of their equipment, the discoveries they enabled and their lasting scientific contributions.

The project addresses the challenge by transforming information about abandoned space equipment into engaging and accessible stories for students and young space enthusiasts. Rather than viewing these objects as discarded machinery, we present them as important parts of humanity's journey of exploration and scientific discovery.

This project is important because it encourages curiosity about space, promotes STEM learning and helps people understand that even when a mission ends, the knowledge gained from it can continue to benefit future generations.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details..

Project Title: Abandoned but Not Forgotten: The Stories Behind NASA's Space Equipment

What does the project do?

Our project explores NASA's equipment left behind during space exploration missions on the Moon, Mars and in deep space. It presents the history, purpose and scientific contributions of these objects through educational storytelling. We focus on missions such as Apollo, Curiosity, InSight, Perseverance, Voyager, Pioneer and New Horizons.

How does it work?

The project organizes space equipment and missions into three main categories:

  • Moon: Apollo lunar experiments, seismometers and laser retroreflectors.
  • Mars: Curiosity, InSight and Perseverance, highlighting their discoveries about the Red Planet.
  • Deep Space: Voyager, Pioneer and New Horizons, exploring humanity's journey beyond the outer planets.

Each story explains what the equipment was designed to do, what discoveries it helped achieve and why its scientific contribution remains valuable.

Benefits and intended impact

The project makes space science easier and more interesting for school students and young space enthusiasts. It encourages curiosity, improves awareness of NASA missions and promotes STEM education. It also communicates an important message: equipment left behind is not necessarily useless or forgotten; it can continue to contribute to scientific knowledge long after its original mission.

Tools and technologies used

Our current project deliverables were prepared using:

  • NASA mission information and educational resources for research.
  • Microsoft PowerPoint for the project demonstration.
  • Digital documentation and content-writing tools for organizing the stories and explanations.

This submission is an educational storytelling concept. It does not claim to include a completed software application, physical prototype or custom hardware.

Creativity and innovation

The creative aspect of our project is presenting abandoned space equipment from a different perspective. Instead of focusing only on spacecraft and successful missions, we highlight the instruments and equipment that remain behind and the discoveries they made possible. By connecting scientific facts with storytelling, we aim to make space exploration more relatable, memorable and inspiring.

Factors considered

Our team considered scientific accuracy, educational value, simplicity of language, accessibility for younger audiences and the importance of highlighting the long-term contributions of NASA missions.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

AI-Powered Astronaut Health Monitoring System

Astronauts face several health challenges during space missions due to microgravity, isolation, and changes in the space environment. Continuous health monitoring is important to identify potential health risks early.

3. Key Features

- Heart Rate Monitoring
- Blood Oxygen Level Monitoring
- Body Temperature Tracking
- Stress Index Monitoring
- Health Status Dashboard
- Automatic Status Updates
- Abnormal Reading Alerts

4. Technology Used

- HTML
- CSS
- JavaScript
- AI-assisted development

5. Innovation

The project combines health monitoring indicators into a simple dashboard to support astronaut health awareness and mission monitoring.

6. Expected Impact

ASTRO HEALTH aims to support astronaut safety, improve health awareness, and encourage early identification of potential health concerns during space missions.

7. Future Improvements

- Integration with real health sensors.
- NASA astronaut health datasets.
- AI-based health risk prediction.
- Real-time monitoring and notifications.
- Cloud-based health data storage.

8. Project Objective

To develop an accessible and intelligent monitoring interface that supports astronaut health management and contributes to safer space exploration.

projectDetails.summary:
Forgotten Horizons – Abandoned but Not Forgotten

Forgotten Horizons is an interactive 3D storytelling experience that explores the history of human exploration beyond Earth by bringing attention to the spacecraft, rovers, and equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars.

Inspired by NASA's challenge, "Abandoned but Not Forgotten," our project transforms forgotten space exploration hardware into meaningful stories. Through an immersive 3D explorer, users can discover eight historical missions, including Surveyor 3, Mars Pathfinder, Sojourner, Viking 1 and 2, Spirit, Opportunity, and the Apollo Lunar Module.

The platform features interactive 3D environments, mission information, historical timelines, a Mission Connection Network, and educational quizzes. Users can explore individual objects, understand their missions, discover their scientific contributions, and learn how these abandoned artifacts remain connected to humanity's journey into space.

Our goal is to make space history engaging, accessible, and educational, especially for students and future explorers. These objects may no longer be active, but their stories, discoveries, and contributions continue to inspire scientific curiosity.

Forgotten Horizons reminds us that exploration does not end when a mission is over. Every object left behind has a story worth remembering.
projectDetails.details:
Forgotten Horizons – Abandoned but Not Forgotten

1. What Does Our Project Do?

Forgotten Horizons is an interactive 3D storytelling and educational platform that explores the history of human space exploration by focusing on spacecraft, rovers, landers, and equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars.

The project was developed in response to NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 and its challenge, "Abandoned but Not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars."

Instead of treating abandoned space equipment as forgotten objects, Forgotten Horizons gives each object a story. It helps users understand why these missions were launched, what they achieved, and how their contributions continue to influence space exploration.

2. How Does It Work?

The platform provides several interactive sections:

3D Space Explorer: Users can explore 3D Moon and Mars environments, interact with markers, select historical objects, and discover information about their missions.

Mission Archive: The platform presents eight historical missions: Surveyor 3, Mars Pathfinder, Sojourner Rover, Viking 1, Viking 2, Spirit, Opportunity, and the Apollo Lunar Module.

Mission Connection Network: An interactive network connects the eight missions, allowing users to explore relationships between missions through nodes, filters, and detailed information.

Mission Control Dashboard: A central dashboard provides access to mission information, interactive features, and educational quizzes.

Historical Stories and Timelines: Users can learn about the history, achievements, and scientific importance of the selected missions.

3. Benefits and Intended Impact

Forgotten Horizons aims to make space exploration history more engaging and accessible, particularly for students and people interested in astronomy and science.

Its main benefits include:

- Making historical space missions easier to understand.
- Encouraging curiosity about NASA's exploration of the Moon and Mars.
- Connecting historical missions with their scientific contributions.
- Providing an interactive alternative to traditional text-based learning.
- Helping younger audiences appreciate the importance of past space exploration.

Our intended impact is to inspire people to look beyond the present and recognize the scientific value of missions that have already ended.

4. Tools and Technologies Used

Forgotten Horizons was developed using web technologies and interactive 3D visualization tools.

The technologies include:

- HTML – Structure of the website.
- CSS – Visual design, layouts, animations, and responsive styling.
- JavaScript – Interactive functionality and user experiences.
- Three.js – 3D visualization and interactive space environments.
- Git and GitHub – Version control and project development.
- GitHub Pages – Public website hosting.

The project was developed and tested using a personal computer and a web development environment.

5. Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of Forgotten Horizons is its storytelling approach.

Space exploration is often presented through successful launches, discoveries, and active missions. However, the equipment left behind after missions also represents an important part of human exploration.

Our project transforms these historical artifacts into interactive learning experiences. By combining 3D environments, mission stories, timelines, educational quizzes, and a mission connection network, we create a platform where users can explore space history rather than simply read about it.

6. Factors Considered During Development

During development, we considered:

- Historical accuracy and reliable mission information.
- Simple and accessible navigation.
- An engaging visual experience.
- Educational value for students and beginners.
- Compatibility with modern web browsers.
- Performance and usability across different screen sizes.
- Clear connections between historical missions and their contributions.

7. Our Vision

Forgotten Horizons is built around one simple idea:

"Exploration does not end when a mission is over."

The spacecraft, rovers, and equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars are more than abandoned hardware. They are reminders of human curiosity, engineering, scientific discovery, and the courage to explore beyond Earth.

Through Forgotten Horizons, we want to ensure that these stories continue to inspire future generations of explorers.

Forgotten Horizons – Abandoned but Not Forgotten.

Project Redline – Mars Escape Mission

Project Overview

Project Redline is an interactive space mission survival game set on Mars. Players take on the role of an astronaut stranded on the Red Planet, where they must navigate dangerous surroundings, overcome challenges, manage their mission, and find a way to escape safely. The game creates an immersive experience that introduces players to the difficulties and uncertainties of surviving in an extraterrestrial environment.

How It Works

The game places players in a Mars-based mission scenario where they must make decisions, explore their surroundings, and complete objectives to progress toward escape. Through interactive gameplay and a visual interface, players experience the challenges of operating in an unfamiliar planetary environment. The mission is designed to encourage strategic thinking, problem-solving, and decision-making under pressure.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Project Redline makes space exploration more engaging and accessible through interactive gaming. It helps players develop an appreciation for the challenges astronauts may face during missions to Mars, including environmental hazards, limited resources, navigation, and survival decisions. Its intended impact is to inspire curiosity about Mars exploration, encourage interest in space science, and make learning about planetary exploration more enjoyable.

Tools and Technologies Used

The project was developed using:

  • HTML – for the structure of the game.
  • CSS – for visual design, styling, and the user interface.
  • Vanilla JavaScript – for gameplay logic, interactions, and mission mechanics.
  • Vite – as the development server and build tool.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of Project Redline is its combination of space exploration and survival-based gameplay. Instead of presenting Mars exploration only through text or static information, the project places the player directly inside a fictional Mars escape mission. This interactive approach turns space-related challenges into an engaging experience where players actively participate in the mission.

Factors Considered During Development

The project considers the importance of an engaging user experience, intuitive controls, clear mission objectives, visual consistency, and an immersive Mars-inspired environment. We also considered accessibility, gameplay flow, and performance to make the experience enjoyable and easy to explore through a web browser.

projectDetails.name: Project GeoGuard Kerala
projectDetails.summary: GeoGuard Kerala is a free web app that helps Kerala families understand and prepare for flood and storm risk. For any of Kerala’s 14 districts, it uses 25 years of NASA POWER rainfall data to show the wettest months, heavy-rain days per year, the longest wet streaks and how this year compares with normal, so people can see long-term trends in their own area. A Now tab maps open natural hazard events from NASA EONET over NASA GIBS satellite imagery and ranks them by distance. An Act tab turns the data into before, during and after checklists for floods, landslides and cyclones, in English and Malayalam, printable for families. It addresses the Earth System Trend Detective challenge by making NASA Earth data usable for local decisions.
projectDetails.details:
What it does: GeoGuard Kerala has three tabs. Risk: for each Kerala district, it analyses daily rainfall from NASA POWER (2001 to now) to show average monthly rainfall against this year, heavy-rain days per year, the longest wet streak per year, and a relative flood-prone-season indicator. Now: an interactive map shows open hazard events from NASA EONET, ranked by distance from the chosen district, over NASA GIBS satellite imagery with a date picker. Act: before, during and after checklists for floods, landslides, cyclones and emergency basics, saved in the browser, printable, and available in English and Malayalam.

Impact: Kerala families get alerts but rarely see their own long-term pattern or know what to do. GeoGuard turns open NASA Earth data into plain-language trends and actions.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Leaflet (maps) and Chart.js (charts). No backend.

Creativity: it combines long-term trend analysis (POWER) with current events and imagery (EONET, GIBS) and an action layer in the local language.

Limits we state openly: POWER data is historical, not a forecast, and is gridded (about 50 km), so it smooths local extremes. EONET lists only significant events. The risk levels are relative indicators, not warnings. It does not replace IMD or KSDMA alerts. The Malayalam text has not been reviewed by a native speaker.

AI use: the code and checklist text were written with help from an AI assistant (Claude by Anthropic) and tested by the team owner.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: EARTH MISSION CONTROL: The 20-Minute Decision
projectDetails.summary:
Earth Mission Control: The 20-Minute Decision is an interactive browser-based Mars mission-control simulation developed to demonstrate the challenges of sustaining human life on Mars.

What we developed: We created a 2D interactive game in which players act as Earth-based mission controllers responsible for the survival of four astronauts at a fictional Mars outpost. Players investigate a previous outpost failure, analyze clues, identify the root cause, and respond to a new emergency involving solar power, oxygen, food, water, and radiation protection.

How it addresses the challenge: The game uses real NASA Mars Science Laboratory (Curiosity) dust-opacity observations to drive its dust and solar-power mechanics. It also simulates Earth–Mars communication delays, showing how commands cannot reach astronauts instantly and why mission controllers must plan ahead using limited resources and scientific information.

Why it is important: Future human missions to Mars will face communication delays, dust storms, power limitations, and life-support risks. This simulation turns these complex challenges into an interactive learning experience, helping players understand the importance of scientific data, resource management, teamwork, and critical decision-making in future space exploration.

projectDetails.name: NISAR-InSAR Explorer
projectDetails.summary:
**NISAR InSAR Explorer – Satellite-Based Surface Change Monitoring**

NISAR InSAR Explorer is an interactive web-based platform developed to visualize and analyze changes in Earth's surface using Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) technology. Inspired by the NASA–ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission, the platform allows users to explore global hotspots, compare satellite observation dates, generate surface-change maps, and monitor ground displacement over time.

The project addresses the challenge of identifying and understanding gradual ground movements and environmental changes that may not be easily detected through conventional optical satellite imagery. It provides interactive mapping, customizable analysis regions, time-series visualization, additional environmental data layers, and support for uploading geospatial datasets.

This project is important because monitoring ground deformation, landslides, glacier movement, flooding, deforestation, and land subsidence can support environmental research, disaster preparedness, and informed decision-making. It also makes complex satellite radar concepts more accessible to researchers, students, resource managers, and the general public.

**Note:** The current platform uses physics-based simulated NISAR-like data for demonstration and educational purposes rather than actual NISAR observations.
projectDetails.details:
NISAR InSAR Explorer – Satellite-Based Surface Change Monitoring

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

NISAR InSAR Explorer is an interactive web-based platform inspired by the NASA–ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission. It uses the concept of Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) to visualize and analyze changes occurring on Earth's surface. Users can explore global geographical hotspots, select regions, compare different observation dates, generate surface-change maps, and monitor ground displacement over time. The platform also supports uploading geospatial datasets in formats such as GeoJSON, KML, CSV, SHP, and HDF5 for additional analysis.

2. What benefits does it have?

The platform simplifies complex satellite radar information through interactive maps, visual representations, time-series graphs, and understandable analytical summaries. It helps identify potential environmental changes such as land subsidence, glacier movement, flooding, deforestation, and ground deformation. It also allows users to combine different environmental data layers and export analytical results for further study.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The primary objective is to make satellite-based Earth observation more accessible and understandable. The project aims to support environmental awareness, scientific education, disaster preparedness, and informed resource management. In the future, integrating actual NISAR observation products could help researchers and authorities monitor environmental changes and identify potentially vulnerable regions more effectively.

4. What tools, programming languages, and software were used?

The project was developed using:

  • HTML5: For the structure and layout of the application.
  • CSS3: For styling, responsive layouts, and visual presentation.
  • JavaScript: For application logic, interactive features, and data processing.
  • Leaflet.js: For interactive geographical maps.
  • Chart.js: For time-series graphs and data visualization.
  • NASA GIBS: For additional environmental and satellite data layers.
  • Esri/CARTO: For geographical basemaps.

The project is primarily software-based and does not require dedicated hardware for its current demonstration.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

The creative aspect of this project is the integration of satellite radar concepts, geographical visualization, and interactive analytical tools into a single platform. Instead of presenting complex scientific datasets as raw numerical information, it transforms them into understandable visual insights. Features such as customizable analysis regions, observation-date comparisons, animated time-series exploration, multiple environmental layers, user-data uploads, and audience-specific insights make the platform interactive and educational.

6. What factors did the team consider?

During development, we considered usability, accessibility, geographical accuracy, data compatibility, visualization quality, and the scientific principles behind InSAR technology. We also considered the importance of presenting analytical results in a simple and meaningful manner for different audiences, including students, researchers, scientists, and resource managers. Data reliability and transparency were important considerations, so the platform clearly distinguishes simulated NISAR-like observations from actual satellite data.

Conclusion

NISAR InSAR Explorer demonstrates how satellite radar technology and web development can be combined to create an accessible Earth-observation platform. By connecting scientific concepts with interactive visualization, the project aims to encourage the use of technology for environmental monitoring, research, and disaster awareness.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized.
