projectDetails.name: TerraSleuth
projectDetails.summary:
Earth’s climate is constantly shifting, but raw satellite tables and complex climate models make it difficult for students and everyday citizens to see what is actually changing in their own backyard—and whether those shifts are real trends or just normal weather swings.

**TerraSleuth** solves this by turning users into Earth System Trend Detectives. Through an interactive world map, anyone can click any location on Earth—or explore curated NASA case studies like Kochi’s warming monsoon, Amazon drying, and Arctic climate variability—to inspect multi-decade temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, and humidity records from NASA’s POWER API and MERRA-2 reanalysis datasets.

Instead of leaving users to guess at noisy graphs, TerraSleuth automatically strips away seasonal cycles using a 12-month rolling average and runs real statistical forensics, including Mann-Kendall significance tests, Sen’s slope decade rates, confidence intervals, and changepoint detection. It even lets users compare two regions side by side to see how the same global forces can push different parts of the planet in opposite directions. Finally, TerraSleuth translates the math into a clear, plain-English **Detective Verdict**, helping anyone understand what is changing, where it is happening, and why it matters.
projectDetails.details:
TerraSleuth is an interactive web application designed to turn students, researchers, and everyday citizens into Earth System Trend Detectives. Users can click anywhere on an interactive global map—or select from curated regional case files—to fetch 30 to 40+ years of monthly Earth science data, including 2m air temperature (T2M), precipitation (PRECTOTCORR), surface solar radiation (ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN), and relative humidity (RH2M).

Rather than displaying raw, noisy weather tables, TerraSleuth automatically strips out seasonal cycles using a 12-month rolling average and runs an in-browser statistical forensics engine. It computes the rate of change per decade (Sen’s slope), runs a non-parametric Mann-Kendall trend test ($S$, $Z$-score, and $p$-value), calculates 95% confidence intervals, and pinpoints the exact changepoint year where the largest historical shift occurred. It also includes a guided 3-step Investigation Wizard and a Compare Opposite Regions split-screen mode that demonstrates how the same global climate drivers can push two different regions in opposite directions.

Benefits & Intended Impact Scientific climate datasets are often locked behind complex file formats and specialized statistical software, creating a barrier for high school and college students. TerraSleuth bridges that gap by pairing accessible, plain-English variable definitions with real statistical rigor. By translating statistical significance ($p < 0.05$) into a clear Detective Verdict (Clue, Suspect, and Why It Matters), the tool empowers learners to distinguish true long-term environmental shifts from short-term natural variability—promoting scientific honesty and data literacy.

Tools, Languages, Software & NASA Resources Used

  • Languages & Libraries: HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), Leaflet.js (interactive mapping), and Chart.js (time-series visualization and changepoint markers).
  • Development & Hosting: Developed using Google Antigravity IDE (used as an AI coding collaborator to accelerate UI scaffolding and statistical module implementation), version-controlled on GitHub ([github.com/arjid200/TerraSleuth](https://github.com/arjid200/TerraSleuth)), and deployed as a zero-backend static web application via GitHub Pages.
  • NASA Data Resources: Live global pin-drops query the NASA POWER Temporal API (1985–2025), backed by NASA MERRA-2 assimilation data. Pre-loaded regional case files use verified 30-year monthly NASA POWER / MERRA-2 CSV datasets (1995–2024, 0.5° × 0.625° spatial resolution) alongside support for user-uploaded CSV exports from NASA Giovanni and AppEEARS (covering missions and models such as GPM, MODIS, OMI, AIRS, and GLDAS).

Creativity & Design Considerations

  • Detective Framing: Reframing statistical hypothesis testing as an environmental "crime scene investigation" makes abstract metrics like $p$-values and deseasonalization intuitive and engaging for students.
  • Scientific Honesty & Spatial Scale: Our team explicitly designed TerraSleuth to highlight non-significant trends alongside significant ones—for example, showing how high year-to-year polar variability at a single Arctic grid point (80.00°N, 0.01°E) masks long-term warming over a 30-year window, whereas Kochi, Kerala (9.93°N, 76.27°E) exhibits statistically significant warming (+0.27°C/decade, $p < 0.0001$) alongside highly variable monsoon rainfall, and the Amazon Basin (3.10°S, 60.00°W) experiences both significant warming (+0.35°C/decade) and drying (-0.52 mm/day/decade). We also explicitly note the ~50–70 km MERRA-2 grid-cell footprint so users understand spatial resolution limits.
  • Zero-Friction Accessibility: By running all statistical calculations purely client-side in JavaScript and bundling pre-verified CSV case studies locally, TerraSleuth requires zero installation, zero server overhead, and loads instantaneously even on low-bandwidth connections.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.details:
LUNAR LEGENDS 🚀

Three friends. One dream. A universe to explore.

What is Rocket Quest?

Rocket Quest is a 3D space-adventure game that you play in your browser. You are the pilot, the engineer and the astronaut all at once.

Every level is one complete space mission:

  1. Design a rocket with a limited money budget.
  2. Launch it from an Earth launch site after a 10-second countdown.
  3. Fly through an asteroid field where rocks and debris come at you from every direction.
  4. Land on the Moon or on Mars.
  5. Survive on foot or in a rover: find oxygen, food and water, repair a probe, collect rock samples and plant a flag that says LUNAR LEGENDS.
  6. Lift off and fly back to Earth, dodge another asteroid field, and land safely.

Only a landing back on Earth completes the mission and pays you. Then you spend your earnings on a stronger rocket and take on the next, harder level. There are 50 levels, and the last stretch is genuinely tough.

Getting Started

Creating your pilot profile

When the game opens you create a profile:

  • Username – the name other pilots see above their screens and in chat.
  • Squad password – pilots who type the same squad password are put in the same room and fly together. Think of it as a room key for you and your friends.

Please note: the squad password only groups players together. It is not a secure account password, so never use a password you use anywhere else. The page itself is already protected by your sign-in to the platform.

The tutorial

First-time players go through a 7-step tutorial covering building, launching, asteroids, landing, the Moon, missions and playing together. You can replay it any time from the main menu.

The main menu

  • Continue campaign (level N) – jump back in where you left off.
  • Level select – replay any level you have already unlocked.
  • Restart from level 1 – wipes your progress (you must click twice to confirm).
  • Mission editor – design your own custom missions.
  • Co-op and friends – add friends, see who is online and invite people.
  • Tutorial – replay the how-to-play steps.

Rocket Quest: Quick Player Guide

What is it? A 3D browser space-adventure game where you design, launch, fly, land, and survive across 50 challenging levels on the Moon and Mars with your squad.

1. Build Your Rocket

  • Starting Budget: $6,000.
    • Engine Power ($500/step): Boosts thrust for faster liftoff and stronger braking.
    • Fuel Tanks ($300/step): Extends your range for launch, dodging, and the trip home.
    • Hull Shield ($400/step): Strengthens your armor against asteroid hits and hard landings.
  • Tip: A balanced build wins. Fuel runs out fast, and shields save you from mistakes!

2. Launch From Earth

  • Watch the 10-second countdown, then hold ▲ Up at liftoff.
  • Tilt with ◀ ▶ to steer and reach 1,200 m to enter space.

3. The Asteroid Field

  • Cruise through 3,400 m of rocks and debris using inertial arrow-key movement.
  • Survival Tools: Use your radar and warning lines to track incoming threats.
  • Hit Limit: You can take 3 asteroid hits (levels 1–39) or 2 hits (level 40+) before crashing back to the pad. Stay out of the edges or an aggressive asteroid swarm will hunt you down!

4. Landing & Surface Survival

  • Landing: Touchdown safely keeping descent under 4 m/s and sideways drift under 3 m/s.
  • Life Support: Keep an eye on your Oxygen, Food, and Water bars. Refill oxygen at your rocket or via caches.
  • Surface Transport: Walk or deploy/call your Rover (R) to save oxygen.
  • Surface Missions: Survive 2 minutes, repair the red probe, collect 3 amber rock samples, plant the LUNAR LEGENDS flag (F), and gather water ice (level 30+). Avoid red meteor rings and get to the rocket during solar flares!

5. Fly Home

  • Board your rocket (E) once missions are done, dodge the return asteroid field, and land safely on Earth to collect your cash reward ($2,500 + $500 per level).

6. Multiplayer & Custom Maps

  • Co-op: Enter the same squad password with friends (like Bryan and Aiden) to see each other's rockets, chat, and fly together in real time.
  • Mission Editor: Design custom challenges with unique seeds, gravity, and asteroid densities, then share them using Make code.

50 LEVELS

  • Levels 1–9 (Moon & Mars on 3,6,9): Very gentle start, 3-hit limit, learn the basics.
  • Levels 10–19: Gentle asteroid field, 3-hit limit; life support drains faster.
  • Levels 20–29: Moderate asteroid field, 3-hit limit; frequent meteors and flares.
  • Levels 30–39: Challenging asteroid field, 3-hit limit; water ice mission added.
  • Levels 40–45: HARD mode, strict 2-hit limit; dense, fast asteroids.
  • Levels 46–50: Very hard, 2-hit limit; only 1 oxygen cache leading up to the Level 50 final boss test.

Space Credits and Upgrades

  • Every completed mission indicates a payment of $2,500 + $500 for each level. Level 1 pays $3,000, level 10 pays $7,500 and level 50 pays $27,500.
  • Bonus +$1,000 if you land on Earth without any damage.
  • Your money pays for the stronger parts you choose on the build screen. As your budget grows you can afford bigger engines, more fuel and thicker armor, and the sliders themselves allow bigger numbers as you rise.
  • Missions from the mission editor earn money too, but they do not move your campaign level.

Co-op Multiplayer and Chat

Rocket Quest is better with friends.

  • Join the same squad: enter the same squad password as your friends.
  • See each other: you see your friends’ rockets during launch, the asteroid field and landing, and their astronauts with name tags on the surface. They also show up as dots on your map, and a “Pilots online” counter appears in the HUD.
  • Same level, same world: you only see pilots who are on the same level and destination as you. Use Join level on the Co-op screen to jump to a friend’s level.
  • Add friends: type a username on the Co-op screen to add a friend and see when they are online.
  • Invite: copy a ready-made invite message with the link and the squad password.
  • Chat: press Enter, type, then Enter again to send (Esc cancels). Messages appear in the bottom-left corner and fade after about 15 seconds

Mission Editor

Want a custom challenge? Open the Mission editor and choose:

  • Destination – Moon or Mars
  • Seed – a number that creates a whole unique world (try different ones!)
  • Asteroid density and space debris density
  • Supply crates
  • Survival drain
  • Gravity multiplier

Use Make code to get a share code, and Load code to play a mission a friend made. Great for challenges and for endless replay.

Controls Cheat Sheet

  • Arrow Keys (▲ ▼ ◀ ▶): Fly, tilt, walk, or drive.
  • Shift: Run on foot or boost the rover.
  • Space: Get out of or into the rover.
  • R: Call the rover to your position.
  • F: Plant a Lunar Legends flag.
  • E: Board the rocket to fly home (when near it and missions are done).
  • Enter / Esc: Open or cancel chat.
  • Mobile / Tablet: On-screen buttons appear automatically with directional arrows on the right, and Run, Exit, E, Flag, and Rover on the left.

Sound and Graphics

  • Sound: engine rumble that deepens with throttle, countdown beeps, deep impact booms, pickup chimes, warning sirens, astronaut footsteps, breathing, an ambient space pad and button clicks. Sound starts after your first click or key press.
  • Graphics: a coastal launch site built from real photo textures, a cratered Moon and a rusty Mars, a real-photo Earth, soft sun shadows, a glowing sun, colorful nebulas, and a rocket with live engine glow.

✅ Do’s

  • Do build a balanced rocket: fuel and hull matter as much as engine power.
  • Do watch the radar and the warning line in the asteroid field.
  • Do return to the center lane to avoid the swarm.
  • Do keep your descent under 4 m/s when landing.
  • Do top up oxygen at your rocket often.
  • Do use the rover and call it with R to save time and oxygen.
  • Do run away from red meteor rings and get to the rocket during solar flares.
  • Do team up with friends and chat.

❌ Don’ts

  • Don’t hide at the edge of the flying area; the swarm will find you.
  • Don’t burn all your fuel on the way up.
  • Don’t ignore the asteroid hit counter in the HUD.
  • Don’t sprint everywhere on foot when oxygen is low.
  • Don’t forget the 2-minute survival rule before you press E.
  • Don’t reuse a real password as your squad password.
  • Don’t relax on the way home; the return flight is as dangerous as the way out.

The Mission

Combine curiosity, creativity, and problem-solving to go farther with every flight.

Dream big. Land smart. Become a Lunar Legend.

projectDetails.name: Dustfall
projectDetails.summary:
It is an Interactive Mars Survival and Mission Training Simulator. DUSTFALL combines story-driven gameplay with NASA's Martian environmental science to help young explorers understand the challenges of operating a planetary outpost.
Through MARS-EIS, real scientific observations can inform environmental conditions, while interactive survival mechanics teach resource management, engineering trade-offs, and scientific decision-making.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, DUSTFALL, powered by the Mars Environmental Intelligence and Simulation Engine (MARS-EIS), is an interactive Mars survival simulation developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, Kochi. It combines scientific environmental modelling, artificial intelligence, and gameplay to demonstrate the challenges of sustaining human life on Mars.

MARS-EIS simulates Martian atmospheric conditions, dust storms, solar radiation, temperature variations, and habitat infrastructure using physics-based models and real observational data from NASA missions. AI models (GRU and Isolation Forest) provide environmental forecasting and anomaly detection. DUSTFALL presents these simulations through a 2D survival game where players respond to emergencies, repair infrastructure, manage resources, and protect the crew.

The project uses Python, Pygame, NumPy, SciPy, PyTorch, FastAPI, WebSockets, NetworkX, SQLite, and with optional CUDA GPU acceleration.

Its key innovation is modelling cascading environmental consequences rather than relying on scripted events. For example, dust storms reduce solar power generation, causing battery depletion and threatening habitat operations.

Our intended impact is to promote planetary science education and provide a foundation for exploring Mars habitat resilience, environmental risks, and sustainable human exploration. We prioritised scientific accuracy, computational efficiency, modularity, scalability, and accessibility.

projectDetails.name: MonsoonLens – Earth System Trend Detective
projectDetails.summary:
MonsoonLens is an interactive climate trend investigation dashboard developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It uses monthly climate data from NASA POWER to explore long-term changes in temperature, precipitation and relative humidity across selected locations in India, including Kochi, Thiruvananthapuram, Kozhikode, Bengaluru, Mumbai and New Delhi.

The platform transforms monthly observations into annual climate indicators and visualizes changes through interactive charts. It includes annual temperature trends, accumulated rainfall, June–September monsoon rainfall and annual relative humidity. Users can compare multiple locations, examine trend estimates and statistical significance, and explore geographical patterns through an interactive map.

By making climate data easier to visualize and compare, MonsoonLens helps users investigate how environmental indicators change over time and how these patterns differ between regions. It uses NASA POWER data to make Earth system trends more accessible and understandable.
projectDetails.details:
MonsoonLens – Earth System Trend Detective

What does the project do and how does it work?

MonsoonLens is an interactive climate trend investigation dashboard that helps users explore how climate indicators change over time and differ across geographical locations in India.

The project retrieves monthly climate data from NASA POWER through its API, focusing on three indicators: air temperature (T2M), precipitation (PRECTOTCORR) and relative humidity (RH2M). The monthly data is processed into annual indicators and presented through interactive visualizations.

Users can select a study location and time period, investigate annual temperature trends, accumulated rainfall, June–September monsoon rainfall and annual relative humidity. The dashboard also provides trend estimates, statistical analysis, comparisons between multiple locations and an interactive map showing the selected study regions.

What benefits does it have?

MonsoonLens makes climate data easier to understand without requiring users to download datasets or perform statistical calculations themselves. It brings multiple climate indicators together in one accessible interface and allows users to compare geographical differences. This helps students, educators and other interested users explore environmental patterns using NASA's Earth science data.

What is the intended impact?

The intended impact is to improve awareness and understanding of regional climate variability and long-term environmental changes. By making Earth science data more accessible, MonsoonLens encourages data-driven exploration, environmental education and curiosity about interconnected Earth systems.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed primarily using Python. Streamlit was used to build the interactive dashboard, Pandas and NumPy for data processing, Plotly for interactive charts and geographical visualizations, SciPy for statistical analysis, and Requests for retrieving data from the NASA POWER API. Development and testing were performed on a Linux-based computer. No dedicated external hardware is required.

How is the project creative?

MonsoonLens combines several climate indicators, statistical trend analysis, geographical visualization and multi-location comparison in a single investigation tool. Rather than presenting climate data as isolated tables, it allows users to interactively explore relationships between time, location and environmental change. Its focus on Indian locations also provides a regional perspective on climate patterns.

What factors did the team consider?

The development considered data availability, reliability of monthly observations, missing values, appropriate annual aggregation methods, ease of use and geographical coverage. Minimum valid-month requirements were applied to annual calculations to reduce misleading results from incomplete data. Rainfall accumulation accounts for the number of days in each month, while annual humidity uses day-weighted averaging. Statistical significance is interpreted cautiously because correlation does not establish causation, and autocorrelation may affect p-values.

MonsoonLens aims to turn publicly available NASA climate data into an accessible and interactive experience for investigating changes in our environment.

projectDetails.summary:
ORBITAL FRONTIER is a web-based space exploration and rocket simulation experience designed around the concept of becoming a spacecraft engineer and astronaut. The project combines a futuristic mission-control interface with 3D spaceflight, rocket engineering, planetary exploration, and astronaut-oriented gameplay.

The core idea is to let the player progress through a space mission by designing and configuring a spacecraft, preparing it for launch, controlling the mission, exploring space/planets, and completing scientific and engineering objectives.

For a hackathon presentation, you could describe it like this:
ORBITAL FRONTIER is an immersive 3D space exploration and rocket engineering simulator that transforms the player into both a spacecraft engineer and astronaut. Players can design and customize spacecraft, prepare missions, launch rockets, monitor flight telemetry, navigate through space, explore planetary environments, and complete engineering and scientific challenges. The project combines interactive 3D graphics, spacecraft systems, mission progression, and scientifically informed space data into a single browser-based experience.
projectDetails.details:
ORBITAL FRONTIER — BEYOND EARTH. BEYOND LIMITS.

Project Overview

ORBITAL FRONTIER is an interactive 3D space exploration and rocket engineering simulator that puts the player in the role of both a spacecraft engineer and astronaut.

The player can select a mission and destination, study environmental conditions, design and customize a spacecraft, select engines, fuel systems, structural components, thermal protection and scientific equipment, and perform pre-launch inspections.

The configured spacecraft is then used in a simulated mission involving rocket launch, atmospheric ascent, flight telemetry, stage separation, orbital navigation, spacecraft deployment, planetary missions, astronaut exploration, spacecraft repair, scientific sample collection and mission scoring.

The spacecraft configuration is connected to the simulation. For example, changing engines can affect thrust and fuel consumption, while adding additional protection increases vehicle mass. This makes engineering decisions part of the actual gameplay rather than purely cosmetic customization.

The first complete mission is designed around the Moon, where the player progresses from spacecraft preparation and launch through lunar operations, repairs and scientific objectives.

Benefits and Educational Value

ORBITAL FRONTIER combines education, engineering concepts and interactive gameplay.

Players can learn simplified concepts related to rocket propulsion, mass and thrust, fuel management, orbital mechanics, spacecraft systems, thermal protection, radiation, life support, planetary environments and mission planning.

Instead of simply reading about spaceflight, players make engineering decisions and see their consequences in the simulation.

For example:

  • More fuel increases capacity but also increases vehicle mass.
  • Different engines provide different thrust and fuel-consumption characteristics.
  • Additional shielding improves protection while adding mass.
  • Different spacecraft configurations can be better suited to different missions.

The project is also designed to incorporate reliable information from NASA, NOAA, JPL, ESA and other authoritative scientific sources rather than presenting fabricated scientific information.

Intended Impact

The intended impact of ORBITAL FRONTIER is to make space science and spacecraft engineering more accessible, interactive and engaging.

Many people experience space science through videos, articles or static educational material. ORBITAL FRONTIER attempts to bridge that gap by allowing users to experience the process themselves:

Design → Inspect → Launch → Fly → Explore → Discover

The project aims to encourage:

  • Interest in STEM
  • Curiosity about space science
  • Understanding of engineering trade-offs
  • Interest in aerospace engineering
  • Scientific thinking
  • Problem solving
  • Mission planning
  • Experimentation

The long-term vision is to expand the Moon mission architecture into missions involving Mercury, Venus, Mars and the outer planets, using appropriate orbital, atmospheric or robotic missions where conventional landing is scientifically inappropriate.

Technology and Development

ORBITAL FRONTIER is designed as a browser-based 3D application, allowing users to experience the project without installing a traditional desktop game.

The planned technology stack includes:

  • React — application and UI architecture
  • TypeScript — strongly typed application and game logic
  • Three.js — real-time 3D rendering
  • React Three Fiber — React integration for Three.js
  • Drei — reusable 3D utilities
  • Tailwind CSS — responsive interface styling
  • Zustand — centralized game-state management
  • Rapier or an appropriate browser physics system — physics-related simulation
  • GLTF/GLB assets — spacecraft and environmental models
  • Node.js or Python-based backend services, where required
  • NASA and other public scientific APIs/datasets for scientific information
  • Vercel — deployment and hosting

The project is designed to use optimized 3D assets, compression, level-of-detail rendering, frustum culling, lazy loading and adaptive graphics quality to improve browser performance.

Creativity and Innovation

The creativity of ORBITAL FRONTIER comes from combining several traditionally separate experiences into one interactive system.

Instead of creating only a rocket simulator, planet viewer, educational dashboard or astronaut game, ORBITAL FRONTIER combines them into a single mission experience.

The player moves between different roles:

SPACECRAFT ENGINEER — Design and configure the spacecraft.

FLIGHT ENGINEER — Inspect systems and monitor telemetry.

PILOT — Control the spacecraft during flight.

MISSION OPERATOR — Navigate and manage spacecraft systems.

ASTRONAUT — Explore, repair equipment and conduct scientific activities.

Another creative aspect is the modular spacecraft system, where components are intended to have actual consequences within the simulation rather than simply changing the appearance of the vehicle.

The project also combines real scientific information with simulated gameplay.

Information is explicitly distinguished as:

REAL DATA — retrieved from scientific sources.

SIMULATED — calculated by the game.

EDUCATIONAL MODEL — simplified representation of scientific principles.

This allows the project to remain engaging while maintaining scientific transparency.

Design Considerations

Several important factors were considered while designing ORBITAL FRONTIER.

Scientific accuracy: Real scientific information must be distinguished from game simulation, and fictional values should not be presented as actual NASA measurements.

Gameplay feasibility: A complete professional-grade space simulator would be extremely complex, so the project uses simplified educational simulation models while maintaining consistent relationships between variables.

Performance: Because the game runs in a browser, the project considers 3D asset size, rendering performance, loading times, texture optimization, level of detail, lazy loading and responsive design.

Usability: Complex spacecraft information needs to remain understandable, so telemetry, warnings, engineering statistics and mission information are organized into dedicated HUD and dashboard systems.

Modularity: The spacecraft, missions, planets, astronaut systems and simulation logic are designed as modular systems so additional missions can be added without rebuilding the entire application.

Scientific realism versus gameplay: The goal is not to claim that ORBITAL FRONTIER is a professional aerospace simulator. Instead, it aims to create a scientifically informed educational simulation that is also engaging and playable.

Hackathon constraints: The Moon mission was selected as the first complete vertical slice so the project can demonstrate the complete gameplay loop before expanding to additional planetary missions.

Project Vision

ORBITAL FRONTIER aims to transform space exploration from something users simply watch or read about into something they can actively experience.

The core experience is:

DESIGN → BUILD → LAUNCH → FLY → EXPLORE → DISCOVER

BEYOND EARTH. BEYOND LIMITS.

projectDetails.name: SPACE LEFT BEHIND
projectDetails.summary:
Still Out There is an interactive story map of NASA hardware. Since the 1960s NASA has left rovers, landers and probes on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Some still work, some finished their missions, and some have gone quiet. The project tells their stories so school-age space fans can meet the machines and the science they made possible.

Students see 17 machines on one distance map and pick a place to explore. Each machine shows its status, a short story, three facts to remember and a link to the open data behind it. A bonus tool shows how long a radio message to each machine takes. A live countdown follows Voyager 1 reaching one light-day from Earth on 18 November 2026.

The facts come from public NASA pages and partner agency data from ISRO and ESA. The next step is to connect live NASA data, such as official photos and exact distances.
projectDetails.details:
Project details: Still Out There

What does it do and how does it work?
Still Out There is a website that puts 17 NASA machines on one distance map, from the Moon to interstellar space. A student picks a place (Moon, Mars, near the Sun, far out) or a status and taps a machine. The machine's page shows:

  • a status: still working, mission complete, or out of contact
  • a short story and the science it made possible
  • three facts to remember
  • a link to the open data behind it

A "How long would a hello take?" tool shows how long a radio message to each machine takes. A live countdown follows Voyager 1 reaching one light-day from Earth on 18 November 2026. The site works on phones and in light or dark mode.

What are the benefits?

  • A student can answer one question quickly: is it still talking?
  • Each story is short and plain, so it works for school-age readers.
  • Every claim links to a public source, so students can check it.
  • The distance map and radio-delay tool make huge distances easier to grasp.

What impact is intended?
We want students to see space exploration as ongoing, with machines that outlive their plans and keep working. We also want them to learn that NASA's data is free to explore. A teacher could use it as a starting point for lessons on the solar system, light-speed delays and how science is checked.

What tools and software did we use?

  • HTML, CSS and plain JavaScript for the website, with no frameworks. The Voyager countdown and the radio-delay calculator are written in JavaScript.
  • Inline SVG for the machine drawings.
  • Google Fonts (Lexend, Unbounded, DM Mono).
  • Claude to research, write and build the site and the deck.
  • Headless Chrome (Playwright) to capture screenshots, and pptxgenjs to build the PowerPoint.

No special hardware was needed.

What data does it use?
NASA mission pages and news provided the dates and status. Partner data from ISRO (Chandrayaan images of Apollo sites and of India's Vikram lander) and ESA (Huygens, the ExoMars orbiter, Hera) appears in the stories. The prototype uses facts I curated from these sources. It does not call live NASA APIs yet. Connecting the NASA Image and Video Library, the Mars Rover Photos API and JPL Horizons is the planned next step.

How is it creative?

  • It organises the machines by whether they are still talking, which gives a story with a status instead of a plain list.
  • The log-scale map keeps the Moon and Voyager 1 on one screen.
  • The page follows a real event in progress: Voyager 1's light-day milestone.
  • The status uses colour and shape together, so it doesn't rely on colour alone.

What factors did we consider?

  • Accuracy: I checked key facts against sources and marked Voyager 2 and the Pioneers as estimates. Hera's arrival is worded as "was due" because I found no confirmation that it had happened.
  • Audience: plain language, short text, readable type sizes.
  • Access: works on phones, in both themes, with keyboard focus and reduced-motion support.
  • Honesty: the page says which parts are live and which are planned.
  • Scope: 17 machines, which is enough to tell the story without overwhelming a student.

projectDetails.name: SphereXPLORER
projectDetails.summary:
SphereXPLORER is an interactive platform that brings the universe closer through immersive astronomical exploration and scientific visualization.

Built to make complex astronomical data easier to understand, it allows users to explore the sky, inspect celestial objects, and investigate their spectral properties through dedicated interactive tools. But it goes beyond simply displaying data.

With 3D visualizations, multi-view astronomical inspection, spectral analysis, and cross-epoch exploration through the Time Machine, users can examine the universe from different perspectives and uncover connections that might otherwise go unnoticed.

The platform combines scientific depth with an intuitive, story-driven interface. Every section encourages discovery, making the experience engaging rather than overwhelming.

Our vision is simple: turn complex astronomical observations into opportunities for discovery. By bringing data, visualization, and exploration together, SphereXPLORER aims to make astronomical research more accessible to researchers, students, and anyone curious about the universe.
projectDetails.details:
SphereXPLORER is designed to turn NASA's vast SPHEREx infrared survey into an interactive environment for astronomical exploration and citizen science.

At its core, the platform connects with the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) to retrieve genuine SPHEREx observation metadata and calibrated Level 2 FITS images. Users can enter custom Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec) coordinates, search for known celestial objects, or explore curated targets such as Barnard's Star, WISE 0855, Epsilon Indi B, RW Aurigae and R Draconis.

The platform is organized into several interconnected scientific workspaces:

  • Sky Explorer: An interactive all-sky atlas that allows users to navigate celestial regions, inspect coordinates and compare different astronomical survey layers.
  • Object Explorer: Provides detailed information about celestial objects, their observations, positions and available scientific data.
  • Spectral Explorer: Opens up SPHEREx's 102 infrared spectral channels, allowing users to investigate wavelength-dependent features and explore the molecular signatures of astronomical sources.
  • Time Machine: One of the platform's central features. It transforms genuine multi-epoch observations into an interactive time-lapse, with playback, blinking, side-by-side comparisons and difference imaging to help users identify changes in the sky.
  • Discovery Lab: Brings together image stacking, source detection, cross-epoch analysis and a discovery journal.
  • Missions: Introduces guided scientific activities and interactive learning experiences for newcomers.

Scientific reliability is a major consideration. Rather than relying on generated astronomical imagery, SPHEREXPLORER processes authentic FITS data using celestial coordinate transformations, WCS reprojection and calibrated image processing. Catalogue-predicted positions are distinguished from actual source detections, and unavailable observations or insufficient evidence are reported transparently.

Technology and Development

The frontend is developed using React 19, TypeScript, Vite and Tailwind CSS, with Three.js powering interactive 3D experiences, including a model of the SPHEREx spacecraft. Aladin Lite provides astronomical sky visualization.

The backend uses Python and FastAPI, supported by Astropy, Photutils, Reproject and PyVO for astronomical data retrieval, FITS processing, astrometry, image alignment and source detection. NASA/IPAC IRSA provides the primary SPHEREx data source, while Gaia DR3 and other astronomical catalogues provide additional reference information.

We also integrated Driver.js to provide guided walkthroughs, making the scientific tools approachable even for users without an astronomy background.

Creativity, Benefits and Intended Impact

What makes SPHEREXPLORER different is the way it combines scientific functionality with an immersive exploration experience. Instead of presenting users with complicated datasets and expecting them to understand everything independently, we created a platform that guides them through the process of exploring, comparing and interpreting astronomical observations.

We considered scientific accuracy, accessibility, performance, data availability, usability and the needs of both beginners and experienced astronomy enthusiasts throughout development.

Our ultimate goal is to make astronomical discovery more accessible and collaborative. By giving people intuitive tools to examine how the sky changes over time, SPHEREXPLORER aims to encourage citizen-science participation and help more people contribute to exploring the universe.

projectDetails.name: Mars Safe Path: An Interactive Jezero Traverse Planner
projectDetails.summary: Mars Safe Path is an interactive web-based educational prototype developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, focusing on the Jezero Crater region of Mars. It combines three NASA Mars Trek imagery layers—Viking visible imagery, MGS MOLA colour hillshade and THEMIS daytime infrared imagery—using HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Leaflet.js. Users can explore different map layers, select starting and destination points, and compare a direct route with an A* pathfinding algorithm that identifies a lower-cost path using a synthetic 16 × 16 traversal-cost grid. The project addresses the challenge by demonstrating how planetary imagery and intelligent route-planning techniques can support Martian surface exploration. It is important because future Mars exploration requires careful terrain assessment and efficient route planning for robotic and human missions. This prototype provides an educational foundation for developing advanced Mars navigation systems using real terrain and hazard data.
projectDetails.details: Mars Safe Path is an interactive educational web application designed to demonstrate how planetary mapping and intelligent route-planning techniques can support future Mars exploration. Focused on the Jezero Crater region, the application allows users to explore three independently selectable NASA Mars Trek imagery layers: Viking visible imagery, MGS MOLA colour hillshade and Mars Odyssey THEMIS daytime infrared imagery. Users can select starting and destination points, generate routes using the A* pathfinding algorithm, and compare the suggested route with a direct path using approximate distance and traversal-cost metrics. The project helps users understand how different remote-sensing datasets provide complementary views of the Martian surface and how algorithms can balance distance with modelled traversal costs. Its intended impact is to improve awareness of planetary mapping, terrain exploration and computational route planning while inspiring interest in space science and technology. The application was developed using HTML, CSS, JavaScript and Leaflet.js, with NASA Mars Trek WMTS imagery and an A* algorithm operating on a synthetic 16 × 16 cost grid. Its creative aspect lies in combining multiple NASA imagery layers with an interactive route-planning demonstration in a single user-friendly platform. We considered map accessibility, ease of interaction, different visual perspectives of Mars, route comparison and scientific transparency. The current prototype is educational; its synthetic costs are not actual terrain measurements or detected hazards. Future development could integrate real elevation and terrain data to improve route-planning accuracy.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Forgotten Echoes
projectDetails.summary: Forgotten Echoes is a 3D exploration game where students walk the Moon and Mars and uncover the hardware NASA left behind. A scanner and radar show how close a find is without revealing what it is. Players then dig it out and brush the dust off by hand. Each find opens a Catalogue Entry with its mission, year, purpose and current status, plus a short written historical story. Sixteen artifacts are included, three on the Moon (the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle, the Apollo 11 Lunar Module descent stage, and the ALSEP science station) and thirteen on Mars (including Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Viking and Ingenuity). Mars unlocks once the Moon is complete.
projectDetails.details:
What it does. Forgotten Echoes is a 3D exploration game for school-age space fans. You walk the lunar surface and Mars. A scanner and a radar show how close a buried object is, but not what it is. You then dig it out with a short mini-game and brush the dust off by hand with the mouse. Each find opens a Catalogue Entry (mission, year, purpose, current status) and a Journal slot. You can also watch a short written historical story about the hardware. There are 16 artifacts: 3 on the Moon (Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle, Apollo 11 Lunar Module descent stage, ALSEP) and 13 on Mars (Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Viking 1 and 2, Phoenix, InSight, Ingenuity, Perseverance hardware and more). Mars unlocks once the Moon is complete.

Benefits and impact. Players learn by finding things, not by reading a list. Each entry separates documented NASA facts (ARCHIVE) from simulated in-game readings (SIM), so students can tell record from simulation. We want players to leave seeing these machines as the work of real people and still-active science.

Tools. Godot 4 with GDScript and the GL Compatibility renderer. IBM Plex fonts, original SVG icons, and a custom “declassified archive” interface design. Artifact text is data-driven (artifacts.json, flashbacks.json) and checked by automated tests.

Creativity. The mystery scanner turns “abandoned equipment” into treasure hunting. The cleaning mini-game reveals each specimen as the player scrubs. The interface looks like a declassified mission file.

Factors considered. Accuracy and source citation, readability at small screen sizes, accessibility (status is never colour alone, reduced-motion option, key hints read from the real controls), and a short, replayable loop.

projectDetails.name: Project MJ : NASA SPACE SILENT HEROS
projectDetails.summary:
We developed NASA’s Silent Space Heroes, an engaging, kid-friendly educational storytelling presentation designed specifically for school students.
To address the Abandoned, But Not Forgotten challenge, our project transforms complex NASA mission archives into an exciting visual journey across the Moon, Mars, and deep space. Using simple analogies, vibrant illustrations, and relatable storytelling, we introduce students to historic pioneers—from Apollo lunar landers and Mars rovers like Spirit, Opportunity, and Ingenuity, to deep-space probes like Voyager—while explaining space laws, space recycling, and planetary protection.
This project is important because young learners often find space science overly technical. By framing inactive spacecraft as heroic pioneers rather than "space trash"—and highlighting how iconic rovers were named by school students—we spark curiosity, preserve humanity’s cosmic heritage, and inspire the next generation of space explorers.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do & How does it work?

NASA’s Silent Space Heroes is an interactive, storytelling-based educational presentation that I developed individually for school students. It takes young learners on an exciting visual journey across the Moon, Mars, and interstellar space to explore NASA’s inactive landers, rovers, and orbital hardware. Each slide pairs vivid custom illustrations with my own authentic, narrative voiceover that brings historic missions—like Apollo, Viking, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight, Ingenuity, and Voyager—to life.

What benefits does it have & What is the intended impact?

The primary benefit of this project is making complex space science and space law accessible, fun, and memorable for children. My intended impact is to shift how young minds view inactive spacecraft—showing them that these machines are priceless historical monuments ("anthropogenic materials") rather than "space trash." By highlighting that famous Mars rovers were named by school students through essay contests, I aim to spark lifelong curiosity and inspire the next generation of space explorers.

How is the project creative?

As a solo creator, I transformed heavy scientific concepts into relatable, kid-friendly analogies—such as comparing space treaties to "museum velvet ropes," rover upgrades to "leveling up," and lunar artifacts to "hidden Easter eggs." Combining custom visual storytelling with a warm, engaging voiceover keeps students hooked from start to finish.

Tools, Software, Hardware & AI Used:

• Software & Hardware: Microsoft PowerPoint for slide design and audio recording (recorded directly using built-in device audio without external microphones), and Google Drive for cloud hosting.

• Use of Super Intelligence (AI Tools): ChatGPT and Google AI were used to refine my kid-friendly narration scripts and generate custom visual illustrations for the slides, while the presentation structure and voiceover recording were created manually by me.

• Official NASA & Partner Data Used: Official NASA Open Data & Mission Archives (Apollo Program, Mars Exploration Program, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, and Voyager mission data) along with ISRO Chandrayaan mission resources.

What factors did I consider?

Working independently, I prioritized age-appropriate language, visual clarity, scientific accuracy, and global inclusivity. I carefully balanced official NASA mission facts with simple everyday comparisons so school children could easily understand complex topics like planetary protection, space weathering, and space recycling without feeling overwhelmed.

projectDetails.name: FireScope : Satellite-Based Wildfire Monitoring and Early Warning System
projectDetails.summary:
FireScope: Satellite-Based Wildfire Monitoring and Early Warning System

FireScope is a satellite-powered wildfire monitoring and decision-support platform that uses NASA's MODIS and VIIRS active-fire datasets, accessed through NASA FIRMS. It processes near-real-time satellite observations to identify potential fire hotspots, visualize their geographical locations, and assess detection attributes such as confidence and Fire Radiative Power (FRP).

The platform aims to combine satellite observations with environmental data, including weather conditions, rainfall, vegetation and terrain, to provide better context for identifying areas of potential fire risk. Through interactive mapping, historical analysis and hotspot monitoring, FireScope seeks to make wildfire information more accessible and useful for timely decision-making.

The project addresses the challenge of monitoring fires across large and remote areas where ground-based observation may be limited. By leveraging freely accessible NASA Earth observation data, FireScope aims to support environmental monitoring, improve situational awareness and assist communities and emergency responders in making informed decisions.
projectDetails.details:
FireScope: Satellite-Based Wildfire Monitoring and Decision-Support System

FireScope is a wildfire monitoring platform designed to improve the detection, visualization and understanding of potential fire activity using NASA Earth observation data.

How it works

The platform retrieves active-fire observations from NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), primarily using MODIS and VIIRS satellite datasets. VIIRS provides approximately 375-metre spatial resolution, enabling more detailed hotspot monitoring. The system processes geographical coordinates, acquisition timestamps, detection confidence and Fire Radiative Power (FRP) to identify and visualize potential fire activity on an interactive map.

We also explore integrating environmental information such as temperature, rainfall, wind conditions, vegetation and terrain to provide additional context for assessing fire risk. Historical observations can help identify recurring fire activity and monitor changes over time.

Benefits and intended impact

FireScope aims to make satellite-derived fire information easier to understand and access. It can help environmental researchers, forest monitoring authorities and emergency response teams identify areas requiring attention, improve situational awareness and support informed decisions. Its intended impact is to contribute towards more effective wildfire monitoring and environmental protection, particularly in remote areas.

Tools and technologies

  • Data sources: NASA FIRMS, MODIS and VIIRS.
  • Programming: Python for data acquisition and processing.
  • Libraries: Pandas and Requests for data handling and API integration.
  • Visualization: Interactive geographical mapping.
  • Environmental data: NASA Earth observation and weather datasets.

Creativity and innovation

The creative aspect of FireScope lies in combining multiple freely accessible satellite datasets into a unified monitoring platform. Rather than displaying isolated fire detections, it aims to provide geographical context, historical patterns and environmental information to make satellite observations more meaningful.

Factors considered

Our team considered satellite resolution, data availability, observation delays, detection confidence, false positives, cloud interference, geographical coverage and accessibility. We also recognized that a satellite hotspot does not always indicate a wildfire and that intermittent satellite observations cannot guarantee continuous monitoring. These limitations are important when designing a reliable decision-support system.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

projectDetails.name: Vigil-space-health
projectDetails.summary:
Who looks after an astronaut when immediate medical help from Earth is unavailable?

VIGIL began with a simple question: how can we make sure astronauts receive appropriate health monitoring, medical guidance and support during long missions, even when they are far from immediate medical assistance on Earth?

Inspired by a physician's perspective, we set out to explore what healthcare could look like beyond our planet. We wanted to build something that goes beyond collecting health measurements—something that helps astronauts understand their health, keep track of changes and access support when they need it.

Our LUNA-01 demonstration brings this idea to life through synthetic astronaut health records, physiological trends, mission conditions, a Crew Health Map and four simulated Medical Companion roles: Doctor, Nurse, Pharmacist and Psychologist.

But VIGIL is bigger than the software we have today. We imagine it eventually becoming the intelligence and coordination system behind a future space medical bay, bringing together automated laboratory testing, bone-health monitoring, robotic ultrasound, psychological support and specialised medical AI.

Our goal is to explore how reliable, accessible healthcare can travel with people, wherever humanity goes.
projectDetails.details:
VIGIL LUNA-01

Beyond Monitoring: Building a Future for Astronaut Healthcare Beyond Earth

Bringing continuous healthcare and human support to space missions.

PROJECT SUMMARY

Who looks after an astronaut when medical help from Earth is no longer just a phone call away?

VIGIL began with a simple question: how can we make sure astronauts receive proper healthcare during long missions, even when they are millions of kilometres away from Earth?

Inspired by a physician's perspective, we set out to explore what healthcare could look like beyond our planet. We wanted to build something that goes beyond collecting health measurements. Something that can help astronauts understand their health, keep track of changes and access support when they need it.

Our LUNA-01 demonstration brings this idea to life through synthetic astronaut health records, physiological trends, mission conditions, a Crew Health Map and four simulated Medical Companion roles: Doctor, Nurse, Pharmacist and Psychologist.

But VIGIL is bigger than the software we have today. We imagine it eventually becoming the intelligence and coordination system behind a future space medical bay, bringing together automated laboratory testing, bone-health monitoring, robotic ultrasound, psychological support and specialised medical AI.

Our goal is to explore how reliable, accessible healthcare can travel with people, wherever humanity goes.

1. THE PROBLEM: HEALTHCARE BEYOND EARTH

When we think about space exploration, we often focus on rockets, spacecraft and the technology needed to reach distant worlds. But there is another challenge that deserves just as much attention: looking after the people who make those missions possible.

An astronaut is more than a set of numbers on a monitor. They are human beings who can experience fatigue, discomfort, stress, loneliness and illness. During a long-duration mission, these challenges can become even harder to manage because immediate medical support from Earth may not be available.

Spaceflight also brings its own health challenges. Changes in gravity can affect muscles and bones, while disrupted sleep, isolation and demanding schedules can influence both physical and psychological wellbeing.

Monitoring health measurements is important, but it is only part of the picture. Astronauts also need support that considers their medical history, changing circumstances and personal experiences.

This led us to ask:

What if astronauts could carry a healthcare companion with them, one that helps them understand their health and access support even when Earth is far away?

That question became the starting point for VIGIL.

2. OUR SOLUTION: VIGIL

VIGIL is an astronaut health-monitoring and support platform that we are developing around LUNA-01, a fictional mission to the lunar south pole.

Our current demonstration brings several ideas together:

- Mission-aware health monitoring: Tracks synthetic crew health measurements, personal baselines, sleep, activity and wellbeing throughout a simulated mission.

- Physiological trends: Helps users see how health indicators change over time instead of looking at individual readings in isolation.

- Crew Health Map: Shows shared numerical patterns across permitted crew records using predefined demonstration rules.

- Mission-control interface: Includes an interactive 3D lunar environment, mission phases, lander inspection and simulated interruptions in communication with Earth.

- Four Medical Companion roles: Doctor, Nurse, Pharmacist and Psychologist, each representing a different aspect of astronaut healthcare.

- Medical references: Provides access to selected NASA Human Research Program material and links to the original sources.

- Personalised support research: A separate authenticated development prototype explores evidence-based responses and consent-controlled health memories.

We wanted VIGIL to bring together two important things: the awareness and organisation of mission control, and the continuity and understanding of a healthcare team.

3. THE HUMAN SIDE OF SPACE EXPLORATION

Physical health is only one part of an astronaut's wellbeing.

Imagine spending months away from family and friends, living in a confined environment and following demanding schedules with very little privacy. Even the most experienced astronauts can face psychological challenges in these conditions.

This is why we included a simulated Psychologist companion in VIGIL.

It represents our early exploration of how technology could support regular wellbeing check-ins, provide a space for supportive conversations and maintain continuity between interactions.

In the future, we would like to explore more personalised support through consent-based memory, culturally sensitive communication and scientifically reviewed psychological assessment methods.

We also recognise that healthcare is not the same for everyone. Certain needs, including menstrual, reproductive and sexual health, deserve appropriate attention and strong privacy protections rather than being overlooked by general monitoring systems.

Our intention is not to replace human relationships or professional mental healthcare. We want to explore how responsible technology can make support more accessible when direct human assistance is difficult to reach.

4. OUR FUTURE VISION: AN INTELLIGENT SPACE MEDICAL BAY

The current VIGIL application is only the beginning of what we hope to explore.

Our long-term vision is to develop VIGIL into the intelligence and coordination layer of a future space medical bay, bringing different medical technologies and specialised AI systems together in one environment.

With the right research partnerships, equipment and medical oversight, we see several possibilities.

AUTOMATED BONE-HEALTH MONITORING

One of the challenges of spending extended periods in reduced gravity is the effect it can have on bone health.

We would like future versions of VIGIL to bring together different measurements that help track changes in bone metabolism.

These could include blood and urine biomarkers, vitamin and mineral assessments, and validated imaging methods.

Compact laboratory equipment could eventually make it possible to collect and analyse some of these measurements directly during a mission.

Rather than relying on one reading, VIGIL could help organise the results over time and make changes easier for medical professionals and astronauts to understand.

These measurements would support medical assessment, not independently diagnose bone-density loss or fracture risk.

ROBOTIC ULTRASOUND FOR MUSCLE MONITORING

Muscle changes are another important concern during long-duration spaceflight.

We imagine a future system that uses compact ultrasound equipment to monitor muscle structure and size over time.

A robotic or robot-assisted ultrasound system could help position the probe consistently and collect images that can be compared throughout a mission.

Specialised software could then analyse the images, track changes and flag measurements that need further review.

This would require considerable research and testing to establish that the equipment is safe and that its measurements are reliable.

AI-COORDINATED LABORATORY SERVICES

Future space missions may need to carry more of their medical testing capabilities onboard rather than depending on laboratories on Earth.

We envision VIGIL eventually connecting with compact laboratory instruments and automated sample-processing systems.

Specialised AI agents could help coordinate approved testing procedures, check equipment quality, collect results and compare them with an astronaut's previous records.

This could make routine medical investigations more manageable during missions where communication with Earth is limited.

A TEAM OF SPECIALISED MEDICAL AI AGENTS

We believe that one general-purpose AI system should not have to handle every aspect of astronaut healthcare.

Instead, we envision specialised systems working together, each with a clearly defined role.

Doctor: Helps organise medical information, review health trends and support clinical decision-making.

Nurse: Supports regular monitoring, care routines and approved procedural guidance.

Pharmacist: Helps review medication safety, maintain medication records and support inventory management.

Psychologist: Provides structured wellbeing activities, supportive communication and guidance on accessing professional care.

Over time, additional agents could assist with laboratory equipment, ultrasound imaging, nutrition and medical supplies.

The idea is to bring these different capabilities together into one coordinated system rather than having separate tools that cannot communicate with each other.

Any high-stakes medical decision or physical intervention would still require appropriate safety controls and authorised human oversight.

5. DEVELOPMENT ROADMAP

We see VIGIL developing in stages, with each stage building on what came before.

PHASE 1: INTEGRATED MISSION HEALTH MONITORING

This is the foundation of our current prototype.

It brings together synthetic astronaut records, personal health baselines, mission timelines, physiological trends, medical reference retrieval and simulated companion interactions.

PHASE 2: ADVANCED MONITORING AND PERSONALISATION

The next step would be to explore suitable physiological sensors, structured health assessments and more reliable methods of tracking individual health changes.

We also want to investigate specialised medical models and personalised support using carefully selected data and expert-reviewed testing.

PHASE 3: MEDICAL EQUIPMENT INTEGRATION

At this stage, we would explore how VIGIL could work alongside automated laboratory instruments, bone-health monitoring systems and ultrasound-based muscle assessments.

The focus would be on making different medical technologies work together within a single platform.

PHASE 4: EARTH-INDEPENDENT MEDICAL OPERATIONS

Our long-term goal is to research a coordinated medical environment that combines specialised AI agents, robotic systems, medical equipment and clinical decision-support tools.

Each stage would need its own technical, medical, ethical and safety validation before it could be used in real missions.

6. WHAT WE HAVE ACTUALLY BUILT

We believe it is important to distinguish between what VIGIL can demonstrate today and what we hope to achieve in the future.

Our submitted public LUNA-01 demonstration is a working browser application. It uses fictional crew members and synthetic health measurements and does not require users to log in.

The current public version includes:

- An interactive 3D lunar environment.

- A mission dashboard.

- Longitudinal astronaut health records.

- A Crew Health Map.

- Four simulated Medical Companion modes.

- Educational medical references from NASA.

The public demonstration uses predefined rules to select relevant educational excerpts. It does not run a live generative AI model.

We have also developed a separate authenticated prototype that uses Gemma for bounded evidence selection. It includes server-side validation, source governance and consent-based memory controls.

Some of our larger ideas are still at the research and planning stage.

The Earth communication outage is simulated. Automated blood testing, robotic laboratory procedures, diagnostic ultrasound, specialised model fine-tuning and autonomous medical treatment are future research goals, not features we claim to have completed.

Neither version has been clinically validated or authorised to provide autonomous diagnoses or prescriptions.

7. WHY VIGIL MATTERS

As humanity prepares for longer missions and eventually more permanent operations beyond Earth, healthcare will become an increasingly important part of space exploration.

Astronauts will need more than equipment that records their vital signs. They will need systems that help them understand their health, organise medical information and access appropriate support when communication with Earth is limited.

VIGIL is our attempt to explore how these capabilities could come together.

What began as a health-monitoring concept has grown into a broader vision of connected medical technology, specialised AI and future medical robotics.

We know there is a long way to go before such a system could be used in a real space mission. But we believe it is worth starting the conversation and building the foundations today.

Because when humanity begins living beyond Earth, healthcare should not be left behind.

PROJECT LINKS

Interactive demonstration:

https://vigil-space-apps-2026.pages.dev/

27-second project video:

https://vigil-space-apps-2026.pages.dev/space-apps-demo.mp4

RESEARCH FOUNDATIONS

The scientific direction behind VIGIL is informed by the NASA Human Research Program, NASA Exploration Medical Technologies and published research into the health challenges of human spaceflight.

AI-assisted development tools supported our planning, implementation, testing and deployment. The public demonstration uses deterministic reference selection and does not claim autonomous medical capabilities.

projectDetails.name: MARS OUTPOST COMMANDER
projectDetails.summary:
Mars Outpost Commander is an interactive survival and science simulation game developed using PictoBlox for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. The project allows players to experience the challenges of living on Mars by managing a science outpost for 30 Martian days (sols). Players must carefully manage four important resources: Power, Oxygen, Crew Morale, and Science Data, while choosing only two actions per sol.
The game simulates real challenges of Mars exploration, including limited communication with Earth, solar flares, random events, and crew isolation. It uses real space weather data from NASA DONKI to make the simulation more realistic. Players must make strategic decisions to protect the crew, maintain life-support systems, and collect at least 100 Science Data to complete the mission.
This project raises awareness about the difficulties of human space exploration and demonstrates the importance of resource management, decision-making, teamwork, and scientific research for future Mars missions.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Mars Outpost Commander

Mars Outpost Commander is an interactive Mars survival and science simulation game developed using PictoBlox for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It allows players to experience the challenges of managing a human science outpost on Mars.

How does it work?

The player takes the role of a commander responsible for keeping the crew alive and completing scientific research over 30 Martian days (sols). Each sol allows only two actions, so players must make careful decisions. They need to manage four important resources: Power, Oxygen, Crew Morale, and Science Data. Solar flares, random events, communication delays with Earth, and crew isolation create additional challenges. Players must collect at least 100 Science Data and maintain the survival resources to win the mission.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

The project creates awareness about the challenges of human exploration on Mars. It helps players understand the importance of resource management, critical thinking, problem-solving, decision-making, and the psychological well-being of astronauts. It also makes space science more engaging and accessible to students.

Tools and Technologies Used:

  • PictoBlox and Scratch 3 programming environment.
  • Block-based coding with 835 programming blocks.
  • Sprites, costumes, backdrops, and interactive user interface elements.
  • NASA DONKI (Space Weather Database) for real solar flare information.
  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the browser-based demonstration.
  • No additional hardware or extensions are required for the PictoBlox game.

Creativity and Innovation:

The creative aspect of this project is combining space science, survival simulation, and interactive gameplay. Instead of simply learning about Mars, players experience the difficulties of living there through realistic challenges and strategic choices. The project also includes a browser demo with movement and a robotic rover that helps players explore and collect science data.

Factors Considered During Development:

Our team considered the harsh Martian environment, limited resources, solar radiation, communication delays between Earth and Mars, crew isolation, life-support requirements, and the need for scientific research. We also focused on making the game interactive, educational, easy to understand, and suitable for young learners.

Overall, Mars Outpost Commander transforms the challenges of Mars exploration into an engaging learning experience and encourages the next generation to think about the future of human space exploration.

projectDetails.name: SPACE DANCING SARs
projectDetails.summary: “Dancing with the STARs,” is an interactive space animation developed using PictoBlox Block Coding. We created a virtual night sky featuring four sprites: a Dancing Star, Polaris (the North Star), a Star Group and Earth. The Dancing Star changes costumes, bounces up and down, rotates and changes colours while playing music. Polaris twinkles by continuously changing its brightness. The Star Group rotates around the centre, and Earth spins continuously to represent its rotation. Through these animations, our project demonstrates why stars appear to move across the night sky while Polaris remains almost stationary. It addresses the challenge of understanding the apparent movement of stars by transforming an astronomy concept into a fun visual coding experience. This project encourages creativity, computational thinking and scientific curiosity while helping students understand Earth's rotation and explore the wonders of space.
projectDetails.details:
Dancing with the STARs

Dancing with the STARs is an interactive space-themed animation developed using PictoBlox Block Coding. Our project demonstrates how stars appear to dance and move across the night sky because of Earth's rotation.

How Does Our Project Work?

We created a virtual night sky with four main sprites:

  1. Dancing Star: The star plays music, changes its costumes, rotates, moves up and down, and changes colours continuously, creating a dancing effect.
  2. Polaris (North Star): This sprite twinkles by continuously increasing and decreasing its brightness. It represents the North Star, which appears almost stationary in the sky.
  3. Star Group: A group of small stars rotates continuously around the centre, demonstrating the apparent circular movement of stars around Polaris.
  4. Earth: The Earth sprite rotates continuously to represent Earth's rotation.

We also planned interactive explanations using speech and a quiz to help users understand the science behind the animation.

Benefits and Intended Impact

  • Makes astronomy easy and interesting to understand.
  • Explains Earth's rotation through visual animation.
  • Helps students understand why stars appear to move.
  • Develops creativity, logical thinking and computational skills.
  • Encourages students to explore space science through coding.

Tools and Technologies Used

  • Software: PictoBlox
  • Programming Language: Visual Block-Based Coding
  • Coding Concepts: Events, loops, motion, costumes, sound and visual effects.
  • Sprites: Star, Polaris, Star Group and Earth.
  • Platform: Computer-based simulation.

No external hardware was required because the entire project was developed as a software-based simulation.

What Makes Our Project Creative?

Our creativity lies in combining astronomy with animation and coding. Instead of simply explaining Earth's rotation through text, we created a virtual night sky where stars twinkle, rotate and dance with music. The combination of animated characters, sound and scientific explanations makes the learning experience more engaging and interactive.

Factors Considered by Our Team

  • Scientific accuracy of the concept.
  • Correct representation of Polaris and Earth's rotation.
  • Smooth animation and sprite movements.
  • Suitable background, colours and sound effects.
  • Simple explanations that students can easily understand.
  • An engaging and educational user experience.

Our main goal is to combine science, imagination and technology to make learning about the universe fun and meaningful.

projectDetails.name: Martian Training Simulation
projectDetails.summary:
This project is an interactive training simulation designed to prepare young astronauts for their journey to Mars. Created using block-based coding in Scratch, it provides a fun and educational way to understand the challenges of space exploration.

Our challenge was to develop a programme that would test and prepare astronauts for the extreme conditions of Mars and space. We designed multiple challenges that simulate space travel, including Mars' harsh climate, strong winds, difficult take-offs, gravity changes and unexpected emergencies. Each challenge tests astronauts' abilities, improves their problem-solving skills and teaches them to handle difficult situations.

Proper training is essential before astronauts travel to space. Without preparation, they may struggle with unpredictable conditions during their mission. Our simulation offers an engaging way to practise important skills while learning about travelling to and surviving on Mars.

Furthermore, this project could inspire other educational simulations, interactive learning experiences and astronaut training programmes in the future.
projectDetails.details:
This project is a Martian Training Simulation designed to

We developed this project using Scratch block coding. To bring our project to life, we transformed a 2D world into a 3D-like environment using a coding technique called raycasting. The simulation consists of three main training stages, each with different objectives and rules.

Stage 1: Centrifuge Training Challenge

Use the D key or right arrow key to move right.

Use the A key or left arrow key to move left.

Navigate carefully through the training course.

Avoid obstacles along the way.

Maintain control of your movements.

Reach the destination before the timer runs out.

Stage 2: Neutral Buoyancy Lab (NBL)

  • Press the SPACEBAR to float upwards.
  • Learn to control your movements
    in simulated weightless conditions.
  • Navigate through the training area.
  • Avoid obstacles while moving.
  • Practise maintaining control in
    a weightless environment.
  • Complete the challenge within
    the given time.

Stage 3: Mars Rover Survival Challenge

  • Use the rover to navigate through the Martian labyrinth.
  • Collect scrap metal and minerals along the way.
  • Avoid the dangerous entity hunting you.
  • Keep an eye on your health and resources.
  • Avoid getting trapped in the labyrinth.
  • Complete the challenge before the timer runs out.

This simulation is intended not only for astronauts but also for ordinary people who are interested in learning about space and the challenges of travelling to Mars. Through its different stages, players can develop problem-solving skills, improve their ability to react to difficult situations and gain a better understanding of the conditions in space. The challenges are designed to test, train and prepare players for the unpredictable environment of Mars and space exploration.

We hope this project will help inspire young people who dream of becoming future astronauts and encourage them to work towards achieving their goals. We also hope that other students and creators will take inspiration from our work and develop more innovative training simulations, educational games and interactive projects. Ultimately, our goal is to make learning about space exploration more exciting, accessible and inspiring for everyone.

projectDetails.name: COSMIC RUN 3D - BEYOND THE UNIVERSE
projectDetails.summary: COSMIC RUN 3D – Beyond the Universe is an immersive 3D space exploration game that combines endless runner gameplay with space science and educational experiences. Players navigate through challenging cosmic environments, avoid obstacles, collect rewards, and explore simulated journeys to destinations such as the Moon, Venus, Mars, and Jupiter.
