projectDetails.details:
COSMIC RUN 3D – Beyond the Universe is an interactive 3D space exploration game developed to combine entertainment, technology, and scientific learning.

The game features an endless runner-style space environment where players control a spacecraft and navigate through challenging cosmic obstacles. Players can move, jump, slide, avoid laser barriers, and overcome different challenges while progressing through the game.

The project introduces a simulated space exploration journey featuring destinations such as the Moon, Venus, Mars, and Jupiter. Player performance and game scores are converted into simulated exploration distances, allowing players to visualize their progress toward different planetary milestones.

Key Features:

- Immersive 3D space environments.

- Interactive spacecraft movement and controls.

- Obstacle avoidance and laser challenges.

- Simulated planetary exploration.

- Score and distance tracking.

- Coins, XP, and achievement systems.

- Game progression and increasing difficulty.

- Mission reports displaying player progress.

- Mobile-friendly gameplay experience.

The main objective is to transform space science into an engaging gaming experience and encourage curiosity about the universe through interactive learning.

projectDetails.name: ARTEMIS-VIEW
projectDetails.summary:
GRAZE (ARTEMIS-VIEW) is an advanced lunar south pole mission planning and horizon navigation web application designed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.

What we developed: An intuitive flight console featuring a real-time 360-degree local horizon raycasting engine, side-by-side site comparison matrices, an interactive launch-slip shock-test simulator, and a scrubbable 30-day operational timeline.

How it addresses the challenge: By integrating NASA LOLA topographical data with topocentric ephemeris calculations, GRAZE visualizes exact Sun and Earth positions relative to jagged crater silhouettes. It dynamically computes solar power generation efficiency—factoring in mast height adjustments and panel orientations—while tracking Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication visibility.

Why it is important: Lunar south pole operations face extreme environmental constraints where a 500-meter coordinate shift or a minor launch date delay can plunge a lander into multi-day shadow blackouts and communication failure. GRAZE bridges the gap between raw scientific telemetry and rapid scenario evaluation, empowering engineers and planners to make agile, life-or-death mission decisions.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

GRAZE is an interactive lunar south pole mission planning and horizon navigation web application. It bridges the gap between complex orbital mechanics and rapid mission decision-making.

  • How it works:
    1. Topographic Horizon Raycasting: It utilizes pre-computed 360-degree terrain elevation profiles derived from NASA LOLA (Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter) high-resolution digital elevation models. For any selected landing site, it accounts for lunar spherical curvature and local crater/mountain ridges.
    2. Topocentric Ephemeris Engine: It computes the precise topocentric azimuth and elevation of the Sun and Earth in real time, accounting for the Moon's extreme $1.54^\circ$ axial tilt, the synodic solar cycle, and Earth's optical libration (the wobbling figure-8 path Earth traces in the lunar sky).
    3. Interactive Visualizations: It renders a 360° sky-dome panorama, a side-by-side site comparison matrix, a launch-slip shock-test simulator, and a scrubbable 30-day operational timeline tracking sunlight, Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication windows, and optimal overlap periods.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Rapid Scenario Evaluation: Instead of navigating cumbersome enterprise tools like NASA's Quickmap or JPL Horizons separately, planners can evaluate alternative sites or delayed launch dates in seconds.
  • Precision Risk Mitigation: It prevents catastrophic mission failures by accurately predicting multi-day shadow blackouts and communication dropouts caused by towering crater rims.
  • Hardware Trade-off Analysis: Features like the dynamic Solar Mast Height Adjuster (1m rover vs. 10m tower) let engineers instantly test how raising an array clears an obstructing ridge.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

  • For Mission Planners & Engineers: Accelerates coordination between science and engineering teams during NASA CLPS or commercial lunar missions, allowing rapid adaptation when launch delays or hardware changes force site re-evaluations.
  • For Education & Outreach: Serves as an engaging public-facing and educational tool that makes the harsh engineering realities of lunar south pole exploration—such as extreme shadowing and libration—instantly intuitive.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Core Framework & UI: React, Vite, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Lucide Icons.
  • Visualizations & Graphics: HTML5 Canvas and SVG for procedural shadow rendering, interactive 360° horizon panoramas, and responsive layout styling.
  • Data & Astronomy: Selenographic ephemeris calculation modules and curated topographic elevation profiles derived from NASA PGDA / LOLA datasets.
  • Version Control & Hosting: Git, GitHub (ARTEMIS-VIEW repository), and Vercel for instantaneous cloud deployment.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Interactive Hero Simulation: The landing page features an HTML5 canvas where moving the cursor sweeps the Sun's azimuth at a grazing $1.54^\circ$ elevation, casting real-time procedural shadow cones across Shackleton Crater while highlighting elevated ridges in golden light.
  • Scrollytelling Physics Briefing: Instead of static text, the app breaks down complex concepts (axial tilt, horizon occlusion, and Earth libration) through interactive, step-by-step visual cards.
  • High-End Flight Console Aesthetic: Abandoning generic tech styling, it adopts a custom design system ("Selenographic Obsidian & Regolith") featuring frosted basalt glassmorphism, vacuum black foundations (#050608), and tabular telemetry numerals.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Airless Vacuum Physics: Factoring in the total lack of atmospheric refraction, meaning terrain silhouettes dictate the horizon with razor-sharp precision and zero diffuse scattering.
  • Spherical Curvature & Scale: Ensuring long-baseline raycasting accurately accounted for the Moon's rapid horizon drop-off ($R = 1737.4\text{ km}$).
  • User Cognitive Load: Designing a single-screen command view that packs map navigation, sky-dome panoramas, timeline scrubs, and feasibility scorecards into a cohesive, jitter-free interface.

Lunar Outpost Simulator is an interactive educational game that explores the challenges of human survival on the Moon. Players take charge of a lunar outpost and manage essential resources such as oxygen, water, food, and power to keep the crew safe throughout a 30-day mission.

The simulation introduces players to key challenges of lunar exploration, including resource conservation, greenhouse food production, radiation protection, and unexpected emergencies. Every decision matters, as players must balance limited resources and respond to changing mission conditions.

By turning complex space exploration challenges into an engaging interactive experience, the project aims to promote awareness of lunar science, sustainable living, and the technologies needed for future human missions to the Moon.
projectDetails.details: Lunar Outpost Simulator is an interactive educational game designed to demonstrate the challenges of establishing and maintaining a human settlement on the Moon. Players manage a lunar outpost for a 30-day mission, making decisions to keep the crew alive and the base operational. The game includes oxygen, water, food, and power management, greenhouse food production, radiation protection, resource conservation, and unexpected emergency events. The simulation encourages strategic thinking, decision-making, and problem-solving. Players must balance limited resources and respond to changing mission conditions to achieve mission success. The project aims to make lunar exploration and the challenges of human survival in space accessible and engaging, especially for students and people interested in space science. The project was developed as a web-based simulation using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with AI-assisted development support. The team considered resource limitations, crew safety, sustainability, and the importance of reliable life-support systems. Its creative approach is to turn complex lunar survival concepts into an interactive 30-day mission experience.

projectDetails.name: NOVYRA
projectDetails.summary:
Field Shift is an interactive climate-intelligence and farm-planning platform developed by Novyra. It combines regional climate scenarios, crop information, interactive maps, temperature and rainfall visualizations, crop-rotation planning, soil-health projections, seasonal risk checks, and estimated farm impacts in one mission-control-style workspace. The platform also includes a NASA POWER data loader, allowing users to compare historical temperature, rainfall, and root-zone soil-wetness data for selected locations. A dedicated offline-first Kerala Farmers Zone provides crop guides, paddy-season information, and basic answers to common farming questions.

Field Shift addresses the challenge of helping farmers adapt to changing growing conditions. It translates complex Earth-observation and climate data into practical decisions about crop selection, irrigation, rotation, soil health, and heat or rainfall risks. It is especially useful in regions where weather-station coverage and internet access may be limited.

The project is important for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 because it demonstrates how NASA data can support climate resilience and local communities. It connects NASA POWER with potential future layers from SMAP, HLS, and GPM IMERG to turn space-based observations into actionable agricultural insights.
projectDetails.details:
FIELD SHIFT BY NOVYRA

Project Documentation

1. What does the project do, and how does it work?

Field Shift is a climate-intelligence and farm-planning web application designed to help farmers understand how changing climate conditions may affect their crops and farming decisions.

The application works as an interactive Mission Control Workspace. Users can:

Select a farming region and crop.

Explore temperature and rainfall patterns.

Adjust an illustrative scenario year and additional warming level.

View changes in growing degree days, rainfall, and average temperature.

Compare historical and recent climate trends.

Review climate conditions for all crops in a selected region.

Build a crop-rotation plan based on soil texture, organic matter, water conservation, heat tolerance, soil health, and income priorities.

Examine expected soil-health changes over a five-year period.

Check a manually entered seasonal forecast for possible heat, rainfall, or soil-moisture risks.

Estimate the wider impact across a selected number of farms and hectares.

Enter coordinates and fetch historical temperature, rainfall, and root-zone wetness data through the NASA POWER API.

Use an offline farmer-support section for Kerala, including crop guides, paddy-season information, and answers to common questions about waterlogging, soil health, monsoon preparation, and plant problems.

The initial experience uses sample regional data. Users can replace this with location-specific historical information using the NASA POWER data loader.

The project clearly explains that its scenario calculations are for exploration and are not official forecasts or validated climate projections.

---

2. What benefits does the project have?

Field Shift provides several important benefits.

1. Better Farm Planning

It helps users compare crops and make more informed decisions about crop rotation, planting conditions, irrigation, soil management, and climate risks.

2. Easier Access to Complex Climate Data

NASA and Earth-observation data can be difficult for non-specialists to interpret. Field Shift converts this information into visual charts, indicators, sliders, tables, and recommendations that are easier to understand.

3. Climate Adaptation

The platform helps farmers think ahead about increasing temperatures, changing rainfall patterns, drought, waterlogging, and declining soil quality.

4. Improved Water and Soil Management

The rotation planner allows users to prioritize saving water, improving soil health, managing heat and drought, and protecting farm income.

5. Support for Regions with Limited Connectivity

The Kerala Farmers Zone is designed to work offline after the page has been saved. This makes the knowledge assistant more useful in areas where internet access may be unreliable.

6. Local Relevance

The project includes Indian and Kerala-specific farming information, including districts, crops, and broad paddy seasons such as Virippu, Mundakan, and Puncha.

7. Scalability

The platform can potentially support additional locations, crops, data sources, satellite products, and local agricultural knowledge libraries.

---

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is to strengthen the ability of farmers and agricultural communities to adapt to climate change.

Field Shift aims to:

Reduce the gap between scientific climate data and everyday farm decisions.

Help farmers identify climate-related risks before they cause major losses.

Encourage more resilient crop choices and crop rotations.

Support responsible use of water and improvement of soil health.

Make Earth-observation data useful to small and medium-sized farms.

Provide practical information to communities that may not have access to specialist agricultural advice.

Encourage farmers to combine satellite and climate information with local observations and expert guidance.

Support more sustainable and economically resilient agriculture.

The broader goal is to transform climate data into practical action. Instead of presenting information only as scientific measurements, the project connects environmental changes to decisions that farmers can understand and use.

Field Shift is not intended to replace agricultural experts, field observations, soil testing, or official weather and agricultural advisories. It is designed as an educational and decision-support tool that helps users ask better questions and prepare more effectively.

---

4. What tools, coding languages, and software were used?

Based on the project files, Field Shift was developed as a browser-based web application using the following technologies:

1. HTML (HyperText Markup Language): Used for the structure and content of the application.

2. CSS (Cascading Style Sheets): Used for the visual design, layout, responsive interface, colours, typography, and component styling.

3. JavaScript: Used for user interactions, calculations, controls, charts, planners, scenario sliders, crop guides, and the offline knowledge assistant.

4. SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics): Used for visualisations such as temperature and rainfall charts.

5. NASA POWER API: Used to retrieve historical temperature, rainfall, and root-zone soil-wetness data.

6. Python: Used for the included NASA data-processing script, using the requests, collections, and json libraries.

7. OpenStreetMap: Used for the interactive map and location exploration.

8. Netlify: Used for hosting and deploying the web application.

Potential Future Data Sources:

NASA SMAP.

HLS (Harmonized Landsat and Sentinel-2).

Landsat.

Sentinel-2.

GPM IMERG.

These are identified as possible additional data layers rather than fully demonstrated features in the current project.

The project is primarily a lightweight, client-side web application, making it easy to access through a browser without requiring users to install specialised software.

---

5. How is the project creative?

Field Shift is creative in both its concept and its presentation.

1. Mission-Control Approach

Instead of presenting the project as a conventional agricultural dashboard, it uses a space-mission and mission-control theme. This connects farming on Earth with NASA Earth-observation technology and makes the interface more engaging.

2. Climate Twin Concept

The Farm Climate Twin combines climate data, crop information, soil conditions, user priorities, and possible scenarios into one interactive planning environment. This helps users explore how different decisions may affect their farms.

3. Combining Data with Action

Many climate tools only display charts or maps. Field Shift goes further by connecting the information to crop rotation, soil health, water management, seasonal checks, and estimated farm impact.

4. Scenario Exploration

The year slider and additional-warming control allow users to explore how conditions could change. The tool labels these as illustrative scenarios, making the feature educational while avoiding the claim that it is an official prediction.

5. Offline-First Local Support

The Kerala Farmers Zone adds a creative, community-focused element. It does not rely entirely on live data or internet connectivity and provides regional crop information and basic farming guidance in one place.

6. User-Centred Visualisation

The project uses large indicators, interactive controls, comparison tables, colour-coded sections, charts, and simple explanations to make complex environmental data more approachable.

7. Connecting Space Technology to Local Farming

Its most distinctive creative idea is turning NASA data into a tool for local agricultural resilience. It shows how space-based observations can have a direct connection to soil, crops, rainfall, and farmer decision-making.

---

6. What factors did the team consider?

The team considered several important factors during development.

1. Data Accuracy and Transparency

The project distinguishes between sample data, historical data, scenarios, forecasts, and official projections. It explains that NASA POWER uses gridded and reanalysis-supported information rather than direct field sensors.

2. Responsible Interpretation

The application warns users not to treat illustrative climate scenarios as official NASA forecasts. It also recommends checking local observations and official agricultural advice before making important decisions.

3. User Accessibility

The interface is designed for people who may not have advanced climate or data-science knowledge. Charts and indicators are paired with plain-language descriptions and practical recommendations.

4. Local Farming Needs

The team included Kerala-specific districts, crops, paddy seasons, and common farmer questions. This shows consideration for regional agricultural practices instead of creating a completely generic global tool.

5. Limited Connectivity

The offline farmer-support feature reflects the possibility that some users may have unreliable or expensive internet access.

6. Diverse Farmer Priorities

The rotation planner allows users to balance water conservation, heat and drought tolerance, soil health, and farm income. This recognises that farms have different priorities and that one solution will not fit every user.

7. Different Soil Conditions

The planner considers sandy, loamy, and clay soils, as well as low, medium, and high organic matter. This helps make the recommendations more context-sensitive.

8. Practical Decision-Making

The team focused on decisions farmers can actually influence, such as crop selection, crop rotation, water management, soil improvement, and seasonal preparation.

9. Scalability and Future Integration

The project was designed so that future layers from SMAP, HLS, Landsat, Sentinel-2, and GPM IMERG could be added. This creates a path from a prototype using historical climate data towards a more comprehensive Earth-observation platform.

10. Safety and Limitations

The project avoids presenting itself as a replacement for agricultural experts. It states that it cannot diagnose pests from photographs, calculate exact pesticide or fertiliser doses, or replace soil testing and local official advisories.

---

SHORT OVERALL DESCRIPTION

Field Shift by NOVYRA is a browser-based, climate-smart agriculture platform that converts NASA Earth-observation and climate data into practical farming insights.

It combines interactive maps, climate visualisations, crop comparisons, rotation planning, soil-health projections, seasonal risk checks, farm-impact calculations, and an offline Kerala Farmer Support Centre.

Its purpose is to help farmers understand changing environmental conditions and make more resilient decisions about crops, water, soil, and income.

The project is creative because it presents agriculture as a Mission Control Experience and connects space-based data with local farming needs.

Its ultimate goal is to transform space technology and climate intelligence into practical solutions for farmers, promoting sustainable agriculture and climate resilience.

A Message Beyond The Stars is a seven-slide multimedia storytelling that explores the remarkable journey of NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft. It takes the audience through Voyager 1's launch in 1977,its encounter with Jupiter and Saturn, the Golden Record carrying messages from Earth, its entry into interstellar space,and its continuing s identification legacy. 

The presentation combines carefully designed slides,recorded voice over narration, and background music to create an engaging and informative storytelling experience. By presenting Voyager 1's journey from its own perspective, the project aims to make space exploration more interesting and help audiences understand the historical and scientific importance of this extraordinary spacecraft. 

One spacecraft. One message. An endless journey.

projectDetails.name: ASTRION
projectDetails.summary:
**ASTRION: Beyond Earth** is a free educational Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer developed in Minecraft Java Edition to explore the challenges of establishing and sustaining human life on the Moon. It transforms a lunar outpost into an interactive learning environment where players take on astronaut responsibilities through 14 interconnected main quests.

Instead of simply exploring the lunar surface, players must operate and manage essential habitat systems, including oxygen and life support, electrical power, agriculture and food production, water-ice extraction, radiation protection, thermal management, communications, and scientific research. Through mission objectives, players discover how these systems depend on one another and why maintaining each is essential for crew safety and outpost operations. Unexpected events introduce additional challenges, encouraging players to assess situations, make decisions, and apply problem-solving skills.

Using an adapted version of LUNARCRAFT, originally created by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) and used with permission for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, ASTRION combines space science concepts with interactive, experience-based learning.

By making lunar mission concepts accessible through a free educational map, ASTRION aims to bridge the gap between theoretical knowledge and practical exploration, encourage STEM education, and inspire the next generation to contribute to humanity's future beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRION: BEYOND EARTH

A Free Educational Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

1. Project Overview

ASTRION: Beyond Earth is a free educational Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer developed in Minecraft Java Edition 26.3. Its purpose is to transform the challenges of human exploration beyond Earth into an interactive, mission-based learning experience.

The project places players inside a lunar research outpost, where they assume the responsibilities of astronauts and work through 14 interconnected main quests. Through these missions, players explore the systems, technologies, resources, and operational challenges involved in establishing and maintaining a human presence on the Moon.

Rather than presenting lunar exploration as a simple journey across the lunar surface, ASTRION focuses on what happens after astronauts arrive. How do they obtain essential resources? How is breathable air maintained? Where does the electricity come from? How can food be produced? How can astronauts remain protected from the lunar environment?

ASTRION approaches these questions through interactive objectives, simulated equipment, mission progression, and interconnected habitat systems.

Our central idea is to make space science more accessible by allowing learners to experience simplified lunar operations through a familiar gaming environment.


2. What Exactly Does ASTRION Do?

ASTRION transforms a Minecraft lunar environment into an educational mission simulation.

Players are introduced to a lunar outpost containing facilities, equipment, and mission locations. Their responsibility is to complete 14 main quests that introduce different aspects of lunar exploration and habitat operations.

The mission experience covers several major areas:

A. Oxygen and Life Support

Players explore the importance of maintaining breathable air and supporting essential life-support operations. The oxygen-related gameplay introduces the importance of astronaut equipment, designated operational zones, and the systems needed to support human activity inside a lunar habitat.

B. Electrical Power and Energy Systems

The power system introduces the importance of electricity in maintaining a functioning lunar outpost. Players encounter energy infrastructure and mission equipment that represent the role of power generation and distribution in supporting essential habitat operations.

C. Agriculture and Food Production

The agriculture-related missions introduce the challenges of producing food in an environment far removed from Earth. They encourage players to consider the importance of sustainable food production and resource management for long-duration exploration.

D. Water-Ice Extraction

Water is an essential resource for future lunar exploration. ASTRION introduces lunar water-ice exploration through mission objectives that help players understand why locating and utilizing lunar resources could be important for future human settlements.

E. Radiation Protection

The lunar environment presents radiation-related challenges because the Moon does not have the same protective atmospheric and magnetic environment as Earth. ASTRION introduces radiation protection as an important consideration in habitat design and astronaut safety.

F. Thermal Management

Extreme lunar temperature conditions make thermal regulation an important part of mission planning. The thermal-related gameplay introduces the need to manage environmental conditions and maintain suitable habitat operations.

G. Communications and Scientific Research

Communication infrastructure and scientific investigation are important components of lunar missions. ASTRION incorporates communications-related equipment and research objectives to introduce the importance of information exchange, observation, and scientific exploration.

H. Crew Readiness and Mission Operations

Astronauts must be prepared before and during mission activities. Crew-related objectives introduce the importance of readiness checks, equipment, and completing essential operational tasks.

Together, these mission areas introduce players to the different responsibilities involved in maintaining a lunar research outpost.


3. How Does the Mission System Work?

ASTRION is structured around 14 main quests that guide players through the lunar mission experience.

Each quest introduces an objective that players must complete using the available mission environment, equipment, and interactive systems.

The general mission progression follows this approach:

  1. Mission Introduction: The player receives a mission objective.
  2. Exploration and Observation: The player explores the relevant facility or mission location.
  3. Equipment Interaction: The player interacts with designated equipment and mission components.
  4. Objective Completion: The player performs the required tasks to satisfy the mission conditions.
  5. Progression and Feedback: The game recognizes completed objectives and provides mission feedback.
  6. Rewards and Advancement: Quest completion can provide rewards and progression feedback before the next stage.

The quest system is designed to provide a structured experience rather than an unrestricted collection of unrelated activities.

The 14 main quests form the central progression of ASTRION. Mission rewards, advancements, equipment interactions, and progression feedback help players understand their progress and recognize completed objectives.

4. Interconnected Lunar Habitat Systems

One of the important design principles behind ASTRION is that lunar habitat systems should not be understood as completely separate technologies.

A functioning outpost depends on multiple systems working together.

For example, electrical power supports essential habitat equipment. Life-support operations depend on functioning infrastructure. Agriculture requires suitable environmental conditions and resources. Scientific operations depend on equipment, energy, and communication infrastructure.

ASTRION uses these relationships as an educational foundation.

Instead of simply showing players individual technologies, the project introduces the idea that maintaining a lunar habitat requires understanding the relationship between resources, equipment, environmental conditions, and astronaut responsibilities.

This systems-based approach helps learners think about lunar exploration as an engineering and operational challenge.

5. Unexpected Events and Mission Challenges

Beyond the normal quest progression, ASTRION incorporates unexpected-event and breach mechanics in its Extended and OP editions.

These events introduce additional challenges that require players to respond to changing mission conditions instead of following only predictable objectives.

The breach systems include different event types, such as Zombie Breach, Skeleton Breach, and Outpost Cataclysm.

These are fictional Minecraft gameplay scenarios designed to represent unexpected operational challenges. They add a challenge-based dimension to the simulation and encourage players to remain attentive to their mission environment.

Players can approach these events at their own pace. The design does not impose countdowns, time limits, death penalties, or loss of normal quest progress for ignoring an event. This allows players to continue their main mission experience while retaining the option to respond to additional challenges..

6. Three Editions of ASTRION

ASTRION is organized into three editions to provide different experiences while preserving the project's educational purpose.

Scientific Edition

The Scientific Edition focuses on the main educational and scientific mission experience. It preserves the 14 main quests and lunar habitat systems while excluding the breach-event mechanics.

Its purpose is to provide a more focused experience for learners who want to explore the science and operation of a lunar outpost.

Extended Edition

The Extended Edition provides the broader astronaut mission simulation. Along with the main quests and scientific systems, it includes the additional breach and unexpected-event gameplay.

It is designed for players who want a more challenging and expanded mission experience without requiring operator-only controls.

OP Edition — Operator Edition

The OP Edition provides the complete feature set with additional operator controls and administrative functionality.

It is intended for testing, demonstrations, and users who need access to the additional controls available in the original operator-enabled build.

These editions allow ASTRION to support different learning and gameplay preferences without changing its central mission-based concept.

7. Educational Benefits and Intended Impact

ASTRION aims to make space-science education more interactive, accessible, and engaging.

Its educational value comes from presenting scientific and engineering concepts through objectives that players can explore and complete.

The project aims to encourage:

  • Scientific Curiosity: Introducing learners to lunar exploration, resources, habitat systems, and the challenges of living beyond Earth.
  • Critical Thinking: Encouraging players to understand mission objectives and consider how different systems contribute to outpost operations.
  • Problem-Solving: Providing mission tasks and unexpected challenges that require observation and decision-making.
  • Systems Thinking: Demonstrating how life support, power, agriculture, environmental protection, and other technologies depend on one another.
  • STEM Engagement: Encouraging interest in science, technology, engineering, astronomy, and space exploration.
  • Independent Exploration: Providing an interactive environment where players can learn through participation and experimentation.

As a free educational map, ASTRION is intended to make these learning opportunities accessible to a wider audience, particularly students, young learners, Minecraft players, and people interested in space science.

The broader ambition is to encourage more people to understand the challenges of human space exploration and imagine how they might contribute to future scientific and technological developments.

8. Tools, Technologies, and Development Environment

ASTRION was developed using Minecraft technologies, world-conversion and construction tools, and AI-assisted development resources.

Primary Development Platform

Minecraft Java Edition 26.3 serves as the primary environment for the mission simulation.

Datapack Development

The Minecraft datapack system forms the foundation of ASTRION's gameplay logic. It is used to implement the quest structure, mission progression, interactive systems, equipment behaviour, and gameplay mechanics.

Minecraft Commands and Function Files

Minecraft commands and .mcfunction files are used to implement mission objectives, triggers, progression conditions, equipment interactions, rewards, and other gameplay functions.

JSON Configurations

JSON files are used for datapack configuration and related Minecraft game data.

World Conversion and Construction

The original lunar environment was based on LUNARCRAFT, created by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA).

Chunker was used to convert the original Bedrock world into Minecraft Java Edition format. Litematica supported construction planning, structure placement, and integration of project facilities into the lunar environment.

Visual Presentation

The project preserves Minecraft's original vanilla textures, interface, blocks, and items to maintain the familiar Minecraft experience. An optional Complementary shader archive is provided separately for players who want an enhanced visual presentation of the lunar environment. Shader installation and compatibility depend on the player's Minecraft setup.

AI-Assisted Development

ChatGPT and Gemini were used as development assistance tools for planning, generating and refining commands and functions, troubleshooting, and improving implementation.

AI tools supported the development process; the actual mission systems and gameplay experience are implemented within Minecraft.

Hardware

A Windows PC served as the primary development, world-editing, integration, and testing platform.

9. Creativity and Innovation

ASTRION's central creative approach is to combine a familiar sandbox gaming environment with the structure and responsibilities of a lunar astronaut mission.

Minecraft provides a flexible environment in which players can explore facilities, interact with equipment, complete objectives, and experience mission progression.

The project uses this flexibility to represent simplified versions of lunar habitat operations.

Its creativity lies in bringing together several elements:

  • A lunar research outpost as an educational environment.
  • Fourteen interconnected main quests forming a structured mission experience.
  • Multiple simulated habitat systems.
  • Interactive equipment and mission objectives.
  • Unexpected-event mechanics in the expanded editions.
  • Different editions supporting different levels of gameplay and operator functionality.
  • A free educational distribution goal.

Instead of treating space exploration as a distant subject that learners can only observe, ASTRION gives them an opportunity to participate in a simplified mission environment.


10. Design Considerations and Development Challenges

During development, several factors were considered to make the project functional, understandable, and educational.

Educational Relevance: Mission objectives were designed around recognizable challenges associated with human lunar exploration.

Gameplay Clarity: Players need to understand their objectives, interact with equipment, and receive meaningful feedback as they progress.

Technical Compatibility: The datapack and adapted world must work together in Minecraft Java Edition 26.3.

Mission Progression: The 14 main quests must provide a coherent experience and preserve the intended order of mission activities.

System Integration: Different habitat systems must coexist without unnecessarily interfering with one another.

Player Experience: The environment, equipment, objectives, and rewards should make the mission experience understandable and engaging.

Accessibility: The project is designed as a free educational map so that more learners can experience its content.

Working within Minecraft's existing mechanics also creates technical limitations. The project therefore uses simplified in-game representations of scientific and engineering concepts rather than claiming to reproduce complete real-world lunar infrastructure.



11. JAXA LUNARCRAFT Acknowledgement and Permission

ASTRION uses an adapted version of LUNARCRAFT, originally created by the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA).

The JAXA Space Education Center granted permission on October 22, 2026, for the use of LUNARCRAFT in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 project.

The original environment was adapted for ASTRION, and the modifications and additions are the responsibility of the project team.

We acknowledge JAXA as the original creator of LUNARCRAFT. ASTRION is an independent project and is not affiliated with or endorsed by JAXA.

The permission applies to participation in NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, with the conditions specified by JAXA, including no commercial use after the competition. Continued non-commercial educational use is permitted.

12. Current Development Status and Future Vision

The core ASTRION mission experience, including its 14 main quests and major lunar habitat systems, has been developed and tested.

The project continues through additional integration, refinement, gameplay testing, and presentation work. This includes testing the unexpected-event systems, improving the overall player experience, and preparing the project website and demonstration materials.

The original Minecraft textures, interface, blocks, and items are preserved to maintain the familiar vanilla Minecraft experience. An optional shader archive is provided separately for players who want enhanced visuals.

Future development aims to improve the educational experience, expand the presentation of lunar habitat systems, and make the project easier for learners to access and understand.

ASTRION is intended to remain a free, non-commercial educational experience within the permissions granted for the adapted LUNARCRAFT environment.

Our long-term vision is to create an engaging environment where students and space enthusiasts can explore the challenges of living beyond Earth, develop an appreciation for space science and engineering, and imagine humanity's future as a spacefaring civilization.

13. Approach to NASA Data Integration

ASTRION takes an educational approach to integrating NASA research and scientific information into Minecraft.

We recognised that directly importing raw scientific datasets into Minecraft was not the most suitable approach for our project. Instead, we explored how the information contained in relevant datasets could be interpreted, adapted, and translated into interactive gameplay experiences that communicate scientific concepts while working within Minecraft's technical capabilities.

For example, lunar water research is represented through water-ice exploration and extraction missions. Concepts related to life support, lunar infrastructure, radiation protection, and sustainable habitat operations are introduced through mission objectives, simulated equipment, and interconnected outpost systems.

This approach allows players to engage with the scientific ideas behind lunar exploration through observation, interaction, and mission-based learning, rather than simply viewing scientific information.

NASA datasets and scientific resources were used as references during ASTRION's development. Rather than attempting to import raw datasets directly into Minecraft, we interpreted and adapted relevant information from them into educational gameplay elements. This included translating scientific findings and concepts into mission objectives, environmental challenges, simulated systems, and interactive learning experiences. In this way, the information within the datasets was communicated through gameplay, making scientific knowledge more accessible and engaging for players.

Our approach was to transform scientific information into an interactive educational experience. By adapting relevant dataset information to Minecraft's capabilities, we aimed to ensure that NASA-related scientific knowledge was not simply presented to players, but explored and understood through gameplay.

ASTRION: Beyond Earth — Explore. Discover. Beyond Earth.

MARS 360 – NASA Space Apps Challenge Project Summary
MARS 360 is an interactive Mars exploration and survival planning application designed to help future astronauts plan safer Marswalk missions. It combines NASA datasets from MOLA, CTX, THEMIS, and HiRISE into one interactive Mars map.
The application will include four main features:
Mars Explorer: Explore Mars using scientific map layers and select locations.
Terrain Analyzer: Examine elevation, slopes, surface features, and potential hazards.
Route Planner: Create Marswalk routes, calculate distances, and compare alternative paths.
Survival Simulator: Estimate astronauts' oxygen, water, and battery consumption during missions.
projectDetails.details:
MARS 360 – Explore Mars. Plan Your Route. Survive the Mission.

1. Project Overview

MARS 360 is an interactive Mars exploration and astronaut survival planning application that combines NASA scientific datasets into a unified planetary map. It helps users explore Martian terrain, identify potential hazards, plan astronaut routes, and simulate resource consumption during exploration missions.

2. Problem Statement

Planning human missions to Mars is challenging because scientific information about the planet is collected by different spacecraft and instruments. Understanding terrain, elevation, temperature, and environmental conditions is essential for planning exploration routes and future astronaut habitats.

3. Proposed Solution

MARS 360 integrates multiple NASA datasets into one interactive platform. Users can explore Mars, analyze surface conditions, create exploration routes, and evaluate whether astronauts have sufficient resources to complete their missions.

4. Main Features

1. Interactive Mars Explorer

  • Explore the Martian surface.
  • Zoom and select geographical locations.
  • Display different scientific map layers.

2. Terrain and Hazard Analyzer

  • Examine surface elevation and slopes.
  • Visualize terrain characteristics.
  • Identify areas requiring further investigation.

3. Marswalk Route Planner

  • Select starting and destination locations.
  • Create routes with intermediate points.
  • Calculate approximate travel distances.
  • Compare alternative routes.

4. Astronaut Survival Simulator

  • Calculate estimated oxygen consumption.
  • Monitor water and battery resources.
  • Simulate missions lasting 1, 7, or 30 days.
  • Generate resource warnings.

5. Mission Report

  • Display route information.
  • Summarize environmental evidence.
  • Show resource consumption and remaining supplies.

5. NASA Data Sources

  • MOLA – Mars elevation and topography.
  • CTX – Mars surface imagery.
  • THEMIS – Thermal infrared observations.
  • HiRISE – High-resolution surface imagery.

6. Technology Stack

  • Google Antigravity – AI-assisted development.
  • React – Frontend application.
  • Tailwind CSS – User interface design.
  • OpenLayers – Interactive planetary mapping.
  • JavaScript – Route and survival calculations.
  • Recharts – Data visualization.
  • Netlify – Application deployment.

7. Target Users

  • Future Mars astronauts.
  • Space researchers.
  • Planetary scientists.
  • Space exploration enthusiasts.
  • Students and educators.

8. Expected Impact

MARS 360 aims to make planetary scientific information easier to explore and understand by bringing multiple datasets together. It demonstrates how NASA open data can support informed Mars exploration planning and educational simulations.

9. Innovation

The main innovation is combining scientific Mars mapping, route planning, terrain analysis, and astronaut resource simulation into one interactive application.

10. Development Plan

The application will be developed using Google Antigravity AI. Our team will research NASA datasets, build the interface, integrate map services, implement route and survival calculations, test the application, and deploy the final prototype.

11. Project Goal

Our goal is to create a functional, interactive, and scientifically grounded Mars exploration platform that demonstrates how NASA data can help people understand and plan future human exploration of Mars.

projectDetails.name: EcoPulse Kerala
projectDetails.summary: EcoPulse Kerala is an interactive Earth observation analytics dashboard developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to evaluate 20-year hydro-climatic shifts and micro-climate thermal stress across two contrasting ecological zones in Kerala, India: the Idukki Highlands (Western Ghats) and the Alappuzha Coast (Arabian Sea). Powered by live satellite telemetry from the NASA POWER API v2.0 (2005–2025), the platform uses Python, Streamlit, and Plotly alongside non-parametric Mann-Kendall trend tests and Theil-Sen slope estimators to analyze precipitation, root zone soil moisture, mean temperature, and extreme heat-humidity stress. Our findings reveal statistically significant warming across both regions, with the coastal belt warming roughly 30% faster (+0.045 °C/year) than the montane highlands (+0.03472 °C/year). By transforming raw NASA satellite data into accessible geospatial insights, EcoPulse Kerala supports regional climate resilience, agricultural water planning, and ecological monitoring.
projectDetails.details:
EcoPulse Kerala is an interactive Earth observation analytics dashboard that tracks 20-year hydro-climatic shifts (2005–2025) and micro-climate thermal stress across two contrasting ecological zones in Kerala, India: the Idukki Highlands (Western Ghats, ~1,500m elevation) and the Alappuzha Coast (Arabian Sea, ~1m elevation). The app fetches live daily satellite telemetry via the NASA Langley Research Center (LaRC) POWER API v2.0 (0.5° × 0.625° grid) across key parameters including Corrected Precipitation (PRECTOTCORR), Root Zone Soil Moisture (GWETROOT), Mean Air Temperature (T2M), and Daily Thermal-Humidity Stress (T2M_MAX ≥ 31°C and RH2M ≥ 70%).

Statistical Engine & Key Findings: Using Python (Pandas, NumPy, and PyMannKendall), the dashboard runs non-parametric Mann-Kendall monotonic trend tests alongside Theil-Sen robust slope estimators to separate statistically significant climate signals from natural inter-annual variability. Our analysis reveals that both regions are experiencing statistically significant warming, with the Alappuzha Coast warming at +0.045 °C/year (p < 0.0001)—roughly 30% faster than the Idukki Highlands (+0.03472 °C/year, p = 0.0102).

Benefits, Creativity & Intended Impact: By pairing rigorous hydro-climatic trend analysis with interactive Plotly time-series charts, Carto geospatial mapping, and a transparent data provenance audit tab, EcoPulse Kerala translates raw NASA satellite data into actionable insights for agricultural water planning, coastal heat resilience, and ecological conservation—hosted completely free and open-source for zero-barrier public access.

Tools, Languages & AI Disclosure: Developed using Python, Streamlit, Plotly, Carto, Pandas, NumPy, PyMannKendall, and GitHub, and deployed on Streamlit Community Cloud. Large Language Model (LLM) assistance was utilized during development to help structure code, documentation, and text descriptions in accordance with NASA Space Apps Challenge guidelines.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

Orbit Odysseys is an interactive space exploration and mission design platform developed to make space science and spacecraft engineering more engaging and accessible.

Users can also explore spacecraft design by selecting and configuring different spacecraft components while understanding important engineering concepts such as payload mass, structural requirements, power systems, communication systems, and orbital mechanics.

projectDetails.details:
Project Details – ORBIT ODYSSEYS

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026

ORBIT ODYSSEYS is an interactive space exploration and spacecraft design platform that combines 3D Solar System visualization with practical spacecraft engineering concepts.

Our project allows users to explore the Solar System through an interactive 3D environment featuring , their rotations and revolutions, orbital paths, and asteroids. Users can observe planetary movements and develop a better understanding of our cosmic neighbourhood.

The platform also includes a spacecraft design and rocket selection experience. Users can explore different launch vehicles and select spacecraft components, scientific instruments, equipment, and payloads. Each component has an individual weight, and the system automatically calculates the total payload mass whenever components are added or removed. It also checks the selected rocket's payload capacity to prevent incompatible configurations.

- Makes space science more interactive and accessible.

- Introduces real-world spacecraft engineering concepts.

- Encourages creativity, scientific curiosity, and problem-solving.

- Provides an engaging educational experience for aspiring space enthusiasts.

Our creativity lies in combining Solar System exploration with spacecraft engineering in one interactive platform. We considered scientific accuracy, realistic payload limitations, usability, visual experience, and educational value while developing the project.

projectDetails.name: FireScope-Kerala
projectDetails.summary:
FireScope – Kerala is an interactive satellite-based wildfire monitoring and analysis platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots.
The project integrates active-fire observations from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS instruments aboard Terra, Aqua, Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 to explore wildfire activity across Kerala, India.
FireScope processes and harmonizes these datasets through geographical filtering, attribute standardization and timestamp preparation. It applies spatial-temporal matching using a mutual nearest-neighbour approach, with exploratory thresholds of 500 metres and 60 minutes, to identify potential relationships between observations from different satellite platforms.
The platform also explores Fire Radiative Power (FRP), matched and unmatched observations, satellite platform distributions, daytime and nighttime activity, and daily and monthly detection trends.
Through an interactive web dashboard, users can explore hotspot locations, filter observations by satellite platform and match status, examine analytical visualizations, and download observation data in CSV format.
Built using Python, FastAPI, Pandas, GeoPandas, JavaScript, Leaflet and Chart.js, FireScope aims to make multi-satellite fire observations more accessible and support comparative analysis of wildfire activity.
The matching results represent potential observation relationships, not confirmed duplicate detections or unique fire incidents.
projectDetails.details:
FireScope – Kerala

FireScope – Kerala is an interactive satellite-based wildfire monitoring and analysis platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 challenge, “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots.”

The project integrates active-fire observations from NASA's MODIS and VIIRS instruments aboard Terra, Aqua, Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 to explore wildfire activity across Kerala, India. It processes the datasets through geographical filtering, attribute standardization and timestamp preparation. A spatial-temporal matching method based on mutual nearest neighbours, using exploratory thresholds of 500 metres and 60 minutes, identifies potential relationships between observations from different satellite platforms.

FireScope provides an interactive dashboard where users can view hotspot locations on a map, explore daily and monthly fire trends, compare satellite platform distributions, examine daytime and nighttime observations, filter records by satellite platform and match status, and download data in CSV format. It also supports analysis of Fire Radiative Power (FRP).

The project aims to make multi-satellite fire observations easier to explore and compare, helping users better understand patterns in wildfire activity and supporting further research and environmental monitoring.

The platform was developed using Python, FastAPI, Pandas, NumPy, GeoPandas, Shapely, SciPy, HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Leaflet.js and Chart.js.

Its creative approach combines observations from multiple satellite missions into one interactive analytical platform. The team considered geographical accuracy, observation timestamps, spatial distance, time differences, satellite characteristics and clear data visualization. Matching results indicate potential observation relationships, not confirmed duplicate detections or unique fire incidents.

projectDetails.summary: FarmShift is a free web app for the Field Shift challenge that helps farmers see the climate conditions at their own fields. A farmer pins a farm on an interactive satellite map by clicking the map, searching a place name, or typing coordinates. The app then pulls NASA POWER climate data for that exact location: temperature, rainfall, humidity, soil wetness (surface and root zone) and solar radiation. It shows summary numbers and charts over a chosen period and lets the farmer download the data as CSV. Farms can be saved and reloaded, and each farm can be viewed on satellite imagery, including NASA MODIS true-colour imagery from NASA GIBS. FarmShift matters because farmers planning crops for a changing climate need local rainfall, heat and soil-moisture information in a simple form, not raw datasets. It needs no login and runs in any browser.
projectDetails.details:
FarmShift is a lightweight, zero-login web application built with Streamlit that empowers users to pin farm locations on an interactive satellite map and analyze historical climate and weather data using the NASA POWER API. It is designed to be run locally or deployed quickly, storing farm data entirely within the current browser session with manual CSV backup options.

Core Features

  • Interactive Satellite Mapping:
    • Powered by folium and streamlit-folium.
    • Supports multiple switchable map layers including Esri World Imagery, NASA MODIS True Color imagery, OpenStreetMap, and geographical boundary overlays.
    • Click-to-pin functionality to easily record farm coordinates.
  • Global Place Search:
    • Integrated with the Open-Meteo Geocoding API to search locations worldwide and automatically populate latitude, longitude, and map views.
  • NASA POWER Climate Analytics:
    • Fetches real agro-meteorological parameters (e.g., temperatures, rainfall, root-zone and surface soil wetness, solar radiation, and relative humidity) for custom date ranges (7 to 365 days).
    • Calculates averages and totals dynamically, rendering interactive line charts and summary metric cards.
  • Session Management & CSV Persistence:
    • Maintains state locally per browser session (preloaded with a sample farm in Kottayam, Kerala).
    • Allows users to download and upload their farm datasets via CSV files for seamless portability without needing a database backend.

projectDetails.summary:
Valhalla—Mars  is an interactive educational website developed to showcase humanity's journey of exploring the Red Planet. Inspired by Valhalla, the legendary hall of heroes, the project celebrates the pioneering missions and achievements that have advanced our understanding of Mars.

The website features a visual timeline of Mars exploration and an interactive Artifact Archive, where users can discover historic rovers, landers, orbiters, and other space missions. It highlights their objectives, discoveries, technological contributions, and even unsuccessful attempts.

The project addresses the challenge of making the history of space exploration accessible, engaging, and easier to understand by presenting complex historical and scientific information through visual storytelling and an interactive interface.

Valhalla—Mars is important because it promotes awareness of space exploration, celebrates scientific innovation, and inspires curiosity about planetary science and humanity's future beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Valhalla-Mars is an interactive educational website designed to present the history of humanity's exploration of Mars in an engaging and accessible way. Inspired by Valhalla, the legendary hall of heroes, the project celebrates the achievements, discoveries, and challenges of the missions that have explored the Red Planet.

How does it work?

The website allows users to explore the evolution of Mars exploration through a visual timeline and an interactive Artifact Archive. The archive showcases important spacecraft, rovers, landers, and orbiters, providing information about their history, objectives, and contributions. It also highlights unsuccessful missions, helping users understand the challenges involved in space exploration.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The project makes space exploration history easier to explore and understand by organizing information into an interactive visual experience. It aims to:

  • Promote awareness of Mars exploration and planetary science.
  • Make scientific and historical information accessible to a wider audience.
  • Encourage curiosity about astronomy, space technology, and future missions.
  • Highlight the importance of innovation, experimentation, and learning from failures.

Technologies Used

The project was developed using:

  • React and JavaScript – for building the website and its functionality.
  • Vite – for the development environment and build process.
  • Tailwind CSS – for responsive styling and interface design.
  • React Router – for navigation between different sections.
  • Framer Motion – for animations and interactive transitions.
  • Lucide React – for interface icons.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of Valhalla-Mars lies in combining the history of space exploration with an immersive, visually engaging presentation. Rather than displaying information as ordinary text, the website uses interactive elements, visual storytelling, and an organized archive to make each mission part of a larger exploration journey.

Factors Considered

During development, the team considered:

  • Accuracy and clarity of historical and scientific information.
  • Ease of navigation and user experience.
  • Responsive design across different screen sizes.
  • Visual consistency and accessibility.
  • Effective organization of missions and artifacts.
  • Performance and usability of the website.

Ultimately, Valhalla-Mars aims to turn the history of Mars exploration into an engaging digital journey that educates, inspires curiosity, and celebrates humanity's continued pursuit of discovery.

The prototype is designed for a remote hackathon where physical biomedical hardware is unavailable and the submission deadline is short.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRA is a software-only prototype concept for astronaut health surveillance. It demonstrates a local desktop-style console that generates synthetic physiological telemetry, compares readings against illustrative baseline values, flags configured deviations, visualizes trends and exports mission reports. The prototype is designed for a remote hackathon where physical biomedical hardware is unavailable and the submission deadline is short.

1. Problem Statement

Astronauts can experience physiological and operational stressors during spaceflight, including cardiovascular adaptation, muscle and bone changes, sleep disruption, fatigue and elevated cognitive workload. A monitoring system should help organize health-related telemetry, surface unusual trends and support timely review by qualified medical personnel.

2. Objectives

·         Demonstrate a simulated astronaut telemetry pipeline.

·         Provide a single-astronaut mission dashboard.

·         Compare current readings with illustrative personal baseline values.

·         Show explainable deviation flags and an emergency review workflow.

·         Visualize historical trends and export telemetry and reports.

·         Run locally without physical sensors or a cloud dependency.

3. Proposed System

ASTRA uses a Python-based simulation engine as a stand-in for a future wearable sensor node. The engine generates time-series values for heart rate, oxygen saturation (SpO₂), temperature, activity and a synthetic stress index. Streamlit presents the data in six modules: Mission Overview, Live Telemetry, AI Risk Analysis, Health Analytics, Emergency Centre and Mission Reports.

4. Architecture

Synthetic telemetry generator → data processing (NumPy/Pandas) → configurable deviation screening → Streamlit dashboard and Plotly charts → CSV/JSON exports.

5. Implementation and Technology

·         Python: application logic and simulation.

·         Streamlit: interactive user interface.

·         NumPy and Pandas: synthetic data generation and tabular processing.

·         Plotly: time-series visualization.

·         JSON and CSV: report and telemetry export formats.

·         Scikit-learn is a potential next step for offline anomaly detection after suitable representative data and validation are available.

6. Demonstration Scenarios

·         Nominal: values fluctuate around illustrative baseline values.

·         Cardiovascular stress: simulated rise in heart rate and stress index.

·         Oxygen desaturation: simulated downward SpO₂ trend.

·         Elevated temperature: simulated increase in temperature.

·         Motion artefact: noisy sensor-like readings to demonstrate data-quality concerns.

7. Risk Screening Logic

The current prototype uses transparent, configurable screening rules that compare generated values with illustrative baseline values. A rule may flag a large deviation in heart rate, low SpO₂, elevated temperature, or a high synthetic stress index. The interface displays contributing signals. These rules are not clinical thresholds, are not a trained predictive model, and must not be used for diagnosis or medical decisions.

8. Limitations and Safety

·         All readings and astronaut identity are fictional and simulated.

·         No physical sensors or biomedical hardware are connected.

·         No validated AI model or clinical prediction capability is claimed.

·         Baseline values and alert rules are illustrative only.

·         The prototype is not certified for spaceflight or medical use.

·         A real system requires sensor calibration, signal-quality assessment, astronaut-specific validated baselines, secure data handling, clinical oversight and aerospace qualification.

9. Future Scope

·         Connect validated wearable sensors and an embedded ESP32 gateway.

·         Add persistent encrypted storage and role-based access for astronaut, physician and mission-control views.

·         Introduce sensor-quality and motion-artifact rejection methods.

·         Evaluate time-series anomaly detection using representative, ethically sourced and validated data.

·         Add store-and-forward synchronization for intermittent communication.

·         Conduct usability, reliability, cybersecurity and aerospace environmental testing.

10. Conclusion

ASTRA demonstrates a feasible software prototype for organizing simulated astronaut health telemetry, identifying configured deviations and supporting a review workflow. It provides a reproducible hackathon demonstration and a clear path toward future hardware integration and validation.

projectDetails.name: Project Perseverantia
projectDetails.summary:
An interactive 14-Sol lunar and Martian outpost mission trainer built for young learners and STEM classrooms. Players balance real-time solar power across Life Support (ECLSS), Active Radiation Shielding, Hydroponics Bio-Dome, and ISRU Maintenance while responding to space weather alerts, radiation spikes, and crew health trade-offs grounded in NASA and CSA open science data.
Key Features:
Dual-Site Simulation: Command Shackleton Rim Outpost (Moon — cosmic radiation, crater shadow dips, water-ice mining) or Jezero Delta Station (Mars — global dust attenuation, 14–22 min comms delay, closed-loop farming) across Cadet and Commander difficulties.
Interactive Habitat Telemetry Canvas: Live animated outpost showing solar tracking, rotating ECLSS scrubbers, active proton-deflecting radiation shields, Bio-Dome LED crops, ISRU drills, surface rover patrol, and clickable module focus controls.
Strategic Planning HUD: Live resource meters (HP, O₂, BAT, FOOD, H₂O, DOSE) with educational interpretation tooltips, a 3-Sol Space Weather & Power Forecast strip, Sol-by-Sol telemetry sparklines, and a filterable Outpost Operations Log (All, Critical, Decisions, Flavor).
Mission Pacing & Audio Feedback: Procedural orbital ambient music, authentic NASA Quindar (2524 Hz / 2475 Hz) achievement chimes, mission badges/medals, 5-Sol milestone banners, and a 1-second Sol transition overlay.
NASA Data Lab: In-app scientific reference modal connecting gameplay trade-off
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works

Outpost Command: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive 14-Sol lunar and Martian habitat simulator designed to teach young learners how real off-world survival systems depend on one another.

Players choose between two authentic mission environments—Moon · Shackleton Crater (high cosmic radiation, solar particle storms, crater rim shadows, and abundant water-ice) or Mars · Jezero Crater (dust accumulation on solar panels, global dust storms, and 14–22 minute Earth communication delays)—and train across Cadet (Guided) or Commander (NASA Margins) difficulty.

Each Sol, players allocate finite solar and RTG kilowatts (kW) across four core subsystems via interactive sliders or by clicking directly on the animated habitat canvas:

  • Life Support (ECLSS): CO₂ scrubbing and O₂ electrolysis.
  • Radiation Shielding: Active magnetic and hydrogen-rich water-wall baffling (plus an emergency Storm Shelter mode during flares).
  • Hydroponics Bio-Dome: LED crop growth that produces fresh food, recycles O₂, and boosts crew morale.
  • ISRU & Maintenance: Ice-water mining and clearing dust off solar arrays.

Players plan ahead using a 3-Sol Space Weather & Power Forecast, inspect educational tooltips on all six telemetry meters (HP, O₂, BAT, FOOD, H₂O, DOSE), resolve real-science mission dilemmas, track trends via Sol-by-Sol charts, and review mission updates in a filterable Operations Log (All, Critical, Decisions, Flavor).

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Turns Abstract STEM Into Hands-On Cause & Effect: Instead of memorizing isolated facts about oxygen or radiation, students immediately see how diverting power to survive an X2.8 solar flare reduces crop yields or drains battery reserves.
  • Built for Classrooms & Self-Guided Learning: Guided tooltips explain safe vs. critical telemetry thresholds in plain language, while 5-Sol milestone popups, 6 unlockable achievements, and tiered Mission Badges encourage replayability and experimentation.
  • Real Space Science Literacy: The built-in NASA Data Lab connects every gameplay rule to NASA DONKI solar flares, NASA RadLab / MSL-RAD radiation benchmarks, NASA OSDR human-health studies, CSA hydroponic research, and Mars Trek surface conditions.

Creativity & Design Craft

  • Living Habitat Telemetry Canvas: Features sun-tracking solar wings, spinning ECLSS turbines, active proton-deflecting shields, swaying Bio-Dome plants, ISRU drill sparks, orbiting telemetry satellites, walking crew members, and a patrolling surface rover.
  • Sensory Time & Audio Design: A 1-second Sol Transition overlay with analog grain texture and subtle screen-shake marks each day's passage. Background orbital music adapts dynamically during solar storms, and unlocking achievements triggers authentic Apollo-era NASA Quindar tones (2524 Hz / 2475 Hz) synthesized completely in code.

Tools, Languages & Technologies Used

  • Languages & Frameworks: TypeScript, React 19, HTML5, CSS3, Tailwind CSS v4
  • Build & Runtime Tooling: Vite, Node.js, Lucide Icons
  • Graphics & Audio: HTML5 2D Canvas API (requestAnimationFrame), Web Audio API (zero external audio asset dependencies)
  • Verification & Testing: Automated simulation, forecasting, tooltip, achievement, and audio unit tests (node:test + tsx), TypeScript static checking (tsc --noEmit), and headless Chromium UI verification

Key Factors Our Team Considered

  • Scientific Fidelity vs. Accessibility: Real orbital/surface radiation (0.67 mSv/day on Mars vs. 1.37 mSv/day unshielded on the Moon) and power trade-offs were balanced so Cadet mode stays approachable for younger learners while Commander mode challenges advanced students.
  • Zero-Dependency Reliability: Audio synthesis and core NASA/CSA reference data work out-of-the-box offline with deterministic fallback benchmarks, so classrooms and judges never hit broken external media or API lockouts.
  • Inclusive, Responsive UX: Designed for both desktop and mobile viewports with non-color-only status indicators, keyboard shortcuts (B, P, M, Space), and reduced-motion safeguards.

projectDetails.name: Sol30
projectDetails.summary:
SOL30: is a 2D pixel-art Mars survival and space mission design game developed by Team Pink Sheep for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.

Players take on the role of an astronaut stranded on Mars after a catastrophic landing, with only 30 Sols to repair their damaged spacecraft and return home. They must explore the Martian surface and underground caves, collect ice and valuable ores, refine materials, and build essential infrastructure for oxygen, water, food, and power. Players must also survive dust storms and radiation while restoring six critical spacecraft systems before the deadline.

Inspired by NASA's Mars exploration, MOXIE oxygen-production technology, and research into Martian water ice and environmental conditions, the game turns real space-exploration challenges into interactive decisions. It highlights the importance of resource management, engineering, resilience, and sustainable mission planning for future human exploration of Mars.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details — Sol30

What does it do and how does it work?

Sol30 is a 2D pixel-art Mars survival and space mission design game developed using Godot. Players take the role of an astronaut stranded on Mars after a spacecraft crash. They have 30 Martian days (Sols) to survive and repair the spacecraft before the return window closes.

Players explore the Martian surface and underground caves, collect resources such as ice, iron, aluminum, sulfur, and electronics, refine ores, craft components, and build essential infrastructure for oxygen, water, food, and power. They must also prepare for environmental threats such as dust storms and radiation. The mission is completed by restoring and installing all six essential spacecraft systems.

Benefits and intended impact

Sol30 makes the challenges of planetary exploration interactive and engaging. It introduces players to resource management, engineering decisions, environmental hazards, and the complexity of sustaining human life on Mars. Our aim is to encourage interest in space science, engineering, and future human exploration missions.

Tools and technologies

- Game Engine: Godot 4.7

- Programming Language: GDScript

- Development: Visual Studio Code

- Design: 2D pixel-art assets and custom game interfaces

Creativity and innovation

Sol30 combines survival mechanics with spacecraft engineering and resource management. Its interconnected systems make every decision important. For example, dust storms reduce solar power generation, requiring players to manage batteries and seek shelter. The game also features explorable cave systems, ore refining, crafting, a cinematic introduction, dynamic environmental hazards, and animated endings.

Factors considered

Our team considered the challenges of the Martian environment, limited resources, oxygen and water consumption, power generation, radiation exposure, dust storms, day-night cycles, player experience, and the 30-Sol mission deadline. NASA's Mars exploration research and technologies such as MOXIE inspired several gameplay concepts. The environmental events are simulated within the game and are not live NASA data feeds.
