projectDetails.name: Podium
projectDetails.summary:
ODIUM: Grand Prix of the Solar System is an interactive, browser-based space mission design game built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Players step into the role of a mission director under a strict budget cap, designing an interplanetary probe across real aerospace trade-offs—propulsion architectures, launcher payload capacities, solar flux inverse-square decay, eclipse battery reserves, and deep-space Friis comms bandwidth.

Rather than calculating in isolation, PODIUM pits the player against two distinct AI rival agencies—cautious, over-margined Helios Dynamics and aggressive, high-risk Vanta Aerospace—launching on the same day in a race across interplanetary space. With switchable 3D orbital cameras, live F1-style timing towers, mid-flight pit-wall decision calls, and an interactive telemetry flight recorder, players see firsthand how an early aggressive burn or an under-sized battery directly impacts mission survival and arrival order.

By framing authentic orbital mechanics (Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, power margins, and radiation faults) through high-stakes competitive racing and a 3-step podium ceremony, PODIUM demystifies mission design engineering, transforming complex multidisciplinary tradeoffs into an accessible, intuitive, and unforgettable educational experience.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do and how does it work?

PODIUM is a browser-based aerospace trade-off game that reframes interplanetary mission design as a high-stakes Grand Prix. Players design a spacecraft under a strict budget cap to reach destinations like Mars or Europa, balancing propulsion architectures, wet mass, power generation, battery eclipse reserves, deep-space comms, and redundancy. Instead of calculating in isolation, the player launches alongside two deterministic AI rivals: cautious Helios Dynamics and aggressive Vanta Aerospace. The mission unfolds in real-time through an interactive 3D WebGL scene featuring an F1-style live Timing Tower, dynamic mid-flight Pit-Wall decision prompts, an interactive Flight Recorder telemetry chart, and a 3-step podium awards ceremony.

What benefits does it have and what is the intended impact?

PODIUM makes complex aerospace systems engineering intuitive. Adding a heavier instrument increases dry mass, which exponentially multiplies propellant requirements via the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, forcing a costlier launcher that threatens the budget cap. Instead of generic failure screens, the game provides transparent root-cause analysis chains explaining the exact engineering fault behind every delay or anomaly. By combining real orbital mechanics with the drama of motorsport, PODIUM turns intimidating equations into an engaging, accessible STEM learning experience.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

PODIUM was built with TypeScript, React 18, and Vite for a fast, responsive user interface. The 3D planetary orbits and racing spacecraft are rendered with Three.js and React Three Fiber. Interface styling and motion use Tailwind CSS, Framer Motion, Lucide Icons, and Canvas Confetti. Headless automated test suites were built with Vitest to rigorously verify rocket equations, inverse-square solar decay, and rival AI generation. The client-side application is deployed globally on the Vercel Edge Network.

How is your project creative?

PODIUM blends authentic orbital physics with motorsport race culture. Trajectory correction burns act as Pit Stops; radiation safe modes act as Safety Cars; coronal mass ejections act as Adverse Weather; and interplanetary transit choices mirror Sprint versus Endurance fuel strategies. Live interval gaps, animated timing tower position swaps, tactical auto-pausing pit-wall calls, and distinct AI rival personalities transform a technical engineering simulator into a gripping competitive spectacle.

What factors did your team consider?

Our team prioritized scientific rigor, implementing real mathematical formulas for Tsiolkovsky delta-V, inverse-square solar flux attenuation (explaining why solar works at Mars but requires nuclear RTGs at Europa), 70% battery depth-of-discharge limits during shadow passes, and Friis comms downlink bandwidth scaling. We also built in deterministic reproducibility using a 32-bit mulberry32 pseudo-random number generator for identical daily challenge seeds, alongside accessibility support for reduced motion, bloom toggles, and high-contrast telemetry dials.

projectDetails.name: MARSBOUND: Tactical Martian Map & Jezero EVA Survival Guide
projectDetails.summary:
Setting foot on Mars shouldn't mean walking into the unknown. We developed MARSBOUND, an interactive first-person Marswalk simulation paired with a multi-layered Tactical GIS navigation system designed for the first human explorers of Jezero Crater.

To solve the challenge, MARSBOUND synthesizes decades of open NASA data into one unified, field-ready survival map. We integrated high-resolution MRO HiRISE surface imagery, MOLA topographic contours, CRISM hyperspectral mineralogy, and Perseverance’s RIMFAX subsurface radar echograms. Explorers can plan safe traverses across steep delta scarps, navigate low-gravity terrain (0.38g) with real-time solar atmospheric scattering, monitor vital life-support telemetry (O2 consumption and suit power), and investigate authentic rock outcrops using handheld Raman spectrometry and core drilling.

Robotic missions laid the groundwork; humans will take the next steps. MARSBOUND transforms complex satellite datasets into an intuitive, life-saving guide—empowering future astronauts to explore safely and conduct high-yield planetary science on the Martian frontier.
projectDetails.details:
The Inspiration & Concept

When our team sat down to tackle the Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map challenge, we asked ourselves a simple question: If human astronauts set foot on Mars tomorrow, what would their dashboard actually look like?

Robotic rovers and orbiters have gathered extraordinary troves of Martian data over the last three decades, but that data lives in siloed archives, planetary databases, and static research papers. On Mars, 140 million miles from Earth, with radio signals taking up to 24 minutes for a round-trip, an astronaut standing at the edge of Jezero Crater cannot wait for mission control. They need immediate, real-time, life-or-death spatial awareness.

We built MARSBOUND to transform static orbital science into an intuitive, living survival companion for human Marswalks.

MARSBOUND is a zero-install, browser-based 3D exploration and tactical GIS platform designed as an operational survival and mapping companion for humanity's first crewed Marswalks. Built for the "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map" challenge, MARSBOUND bridges over twenty years of NASA robotic planetary science into an interactive, synchronized dual-view dashboard: a boots-on-the-ground 0.38g EVA simulation paired with an orbital telemetry GIS console centered on Jezero Crater (18.4447∘N, 77.4508∘E).

What Does It Do & How Does It Work?

MARSBOUND is a zero-install, browser-native 3D exploration and tactical GIS platform that drops users into a synchronized dual-view experience:

  1. Boots-on-the-Ground 3D Simulation: An astronaut's first-person Extravehicular Activity (EVA) view of Jezero Crater's ancient lake delta, operating under realistic 0.38g0.38g0.38g Martian gravity, terrain physics, and dynamic solar illumination.
  2. Tactical GIS Console: An interactive geospatial heads-up display synchronizing orbital satellite telemetry directly with surface navigation. Explorers can view live breadcrumb trails, measure real distance vectors with an interactive ruler, set objective waypoints, and monitor life-support telemetry (oxygen draw rate, suit battery power, and heart rate).
    • MRO HiRISE: High-resolution visible light surface orthomosaics for boulder recognition and terrain roughness.
    • MGS MOLA: Laser altimeter digital elevation models with contour lines and hazardous slope warnings.
    • MRO CRISM: Hyperspectral mineralogy mapping ancient lacustrine clays, carbonates, and olivine.
    • Mars 2020 RIMFAX: Subsurface ground-penetrating radar echograms revealing stratified layers down to 10 meters beneath the Martian regolith.
  3. Surface Operations & Field Laboratory: Explorers can traverse steep terrain on foot or pilot a pressurized rover at 60–80 km/h with responsive Ackermann steering. At 25 georeferenced NASA sample cache sites, users deploy drill tools and examine cores in an onboard laboratory equipped with simulated PIXL (X-ray fluorescence) and CheMin (X-ray diffraction) instruments.

What Factors Did Our Team Consider?

We grounded every design decision in the real physical constraints of Martian exploration:

  • Human Physiological Limits: Mars offers no breathable air (6.1 hPa, 95% CO2​) and freezing temperatures (−63∘C). Our HUD tracks realistic consumables consumption where running consumes oxygen faster, forcing the explorer to plan safe turnaround margins.
  • Topographical Hazards: The Jezero river delta has vertical scarps and loose scree. We incorporated MOLA-derived slope-hazard alerts so explorers don't drive into steep dead ends.
  • Cognitive Load Under Stress: An astronaut in an EVA suit cannot decipher complex GIS software with tiny menus. We designed high-contrast, glanceable telemetry, color-coded symbology, and intuitive interactive tools.
  • Accessibility & Device Parity: Real field crews use handheld tablets; classroom students use Chromebooks or phones. We built a custom touch-native mobile landscape interface with dual virtual thumbsticks and pinch-to-zoom mapping so anyone can explore without dedicated gaming hardware.

How Is Our Project Creative?

Most mapping tools are either purely 2D top-down maps or disconnected 3D tech demos. MARSBOUND bridges both worlds seamlessly.

We created an editorial-grade narrative framework styled like an authentic expedition dossier—connecting historical robotic discoveries with future human footsteps. By overlaying real RIMFAX radar radargrams alongside 3D surface boulders and CRISM mineral signatures, users don't just see a terrain map; they understand why Perseverance stopped at Octavia E. Butler Landing or Skinner Cove, and what it feels like to conduct fieldwork at those exact coordinates.

Tools, Languages, & Technologies Used

  • Frontend & UI: React 18, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Lucide Icons, Canvas API.
  • 3D Graphics & Physics: Three.js (WebGL), custom procedural shaders for atmospheric dust scattering, low-gravity kinematic controllers, and responsive vehicle physics.
    • NASA MRO HiRISE (High Resolution Imaging Science Experiment) Jezero DTM and mosaic tiles.
    • NASA MGS MOLA (Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter) topographic elevations.
    • NASA MRO CRISM (Compact Reconnaissance Imaging Spectrometer for Mars) mineralogy data.
    • NASA Mars 2020 Perseverance Rover RIMFAX (Radar Imager for Mars' Subsurface Experiment) radargrams and official published sample cache dossiers.
  • Audio & Spatial Ambience: Web Audio API synthesizing Martian wind resonance and suit biometrics.

Intended Impact

MARSBOUND has a dual horizon:

  • For Space Exploration: It serves as a proof-of-concept for how NASA's Artemis Moon-to-Mars missions can package multi-instrument orbital telemetry into lightweight, astronaut-operable tactical HUDs that function completely offline on local compute nodes.
  • For Global STEM Education: Millions of students around the world know that Perseverance is on Mars, but very few have interacted with its raw scientific data. MARSBOUND democratizes planetary science, turning complex PDS (Planetary Data System) archives into an exciting, accessible expedition that sparks the next generation of planetary scientists and astronauts.

projectDetails.name: TerraLens
projectDetails.summary: TerraLens is an interactive multi-spectral workbench designed to identify and characterize terrestrial analogs for Lunar and Martian exploration beyond simple visual similarity. By fusing open satellite datasets from NASA, CSA, ESA, and JAXA across four sensor regimes—Optical, SAR Radar, Thermal, and Elevation—the platform pairs extraterrestrial targets like Shackleton and Jezero Crater with lesser-known Earth environments. Mission planners can inspect terrain through a synchronized full-screen Split-Scope and X-Ray lens, adjust engineering priority weights to dynamically rank sites, evaluate where physical analogies break down, and export comprehensive flight dossiers to guide real-world hardware testing.
projectDetails.details:
How It Works: The platform pairs extraterrestrial targets (Shackleton Crater on the Moon and Jezero Crater on Mars) with five lesser-known Earth sites across four paired sensor regimes: Optical, SAR Radar, Thermal, and Topographic Slope. Users explore terrains through a 10 km × 10 km scale-locked Split-Scope with synchronized pan/zoom, an X-Ray Magnifying Lens for peering through sensor layers, and live `<canvas>` pixel telemetry. A Mission Priority Weighting Engine ($S = \sum w_i m_i$) lets engineers adjust sliders for slope, radar roughness, thermal regime, and geochemistry to dynamically re-rank sites and export printable Flight Dossiers (PDF, JSON, Markdown, and custom SVG Mission Patches).

Creativity & Factors Considered: Instead of relying on overused red deserts, we paired planetary instruments directly with Earth sensors . Recognizing that no Earth site is perfect, we built a 3-Tier Diagnostic Matrix and 4-Axis Radar Chart that explicitly highlight High-Fidelity Matches, Where the Analogy Breaks Down (such as 1G gravity, 1 bar atmosphere, or high rainfall in Newfoundland's ultramafic Tablelands), and Engineering Mitigations to compensate during testing.

Benefits & Impact: TerraLens de-risks hardware testing for Artemis and Mars missions by matching specific engineering needs (like rover wheel slip or cryo-drilling) to physical satellite measurements, while making multi-agency planetary science accessible to researchers and students.


Tools & Tech Stack: Built using React 19, Vite, JavaScript, HTML5 Canvas, CSS3 Spatial Glassmorphism, and SVG on the frontend; Python, FastAPI, and Pydantic with custom raster/histogram processing scripts on the backend; integrating open data from NASA (LRO LROC/Mini-RF/Diviner/LOLA, Mars HiRISE/SHARAD/THEMIS/MOLA, Earthdata MODIS), CSA (RADARSAT), ESA (Sentinel-2), and JAXA (ALOS PALSAR, AW3D30 DEM).

projectDetails.name: Project Project Zelestial
projectDetails.summary:
"Where Did the Space Robots Go?" is an interactive digital storybook developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 theme, "Abandoned but Not Forgotten." Designed to make space exploration engaging and accessible for young readers, the project brings to life the fascinating journeys of eight robotic explorers across the Moon, Mars, and deep space, including Surveyor 3, Sojourner, Spirit, Phoenix, Pioneer 10, and Voyager 1.

Through illustrated storytelling and interactive features such as page navigation, background music, read-aloud functionality, clickable explorer maps, informative tabs, and quizzes, the project transforms real space mission histories into an engaging and educational experience. Readers can discover what these robotic explorers accomplished, what happened to them after their missions, and how their discoveries continue to contribute to our understanding of the universe.

Our goal is to make space exploration accessible, enjoyable, and memorable while celebrating the remarkable contributions of robotic explorers. By bringing their stories back into the spotlight, we hope to inspire curiosity about space and remind readers that even when a mission ends, its legacy is never forgotten.
projectDetails.details:
Project Description: Where Did the Space Robots Go? Presented by Project Zelestial

Curious Stories of the Machines We Sent Beyond Earth

1. What does the project do or how does it work?

Our project is an interactive digital storybook designed to teach children about space exploration and the journeys of spacecraft and robots sent beyond Earth.



It explores the stories of eight real space explorers, including Surveyor 3, Lunar Roving Vehicle, ALSEP, Sojourner, Spirit, Phoenix, Pioneer 10 and Voyager 1.

The complete map is as shown below:




Every explorer’s chapter has two parts.

1. Interactive story
Meet the explorer through an animated, illustrated story. It speaks in its own voice, and you can lift the flaps, pull the tabs and tap the explorer to hear its tale.



2. The real science
Discover the facts behind the story: a real NASA photo, key dates, mission facts, and a labelled machine with tappable parts.



3. Quick quiz
After each world, the Moon and then Mars, there is a short quiz to check what you’ve learned. At the end, a final explorer challenge covers all eight explorers.


In this way the project explains what these machines were designed to do, how they worked, what scientific discoveries they made and what happened to them after their missions.

Users can explore the digital storybook through interactive animations, illustrated spacecraft, moving components, clickable hotspots, information cards, audio narration, sound effects and quizzes. Readers can turn pages, explore different parts of spacecraft and test their knowledge through interactive questions.

2. What are the benefits of the project?

- Makes space science interesting and enjoyable for children.
- Explains complex scientific concepts in simple, child-friendly language.
- Improves scientific curiosity and knowledge about space exploration.
- Encourages interactive and self-paced learning.
- Helps children understand real NASA missions and technological achievements.
- Combines storytelling, visuals, audio and quizzes to improve learning and memory.
- Introduces children to robotics, engineering and scientific instruments.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our main aim is to inspire the next generation of young scientists, engineers and space explorers.

Many children know about rockets and astronauts, but they may not know what happens to spacecraft and robots after completing their missions.

Through this project, we want children to understand that some space robots remain on the Moon or Mars, some continue travelling silently through space, and some are still sending scientific information to Earth.

We hope to develop curiosity about the universe, encourage scientific thinking and make space education more accessible, engaging and enjoyable for young learners.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

This project was developed as a browser-based interactive digital experience.

The main technologies used include:

- HTML5: To create the structure and pages of the digital storybook.
- CSS3: To design the interface, colourful backgrounds, animations, layouts and interactive visual effects.
- JavaScript: To control page navigation, interactive spacecraft components, quizzes, sound effects and user interactions.
- SVG: To create illustrated spacecraft, robots and animated scientific components.
- HTML Canvas: To support the visual background effects.
- Web Speech API: To provide audio narration and read-aloud functionality.
- Web Audio API: To create interactive sound effects.

The project is designed to run in a web browser and does not require specialised physical hardware.

5. How is your project creative and innovative?

The creativity of our project comes from presenting real space missions through an interactive storytelling experience.

Instead of simply providing facts about spacecraft, we allow each space explorer to tell its own story using an imaginative first-person voice.

Some unique features include:

- Interactive digital book with page-turning animations.
- Animated illustrations of real spacecraft and robots.
- Clickable hotspots that explain different spacecraft components.
- Interactive tabs and sliders that demonstrate how certain parts work.
- Audio narration that allows children to listen to the stories.
- Knowledge-testing quizzes with instant feedback.
- A visual explorer map connecting missions across the Moon, Mars and deep space.

The combination of storytelling, science, technology and interactive learning makes the project different from an ordinary educational website.

6. What factors did our team consider?

While developing this project, we considered several important factors:

- Scientific accuracy: Using real space missions, equipment, dates and discoveries as the foundation of the stories.
- Age appropriateness: Keeping the content simple and understandable for young learners.
- User engagement: Including animations, sounds, interactive activities and quizzes.
- Educational value: Ensuring that every explorer teaches something about science and technology.
- Accessibility: Including audio narration and easy navigation.
- Creativity: Making scientific information entertaining through storytelling.
- Technical performance: Designing a browser-based experience that does not depend on specialised hardware.
- Learning outcomes: Encouraging children to ask questions, explore independently and develop an interest in space science.

Conclusion

“Where Did the Space Robots Go?” is more than a digital storybook. It is an interactive journey through the history of space exploration.

Our goal is to turn children's curiosity into scientific understanding and inspire them to imagine themselves as the scientists and explorers of tomorrow.

projectDetails.name: ASTRA: Astronaut Safety Tracking & Real-time Analytics
projectDetails.summary:
During deep-space missions to the Moon and Mars, communication delays of up to 20 minutes make real-time telemedicine from Earth impossible. Astronauts must have complete medical autonomy. 

To solve this challenge, we developed ASTRA (Astronaut Safety Tracking & Real-time Analytics) — an offline-first, mission-critical health dashboard designed for long-duration spaceflight. ASTRA tracks 8 essential biometric and behavioral telemetry indicators (including blood pressure, heart rate, SpO2, sleep duration, and hydration) linked to the 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight defined by the NASA Human Research Program (HRP).

The platform features an interactive 3D astronaut digital twin, real-time Chart.js physiological trend analytics, autonomous emergency diagnostic alerts (such as microgravity hypotension and SANS risk detection), and guided clinical countermeasures. To combat mission-induced cognitive fatigue and sensory-vestibular discordance, ASTRA also integrates a gamified 3D neuro-cognitive flight simulation for non-invasive stress de-escalation.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do and how does it work?

ASTRA is an autonomous health management platform tailored for exploration-class spaceflight:

  • Daily Biometric Check-in: Astronauts rapidly record vitals (Blood Pressure, Heart Rate, Core Temperature, Blood Glucose, SpO2, Sleep Hours, Mood, Hydration) with an intuitive stepper interface that awards daily mission XP and maintains habit streaks.
  • Autonomous Clinical Issue Alerts: When vitals enter caution or critical zones (e.g., blood pressure < 85 mmHg due to cephalad fluid shift, or SpO2 <= 90%), ASTRA triggers high-visibility HUD emergency alert banners with clinical diagnostic explanations and step-by-step countermeasure protocols.
  • Interactive 3D Physiological Digital Twin: A WebGL/Three.js 3D astronaut model visualizes organ-level impacts across 7 physiological systems (Cardiovascular, Respiratory, Neurological, Metabolic, Immune, Musculoskeletal, and Behavioral).
  • Chart.js Historical Telemetry: Multi-day historical graphs with normal physiological threshold bands, moving averages, and Sol-time hover diagnostics.
  • Stress Relief Combat Therapy: A high-speed 3D flight simulation targeting vestibular-ocular recalibration and acute cortisol reduction through flow-state pursuit mechanics.

2. What benefits and impact does it have?

  • Medical Autonomy: Enables crews to independently diagnose and mitigate health threats during communication blackouts.
  • Early Intervention: Prevents acute escalation of spaceflight-specific conditions like orthostatic intolerance, Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS), and dehydration-induced renal calculi.
  • Cognitive Resilience: Combines gamification mechanics (ranks, badges, XP) and neuro-sensory flight decompression to combat astronaut isolation and mission burnout.

3. Tools, Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Frontend Core: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS 4.
  • 3D Graphics & Shaders: Three.js (r187), GLTF Loader, UnrealBloomPass post-processing shaders, ACESFilmic tone mapping.
  • Data Visualization: Chart.js, react-chartjs-2.
  • Animations: Framer Motion.
  • Data & Persistence: Supabase real-time database with offline-first LocalStorage fallback and PWA Service Workers.
  • Deployment: Vercel with automated continuous deployment.

4. Spaceflight Factors Considered

  • Microgravity Fluid Redistribution: Cephalad venous engorgement causing lower-limb hypotension and intracranial pressure spikes.
  • Blunted Thirst Reflex: Decreased hydration perception in microgravity compounded by calcium bone resorption.
  • Circadian & Sleep Disruption: Spacecraft noise and 90-minute orbital light-dark cycles causing chronic sleep debt.
  • Sensory-Vestibular Discordance: Space Motion Sickness (SMS) during initial adaptation and re-adaptation.

projectDetails.name: PYROTRACE
projectDetails.summary:
PYROTRACE harmonizes active-fire observations from four NASA satellite 
sensors — MODIS Terra, MODIS Aqua, VIIRS NOAA-20 and VIIRS NOAA-21 — 
into one consistent, comparable fire-activity record for Kerala, India.

The core problem: VIIRS pixels are 375 m versus MODIS at 1 km. VIIRS 
detects smaller fires, making raw detection counts 3–5× higher for the 
same burning activity. Every historical fire trend built from raw counts 
carries this artifact silently. NASA's Suomi NPP satellite stopped 
transmitting on November 1, 2026 — fourteen days before this hackathon — 
creating a third sensor transition in the 24-year record.

PYROTRACE addresses this by aggregating MODIS and VIIRS detections onto 
a common 0.05° spatial grid, counting unique active cell-days per sensor, 
and applying regional calibration using the sensor overlap period. A 
Sensor Truth Lab displays raw versus harmonized records side by side, 
making the correction visible rather than hidden.

The platform uses real NASA FIRMS data: 25 Kerala fire detections across 
all four sensors from November 2026, correctly showing Kerala's low 
pre-season baseline with transparent uncertainty at every step.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

PYROTRACE is a satellite fire-intelligence platform that solves a concrete scientific problem: NASA MODIS and VIIRS sensors observe fires differently, making their raw detection counts incomparable across time.

VIIRS pixels are 375 m versus MODIS at 1 km — VIIRS detects smaller fires, inflating counts 3–5× for identical burning activity. Every raw historical fire trend carries this artifact. With Suomi NPP ending science data delivery on November 1, 2026 and MODIS missions nearing their end, cross-sensor continuity is an urgent operational problem happening right now.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data ingestion — MODIS C6.1, VIIRS NOAA-20 C2 and VIIRS NOAA-21 C2 active-fire observations downloaded from NASA FIRMS for Kerala, India

2. Grid aggregation — detections mapped to a common 0.05° spatial grid; unique active cell-days counted per sensor per day, eliminating pixel-size inflation

3. Sensor calibration — regional calibration factor calculated from the MODIS–VIIRS overlap period using median ratio and MAD uncertainty

4. Sensor Truth Lab — raw versus harmonized records displayed side by side so the correction is visible, not hidden inside a finished chart

5. Historical calendar — seasonal fire patterns visualized with anomaly detection using robust median and MAD statistical methods

6. Methodology page — every formula documented with known limitations stated transparently

REAL DATA

25 Kerala fire detections from November 7–13, 2026 across all four sensors: MODIS Terra, MODIS Aqua, VIIRS NOAA-20 and VIIRS NOAA-21. November is correctly shown as Kerala's low pre-season baseline. The February–April peak fire season is documented in the historical calendar view. Source: NASA FIRMS active fire data.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

PYROTRACE makes the sensor transition problem visible and correctable for researchers, forest officers and disaster-response teams who rely on historical fire records. By showing raw versus harmonized records side by side with transparent uncertainty, it builds trust in the corrected output. The methodology is documented and reproducible. The platform architecture supports extension to any global region using the same NASA FIRMS data pipeline.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

  • Frontend: React 18, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS
  • Charts: Recharts
  • Maps: Leaflet, React-Leaflet, OpenStreetMap
  • Data processing: Python, Pandas
  • Data source: NASA FIRMS API — MODIS C6.1, VIIRS NOAA-20 C2, VIIRS
  • NOAA-21 C2 (CSV format, South Asia region)
  • Deployment: Vercel
  • Source control: GitHub

CREATIVE APPROACH

Instead of building another fire hotspot map, PYROTRACE makes the measurement problem the central experience. The Sensor Truth Lab lets any user — researcher, judge or student — see exactly where the artificial sensor gap comes from, what the correction does, and how reliable that correction is. The science is not hidden. Scientific honesty is treated as a feature, not a disclaimer. Every statistic on the platform is calculated from loaded NASA data — no fabricated numbers appear anywhere in the application.

SCIENTIFIC PRINCIPLES FOLLOWED

  • Active cell-days formula: A(s,t) = Σ I(cell g has ≥1 detection from sensor s on date t), summed over all grid cells in the AOI
  • Calibration: R = median(A_MODIS / A_VIIRS) during overlap period
  • Anomaly score: z = (observed − median_historical) / MAD_historical
  • Active cell-days are satellite observations, not confirmed wildfires
  • Cloud cover, overpass time, confidence flags and grid resolution all affect results and are documented as limitations

Source code: https://github.com/sanjay-sanju-03/PYROTRACE.git

Live application: https://pyrotrace.vercel.app/

projectDetails.details:
MISSIONFORGE — Educational Space Mission Design & Simulation Game

https://missionforge.qorvode.co.in/

What It Does & How It Works

MISSIONFORGE is an interactive, browser-based space mission design and simulation platform where players step into the roles of Spacecraft Mission Engineer and Mission Director to design, configure, launch, and operate robotic exploration missions across the Solar System.

Rather than simply selecting a destination and clicking launch, players manage end-to-end aerospace trade-offs across nine flight phases:

1. Explore & Plan: Navigate a 3D Solar System to inspect planetary telemetry, select a destination, define scientific objectives, and set mission duration and budgets.

2. Build the Spacecraft: Assemble a modular 3D spacecraft—configuring the structural bus, solar arrays or RTGs, high-gain antennas, propulsion systems, propellant tanks, and scientific instruments—while watching mass, power, thermal, and cost metrics update in real time.

3. Select Launch & Trajectory: Match the spacecraft's wet mass to an appropriate launch vehicle (such as Falcon 9, Falcon Heavy, SLS, Atlas V, Ariane 6, Starship, or Electron) and plan interplanetary Hohmann transfer windows and delta-v budgets.

4. Launch & Operate: Execute a nine-phase mission from pre-launch countdown and orbital insertion through interplanetary cruise, mid-course corrections, arrival capture burns, and scientific operations.

5. Handle Dynamic Anomalies: Respond under pressure to real-time engineering events—such as solar particle events, micrometeoroid impacts, communication blackouts, thermal extremes, and sensor glitches—by making calculated operational trade-offs.

6. Mission Debrief: Receive a weighted post-flight evaluation across five pillars—Scientific Objectives (30%), Engineering Performance (25%), Mission Completion (20%), Budget Efficiency (15%), and Resource Management (10%)—with exportable JSON and printable mission reports.

Benefits & Intended Impact

- Bridges Theory and Intuition: Transforms abstract orbital mechanics and systems engineering formulas into hands-on, cause-and-effect decision-making where every kilogram, watt, and dollar has a direct impact on mission survival.

- Accessible STEM Education: Runs completely in the browser as an offline-first application with zero installation or heavy hardware requirements, making authentic space mission engineering accessible to students, educators, and space enthusiasts anywhere.

Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

- Core Framework & Languages: React 19, TypeScript (Strict mode), and Vite.

- 3D Graphics & Visualization: Three.js, React Three Fiber, @react-three/drei, procedural HTML5 Canvas planetary textures, and Recharts for real-time telemetry graphs.

- State, Styling & Testing: Zustand (with localStorage persistence), Tailwind CSS v4, Framer Motion, Lucide React, and Vitest for deterministic physics verification.

- Data Sources: Adapted from public NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (GSFC) Planetary Fact Sheets, NASA Launch Services Program (LSP) performance curves, and deep-space mission heritage (Voyager, Cassini-Huygens, New Horizons, Perseverance, Europa Clipper, and Parker Solar Probe).

How Our Project Is Creative

- Authentic SI-Unit Physics Inside Interactive Gameplay: Instead of arbitrary game stats, MISSIONFORGE runs a deterministic, fixed-step engineering engine modeled on real physics—including coplanar Keplerian orbits, the vis-viva equation, the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation (with a 12% structural mass margin), inverse-square solar irradiance (1361 W/m² at 1 AU), Stefan-Boltzmann radiative thermal equilibrium, and speed-of-light deep-space signal delays.

- Procedural & Offline-First Architecture: All planetary surfaces, starfields, and spacecraft assemblies are procedurally generated on the client side with zero runtime CDN dependencies, ensuring smooth performance and full offline capability.

Factors Our Team Considered

- Realism vs. Accessibility: We balanced authentic aerospace constraints (delta-v budgets, duty cycles, thermal sink limits, and downlink path loss) with intuitive visual feedback and simplified two-impulse transfer classes so newcomers can grasp orbital mechanics without needing an aerospace degree.

- Client-Side Reliability: Designed as a zero-backend static Single Page Application with hash routing and deterministic seeded RNG so users can save mission archives locally and run repeatable simulations on standard laptops.

projectDetails.name: OrbitOps
projectDetails.summary:
OrbitOps is a 3D, character-driven space engineering game built with React, Three.js and Google AI Studio. Players pick one of 5 NASA-inspired missions (Earth, Moon, Mars, Asteroids, Sun). They build a spacecraft from 5 subsystems and pair it with a real rocket (Falcon 9, Vulcan Centaur, Electron, SLS) and a GMAT-inspired orbit. Then they fly it through a 7-stage flight or a 14-day campaign. A physics and scoring engine checks mass, power, eclipse battery margin and data-link limits, and players need 65/100 to pass. Along the way they face three live emergencies: a solar storm, an eclipse power shortage, and a communication blackout.
How it addresses the challenge
Real systems engineering: players balance mass, power and data budgets, as real mission designers do.
Official NASA resources: it tracks the four mission segments (Launch, Space, Ground, User), shows JPL Concept Maturity Levels (CML 1-4), models GMAT-style orbits and solar irradiance, and cites real instruments such as Landsat 9, MODIS, NISAR, LRO and MRO.
Learning from failure: every lost point comes with what failed, why it happened, and how to fix it. 
Judge-friendly demos: two one-click benches show a 94/100 build and a 32/100 build.
Why it matters
Professional tools like GMAT are hard for beginners, and arcade games teach no real physics. OrbitOps sits in between, so students learn why spacecraft need eclipse batteries, radiation shielding and high-gain dishes, and they can save, compare and improve designs.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does the project do and how does it work?

OrbitOps is a 3D, character-driven space engineering game designed to teach students the fundamentals of spacecraft design and space mission planning through interactive simulation. Players can choose from five NASA-inspired missions: Earth observation, Moon exploration, Mars exploration, asteroid exploration and solar observation.

Players design their own spacecraft by selecting and combining five essential subsystems. They then choose a suitable launch vehicle, such as Falcon 9, Vulcan Centaur, Electron or SLS, and configure an orbit inspired by real orbital mechanics.

The game features a seven-stage flight simulation or a 14-day mission campaign. A physics-based engine evaluates spacecraft performance by checking mass limits, power consumption, battery capacity during eclipses and communication/data-link limitations.

During the mission, players encounter three major emergencies: solar storms, eclipse-related power shortages and communication blackouts. Their decisions directly affect mission performance and the final score. Players need to achieve at least 65/100 to successfully complete a mission. The game also provides explanations for failures, including their causes and possible solutions, helping players improve their spacecraft designs.

2. What benefits does the project have?

- Practical STEM Learning: Helps students understand spacecraft engineering, orbital mechanics, power systems and communication networks through hands-on simulation.

- Problem-Solving Skills: Encourages logical thinking, decision-making and resource management.

- Learning from Failure: Explains why a spacecraft design fails and provides suggestions for improvement.

- Scientific Awareness: Introduces students to real NASA missions, spacecraft instruments and scientific resources.

- Accessible Education: Makes complex space engineering concepts easier to understand without requiring expensive professional simulation software.

- Creativity and Innovation: Allows students to experiment with different spacecraft configurations and mission strategies.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The main objective of OrbitOps is to make space engineering more accessible, engaging and understandable for students and beginners.

Professional tools such as GMAT can be challenging for beginners, while conventional space-themed games often focus more on entertainment than scientific accuracy. OrbitOps aims to bridge this gap by combining interactive gaming with simplified engineering principles.

The project intends to develop students' interest in space science, encourage STEM education and help young learners understand the challenges involved in designing and operating real spacecraft. In the long term, it aims to inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers and space explorers.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware or software were used?

Development tools and technologies:

- React.js: Used to develop the interactive user interface and manage the game's components.

- Three.js: Used to create 3D spacecraft, space environments and interactive visualizations.

- JavaScript: Used to implement game mechanics, mission logic, physics calculations, scoring and emergency scenarios.

- HTML5 and CSS3: Used to structure and style the application.

- Google AI Studio: Used to support AI-assisted development and experimentation.

- GMAT-inspired orbital modelling: Used as a reference for representing orbital mechanics in a simplified educational simulation.

Hardware requirements:

OrbitOps is a browser-based software project and does not require specialized hardware. It can run on a computer with a modern web browser.

5. How is the project creative and what factors did the team consider?

OrbitOps is creative because it transforms complex spacecraft engineering concepts into an interactive, character-driven 3D learning experience. Instead of simply presenting scientific information, it allows players to experience the challenges of designing and operating a space mission.

Some of its unique features include:

- Five Mission Environments: Players can explore Earth, Moon, Mars, Asteroids and the Sun through different mission objectives.

- Realistic Engineering Trade-offs: Every spacecraft component affects mass, power consumption and data requirements.

- Real-World Rocket Selection: Players choose from real launch vehicles, introducing them to actual spaceflight capabilities.

- Dynamic Emergency Scenarios: Solar storms, eclipses and communication failures challenge players to make critical decisions.

- Learning Through Failure: Every lost point is accompanied by an explanation of what went wrong and how it can be corrected.

- Performance Comparison: Two one-click demonstration builds, scoring 94/100 and 32/100, help players compare successful and unsuccessful spacecraft designs.

- Scientific References: The project incorporates NASA-related resources, real instruments such as Landsat 9, MODIS, NISAR, LRO and MRO, and JPL Concept Maturity Levels (CML 1–4).

During development, the team considered scientific accuracy, beginner accessibility, user engagement, realistic engineering constraints, educational value and ease of use.

The ultimate goal was to create a project that is not just a space game, but an educational platform where students can experiment, make mistakes, understand scientific principles and improve their engineering decisions.

projectDetails.name: CropCycle AI – NASA-Powered Smart Crop Rotation Planner for Kerala
projectDetails.summary:
CropCycle AI is a NASA-powered smart crop rotation planning platform designed to support farmers in Kerala, India. We developed a web application with an interactive map that allows users to select or draw their agricultural fields, analyze field conditions, and generate suitable crop rotation plans based on factors such as land area, soil type, water availability, and crop preferences.

The platform combines soil information and NASA POWER climate data to support informed agricultural decisions. It provides multiple crop rotation options, helping farmers consider soil health, water efficiency, climate resilience, and potential income.

CropCycle AI addresses the challenge of sustainable agriculture by helping farmers move beyond traditional monocropping and make better-informed crop rotation decisions. It is important because Kerala's farmers face changing weather patterns, soil degradation, and water management challenges. Our goal is to make data-driven, climate-smart farming recommendations more accessible and practical for local farmers.
projectDetails.details:
CropCycle AI is a web-based smart crop rotation planning platform developed to promote sustainable and climate-resilient agriculture in Kerala, India.

How it works:
Farmers can use the interactive map to select their agricultural field or draw its boundaries. The application calculates the field area and allows users to provide information such as soil type, water availability, preferred crops, and farming priorities. It uses soil information and NASA POWER climate data to support field analysis. Based on these inputs, the system generates three alternative crop rotation plans, focusing on soil health, water efficiency, climate resilience, and farming income.

Benefits and intended impact:
CropCycle AI helps farmers make more informed crop selection and rotation decisions instead of depending only on traditional monocropping practices. It aims to improve soil health, encourage efficient water use, reduce climate-related agricultural risks, and support better long-term farm productivity. The project is designed with Kerala's diverse agricultural conditions in mind.

Tools and technologies:
We developed the application using React and JavaScript for the frontend, Python and FastAPI for the backend, Google Maps API for interactive field mapping, and Google Cloud Run for deployment. NASA POWER climate data and soil information are used to support agricultural analysis.

Creativity and innovation:
The creative aspect of CropCycle AI is the integration of interactive field mapping, environmental data, and AI-assisted crop rotation planning in one platform. Instead of giving farmers a single generic recommendation, it provides three alternative rotation strategies so they can consider different priorities.

Factors considered:
Our team considered Kerala's climate, soil conditions, seasonal water availability, field size, farmer crop preferences, soil health, climate risks, and economic priorities while designing the solution. Our aim is to make data-supported sustainable farming decisions easier and more accessible to farmers.

projectDetails.name: Agri Nova: AI Crop Prediction and Rotation Planning from NASA Earth Data
projectDetails.summary: Agri Nova is an AI-powered web platform that helps farmers decide what to grow each season and how to rotate crops for long-term soil health. It combines NASA POWER daily and long-term climate data with the farmer’s own soil test. A machine-learning model, 99.6% accurate on records it never saw during training, then ranks the most suitable crops for each season and explains every recommendation. A suitability engine checks each crop against temperature, rainfall, water and soil limits. A rotation planner then builds several strategies and simulates five years of soil carbon, nutrient balance, water demand and climate risk, with downloadable reports for farmers and researchers. This turns NASA Earth observations into practical decisions at the farm level, replacing habit and guesswork with clear, evidence-based guidance. As rainfall grows less predictable, heat rises and soils degrade from repeated cropping, Agri Nova helps farmers, especially smallholders, protect their land, plan their water use and adapt to a changing climate. It’s honest about uncertainty and never invents data.
projectDetails.details:
Agri Nova helps farmers decide what to grow each season and which crop rotation will keep their land healthy. A farmer pins their farm on a map and adds a soil test, and the platform pulls NASA POWER daily and 10-year climate data for that location. A machine-learning model then ranks the best crops for each season and explains each pick. Agri Nova also generates rotation strategies and simulates five years of soil carbon, nutrient balance, water demand and climate risk, with downloadable PDF reports.

Farmers get clear, explained advice instead of guesswork, can plan water use before the season starts, and can compare rotations by what matters to them: soil health, water, climate resilience, income or diversity. Researchers and agricultural organisations get data exports, model details and regional views. The goal is healthier soil, lower risk and more climate-resilient farming, especially for smallholder farmers in India.

We built the frontend with Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS and Leaflet maps, and the backend with Python, FastAPI and PostgreSQL/PostGIS. The AI uses scikit-learn and pandas, PDF reports use ReportLab, and uploaded soil reports are read with Tesseract OCR. The data comes from NASA POWER, with optional GPM IMERG, SMAP, MODIS, HLS, ECOSTRESS and SRTM. No special hardware is needed; it runs in any web browser.

Agri Nova goes beyond picking a single crop: it plans multi-season rotations and simulates how the soil changes year by year. We compared six algorithms, and the chosen model is 99.6% accurate on records it never saw. Every prediction shows its confidence, each crop’s typical conditions, and a warning when inputs are unusual.

Throughout, we focused on accuracy and honesty. The platform never invents data, labels demonstration data clearly, and leaves out yield prediction because our data couldn’t support it. We also kept the language simple for farmers, let them confirm every value read from a soil report, and kept all credentials on the server.

projectDetails.name: Last Light
projectDetails.summary:
LAST LIGHT 🚀

Earth is fading. Humanity's future lies beyond the stars.

Take command of AURORA-1, navigate the unknown, overcome critical emergencies, and explore Lumen-b, a mysterious planet that could become humanity's next home.

Manage resources, make life-changing decisions, and uncover the secrets of an alien world in this immersive 3D space exploration and survival simulator.

The mission is yours. The future is unknown. Will you find a new home? Play the game to find out!
projectDetails.details:
LAST LIGHT – An Immersive 3D Space Exploration and Survival Simulator

LAST LIGHT is an interactive 3D space exploration and survival simulator that places players in command of AURORA-1, an advanced fictional spacecraft sent on a mission to investigate Lumen-b, a potentially habitable planet, as Earth faces an environmental crisis.

The game takes players through seven mission phases: launch, Earth orbit, departure, cruise, emergency response, arrival, and planetary survey. Throughout the journey, players must monitor and manage essential spacecraft systems, including oxygen, power, fuel, communications, and hull integrity. During the mission, unexpected emergencies such as oxygen faults, meteorite encounters, battery failures, and communication blackouts challenge players to make critical decisions. Each choice has consequences that affect the spacecraft's condition and the mission outcome.

Upon reaching Lumen-b, players conduct scientific scans of its atmosphere, surface, and water indicators before assessing its potential habitability. The mission concludes with a final report based on the player's decisions, resource management, and survey results.

The project aims to make space science more engaging and accessible through interactive learning. It introduces concepts related to planetary exploration, orbital motion, spacecraft systems, resource management, and habitability assessment. It also encourages critical thinking, problem-solving, decision-making, and an understanding of the challenges involved in long-duration space missions.

Technology and Development: The project was developed as a browser-based application using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with Three.js and WebGL for its interactive 3D environment. Procedurally generated planetary textures, nebulae, starfields, orbital paths, spacecraft animations, and interactive camera controls create an immersive visual experience.

Creativity and Innovation: Rather than presenting space science as static information, LAST LIGHT transforms it into a playable mission where every decision matters. It combines scientific concepts with storytelling, simulation, interactive exploration, and multiple possible endings. The fictional planetary system and spacecraft are designed to create an original science-fiction experience while distinguishing fictional elements from established scientific facts.

During development, our team considered scientific relevance, gameplay balance, resource limitations, user interaction, visual clarity, accessibility, and the importance of making the experience both educational and enjoyable. The ultimate vision is to inspire curiosity about space exploration and demonstrate how technology, scientific thinking, and decision-making could contribute to humanity's search for habitable worlds.

projectDetails.name: project life on mars
projectDetails.summary: Life on Mars is a free browser game for kids aged 7 to 12. You play a junior astronaut running a small Mars outpost for 7 sols (Mars days). Four bars (Power, Air, Food and Shield) start at 75. Every action helps one bar but costs another, so kids see the result of each choice straight away. The game warns you the evening before a solar flare and a dust storm. After each event, a short science note shows its source link. It answers the Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer challenge by turning mission planning, limited resources and space weather into a living simulation instead of a quiz. It matters because kids learn to plan, make trade-offs and understand why astronauts need protection, just by playing, with nothing to install.
projectDetails.details:
The player walks around a 3D Mars outpost, goes to a station and presses E. Each of the four stations changes the bars: Solar panels, Air recycler, Greenhouse and Shield wall. Each sol has one action, then a night that drains every bar. A “tomorrow” number under each bar shows the cost ahead. A solar flare hits on Sol 3 and a dust storm on Sol 5, and both are warned the evening before. The player loses if any bar reaches 0 and wins by surviving 7 nights. Stars are given for how few bars ended in the red. The game also has a rover you can drive, four places to explore, small missions and a phone screen.

Benefits. Kids practise planning ahead, weighing trade-offs and reading simple numbers. There is no reading-heavy text, and it runs in a normal desktop browser.

Intended impact. We want kids to feel that being an astronaut is about careful choices and teamwork with real science, and to get curious about space weather.

Tools and languages. HTML, CSS and JavaScript in one file, with no build tools. Three.js (3D graphics) and the browser’s Pointer Lock feature for mouse look. All art is made in code: no image, audio, video or 3D model files. Developed on one laptop. Hosted on GitHub Pages. Code was written with AI assistance (Claude by Anthropic).

Creativity. A simulation where every choice has a visible cost, an astronaut you can steer and a rover you can drive, a story intro, places to explore, and a dancing astronaut when you win.

Factors we considered. Kid-friendly text sizes (at least 20px) and colors, about 60 fps on school laptops, no people under 18 shown, and no NASA logos. We kept the science honest: we use only facts we can link to and mark the made-up story as made-up.

projectDetails.name: TerraScope
projectDetails.summary:
TerraScope is an Earth-observation dashboard that helps people explore how radar and other satellites observe a changing landscape. Its current study focuses on Madhya Pradesh, India. Users can explore dated NASA/ISRO NISAR radar imagery, NASA FIRMS heat detections, and supporting Sentinel-1, MODIS, rainfall, and soil-moisture context on a district-level map. The site explains how to interpret these different signals.

Next, TerraScope aims to add stronger radar comparisons using compatible calibrated NISAR data and independent validation. It also plans to develop studies of water, crops, vegetation, and other land changes. The longer-term goal is to expand the project’s methods beyond Madhya Pradesh to wider India as suitable data and analysis methods become available.
projectDetails.details:
1. What exactly does it do?

Dancing with the SARs is an Earth-observation project presented through the TerraScope web dashboard. It helps people explore satellite heat-detection reports in Madhya Pradesh alongside radar imagery and other environmental context.

On the interactive map, users can select a date or district, view reports as clusters or individual records, and explore summaries and charts by date and district. The dashboard also has a live-data page for recent NASA FIRMS detections and NISAR catalog scenes, plus learning pages that explain radar and the project’s data sources.

The snapshot I reviewed covers 35 observation dates from September 29 to November 4, 2026. It contains 4,701 detection records statewide and 2,014 in the smaller project footprint. These are satellite reports, not confirmed or unique fires. We plan to expand the dashboard to the full historical record available from each data source; the current snapshot counts and date range will change as that archive is added.

2. How does it work?

The project combines satellite data, geospatial processing, and an interactive website:

  1. Prepare the observation records: Python scripts combine archived NASA FIRMS VIIRS records, filter them to the study area, and associate them with Madhya Pradesh districts. The map uses GeoJSON boundary and detection files.
  2. Explore the map: Users can choose dates, districts, and display options to inspect the records. Charts summarize how the number of reports varies over time and by district.
  3. View satellite context: The site displays date-based NISAR L-band radar browse imagery and other satellite imagery for comparison. It includes a separate monthly MODIS burned-area layer and regional rainfall and soil-moisture context from NASA POWER/SMAP.
  4. Refresh recent feeds: Supabase Edge Functions connect to NASA FIRMS and the ASF NISAR catalog for recent reports and scene information. An optional EchoGuide assistant can explain project context and sources when its service is configured.
  5. Support future analysis: A separate Python workflow can calculate radar backscatter differences from a compatible pair of calibrated NISAR GCOV measurement rasters. That workflow requires suitable matched inputs; it is not the calculation shown on the current map.

Radar browse images are previews, not calibrated change measurements. The dashboard does not confirm fires, map fire perimeters, measure burned area from FIRMS reports, or determine that fire caused a radar pattern.

3. What benefits does it have?

TerraScope brings several satellite data sources into one place and makes them easier to explore through a date-driven map, district summaries, and plain-language explanations. It can help users find dates and locations for closer investigation and understand what different sensors contribute.

The project also emphasizes careful interpretation. Multiple reports may relate to one event, and a thermal detection does not by itself confirm a fire or show how much land burned. Radar signals can also be influenced by moisture, surface structure, viewing geometry, and processing. Explaining these limits helps users treat the dashboard as a research and learning tool rather than a fire-warning or confirmation system.

4. What do we hope to achieve?

We hope to make satellite observations more accessible and useful for people studying environmental change in Madhya Pradesh. A key next step is to expand the current limited snapshot to include the full historical archive available from each data source, so users can explore a longer record over time. Historical coverage will differ by satellite and dataset.

We also plan to strengthen the analysis by comparing compatible calibrated NISAR measurements with independent burned-area data and, where possible, field observations. Longer term, we hope to extend the project to other regions and develop separate studies of vegetation, crops, flooding, water, and other land-surface changes.

5. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

  • Website: React, TypeScript/JavaScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, and Lucide icons.
  • Data processing: Python scripts for combining FIRMS records, filtering geographic areas, preparing map data, and supporting the separate NISAR GCOV analysis workflow.
  • Geospatial tools and formats: QGIS and GeoJSON, with administrative boundaries from the 2021 geoBoundaries India ADM2 dataset.
  • Backend and hosting: Supabase Edge Functions for live data requests and Netlify for the website. The optional EchoGuide assistant uses Gemini when configured.
  • Earth-observation sources: NASA/ISRO NISAR, NASA FIRMS VIIRS, MODIS, NASA GIBS, OPERA Sentinel-1 context, and NASA POWER/SMAP.
  • Hardware: No custom hardware or field sensors were built. The project was developed on a standard computer and uses data collected by satellite missions.

projectDetails.name: EARTHSCOPE– Understand Earth's Changing Systems
projectDetails.summary:
Earth System Trend Detective is an interactive web application that helps students and the public explore how our planet is changing using NASA data. Users can select an environmental variable and region to see how it has changed over time.
Our project uses NASA POWER data, based on MERRA-2 reanalysis and GPM satellite observations, to study monthly air temperature and rainfall from 2001 to 2024 across eight regions, including Kerala, Rajasthan, Assam and the Central Amazon.
The application calculates Sen's Slope to measure the rate of change and uses the Mann-Kendall test to determine whether a trend is statistically significant. We also apply False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction to improve reliability when comparing multiple regions.
Results are displayed through interactive maps, graphs and simple explanations. Users can see whether a variable is increasing, decreasing or showing no clear trend.
The same environmental variable may increase in one region and decrease in another. Even when a trend is not statistically significant, it is worth monitoring because changes may become important over time.
Our goal is to make NASA Earth science data easier to understand and help people explore environmental changes around them.
projectDetails.details:
EarthTrend Dashboard – Be an Earth System Trend Detective!

1. What does our project do?

EarthTrend Dashboard is an interactive, student-friendly website designed to help users understand how Earth's environment changes over time. It allows users to explore historical environmental data, select geographical locations, compare different years, and identify increasing or decreasing environmental trends.

Our main aim is to make complex Earth observation data easier to understand through visual representations such as charts, graphs, and maps.

2. How does it work?

Users can visit our website, select a geographical location, choose an available time period, and explore environmental information. The website presents the available data through visualisations, helping users compare different years and observe environmental patterns.

We use NASA's GIOVANNI platform as a source for collecting Earth observation datasets. These datasets help us explore environmental changes over time.

3. What are its benefits?

  • Makes complex environmental data easier to understand.
  • Helps students explore real-world environmental information.
  • Encourages data analysis and scientific thinking.
  • Helps users identify environmental patterns and changes.
  • Creates awareness about Earth's changing systems.
  • Makes environmental learning more interactive.

4. Intended impact

Our project aims to make Earth science more accessible to students and young learners. It encourages students to explore scientific data, understand environmental changes, and develop curiosity about our planet. It can be useful for educational activities, classroom learning, science projects, and environmental awareness.

5. Tools and technologies used

  • NASA GIOVANNI – Environmental data collection.
  • Python – Data processing and analysis.
  • Visualisation tools – To present environmental information through charts and graphs.
  • Vercel – Website hosting and deployment.

6. What makes our project creative?

Our project connects NASA Earth observation data with student-friendly interactive learning. Instead of presenting environmental information only as numbers, we aim to make it easier to explore and compare through visualisations.

EarthTrend Dashboard transforms environmental data exploration into an engaging learning experience.

Our Vision: Explore the past, understand the present, and discover how our Earth is changing.

projectDetails.name: Project Lunar Landing Site Navigator
projectDetails.summary:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator answers a question every south-pole mission planner faces: will this site, on this date, actually have sunlight and Earth contact — once real terrain gets in the way? Most tools stop at geometric sun/Earth angles. We go further: using NASA LOLA elevation data and JPL SPICE ephemeris, we compute the actual local horizon at each site and determine when the Sun or Earth clears real crater rims and ridges, not just an idealized flat horizon.

The centerpiece is a Mission Delay Simulator — move a landing date and instantly see how sunlight, communication windows, and solar power change, which directly addresses NASA’s call to handle schedule slips and hardware delays. We validated this against real landing sites (IM-1, IM-2, Chandrayaan-3), with every result traceable to its data source, resolution, and assumptions — and sites with insufficient terrain data are labeled honestly rather than given a fabricated number.

It matters because mission planning decisions shouldn’t rest on optimistic geometry when the Moon’s terrain says otherwise.
projectDetails.details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator answers two questions that decide a south-pole landing: when does sunlight reach the lander, and when is Earth in view for a direct link? It then shows how far each answer can be trusted.

How it works. Pick a site and dates. The Python engine computes the Sun and Earth directions from NASA/JPL SPICE (DE440). It builds the terrain horizon at every compass direction from real LRO LOLA elevation data (20 m at IM-2), by tracing rays over the Moon's curved surface. It then finds when each body is visible, to 1-second resolution, as intervals, fractions of time, the longest dark stretch, and a countdown to sunset and Earthset. Everything is recomputed at 8 displaced positions (default ±100 m), so every number comes with a band. The browser only displays what the engine computed.

What you get. Terrain-corrected and geometric (no terrain) results are shown side by side. For IM-2 Athena (15 Jan 2027, 30 days) the Sun is visible 48.6 % of the time (band 45.4–48.9 %) against 53.3 % geometric, and Earth 80.8 % against 73.5 %. A delay simulator shows how a schedule slip moves the window, and a comparison view puts sites and dates side by side. A time player, click-to-pick map on NASA imagery, Learn mode and glossary make it usable by non-specialists.

Intended impact. Mission planners, educators and the public can compare sites and dates in seconds, instead of working through several specialist tools for each combination.

What makes it creative. The design is honesty-first. Where terrain data is insufficient (IM-1), the tool says "terrain data insufficient" and gives no number. Every result states its status: "validated" means reviewed and approved by the project owner, not proven against measurement, and the Chandrayaan-3 terrain is labelled "implemented unvalidated". It is geometry only: no link budget, thermal or power model.

Tools. Python 3.12, FastAPI, SpiceyPy/NAIF SPICE, rasterio/GDAL, NumPy; React, TypeScript, Vite; pytest, Vitest, axe-core and a real-browser end-to-end suite (404 backend, 188 frontend and 26 browser checks pass); Docker. Data: NASA LOLA elevation models (PGDA), NAIF kernels, LROC imagery via NASA Moon Trek, and JPL Horizons as an implementation check. It runs on an ordinary laptop with no special hardware.

What we considered. Scientific accuracy over visuals: no invented data, typed errors, and checksum-verified data. The ephemeris matches JPL Horizons to 1.4×10⁻⁸° and the horizon matches an independent implementation to 1.1×10⁻⁹°. We documented 39 limitations and made setup reproducible with a verified data bundle and Docker.

Code and docs: github.com/Dhinu-2001/NASA-Space-Apps-2026 (MIT licence). Independent project, not endorsed by NASA.

projectDetails.name: Fieldwise AI
projectDetails.summary:
FIELDWISE AI is a web-based decision tool designed for NASA’s Space Apps Challenge 2026: “Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data.” The tool analyzes the effects of climate change on the selected plot and suggests suitable crop rotation strategies.

First, users choose or sketch a farm on the satellite map, and real NASA’s data such as POWER weather observations, Landsat vegetation condition, GPM IMERG precipitation data, and SMAP soil moisture are retrieved for the input coordinates. Because satellites cannot estimate soil composition, farmers need to insert laboratory results about soil chemistry manually. The tool measures the five risks related to agriculture: water stress risk, heat risk, flood risk, decrease in vegetation risk, and soil erosion risk.

The web application works without using AI chatbot. Instead, it utilizes an open two-step system that consists of rigid agricultural filters and the calculation of weighted score. The software analyzes three possible crop rotation approaches in different climate scenarios and creates the final PDF report for the user. For the demonstration example, Pokkali rice-prawn cultivation in Kumbalangi, Kerala is used.
projectDetails.details:
FIELDWISE AI is a web application that helps a farmer assess climate impacts on the specific area and choose suitable crop rotation strategy. After selecting the demo farm "Kumbalangi Pokkali" or drawing his field borders using an interactive satellite map, the backend extracts the data from NASA: POWER for temperature, precipitation and solar irradiance, Landsat 8/9 via Google Earth Engine for NDVI and EVI vegetation health indicators, IMERG for precipitation and SMAP for soil moisture. However, satellites cannot provide any information on soil chemical composition, thus, a user manually provides lab results (pH, salt content, nutrients: nitrogen, phosphorous and potassium, organic carbon, drainage).

The program evaluates five vulnerabilities (water stress, heat stress, flooding probability, reduction of vegetation and soil degradation) and gives their rating depending on a degree of certainty. Then in the Rotation Lab section it contrasts the performance of three rotation strategies: current state of the farm, a soil improvement strategy and a climate adaptation strategy. It is possible to alter the rainfall, temperature, water supply and season start date in the Climate Simulator section in order to observe the differences in ranking of strategies. Finally, the user obtains a downloadable PDF report containing all data and limitations.

projectDetails.name: Abandoned, but Not Forgotten
projectDetails.summary: Abandoned but Not Forgotten is a scrolling story told in the first person by NASA’s Opportunity rover, left behind on Mars. It was designed for 90 sols and instead worked for 5,111. The story follows five short acts: landing in Eagle Crater, finding hematite “blueberries” that show Mars was once wet, driving 28.06 miles, going silent in the 2018 global dust storm, and the question of what we leave behind on other worlds. Real NASA numbers (distance, sols, dust opacity, final power) are woven into the story. Narration, animations and illustrations make it feel like a short film you scroll through. It works on phones, in classrooms and at outreach events.
projectDetails.details:
What it does
Abandoned, but Not Forgotten is a scrolling story told by NASA’s Opportunity rover, left behind on Mars. Opportunity was designed for 90 sols and worked for 5,111. Over five short acts, the rover narrates its landing in Eagle Crater, its discovery of hematite “blueberries” that show Mars was once wet, its 28.06-mile drive, the 2018 global dust storm that silenced it, and the question of what we leave behind on other worlds. Real mission numbers appear inside the story.

How it works
The story is one continuous web page. As the reader scrolls, each act brings its own effect: a starfield and Martian horizon on the title screen, an image that bounces in like a ball for the “hole in one” landing, a trail that draws itself behind the traverse map, a dust storm that builds in the dark act, and a quiet, breathing ending. Narration plays for each act, and a small rover drives across the screen as the page scrolls.

Benefits and intended impact
It turns an abandoned machine’s mission into something readers can feel, not just read about, which helps students and general audiences connect with space exploration history. It needs no sign-in or app and works on a phone, so it can be used in classrooms, libraries and outreach events.

Tools
HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript (no framework), Canvas and SVG animation, scroll-triggered effects, MP3 narration, Netlify hosting and GitHub for the code.

How it is creative
The abandoned machine tells its own story, and the mood of the visuals follows the story, from busy and warm at landing to dark in the storm to quiet at the end. The reader controls the pace by scrolling.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: we checked key facts against NASA pages. For example, the rover’s distance is 28.06 miles, and the final power reading is given as “about 22 W” because sources differ slightly.
  • Accessibility and comfort: narration is optional, the site is mobile-first, and motion effects respect “reduce motion” settings.
  • Transparency: AI use is acknowledged (Claude for text and code, Narakeet and fish audio for the narration voice), and no AI-generated images are used.
  • Branding: the project uses no NASA logos or mission patches.

projectDetails.name: Project Skycolony
projectDetails.summary:
Project Summary: Abandoned, But Not Forgotten

Space exploration leaves behind more than discoveries. It also leaves scientific instruments, spacecraft components and equipment on the surfaces of the Moon and Mars. Although these objects may no longer be operational, they represent important milestones in humanity's journey into space. However, their contributions and stories often remain overlooked.
Abandoned, But Not Forgotten is a proposed educational digital comic book that aims to bring these forgotten objects to life through creative storytelling. The project transforms real space equipment into fictional characters, allowing them to narrate their missions, purposes and experiences through engaging comic-style conversations and illustrations.
Beginning with the Apollo 11 mission, the comic explores equipment such as the Early Apollo Surface Experiments Package (EASEP) and the Lunar Module descent stage. It then extends to Mars, highlighting components of NASA's Perseverance landing system, including the heat shield, backshell, parachute and descent stage.
The stories will be developed using authentic NASA archives, mission records and scientific information, ensuring that creative narratives remain grounded in historical facts.
Our objective is to make space exploration history more accessible and engaging for students and the general public while encouraging curiosity about science, technology and engineering.
projectDetails.details: Abandoned, But Not Forgotten is an educational digital comic book that brings attention to scientific equipment and spacecraft components left behind on the Moon and Mars. It transforms these objects into fictional characters that share their stories through creative conversations and illustrations. Using NASA's official archives and mission records, the project explores equipment from the Apollo 11 mission and landing components of the Perseverance rover mission on Mars. It combines factual research with imaginative storytelling to make space science more engaging and accessible to students and the general public. We use NASA resources for research and digital design tools to develop the comic. Our team focuses on creativity, scientific accuracy, visual appeal and educational value. The project aims to inspire curiosity about space exploration and remind people that even after their missions end, these objects remain part of humanity's achievements.
