projectDetails.name: Project Sleepy heads
projectDetails.summary:
ORBITAL ARCHITECT is a browser-based 3D space mission engineering game modeled after NASA JPL’s Mission Design Lab (MDL) and General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT). Players act as mission architects to plan, assemble, launch, and operate complete space missions across progressive destinations from Low Earth Orbit to the Moon, Mars, and Europa.   

Space mission engineering is typically taught through isolated theoretical exercises, leaving students disconnected from how real spacecraft subsystems interact. ORBITAL ARCHITECT bridges this gap through a coupled systems-engineering engine and real-time 3D WebGL visualizer. Every component choice triggers authentic trade-offs: heavier instruments demand larger launch vehicles, outer-planet distances reduce solar flux via the inverse-square law, planetary eclipses drain battery reserves, and high-rate sensors require high-gain Deep Space Network antennas.   

Featuring Solo, 4-Player Team Sync, Sandbox, and Custom Architect modes—alongside interactive mid-flight solar storm decisions, root-cause engineering audits, and real NASA flight-heritage comparisons—the game turns complex systems engineering into an accessible, hands-on experience for students, educators, and aspiring aerospace engineers.
projectDetails.details:
ORBITAL ARCHITECT

3D SPACE MISSION ENGINEERING SIMULATION GAME

ORBITAL ARCHITECT is a browser-based 3D space mission engineering game inspired by NASA JPL’s Mission Design Lab (MDL) and General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT).

Rather than teaching orbital mechanics, rocket propulsion, and spacecraft subsystems as isolated textbook concepts, the game puts players in the role of mission architects. Players must design, balance, launch, and operate a complete space mission, progressing from initial mission planning to orbital operations.

1. Mission Briefing & Mode Selection

Players begin by selecting a game mode and choosing a mission contract.

Available Game Modes:

  • Solo Architect: Design and operate missions independently.
  • 4-Player Team Sync: Collaborate with three other players to complete a mission.
  • Sandbox Lab: Experiment freely with spacecraft configurations and mission parameters.
  • Custom Architect Mode: Create missions with customizable objectives and constraints.

2. Four-Step Interactive Assembly Hangar

Players configure their spacecraft through four interactive engineering stages:

  1. Launch Vehicle & Orbit: Select the launch vehicle, configure payload capacity, and determine the target orbit.
  2. Scientific Instruments: Choose scientific payloads based on mission objectives and data-generation requirements.
  3. Power & Thermal Systems: Configure solar panels, batteries, nuclear power sources, and thermal management systems.
  4. Deep Space Network (DSN) Communications: Select communication bands and antennas to establish reliable spacecraft-to-ground communication.

Real-Time Coupled Physics Engine

The physics.js engine continuously evaluates spacecraft configurations and calculates the consequences of engineering decisions.

Core Engineering Simulations:

- Mass vs. Booster Capacity: Calculates the combined mass of the spacecraft bus, scientific instruments, power systems, and communication antennas against the launch vehicle's payload capacity.

- Inverse-Square Solar Flux (\(1/r^2\)): Dynamically calculates available solar energy based on the spacecraft's distance from the Sun. Solar power decreases from 100% at Earth and the Moon to approximately 43% at Mars (1.52 AU) and 3.7% at Europa (5.2 AU), making nuclear MMRTG power sources essential for outer-planet missions.

- Orbital Eclipse Survival: Simulates battery discharge during planetary shadow passages and determines whether the spacecraft can maintain essential operations without sunlight.

- RF Downlink Bandwidth: Compares the total scientific instrument data-generation rate (Mbps) against S-Band, X-Band, and Ka-Band communication capacities to prevent data overflow.

3. 3D Launch & Accelerated Orbital Flight Simulation

Once spacecraft assembly is complete, players initiate the launch sequence with a T-3 countdown, transitioning into a real-time 3D orbital simulation.

Powered by scene3d.js, the visualizer features:

  • Planetary Shadow Cones: Visual representations of planetary shadows and orbital eclipse conditions.
  • Surface Target Zones: Interactive mission destinations and designated observation regions.
  • DSN Telemetry Beams: Live cyan communication beams representing spacecraft-to-ground data transmission.
  • Accelerated Orbital Flight: Experience mission progression without waiting for actual orbital durations.
  • Interactive Mid-Flight Anomalies: Encounter unexpected events, such as a Coronal Mass Ejection (CME) solar storm, that require immediate engineering decisions.

Players must act as flight directors, making real-time trade-offs to protect spacecraft systems, preserve mission objectives, and maintain operational stability.

4. Post-Flight Engineering Audit

At mission completion, the game generates a comprehensive engineering performance report.

Mission Evaluation Includes:

  • Final Mission Rank: A performance grade ranging from S to FAILED.
  • Root-Cause Engineering Breakdown: Identifies the exact engineering decisions responsible for mission successes, inefficiencies, and failures.
  • Subsystem Performance Analysis: Evaluates spacecraft mass, power availability, thermal stability, orbital survival, and communication efficiency.
  • Mission Heritage Comparison: Compares the player's spacecraft design and mission outcomes against real NASA flight-heritage missions.

5. Benefits & Intended Impact

Bridging the Systems-Engineering Gap

Traditional educational tools often teach orbital trajectories, rocket launches, and spacecraft subsystems as separate concepts. ORBITAL ARCHITECT bridges this gap by demonstrating how spacecraft subsystems interact and compete for limited resources, including mass, power, budget, and data transmission capacity.

Students experience the engineering trade-offs involved in designing a spacecraft, understanding that there is no universally perfect design—only designs optimized for specific mission objectives and constraints.

Accessible Across Skill Levels

The game incorporates beginner-friendly learning features without compromising the authenticity of its aerospace engineering concepts.

  • Flight Director Onboarding: A guided 3-step introduction familiarizes new players with mission planning and spacecraft operations.
  • Plain-English Engineering Callouts: Explains engineering trade-offs and their consequences in an understandable manner.
  • One-Click Starter Blueprints: The Load Baseline feature provides ready-made spacecraft configurations that players can modify and improve.
  • Smart Launch-Blocker Hints: Identifies configuration problems and provides actionable guidance before launch.

These features make the experience accessible to middle and high school students while retaining meaningful engineering challenges for aspiring aerospace engineers.

Zero-Barrier Classroom & Workshop Deployment

ORBITAL ARCHITECT operates entirely within a standard web browser, requiring no software installation or backend server infrastructure.

This makes it suitable for:

  • School and college classrooms.
  • STEM education programs and aerospace outreach clubs.
  • Hackathons and engineering workshops.
  • Collaborative mission-design challenges.
  • Self-guided learning on laptops and Chromebooks.

Its lightweight deployment model allows educators and participants to start designing missions without complicated setup procedures.

6. Tools, Coding Languages & Software Used

Programming Languages

  • HTML5: Provides the application structure and interface.
  • CSS3: Handles styling, responsive layouts, animations, and the JPL-inspired telemetry aesthetic.
  • JavaScript (ES6+): Implements the application logic through modular architecture, including physics.js, scene3d.js, and app.js.

3D Graphics & Visualization

Celestrak Visualizer | Noelkawano

Three.js (WebGL)

Powers procedural 3D spacecraft assembly, structural over-mass wireframe alerts, three-point studio and solar lighting, orbital trajectory splines, and planetary eclipse shadow geometry.

Retro Futuristic Satellite Control Center Interface Display

HTML5 2D Canvas

Renders tactical radar sweeps, telemetry oscilloscopes, and floating real-time statistical popups.

Audio & User Interface

  • Web Audio API: Generates procedural NASA-style Quindar tones, telemetry clicks, and launch rumble effects without relying on external audio files.
  • Google Fonts: Uses Inter and JetBrains Mono for a modern, technical interface.
  • Material Symbols Outlined: Provides consistent icons throughout the application.

Development & Hosting

Tool

Purpose

Visual Studio Code

Development environment

Git & GitHub

Version control and source-code hosting

GitHub Pages

Browser-based application deployment

7. Creativity & Key Design Considerations

Custom Architect Mode for Educators & Engineers

Unlike fixed-scenario simulations, Custom Architect Mode provides extensive mission customization capabilities.

Users can:

  • Define custom mission budgets and scientific targets.
  • Adjust solar flux percentages to simulate different mission environments.
  • Edit the $M cost of existing spacecraft subsystems directly.
  • Create entirely new hardware components across all four assembly stages.
  • Dynamically integrate custom components into the 3D spacecraft model.

This transforms the application from a predefined game into a flexible mission-design environment suitable for experimentation, education, and engineering demonstrations.


Lightweight 4-Player Team Collaboration

The Team Sync system enables up to four players to collaborate using Base64-encoded configuration tokens.

Each participant can take responsibility for a different engineering discipline:

  1. Flight Director: Oversees mission objectives, launch readiness, and overall mission decisions.
  2. Payload Lead: Manages scientific instruments, payload mass, and data-generation requirements.
  3. Power Engineer: Handles electrical power generation, battery capacity, and thermal considerations.
  4. Communications Officer: Manages antennas, communication bands, and downlink bandwidth.

Each teammate operates from a separate console, contributing to the overall spacecraft configuration without requiring an external database or backend infrastructure.

projectDetails.name: THE SILENCE BENEATH: Exploring the Hidden Ocean of Enceladus
projectDetails.summary:
THE SILENCE BENEATH is an interactive 3D space exploration game that takes players on a scientific expedition to Enceladus, one of Saturn's most fascinating moons. Inspired by discoveries from NASA's Cassini mission, the project transforms real planetary science into an immersive spacecraft exploration experience.

Players explore Enceladus, investigate its mysterious south-polar water plumes, interact with scientific instruments, and examine evidence related to its hidden subsurface ocean. Through exploration and scientific analysis, the game introduces concepts such as organic compounds, molecular hydrogen, chemical energy sources, and planetary habitability.

The project aims to make complex scientific discoveries more accessible and engaging through interactive gameplay rather than traditional information-based presentations.

By combining 3D technology, space exploration, and scientific storytelling, THE SILENCE BENEATH encourages curiosity about ocean worlds and the search for environments beyond Earth that could potentially support life.

Importantly, the project explores habitability, not confirmed extraterrestrial life.
projectDetails.details:
THE SILENCE BENEATH: Exploring the Hidden Ocean of Enceladus is an interactive 3D space exploration game created by Team Smallville. Our idea is to take players on a virtual journey to Enceladus, one of Saturn's most interesting moons, and help them discover what makes it so special.

In our game, players can explore Enceladus, investigate its south-polar water plumes, and learn about the hidden ocean beneath its icy surface. As they explore, they get introduced to scientific concepts such as organic compounds, molecular hydrogen, chemical energy, and the possibility of habitable environments beyond Earth.

We wanted to make learning about space more interesting and enjoyable. Instead of just showing scientific facts through text or slides, we decided to turn them into an interactive experience where players can explore and learn at the same time.

Through this project, we hope to create curiosity about space science, especially about ocean worlds and the possibility of life beyond Earth. Enceladus has some interesting conditions that scientists study when exploring the possibility of habitability, although life has not been confirmed there.

We built the project using React, JavaScript, Three.js, Vite, HTML, and CSS. We used GitHub to manage our project files and Vercel to make the game available online.

What makes our project creative is the way we combine 3D exploration, gaming, and scientific learning. We wanted players to feel like they were exploring a mysterious moon rather than simply reading about it.

While developing the project, we focused on making it interesting, easy to use, educational, and scientifically meaningful. Our goal was to create an experience that makes people curious about what lies beneath the icy surface of Enceladus.

Mission Control: Mars Outpost is an interactive Mars colony survival simulation developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge.

Players take command of ARES-01, a fictional four-person research outpost at Jezero Crater, and must keep their crew alive for 30 Martian sols. They manage essential life-support resources, assign astronaut duties, maintain habitat systems, respond to unpredictable environmental emergencies, and complete scientific exploration objectives.

The simulation features dynamic weather, decision-based events, resource management, crew specializations, mission telemetry, and an AI-assisted mission advisor. Every decision affects the mission's survival and scientific progress.

Our goal is to make the engineering challenges of human exploration on Mars accessible and engaging through an interactive experience that encourages strategic thinking, resource management, and curiosity about planetary science.
projectDetails.details:
Overview

Mission Control: Mars Outpost is a browser-based interactive simulation designed to introduce users to the challenges of establishing and maintaining a human research outpost on Mars.

The player assumes the role of commander of ARES-01, a fictional four-person research mission located at Jezero Crater. The objective is to survive 30 Martian sols while maintaining essential life-support systems, protecting the crew, and completing scientific exploration objectives.

How It Works

The simulation revolves around interconnected resource-management and decision-making mechanics.

1. Life Support Management

Players manage six essential resources: energy, water, oxygen, food, radiation protection, and crew health. Habitat integrity and supporting subsystem conditions are tracked separately.

2. Crew Management

Four astronauts have different specializations, including mission command, medicine, engineering, and geology. Players assign activities to crew members, and their specializations influence mission outcomes.

3. Dynamic Environmental Events

The simulation features 13 events, including dust storms, solar particle events, oxygen leaks, equipment failures, and unexpected scientific discoveries. Players must evaluate available options and manage their consequences.

4. Scientific Exploration

Players collect geological samples and conduct scientific experiments. Completing research objectives contributes to the final mission evaluation.

5. Mission Intelligence

A mission advisor analyses the current simulation state and provides recommendations based on resource levels, crew health, environmental threats, and mission progress. A rule-based advisor works without requiring an external API.

6. Mission Telemetry

Interactive charts track resource trends and mission conditions, helping players understand how their decisions influence the outpost over time.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The project transforms abstract space-exploration challenges into an interactive learning experience. Instead of simply reading about the difficulties of living on Mars, users experience the trade-offs involved in maintaining life-support systems, managing limited resources, responding to emergencies, and prioritizing scientific objectives.

It encourages strategic thinking, problem-solving, resource allocation, and interest in planetary science and human space exploration.

Technology Used

  • React and TypeScript
  • Vite
  • Tailwind CSS
  • Framer Motion
  • Recharts
  • Lucide React
  • LocalStorage
  • Procedural Web Audio

The application uses a modular simulation engine with game logic separated from the user interface.

Creativity and Innovation

The project combines educational content with strategy-game mechanics. Environmental events, astronaut specializations, resource dependencies, and evolving mission conditions ensure that decisions have consequences.

The interface is designed as a futuristic mission-control system to make the player feel responsible for operating a Mars research outpost.

The simulation is intentionally simplified for educational gameplay and is not intended to represent a real engineering or life-support model.

Scientific Foundation

Environmental concepts and Martian facts are informed by publicly available NASA resources. The game references Martian weather, atmospheric conditions, temperature, radiation challenges, and communication delays.

ARES-01, its astronauts, and its mission scenarios are fictional.

projectDetails.name: Project SONIONS
projectDetails.summary:
Spacey — Space Biology Knowledge Engine

Summary

Spacey is a research prototype that helps students and researchers explore space biology literature through natural-language search and evidence-linked answers. We developed a web interface and API connecting publication discovery, semantic retrieval, and a graph of scientific claims. The ingestion pipeline uses NASA’s Space Biosciences publications page, enriches records through PubMed and Crossref, and stores publication excerpts and extracted claims for exploration.

Users can search topics such as microgravity and bone density, inspect supporting excerpts, ask questions, and explore opposing claim directions and relative research coverage. Local language models support embeddings, claim extraction, and citation-backed answer generation.

Spacey aims to make space biology research easier to navigate and compare. Its claim counts and coverage indicators are exploratory measures, rather than validated assessments of evidence quality or mission readiness.
projectDetails.details:
Spacey combines semantic search, evidence-linked Q&A, and graph exploration in a space biology research interface.

The ingestion service discovers publication links from NASA’s Space Biosciences publications page and retrieves available titles, abstracts, and metadata through PubMed and Crossref. Qdrant stores text embeddings for retrieval, while Neo4j connects publications, excerpts, and extracted claims. Ollama supplies local models for embeddings, claim extraction, and answer generation.

The interface uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, SWR, and Vega-Lite. The Python backend uses FastAPI, and Docker Compose coordinates the services.

The creative approach connects relevant excerpts with structured claim relationships, helping users investigate findings and opposing directions while retaining access to source material. Intended benefits include easier literature navigation and comparison; improvements in research speed or accuracy have not yet been measured.

The prototype requires further validation. Generated answers and claims need source review, consensus values are claim counts, coverage describes observed combinations, and mission cards remain examples.

projectDetails.name: EARTHSCOPE
projectDetails.summary:
EARTHSCOPE: Discover Changes. Connect the Signals. Understand Our Planet.

EARTHSCOPE is a free, open-source web app that turns NASA POWER monthly climate data into evidence-based environmental investigations. A user picks any location, chooses temperature, precipitation and relative humidity, and selects a period (2001 to the last full year). One click retrieves the data and tests for long-term trends with Mann-Kendall and Sen’s slope. It shows the rate of change and its significance, flags unusual months against each calendar month’s historical average, and scores how strong the evidence is.

Its distinctive features are the Environmental Fingerprint, which analyses the three indicators together to name change patterns such as warming with drying, and Similar Earth Regions Discovery, which finds distant places with matching trends. It also finds locations whose trends run in opposite directions. Findings are written in plain language from fixed templates, with no paid AI or APIs. The app labels data provenance and never claims causation.

It matters because raw climate data is hard for non-specialists to interpret. EARTHSCOPE shows what the data says, how strong the evidence is and where it is uncertain, and the whole analysis runs on Python, Streamlit and open data.
projectDetails.details:
EARTHSCOPE – Environmental Change Detection and Investigation Platform

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

EARTHSCOPE is a web app that investigates how the local environment at any place on Earth has changed. You pick a location, choose indicators (temperature, precipitation, relative humidity) and a period (2001 to the last full year). The app then runs a fixed pipeline: retrieve, clean, analyse, compare and explain.

  1. Retrieve. It pulls monthly NASA POWER data for the location. It never fills or interpolates missing values.
  2. Detect change. It tests each indicator for a trend using the Mann-Kendall test and measures the rate with Sen’s slope. It reports the rate per decade and the significance separately. It also runs seasonal trend tests as supporting evidence.
  3. Environmental Fingerprint. It looks at the indicators together. A fixed rule table (12 named patterns) turns the combination of trends into a pattern such as “warming–drying”. A correlation heat-map shows which indicators move together. It describes co-occurring trends and never claims one causes another.
  4. Compare regions. The Opposite Trend Finder lists places where the same indicator is significantly rising in one and falling in another. Similar Earth Regions Discovery ranks places by how similar their pattern of change is, using plain maths over a fixed pool of 30 locations.
  5. Anomalies and timeline. It flags unusual months against each calendar month’s own history, kept separate from trends.
  6. Evidence score and report. Each finding gets a transparent 0–100 evidence score with its three components shown. The findings are written in plain language from fixed templates, and the full report downloads as CSV.

2. What are the benefits?

  • Makes complex environmental data accessible through statistically sound, easy-to-understand findings instead of raw time series.
  • Ensures transparency by allowing users to trace results to NASA data, with the request URL, grid cell, units and data-quality information displayed.
  • Provides free access without requiring API keys, user accounts or paid services, and runs on standard laptops.

3. What is the intended impact?

EARTHSCOPE aims to make environmental investigation more accessible to students, educators, researchers and community groups by helping them explore NASA's open data and understand how environmental conditions change over time and differ across regions.

It helps users ask: "Is my region changing, how strongly do we know, and where else is changing in a similar way?"

The project also promotes responsible use of scientific data by clearly communicating limitations, such as the use of gridded model data rather than ground-based station records. It is intended to support environmental education and preliminary investigation, not replace scientific monitoring or official early-warning systems.

4. What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed as a software-only solution using the following technologies:

  • Programming Language: Python 3.13
    • Pandas and NumPy for data processing and numerical calculations.
    • SciPy for Sen's slope and correlation analysis.
    • PyMannKendall for statistical trend testing.
    • Plotly for interactive charts, graphs and maps.
    • Requests for NASA API communication.
  • Data Source: NASA POWER Monthly Point API for historical environmental data.
  • Testing: pytest (77 tests) and Streamlit AppTest.
  • Development Environment: Visual Studio Code (VS Code).
  • Additional Implementation: On-disk caching and retry/backoff mechanisms for efficient and responsible API usage.
  • Hardware: Standard laptops. No GPU, paid API or cloud service is required.

The application uses freely available tools and technologies, making it accessible without specialised hardware or paid services.

No specialised hardware or paid APIs are required for the current prototype.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

EARTHSCOPE focuses on environmental investigation rather than simply displaying environmental statistics. Its innovative approach combines multiple analytical capabilities into a single interactive platform.

  • Environmental Change Fingerprinting: Combines multiple environmental indicators into a single pattern, helping users understand how different environmental conditions change together.
  • Similar Earth Regions Discovery: Identifies locations with similar patterns of environmental change rather than simply comparing their climates. It standardises indicator trends so different measurement units can be compared.
  • Transparent Evidence Scoring: Assigns each finding an explainable evidence score based on three components, allowing users to understand the strength of the supporting evidence.
  • Explainable and Deterministic Analysis: Uses predefined statistical methods and rules rather than a black-box AI model, ensuring that findings are reproducible and understandable.
  • Integrated Environmental Investigation: Combines trend detection, anomaly identification, regional comparison and report generation into one platform.

These features make EARTHSCOPE more than a conventional environmental data visualisation tool. It transforms historical environmental data into structured, interpretable investigations.

6. What factors did the team consider?

During development, we considered the following factors:

  • Data Limitations: NASA POWER provides model-derived environmental data at approximately 0.5° × 0.625° grid resolution. Therefore, the data represents an area rather than an exact ground-level measurement at a location.
  • Statistical Reliability: Trends require at least 10 complete years of data. Years with missing months are excluded, and serial correlation is flagged. The application also communicates that no multiple-testing correction is applied and that the evidence score is not a probability.
  • Scientific Interpretability: Correlation does not imply causation. Environmental fingerprints and regional similarities are presented as descriptive patterns rather than causal relationships.
  • Development Constraints: The project was developed within a limited timeframe using free tools and technologies. Caching and request-pacing mechanisms were included to ensure responsible use of NASA's API.
  • Accessibility: The interface is designed for non-specialist users, with understandable visualisations and maps that use symbols alongside colours.

These considerations helped ensure that EARTHSCOPE remains accessible, transparent and responsible in presenting environmental findings.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: SPACEBOUND: Design It, Test It, Fly It
projectDetails.summary: We developed SPACEBOUND, a 3D mission design game that puts players inside a space station as its newest mission designer and shows them how real space missions are planned, built and flown, by allowing them them to experience it firsthand. It directly addresses the challenge by turning the real mission lifecycle into gameplay: across four missions of rising difficulty (a wildfire-monitoring satellite, a student CubeSat, a lunar ice-hunting orbiter and a sample grab from asteroid Bennu), the players write requirements, design their spacecraft and live with real tradeoffs where every kilogram, watt and dollar counts. Before launch, the station crew puts each design through ground testing that catches weak spots, and after the flight a verification report shows exactly which requirements passed or failed, and why. Built on NASA's OSIRIS-REx, LRO and LCROSS missions, with the Moon's south pole recreated from NASA's LOLA elevation data, SPACEBOUND lets players feel real engineering problems like limited power, minutes of radio contact, and an 18.5-minute signal delay that forces a spacecraft to land itself. In online crews, every player owns a role, just like a real mission team. Its importance is simple: mission design shouldn't be a closed room for engineers. SPACEBOUND gives students the chance to design a mission, watch it fail safely, and understand why.
projectDetails.details:
SPACEBOUND is a 3D mission design game built in Godot. The player joins a space station as its newest mission designer and takes four missions from an idea on paper to a real flight. Instead of only watching launches, players do the work behind them: setting requirements, making design trade-offs, getting the design tested, flying it and checking whether it met its goals.

How It Works:
The player explores a station with a Mission Design Bay, crew decks and specialists to talk to. Four missions unlock in order of difficulty: a training mission to fix a wildfire-monitoring satellite, a student CubeSat, a lunar orbiter hunting for ice at the Moon's south pole, and a sample grab from asteroid Bennu. Each mission follows the real mission lifecycle: requirements → design → ground testing → flight → verification. During design, every part costs mass, power or money. Before launch, the player walks the design to specialists who find weak spots, and can fix them or fly anyway. Each flight is a hands-on mini game: tracking a CubeSat from a ground station in Kochi, braking into lunar orbit, drilling for ice in a crater built from NASA LOLA elevation data, or touching Bennu without hitting a boulder. A report then shows which requirements passed or failed, and why. After all four missions, a Mission Review Board judges the player's portfolio.

Benefits:

  • Hands-on Learning: Students learn how missions are designed by doing it, not by reading about it.
  • Systems Thinking: Teaches requirements, trade-offs, margins and testing through play.
  • Safe Failure: Players can fail a mission and learn exactly why it failed.
  • Teamwork: In online crew mode, each player gets their own role, so no one sits idle.
  • Accessible: Free to play on an ordinary Windows laptop, with no engineering background needed.

Intended Impact:
SPACEBOUND aims to make mission design understandable for school and college students, who usually only see the launch and not the years of decisions behind it. It can be used in classrooms, science clubs and outreach events to spark interest in space engineering, especially among students who don't yet see themselves as engineers.

Development Tools and Technology Stack:

  • Game Engine: Godot 4.7 (GDScript)
  • Multiplayer: Node.js + WebSockets server hosted on Render
  • Data Processing: Python, used to turn NASA LOLA elevation data into game terrain and to prepare audio
  • 3D Assets: NASA 3D Resources (spacecraft), Creepy Cat Sci-Fi Starter Kit (free, station), Tripo Astronaut 2 by Jungle Jim (CC BY 4.0)
  • Animation: Mixamo
  • Font: Rajdhani (Google Fonts)

Creativity and Innovation:
The project turns each step of mission design into something you physically do: walking your design to the test team, aiming a ground station dish, watching a requirement turn green. The missions are built around real engineering problems, such as limited power, only minutes of radio contact per pass, and the 18.5-minute signal delay that forced OSIRIS-REx to land on its own. Online crews split the work so each player is responsible for one system, just like a real mission team.

Design Considerations:

  • Accuracy: Real mission values (from OSIRIS-REx, LRO, LCROSS and CubeSat 101) are kept separate from values simplified for gameplay.
  • Performance: A Safe Graphics mode and DirectX 12 support let it run on low-power and ARM (Snapdragon) laptops.
  • Fair Roles: Each player's role changes with the number of people in the crew.
  • Responsible Content: No NASA logos or branding, and every asset licence is credited.

Use of SI:
Claude (Anthropic) helped write most of the game's code and drafts of the dialogue, all reviewed and play-tested by our team. ChatGPT (OpenAI) and Gemini (Google) were used for brainstorming and feedback. Character voices were made with Chatterbox (from recordings of adult family members, with permission) and Kokoro, and each voice file is tagged as AI-generated in its metadata. No AI image generators were used for artwork. The only exception is the astronaut model's textures, which were edited with AI help. All SI use is also listed in the game's credits.

In essence, SPACEBOUND is more than a game about space. It is a way for any student to design a mission, watch it succeed or fail, and understand why.

projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Space Time Capsule

Space Time Capsule is a web-based platform designed to help users preserve meaningful memories, personal thoughts, and messages for the future. It provides an interactive website where users can explore the concept of creating digital time capsules and preserving special moments. The platform aims to make memory preservation simple, engaging, and accessible.

projectDetails.name: Project SPACENCODE
projectDetails.summary:
We developed SpaceExploit, an interactive real-time astronaut bio-telemetry and mission hazard monitoring dashboard built with Python, Streamlit, and Plotly. Designed to address the challenge of autonomous crew health monitoring during deep-space missions, the software continuously tracks critical physiological vitals—including heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), and core body temperature—alongside ambient suit radiation levels.

Using automated threshold-based anomaly detection, the system immediately flags physiological overheating, cardiovascular strain, and Solar Particle Events (SPE), providing actionable shelter or EVA-pause protocols without waiting for delayed Earth-to-space communications. Additionally, the platform integrates SHA-256 cryptographic hashing to verify telemetry payload integrity between suit sensors and habitat consoles. By combining predictive health alerts, intuitive telemetry visualization, and secure data verification, SpaceExploit helps protect astronaut safety and mission continuity in high-risk extraterrestrial environments.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works:

SpaceExploit is an autonomous astronaut bio-telemetry and mission hazard support dashboard built to monitor crew health and suit microclimate safety in real time. Using a dynamic physiological telemetry engine, the platform continuously tracks four critical parameters across multiple crew members: Heart Rate (60–120 bpm), Blood Oxygen Saturation (SpO2: 94%–100%), Core Body Temperature (36.2°C–38.5°C), and Ambient Radiation Exposure (0.10–0.75 mSv/h). An automated rule-based anomaly engine evaluates every sensor reading against safety thresholds, instantly classifying mission status into Nominal, Warning (physiological overheating and cardiovascular strain when Heart Rate > 105 bpm and Core Temperature > 37.8°C), or Critical (Solar Particle Event alert when radiation exceeds 0.50 mSv/h).

Benefits & Intended Impact:

During deep-space, lunar, or Martian Extravehicular Activities (EVAs), communication latency between spacecraft and Earth mission control can delay emergency medical guidance by several minutes. SpaceExploit enables immediate, onboard decision-making by delivering clear, actionable safety protocols—such as pausing an EVA or seeking radiation shelter—directly to crew consoles without relying on ground-station round trips.

Tools, Languages & Software Used:

- Programming Language: Python 3.10+

- Web Framework & UI: Streamlit

- Data Visualization & Processing: Plotly, Pandas, NumPy

- Security & Data Integrity: Python hashlib (SHA-256 cryptographic payload hashing)

- Version Control & Hosting: GitHub

Creativity & Design Considerations:

Rather than displaying raw numerical tables that cause cognitive overload during high-stress mission phases, SpaceExploit combines color-coded visual telemetry trends with instant triage banners. A key engineering factor we considered was telemetry integrity: every simulated sensor packet generates a real-time SHA-256 cryptographic hash to demonstrate tamper-proof verification between suit sensors and habitat consoles. Super Intelligence (SI) tools were utilized to assist with initial Python code scaffolding, documentation drafting, and slide deck visual generation, with all threshold logic and system architecture reviewed and integrated by the team.

projectDetails.name: MARS: OUTPOST SURVIVAL
projectDetails.summary: MARS: OUTPOST SURVIVAL is a browser-based 2D educational strategy game designed for children aged 7–12. Stepping into the role of Mars Outpost Commander, players lead a crew of four astronauts through a 10-day mission on the Red Planet. Built with plain HTML, CSS, and modular JavaScript requiring no installs, frameworks, or backend servers, the game challenges young learners to balance five core resources—Oxygen, Energy, Food, Water, and Shielding—alongside Crew Health and Research progress.   The project addresses the challenge by transforming real mission planning into interactive daily decisions where every choice carries a visible cost and benefit. Gameplay scenarios are grounded in authoritative NASA sources, including the DONKI space-weather database for solar flare alerts, the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) for space-biology plant research, NASA Mars exploration facts, and Earth–Mars signal travel time calculations. To succeed, players must keep their crew safe through Day 10 and complete at least two of three mission goals: conducting research, growing food in the greenhouse, and sending a report to Earth.   This project is important because it makes space systems engineering accessible to young students, teaching resource interdependence, critical thinking, and scientific honesty through hands-on play.
projectDetails.details:
MARS: OUTPOST SURVIVAL is an interactive, browser-based 2D simulation that places children aged 7–12 in the role of a Mars Outpost Commander. Over a simulated 10-day mission, players must keep a crew of four astronauts alive by managing five interdependent resources: Oxygen, Energy, Food, Water, and Radiation Shielding.

The core gameplay loop centers on daily engineering trade-offs. Each day introduces a scenario grounded in real Mars operational hazards—such as a Coronal Mass Ejection, clogged oxygen scrubbers, or deep-space communication delays. Players are presented with multiple solutions, but every choice has a cost. Boosting life support or repairing a water recycler might consume the electrical energy needed to conduct scientific research or harvest greenhouse crops. To win, players cannot simply hoard one resource; they must survive all 10 days while completing at least two of three mission objectives (Science, Food, and Earth Telemetry).

Benefits & Intended Impact

The primary benefit of the project is translating highly complex aerospace systems engineering into an accessible, low-stakes learning environment. It teaches young students that in space exploration, there are rarely perfect answers—only calculated trade-offs.

Our intended impact is to inspire the Artemis Generation to pursue STEM careers by fostering critical thinking and resource management skills. Furthermore, the game reframes failure: if a player runs out of critical life support, the crew safely evacuates to orbit, and the player is presented with a debriefing screen explaining the science of what went wrong. This encourages iterative learning rather than frustration. Because the application requires zero installations and works completely offline, its impact can reach global classrooms regardless of internet bandwidth.

Tools, Languages & Technologies Used

We engineered the application using a "zero-dependency" philosophy to ensure maximum accessibility and performance.

  • Frontend Languages: Semantic HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla ES6 JavaScript (Modules). We avoided heavy frameworks (like React or Unity) to keep the file size minimal and ensure 100% offline playability.
  • Architecture: A custom-built pure-function rootReducer and a publish/subscribe (pub/sub) state store. This decouples the game math from the DOM rendering, making the resource calculations bug-free and predictable.
  • Development Tools: Visual Studio Code (with the Live Server extension) for rapid local testing and development.
  • Deployment & Hosting: Git and GitHub Pages for seamless, free public hosting and continuous deployment.
  • NASA Data Integrations: NASA's Open APIs (Specifically the DONKI Solar Flare FLR endpoint) accessed via standard JavaScript fetch() promises, supplemented by published research from the Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) and Mars Exploration Program telemetry.

Creativity & Innovation

Instead of relying on heavy text or confusing spreadsheets to teach resource balancing, we designed a highly visual "Ghost Bar" UI system. When a player hovers over a decision, GPU-accelerated ghost bars render directly over their outpost meters, showing exactly how much of a resource will be gained or lost before they commit to the action. This creatively turns complex subtraction and addition into intuitive visual spatial reasoning for young minds.

Additionally, we utilized a Reactive Living SVG Scene. Instead of static images, the 2D Mars outpost dynamically changes based on the game's mathematical state. If a dust storm rolls in, the sky turns a hazy orange; if energy levels drop below critical, the habitat windows dim; and if the greenhouse objective is met, the hydroponic crops visibly glow.

Factors Our Team Considered

  • Scientific Honesty & Transparency: We wanted to ensure kids knew the difference between real science and a game mechanic. We built a dedicated "Science & Data" screen that explicitly separates Real NASA Data, Derived Orbital Math, Fictional Story Events, and Game Assumptions.
  • Accessibility (a11y): We ensured the game could be played by everyone. Every color-coded status (like green for OK or red for Empty) is paired with a distinct emoji icon and text label for colorblind users. The entire UI supports keyboard-only navigation with visible focus rings, and ARIA live regions announce critical alerts to screen readers.
  • Network Resilience: Hackathons and classrooms often suffer from spotty Wi-Fi. We designed the live NASA DONKI space-weather API fetch with a graceful fallback. If the network drops or the API rate-limits, the game instantly switches to a curated NASA archive record, guaranteeing the presentation and gameplay never break.

projectDetails.name: COSMOLLOKUP
projectDetails.summary:
COSMOLOOKUP is an astronaut health monitoring and decision-support platform designed to help monitor physiological changes and identify potential health risks during space missions. It combines astronaut health indicators, historical trends, personalized exercise guidance, alerts, and an interactive 3D anatomical model to make complex health information easier to understand.

AI-assisted development tools were used for software architecture, coding, debugging, and integration. The platform incorporates NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) as a scientific research source, using publicly available spaceflight research datasets and metadata to inform health-risk analysis and provide scientific context. These research findings complement simulated astronaut monitoring data; they are not presented as live astronaut telemetry.

By bringing health indicators, research evidence, and explainable assessments together, COSMOLOOKUP aims to support timely, informed health-monitoring decisions and contribute to safer, longer-duration human space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
COSMOLOOKUP is an AI-assisted astronaut health monitoring and decision-support platform designed to address the challenges of maintaining astronaut health during long-duration space missions. It brings physiological monitoring, historical health trends, scientific research evidence, and interactive anatomical visualization into a unified mission-control interface.

The platform organizes astronaut health information into an interactive dashboard featuring a rotatable 3D human anatomical model. Users can explore different body systems, inspect relevant health indicators, identify potential concerns, view alerts, and access personalized exercise guidance. Its assessment system uses historical baselines, trend analysis, data freshness, and contextual health indicators to support explainable decision-making rather than autonomous diagnosis.

NASA's Open Science Data Repository (OSDR) is integrated as a source of publicly available spaceflight biological research datasets and metadata. These resources provide scientific context for understanding physiological changes associated with spaceflight. They complement clearly identified simulated astronaut monitoring data rather than being misrepresented as live telemetry.

AI tools assisted our development process through architecture exploration, code generation, debugging, testing, and integration. The technology stack includes React, TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Python, FastAPI, SQLAlchemy, SQLite, and NASA's research APIs. We also use Git and GitHub for version control and collaborative development.

The project's creativity lies in combining interactive 3D anatomy with explainable health assessments and research-backed context, making complex physiological information more accessible. Our team considered scientific accuracy, data reliability, usability, privacy, performance, and the limitations of spaceflight monitoring systems throughout development.

Our intended impact is to support better-informed health-monitoring decisions, encourage early attention to potential health risks, and contribute to safer and more sustainable human exploration beyond Earth.

projectDetails.name: A.I.M.S. – Astronaut Integrity & Mission Support: A Wearable Health Monitoring and Continuous Data Logging Platform for Space Missions
projectDetails.summary:
A.I.M.S. (Astronaut Integrity & Mission Support) is an ESP32-based wearable health-monitoring and mission-support platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026.

Combining physiological and motion sensors with an onboard REST API and a browser-based mission dashboard, A.I.M.S. collects, processes, visualizes and locally logs astronaut health indicators.

Its primary objective is continuous health-data harvesting and longitudinal monitoring to support research into the physiological effects of long-duration spaceflight. The platform currently supports heart-rate and SpO2 monitoring, motion and acceleration tracking, health alerts, routine checkups, mood logging and persistent data storage.

Designed with extensibility in mind, A.I.M.S. provides a foundation for future integration of immune biomarkers, additional cardiovascular measurements and radiation-monitoring instruments, including MOSFET dosimetry and CANS-related data.

The project aims to transform individual health readings into a persistent, structured record that can help astronauts and researchers understand physiological changes throughout a mission.
projectDetails.details:
A.I.M.S. – Astronaut Integrity & Mission Support

The Problem

Long-duration space missions expose astronauts to multiple physiological challenges, including cardiovascular changes, immune-system alterations, muscle and bone loss, sensorimotor disturbances, radiation exposure and behavioural health challenges.

These conditions can develop progressively. Individual readings or occasional health checkups may not provide enough information to understand how an astronaut's physiological condition changes throughout a mission.

A continuous, accessible and persistent health-data collection system can help address this gap.

Our Solution

A.I.M.S. is a wearable astronaut health-monitoring and mission-support platform developed using an ESP32 microcontroller and a standalone web dashboard.

The system is built around one primary objective: continuous health-data harvesting, structured logging and longitudinal monitoring.

The wearable collects physiological and motion-related information, processes measurements locally and makes the telemetry available through an API hosted directly on the ESP32.

A browser-based dashboard connects to this API and presents the collected information through health indicators, crew visualizations, event logs and mission-support interfaces.

Hardware Architecture

The current prototype consists of:

  • ESP32 DevKit – Main microcontroller, onboard processing, Wi-Fi communication and REST API hosting.
  • MPU6050 Accelerometer – Motion, acceleration and activity-related measurements.
  • MAX30102 IR Sensor – Optical heart-rate and SpO2 monitoring through photoplethysmography.
  • 0.96-inch I2C OLED Display – On-device health information and interactive checkups.

Implemented Features

Physiological Monitoring

  • Heart-rate monitoring.
  • SpO2 monitoring.
  • PPG sensor support.
  • Motion and activity tracking.
  • Acceleration and experimental force estimation.
  • Configurable abnormal-vital alerts.

Crew Health Support

  • Guided health checkups.
  • Mood check-ins.
  • Hydration reminders.
  • Exercise reminders.
  • Routine health reminders.
  • Health-event detection and logging.

Persistent Data Collection

The ESP32 uses LittleFS flash storage to maintain CSV records of:

  • Vital-sign measurements.
  • System and health events.
  • Mood assessments.
  • Reminder completion.
  • Health checkup results.

This provides a persistent history that can be used to compare measurements over time.

Mission Dashboard

The standalone HTML dashboard connects directly to the ESP32 through its native REST API.

It provides:

  • Live telemetry visualization.
  • Crew health status.
  • Astronaut injury-region visualization.
  • Mission event logs.
  • EVA safety simulation.
  • Communication-status visualization.
  • Emergency scenario demonstrations.

The dashboard also supports USB serial communication.

Research Alignment

A.I.M.S. is designed to complement research interests associated with NASA's ARCHeR program and the broader Spaceflight Standard Measures framework.

Its physiological monitoring and activity-recording architecture can support future research into:

  1. Immune-system changes through regular health assessments and future biomarker integration.
  2. Cardiovascular changes through heart-rate, PPG and oxygen-saturation records.
  3. Sensorimotor adaptation through motion and acceleration history.
  4. Gastrointestinal health through future nutrition and symptom-record integration.
  5. Musculoskeletal deconditioning through activity and exercise records.
  6. Radiation exposure through proposed integration of MOSFET dosimetry and CANS-related measurements.

These represent a combination of implemented capabilities and proposed research extensions. The prototype does not currently measure all six physiological areas directly.

Data Architecture

A key design decision is that the ESP32 hosts its own REST API.

The browser dashboard communicates directly with the wearable over Wi-Fi, avoiding the need for a separate backend server in the standard setup.

The architecture is:

Wearable Sensors → ESP32 Processing → Local Data Storage → Native REST API → Web Dashboard → Historical Health Visualization.

This approach is intended to support modular sensor integration and reduce dependence on external connectivity for local data retention.

NASA Data and Research Context

The team researched NASA astronaut-health research resources, including ARCHeR-related activity and well-being research, Spaceflight Standard Measures and relevant space-biology datasets.

These resources informed the project's research direction and the selection of health indicators and potential future integrations.

The current hardware demonstration is based on sensor telemetry and locally generated records; it does not claim to directly ingest NASA research datasets.

Future Development

Potential future extensions include:

  • Immune biomarker integration.
  • Sleep and circadian monitoring.
  • Expanded cardiovascular measurements.
  • Dedicated balance assessments.
  • Nutrition and gastrointestinal symptom tracking.
  • Muscle-strength and bone-density data integration.
  • MOSFET radiation dosimetry.
  • CANS-compatible neutron radiation records.
  • Multi-crew monitoring.
  • Advanced longitudinal analysis and predictive health models.

Impact

A.I.M.S. demonstrates a practical approach to integrating wearable hardware, embedded data processing, persistent storage and mission-oriented visualization.

By prioritizing continuous data acquisition over isolated readings, it aims to establish a foundation for better understanding astronaut health changes throughout long-duration space missions.

A.I.M.S. – Monitor continuously. Record intelligently. Understand astronaut health over time.

projectDetails.name: MARSCOPE: Explainable AI-Powered Mars Terrain Intelligence and Route Planning
projectDetails.summary:
MARSCOPE is an interactive Mars exploration and decision-support platform designed to help future human explorers evaluate terrain and plan safer surface traversals. Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, it combines interactive 2D mapping, 3D terrain visualization, terrain analysis, and intelligent route optimization in a unified interface.

Using the A* pathfinding algorithm, MARSCOPE generates and compares two route alternatives: a risk-aware route that considers terrain-related risks and a distance-focused route that prioritizes shorter traversal. Explainable route metrics, including distance and average terrain roughness, help users understand the trade-offs between safety and efficiency.

The platform aims to make complex planetary terrain information easier to interpret and turn it into actionable exploration insights. Its modular architecture also provides a foundation for future predictive hazard intelligence as suitable validated datasets become available.
projectDetails.details:
MARSCOPE: Project Details

1. Overview

MARSCOPE is an interactive planetary exploration and mission-planning platform designed to support future human exploration of Mars. It provides an integrated environment where users can visualize Martian terrain, examine surface characteristics, and compare potential traversal routes.

The initial focus is Jezero Crater, a scientifically important region explored by NASA's Perseverance rover.

2. Interactive 2D and 3D Terrain Visualization

MARSCOPE combines an interactive 2D Mars map with a 3D terrain visualization environment. Users can explore the selected region, understand elevation variations, and observe the relationship between terrain features and potential traversal paths.

The 3D environment is built using Three.js and React Three Fiber, while the 2D mapping interface uses React Leaflet.

3. Intelligent Route Planning Using A*

The platform implements the A* pathfinding algorithm to identify alternative routes between a selected starting point and destination.

Two route alternatives are generated:

  • Risk-aware route: incorporates terrain-related risk factors into route evaluation to prioritize comparatively safer traversal.
  • Distance-focused route: prioritizes a shorter traversal path.

This comparison helps users understand that the shortest route is not necessarily the most suitable route for exploration.

4. Explainable Route Intelligence

MARSCOPE provides a route comparison interface that presents useful metrics, including:

  • Total route distance
  • Average terrain roughness
  • Comparative route characteristics

These metrics make the route-planning process more interpretable and help users evaluate the trade-offs between traversal efficiency and terrain-related risk.

5. Terrain and Hazard Intelligence

Terrain analysis contributes to the assessment of surface conditions and route suitability. The platform also includes environmental and hazard information panels.

Future development will expand this component into predictive hazard intelligence using validated historical and spatial datasets. Potential extensions include identifying hazardous terrain conditions and estimating changing environmental risks. These predictive capabilities are a planned extension rather than a fully validated forecasting system in the current prototype.

6. Technology and Architecture

Frontend

  • React
  • TypeScript
  • Vite

3D Visualization

  • Three.js
  • React Three Fiber
  • Drei

2D Mapping

  • React Leaflet
  • Leaflet

Backend

  • Python
  • FastAPI
  • NumPy
  • Rasterio
  • SciPy

Algorithms and Analysis

  • A* pathfinding
  • Terrain analysis
  • Risk-based route evaluation
  • Route comparison metrics

Development Tools

  • Visual Studio Code
  • Git and GitHub
  • npm
  • Python

7. Creativity and Innovation

The main innovation of MARSCOPE is the integration of interactive planetary visualization, terrain-aware pathfinding, and explainable route comparison in a single exploration platform.

Rather than presenting only a map or a shortest-path result, MARSCOPE allows users to compare alternative traversal strategies and understand the factors influencing route selection.

Its modular architecture is designed to support future integration of additional planetary datasets and predictive intelligence.

8. Intended Impact

MARSCOPE aims to make planetary terrain information more accessible and useful for exploration planning. It provides a prototype foundation for evaluating surface conditions, comparing traversal alternatives, and supporting more informed decisions during future human Mars missions.

The system is a research and planning prototype, not a certified operational navigation or astronaut safety system.

projectDetails.summary: Stellarchive: Far Away from Home is an illustrated storytelling project about the machines that remain on the Moon and Mars after their missions. Through first-person narratives, it brings the journeys of NASA’s Opportunity rover and the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicles to life. The project makes space history and planetary science easier to understand, encourages interest in exploration and engineering, and shows how past missions guide future discovery. STELLARIX – MarsPath

MarsPath is an interactive Mars exploration and route-planning platform developed by Team STELLARIX. It brings multiple exploration tools together in one accessible workspace, helping users understand the Martian environment and explore mission-planning concepts.

The platform features an interactive Mars Explorer with selected Martian locations, a prototype A* route planner, Mars discoveries, a simulated rover telemetry dashboard, a Mars sol time estimator, a controlled Mars cultivation research concept called MarsGrow, and Mission Memory for recording exploration notes.

MarsPath aims to make planetary exploration more understandable and engaging by connecting terrain exploration, route planning, rover simulations, and research in a single platform. It provides an educational environment for exploring the challenges of operating on Mars and encourages interest in planetary science, space technology, and future exploration missions.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – STELLARIX: MarsPath

MarsPath is an interactive Martian exploration and mission-planning platform designed to bring multiple exploration tools into one unified workspace.

The platform includes:

  1. Mars Explorer: An interactive map featuring selected Martian locations and terrain imagery.
  2. Route Planner: A prototype A* pathfinding system that demonstrates route planning across a sample terrain grid.
  3. Mars Discoveries: An exploration section presenting discovery-related information.
  4. Rover Simulator: A simulated rover telemetry dashboard displaying rover parameters.
  5. MarsTime: An estimator based on the duration of a Martian sol.
  6. MarsGrow: A controlled cultivation concept exploring the challenges of growing plants in Martian conditions.
  7. Mission Memory: A feature for recording and managing exploration notes.

Technology Stack: React.js, Vite, Leaflet, Python, FastAPI, and REST APIs. The frontend is deployed using Vercel, and the backend is hosted on Render.

MarsPath aims to make Mars exploration concepts more accessible and interactive. It combines geographical exploration, prototype route planning, rover simulation, and research concepts to help users understand the challenges of future Martian missions.

The current platform is an educational prototype. Its route planner uses a sample terrain grid, rover telemetry is simulated, and its cultivation content is illustrative rather than experimentally validated.

projectDetails.name: Strangelets
projectDetails.summary:
We developed an interactive, story-driven web experience that chronicles the history of NASA’s discarded hardware on the Moon and Mars. Designed for school-age space enthusiasts, our project transforms dense historical data into engaging, character-driven narratives. Instead of dry fact lists, users explore a cinematic timeline featuring interactive 3D models, scroll-triggered animations, and immersive storytelling about missions.

This directly addresses the challenge by making the "graveyard" of space hardware emotionally resonant and accessible. It is important because it reframes abandoned equipment not as forgotten trash, but as silent monuments to human curiosity. By highlighting how these robotic pioneers proved the Moon was safe and discovered hidden water ice, we inspire the next generation to see that every piece of hardware left in the lunar dust paved the way for humanity's return.
projectDetails.details:
Overview

Strangelets is an interactive, 3D-based space exploration platform designed to showcase the history and stories of NASA's abandoned, retired, and non-operational space equipment on the Moon and Mars. Over the decades, numerous space missions have left behind scientific instruments, landers, rovers, and other equipment on these celestial bodies. Although these machines are no longer actively functioning, they played an important role in advancing our understanding of space.

The project transforms this often-overlooked part of space exploration into an interactive digital museum. Users can explore the Moon and Mars through immersive 3D environments, discover different pieces of abandoned equipment, and learn about their missions, purposes, and scientific contributions. The platform presents the information through visual storytelling, allowing users to understand the journey and significance of these machines rather than simply reading historical facts.

Benefits of the Project

The project provides an engaging and educational way to learn about the history of space exploration. It brings attention to space equipment that is often forgotten after its mission ends, highlighting the important scientific contributions made by these machines. Through interactive 3D visualizations, users can develop a better understanding of the Moon and Mars missions and the technologies used in them.

It also makes space-related information more accessible to students, educators, astronomy enthusiasts, and the general public. Instead of relying entirely on lengthy articles or traditional presentations, users can explore a visually engaging environment at their own pace. This approach improves curiosity, encourages independent learning, and makes scientific information easier to understand and remember.

Intended Impact of the Project

The primary objective of this project is to change the way people perceive abandoned space equipment. These machines are not merely discarded objects; they represent years of research, engineering, innovation, and human curiosity. Every rover, lander, and scientific instrument has a story behind it and contributed something valuable to space exploration.

The project aims to preserve these stories digitally and create awareness about the historical and scientific importance of NASA's missions. It also encourages people to appreciate the efforts of scientists and engineers who made these missions possible. Ultimately, the project seeks to connect technology, science, history, and storytelling through an interactive educational experience.

Tools, Programming Languages, and Technologies Used

The project was developed as a web-based application using modern frontend technologies and 3D visualization libraries. The major technologies used include:

  • React 19: Used to build the interactive user interface and manage the different pages and components.
  • JavaScript: Used to implement the application logic and interactive functionalities.
  • Three.js: Used for rendering and displaying 3D environments and space-related objects.
  • React Three Fiber: Used to integrate Three.js with React and create interactive 3D scenes.
  • React Three Drei: Used to simplify 3D development through reusable components and utilities.
  • Tailwind CSS 4: Used for styling and creating a responsive, modern interface.
  • Framer Motion and Anime.js: Used to create animations and smooth visual transitions.
  • Vite 8: Used as the development server and build tool.
  • React Router DOM: Used for navigation between different sections of the application.
  • Lucide React: Used for interface icons.

Additionally, GLB-based 3D models are used to represent celestial bodies and space equipment, including the Moon, Mars, rovers, and landers. GitHub is used for source-code management and project collaboration.

The project is entirely software-based and does not require any dedicated physical hardware or external devices. It can be accessed through a web browser.

Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of this project lies in presenting an unusual perspective on space exploration. Most space-related platforms focus on successful missions, active rovers, upcoming launches, and major scientific discoveries. However, this project focuses on the equipment left behind after missions and gives importance to the stories that are often overlooked.

The idea of transforming this information into an interactive 3D space museum makes the project different from conventional educational websites. Instead of presenting the Moon and Mars as static images, it allows users to explore visually represented environments and discover the equipment associated with different missions.

Combining 3D visualization, animations, historical information, and storytelling creates an experience that connects technical achievements with human curiosity. The project demonstrates how modern web technologies can be used creatively to preserve scientific history and make learning more immersive.

Factors Considered During Development

During the development of the project, several factors were considered to ensure that the platform provides an effective and engaging experience. Historical and scientific relevance was an important consideration, as the information presented needed to reflect the actual missions and equipment associated with NASA's Moon and Mars exploration programs.

User experience and accessibility were also considered while designing the interface. The navigation was structured to make exploration simple, while visual elements and animations were incorporated to maintain user engagement. The 3D models and environments were selected to make the experience more realistic and informative.

Performance and responsiveness were additional considerations because rendering 3D environments can require significant browser resources. The application was developed using reusable React components and modern frontend tools to maintain a structured codebase and support efficient development. The overall design was intended to balance visual creativity, educational value, usability, and technical performance.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

Earth Trend Detective is a beginner-friendly, no-code project that helps users explore how precipitation changes over time in two contrasting Indian regions: Kerala and Rajasthan. It turns satellite-derived Earth science data into an accessible trend-exploration experience. Users select a region, view a time series, compare annual precipitation, inspect a fitted trend and read an explanation of statistical significance.

The scientific foundation is NASA precipitation data. The team verifies the exact product, version, temporal resolution, units, date coverage and spatial selection before analysis. Monthly data is quality-checked and converted to annual summaries only when the variable is a monthly accumulation. The working tool is built in Google Sheets, so a team with no programming background can create a functional prototype.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Aria Earth Sonification
projectDetails.summary:
ARIA — Earth Sonification System is an interactive web-based platform that transforms environmental and climate data into visual and audio experiences. It features an interactive 3D Earth, allowing users to explore environmental indicators, geographical regions and changes over time. Through sonification, scientific measurements are mapped to sound properties such as pitch, tempo and stereo position, helping users experience patterns beyond traditional charts and graphs.

ARIA addresses the challenge of making complex Earth data easier to understand and more accessible by combining visualization with sound. It aims to provide an additional way for people, including users with visual impairments, to explore environmental changes. Open scientific data and technologies from NASA, along with relevant NOAA datasets, can support the platform with information about temperature, atmosphere, oceans and other Earth systems.

ARIA is important because understanding our planet's changing environment should be engaging, inclusive and accessible. It turns scientific information into an experience people can both see and hear.
projectDetails.details:
ARIA — Earth Sonification System

ARIA is an interactive web-based Earth observatory that transforms scientific environmental and climate data into visual and audio experiences. It allows users to explore different regions of Earth, select environmental data channels, navigate historical timelines from 1980 to 2025, and listen to changes through real-time browser-based sound synthesis.

The platform uses open scientific data from NASA, NOAA and other research organizations. Its data sources include NASA GISTEMP for global temperature anomalies, NASA POWER for regional meteorological information, NASA GIBS for satellite imagery, NOAA measurements for atmospheric CO₂ and methane, and satellite-altimetry data for sea-level changes. The website also identifies forest and cryosphere indicators as empirical benchmarks rather than direct live data feeds.

ARIA's main benefit is making complex scientific information more engaging and accessible. Through sonification, measurements are mapped to sound properties such as pitch, tempo, resonance and stereo positioning. This provides another way to recognize environmental patterns, including for people who may have difficulty interpreting visual charts.

We developed ARIA using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js, Python and FastAPI, along with Web Audio API technology for sound generation. The project combines interactive mapping, scientific data processing and creative audio design in one platform.

Its creativity lies in turning environmental measurements into an experience that users can both see and hear. During development, we considered scientific accuracy, data transparency, accessibility, usability, performance and the distinction between real scientific observations and empirical or simulated information.

Our intended impact is to make understanding Earth's changing environment more interactive, inclusive and engaging, encouraging greater awareness of climate change and the importance of protecting our planet.

projectDetails.name: Astronaut Health Assessment Tool
projectDetails.summary:
AstroHealth OS is an autonomous deep-space health assessment and clinical decision support system built for Artemis lunar and Mars transit missions.

What we developed: An interactive aerospace medical suite featuring a holographic bio-digital twin, an autonomous clinical triage engine, a simulated ultrasound/retinal imaging lab with digital calipers, a psychomotor vigilance cognitive test (PVT-B), and gamified daily health tracking.

How it addresses the challenge: With 10-to-44-minute Earth communication delays making live flight surgeon support impossible in emergencies, AstroHealth OS acts as an onboard "virtual flight surgeon." It maps crew vitals to NASA’s five spaceflight hazards (R.I.D.G.E.) and recommends immediate hardware and medical countermeasures (like Chibis LBNP for fluid shifts and ARED resistive workouts for bone loss).

Why it is important: It enables medical self-sufficiency, prevents irreversible spaceflight conditions like permanent vision loss (SANS) and kidney stones, and protects crew survival far beyond Earth's orbit.
projectDetails.details:
AstroHealth OS is an autonomous deep-space medical suite and clinical decision support system built with TypeScript, React, SVG, HTML5 Canvas, and Web Audio API for Artemis lunar and Mars transit missions.

  • What it does: Acts as an onboard "virtual flight surgeon" featuring a holographic bio-digital twin, an autonomous triage engine, a simulated ultrasound/retinal imaging lab with digital calipers, a cognitive vigilance test (PVT-B), and gamified daily health quests ("AstroFit").
  • Benefits & Impact: Overcomes 10-to-44-minute Earth communication delays by enabling immediate, autonomous medical care. It catches critical spaceflight conditions early—such as vision-threatening fluid shifts (SANS), bone loss, and kidney stones—and pairs them with real flight countermeasures (like Chibis LBNP suits and ARED workouts) to keep crews safe and mission-ready.
  • Key Design Factors: Combines intuitive spatial visuals, synthesized audio alerts, and single-click workflows to reduce crew cognitive load during high-stress emergencies while strictly respecting spacecraft medical kit limits.
