projectDetails.name: Project Abandoned But Not Forgotten
projectDetails.summary: **Abandoned but Not Forgotten** is a 10-scene illustrated comic that makes robotic space exploration engaging and accessible through emotional storytelling. Following a young space enthusiast named Alex and his fictional exploration robot, B.O.B., the story pairs original artwork with authentic NASA imagery and verified data to spotlight real missions—including Apollo’s ALSEP, the Mars rovers Sojourner and Opportunity, and Voyager 1 and 2. By framing these spacecraft as silent pioneers rather than mere technical hardware, the project addresses the challenge of communicating complex space science to general audiences. This matters because robotic explorers often go unrecognized compared to human spaceflight; honoring their lasting scientific legacy reminds readers that even when these machines never return home, their discoveries permanently expand humanity’s understanding of the universe.
projectDetails.details:
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is a 10-scene illustrated comic designed to make robotic space exploration accessible, engaging, and emotionally resonant for general audiences. Through the conversations between a curious young space enthusiast named Alex and his fictional exploration robot, B.O.B., the story introduces readers to real NASA missions—including the Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP), the Mars rovers Sojourner and Opportunity, and the Voyager 1 and 2 spacecraft.

By pairing original illustrations with authentic archival NASA imagery and verified mission data, the comic addresses the challenge of communicating complex scientific achievements through human-centered storytelling. Rather than presenting technical specifications in isolation, it frames these spacecraft as silent pioneers that ventured into the unknown and continued gathering vital data long after their missions ended or human crews departed.

This project matters because public interest in space often focuses on human spaceflight, overlooking the robotic explorers that paved the way. By honoring the enduring scientific legacy of machines left behind on the Moon, Mars, and in interstellar space, Abandoned but Not Forgotten inspires curiosity and reminds audiences that while these explorers never return home, their discoveries permanently expand humanity’s understanding of the universe.

projectDetails.name: Beyond the Stars
projectDetails.summary:
VOYAGER – BEYOND THE STARS
“The journey never ends.”
Voyager – Beyond the Stars is an interactive digital space museum that brings NASA's historic Voyager 1 mission to life through visual storytelling, interactive timelines, animations and authentic NASA photographs. Visitors explore Voyager 1's journey from its 1977 launch to its encounters with Jupiter and Saturn, the iconic Pale Blue Dot photograph and its entry into interstellar space. Guided by Cosmo, our astronaut cat, they discover its scientific instruments, Golden Record and continuing mission. Developed using React, JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3 and Vite, with the assistance of SI, Claude and Visual Studio Code, the project aims to preserve Voyager's scientific legacy, inspire curiosity about space and encourage STEM learning among younger generations.
projectDetails.details:
VOYAGER – BEYOND THE STARS


1. Purpose and Overview:
Voyager – Beyond the Stars is an interactive digital space museum that brings NASA's Voyager 1's mission to life through cinematic storytelling, animated space environments and educational exploration. Visitors can follow Voyager 1's journey from its 1977 launch through its encounters with Jupiter and Saturn, its famous Pale Blue Dot photograph and its entry into interstellar space.
Key Features:

  • Cinematic space introduction.
  • Interactive historical timeline.
  • Planetary journey visualization.
  • Scientific instrument explorer.
  • NASA images and facts.
  • Cosmo, the astronaut cat guide.
  • Golden Record exploration.
  • One-light-day milestone finale.

2. How it works
The website follows Voyager 1's mission chronologically, from launch to interstellar space.

Visitors explore planetary encounters, historical events, NASA photographs and scientific instruments through interactive timelines and animations.

Cosmo, the astronaut cat, guides visitors through key discoveries, including the Pale Blue Dot, interstellar entry and the projected one-light-day milestone.

The journey concludes with the Golden Record and its timeless message. Voyager 2 appears as supporting historical information, while Voyager 1 remains the focus.

 3. The Perks

  • Makes space science accessible and engaging.
  • Inspires interest in astronomy and STEM.
  • Simplifies science through interactive learning.
  • Preserves Voyager's scientific legacy.
  • Promotes NASA's educational resources.
  • Creates an immersive learning experience.

4. Our Vision

Our aim is to preserve Voyager's legacy, inspire future explorers and make its historic mission accessible through interactive storytelling.

We highlight how decades-old spacecraft continue to advance science and inspire future exploration.

 5. Tools Used

Development platform and tools:

·        SI (Superintelligence) – Assisted in the development and creation of the project.

·        Claude – Assisted with development, code generation and refinement.

·        Visual Studio Code – Code editing and project management.

·        Node.js and npm – Development environment and dependency management.

·        Vite – Development server and build tool.

Programming languages and technologies:

·        HTML5 – Website structure.

·        CSS3 – Styling, animations and responsive layouts.

·        JavaScript – Interactive functionality and animations.

·        React – Component-based development was used in the project.

Resources:

·        Official NASA/JPL photographs and mission information.

·        Animated spacecraft and planetary visualizations.

·        Original Cosmo character and storytelling content.

Hardware: Developed and tested using an ordinary laptop and modern web browser, without requiring specialized hardware.

 6. Key Impact

Voyager transformed our understanding of the outer planets and interstellar space, but its scientific achievements risk becoming unfamiliar to younger generations.

Our project preserves this legacy through interactive learning, highlighting how Voyager's discoveries continue to inspire future exploration.

7. Our Approach to the Challenge

The project brings NASA's historic space hardware into focus, introducing younger generations to Voyager 1's engineering and scientific achievements.

Through interactive timelines, instrument panels, NASA photographs and Cosmo's narration, we explore its technology, discoveries and planetary encounters.

The experience highlights the Voyagers' entry into interstellar space, building towards Voyager 1's projected one-light-day milestone.

By combining science, technology and storytelling, we make this historic mission engaging and accessible to a new generation.

VOYAGER – BEYOND THE STARS

‘The journey never ends.’

projectDetails.name: Abandoned But Not Forgotten: Interactive Bilingual Space Storybook & Educator Kit
projectDetails.summary: Abandoned But Not Forgotten is an interactive, bilingual (English & Malayalam) digital children's storybook and educator kit created for school-age space enthusiasts (ages 7–11). Across the Moon, Mars, asteroids, and deep space, dozens of NASA landers, rovers, helicopters, and telescopes rest silently after completing groundbreaking missions. While young learners often hear only about active launches, our storybook brings 13 real off-world explorers to life—connecting their engineering designs directly to the scientific discoveries they made possible. Built from 10 official NASA Science and NSSDCA datasets, every chapter pairs whimsical storytelling with verified mission facts, clickable links to real NASA Martian wind audio, 360° panoramas, and 3D spacecraft models. To maximize hands-on learning and classroom accessibility, the book also includes a printable cut-and-fold MarCO CubeSat model, coloring and word-search puzzles, a Junior Space Explorer certificate, and a two-page Parent & Educator Guide.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works:

"Abandoned But Not Forgotten" translates dense planetary archive records into an engaging, story-driven educational package for ages 7–11. Guided by a curious young stargazer named Mia, readers journey through four cosmic chapters covering 13 real NASA spacecraft:

1. The Moon: Surveyor 3 (1967 soil trench tests), Apollo 11 Eagle & Laser Ranging Retroreflector (still measuring the Moon's 3.8 cm/year drift), Apollo 12 Intrepid & ALSEP, and Apollo 15 Falcon & the first Lunar Roving Vehicle (27.9 km drive).

2. Early Mars Pioneers: Viking 1 (1976 first successful Mars landing) and Mars Pathfinder & Sojourner (1997 15-bounce airbag landing and first Mars rover in Ares Vallis).

3. Modern Mars Explorers: Twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity (proving ancient liquid water on Mars across 7.7 km and 45.16 km), InSight & MarCO CubeSats (recording 1,300+ marsquakes and Martian wind), and Ingenuity Mars Helicopter (completing 72 powered flights).

4. Asteroids & Deep Space: NEAR Shoemaker (first asteroid orbit and landing on 433 Eros), Dawn (orbiting Vesta and Ceres), Kepler/K2 (discovering 2,600+ exoplanets), and Pioneer 10 (carrying Earth's plaque toward interstellar space).

Educational Impact & Accessibility:

- Bilingual Storytelling (English & Malayalam): Makes NASA planetary science accessible to both English-speaking readers and Malayalam-speaking communities in Kerala, India, and worldwide.

- Interactive NASA Media Integration: Embeds clickable links to real NASA Martian wind audio (InSight), 360° landing-site panoramas (Pathfinder), and interactive 3D spacecraft models (Ingenuity).

- Hands-On STEM Activities: Includes a printable cut-and-fold MarCO CubeSat paper model, a Mars coloring page and 10-mission word search, a bilingual Junior Space Explorer Certificate, and a 2-page Parent & Educator Guide with NGSS-aligned discussion prompts and an exoplanet transit flashlight experiment.

Tools & Workflow:

We synthesized mission timelines, instrument specs, and scientific highlights from 10 official NASA Science and NSSDCA mission records, drafted and translated the bilingual narrative, and designed both the 13-page storybook package and 7-slide demo presentation using Canva.

projectDetails.name: FireSync: Global Harmonization of MODIS & VIIRS Hotspots
projectDetails.summary: Developed by Team ASTROLYTICS, FireSync is an intelligent wildfire analytics platform designed to solve the critical cross-sensor discrepancy between NASA’s MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m) active fire datasets. When raw detections from both satellite constellations are combined without calibration, emergency responders face duplicate fire alerts, inflated hotspot counts, and blurred boundaries. FireSync applies spatio-temporal clustering and resolution prioritization to eliminate redundant detections by ~36%, consolidating raw multi-satellite telemetry into a single, accurate Unified Burning Activity Calendar for global disaster management and forest monitoring teams.
projectDetails.details:
1. Project Overview & Problem Statement

Developed by Team ASTROLYTICS, FireSync is a wildfire intelligence platform designed to solve the cross-sensor discrepancy between NASA’s MODIS (1 km resolution) and VIIRS (375 m resolution) active fire datasets. When raw detections from both satellite constellations are combined without calibration, emergency responders face duplicate fire alerts, inflated hotspot counts, and blurred perimeter boundaries. FireSync applies spatio-temporal clustering and resolution prioritization to eliminate redundant detections by ~36%, consolidating raw multi-satellite telemetry into a single, accurate Unified Burning Activity Calendar for global disaster management and forest monitoring teams.

2. Solution Details (How It Works)

FireSync processes raw thermal anomaly detections through a three-stage harmonization pipeline:

- Spatial Grid Alignment: Maps coarse 1 km MODIS pixels against finer 375 m VIIRS sub-pixels using a standardized geographic bounding grid.

- Spatio-Temporal Deduplication: Identifies overlapping detections occurring within a 1 km spatial radius and a 60-minute satellite overpass window. When both sensors detect the same thermal event, FireSync merges the records and prioritizes the higher-precision 375 m VIIRS coordinates and Fire Radiative Power (FRP) metrics.

- Unified Burning Activity Calendar: Outputs clean, deduplicated daily fire logs filtered by global regions (including the Western Ghats, Amazon Basin, California, New South Wales, and Wayanad Forest Belt) so local authorities can track true wildfire progression without sensor noise.

3. Impact & Global Scalability

By eliminating ~36% of duplicate sensor noise from raw multi-satellite feeds, FireSync prevents false alarm fatigue and enables forest departments, environmental researchers, and emergency response units to allocate firefighting resources accurately across both local ecosystems and global wildfire hotspots.

4. Technology Stack Used

- Frontend & Interactive Web Dashboard: HTML5, Tailwind CSS, JavaScript (hosted live via CodePen Projects)

- Data Processing & Prototyping: Python, Pandas, Gradio, Google Colab

- Presentation & Documentation: Digital Slide Deck & Technical Architecture Diagrams

5. NASA & Partner Open Data Sources

- NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System): Near Real-Time (NRT) active fire and thermal anomaly data feeds.

- MODIS (Moderate Resolution Imaging Spectroradiometer): Terra & Aqua Active Fire Products (MOD14 / MYD14, 1 km spatial resolution).

- VIIRS (Visible Infrared Imaging Radiometer Suite): Suomi NPP & NOAA-20 Active Fire Products (VNP14IMGTDL_NRT, 375 m spatial resolution).

- NASA Worldview & EOSDIS: Global satellite imagery and geospatial visualization reference layers.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

ArtemisQuest: Beyond Earth – Lunar & Martian Survival Simulator

ArtemisQuest: Beyond Earth is an interactive Lunar and Martian outpost survival simulator that places players in the role of mission commander. Players choose a Shackleton Rim lunar expedition or a Martian surface mission, explore the outpost, operate specialized facilities and complete engineering mini-games. They balance resources including power, oxygen, water and food, while monitoring crew health and responding to equipment failures and emergency events. Solar arrays, water recovery, oxygen production, carbon-dioxide processing, research and habitat systems introduce mission decisions. By combining exploration, resource strategy and consequence-based gameplay, ArtemisQuest makes the challenges of sustaining human life beyond Earth engaging and accessible.
projectDetails.details:
ArtemisQuest is an interactive space-outpost survival simulator that explores the challenges of sustaining human life on the Moon and Mars.

Players take on the role of an astronaut mission commander, managing a five-Sol survival mission. They explore planetary outposts, operate specialized facilities, complete engineering mini-games and manage essential resources, including oxygen, water, electricity and food.

The Lunar and Martian environments feature unique challenges such as water and oxygen production, power management, radiation protection, dust storms and equipment failures. Players must maintain life-support systems, monitor crew health and respond to emergencies.

Developed using JavaScript, HTML5, CSS3 and Vite, ArtemisQuest combines interactive gameplay with space science concepts.

The project aims to promote STEM education, critical thinking and problem-solving by allowing students to experience the engineering and survival challenges of human exploration beyond Earth.

projectDetails.name: Echoes in the Dust
projectDetails.summary:
Echoes in the Dust – The Last Transmission of Opportunity

This project focuses on NASA's Mars Exploration Rover Opportunity, also known as MER-B, which explored the surface of Mars from January 25, 2004, to June 10, 2018. The project presents the journey, scientific objectives, achievements, and final days of the Opportunity rover through an informative and visually engaging presentation.

Opportunity was one of NASA's two twin Mars exploration rovers, with Spirit being the other. Its main objectives were to search for evidence of water, study Martian rocks and soil, and survive and operate in the challenging Martian environment.

The project highlights Opportunity's exploration of Perseverance Valley in Endeavour Crater and explains how a massive global dust storm blocked sunlight from reaching its solar panels, eventually ending the mission.

The central theme of the project is the remarkable journey of a robotic explorer that helped scientists understand Mars and provided valuable information about the possibility of water on the planet.
projectDetails.details:
Echoes in the Dust – The Last Transmission of Opportunity

1. Introduction

Mars is one of the most fascinating planets in our solar system and has been a major subject of scientific exploration. NASA launched robotic missions to study its surface, atmosphere, geological structure, and the possibility of past water.

One of these important missions was the Mars Exploration Rover Opportunity, also known as MER-B. The project, titled "Echoes in the Dust – The Last Transmission of Opportunity," describes the journey and achievements of this rover, which explored Mars for more than 14 years.

The project presents the mission through an interactive and visually appealing format, helping viewers understand the history, objectives, challenges, and conclusion of Opportunity's exploration.

2. Project Overview

The project is based on the NASA Mars Exploration Rover Opportunity mission.

Mission Details:

  • Mission Name: Mars Exploration Rover B (Opportunity)
  • Agency: NASA
  • Rover Name: Opportunity
  • Mission Period: January 25, 2004 – June 10, 2018
  • Resting Place: Perseverance Valley, Endeavour Crater
  • Coordinates: 2.33° S, 354.4° E
  • Mission Status: Ended in 2018

Opportunity was the second of NASA's two twin rovers. It landed on Mars approximately three weeks after its twin rover, Spirit.

3. Objectives of the Mission

The Opportunity mission had three primary objectives:

3.1 Find Water

One of the main objectives was to search for evidence of water on Mars. The rover investigated Martian rocks and soil to understand whether water had existed on the planet in the past.

3.2 Grind Rocks

Opportunity was equipped with scientific instruments that allowed it to examine and study rocks. By examining the internal structure and composition of rocks, scientists could understand the geological history of Mars.

3.3 Survive

The rover was designed to operate in the harsh Martian environment. Its mission involved surviving extreme temperatures, dust, and other environmental challenges while continuing its scientific exploration.

4. History of Opportunity

Opportunity was one of two twin rovers sent by NASA to explore Mars. Its twin, Spirit, arrived on Mars approximately three weeks earlier.

Both rovers were designed to investigate the Martian surface and search for geological evidence of water.

Opportunity began its mission on January 25, 2004. Although it was initially designed for a much shorter mission, it continued operating and exploring Mars for more than 14 years.

During this period, it travelled across the Martian surface, studied rocks, collected scientific information, and sent valuable data back to Earth.

Its final resting place was Perseverance Valley in Endeavour Crater.

5. Scientific Exploration

Opportunity played an important role in understanding the geological history of Mars.

Its scientific investigations focused on:

  • Studying the composition of Martian rocks.
  • Examining the Martian soil and surface.
  • Searching for geological evidence of ancient water.
  • Collecting images and scientific information about the Martian environment.
  • Helping scientists understand the planet's past conditions.

The rover's findings contributed significantly to scientific knowledge about Mars and its history.

6. Challenges Faced by Opportunity

Exploring Mars was not an easy task. Opportunity faced several environmental and technical challenges during its long mission.

One of the major challenges was Martian dust.

Mars experiences large dust storms that can cover the planet and reduce the amount of sunlight reaching its surface.

Since Opportunity depended on solar panels for electrical power, the dust storm created a serious problem.

7. The End of the Mission

In 2018, a massive global dust storm spread across Mars. The thick dust in the atmosphere blocked sunlight from reaching Opportunity's solar panels.

As a result, the rover could not generate enough electrical power to continue its operations.

NASA made repeated attempts to establish communication with Opportunity. However, the rover did not respond.

The mission officially ended on June 10, 2018, marking the conclusion of an extraordinary exploration journey.

The title "Echoes in the Dust" represents the rover's final communication and the end of its journey across the Martian surface.

8. Importance of the Mission

The Opportunity mission was an important achievement in space exploration.

Its contributions include:

  • Improving scientific understanding of Mars.
  • Providing evidence about the presence of water in the planet's past.
  • Studying Martian rocks and geological formations.
  • Demonstrating the ability of robotic rovers to operate for extended periods on another planet.
  • Providing valuable images and scientific data for future Mars missions.

9. Project Design and Presentation

The project presents the Opportunity mission using a visually engaging layout.

The presentation includes:

  • A title section introducing the mission.
  • A mission overview containing important dates, coordinates, and location details.
  • A historical section explaining the relationship between Opportunity and its twin rover, Spirit.
  • A section describing the three primary mission objectives: Find Water, Grind Rocks, and Survive.
  • Illustrations of the rover and the Martian landscape.

The use of dark backgrounds, orange headings, blue highlights, and space-themed illustrations creates a visual connection with the Martian environment.

The presentation is designed to communicate scientific information in a simple and understandable manner.

10. Conclusion

The Opportunity mission represents one of the remarkable achievements of robotic space exploration. What began as a mission to explore Mars and study its geological history became an extraordinary journey lasting more than 14 years.

Opportunity helped scientists investigate the possibility of ancient water on Mars, study its rocks and soil, and understand the planet's environmental history.

Although a global dust storm eventually ended its mission, the information collected by the rover continues to contribute to our understanding of Mars.

"Echoes in the Dust – The Last Transmission of Opportunity" celebrates the achievements, challenges, and scientific contributions of a rover that explored Mars far beyond its original mission expectations.

Opportunity's mission ended, but its discoveries continue to inspire future space exploration.

projectDetails.name: ASTROVITAL: An Integrative Astronaut Health Intelligence & Wellness System
projectDetails.summary:
ASTROVITAL is an offline-capable astronaut health and wellbeing dashboard prototype for long-duration space missions. It combines two complementary layers: AstroVitals, for crew-entered physiological observations and mission-day records, and AyurSpace, an optional
Ayurveda-inspired, non-clinical wellness reflection layer.

The integrated prototype brings together manually entered heart rate, oxygen saturation (SpO₂), sleep and fatigue observations; daily water and food intake; work, exercise, sleep and rest routines; mission environment and exposure records (space station, spacecraft transit, spacewalk/EVA and planetary-surface activity); and mood, stress and energy check-ins approximately every 12 hours. A mission overview displays recent entries and transparent, illustrative review prompts.

AyurSpace adds optional reflections inspired by Dinacharya (daily activities), Ahara and Agni (food and digestive comfort), Nidra (sleep and recovery), and Manas (mood and perceived stress). Tridosha concepts are presented only as traditional cultural lenses. They are not
biomarkers, diagnoses or validated spaceflight measurements. 

All sample values are synthetic and all new records are manually entered and stored locally in the browser. The prototype does not connect to NASA telemetry, sensors or astronaut medical records. It is intended to explore structured self-observation and communication—not to diagnose, prescribe or make mission decisions.
projectDetails.details:
The problem

Long-duration space missions create a complex environment in which physiological observations, sleep-wake patterns, nutrition, hydration, workload, physical activity, mission exposure and psychological wellbeing may all matter. A crew-friendly way to record these domains together may help astronauts review their own patterns and communicate observations to authorised support teams.

What the integrated ASTROVITAL prototype does

  1. AstroVitals - physiological observations: manual entries for heart rate, SpO₂, sleep duration, fatigue rating and activity context. Recent observations appear in the overview.
  2. Ilustrative trend and review prompts: displays recent manually entered readings and simple, transparent demonstration prompts based on broad example rules. These are not clinical thresholds, diagnoses, risk predictions or autonomous alerts. No prompt establishes fitness for duty or replaces mission procedures.
  3. Daily intake log: records water volume, number of food/meal entries, optional food summary and self-reported appetite/ digestive comfort. It does not prescribe a hydration target or diet.
  4. Work, activity and rest log: Records mission duty hours, exercise/activity and sleep/rest hours.
  5. Mission environment and exposure log: records context such as space station/orbital habitat, spacecraft transit, planetary surface, lunar surface or Mars surface; activity types include routine habitat operations, spacewalk/EVA, planetary surface EVA and recovery; duration is recorded where relevant.
  6. 12-hour mood check-in: supports start- and end-of-wakingperiod (AM/PM) self-reports of mood, perceived stress and energy/alertness, with an optional note. These are subjective selfreports, not psychological assessments.
  7. AyurSpace: a separate optional reflection layer using Dinacharya, Ahara, Agni, Nidra and Manas. Vata/Pitta/Kapha are described only as traditional lenses for reflection—not medical categories, biomarkers or validated space-health indicators.
  8. Crew log and export: records are stored in the current browser using localStorage and can be exported as CSV.

How it works

The prototype is a single-page HTML5, CSS3 and vanilla JavaScript application. Users manually enter observations through forms. The dashboard updates and stores records in browser local Storage. It works locally without an account, server or network connection. It has no live sensors, no live telemetry, no NASA API connection, no multi-user account system and no clinical decision model.

Benefits and hoped-for outcomes

ASTROVITAL explores whether combining physiological observations with daily routine, intake, mission exposure and periodic mood check-ins can make self-observation more structured and support communication. AyurSpace tests whether an optional culturally informed reflection layer can complement—but remain clearly separate from—space-medicine monitoring. These potential benefits require usability research and evaluation with astronauts, clinicians, behavioural-health specialists and human-factors experts.

Tools and technologies

HTML5, CSS3, vanilla JavaScript, browser localStorage and browsergenerated CSV export. No external code library, live NASA API or external data service is used in the current prototype.

Current limitations

All preloaded values are synthetic. Physiological entries are manual demonstration values, not sensor measurements. Review prompts use illustrative rules and are not medically validated. Water, food, work and rest entries are descriptive records, not recommended targets. Mood and fatigue ratings are subjective self-reports. Local browser storage is not an approved secure system for real astronaut health information. The application has not been validated for operational or clinical use.

projectDetails.name: MARSCOPE
projectDetails.summary:
Martian Map - Interplanetary Survival Guide

Martian Map is an interactive exploration and traverse-planning platform designed to support safer and more informed exploration of Mars. It allows users to explore notable Martian regions, inspect NASA imagery, retrieve elevation and slope information from the Mars MGS MOLA 463m Digital Elevation Model, and compare environmental conditions across candidate locations.

The platform incorporates a terrain-aware route planner using the A* least-cost pathfinding algorithm. It analyses elevation and terrain slope to generate potential traverses, avoid excessively steep terrain, and compare optimized routes with direct paths. Users can also explore illustrative slope, rock and thermal overlays, examine estimated terrain-risk scores, and export mission plans for further analysis.

By bringing planetary datasets, terrain analysis and interactive route planning together, Martian Map makes complex Martian surface information easier to understand and use. It aims to support preliminary exploration planning, helping researchers and future mission planners identify promising regions and evaluate potential terrain challenges before detailed mission assessment.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details - Martian Map: Interplanetary Survival Guide

1. Project Overview

Martian Map is an interactive Mars exploration and terrain-aware traverse-planning platform developed to make planetary surface exploration more informed and accessible. It combines NASA planetary datasets, interactive mapping, terrain analysis, and pathfinding algorithms to help users explore Martian regions and identify potential routes between locations.

2. How Does It Work?

The application provides an interactive map of Mars featuring notable locations such as Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris, and Arcadia Planitia. Users can explore different map layers, inspect locations, and retrieve elevation and slope information.

A key feature is its terrain-aware route planner, which uses the A* (A-star) least-cost pathfinding algorithm. Instead of simply calculating the shortest geographical distance, the system analyses terrain elevation and slope to identify potential traverses while avoiding excessively steep areas. It also compares the generated route with a direct path, helping users understand how terrain influences route selection.

The platform additionally includes illustrative slope, rock, and thermal overlays, estimated terrain-risk scores, and an option to export mission plans in JSON format.

3. Data Sources and Technologies

The project uses NASA's Mars Global Surveyor (MGS) Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) 463-metre Digital Elevation Model (DEM) for elevation and terrain analysis.

The technologies used include:

  • Frontend: HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the interactive user interface and map functionality.
  • Backend: Python and Flask for server-side processing and API endpoints.
  • Terrain Processing: Rasterio and NumPy for reading and processing elevation data.
  • Pathfinding: A* least-cost search algorithm for terrain-aware route planning.
  • Deployment: Gunicorn for serving the Flask application.
  • Planetary Data and Imagery: NASA MOLA elevation data and Mars imagery, including Mars Trek visual resources.

4. Benefits and Intended Impact

Martian Map brings planetary terrain information and route-planning capabilities together in a single interactive platform. It helps users understand how elevation and slope can influence surface traversal, explore scientifically interesting Martian regions, and compare potential routes.

Its intended impact is to support preliminary mission exploration and educational understanding of Mars, making complex planetary datasets easier to interpret for students, researchers, and future mission planners.

5. Creativity and Innovation

The project's key innovation is its integration of planetary elevation data with terrain-aware pathfinding. Rather than treating Mars as a flat map, it considers terrain characteristics when generating potential routes. The combination of interactive map layers, location exploration, route comparison, estimated risk indicators, and mission-plan export creates an accessible exploration experience.

6. Factors Considered During Development

The team considered the importance of terrain elevation, slope, geographical distance, map usability, and accessibility of planetary datasets. The application was designed to provide an understandable interface while incorporating actual NASA elevation data into its route-planning process.

The platform is a preliminary planning prototype. Its estimated risk scores and illustrative hazard overlays are not validated NASA hazard measurements, and its routes should not be interpreted as operationally certified navigation guidance.

projectDetails.name: Space Explorer - Forgotten Missions
projectDetails.summary:
Space Explorer – Forgotten Missions is an interactive web-based educational platform developed to highlight the abandoned equipment, historical missions, and forgotten stories of human exploration on the Moon and Mars.

Our project addresses the NASA Space Apps Challenge theme, "Abandoned but Not Forgotten," by bringing attention to the spacecraft, rovers, landing hardware, and scientific equipment left behind during space missions. Using an interactive mission explorer, visitors can explore the Moon and Mars, discover equipment stories, learn about mission histories, view historical images, and explore landing locations with coordinates and links to official NASA resources.

The project is important because space exploration is not only about successful landings and discoveries but also about the objects and scientific history left behind. By presenting this information in an engaging and accessible way, Space Explorer encourages curiosity, scientific awareness, and appreciation for humanity's achievements in space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Space Explorer – Forgotten Missions is an interactive, web-based educational platform created to bring attention to abandoned space equipment and the forgotten stories of human exploration on the Moon and Mars.

The project allows users to explore historic space missions through an interactive interface. Users can switch between the Moon and Mars, discover important mission locations, view their coordinates, and access location links. Each mission provides information about its history, landing site, and equipment left behind. The platform also includes mission timelines, image galleries, detailed story panels, historical information, and mission statistics to make space exploration easier and more engaging to understand.

Our project addresses the NASA Space Apps Challenge theme, "Abandoned but Not Forgotten," by highlighting the spacecraft, lunar rovers, landing hardware, and other equipment that remain on celestial bodies after missions. It helps users understand that even when a mission ends, the objects and scientific contributions left behind continue to have historical and scientific value.

The project was developed using React, TypeScript, Vite, HTML, and CSS. Visual assets and mission information were referenced from NASA and NASA/JPL-Caltech resources. The website was deployed using Vercel to make it publicly accessible.

The creative aspect of our project is its combination of space exploration, interactive mission discovery, historical storytelling, and educational content in one platform. Instead of simply presenting mission facts, it encourages users to explore the forgotten objects and understand the stories behind them.

The intended impact is to increase public awareness of space exploration history, inspire students and space enthusiasts, and preserve interest in the scientific and historical importance of equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars.

ChatGPT was used as an AI assistance tool during project development for brainstorming, coding guidance, debugging support, and preparation of descriptive content. The team reviewed, tested, and adapted the suggestions while developing the final project.

projectDetails.name: SPHEREx SkyTime: An Interactive Explorer for Spectral and Temporal Analysis of the Universe
projectDetails.summary:
SPHEREx SkyTime is a web-based astronomical data exploration platform designed to make NASA's SPHEREx observations easier to access, visualize, and understand.

The platform connects to the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) to retrieve real SPHEREx Data Release 1 (DR1) observation metadata and astronomical image files. It processes FITS-format scientific data into browser-viewable images and provides an interactive interface for exploring observations using sky coordinates and spectral information.

The project aims to simplify access to infrared astronomical observations, support comparative exploration of the universe, and make scientific space data more accessible to students, researchers, and astronomy enthusiasts.
projectDetails.details:
SPHEREx SkyTime – Exploring a Changing Universe

SPHEREx SkyTime is a web-based astronomy exploration platform designed to help users explore infrared observations collected by NASA's SPHEREx mission. It retrieves astronomical observation records from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive using user-entered sky coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination). The platform displays real SPHEREx image data and allows users to view and compare different image products from the same observed region.

The project aims to make astronomical data easier to access and understand. Instead of requiring users to manually search through complex scientific archives and FITS files, SPHEREx SkyTime provides a simple interface where users can enter sky coordinates, retrieve available observations, and view processed astronomical images. This can support students, astronomy enthusiasts, and researchers in exploring infrared sky data.

The intended impact is to improve public access to space-science data, encourage interest in astronomy, and provide a foundation for studying how astronomical objects and regions change over time. In future development, the platform aims to support observations from different dates, image blinking, image-difference analysis, and the identification of possible moving-object candidates. These advanced analysis features are planned and are not yet fully implemented.

The project was developed using React.js and JavaScript for the frontend, HTML and CSS for the user interface, and Python with FastAPI for the backend. Python libraries including Astropy, NumPy, and Pillow are used to read and process FITS astronomical image data and convert it into viewable images. The project retrieves SPHEREx data through the NASA/IPAC archive services. Vite is used as the frontend development tool, and Visual Studio Code is used for development.

The creative aspect of SPHEREx SkyTime is its focus on exploring the sky through time rather than simply displaying static astronomical images. It combines real mission data, coordinate-based archive searching, image processing, and an accessible web interface in one platform. The project was designed with usability, scientific data accessibility, accurate presentation of real observations, and future expansion in mind.

During development, important factors included the availability and format of NASA SPHEREx data, valid astronomical coordinates, FITS image processing, communication between the frontend and backend, loading performance, and the need to distinguish currently implemented features from planned capabilities. The overall goal is to turn complex space-mission data into an accessible and engaging experience for everyone.

projectDetails.name: Life On Mars
projectDetails.summary:
The project is an interactive, space-themed educational game designed to introduce children aged 7–12 to the challenges of establishing and maintaining a human presence on Mars.
The game features four mini-games that simulate key aspects of Martian exploration: maintaining outpost systems, protecting the base from radiation hazards and incoming asteroids, collecting valuable resources such as lithium, gold and water ice, and navigating a rover through challenging terrain during a dust storm.
The project transforms complex space-science concepts into engaging, interactive missions that encourage problem-solving, decision-making and scientific awareness, while helping young learners understand the challenges of future human exploration of Mars.
projectDetails.details:
Our project is an interactive educational game designed to introduce children aged 7–12 to the challenges of living and working on Mars.

The game has four mini-games, each focusing on a different challenge that astronauts might face during space exploration:

  1. Systems check: Players have to monitor the martian outpost's systems and keep them working without allowing any system to fail.
  2. Martian Defence: Players must destroy incoming asteroids carrying radiation to protect the Martian Base and the astronauts.
  3. Resource Collection: Players explore Mars and collect lithium, gold and water ice, learning how these resources could be useful for future missions.
  4. Rover Rescue: Players control a Mars rover and avoid boulders while navigating through difficult terrain during a dust storm.

We wanted to make learning about space more interesting by turning scientific concepts into games rather than simply presenting facts. Through these mini-games, players get to understand some of the difficulties of maintaining a human settlement on Mars, such as radiation exposure, managing resources, maintaining equipment and dealing with extreme weather conditions.

We developed the game using Scratch, a block-based coding platform, and designed our presentation using Canva. The game includes interactive controls, timed challenges and different objectives to keep players engaged.

What makes our project creative is that we combined four different mini-games into one larger space mission. Each game gives the player a new responsibility and introduces a different aspect of space exploration.

While developing the game, we considered our target audience, which is kids aged 7–12. We wanted the controls to be simple, the instructions easy to understand and the challenges interesting without being too difficult. Most importantly, we wanted to maintain a balance between making the game fun and ensuring that players actually learn something about space exploration.

But there's more than meets the eye: hidden clues are scattered throughout the mini-games, waiting to be discovered, challenging players to unravel the mystery behind the missions. Try to find the clues, Astronaut.

PROJECT ARTEMIS GENESIS: A Guide for Future Generations
Team: THE ARTEMIS AVIONICS
High-Level Project Summary:
Project Artemis Genesis is an interactive space-awareness game developed by THE ARTEMIS AVIONICS, a team of three enthusiastic Grade 8 students (Adina Somie Thomas, Adiya Grace Thomas, and Theertha Girish), for the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge. It introduces young learners to space exploration through an engaging, educational gaming experience. Players guide Zora, a young astronaut, on a lunar mission featuring three progressive levels simulating real astronaut hazards:

Level 1 – Life Support Emergency
Zora faces a critical life-support emergency as oxygen levels drop dangerously low. Players must help her overcome the shortage to survive, highlighting oxygen supply and resource management.

Level 2 – Solar Radiation
Zora encounters intense solar radiation on the lunar surface. Players must deploy a protective shield against harmful rays to avoid losing life points, emphasizing astronaut safety.

Level 3 – Meteor Threat
Zora must dodge incoming meteors to survive a dangerous attack. This level introduces space debris hazards while building alertness and quick decision-making.

Featuring an optional trivia quiz at the end, Project Artemis Genesis makes space science accessible and inspires scientific curiosity. Join Zora and discover the wonders of space!
projectDetails.details:
THE ARTEMIS AVIONICS - Detailed Description

 

Project Name: PROJECT ARTEMIS GENESIS - A Guide for Future Generations

Developers: THE ARTEMIS AVIONICS (Adina Somie Thomas, Adiya Grace Thomas and Theertha Girish

Challenge: Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
Project Platform: PictoBlox

 

Project Artemis Genesis is an interactive educational game designed to introduce young learners to the exciting challenges of space exploration and survival of astronauts in space conditions. Developed by THE ARTEMIS AVIONICS, a team of three Grade 8 students from Mar Thoma Residential School, Tiruvalla. This project combines science, technology, creativity, and gaming to create an engaging learning experience. The game is designed as a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer, in which players take on the role of Zora, a young girl astronaut on an adventurous mission to explore the Moon. Although lunar exploration offers exciting opportunities for scientific discovery, surviving on the Moon's harsh environment requires careful planning, scientific knowledge, quick thinking, and effective decision-making. During her mission, Zora encounters three major survival challenges involving oxygen shortage, harmful solar radiation, and incoming meteors. Players must help her overcome these dangerous situations by choosing appropriate actions and responding to unexpected emergencies.

The story begins with Zora embarking on an exciting lunar exploration mission. Her objective is to explore the Moon while overcoming various environmental challenges that threaten her safety. Unlike Earth, the Moon has no breathable atmosphere, exposes astronauts to harmful radiation, and experiences frequent impacts from space debris and meteors. Therefore, astronauts require specialized equipment, protective systems, and carefully designed survival strategies. As Zora explores the lunar surface, she encounters a series of emergencies. Each emergency represents a real scientific challenge associated with human space exploration. The player becomes responsible for helping Zora make the right decisions and complete her mission successfully.

The game progresses through three increasingly challenging levels. Each level introduces a different survival situation;

Level 1 – Life Support Emergency: Oxygen Crisis

In the first level, Zora encounters a critical life-support emergency when the oxygen supply becomes dangerously low. Since the Moon has no breathable atmosphere, astronauts cannot survive without a continuous supply of oxygen. 

Through this challenge, players learn that even a small failure in the life-support system can become a serious threat to an astronaut's survival. Players are tasked with excavating lunar ice to feed to an oxygen converter machine on the mission to make oxygen reserves available for consumption. This level has been developed by Adina Somie Thomas.

Level 2 – Solar Radiation Emergency: Activate the Protective Shield

In the second level, Zora faces another serious threat: harmful solar radiation. Unlike Earth, which is protected by its atmosphere and magnetic field, the Moon has very little natural protection against radiation from the Sun.

During a sudden increase in solar activity, Zora becomes exposed to dangerous radiation. Players must help her activate a protective shield to minimize the effects of radiation exposure.

The protective shield acts as a defence mechanism against the incoming radiation. Players must respond quickly and activate the shield at the appropriate time. If Zora is hit by radiation, she loses 10 life points, making the challenge more difficult. The challenge demonstrates why radiation protection is an essential component of future lunar exploration missions. This level has been developed by Adiya Grace Thomas.

Level 3 – Space Hazard Emergency: Dodge the Meteors

The third level introduces Zora to one of the unpredictable dangers of space exploration: incoming meteors.

As Zora continues exploring the lunar surface, meteors begin approaching her lunar outstation. These space objects can strike the lunar surface at high speeds, creating impact craters and posing serious risks to astronauts and lunar equipment.

A swarm of meteors begins approaching her lunar outpost, putting her spacecraft and its equipment at serious risk. These space rocks travel at high speeds and can cause severe damage if they collide with the ship.

Zora must now take charge and defend her spacecraft from the incoming meteors. Players must help her identify the approaching threats, aim carefully ,and  must guide Zora carefully and help her destroy the incoming meteors. The challenge becomes increasingly demanding as players must observe the movement of the meteors, anticipate their paths, and respond quickly to avoid collisions. This level has been developed by Theertha Girish.

 

Trivia & Quiz:

The Lunar Odyssey also contains a trivia and quiz. Players will be able to experience this part once they have completed all the 3 levels. But, we acknowledged the fact that the young learners will be exhausted and tired after they have played the game, so, we ensured that this feature is completely optional and that they can stop after the 3 levels. The quiz is also optional once they are done with the trivia. 

Elements:

Project Artemis Genesis is designed to provide an engaging gaming experience through interactive challenges and progressive difficulty.

The major gameplay elements include:

1. Character-based gameplay: Players control Zora, the astronaut, and guide her through different lunar survival situations.

2. Three progressive levels: Each level introduces a new challenge, beginning with oxygen management, followed by radiation protection and finally meteor avoidance.

3. Survival-based challenges: Players must make appropriate decisions and respond to emergencies to ensure availability of Oxygen reserves to continue the lunar mission

4. Protective mechanisms: The second level introduces a protective shield to defend Zora against harmful solar radiation.

5. Life-point system: Radiation exposure results in the loss of one life point, encouraging players to respond carefully and protect the astronaut.

6. Increasing difficulty: Each level presents a different type of environmental threat, requiring improved attention, coordination, and problem-solving skills.

7. Educational interaction: The game connects the challenges faced by Zora with real scientific concepts associated with lunar exploration and astronaut safety.

Conclusion

Project Artemis Genesis is more than an ordinary game; it is an exciting journey into the world of space science. Through Zora's lunar adventure, players learn about astronaut safety, life-support systems, radiation protection, and space hazards while enjoying an interactive gaming experience. The project reflects the creativity, teamwork, and technological skills of young innovators. Do you want to find out what the questions in the quiz are? Want to find out what all trivia lies for you? Play The Lunar Odyssey to find out!

projectDetails.name: Infinite Orbit
projectDetails.summary: FORGOTTEN ON THE MOON is an interactive educational website developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The project aims to bring attention to the equipment and scientific instruments left behind during space exploration missions and help people understand their historical and scientific importance. The website features six interactive equipment icons representing Apollo 11, Apollo 15, Viking 1, Spirit & Opportunity, Surveyor and Kepler. Visitors can click on each icon to explore dedicated sections containing information about the equipment, its mission and its contributions to space exploration. The platform also includes COSMO, an AI-powered assistant that guides visitors, answers questions about space missions and explains complex concepts in simple language. To make learning more engaging, the website features an interactive quiz  project are sourced exclusively from NASA's official website. The website was developed with the help of Google Antigravity for AI-assisted development and coding, Lovable for website creation and design, and GitHub for version control, project management and team collaboration. Overall, FORGOTTEN ON THE MOON combines space history, interactive storytelling and AI-assisted technology to make lunar and planetary exploration more accessible, interesting and memorable, while celebrating the scientific achievements of equipment that is often forgotten. Its central message is: "Some missions end. Their stories remain."
projectDetails.details:
Infinite Orbit – An Interactive NASA Space Exploration and Learning Platform

Infinite Orbit is an interactive educational platform designed to make space exploration and NASA's achievements more engaging, accessible, and enjoyable. It allows users to explore the history of six important NASA missions through interactive stories, mission archives, educational quizzes, and an exciting space exploration game.

The platform includes a four-level Space Relic Expedition game in which players explore simulated planetary environments, including the Moon and Mars. Players must overcome obstacles such as lunar craters, dust storms, canyons, and boulder fields while experiencing different gravity conditions. By reaching mission artifacts, users can unlock information about historic NASA spacecraft and discoveries.

The website also features an interactive quiz to test users' knowledge, a space assistant named Cosmo to answer questions about NASA missions and space science, and links to NASA's official resources, including NASA Image Library, NASA Open APIs, and NASA Open Data.

Benefits and Intended Impact

Our project makes space science and astronomy easier to understand, especially for students and young learners. It encourages curiosity, scientific thinking, interactive learning, and interest in space exploration. Instead of simply reading about space missions, users can actively participate in a learning experience.

Creativity and Innovation

The main creative aspect of Infinite Orbit is the combination of historical storytelling, educational content, gamification, and an interactive space assistant in one platform. It transforms NASA's mission history into an engaging digital experience and helps users understand the importance of past space missions and their discoveries.

Development Approach and Tools

The project is developed as a web-based platform and hosted using GitHub Pages. It brings together interactive website features, game mechanics, educational content, and NASA-related resources. The platform is designed to be accessible through a web browser on different devices.

Factors Considered

During development, we considered user accessibility, educational value, ease of navigation, engagement, scientific relevance, and the importance of connecting users with authentic NASA information. Our goal is to make learning about space exploration both informative and enjoyable.

Infinite Orbit represents our vision of connecting space history with interactive technology and inspiring the next generation of space explorers.

projectDetails.name: Project Orbit by TheDawgInMe
projectDetails.summary: Project Orbit is an interactive, space-themed educational game that challenges players to design, launch, and operate an Earth-observation satellite. Players take on the role of a spacecraft engineer, making decisions about satellite components, power requirements, fuel capacity, communication systems, and launch vehicles. Through a series of progressively challenging missions, the game introduces fundamental concepts of satellite engineering, orbital operations, and Earth observation in an engaging, hands-on environment. By combining interactive 3D environments with mission-based gameplay, Project Orbit makes complex space science concepts more accessible and enjoyable.
projectDetails.details: Project Orbit features a multi-stage gameplay experience that takes players from spacecraft assembly to live orbital operations. Players begin by selecting and configuring satellite components, including imaging instruments, solar arrays, batteries, antennas, and propulsion systems. Each configuration must satisfy specific mission requirements, such as payload mass limits, electrical power demands, and budget constraints, before an appropriate launch vehicle can be selected. Once launched, players operate their spacecraft in a simulated low Earth orbit, where they must identify survey zones, collect observation data, manage available power and fuel, and transmit collected information during designated ground communication windows. The game includes six missions of increasing difficulty, covering scenarios such as coastal mapping, wetland monitoring, storm response, wildfire observation, and glacier profiling. A mission evaluation system provides performance scores and engineering feedback, allowing players to understand the consequences of their design and operational decisions.

projectDetails.name: Project THE PROJECT EXODUS
projectDetails.summary:
DRIFT (Dynamic Rapid Infrared Frame-Tracking & Blink Comparator) is an advanced web application developed to bridge the gap between archival NASA sky surveys and rapid astronomical discovery. Built using a React frontend and a Python FastAPI backend, DRIFT interfaces directly with NASA's public SkyView and Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) APIs to ingest multi-epoch infrared imagery from premier missions like WISE and 2MASS.

To address the challenge of shifting through massive repositories of celestial data, DRIFT features a high-precision optical blink comparator equipped with variable-frequency frame alternation, split-screen wipe sliders, difference imaging, and sub-pixel astrometric alignment tools. These features allow users to instantly isolate moving objects, proper-motion stars, and transient infrared phenomena that would otherwise remain hidden in static frames.

This project is important because it democratizes access to complex space science data, empowering researchers, students, and citizen scientists to perform efficient data-driven visual analysis, preliminary planetary defence screening, and multi-wavelength astronomical research
projectDetails.details:
The universe is in constant motion, yet the most critical dynamic events—near-Earth asteroids, high-proper-motion brown dwarfs, and transient infrared phenomena—often hide in plain sight within vast petabytes of archival sky surveys. DRIFT bridges the gap between raw NASA infrared survey archives and rapid human-in-the-loop anomaly detection. Engineered as a modern, browser-based astrometric blink comparator, DRIFT empowers researchers, citizen scientists, and students to retrieve, align, and visually interrogate multi-epoch, multi-wavelength NASA infrared imagery in real time—transforming static archival data into actionable astronomical discoveries.

Technical Architecture & Core Capabilities

  • Direct NASA Survey Archive Integration: DRIFT interfaces directly with NASA’s public SkyView Virtual Observatory and Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) APIs to ingest uncalibrated and unaltered FITS/JPEG imagery across premier infrared missions, including the Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer (WISE) (3.4µm, 4.6µm, 12µm, and 22µm bands) and the Two Micron All-Sky Survey (2MASS) (J, H, and K near-infrared bands). Users can query targets by common astronomical nomenclature or precise Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec) coordinates, with full access to native mission metadata and original source files.
    • Variable-Frequency Blink Alternation: Rapidly cycles between Epoch/Band A and Epoch/Band B at user-defined intervals (0.1s to 3.0s), leveraging human visual motion sensitivity to isolate moving bodies and variable flux sources.
    • Interactive Split-Screen Wipe & Difference Blending: Allows continuous spatial comparison via a real-time split-screen divider, alongside difference-imaging and false-color overlay modes that suppress static background starfields while amplifying thermal dust structures and transient anomalies.
  • Sub-Pixel Astrometric Alignment & Radiometric Scaling: To account for spacecraft roll-angle variations and multi-mission astrometric offsets, DRIFT incorporates sub-pixel X/Y translation controls and synchronized pan-and-zoom locking. Researchers can dynamically toggle between linear, logarithmic (log), and square-root (sqrt) pixel intensity stretches to resolve faint interstellar nebulosity alongside high-luminosity stellar cores.
  • Transient Logging & Hybrid Local/Cloud Processing: DRIFT includes an integrated annotation suite that enables users to tag candidate anomalies directly on the celestial canvas, automatically recording celestial/pixel coordinates and generating exportable session logs for follow-up observation. Built on a decoupled React/TypeScript frontend with a dual-mode architecture, DRIFT operates seamlessly in Direct NASA Live Mode for zero-latency cloud access while supporting a Local Python FastAPI Backend for custom automated image-processing pipelines.

Scientific Impact & Alignment with NASA Objectives

By lowering the computational barrier to multi-band infrared analysis, DRIFT democratizes access to NASA’s open-science data repositories. Whether used for preliminary planetary defense screening, comparative stellar evolution studies, or STEM education, DRIFT accelerates the path from archival observation to scientific discovery.


Tools, Technologies & Data Resources Used

1. NASA Data Archives & Astronomical APIs

  • NASA SkyView Virtual Observatory (GSFC HEASARC): Used for real-time retrieval and rendering of multi-wavelength sky cutouts via target names or J2000 RA/Dec coordinates.
  • NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA): Utilized as the primary repository for calibrated infrared science products and archival mission metadata.
  • WISE / NEOWISE (Wide-field Infrared Survey Explorer): Ingested mid-infrared survey imagery across four bands (W1: 3.4 µm, W2: 4.6 µm, W3: 12 µm, W4: 22 µm) to detect thermal dust, brown dwarfs, and moving objects.
  • 2MASS (Two Micron All Sky Survey): Ingested near-infrared survey imagery across three channels (J: 1.235 µm, H: 1.662 µm, Ks: 2.159 µm) to peer through dense interstellar dust clouds.
  • NASA FITS Format & World Coordinate System (WCS): Used for raw astronomical pixel analysis, header inspection, and celestial coordinate mapping (supported via SIMBAD and NASA/IPAC Extragalactic Database (NED) name resolution).

2. Frontend Coding & UI Frameworks

  • React & TypeScript: Core libraries used to build the interactive browser-based blink comparator dashboard and user interface.
  • Vite: Frontend build tool and development server for fast application bundling.
  • Tailwind CSS & Lucide Icons: Used for responsive dark-mode observatory styling and clean scientific iconography.
  • TanStack Start: Used for client-side routing and data fetching architecture.

3. Backend, Scientific Analysis & Deployment

  • Python: Primary backend programming language for scientific data handling.
  • FastAPI: High-performance Python API framework used for backend astronomical processing endpoints.
  • Astropy: Core astronomy library used for parsing FITS files, handling WCS transformations, and performing astrometric alignment calculations.
  • GitHub: Used for source code version control and repository hosting.
  • Vercel: Used for continuous deployment and global public hosting of the live web application.

4. AI Assistants, Research & Presentation Tools

  • Lovable: Used for rapid full-stack web prototyping and UI component scaffolding.
  • Google Gemini, Claude, & ChatGPT: Used as AI development co-pilots for debugging API integrations, refining astrometric math logic, and structuring technical documentation.
  • Perplexity: Used for rapid astrophysics literature lookups, mission band specifications, and technical verification.
  • Gamma: Used to design and structure the 7-slide visual presentation deck for the project demonstration.

AI Usage Disclosure: AI tools (Google Gemini, Claude, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Lovable, and Gamma) were used to assist with frontend prototyping, debugging API workflows, astrophysical research, and structuring presentation materials. All astronomical imagery and scientific data are sourced directly from official NASA open archives.

projectDetails.summary: ULTRON MK7 Space Station is a NASA Space Apps 2026 astronaut health-monitoring prototype designed to simulate a futuristic spacecraft health-monitoring system. The project consists of four development boards: a Wearable ESP32 equipped with a MAX30102 sensor, OLED display, and SOS button to monitor heart rate and blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂); a Space Station ESP32 that receives wearable health data through ESP-NOW and forwards it through Wi-Fi; a Station Arduino UNO R4 WiFi with an LCD Keypad Shield, DHT11 temperature and humidity sensor, and buzzer for displaying health information, environmental conditions, and emergency alerts; and a Laptop Arduino UNO R4 integrated with the Python-based ULTRON MK7 AI system for computer interaction and intelligent processing. The system aims to provide real-time health monitoring, wireless communication, environmental monitoring, emergency signaling, and AI-assisted analysis through a connected dashboard, all housed in a custom-built prototype enclosure. The ultimate goal is to develop an innovative, interactive astronaut health-monitoring solution that demonstrates how embedded electronics, wireless networking, and artificial intelligence can work together to support astronaut safety and mission awareness.
projectDetails.details:
ULTRON MK7 Space Station aims to improve astronaut safety by demonstrating how wearable sensors, wireless communication, and artificial intelligence can work together to monitor health in space environments. Astronauts experience demanding conditions such as microgravity, isolation, and physical stress, making continuous health monitoring important. Our prototype demonstrates a compact, affordable, and interactive monitoring system that could inspire future intelligent astronaut-support technologies. It also promotes STEM education by combining Arduino, ESP32, sensors, networking, and Python AI into a single working project.

How Does It Work?

The wearable ESP32 measures heart rate and blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂) using the MAX30102 sensor and allows astronauts to trigger an SOS emergency signal. The wearable transmits this information wirelessly using ESP-NOW to the Space Station ESP32, which acts as a communication gateway and forwards the data over Wi-Fi. The Station Arduino UNO R4 WiFi receives the health information and displays it on its LCD Keypad Shield alongside temperature and humidity measurements from the DHT11 sensor. Emergency signals can activate the station's alert system. The laptop runs the ULTRON MK7 Python AI software, which can be integrated with the monitoring system to provide health-data analysis and a dashboard for visualizing station information.

What Are Its Uses?

- Astronaut Health Monitoring: Demonstrates monitoring of heart rate and blood oxygen levels.

- Emergency Signaling: Provides an SOS mechanism for communicating emergency situations.

- Environmental Monitoring: Measures temperature and humidity around the station.

- AI-Assisted Analysis: Enables health-data visualization and potential intelligent anomaly detection.

- Space Research Education: Demonstrates spacecraft-inspired monitoring architecture.

- Remote Monitoring: Shows how sensor data can be transmitted wirelessly to a central station.

- Future Applications: Could inspire similar monitoring concepts for remote research stations, isolated environments, and wearable health-monitoring systems.

How to Use the Project

1. Wear the sensor device and place your finger correctly over the MAX30102 sensor.

2. Power on the wearable ESP32 and Space Station ESP32.

3. Power on the Station UNO R4 WiFi and allow the system to connect to Wi-Fi.

4. Wait for the wearable sensor to begin transmitting health readings.

5. Navigate the Station LCD Keypad Shield using UP, DOWN, LEFT, RIGHT, and SELECT buttons.

6. View heart rate, SpO₂, temperature, humidity, and SOS information on the station display.

7. Use the wearable SOS button to send an emergency signal to the station.

8. Open the ULTRON MK7 laptop dashboard to view or analyze available health data.

9. Monitor the system and observe how information moves between the wearable, station, and laptop.

projectDetails.name: The Silent Explorers: Stories Beyond the Mission
projectDetails.summary:
**The Silent Explorers** is an interactive digital space museum created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, in response to the challenge *“Abandoned but Not Forgotten.”*

Space missions are often remembered for their launches, discoveries and historic achievements, but the stories of the spacecraft, machines and engineering that made these journeys possible can receive less attention once missions end.

Our project addresses this by creating a digital museum that brings these stories together through interactive exhibits, mission timelines and visual storytelling. Featuring historic missions such as Apollo 11 and Mars Pathfinder, the website allows visitors to explore their journeys, milestones and contributions to space exploration.

The goal of The Silent Explorers is to preserve the legacy of past missions, make space history more accessible and encourage curiosity about the technology and people behind exploration.

**The mission may end. The story doesn't.**
projectDetails.details:
Project Details — The Silent Explorers

What does the project do and how does it work?

The Silent Explorers is an interactive digital space museum designed to preserve and showcase the stories of historic space missions, particularly the technology and engineering that remain part of space exploration even after a mission has ended.

The website is organised into different sections, allowing visitors to explore the purpose of the project, a historical mission timeline, individual mission exhibits, and educational information through FAQs and additional resources.

It currently features two major missions:

  • Apollo 11 (1969): An interactive storytelling experience following humanity's first crewed Moon landing, from launch and lunar orbit to the Moonwalk and return to Earth.
  • Mars Pathfinder (1997): An exhibit exploring the mission and its contribution to robotic exploration of Mars.

Visitors can navigate between the main museum and individual exhibits to discover mission milestones, historical information, and visual representations of space exploration.

What benefits does it have?

Space exploration is often remembered through major achievements, but the machines, instruments, engineering and historical stories behind these missions deserve attention too.

The project makes these stories easier to discover in one accessible digital space. It combines educational information with visual storytelling, making the subject more engaging for people who may not usually explore detailed space mission histories.

It also encourages visitors to think about the lasting significance of past missions and the importance of preserving their history.

Intended impact

The intended impact is to make the history of space exploration more accessible, encourage curiosity about science and engineering, and help preserve the legacy of missions that have contributed to humanity's understanding of space.

The project hopes to inspire younger audiences to explore astronomy, technology, robotics and scientific discovery.

Its central message is that the end of a mission does not mean the end of its story or significance.

Tools and technologies used

The project was developed as a browser-based website using:

  • HTML — to structure the website, its sections, exhibits and content.
  • CSS — to design the visual appearance, layouts, animations, typography and space-inspired atmosphere.
  • JavaScript — to implement interactive website elements and dynamic visual effects.
  • CodePen — as the online development and testing environment.

The website uses a dark cosmic visual theme, starfield effects, space-inspired typography, visual transitions and interactive navigation to create an immersive museum experience.

No specialised physical hardware was required; the project was developed using web technologies.

NASA mission information and historical resources were consulted to support the educational content. Relevant sources are credited within the project.

What makes the project creative?

Rather than presenting space mission information as a conventional article or collection of facts, The Silent Explorers transforms it into a digital museum.

Its creative approach combines historical storytelling, interactive exhibits, cinematic visual design and connected mission pages. Each mission is presented as a journey, allowing visitors to explore its milestones in sequence.

The visual design was also developed around the theme of space exploration, using a cosmic atmosphere to make the experience feel like an exploration of a digital museum.

The connection between Apollo 11 and Mars Pathfinder demonstrates how different generations of exploration can be presented together while preserving their individual stories.

Factors considered during development

Several factors influenced the design and development:

  • Educational value: Information needed to be understandable and meaningful rather than simply decorative.
  • Historical accuracy: Mission details were checked against NASA and other relevant historical sources.
  • Accessibility: Navigation and information were organised so visitors could explore the exhibits without needing specialised knowledge of space science.
  • User experience: The website was designed to guide visitors between the museum, timeline and individual mission exhibits.
  • Visual communication: The space-inspired design needed to support the educational content rather than distract from it.
  • Feasibility: The project was developed using accessible web technologies without requiring specialised hardware.

AI Tools and Assistance

ChatGPT (OpenAI) was used as an AI-assisted development tool throughout the project. It helped with understanding and writing code, debugging HTML, CSS and JavaScript, refining website content, and improving the overall structure and presentation.

The project concept, creative direction, design decisions, development process, testing and final selections were guided and carried out by the participant, with AI assistance used as a supporting tool.

AI-generated suggestions were reviewed and adapted during development rather than being treated as a substitute for independent decision-making.

Conclusion

The Silent Explorers is an attempt to give the stories of past space missions a place where they can continue to be explored and appreciated.

It celebrates not only the achievements of reaching new worlds, but also the engineering, technology and human curiosity that made those achievements possible.

The mission may end. The story doesn't.
