projectDetails.name: FlameAtlas
projectDetails.summary: FlameAtlas is a web dashboard that makes decades of NASA microgravity combustion research easy to search, compare and rank. NASA’s ISS combustion experiments matter for fire safety on future Moon and Mars missions, but they are hard to find and interpret. FlameAtlas organizes 20 investigations (including FLEX, BASS, SoFIE, SAME and ACME) with search, category filters and a detail page for each showing objectives, fuels, hardware, test conditions, key findings and Earth applications. A Moon Base relevance score ranks investigations against planned lunar habitat conditions (30% or more oxygen, 10.2 psi or less) and explains every score criterion by criterion. Missing data is shown as “Not reported” and never guessed, and the score is labeled a heuristic, not a NASA metric.
projectDetails.details:
What it does: FlameAtlas turns NASA’s microgravity combustion research into an interactive dashboard for students, researchers and engineers. Users can search and filter 20 investigations, open a detail page for each (objective, fuel, hardware, oxygen and pressure conditions, key findings, Earth applications), and sort by a Moon Base relevance score.

How the score works: it combines oxygen level (50%), pressure (30%) and fire-safety category (20%), compared against planned lunar habitat conditions (30%+ oxygen, 10.2 psi or less). If data is missing for a criterion, it is skipped and the other weights are rescaled. If both oxygen and pressure are missing, the investigation shows “Not scored.” Every score has a “Why this score” panel, and it is labeled a heuristic, not a NASA metric.

Data: compiled from NASA’s “A Researcher’s Guide to ISS Combustion Science” (2015) and the challenge description. Every value that is not stated in the sources is shown as “Not reported.” Some statuses (such as ACME and SoFIE “planned”) are as of the 2015 guide and are labeled that way.

Tools: Next.js, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, hosted on Vercel.

Use of SI: the code was written with AI coding assistance (Cline with DeepSeek models), and the dataset and project plan were prepared with help from an AI assistant (Claude), then checked against NASA sources. The app contains no AI-generated images or video.

Limitations and next steps: PSI links still need to be added per investigation, and a partial-gravity gap view and an AI research assistant that answers only from the dataset are planned. NASA’s database currently has no partial-gravity combustion data.

projectDetails.name: Project Top SAPASTRA-MED, the AI-driven astronaut health monitoring and space-environment intelligence platform.
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRA-MED is an AI-driven astronaut health monitoring and space-environment intelligence platform designed to support crew health awareness during long-duration space missions. It integrates physiological monitoring, personalized health baselines, predictive analytics, and environmental intelligence into a unified mission control system.

The platform monitors vital indicators such as heart rate, SpO₂, respiratory rate, body temperature, sleep, and physical activity. Its AI engine detects unusual physiological patterns, forecasts potential trends, and generates explainable health alerts. An astronaut digital twin provides an evolving view of individual health profiles, while NASA space-science resources offer environmental context through space weather, radiation-related information, and available ISS research datasets.

ASTRA-MED also features an AI-powered medical information assistant, mission timeline, emergency simulation, and interactive analytics dashboard. By combining astronaut health information with space-environment data, ASTRA-MED demonstrates an integrated approach to improving crew health awareness and supporting medical decision-making in future space exploration.
projectDetails.details: ASTRA-MED is an AI-driven astronaut health monitoring and space-environment intelligence platform designed to support astronaut health awareness and medical decision-making during long-duration space missions. HOW IT WORKS: ASTRA-MED collects and analyzes physiological indicators, including heart rate, SpO₂, respiratory rate, blood pressure, body temperature, sleep patterns and physical activity. Its AI-powered analytics engine uses personalized baselines, machine learning-based anomaly detection and time-series forecasting to identify unusual physiological patterns and generate explainable alerts. The Astronaut Digital Twin maintains an evolving representation of individual astronaut health profiles. The Space Environment Intelligence module incorporates relevant NASA space-science resources, including space weather, solar activity, radiation-related information and available ISS environmental research datasets. A mission timeline combines physiological and environmental events to support exploratory correlation analysis. The platform also includes an AI-powered medical information assistant using Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), an interactive emergency scenario simulator, mission control dashboard, predictive analytics and incident reporting. BENEFITS AND IMPACT: ASTRA-MED aims to improve crew health awareness, support early identification of unusual physiological trends, provide personalized health insights and help mission operators explore potential relationships between astronaut health and space-environment conditions. Its modular architecture offers potential applications in future long-duration missions, space medicine research and remote health monitoring. TECHNOLOGY: The software architecture uses modern web development technologies, including Next.js, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, Python, FastAPI, machine learning frameworks, PostgreSQL and interactive data visualization libraries. AI-assisted development tools, including Claude and ChatGPT, supported architecture design, coding, debugging and documentation. No dedicated medical hardware is required for the current software prototype; simulated physiological telemetry is used where real astronaut measurements are unavailable. CREATIVITY AND INNOVATION: The central innovation is integrating personalized astronaut health monitoring, predictive AI, digital twins and space-environment intelligence into one mission-oriented platform rather than treating these systems independently. DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS: The project considers data reliability, scientific validity, privacy, explainability, uncertainty, interoperability and the distinction between real measurements, historical research data, estimates and simulated scenarios. ASTRA-MED is an experimental research prototype, not a clinically validated diagnostic system or a replacement for professional medical judgment.

Space Legacy is an interactive educational web platform that explores the history and legacy of space exploration equipment. It showcases important spacecraft, landers, and rovers from historic space missions, explaining their original purposes, technologies, scientific contributions, and what happened to them after their missions.

Through images, informative descriptions, and an easy-to-navigate interface, the platform helps users understand how early space exploration missions contributed to modern space science and technology.

By bringing these historical missions together in one place, Space Legacy makes space exploration more accessible, engaging, and educational.
projectDetails.details:
About the Project

Space Legacy aims to preserve and present the history of important space exploration equipment through an interactive digital platform.

Many spacecraft and robotic explorers played significant roles in advancing our understanding of the Moon and Mars. However, the stories behind these machines, their technological contributions, and their final locations are not always widely known.

Our platform brings these stories together in an organized and visually engaging format.

Key Features

  • Interactive Equipment Dictionary: Explore important space exploration equipment through images and descriptions.
  • Mission Information: Learn about the missions, their objectives, and their historical significance.
  • Technology and Instruments: Understand the technologies and scientific instruments used.
  • Scientific Contributions: Discover how each mission helped advance space research.

  • Visual Learning: Use images and structured information to make learning about space exploration easier.

Featured Missions

  3. Surveyor 3 (1967)
  4. Sojourner Mars Rover (1997)

Our Goal

Our goal is to create an accessible digital collection that connects the achievements of early space exploration with the future of scientific discovery.

projectDetails.summary:
ASTRA — Astronaut Health Intelligence & Monitoring Platform
ASTRA is an AI-powered platform that helps astronauts and mission teams monitor health, detect unusual patterns, assess potential risks, and make informed decisions during space missions.

CORE FEATURES:
- Mission dashboards with astronaut status, alerts, and health trends.
- Astronaut profiles with individual measurements and health history.
- Analytics for heart rate, SpO2, blood pressure, temperature, respiration, sleep, and activity.
- PDF, CSV, and JSON data upload and validation.
- Anomaly detection using Isolation Forest, Z-scores, and NASA-based thresholds.
- Gemini AI assistant for health insights and anomaly explanations.
- Alert management with severity levels and acknowledgment.
- Downloadable PDF health reports.

SCIENTIFIC FOUNDATION:
NASA research on microgravity, cardiovascular changes, sleep, circadian rhythms, radiation, and astronaut health.

DEMO MODE:
Three fictional astronaut profiles, simulated telemetry, historical data, intentional anomalies, and interactive controls.

TECH STACK:
Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, Lucide, Motion.
Backend: Node.js, Express, TypeScript.
Data: csv-parse, pdf-parse, JSON storage.
ML: Custom Isolation Forest, Rolling Z-score.
AI: Google GenAI SDK, Gemini API, NASA references.
Reports: jsPDF.

VISION:
Turning astronaut health data into actionable intelligence for safer space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRA — Astronaut Health Intelligence & Monitoring Platform

ASTRA is an AI-powered astronaut health-monitoring platform designed to help astronauts and mission teams monitor physiological indicators, identify unusual health patterns, understand potential risks, and make informed decisions during space missions.

How it works:
ASTRA brings astronaut health information together in a centralized dashboard. It processes uploaded PDF, CSV, and JSON files, extracts relevant health records, and presents the information through interactive charts and analytics. Its anomaly detection engine combines a custom Isolation Forest implementation, Rolling Z-score analysis, and NASA-based reference thresholds to identify unusual patterns. A Gemini-powered AI assistant helps interpret these findings, explain potential concerns, and provide insights grounded in NASA research. The platform also supports alerts, historical trend analysis, and downloadable PDF reports.

Benefits and intended impact:
ASTRA aims to make astronaut health information easier to monitor, interpret, and act upon. By highlighting unusual physiological patterns and presenting explainable insights, it can support more informed health-monitoring decisions, reduce the effort required to analyse complex records, and contribute to safer human space exploration. It is designed as a decision-support platform, not a medical diagnostic system.

Technology used:
The frontend uses React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts, Lucide React, and Motion. The backend is built with Node.js, Express, and TypeScript. Data processing uses csv-parse and pdf-parse, with JSON-based persistence. Machine learning is implemented through a custom TypeScript Isolation Forest and Rolling Z-score engine. Google GenAI SDK and Gemini power the AI assistant, while jsPDF generates reports.

Creativity and innovation:
ASTRA combines machine learning, AI-assisted interpretation, interactive health analytics, and scientific research into one integrated astronaut-monitoring platform. Its demonstration mode includes three fictional astronaut profiles, simulated telemetry, historical records, and intentionally introduced anomalies, allowing users to explore how the system responds to changing health patterns.

Factors considered:
We prioritised scientific credibility, data accuracy, explainability, usability, and reliability. NASA research and reference standards inform the monitoring logic. We also distinguish simulated data from actual records, avoid presenting statistical anomalies as confirmed medical conditions, and provide fallback functionality when the AI service is unavailable.

projectDetails.details:
LUNARIS

VEXORA COSMOS developed an intuitive Lunar Site Landing Navigator for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The project addresses the difficulty of evaluating potential landing sites near the Moon’s south pole, where extreme lighting conditions, challenging terrain, and limited communication visibility create significant mission-planning constraints.

The navigator helps users compare candidate lunar landing sites across different dates and understand how the positions of the Sun and Earth change relative to the local horizon.

1. What does the project do, and how does it work?

The Lunar Site Landing Navigator is an interactive web-based application for exploring environmental conditions at possible lunar south-pole landing locations.

Users can select or compare candidate landing sites and examine conditions for different dates. The application presents astronomical information in a visual and accessible form, including:

The Sun’s position relative to the local lunar horizon

The Earth’s position relative to the horizon

Potential sunlight availability for solar power generation

Possible direct-to-Earth communication windows

Changes in lighting and visibility over time

Comparisons between different candidate locations

At a high level, the application takes a selected lunar location and date as inputs. It then presents the relevant Sun and Earth position information through visual indicators, charts, horizon diagrams, or other interface elements. Instead of requiring users to interpret complex astronomical data manually, the navigator translates that information into clear visual insights.

This allows mission planners, educators, and members of the public to evaluate how suitable a landing site may be under different lighting and communication conditions.

2. What benefits does the project have?

The project provides several important benefits.

Faster site comparison

Users can compare multiple landing sites and dates more efficiently instead of relying on complicated tools or interpreting large amounts of raw data.

Improved mission planning

The application supports early-stage decisions about:

Solar power availability

Visibility of Earth for communication

Lighting conditions at the landing site

Timing of scientific or engineering activities

Potential operational constraints

More accessible astronomical information

Many existing tools are designed for specialists and may have complicated interfaces. VEXORA COSMOS presents the information in a simpler and more visual format, making it easier for a wider audience to understand.

Better communication between disciplines

Lunar missions require cooperation between science, engineering, operations, and mission-planning teams. A shared visual interface can help team members discuss the same information more easily.

Educational value

The tool can be used by students, educators, and the public to learn about:

Lunar geography

Orbital and astronomical motion

Solar illumination

Communication geometry

The challenges of returning to the Moon

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The intended impact is to make lunar south-pole mission planning more understandable, efficient, and accessible.

Lunar south-pole missions are especially challenging because the region contains areas of near-permanent shadow as well as elevated locations that may receive sunlight for extended periods. At the same time, communication with Earth depends on whether Earth is visible above the local horizon. A landing site may therefore have strong scientific value but limited power or communication opportunities.

By visualizing these factors together, the project aims to help users make more informed assessments of possible landing sites.

The project could contribute to:

Safer and more informed mission planning

More effective coordination between science and engineering teams

Improved understanding of lunar environmental constraints

Greater public interest in lunar exploration

More accessible STEM education

Better communication of complex space-science concepts

The long-term goal is not to replace professional mission-analysis systems, but to provide an intuitive first layer for exploration, comparison, education, and early decision-making.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

The project is presented as a web-based application. Based on the provided project description, the confirmed software elements are:

A web interface

Astronomical and lunar-location data

Interactive visualization

A browser-based application hosted at https://vexoracosmos.netlify.app/

However, the specific programming languages, libraries, development environments, and hardware were not included in the project description. Those details should be confirmed before submitting the final response.

You can use the following version if it accurately reflects your actual development process:

The project was developed as a browser-based web application using standard front-end web technologies. The interface was designed to make astronomical and mission-planning data easy to explore interactively. The application uses computational logic to determine the relative positions of the Sun and Earth at selected lunar locations and dates, then presents the results through visual diagrams and comparison elements.

The project was tested using standard computers and web browsers. Development and deployment were carried out using software development tools, source-code management, browser testing tools, and a web-hosting platform. The application is hosted through Netlify, allowing users to access it online without installing specialized software.

Data sources

Development tools

Visual Studio Code, GitHub, Git, Figma, or other tools

Hosting

Netlify

Hardware

Testing

Desktop browsers, mobile browsers, responsive testing tools, or other methods

It is important not to list a framework, language, data source, or library unless the team actually used it.

5. How is the project creative?

The creativity of VEXORA COSMOS comes from how it transforms a complex technical problem into an accessible interactive experience.

Instead of presenting users with dense astronomical tables or specialist interfaces, the project focuses on visual explanation. It connects several different types of information in one place:

Lunar location

Date and time

Sun position

Earth visibility

Lighting conditions

Power-generation potential

Communication opportunities

This combination makes the project more than a static information page. It functions as an exploratory tool that allows users to investigate different possibilities and immediately see how changing the location or date affects mission conditions.

The project is also creative because it serves multiple audiences. A mission planner may use it to compare operational conditions, while a student or member of the public may use it to understand why the lunar south pole is difficult to explore.

Its creativity can be summarized as:

Turning technical data into visual insights

Combining science and engineering considerations

Making lunar mission planning more intuitive

Supporting both expert exploration and public education

Using interaction rather than static explanations

Presenting a difficult space-science challenge through a clear user experience

6. What factors does the team consider?

The team considers both technical mission requirements and user-experience requirements.

Scientific and engineering factors

The project considers:

Sun elevation above or below the local horizon

Earth visibility from a selected lunar location

Duration and availability of sunlight

Potential solar power generation

Direct-to-Earth communication opportunities

The effects of location and date on mission conditions

The extreme lighting environment of the lunar south pole

The need to coordinate science and engineering priorities

User-experience factors

The team also considers:

Ease of navigation

Clarity of visual information

Simple comparison between locations and dates

Accessibility for non-specialists

Readability of charts and horizon diagrams

Minimizing unnecessary complexity

Making the interface useful on different screen sizes

Helping users understand the meaning of the data, not just displaying numbers

Mission-planning factors

A suitable landing site cannot be judged by a single factor. The team therefore considers the balance between:

Scientific value

Solar illumination

Communication visibility

Operational safety

Accessibility of the site

Duration of useful mission conditions

The needs of different mission teams

The design recognizes that lunar exploration involves trade-offs. A location with good scientific potential may have limited sunlight, while a location with strong solar exposure may present other operational or communication challenges.

Conclusion

VEXORA COSMOS developed an interactive Lunar Site Landing Navigator for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. The application helps mission planners, educators, and the public compare potential landing sites near the Moon’s south pole across different dates. It visualizes the positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the lunar horizon, allowing users to assess sunlight availability for solar power and identify possible direct-to-Earth communication windows.

The project benefits users by simplifying complex astronomical and mission-planning information. Instead of requiring specialist knowledge or difficult interfaces, the navigator presents important information through clear visual comparisons. This can support early landing-site evaluation, improve communication between science and engineering teams, and make lunar exploration concepts easier for students and the public to understand.

The intended impact is to contribute to safer and more informed planning for future lunar south-pole missions. The tool highlights the trade-offs between scientific value, solar illumination, power generation, and communication visibility.

The project was developed as a browser-based web application and deployed through Netlify. The team used web-development tools, astronomical or lunar-location data, computational logic, and interactive visualization techniques. The exact programming languages and libraries should be listed according to the team’s actual implementation.

The project is creative because it turns complex space-science data into an intuitive exploration tool. It combines location, date, sunlight, and Earth visibility in one interface and makes the information useful to both technical and non-technical audiences. In developing the project, the team considered scientific accuracy, mission-planning needs, communication constraints, power-generation potential, accessibility, simplicity, readability, and the different needs of engineers, researchers, educators, and the public.

projectDetails.name: Lunar Navigator
projectDetails.summary:
Lunar Navigator is an interactive mission planning platform that simplifies lunar exploration. Currently, evaluating Moon landing sites requires manually cross-referencing complex elevation maps with dense astronomical data.

To solve this, we developed a 3D lunar globe with a built-in AI assistant that translates this heavy data into clear, side-by-side visual comparisons. Instead of wrestling with spreadsheets, mission teams can rapidly test multiple scenarios, simulate rover paths, and quickly find backup options if launch dates shift.

This tool is vital for upcoming missions to the lunar South Pole, where the Sun hovers just 1.5 degrees above the horizon. In this extreme environment, a single crater shadow can freeze a lander or cut off communications with Earth. If plans change, Lunar Navigator instantly recalculates sunlight windows and radio signals across dozens of landing sites.

By turning weeks of manual calculations into instant visual insights, Lunar Navigator helps planners, scientists, and engineers safely and confidently map out humanity’s return to the Moon.
projectDetails.details:
Project Description & Mechanics

  • Unified Simulation Platform: Combines 3D lunar mapping with real-time solar system tracking to evaluate safe landing zones and surface operations.
  • Shadow & Line-of-Sight Mapping: Instantly checks Sun and Earth positions against local crater topography to flag dangerous shadows or communication blackouts.
  • Real-Time Time Scrubber: A smooth, lag-free timeline controller that lets users scrub through a full lunar month, watching shadows, temperatures, and Earth visibility shift dynamically.
  • Comparative Analysis Deck: Allows users to view multiple candidate landing sites side-by-side, comparing terrain slopes, solar energy availability, and radio link strength.
  • Deep-Dive Telemetry Inspector: Features cross-section views of craters to identify safe, flat landing shelves and check precise radio signal margins.
  • Dynamic Mission Modeling: Simulates battery life, power drain, and rover driving speeds based on the selected mission profile (e.g., crewed, rover, static lander) and local terrain.
  • Integrated AI Assistant: Features "Dr. Raj, Ph.D Astrophysicists " an AI advisor powered by live map telemetry to help planners identify hazards and answer operational queries on the fly.

Key Benefits

  • Consolidated Workflow: Replaces the need to jump between separate NASA databases and complex math scripts by computing everything instantly in one dashboard.
  • Instant Adaptability: Allows planners to simply slide the timeline to a new date to see the immediate impact on sunlight and communications if a launch gets delayed.
  • Offline Reliability: Runs core physics directly on the user's device, ensuring the timeline and site analysis function smoothly even if the internet connection drops.
  • Broad Accessibility: Uses an intuitive, color-coded interface for students and educators while maintaining the strict decimal-precision physics required by actual aerospace engineers.

Intended Impact

  • Mission Safety: Protects multi-million-dollar equipment and astronauts at the treacherous lunar South Pole by clearly visualizing when life-threatening shadows will occur.
  • Accelerated Planning: Helps science teams rapidly balance their desire to explore difficult, icy terrain with the engineering need for safe, flat, well-lit landing spots.
  • Educational Outreach: Democratizes space exploration by giving students and enthusiasts access to the same data and planning challenges faced by NASA professionals.

Tools & Technologies

  • Frontend: JavaScript, HTML, and CSS, paired with Three.js for an interactive 3D Moon globe using high-resolution surface textures.
  • Backend: Python using the FastAPI framework to manage data requests and routing.
  • AI Integration: Google Gemini API customized to interpret live aerospace telemetry.
  • Authentic Data Sources: Powered by real NASA datasets, including LROC imagery, LOLA elevation models, Diviner temperature data, and JPL Horizons planetary tracking.

Creative Innovations

  • Visualized Geometry: Transforms complex 3D math into simple, 2D "skyline" graphs where users can literally watch the Sun and Earth dip behind local crater peaks.
  • Immersive Interface: Designed to mimic a real mission control console, featuring target crosshairs, live readouts, and clear safety warnings.
  • On-the-Fly Synthesis: Allows users to click anywhere on the 3D globe—not just pre-selected sites—to instantly generate local terrain, temperature, and sunlight data for that exact spot.
  • Dual-Persona AI: The AI dynamically switches tones, acting as a strict, data-driven Flight Director for engineers or a friendly Planetary Scientist for educational use.

Design Considerations

  • Harsh Environmental Factors: Accounted for the Moon's natural wobble (libration), freezing crater temperatures, and far-side communication blackouts requiring relay satellites.
  • Hardware Limitations: Programmed with strict landing gear tilt constraints, flagging slopes as safe, risky, or hazardous based on real spacecraft engineering limits.
  • System Reliability: Built with a decoupled software architecture where the globe, timeline, and data cards communicate seamlessly without slowing down the application, backed by rigorous automated math testing.

projectDetails.name: MarsWalk Route Planner
projectDetails.summary:
MarsWalk Route Planner is an interactive, web-based Martian surface navigation tool built for future human explorers in Jezero Crater (18.44°N, 77.45°E). Using Leaflet.js and real orbital elevation tiles from NASA’s Mars Trek (MGS MOLA/HRSC), we developed a layered map dashboard that integrates terrain topography, a verified 9.2 km low-slope EVA traverse route, geological hazard zones, and high-priority science sample waypoints into a single view.

It directly addresses the Interplanetary Survival Guide challenge by allowing astronauts to toggle hazard zones—such as steep crater rims (>25° slope) and deep sand ripple fields—against safe basalt corridors and Mars 2020 Perseverance science targets like the ancient river delta and Neretva Vallis channel. This unified spatial awareness is critical for keeping crewed Marswalks safe from terrain entrapment while maximizing scientific return during time-limited surface missions.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works:

MarsWalk Route Planner is an interactive, web-based Martian surface navigation dashboard centered on Jezero Crater (18.44°N, 77.45°E). Using Leaflet.js configured in planetary Equirectangular projection (EPSG:4326) and live orbital elevation tiles from NASA’s Mars Trek (MGS MOLA + HRSC Color Hillshade), the application overlays three toggleable mission layers onto real Martian terrain:

1. Safe EVA Traverse Route: A verified 9.2 km low-slope (<8°) basalt corridor connecting the Octavia E. Butler Landing habitat hub to the western river delta front and Neretva Vallis inlet.

2. Terrain & Slope Hazards: Interactive hazard polygons marking steep crater rim walls (>25° slope, high rockfall and traction risk) and the Séítah boulder and aeolian sand field (high boot and rover entrapment risk).

3. Science Sample Waypoints: Clickable mission markers detailing priority geological sites for mudstone biosignature and fluvial conglomerate core sampling.

Benefits & Intended Impact:

Future human explorers on Mars will operate under strict oxygen and time limits where stepping into deep aeolian sand ripples or steep crater walls can be mission-critical. Instead of cross-referencing disconnected orbital datasets, MarsWalk Route Planner unifies elevation relief, terrain hazards, and high-value science targets into a single browser interface—helping astronauts plan safer routes while maximizing scientific return.

Tools, Languages & Software Used:

- Languages & Libraries: HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6), and Leaflet.js (v1.9.4)

- Development & Hosting: Google Antigravity, GitHub, and Vercel (deployed as a static web app)

- Data Sources: NASA Mars Trek WMTS Tile Service (MGS MOLA/HRSC) and NASA Mars 2020 (Perseverance) Jezero Crater geological coordinates

Creativity & Design Factors Considered:

Rather than building a generic 2D map, we aligned the web GIS projection (EPSG:4326) directly with NASA’s planetary tile servers and modeled real operational EVA constraints—specifically slope thresholds (<8° safe traverse vs. >25° hazard zones) and surface traction hazards documented by the Mars 2020 mission.

projectDetails.name: Space legends
projectDetails.summary:
SPACE LEGENDS
Their missions ended. Their discoveries live forever.

Space Legends is an educational adventure game that introduces school-age learners and casual space enthusiasts to the machines behind historic space exploration. Guided by Nova the Astronaut and Beep-Bop the Robot, players explore artifacts across the Moon, Mars, and deep space through storytelling, interactive maps, and mission profiles.

The experience features 14 machines, including Apollo’s Eagle descent stage, Lunar Roving Vehicles, and ALSEP science stations; Mars explorers such as Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Viking, Phoenix, InSight, and Ingenuity; and deep-space missions including Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Kepler, and Pioneer 10 and 11. Profiles explain each machine’s purpose, mission, scientific contributions, and current status.

Three mini-games—Who Am I?, Mission Memory, and Science Detective—make learning interactive. An Explorer Journal, badges, and a Space Guidebook encourage players to keep exploring.

Mission details are cross-referenced with NASA’s Space Science Data Coordinated Archive. Space Legends is an independent student project inspired by the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It is not an official NASA website and is not endorsed by NASA.
projectDetails.details:
Space Legends is an educational adventure game that helps school-age learners and casual space enthusiasts discover the machines left behind by historic missions. Guided by Nova the Astronaut and Beep-Bop the Robot, players explore interactive maps and artifact profiles covering 14 missions and machines across the Moon, Mars, and deep space. The profiles explain each machine’s purpose, mission, scientific contributions, location, and current status, including the distinction between surface artifacts, inactive orbiters, and probes still traveling through space.

Players can reinforce what they learn through three mini-games: Who Am I?, a mission timeline challenge, and Science Detective, which connects scientific instruments to their discoveries. An Explorer Journal, badges, a guidebook, and NASA archive links support continued learning.

The project aims to make space history approachable and memorable, helping learners see how engineering enabled scientific discovery and how past missions paved the way for later exploration. Its storytelling approach gives historic hardware a distinct voice while keeping mission facts tied to NASA’s Space Science Data Coordinated Archive.

The team created original cartoon characters and artwork and built the website using React. The project combines interactive maps, game mechanics, and beginner-friendly narratives in a format designed to invite exploration. In developing it, the team considered audience age, accessibility, factual accuracy, clear explanations, and the need to distinguish artifacts by their actual location and operational status.

Space Legends is an independent educational student project inspired by the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It is not an official NASA website and is not endorsed by NASA.

projectDetails.summary:
VYOMED is an astronaut health-monitoring platform designed to support health awareness during space missions. Its central innovation, Personal Baseline Intelligence, compares an individual's recorded physiological measurements against their own historical patterns to identify meaningful changes rather than relying exclusively on generic population reference values.

The platform features an interactive 3D physiological digital twin, cardiovascular and immune-health monitoring context, historical trend visualisations, and a NASA OSDR-575 research explorer featuring Inspiration4 blood-serum observations. It distinguishes user-entered measurements from synthetic demonstration data and actual NASA laboratory research observations.

VYOMED aims to make personal health trends easier to understand and monitor during space missions. It is a research-informed prototype, not a clinically validated diagnostic system or live spacecraft telemetry service.

projectDetails.name: VitalOrbit - Astronaut Health Monitoring System
projectDetails.summary: VitalOrbit is an autonomous real-time astronaut health monitoring web application that tracks radiation exposure, cardiovascular fitness, musculoskeletal health, behavioral well-being, immune function, and habitat environment—empowering deep-space crews to detect early physiological shifts, execute guided self-assessments, and trigger evidence-based countermeasures independently during long communication delays with Earth.
projectDetails.details:
THE CHALLENGE & INSPIRATION

Long-duration missions to the Moon, Mars, and beyond expose astronauts to the five primary hazards of human spaceflight: space radiation, isolation and confinement, distance from Earth, altered gravity fields, and hostile/closed environments. On these deep-space voyages, multi-minute communication latencies prevent real-time clinical intervention from ground flight surgeons. Astronauts must take primary responsibility for monitoring their own health, spotting early physiological deterioration, and initiating countermeasures before minor issues become catastrophic emergencies.

WHAT VITALORBIT DOES

VitalOrbit is an autonomous, browser-based physiological telemetry and environmental monitoring system built specifically for deep-space crews. It consolidates six physiological and environmental domains into a cohesive, mission-critical dashboard:

1. Radiation Dosimetry: Tracks cumulative career dose (against NASA's 1,000 mSv career REIC standard), daily exposure rates, and organ-equivalent doses (blood-forming organs, eye lens, skin, and central nervous system). It provides space weather tracking and Solar Particle Event (SPE) storm-shelter advisories based on Canadian Space Agency (CSA) dosimetry research.

2. Cardiovascular & Hemodynamics: Features a live 500 Hz animated Lead-II ECG waveform, resting heart rate, non-invasive blood pressure, continuous heart rate variability (rMSSD) reflecting autonomic nervous tone, VO2 max trend tracking, and an interactive 3-minute Orthostatic Intolerance Protocol to assess post-microgravity cardiovascular deconditioning.

3. Musculoskeletal Health: Monitors regional Bone Mineral Density (BMD) loss across the lumbar spine, femoral neck, and wrist alongside lean muscle mass index. It tracks compliance against NASA's mandatory 2.5-hour/day exercise prescription across ARED (resistance loading), T2 (treadmill), and CEVIS (cycle ergometer).

4. Behavioral Health & Sleep Architecture: Combines continuous actigraphy sleep stage breakdown (Deep N3, Light, REM, Awake), daily psychological mood tracking, an embedded PHQ-2 depression screener, an on-board reaction-time test (WinSCAT PVT), and an encrypted private mission journal.

5. Immune Competence & Biomarkers: Surfaces on-board hematology metrics (WBC differential breakdown, neutrophils, lymphocytes), systemic inflammation markers (hs-CRP, IL-6), and salivary PCR latent virus reactivation surveillance (EBV, VZV, CMV) to preempt immune dysregulation.

6. Habitat Environment (ECLSS): Monitors cabin partial pressure of CO2 (ppCO2 with active CDRA scrubber cycle controls), atmospheric pressure, internal temperature, relative humidity, acoustic levels, and water reclamation potability.

7. Autonomous Self-Assessment Wizard: An interactive clinical decision-support engine featuring Visual Analog Scales (VAS) for headache, nausea, and fatigue, body symptom tagging, and a Space Flight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS) near-vision screener. Submitting an assessment generates clinical severity scoring and evidence-based countermeasure protocols.

HOW IT WORKS

VitalOrbit is built with clean HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript, leveraging Chart.js for data visualization. It requires zero server backend, runs client-side, operates completely offline in spacecraft cabins, and supports one-click JSON clinical telemetry export for ground synchronization.

projectDetails.name: Project Whispers Of Spaces
projectDetails.summary: Hi, we’re Team Whispers of Space, and we created an audio drama for kids. Through 12-year-old Tara’s homemade ham radio in Kumbalangi, listeners tune into real NASA NSSDCA missions—like Apollo 11, 12, and 15—turning dense telemetry into unforgettable bedtime stories.
projectDetails.details:
Whispers of Space is a three-part narrative audio mini-series created by Team Whispers of Space for young learners (ages 8–13) and curious space enthusiasts. Set on a quiet rooftop terrace in the backwater village of Kumbalangi, Kochi, the series follows 12-year-old Tara as she tinkers with her grandfather’s vintage ham radio and accidentally tunes into Frequency 1957—a mysterious deep-space channel where silent NASA spacecraft wake up once a year to share their stories.

Through immersive sound design and character-driven dialogue, each episode translates real archival telemetry from the NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA) into vivid, accessible storytelling.

Dense technical catalogs and dry historical summaries often make space exploration feel distant or overly intimidating to children. Ghost Signals bridges that gap by turning engineering milestones into relatable, bedtime-friendly audio adventures. Because it is audio-first and low-bandwidth, it is highly accessible for classrooms, mobile devices, and communities with limited screen or internet access—empowering kids from rural backwater villages to bustling cities to see themselves as part of humanity's space story.

Giving distinct personalities to landers, rovers, and surface experiments transforms static "space hardware" into memorable mentors. Complex concepts like laser ranging, thermoelectric nuclear power, and lunar seismology are anchored in familiar comparisons (fingernail growth, a household light bulb, and ringing a bell). Centering the series in Kumbalangi highlights that curiosity about the cosmos belongs to everyone, everywhere—no telescope or mission control badge required.

Official spacecraft trajectories, mission timelines, coordinates, and instrument logs from the NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA Master Catalog).

Google Docs and Google Slides for scriptwriting and visual presentation, standard digital audio recording and editing software for voice mixing and radio-frequency sound effects, and large language model assistance for script structuring and brainstorming.

projectDetails.name: BioSentinel: Autonomous Health Monitoring & Countermeasure System
projectDetails.summary:
BioSentinel is an offline-first autonomous clinical health monitoring system engineered for astronauts on long-duration exploration missions, such as Mars transit. When interplanetary distances impose communication delays of up to 22 minutes each way, astronauts cannot rely on real-time ground control to diagnose and manage medical crises.

To address this, we developed a system that continuously gathers multi-modal health indicators: real-time biometric vitals (heart rate, HRV, continuous blood pressure, SpO2), environmental life-support telemetry (cabin CO2, radiation dosimeters), and interactive self-assessment tools—specifically an in-browser Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT) for cognitive fatigue and an interactive Amsler Grid for Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS).

Using a clinical decision engine aligned with NASA Human Research Program (HRP) thresholds, BioSentinel autonomously evaluates cross-system hazards and prescribes immediate, actionable countermeasures. These include adapted ARED axial-load resistance protocols for bone remodeling, Lower Body Negative Pressure (LBNP) for ocular decompression, solar storm shelter lockdowns, and circadian phototherapy. BioSentinel bridges the gap between deep-space isolation and digital medicine, ensuring crew autonomy and survivability on humanity's journey beyond Earth orbit.
projectDetails.details:
1. How It Works & What It Does

BioSentinel is an offline-first, autonomous digital health system designed to support astronauts on long-duration interplanetary exploration missions (such as Earth-Mars transit). Because deep-space communication delays can reach up to 22 minutes each way, astronauts cannot rely on real-time telemedicine from Mission Control Houston.

BioSentinel operates entirely onboard within the spacecraft’s local network, continuously performing three core functions:

- Multi-Modal Data Ingestion: Gathers continuous physiological telemetry (heart rate, HRV RMSSD, continuous blood pressure, SpO2, core temperature, and sympathovagal stress), environmental life-support sensors (ambient CO2, cabin pressure, and active radiation dosimetry in µGy/hr and cumulative mSv), and daily biochemical markers (urinary NTx for bone resorption and hydration specific gravity).

- Interactive Self-Assessment Suite: Provides astronauts with in-browser diagnostic tools, including a tactile 60-second Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT) that quantifies reaction times and attentional lapses (>500 ms) to detect cognitive fatigue, alongside an interactive Amsler Grid canvas to map visual scotomas and globe flattening caused by cephalad fluid shifts.

- Autonomous Clinical Risk Engine: Evaluates cross-system telemetry against NASA Human Research Program (HRP) thresholds, generating holistic health scores and immediate multi-hazard risk categorizations.

2. Benefits & Actionable Countermeasures

Unlike passive telemetry dashboards, BioSentinel immediately closes the loop between diagnosis and treatment. When physiological drift or environmental spikes are identified, the system generates targeted, astronaut-executable countermeasure checklists:

- Bone & Muscle Remodeling: Prescribes adapted axial-load resistance protocols on the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device (ARED)—such as 1.8x Earth bodyweight squats and deadlifts—coupled with calcium and vitamin D3 titration to combat microgravity bone mineral density loss.

- SANS Ocular Decongestion: Detects early optic disc edema and schedules Lower Body Negative Pressure (LBNP) chamber sessions (-25 mmHg) to draw pooled cephalad venous blood back into the lower extremities.

- Radiation Protection: Automatically triggers storm-shelter lockdown protocols and radioprotective antioxidant administration during Solar Particle Events (SPEs).

- Circadian Realignment: Schedules targeted blue-enriched 480 nm phototherapy and micro-rest periods to counteract sleep loss and circadian desynchronization.

3. Creativity & Innovation

- Active Interactive Diagnostics: Rather than relying only on wearable sensors, astronauts actively participate in their health evaluations through gamified, scientifically validated tests (PVT and interactive Amsler eye exams) embedded directly into the flight deck HUD.

- Integrated Mission Crisis Simulator: Includes an onboard scenario injector allowing astronauts (and evaluators) to simulate spaceflight anomalies—such as coronal mass ejections, CO2 scrubber bed saturation, or acute SANS spikes—to verify and rehearse emergency response protocols in real time.

- Hardware-Agnostic Web Audio Alerts: Synthesizes audible aerospace alert chimes natively via the browser's Web Audio API oscillators, eliminating external media dependencies.

4. Factors Considered

- The 5 Hazards of Spaceflight: Structured comprehensively around NASA’s Human Research Program framework: Space Radiation, Altered Gravity, Isolation/Confinement, Hostile Closed Environments, and Distance from Earth.

- Zero-Cloud Resilience: Built with zero external API calls or cloud dependencies, ensuring complete operational reliability in deep-space autonomous isolation.

- Cockpit Ergonomics: Designed with a high-contrast dark flight-ops UI optimized for spacecraft lighting conditions, supporting touchscreens, mouse controls, and tactile keyboard shortcuts.

5. Tools, Languages, & Technologies Used

- Backend: Python 3.11, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic, NumPy, SciPy, Scikit-learn.

- Persistence: Embedded SQLite for offline time-series biometric logging and clinical audit trails.

- Frontend: HTML5, Tailwind CSS, Chart.js (for high-frequency cardiovascular waveforms), Lucide Icons, and HTML5 Canvas API.

- Version Control: Git and GitHub (open-source MIT License).

6. Intended Impact & Terrestrial Dual-Use

Beyond securing astronaut survival on Artemis and Mars transit missions, BioSentinel offers substantial terrestrial spin-offs. Its lightweight, offline-first autonomous architecture is directly transferable to extreme isolated environments on Earth—including Antarctic research stations, commercial maritime and submarine crews, deep-sea exploration, and remote rural clinics where access to specialized physicians is severely restricted.

Planet X – Exploring the Changing Universe

Planet X is an interactive, public-facing web platform designed to make NASA's SPHEREx space mission data easier for everyone to explore and understand. It allows users to view sky images captured at different times and compare them to discover changes in celestial objects such as stars, comets, asteroids, and other fascinating objects in space.

Our platform aims to simplify complex astronomical data through a user-friendly interface, visual comparisons, and time-based exploration. By helping users notice changes in the sky, Planet X makes it easier to identify objects that move or change over time and encourages people to take part in space exploration.

This project is important because SPHEREx collects an enormous amount of valuable data that is difficult for individuals to examine manually. Planet X connects science and technology with public participation, making astronomy more accessible, interactive, and exciting for everyone.

The main goal is to help users view sky images captured at different times and compare observations to notice changes in celestial objects. The platform aims to provide a simple and user-friendly experience for exploring astronomical images.

Users will be able to explore observations, compare images from different periods, and learn how objects in the universe change over time.

The project focuses on accessibility, interactive visualization, and public participation in space science. It aims to connect technology and astronomy while encouraging students and space enthusiasts to explore the universe.

Our vision is to make complex space data easier to understand and inspire more people to participate in scientific discovery.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: FIELD SHIFT: Satellite Crop Health for Adaptive Farming
projectDetails.summary: FIELD SHIFT is a web app that turns free NASA satellite data into a simple crop-health picture for small farms. A farmer saves a field, and the app requests its vegetation history from NASA's MODIS MOD13Q1 product through NASA AppEEARS. It then shows NDVI and EVI scores, valid-pixel and coverage figures, a field map, a time-series chart, plain-language recommendations and a one-page PDF report. By making a reading that arrives every 16 days as easy to read as a weather forecast, FIELD SHIFT helps farmers, starting with paddy growers in Kerala, catch a decline early and adapt water, nutrients and timing as the season unfolds.
projectDetails.details:
FIELD SHIFT turns free NASA satellite data into a simple field health picture for small farms. A user saves a field once, requests its vegetation history from NASA, and reads four numbers (mean NDVI, mean EVI, valid pixels and coverage), a boundary map, a time-series chart and a short recommendation with the evidence behind it. Nothing is guessed or simulated: every reading comes from NASA’s MODIS MOD13Q1 vegetation product (250 m, one reading per 16 days), retrieved through NASA AppEEARS.

How it works: The user chooses a farm and date range. FIELD SHIFT files an AppEEARS request, and NASA cuts out only that field from the satellite product. FIELD SHIFT then averages the usable pixels for each date, and the dashboard, recommendations and a PDF report update themselves. A request usually takes 5 to 45 minutes and keeps running on the server if the user closes the page. Users can upload a GeoJSON or KML boundary, or measure a single pixel at the farm’s centre.

Benefits and intended impact: It was built for paddy fields in Kerala, where plots are small, monsoon cloud hides the ground for weeks, and extension officers cannot visit every field. It supports adaptive farming by letting farmers do five things:

  • catch a decline early
  • tell a bad week from a bad season
  • save fertiliser and spraying on healthy fields
  • avoid mistaking a nutrient or pest problem for a water shortage
  • keep a dated record to compare seasons

Distant and tiny plots still get measured every 16 days, at no cost. The same method works for any crop wherever MODIS covers.

Tools and technology: NASA MODIS (Terra), the MOD13Q1 product, NASA AppEEARS and NASA Earthdata Login, with data courtesy of NASA LP DAAC. [Add your frontend, backend, language and hosting here, e.g. HTML/CSS/JavaScript, Python, hosting platform.] NASA credentials are stored on the server only, so the browser never sees them.

Creativity: Instead of showing raw satellite indices, FIELD SHIFT translates them into plain-language advice. Every technical term in the app links to a glossary written for farmers, and each recommendation shows its supporting numbers so the advice can be checked.

Factors considered: The satellite pixel is about 6 hectares, so a small field is averaged with its surroundings. Monsoon cloud leaves gaps, so the app reports valid pixels and coverage and warns when coverage is below about 50%. A pixel quality filter lets users trade reliability against the number of dates. The app is also honest that it is one input, not a verdict, and should be combined with what the farmer sees in the field.

node.excerpt:
Our Project Vision
We are building an advanced decision-support tool to help farmers adapt to shifting climates using NASA Earth observations.

projectDetails.name: Yieldary AI
projectDetails.summary:
Yieldary AI, a precision agriculture and farm-adaptation platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge (Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data). Using a Django and React/TypeScript stack integrated with Google Earth Engine, Yieldary AI transforms orbital datasets—including SMAP L4, GPM IMERG, MODIS, Sentinel-2, Landsat 8/9, SRTM 90m, GEDI LiDAR, and NASA POWER—into actionable farm intelligence without requiring on-farm IoT hardware.

The platform addresses the challenge through three core modules: Space-to-Soil Telemetry (tracking soil moisture, water stress, VPD, and vegetation vigor), Terrain & Erosion Analysis (computing a LiDAR-adjusted RUSLE topsoil erosion score), and a Gemini-powered Crop Rotation & Climate What-If Engine with deterministic fallbacks. It also includes a 3-season rotation simulator, leaf/soil diagnostics, subsidy matching, and a multilingual voice helpdesk in English, Malayalam, Tamil, and Hindi.

This is important for smallholder farmers in climate-vulnerable regions like Kerala, helping them prevent topsoil loss, adapt to erratic rainfall, and protect yields and livelihoods.
projectDetails.details:
Yieldary AI is a precision agriculture and farm-adaptation platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge ("Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data"). It translates raw orbital Earth observation data into localized crop rotation strategies, erosion risk assessments, and cluster-level farm management.

5-Step Operational Pipeline

  1. Farmer Onboarding & Geolocation: Farmers search their village via OpenStreetMap Nominatim to capture exact GPS coordinates, verify their email with a 6-digit OTP, and register securely (Argon2 password hashing + SimpleJWT). Registration triggers a background thread that precomputes satellite reports for their plot.
  2. Module 1 — Space-to-Soil Telemetry: Queries Google Earth Engine (GEE) and NASA POWER in a batched server call to compute monthly soil moisture (SMAP L4), rainfall (GPM IMERG), evapotranspiration (MODIS MOD16A2GF), Water Stress Index (WSI), vegetative vigor (Sentinel-2 & Landsat 8/9 NDVI, EVI, NDWI), Vapor Pressure Deficit (GLDAS-2.1 VPD), and Frost Risk.
  3. Module 2 — Terrain, Canopy & Soil Erosion Analysis: Combines NASA/CGIAR SRTM 90m slope, GPM wettest-month rainfall intensity, OpenLandMap USDA soil texture, ESA WorldCover 10m land cover, and NASA GEDI ISS LiDAR canopy height (rh98) to compute an adjusted RUSLE Topsoil Erosion Risk Score (0–100).
  4. Module 3 — Crop Rotation & Climate What-If Engine: Feeds telemetry, erosion metrics, 3-year ERA5/MODIS history, farmer constraint sliders (water, budget, market demand, equipment), and climate perturbations ($\pm 50\%$ rainfall, $+0\text{–}4^\circ\text{C}$ temperature) into Google Gemini (gemini-2.0-flash $\rightarrow$ gemini-2.5-flash-lite $\rightarrow$ gemini-2.5-flash) with a strict Pydantic schema (RotationResponseSchema). It outputs 3 strategies—Baseline, Soil-Resilience Intercrop, and Low-ET Water-Saver—in English, Malayalam, Tamil, or Hindi. If the LLM is unreachable or quota-limited, a deterministic _fallback_decision_matrix() computes all scores and translations locally so the endpoint always returns HTTP 200 OK.
  5. Precision Agriculture Suite: Adds 6 integrated operational tools in the same Yieldary AI dashboard: a Cluster Command Heatmap & One-Tap Satellite Field Profiler, a 3-Season Kharif-Rabi-Zaid Pareto Simulator, an AI Visual Leaf & Soil Card Scanner, an AI4Bharat Multilingual Voice Helpdesk, a Cadastral Farmer CRM, and a Government Subsidy Scheme Match Wizard.

Core Technical Innovations

  • Multi-Sensor Orbital Fusion for Erosion Modeling: Instead of relying on static slope maps alone, Module 2 fuses SRTM 90m topography, GPM rainfall erosivity, ESA WorldCover bare-ground ratios, and NASA GEDI 98th-percentile LiDAR canopy height into a dynamic RUSLE proxy.
  • Interactive "What-If" Climate & Economic Sandbox: Farmers can stress-test crop rotations in real time against hypothetical rainfall shifts, temperature spikes, and personal capital/equipment constraints, or optimize 3-season Kharif-Rabi-Zaid sequences via a multi-objective Pareto fitness equation.
  • Hybrid Generative + Deterministic AI: Pairing structured Gemini JSON outputs with a mathematically grounded _fallback_decision_matrix() combines natural-language regional agronomy with guaranteed numerical reliability.
  • Unified Mission Control & Precision Ag Suite: Seamlessly connects individual farm telemetry, leaf/soil card computer vision, multilingual voice synthesis, and government scheme matching inside a single bento-grid interface.

Benefits

  • Zero-Hardware Sensing: Delivers root-zone soil moisture, canopy height, slope, and microclimate telemetry using orbital satellites rather than expensive on-farm IoT sensors.
  • Proactive Disease & Climate Resilience: Detects 48-hour Fungal Blast Epidemic windows ($\text{RH} \ge 85\%$ and $22.0^\circ\text{C} \le T \le 28.5^\circ\text{C}$) and stomatal closure stress ($\text{VPD} > 1.6\text{ kPa}$) before crop damage escalates, enabling SMS/IVR broadcasts to 1,280+ farmers.
  • Actionable, Non-Technical Decisions: Converts complex biophysical indices into clear 0–100 suitability scores, visual gauges, and native-language advisories with read-aloud audio.
  • 100% Uptime Guarantee: Deterministic mathematical fallbacks (for both the Gemini rotation advisor and the Scikit-Learn Random Forest / Gaussian Mahalanobis 22-crop classifier) ensure farmers never face broken screens during API outages.

Impact of the Project

The project aims to bridge the gap between complex NASA/ESA Earth observation datasets and everyday decision-making for smallholder farmers and agricultural clusters—especially in climate-vulnerable, steep-terrain regions such as Kerala (e.g., Idukki). By helping farmers anticipate water deficits, prevent monsoon-driven topsoil erosion, disrupt pest cycles through 3-season crop rotation, and match directly with Central and State government subsidies, Yieldary AI seeks to protect soil health, stabilize yields, and improve farm profitability under shifting climate conditions.

Factors Considered

  • Regional & Tropical Accuracy: Standard NDVI saturates in dense tropical plantations (such as Idukki), so the team included EVI to correct for aerosols and dense canopy, alongside GLDAS psychrometrics to catch fungal blast incubation windows.
  • Accessibility & Language Inclusion: Recognizing that smallholder farmers may not read English or complex charts, the team built native Malayalam, Tamil, Hindi, and English support, Web Speech API read-aloud, and a 16kHz WAV voice helpdesk.
  • Fault Tolerance & Latency: To prevent slow satellite queries or API rate limits from blocking users, the team implemented async post-signup precomputation, single-call .getInfo() GEE batching, and deterministic local fallbacks.
  • Data Security & Practical Viability: Protected user accounts with Argon2 hashing, OTP verification, and JWT bearer tokens, while grounding crop recommendations in real-world constraints (water availability, capital budget, labor, equipment, and subsidy eligibility).

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, and Software Used

  • Development Environment & AI Coding Tools: Antigravity, Visual Studio Code (VS Code), and Google Gemini for architecture, code generation, and debugging.
  • Backend & Database: Python, Django, Django REST Framework, SimpleJWT, Argon2 (Argon2PasswordHasher), Pydantic, and SQLite (db.sqlite3).
  • Frontend & Visualization: TypeScript, React, Vite, Axios, custom SVG Cubic Bezier charts and radial gauges, OpenStreetMap terrain/heatmap layers, and the Web Speech API.
  • Geospatial & Climate APIs: Google Earth Engine (GEE), NASA POWER API, ISRIC SoilGrids v2.0, OpenStreetMap Nominatim, and orbital datasets including Copernicus Sentinel-2, NASA/USGS Landsat 8 & 9, NASA MODIS (NDVI, ET, Land Cover), NASA SMAP L4, NASA/JAXA GPM IMERG, ECMWF ERA5-Land, NASA GLDAS-2.1, NASA/CGIAR SRTM 90m, OpenLandMap, ESA WorldCover 10m, and NASA GEDI LiDAR.
  • AI, ML & Speech Engines: Google Gemini GenAI (google-genai), Scikit-Learn Random Forest + Gaussian Mahalanobis classifier (trained on 2,200 records across 22 crop classes), LLaVA multi-modal vision diagnostics, AI4Bharat Indic ASR/IndicTrans2, and a custom 16kHz 16-bit mono PCM WAV synthesizer.
  • Hardware: Standard developer workstations for building and hosting, paired with spaceborne Earth observation satellites and ISS LiDAR (GEDI) as the remote-sensing layer.

projectDetails.name: TERRASCAN
projectDetails.summary:
TERRASCAN is an AI-powered geospatial platform that identifies Earth locations resembling potential Moon base sites and Mars landing environments. It uses terrain, geological and environmental analysis to support planetary exploration research.

The platform includes modules for planetary exploration, analog discovery, Earth location mapping, environmental comparison, mission suitability analysis and reporting.

It uses React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS and MapLibre for the frontend, with Python and FastAPI for the backend. Geospatial and AI technologies include GeoPandas, Rasterio, NumPy, Pandas and Scikit-learn, with SQLite for database management. NASA, ESA and USGS are the intended scientific data sources.

The analysis workflow includes data acquisition, preprocessing, feature extraction, similarity analysis and visualization. Key comparison factors include slope, elevation, surface roughness, thermal conditions and geology.

Potential Earth analog locations include the Atacama Desert, McMurdo Dry Valleys, Death Valley, Haughton Crater and Icelandic volcanic landscapes.

Future development will focus on integrating verified scientific datasets, improving similarity analysis, validating machine learning models and enhancing terrain assessment.

TERRASCAN aims to connect Earth-based geospatial intelligence with planetary exploration by helping researchers study terrestrial environments that share characteristics with the Moon and Mars.
projectDetails.details:
TERRASCAN: AI-Powered Planetary Analog Intelligence Platform

1. Project Overview

TERRASCAN is an AI-powered geospatial intelligence platform designed to identify and evaluate locations on Earth that resemble potential permanent lunar base sites and Mars landing environments. The project addresses an important challenge in future space exploration: finding suitable terrestrial environments that can serve as analogues for studying extraterrestrial terrain, geological conditions, and environmental characteristics.

Earth contains several extreme environments, including deserts, volcanic landscapes, polar regions, and impact craters, that share certain characteristics with the Moon and Mars. TERRASCAN aims to analyze these environments using geospatial data, terrain analysis, environmental indicators, and AI-assisted comparison techniques.

The platform brings together planetary exploration data and Earth observation information to help researchers explore potential analog locations, compare environmental characteristics, and assess their relevance to future space missions.

2. Problem Statement

Selecting suitable locations for permanent lunar bases and Mars landing missions requires extensive analysis of terrain, geological characteristics, environmental conditions, and surface properties.

However, identifying Earth locations that resemble these extraterrestrial environments involves working with multiple scientific datasets and complex geospatial information. Manually comparing these datasets is time-consuming and makes large-scale analysis difficult.

TERRASCAN aims to address this challenge by providing a centralized platform for exploring, analyzing, and comparing terrestrial environments with selected lunar and Martian reference conditions.

3. Project Objectives

The primary objectives of TERRASCAN are:

  • Identify Earth locations that resemble selected lunar and Martian environments.
  • Analyze terrain characteristics, including slope, elevation, and surface roughness.
  • Evaluate thermal, geological, and environmental similarities.
  • Integrate scientific datasets from organizations such as NASA, ESA, and USGS.
  • Apply geospatial processing and machine learning techniques to support location analysis.
  • Provide interactive maps and visual comparisons of potential analog locations.
  • Support research and preliminary mission-site suitability studies.

4. Key Features and Modules

Overview Dashboard: Provides a centralized view of the platform, its analytical capabilities, and important project information.

Planetary Explorer: Allows users to explore Moon and Mars environments and understand the reference conditions used for terrestrial comparisons.

Analog Discovery: Identifies potential Earth locations based on selected planetary environmental and terrain characteristics.

Earth Locations: Provides information about candidate terrestrial environments, including their geographical and physical characteristics.

Comparison Module: Supports comparisons between selected Earth locations and planetary reference environments.

Mission Suitability Analysis: Organizes mission-relevant characteristics to help assess the potential usefulness of different terrestrial analog environments.

Reports Module: Provides a framework for presenting analytical findings, comparisons, and location assessments.

5. Technology Stack

The project follows a modular frontend and backend architecture.

Frontend:

  • React
  • TypeScript
  • Vite
  • Tailwind CSS
  • MapLibre
  • Recharts

Backend:

  • Python
  • FastAPI

Geospatial Processing and Analysis:

  • GeoPandas
  • Rasterio
  • NumPy
  • Pandas
  • Scikit-learn

Database:

  • SQLite

Scientific Data Sources:

  • NASA
  • European Space Agency (ESA)
  • United States Geological Survey (USGS)

6. Analytical Methodology

TERRASCAN follows a structured analytical workflow:

  1. Data Acquisition: Collect relevant planetary and terrestrial geospatial datasets.
  2. Data Preprocessing: Validate datasets, handle missing information, and standardize spatial references and data formats.
  3. Feature Extraction: Extract relevant characteristics such as elevation, slope, roughness, thermal conditions, and geological information.
  4. Similarity Analysis: Compare terrestrial environmental characteristics against selected lunar and Martian reference conditions.
  5. Candidate Evaluation: Organize potential analog locations based on their measured similarities and available evidence.
  6. Visualization: Present geographical information, comparisons, and analytical findings through interactive interfaces.

The analytical framework is designed to distinguish similarity scores from data completeness and confidence, ensuring that users can understand the reliability and limitations of individual comparisons.

7. Potential Earth Analog Locations

The initial candidate environments considered by the project include:

  • Atacama Desert, Chile: An extremely arid environment relevant to studying Mars-like conditions.
  • McMurdo Dry Valleys, Antarctica: A cold, dry environment useful for investigating certain Martian analog conditions.
  • Death Valley, USA: An environment with distinctive desert terrain and geological characteristics.
  • Haughton Crater, Canada: An impact crater environment relevant to planetary geology research.
  • Icelandic Volcanic Landscapes: Volcanic terrain that provides opportunities for studying geological analogues.

These locations are candidate research environments, not scientifically validated equivalents of specific lunar or Martian landing sites.

8. Development and Implementation

TERRASCAN has been developed through a staged implementation process. The project architecture, frontend foundation, interactive mapping components, planetary exploration interface, and several supporting application modules have been addressed during development.

The initial implementation includes candidate-location visualization and the structural foundations for geospatial analysis and planetary comparisons.

Further validation is required to establish reliable real-world data integration, scientifically calibrated similarity rankings, complete frontend-backend functionality, and machine learning performance using representative scientific datasets.

9. Applications and Significance

TERRASCAN can support:

  • Planetary science and geological research.
  • Lunar and Martian analog environment studies.
  • Preliminary extraterrestrial mission-site research.
  • Geospatial intelligence and environmental analysis.
  • Educational demonstrations of planetary exploration technologies.
  • Research into terrestrial environments that simulate selected extraterrestrial conditions.

By combining geospatial technologies with AI-assisted analytical methods, the project provides a foundation for exploring the relationship between Earth's extreme environments and the challenges of future planetary exploration.

10. Future Scope

Future development will focus on integrating verified scientific datasets, improving geospatial processing capabilities, validating similarity calculations, developing reliable machine learning models, and expanding interactive visualization features.

Additional improvements may include advanced terrain classification, more detailed environmental comparisons, mission-specific evaluation criteria, and automated scientific report generation.

11. Conclusion

TERRASCAN aims to bridge terrestrial geospatial analysis and planetary exploration research through an integrated AI-powered platform. By identifying and evaluating Earth environments that share selected characteristics with the Moon and Mars, it provides a framework for studying planetary analogues and supporting preliminary research for future space exploration missions.

The long-term vision is to develop TERRASCAN into a reliable, transparent, and extensible planetary analog intelligence platform that makes complex environmental comparisons more accessible to researchers, students, and space exploration enthusiasts.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

**The Explorers That Never Came Home** is an interactive, comic-style NASA space exploration flipbook that tells the stories of spacecraft, rovers, landers, and scientific instruments that remained in space after completing their missions. The project covers famous missions such as Apollo, Spirit and Opportunity, Sojourner, Viking, Dawn, Pioneer, Ingenuity, and Kepler.

This project is important because it highlights the achievements of NASA's past missions, explains their scientific contributions, and inspires curiosity about space exploration. It also demonstrates how digital storytelling and multimedia technology can transform educational content into an interactive learning experience.

projectDetails.name: GHOSTS OF SPACE
projectDetails.summary:
GHOSTS OF SPACE — The Machines We Left Behind

GHOSTS OF SPACE is an interactive, animated educational documentary series that brings the stories of forgotten human-made machines left on the Moon, Mars, and other parts of space to life.The project aims to make space exploration interesting and easy to understand, especially for students. Through colourful 3D cartoon storytelling, viewers meet ORBIT, a friendly robot guide who takes them on journeys through real historical space missions, including Mars 3, Sojourner, Opportunity, and Cassini-Huygens.Unlike traditional documentaries, GHOSTS OF SPACE allows viewers to participate in the stories through interactive decisions and branching storylines. They can choose what a rover investigates, explore different scientific possibilities, and learn about the discoveries, challenges, and technology behind each mission.
The project uses publicly available NASA images, videos, scientific datasets, and mission information to ensure that the educational content is based on real space exploration.Technologies such as HTML, CSS, and JavaScript bring the interactive website, animations, and decision-based experiences together.Our goal is to turn forgotten space missions into exciting learning experiences, inspire curiosity about science and technology, and show how even machines that have stopped working can leave behind discoveries that change our understanding of the universe.
Their missions ended.Our curiosity never will.
projectDetails.details:
1. Project Title

GHOSTS OF SPACE: The Machines We Left Behind

2. Team Name

Zero Gravity X

3. Team Members

  • Anakha A
  • Geethika Vinod
  • Christine Julia Danie
  • Nora Susan Mathew
  • Aleena Binoy

4. Challenge Selected

Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars.

5. Project Type

Interactive educational website and animated documentary series.

6. Project Description

GHOSTS OF SPACE is an interactive storytelling platform that explores human-made machines left behind after space missions. It presents their journeys, discoveries, scientific importance, and mission endings through animated episodes and interactive choices.

7. Main Features

  • Interactive Homepage: A space-themed homepage introducing the project.
  • ORBIT: A friendly robot character who guides viewers through the series.
  • Animated Episodes: Cartoon documentaries based on real space missions.
  • Branching Storylines: Viewers make decisions that lead to different exploration paths.
  • Educational Content: Simple explanations of space science, robotics, and planetary exploration.
  • Historical Reconstructions: Visual recreations of important mission events, clearly distinguished from real footage.

8. Featured Space Missions

  1. Mars 3: The Soviet lander that transmitted from Mars for approximately 14.5 seconds.
  2. Moon Exploration Machines: Human-made equipment and robotic missions left on the lunar surface.
  3. Sojourner: NASA's first successful Mars rover.
  4. Opportunity: The Mars rover that operated for almost 15 years.
  5. Cassini-Huygens: The mission that explored Saturn and its moons.

9. Technologies Used

  • HTML — Website structure.
  • CSS — Design, animations, and visual effects.
  • JavaScript — Interactive buttons and branching storylines.
  • AI-assisted creative tools — Character, scene, and animation creation.
  • Browser text-to-speech — Narration.
  • NASA public resources — Mission images, videos, and scientific information.

10. NASA and Open Data Resources

  • NASA Image and Video Library.
  • NASA Planetary Data System (PDS).
  • NASA mission archives and educational resources.
  • Publicly available images and scientific mission records from other space agencies where relevant.

11. Target Audience

School students, young learners, space enthusiasts, and anyone interested in astronomy and robotics.

12. Main Objective

To make space exploration easier to understand through interactive storytelling while encouraging curiosity about science, technology, engineering, and the universe.

13. Expected Outcome

A user-friendly interactive website that transforms historical space missions into engaging educational experiences and helps students understand the importance of robotic space exploration.
