It allows users to ask questions through an AI Copilot, understand complex scientific concepts, explore educational knowledge, generate short notes, and discover space-related information such as ISS tracking and upcoming launches.

The platform makes learning easier, more engaging, and accessible by bringing multiple learning features together in one place. It aims to inspire students and curious learners to explore science, technology, and space.

GrandNexa was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with AI integration and online data sources. It is designed to work through a web browser without requiring users to install a separate application.

Its creativity lies in combining AI-assisted learning, educational resources, and real-world space information into a single platform. During development, we focused on user-friendly design, accessibility, educational value, performance, and future expansion.

Our vision is to develop GrandNexa into a comprehensive space learning environment that encourages curiosity, supports education, and inspires the next generation of scientists, engineers, and space explorers.

It aims to inspire students and curious learners to explore science, technology, and space. GrandNexa was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with AI integration and online data sources. It is designed to work through a web browser without requiring users to install a separate application. Its creativity lies in combining AI-assisted learning, educational resources, and real-world space information into a single platform. During development, we focused on user-friendly design, accessibility, educational value, performance, and future expansion. Our vision is to develop GrandNexa into a comprehensive space learning environment that encourages curiosity, supports education, and inspires the next generation of scientists, engineers, and space explorers.

projectDetails.name: Ghosts of the Solar System
projectDetails.summary:
Ghosts of the Solar System is an interactive, story-driven web experience that introduces school-age and casual space enthusiasts to the hardware NASA has left on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space. Users choose a world, tap a glowing marker, and hear each machine tell its own story in the first person, from the Apollo 15 rover parked with its camera aimed at the sky to Insight listening to Mars’s heartbeat until its power faded. Each story pairs the engineering of the machine with the scientific discoveries it made possible, such as Opportunity’s evidence of ancient water or Pioneer 10’s first close-up views of Jupiter.

It addresses the challenge by turning dense mission histories into short, personal narratives rather than lists of facts. Most people hear only about active missions, so these stories show that silent explorers helped pave the way for today’s achievements. The page is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, works on phones and desktops, supports keyboard navigation, and respects light, dark, and reduced-motion settings.

It matters because stories make science memorable, and curiosity about past missions can inspire the next generation of explorers.
projectDetails.details:
An interactive web page where NASA’s retired machines tell their own stories. Pick the Moon, Mars, or Deep Space, tap a marker, and read a first-person story with what the machine discovered and a fun fact. It covers 8 machines.
It turns complex mission history into short, memorable stories for students and casual space fans. It works in any browser, on phones and computers, with no download needed, and it supports keyboard use and light and dark mode
To show young people that missions don’t end when the signal stops, and to inspire curiosity about past and future space exploration.
HTML, CSS, and JavaScript in a single file, a code editor and browser, Netlify or GitHub Pages for hosting, Google Slides or PowerPoint for the demo, and public NASA mission information. We also used an AI assistant (Claude) for drafting, and our team reviewed the results. Check this against the Space Apps rules on AI use.
Each machine speaks in its own voice, so facts become characters and stories. Pulsing markers act like waiting signals, and Voyager 1 appears as a “still talking” contrast to the silent ghosts. Audience age (8–14), accuracy against NASA records, accessibility, a lightweight format that works anywhere, and a data structure that makes adding new stories easy.

projectDetails.name: Lunar VISTA (Visibility & Illumination Site Trade-off Analyzer)
projectDetails.summary:
Lunar VISTA (Visibility & Illumination Site Trade-off Analyzer) is a web app for comparing lunar south-pole landing sites and dates in seconds. Users choose from 65 curated sites (Artemis III candidates, CLPS, other commercial, Apollo and other nations' missions) or enter custom coordinates, and pick a landing time. The app plots the Sun and Earth against the real terrain horizon, built from LRO LOLA elevation data and JPL Horizons ephemerides for 2024–2032. For each site it shows time to sunset and Earth-set, 30-day sunlight and Earth-visibility timelines, libration, and 13 metric categories covering power and direct-to-Earth communication. Up to three site-and-date scenarios can be compared side by side, each rated 1–10, with plain explanations of why small changes matter. A toggle adapts the same views for enthusiasts, educators and mission planners.

Why it matters: at the south pole, a few kilometres or a few days can decide whether a lander has sunlight and contact with Earth or neither. Answering that today means working across Horizons, QuickMap and Moon Trek. Lunar VISTA puts this answer at one place, and every number links to its NASA source, so science & engineering teams can re-plan quickly when a schedule slips.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do, and how does it work?

Lunar VISTA is a web app for comparing landing sites and landing dates near the lunar south pole. It has three main pages:

  1. Site selection. You pick a site on a south-pole map, a flat whole-Moon map or a 3D globe. The 65 curated sites cover Artemis candidate regions, CLPS and other commercial missions, Apollo, other nations' landers and named south-pole features. You can also enter custom coordinates. You also choose a landing date and time in UTC.
  2. Site details. This shows the terrain horizon at the site with the Sun and Earth drawn against it. It gives the time to sunset and Earth-set and a 30-day timeline you can scrub or play. There are lanes for sunlight, Earth in view, each Deep Space Network complex, and combined contact time. It also shows libration, a battery and array-power model, and metrics in 13 categories.
  3. Compare. Two or three site-and-date scenarios sit side by side. Each is rated Favourable, Conditional or Unfavourable. A "Why these scenarios differ" row is written from the computed geometry, for example the horizon height toward the Sun at each site.

How it works. Two steps run offline:

  • We pulled hourly Sun and Earth geometry for 2024–2032 from JPL Horizons (DE441) into compact tables. The browser converts these tables into the Sun's and Earth's position in the sky at any site. That conversion matches Horizons' own output to within 0.0002°. Years outside 2024–2032 are fetched live through the server.
  • For each site, we trace 360 rays across the LOLA 120 m polar elevation model out to 200 km. This builds the terrain horizon, including the Moon's curvature and no atmospheric refraction.

The Sun is treated as a disk, so the app shows how much of it clears the ridge, not just whether its centre does. All metric calculations run in the browser, so changing the date or an assumption updates the results straight away.

What are its benefits?

  • One screen instead of several tools. Today you would combine Horizons, QuickMap and Moon Trek and read their raw output yourself. Here, site, date, horizon, Sun, Earth and DSN coverage are in one place.
  • Fast re-planning. There are ±1-day and ±7-day steps, a side-by-side comparison, and sensitivity metrics: how much sunlit time changes with even a 1-day shift, or a 1 km move.
  • Values you can check. Every number has a tooltip naming its source and status: computed, modelled, reference, assumption or unavailable. Hovering a computed value shows the calculation steps. A metric that can't be backed by data is not shown, rather than estimated.
  • Planners can adjust the model. There are 26 mission assumptions (array, battery, loads, mast height, slope tolerance, link parameters) and 15 sets of rating thresholds. Edits are saved in the browser.
  • Shareable. The site, time and comparison are kept in the URL. There are no accounts, and the history of pages you opened stays in your browser.

What is the intended impact?

For mission planners, the aim is to make "what if we land three days later, or 2 km away?" a question that takes seconds to answer. For educators and the public, the aim is to show why the south pole is so hard: the Sun stays only a few degrees above the horizon, so a ridge a fraction of a degree high can decide whether a site is in light or shadow.

From mission planners to educators to enthusiasts, the level of technicality decreases and the level of explanation increases.

What tools, languages, hardware and software did we use?

  • Languages: TypeScript (app and data pipeline), Python (standard-library scripts that build the metric catalog and site list), CSS, Bash.
    • JPL Horizons (DE441), including Goldstone, Canberra and Madrid as observers for DSN visibility
    • LRO LOLA elevation models, plus the LOLA average-illumination maps (used only for validation)
    • LROC permanently shadowed region polygons and the anthropogenic-objects catalogue
    • LRO Diviner polar temperature maps
    • NASA Moon Trek basemap tiles
    • USGS Gazetteer of Planetary Nomenclature
    • DSN 810-005 handbook (station coordinates, antenna gain)
    • NSSDCA fact sheets
    • 123 quoted values from cited literature
  • Other tools: Git and GitHub, Cursor, Vercel, and Claude Code (AI coding assistant).
  • Hardware: none beyond a laptop.

How is the project creative?

  • One app, three depths. A toggle switches between Enthusiast, Educator and Mission planner. The page structure stays the same and only the level of detail changes. Enthusiasts see 27 metrics framed as plain questions, educators see 89 with explanations, and planners see every available metric plus the assumptions and threshold editors.
  • A horizon you can read. The real skyline, with a partly clipped Sun disk and the Earth on top of it, makes grazing light visible in a way a table of angles doesn't.
  • Communications shown as a timeline. One lane per DSN complex and a combined Contact lane, with handover gaps marked in red.
  • Explanations generated from the data. The comparison explains differences between scenarios using that scenario's own numbers, not fixed text.
  • The app checks itself in public. The Data & methods page shows our results next to an independent NASA product, including where they disagree.

What factors did we consider?

  • Accuracy and authenticity first. No values from memory and no placeholders. 6 candidate sites were left out because I couldn't find a cited coordinate for them.
  • South-pole physics: terrain-limited horizons, the Sun as a disk, no refraction, libration (already included in the Horizons geometry, so it isn't added twice), Earth eclipses of the Sun, and permanently shadowed regions.
  • The schedule-slip scenario from the challenge brief, which shaped the date steps, sensitivity metrics and comparison.
  • Speed and reliability: precomputed tables, because Horizons can't be called directly from a browser, and a 127 MB committed terrain bundle so custom coordinates work without downloading roughly 500 MB of raw data.
  • Readability: light and dark themes, text no smaller than 14 px, and tooltips that open on hover, keyboard focus or tap.
  • Privacy: no accounts or tracking. Preferences and history are stored only in the browser.

How do we know the results are right?

  • The Sun and Earth positions match Horizons' own topocentric output to within 0.0002°.
  • For 35 sites, I compared the share of time the Sun and Earth are above the terrain horizon against LOLA's independent average-illumination maps. The median difference is 0.24 percentage points for the Sun and 0.19 for the Earth. 34 of 35 sites agree within 2 points for the Sun, and 32 of 35 for the Earth.
  • The largest gap is at Malapert Massif: about 9 points for the Sun and 8 for the Earth. LOLA's own map varies from about 15% to 61% within 240 m of that pin, so the result there depends heavily on the exact location.

What are the limitations?

  • The terrain is a 120 m grid, so boulders and metre-scale relief are not modelled.
  • The Artemis region pins are the centres of LROC image mosaics, because NASA does not publish official region centres.
  • The power and link figures are models driven by editable assumptions with example defaults. They don't describe any real lander's hardware.
  • Some rating thresholds follow NASA criteria. Others are planning bands set by this tool, and they are labelled as such.
  • 38 of the 196 metrics are hidden at the reference site because they need mission-specific inputs or measurements taken on the surface.
  • The phone layout isn't finished: the header overflows at about 390 px wide.

Was AI used?

Yes. I built the app with Claude Code, inside Cursor, under my direction. I made the product and design decisions and logged each one in the repo (LOGS.md). Research on site coordinates and reference values was AI-assisted. Every value is stored with its source URL and the quoted text, so it can be checked. No data values are generated by AI.

Who built it?

A one-person team, me, Rounak.

What's next?

  • Finishing the mobile layout.
  • Adding cited sources for metrics that are still unavailable, such as the USGS geologic map and LEND neutron data.
  • Adding the remaining excluded sites once cited coordinates are found.

Where can you try it?

At https://lunar-landing-site-navigator-2026.vercel.app/. It needs no account and no installation. It works best on a desktop browser, because the phone layout hasn't been looked into. The source code is in a public GitHub repo: https://github.com/Not-A-Builder/lunar-landing-site-navigator-2026

Data

You can find all data used in the platform, at https://lunar-landing-site-navigator-2026.vercel.app/sources#sources
Please note: Some data couldn't be attached to the data links for this project due to a cap on the number of links that can be added.

Thank you!

projectDetails.name: Project 77_456
projectDetails.summary:
Objective
The goal was to give astronauts a quick, visual way to check their own health during long missions and know what to do next, without needing medical training.
What I developed
I built an interactive web tool with a clickable body map covering nine areas: eyes, brain, lungs, heart, kidneys, muscles, bones, immune system and radiation. Astronauts log simple readings such as sleep hours, blood oxygen, grip strength and radiation dose. Each reading is color-coded, charted over 14 days and combined into a readiness score. The tool adapts to four settings: space station, deep-space transit, lunar base and Mars surface. XP, levels and badges reward daily logging.
How it addresses the challenge
Each indicator comes with measurement steps, an explanation of how spaceflight affects it, and clear actions for on-track, attention and urgent states. Red results tell the crew when to contact the flight surgeon, adjusted for communication delay.
Why it matters
Missions to Mars will be too far for real-time medical help. Bone loss, vision changes and radiation build up slowly and are easy to miss. Early self-assessment lets crews act sooner, supports flight surgeons with better data, and keeps astronauts healthier and mission-ready.
projectDetails.details: **What it does and how it works** The Crew Health Console is a single web page. Astronauts tap a body map (eyes, brain, lungs, heart, kidneys, muscles, bones, immune system, radiation) and see that area's function and current status. They log a reading with a slider or number box. The tool compares it to a healthy range, colors it green, amber or red, and updates a 14-day trend chart and an overall readiness score. Every indicator includes step-by-step measurement instructions, why spaceflight affects it, and what to do for each status. Data is saved on the device. **Benefits** - Needs no medical knowledge: plain language and clear instructions - Status is readable at a glance through color - Shows trends, so slow changes like bone loss, vision change and rising radiation dose are caught early - Gives flight surgeons better data - Gamification (XP, levels, badges) encourages consistent daily checks **Intended impact** Missions to the Moon and Mars will have communication delays of seconds to over 20 minutes, so crews must manage their own health. The goal is earlier detection, faster action, fewer emergencies and better mission readiness. **Tools and technology** - HTML, CSS and JavaScript with no frameworks - SVG for the body map and charts - IBM Plex Sans via Google Fonts - Browser localStorage for saving readings - Claude's artifact publishing for the web page and the 7-slide deck - No hardware used, but the design accepts readings from devices such as a pulse oximeter, thermometer, dosimeter and dynamometer **Creativity** - A clickable body map doubles as a live dashboard, with pulsing alerts - The environment selector changes which areas are flagged and how urgent advice is worded, for example a Mars comms delay - Missions and a readiness score turn routine checks into a habit **Factors considered** - Which measurements astronauts can realistically take in space - Hazards from NASA Human Research Program topics: bone and muscle loss, SANS eye changes, radiation, sleep, fluid shifts, kidney stones - Different mission environments and communication delays - Mobile and desktop screens, dark and light themes, and reduced-motion settings - Safety: the ranges are simplified examples, not clinical limits, and need validation by flight surgeons before real use

projectDetails.details:
TerraSpace Analog Explorer

TerraSpace Analog Explorer is an interactive web application designed to explore Earth environments that may serve as analogues for future human exploration and research on the Moon and Mars.

The project helps users investigate and compare different Earth locations using environmental information such as temperature, humidity, precipitation, and solar radiation. It brings environmental data and geographical information together in one platform, helping users explore how different regions on Earth compare in their environmental characteristics.

The application identifies and organizes 192 candidate Earth locations and presents their geographical information, including latitude, longitude, and distance. Users can explore environmental groupings, select date ranges, examine available environmental records, and compare locations through interactive visualizations. The platform also provides information about its methodology and data sources to help users understand how the comparisons are made.

Benefits and intended impact:
TerraSpace makes environmental and geographical information easier to explore and understand through an accessible, interactive platform. It can support students, educators, researchers, and space enthusiasts in studying Earth environments that may be useful for planetary analogue research. By bringing multiple environmental indicators together, the project encourages data-informed exploration and provides a foundation for future research into potential Moon and Mars analogue environments.

Tools and technologies:
The project was developed using Python as the main programming language, Streamlit for the interactive web application, and Pandas for handling and organizing environmental datasets. NASA POWER data is used to obtain environmental information. The application is deployed as a web-based platform, allowing users to access it through a browser.

Creativity and innovation:
The creative aspect of TerraSpace is the integration of geographical exploration, environmental data, date-based analysis, and interactive comparisons in a single platform. Instead of presenting isolated datasets, it gives users an opportunity to explore multiple candidate locations and understand their environmental characteristics together. The project also establishes a foundation for a future feature called **MissionTwin**, which aims to support more advanced matching between Earth environments and selected lunar or Martian conditions.

Factors considered:
Our team considered the relevance of environmental conditions to planetary analogue research, the availability of accessible scientific data, geographical coverage, the ability to compare multiple locations, usability, and transparency of the methodology. We also considered the importance of distinguishing descriptive environmental comparisons from confirmed conclusions about the suitability of a location for an actual space mission.

TerraSpace Analog Explorer aims to make Earth analogue exploration more accessible today while creating a foundation for more advanced planetary research in the future.

projectDetails.name: Project Aakaasham
projectDetails.summary:
We built Still Listening-for our project Aakaasham, an interactive scrollytelling story with a companion slide deck. You play a radio signal leaving Earth and meet the hardware NASA left behind: Apollo landers, moon buggies and laser mirrors on the Moon, then Viking, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity and Ingenuity on Mars. At a fork, you choose between answering Opportunity in its 2018 dust storm and following Pioneer 10 into deep space. Each path ends in an epilogue on other machines that went quiet, including InSight, Kepler, NEAR Shoemaker and Dawn. The page uses animated line art, parallax and a color palette that shifts with each chapter.

It turns dry mission facts into a personal journey, so people learn through exploration and choice instead of a list. It reframes “dead” spacecraft as lasting legacies that still shape science. This matters because it makes space history emotional, accessible and memorable for general audiences. It is also designed to be inclusive, with readable type, reduced-motion support and mobile layouts.
It answers Abandoned but Not Forgotten by treating NASA’s discarded equipment as characters, not junk. Mirrors still work, rovers outlived their 90-day missions, and a helicopter built for five flights flew 72. Each silent machine taught engineers how to build the next one, so what was left behind is remembered.
projectDetails.details:
Still Listening is an interactive scrollytelling website about NASA hardware left on the Moon and Mars. The reader is a radio signal leaving Earth, and scrolling moves them through five chapters: the Moon (Apollo landers, moon buggies, laser mirrors, Surveyor 3), Mars (Viking 1, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Ingenuity), a choice at a fork, then an epilogue. At the fork the reader picks between answering Opportunity in its 2018 dust storm and following Pioneer 10 into deep space. Each path ends with other machines that went quiet: InSight, Kepler, NEAR Shoemaker and Dawn. A companion 7-slide deck summarizes the story.

Benefits and intended impact
It turns dry mission facts into a personal journey, so people learn through exploration and choice. It reframes “abandoned” spacecraft as lasting legacies that still shape science, and it makes space history emotional, accessible and memorable, especially for young space fans.

Tools and technology
HTML, CSS and JavaScript; GSAP with ScrollTrigger for scroll animation; HTML Canvas for the particle background; hand-drawn inline SVG illustrations; Google Fonts (Fraunces and Atkinson Hyperlegible); GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting. No special hardware was needed. Mission facts come from NASA’s Space Science Data Coordinated Archive and science.nasa.gov. Add any other tools your team used.

Creativity
The reader is the radio signal, so the story is told from a new point of view. The branching choice means no two journeys are identical. Line-art illustrations draw themselves as you scroll, and the color palette and background motion change with each chapter.

Factors we considered
Accuracy of mission facts, accessibility (readable fonts, reduced-motion support, high contrast), mobile-friendly layouts, no installs or logins, and a clear, age-friendly tone.

projectDetails.summary:
Backscatter is an interactive Earth-observation platform developed by Team Afterimage for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It uses NASA–ISRO NISAR Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) data to investigate changes on Earth's surface, even in cloudy conditions.

Focusing on Kuttanad, Kerala, a region vulnerable to flooding and waterlogging, we developed a web application that compares satellite observations from different dates. Users can explore radar backscatter changes, switch between polarization layers, and inspect individual locations. We also integrated NASA's OPERA surface-water products to provide independent supporting evidence and highlight uncertainties.

Backscatter addresses the Dancing with the SARs challenge by turning complex satellite measurements into accessible, interactive visualizations that help users investigate environmental changes.

This matters because timely information about changing water conditions can support research, environmental monitoring, and disaster preparedness. Rather than making unsupported flood predictions, Backscatter emphasizes transparent, evidence-based interpretation of real satellite observations.
projectDetails.details:
Backscatter

Backscatter, developed by Team Afterimage, is an interactive satellite radar analysis platform that helps users investigate changes on Earth's surface using real NASA–ISRO NISAR data. Our project focuses on Kuttanad, Kerala, a low-lying region vulnerable to flooding and waterlogging.

How does it work?

Backscatter compares Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) observations captured on different dates to identify changes in radar backscatter. Unlike conventional optical imagery, SAR can observe Earth's surface even through clouds and without sunlight.

We developed an interactive web application where users can explore before-and-after satellite observations, visualize changes, switch between HH and HV radar polarization layers, and click individual locations to examine actual measurements. We also compare our results against NASA's OPERA surface-water products to provide supporting evidence and assess reliability.

Tools and technologies

Our project was developed using:

  • Frontend: React, JavaScript, MapLibre GL JS, Vite, HTML and CSS.
  • Data processing: Python, NumPy, Rasterio, GDAL and Matplotlib.
  • Satellite data: NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band SAR and NASA OPERA surface-water datasets.
  • Data services: NASA Earthdata, ASF, NASA Harmony and Common Metadata Repository (CMR).
  • Development: Git, GitHub and an Apple Silicon Mac for processing and testing.

Creativity and innovation

Backscatter goes beyond simply displaying satellite imagery. It combines real radar measurements, multiple polarization channels, interactive visualization and independent reference data in one accessible interface.

A key aspect of our approach is scientific transparency. Our experiments demonstrated strong agreement between NISAR measurements and OPERA classifications for existing open water. However, detecting newly flooded or receding areas proved significantly harder. Rather than hiding these limitations, our platform distinguishes measured radar changes from interpretations that require further validation.

Benefits and intended impact

Backscatter makes complex satellite observations easier to understand for students, researchers, environmental organizations and disaster-management teams. It can help users investigate changing water conditions, explore environmental patterns and identify areas that deserve closer examination.

Our goal is to make satellite-based environmental monitoring more accessible, reproducible and trustworthy, particularly for regions affected by seasonal flooding.

Factors we considered

During development, we prioritized data authenticity, scientific reliability, geographical relevance, processing efficiency and ease of use. We also considered cloud cover, differences in satellite acquisition dates, radar calibration, agricultural land-use changes and uncertainty in water classification.

Ultimately, Backscatter transforms complex SAR data into an interactive, evidence-driven experience that helps people understand how Earth's surface is changing—without presenting uncertain interpretations as established facts.

projectDetails.details: MISSION: ORBIT — Design. Launch. Learn. Project Overview MISSION: ORBIT is an interactive educational space mission design game that helps users understand the challenges involved in planning a space mission. Players can design a spacecraft, select a destination, choose a launch vehicle and propulsion system, and select scientific instruments to achieve mission objectives. How It Works The game allows users to explore different mission destinations, including the Moon, Mars, and asteroid 433 Eros. Players make spacecraft design decisions while considering important mission constraints such as spacecraft mass, power demand, fuel requirements, and estimated cost. After configuring the spacecraft, users run a mission simulation. The game calculates resource usage, checks engineering constraints, evaluates the scientific value of the selected instruments, and displays a mission score and result. If a resource limit is exceeded, the mission requires redesign. Users can modify their choices and run the simulation again to understand how different decisions affect mission feasibility. Benefits and Intended Impact MISSION: ORBIT makes space mission planning easier and more engaging for students and beginners. It introduces important concepts in spacecraft design, scientific exploration, resource management, and engineering trade-offs through interactive learning. The project aims to encourage curiosity about space exploration, develop problem-solving skills, and help learners understand why careful planning is essential for successful space missions. Tools and Technologies Used - HTML for the webpage structure. - CSS for the visual design and user interface. - JavaScript for mission calculations, simulation logic, and interactive features. - GitHub for source code hosting and version control. - GitHub Pages for public website hosting. - NASA/JPL Small-Body Database resources for background information about asteroid 433 Eros. Creativity and Innovation The creative aspect of MISSION: ORBIT is its game-based approach to understanding complex space mission planning. Instead of only reading about spacecraft engineering, users can experiment with different spacecraft configurations and immediately see the consequences of their decisions. The simulation combines scientific objectives with engineering constraints, creating an interactive experience where users learn through experimentation, comparison, and redesign. Factors Considered During development, the main factors considered were: - Mission destination and scientific objectives. - Spacecraft mass and launch vehicle capacity. - Power requirements of scientific instruments. - Fuel requirements and propulsion selection. - Estimated mission cost and available budget. - Scientific value of the selected payload. - Overall mission feasibility. Project Scope MISSION: ORBIT is a simplified educational simulation. Its calculations and mission scores are intended for learning and experimentation and should not be interpreted as real-world spacecraft engineering predictions or guarantees of mission success.

projectDetails.name: Sphery
projectDetails.summary:
The Sphery Project helps anyone, irrespective of field, look at, understand and personally use official data from the NASA SPHEREx satellite. It's divided into two parts: the Dome view and the Pro view. The Dome view drops you into a grassy field under a dome that simulates the night sky in optical, near-infrared, and mid-infrared views. Click any point to take it to the Pro view, where you can explore the details. The Pro view is a dashboard for the selected point. You can search the IRSA archive by object name or position, open real SPHEREx FITS images, and compare the six detector bands. You can also measure brightness and identify the object.

. A landing page precedes these two parts and contains general information about the project and the satellite itself, letting the user explore how the satellite works, its images and what each part does in high detail.
projectDetails.details:
The problem

SPHEREx is mapping the whole sky in infrared, and its data is public, but most professional astronomy software looks like an aircraft control panel. A student who is interested in astronomy and wants to get into the field opens one of these tools, sees hundreds of buttons and gives up before they ever see a real image. The Sphery Project is made for those students. It lets anyone look at, understand and personally use official data from the NASA SPHEREx sattelite without learning a whole professional tool first.

What it does

The user starts in the dome and clicks any patch of sky that interests them. They then take that exact point to the Pro view to find out more about it. A landing page comes before both of these and explains the satellite itself.

The three parts

Landing page - has general information about the project and the SPHEREx satellite. It includes a 3D model of the satellite that we made with GLM 5.3 (the shapes are approximate). It lets the user explore how the satellite works, how one exposure becomes six pictures and a full spectrum, the mission timeline and what each part does in high detail.

Dome view – puts the user in the centre of a grass field covered by a dome that simulates the night sky. The sky can be switched between optical (DSS2), near-infrared (2MASS) and mid-infrared (AllWISE) views. Clicking any point shows its coordinates and how many SPHEREx frames are nearby. You can also type an object name like M42 or Sirius and go straight to it.

Pro view is a dashboard for the point you clicked. You can search the IRSA archive by object name or position in the sky and open the real SPHEREx FITS images. FITS is the standard image format astronomers use; it stores the pixel values and a header that describes them. You can blink between the six detector bands to compare the same spot at different wavelengths. You can also measure how bright something is with aperture photometry (the total light inside a small circle with the background taken out) and see which catalogued object is actually sitting there.

Try it.

Open the link and look around the dome.

Switch the sky layers and click a point, or type an object name like M42.

Press “Investigate this region”.

In the Pro view, search an object like M31 or Orion, open an image, compare the bands and measure the brightness.

What is real, and what is simulated?

We want to be clear about this. The Dome sky is survey imagery (DSS2, 2MASS, AllWISE); it is not SPHEREx data. The Dome observer is simulated at latitude 30° S at a fixed moment, so it is not the user's location or the live sky. “Frames nearby” counts frame centres close to the point, not exact coverage. The 3D spacecraft, the orbit position and the clouds on Earth are illustrative, not live. The real SPHEREx data only appears in the Pro view.

Who it helps

Mainly students who are interested in astronomy and want to help in the field but are put off because the professional software looks so complicated. The Dome gives them an easy way in, and the Pro view lets them touch real data the same way a professional does.

Limits and setbacks

The traffic limit is 2,500 people, so the app can only handle that many users at a time.

The Dome fell below our expectations because we ran out of time. The sky is soft when you zoom in, so the Dome is for finding your way around, and the detail is in the Pro view.

The data comes from older NASA data and is not updated live. Updating it is hard because the backend is heavy and slow to work with, and this was a real pain for us during the hackathon.

Tools

JavaScript, Three.js, Python (numpy, astropy, scipy) and GLM 5.3 for the 3D model.

projectDetails.name: ASTRO HEALTH CHECK
projectDetails.summary:
"ASTRO HEALTH CHECK" is a little software I built to make daily health checks easy for astronauts, for the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge. It works without internet, and everything stays on your own device.

When you open it, you see three big buttons: add your daily log, see your health report, or open the emergency guide. If more than one person shares the app, each crew member gets their own history.

The daily log asks one simple question at a time: heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, oxygen, breathing, sleep and exercise. If you don't have the right device, it doesn't leave you stuck. It shows an easy way to measure by hand, like counting your pulse, or just asks how you're feeling. You can skip anything you can't do.

The health report tells you how you're doing in plain words. A body figure lights up green, yellow or red, and you can tap any part to see what it means. Below that are the actions you should take, and a graph that shows how your health is changing over time.

If something serious comes up, the emergency guide walks you through what to do, starting with a heart attack. Temperature works in °C or °F, and the app remembers your choice.

You can add a shortcut for this in a web browser, so it opens like a normal app.
projectDetails.details: Astro Health Check is a small offline software I built for the NASA Space Apps 2026 Health Monitoring challenge, to help astronauts look after their health on long missions when a doctor on Earth isn’t always a quick call away. It needs internet for first opening though. Each day, the app asks simple questions about heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, oxygen, breathing, sleep and exercise, and if a device isn’t available it shows an easy way to check by hand. It then turns the answers into a health report: a body figure that lights up green, yellow or red, clear next steps, and a graph of how your health is changing over time. If something serious happens, an emergency guide gives calm, step-by-step help for situations like a heart attack or trouble breathing. Each crew member keeps their own history, and everything stays on the device. It installs on a phone like a normal app and works without internet.

projectDetails.name: THE SILENT EXPLORERS
projectDetails.summary:
THE SILENT EXPLORERS is an interactive educational web experience that tells the stories of spacecraft, rovers, landers and scientific instruments left across the Moon, Mars and deep space. It explores how machines that have completed their missions, become inactive or continued travelling have contributed to humanity's understanding of the universe.

Organised into seven chapters, the project transforms space history into an engaging journey through storytelling, authentic NASA photographs, interactive 3D spacecraft models, narrated experiences, mission timelines and educational activities.

Developed using HTML, CSS and JavaScript, the website integrates NASA's Image and Video Library API for discovering mission photographs and uses Google's model-viewer component to display GLB-format 3D models. It also features a searchable Mission Atlas and an Explorer Constellation where visitors collect stars and earn milestone badges as they complete chapters.

The project uses resources from NASA's Image and Video Library, NASA 3D Resources, NASA Science, the National Space Science Data Center and other credited sources. It is deployed through Netlify, making the experience accessible online.

Our mission is to make space science engaging for students while preserving the stories and scientific legacies of humanity's robotic explorers.
projectDetails.details:
THE SILENT EXPLORERS is an interactive educational web experience that brings the stories of humanity's robotic explorers back to life. It focuses on spacecraft, rovers, landers and scientific instruments left on the Moon, Mars and throughout deep space. The project explores what these machines were designed to do, what they discovered and how their scientific contributions continue to influence our understanding of the universe.

What does it do and how does it work?

The website takes visitors on a seven-chapter journey through space exploration. Each chapter combines scientific explanations, storytelling, NASA photographs, narrated scenes, interactive 3D models, mission timelines and educational activities.

Visitors can explore spacecraft models by rotating and zooming, discover mission photographs through NASA's Image and Video Library API, and investigate additional missions through the Mission Atlas. An Explorer Constellation allows visitors to collect stars and unlock milestone badges as they complete chapters.

What benefits does it have?

The project makes complex space science more accessible and engaging, particularly for school students. It encourages independent exploration, improves awareness of historical space missions and introduces scientific concepts through interactive experiences rather than conventional text-based learning.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to inspire the next generation of scientists, engineers and explorers. We want visitors to understand that even when a spacecraft becomes inactive or completes its mission, its discoveries and engineering legacy can continue benefiting humanity. The project also encourages appreciation of Earth's uniqueness and the importance of scientific exploration.

What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed using HTML, CSS and JavaScript. NASA's Image and Video Library API provides access to mission photographs, while NASA's 3D Resources collection supplies GLB models. Google's model-viewer component, delivered through jsDelivr, enables browser-based 3D visualisation. The Web Speech API provides narration, JavaScript manages interactions and progress tracking, and Netlify hosts the finished website. Additional research resources include NASA Science, the NASA National Space Science Data Center and NASA's Scientific Visualization Studio.

How is the project creative?

Our creativity lies in transforming space hardware into an interconnected storytelling experience. Instead of simply listing technical specifications, we present missions through a cinematic seven-chapter narrative. Real space imagery, interactive 3D exploration, narration, science activities and the collectible constellation combine education with discovery and engagement.

What factors did our team consider?

We considered scientific accuracy, educational value, accessibility, ease of navigation, visual engagement, performance and reliability. We distinguished between inactive spacecraft, completed missions and spacecraft still operating or travelling. projectDetails.summary:
This project, **“Abandoned but Not Forgotten: The Legacy of NASA’s Equipment on the Moon,”** explores four important pieces of equipment left behind on the lunar surface during NASA’s Apollo missions: the Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV), Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP), Lunar Module Descent Stage, and Lunar Laser Ranging Retroreflector (LRRR).

The project explains the purpose, design, working principles, and scientific importance of each piece of equipment. It also describes why these machines and instruments were left on the Moon after completing their missions. While some equipment helped astronauts explore the lunar surface, other instruments collected valuable scientific data about the Moon and its environment.

Although these objects are no longer actively used by astronauts, they remain important evidence of human achievements in space exploration. Their contributions continue to support our understanding of the Moon and inspire future missions.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Abandoned but Not Forgotten: The Legacy of NASA’s Equipment on the Moon

This project focuses on four important pieces of equipment left behind on the Moon during NASA’s Apollo missions: the Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV), Apollo Lunar Surface Experiments Package (ALSEP), Lunar Module Descent Stage, and Lunar Laser Ranging Retroreflector (LRRR).

Through storytelling, the project explores the history, purpose, construction, working principles, and contributions of these objects to lunar exploration. It explains how each piece of equipment helped astronauts explore the Moon, conduct scientific experiments, land safely, or support long-term research. The project also highlights why these objects were left on the lunar surface after their missions ended.

By presenting their stories in a simple and engaging way, the project aims to help people understand that these objects are not merely abandoned equipment. They are valuable reminders of human curiosity, scientific progress, and the achievements of space exploration.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project ASTR0-NEX
projectDetails.summary:
Project Summary

We are developing a web-based platform that harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS satellite active fire hotspot data to create a unified Burning Activity Calendar. The application integrates historical fire observations spanning more than two decades and processes them into a consistent format for meaningful comparison and analysis. Users can explore fire activity through interactive maps, calendar-based heatmaps, historical trends, and regional analytics. The platform also identifies unusual increases in burning activity and highlights recurring high-risk periods by comparing current observations with historical patterns.

By addressing differences in satellite sensors, spatial resolutions, and detection characteristics, our solution aims to provide a more consistent understanding of global burning activity, including wildfires and agricultural burns. This platform can support emergency responders, scientists, and land managers in monitoring fire patterns, anticipating critical periods, improving preparedness, and making more informed decisions for fire management and environmental protection.
projectDetails.details: Project Details – Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hotspots 1. What does the project do and how does it work? Our project is a web-based platform designed to harmonize active fire hotspot data collected by NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite sensors. It integrates historical satellite observations spanning more than two decades into a consistent dataset for analyzing global burning activity, including wildfires and agricultural burns. The system collects hotspot data from NASA FIRMS, processes and cleans the datasets, standardizes their temporal and spatial information, and applies harmonization techniques to address differences between the satellite sensors. The processed data is presented through an interactive map, a burning activity calendar, historical trend charts, and regional analytics. Users can select an area of interest, explore historical burning patterns, compare different time periods, and identify unusual increases in fire activity. 2. What are the benefits? - Combines MODIS and VIIRS observations into a more consistent analytical dataset. - Provides access to historical burning activity patterns. - Helps identify seasonal burning trends and critical periods. - Highlights unusual changes in hotspot activity. - Makes complex satellite data easier to understand through interactive visualizations. - Supports better monitoring and data-driven decision-making. 3. What is the intended impact? Our goal is to support emergency responders, scientists, environmental researchers, and land managers by providing a better understanding of when and where burning activity occurs. The platform aims to improve fire monitoring, help identify periods of unusually high burning activity, support early preparedness, and contribute to more informed fire management strategies. It can also help researchers study long-term changes in global burning patterns and their environmental implications. 4. What tools, programming languages, and software are used? Frontend: - React.js - HTML5 - CSS3 - JavaScript - Tailwind CSS Backend: - Python - FastAPI Data Processing and Analysis: - Pandas - NumPy - GeoPandas Database: - PostgreSQL - PostGIS Data Visualization and Mapping: - Leaflet.js - Recharts Machine Learning and Analysis: - Scikit-learn Data Source: - NASA FIRMS (Fire Information for Resource Management System) - MODIS and VIIRS active fire datasets The platform uses satellite datasets and software-based data processing; no specialized physical hardware is required for the proposed system. 5. How is the project creative and innovative? The innovative aspect of our project is transforming fragmented satellite fire observations into a unified, interactive burning activity calendar. Instead of simply displaying individual satellite hotspots, our platform focuses on harmonizing observations, revealing long-term patterns, and making historical comparisons easier. The combination of: - A unified MODIS and VIIRS data analysis approach. - An interactive geographical burning activity calendar. - Historical and seasonal pattern analysis. - Unusual burning activity detection. - Region-specific insights. creates a more accessible way to explore satellite-based fire information and understand changes in burning activity over time. 6. What factors did our team consider? During the design of the project, we considered: - Differences in spatial resolution and detection capabilities between MODIS and VIIRS. - Data quality, confidence levels, and possible duplicate observations. - Consistent spatial and temporal aggregation. - Historical data availability and sensor coverage periods. - Usability and accessibility for different types of users. - Accuracy and reliability of analytical results. - Scalability to support different geographical regions. - The importance of distinguishing unusual hotspot activity from confirmed wildfire emergencies. We designed the project with the aim of making complex satellite observations more understandable, comparable, and useful for real-world environmental monitoring and decision-making.

projectDetails.name: M&M Family By ASTRA4
projectDetails.summary: M&M FAMILY – Moon & Mars is an interactive educational website developed by Team ASTRA4 to address NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026's theme, "Abandoned but Not Forgotten." We developed a digital exploration archive that brings together the stories of NASA's lost, unsuccessful, and abandoned Moon and Mars missions. The website features separate Moon and Mars exploration sections, individual spacecraft pages, historical timelines, animated stories for children, narrated documentaries for adults, detailed research reports, original NASA/JPL archival references, and interactive quizzes. By transforming scattered technical information and mission records into an engaging storytelling experience, our project directly addresses the challenge of making forgotten space mission stories accessible and understandable, especially for school-age students and space enthusiasts. It is important because unsuccessful missions are also valuable parts of space exploration history. Their failures provide important scientific and engineering lessons that can help improve future missions. Through this platform, we aim to preserve these stories, increase awareness of past space exploration efforts, encourage curiosity about science and technology, and inspire younger generations to explore the mysteries of space. Our central message is that even when a mission fails, the knowledge it leaves behind should never be forgotten.
projectDetails.details:
M&M FAMILY – Moon & Mars is an interactive educational website developed by Team ASTRA4 for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, based on the challenge “Abandoned but Not Forgotten.” The project aims to preserve and share the stories of NASA's lost, unsuccessful, and abandoned Moon and Mars missions in an engaging and educational way. It brings together mission histories, spacecraft details, research reports, NASA/JPL archival documents, and photographs in a single platform. Users can explore different Moon and Mars missions through animated storytelling for children, narrated documentaries for adults, detailed text reports, historical timelines, and interactive quizzes. The website is developed using React, HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with browser-based SpeechSynthesis for narration and the Web Audio API for sound effects. We used Google Gemini as an AI assistant for code structure, summaries, and quiz content, while referring to authentic NASA/JPL resources for mission information. The creativity of our project lies in transforming complex technical information into an interactive storytelling experience that makes space science accessible and interesting for different age groups. While developing the project, we considered factors such as educational value, accessibility, user experience, authenticity of information, engagement, and preservation of mission history. The project benefits students, educators, and space enthusiasts by making scientific information easier to understand, encouraging curiosity about space exploration, and highlighting the valuable lessons learned from unsuccessful missions. Our intended impact is to inspire future generations, increase awareness of forgotten space missions, and demonstrate that even missions that fail can contribute to scientific progress and future exploration.

"Missions may fail, spacecraft may be lost, but the knowledge they leave behind helps humanity explore further."

projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Left Behind: Stories from the Moon and Mars

Left Behind: Stories from the Moon and Mars is an interactive educational website that explores NASA hardware left behind on the Moon and Mars after space missions. It helps users discover the history and importance of these objects through an engaging storytelling experience.

The website features interactive Moon and Mars maps with clickable markers representing mission locations, including Apollo 11, Apollo 15, Viking 1, Spirit, Opportunity, and Ingenuity. When users select a location, they can explore information about the mission, the hardware left behind, why it remained there, and its current status. Each object is presented through a first-person storytelling approach, making the experience more interesting and understandable. The website also includes voice narration using the browser's Web Speech API, a guided tour, and navigation between locations.

The project was developed using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and SVG for the interactive maps and website interface. The Web Speech API is used for voice narration, and Netlify is used for hosting and deployment.

The creative aspect of our project is its storytelling approach. Instead of presenting only facts and timelines, we allow users to explore the stories of abandoned space hardware as if the objects themselves are speaking. We considered ease of use, educational value, accessibility, simple navigation, and engagement while designing the website.

Our intended impact is to create curiosity about space exploration, improve awareness of NASA's past missions, and encourage students to learn more about the history and legacy of human exploration beyond Earth.

Through scientific information, real photographs, and creative storytelling, this project brings these forgotten machines back to life. It reminds us that although their missions have ended, their discoveries and contributions will remain part of human history.

projectDetails.name: ASTRIS & ASTRA
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRIS: Onboard Crew Health Monitoring and Triage System

ASTRIS is a health monitoring platform designed to support astronauts during space missions, especially when communication with Earth is limited. In space, astronauts may face health issues that need immediate attention, so having a reliable onboard health system is important.

Our project provides a single platform where crew members can enter and monitor their vital signs, such as heart rate, blood oxygen, body temperature, blood pressure and glucose levels. Its main innovation is ASTRA AI, an intelligent health assistant that analyses the entered health data, identifies possible health risks and provides quick guidance on what to do next.

ASTRIS also includes features such as health history tracking, body system monitoring, triage levels, check-up scheduling, response logs and printable medical reports. It also provides information about solar radiation using NASA's space-weather data.

Our aim is to make health monitoring easier and help astronauts respond to possible medical emergencies, even without continuous support from Earth.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRIS & ASTRA [Autonomous Space Telemetry & Response Assistant]

An Offline-First Astronaut Health Monitoring and Triage System

1. Project Overview

Our Team ASTRIS presents ASTRA (Autonomous Space Telemetry & Response Assistant) which is an offline-first astronaut health monitoring and triage platform designed to support crew members during space missions, particularly missions to the Moon and Mars.

During long-duration space missions, astronauts may experience health-related problems due to isolation, radiation exposure, changes in their environment and limited access to immediate medical assistance. Communication delays between Earth and distant space missions can also make it difficult to receive timely medical guidance.

ASTRIS aims to address this challenge by providing an onboard platform that helps astronauts monitor their health, identify unusual changes in vital signs and receive immediate guidance without depending on continuous communication with Earth.

The platform combines health monitoring, rule-based analysis, an intelligent assistant, medical response logging and environmental information in one dashboard.

2. Our Main Innovation – ASTRA AI

The most important innovation of our project is ASTRA AI (Autonomous Space Telemetry & Response Assistant), an intelligent onboard health assistant designed specifically for astronaut healthcare.

ASTRA helps astronauts understand their health condition by analyzing the readings entered into ASTRIS. It can answer questions about health parameters, explain active alerts, identify the current triage status and provide guidance on the next steps.

Unlike a system that depends entirely on cloud-based AI services, ASTRA is designed to work using information available on the device itself. This makes it useful in situations where communication with Earth is delayed or unavailable.

ASTRA includes quick actions such as:

  • Checking the astronaut's current health status.
  • Explaining the reason behind a particular triage level.
  • Identifying active health alerts.
  • Providing information about individual vital signs.
  • Explaining how to measure parameters such as SpO₂.
  • Suggesting the next health check.
  • Explaining how the analysis model works.

ASTRA currently uses a rule-based approach rather than a medically validated AI diagnostic model. Its purpose is to provide understandable triage guidance, not to replace doctors or flight surgeons.

3. Website Features and Functionality

Our website is designed as a central control dashboard where astronauts can access all the health monitoring and response features.

A. Overview Dashboard

The overview page provides a quick summary of the crew member's health status. It displays the current triage level, available health readings, alerts and check-up schedule. It also provides shortcuts to save a check-in, ask ASTRA, contact a medical officer and generate a handover report.

B. Crew Member Management

The platform allows users to create, select, rename and remove crew member profiles. This makes it possible to maintain separate health records for different astronauts.

C. Health Monitoring and Check-ins

Astronauts can manually enter or update their health readings. The system supports important parameters such as:

  • Heart rate
  • Blood oxygen level (SpO₂)
  • Body temperature
  • Systolic blood pressure
  • Blood glucose
  • Sleep and mood information

The readings are saved as check-ins, allowing the system to maintain a history of health information. Sample normal and emergency drill readings are also available for demonstration.

D. Triage and Alert System

This feature evaluates the entered readings and identifies possible health concerns. It uses different levels of response, including normal monitoring, rechecking readings and escalation when necessary.

The system explains why a particular triage level has been assigned and highlights readings that require attention. This helps astronauts understand when they should recheck a measurement or seek medical assistance.

E. ASTRA AI Assistant

ASTRA acts as the onboard health assistant. Users can interact with it through a chat interface and ask questions about their readings, alerts and recommended next steps. It uses the available health data on the device to provide contextual guidance.

F. Body Systems Map

The body systems section provides a visual representation of different body systems and their monitoring status. It helps users identify which systems may require attention.

It uses status indicators such as Normal, Recheck, Escalate, Check Sensor and No Data to make health information easier to understand.

G. Model Analysis and Evaluation

This section explains how the health analysis system works. It considers reference ranges, unusual readings, personal baselines and changes in readings over time.

The website also provides options to:

  • Add simulated health history.
  • Import baseline reference data.
  • Run model benchmarks.
  • View per-measure statistics.
  • Evaluate how the model responds to different sample readings.

The system uses simulated data for demonstration and testing. It does not claim to have been validated using actual astronaut medical records.

H. Health History and Trend Analysis

ASTRIS stores previous check-ins and allows users to view changes in their health readings over time. Trend graphs display the last 12 saved values for a selected parameter.

This helps identify repeated unusual readings or gradual changes that might otherwise go unnoticed.

I. Check-up Scheduling

The check schedule feature allows users to set intervals for regular health check-ins. The system keeps track of missed checks and includes an escalation window following a critical check-in.

This encourages regular monitoring rather than waiting until a health problem becomes serious.

J. Response Log and Medical Handover

The response log records actions such as saved check-ins, acknowledgements, rechecks and medical officer contacts.

Users can also generate printable handover reports containing relevant information that can assist in communicating the astronaut's health status to medical personnel.

These records help maintain a history of actions taken during a health-related event.

K. Solar Radiation Monitoring

Space radiation is an important environmental risk for astronauts. ASTRIS includes a solar radiation section that connects with NASA's DONKI (Space Weather Database of Notifications, Knowledge, Information).

It allows users to check available solar flare and space-weather information, helping them remain aware of potential radiation-related environmental events.

ASTRIS does not directly measure radiation dose. Actual radiation monitoring requires appropriate onboard dosimeters.

L. Data Import and Export

The platform supports importing and exporting health records in CSV and JSON formats. This makes it easier to maintain, transfer and analyze health information when required.

The records and response logs are stored locally on the device, supporting the platform's offline-first approach.

4. How the System Works

The basic working process of ASTRIS can be explained in five steps:

  1. Data Entry: The astronaut enters health readings through the website.
  2. Data Analysis: The system compares readings with expected reference ranges and available personal health baselines.
  3. Risk Identification: Unusual readings, repeated changes and possible sensor errors are identified.
  4. Triage and Guidance: The system determines an appropriate triage level and ASTRA provides understandable guidance.
  5. Record Keeping: The check-in, alerts and actions taken are stored in the health history and response log.

Technologies Used

  • Frontend Development: HTML for building the website structure and user interface.
  • Deployment: Vercel for hosting and making the website accessible online.
  • Data Management: CSV and JSON formats for importing and exporting health records.
  • NASA Data Source: NASA DONKI API for accessing solar flare and space-weather information.
  • Hardware: Currently a software-based prototype. Bluetooth wearable sensors are planned for future integration.

5. What Makes ASTRIS Different?

The main strength of ASTRIS is that it brings several important functions together in a single onboard platform.

Instead of having separate systems for health readings, alerts, medical guidance and record keeping, ASTRIS combines them into one interface.

Its offline-first design reduces dependence on continuous communication with Earth. Its personal baseline and trend analysis features also help identify changes rather than looking at individual readings alone.

The integration of ASTRA, health triage, response logging and NASA space-weather information makes it a useful prototype for exploring the future of astronaut healthcare.

6. Future Scope

Although the current version is a functional website prototype, several improvements can make ASTRIS more suitable for actual space missions.

  • Wearable Sensor Integration: Connecting Bluetooth-enabled devices to automatically collect heart rate, SpO₂, skin temperature and other available health readings.
  • Real-Time Monitoring: Continuously monitoring astronaut health without requiring manual data entry.
  • Advanced AI Models: Developing more advanced predictive models using validated medical datasets.
  • Radiation Sensor Integration: Connecting appropriate radiation monitoring hardware to track actual radiation exposure.
  • Improved Medical Support: Developing better communication and reporting systems for astronauts and medical officers.
  • Mission-Specific Customization: Adapting the platform to the requirements of future Moon and Mars missions.

7. Expected Impact

ASTRIS aims to improve how astronaut health information is monitored and managed during space exploration. By combining continuous monitoring as a future goal, early identification of unusual readings, triage guidance and organized medical records, the system can help astronauts respond more effectively to potential health concerns.

It is particularly relevant to long-duration missions where communication delays and limited medical resources make onboard health support important.

8. Conclusion

ASTRIS is our attempt to address one of the important challenges of future space exploration: keeping astronauts healthy and safe when immediate medical support from Earth may not be available.

Through its health monitoring dashboard, ASTRA intelligent assistant, triage system, trend analysis and space-weather monitoring, ASTRIS provides a unified approach to astronaut health management.

Our vision is to develop ASTRIS into a reliable onboard health support platform that helps astronauts make informed decisions and supports safer missions to the Moon, Mars and beyond.

projectDetails.name: AstroCare
projectDetails.summary: My team created a software in which you could keep track of your health while you are in space.The project is called AstroCare.Our challenge was to create a software through which astronauts could monitor their health while in space missions.I think this is important because many astronauts suffer from health issues after going to space
projectDetails.details:
AstroCare – Astronaut Health Companion

1. What does the project do, and how does it work?

AstroCare is a web-based health companion designed to help astronauts keep track of their health during space missions. Astronauts can enter important health information, such as heart rate, blood pressure, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep hours, and mood.

The website provides a daily health check-in, displays health trends, and gives simple educational feedback based on the information entered. It also includes information about different body systems, a mission checklist, and a spaceflight health guide. Users can save their records in the browser and export them as CSV files for later use.

2. What benefits does it have?

Living in space can be challenging for the human body and mind. AstroCare aims to make health tracking easier and more convenient for astronauts.

It helps them keep their health information organised, notice changes in their health over time, and pay attention to important areas such as sleep and mood. The health guides also help astronauts understand how space conditions can affect their bodies. Overall, the project encourages astronauts to take an active role in looking after their well-being.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The main goal of AstroCare is to support astronauts in staying healthy and well during long-duration space missions. We hope it will encourage regular health check-ins, improve awareness of physical and mental well-being, and help astronauts keep useful health records.

By making health information easier to track and understand, AstroCare could also support better communication with the crew's medical team when health concerns arise.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

We developed AstroCare using common web development technologies:

  • HTML5 – to build the structure of the website.
  • CSS3 – to create the design and layout.
  • JavaScript – to make the features interactive.
  • Browser Local Storage – to save health records and checklist progress on the user's device.
  • Canvas API – to display health trend charts.
  • CSV export – to allow users to download their health records.

The project runs in a web browser, so it does not require specialised hardware or medical sensors. Health information is entered manually, and the sample dashboard values are for demonstration purposes.

5. How is the project creative?

What makes AstroCare different is that it brings health tracking and space exploration together in one simple platform. Instead of focusing only on physical health, it also considers sleep, mood, and the mental challenges astronauts may experience in space.

We designed it with a modern, space-inspired interface and included interactive features such as health check-ins, charts, a mission checklist, and educational guides. Our aim was to make health monitoring feel simple, engaging, and relevant to the unique needs of astronauts.

6. What factors did the team consider?

While developing AstroCare, we considered the challenges astronauts may face during space missions, including:

  • Microgravity: How spending time in low gravity can affect the human body.
  • Radiation: The possible health risks of exposure to radiation in space.
  • Isolation: The effects of being away from family, friends, and Earth.
  • Physical health: The importance of monitoring basic health indicators.
  • Mental well-being: The role of sleep and mood in maintaining overall health.
  • Ease of use: Making the website simple and easy to navigate.
  • Accessibility: Keeping it lightweight and usable through a web browser.
  • Data management: Allowing users to save and export their records.
  • Medical safety: Making it clear that AstroCare is an educational prototype, not a certified medical device or a replacement for professional medical advice.

Our overall vision

With AstroCare, we wanted to create more than just a health-tracking website. We wanted to develop a simple and useful companion that reminds astronauts to look after themselves while exploring space. We believe that taking care of the people behind every space mission is just as important as the mission itself.

Project Astro Space

Project Astro Space is a digital storytelling project that explores the abandoned equipment and human-made objects left behind on the Moon and Mars during space exploration missions. The project aims to highlight the history, purpose, and importance of these objects through informative content and visual storytelling.

It presents how different space missions have used equipment such as landers, rovers, scientific instruments, and other mission hardware, and explains why some of them remain on planetary surfaces after their missions are completed.

By combining space science, historical information, images, and interactive storytelling, Project Astro Space aims to create awareness about humanity's exploration of other worlds. It also encourages people to understand the legacy of past missions and their contribution to future space research.

Our goal is to make space exploration history interesting, educational, and accessible to everyone.
projectDetails.details:
Our project, Astro Space, focuses on exploring abandoned human-made equipment and objects on the Moon and Mars. It aims to create awareness about space exploration history by explaining what equipment has been left behind, why it was abandoned, and how it may affect future space missions.

The project will present information through a simple and interactive digital storytelling platform. Users can explore different abandoned objects, understand their original purposes, learn why they are no longer in use, and discover their importance for future space exploration.

The main benefit of this project is to make space science and planetary exploration easier and more interesting for students and the general public. It also highlights the importance of responsible space exploration and the challenges of managing human-made objects beyond Earth.

We plan to use NASA's publicly available information, images, and educational resources, along with Google Sites for presenting the project. ChatGPT will assist with organizing information and developing project content.

The creative aspect of our project is presenting space exploration history in a simple, educational, and engaging storytelling format. Our team considers scientific accuracy, educational value, user accessibility, environmental awareness, and the future of space exploration.

projectDetails.name: Echoes of Exploration
projectDetails.summary:
Echoes of Exploration is an interactive website that tells the stories behind the equipment humanity has sent to the Moon and Mars. Instead of listing technical specifications, it lets visitors explore each piece of hardware as a character in the story of exploration. Equipment cards for Apollo lunar modules, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, ALSEP, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, and Ingenuity each open a story popup. These popups cover why the machine was built, what it faced, and what it achieved. All stories are drawn from NASA's own published material and use NASA imagery and our own visuals.

The project makes space history approachable for students and the general public, and shows how each mission built on the one before it. It is built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript and hosted on GitHub Pages, so anyone can open it in a browser without installing anything.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works
Echoes of Exploration is a website that presents the Moon and Mars equipment humanity has sent into space as stories. Visitors browse equipment cards divided into Moon and Mars sections. These include the Apollo lunar modules, the Lunar Roving Vehicle, ALSEP, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, and Ingenuity. Clicking a card opens a popup that tells the story of that machine: why it was built, the challenges it faced, and what it achieved.

Benefits and intended impact
The site makes space exploration history easy to understand for students and the general public. Presenting each machine as a story, instead of a list of specifications, helps people connect with the missions. It also shows how each generation of equipment built on the work of the one before it.

Tools and technologies

  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with no frameworks
  • Mission data stored in a separate JavaScript data file, so new equipment can be added without changing the page code
  • Content sourced from NASA's official mission pages
  • Images from the NASA Image and Video Library, plus our own visuals for the lunar rover, Spirit and Opportunity, and Ingenuity
  • Version control with Git, hosted on GitHub Pages so it works in any browser

Creativity
The creative idea is to treat the equipment as characters, so each machine's "echo" of exploration is heard through its own story. The card-and-popup layout keeps the page clean while letting visitors choose how deep to go.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy: all facts come from NASA sources
  • Accessibility: the site is lightweight, works on any device, and needs no installation
  • Scalability: the data-driven structure lets us add more missions later
  • Clarity: the stories use simple language so non-experts can follow them
