projectDetails.name: Project ASTRO-X
projectDetails.summary:
Project ASTRO-X is an interactive 3D educational simulator designed to introduce users to the fundamentals of space mission planning and spacecraft design. Users can explore different mission objectives, assemble spacecraft using various components, monitor mass, power, cost and scientific capabilities, select orbital paths and launch vehicles, and experience a simulated launch with unexpected events.

The project transforms complex aerospace concepts into an engaging, hands-on learning experience. By allowing users to experiment with different spacecraft configurations and mission choices, it demonstrates how engineering decisions can influence mission outcomes. ORBIT ARCHITECT aims to make space exploration and mission design more accessible, encourage interest in aerospace engineering, and inspire users to understand the challenges behind real-world space missions.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRO-X is an interactive, browser-based 3D space mission design simulator that introduces users to the fundamentals of spacecraft engineering and mission planning. It allows users to experience the process of planning a space mission through a series of interactive stages.

Users begin by selecting a mission objective, such as Earth observation, deep-space communication, lunar orbit or a Mars flyby. They then assemble a spacecraft using different components, including solar panels, batteries, onboard computers and scientific instruments. The simulator provides mission diagnostics to help users consider important factors such as spacecraft mass, power requirements, budget and scientific capabilities. Users subsequently select an orbit and a suitable launch vehicle before entering a simulated launch sequence. During the simulation, unexpected events and anomalies require users to make decisions. A final mission report evaluates the outcome and provides a score.

The main benefit of ASTRO-X is that it makes complex aerospace engineering concepts more accessible through interactive experimentation rather than passive learning. It encourages users to understand how engineering decisions, resource limitations and mission requirements influence mission planning.

The project aims to promote interest in space exploration, aerospace engineering and STEM education, especially among students and beginners. Its creative approach combines a 3D space environment, spacecraft customization, interactive decision-making and mission evaluation into one educational experience.

The simulator was developed using HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Three.js for 3D graphics, Tailwind CSS for interface styling and the Web Audio API for sound effects. Google Fonts is used for typography. The project was designed with usability, visual engagement, interactive learning and the balance between mission objectives and limited resources in mind.

ASTRO-X is an educational simulation, not an operational spacecraft control system or a substitute for professional mission-planning software.

projectDetails.name: Project ASTROXZIA
projectDetails.summary:
Earth Information Jukebox is an accessibility or first Earth science platform that transforms real NASA and partner climate datasets into interactive sound. Instead of relying only on charts and graphs, the platform enables users to hear long term changes in Earth's systems through a custom "Earth Orchestra" sonification engine.

The project uses global temperature, atmospheric CO₂, Arctic sea ice, and sea level datasets to create a synchronized audio and visual experience. Each dataset is assigned a unique musical role , allowing users to hear how Earth's systems evolve and interact over time. The platform also includes live visualizations, transcript generation, voice narration, keyboard navigation, and WCAG-inspired accessibility features to support a wide range of users , including blind and low-vision audiences.

Earth Information Jukebox addresses the challenge by making complex Earth science data more understandable, engaging, and inclusive. By combining scientific accuracy, accessibility, and creative data sonification, the project helps transform environmental measurements into a human experience. Our goal is to help people not only see Earth's changing systems, but also hear and understand them in a completely new way.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

Earth Information Jukebox is an accessibility-first Earth science platform that transforms real climate and environmental datasets into interactive soundscapes. Instead of only displaying charts and graphs, the project allows users to hear changes in Earth's systems through sonification while simultaneously exploring synchronized visualizations, transcripts, and scientific context.

The platform uses verified datasets from NASA, NOAA, NSIDC, and the NASA Sea Level Change Team, including Global Surface Temperature, Atmospheric CO₂ Concentration, Arctic Sea Ice Extent, and Global Sea Level Rise records. These datasets are converted into sound using a custom Earth Orchestra sonification engine.

Each Earth system is assigned a unique musical role:

  • Global Temperature → Lead Voice
  • Atmospheric CO₂ → Harmony Layer
  • Arctic Sea Ice → Crystal Texture Layer
  • Sea Level Rise → Deep Bass Foundation
  • Climate Acceleration → Dynamic Trend Layer

As users move through time, they can hear Earth's changing systems evolve together while viewing synchronized charts, a planetary data orb, waveform analysis, and live transcripts.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The project is designed to make Earth science more accessible, engaging, and intuitive for a broader audience.

Key benefits include:

  • Improves accessibility for blind and low-vision users through sound and spoken narration.
  • Helps students and the general public understand long-term climate trends in a more intuitive way.
  • Creates a stronger emotional connection to Earth science data.
  • Provides an alternative method of scientific communication beyond traditional graphs and tables.
  • Demonstrates how multisensory experiences can increase engagement with climate education.

Our goal is to help people not only see Earth's changing systems, but also hear and experience them.

Tools and Technologies Used

Languages

  • HTML5
  • CSS3
  • JavaScript (ES6)

Web Technologies

  • Web Audio API
  • HTML Canvas API
  • Speech Synthesis API
  • Responsive Web Design

Data Sources

  • NASA GISS GISTEMP
  • NOAA Global Monitoring Laboratory
  • NSIDC Arctic Sea Ice Index
  • NASA Sea Level Change Team

Design and Development

  • GitHub
  • GitHub Pages
  • PowerPoint
  • WCAG 2.1 Accessibility Principles

Creativity and Innovation

Rather than mapping scientific values directly to simple tones, Earth Information Jukebox introduces the concept of an Earth Orchestra, where multiple planetary systems interact simultaneously as components of a living soundscape.

This approach turns climate data into a multisensory experience that combines science, accessibility, education, and sound design. Users can hear warming temperatures, increasing atmospheric CO₂, shrinking Arctic sea ice, and rising sea levels as interconnected parts of the same planetary story.

Factors Considered During Development

Our team focused on several key priorities:

  • Scientific accuracy and trustworthy data sources.
  • Accessibility for users with different abilities.
  • Educational value for students and the public.
  • Intuitive user experience and navigation.
  • Performance on low-spec devices.
  • Real-time audio generation without external services.
  • Visual and auditory synchronization.
  • Scalability for future Earth science datasets.

Earth Information Jukebox demonstrates how science, technology, accessibility, and creativity can work together to transform complex Earth observations into a human experience that is easier to understand, remember, and share.

projectDetails.summary: FireWatch is a web-based platform designed to harmonize MODIS and VIIRS satellite active fire hotspot data into a unified system for monitoring global burning activity. The platform aims to overcome differences between satellite sensors by standardizing fire observations and organizing them into a consistent spatial and temporal dataset. Users can explore historical fire patterns through an interactive map, a burning activity calendar, and visual analytics that compare fire activity across different regions and time periods. The system also highlights unusual increases in hotspot activity by comparing current observations with historical patterns. By transforming complex satellite observations into accessible and meaningful insights, FireWatch supports early awareness, wildfire monitoring, and informed decision-making. It is designed to assist emergency responders, scientists, environmental researchers, and land managers in identifying critical fire periods, understanding long-term burning trends, and improving fire management strategies.
projectDetails.details:
FireWatch: Harmonizing MODIS and VIIRS Satellite Data for Global Fire Activity Monitoring

FireWatch is a web-based platform designed to bring MODIS and VIIRS satellite active-fire observations together into a common format for easier visualization and analysis.

The platform aims to help users explore fire activity across different locations and time periods using interactive maps, daily fire activity calendars, and historical data visualizations. By combining observations from two satellite sources, FireWatch helps users understand fire patterns and compare the information provided by different satellite sensors.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

  • Makes satellite fire observations easier to explore and understand.
  • Helps identify geographical and temporal patterns in fire activity.
  • Supports awareness of wildfire activity and potential environmental risks.
  • Provides an accessible way for students, researchers, and interested users to explore satellite fire data.

Tools and Technologies:

  • Programming Language: Python
  • Framework: Streamlit
  • Data Processing: Pandas
  • Visualization: Plotly
  • Data Sources: NASA FIRMS MODIS and VIIRS active-fire datasets.
  • Development Environment: Visual Studio Code
  • Version Control: Git and GitHub

Creativity and Innovation:

The creative aspect of FireWatch is its focus on bringing observations from two different satellite systems into one accessible visualization platform. Instead of examining separate datasets independently, users can explore their observations through a unified interface while retaining information about their original satellite sources.

The project considers differences in satellite observations, data quality, spatial resolution, timestamps, and the importance of avoiding misleading duplicate fire counts.

FireWatch aims to make satellite-based fire monitoring more understandable, accessible, and useful for environmental awareness and further research.

challengeDetails.title: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots
challengeDetails.excerpt: Understanding how burning activity is distributed across our planet over time, including wildfires and agricultural burns intense enough to be detected by satellite sensors, enables us to anticipate critical periods, guide monitoring efforts, and improve fire response.  Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly, leaving fire managers without a consistent picture of when and where burning has occurred. Your challenge is to build a web application that harmonizes these records into a burning activity calendar based on active fire hotspots,  enabling early warning and emergency responders, scientists, and land managers to examine historical fire patterns, unusual conditions, and critical periods within a selected area of interest.

projectDetails.name: Project Axeell
projectDetails.summary:
Echoes Beyond Earth by Team AXEELL is a mobile-first, interactive web field journal built for the "Abandoned, but Not Forgotten" challenge. Developed using open web technologies (HTML, CSS, and JavaScript) and powered by verified NASA open data, the platform transforms discarded space hardware into accessible human stories.
Rather than treating retired equipment as mere space debris, our application guides users through a five-step interactive journey across the Moon, Mars, and deep space. Users can explore a curated Field Archive featuring five iconic artifacts—including Apollo lunar rovers and laser retroreflectors, Mars Pathfinder and Sojourner, and Voyager 1—trace their missions through an interactive chronological timeline, test their knowledge with a clue-based quiz, and verify every fact against linked NASA archival records.
By turning complex archival datasets into a cohesive, accessible digital experience that runs on any device without installation, Echoes Beyond Earth preserves humanity’s off-world heritage and makes space exploration inspiring and easy for anyone to follow.
projectDetails.details:
AXEELL: Echoes Beyond Earth is a mobile-first interactive field journal about hardware NASA left on the Moon, Mars and in deep space. Visitors follow a photo-story trail, explore an artifact archive (Lunar Roving Vehicle, Apollo laser retroreflector, Sojourner, Pathfinder and its airbags, Voyager 1), travel a 1969–1997 timeline, and take a short quiz that reveals field-note clues. Every field note links to its NASA source record.

Benefits and intended impact: it makes space heritage easy to understand for students and the public. It shows that “abandoned” equipment still carries science (the Apollo reflectors are still used for lunar laser ranging) and human stories. It also builds the habit of checking sources.

Tools: HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single mobile-first web page, using Google Fonts (Space Grotesk, DM Sans, DM Mono). Our submission slides were made with PptxGenJS and the demo video with Python (Pillow) and FFmpeg.

Creativity: we treat each object as “a message in place” and tell the story as a field journal, not a data dashboard. It combines archival photos, short original notes and a quiz.

Factors considered: accuracy (facts only from NASA records), readability on phones, no install needed, short text, and credit for every image.

projectDetails.name: DeltaPulse
projectDetails.summary: DeltaPulse is a web-based coastal monitoring and visualization platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to explore shoreline changes and environmental conditions in the Sundarbans. Built using React, Vite, JavaScript, MapLibre GL JS, and Recharts, it integrates satellite imagery, geographic information, and environmental datasets. The platform uses NASA GIBS (VIIRS NOAA-20), ASF DAAC (NISAR GCOV), Open-Meteo Marine and Weather APIs, Esri World Imagery, and CARTO. GeoJSON represents shoreline boundaries and geographic features, while raster and vector layers display satellite imagery and spatial data. Interactive maps, layer controls, location selection, coherence filtering, and time-series charts help users compare shoreline positions from 2015 to 2025 and explore coastal changes. Deployed through Cloudflare, DeltaPulse brings diverse data sources into one interface, making complex environmental information more accessible and easier to understand.
projectDetails.details:
DeltaPulse

Continuous Coastal Monitoring of the Sundarbans

DeltaPulse is a web-based coastal monitoring platform built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge. It lets users select a coastal area, with the Sundarbans as our focus, and continuously monitor shoreline change, land subsidence, wave height, sea-surface temperature, wind and precipitation. It is designed to record these changes and connect automatically with NASA’s NISAR data.

How It Works

Users see satellite imagery, shoreline boundaries and environmental data on one interactive map. They can toggle layers, filter by coherence, compare shorelines from 2015 to 2025, and view changes in charts.

Data Sources

NASA GIBS, ASF DAAC (NISAR GCOV products), Open-Meteo Marine and Weather APIs, Esri World Imagery and CARTO.

Impact

DeltaPulse brings scattered coastal data into one place, helping researchers, planners and local communities track erosion and subsidence in the Sundarbans and protect people and mangroves.

Tools

React, Vite, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, MapLibre GL JS, Recharts, GeoJSON, Python and Java, deployed on Cloudflare.

Creativity

It combines satellite and vector map layers with ocean and weather data in one interface, making complex NISAR radar data easy for non-experts to explore.

Factors Considered

Reliability, availability and update frequency of the data sources

Ease of use for non-technical users

The Sundarbans’ vulnerability to sea-level rise, erosion and storms

Automatic connection to NISAR data for continuous monitoring

projectDetails.name: Project Bhairava
projectDetails.summary:
We developed an interactive educational website called NASA's Forgotten Machines to introduce school-age students to the spacecraft, rovers, landers, and scientific instruments left across the Solar System. The platform features an interactive machine explorer covering the Moon, Mars, and deep space, with mission histories, scientific discoveries, images, timelines, and operational statuses.

The project addresses the challenge by transforming complex space exploration information into an engaging and easy-to-understand digital experience. Students can explore individual machines, learn why they were sent into space, discover what scientific knowledge they contributed, and understand whether they are still operating or inactive. An interactive quiz further encourages learning.

This project is important because these machines represent decades of human innovation and scientific discovery. By preserving and sharing their stories, we inspire the next generation to develop curiosity about space, science, engineering, and exploration.
projectDetails.details: NASA Hardware Explorer is an interactive website that tells the story of the equipment NASA has left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. A year slider (1960 to today) animates the planets and shows each spacecraft’s position, and clicking one reveals its status, its distance from Earth and how long a radio message takes to reach it, calculated from distance and the speed of light. It also includes a searchable mission library, a Voyager power simulator, a chart of how much longer the rovers lasted than planned, and a quiz, all supported by a written report. It helps school-age space enthusiasts explore ideas like light-travel time, nuclear power in space and mission lifetimes in a way a list of facts cannot, and it aims to spark curiosity about space engineering. I built it with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, drawing the map on the HTML canvas with no external libraries, using a laptop and a web browser, with help from Claude, an AI assistant, for drafting the code and report. Its creative idea is to turn hardware into a timeline you can scrub, so students can feel distance instead of reading numbers. I considered accuracy by using simplified orbits and approximate data that I label clearly, a plain-language style for the audience, and a lightweight single-file design that works on phones. The site also states that it is an independent educational project and not an official NASA website.

projectDetails.name: Mission Control
projectDetails.summary:
Mission Control is a browser based design game built for the Space Mission Design Game challenge. Players take on the role of mission architect, allocating a limited pool of mass, power, fuel, and budget across a lunar landing, Mars rover, or satellite deployment scenario, then find out whether their design actually survives the trip.

What sets it apart is what happens next. Mid-mission, an unscripted event tests whatever margin the player kept in reserve, and every result — success or failure — gets matched to a real NASA mission that faced the same pressure. Cut your power margin too thin, and you might see echoes of a mission that hit the same problem decades earlier.

The constraints aren't invented. They're calibrated against NASA's General Mission Analysis Tool, the Small Spacecraft Technology State-of-the-Art Report, and mission data from the NSSDCA. We built this because the hardest part of engineering has never been the math — it's learning to feel a trade-off before you've made one.
projectDetails.details:
What it does: players pick an objective — lunar landing, Mars rover deployment, or satellite placement — then divide a fixed resource pool across mass, power, fuel, and budget using a slider interface. The game checks that allocation against the physical and financial limits a real mission would face.

How it works: partway through a run, an unscripted event — a solar flare, an underperforming launch, a late payload increase — forces a response using whatever margin the player built in. The outcome is then matched to a real NASA mission that faced the same pressure, so losing teaches something specific instead of just telling the player to try again.

Benefits: for students, it builds intuition for systems-engineering trade-offs before they ever see the formulas. For educators, it's a classroom activity that needs no lab and no aerospace background. For us, it turned a hackathon idea into something we think keeps teaching value after the event ends.

What we hope to achieve: a lightweight, approachable way to make the hardest part of mission design — trading one constraint for another under pressure — something anyone can feel, not just read about.

Tools used: the constraint logic is grounded in NASA's General Mission Analysis Tool (GMAT) for trajectory and fuel cost, NASA's Small Spacecraft Technology State-of-the-Art Report for mass and power ranges, and NSSDCA mission data for lunar and Mars budget figures. The demo presentation was built with help from an AI assistant (Claude, by Anthropic), used for drafting text and generating the slide layout — the challenge selection and design decisions were our own.

Creativity: most resource trade-off tools stop at pass or fail. We wanted losing to be as informative as winning, so every outcome is tied to a real NASA mission that faced the same choice — the margin that saved it, or the shortfall that didn't.

projectDetails.name: Project BigX
projectDetails.summary:
Silent Sentinels: The Off-World Heritage & Telemetry Archive

Over the past six decades, humanity has left hundreds of tons of spacecraft, rovers, and rocket stages across the Moon, Mars, and deep space. Often dismissed as "space junk," these silent machines are actually monuments of human ingenuity. Silent Sentinels is an interactive digital museum that transforms raw NASA telemetry into vivid, human-centered stories.

Built with React, Tailwind CSS, and custom CAD vector blueprints, the platform features:

Dual-Planet Surface Explorer (Luna & Mars): Interactive topographic maps with live coordinate tracking and precision reticles for historic hardware—from the Apollo 11 Eagle Descent Stage and Surveyor 3 to Opportunity, Ingenuity, and Perseverance’s Skycrane.

Three-Lens Dossiers: Every artifact includes a first-person hardware log ("The Voice"), engineering telemetry explaining the physics of why it stayed behind, and a Personnel Roster honoring pioneers like Margaret Hamilton, Neil Armstrong, Swati Mohan, and MiMi Aung.

Rockets & Observatories Wing: Architectural scale comparisons and end-of-life histories for Saturn V, Space Shuttle, SLS (Artemis II), Hubble, Spitzer, JWST, and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview: What It Does & How It Works

Silent Sentinels: The Off-World Heritage & Telemetry Archive is an interactive digital museum and spaceflight telemetry explorer that documents NASA’s retired, impacted, and expended hardware across the Moon, Mars, and orbital space.

Instead of presenting historical missions as static tables of coordinates and mass figures, the web application turns off-world hardware into an explorable exhibition across three integrated views:

  1. Dual-Planet Surface Archive (Luna & Mars): Users toggle between equirectangular topographic maps of the Moon and Mars featuring real geological landmarks (Mare Tranquillitatis, Hadley Rille, Jezero Crater, Meridiani Planum) and live latitude/longitude cursor tracking. Clicking precision surveyor reticles locks onto iconic hardware—such as the Apollo 11 Eagle Descent Stage, Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, Surveyor 3, LCROSS Centaur Impactor, Opportunity Rover, Ingenuity Helicopter, Perseverance Skycrane, and Viking 1 Lander.
    • The Voice: First-person narrative logs written from the perspective of the hardware itself, capturing physical milestones like extreme lunar thermal cycles, Martian dust storms, and final telemetry transmissions.
    • Mission & Engineering Specs: Launch vehicles, mission timelines, critical turning points, custom CAD-style vector schematics, and the orbital physics rationale explaining why each piece remained behind (such as delta-v fuel budgets, planetary protection rules, or kinetic impact science).
    • Personnel Roster: Profiles highlighting the astronauts, flight directors, software leads, and principal investigators behind each mission—connecting cold metal back to pioneers like Margaret Hamilton, Neil Armstrong, Swati Mohan, MiMi Aung, and Steve Squyres.
  2. Launch Vehicles & Observatories Wing: A dedicated architectural scale comparison documenting the life cycles and end-of-life fates of NASA’s heavy-lift rockets (Saturn V, Space Shuttle, SLS/Artemis II) and deep-space telescopes (Hubble, Spitzer, James Webb, and Nancy Grace Roman), alongside a Chronological Scrubber (1969–2026) and Mass & Scale Visualizer.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Reframing "Space Junk" as Off-World Heritage: Public conversations around retired spacecraft often reduce them to orbital or planetary debris. Silent Sentinels educates students, educators, and space enthusiasts on the scientific triumphs, engineering trade-offs, and international preservation guidelines (such as NASA’s Lunar Heritage protocols) surrounding these historic sites.
  • Making Telemetry Accessible: By pairing raw coordinates, dry mass metrics, and physics explanations with relatable scale comparisons and first-person storytelling, the platform bridges the gap between dense aerospace archives and classroom-friendly STEM engagement.
  • Honoring the Human Element: Highlighting the engineers, software architects, and flight controllers alongside astronauts inspires learners to see the diverse STEM careers required to explore other worlds.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Languages & Core Web Technologies: JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, CSS3, and Scalable Vector Graphics (SVG) for custom cartographic projections and CAD-style spacecraft blueprints.
  • Frameworks & Libraries: React (built with Vite for fast bundling), Tailwind CSS for responsive layout and typography, and Lucide Icons for minimalist telemetry controls.
  • NASA Data & Archival Sources: Synthesized verified landing coordinates, dry mass figures, and mission logs from the NASA Planetary Data System (PDS), NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA), Apollo Lunar Surface Journal, and NASA Lunar Heritage Preservation Guidelines.
  • Development & Deployment Environment: Built in VS Code on a Windows 11 development workstation, utilizing browser-based responsive testing and static cloud hosting for zero-latency access without external API dependencies.

Creativity & Design Philosophy

  • Authentic Telemetry Aesthetic: Rather than using generic neon sci-fi templates, we modeled the interface after a 1970s–2020s NASA JPL Flight Telemetry Console paired with a Smithsonian archival exhibition—combining matte instrument-black panels, hairline grid borders, editorial serif storytelling typography, and tabular monospace coordinates.
  • Empathy Through Perspective: Writing hardware logs in the first person gives silent machines an emotional voice grounded in real physics, transforming a rover’s dead battery or a spent rocket stage’s lunar impact into a memorable story.
  • Bespoke Technical Wireframes: Every spacecraft, rocket, and telescope features a unique architectural line drawing rather than generic icons, allowing users to visually compare structural designs alongside real-world mass and height scales.

Key Factors Considered by Our Team

  • Scientific & Historical Accuracy: Every coordinate, dry mass figure, mission duration, and personnel attribution was cross-checked against official NASA mission records—including up-to-date 2026 milestones such as Artemis II and the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.
  • Performance & Accessibility: By structuring verified NASA datasets into a lightweight, zero-backend client architecture, the app loads instantaneously even on low-bandwidth connections or classroom devices, while high-contrast typography ensures readability.
  • Balanced Storytelling: We carefully balanced emotional narrative with hard engineering facts so that the platform appeals equally to casual space fans, history buffs, and technical judges.

projectDetails.name: Smart Earth Information Jukebox
projectDetails.summary:
Smart Earth Information Jukebox – Project Summary

What do we develop?

We propose to develop a Smart Earth Information Jukebox, an interactive web application or digital kiosk that converts real Earth data into music and sound. It uses information such as temperature, rainfall, ocean conditions and forest changes to generate different musical patterns.

How does it address the challenge?

The system transforms complex scientific data into simple audio and visual experiences. Users can select different environmental topics, listen to data-based sounds and explore related graphs and maps. It also provides an alternative way for visually impaired people to understand Earth information.

Why is it important?

This project promotes environmental awareness, improves accessibility and makes science education more engaging. By combining NASA Earth data, technology and sound, it helps people understand climate change and environmental conditions in an innovative way.

Our vision is to make people not only see how Earth changes but also hear its story.
projectDetails.details: Project Details – Smart Earth Information Jukebox (Earth Beats) Our project, Smart Earth Information Jukebox, is an interactive system that transforms Earth-related scientific data into sounds, music and visual information. It uses environmental data such as temperature, rainfall, ocean conditions and forest cover to create meaningful audio experiences. Users can select an environmental topic, explore graphs and maps, and listen to how different environmental conditions change over time. Benefits and Intended Impact: The project makes complex Earth science information easier to understand and more interesting. It promotes environmental awareness, supports science education and provides an alternative method of accessing information for visually impaired people. Our aim is to encourage people, especially students and young generations, to understand climate change and become more responsible towards protecting our planet. Tools and Technologies: We plan to use NASA Earth data sources for environmental information, Python for data processing, HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the user interface, and Web Audio API for generating sounds. The system can operate as a web application or a touchscreen kiosk with speakers or headphones. Creativity and Team Considerations: The creative aspect of our project is converting scientific measurements into musical patterns using pitch, rhythm and sound intensity. Instead of only displaying numbers and graphs, we allow users to hear environmental changes. Our team considered data accuracy, accessibility, user-friendliness, affordability, technical feasibility and educational value while planning the project. We aim to make Earth information accessible, interactive and memorable for everyone.

projectDetails.name: Mission Architect
projectDetails.summary: Mission Architect, built by team BUG E, is a browser game where students design and fly a complete space mission. Players choose a destination (Moon, Mars or Europa), a launch vehicle, a power system, an antenna, science instruments and a propellant load. Live meters show how each choice changes cost, launch mass, delta-v, power and data return. The game then simulates launch, cruise, orbit insertion and science operations, with risks such as launch failure and solar storms, and gives a score. It makes mission trade-offs concrete: bigger rockets cost more, extra propellant adds mass, solar power fades far from the Sun, and distant missions return less data. Failures teach as much as successes, so players can redesign and try again.
projectDetails.details: The game is a single HTML, CSS and JavaScript file with no backend. It uses the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation for delta-v, inverse-square solar flux for power at each destination, and a link-budget-style limit on data return. Players balance a fixed budget, launcher capacity, instrument power draw and communication capacity. Each mission faces probabilistic events, so the same design can succeed or fail. The score rewards science return and unspent budget. It is aimed at students who rarely get to see a whole mission from concept to operation, and it works on phones and laptops with nothing to install.

projectDetails.name: Halfway Rescuer
projectDetails.summary: Halfway Rescuer is an offline-first web app that helps astronauts assess their own health and act in an emergency when no doctor is aboard. It is inspired by the challenge scenario of a crewmate collapsing halfway to Mars. Its Emergency Protocol guides the rescuer one step at a time: check response, call the crew, check breathing, and run CPR with a live compression pacer and swap timer. It then builds a summary for Earth. A health console tracks eight indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen, temperature, glucose, sleep, mood and radiation. Each card explains how to measure it, why it matters in space, and what to do if a value looks abnormal, with colour-coded status and trend charts. A clickable body map links NASA’s five hazards to the body systems affected. A delay-tolerant outbox queues reports for Earth when the link is lost, with environment profiles for transit, station, Moon and Mars. All data is simulated and medical content is marked to be verified. It is a training prototype, not a medical device.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Halfway Rescuer is a website that helps astronauts when no doctor is on board. Its idea comes from the challenge video, where a crewmate suddenly collapses halfway to Mars and the person next to them has no medical experience.

If a crewmate collapses, the rescuer taps one big red button. The app then gives one simple instruction per screen: check if the person responds, call the crew, check breathing, and start CPR with a live beat to follow, a counter and a timer for swapping rescuers. At the end it builds a short summary for doctors on Earth.

The app also has a health console with eight indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen, temperature, blood sugar, sleep, mood and radiation. Each one explains how to measure it, why it matters in space, and what to do if the number looks wrong. Colours show green, amber or red, and charts show the trend. A clickable body figure shows how NASA’s five spaceflight hazards affect each body system.

Benefits

It guides people who are not doctors, works without internet, and saves a report for Earth even when the link is down.

Intended impact

The aim is that on long missions, astronauts can act quickly and safely, and that doctors on the ground get clear information. The same idea could help remote communities with little access to healthcare.

Tools used

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no backend), SVG and canvas for graphics, and the browser’s audio for the CPR beat. [Add the AI tools you used, for example Claude, because the form usually asks you to disclose them.]

How is it creative?

Most projects only show health numbers. Ours is built for the rescuer, step by step, in a real emergency. It also adds a delay-tolerant outbox for Earth, a clickable body map tied to NASA’s hazards, and a premium cinematic design.

What did the team consider?

Astronauts are not doctors, so every instruction is short and plain.

Earth help can be many minutes away, so the app works offline.

The medical thresholds are simple demo values, so we mark them “to be verified.”

All data is simulated, and the app says clearly that it is a training aid, not a medical device.

NASA’s hazards, Mars gravity and radiation facts come from NASA’s Human Research Program and the Canadian Space Agency.

projectDetails.name: The Silent Witnesses – Abandoned but Not Forgotten
projectDetails.summary: The Silent Witnesses is a digital storytelling project by Team CASIO that explores the human-made equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars during space exploration missions. Through an interactive presentation, we highlight real examples such as Apollo lunar landing stages, scientific instruments, and the parachute and backshell from NASA's Perseverance rover landing. Our project explains the purpose of this equipment, why it was left behind, and how these objects continue to hold scientific, engineering, and historical value. By combining space science, research, and storytelling, we aim to bring attention to the forgotten remains of exploration and show how they represent human innovation, technological progress, and the journey of discovering other worlds.
projectDetails.details:
THE SILENT WITNESSES – ABANDONED BUT NOT FORGOTTEN

Project Overview

The Silent Witnesses is a digital storytelling project developed by Team CASIO to explore the equipment and human-made objects left behind during space exploration missions on the Moon and Mars.

Space missions require several types of equipment, including landing stages, scientific instruments, parachutes, protective shells and other mission hardware. Some of these objects remain on planetary surfaces even after their primary missions are completed.

How Our Project Works

Our project presents real examples of discarded space equipment through an informative digital presentation and interactive website. It focuses on historical Apollo lunar mission equipment and the parachute and backshell separated during NASA's Perseverance rover landing on Mars. It explains why these objects were used, why they remained behind and what scientific or historical value they hold.

Benefits and Intended Impact

The project helps people understand the lesser-known side of space exploration. It increases awareness of space history, engineering achievements and the importance of preserving significant locations on the Moon and Mars for future exploration. It also encourages students to explore planetary science and aerospace engineering.

Tools and Technologies

The project uses digital research, HTML, CSS, web technologies and presentation software to organize information and communicate the story. NASA-related public resources and scientific datasets are used as references.

Creativity and Innovation

Instead of focusing only on successful space missions, our project tells the story of the equipment that remains after those missions. By presenting these objects as silent witnesses to human exploration, we connect engineering, science and history through storytelling.

projectDetails.details: Echoes Beyond Earth is an interactive website developed to explore and showcase the history, achievements, and technological advancements of space exploration missions to the Moon and Mars. The website provides information about important space missions, including lunar landers, rovers, and Mars landers, through detailed descriptions, images, individual mission story pages, and a chronological timeline. The website was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, with JSON files to store and organize mission information. The creative aspect of the project lies in combining visual storytelling, interactive exploration, mission-based information, and a chronological timeline to create an engaging learning experience. During development, the team considered factors such as information accuracy, reliable sources, user-friendly navigation, visual presentation, responsive design, accessibility, and proper organization of mission data. The intended impact is to increase awareness of space exploration, encourage interest in astronomy and space science, and inspire curiosity about humanity's continuing efforts to explore beyond Earth.

projectDetails.name: MarsWalk: An Integrated Mars Surface Exploration and Safety Planner
projectDetails.summary:
MarsWalk is an interactive Mars exploration planning platform designed to support future astronauts during surface exploration missions. Focusing on Jezero Crater, the application brings together different types of planetary science information, including surface imagery, elevation, temperature, mineral composition and rover observations.

The platform provides an interactive map, scientific points of interest, potential terrain hazard indicators and a route planning interface. It aims to help explorers understand the surrounding environment, identify scientifically interesting locations and plan their surface activities more effectively.

By combining information from multiple NASA missions into a unified interface, MarsWalk demonstrates how existing robotic exploration data can support future human missions to Mars. Its primary goal is to make planetary information more accessible, understandable and useful for safer exploration and scientific discovery.
projectDetails.details:
MarsWalk is a web-based Mars surface exploration and safety planning application developed to address the challenges of future human exploration of Mars.

The application focuses on Jezero Crater, a scientifically important region explored by NASA's Perseverance rover. It provides an interactive map interface where users can explore locations, examine scientific information, view different planetary data categories and plan hypothetical surface exploration routes.

The main features include:

• Interactive Mars exploration map with location markers and navigation.
• Scientific data layer controls for optical imagery, elevation, thermal information, mineral composition and rover observations.
• Scientific points of interest with geological information.
• Potential terrain hazard indicators for identifying challenging areas.
• A basic route planner showing suggested exploration paths, estimated distance and travel duration.
• An astronaut safety dashboard displaying terrain risk and environmental information.

The project is designed to bring different types of planetary science information into one accessible interface instead of requiring explorers to consult multiple separate sources.

We use React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS and Leaflet to develop the web application. The project uses NASA planetary science resources as its scientific foundation, with demonstration and estimated values clearly distinguished wherever actual measurements are unavailable.

MarsWalk demonstrates how existing robotic mission observations can be transformed into a practical exploration-planning interface for future human missions. It aims to support safer decision-making, efficient exploration and new scientific discoveries on the Martian surface.

projectDetails.name: SAR-Based AI-Powered Maritime Awareness and Ship Tracking System
projectDetails.summary: The system uses AI-based image processing and deep learning techniques to detect ships in SAR images, including during nighttime and cloudy weather conditions. It integrates AIS data to identify vessels, compare reported positions with satellite detections, and track their movements. It also aims to identify unmatched SAR detections, analyze ship movement patterns, and flag unusual maritime activities for further investigation.
projectDetails.details:
Illegal fishing, smuggling and vessels that switch off their AIS transponders are hard to catch. Optical satellites cannot see at night or through cloud, but synthetic aperture radar (SAR) can. Our project detects ships in SAR satellite images and checks each one against AIS broadcasts. It flags vessels that do not add up.

The system works in stages. First, it detects ships in a SAR scene using a classic CFAR detector or a trained YOLO model. Second, it estimates each ship’s heading from its wake, because SAR shows position but not direction. Third, it matches detections to AIS messages in a time-aware way. The satellite pass and AIS reports rarely share a timestamp, so a Kalman filter projects each AIS track to the moment the image was taken. Finally, an anomaly scorer raises alerts for dark vessels (seen by radar but silent on AIS), vessels reporting a false course, and AIS-only reports with no ship in the image. The results appear in a web mission console with a tactical fusion map.

The benefit is a clear answer to the question “is every ship I can see also telling me where it is?” This supports fisheries enforcement, marine protected areas, and search and rescue. It works day and night and in any weather. The intended impact is to give coastal authorities and researchers an open, low-cost way to find vessels that are hiding.

We built the system in Python, using NumPy, pandas, SciPy, OpenCV, Matplotlib and Folium for processing and mapping, and Ultralytics YOLO for learned detection. A Tkinter desktop app and an HTML/JavaScript mission console make it usable without coding. We trained models in Kaggle and Colab notebooks on public SAR ship datasets (SSDD, SL-SSDD and SARscope). Our SAR data comes from Sentinel-1, accessed through NASA’s ASF DAAC.

The project is creative in combining three things that are usually separate: radar detection, wake-based heading, and time-aware AIS fusion. Heading from wakes lets us catch vessels that spoof their reported course, not just ones that go dark.

We considered accuracy, honesty and usability. So far we have measured the pipeline on 50 simulated scenes, where it found all ships and flagged 94% of spoofed-course vessels. We are clear that this is a best case, and we are validating on real Sentinel-1 scenes. We also considered that AIS coverage varies by region, and that wake visibility depends on sea state. All code, notebooks and a demo video are open in our GitHub repository.

Team: Alex J Mathew, Jerin Francis, and an NPOL (DRDO) apprentice.

projectDetails.name: Project Civilianz
projectDetails.summary:
What we developed: a 12-slide pitch deck for a concept called PolarView, a web tool for comparing lunar south pole landing sites and dates. We built the presentation and an interface mock-up, not a working application. The chart numbers and Sites A/B/C are illustrative.
How it addresses the challenge:
Simple interface: pick sites, drag a date timeline, and read the result on one screen, replacing complicated tool interfaces.
Sun and Earth vs. the horizon: a sky view draws both over the local terrain horizon.
Power: a timeline shows sunlit windows and long dark gaps.
Communications: a second timeline shows when Earth is above the horizon for direct-to-Earth links.
Quick comparison: side-by-side site bars let planners, educators and the public compare options in seconds.
Feasible build: it uses public NASA data (SPICE ephemerides, LRO LOLA terrain), with the heavy computation done in advance so the browser stays fast.
Why it matters:
At Artemis candidate regions the Sun never rises above about 7°, so shadows are long and sunlight comes and goes.
Without relays, a lander needs Earth in view, so power and communications decide which sites and dates are workable.
A fast, visual tool helps planners shortlist options sooner, and it lets students and the public understand the pole's unusual lighting
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

PolarView is a web tool that lets mission planners, educators and the public compare lunar south pole landing sites and dates in seconds. The user picks one or more sites and drags a date timeline. The tool then draws the Sun and Earth over the site's real terrain horizon. Two timelines show sunlit periods for power and Earth-visible periods for direct-to-Earth communication. Sun and Earth positions come from NASA ephemerides. Each site's horizon comes from lunar terrain data. The tool compares each body's elevation to the horizon at its direction. The heavy calculations are done in advance, so the browser responds instantly.

Benefits

It replaces complicated interfaces with one clear screen.

Side-by-side comparison speeds up site and date shortlisting.

Power and communication trade-offs are visible at a glance.

It runs in any browser with no install, so non-experts can use it too.

Intended impact

Help teams choose landing sites and dates faster and with more confidence. It also makes the pole's extreme lighting (the Sun never above about 7° at candidate regions) understandable to students and the public.

Tools and technology (planned stack)

Data: NASA NAIF SPICE kernels for Sun and Earth positions, and LRO LOLA topography for horizon profiles

Precomputation: Python with SpiceyPy

Front end: JavaScript with React and D3/Canvas, using static JSON files per site and static hosting

Pitch deck: pptxgenjs, a JavaScript library for building PowerPoint files

Creativity

The sky is shown as a horizon view, as a person on the surface would see it, instead of as tables of angles.

Power and comms windows sit on one shared timeline, so conflicts show up immediately.

One interface scales from expert planning to public education.

Factors considered

Accuracy: terrain horizons matter a lot at such low Sun angles.

Speed: precomputing keeps the interface fast.

Audience: three groups with different needs.

Data openness: only public NASA data is used.

Limits: no relay satellites are assumed, and coverage starts with a few sites before all 13 candidate regions.

projectDetails.name: Field Shift Agroclimatic Engine
projectDetails.summary: Field Shift is a decision-support tool that helps rainfed farmers and extension advisers in Solapur, Maharashtra, explore crop-rotation options under uncertain monsoons. Using 41 years (1985–2025) of NASA POWER daily weather (MERRA-2 and CERES-derived rainfall, temperature, humidity, wind and solar radiation), it runs an FAO-56 daily soil-water balance for three rotations on shallow, medium and deep black soils: fallow then rabi sorghum, sole pigeon pea, and pearl millet then chickpea. Instead of a single winning answer, it shows how much water stress each rotation faces in typical and bad years, how often the planting window is missed, and how stable each comparison is across 500 plausible parameter combinations. Parameters carry source and status labels, and assumptions are stated openly. Field Shift supports, not replaces, farmer judgment: it models water stress, not yield or income.
projectDetails.details:
Problem. Rainfed farmers in Solapur’s semi-arid Deccan face erratic monsoon rainfall. Choosing a rotation depends on soil depth, the date monsoon rain arrives, and moisture stored for rabi crops. CRIDA’s district plan shows about 68% of the district has shallow black soils. Existing tools rarely show how uncertain a comparison is.

Solution. Field Shift is a self-contained web tool with a precomputed engine. Farmers or advisers pick a soil depth, an existing rotation, and priorities. The tool shows each rotation’s water stress, planting-window risk, where the rain goes, and how robust each comparison is.

How it works.

  • Data: NASA POWER daily point data for a 55 km grid cell near Pandharpur in western Solapur district (17.68°N, 75.32°E), 1984–2025. 1984 is spin-up, and 1985–2025 (41 years) is evaluated.
  • Evapotranspiration: FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference ET, tested against FAO’s worked Example 18 and a hand calculation.
  • Water balance: a daily root-zone balance with FAO-56 crop coefficients, a two-stage bare-soil evaporation model, and optional runoff. Rainfall equals crop ET, soil evaporation, losses, and storage change, with closure under 1e-6 mm.
  • Rotations: (R1) fallow then rabi sorghum, (R2) sole pigeonpea, (R3) pearl millet then chickpea.
  • Soils: shallow 0.20 m, medium 0.375 m, deep 1.0 m, from CRIDA depth classes, with an assumed available water of 190 mm/m.
  • Sowing: kharif crops sow at the first 3-day rainfall of at least 25 mm inside the CRIDA window (an assumed trigger). Rabi crops sow when stored moisture reaches 40% of capacity.
  • Two views of a missed planting window: one assumes late planting always works, and the other treats a missed window as total loss. They are optimistic and pessimistic bounds.
  • Uncertainty: 500 Monte Carlo draws over assumed (not measured) ranges for water capacity, sowing date, rain trigger, runoff, humidity method, evaporation settings, crop coefficients, and cultivar duration. The output is how often each ordering holds, not a probability of real outcomes.
  • Extras: a season calendar of soil water, ET₀ trend tests (Mann-Kendall, Theil-Sen, Pettitt), and parameter-source labels.

Findings so far [verify against docs/key-results.md]: soil depth dominates the results. When late planting always works, pigeon pea and millet-chickpea show lower mean deficit than fallow-sorghum in 95% to 98% of draws on deep soil, and 100% on medium and shallow soils. When a missed window counts as total loss, on deep soil fallow-sorghum is lower in about 71% and 65% of draws, while on medium and shallow soils the alternatives stay lower in 88% to 100%.

Tools. JavaScript on Node.js with no runtime dependencies, node:test (55 tests), static HTML/CSS/JS with inline SVG, git. Statistical tests are our own implementations, hand-checked against a published textbook benchmark.

Creativity. The distinctive features are showing when the tool cannot separate options, stating both missed-planting treatments openly, and labelling every parameter as cited, proxy, assumption, or pending. We make no claim of being the only tool that does this.

Benefits and intended impact. The tool is meant to help extension officers and farmers frame rotation discussions, see which options are plausible at which soil depth, and see where planting risk and bare-field periods fall. The impact is potential and has not been field-tested.

Limitations and future work.

  • The reanalysis grid is 55 km and gridded rainfall smooths storm peaks.
  • It models water stress, not yield, income, or markets.
  • No farmer or expert has validated it.
  • Soil health and pest cycles are qualitative: crop family and legume flags only.
  • Early-season crop evaporation uses a fixed initial coefficient, and fallow is modelled as bare soil.
  • Next steps: expert review with local extension (KVK), additional NASA products (SMAP, GPM, MODIS), more districts, and a dual-coefficient crop evaporation model.

projectDetails.name: THE LEGEND OF OM
projectDetails.summary:
The Legend of Om - is an interactive, story-driven web application that transforms NASA Earth observation data into a captivating musical and visual experience. Developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge: Earth Information Jukebox, the project explores how our planet's natural phenomena can be experienced through sound.

The experience follows a fictional Traveller–Musician who discovers that Earth's oceans and lightning storms contain patterns that can be interpreted musically. Through cinematic illustrations, interactive narration, and original soundscapes, users explore how ocean-current visualizations inspire flute melodies and lightning observations inspire electric guitar compositions.

By combining environmental data visualization with sonification—the process of translating data into sound—the project makes complex Earth science more approachable, engaging, and memorable.

Unlike conventional data dashboards, The Legend of Om presents scientific information through an interactive adventure where users progress through illustrated scenes, discover musical interpretations, and learn about NASA's Earth observations.

Our goal is to make Earth science accessible to wider audiences by connecting scientific curiosity, storytelling, art, and music.
projectDetails.details:
The Legend of Om — Project Details

Project Overview

The Legend of Om is an interactive cinematic storytelling application developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, addressing the Earth Information Jukebox challenge.

The project explores an imaginative question: What if Earth itself were the greatest musician, and we could translate its natural patterns into music?

Our application combines NASA Earth observation visualizations, data-inspired musical compositions, interactive storytelling, and cinematic artwork to create an educational experience that allows users to discover the hidden rhythms of our planet.

How Does It Work?

The application follows a Traveller–Musician on a journey to discover the music of nature. The experience is divided into six interconnected chapters.

Chapter 1 — The Call of the Wind

The traveller discovers mysterious sounds carried by the wind and begins searching for their origin.

Chapter 2 — The Ocean Shoreline

At the coastline, the traveller encounters the natural rhythms of wind and waves, inspiring him to explore how environmental patterns might be represented through music.

Chapter 3 — The Ocean Symphony

Inspired by NASA ocean-current visualizations, the traveller creates a wooden flute. Ocean circulation patterns are artistically interpreted as melodic variations, introducing users to the concept of sonification.

The application illustrates how properties extracted from environmental data can be mapped to musical characteristics such as pitch, tempo, and melodic movement.

Chapter 4 — The Arrival of the Storm

The traveller encounters a powerful lightning storm, revealing an entirely different natural rhythm.

Chapter 5 — The Lightning Symphony

The traveller constructs an electric guitar and explores how lightning observations can inspire musical compositions.

Lightning activity is represented through energetic guitar sounds, with variations in the observed patterns influencing the musical interpretation.

The traveller also creates maps to illustrate geographical variations in environmental activity.

Chapter 6 — The Earth Jukebox

The journey concludes with an Earth Jukebox that brings the ocean-inspired flute and lightning-inspired guitar compositions together.

Users discover how different environmental phenomena can produce distinct musical interpretations, demonstrating the relationship between scientific observations and sound.

Interactive Web Application

Rather than presenting scientific data through conventional charts alone, our project introduces an interactive storytelling experience.

Users begin by opening a traditional parchment scroll sealed with wax, entering the world of The Legend of Ohm.

The experience includes:

  • Interactive storytelling: Users progress through individual cinematic frames and chapters.
  • Illustrated narrator: A dedicated narrator character guides users through the story and explains scientific concepts.
  • Audio experiences: Musical soundscapes accompany the ocean and lightning chapters.
  • Environmental visualizations: NASA-inspired imagery illustrates ocean currents and lightning activity.
  • Educational explanations: Scientific concepts are introduced naturally during the traveller's discoveries.
  • Cinematic presentation: Painterly, cel-shaded illustrations, atmospheric lighting, and subtle transitions create an immersive experience.

NASA Data and Sonification

The project draws inspiration from NASA's Earth Information Center visualizations, particularly ocean circulation and lightning activity.

These two environmental phenomena were selected because they offer contrasting musical characteristics.

Ocean Currents — Flute Sonification

Ocean circulation is represented through flowing melodies. Changes in visualized environmental patterns can be interpreted through musical parameters such as pitch, note duration, and melodic progression.

The flute represents the smooth and continuous movement of ocean currents.

Lightning — Electric Guitar Sonification

Lightning activity is represented through energetic guitar compositions. Variations in the observed lightning patterns can be translated into changes in musical intensity, rhythm, and pitch.

The electric guitar symbolizes the sudden, powerful, and irregular nature of lightning events.

These sonifications are artistic interpretations of environmental observations rather than recordings of physical sounds emitted by the datasets.

Technologies and Tools

The application is designed as a lightweight, browser-based experience using accessible web technologies.

Frontend Development

  • HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript
  • Responsive web design
  • Interactive frame navigation and scene transitions
  • Browser-based audio playback and narration

Deployment

  • Netlify for free static website hosting
  • Git and GitHub for version control and project management, where applicable

Creative Production

  • AI-assisted character and storyboard illustration
  • Digital audio editing and soundscape preparation
  • Custom environmental data-inspired musical arrangements

Scientific Resources

  • NASA Earth Information Center visualizations
  • Ocean-current visualization imagery
  • Lightning observation visualizations

The project is designed to operate without paid APIs or specialized hardware, making it practical to host and share online.

Creativity and Innovation

The primary innovation of The Legend of Ohm is its combination of scientific data interpretation with character-driven storytelling.

Instead of requiring users to understand complex scientific charts before engaging with Earth observation data, the project introduces these concepts through a fictional musician's discoveries.

The two environmental phenomena are assigned contrasting instruments, creating a recognizable relationship between natural patterns and musical expression.

The project also uses an illustrated narrator, a parchment-scroll introduction, hand-drawn maps, and cinematic transitions to make scientific exploration feel like an unfolding adventure.

This approach combines science, technology, storytelling, visual art, and music in a single interactive experience.

Design Considerations

During development, our team prioritized scientific clarity, visual consistency, accessibility, storytelling, and performance.

We aimed to preserve the distinction between observed environmental data and the artistic decisions used to represent that data musically.

We also focused on creating an experience that can run directly in a web browser, without requiring users to install specialized software.

Conclusion

The Legend of Om transforms Earth observation into an interactive musical adventure.

By connecting NASA environmental visualizations with sound, storytelling, and cinematic artwork, the project demonstrates a creative way to communicate Earth science.

Our vision is to help audiences experience the planet not only as something to observe, but also as something to listen to, interpret, and understand.

The Earth has patterns. We turn them into music.

projectDetails.name: Astra Health
projectDetails.summary:
ASTRA (Autonomous Astronaut Health Monitoring and Decision Support System) is a project developed to monitor astronauts' health and safety during space missions. It provides a centralized platform where astronauts and medical officers can access important health and mission-related information through separate portals with role-based access.

The system monitors various health parameters, including heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), body temperature and respiratory rate. It also tracks environmental conditions such as oxygen and carbon dioxide levels, humidity, temperature and cabin pressure. In addition, ASTRA includes radiation monitoring to track personal exposure and radiation levels in the surrounding environment. A rule-based alert system identifies measurements that exceed predefined limits and notifies medical officers so they can review the situation and take appropriate action.

The application also provides features for viewing historical records, monitoring crew health, analysing measurements through graphical representations and generating reports. Developed using Python, Flask, SQLite, HTML, CSS and JavaScript, ASTRA follows an offline-first approach, allowing data to be stored and accessed even when internet connectivity is limited. The main aim of this project is to make astronaut health monitoring more organized and accessible while helping medical officers identify potential health and environmental risks during space missions.
projectDetails.details:
ASTRA (Autonomous Astronaut Health Monitoring and Decision Support System) is a project developed to help monitor astronauts' health and safety during space missions. Since astronauts work in an environment where even small changes in health or surroundings can become serious, the project aims to bring important monitoring information together in one place.

The system has separate portals for astronauts and medical officers. It monitors health parameters such as heart rate, blood oxygen level (SpO2), body temperature and respiratory rate. It also tracks environmental conditions, including oxygen and carbon dioxide levels, humidity, temperature and cabin pressure, along with radiation exposure. When a recorded value crosses a predefined threshold, the system generates an alert so that medical officers can review the situation. Users can also view historical records, analyse data through graphs, monitor crew health and generate reports.

The main benefit of ASTRA is that it makes health and environmental information easier to access and manage. It can help medical officers identify unusual changes early and make better-informed decisions. The project follows an offline-first approach, allowing data to be stored and accessed even with limited internet connectivity.

ASTRA was developed using Python, Flask, SQLite, HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Chart.js for data visualization. Its creative aspect lies in combining astronaut health monitoring, environmental monitoring, radiation tracking and alert management into a single platform. During development, factors such as data accuracy, security, ease of use, accessibility, reliability and limited connectivity were considered. The overall aim is to contribute towards safer and more organized health monitoring during space missions.

projectDetails.name: SPACEVERSE
projectDetails.summary:
SpaceVerse is an interactive 3‑D web application that lets users explore a virtual solar system and conduct scientific missions on planets, moons, and spacecraft. Built with Vite, React, and Three.js, the app provides a realistic physics‑based environment where users can launch rockets, operate orbital labs, and manage resources such as fuel and power. The codebase includes a rich component library (e.g., LunarFlybyLab, RocketAssemblyStage, SpaceCampaignMap) alongside data modules that define celestial bodies and mission parameters.

The challenge addressed by SpaceVerse is to make complex space‑flight concepts accessible through an engaging, browser‑based experience without requiring heavyweight desktop software or specialized hardware. By bundling the simulation logic, visual assets, and UI into a single, easily deployable project, the app enables educators, hobbyists, and developers to demonstrate orbital mechanics, mission planning, and spacecraft design in real time. Its open‑source nature encourages community contributions, fostering a collaborative platform for learning and prototyping future space‑technology ideas.
projectDetails.details:
SpaceVerse // GALAXY-X
Interactive 3D Aerospace Mission Campus & Flight Simulation Platform

  1. What Does It Do or How Does It Work?

SpaceVerse is a browser-based, interactive 3D aerospace mission campus and flight simulation platform. Rather than presenting static quiz cards or flat menus, SpaceVerse places the user in the boots of an aerospace engineer and flight director inside a live NASA Space Center Campus built with Three.js and React.

How It Works:

  1. Interactive 3D Campus Navigation: Players navigate in real-time across six specialized aerospace campus sectors:
  • SAH (Spacecraft Assembly Hangar): Cleanroom bays for satellite staging and mechanical integration.
  • LCC (Launch Control Complex & Pad 39X): Multi-stage launch vehicle assembly, pad staging, and countdown sequencing.
  • GSC (Ground Station & Deep Space Network): Antenna array telemetry tracking, orbit power monitoring, and interplanetary signal downlink.
  • MPR (Mission Planning Room): Trajectory calculation holo-tables and environmental stress testing.
  • PNL (Propulsion & Navigation Lab): Fuel-mass ratio calibration and orbital delta-V calculations.
  • MCC (Mission Control Center): Real-time orbital monitoring, telemetry consoles, and emergency response.
  1. Eight Scaffolding Mission Levels:
  • Level 1 - Satellite Assembly (SAH): Snap-fitting 9 essential subsystems (Bus frame, Solar wings, Battery pack, S-Band antenna, Multispectral camera, Propulsion thrusters, On-Board Computer, ADCS reaction wheels, Thermal radiator louvers) with live validation of mass, power, and telemetry tags.
  • Level 2 - Rocket Assembly & Launch (LCC & Pad 39X): 10-module multi-stage rocket construction (boosters, cryogenic tanks, interstage, avionics, payload fairing), pad staging, ignition sequence, aerodynamic ascent, and orbital insertion.
  • Level 3 - Orbit & Power Management (GSC): Balancing solar panel power generation against battery capacity to ensure spacecraft survival through the dark eclipse of Earth's shadow.
  • Level 4 - Environmental Shake & Freeze Test (MPR): Acoustic/vibration qualification on a shaker table (70 pts or higher target) and thermal vacuum cryogenic chamber testing (-20°C survivability) within strict mass limits (500 kg or less).
  • Level 5 - Lunar Flyby Fuel Math (PNL): Calculating the optimal propellant balance (45-65 kg) to generate sufficient delta-V for a 238,000-mile lunar transfer without exceeding rocket payload lift limits.
  • Level 6 - Thermometer Telemetry Probe (Europa Discovery): Deep-space mission over 628 million km to Jupiter's icy moon Europa; landing on a procedural 3D ice basin, calibrating sensors, drilling into cryo-fissures, and downlinking thermal readings to Earth.
  • Level 7 - Lunar Water Hunt (Moon South Pole Expedition): Exploring permanently shadowed craters (Cabeus, Shackleton, Faustini) using neutron spectrometers and ice-penetrating radar to confirm subsurface water ice.
  • Level 8 - Astronaut EVA Rescue (ISS Low Earth Orbit): Emergency spacewalk rescue 408 km above Earth. Radar-locking a drifting astronaut, dodging space debris, matching orbital velocity, and deploying the robotic arm for capture.
  1. In-Game Engineering Handbook & Dialogue:
  • Flight Director Vance: Features a voice-briefed mission commander avatar providing spoken situational updates and mission context.
  • Spacecraft Engineering Handbook: An illustrated technical guide explaining aerospace principles through intuitive analogies, troubleshooting cheatsheets, and concept mastery quizzes.
  1. What Benefits Does It Have?
  • Hands-on STEM Experiential Learning: Replaces abstract textbook formulas with interactive cause-and-effect simulations (for example, if you undersize your battery pack, your satellite de-powers during eclipse; if you overload fuel, the rocket fails to lift off).
  • Zero Barrier to Entry: Operates entirely in modern web browsers via WebGL—no high-end flight sim rigs, expensive software licenses, or gigabyte-heavy installations required.
  • Systems-Thinking Mastery: Teaches players how aerospace disciplines interconnect: mechanical structures, electrical power, thermodynamics, orbital mechanics, communication link budgets, and cost/weight optimization.
  • Immediate Telemetry & Failure Scaffolding: Provides real-time feedback with explicit diagnostic notes explaining why an assembly failed or why an orbit decayed, fostering scientific inquiry and resilience.
  1. What Is the Intended Impact of the Project?
  • Democratizing Aerospace Education: Giving K-12 students, university engineering recruits, and space enthusiasts worldwide equal access to high-fidelity space mission design tools.
  • Inspiring the Artemis Generation: Cultivating interest in lunar exploration, deep-space planetary science (Europa Clipper), and orbital space safety (debris mitigation and astronaut rescue).
  • Bridging Theory and Practice: Demonstrating how physics, mathematics, and computer science apply directly to real missions conducted by NASA, ESA, and commercial spaceflight organizations.
  1. What Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware, or Software Were Used?
  • Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript (ESNext), HTML5, CSS3, GLSL shader techniques
  • 3D Engine & Graphics: Three.js (WebGL renderer, RoomEnvironment PBR lighting, custom procedural geometry, camera controls, Raycasting)
  • UI & Animation: React 19, Tailwind CSS v4, Motion (Framer Motion), Lucide React icons, custom SVG technical diagrams
  • Audio Engine: Custom Web Audio API procedural synthesizer (real-time sound synthesis for rocket roar, ignition rumble, radio static, and telemetry beeps)
  • Build & Tooling: Vite, tsx, Node.js
  • Backend & APIs: Node.js Express, RESTful endpoints, local persistence registry
  • Database & Cloud: Google Firebase Authentication & Google Cloud Firestore with local JSON fallback (galaxyx-db.json)
  • AI Capabilities: Configured with Google Gemini API (@google/genai) for dynamic mission intelligence
  • Target Hardware: Runs cross-platform on standard consumer laptops, desktops, and Chromebooks with WebGL-capable GPUs
  1. How Is Your Project Creative?
  • The 3D Campus Metaphor: Instead of traditional menu dropdowns, users interact with a physical 3D space center campus featuring sector signage, walking navigation, and proximity-activated workstations.
    • Chassis/Bus = Skeleton
    • On-Board Computer = Brain
    • Solar Panels & Batteries = Heart & Metabolism
    • Multispectral Sensors = Eyes
    • High-Gain Antenna = Voice
  • Procedural Planetary Surface Explorers: Custom 3D heightmapped terrain renderers for both the Moon's South Pole and Europa's fractured icy crust.
  1. What Factors Did Your Team Consider?
  2. Scientific Fidelity vs. User Accessibility:
  • Consideration: Real orbital mechanics and thermal calculations involve advanced differential equations that could intimidate beginners.
  • Solution: We preserved the real physics (mass trade-offs, cryogenic temperatures in Celsius/Kelvin, solar flux vs. battery watt-hours, delta-V limits) while encapsulating them into intuitive visual sliders, gauges, and instant telemetry cards.
  1. Web Performance & Load Times:
  • Consideration: Heavy 3D assets often cause long loading screens and lag on classroom computers or mobile devices.
  • Solution: Built lightweight procedural 3D meshes and procedural textures directly in Three.js code, keeping the initial bundle fast, responsive, and lightweight.
  1. Resilience & Offline-First Architecture:
  • Consideration: Unstable internet connections in classrooms or remote environments shouldn't interrupt learning.
  • Solution: Implemented dual data storage: seamless cloud synchronization via Firebase/Firestore when connected, paired with an automatic offline local JSON database fallback.
  1. Multimodal Learning (Audio, Visual, Kinesthetic):
  • Consideration: Different learners absorb information differently.
  • Solution: Integrated audio cues (Director Vance voice briefings, sound effects), visual diagrams (SVG schematics, 3D orbits), and interactive kinesthetic labs (dragging modules, snapping parts, dialing fuel values).
  1. Progressive Cognitive Scaffolding:
  • Consideration: Space exploration is vast and complex.
  • Solution: Structured the campaign into 8 clear stages, gradually ramping from elementary modular assembly to orbital mechanics, deep-space planetary science, and emergency spacecraft control.

projectDetails.name: The Silent Legacy

Instead of treating these objects simply as discarded hardware, our project explains the purpose, engineering role, and lasting significance of each component. projectDetails.details: The Silent Legacy: Humanity’s Footprints on the Moon and Mars The Silent Legacy is an interactive digital storytelling project that explores human-made spacecraft hardware left on the Moon and Mars after successful space missions. The project presents this equipment as a virtual museum, helping visitors understand why these objects remain on other worlds and what they tell us about exploration. The project focuses on two major mission stories: Apollo 11 on the Moon and NASA’s Perseverance mission on Mars. The Moon section explains the Apollo 11 Lunar Module descent stage and the lunar laser-ranging retroreflector. The Mars section explores landing-system components associated with Perseverance, including the heat shield, parachute, backshell, and powered descent stage. Rather than presenting these objects simply as “space junk,” the project explains their different purposes. Some were mission hardware designed for one-time use, while others were intentionally deployed for scientific research. The website connects these objects with the engineering decisions, scientific goals, and historical importance of planetary exploration. The project is designed for students, teachers, families, and anyone interested in space science. It uses simple explanations, visual storytelling, object cards, timelines, comparisons, and an easy-to-navigate virtual museum structure to make the subject accessible to beginners. The project also highlights an important idea for future exploration: as humans continue sending missions to the Moon and Mars, the hardware left behind can become part of the scientific and historical record of exploration. Understanding what is intentionally left behind helps us think about responsible exploration and the long-term legacy of human activity beyond Earth. Technologies and tools: HTML, CSS, digital presentation tools, online research resources, and NASA mission information. Creativity and innovation: The project transforms technical mission information into a virtual museum experience. Instead of only listing spacecraft components, it tells the story of each object, its purpose, and its connection to human exploration. Expected impact: The project aims to improve awareness of planetary exploration, encourage interest in STEM subjects, and help students understand the engineering and scientific significance of spacecraft hardware beyond Earth. Tagline: “The machines may stop. The discoveries continue.”
