projectDetails.name: Project Tonitrus Luna
projectDetails.summary:
Tonitrus Luna – Lunar Landing Site Navigator

Tonitrus Luna is an interactive lunar mission planning platform designed to identify and evaluate suitable landing sites near the Moon’s South Pole. Our project addresses the challenges of lunar exploration by combining scientific data, visualization, and mission-planning tools in one integrated platform. It features a 3D lunar globe, solar illumination analysis, landing site comparison, and a horizon radar to evaluate sunlight availability and terrain obstructions. It also calculates potential solar power generation, Earth visibility, and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication windows using lunar libration data. Additionally, it integrates with space-tracking applications such as Celestia and Orbitrack, providing downloadable mission data for further analysis. This project is important because selecting a safe and sustainable lunar landing site is essential for future human exploration. By helping assess power availability, communication reliability, and environmental conditions, Tonitrus Luna supports better-informed decisions for future lunar missions, including Artemis.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do & how does it work?

Tonitrus Luna is an interactive mission planning tool that models extreme solar illumination and Direct-to-Earth (DTE) communication constraints at the Moon’s South Pole:

  • Topocentric Astronomical Engine: Computes real-time Sun and Earth positions using Meeus algorithms and JPL ephemerides, calculating topocentric azimuth and elevation for any lunar coordinate.
  • Grazing Sunlight & Solar Power: Sunlight at the poles grazes the horizon between −1.54∘-1.54^\circ−1.54∘ and +1.54∘+1.54^\circ+1.54∘. The tool models solar flux (W/m2W/m^2W/m2) and proves why vertical solar arrays capture up to 12×12\times12× more energy than horizontal panels, estimating power output for a 10 m210\text{ m}^210 m2 GaAs array (3.8 kW3.8\text{ kW}3.8 kW peak).
  • Libration & DTE Communication Windows: Models Earth’s ±7.9∘\pm 7.9^\circ±7.9∘ longitude and ±6.7∘\pm 6.7^\circ±6.7∘ latitude libration cycle, predicting when Earth dips behind crater rims to trigger communication blackouts.
  • LOLA Terrain Obstruction: Incorporates 360∘360^\circ360∘ elevation masks from NASA Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter data for candidate Artemis landing sites (Shackleton, Malapert, Nobile, Chandrayaan-3, IM-1 Odysseus, etc.).
  • Interactive Visuals: Features a 360° Polar Horizon Radar with a −5∘-5^\circ−5∘ dip ring, a scrubbable dual-axis ephemeris timeline (1×1\times1× to 1,500×1,500\times1,500× speed), and an interactive 3D lunar globe with dynamic terminator shadows.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Replaces Complex Tools: Eliminates the steep learning curve of fragmented SPICE command-line tools with a unified, zero-install web interface.
  • Instant Site Trade Studies: Side-by-side Landing Sites Comparator evaluates illumination %, longest continuous darkness, and DTE availability in seconds.
  • Mission Risk Reduction: Helps mission planners choose launch and landing epochs that maximize solar power and prevent communication loss.
  • Zero-Install Portability: Runs completely offline in any modern browser on desktop or mobile.

3. What is the intended impact?

  • Artemis & Commercial Lunar Missions: Assists mission design for NASA Artemis III, international agencies (ESA, ISRO, JAXA), and commercial CLPS landers (Intuitive Machines, Astrobotic).
  • STEM & Higher Education: Demystifies complex orbital mechanics (librations, anomalistic months, polar grazing geometry) for university classrooms and museums.
  • Public Engagement: Connects surface mission design directly with ground-based amateur astronomy.

4. What tools, languages, and software were used?

  • AI Architecture: Google Antigravity (ephemeris formulation, code generation, UI engineering, and automated browser testing).
  • Languages & Web Stack: JavaScript (ES6+) for zero-dependency astronomical math; HTML5 Canvas 2D for custom vector rendering of radar, timeline, and 3D globe; CSS3 for a space-grade dark glassmorphism design system.
  • Scientific Data: NASA LOLA topographic profiles, Jean Meeus astronomical algorithms, and NASA/ISRO/CNSA mission archives.
  • Hosting & Packaging: Netlify for global CDN deployment; PowerShell for POSIX-compliant forward-slash ZIP packaging and single-file bundling.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Celestial Synergy Hub: Cross-platform interoperability bridging surface planning with 4 popular space tracking tools:
    • Celestia: Exports .ssc Solar System Catalogs and .cel camera fly-to scripts.
    • Orbitrack: Exports .csv target databases and cislunar orbital elements.
    • ISS Detector & Star Walk: Generates standard 69-character NORAD TLEs for lunar orbiters (LRO, CAPSTONE, Gateway) and real-time Earth observer pointing coordinates (RA/Dec, Az/El) for Augmented Reality (AR) night-sky spotting.
    • CCSDS OEM XML: Exports standardized inter-agency navigation ephemerides.
  • Self-Contained Architecture: Entire app runs from a single 171 KB HTML file (tonitrusluna.html) with zero external network requests.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • Extreme Lunar Polar Physics: Grazing sunlight angles (±1.54∘\pm 1.54^\circ±1.54∘), 27.3-day libration cycles, and cryogenic cold traps (<40 K<40\text{ K}<40 K).
  • Crater Topography: NASA LOLA elevation profiles to determine whether towering mountain peaks (e.g., Malapert Mons at +5,000 m+5,000\text{ m}+5,000 m) shield or block the Sun and Earth.
  • Human Factors & Telemetry: Color-coded status alerts (Green Optimal, Yellow Grazing, Red Blackout) and quick-jump date presets (Solstices, Artemis III, Chandrayaan-3, IM-1).
  • Comprehensive Lunar History: Curated a database of 50+ lunar missions (1959–2026+) documenting launch dates, power systems, communications bands, rover wheel mechanics, science instruments, and mission milestones.

projectDetails.details:
A Sojourner Tale: An Interactive Digital Story Inspired by NASA's Mars Pathfinder Mission

A Sojourner Tale is an interactive storytelling website based on NASA's Mars Pathfinder mission and its small rover, Sojourner. Sojourner tells the story itself, in the first person, so visitors follow the trip from Earth to Mars through the rover's eyes. I didn't want the site to be another list of dates and facts. It mixes storytelling with science, illustrations, animations and interactive features to make space exploration feel more alive and easier to follow.

The story moves through the main stages of the mission. It starts with the launch from Earth, then goes through the landing on Mars, the rover's first movements, its study of rocks and soil, what it discovered, and how it shaped later Mars missions. Mars Pathfinder launched on December 4, 1996, and landed in Ares Vallis on July 4, 1997. The site explains the airbag system that cushioned the landing and introduces some of the rocks Sojourner studied, including Barnacle Bill, Yogi and Scooby-Doo. Visitors also learn about the rover itself: it weighed only about 10.6 kg, stood around 30 cm tall and moved on six wheels.

The project runs in any web browser. Visitors scroll through the story chapter by chapter. They can also click hotspots on the rover illustration to explore its parts: the solar panel, cameras, APXS instrument, wheels and body. Information cards and pop-ups give extra details about the mission, the instruments and the discoveries. Animated backgrounds, smooth transitions, a scroll progress bar and a read-aloud option make the site more engaging and more accessible.

I built the website with HTML, CSS and JavaScript:

  1. HTML gives the site its structure and splits the story into sections.
  2. CSS handles the layout, colours, animations, transitions and responsive design.
  3. JavaScript runs the interactive parts, including chapter navigation, hotspots, pop-ups, scroll tracking and the animated backgrounds.
  4. SVG illustrations draw the rover and the Martian landscape.
  5. The Canvas API creates the moving star background.
  6. The browser's Web Speech API provides the read-aloud narration.

Together, these let the site work without special hardware or any software to install.

One of the project's biggest strengths is how it makes scientific and historical information simple to take in. Space missions, scientific instruments and planetary exploration can feel overwhelming, but they become much easier to understand when they're told as a story with visuals you can interact with. The site can be useful for school and college students, teachers, and anyone curious about space. Because the design is responsive, it works on computers, tablets and phones.

The main goal of A Sojourner Tale is to spark interest in planetary exploration. It shows how a rover weighing only about 10.6 kg made a big difference to our understanding of Mars. It also tested technologies that later missions built on. By combining real science with a story, I hope the project encourages people, especially students, to get curious about science, technology, engineering and space.

The creative side of the project comes from telling the mission from Sojourner's point of view. Instead of treating it as just a machine, the website gives the rover a voice, so visitors feel like they're travelling with it. Space-themed visuals, Martian scenery, interactive illustrations, animations and narration make the mission more memorable. The story also links Sojourner's work to the rovers that followed it: Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity and Perseverance.

While building the site, I focused on keeping the science accurate, ordering the story so it made sense, making the interactions smooth and keeping it easy to navigate on any device. No physical rover or electronic hardware is needed; a browser is enough. In the future, I'd like to add more detailed animations, interactive maps, quizzes, more information about the scientific instruments, and narration in other languages.

In short, A Sojourner Tale brings together technology, creativity, education and storytelling to share what the Mars Pathfinder mission achieved. A rover small enough to carry in your arms helped change how we explore space, which shows that even a small step on another planet can help us understand the universe.

projectDetails.name: PROJECT ASTROHEALTH
projectDetails.summary:
ASTROHEALTH – An Intelligent Wearable-Based Health Monitoring and Decision Support System for Astronauts

ASTROHEALTH is an AI-powered health monitoring system designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. It integrates wearable sensors with intelligent software to collect and analyse vital health indicators such as heart rate, ECG, blood oxygen levels, body temperature, sleep patterns and physical activity. The system monitors changes in astronauts' health, identifies potential risks associated with microgravity, radiation exposure, isolation and the space environment, and provides personalised health recommendations and real-time alerts. It also maintains individual health records and provides a dashboard for monitoring health trends. The primary objective is to empower astronauts to independently assess, manage and respond to their health conditions, improving crew safety and well-being during space missions.
projectDetails.details: ASTROHEALTH is an intelligent wearable-based health monitoring and decision support system designed to monitor and improve the health, safety and well-being of astronauts during long-duration space missions. Astronauts face several health challenges due to microgravity, radiation exposure, isolation, confinement and changes in their daily routines. To address these challenges, ASTROHEALTH combines wearable sensors with an AI-powered software platform to collect and analyse important health parameters such as heart rate, ECG, blood oxygen level (SpO₂), skin temperature, physical activity and sleep patterns. Environmental sensors can also monitor cabin conditions such as temperature, humidity and carbon dioxide levels, while a dedicated radiation dosimeter can measure radiation exposure. The collected data is transmitted to the software platform, where it is analysed and compared with each astronaut's personal health baseline to identify unusual patterns and potential health risks. The system provides real-time alerts, personalised recommendations and a digital dashboard displaying health status, trends and medical history, helping astronauts monitor their condition and take appropriate action. The major benefits include continuous health monitoring, early identification of potential health problems, personalised health analysis, improved self-management, long-term health records and better health-related decision-making during missions. The intended impact is to reduce health risks, support astronaut independence and contribute to safer and more sustainable space exploration, including future lunar and Mars missions. The proposed development technologies include an ESP32 microcontroller, MAX30102 sensor for heart rate and SpO₂ monitoring, AD8232 ECG sensor, temperature sensors, environmental sensors and a radiation dosimeter. Python is proposed for data analysis and AI development, C/C++ for embedded programming, Scikit-learn or TensorFlow for machine learning, Streamlit for the health dashboard and SQLite or PostgreSQL for storing health records. Bluetooth or Wi-Fi may be used for communication in the prototype. The creativity and innovation of ASTROHEALTH lie in its integration of wearable health monitoring, artificial intelligence and personalised health analysis into a single platform. Unlike basic health monitoring systems that only display measurements, ASTROHEALTH compares readings with individual health baselines, identifies unusual changes and provides useful alerts and suggested actions. During development, the team considered factors such as sensor accuracy, system reliability, astronaut safety, space environmental conditions, power efficiency, wearable comfort, data security, real-time performance, individual health differences, scalability and cost. The system also recognises the limitations of wearable technology, as conditions such as bone-density loss and immune-system changes require specialised tests or validated indirect indicators rather than ordinary smartwatch sensors. The project is currently a prototype concept demonstrated using simulated health readings, and further development, testing and validation would be required before actual spaceflight use. Overall, ASTROHEALTH aims to make astronaut health monitoring smarter, more personalised and more reliable, helping astronauts maintain their health and safety throughout long-duration space missions.

projectDetails.name: Regolith
projectDetails.summary: Regolith is a browser game where students design and run a Moon or Mars outpost for 60 sols, balancing power, radiation shielding, life support, food and mass. Every choice has a cost, and a post-mortem traces failures to the decision that caused them. A rover mission layer logs open, structured data that can train rover navigation and planning AI.
projectDetails.details:
What it is. Regolith is a browser game where students design and run a Moon or Mars outpost for 60 sols. Before launch, players split a fixed mass budget across solar arrays, fission units, batteries, radiation shielding, life-support recycling, greenhouse beds and stored rations. Then they run the outpost, spending 12 crew-hours per sol on greenhouse tending, life-support maintenance, panel cleaning, regolith excavation, a rover EVA, or hibernate mode, while random events strike: solar particle events, recycler faults, dust build-up, and Martian dust storms. Three sites change the constraints: Moon (polar ridge), Moon (equatorial, with a 14-day night) and Mars. If the mission fails, a post-mortem traces the failure back to specific decisions with numbers.

How it works. One deterministic resource model links power, oxygen, water, food, radiation dose, dust and mass, so no choice is free. A rover EVA minigame adds scouting (tagging rocks and craters), terrain driving with slope, tilt and battery drain, and a self-righting decision after a tip-over. Everything runs in a single HTML/JavaScript file with canvas graphics and needs no install.

NASA data and resources. Our life-support model is parameterized with NASA published values: crew oxygen use from NASA’s Life Support Baseline Values and Assumptions Document (BVAD), baseline drinking water intake and food planning values from NASA Johnson Space Center and NTRS publications, and Mars surface radiation from the Curiosity rover’s Radiation Assessment Detector (RAD) measurements. [Add only the sources you finish verifying; see below.]

Benefits and impact. Students feel why a mission fails or succeeds instead of reading about it. The same simulation produces open, structured data, with every outpost decision, rover drive trace, hazard label and self-righting choice stored as JSONL. This data is intended to train rover navigation, perception and planning AI, and to benchmark resource-allocation agents. It supports high-level policy and perception, not low-level servo control. Our own rover project is the first user of the data.

Creativity. The game is both a learning tool and a data-collection pipeline: each lesson a student learns also becomes labelled human-decision data.

Tools. HTML, CSS, JavaScript, canvas, Google Fonts, GitHub Pages. The code was generated with Claude (Anthropic) AI and edited by our team; the concept and rover integration are ours.

Factors we considered. Scientific accuracy vs playability (simplified physics, real parameters), mobile controls for classrooms, privacy (anonymous data only, no personal information), honest limits of what game data can teach a robot, and a roadmap: real LRO and HiRISE imagery for hazard labelling, cloud collection across schools, and a digital twin of our rover.

projectDetails.name: Project csetechies1
projectDetails.summary:
We developed an **Autonomous Astronaut Health Monitoring System** designed to protect astronauts during long-duration space missions. The system combines a wearable wrist monitoring device and an ESP32-S3-based cabin monitoring hub. It uses sensors such as MAX30102 for heart rate and SpO₂, MAX30205 for body temperature, MPU6050 for movement, SCD41 for CO₂, BME680 for environmental monitoring, and BG51 for radiation monitoring.
The system continuously collects health and cabin data, analyzes readings using filtering and baseline checks, and generates alerts when abnormal conditions are detected. It also stores health records locally and continues operating during communication blackouts, synchronizing data with ground control when connectivity returns.
This solution addresses the challenges of microgravity, radiation exposure, health risks, and communication delays. It is important because it supports early detection of potential health problems, improves astronaut safety, and enables more reliable health monitoring during future deep-space missions.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details: Autonomous Astronaut Health Monitoring System

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Our project, the Autonomous Astronaut Health Monitoring System, is designed to continuously monitor astronauts' health and cabin environmental conditions during long-duration space missions.

The system consists of two main components: a wearable wrist monitoring device and an ESP32-S3-based cabin monitoring hub. The wearable device uses sensors to measure heart rate, blood oxygen levels, body temperature and movement. The cabin hub monitors carbon dioxide levels, pressure, environmental conditions and radiation.

The collected data is processed by the ESP32-S3, which filters sensor noise, checks readings against configured limits and compares them with the astronaut's normal health baseline. If abnormal readings are detected, the system generates local warnings or critical alerts. It also stores health records locally and continues working during communication blackouts. When communication is restored, stored information can be synchronized with ground control.

2. What are its benefits?

  • Continuous monitoring of astronaut health and cabin conditions.
  • Early identification of possible health abnormalities.
  • Immediate alerts for potentially dangerous conditions.
  • Independent operation during communication blackouts.
  • Local storage of health records for later analysis.
  • Improved awareness of environmental risks during space missions.
  • Better support for astronauts and ground medical teams.

3. What is the intended impact?

The main goal is to improve astronaut safety during long-duration missions, especially deep-space missions where immediate communication with Earth may not always be possible.

The system aims to reduce delays in identifying potential medical problems, support faster onboard responses and provide reliable health records for medical teams. It can contribute to safer future missions to the Moon, Mars and beyond.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware and software were used?

Hardware and sensors:

  • ESP32-S3 – Main processing and control unit.
  • MAX30102 – Heart rate and blood oxygen monitoring.
  • MAX30205 – Body temperature monitoring.
  • MPU6050 – Motion and movement detection.
  • SCD41 – Carbon dioxide monitoring.
  • BME680 – Environmental monitoring and pressure-related measurements.
  • BG51 – Radiation monitoring component.

Software and technologies:

  • Embedded programming for sensor integration and data processing.
  • Kalman filtering for reducing sensor noise.
  • SQLite for local data storage.
  • ESP32-S3 firmware for processing readings and generating alerts.
  • NASA Open Spaceflight Data (OSDR) for research and understanding spaceflight health conditions.
  • NASA-STD-3001 and Delay/Disruption Tolerant Networking (DTN) concepts for informing system requirements and communication design.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

The creative aspect of our project is the combination of wearable health monitoring and cabin environmental monitoring in one autonomous system.

Instead of depending entirely on continuous communication with Earth, the system can process information, identify unusual readings, alert astronauts and store important records directly onboard. Combining personal health data with environmental information provides a broader understanding of possible risks to astronauts.

6. What factors did the team consider?

Our team considered:

  • Astronaut safety and health risks.
  • Radiation exposure and microgravity-related effects.
  • Reliability and accuracy of sensor readings.
  • Low-power and compact hardware requirements.
  • Communication delays and blackouts.
  • Offline processing and secure data storage.
  • Ease of use for astronauts.
  • The need for medical-specialist validation of alert thresholds and response procedures.

Overall, our project aims to make long-duration space missions safer through autonomous health monitoring, early warnings and reliable onboard data management.

Space missions depend on many connected decisions. A bigger science payload adds value but also adds mass, needs more power and may require a larger rocket, which costs more. WHAT IT DOES AND HOW IT WORKS

MISSION X is a browser-based game in which the player designs a spacecraft for a Moon, Mars or Deep Space mission. projectDetails.name: EarthBeat — Hear the Pulse of Our Planet
projectDetails.summary:
EarthBeat is an interactive climate sonification experience developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026: The Earth Information Jukebox. It transforms NASA's monthly global temperature anomaly data from the GISTEMP v4 dataset into sound, allowing users to explore the changing climate record through both visualization and listening.

By mapping real temperature anomaly values to musical tones using browser-based audio synthesis, EarthBeat creates an alternative way to experience long-term climate patterns. Users can explore the data timeline, view the corresponding chart, and hear how the signal changes over time. The project connects NASA's Climate Spiral visualization with data-driven sonification to make climate information more engaging, accessible, and memorable.

EarthBeat demonstrates how scientific data can become an interactive sensory experience without losing its connection to the underlying measurements.
projectDetails.details:
What EarthBeat does

EarthBeat explores climate change through data-driven sonification. It connects NASA's Earth Information Center visualization context with monthly global temperature anomaly observations from NASA's GISTEMP v4 dataset.

The application processes the monthly data and maps temperature anomaly values to sound parameters. Using the Web Audio API, it generates tones directly in the browser, allowing users to listen to how the climate signal changes across the available historical timeline.

How it works

  1. Data source: Monthly global Land-Ocean Temperature Index (LOTI) anomalies are obtained from NASA GISTEMP v4.
  2. Data processing: The application parses the observations, handles missing values, and uses the historical period corresponding to the NASA Climate Spiral visualization (1880–2022).
  3. Sonification: A deterministic mapping translates the temperature anomaly values into audio parameters.
  4. Interactive exploration: Users can play, pause, and navigate the timeline while viewing the corresponding data and mapped frequency readout.

Technology

  • React and TypeScript
  • Vite
  • Web Audio API for browser-based sound synthesis
  • NASA GISTEMP v4 scientific dataset
  • NASA Scientific Visualization Studio Climate Spiral
  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript

Innovation and impact

EarthBeat offers an alternative way to engage with climate information by combining visual exploration with sound. It aims to make long-term scientific patterns more intuitive and memorable, particularly for people who may find conventional charts and numerical datasets difficult to interpret.

The sonification is an artistic representation of measured scientific values, not a recording of sounds produced by Earth. The application retains the original data context, units, baseline information, and source attribution to encourage responsible interpretation.

EarthBeat is an independent educational project created for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 and is not an official NASA product.

projectDetails.name: TerraFlame
projectDetails.summary:
TerraFlame: one consistent fire record for India, 2000 to today

Satellite fire data is hard to compare fairly. MODIS has counted fires since 2000 and VIIRS since 2012, and they see fires differently. When the newer sensor arrives, raw counts jump and year-to-year comparisons break.

TerraFlame, built by team DarkNova, is a fire hotspot calendar for any area in India. Users pick a state, the whole country, a drawn shape or a point and radius. They see detections by year, month or day since November 2000, and whether a period is unusual compared with the same dates in earlier years. A live map shows detections from the last 24 to 72 hours.

We harmonize NASA FIRMS data into one MODIS-equivalent record with an uncertainty band, calibrated by state and month. After conversion, monthly correlation is 0.99 and VIIRS drops from 5.7 times MODIS to 1.03 times. Fresh data arrives every 3 hours, and results can be exported as CSV.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

TerraFlame is a web app that gives one consistent record of fire hotspot detections for any area of India, from November 2000 to today. A user picks an area: a state, the whole country, a shape drawn on the map, or a point with a radius. They then see detections and fire radiative power (fire intensity) by year, month or day, and whether a chosen period is unusual compared with the same dates in earlier years, shown as a median, percentile and rank. A live map shows individual detections from the last 24, 48 or 72 hours. Results can be downloaded as CSV for an area, a map cell or individual points.

Behind this is a harmonization pipeline. NASA FIRMS has two sensor families that count fires differently: MODIS since 2000 and VIIRS since 2012. When VIIRS arrives, raw counts jump and long-term comparison breaks. We clean the detections, count them per H3 hexagon cell (about 250 km²), per state and per day, and calibrate conversion ratios by state and month using the years both sensors flew. The result is one MODIS-equivalent record with a low-to-high uncertainty band. A scheduled job fetches new detections every 3 hours, harmonizes them the same way, and stores them in PostgreSQL. The website reads only that database, never FIRMS directly.

Benefits

  • History you can compare: old and new satellites sit on one scale, so a jump in the chart is a change in fire activity, not a change of sensor.
  • Answers, not raw data: users get clear readings for their own area and period, like “higher than 96% of earlier years”, instead of files to process.
  • Built-in trust: a Proof page shows how well the converted VIIRS record matches MODIS.
  • Recent and history in one place: the live view and the long-term record sit side by side.

Intended impact

TerraFlame is for emergency managers, forest and agriculture officials, researchers and journalists. They can see quickly whether this season is normal for their area and back decisions with a consistent 25-year record. Open data and an open method mean others can check and reuse the work.

Tools, languages and software

  • Languages: Python and TypeScript.
  • Data and backend: NASA FIRMS API (MODIS and VIIRS), pandas, the H3 hexagon grid, PostgreSQL, FastAPI, and a scheduled ingest job every 3 hours.
  • Frontend: React, TypeScript, Vite, ECharts for charts, MapLibre and deck.gl for maps, OpenStreetMap basemap.
  • Design: Figma.

What makes it creative

Most fire tools show either raw recent points or a single sensor’s history. TerraFlame joins the two sensor eras into one record and then shows its own evidence. After conversion, monthly correlation is 0.99 and the typical monthly difference is 8%. VIIRS goes from 5.7 times MODIS to 1.03 times, and 88% of states share the same peak month. A calendar heatmap of years by months makes 25 years of fire seasons readable at a glance. The “is this period unusual” comparison turns statistics into a plain sentence.

Factors our team considered

  • Fairness of comparison: conversion is calibrated per state and per month, not with one national factor.
  • Honesty about uncertainty: every estimate has a low-to-high band. The checks describe the overlap years and are not a forecast.
  • Clear limits: counts are detection events, not unique fires or burned area; clouds, smoke and orbit gaps can hide fires; daily values are noisier than monthly ones.
  • Raw versus converted: map dots are raw FIRMS points, while daily totals are harmonized like the history.
  • Reliability: the app reads only from our own database, so it keeps working if the FIRMS service is slow.
  • Usability and accessibility: plain-language wording, colour-blind-safe chart colours, and light and dark themes.

projectDetails.name: Project DEKEX
projectDetails.summary:
**Lunar Landing Site Navigator**

Lunar Landing Site Navigator is an interactive web-based prototype developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge to simplify the evaluation of potential landing sites near the Moon's south pole. The project addresses two major challenges in lunar exploration: limited sunlight availability and direct-to-Earth communication opportunities.

Built using Python, Streamlit, and Plotly, the application is designed to use NASA's JPL Horizons astronomical data to analyze the positions of the Sun and Earth at selected lunar locations. Users can choose candidate landing sites and observation dates, visualize elevation angles, and compare estimated sunlight and Earth visibility conditions.

By presenting complex astronomical information through an accessible interface, the project aims to support preliminary mission analysis, scientific education, and public engagement in lunar exploration. Future improvements include terrain-aware horizon calculations, interactive lunar maps, and advanced landing-site recommendations.

Our goal is to make lunar exploration planning more accessible, understandable, and data-driven.
projectDetails.details:
Lunar Landing Site Navigator is a rapid prototype designed to help users explore sunlight and Earth visibility conditions at candidate locations near the Moon's south pole.

The project uses Python, Streamlit, Plotly and NASA JPL Horizons to provide a simple interface for analyzing the Sun's and Earth's apparent positions over a selected observation period.

Users can select from three sample lunar south pole coordinates, choose a date and analysis duration, and request astronomical position data. The application is designed to display elevation graphs and compare the percentage of sampled times during which the Sun and Earth are above the geometric horizon.

The project aims to make complex astronomical information more accessible to students, educators and early-stage mission planners.

Our prototype uses a simplified horizon model and does not yet account for terrain obstructions, landing hazards or actual radio-link performance. Future development will incorporate lunar elevation data, terrain-aware visibility calculations and improved landing-site comparison tools.

The project was developed with AI assistance for coding, architecture and documentation. Scientific results require validation against NASA's published ephemerides.

projectDetails.name: SuitOS: AI-Driven Spacesuit Telemetry & Flight Surgeon
projectDetails.summary:
During deep-space missions, communication delays of up to 20 minutes make real-time medical support from Earth impossible. To address this, we developed SuitOS: a localized, AI-driven Flight Surgeon built directly into the spacesuit's telemetry loop.

SuitOS processes real-time biometric hardware inputs—including optical webcam extraction and wearable sensor uploads—and monitors them against strict NASA-STD-3001 physiological limits. When anomalies like hypoxia, hyperthermia, or tachycardia are detected, the onboard AI instantly generates offline, actionable emergency medical protocols. This project is critical because it ensures astronaut survivability during communication blackouts, empowering them with autonomous, real-time medical interventions without relying on an Earth-uplink.
projectDetails.details:
SuitOS acts as an autonomous medical assistant inside an astronaut's HUD. The system ingests real-time telemetry across 12 distinct physiological metrics. We integrated multiple hardware input methods to ensure robust monitoring: manual sensor overrides, wearable packet uploads (JSON/CSV), and optical biometric extraction via webcam frame data. The system continuously monitors these baselines against strict NASA-STD-3001 parameters. Upon detecting a critical anomaly, the onboard LLM instantly streams a diagnostic status update and generates two immediate, actionable countermeasures for the astronaut to execute, completely independent of Earth. The impact is enhanced autonomy and survivability for deep-space missions (Mars and beyond).

Tools, Languages, and Software: We built this web application using Python and Streamlit for the responsive, glassmorphism UI. We utilized the OpenAI SDK connected to Groq's API to power the local LLM inference, ensuring lightning-fast response times. The application relies on Pandas for data structuring, session-state caching for zero-reload AI streaming, and the Requests library for real-time NASA API integrations.

Creativity and Factors Considered: We recognized that spaceflight causes extreme psychological stress, so we integrated a "Mental Health & Morale" module that streams live Earth imagery from the ISS Cupola to act as an active psychological countermeasure. Furthermore, we built a fallback failover chain for the AI models to ensure the system remains online even if one model degrades.

Second Chance is a mission-design game built on a real failure. In 1999, NASA’s Mars Polar Lander was lost, and the investigation traced it to a missing line of software logic, inadequate testing and a mission underfunded by about 30%. Players take over the redesign: they choose instruments, landing logic, communications and power for a Mars lander, balance cost, mass, power and schedule under monthly funding limits, then fly the mission through launch, transfer, landing and surface operations. A review board scores the result and reveals the hidden risks they carried. The game teaches integrated systems engineering and the human pressures behind real decisions. Sources: NASA/JPL report D-18709, Phoenix press kits and NSSDCA records.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does it do or how does it work?

SECOND CHANCE is an interactive, pixel-art 2D space mission design game inspired by the Mars Polar Lander mission. Players take the role of a mission director, making engineering decisions, selecting spacecraft systems, managing resources and planning an Earth-to-Mars journey. They then experience the launch, landing and Martian rover exploration while facing the consequences of their decisions.

2. What benefits does it have?

The project makes complex aerospace engineering concepts easier to understand through interactive learning. It develops critical thinking, problem-solving and decision-making skills while introducing players to spacecraft design, robotics, orbital mechanics and planetary exploration.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our goal is to make space science and engineering more accessible and engaging, especially for students. We hope to inspire the next generation of scientists and engineers by turning real-world space mission challenges into an enjoyable educational experience.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

The game was developed using HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript. SVG graphics and CSS animations are used to create spacecraft visuals, orbital diagrams and interactive environments. Development was carried out using Visual Studio Code. The project is browser-based and does not require specialised physical hardware.

5. How is your project creative?

SECOND CHANCE combines retro pixel-art gaming with space mission engineering. Instead of simply explaining mission failures, it allows players to investigate challenges, redesign spacecraft, make decisions and experience different mission outcomes. Its interactive storytelling and simulation-based gameplay make engineering concepts more engaging.

6. What factors did your team consider?

We considered engineering accuracy, educational value, accessibility, cost, usability and player engagement. Important mission constraints such as mass, power, budget, reliability, payload capacity and time were incorporated into the gameplay to demonstrate the trade-offs involved in real space exploration.

projectDetails.name: Earth Jukebox
projectDetails.summary:
Earth Jukebox — hear 46 years of NASA Earth science as music

NASA's Earth Information Center produces extraordinary visualisations of our changing planet, but presenting Earth science only as images excludes blind and low‑vision audiences. Earth Jukebox turns those visual frames into sound in real time. We pull NASA GIBS MERRA‑2 monthly rasters, decode every pixel back into a physical value using NASA's own published colour bars, and aggregate them onto a 10° global grid — 560 monthly frames from January 1980 to August 2026 across five variables: air temperature, precipitation, wind speed, aerosol optical depth and root‑zone soil moisture. Two places then sound simultaneously, one in each ear, as a browser‑synthesised ensemble in which each variable is played by the sound of the physical process it measures: rain falls as droplets, wind breathes as filtered noise, dust thickens a chord‑tuned sub‑bass, soil moisture becomes a fingerpicked guitar arpeggio, and temperature sets the register of a plucked nylon‑guitar melody built from Karplus‑Strong strings. A listener can scrub through 46 years of climate history and hear the Arctic warm, the monsoon arrive and the Sahara fall silent — no installation, no audio files, no server.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works. Earth Jukebox is a single web app that sonifies NASA Earth science data in real time. The pipeline has three stages:

  1. Ingest (offline, Python). tools/ingest.py requests NASA GIBS WMS GetMap rasters for five MERRA‑2 monthly layers for every month from 1980‑01 to 2026‑08 (560 frames). Each pixel is converted back to a physical number by inverting NASA's own published colour bar for that layer (tools/make_ramps.py), then aggregated onto a 36×18 grid at 10° resolution. The result is a 2.4 MB dataset (data/dataset.json → packed to app/data/dataset.js).
    • Temperature → the register of a plucked guitar melody (10 scale steps ≈ 1.5 octaves) plus note length and brightness.
    • Precipitation → droplet hits whose rate (0.35→10/s), pitch and level follow rainfall; a dry month is genuinely silent.
    • Wind speed → a band of breathing noise; level, centre frequency (300→1200 Hz) and LFO rate all follow speed, and wind also triggers a high "sparkle" layer.
    • Aerosol optical depth → a warm sub‑bass tuned to the chord root, so dust thickens the harmony from below.
    • Soil moisture → the density of a fingerpicked guitar arpeggio inside the chord.
    • A shared four‑chord progression keeps both ears consonant: side A is Dorian on A2, side B is Lydian on E3, a fifth apart. Nothing is sustained — every voice is struck and decays, so a 46‑year scan never turns into a drone.

Benefits. For blind and low‑vision users it converts a visualisation they cannot access into a continuously listenable stream that carries the actual numbers, with a screen‑reader live region narrating date, both places, all five values and the musical register. For sighted users it makes 46 years of climate change perceptible in about 100 seconds — the Arctic's warming is audible as a rising register, and the Arctic/global contrast is audible as a difference between the two ears. Because both sides obey identical mapping rules, any difference you hear is a real difference in the data.

Intended impact. A demonstration that accessibility is not a retrofit: a sonification can be a genuine instrument, not a beeping chart. The technique generalises to any NASA variable that has a published colour bar — the app is a template for turning EIC imagery into an accessible, broadcastable, museum‑loopable channel.

Tools, languages, software. Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no frameworks, no bundler, no CDN, no third‑party libraries). Web Audio API (OscillatorNode, AudioBufferSourceNode, BiquadFilterNode, StereoPannerNode, ConvolverNode, DynamicsCompressorNode) and Canvas 2D. Ingest and QA in Python 3 with numpy, pillow and playwright (headless Chromium). No hardware beyond the listener's browser.

How it is creative. The creative decision was to make each variable sound like itself rather than like a parameter. Dust does not get a tune — it thickens the bass. Heat does not raise a beep — it moves the melody into a higher register inside a shared harmony. Two places are heard as two characters in one key rather than two data streams, so the piece can be listened to for hours. It also documents its own failures: the design notes record six earlier versions (sawtooth drone, sustained pad, fixed motif, organ, physical models, guitar) and why each was rejected — the tune that was "ours rather than the planet's" was the hardest one to give up.

Factors considered. Data fidelity vs. musicality (quantising a continuous curve onto a scale loses precision — documented honestly); accessibility as a first‑class path (keyboard‑only operation, ARIA slider, narrated live region, reduced‑motion and contrast support); performance (a 46‑year scan on a laptop, cached strings, compressor + limiter so nothing clips); honesty of representation (the app is explicit that it is reanalysis data on a 10° display grid, ~0.2 K colour‑bar quantisation, monthly resolution); and licensing/attribution (NASA data credited, MIT code, no copyrighted assets).

projectDetails.name: MarScope
projectDetails.summary: Martian Map is a turn-by-turn EVA surface navigation system — essentially "Google Maps for Mars" — that layers six NASA datasets (HiRISE imagery, MOLA topography, Viking mosaics, USGS nomenclature, Curiosity 360° panoramas, and REMS meteorology) into a single astronaut-ready interface for hyperlocal Marswalk planning in Gale Crater. It fills the gap between NASA's existing global-scale tools (like Mars Trek) and what the first human explorers will actually need: route-level, slope-aware, obstacle-conscious guidance they can use while wearing spacesuits on an alien surface.
projectDetails.details:
MarScope  

What It Does & How It Works  

Martian Map is a turn-by-turn EVA surface navigation system—essentially a Mars counterpart to familiar mapping tools—built as a spacecraft tablet application for planning and carrying out a Marswalk. It centres on Gale Crater, the zone used by NASA’s Curiosity rover, and combines six real NASA datasets into one tactical interface.  

The application offers four integrated views sharing a single reactive state store:  

  • 3D Terrain HUD (Three.js)  
  • First-person surface view at 1.7 m astronaut eye height, using DEM geometry draped with HiRISE orthophoto imagery  
  • Physically accurate Mars sky model—butterscotch daytime CO₂-scattered atmosphere, blue forward-scattering sunrise/sunset glow, dust haze horizon band driven by optical depth tau, stars at night, and a 0.35° sun disc  
  • Curiosity rover 3D model enabling a third-person camera option  
  • Ground-anchored route lines with chevron indicators, destination beacon poles, and arrival rings  
  • 2D Tactical Mini Map (Leaflet)  
  • High-resolution Gale Crater map from 25 cm/px HiRISE imagery  
  • Switchable among three layer styles: satellite orthophoto, MOLA elevation hillshade, and slope hazard heatmap  
  • Shows astronaut position, heading, and route overlay with heading-up or north-up orientation  
  • Mars Planetary Globe & Flat Map (Three.js)  
  • Interactive 3D globe textured with the Viking MDIM 2.1 colourised global mosaic- Labeled 30° graticule, atmospheric rim glow, and 2,055 USGS/IAU planetary nomenclature features include level-of-detail decluttering.  
  • A pannable flat equirectangular projection offers multiple base layers.  
  • Mars “Street View”  
  • A 360° panoramic viewer uses real Curiosity Mastcam panoramas from multiple sols.  
  • It lets the astronaut preview the surface at waypoints before arrival.  
  • Drag-to-look and pinch-to-zoom follow the Google Street View model.  

Turn-by-Turn Navigation Engine  

  • Great-circle distances and forward azimuths are computed on the IAU 2000 Mars sphere (R = 3,396,190 m) using the Haversine formula.  
  • Human-readable tactical instructions such as “Move forward 40 m” or “Move forward right 285 m” use turn reasoning based on relative bearing from the current heading.  
  • An instruction bar shows remaining distance, estimated walking time at a 1.4 m/s suited astronaut pace, live DEM elevation, and Horn-method ground slope with safety grading below 15°.  
  • A directional waypoint arrow in the 3D HUD points toward the next waypoint; a destination beacon overlay shows the target name and live distance.  
  • Arrival is announced within 5 m of the destination.  

Mars Solar Time & Sun Geometry Simulator  

  • The Allison & McEwen (2000) / Mars24 solar geometry formula is implemented.  
  • Adjusting Local True Solar Time (00:00–24:00 LTST) via slider or quick-jump buttons drives the 3D sun position, surface shadows, sky dome coloring, and lighting in real time.60× playback mode advances one Martian hour every 60 seconds, allowing the astronaut to preview shadow conditions and visibility across a sol before choosing a route.  

Weather & Climate Panel  

  • Modeled on the Google Weather card layout, it presents surface meteorology using Curiosity REMS baseline data.  
  • Current temperature (°C/°F toggle) includes diurnal cycle modeling, peaking at −18°C at 14:00 LTST and dropping to −78°C at 05:00.  
  • Atmospheric pressure shows semi-diurnal thermal tide modeling (~725–770 Pa).  
  • Surface wind speed and direction follow daytime thermal upslope and nighttime downslope cycles.  
  • Dust visibility (optical depth tau) uses an adjustable slider.  
  • Hourly forecast pills and a 5-sol outlook are provided.  
  • Interactive charts track diurnal temperature, pressure, and wind.  
  • Gale Crater rim depth analysis shows current depth below the 5,500 m crater rim.  

Terrain Measurement Tool  

  • Click two points on the map to compute terrain distance, straight-line 3D distance, elevation gain or loss, maximum slope angle with safety assessment, and an elevation profile cross-section. This is vital for route planning in unfamiliar terrain where obstacles may not be visible from a distance.  

Places Catalog & Feature Inspection  

  • A searchable, filterable catalog lists Mars locations, including active rovers (Perseverance, Curiosity), historic missions (Opportunity, Spirit, Pathfinder/Sojourner, Phoenix, InSight, Viking landers), and geographic features.Each entry serves as a detailed “mission dossier” containing coordinates, elevation, scientific instruments, key discoveries, narrative storytelling, and high-resolution imagery carousels. Entries may be set as navigation destinations or viewed on the globe. Filter chips include All Targets, Rover Expeditions, Walkable EVA, and Verified sites.

Benefits  

  • Safety-First Design — Slope hazard heatmaps, live slope grading in the instruction bar (with a 15° EVA safe limit), elevation profile measurement, and weather forecasting provide astronauts with the information needed to avoid terrain hazards and plan around environmental conditions — NASA’s primary priority.  
  • Hyperlocal Scale — Unlike existing tools built for regional or global views, Martian Map operates at the individual Marswalk scale — meter level resolution where route planning decisions occur.  
  • Familiar UX Paradigm — By modeling the interface on Google Maps (turn-by-turn directions, Street View, weather cards, measurement tools), the system uses navigation patterns every astronaut already knows, reducing training time and cognitive load in a high-stress environment.  
  • Multi-Data Fusion — Layers optical, topographic, slope, atmospheric, meteorological, and nomenclature data together in context, so the astronaut sees the full picture rather than consulting separate tools.  
  • Zero-Infrastructure Deployment — Runs entirely client-side with no backend, no API keys, no accounts, and no internet dependency crucial for a Mars habitat where connectivity to Earth has 4–24 minute light-speed delays.  

Intended Impact  

  • Mission Planning — Provide a template for the type of integrated surface navigation system that will be essential when humans reach Mars, showing what is possible with current data and what gaps remain.  
  • Public Engagement — Make Mars exploration tangible and accessible — anyone can open the tool and experience what it would feel like to walk across the Martian surface, building public understanding of and support for human Mars exploration.Data Integration Proof of Concept Demonstrating that combining HiRISE imagery, MOLA topography, REMS meteorology, Mastcam panoramas, and USGS nomenclature into one interface yields value beyond the individual components.

Tools, Languages, Hardware & Software  

Languages & Frameworks  

  • JavaScript (ES Modules) — all application logic (~7,000 lines of source code)  
  • HTML5 & CSS3 — custom dark aerospace mission-control theme (1,188 lines of CSS), fully responsive layout  

3D & Mapping Libraries  

  • Three.js v0.187 — WebGL terrain rendering, sky simulation, planetary globe, and Street View panoramas  
  • Leaflet v1.9.4 — 2D Mars equirectangular tactical mini-map with custom coordinate reference system  

Build & Test Tooling  

  • Vite v8.3.8 — modern frontend development server and production bundler  
  • Puppeteer Core v25.17 — headless browser regression testing across multiple viewports (1280×800, 1024×768, 768×1024)  

Deployment  

  • GitHub Pages — static hosting, 88 MB total bundle, zero backend services  

Scientific Models & Standards  

  • IAU 2000 Mars Sphere — Haversine great-circle distance, forward azimuth, East-North-Up local tangent plane coordinates  
  • Allison & McEwen (2000) / Mars24 — Mars solar geometry (elevation, azimuth, declination, hour angle)  
  • Horn (1981) Method — 3×3 window slope computation over ≥5 m baseline for terrain safety grading  
  • Lucide (inline SVG) — tactical UI iconography  

NASA Data Sources Used  

  • Mars Viking Colorized Global Mosaic — Viking Orbiters 1 & 2 (MDIM 2.1) — optical imageryMOLA Global Elevation & Hillshade Mars Global Surveyor / Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter topographic data  
  • Gale Crater Color Orthophoto Mosaic — Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter / HiRISE (25 cm/px native) optical imagery  
  • Gale Crater Topographic DEM & Slope — MRO HiRISE Stereo DTM / HRSC Blend topographic data  
  • Planetary Nomenclature Gazetteer — USGS / IAU Working Group (2,055 named features) — geospatial reference  
  • Curiosity Mastcam 360° Panoramas — MSL Curiosity / Mastcam surface optical imagery  
  • Curiosity REMS Surface Meteorology — MSL / Rover Environmental Monitoring Station — atmospheric data  

All data is NASA Public Domain (17 U.S.C. §105), sourced from USGS Astrogeology, NASA PDS, JPL, and the University of Arizona.  

Creativity  

  • "Google Maps for Mars" Paradigm — Rather than constructing another scientific viewer, we reimagined navigation through the most familiar mapping interface on Earth —turn by turn directions, Street View, weather cards, and measurement tools applied to an alien world. This approach makes the tool instantly intuitive for anyone who has used a smartphone.  
  • Mars "Street View" from Real Panoramas — We adapted Curiosity's Mastcam 360° panoramas into an immersive preview system an astronaut can survey their destination before moving there, a capability absent from current Mars tools.Dynamic Mars Sky Simulation — The sky dome is not a fixed backdrop; it is a physically informed model with butterscotch CO₂scattered daylight, blue forward-scattering sunset glow (the reverse of Earth), dust haze that varies with optical depth, and a star field visible at night. Paired with the solar time simulator, you can experience a complete Martian sol.  
  • Minecraft F3-Style Live Coordinates — Drawing from the real-time debug overlay in Minecraft, we included a persistent HUD showing live planetocentric coordinates, MOLA elevation, and compass heading offering the astronaut steady spatial awareness without opening any panel.  
  • Mission Storytelling Dossiers — Each rover and lander is more than a map pin; it carries a detailed narrative with the full mission story, scientific discoveries, instrument payloads, and telemetry data. This shifts navigation into exploration and learning.  
  • Zero-Backend Architecture — The whole system operates with no servers, no API keys, no user accounts, and no internet reliance. Every byte is bundled and served from the same origin, enforced by a strict Content Security Policy. This is not merely a technical choice; it is a design philosophy for a tool that must function 225 million kilometres from the nearest server.  

Factors the Team ConsideredAstronaut Safety as Priority #1 — Each feature was assessed through the question of whether it aids crew movement. Slope hazard maps, elevation profiles, weather forecasting, and real-time terrain grading support this aim.  

  • Spacesuit Mobility Constraints — A 1.4 m/s EVA pace, a 15° slope limit, and step-based controls mirror the physical limits of a pressurized suit carrying scientific gear.  
  • Mars-Specific Environmental Physics — The solar geometry model uses Mars’s 25.19° obliquity; the weather model reflects a thin CO₂ atmosphere (~748 Pa versus Earth’s 101,325 Pa); and the sky model shows blue sunsets from forward-scattering dust.  
  • Data Transparency — Every dataset is marked REAL or SIMULATED in the interface and code registry. Simulated values such as weather curves and micro-terrain detail carry badges, since clear provenance builds trust in a tool astronauts rely on.  
  • Offline-First Design — Because Earth, Mars delays range from 4–24 minutes, the tool avoids real-time links. A static, self-contained design lets it function without any network.  
  • Responsive Design — Tested across viewports (1280×800, 1024×768, 768×1024), it serves as a workstation display, handheld tablet, or portable device during EVA.  
  • WebGL Resource Discipline — Exactly 2 WebGL contexts (terrain HUD plus globe/minimap sharing one renderer) prevent GPU strain on tablet hardware an astronaut might carry.  
  • Accessibility & Discoverability — An 8-step guided tour introduces features; ARIA labels support screen readers; and consistent color language uses cyan for science data, orange for Mars/destination markers, and green for safe status.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Elyra
projectDetails.summary:
Beyond Earth: The Forgotten Footprints of Space is an interactive educational website built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript that explores human-made spacecraft, landers, rovers, and scientific instruments left behind on the Moon, Mars, Venus, and deep space.
Users can select different celestial destinations to discover the artifacts resting there, learn why they were launched, and explore their scientific achievements. Each object features mission facts, animated visuals, and engaging first-person voice-narrated storytelling, allowing the machines themselves to share their journeys. The platform also includes a chronological mission timeline and an interactive quiz to reinforce learning.
By transforming space history into an audio-visual, story-driven experience rather than plain textbook articles, Beyond Earth makes space science accessible and memorable for students and space enthusiasts. While many know about famous launches, few realize how much historic equipment remains on other worlds—and how some instruments still send data today. Beyond Earth preserves awareness of these remarkable engineering milestones and inspires curiosity about astronomy and space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Beyond Earth is an interactive storytelling website that shows the real spacecraft, rovers, and scientific tools humans have left behind on the Moon, Mars, Venus, and deep space.

How it works:

Watch & Listen Story: Users start with a short, animated story with a human-like voice narrator and space music that introduces famous machines like the Apollo 11 Moon mirror, the Ingenuity Mars helicopter, and Voyager 1.

Explore by Planet: Users can click on different worlds (Moon, Mars, Venus, and Deep Space) to see 11 real space artifacts, their mission facts, and whether they are still active today.

Machines Tell Their Own Stories: Clicking any artifact lets users read and listen to a first-person story where the spacecraft itself explains why it was sent to space and what it discovered.

Timeline & Quiz: Users can scroll through a simple mission timeline from 1959 to today and take a quick 4-question quiz to test what they learned.

What Benefits Does It Have?

  • Makes Learning Fun and Easy: Instead of boring textbook paragraphs, students learn space history through animated visuals, voice narration, and interactive quizzes.
  • Builds Emotional Connection: Letting spacecraft tell their own stories in the first person helps users remember the science and feel connected to space exploration.
  • Uncovers Hidden Space History: Most people only hear about rocket launches, not the real machines still sitting on the Moon, Mars, and Venus—or the ones still sending data today.
  • Accessible to Everyone: With built-in voice narration, adjustable reading speeds, and simple controls, it works smoothly on any phone or computer with no downloads needed.
  • Inspires Future Explorers: Sparks curiosity about astronomy, engineering, and space science among school students and casual learners.

What Is the Intended Impact?

  • Inspire Young Learners: Encourage school students to take an interest in space science, engineering, and astronomy by turning dry history into an emotional, interactive story.
  • Preserve Off-World Heritage: Help people recognize and appreciate the real machines still resting on the Moon, Mars, Venus, and deep space as historic human achievements—not just forgotten hardware.
  • Make Space Education Accessible Anywhere: Provide a free, browser-based learning tool with voice narration and simple visuals that teachers, students, and casual space fans around the world can use on any device.
  • Shift How People Learn Science: Show that complex space missions and scientific discoveries are easier to understand and remember when told through human-like storytelling and interactive exploration.

Tools & Technologies Used

  • Coding Languages: HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript (ES6+) to build the interactive website and storytelling logic.
  • Design & Styling: Tailwind CSS, custom CSS animations, Google Fonts, and Font Awesome icons for a clean, space-themed look that works on both phones and computers.
  • Graphics & Visuals: HTML5 Canvas for the moving starfield background and custom SVG vector graphics for the animated planets, lasers, and spacecraft.
  • Voice & Sound Software: Built-in browser Web Speech API for the human-like voice narrator and Web Audio API to generate soft background space ambience.
  • Development & Hosting Tools: Visual Studio Code (or standard code editor), modern web browsers for testing, and Netlify for publishing the live website link.

What Factors Did Your Team Consider?

  • User Accessibility & Ease of Use: We designed Beyond Earth to work seamlessly on any device (smartphones, tablets, and computers) through a web browser with zero downloads required.
  • Emotional Connection & Engagement: We considered how to make history memorable, choosing a first-person storytelling perspective where spacecraft "speak" their own journeys so users feel a deeper connection to the science.
  • Inclusivity & Comfortable Listening: We added natural human voice pacing and adjustable speed controls so users of all reading levels and learning styles can easily follow along with the audio narration.
  • Technical Simplicity & Reliability: We built the project using clean HTML, CSS, and JavaScript without complex external plugins, ensuring the site loads instantly and runs smoothly during presentations.

projectDetails.name: AFTERLIGHT
projectDetails.summary:
AFTERLIGHT is an interactive 3D planetary archaeology and spatial storytelling platform that preserves and contextualizes humanity’s physical exploration heritage across the Moon, Mars, and the Solar System.

We developed a real-time WebGL simulation engine (Three.js and React 19) coupling ground-truth NASA Planetary Data System (PDS), LROC, and USGS MOLA coordinates with a 14-chapter mission choreographic cinema, a 48 kHz physically grounded space acoustic suite, and a 0%–100% CAD exploded-view hardware inspector across 22 natural satellite worlds.

AFTERLIGHT addresses the challenge by resolving the fragmentation and static nature of space history archives. It replaces disconnected 2D tables with centimeter-accurate 3D coordinate provenance tracking initial touchdown, final operating, orbital reconnaissance, and impact sites with explicit uncertainty radii and authentic aerodynamic flight telemetry.

This project is vital as humanity enters the Artemis era and prepares for crewed Martian exploration. Over 70 historic landers, rovers, and probes face severe physical degradation from micrometeorite impacts, thermal stress, and solar radiation. AFTERLIGHT creates an immutable, educational digital twin that safeguards humanity's first extraterrestrial footprints, ensuring our cosmic heritage remains permanently accessible and inspiring to future generations.
projectDetails.details:
### What It Does & How It Works

AFTERLIGHT is a real-time 3D spatial simulation and planetary archaeology platform. It maps humanity’s physical exploration artifacts across the Solar System using four distinct coordinate disciplines: Initial Touchdown, Final Operating, Modern Documented Reconnaissance (LROC NAC / MRO HiRISE), and Impact Coordinates, each bound to ground-truth uncertainty radii.

Key capabilities include:

1. **Interactive 3D Spatial Canvas**: A heliocentric Solar System and centimeter-resolution 3D globes for the Moon and Mars with authentic topographical graticules and real rover traverse routes (Apollo 15 LRV, Lunokhod 2, Opportunity, and Perseverance).

2. **22 Natural Satellite Worlds**: Accurate modeling of moons across Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune, supporting true 1:1 physical scale and computing real-time parent-planet sky visibility and angular subtense.

3. **14-Chapter Story Cinema Engine**: 70 synchronized micro-beats calculating live aerodynamic telemetry (altitude, velocity, dynamic pressure, g-force, thermal load) with exact 12.0-second archival video timing.

4. **Physically Grounded Space Acoustics**: Emulates vacuum structural sound conduction, featuring a 24-second dual-part soft increasing thruster sound that cushions touchdown impact, with zero-latency immediate pause.

5. **3D Hardware CAD Inspector**: Damped exploded-view radial disassembly (0%–100%) with aerospace PBR materials (wrinkled golden Kapton foil, anodized aluminum, and solar arrays).

### Tools, Coding Languages & Software

- **Frontend & 3D**: React 19, TypeScript (Strict Mode), Three.js (r187), WebGL 2.0, Tailwind CSS v4, Lucide Icons.

- **Audio Engine**: Web Audio API with generation-token gating against asynchronous race conditions.

- **Backend & Security**: Node.js, Express 4, Vite 8, OWASP-compliant Content Security Policy (CSP).

- **Media Worker Pipeline**: Sandboxed FFmpeg / FFprobe subprocess worker with path-traversal prevention.

- **Testing & Verification**: 10 automated unit test suites (`node:test`) verifying coordinate transforms, spherical Haversine distances, and astronomical scale ratios.

### Benefits & Intended Impact

With NASA’s Artemis campaign returning humanity to the Moon and preparing for Mars, protecting historic landing sites from rocket plume exhaust and accidental disturbance is urgent. AFTERLIGHT bridges aerospace engineering, historical preservation, and public education by providing an open, interactive, mathematical standard for planetary archaeology.

### Creativity & Design Factors

Rather than presenting flat tables or static 2D images, AFTERLIGHT integrates physical vacuum acoustics, authentic 16mm archival camera timings, real-time parent-planet sky subtense, and CAD exploded-view inspection into a single cinematic web experience accessible on desktop, tablet, and mobile devices.

projectDetails.name: Crew Health Monitor: Neurocognitive and Behavioral Health Monitoring for Astronauts
projectDetails.summary:
In deep space, protecting an astronaut's health means protecting their ability to think, react and make critical decisions.

Crew Health Monitor (CHM) is an offline-capable neurocognitive and behavioral health monitoring platform designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. Through four quick daily assessments—reaction time, visual working memory, fine motor coordination and psychological wellbeing—CHM tracks changes in an astronaut's performance against their personal baseline.

Its transparent statistical analysis identifies unusual performance changes and classifies them into clear alert levels. A seven-session trend dashboard helps reveal gradual changes that a single check-in might miss. Going beyond monitoring, MAYA-V, an AI crew companion, offers motivational and wellbeing support, while the BH-01 protocol is designed to escalate serious behavioral distress for human medical attention.

By combining early monitoring, personalized insights and offline functionality, CHM aims to help crews stay aware, supported and better prepared for the challenges of spaceflight.
projectDetails.details:
FROM HEALTH MONITORING TO MISSION READINESS: THE ENGINEERING BEHIND CREW HEALTH MONITOR

The most dangerous change in an astronaut may be the one nobody notices.

A crew member can appear physically healthy while experiencing subtle deterioration in reaction speed, working memory, motor coordination or psychological wellbeing. In a long-duration Mars mission, these changes are not merely personal health concerns; they can become operational risks. Our team approached this challenge from a different perspective: instead of simply monitoring an astronaut's health, can we continuously assess whether they are cognitively and behaviourally prepared to perform mission-critical duties?

This question became the engineering foundation of Crew Health Monitor (CHM).

1. How the System Works: From Human Performance to Mission Readiness

CHM transforms a short daily assessment into a structured flight-readiness screening process. Its four assessment modules examine different dimensions of human performance:

- Reaction Time: A visual stimulus test measures response speed and attention. Changes from an astronaut's normal performance can indicate reduced alertness or fatigue.

- Working Memory: A progressively challenging spatial sequence-recall test evaluates the ability to retain and reproduce information, an essential cognitive function during complex mission operations.

- Fine Motor Coordination: A 20-second moving-target tracking assessment evaluates hand-eye coordination and precision, particularly relevant to robotic operations, docking and extravehicular activities.

- Behavioural Wellbeing: A structured self-assessment records mood, sleep, stress and energy on a five-point scale, bringing psychological wellbeing into the same monitoring framework as cognitive performance.

The key innovation is that these assessments are not interpreted independently. Their results contribute to a unified picture of the astronaut's daily performance.

2. The Intelligence Behind the Decision: Personal Baselines, Not Generic Scores

One of our central engineering decisions was to avoid judging every astronaut against the same fixed performance standard.

Human performance naturally differs between individuals. Therefore, CHM compares daily assessment results against the astronaut's own pre-launch baseline, using statistical z-score calculations to identify meaningful deviations.

A two-tier baseline approach is incorporated: individual pre-launch measurements are preferred, while NASA population norms provide a fallback where individual baseline data are unavailable.

The system translates these calculations into three understandable readiness categories:

- ON TRACK (z > -1): Performance remains within the expected range.

- WATCH (-2 to -1): A noticeable decline prompts a recommended 20–30-minute cognitive recovery period, hydration and stretching.

- BELOW BASELINE (z < -2): A significant decline triggers a mandatory pause and a Flight Surgeon notification workflow.

Reaction time uses an appropriately adjusted calculation because lower response times indicate better performance, whereas memory and coordination use higher-is-better scoring.

We deliberately chose transparent statistical assessment over an unexplained black-box prediction model. Every classification has an interpretable mathematical basis, allowing medical personnel to understand why an alert was generated.

3. MAYA-V: Addressing the Human Side of Deep-Space Exploration

We recognised that monitoring performance alone does not address the psychological challenges of prolonged isolation. An astronaut may need more than a dashboard; they may need a consistent source of encouragement and behavioural support.

This led to MAYA-V (Mission Auxiliary Yielding Assistance – Version 5), an AI-powered crew companion integrated into CHM.

MAYA-V provides conversational engagement, humour, motivational support and reminders for hydration, eye rest and sleep. However, we designed it with a more important responsibility: recognising situations that require human intervention.

Its dedicated safety mechanism, Protocol BH-01, responds to messages indicating hopelessness or self-harm. It disables humour, switches to an empathetic response, locks the conversation to prioritise the emergency workflow, displays a prominent alert, records a critical event with mission-time information and initiates priority notification to the Flight Surgeon.

The companion also incorporates an offline fallback library of more than 50 curated responses when cloud AI services are unavailable.

This makes MAYA-V more than a conversational feature. It represents our attempt to integrate psychological support and safety escalation into an astronaut-monitoring environment.

4. Resilience by Design: Engineering for the Reality of Space

A major constraint considered by our team was communication reliability. A system designed for deep-space missions cannot assume continuous internet access or uninterrupted communication with Earth.

Accordingly, we developed the core screening application using a lightweight, single-file architecture in HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Its essential assessment, scoring and monitoring functions operate locally without requiring an internet connection, external server or continuous cloud dependency.

The AI companion uses cloud-based language-model functionality when available and switches to predefined offline responses when connectivity is lost.

We also incorporated seven-session trend visualisations. Rather than focusing exclusively on an isolated poor assessment, CHM allows performance changes to be observed over successive sessions. Its demonstration mode uses simulated astronaut profiles and accelerated mission timelines to illustrate how different performance patterns can develop over a mission week.

5. Technology, Tools and Development Approach

The prototype was developed using:

- HTML5: Application structure and assessment interfaces.

- CSS3: Responsive layouts, visual feedback and monitoring dashboards.

- JavaScript: Assessment logic, statistical calculations, local functionality, alert workflows and performance visualisations.

- Groq and Qwen 3.8 27B: Cloud-based AI infrastructure and language-model support for MAYA-V.

- Offline response library: More than 50 curated responses for basic companion functionality during cloud-service interruptions.

- Browser-based architecture: A single HTML application that can run on standard computing devices without dedicated monitoring hardware.

No dedicated physiological sensors are required for the current prototype. Integration with wearable measurements such as heart-rate variability (HRV), oxygen saturation (SpO₂) and activity monitoring is identified as a future development direction.

6. What Makes Our Approach Creative and Different?

The creativity of CHM lies not in introducing another health dashboard, but in connecting multiple dimensions of astronaut performance into a single mission-readiness framework.

Our approach brings together:

Performance + Wellbeing + Individual Baselines + Human Oversight + Operational Resilience.

Most importantly, we address three interconnected questions:

1. Is the astronaut performing at their normal cognitive and motor level?

2. Are behavioural and wellbeing indicators suggesting a developing problem?

3. Does the observed decline require recovery, closer monitoring or medical attention?

The combination of objective performance assessments, subjective wellbeing indicators, personalised statistical comparisons and a safety-focused AI companion gives CHM a broader perspective on crew readiness.

We also considered interpretability, limited communication, individual differences, continuity of essential functions, ease of use and the importance of keeping medical decisions under human supervision.

7. Intended Impact: Protecting the Human Element of Space Exploration

Our intended impact extends beyond identifying fatigue. We aim to contribute to a future in which potential declines in astronaut performance can be recognised earlier, recovery can be encouraged at the appropriate time and mission-support personnel can receive meaningful information for human-led decisions.

For future Mars missions, where immediate medical assistance cannot always be guaranteed, an accessible and resilient crew-monitoring tool could become a valuable part of the broader astronaut-support ecosystem.

CHM is currently a functional prototype, not a clinically validated medical device or an autonomous flight-authorisation system. Its classifications are intended as decision-support indicators requiring appropriate human oversight and further validation.

At ERGOXIS, we believe that the future of space exploration depends not only on how far humans can travel, but also on how well we can protect the minds and capabilities of those making that journey.

Our vision is simple: detect the decline before it becomes a mission-critical failure.
