challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.summary:
LUNAVISTA – Lunar Landing Site NavigatorLUNAVISTA – Lunar Landing Site Navigator

LUNAVISTA is an interactive lunar mission-planning and landing-site assessment platform designed to support the identification and evaluation of potential lunar landing regions, particularly near the lunar south pole. It integrates NASA Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO) and Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) terrain data with JPL SPICE ephemerides to provide terrain visualization, elevation and slope assessment, 360° horizon analysis, and time-dependent Sun and Earth visibility calculations.

The platform allows users to explore lunar terrain in 2D and 3D, evaluate candidate landing locations, assess illumination and communication line-of-sight opportunities, and compare mission scenarios against defined engineering requirements. Its mission-planning tools also aim to identify suitable mission windows by evaluating actual celestial geometry and terrain constraints over time.

By combining terrain analysis, orbital geometry, visibility modelling, and mission decision support in one platform, LUNAVISTA aims to make lunar landing-site evaluation more accessible, transparent, and data-driven, helping future lunar exploration missions make better-informed decisions.
projectDetails.details:
LUNAVISTA – Lunar Landing Site Navigator

Website URL

1. Project Overview

LUNAVISTA is an interactive lunar terrain exploration, landing-site assessment and mission-planning platform designed to support future lunar exploration, particularly missions targeting the Moon's south polar region.

Selecting a suitable lunar landing site is challenging because the terrain is uneven, sunlight conditions vary significantly over time, and communication opportunities depend on the visibility of Earth. LUNAVISTA addresses these challenges by integrating lunar terrain data, celestial ephemerides, terrain-aware visibility analysis and mission decision-support tools into a unified platform.

2. How It Works

LUNAVISTA combines several scientific and computational systems:

Lunar Terrain Exploration: The platform processes NASA Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) digital elevation models to generate interactive 2D and 3D terrain visualizations. Users can explore surface elevation, slope, terrain profiles and local topography.

Terrain and Landing Assessment: Users can define candidate landing locations and evaluate their surrounding footprints using elevation and slope measurements. The system checks engineering requirements and identifies compliant, non-compliant and indeterminate conditions based on available data.

Celestial Ephemeris: Using NASA/JPL SPICE and the DE421 planetary ephemeris, LUNAVISTA calculates the apparent positions and directions of the Sun and Earth relative to selected lunar surface locations.

Terrain-Aware Visibility: By combining celestial positions with calculated terrain horizons and finite-disk visibility geometry, the platform evaluates solar illumination opportunities and geometric Earth visibility. It calculates full, partial and obstructed visibility periods over selected time intervals.

Mission Planning and Comparison: Users can create mission profiles, define engineering constraints, screen candidate regions, compare alternatives and evaluate possible mission windows using calculated terrain and visibility metrics.

3. Technologies and Tools

  • Frontend: React, TypeScript and Vite.
  • 3D Visualization: Three.js, React Three Fiber and Drei.
  • 2D Mapping: OpenLayers.
  • Backend: Python and FastAPI.
  • Scientific Computing: NumPy, SciPy, Rasterio, GDAL and PyProj.
  • Celestial Mechanics: NAIF SPICE Toolkit and JPL DE421.
  • Data Sources: NASA LOLA elevation products, Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter datasets and NASA lunar mapping resources.

4. Innovation and Creativity

The key innovation of LUNAVISTA is the integration of multiple lunar mission-planning capabilities into a single interactive environment.

Rather than evaluating terrain, sunlight and Earth visibility independently, the platform connects these calculations to support location-specific and time-dependent mission assessment. Its finite solar and Earth disk visibility modelling accounts for terrain obstruction beyond simple horizon or central-body visibility checks.

The mission decision-support system also distinguishes hard engineering constraints from soft preferences, handles incomplete measurements explicitly and avoids treating unavailable scientific data as zero or as a successful result.

5. Benefits and Expected Impact

LUNAVISTA aims to make lunar landing-site exploration more accessible, reproducible and data-driven. It can help researchers, students and mission planners investigate candidate locations, understand terrain-related risks, evaluate illumination and communication opportunities, and compare potential mission windows.

By bringing terrain analysis, celestial geometry and mission planning together, LUNAVISTA provides a foundation for more informed lunar exploration decisions, particularly in the scientifically challenging south polar environment.

6. Design Considerations

The platform is designed around scientific traceability, data provenance, coordinate-system consistency and transparent uncertainty handling. It distinguishes geometric visibility from actual electrical power generation and radio communication performance. It also accounts for limitations in DEM coverage and ephemeris data rather than presenting unsupported measurements as verified results.

projectDetails.name: Apollo 11 Simulation
projectDetails.summary:
Apollo 11: A Journey to the Moon – Interactive Space Simulation

Our project is an interactive 3D space simulation game that recreates the historic Apollo 11 mission, taking players on a journey from Earth to the Moon. It allows players to experience key stages of the mission, including rocket launch, spacecraft separation, docking, lunar orbit, challenges faced during the mission, lunar descent, landing and the historic Moonwalk.

The simulation combines interactive gameplay, cinematic cutscenes and educational information to make the Apollo 11 mission engaging and immersive. We use 3D models obtained from NASA's official website, along with selected audio recordings from official NASA resources, to improve historical authenticity. The spacecraft flight trajectory is also partially based on official Apollo 11 mission data.

The project aims to make space exploration more accessible by allowing users to experience the complexity, engineering and challenges of a real lunar mission rather than simply learning about it through text or videos. It combines education, historical storytelling and simulation to bring one of humanity's greatest achievements to life.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Apollo 11: An Interactive Journey to the Moon

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Our project is an interactive 3D space simulation that recreates the historic Apollo 11 mission, allowing users to experience the journey from Earth to the lunar surface. Rather than simply presenting the mission as a documentary, we aim to make users feel as though they are participating in the mission.

The simulation follows the major stages of Apollo 11, including the Saturn V rocket launch, spacecraft separation, transposition and docking, translunar journey, lunar orbit insertion, lunar module separation, descent, landing and the historic Moonwalk.

The experience combines interactive simulation, cinematic cutscenes, historical information and mission-related challenges. Users can understand spacecraft operations, follow the flight trajectory and experience some of the difficulties encountered during the actual mission.

2. Use of Artificial Intelligence and Advanced Video Generation

One of the major creative aspects of our project is the extensive use of generative AI for cinematic storytelling.

We use AI-powered video generation to create historical-style 3D cinematic sequences depicting important moments of the Apollo 11 mission, including presidential announcements, NASA engineering activities, spacecraft preparation, rocket launches, docking procedures and the journey towards the Moon.

We treat generative AI as an advanced creative intelligence tool that assists us in transforming historical information and visual references into cinematic experiences.

Our process involves:

  • Researching historical events and collecting authentic visual references.
  • Preparing detailed scene descriptions and camera movement instructions.
  • Using AI video generation to produce individual cinematic shots.
  • Maintaining visual consistency across characters, spacecraft and environments.
  • Combining generated clips with narration, sound effects and historical audio.
  • Integrating the finished cutscenes into the simulation.

This approach allows a relatively small development team to create cinematic sequences that would otherwise require extensive animation, modelling and filmmaking resources.

3. Tools, Technologies and Resources

Our project combines 3D game development, AI-assisted content generation and authentic historical resources.

Game Development

  • Unity Engine – Used to build the interactive 3D simulation, integrate spacecraft models, develop game environments and create the overall gameplay experience.

Artificial Intelligence and Content Creation

  • Google Flow and generative AI tools for producing cinematic video sequences.
  • AI-assisted visual development, scene planning and storyboard creation.

3D Assets and Historical Resources

  • Official NASA website resources for spacecraft and other 3D models.
  • NASA historical photographs and mission documentation for visual references.
  • Selected audio recordings from official NASA resources.
  • Official Apollo 11 mission information for reconstructing important flight events.

Flight Trajectory and Mission Simulation

  • The spacecraft trajectory is partially based on official Apollo 11 flight data.
  • Historical mission stages and orbital manoeuvres are used as references.
  • The simulation aims to represent the actual sequence of spacecraft operations, from Earth departure to lunar landing.

4. Benefits and Intended Impact

The project aims to make space exploration more accessible, interactive and engaging.

Its major benefits include:

  • Experiential learning: Users can experience the different stages of a historical lunar mission rather than only reading about them.
  • Scientific awareness: Introduces concepts such as orbital mechanics, spacecraft propulsion, docking, lunar descent and navigation.
  • Historical education: Helps users understand the Apollo 11 mission, its achievements and the challenges faced by astronauts.
  • Interactive exploration: Encourages users to understand the engineering and operational complexity behind space missions.
  • Accessibility: Presents complex scientific and historical information through visual storytelling and simulation.

Our intended impact is to bridge the gap between theoretical learning and practical understanding by transforming one of humanity's greatest achievements into an immersive educational experience.

5. Creativity and Innovation

The main innovation of our project is the combination of historical spaceflight simulation and AI-assisted cinematic storytelling.

Instead of developing a conventional space game or presenting a series of historical videos, we combine both approaches. AI-generated cinematic sequences establish the historical context, while Unity-powered interactive simulation allows users to experience the mission themselves.

We also incorporate authentic NASA spacecraft models, historical audio resources and mission-based trajectory information to improve the connection between the simulation and the actual Apollo 11 mission.

6. Factors Considered During Development

Our team considered several important factors:

  • Historical accuracy: Using official NASA resources and mission documentation wherever possible.
  • Scientific authenticity: Following the actual sequence of Apollo 11 mission operations and partially basing the trajectory on official flight data.
  • Visual consistency: Maintaining consistent spacecraft appearances, environments and cinematic styles across AI-generated videos.
  • User experience: Making the simulation understandable and engaging for users without requiring advanced aerospace knowledge.
  • Technical feasibility: Using Unity Engine, existing NASA 3D assets and AI-generated video content to reduce the time and resources required for development.
  • Educational value: Ensuring that each stage communicates something meaningful about spaceflight, engineering or the history of Apollo 11.

Ultimately, our goal is to transform the Apollo 11 mission from something people simply learn about into something they can experience through an interactive simulation.

projectDetails.name: Project Embertrace
projectDetails.summary:
EMBERTRACE is a satellite-powered research platform designed to investigate persistent underground smouldering fires in peatlands, even after visible surface-fire activity has disappeared. The project combines NASA and other Earth-observation datasets, including NISAR synthetic aperture radar, Landsat thermal imagery, NASA FIRMS fire detections, and SMAP soil-moisture observations, to analyse changes in fire activity and peatland conditions over time.

By integrating radar observations, thermal anomalies, historical fire records, and environmental indicators, EMBERTRACE aims to identify regions showing evidence consistent with persistent underground burning and assess conditions that could favour renewed surface fires. An interactive geospatial dashboard will visualise fire history, recurring anomalies, and potential areas requiring further investigation.

The project addresses the Dancing with the SARs challenge by exploring how NISAR radar observations can contribute to monitoring environmental changes associated with peatland fires. EMBERTRACE is important because underground peat fires can remain undetected, release significant amounts of carbon, and reignite under favourable conditions. Our goal is to make these hidden threats easier to investigate and support more informed environmental monitoring and fire-management decisions.
projectDetails.details:
EMBERTRACE is a proposed satellite-based platform that aims to investigate persistent underground smouldering fires in peatlands, even after visible surface-fire activity disappears.

The platform could integrate multiple Earth-observation datasets, including NASA–ISRO's NISAR synthetic aperture radar observations, Landsat thermal imagery, NASA FIRMS fire detections and SMAP soil-moisture data. By analysing these complementary observations over time, it could identify regions showing patterns consistent with persistent underground smouldering and examine environmental conditions that may favour renewed surface fires.

The proposed platform would feature an interactive geospatial dashboard displaying historical fire activity, recurring thermal anomalies, radar-derived environmental changes and areas requiring further investigation.

Its potential benefits include improving awareness of hidden peatland fires, supporting environmental monitoring and helping researchers and fire-management authorities prioritise areas for investigation. The project's creative approach lies in combining radar, thermal, fire-history and environmental indicators rather than relying on individual satellite observations.

The concept considers data availability, spatial and temporal resolution, cloud interference, sensor limitations and the importance of distinguishing confirmed fire observations from suspected underground smouldering.

Proposed technologies: Python, Google Earth Engine, Rasterio, GeoPandas, React, FastAPI and Leaflet.

projectDetails.name: Analog Finder
projectDetails.summary: Analog Finder takes a landing region on the Moon or Mars and finds the places on Earth whose measured environment comes closest. A Python pipeline pulls NASA POWER climate data and LOLA and MOLA topography, builds a 0.1 degree grid over about 2.2 million land cells, and scores every cell against the target with a Gaussian similarity kernel on seven features: slope, relief, roughness, mean surface temperature, day to night swing, coldest surface temperature and annual precipitation. A Monte Carlo over perturbed weights reports how stable each rank is, so a site that only appears because of one weighting choice is visible as such. The results drive a 3D web terminal with Earth, Moon and Mars globes, similarity heatmaps for every target and preset, and a dossier per site holding the feature breakdown, an elevation profile and satellite links. Every value carries its source. The aim is to build physical intuition about which earthly places resemble a given landing region, and to show the working.
projectDetails.details:
What it does

Pick one of 12 landing regions, eight Artemis III candidate regions near the lunar south pole and four Mars sites (Jezero, Gale, Oxia Planum, Mawrth Vallis), then pick a weighting preset. The app returns the 50 best matching places on Earth, each with a score, the similarity for all seven features, the measured values behind that score, a rank-stability percentage from the Monte Carlo, an elevation transect and a hillshade chip. A 3D globe shows the target and the candidates together, a heatmap view shows the whole planet for that target and preset, and a split view puts the target terrain next to the Earth site. Satellite deep links open the same coordinates in Google Earth and NASA Worldview.

How it works

The Earth grid is built once. ETOPO 2022 bedrock elevation provides terrain and NASA POWER daily reanalysis provides climate, resampled to a 0.1 degree grid over land only. Terrain features are computed at a 28 km radius so that Earth and the target are compared at the same physical scale.

For each target, the pipeline reads a 28 km window of the global LOLA or MOLA elevation model and computes the same terrain features. A median despike removes single-pixel artefacts left by gaps between laser tracks; without it the de Gerlache window reports 27 km of relief instead of 11.5 km. Thermal values for the target come from published measurements, each with a citation recorded in config/targets.yaml, and the app displays that citation next to the number.

Scoring uses one Gaussian kernel per feature. A difference equal to the feature tolerance scores 0.61, twice the tolerance scores 0.14, and the weighted mean of the seven similarities is the site score. Weights come from four presets (polar, volcanic, dry basalt, cold desert) and are normalised inside the scorer.

Duplicate suppression removes candidates closer than 200 km and keeps a spread across continents, so the top ranks are not fifty cells on one ridge. The Monte Carlo perturbs every weight by up to 30 percent across 400 seeded draws and reports the share of runs in which a site stays in the top ten. The whole run is deterministic and reproducible.

The interface

React and TypeScript on Vite, with Three.js through globe.gl for the globes, D3 for charts, Palantir Blueprint for controls and Zustand for state. The build is entirely static: JSON, heatmap PNGs, hillshade chips and globe textures are bundled, and a SHA-256 manifest lists every file, so the app runs with the network switched off. It is deployed as a static site on Vercel and can be served from any CDN.

What we deliberately left out

Gravity, atmospheric pressure, radiation, the dust regime and Sun geometry are displayed but never scored. Adding them would reward an Earth site for having an atmosphere, which no Earth site can change. The score answers which environment is closest, and the app labels the non-scored values as context.

Solar elevation is computed against a flat horizon. At the lunar poles the Sun stays within about six degrees of the horizon, so real terrain shadows decide whether a site is lit, and every solar figure in the app carries that caveat.

Validation against eight known analog testbeds (Devon Island, McMurdo Dry Valleys, Atacama, MDRS, HI-SEAS, Askja, Danakil, Lanzarote) put a testbed in the top 5 percent of Earth cells in 24 of 144 site, target and preset checks. Those testbeds were chosen in the literature partly for logistics, so a miss says the model did not rank a site highly, and it does not prove the site is a poor physical analog. The report is visible in the app.

One Artemis III region is missing. NASA lists nine, and the IAU Gazetteer gives a single centre point for the Mons Mouton massif, so the massif and the plateau cannot be anchored to distinct authoritative coordinates. We dropped that region rather than invent a coordinate.

Tools and languages

Python 3.13 with NumPy, SciPy, pandas, xarray, rasterio, netCDF4, Pillow, PyYAML, requests, SciPy-based scoring, scikit-learn and SpiceyPy for ephemerides. The app is React 18, TypeScript, Vite, globe.gl and Three.js, D3, Blueprint and Zustand, with Vitest for the frontend and pytest for the pipeline. Data comes from NASA, USGS, NOAA, Natural Earth and the IAU.

Why it matters

Analog sites are used to test instruments, suits and procedures before launch, and the reasoning behind a choice is usually buried in a report. This tool makes the comparison explicit: which features matched, by how much, with which source, and how sensitive the ranking is to the weights. It is useful for teaching, outreach and early mission-concept work, and it is honest about its own limitations.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: ASTRA Twin
projectDetails.summary: ASTRA Twin is a prototype that builds a personal digital twin of each astronaut's health. It compares each astronaut to their own baseline instead of generic limits, so slow drifts in heart rate, sleep, mood and other signals can be noticed earlier. It suggests likely causes, and writes delay-aware action guidance and reports for the flight surgeon. It uses simulated data.https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1fxmBPK9N-NMz6BnRBF_7xzFKwFkvTSmR/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=114333236277418179903&rtpof=true&sd=true
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

ASTRA Twin is a decision-support prototype (a Google Colab notebook) for monitoring astronaut health on long missions. It simulates a 30-day mission for a 4-person crew (all data is simulated) with 8 indicators: resting heart rate, HRV, systolic blood pressure, body temperature, blood glucose, sleep, mood and reaction time.

For each astronaut, the first 7 days set a personal baseline. A Kalman filter smooths the data and tracks slow drift from that baseline. Changes are grouped into four body systems (cardiovascular, sleep and cognition, immune and metabolic, behavioural) and rated Green, Yellow, Orange or Red, with a 0-100 readiness score. An Isolation Forest model adds an anomaly score that catches unusual combinations of signals.

The notebook also includes: a simple correlation-based check that suggests a likely cause (radiation, isolation drift or low exercise); an illustrative what-if model for exercise vs bone density and aerobic fitness; a rule-based decision guide that depends on Earth communication delay; an automatically generated SBAR (Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation) report; a crew readiness heatmap; and a signal-processing demo that estimates heart rate from a synthetic video-style signal (rPPG). It also contains code that downloads solar energetic particle events from the NASA DONKI API.

BENEFITS

The idea is to compare each astronaut to their own baseline instead of generic limits, so slow personal drifts can be noticed earlier. Reports and suggested actions are generated automatically to support crews who face communication delays with Earth.

INTENDED IMPACT

A starting point for personalised, delay-aware health monitoring on long missions to the Moon and Mars. It is a decision-support prototype only, not a medical diagnosis tool. The health data is simulated and the what-if model is illustrative, not clinically validated.

TOOLS

Python, Google Colab, NumPy, pandas, matplotlib, scikit-learn (Isolation Forest), ipywidgets and the Requests library. No special hardware is needed.

CREATIVITY

It combines a per-astronaut baseline, cause suggestions, a what-if simulator, delay-aware decision guidance and automatic reports in one notebook.

FACTORS CONSIDERED

Individual differences between astronauts, Earth communication delay, space radiation, isolation and reduced exercise as mission stressors, and clear labelling of simulated data and prototype limits.

projectDetails.name: Project EARTHPULSE
projectDetails.summary: EARTHPULSE is an interactive environmental data analysis platform that identifies and visualizes long-term changes in Earth's environmental systems using NASA satellite observations and scientific models. The application focuses on analyzing land surface temperature, precipitation, vegetation and soil moisture across different geographical regions. Users can select locations, variables and time periods to explore environmental changes through interactive maps, graphs and statistical analysis. Using trend detection methods, including Sen's slope and the Mann-Kendall test, EARTHPULSE estimates the rate of change and evaluates its statistical significance. By integrating Earth observation data with software and engineering concepts, the project aims to make complex environmental trends easier to investigate, compare and understand.
projectDetails.details:
EARTHPULSE is a web-based environmental trend detection platform developed to analyze long-term changes in Earth's environmental systems using NASA satellite observations and scientific datasets.

The platform focuses on four important environmental variables: land surface temperature, precipitation, vegetation and soil moisture.

Users can select a geographical location, choose environmental variables and specify a study period. The system processes the selected data and presents the results through interactive graphs, maps and comparative visualizations.

Statistical methods such as Sen's slope and the Mann-Kendall test are used to identify the direction and rate of environmental changes and evaluate their statistical significance.

The main objective is to identify what is changing, where the changes are occurring, how much change is taking place and whether the observed changes are statistically significant.

The project combines Electrical Engineering concepts, including data processing, numerical analysis and software development, with Civil Engineering concepts such as geographical analysis and environmental assessment.

The proposed system uses Python for data processing and statistical analysis, HTML, CSS and JavaScript for the user interface, and NASA open-access Earth science datasets.

EARTHPULSE aims to make complex environmental data easier to understand and encourage scientific investigation of changes in Earth's interconnected environmental systems.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project Gladieters
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, Project Gladiators, focuses on exploring and documenting the abandoned equipment left behind by NASA missions on the Moon and Mars. These objects include scientific instruments, landers, rovers, and other mission hardware that played important roles in space exploration.

We aim to develop an educational storytelling experience that highlights the history, purpose, and significance of these discarded objects. By presenting their stories, we help people understand why this equipment was sent into space, what scientific contributions it made, and why it remains on the lunar and Martian surfaces.

This project addresses the challenge by bringing attention to forgotten equipment and preserving the legacy of space exploration through engaging and informative storytelling. It is important because these objects are not just discarded materials; they represent human curiosity, scientific achievements, technological progress, and the history of our journey beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
SPACE RELICS – An Interactive Space Museum

SPACE RELICS is an interactive educational website developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 under the challenge "Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars."

Our project explores the historical and scientific importance of equipment left behind by NASA's lunar and Martian missions. It transforms space exploration history into an engaging digital museum where visitors can discover the stories, purposes and contributions of these objects.

The website features an interactive collection of space equipment with search and filtering options, a historical mission timeline (1966–2021), and a Planetary Atlas highlighting important mission locations. The 3D Model Bay allows users to explore an Apollo Lunar Module model interactively. The Science Wing presents information about lunar instruments, laser retroreflectors and Mars exploration equipment. An interactive quiz allows visitors to test their knowledge.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

SPACE RELICS makes space exploration history accessible to students, educators and space enthusiasts. It increases awareness of past NASA missions, encourages scientific curiosity and preserves the historical legacy of planetary exploration.

Tools and Technologies:

The website was developed using HTML for structure, CSS for styling and JavaScript for interactive functionality. It is hosted on Netlify and incorporates NASA-related educational resources and 3D models.

Creativity and Innovation:

Our project combines digital storytelling, interactive 3D visualization, historical timelines, planetary exploration maps and educational quizzes in one platform. Rather than simply listing abandoned equipment, it gives each object a story and explains its contribution to space exploration.

Factors Considered:

We considered historical accuracy, scientific relevance, accessibility, user experience and educational value. We also distinguish between equipment that is retired and equipment whose operational status is uncertain, helping visitors understand the history without making unsupported assumptions.

projectDetails.name: Argus
projectDetails.summary:
Spotting moving objects in SPHEREx data? Argus will blink sequences, allow you to point out potentially interesting changes and generate summary reports.
Argus is a web-based portal for analyzing SPHEREx data and searching for variable or moving objects.
Using Argus you can: Explore SPHEREx data with the Sky Explorer tool: overlay SPHEREx data from different observations or with other datasets on top of each other.
Consider possible variables with the Spectral Lab tool: make sure that what looks like variable behaviour isn’t caused by spectral features.
Investigate changes with the Change Lab tool: spot movement by eyeballing difference images, stacking observations to improve your signal-to-noise, or by indicating when you spot potentially interesting behaviour.
Evaluate data quality with the Evidence Lens tool: see metadata like flags and uncertainties as well as contextual information from other surveys (Gaia, WISE). Rate the quality of your evidence as “Not assessed”, “Review needed” or “Comparable”.
Argus helps you conduct morphological analysis of SPHEREx data in a reproducible way. Argus will warn you if a dataset is unsuitable for morphological analysis, and will allow you to save and share your analysis results as evidence reports. Argus is built with Django, Celery and Astropy.
projectDetails.details:
**Argus** is an interactive, web-based astronomy platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge, focusing on the *Planet X and SPHEREx* challenge. Our project aims to make astronomical exploration and scientific investigation accessible to students, amateur astronomers, citizen scientists, and researchers.

**What does our project do?**

Argus allows users to explore real infrared observations collected by NASA's SPHEREx space telescope. Users can search for celestial objects by name or sky coordinates, select a region of the sky, and retrieve available observations from different dates.

The platform's interactive 2D Sky Explorer enables users to zoom, pan, and compare observations through time-lapse playback, image blinking, and side-by-side comparisons. This helps identify possible changes in an object's position or brightness.

Argus also includes several specialized features:

- **Spectral Lab:** Explore infrared wavelengths, compare spectral observations, and analyze how celestial objects behave across different wavelength ranges.

- **Change Lab:** Investigate possible moving objects, brightness variations, and other changes using motion tracking, image stacking, and difference imaging.

- **Evidence Lens:** Examine observation dates, scientific quality indicators, uncertainties, and reference data from astronomical surveys such as Gaia and WISE.

- **Observation Reports:** Document potential findings, annotate observations, and generate reproducible reports that can be shared for independent review.

**Benefits and intended impact**

Astronomical research often requires specialized software, technical knowledge, and complicated data-processing workflows. Argus aims to simplify these processes through an intuitive browser interface while maintaining scientific accuracy.

Our project encourages public participation in astronomy, promotes scientific curiosity, and helps students develop skills in data analysis, observation, and critical thinking. It also supports citizen science by enabling users to investigate possible astronomical changes and share evidence for further examination.

Rather than claiming to automatically discover new celestial objects, Argus provides tools that help users identify and evaluate potential candidates responsibly.

**Technologies and tools**

Argus is designed as a full-stack web application using Python and Django for backend development, JavaScript and Canvas 2D for interactive astronomical visualization, and HTML and Tailwind CSS for the user interface.

The technical architecture includes PostgreSQL for data storage, Redis and Celery for background processing, and Docker for deployment. Scientific processing uses Python libraries such as Astropy, Astroquery, NumPy, SciPy, Reproject, and Photutils.

The platform is designed to integrate real SPHEREx observations from NASA's astronomical archives, with Gaia and WISE providing additional reference information. These technologies form our planned implementation stack, with actual integration and validation tracked during development.

**Creativity and innovation**

The innovation of Argus lies in combining astronomical visualization, time-based observation comparison, spectral exploration, scientific analysis, and evidence reporting within a single accessible platform.

Instead of simply displaying static space images, Argus allows users to actively investigate the sky, explore changes across time and wavelength, and document their observations.

Its emphasis on reproducible evidence and scientifically valid comparisons makes it different from conventional astronomy visualization websites.

**Factors considered during development**

Our team prioritized accessibility, scientific reliability, performance, scalability, and ease of use. We designed the application to work through a web browser without requiring users to install specialized astronomy software.

We also considered the challenges of handling large astronomical datasets, differences in observation wavelengths, image alignment, measurement uncertainty, data availability, and server resource limitations.

To address these challenges, Argus uses a modular architecture, background processing, caching, scientific validation, and clear reporting of data limitations.

**Our vision**

Our ultimate goal is to bridge the gap between professional astronomical data and public exploration. By transforming complex SPHEREx observations into an accessible and interactive experience, Argus aims to empower more people to explore the universe, investigate potential astronomical changes, and contribute to scientific learning and citizen science.

challengeDetails.title: Planet X and SPHEREx

Comets, asteroids, stars, brown dwarfs, and even new planets reveal themselves by shifting position between images, but no one person can sift through all that data alone. projectDetails.name: Ocean notes
projectDetails.summary:
The Earth Information Jukebox turns NASA ocean-surface-current data into music you can see and hear. Using NASA OSCAR near-real-time currents for the Indian Ocean (10°S to 10°N, 60°E to 90°E) in October 2026, we built a static website that flies from a globe into the region and plays a 4.5-minute piece generated from the data. Current direction sets pitch, speed sets loudness, and longitude sets stereo position, so the music grows as the month's currents strengthen (mean cell speed rose from about 0.16 to 0.24 m/s). A Research Lab lets anyone trace every note to its grid cell, date and value, with CSV and JSON export. Sound is optional and off by default; live captions, keyboard grid navigation and text readouts give blind and low-vision users the same information. The project makes satellite-derived ocean data approachable for the public while staying verifiable for researchers.

Access the site: https://eberjohns.github.io/ocean-notes/
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

When you press Play, current particles flow across a relief(height) map while a 4:30 min long piece plays: one day of October 2026 is four bars at 110 BPM, so the month is one composition and the timeline slider is the playhead. Research Lab page shows exact u, v, speed and direction for any cell and date, time series, and exports.

HOW IT WORKS

Offline Python scripts read the 31 daily OSCAR files, crop to the region, and write (1) an 8x8 grid for audio and readouts and (2) a 0.25-degree binary grid for the particles. In the browser, a Web Audio synthesizer maps data to sound: direction to pitch (16 sectors on a scale), latitude to register, mean speed to loudness and note density, longitude to stereo pan. All voices are synthesized; no samples or recordings are used. The same data always produces the same notes.

WHY IT MATTERS

Surface currents carry heat, nutrients and pollution, but a vector map is hard to read for many people. Sound adds a second channel, and the text and keyboard path makes the data usable by blind and low-vision users. Because every note is traceable, the music is an honest view of the data and not a decoration.

TOOLS

Python and NumPy (data preparation), TypeScript, Vite, three.js (rendering), Web Audio API (synthesis), Static hosting - GitHub Pages.

WHAT IS CREATIVE

The month is composed as one piece with a natural crescendo taken from the data. A globe-to-region dive and synchronized particles and music form the signature moment. Data encoding (fixed by the numbers) is kept separate from arrangement (instrument choices), and the interface labels both.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

OSCAR is model-derived from satellite and in situ inputs, not a direct measurement, and the site says so. We use a fixed 0 to 1.0 m/s color and loudness scale so days can be compared. Sound is off by default and no information exists only in sound or only in color.

projectDetails.name: Project Gravitians
projectDetails.summary: This project explores using extreme Earth environments as field analogs to test hardware, drills, and rovers before launching space missions. Specifically, it pairs the Lunar South Pole with Antarctica's Dry Valleys to test cryogenic drills and thermal suits, and Mars' Jezero Crater with the Atacama Desert to evaluate rover traversal, drilling tools, and life-detection sensors. Ultimately, these field tests validate rover autonomy and hardware reliability, significantly de-risking missions before expensive launches.
projectDetails.details:
• What it does and how it works: The project bridges orbital planetary data and surface operations by pairing extreme environments on Earth with target sites on the Moon and Mars to enable immediate field testing of hardware and mission strategies. It utilizes terrestrial analogs—such as Antarctica's Dry Valleys for the Lunar South Pole, the Atacama Desert for Mars' Jezero Crater, and Devon Island as a unified Canadian Arctic testbed—to simulate planetary conditions.
  • Benefits and intended impact: The primary impact of the project is de-risking lunar and Martian hardware failures before expensive, billion-dollar space launches. It validates rover autonomy, life-detection sensor logic, ice-drilling efficiency, dust-mitigation, and crew isolation endurance.
  • Tools, hardware, and equipment used: While specific programming languages or software tools are not detailed in the source, the project focuses on testing advanced physical hardware and scientific instrumentation. This includes cryogenic drills, thermal suits, quiet/deep-space communications, 80 cm to 1 m TRIDENT drilling systems, rover wheels and traction setups, life sensors, and biosignature suites (SOLID, PISCES, and WCL).
  • Creativity and team considerations: The project's creativity lies in its strategic dual-site and single-site terrestrial matching, pairing planetary features (like Shackleton Crater's permanent shadowed regions and Jezero's paleolake basin) with corresponding Earth counterparts featuring volcanic basalt, hyper-arid playas, and impact blockfields. The team carefully considered empirical fidelity boundaries, including surface pressure differentials, gravity, mean temperatures, cosmic radiation, operational challenges like dust optics fouling, command cycles per sample, and 72 cm drill jam recovery limits.

projectDetails.name: Mission Desk: Space Mission Design Game
projectDetails.summary: Mission Desk is a browser game where players design a space mission and a three-stage rocket. They choose a destination (Moon, asteroid Bennu, Mars or Jupiter and Europa), engines, propellant and science instruments. The game then checks the design against real physics: the rocket equation, thrust-to-weight ratio and Hohmann transfer orbits. A player learns why a mission fails, for example because it is short on Δv or overweight, and can fix the design within a $1500M budget. We built it with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no extra libraries.
projectDetails.details:
What it does. Mission Desk teaches mission design through play. The player picks a destination and builds a three-stage launch vehicle by choosing the engine type, engine count and propellant mass for each stage. They then add instruments, each with its own mass, cost and science value.

How it works. Each stage’s Δv is calculated with Δv = Isp·g0·ln(m0/mf), including structural mass and engine mass. Thrust-to-weight ratio is checked at each stage ignition. Mission Δv comes from Hohmann transfer equations. The page shows the burn budget step by step (departure, then orbit insertion) and the transfer time. A mission succeeds only if it reaches orbit, completes the mission with 5% margin, stays in budget, and carries at least one instrument.

Benefits. Players learn mission trade-offs: more fuel adds Δv but also mass and cost, and efficient engines cost more.

Goals. Make orbital mechanics and mission planning easy to understand for students.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript only.

Limits. The model uses impulsive burns and circular, coplanar planet orbits, and a fixed ascent Δv of 9.4 km/s. It is a teaching model, not a flight-ready design.

projectDetails.summary:
## Project Summary – SpaceCare: Astronaut Health Monitoring System

SpaceCare is an advanced web-based health monitoring application designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. It provides a centralized dashboard to monitor important health indicators, including heart rate, blood pressure, sleep duration, physical activity, radiation exposure, and mental well-being.

The application allows astronauts to enter health readings, record mood and stress levels, view health trends through graphs, maintain health records, and receive automatic alerts when certain readings require attention. It also supports exporting health reports for further review.

SpaceCare addresses the challenges of spaceflight by helping astronauts identify unusual health changes early and make informed decisions about seeking medical assistance. It is important because prolonged exposure to microgravity, radiation, isolation, and confinement can affect astronauts' physical and psychological health. By bringing multiple health indicators together in one accessible platform, SpaceCare aims to improve health awareness, support early intervention, and contribute to safer and healthier space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – SpaceCare: Astronaut Health Monitoring System

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

SpaceCare is a web-based Astronaut Health Monitoring System developed to help astronauts monitor their physical and mental health during long-duration space missions. It provides a centralized dashboard to record and review important health indicators, including heart rate, blood pressure, sleep duration, physical activity, radiation exposure, mood and stress levels.

Astronauts can manually enter their health readings and wellbeing information. The software stores these records in the browser, displays health trends through graphs, maintains a health history and generates automatic alerts when certain readings fall outside predefined demonstration ranges. It also allows users to export their health records as CSV files for further review.

2. What are the benefits of the project?

  • Helps astronauts monitor multiple health indicators in one place.
  • Encourages regular physical and mental health check-ins.
  • Helps identify unusual changes in health readings.
  • Provides graphs to understand health trends over time.
  • Maintains health records for future reference.
  • Supports sharing health information with medical teams through exported reports.

3. What is the intended impact?

The main aim of SpaceCare is to improve astronaut health awareness and support early identification of potential health concerns during long-duration space missions. It addresses challenges associated with microgravity, radiation exposure, isolation and confinement. Ultimately, the project aims to contribute to safer missions, better health management and improved astronaut wellbeing during space exploration.

4. What tools, programming languages and software were used?

The project was developed using:

  • HTML5: To create the structure of the web application.
  • CSS3: To design the dashboard and provide a modern, responsive interface.
  • JavaScript: To implement health-data entry, calculations, alerts, graphs and interactive features.
  • HTML Canvas: To display health trend graphs.
  • Browser Local Storage: To save health records locally.
  • CSV: To export health records for further analysis.
  • Microsoft Edge: To run and test the application.

No additional hardware or external sensors were required for the current prototype. Health readings are entered manually. Future versions could integrate wearable health sensors and radiation dosimeters.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

SpaceCare combines physical health monitoring, mental wellbeing tracking, health history and automatic alerts in a single astronaut-focused dashboard. Instead of displaying isolated measurements, it organizes different health indicators to help astronauts observe changes over time.

Its responsive interface, interactive graphs, wellbeing check-ins and downloadable health reports make health monitoring more accessible. The project also provides a foundation for future AI-based health trend analysis and integration with space-grade monitoring equipment.

6. What factors did the team consider?

The following factors were considered during development:

  • Space environment: The effects of microgravity, radiation and isolation on astronaut health.
  • Ease of use: A simple interface that astronauts can operate independently.
  • Reliability: Clear recording and presentation of health information.
  • Early awareness: Alerts for readings that require further attention.
  • Privacy: Local storage of demonstration records without transmitting them to external servers.
  • Accessibility: A browser-based application that does not require specialized hardware to demonstrate.
  • Future expansion: The possibility of integrating wearable sensors, medical equipment and AI-based analysis.

Conclusion

SpaceCare demonstrates how software technology can support astronaut health management during long-duration space missions. By combining health tracking, mental wellbeing check-ins, trend visualization and alerts, it provides a practical foundation for improving health awareness and supporting safer human space exploration.

Note: SpaceCare is currently an educational software prototype using manually entered and sample data. Its alerts are illustrative and are not medically validated diagnostic tools.

projectDetails.name: ALEX & FireLens: Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Earth Observation Hotspots
projectDetails.summary:
When analyzing multi-decadal satellite fire records, apparent hotspot counts often show dramatic upward spikes. For example, in the Nilgiris Biosphere study window (2019–2026), raw NASA detections jumped by +29.2%. A naive analysis attributes this entirely to climate change or catastrophic ground burning. 

However, the spaceborne observing system is non-stationary: NOAA-20 and NOAA-21 increased equatorial daily overpasses by +25%, VIIRS 375m I-band reduced minimum detectable Fire Radiative Power from ~10 MW down to ~1 MW, and Terra’s morning crossing drifted 1.14 hours earlier.

We built ALEX (Autonomous Live Environmental eXpert) and the FireLens scientific engine to answer NASA’s core challenge question: "Are we observing more burning, or are changes in the observing system influencing what we see?"

FireLens mathematically separates constellation expansion from true ground burning using scan-angle geometry correction, footprint-aware ellipse matching, SGP4 orbital propagation, and USDA Rothermel fire physics. Our causal decomposition proves 91.6% of apparent hotspot growth is attributable to observing system expansion, leaving true physical burning at +7.4%—providing scientists and wildfire incident commanders with truthful, unskewed environmental intelligence.
projectDetails.details:
### 1. What does it do and how does it work?

**ALEX (Autonomous Live Environmental eXpert)** is an operational Earth observation intelligence platform engineered to resolve the central remote sensing dilemma of the NASA Space Apps Challenge:

> *"Are we observing more burning, or are changes in the satellite observing system influencing what we see?"*

ALEX processes active-fire observations across a four-tier scientific pipeline:

* **Tier 1 (Geometric Sensor Normalization)**: Corrects scan-angle distortion by modeling sensor Instantaneous Field of View (IFOV). It accounts for MODIS scan-angle bowtie expansion ($1.0\text{ km}$ at nadir expanding to $4.8\text{ km} \times 2.0\text{ km}$ at swath edge) and VIIRS onboard 3:1/2:1 pixel aggregation ($\le 750\text{ m}$ edge footprint), preserving sensor-native confidence categories without lossy conversions.

* **Tier 2 (Footprint-Aware Spatial Association)**: Replaces arbitrary Euclidean distance buffers with physical bounding ellipse intersections. Detections are strictly temporal-pass gated ($\le 30\text{ minutes}$); Fire Radiative Power (FRP) is never averaged across distinct overpasses to avoid masking peak thermodynamic intensity.

* **Tier 3 (Physical Fire Event Clustering)**: Aggregates contiguous thermal detections into physical fire complexes bounded by dynamic convex hulls, tracking perimeter expansion rates, centroid drift, and multi-sensor coverage histories.

* **Tier 4 (Causal Observing Effort Decomposition)**: Decomposes multi-decadal fire trends using 1,000 Monte Carlo bootstrap resampling iterations validated against independent NASA MCD64A1 burned-area datasets. It decouples real fire activity from constellation additions (NOAA-20/21 infill, $+25\%$ equatorial pass frequency) and Terra's 1.14-hour Mean Local Solar Time (MLST) orbital drift.

For incident response, ALEX couples satellite detections with USDA Forest Service Rothermel (1972) / Albini (1976) surface spread equations (Anderson 13 fuel models), Nelson (2000) fuel moisture mechanics, SGP4 NORAD orbital mechanics, and an immutable HMAC-SHA256 audit ledger.

---

### 2. Benefits & Intended Impact

* **Eliminating Multi-Decadal Climate Bias**: Proves mathematically that in target study windows (e.g., Nilgiris Biosphere 2019–2026), $+91.6\%$ of apparent raw hotspot increases ($+29.2\%$) stem directly from sensor constellation expansion and higher spatial resolution rather than true ecological fire acceleration ($+7.4\%$).

* **Tactical Responder Safety**: Replaces static, uncalibrated satellite dots with physical fireline intensity ($I_B\text{ kW/m}$), Byram flame lengths, and dynamic evacuation corridor re-routing based on real-time terrain slopes, fuel moisture, and wind vectors.

* **Zero Synthetic Truthfulness**: Implements a zero-trust architecture where missing remote sensing telemetry remains truthfully `null` rather than artificially imputed, and unverified thermal anomalies cannot trigger emergency dispatches without multi-source field corroboration.

* **Multi-Agency Interoperability**: Integrates OpenSky ADS-B aerial firefighting asset tracking (air tankers/helitack), automated Telegram incident dispatches, and cryptographically signed chain-of-custody logging.

---

### 3. Tools, Coding Languages & Hardware

* **Languages & Core Runtimes**: TypeScript 5.8+ (Strict Mode), Node.js 20+ LTS, HTML5/Tailwind CSS v4.

* **Frontend Visualization**: React 19, Vite, Three.js & React Three Fiber (interactive 3D geocentric orbital globe), Canvas 2D GIS Engine.

* **Scientific & Mathematical Libraries**: `satellite.js` (NORAD SGP4 orbital propagation), custom Rothermel (1972) / Albini (1976) / Nelson (2000) numerical physics engine, D3.js.

* **Backend Architecture**: Express 4.21, PostgreSQL 16 + PostGIS (SRID 4326), HMAC-SHA256 Cryptographic Event Ledger, WebSocket streaming.

* **AI & Voice Reasoning**: Google GenAI SDK (`gemini-2.0-flash` & `gemini-3.8-live` bidirectional 24 kHz PCM voice worklet), Groq SDK (`llama-3.3-70b-versatile` multi-key rotation pool).

* **Automated Quality Assurance**: 75 automated unit and integration tests passing with 100% code integrity, zero TypeScript diagnostic errors.

---

### 4. Creativity & Human Factors Considered

* **Decoupling System Artifacts from Reality**: Rather than treating satellite detections as ground truth perimeters, ALEX labels clusters as *"Harmonized Thermal Anomaly Hypotheses"*, strictly distinguishing observing system capacity from verified ground reality.

* **Orbital Drift Modeling**: Accounts for Terra’s morning equatorial overpass shift from 10:30 AM to ~09:00 AM, correctly quantifying the diurnal attenuation caused by observing before peak afternoon solar heating.

* **Multi-Modal Crisis Voice Studio**: Field incident commanders can query fire behavior hands-free via a low-latency 24 kHz raw PCM audio worklet that translates spoken tactical queries into authenticated API tool executions.

* **Resilient Graceful Degradation**: If external APIs face rate limits or network dropouts, the system fails closed securely, transitioning from cloud LLM reasoning to deterministic onboard physics and cached local geospatial records.

projectDetails.summary:
**Project Summary – Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data**

Our project, *Flame in Freefall*, explores how flames behave in microgravity and how scientific data from space-based combustion experiments can improve fire safety on Earth and in space. We developed a concept for an SI-powered fire safety insight system that uses microgravity combustion data to understand flame behaviour, heat release, oxygen consumption and fire propagation under different conditions. By analysing these patterns, the project aims to identify potential fire hazards and support better fire detection, prevention and emergency response strategies. Unlike normal gravity, microgravity changes flame shape, airflow and combustion behaviour, making fire prediction more challenging, especially inside spacecraft. This project is important because it connects space research with real-world safety applications, helping engineers develop smarter fire protection systems, improve astronaut safety and contribute to safer buildings and enclosed environments on Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

Flame in Freefall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data

1. Project Overview and Working Principle

Flame in Freefall is a space-science-based fire safety concept that explores how combustion behaves in microgravity and how this knowledge can improve fire safety in spacecraft and on Earth. The project focuses on understanding flame shape, flame propagation, heat release, oxygen availability and combustion behaviour under reduced-gravity conditions.

The proposed system follows a data-driven approach. It uses observations and measurements from microgravity combustion experiments to identify changes in flame behaviour. These observations can be compared with normal-gravity combustion patterns to understand the influence of gravity on fire development. The analysed information can then be translated into useful fire safety insights for monitoring, prevention and emergency response.

2. Benefits of the Project

  • Improves understanding of fire behaviour in microgravity environments.
  • Supports research into fire prevention and detection in spacecraft.
  • Helps identify the importance of oxygen availability and ventilation in combustion.
  • Provides insights that can contribute to safer enclosed environments.
  • Connects space research with practical civil engineering and safety applications.

3. Intended Impact

The main objective is to contribute to safer space missions by improving our understanding of combustion in spacecraft cabins. Fire incidents in enclosed space environments can be extremely dangerous because evacuation and firefighting options are limited.

The knowledge gained through this concept may also benefit buildings, laboratories, industrial facilities and other enclosed environments on Earth. Our long-term vision is to support the development of smarter fire detection, monitoring and prevention strategies.

4. Tools and Technologies

Our project is designed around scientific data interpretation and a conceptual engineering workflow.

  • NASA microgravity combustion research: Scientific background and experimental observations.
  • Microsoft PowerPoint: Presentation and visual explanation of the project.
  • Data analysis approach: Comparing flame characteristics and identifying combustion patterns.
  • Engineering concepts: Fire behaviour, oxygen supply, heat transfer, ventilation and fire safety principles.

Note: This is a conceptual data-analysis project. No physical fire detection hardware or fully operational software prototype has been developed.

5. Creativity and Innovation

The creative aspect of Flame in Freefall is its connection between space-based combustion research and real-world fire safety. Instead of considering fire behaviour only under normal gravitational conditions, our project focuses on the unusual flame patterns and combustion characteristics observed in microgravity.

It transforms complex scientific observations into understandable engineering insights that can support future fire safety solutions.

6. Factors Considered by Our Team

Our team considered:

  • Differences between normal gravity and microgravity.
  • Flame shape, size and propagation.
  • Oxygen availability and diffusion.
  • Heat transfer and combustion behaviour.
  • Ventilation and airflow in enclosed spaces.
  • Astronaut safety and emergency response limitations.
  • Practical applications of space research on Earth.
  • Scientific accuracy and the limitations of available experimental data.

7. Conclusion

Flame in Freefall demonstrates how understanding fire in space can contribute to safer environments both beyond Earth and on our planet. By connecting microgravity combustion observations with engineering-based fire safety insights, our project highlights the importance of scientific research, innovation and interdisciplinary thinking in solving real-world challenges.

projectDetails.name: Ember: one 25-year fire calendar for India from NASA satellites
projectDetails.summary:
Ember is a web app that joins NASA's two fire-detection records, MODIS (from 2001) and VIIRS (from 2012), into one consistent burning calendar for India. VIIRS sees small fires that MODIS misses, so simply joining the records makes fire counts appear to jump 5.7 times in 2012. Ember learns that gap for each place and each month from the years both satellites flew (2012 to 2019), applies it to the MODIS-only years, and tests the result on 2020 to 2025, years it never saw. After correction the 2012 jump falls to 1.1 times, and India's corrected total sits within 3% of the real VIIRS count.
Anyone can search a town, district or state and see a typical year week by week, every year from 2001 to 2025, the usual reason fires happen at that time, and an accuracy readout for that area. Early-warning teams, emergency responders, scientists and land managers can see when burning usually starts, peaks and ends, and spot unusual years
projectDetails.details:
The problem. Satellites have tracked active fire hotspots for more than two decades, but the record is split across sensors whose data cannot be compared directly. MODIS (Terra from 2000, Aqua from July 2002) sees mostly large fires at 1 km. VIIRS (from 2012) sees small fires too at 375 m. Joined as they are, India's counts jump 5.7 times in 2012. Fire managers are left without a consistent picture of when and where burning happens.

What Ember does. Ember harmonizes the two records into one burning-activity calendar for India, 2001 to 2025, covering 9.2 million corrected detections on a 27 km (0.25 degree) grid. A user searches any town, district or state and gets:

  • the busiest weeks of a typical year and the wider fire season;
  • a bar for every year from 2001 to 2025, marked "estimated from MODIS" (2001 to 2011) or "measured by VIIRS" (2012 on);
  • a map you can play year by year, with a before and after correction toggle;
  • the usual reason fires happen then, each with a cited news or research source;
  • an accuracy rating for that area, so users know how far to trust it.

How it works.

  1. Take the NASA FIRMS active fire records for India from both sensors and remove year-round heat sources such as coal fields (about 4% of the record, 308,099 detections).
  2. Count detections per grid cell per week, 52 weeks a year.
  3. In 2012 to 2019, when both satellites flew, learn how many VIIRS detections correspond to each MODIS detection, separately for each place and calendar month, leaning on the all-India ratio (about 5.6 times) where a place has few detections.
  4. Apply those ratios to the MODIS-only years, 2001 to 2011, so all 25 years sit on the VIIRS scale.
  5. Test on 2020 to 2025, six years the method never saw, comparing the corrected MODIS count with the real VIIRS count.

Results. The 2012 step falls from 5.7 times to 1.1 times (MODIS alone gives 1.0). On held-out years India's corrected weekly total is within 3% of VIIRS, against 82% too low with no correction.

projectDetails.name: Mission mars
projectDetails.summary:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer

I developed an interactive educational game called Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer. It allows players to experience the responsibilities of an astronaut managing a space outpost on Mars or the Moon. Players must balance four important resources: power, food, radiation shielding, and life support.

The game includes interactive controls, environmental conditions, equipment maintenance, mission alerts, and decision-making challenges across five mission days (sols). Every decision affects the outpost's performance and survival.

This project addresses the challenge by helping students understand the difficulties of living and working in space through an engaging simulation. It combines science, technology, and problem-solving to make space exploration easier to understand. The project is important because it encourages young learners to think like astronauts and explore the science behind future space missions.
projectDetails.details: How the Project Works The Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive browser-based simulation that allows players to manage a space outpost on Mars or the Moon. Players control four important resources: solar power, food, radiation shielding, and life support. They must balance these resources and complete a five-sol mission. The game includes equipment maintenance, environmental monitoring, weather forecasts, mission alerts, radio communications, and decision-making events. Players can monitor their progress through a flight log and receive a mission debrief and completion certificate. Benefits and Intended Impact The project helps students understand the challenges of space exploration through interactive learning. It develops problem-solving, decision-making, and resource-management skills while creating interest in astronomy and space science. Technology Used The project was developed as a web-based game using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It runs in a web browser and does not require special hardware. Creativity The project combines astronaut training concepts with interactive gameplay. Players experience different mission situations and learn how decisions affect the stability of a space outpost. The resource values are simplified for educational purposes and are not real mission-planning data.

projectDetails.name: EARTHSONA
projectDetails.summary:
**EARTHSONA — Hear the Earth, Understand the Planet**

EARTHSONA is an interactive 3D Earth information and sonification platform developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge's "The Earth Information Jukebox." It allows users to explore our planet through an interactive globe, select geographical regions and investigate environmental information through four layers: Natural, Ocean, Forest and Lightning.

The platform transforms available numerical Earth science data into sound, allowing users to experience environmental information through both visual and auditory representations. Region-specific sound generation and animated audio visualizations make scientific information more engaging and accessible, particularly for people who are blind or have low vision. Users can also explore geographical details, including country, region and coordinates, alongside available scientific information and its sources.

EARTHSONA aims to make complex Earth science easier to explore, understand and experience. By combining interactive visualization with sonification, it creates a more inclusive way to connect people with our planet and its changing environmental systems.
projectDetails.details:
How EARTHSONA Works

EARTHSONA is an interactive 3D Earth exploration platform that combines geographical visualization, environmental information and sound to make Earth science more engaging and accessible.

Users can interact with a realistic 3D globe, select geographical locations and explore four information layers: Natural, Ocean, Forest and Lightning. When a location is selected, the application displays relevant geographical details, including its country, region, latitude, longitude and available environmental information.

One of EARTHSONA's main features is data sonification. It transforms available numerical environmental information into sound, allowing users to experience selected Earth data through audio as well as visual representations. Animated audio visualizations help users follow the sound as it plays.

Benefits and Intended Impact

EARTHSONA provides an alternative way to explore and understand Earth science. By combining visual and auditory experiences, it aims to make environmental information more accessible, particularly for people who are blind or have low vision. It also encourages students and the general public to explore geographical locations and develop a greater interest in our planet.

Technology and Tools

The project was developed using Google AI Studio Build mode with AI-assisted application development. It uses interactive 3D globe visualization, web-based application technologies and browser audio capabilities to provide geographical exploration and sound generation. NASA Earth science resources and datasets are used where integrated and available.

Creativity and Design Considerations

The creative aspect of EARTHSONA is its combination of an interactive Earth globe and data sonification in one experience. Instead of only displaying environmental information through maps and visualizations, it allows users to hear representations of available scientific data.

During development, we considered accessibility, ease of navigation, geographical accuracy, scientific data reliability, audio clarity and the importance of distinguishing actual scientific measurements from illustrative representations. The goal is to make exploring our planet an experience that can be seen, heard and understood.

projectDetails.name: Ghost Rovers: Abandoned but Not Forgotten
projectDetails.summary: Ghost Rovers is an interactive storytelling website that introduces children aged 10–14 to 20 NASA machines left behind on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Each machine is a character that tells its own story in a first-person diary, read aloud in its own voice. Older machines from the 1960s and 70s sound like crackly old radio broadcasts, while newer ones sound clear and modern. Kids spin 3D globes of the Moon and Mars to find machines at their real landing spots, explore a 3D solar system to find deep-space probes, take a quick quiz on every machine, follow a 57-year timeline, and play a game where they drive the Spirit rover through dust storms, a broken wheel and the sand trap that ended its mission. Every card links the engineering ("why I was sent") to the science ("what I found"). Ghost Rovers turns "space junk" into heroes, so kids learn that today's missions stand on the shoulders of these forgotten explorers.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT IT DOES

Ghost Rovers is a free website where 20 retired NASA machines tell their own stories to kids aged 10–14. It covers 7 machines on the Moon (Apollo 11's Eagle, the Apollo 11 laser reflector, Surveyor 3, an ALSEP science station, Alan Shepard's golf balls and two Lunar Roving Vehicles), 8 on Mars (Viking 1 and 2, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight and Ingenuity) and 5 in deep space (NEAR Shoemaker, Dawn, Kepler, Pioneer 10 and Pioneer 11).

3D Moon: each picture sits at the machine's real landing spot. Grandma Moon shares extra facts.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Spin a 3D world. Kids drag to spin the Moon and Mars. The surfaces are drawn by our code using real map features (lunar maria, Olympus Mons, Valles Marineris, polar ice caps).

3D Mars with 8 machines, hosted by Uncle Mars (who sneezes dust storms).

2. Meet a machine. Clicking a machine opens its diary card. The machine tells its story in first person, read aloud in its own voice. The card links engineering to science: "Why I was sent", "What I found", "Where I am now", plus a fun fact, a quiz question and a link to its NASA page.

Surveyor 3's diary: it bounced on landing, and two years later Apollo 12 astronauts took its camera home.

3. Voices that age. Machines from the 1960s and 70s sound like crackly old radio, 2000s machines sound like light radio, and new machines sound clear.

4. Deep space in 3D. A 3D solar system shows where the deep-space probes are now: Dawn circling Ceres, NEAR Shoemaker on asteroid Eros, Kepler trailing Earth, and Pioneer 10 and 11 leaving the solar system.

5. Timeline. All 20 machines from 1967 to today, from launch or landing to last signal. The Apollo 11 laser reflector is still working!

6. Game: Spirit's Sand Trap. Kids drive Spirit across Gusev Crater, manage battery and dust, get cleaned by a dust devil, lose a wheel in 2006, discover silica soil with the dragging wheel in 2007, and get stuck at Troy in 2009, just as it really happened.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Kids usually hear only about today's missions. Ghost Rovers shows that every "abandoned" machine made a discovery that made later missions possible. Surveyor 3 proved the Moon was safe to land on, and the laser reflector still measures the Moon's distance today. It works in classrooms, at home and at outreach events, with no login or install.

TOOLS AND LANGUAGES

HTML, CSS and JavaScript; three.js for 3D; the Web Audio API for sound effects; Python for building the content and voices; hosted on GitHub Pages.

CREATIVITY

Machines become characters with personalities that match their real history: Ingenuity is hyper because it flew 72 times instead of 5, and Opportunity is a show-off because it drove a marathon. The voices "age" like old radio, and the game lets kids live a real mission instead of reading about it.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Accuracy: facts are based on NASA and NSSDCA pages, linked on every card.

- Age 10–14: simple words, humour, quizzes, a game and a certificate for meeting all 20 machines.

- Accessibility: every story is read aloud, machines can be opened from a list without the 3D view, and it works with keyboard, mouse and touch.

- Honest AI use: every AI image carries a visible watermark, AI voices are labelled on the page and in each audio file, and no NASA logos or flags are used in AI content.

Every AI-generated 3D image is clearly watermarked, next to real mission pictures.

projectDetails.details: Project Details – Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data FieldWise Kerala is a bilingual web-based prototype designed to help farmers explore suitable crop rotation ideas using NASA Earth observation data and local farm information. The website uses NASA POWER data to display temperature and rainfall information based on the farm's location. Farmers can enter details such as soil type, water availability, current crop, and farming priorities. Based on these inputs, the website provides illustrative crop rotation options to help farmers compare different possibilities. The main benefit of this project is that it helps farmers understand local weather conditions and explore different crop rotation strategies. It aims to support better farming decisions, encourage sustainable agriculture, improve soil health, and promote efficient water use. We developed the prototype using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. NASA POWER API is used to retrieve weather information, and GitHub Pages is used to host the website publicly. The creative aspect of our project is the combination of NASA Earth observation data with local farming information in one simple platform. It also supports both English and Malayalam, making it easier for farmers in Kerala to understand and use. While developing this project, we considered Kerala's local farming conditions, soil types, water availability, weather variations, farmers' priorities, and ease of use. The project is an educational prototype, and the suggested crop rotations should be confirmed with local agricultural experts before practical use.
