projectDetails.name: NOVALITHA
projectDetails.summary:
Earth Jukebox is a single-file, browser-based instrument that turns Earth-observation image 
frames into live sound. A playhead sweeps across a frame from west to east. Each band of 
latitude becomes a musical note, and the strength of the signal in that band sets how loud it is. 
Colour changes the instrument, and the amount of fine detail changes the rhythm. Because the 
sound is generated in real time from the pixels, any frame a person loads can be heard.
We built it so that people who cannot see a map, or who find dense maps hard to read, can still 
follow what a satellite sees. We also built it so that anyone can hear change: step through 
consecutive days and listen to haze spread, thin and move.
projectDetails.details:
Earth Jukebox: Hearing a Changing Planet

NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 · Challenge: The Earth Information Jukebox · Project

NOVALITHA

Team: NOVALITHA · Members: Anna Rose, Binitta Rose, Cleetus T J, Mebin Babu, Niya Maria

1. Summary

Earth Jukebox is a single-file, browser-based instrument that turns Earth-observation image

frames into live sound. A playhead sweeps across a frame from west to east. Each band of

latitude becomes a musical note, and the strength of the signal in that band sets how loud it is.

Colour changes the instrument, and the amount of fine detail changes the rhythm. Because the

sound is generated in real time from the pixels, any frame a person loads can be heard.

We built it so that people who cannot see a map, or who find dense maps hard to read, can still

follow what a satellite sees. We also built it so that anyone can hear change: step through

consecutive days and listen to haze spread, thin and move.

2. The challenge

The challenge asks for an "Earth Jukebox": an interface, script or application that pairs Earth

Information Center (EIC) visual frames with dynamic sonifications generated in real time, so

that complex Earth science becomes accessible, engaging and multi-sensory. It encourages

computer-vision-style analysis of colour, shape and pixel density, mapped to pitch, tempo and

instrumentation. It asks teams to balance data translation with musicality, to treat accessibility

as a core theme, and to tell the story behind the choices.

3. What we built

A self-contained web page (one HTML file, about 220 KB, no external libraries, works offline)

that:

• Opens with three real NASA satellite frames already loaded, so a judge can press Play

immediately.

• Offers six sound styles, Side A to Side F. They use the same satellite frames and change

only the scale and tone.

• Lets anyone load their own frames (one or several) and plays them as a time sequence.

• Records the result as a downloadable audio file.

4. Data used

Item Detail

Imagery Three true-colour satellite frames

over South Asia from consecutive

Item Detail days Dates Day 1: 11 Nov 2026. Day 2: 12 Nov 2026. Day 3: [confirm the date] Layer / instrument Terra / MODIS, Corrected Reflectance (True Color); layer name MODIS_Terra_CorrectedReflectance_T rueColor Source NASA Worldview (worldview.earthdata.nasa.gov) Preparation Each frame was cropped to a 2:1 strip (keeping the Himalayan foothills and the northern plains), resized and compressed as JPEG, then embedded in the page The frames show winter-season haze lying over the northern plains, snow and cloud over the Himalaya and Tibetan Plateau, cloud over the Bay of Bengal, and black wedges where the satellite did not cover the ground. Seasonal haze in this region is a recurring public-health concern, which made it a meaningful subject for a first demonstration. All data in the project is real NASA imagery. Nothing in it is synthetic. 5. How the sonification works Every frame is drawn onto a 360 × 180 grid. The sound engine then reads that grid as a moving window. Image property Sound property Why Position left to right Time (one pass takes 30 seconds at normal speed; speed is adjustable) Reading order matches how maps are read Position top to bottom, in 12 bands Pitch: higher in the frame is higher in pitch A natural "up is high" metaphor Brightness or signal strength in a band Loudness, and how bright the tone sounds (filter opening) Stronger signal is louder Dominant colour in a column Instrument: warm tones play a bright sawtooth, green a soft triangle, blue a pure sine Colour becomes timbre; low-colour areas keep the default voice Amount of fine detail in a column Pulse rate, from about 48 to 180 beats per minute Busy areas feel busy Image property Sound property Why Black (no data) Silence Missing data should not be mistaken for a quiet Earth To keep the result musical rather than chaotic, all twelve voices are tuned to a pentatonic or similar scale, so any combination of loud and quiet bands sounds consonant. A gentle low-pass filter and an echo smooth the output. The engine is built on the Web Audio API and generates every sound live; there are no pre-recorded clips. Sides A to F The six sides are sound styles applied to the same data: Side A (bright major pentatonic), Side B (high, glassy lydian bells), Side C (soft strings), Side D (low, dark minor), Side E (light, airy suspended tones) and Side F (deep dorian swells). They change how the data sounds, not what the data is. Two analysis modes • Haze mode (approximate). Instead of raw brightness, it scores each pixel with a colour rule that favours grey-beige, mid-brightness, low-saturation pixels, which is how thin haze looks in true colour, and plays that score. It also shows the score as a heat map so people can see what they are hearing. • Hear change between days. It subtracts one day from the next and plays the size of the difference. Louder means more change. It combines with haze mode to play change in the haze estimate. Time-lapse With time-lapse on, each sweep moves on to the next day, so one listen takes the audience through the whole sequence. A slider and the N and P keys step through frames manually. 6. Accessibility The challenge names accessibility as a core theme, so we treated it as part of the design, not an add-on: • The page works without sight: everything important is audible, and every frame has an automatically generated text description (which band is strongest and weakest, where the peak is, how detailed the frame is, and whether black gaps are present). • A Read description button speaks the description. Day changes are announced to screen readers, and spoken announcements are optional. • Full keyboard control: Space for play and pause, arrows to scrub, N and P for frames, H for haze mode, C for change, T for time-lapse, R to record, and ? for the shortcut list. • A high-contrast mode, a visible focus outline, larger touch targets on phones, and reduced-motion support. • Optional vibration on supported phones, pulsing with the rhythm, as a tactile channel. • A short "Start here" guide and an on-page legend for first-time visitors. 7. Telling the story Maps are silent. A person who is blind or has low vision, or a person who simply cannot read a dense colour map at a glance, is shut out of the picture that satellites provide. Sound can carry the same pattern: where the signal is strong, where it is weak, and how it shifts from one day to the next. We chose haze over South Asia as our demonstration because it is a changing system that people live inside. When the time-lapse plays, the listener hears the loudest regions drift and spread from day to day. We wanted the experience to carry some of the urgency of a changing planet without claiming more than the data supports, which is why the limits below are part of the project and not a footnote. 8. Limitations and honesty about the data • The sound follows brightness, not true measured values. In the default mode, bright clouds and snow are as loud as haze. The instrument shows where an image is bright or colourful, not how much pollution is present. • Haze mode is an estimate. It is a colour rule we designed, not a validated aerosol measurement. It is imperfect, and thin cloud or bright land can be mistaken for haze. • Change mode shows size, not direction. It does not say whether haze increased or cleared. • Resolution is low. Frames are reduced to a 360 × 180 grid, and the embedded samples are compressed, so fine features are lost. • The samples are cropped. The three frames were cut to a 2:1 strip, so the southern part of the peninsula is not included. • Regional frames are not a whole-world map. For regional images the page reports position as a percentage across and down the frame, not as latitude and longitude, to avoid false precision. • Missing data is silent. Black satellite-swath gaps are treated as no data, but they can look like quiet areas to a listener unless the description is read. For a research-grade version, the colour-to-value step should be replaced with real data values, such as an aerosol optical depth layer, instead of colour. 9. How to run it 1. Open the project link, or open earth-jukebox.html in a modern browser such as Chrome. No installation or internet connection is needed for the file. 2. Press Play. The three sample days load automatically. 3. Choose Side A to Side F to change the sound style. 4. Drag across the map to hear any single spot. 5. Try Haze mode and Hear change between days. 6. To use new imagery, choose one or more image files under Load EIC frame(s). Name multiple files in order, such as frame01.png, frame02.png. Use flat map views, and crop out legends and labels. 7. Press Record full sequence to save the soundtrack as a WAV file. 10. Future work • Use real data values (for example aerosol optical depth) and a sign-aware change mode that distinguishes increase from decrease. • Add more EIC layers, such as temperature, sea ice and chlorophyll, and a built-in picker. • Support global map frames and animated sequences directly, and sync stereo position to longitude. • Run listening sessions with blind and low-vision users to tune the mappings. • Offer a server version that generates audio files in bulk for a curated playlist. 11. Tools, credits and Super Intelligence (SI) disclosure • Imagery: NASA satellite imagery obtained through NASA Worldview (Terra / MODIS, Corrected Reflectance (True Color)). We thank the NASA Earth Information Center and the Space Apps organisers for the challenge. • Built with: plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, and the browser's Web Audio API. No third-party libraries. The demo video was recorded with Playwright and encoded with FFmpeg, and the frames were cropped with Pillow. • SI use: Claude (by Anthropic), a Super Intelligence tool, helped write the code, the on- page text, this document and the demo video script. The team directed the design and reviewed the results. • Where SI is acknowledged: the demo video carries a visible "SI-generated video" watermark and file metadata. The code has a comment, a meta tag and a visible notice. Soundtracks recorded from the page carry an SI acknowledgment in their file metadata. • Not SI-generated: the satellite imagery itself, which is NASA data.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.details:

projectDetails.name: LEFT BEHIND
projectDetails.summary:
LEFT BEHIND – An Atlas of Humanity in Space

Left Behind is an interactive digital storytelling platform that explores the human footprint across the Solar System through spacecraft, mission remnants, abandoned equipment, and lost communications. We developed a web-based experience featuring a Solar System Atlas, an interactive spacecraft exploration guide, mission histories, last transmissions, spacecraft status information, visual galleries, 3D visualizations, and a historical timeline.

The project addresses the challenge “Abandoned but Not Forgotten” by transforming space mission data and historical records into engaging, accessible stories. It highlights the objects and spacecraft that remain on the Moon, Mars, and beyond, revealing their original purposes, journeys, achievements, and final states.

Our goal is to make space exploration more meaningful by connecting scientific information with human stories. By preserving the legacy of these missions, Left Behind reminds us that even when a mission ends, its contribution to humanity's exploration of the universe should never be forgotten.
projectDetails.details:
LEFT BEHIND – An Atlas of Humanity in Space

Left Behind is an interactive digital storytelling platform designed to document and explore the objects, spacecraft, mission remnants, and lost communications that represent humanity's presence across the Solar System. It transforms space exploration history into an engaging, educational, and visually immersive experience.

What does it do and how does it work?

The platform allows users to explore humanity's space exploration legacy through several interactive features:

Solar System Atlas: Provides a visual overview of celestial bodies and the spacecraft associated with their exploration.

Explore the Darkness: Presents spacecraft profiles and mission histories, explaining their purpose, journey, achievements, and final status.

Last Transmission: Explores the final communications and lost signals of spacecraft, bringing attention to missions that have gone silent.

Spacecraft Behaviour: Categorizes spacecraft based on their operational status, including active, inactive, retired, and crashed missions.

Image Album: Showcases visual records and historical photographs of spacecraft and mission remnants.

3D Visualizations: Offers a more immersive way to understand spacecraft and their structures.

Historical Time Machine: Allows users to explore important milestones in space exploration through time.

Benefits and intended impact

Left Behind makes space exploration history accessible to students, educators, space enthusiasts, and the general public. It encourages curiosity about planetary exploration, spacecraft engineering, scientific discoveries, and the challenges of operating in extreme environments.

Its intended impact is to preserve awareness of humanity's achievements in space, promote STEM education, and encourage a deeper appreciation of the scientific and historical value of space mission remnants.

Tools and technologies used

The project was developed as a web-based application using web development technologies, including HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, along with interactive visualization techniques and web-based 3D components. We also incorporated space mission information, historical records, and publicly available space exploration resources to develop the content.

Creativity and innovation

The creative aspect of Left Behind is its storytelling approach. Instead of presenting spacecraft as technical objects or displaying mission data as ordinary information, the platform encourages users to view them as silent witnesses to humanity's exploration of other worlds.

Each spacecraft has a story: why it was launched, what it accomplished, what happened at the end of its mission, and what remains of it today. The combination of interactive exploration, historical timelines, visual storytelling, and mission information creates a unique experience.

Factors considered during development

Our team considered scientific accuracy, historical reliability, user accessibility, visual clarity, educational value, and the distinction between abandoned equipment, intentionally discarded mission hardware, retired spacecraft, and spacecraft that have lost communication.

Ultimately, Left Behind aims to remind the world that the end of a space mission does not mean the end of its story. Every object left beyond Earth represents a chapter in humanity's journey into the universe.

LUNAR EXPLORER: Interactive Lunar Landing Site Explorer

LUNAR EXPLORER is an interactive web-based platform developed to help users explore the Moon and identify potential landing locations by understanding lunar surface conditions. The platform provides a visual and user-friendly interface for exploring lunar locations, viewing latitude and longitude coordinates, and examining environmental conditions that may affect landing-site selection.

The project addresses the challenge of making complex lunar information easier to understand and use. By allowing users to select locations on the Moon and explore relevant data, LUNAR EXPLORER helps highlight potential hazards and supports preliminary assessment of landing-site suitability.

This project is important because selecting an appropriate lunar landing site is essential for astronaut safety, rover mobility, scientific research, and future lunar missions. By presenting lunar information in an accessible and interactive format, LUNAR EXPLORER aims to make space science more understandable and demonstrate how web technology can support lunar exploration and mission planning.
projectDetails.details:
1. What does the project do, and how does it work?

LUNAR EXPLORER is an AI-based lunar navigation platform designed to help users explore the Moon and identify potential lunar landing locations. Through an interactive lunar interface, users can select locations, examine latitude and longitude coordinates, and explore information relevant to landing-site selection. The platform aims to make lunar exploration more interactive and understandable.

2. What are the benefits?

The project makes lunar location exploration accessible through a web-based interface. It helps users understand how geographical coordinates, surface conditions, and potential hazards can influence landing-site selection. It also provides an educational way to learn about lunar geography and space exploration.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to support the understanding of safer and more informed lunar landing-site selection. By presenting lunar information in an interactive format, LUNAR EXPLORER aims to make space science more accessible to students, educators, and space enthusiasts while demonstrating how digital technology can contribute to future lunar exploration.

4. What tools and technologies were used?

We developed the project as a web application using web development technologies, including TypeScript, HTML, and CSS, along with a modern frontend development environment. We used GitHub for source-code management and Vercel for deployment, making the platform accessible through a web browser.

5. How is the project creative?

LUNAR EXPLORER combines lunar exploration with an interactive navigation experience. Instead of presenting lunar information only through static maps or text, the project aims to let users explore locations directly and understand their significance visually. This makes the concept engaging, practical, and educational.

6. What factors did the team consider?

We considered usability, accessibility, geographical accuracy, potential landing hazards, coordinate interpretation, and the importance of presenting lunar information clearly. We also considered how the platform could help users understand the challenges of exploring the Moon and how it could be improved with reliable scientific data and more advanced analysis in the future.

**Ksheti – Hyper-Local Climate Intelligence & Precision Agriculture Decision Support**

Ksheti is an AI-powered precision agriculture platform that combines multispectral satellite imagery, IoT sensor data, weather intelligence, laboratory soil tests, and cultivation history to deliver field-level agricultural insights.

The platform analyzes satellite vegetation indices such as NDVI, EVI, SAVI, NDWI, and NDRE to monitor crop health, detect changes, and identify potential environmental risks. It provides crop yield forecasts, pest and disease risk assessments, drought and flood predictions, and personalized irrigation and fertilizer recommendations.

Ksheti uses machine learning, geospatial visualization, and agricultural science to make recommendations more reliable and explainable. Each prediction includes a confidence score, supporting environmental indicators, historical comparisons, satellite evidence, and explanations of the factors influencing the result.

The platform also supports offline operation, multilingual advisory in English, Hindi, and Malayalam, SMS-based recommendations, and a digital farm twin for exploring alternative farming decisions.

Ksheti aims to improve crop productivity, conserve water and resources, reduce agricultural risks, and support sustainable farming through accessible, data-driven decision-making.

Future possibilities include expanded satellite integration, automated smart irrigation, and advanced digital farm simulations.
projectDetails.details:
Ksheti – Hyper-Local Climate Intelligence & Precision Agriculture Decision Support

Ksheti is an AI-powered precision agriculture platform designed to help farmers make informed decisions using localized environmental and agricultural data. General weather forecasts often fail to capture the conditions of individual farms. Ksheti addresses this problem by combining multispectral satellite imagery, IoT field telemetry, weather intelligence, laboratory soil tests, and cultivation history to provide field-level insights and recommendations.

How Does It Work?

Ksheti collects and analyzes data from multiple sources, including Sentinel-2 satellite imagery, weather information, soil test results, IoT sensors, and historical cultivation records. It uses satellite vegetation indices such as NDVI, EVI, SAVI, NDWI, and NDRE to monitor crop health, identify changes, and assess vegetation conditions.

Machine learning models support crop yield forecasting, pest and disease risk assessment, and drought and flood risk prediction. The platform also provides irrigation and fertilizer recommendations using agricultural models and soil nutrient information.

Each prediction includes a confidence score, supporting environmental indicators, historical comparisons, satellite evidence, and an explanation of the factors influencing the result. This makes the recommendations more transparent and understandable.

Benefits and Intended Impact

  • Helps farmers monitor crop health and identify potential risks earlier.
  • Provides localized agricultural and climate insights.
  • Supports efficient irrigation and fertilizer management.
  • Helps reduce unnecessary water and fertilizer consumption.
  • Assists farmers in making informed cultivation decisions.
  • Supports sustainable agriculture and improved resource management.

Our intended impact is to make precision agriculture more accessible, improve agricultural productivity, reduce climate-related farming risks, and support informed decision-making among farmers, agronomists, and policymakers.

Tools and Technologies Used

Programming Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML, CSS.

Backend: FastAPI and Python's built-in HTTP server.

Frontend: React and JavaScript.

Machine Learning: Scikit-learn, XGBoost, and Joblib.

Satellite and Weather Data: Sentinel-2 imagery and Open-Meteo weather integration.

Geospatial Visualization: Leaflet.

Database: PostgreSQL with PostGIS.

Hardware: ESP32-based IoT sensors for field data collection.

Agricultural Methods: FAO-56-based water requirement estimation and soil-test-based fertilizer recommendations.

What Makes Ksheti Creative and Innovative?

Ksheti combines multiple agricultural data sources into a unified, hyper-local decision-support system. Instead of providing only general predictions, it focuses on individual farm conditions.

One of its key innovations is explainable AI. Every prediction provides its confidence score and the environmental factors influencing the result. It also distinguishes between machine-learning predictions and physics-based recommendations, helping users understand where the advice comes from.

The platform supports offline operation, low-bandwidth usage, and multilingual advisory in English, Hindi, and Malayalam. Its digital farm twin also allows users to explore alternative farming decisions through what-if scenarios.

Factors Considered by Our Team

During development, we considered the practical challenges faced by farmers, including changing weather conditions, soil variability, limited internet connectivity, language barriers, and the need for understandable recommendations.

We also considered prediction reliability, data integration, affordability, scalability, resource conservation, and transparency. Since demonstration training data is generated using an agronomic process model rather than observed field records, we distinguish prototype model performance from real-world agricultural accuracy.

Future Scope

Future improvements include expanded real-world agricultural datasets, drone-based crop monitoring, automated smart irrigation, improved satellite data integration, and advanced digital farm simulations.

Ksheti aims to bridge the gap between climate intelligence and practical farming decisions, helping build a more sustainable and climate-resilient agricultural future.

FIRETRACE: The Living Combustion Explorer is a React 19 / TypeScript analytics dashboard built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 (Microgravity Fire Safety). 

It ingests, validates, and visualizes real spaceflight data from NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI-69 FLEX investigation), conducted aboard the International Space Station’s Combustion Integrated Rack. FIRETRACE analyzes 274 combustion runs—tracking fuel types, atmospheric composition, burn rates, and droplet extinction limits.

projectDetails.details:
Project Details: FIRETRACE

What it does and how it works:

FIRETRACE is a web-based data dashboard that analyzes microgravity fire behavior to improve spacecraft fire safety. It directly ingests, cleans, and visualizes raw flight data from NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI-69 FLEX investigation) recorded aboard the International Space Station. The platform parses 274 combustion tests across varying fuels, pressures, and gas mixtures to analyze droplet burning rates, flame geometry, and extinction limits.

Benefits and intended impact:

It transforms static spaceflight records into an interactive research tool. By revealing how flames burn and extinguish in low gravity without buoyant air currents, it helps mission planners evaluate spacecraft fire-suppression protocols, improve material safety standards like NASA-STD-6001B, and design safer habitats for long-duration Moon and Mars exploration.

Tools, languages, and software:

Built using React 19, TypeScript, Vite 8, Oxlint, and custom CSS. It runs in any modern web browser without requiring external database setups or specialized hardware.

Creativity and factors considered:

The design translates complex flight telemetry into an intuitive mission-control interface. The team prioritized strict scientific integrity over visual fluff, ensuring zero fabricated data is shown, missing sensor readings are preserved accurately, and the unique physics of spherical microgravity flames are faithfully represented.

projectDetails.name: Earth Jukebox: Turning NASA Climate & Satellite Data into Sound
projectDetails.summary:
Earth Jukebox is an accessible web application that transforms NASA Earth observations and climate records into synchronized musical soundscapes. Modeled on NASA’s Caldwell 73 sonification principles, it pairs live NASA GISS global surface temperature anomalies (1880–present) with NASA GIBS and Worldview satellite imagery—covering land temperature, ocean gradients, forest vegetation, atmospheric aerosols, and nighttime lights—plus an importer for downloaded NASA Earth Information Center and Scientific Visualization Studio frames.
Using real-time pixel analysis and dynamic audio synthesis, Earth Jukebox converts measured warming and thermal colors into pitch, brightness into volume, East–West distribution into stereo panning, and frame changes into rhythm. Listeners can toggle between Scientific Mode for consistent precision and Artistic Mode for expressive soundscapes, supported by plain-English explanations, keyboard shortcuts, screen-reader announcements, optional spoken narration, and a High-Contrast theme.
By turning sight-dependent planetary data into sound, Earth Jukebox makes Earth science accessible and engaging for blind, low-vision, and sighted audiences alike.
projectDetails.details:
What Earth Jukebox Does & How It Works Earth Jukebox (Hear the Earth. Understand the Change.) is an accessible, interactive web application that transforms genuine NASA Earth observations and climate records into synchronized, meaningful musical soundscapes. The application operates through a real-time four-stage pipeline: Official NASA Data Retrieval: A lightweight proxy server fetches live NASA GISS Surface Temperature Analysis (GISTEMP v4) numerical anomalies (1880–present) and NASA GIBS / Worldview Snapshots satellite imagery across five Earth science datasets—Global Temperature Changes (MODIS_Terra_Land_Surface_Temp_Day), Ocean Currents & Thermal Gradients (GHRSST_L4_MUR_Sea_Surface_Temperature), Forest Coverage & Vegetation Pulse (MODIS_Terra_NDVI_8Day), Atmospheric Aerosols (OMPS_Aerosol_Index), and Earth at Night (VIIRS_Black_Marble). Users can also upload downloaded PNG/JPG image sequences from the NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) and Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) (such as Perpetual Ocean 2, GEOS Aerosols, DYAMOND CO₂, ISS Lightning Events, or GEDI Forest Height). Computer Vision & Scientific Analysis: An HTML5 Canvas analyzer extracts Red, Green, and Blue color intensities, perceived luminosity, East–West spatial center-of-mass, coverage, 8 longitudinal energy bands, and frame-to-frame changes. When measured scientific data is available (such as GISTEMP °C anomalies), the engine prioritizes exact numerical measurements over visual color estimates. Configurable Sonification Engine: Modeled after NASA’s Caldwell 73 sonification principles, extracted metrics drive real-time Web Audio synthesis: higher temperatures and warm red intensity raise musical pitch, cooler baselines and blue zones lower pitch, brightness controls volume, East–West spatial distribution controls stereo panning, and frame-to-frame changes modulate rhythm and tempo (BPM). Synchronized Studio Player: Displays the visualization alongside an interactive timeline scrubber, a live audio waveform and tabular telemetry bar, a hover Lat/Lon/RGB probe, and an Understand the Sound guide explaining what every sound represents. Benefits & Intended Impact Breaking Accessibility Barriers: Most climate visualizations rely exclusively on sight. Earth Jukebox makes planetary change audible and navigable for blind and low-vision users through aria-live announcements, full keyboard shortcuts (Space, S, ←/→, M, H), plain-English frame descriptions, optional spoken audio narration, and a dedicated High-Contrast display theme. Intuitive Climate Storytelling: Hearing 146 years of NASA GISTEMP global temperature anomalies climb from low, calm 19th-century bass notes into bright, rapid modern pitches communicates the pace of climate change emotionally and immediately—useful for classrooms, museums, outreach, and public education. Scientific Transparency: Every dataset clearly distinguishes between directly measured scientific data (°C anomalies) and image-derived color/brightness proxies so users understand both the insights and limitations of visual sonification.

Tools, Languages & Technologies Used Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML5, CSS Frontend & Visualization: React, Tailwind CSS, HTML5 2D Canvas (pixel-level computer vision analysis), SVG data visualization, Web Speech API (optional spoken narration) Audio Synthesis: Tone.js and the browser Web Audio API (multi-voice synthesis, stereo panning, harmonic scales, and real-time waveform/FFT analysis) Backend Proxy & Build Tooling: Node.js, Express (CORS-clean caching proxy for NASA APIs), Vite Official NASA Data Sources: NASA GISS (GISTEMP v4), NASA GIBS / Worldview Snapshots API, NASA JPL PO.DAAC, NASA LP DAAC, NASA Suomi NPP OMPS, and NASA EIC / SVS conceptual resources

How the Project Is Creative Dual Listening Modes: Users can switch instantaneously between Scientific Mode (a dry, calibrated triangle-wave signal with optional continuous Chromatic Hz output for analytical repeatability) and Artistic Mode (expressive harmonic pad chords, 8-band longitudinal FM melodic sweeps, and bright-spike shimmers that preserve the exact underlying data trends). Interactive Crosshair Spatial Probe: Hovering over any satellite map samples exact Latitude, Longitude, RGB values, and local luminosity in real time. Bring-Your-Own NASA SVS Frames: Beyond the 5 live datasets, the built-in frame importer turns any downloaded NASA SVS animation sequence into an instant musical instrument. Key Factors Considered Accessibility First: Designing controls that work seamlessly without sight (semantic landmarks, ≥44px touch targets, reduced-motion support, keyboard-only playback, and spoken summaries). Scientific Honesty: Prioritizing numerical °C records over approximate pixel colors and explicitly documenting color-palette limitations inside the Understand the Sound section. Reliability for Live Demos: Caching NASA API responses in the Express proxy with an offline GISTEMP backup ensures smooth, lag-free playback even on slow connections. Pleasant, Understandable Audio: Mapping values onto curated musical scales (Pentatonic Major, Lydian, Dorian, Natural Minor, Chromatic) so data trends sound musical and distinguishable rather than harsh random noise.

projectDetails.name: Flame in Free Fall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data
projectDetails.summary: Flame in Free Fall is an SI-powered interactive dashboard designed to explore, analyze, and interpret NASA's microgravity combustion research. The platform brings together findings from space-based fire experiments to help users understand how flames behave in reduced-gravity environments. It summarizes and compares experimental results, identifies important fire-safety factors, and provides intelligent insights into flame behavior, fuel flammability, oxygen levels, airflow, and fire detection and suppression. By converting complex scientific data into accessible visualizations and actionable insights, the project aims to support safer spacecraft, space stations, lunar habitats, and future Mars missions. It also highlights how research in space can contribute to improved fire safety on Earth.
projectDetails.details:
Flame in Free Fall: SI-Powered Fire Safety Insights from Microgravity Combustion Data

Our project, Flame in Free Fall, proposes an intelligent web-based research platform designed to make NASA's microgravity combustion research easier to explore, understand and compare. In space, flames behave differently because the effects of gravity and natural convection are greatly reduced. Understanding these changes is essential for developing effective fire prevention, detection and suppression strategies for future space missions.

The platform provides a central interface to explore relevant NASA combustion investigations, including BASS, BASS-II, SAFFIRE, SAME, SAME-R, FLEX, FLEX-2 and other related experiments. Users can search investigations by name, research objective, fuel, material and experimental conditions. The proposed SI-powered features include automatic research summaries, relevance-based investigation ranking, comparison of experimental parameters and visual presentation of research information. Parameters of interest include fuel type, flame shape and size, oxygen concentration, airflow, experimental variations and sensor measurements.

The main benefit is to reduce the difficulty of finding and interpreting large volumes of scientific information. It aims to help students, researchers, professors and aerospace engineers identify relevant experiments and understand their contributions to spacecraft fire safety. Its intended impact is to support safer spacecraft, space stations, lunar habitats, pressurised rovers and future Mars missions. The research may also provide useful insights for fire-safety applications on Earth.

The website prototype was developed using HTML, CSS and JavaScript. HTML provides the structure, CSS handles the visual design and responsive layout, and JavaScript supports search, filtering and interactive investigation details. The project is designed as a web-based software solution and does not require special hardware for its current prototype. NASA's Open Science Data Repository and Physical Sciences Informatics resources are considered reference sources for the research data.

The creative aspect of this project is the combination of space-combustion research with an intelligent, user-friendly data exploration approach. Instead of treating each experiment as isolated information, the platform aims to connect related investigations and make their findings easier to compare. Important factors considered include microgravity flame behavior, oxygen concentration, atmospheric pressure, fuel and material properties, airflow, detection methods, suppression techniques and the reliability of scientific sources.

The current website is a prototype with demonstration investigation records. Connecting verified NASA datasets and implementing the proposed SI-powered analysis features are planned development steps.

projectDetails.details:
ASTRAGUARD is a web-based astronaut health-monitoring support platform developed to demonstrate how crew health information can be organised and reviewed during long-duration space missions.

The application provides separate views for astronauts and crew medical officers. Users can record physiological readings such as heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation and body temperature, complete daily wellness check-ins, and review historical records. A dashboard presents key readings and trends, while an interactive 2D human-body map lets users explore cardiovascular, respiratory, neurological and thermal monitoring categories. A configurable demonstration rule system highlights readings that fall outside the project's example ranges, and alerts can be reviewed and acknowledged.

The project is designed to make health information easier to access, understand and communicate. Its creative element is the combination of a visual 2D body map, individual health records, trend views and crew-oriented monitoring in one interface.

The application is developed using React, Vite, Tailwind CSS, JavaScript, Node.js, Express.js and MongoDB. The team considered usability, clear visual feedback, role-based access and the limitations of remote health monitoring. The current demonstration uses synthetic data and is not a medical diagnostic or treatment system.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: AeroCrop Q-BRIX ROBOTICS
projectDetails.summary:
AeroCrop Sentinel shows that a low-cost, field-ready device can turn raw environmental data into clear decisions for farmers. The system combines on-site sensing (soil moisture, soil temperature, air temperature, and humidity) with a 3-day weather forecast and NASA’s EONET feed of nearby storms and floods. From these, it produces simple advice such as plant now, irrigate soon, hold for rain, or halt crops during drought risk. A Gemini-based advisor and voice assistant explain that guidance in plain language, while the dashboard, on-device screen, and WhatsApp alerts deliver it directly—including to farmers who prefer asking aloud.
The project addresses key pressures farmers face today: shifting temperatures, erratic rainfall, water shortages, and extreme weather. Tying irrigation and planting timing to live soil conditions and incoming weather helps conserve water and reduce crop stress. Its modular design—one board for sensing and the web service, and one for display and voice—keeps costs low and makes adding sensors or locations simple.
The next step extends this foundation into full crop-rotation planning. By integrating NASA Earth observation datasets—such as SMAP soil moisture, GPM rainfall, and NASA POWER climate data—with local soil records and each farmer’s priorities, the tool can compare rotation options across multiple seasons. In this way, AeroCrop Sentinel grows from a daily decision aid into a long-term partner for building soil health and farm resilience.
projectDetails.details: AeroCrop Sentinel v3.0 is an AI-powered, dual-node agricultural monitoring and decision-support system that helps farmers optimize irrigation, monitor crop health, predict weather conditions, and prevent crop losses using real-time sensor data, satellite alerts, and voice-based AI assistance. 1. Working Principle The system uses two ESP32 microcontrollers connected through a 115200-baud UART link. Node A – ESP32-C3: Collects soil moisture, soil temperature, air temperature, and humidity using sensors. Calculates VPD, dew point, and heat index. Fetches 3-day weather forecasts from Open-Meteo and disaster alerts from NASA EONET. Generates smart recommendations such as IRRIGATE NOW, HOLD: RAIN, PLANT NOW, and HALT CROPS. Hosts a web dashboard and sends WhatsApp alerts. Provides an offline Wi-Fi hotspot when internet connectivity fails.

projectDetails.name: HEARTBEAT OF EARTH- The Earth Information Jukebox
projectDetails.summary:
HEARTBEAT OF EARTH is an interactive web platform that brings together Earth science, music, and storytelling to help people connect with our planet.
We wanted to find a creative way to make scientific information more interesting and easier to understand. Our project uses NASA Earth observations and environmental data, including temperature changes, atmospheric CO₂ levels, and historical sea-ice changes, to help users explore what is happening to our planet.
Through an interactive experience, users can discover important Earth events, explore scientific information, and connect environmental changes with music through data-inspired soundscapes.
We believe that science doesn't always have to be explained through numbers and graphs. By combining technology, music, and real-world data, we hope to make people more curious about Earth, help them understand environmental changes, and remind everyone why protecting our planet matters.
projectDetails.details:
HEARTBEAT OF EARTH – The Earth Information Jukebox is a project we created with the idea of bringing science and music together. We wanted to find a different way for people to understand our planet and learn about the changes happening around it. Our website allows users to explore Earth through information about temperature changes, atmospheric CO₂ levels, sea-ice variations, and NASA's Earth observation missions. We have brought these different elements together in an interactive platform where users can explore environmental events and experience the connection between scientific data and music. The idea behind our project is simple: scientific information should not feel difficult or boring to explore. Instead of showing people only numbers and graphs, we wanted to make the experience more interesting through visuals, music, and storytelling. We hope this will encourage more people, especially students, to become curious about Earth and understand the importance of protecting it.

We developed the project using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Node.js, and web-based development tools. We also used GitHub for managing our code and Vercel to host our website. Our project is completely software-based and does not require any additional hardware. What makes this project special to us is the combination of two things that people connect with in different ways: science and music. While developing it, we considered how easy the website would be to use, how the information could be presented clearly, and how it would work on different devices.

Through HEARTBEAT OF EARTH, we hope to make people look at our planet a little differently. We don't just want users to see environmental changes through data; we want them to connect with the story behind that data and understand why our Earth deserves attention and care.

projectDetails.details:
Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer – Que Sera Sera

The Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is an interactive educational simulation designed to introduce students and young learners to the challenges of living and surviving in space. It provides a simple and engaging way to understand the basic requirements of establishing a human outpost on the Moon or Mars.

The project allows users to select between the Moon and Mars and begin a simulated seven-day space mission. During the mission, users monitor and manage essential resources such as oxygen, water, food, and power. They can perform astronaut activities, respond to unexpected events, and make decisions that influence the success of their mission.

Benefits and Intended Impact:

The project makes space exploration more accessible and interesting for students. It encourages critical thinking, problem-solving, decision-making, and an understanding of the difficulties astronauts face in extraterrestrial environments. It also promotes interest in STEM education, space science, and future space exploration.

Tools and Technologies Used:

The project was developed using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. HTML provides the structure, CSS handles the visual design and layout, and JavaScript implements the interactive mission simulation and resource management features. The project was tested in a web browser and deployed using GitHub and GitHub Pages, making it accessible online.

Creativity and Innovation:

The creative aspect of this project is its interactive, decision-based learning approach. Instead of simply reading about space missions, users actively participate in a simulated mission where their choices and resource management affect the outcome. Combining educational content with a simple game-like experience makes learning about space exploration more engaging.

Factors Considered:

The project considers the importance of resource management, astronaut survival, mission duration, unexpected challenges, and the differences between Moon and Mars environments. Simplicity, accessibility, user engagement, and educational value were also considered during development.

Our goal is to inspire young learners to explore space science by giving them an opportunity to experience some of the challenges of being an astronaut through an interactive simulation.

The main benefit of this project is to make space science more accessible and engaging, especially for students and young learners. It encourages curiosity about astronomy, engineering, robotics, and future space missions.

Our goal is to remind people that a space mission's story does not end when communication stops or the mission is over. The machines left behind remain part of humanity's journey into space.

projectDetails.name: Orbit Pulse
projectDetails.summary:
OrbitPulse is an interactive astronaut self-health monitoring tool, built as a Python notebook, for long-duration missions where help from the ground is delayed. It tracks eight daily indicators: heart rate, blood pressure, SpO₂, glucose, temperature, sleep, mood and exercise. Each indicator is colour-coded as normal, caution or alert. It also pulls recent solar flare and solar energetic particle events from NASA’s CCMC DONKI space-weather service and turns them into a daily radiation hazard index.

Crew members get a 30-day trend dashboard, an interactive body map showing which organ systems are affected, and a daily check-in. For every out-of-range reading, the check-in explains why it can happen in space and suggests what to do. It flags when to contact the flight surgeon. A health score, streaks and badges encourage daily use.

This addresses the challenge by giving astronauts a clear, visual way to assess and act on their own health. It matters because Moon and Mars crews will need to manage their health autonomously, and linking vitals to the radiation environment supports earlier detection of problems. Crew vitals are synthetic demo data, and the reference ranges are not medical advice.
projectDetails.details:
What it does and how it works

OrbitPulse is an interactive Python notebook that helps astronauts monitor their own health on long-duration missions. It works in five steps:

  1. Space-weather data: It pulls the last 30 days of solar flares and solar energetic particle (SEP) events from NASA’s CCMC DONKI service. It weights each event (X-class flares count most, then M, then C, and SEP events count heavily) and combines them into a daily radiation hazard index rated Low, Elevated or High.
  2. Vitals tracking: It tracks eight daily indicators: heart rate, systolic blood pressure, SpO₂, blood glucose, body temperature, sleep, mood and exercise. Each has a normal range and a caution range. Anything outside the caution range is an alert.
  3. Dashboards: A 30-day trend dashboard shows each indicator with its normal-range band and colour-coded points. An interactive body map lets the user hover over the brain, lungs, heart, blood, core/immune system and bones/muscle to see each one’s status, why it is affected in space and what to do.
  4. Daily check-in: An interactive form lets the astronaut enter the day’s values and click “Evaluate my health”. Every out-of-range reading comes with a short explanation (for example, fluid shifts in microgravity) and a concrete action. Red readings trigger an alert to contact the flight surgeon. High solar activity triggers a reminder to follow the radiation-shelter protocol.
  5. Motivation: A daily health score, green-day streaks and badges (Mission Fit, Bone Guardian, Sleep Master, Steady Mind) encourage consistent monitoring and exercise.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Supports crew autonomy when communication with Earth is delayed, as on Moon and Mars missions.
  • Links the space environment to physiology, so the astronaut can see how radiation relates to heart rate, sleep and mood.
  • Gives plain-language explanations and next steps instead of raw numbers, which reduces guesswork under stress.
  • Helps catch problems early through trends and a clear escalation path.
  • Covers physical and behavioural health in one view.

The intended impact is safer, more self-reliant crews on future deep-space missions. The same approach could also adapt to remote, isolated settings on Earth, such as polar stations and submarines.

Tools and technologies

  • Language and environment: Python in Google Colab / Jupyter
  • Data: NASA CCMC DONKI API (ccmc.gsfc.nasa.gov/DONKI-API) via requests
  • Analysis: pandas and numpy
  • Visualisation: plotly for the trend dashboard, body map and score chart, and matplotlib for the radiation chart
  • Interface: ipywidgets for the interactive check-in
  • Demo slides: PptxGenJS
  • Hardware: None required. It runs in a browser or on a laptop, so it is easy to deploy.
  • AI assistance: The code was generated with AI assistance (Claude, Anthropic), as disclosed in the notebook.

Creativity

  • The body map turns abstract numbers into an intuitive picture of which organ systems need attention.
  • It couples live NASA space-weather data to crew health indicators, rather than treating vitals in isolation.
  • Gamification, such as streaks and badges, addresses the real problem of keeping crews engaged with routine self-monitoring.
  • Every alert pairs a “why” with an “action”, which makes it an educational coach and not just a monitor.
  • A dark mission-control look with a consistent traffic-light colour scheme makes status readable at a glance.

Factors considered

  • Realistic space health risks: microgravity fluid shifts, bone and muscle loss, radiation exposure, disrupted sleep and isolation.
  • Safety: A clear escalation path for red alerts, and caution-level readings prompt re-measurement.
  • Usability: Colour coding, hover details and one-click evaluation keep it simple under mission workload.
  • Reliability: The tool handles API failures gracefully and falls back to demo values if NASA data is unavailable.
  • Ethics and transparency: Crew vitals are synthetic demo data, the reference ranges are general values and not medical advice, and the use of AI assistance is disclosed.
  • Future work: Real wearable and biosensor integration, personalised baselines per astronaut, predictive alerts from radiation forecasts, and an offline mode for deep space.

projectDetails.name: SECTOR 17 — THE LAST EXPEDITION
projectDetails.summary:
SECTOR 17 — THE LAST EXPEDITION is a browser-based Space Mission Design Game that puts players in command of EXPEDITION-V, a fictional mission to Jupiter’s icy moon Europa. Players select mission objectives, configure the AETHON spacecraft, balance propulsion, power, mass and thermal constraints, plan orbital manoeuvres, operate the spacecraft, communicate across deep space and process simulated scientific observations.

The game uses real aerospace concepts and equations, including the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, Vis-Viva orbital mechanics, Hohmann transfers, inverse-square solar irradiance, radiative thermal balance and deep-space communication models. Its guided campaign turns these interconnected engineering challenges into an interactive learning experience.

By combining 3D visualisation, a deterministic simulation runtime, mission decisions and a multi-stage science data pipeline, SECTOR 17 aims to make complex space exploration concepts more accessible, engaging and understandable.
projectDetails.details:
SECTOR 17 — THE LAST EXPEDITION is an interactive Space Mission Design Game built around EXPEDITION-V, a fictional robotic survey mission to Europa, Jupiter’s icy moon. The player takes the role of mission director and flight operations lead, making engineering and operational decisions throughout the expedition.

The experience follows six main stages: Main Menu, Mission Selection, Spacecraft Workshop, Trajectory Planner, Mission Operations and Mission Debrief. In the Workshop, players configure the fictional AETHON spacecraft by selecting propulsion, electrical power and scientific payload components while monitoring mass, power and thermal budgets. The Trajectory Planner introduces orbital transfer planning and manoeuvre decisions. Mission Operations presents spacecraft telemetry, communications and science-processing controls. The Debrief records mission outcomes and player decisions.

The simulation incorporates established aerospace concepts, including the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation, Vis-Viva equation, Hohmann transfers, inverse-square solar irradiance, Stefan–Boltzmann radiative balance, Friis transmission loss and Shannon channel capacity. Orbital mechanics uses a classical Keplerian two-body approximation, while the thermal subsystem uses a simplified single-node model. Science observations are simulated: the data pipeline demonstrates Level 0 ingestion, Level 1 calibration and Level 2 analysis, including illustrative candidate chemical matches and radar echo horizons. These are not real scientific discoveries.

The application was developed using React, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Three.js and React Three Fiber. Its architecture includes a deterministic simulation runtime, an 18-stage campaign state machine, spacecraft subsystem models, browser-based persistence and Web Audio API sound effects.

The project aims to make the engineering trade-offs of deep-space exploration accessible through hands-on experimentation rather than passive reading. Players learn how mass, propulsion, power, thermal constraints, communication delays and scientific objectives interact in a complex mission.

The project was informed by NASA planetary imagery, Europa Clipper mission and instrument references, and Deep Space Network technical resources. AI tools assisted parts of software engineering, testing, technical writing and concept artwork; these contributions are disclosed in the project. The simulation logic and physics calculations execute as deterministic code.

Live project: https://sector-17.vercel.app

projectDetails.name: Project silent cosmos
projectDetails.summary:
Our project, “Abandoned but Not Forgotten: Storytelling About NASA’s Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars,” explores the stories behind spacecraft, scientific instruments and other hardware left behind by NASA during space exploration.

We developed an educational presentation highlighting three major examples: Apollo mission equipment left on the Moon, Mars landers and discarded landing components, and the Pioneer 10 spacecraft travelling through deep space. The project explains why this equipment was left behind, its original purpose, the scientific discoveries it enabled and its present status.

Our project addresses the challenge by transforming the history of discarded space hardware into an engaging and informative story for school-age space enthusiasts. It demonstrates that these objects are not simply waste but valuable reminders of scientific achievement, engineering innovation and human curiosity.

This project is important because it helps people understand the legacy of space exploration and appreciate how even equipment left behind can continue to contribute to science and inspire future generations.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Abandoned but Not Forgotten

What does the project do and how does it work?

Our project explores NASA's discarded and abandoned space equipment on the Moon, Mars and in deep space. It tells the stories of spacecraft, landers, rovers and scientific instruments that were left behind after completing their missions or becoming inactive. Through an educational presentation, we explain their original purposes, how they worked, why they were abandoned and what scientific contributions they made. We highlight examples such as Apollo lunar equipment, Mars landing systems and the Pioneer 10 spacecraft.

What are its benefits?

The project makes space science easier and more interesting to understand, especially for school-age students. It introduces audiences to real NASA missions, space technology, engineering challenges and scientific discoveries. It also helps people understand that abandoned equipment can have historical, scientific and educational value.

What is the intended impact?

Our aim is to inspire curiosity about space exploration and encourage the next generation to learn more about science, technology and engineering. We also want to raise awareness about preserving historic space exploration sites and recognising the importance of past missions in shaping future discoveries.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software were used?

We developed the project using presentation and research tools. We used PowerPoint-compatible presentation software to create the slides, along with information and reference materials from NASA and other scientific sources. No physical hardware or specialised coding languages were required because this is an educational storytelling project rather than a hardware prototype or software application.

How is the project creative?

Instead of presenting space exploration only through successful missions and discoveries, we focus on the lesser-known stories of equipment left behind. We connect different missions across the Moon, Mars and deep space to show how each object represents a part of humanity's journey into the universe. This storytelling approach makes forgotten technology interesting and meaningful to younger audiences.

What factors did the team consider?

Our team considered scientific accuracy, educational value, audience engagement, historical importance and clarity of presentation. We selected examples that demonstrate different types of space equipment and missions. We also considered why the equipment was left behind, whether it is still functioning, its contribution to science and how its story could inspire future space explorers.

projectDetails.name: Silent Sentinels: NASA's Off-World Monuments
projectDetails.summary: Silent Sentinels: NASA’s Off-World Monuments is an interactive, story-driven web application designed for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge to inspire school-age space enthusiasts. Moving beyond dense technical archives, the platform transforms historic spacecraft left on the Moon, Mars, and deep space into relatable first-person narrators. Users explore clickable orbital radar maps featuring nine iconic artifacts from Apollo’s Lunar Roving Vehicle to Mars’s Opportunity and Ingenuity. Each monument pairs audio-narrated "Voices from the Dust" with an Engineering-to-Science Decoder, interactive field-check quizzes that unlock Junior Space Historian badges, and an Endurance Timeline showing how NASA’s hardware outlasted its warranties to reshape planetary science.
projectDetails.details:
Silent Sentinels: NASA’s Off-World Monuments is an interactive, story-driven web application created for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge to bridge the gap between dense archival mission logs and young, curious minds.

What It Does & How It Works

The platform turns the Moon, Mars, and deep space into an explorable digital museum. Users switch between three celestial regions on an interactive Orbital Radar Map dotted with glowing "Ghost Hardware" beacons. Selecting any of the nine featured monuments—such as Apollo 11’s Eagle & Retroreflector, Surveyor 3, Sojourner, Opportunity, InSight, Ingenuity, Pioneer 10, or NEAR Shoemaker—opens a three-part interactive story experience:

  • Voices from the Dust (First-Person Narratives & Audio): Each spacecraft tells its own story in an accessible, emotional first-person voice, accompanied by built-in browser text-to-speech narration so younger learners can listen along.
  • Engineering-to-Science Decoder: Connects what the hardware was physically built to do with the groundbreaking planetary discoveries it achieved.
  • Field Check Quizzes & Badge Progression: Short interactive challenges test comprehension and award collectible Junior Space Historian badges, alongside an Endurance Legacy Timeline comparing planned mission lifespans against actual survival times.

Benefits & Intended Impact

Traditional space archives are often overwhelming for school-age learners, focusing heavily on active missions while leaving historic hardware buried in technical PDFs. Silent Sentinels humanizes robotic explorers, helping students build an emotional connection with space history while clearly understanding why engineering choices matter for scientific discovery. By making historical mission data tactile, auditory, and game-like, the project aims to spark long-term curiosity in STEM, planetary science, and aerospace engineering among school-age students and casual space fans.

Tools, Languages & Technology Used

  • Languages: HTML5, CSS3, and Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+).
  • APIs & Web Standards: Browser Web Speech API (window.speechSynthesis) for zero-dependency voice narration, SVG graphics for custom orbital radar maps and spacecraft schematics, and CSS Grid/Flexbox with custom keyframe animations for responsive telemetry styling.
  • Data Sources: Historical mission specifications, landing coordinates, and scientific outcomes sourced from NASA’s NSSDC (National Space Science Data Center), Apollo Lunar Surface Journal, and JPL Mars Exploration archives.

Creativity & Key Design Considerations

Instead of presenting a static encyclopedia or timeline, the project gives silent machines a voice—framing retired rovers and landers as enduring monuments still standing watch across the solar system. In designing the experience, we prioritized age appropriateness (clear, vivid storytelling tailored for ages 8–15 without sacrificing scientific accuracy), accessibility (high-contrast mission-control visuals, audio narration for developing readers, and filterable views by mission status and era), and zero-friction deployment (built as a lightweight, single-file web app that runs smoothly on any classroom computer, tablet, or smartphone without installations or external servers).

projectDetails.details:
FIREWISE is an interactive Microgravity Combustion Intelligence Dashboard designed to make NASA combustion research easier to explore and understand.

The platform features an investigation explorer covering BASS-II, FLEX, SAFFIRE and SAME. Users can search and filter investigations, explore research summaries, compare research themes and view their relevance to spacecraft fire safety.

projectDetails.name: SkyPages: Abandoned but not Forgotten
projectDetails.summary: SkyPages is an interactive, child-friendly storybook website about NASA equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars. Children turn the pages of a flipbook to meet the Apollo lander bases and Lunar Rovers, and the Mars robots Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Ingenuity and InSight. Each page combines a real NASA photograph, a short story, animation, background music, read-aloud narration and quizzes. SkyPages answers the challenge "Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars" by turning forgotten machines into characters that school-age learners can meet. It matters because stories make space science memorable and accessible, and they inspire the next generation of explorers.
projectDetails.details:
SkyPages is a free, interactive storybook website that introduces school-age learners to NASA equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars.

What it does: Children turn the pages of a 16-page flipbook. On the Moon they see the Apollo lander bases, footprints, the Lunar Rover and a rover parked for good. On Mars they meet Sojourner, the twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity, the Ingenuity helicopter (shown with Perseverance) and the InSight lander. Every page pairs a real NASA photograph with a short, simple story and a fun fact. Two quizzes and a storyteller activity invite children to draw, write or act out a robot's story.

How it works: SkyPages is a single web page that runs in any phone or computer browser, with no login or install. Pages turn by tapping the left or right side, swiping or dragging, using the arrow buttons or the keyboard. Sound effects and background music are generated in the browser, and a read-aloud button uses the browser's built-in speech so early readers can listen to each page.

Benefits and impact: It makes space history friendly and memorable, supports listening as well as reading, and works on low-cost phones. We hope teachers and families use it, and we plan to add more missions, languages and classroom activities.

Creativity and design choices: We chose a storybook format, page-flip animation, a calm space soundtrack and large, simple text because young learners respond to stories, motion and sound. Facts were checked against NASA mission pages, and every NASA photo is credited on its page.

Tools: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Web Audio API, Web Speech API, Google Fonts (Fredoka and Nunito), Python and ffmpeg for the demo video.

AI use: This project was built with AI assistance. Claude (Anthropic), a large language model, helped write the code, simplify the text, and create the illustrations (drawn in code), the music and sound effects (generated in code) and the demo video. The narration voice was generated with an AI text-to-speech tool: GOOGLE AI STUDIO. The SkyPages logo was generated with an AI tool: CHATGPT. The project idea and the choice of challenge were made by our team. AI-assisted content is labeled "AI-assisted • made with Claude" in the video and images, "AI-assisted" in the website footer, and in the file metadata. The NASA photographs are real NASA images and are not AI-generated.

projectDetails.summary:
Our project aims to create an interactive digital storytelling platform that brings NASA's abandoned and retired space hardware on the Moon, Mars, and beyond back into the spotlight. Through engaging stories, visuals, 3D models, timelines, and mission details, users can explore different spacecraft, rovers, landers, and scientific instruments, discovering their original purposes, achievements, and the science they made possible.

The platform transforms technical mission data into an exciting and easy-to-understand learning experience, especially for school-age space enthusiasts. By highlighting the history, contributions, and current status of these forgotten machines, we aim to inspire curiosity about space exploration, demonstrate the importance of scientific innovation, and help the next generation appreciate the technology behind humanity's journey beyond Earth.
projectDetails.details:
RelicVoyager – Exploring the Forgotten Legacy of Space Exploration

Developed by Team smAsh

RelicVoyager is an interactive digital storytelling and educational platform developed in response to NASA's challenge, "Abandoned but not Forgotten: Storytelling about NASA's Discarded Equipment on the Moon and Mars."

The project explores the history and scientific legacy of human-made hardware left behind on the Moon and Mars. Instead of treating these objects as abandoned debris, RelicVoyager presents them as important technological and historical artifacts that represent humanity's journey into space.

How It Works

RelicVoyager combines interactive visualization, technical information, historical storytelling and gamified learning into a single web-based experience.

The platform consists of several interconnected sections:

  1. 3D Celestial Map: An interactive visualization that allows users to explore extraterrestrial locations and discover the hardware left behind. Users can rotate the view, interact with markers and inspect individual artifacts.
  2. Relic Archives & Dossiers: A searchable archive containing information about space exploration hardware, including Opportunity, Ingenuity, Apollo 11 and InSight. Each dossier presents technical specifications, landing locations, mission timelines, scientific contributions and engineering details.
  3. Echoes from the Dust: A creative storytelling experience that presents first-person narratives from the perspective of retired spacecraft and exploration hardware. It transforms technical mission histories into engaging stories that help users emotionally connect with these machines.
  4. The Trail of Silent Pioneers: An interactive chronological timeline showcasing the evolution of robotic exploration, from early missions in the 1960s to modern planetary exploration.
  5. Junior Space Archaeologist Challenge: An educational quiz experience where users answer mission-related questions, earn collectible badges and work towards a Space Archaeologist Certificate of Achievement.
  6. The Space Heritage Charter: An awareness section highlighting the importance of preserving extraterrestrial historical sites, protecting scientific artifacts and recognizing the cultural and engineering significance of humanity's presence beyond Earth.

Benefits and Intended Impact

RelicVoyager makes space exploration history more accessible, interactive and engaging, particularly for students and young space enthusiasts.

Its primary benefits include:

  • Promoting STEM education through interactive exploration and gamified learning.
  • Increasing awareness of NASA's historical missions and technological achievements.
  • Making complex engineering and scientific information easier to understand.
  • Encouraging interest in robotics, aerospace engineering, planetary science and space exploration.
  • Highlighting the importance of protecting extraterrestrial heritage from future exploration and commercial activities.

Our intended impact is to encourage people to look beyond the achievements of successful missions and recognize the scientific, historical and cultural value of the hardware they leave behind.

Tools and Technologies

RelicVoyager was developed as a browser-based interactive web platform.

The development involved:

  • HTML, CSS and JavaScript for website structure, styling and interactive functionality.
  • Interactive 3D visualization for exploring extraterrestrial artifacts.
  • NASA's publicly available scientific and mission information.
  • GitHub for source-code management and collaboration.
  • GitHub Pages for hosting and deployment.

Data sources: NASA National Space Science Data Center (NSSDCA), NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) and JPL Horizons.

Creativity and Innovation

The most distinctive aspect of RelicVoyager is its approach to storytelling. Rather than presenting abandoned spacecraft as static objects in a conventional database, we transform them into historical characters with stories, missions and scientific legacies.

The combination of 3D exploration, technical dossiers, first-person storytelling, chronological visualization and gamified STEM education creates a multi-dimensional learning experience.

We wanted users to experience space archaeology rather than simply read about it.

Factors Considered During Development

Our team considered several important factors while developing the project:

  • Educational accessibility: Information should be understandable and engaging for users with different levels of scientific knowledge.
  • Scientific accuracy: Mission histories and technical information should be grounded in credible NASA data sources.
  • User experience: Navigation and interactions should make exploration intuitive and enjoyable.
  • Historical preservation: The platform should communicate why extraterrestrial artifacts deserve recognition and protection.
  • Engagement: Interactive elements, storytelling and challenges should encourage users to explore further.
  • Accessibility: The platform should be accessible through a standard web browser without requiring specialized hardware.

Ultimately, RelicVoyager aims to change how people perceive abandoned space hardware. Every forgotten lander, rover and spacecraft component represents a chapter in humanity's exploration history. Through this project, Team smAsh hopes to ensure that these silent pioneers are never forgotten.

projectDetails.name: Abandoned but Not Forgotten
projectDetails.summary: Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an educational storytelling project that explores the human-made equipment remaining on the Moon and Mars after NASA missions. It focuses on the Apollo Lunar Module descent stages, Lunar Roving Vehicles and scientific instruments on the Moon, as well as the landing equipment from the Perseverance mission on Mars, including its heat shield, parachute, backshell and descent stage. The project describes why certain mission components are not brought back to Earth and compares the equipment found on both planetary surfaces. To make the subject more engaging, it includes imaginative stories narrated from the perspectives of a lunar rover, a heat shield and a descent stage. These objects are valuable records of scientific progress, technological development and space exploration. The project also discusses the need to preserve these historical remains through location documentation, satellite-based observation and responsible protection of landing sites.
projectDetails.details: The main aim of this project is to introduce space heritage in a simple and engaging way through storytelling. The presentation is organised into seven slides and examines why spacecraft leave certain components behind after completing their missions. Factors such as restricted storage capacity, equipment weight, landing-specific components and scientific devices intended to remain on the surface are explained. The project describes the important objects found on the Moon, including Apollo Lunar Module descent stages, Lunar Roving Vehicles and scientific research instruments. It also examines the remains of the Mars 2020 Perseverance landing system, such as the heat shield, parachute, backshell and descent stage. The sequence of events involved in the rover's landing on Mars is also presented. A comparison between the Moon and Mars highlights the different types of exploration and equipment associated with each world. In addition, three fictional first-person narratives describe the experiences of a Lunar Rover, a heat shield and a descent stage. These narratives are creative interpretations and should not be considered actual recorded statements. The concluding section explains the historical and technological value of these objects and recommends methods for safeguarding space heritage, including documenting artifact positions, examining landing areas through satellite imagery and avoiding unnecessary contact with historic remains. PowerPoint slides with simple diagrams and shapes are used to communicate the information. AI assistance was used in developing the presentation content and design. The project aims to encourage students and the wider public to understand the achievements of space missions and recognise the importance of protecting their historical remains.
