projectDetails.name: THE LAST NIGHT OF EAGLE
projectDetails.summary: The Last Light of Eagle is an educational storytelling project that explores the Apollo 11 Lunar Module and the scientific equipment left on the Moon in July 1969. It highlights the design and functions of Eagle's descent and ascent stages, along with the Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package (EASEP). The project explains how instruments such as the passive seismometer, lunar dust detector and laser ranging retroreflector contributed to lunar research. It also describes their operating principles, mission duration and eventual shutdown. Through this story, the project demonstrates how space technology continues to contribute to scientific knowledge even after its mission ends.
projectDetails.details: The Last Light of Eagle is an educational storytelling project that presents the history, engineering and scientific contributions of NASA's Apollo 11 Lunar Module, Eagle, and the scientific equipment left on the Moon. It works by combining historical information, scientific explanations, timelines and visual illustrations to explain how Eagle landed on the lunar surface, how its two stages functioned, and how the Early Apollo Scientific Experiments Package (EASEP) collected scientific data and communicated with Earth. The project benefits students and space enthusiasts by making complex space technology and lunar exploration easier to understand. Its intended impact is to create awareness about the importance of space research, engineering innovation and scientific exploration. The project was developed using HTML and CSS to create an interactive, visually engaging storytelling webpage, along with PowerPoint for the project demonstration. Its creativity lies in presenting the story from the perspective of abandoned space hardware, highlighting not only the astronauts' achievements but also the scientific legacy of the equipment they left behind. The team considered historical accuracy, scientific relevance, simplicity of explanation, visual presentation, audience engagement and the educational value of the content while developing the project.

challengeDetails.title: Identify Earth Locations that Analog the Permanent Moon Base Locations and Mars
challengeDetails.excerpt: Selecting future landing sites and lunar base locations depends on many factors, including topography, geology, environment, and available resources, to name a few. Places on Earth that have analogous characteristics to the Moon or Mars – the Atacama Desert, Haughton Crater, Death Valley – allow mission teams to test equipment and methods before they fly; however, such terrestrial analog sites are not entirely well characterized. Your challenge is to use open Earth, Moon, and Mars data from NASA and other space agencies to identify and characterize new terrestrial analogs for future bases or landing sites, drawing on deserts, polar regions, volcanic and arid terrains, caves, and other environments that share conditions with the lunar or Martian surface, then present your findings as a map, visualization, or other tool.

projectDetails.name: Project Spacetechx
projectDetails.summary: FIELDSHIFT is a farmer-focused decision-support concept that aims to help farmers adapt to changing climate conditions using NASA Earth observation data. The proposed tool combines information on rainfall, temperature, soil moisture and vegetation health with local soil conditions, crop characteristics and farmers’ needs. It compares different crop rotation strategies, including existing practices, to identify possible alternatives and their benefits, risks and limitations. Designed with Kerala’s agricultural context in mind, FIELDSHIFT aims to make satellite-based information easier to understand and support more informed, climate-resilient farming decisions.
projectDetails.details: FIELDSHIFT – Adapting Farms with NASA Data FIELDSHIFT is a farmer-focused decision-support concept developed by Team SPACETECHX for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Our project aims to connect NASA Earth observation data with local agricultural information to help farmers understand changing environmental conditions and make better crop rotation decisions. 1. Problem We Address Farmers face several challenges due to changing climate conditions, including rising temperatures, unpredictable rainfall, water shortages, soil moisture changes and declining soil health. Choosing the right crop rotation is difficult because different crops have different water requirements, soil needs and growing seasons. NASA provides valuable Earth observation data, but this information can be difficult for farmers to understand and apply in everyday farming. 2. Our Proposed Solution FIELDSHIFT aims to convert complex satellite-based environmental information into simple and useful agricultural insights. It combines NASA Earth observation data, local soil information, crop characteristics and farmer priorities to compare different crop rotation strategies. 3. NASA Data Sources Our proposed system considers eight NASA data sources: - NASA POWER – Temperature, precipitation and solar radiation. - GPM – Rainfall patterns and extreme precipitation. - SMAP – Surface and root-zone soil moisture. - ECOSTRESS – Land surface temperature and evapotranspiration. - Landsat – Vegetation condition and land-use changes. - MODIS – Vegetation indices and seasonal patterns. - GRACE / GRACE-FO – Regional water-storage changes. - SRTM – Elevation and terrain information for erosion-risk screening. These datasets are proposed inputs and have not yet been downloaded or analysed in our current prototype. 4. How FIELDSHIFT Works The proposed workflow has seven stages: 1. The farmer selects the field location and enters soil type, existing crop rotation, water availability and farming priorities. 2. Relevant NASA environmental datasets are collected through official NASA portals and APIs. 3. The collected data is cleaned, checked, standardised and prepared for analysis. 4. NASA observations are combined with local soil characteristics, crop requirements and farmer preferences. 5. Environmental conditions such as rainfall changes, temperature trends, soil moisture, vegetation health and water stress are assessed. 6. Three crop rotation strategies are compared using transparent criteria and farmer-selected priorities. 7. Results are presented through a simple dashboard with explanations, possible benefits, limitations and confidence levels. 5. Crop Rotation Strategies FIELDSHIFT compares three strategies: Strategy A – Existing Rotation: The farmer's current crop rotation, used as the baseline. Strategy B – Legume and Cover-Crop Rotation: Considers nitrogen fixation by legumes, soil protection, organic matter improvement and erosion reduction. Strategy C – Diversified, Deep-Rooted and Drought-Tolerant Rotation: Explores crop diversification, deeper root systems and crops that can better tolerate dry conditions. The strategies are compared based on water requirements, soil health, nitrogen contribution, erosion reduction, pest-cycle disruption, growing-season suitability, market suitability and farmer preferences. 6. Proposed Dashboard Our concept dashboard allows farmers to select their field, enter soil and water information, choose farming priorities and compare the three rotation strategies. It is designed to present environmental indicators and explain why a particular strategy may or may not suit the selected field. The current dashboard is a concept prototype mock-up. Its displayed values, charts and imagery are illustrative and are not actual NASA measurements. 7. Benefits and Expected Impact FIELDSHIFT aims to support better-informed crop rotation planning, improved soil management, more efficient water use, reduced periods of exposed soil and better understanding of seasonal climate risks. It also aims to make NASA Earth observation data more accessible to farming communities and encourage sustainable, climate-resilient agricultural practices. 8. Creativity, Limitations and Future Development The main innovation of FIELDSHIFT is connecting space-based environmental observations with practical crop rotation decisions through a farmer-friendly approach. The project combines satellite information, local agricultural knowledge and individual farming priorities rather than presenting technical satellite data alone. Currently, the project has a concept and dashboard mock-up. NASA data integration, environmental analysis, strategy scoring and farmer and expert testing are planned future developments. Local soil tests, ground observations and agricultural expert review will be essential before providing actual crop recommendations. FIELDSHIFT is designed to support farmers' decisions, not replace their knowledge or professional agricultural advice.

projectDetails.details:
Project Details – Ghosts of Space

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Ghosts of Space is an interactive 3D space archaeology game that transforms the history of abandoned, retired, and inactive space exploration hardware into an engaging learning experience. Players take on the role of a Space Archaeologist and explore three environments: the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space.

Guided by LUNA, a robotic companion, players discover real space artifacts, investigate their components, learn about their missions and scientific contributions, and document their findings in a mission archive. The experience combines exploration, storytelling, educational challenges, resource management, and mission progression to make learning about space history interactive.

2. What benefits does it offer?

- Interactive learning: Makes complex space exploration history easier and more enjoyable to understand.
- Historical awareness: Introduces players to spacecraft and equipment that are often overlooked despite their scientific importance.
- Scientific curiosity: Encourages users to explore engineering, astronomy, planetary science, and space technology.
- Engaging storytelling: Uses LUNA as a companion to make the learning experience more personal and approachable.
- Knowledge retention: Allows players to learn through discovery, investigation, and challenges rather than passive reading.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to make the stories of space exploration hardware accessible to students, young learners, and space enthusiasts. We want players to understand that even when a spacecraft stops functioning or a mission ends, its scientific contributions and engineering legacy remain valuable.

By combining gaming with education, Ghosts of Space aims to inspire curiosity about space science, encourage interest in STEM fields, and preserve awareness of humanity's achievements in space exploration.

4. What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed using web-based technologies:

- Babylon.js: 3D rendering, environments, camera systems, interactions, and visual effects.
- TypeScript: Core game logic, player controls, mission systems, and interactions.
- Vite: Development environment and project build tooling.
- HTML5 and CSS3: User interface, HUD, menus, dialogue, and visual styling.
- Blender: Preparation and modification of 3D assets, where applicable.
- Git and GitHub: Version control and collaborative development.
- Render: Web deployment and hosting.

The game is designed to run in a web browser, making it accessible without requiring users to install a dedicated game application.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

The creative aspect of Ghosts of Space lies in presenting space history through the perspective of a space archaeology adventure.

Instead of simply displaying information about spacecraft, the project allows players to discover their stories through exploration and investigation. LUNA adds a conversational and narrative dimension, acting as both a guide and a companion. The three environments also create a sense of progression, taking players from the familiar lunar surface to Mars and eventually into deep space.

The project also recognizes that not every artifact can be physically explored. Deep-space missions are approached through signals, mission records, telemetry, and trajectory information rather than treating distant spacecraft as objects that can be retrieved.

6. What factors did the team consider?

During development, we considered:

- Historical accuracy: Keeping mission histories, scientific contributions, and current artifact statuses as accurate as possible using available mission information.
- Educational value: Presenting technical information in a way that is understandable to younger audiences and non-specialists.
- Accessibility: Developing a browser-based experience that does not require specialized hardware or installation.
- User engagement: Combining exploration, storytelling, challenges, and progression to maintain interest.
- Performance: Optimizing 3D environments and assets to support smoother gameplay on commonly available computers.
- Usability: Designing clear controls, readable interfaces, and intuitive interactions.
- Scalability: Structuring the experience around multiple environments and artifacts so that additional missions and discoveries can be incorporated in the future.

Ultimately, Ghosts of Space aims to show that abandoned space hardware is not simply forgotten machinery. Each artifact represents a mission, a scientific achievement, and a story worth preserving.

projectDetails.name: Spaizone Vitals
projectDetails.summary: Spaizone Vitals is a health monitoring dashboard that helps astronauts on long missions spot health changes early, without waiting for Earth. It learns each astronaut’s own normal baseline, uses rules and a machine learning anomaly model to flag drift in heart rate, oxygen, sleep, temperature, mood and radiation, and tells the astronaut what to do next.
projectDetails.details:
Problem. On missions to the Moon and Mars, astronauts face radiation, microgravity, isolation and stress. These cause slow changes such as bone loss, cardiovascular strain, immune changes and mental health decline. Communication delays mean astronauts must often notice these changes themselves.

Solution. Spaizone Vitals is a health monitoring dashboard that runs on board and needs no connection to Earth. It tracks six indicators every day: resting heart rate, blood oxygen, sleep, core temperature, mood check-ins and radiation dose rate.

How it works.

  1. Personal baseline. Each astronaut’s first 14 days set their own normal, because healthy ranges differ between people.
  2. Drift detection. A 5-day rolling average smooths daily noise. A move of 2σ in the unwanted direction raises a Watch, and 3σ raises an Alert. Radiation is also checked against a 250 mSv 30-day limit.
  3. Anomaly model. A k-nearest-neighbour model learns the astronaut’s normal combination of all six readings from the first 30 days. It scores how far each new day is from that normal. It catches several small shifts that happen together, even when no single reading has crossed its own limit.
  4. Guidance. Each warning comes with plain actions, such as a heart check, protecting sleep, calling behavioral health, or moving to shielded areas during a solar event.
  5. Ground report. A summary for the ground medical team is generated automatically on board.

Data input. Users can upload or paste a CSV, or add one day at a time, so the same dashboard works with real sensor data.

Benefits. It is personalized, catches slow changes early, supports crew autonomy during communication delays, and works offline.

Tools. HTML, CSS and JavaScript. All analysis runs in the browser.

projectDetails.name: Silent Explorers
projectDetails.summary: The Museum of Silent Explorers is an immersive, narrative-driven NASA Space Apps Challenge project that reimagines abandoned space hardware as historical storytellers. Instead of a traditional museum, it uses an interactive digital experience to guide users across three galleries: the Moon, Mars, and deep space. Visitors uncover the mysteries behind artifacts like the Apollo Lunar Rover, the resilient Mars rover Opportunity, and the Voyager spacecraft carrying the Golden Record. By combining real missions, rigorous engineering, and scientific discoveries with emotional storytelling, the project connects humanity's past achievements with the next generation of space explorers.
projectDetails.details:
The Museum of Silent Explorers

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

The Museum of Silent Explorers is an interactive educational web experience that tells the story of robotic and scientific machines that explored space but never returned to Earth.

The website is organized into three interactive galleries: the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space. Users explore the stories of different machines, including Apollo-era lunar equipment, the Mars rovers Spirit and Opportunity, and the Voyager spacecraft. The website uses storytelling, interactive sections, timelines, visual illustrations, and information cards to make space exploration more engaging.

The project also explains why some machines are left behind. The main reasons include fuel limitations, mission cost, engineering limitations, and the fact that some spacecraft are designed to continue travelling rather than return to Earth.

The experience ends by asking users to imagine the next generation of space explorers and consider what future machines might discover.

2. What are the benefits of the project?

The project provides several important benefits:

  • Educational: It helps users understand space exploration and the role of machines in scientific discovery.
  • Interactive learning: Instead of presenting information like a traditional textbook, users explore the information through an interactive museum concept.
  • Easy to understand: Complex concepts such as spacecraft missions, fuel requirements, and remote exploration are explained through simple storytelling.
  • Increases curiosity: The project encourages users to think about space, engineering, robotics, and future exploration.
  • Preserves scientific history: It highlights machines that played important roles in exploration even though they never returned to Earth.
  • Engages younger audiences: The visual and interactive approach can make STEM topics more interesting to students.

The website emphasizes that the knowledge collected by these machines returns to Earth even when the physical machines remain in space.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

The main objective is to change the way people learn about space exploration.

Instead of focusing only on astronauts, the project shows that machines are also important explorers. Rovers, scientific instruments, spacecraft, cameras, and communication systems allow humans to investigate environments that are extremely difficult or impossible for people to reach.

The intended impact is to:

  • Increase interest in space science and technology.
  • Encourage students to explore STEM fields.
  • Demonstrate the importance of robotics and autonomous systems.
  • Help users understand the challenges of exploring other worlds.
  • Inspire people to think about the future of human and robotic space exploration.

The website's central message is that the history of space exploration is also written by the machines that remain behind and continue sending knowledge back to Earth.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software were used?

The project is primarily a web-based software project, so it does not require specialized physical hardware for users.

The development can be described in terms of:

Software and technologies

  • HTML5 – for structuring the web pages and content.
  • CSS3 – for the visual design, layout, animations, and responsive interface.
  • JavaScript – for interactive elements and user interactions.
  • Web browser – for accessing and running the project.
  • Netlify – for hosting and deploying the website.
  • Git/GitHub – for managing and deploying the project source code, where applicable.

Hardware

  • A computer/laptop for development.
  • Internet connection for deployment and accessing online resources.
  • A smartphone, tablet, or computer can be used by visitors to access the website.

The final project is hosted as a web application and can be accessed through the Silent Explorers website.

5. How is the project creative?

The project is creative because it presents scientific information as an interactive digital museum rather than a conventional website or presentation.

Some of its creative features include:

  • The concept of a virtual museum located millions of kilometres away from Earth.
  • Three themed galleries representing the Moon, Mars, and Deep Space.
  • A narrative-based approach where users feel like they are discovering exhibits.
  • Interactive identification of the machines.
  • A timeline showing the history of these explorers.
  • A storytelling approach that gives scientific machines a sense of identity and history.
  • The final "Your Turn" section allows users to imagine the next generation of explorers.

The website describes itself as having three galleries and six machines, turning the learning experience into an exploration activity rather than simply displaying information.

6. What factors did the team consider?

While developing the project, the team considered several important factors:

User Experience

The website needed to be simple enough for students and general visitors to understand while still providing meaningful scientific information.

Educational Value

The information was selected to explain not only what the machines are, but also why they were sent, what they achieved, and why they remained behind.

Accuracy

The project uses space-exploration facts based on public NASA records. The website also clearly states that it is not affiliated with or endorsed by NASA.

Visual Design

The team considered how to present scientific information through illustrations, galleries, timelines, cards, and interactive elements instead of large blocks of text.

Accessibility and Usability

The interface was designed so that users can move through the story progressively and understand the information without requiring advanced knowledge of astronomy.

Performance

Because the project is web-based, factors such as page loading, responsive design, browser compatibility, and efficient use of digital assets were important.

Engagement

The team considered how to keep users interested throughout the experience. The final question—asking what a future machine might discover—encourages users to participate creatively rather than simply finish reading.

projectDetails.name: Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer
projectDetails.summary:
Lunar Outpost Academy turns lunar exploration into a guided mission for children ages 7–12. Players choose one of six real Apollo landing sites, mapped with NASA coordinates, then drive a rover through a training route: scan three survey points in order and reach the beacon to unlock the habitat mission.

In mission control, players balance air, power and radiation shielding with simple actions: refresh air, charge batteries, strengthen protection or shelter the crew. Each day brings tradeoffs, points and a chance to recover and try a new strategy.

Captain Luna explains every control with step-by-step narration, highlighted focus cues and replay, previous and skip options. No account is needed, and names, progress and scores are saved locally.

Live NASA DONKI space-weather data adds real solar-storm warnings, while NASA archive photos and clearly labelled simulations separate observed facts from gameplay.

Children learn engineering by making decisions, seeing effects and reflecting, not just memorising facts. By pairing approachable play with traceable science, the game makes planetary exploration understandable and meaningful. Built with React, Three.js and Tailwind CSS, and deployed on Vercel.
projectDetails.details:
Lunar Outpost Academy is a browser-based learning game that introduces children to the challenges of exploring and living on the Moon. Players choose among six real Apollo landing sites, guide a rover along an illustrated training route, and then manage a lunar habitat by balancing air, power, and radiation protection. The game combines Apollo location information, NASA imagery, and space-weather data with clearly labeled simulated gameplay.

It works through a sequence of interactive tasks: players select a destination, scan route points with the rover, and make choices in mission control. Narration and visual guidance help explain what to do, while feedback, points, and mission progress show how decisions affect the crew.

The project aims to build curiosity about space and introduce systems thinking, planning, and problem-solving through play. Its creative element is connecting real lunar exploration information to a guided rover challenge and habitat-management game, rather than presenting space facts as a quiz.

It is built with JavaScript, React, CSS, Vite, Zustand, and Motion. It runs in a web browser without an account or app download. Accessibility-minded features include narration controls, keyboard movement, clear instructions, and options to skip or revisit guidance; the experience has not been formally accessibility-certified. The game uses public NASA resources and open-source tools, so there is no required app purchase, though internet access and any hosting costs may apply.

projectDetails.name: Still
projectDetails.summary:
STILL — Abandoned, Not Forgotten is an interactive archival storytelling experience that chronicles thirteen silent NASA spacecraft resting across the Moon, Mars, and deep space—from the Apollo Lunar Modules, ALSEP retroreflectors, and Surveyor 3 on the Moon to Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Viking, InSight, and Ingenuity on Mars, and outward to Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Kepler, and Pioneer 10.

Addressing the "Abandoned, But Not Forgotten" challenge, STILL pairs first-person spacecraft perspectives and long-form historical narrative with verified NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA) records, orbital coordinates, and real-time light-delay telemetry. Readers can fire a simulated 2.56-second laser pulse to lunar retroreflectors, compare "Then & Now" orbital imagery, and explore mission longevity counters across dual Vacuum and Archival Paper reading modes.

These machines are not space debris; they are humanity’s first off-world archaeological monuments—transforming cold telemetry into an enduring human story of exploration.
projectDetails.details:
What It Does & How It Works

STILL — Abandoned, Not Forgotten is an interactive digital exhibition and archival storytelling platform dedicated to thirteen pioneering NASA spacecraft left behind across the Solar System:

  • Act I · The Moon: Apollo Lunar Module Descent Stages (1969-059C), Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicles (1971-063C), ALSEP & Laser Retroreflectors (1969-099C), and Surveyor 3 (1967-035A).
  • Act II · Mars: Sojourner (1996-068A), Spirit & Opportunity (2003-027A / 2003-032A), Viking 1 & 2 Landers (1975-075C), Phoenix & InSight (2018-042A), and the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter (2020-052B).
  • Act III · Deep Space: Dawn at Ceres (2007-043A), NEAR Shoemaker on Asteroid 433 Eros (1996-008A), the Kepler Space Telescope (2009-011A), and Pioneer 10 (1972-012A).

As readers travel outward from Earth (384,400 km to 24+ billion km), the platform dynamically updates real-time distance and speed-of-light signal delay telemetry (1.28 seconds at the Moon to over 22 hours in interstellar space) and calculates live "Silent for N Days" counters from each mission’s final contact date.

Each chapter weaves together:

  1. First-Person Spacecraft Voice: An evocative opening transmission spoken from the resting hardware’s perspective, paired with a strict historical verification note.
    • Ping the Moon (ALSEP): Fires a simulated laser pulse across 384,400 km to the Apollo corner-cube prisms and times the exact 2.56-second round-trip photon return.
    • Sol Odometer (Spirit & Opportunity): Visualizes Opportunity’s 90-sol warranty stretching into 5,111 sols of exploration.
    • Flight Counter (Ingenuity): Maps all 72 Martian flights against the original 5-flight technology demonstration goal.
    • Send a Message (Pioneer 10): Broadcasts a radio signal into interstellar space at 299,792 km/s to illustrate the immense scale of deep space.
    • Then & Now Archival Sliders: Compares surface photography from active operations with modern orbital reconnaissance imagery from LRO and HiRISE.
  2. Verified NSSDCA Colophon & Master Registry: Links every mission directly to its official NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA) catalog entry.

Creative Design & Dual Reading Modes

Rather than building a conventional dashboard, we designed STILL as a tactile museum monograph with two distinct physical reading environments:

  • Vacuum Mode (Dark): An obsidian zero-gravity canvas (#07080a) featuring a custom HTML5 Canvas 3D starfield with inertial scroll physics and a two-stage radial time-warp interaction when clicking the STILL masthead.
  • Paper Mode (Light): A vintage 1969 cotton-rag archival parchment sheet (#e6dac2) with fine paper grain, Celestial Cartography graticule lines, and high-friction page-turn mechanics.
  • Editorial Rubrication: Key historical dates, chapter numbers, and opening initials are highlighted in archival Rubric Red (--c-rubric) set in calibrated Space Mono typography so critical milestones anchor the reader’s eye effortlessly.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Humanizing Space Hardware: Shifts public perception of decommissioned spacecraft from "discarded equipment" to irreplaceable off-world archaeological monuments and active scientific benchmarks.
  • Accessible Science Communication: Translates abstract astrophysical numbers (light-time delay, sols, heliocentric distances, NSSDCA designators) into intuitive, hands-on interactions for students, educators, and space enthusiasts.
  • Strict Historical Integrity: Separates poetic storytelling from hard telemetry through automated build-time schema validation against NASA/NSSDCA records.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

  • Framework & Content Architecture: Astro 5 (astro:content MDX collections), TypeScript, HTML5, CSS3 Custom Properties.
  • Data Validation: Zod strict schema validation (STRICT_FACTS=true) verifying NSSDCA IDs, coordinates, distances, and mission dates at build time.
  • Motion & Graphics: Custom HTML5 2D Canvas starfield and celestial graticule engine, GSAP + ScrollTrigger, Lenis mode-aware smooth scrolling, and custom SVG schematics.
  • Data & Imagery Sources: NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA), Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC), Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter (HiRISE), and NASA/JPL-Caltech archives.

Key Factors Considered by Our Team

  1. Scientific Accuracy vs. Emotional Resonance: We separated verified NSSDCA facts (data/artifacts.ts) from narrative prose (story/chapters/*.mdx) so poetic storytelling never compromises factual accuracy.
  2. Reading Ergonomics & Universal Responsiveness: We calibrated Space Mono line lengths (70ch), line height (1.92), and word spacing across all screen dimensions (320px mobile viewports to 4K displays).
  3. Accessibility & Performance: Full prefers-reduced-motion support, keyboard navigation (← / →), semantic ARIA live telemetry regions, and zero-overhead static site generation.

projectDetails.name: Orbit-Ops_Astrobase: Junior Flight Director
projectDetails.summary:
Space exploration requires mastering complex engineering trade-offs, but these concepts are often too abstract or complicated for young learners. To bridge this gap, we developed OrbitOps, an interactive web application built with Java that acts as a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer for children ages 7–12.

Our app addresses the challenge by transforming real-world lunar mission constraints into an engaging, gamified experience. Players step into the shoes of a mission commander managing a lunar outpost, where they must carefully balance vital resources like solar power management during lunar night cycles, life support, and radiation shielding. Every decision carries a direct consequence, teaching players authentic systems-thinking and resource management. This project is important because early exposure to STEM through interactive problem-solving sparks curiosity and builds the next generation of space explorers. 
By leveraging Java for a robust, reliable backend, our web app delivers seamless performance and smooth gameplay straight to the browser making lunar mission training accessible, interactive, and fun for classrooms everywhere.
projectDetails.details:
Project OrbitOps: AstroBase – Junior Flight Director

What It Does & How It Works Project OrbitOps is an interactive, browser-based mission simulation game designed to train young learners (ages 7–12) as Junior Flight Directors managing an Artemis lunar outpost. Across a 5-Sol mission cycle, players balance competing survival systems—Power Reserves, Oxygen Supply, Water Reserves, and Science Progress—while managing a three-person crew (Commander, Flight Engineer, and Life Support Specialist) across specialized habitat modules (Habitat, Greenhouse, Science Lab, Solar Array, and Storm Vault).

The simulation dynamically integrates real-world aerospace data—including live space weather telemetry via the NASA DONKI Space Weather API (tracking Coronal Mass Ejections and solar storm activity), surface cartography from the NASA Planetary Data System (PDS), atmospheric telemetry from NASA Mars Rover Environmental Data, and NASA Artemis Base Camp life-support parameters—to scale mission hazards in real time. During each Sol, players face unscripted emergencies such as Solar Particle Events (SEPs), dust-covered solar arrays, water recycler failures, and module oxygen leaks. Players must choose between competing operational trade-offs—such as sheltering the crew to prevent radiation exposure at the cost of halting scientific research, or sealing off a leaking habitat section to preserve air while losing usable workspace. At the end of the mission, players receive a comprehensive Flight Director Decision Log detailing their survival metrics and the real-world engineering science behind each choice.

Benefits & Intended Impact Space-themed STEM content for children often falls into two extremes: overly simplified arcade games that ignore physical constraints, or dense engineering manuals that overwhelm young minds. Project OrbitOps bridges this gap by making systems engineering trade-offs tangible, visual, and fun. By framing failure and resource scarcity as safe, replayable puzzles, the app builds critical thinking, systems-level problem-solving, and authentic aerospace literacy—inspiring the next generation of students to explore STEM and space exploration careers.

Tools, Languages & Software Used

  • Build Tool & Frontend Stack: Vite, HTML5, CSS3, JavaScript (ES6+), responsive UI/UX dashboard design, and custom SVG/2D habitat graphics.
  • Data Used :
    1)NASA Open APIs — DONKI (Space Weather Database Of Notifications, Knowledge, Information) for real-time solar storm and CME telemetry.
    2)NASA Planetary Data System (PDS) for lunar and Martian surface cartography (Ares Planitia and lunar south pole coordinates).
    3)NASA Mars Science Laboratory (REMS) environmental telemetry for Martian Sol cycles and atmospheric conditions.
    4)NASA Artemis Program mission parameters for lunar surface habitat, power, and life-support trade-offs.
  • Hosting & Version Control: GitHub / GitHub Pages for zero-install, cross-platform browser accessibility, also used Vercel.

Creativity & Key Design Factors Considered

  • Zero Barrier to Entry: Built with Vite as a lightweight, fast-loading web application that runs instantly in any modern browser without downloads, installations, or account sign-ups.
  • Cognitive Load Balancing for Ages 7–12: Instead of overwhelming young players with dozens of complex variables, we focused on core interdependent meters (Power, Oxygen, Water, Crew Health) paired with bite-sized, jargon-free "Science Takeaways" after every decision.
  • Real-World Scientific Grounding: Every game mechanic reflects actual lunar mission protocols, teaching concepts like In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU), cumulative astronaut radiation limits, autonomous rover maintenance, and modular habitat isolation.

projectDetails.details: EarthVision is a project concept designed to help people understand environmental changes on Earth using satellite observations and Earth science data from NASA. Our idea is to explore changes in temperature, rainfall, vegetation and land cover over time. By presenting this information through maps, charts and simple explanations, the project aims to make environmental changes easier to understand. The main benefit is to create awareness about climate change, vegetation loss and other environmental challenges. It could help students, researchers and the public understand how our planet is changing. We prepared a demonstration website prototype and a PowerPoint presentation to explain our idea and its proposed workflow. The prototype includes an illustrative trend chart and a map section. These are examples for demonstration, not verified NASA measurements. Our proposed tools include NASA Earth observation data, HTML, CSS, JavaScript and GitHub. We also used AI assistance during the preparation of the project materials. Our creative approach is to present environmental information in a simple and understandable way. Our five-member team considered the importance of climate awareness, accessibility, teamwork and the potential use of satellite data. Our future goal is to connect the prototype with real NASA datasets and develop it into a useful environmental monitoring platform.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: MISSION CONTROL :  Design, Build, Launch, Survive
projectDetails.summary:
MISSION CONTROL is an interactive, browser-based 3D space exploration and aerospace engineering simulator that allows users to experience the complete lifecycle of an interplanetary space mission.

The application enables users to design and assemble modular spacecraft, configure propulsion and power systems, evaluate engineering parameters, perform launch simulations, navigate orbital environments and conduct planetary investigations across four campaigns: Mars, the Moon, asteroid Bennu and Europa.

It addresses the challenge of making complex aerospace engineering and planetary science concepts more accessible through interactive visualization and game-based learning. By combining simplified engineering models, scientific reference information and immersive 3D environments, users can understand how spacecraft design decisions influence mission performance and survival.

MISSION CONTROL aims to bridge the gap between theoretical aerospace education and practical interactive experimentation, making space exploration more engaging and accessible without requiring expensive physical equipment or professional simulation infrastructure.
projectDetails.details:
MISSION CONTROL integrates several engineering and simulation modules to provide an interactive spacecraft operations experience.

Core Functionalities

- Spacecraft Assembly: Modular selection of structural buses, propulsion systems, solar arrays, batteries, thermal management, communication equipment, navigation systems and scientific payloads.

- Engineering Validation: Evaluation of spacecraft mass, available Delta-V, power generation, electrical consumption, thermal conditions and communication link budgets.

- Launch Operations: Pre-launch system checks, countdown sequences, simulated multi-stage launch and orbital deployment.

- Orbital Navigation: Third-person spacecraft control with simulated propulsion, attitude control and navigation.

- Scientific Exploration: Mission-specific investigations using simulated scientific instruments.

- Mission Survival: Dynamic emergency scenarios involving power management, thermal regulation, propulsion and spacecraft control.

Benefits

- Encourages practical understanding of spacecraft engineering.

- Demonstrates how engineering decisions influence mission performance.

- Develops technical problem-solving and decision-making skills.

- Provides an accessible environment for aerospace experimentation without physical prototypes or specialized simulation infrastructure.

Intended Impact

The project aims to encourage interest in aerospace engineering, spacecraft systems and planetary science. It promotes interdisciplinary learning, engineering-based decision-making and a deeper understanding of the technical challenges associated with space missions.

Technology Stack

- Programming Languages: TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML5 and CSS.

- Frameworks and Libraries: React 18, Three.js, Zustand, Tailwind CSS and Lucide React.

- Development Tools: Google Antigravity, Gemini, Vite, Node.js and npm.

- Web Technologies: WebGL, Web Audio API and LocalStorage.

- Deployment: GitHub for source code management and Vercel for hosting.

- Hardware: No dedicated physical hardware is required. The application runs on compatible computers with a modern web browser and WebGL support.

Creative Approach

The project combines spacecraft engineering with interactive simulation and game-based exploration. Engineering dashboards, modular component selection, orbital operations and dynamic survival scenarios allow users to experience the consequences of technical decisions rather than simply study theoretical concepts.

Design Considerations

- Energy Efficiency: Incorporates spacecraft power generation, electrical consumption and variations in solar irradiance.

- Accessibility: Browser-based operation eliminates specialized installation and dedicated laboratory requirements.

- Cost: Avoids expensive physical prototypes and professional simulation infrastructure.

- Environmental Considerations: Encourages virtual experimentation and introduces the importance of energy efficiency, thermal management and resource optimization in spacecraft systems.

projectDetails.name: SARWISE – AI-Powered Earth Change Intelligence
projectDetails.summary:
SARWISE – See the Invisible. Understand the Change.

SARWISE is an interactive Earth-change monitoring platform designed to transform complex NASA-ISRO NISAR Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) observations into meaningful environmental insights. We propose a user-friendly dashboard that allows users to explore surface changes through interactive maps, multi-date satellite comparisons and visual change analysis.

Our initial focus is the Kuttanad–Vembanad region of Kerala, where we aim to demonstrate how SAR data can help identify changes in water coverage, flood inundation patterns and wetland boundaries. Key features include Flood Vision, Wetland Watch, an interactive Earth Time Machine and Change Intelligence, which highlights changing areas and estimates their spatial extent.

By leveraging NISAR's L-band and S-band radar capabilities, SARWISE addresses the challenge of monitoring Earth's surface even through clouds and in darkness. It bridges the gap between advanced satellite data and practical understanding, supporting environmental researchers, farmers and decision-makers. Our vision is to make satellite-based change detection more accessible, understandable and useful for protecting ecosystems and communities worldwide.
projectDetails.details: SARWISE – See the Invisible. Understand the Change. 1. Project Overview SARWISE is an interactive Earth-change monitoring platform designed to transform complex NASA-ISRO NISAR Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) observations into meaningful environmental insights. It helps users identify, visualize and understand changes occurring on Earth's surface, with an initial focus on flood-related water coverage and wetland transformation in Kerala's Kuttanad–Vembanad region. Traditional optical satellites can face difficulties observing Earth's surface during cloudy weather and at night. SAR technology overcomes these limitations by using radar signals to observe the Earth's surface through clouds and in darkness. SARWISE aims to make this powerful technology accessible through an intuitive, interactive platform. 2. How Does It Work? SARWISE follows a satellite-to-insight workflow: 1. Data Acquisition: Obtain NISAR radar observations and relevant supporting geospatial datasets. 2. Data Processing: Prepare radar imagery using appropriate techniques such as calibration, speckle filtering, terrain correction and geospatial alignment. 3. Change Detection: Compare observations from different dates using radar backscatter information to identify changes in surface conditions. 4. Visualization: Display detected changes through interactive maps, colour-coded layers and before-and-after comparisons. 5. Analysis: Estimate the spatial extent of detected changes and highlight areas that may require further investigation. Users can select geographical locations, explore available observation dates and compare how the Earth's surface has changed over time. 3. Main Features SARWISE combines five important capabilities: - Flood Vision: Visualizes changes in water-covered areas and helps identify potential flood-inundation zones. - Wetland Watch: Monitors changes in wetland boundaries, water bodies and surrounding land. - Earth Time Machine: Provides an interactive timeline to compare satellite observations from different dates. - Change Intelligence: Highlights detected changes using colour-coded maps and estimates their geographical extent. - Community Impact: Presents satellite-derived information in an understandable format for farmers, researchers and local authorities. 4. Benefits and Intended Impact Our initial focus is Kuttanad, Kerala, where water distribution, wetlands and agriculture are closely connected. SARWISE aims to support environmental awareness and research by making changes easier to observe and interpret. The platform can help researchers study wetland transformation, provide agricultural communities with useful information about changing water conditions and support local authorities in identifying areas requiring further investigation. In the future, SARWISE can be expanded to applications such as deforestation monitoring, agricultural assessment, soil-moisture studies, glacier monitoring and land-surface deformation. It is designed as a monitoring and decision-support tool, not an operational flood forecasting or emergency-warning system. 5. Tools and Technologies Our proposed development stack includes Python for SAR processing and data analysis, JavaScript and React for the interactive interface, FastAPI for backend services, Leaflet or MapLibre for geographical visualization, ESA SNAP for radar processing, and Rasterio, GeoPandas, NumPy, SciPy and Plotly for geospatial analysis and visualization. NISAR is the primary satellite data source. Supplementary datasets such as Sentinel-1 may be used where necessary and will be clearly distinguished. 6. Creativity and Innovation The uniqueness of SARWISE lies in converting complex radar observations into understandable environmental information. Features such as the Earth Time Machine, interactive before-and-after explorer and Change Intelligence make satellite-based monitoring more intuitive and engaging. Our team considered scientific reliability, data availability, usability, environmental relevance and scalability. We also considered the influence of surface moisture, roughness, vegetation and observation geometry on radar backscatter to avoid misleading interpretations. Our Vision: To bridge the gap between advanced satellite technology and real-world environmental understanding. Team Seblaski: Nirmal C George, P Pranav Krishnan, Neeraj Pallakkat and Gokul Arun Menon.

projectDetails.name: CrewPulse
projectDetails.summary: Crew Check-In is a fictional-data prototype for exploring how astronauts could record everyday wellness information during a space mission. The app brings daily entries—resting heart rate, sleep, optional blood pressure and temperature, mood, hydration, meals, exercise, and notes—together in one place. projectDetails.details:
Introduction

CrewPulse is a browser-based prototype for recording and reviewing fictional astronaut wellness check-ins. It explores how a simple daily log could help crew members keep health-related observations organized during a long-duration mission. The prototype is for demonstration and learning; it is not a medical device and does not provide medical advice, diagnosis, treatment, or emergency alerts.

What the prototype does

  • Records daily check-ins: Users can enter fictional readings and routine details, including resting heart rate, sleep, mood, notes, and other selected wellness fields.
  • Shows check-in history: Saved entries appear in a dated list, so users can review what they recorded over time.
  • Displays trends: A chart presents recorded heart-rate and sleep values across check-in dates. It visualizes the entries; it does not interpret them as healthy or unhealthy.
  • Supports follow-up: A user can mark an entry for review. This is a way to identify an item for attention in the demo, not an automatic medical referral.
  • Provides a Sources section: The app links to NASA materials about human-spaceflight hazards and risks, plus measurement guidance from other health sources. These references provide context and measurement instructions; they are not used to claim NASA has set universal health thresholds for this prototype.
  • Includes measurement guidance: Short instructions explain how a user might take or record selected measurements. They are informational and do not replace professional guidance or mission procedures.

How it works

  • The user fills out the check-in form and saves the entry.
  • Entries are stored in the browser on the device being used. The prototype has no account system or central server, so data is not shared between devices.
  • The history and chart use the saved entries to make the user’s own records easier to review.
  • Sample entries are fictional and labeled as sample data.
  • No sensors, spacecraft systems, NASA databases, or external health services are connected to the app.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Makes routine wellness notes easier to record and revisit.
  • Presents information in a straightforward format that may help users notice what they have logged across multiple days.
  • Demonstrates how a small digital tool could organize self-reported information in a mission setting.
  • Encourages careful use of sources and clear communication about what a prototype can—and cannot—conclude.
  • Provides a starting point for discussion about usability, privacy, measurement consistency, and the needs of crews on long-duration missions.

Tools and development

  • Bolt.new was used to create and develop the web app.
  • The app was built with React and TypeScript, with styling and browser storage for the prototype’s interface and locally saved entries.
  • ChatGPT was used to help plan features, explain development steps, research and summarize source material, and draft project text.
  • The app contains fictional demonstration data. AI-assisted code and text are identified in the project’s Super Intelligence disclosure.

Design considerations

  • Clarity: Labels and short instructions aim to make the check-in understandable to a first-time user.
  • Privacy: Entries stay in the browser rather than being sent to an account or server.
  • Safety: The app avoids diagnosis, treatment recommendations, and unsupported claims about “normal” health values.
  • Source transparency: NASA resources are used for spaceflight-health context. Measurement instructions and any other external references are credited separately.
  • Prototype limits: The app has not been clinically validated and is not designed for real astronaut care or operational mission decisions.

projectDetails.name: AstroCare
projectDetails.summary:
AstroCare is a health monitoring and decision-support application designed to support astronauts during long-duration space missions. Spaceflight conditions such as altered gravity, isolation, radiation exposure, and disrupted sleep can affect an astronaut's physical and behavioral health.

AstroCare brings important health indicators into a single dashboard, including heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), body temperature, sleep duration, and self-reported mental wellness. It presents health trends through interactive visualizations and helps astronauts identify unusual changes through warning indicators and personalized health monitoring.

The application aims to help astronauts become more aware of their health, recognize potential concerns early, and make informed decisions about seeking appropriate support. By combining physical health tracking, wellness check-ins, and trend analysis within an accessible software platform, AstroCare supports the goal of safer, more self-reliant long-duration human space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview

AstroCare is an astronaut health monitoring and decision-support application designed for long-duration space missions. It provides a centralized platform to monitor physical health indicators, track mental wellness, and observe changes in health patterns over time.

How It Works

The application collects or accepts health indicators such as heart rate, blood oxygen saturation (SpO₂), body temperature, sleep duration, and self-reported stress and mood levels.

These indicators are displayed through an interactive dashboard. Historical readings are visualized using graphs to help identify changes from an individual's usual health patterns. The system also provides warning indicators when configured conditions require attention and generates downloadable health reports.

The initial prototype uses simulated health readings to demonstrate the monitoring workflow. It is designed to support future integration with wearable sensors and real astronaut health datasets.

Key Features

  • Physical health indicator monitoring.
  • Sleep and mental wellness check-ins.
  • Interactive health trend visualization.
  • Personal health baseline comparison (planned enhancement).
  • Warning and decision-support indicators.
  • Downloadable health reports.

Technologies Used

Python is used for application development, Streamlit for the interactive interface, Pandas and NumPy for data handling and processing, and Plotly for data visualization.

Creativity and Innovation

AstroCare combines physical health monitoring, behavioral wellness tracking, and historical trend visualization in a single application. Rather than displaying isolated measurements alone, the intended approach focuses on helping astronauts understand changes in their health over time and take appropriate action.

Intended Impact

AstroCare aims to improve astronaut awareness of physical and behavioral health changes, support early identification of potential concerns, and encourage informed self-monitoring during long-duration missions where immediate access to medical assistance may be limited.

The application is a prototype and is not intended to replace professional medical diagnosis or emergency medical support.

projectDetails.name: AstroVital
projectDetails.summary:
AstroVital is an offline-first biomedical monitoring platform designed for astronauts on long-duration space missions, including journeys to Mars. It operates locally, providing essential health monitoring and medical decision support despite communication delays with Earth.

The platform monitors ECG, heart rate, SpO₂, radiation exposure, intraocular pressure, cabin pressure, oxygen, and carbon dioxide levels. Its 16 specialized modules cover cardiovascular health, bone and muscle loss, motion sickness, immune status, dust toxicity, sleep, nutrition, and cognitive performance.

AstroVital provides explainable alerts by identifying abnormal measurements, explaining threshold deviations, and displaying approved medical checklists. Multi-crew profiles enable personalized monitoring, health history tracking, and medical report generation.

Built with React 18, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS, it features an aerospace mission-control interface with interactive dashboards, animated telemetry, and clinical visualizations.

Its goal is to improve astronaut safety through continuous monitoring, early warnings, and reliable offline medical decision support.
projectDetails.details:
1. What It Does & How It Works

AstroVital is an autonomous, offline-first biomedical command and clinical decision-support flight suite engineered for manned deep-space missions, specifically the 1,000-day Ares-V interplanetary transit class to Mars.

  • Offline-First Spacecraft Enclave: Because round-trip radio delays between Earth and Mars range from 4.2 to 48.0 minutes and solar conjunctions cause complete communication blackouts, AstroVital runs 100% locally on radiation-hardened spacecraft hardware (Hermes Transit Hab-03) with zero ground cloud dependency. All biometric records, timelines, and dossiers are stored in an AES-256 encrypted local IndexedDB / SQLite persistence enclave and synchronize asynchronously with Earth's Deep Space Network (DSN) only during intermittent batch downlink windows.
  • Continuous Multi-Channel Telemetry & Deterministic Simulation: Powered by a real-time event engine (telemetryService.ts), AstroVital ingests physiological streams over a 2.4 GHz UWB-44 wearable sensor bus—including 500 Hz Lead-II ECG waveforms, SpO2 plethysmography, bilateral rebound tonometry, and silicon radiation dosimeters—alongside Environmental Control and Life Support System (ECLSS) cabin atmosphere metrics.
  • Explainable Clinical Decision Support (ACDSS): Instead of opaque machine learning predictions, the Autonomous Clinical Decision Support System (ACDSS) evaluates live telemetry against each astronaut's pre-flight 1G baseline and Mission-Elapsed-Time (MET) adaptation curves. Whenever a threshold is breached, it surfaces the exact violating metric, numerical delta, physiological root cause, and flight-rule remediation checklist.
  • 16 Autonomous Subsystem Modules & Live Flight Console: Clinical operations are organized into 16 dedicated subsystems (SYS-01 through SYS-16) covering cardiovascular vitals, GCR/SPE radiation (600 mSv career ALARA limit), cabin pressure/gas scrubbing, ARED musculoskeletal countermeasures, Spaceflight-Associated Neuro-Ocular Syndrome (SANS), Space Adaptation Syndrome (SAS), spinal elongation, immunity, regolith dust, cognitive Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT) testing, flight-rule alerts, and printable Flight Surgeon dossiers. The entry flight deck also features a 4-channel interactive telemetry console (Lead-II ECG, Cosmic Dosimetry, Neuro-Ocular SANS, and ECLSS Atmosphere) and 1-click crew roster authentication (Cmdr. Elena Vance, MD/PhD, Marcus Kane, and Dr. Sarah Lin, PhD).

2. Benefits of the Project

  • Life-Critical Autonomy During Blackouts: Eliminates dangerous delays caused by 4.2–48.0 minute Earth–Mars radio latency by enabling immediate onboard triage and emergency checklist execution without waiting for ground control.
  • Transparent, Auditable Clinical Guidance: Every alert is backed by explicit aerospace flight-rule citations (NASA-STD-3001 and ESA Flight Rule #MED-AUTO-01), exact numerical deltas from baseline, and verifiable standard operating procedures rather than unexplainable "black-box" risk scores.
  • Fewer False Positives via Baseline Differentials: Continuously compares live readings against individualized pre-flight baselines and microgravity adaptation trajectories—preventing false alarms for expected 0-g adaptations such as +4.6 cm spinal elongation or cephalad fluid shifts.
  • High-Legibility Flight-Deck Ergonomics: Tabular-numeral typography (tabular-nums) prevents horizontal number jitter on rapidly updating 500 Hz ECG and sensor readouts, while low-glare dark panels reduce visual fatigue during high-stress crew operations.

3. Intended Impact

  • Enabling Safe Interplanetary Human Spaceflight: Bridges the medical self-sufficiency gap required for multi-year Mars transit missions where real-time terrestrial telemedicine and emergency medical evacuation are physically impossible.
  • Preventing Irreversible Astronaut Deconditioning: Protects long-term crew health by auditing daily countermeasure adherence—including 150-minute daily ARED/CEVIS/T2 exercise sessions to prevent microgravity osteopenia, 45-minute daily Lower Body Negative Pressure (LBNP) regimens to relieve SANS ocular pressure, and cumulative dose tracking against NASA's 600 mSv career ALARA ceiling.
  • Advancing Mission Simulation & Crew Training: Provides an authoritative, production-grade biomedical command platform for deep-space mission simulations, human-factors engineering audits, and astronaut medical officer training.

4. Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Coding Languages: TypeScript (Strict Mode), JavaScript (ES6+), HTML5, and CSS3.
  • Frontend Framework & Build Tools: React 18 for modular UI engineering across all 16 subsystems, Vite 5 (with Rollup bundling and sub-second Hot Module Replacement), Tailwind CSS with custom aerospace display utilities (font-telemetry, font-mono, space-panel), and Lucide React for uniform technical iconography.
  • State, Motion & Storage Software: Custom deterministic telemetry service (telemetryService.ts), browser View Transitions API (animated-theme-toggler.tsx), custom SVG waveform rendering, and local IndexedDB / SQLite encrypted storage.
  • Target Spacecraft Hardware & Biosensor Integrations: Engineered for local radiation-hardened spacecraft nodes (Hermes Transit Hab-03) interfacing over a 2.4 GHz UWB-44 biometric link with CSA Bio-Monitor, Astroskin smart garments, silicon GCR radiation dosimeters, rebound tonometers, ARED vacuum cylinder force transducers, airlock PM2.5 laser photometers, and ECLSS atmospheric sensors.
  • Aerospace Compliance Standards: Built directly around NASA-STD-3001 (Human Integration Design Standards) and ESA Flight Rule #MED-AUTO-01.

5. How the Project Is Creative

  • Replacing "AI Sci-Fi Clichés" with Authentic Aerospace Realism: Rather than relying on superficial sci-fi tropes—such as fake AI chatbot prompt bars, decorative CSS corner HUD brackets, blinking neon tags, and heavy starfields—the interface was modeled on real NASA Mission Control and modern avionics glass cockpits, replacing a faux AI input box with a live 4-channel physiological and ECLSS telemetry console.
  • Explainable Deterministic Autonomy Over Black-Box AI: In safety-critical aerospace medicine, opaque neural networks cannot be easily audited during an emergency; AstroVital pairs real-time physiological simulation with transparent flight-rule provenance and exact delta math.
  • Purpose-Built 60 fps Motion Engineering: Integrates bespoke, hardware-accelerated interactive animations—including a 3D orbital perspective ScrollMorphHero, word-atomic KineticText, dual-direction hardware compatibility marquees (CSA Bio-Monitor, Astroskin, ARED, RadWorks, ECLSS), and circular View Transitions API theme switching—to convey live telemetry flow without sacrificing clinical clarity.

6. Key Factors Considered by the Team

  • Deep-Space Telecommunications Physics: Accounted for 4.2–48.0 minute Earth–Mars light-speed latency and solar conjunction blackouts by making the entire application 100% offline-capable with local encrypted storage and asynchronous DSN batch syncing.
  • Dynamic Microgravity Physiology: Factored in how human baselines shift over a 1,000-day mission—including 1.5–2.0 L cephalad fluid redistribution (SANS), +4.6 cm intervertebral disc spinal lengthening, initial orbital neurovestibular adaptation (SAS), and accelerated bone mineral loss—so clinical alerts adapt to Mission Elapsed Time.
  • Cognitive Ergonomics & Human Factors: Eliminated ALL-CAPS melodramatic headings in favor of clean sentence-case mission-control typography, enforced fixed-width tabular numerals so high-frequency readouts never jitter, and organized complex medical workflows into 16 scannable modules.
  • Regulatory Governance & Crew Data Privacy: Mapped clinical thresholds directly to NASA-STD-3001 and ESA #MED-AUTO-01 flight rules while protecting sensitive mental wellness journals and crew medical histories using AES-256 local encryption.

A.R.V.I.S. is an online decision-support tool designed for agriculture.

This tool helps you identify the best crop rotations for your farm and offers insights into your environmental data.

A.R.V.I.S. efficiently manages all your farming activities by providing a single source of information about your crops, soil data, weather resources, and environmental factors.

Inspired by Earth observation technology, this tool makes accessing agricultural information easy.

projectDetails.details: A.R.V.I.S.—the Agricultural Resilience & Vegetation Intelligence System—is a cutting-edge web-based platform developed by Team Tech Wizards that revolutionizes how farmers make informed decisions. By leveraging advanced data from NASA, A.R.V.I.S. combines satellite observations, environmental information, crop specifics, and farmer-provided soil data into a powerful decision-support tool. This platform incorporates NASA POWER Earth data and satellite imagery from NASA GIBS, enabling farmers to analyze crucial environmental factors such as vegetation patterns, rainfall, and temperature fluctuations. With features designed for optimal crop rotation recommendations, personalized planning, comprehensive soil and crop assessments, scenario comparisons, and timely weather information, A.R.V.I.S. takes agricultural management to the next level . Farmers can confidently explore their farm locations, compare various crop sequences, and assess environmental conditions with ease. The innovative scenario explorer feature empowers users to evaluate crop planning options under a range of conditions, ensuring that every decision is made with precision and foresight. The primary goal of A.R.V.I.S. is to eliminate barriers to agricultural information access, making it straightforward for farmers to utilize essential data. By seamlessly connecting satellite technology with practical agricultural strategies, A.R.V.I.S. promotes resilience in farming, encourages strategic crop rotation, and emphasizes the importance of understanding environmental factors in planning. It is a definitive support tool that complements and enhances local agricultural expertise. Developed as a web application using HTML, A.R.V.I.S. smartly utilizes NASA’s data services to present information engagingly and interactively. The platform features dynamic dashboards, detailed maps, and intuitive data visualizations, presenting recommendations straightforwardly and effectively. What truly distinguishes A.R.V.I.S. is its innovative amalgamation of space-based data and practical farming insights. Rather than simply displaying raw satellite imagery, it synthesizes critical environmental information, crop details, soil characteristics, and scenario analyses into a cohesive platform—directly linking advanced technology to concrete farming decisions. Throughout its development, our team meticulously focused on data availability and specific environmental conditions. We analyzed factors such as vegetation patterns, rainfall, temperature, soil traits, and crop needs, ensuring the platform is not only user-friendly but also delivers clear recommendations while acknowledging the limitations of environmental data. Our mission is clear: to create a pragmatic and accessible resource that unites NASA’s Earth observations with the real-world challenges farmers face every day.

projectDetails.name: Project PLANETARY TIME MACHINE
projectDetails.summary:
**PLANETARY TIME MACHINE- is an AI-assisted platform designed to discover when and where Earth's environments most closely resemble selected regions of the Moon and Mars. Instead of simply identifying places that look similar to planetary landscapes, the project compares measurable environmental characteristics such as geology, elevation, surface roughness, temperature, moisture, dust and ice conditions.

The platform brings together Earth observation data from NASA, ESA, CSA and JAXA with planetary mission data from NASA's Planetary Data System, including Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter observations. Its temporal analysis feature explores seasonal and historical changes to identify periods when terrestrial conditions provide stronger planetary analogues. An explainable similarity engine ranks candidate locations and displays data coverage, confidence and scientific evidence.

By helping researchers identify suitable Earth-based environments and time windows for planetary mission simulations, equipment testing and astronaut training, PLANETARY TIME MACHINE aims to make planetary exploration research more accessible, efficient and evidence-driven.
projectDetails.details:
PLANETARY TIME MACHINE

PLANETARY TIME MACHINE is an AI-assisted platform designed to explore when and where Earth's environments most closely resemble selected regions of the Moon and Mars. It focuses on comparing important environmental characteristics such as geology, elevation, surface roughness, temperature, moisture, dust and ice conditions to identify potential terrestrial analogue locations.

The platform is designed to let users select a planetary target, explore possible matching locations on Earth and examine environmental similarities through an interactive interface. Its time-based approach considers seasonal and historical variations to explore how environmental conditions change and when certain locations may offer stronger planetary analogues.

The project could benefit planetary scientists, researchers, students and space mission planners by helping identify suitable Earth-based environments for mission simulations, equipment testing and astronaut training. Its intended impact is to make planetary analogue discovery more accessible, efficient and data-driven.

The website was developed using Google AI Studio and AI-assisted development tools. Our team used these tools to translate our scientific concept into an interactive web-based platform. The project is designed around the use of Earth observation and planetary datasets from space agencies such as NASA, ESA, CSA and JAXA.

The creative aspect of PLANETARY TIME MACHINE is its focus on both where and when Earth resembles another planetary environment. Rather than depending only on visual similarities, the concept emphasizes measurable environmental characteristics and their changes over time. During development, we considered scientific reliability, data availability, seasonal variations, usability and the limitations of terrestrial analogues. Since Earth cannot fully reproduce conditions such as lunar vacuum, reduced gravity or the thin Martian atmosphere, the platform focuses on identifying useful environmental similarities rather than claiming exact planetary equivalence.

projectDetails.name: Project Tetria_A2
projectDetails.summary:
For the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge, we developed The Silent Guardians of the Stars, an illustrated digital storytelling book that introduces school-age space enthusiasts to NASA's discarded equipment on the Moon, Mars, and deep space.
Addressing the challenge of translating complex historical and scientific data into an engaging narrative, our project brings silent off-world artifacts—such as Apollo lunar modules, Surveyor 3, Sojourner, NEAR Shoemaker, and Pioneer 10—back to life. Rather than relying on dense technical websites or historical textbooks, the book weaves real mission facts, engineering milestones, and telemetry data into an imaginative, accessible story.
This project is vital because students often hear only about active missions; it inspires the next generation by connecting humanity's forgotten robotic explorers to the groundbreaking science that paved the way for today's achievements and tomorrow’s exploration.
projectDetails.details: For over half a century, humanity has sent incredible machines to the Moon, Mars, and deep space. When their missions end, probes, rovers, landers, and scientific instruments are left behind as silent monuments to human exploration. While space agencies know their histories, school-age space enthusiasts often hear only about active missions. To bridge this gap, our project—The Silent Guardians of the Stars—transforms complex historical telemetry and scientific data into an engaging, story-driven digital children’s book and interactive narrative designed for young space enthusiasts. On the Moon, our narrative explores artifacts like Surveyor 3, which landed on April 20, 1967, after bouncing like a pogo stick because reflective rocks confused its landing radar. Equipped with a surface-sampling arm that reached 5 feet and dug 7 inches deep, Surveyor 3 proved that lunar soil had a consistency similar to wet sand with a bearing strength of about 10 pounds per square inch—solid enough to support a human Lunar Module. We also examine the Apollo 11 Lunar Module Eagle descent stage left behind in Mare Tranquilitatis after Armstrong and Aldrin's historic 1969 landing, alongside the Early Apollo Scientific Experiment Package (EASEP). Later, Apollo 12 landed within 180 meters of Surveyor 3 in November 1969, allowing astronauts Pete Conrad and Alan Bean to retrieve its camera and parts to evaluate how 2.5 years of space exposure affected metal. On Mars, the project chronicles pioneering missions such as Mars Pathfinder and its 23-pound rover, Sojourner. Using an innovative airbag landing system, Pathfinder bounced 15 times before resting in Ares Vallis, an ancient flood plain cut by colossal volumes of water. Viking 1 safely touched down on July 20, 1976, returning 4,500 photos and analyzing sulfur-rich soils before its communication ceased in 1982. The story also highlights twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity—which drove an astonishing 28.06 miles—alongside Phoenix, InSight, and the Ingenuity helicopter, which completed 72 historic flights in the thin Martian atmosphere. Venture deeper into space, and the museum expands to asteroids and interstellar trajectories. In February 2001, NEAR Shoemaker became the first spacecraft to land on an asteroid, touching down gently at 4 miles per hour on 433 Eros and returning data for two weeks. The Kepler Space Telescope surveyed over 500,000 stars and revealed that 20 to 50 percent of visible stars likely harbor rocky, Earth-sized planets in their habitable zones. Finally, Pioneer 10—launched in March 1972—braved the asteroid belt and Jupiter's radiation before crossing Neptune's orbit in 1983. In January 2003, it sent its final signal from 7.6 billion miles away, carrying a gold-anodized aluminum plaque as a message from Earth to the stars.
