projectDetails.name: Project The Last Light
projectDetails.summary:
The Last Light

Challenge: Abandoned but Not Forgotten

The Last Light is a digital storybook that explores the journeys and legacies of NASA's spacecraft, instruments, and scientific equipment left across the Solar System.

Through engaging storytelling, the project introduces young space enthusiasts to remarkable missions such as the Apollo lunar experiments, Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, InSight, and Voyager 1 and 2.

Each piece of equipment has a story to tell: discoveries made, mysteries explored, and knowledge sent back to Earth. Although some missions have ended, their scientific contributions continue to shape our understanding of space.

Designed to make space exploration accessible and inspiring to school-age readers, The Last Light celebrates the idea that a mission may end, but its legacy lives on.

A mission can end. Curiosity does not.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details: The Last Light

The Last Light is an educational digital storybook created for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, under the challenge Abandoned but Not Forgotten. It explores the stories of NASA's space hardware that remains on the Moon, Mars, and throughout the Solar System, even after its original mission has ended.

What does the project do and how does it work?

Our project uses visual storytelling to introduce school-age space enthusiasts to the history and scientific contributions of space equipment left behind during space exploration.

Through a series of illustrated slides, we explore:

  • Apollo Lunar Experiments: Scientific instruments and reflectors left on the Moon that helped scientists study its environment.
  • Sojourner: NASA's first successful Mars rover, which demonstrated the potential of robotic exploration.
  • Spirit and Opportunity: Twin Mars rovers that investigated the planet's geology and discovered evidence of past water activity.
  • InSight: A lander that studied the internal structure and seismic activity of Mars.
  • Voyager 1 and 2: Spacecraft that continue to carry the legacy of human exploration far beyond the planets.

Each section tells the story of the equipment, its purpose, its discoveries, and the scientific legacy it leaves behind.

What benefits does it have?

The project makes space science easier and more engaging for young learners. It transforms complex mission information into accessible stories and visual explanations. It also encourages curiosity about robotics, engineering, astronomy, planetary science, and the technology behind space exploration.

What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to help the next generation understand that space exploration does not become meaningless when a spacecraft stops functioning or a mission officially ends. The knowledge, discoveries, and inspiration created by these missions continue to contribute to science.

We hope our storybook encourages students to explore space science, appreciate the engineering behind NASA missions, and imagine the possibilities of future exploration.

What tools and technologies did we use?

We developed the project as a digital presentation and illustrated storybook using:

  • Google Slides: Presentation design and storybook development.
  • Digital illustrations and visual design: To make the missions and their hardware easier to understand.
  • ChatGPT: Used as an AI-assisted tool for brainstorming, organizing the narrative, simplifying scientific explanations, and supporting content development.
  • NASA educational resources and mission information: Used for research and factual reference.

The project does not require a physical hardware prototype or custom-coded software. It is a digital educational storytelling project.

How is the project creative?

Instead of presenting space hardware as abandoned machinery or simply listing mission facts, The Last Light treats each piece of equipment as a storyteller with a history, purpose, and legacy.

We connect different missions across the Moon, Mars, and deep space to create one continuous story about human curiosity and exploration. The visual format and narrative approach help readers connect emotionally and intellectually with the science behind these missions.

What factors did our team consider?

While developing the project, we considered:

  • Scientific accuracy: Keeping mission information and explanations consistent with NASA resources.
  • Accessibility: Making the content understandable for school-age readers and beginners.
  • Visual storytelling: Using illustrations and a clear narrative to maintain interest.
  • Educational value: Explaining not only what the equipment was, but also what scientists learned from it.
  • Mission diversity: Including examples from the Moon, Mars, and deep space.
  • Clarity and simplicity: Presenting information in a concise format without overwhelming readers with technical details.

Our central message is:

A mission can end. Curiosity does not.

Through The Last Light, we want to remind people that even when machines fall silent, their discoveries continue to illuminate our understanding of the universe.

**LUNARIS – Interactive Lunar Exploration and Mission Planning Platform**

LUNARIS is an interactive web-based platform developed to make lunar exploration more accessible through 3D visualization, mission simulations and location-based analysis. It features separate 3D Earth and Moon explorers, an individual satellite database, and a Mission Lab offering different mission scenarios, including thermal mapping, surface analysis and satellite deployment.

Users can select custom lunar latitude and longitude coordinates, investigate potential landing locations and receive indicative landing-compatibility assessments. Additional tools such as Earth Visibility Analysis, Horizon Analysis and Site Comparison introduce important factors involved in lunar mission planning.

Developed using HTML, CSS and JavaScript, LUNARIS combines interactive exploration with preliminary computational assessments. It addresses the challenge by allowing users to visualize, investigate and better understand the complexities of lunar exploration rather than simply reading about them. Its purpose is to encourage scientific curiosity and demonstrate how interactive technology can support space science education and preliminary mission investigation.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details – LUNARIS

LUNARIS is a project I independently conceptualized and developed with the goal of making lunar exploration more interactive, accessible and understandable. Rather than creating another website that simply provides information about space, I wanted to build something that allows users to actively explore the Moon, investigate potential landing locations and experiment with different mission scenarios.

The platform combines several features into one environment. It includes separate interactive 3D Earth and Moon explorers, a satellite database containing individual satellite profiles, and a Mission Lab with different exploration scenarios such as thermal mapping, surface analysis and satellite deployment concepts.

One of the features I particularly focused on was custom lunar coordinate selection. Instead of limiting users to predefined locations, I wanted them to be able to enter their own latitude and longitude and investigate potential landing regions. LUNARIS provides indicative landing-compatibility assessments based on the selected locations. It also incorporates Earth Visibility Analysis, Horizon Analysis and Site Comparison to introduce users to important considerations involved in lunar mission planning.

My approach to developing LUNARIS was also important to me. I independently came up with the concept, planned the platform, designed its interface, developed its features and worked through the technical challenges involved in bringing everything together. I used HTML, CSS and JavaScript to build the application and Netlify to deploy it publicly.

In today's world, where Artificial Intelligence is increasingly capable of generating code and applications, I deliberately wanted to challenge myself by doing the majority of the development independently. I used little to no AI assistance in creating the actual project, prioritizing my own problem-solving, experimentation, coding and learning. I wanted the final result to reflect my own understanding and effort rather than simply relying on an AI-generated application.

The development process involved continuous experimentation, identifying errors, fixing functionality and refining different sections. I particularly focused on making every section serve a distinct purpose rather than creating features that were interactive in appearance but offered little meaningful functionality.

The main factors I considered were usability, scientific relevance, accessibility, visual clarity and the distinction between simulated assessments and scientifically verified mission data. I wanted LUNARIS to be visually engaging while still introducing meaningful concepts related to lunar exploration.

The intended impact of LUNARIS is to encourage curiosity about space exploration and make complex lunar mission concepts easier to understand. It could serve as an educational platform for students, space enthusiasts and anyone interested in understanding the challenges of exploring the Moon.

I see LUNARIS as more than a website. It represents my interest in space technology, my willingness to learn independently and my belief that meaningful projects can be created through curiosity, persistence and experimentation.

My vision is to make space exploration something people do not just read about, but something they can actively explore and understand.

projectDetails.name: TERRATREND AI: Earth System Intelligence Platform
projectDetails.summary:
TERRATREND AI is a full-stack environmental intelligence dashboard designed to decode the planet's changing systems. By integrating NASA POWER historical datasets with real-time Open-Meteo weather feeds and NOAA ocean temperatures, the platform allows users to investigate climate anomalies, identify sudden environmental shifts, and perform rigorous statistical trend analysis (using Mann-Kendall tests and Sen's Slope).
Addressing the challenge of accessible climate data, TERRATREND provides a dynamic "Live Vegetation Suitability" check and a Green/Yellow/Red environmental alert engine based on seasonal historical baselines. Users can explore spatial heatmaps, animate historical timelines, and generate automated AI-driven research summaries. The platform is built to be scientifically honest—every result includes data provenance, confidence scores, and explicit limitations, making complex Earth observation data accessible and actionable for researchers, policymakers, and the public.
projectDetails.details:
What does it do?
TERRATREND AI is a comprehensive web application that transforms raw Earth observation data into actionable environmental intelligence. Users can select specific geographical coordinates and analyze variables like temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind speed, and soil moisture. The platform features a live Vegetation Suitability index, real-time Sea Surface Temperature (NOAA), and a dynamic Alert System (Green/Yellow/Red) that compares live conditions against 10-year historical baselines.

How does it work?
The platform utilizes a React frontend and a Python FastAPI backend. It fetches historical data via the NASA POWER API and real-time weather via Open-Meteo. The backend performs rigorous statistical analysis using SciPy, Statsmodels, and PyMannKendall to calculate linear regression slopes, Sen's slopes, and Mann-Kendall trend significance. Machine learning techniques are simulated via a rule-based AI engine that generates scientific summaries, detects anomalies, and identifies sudden environmental shifts. The frontend visualizes this data using Recharts and React-Leaflet, rendering interactive time-series charts, spatial heatmaps, and animated "Time Machine" timelines.

Benefits and Impact:
The project democratizes access to complex climate data. By translating dense scientific metrics into intuitive UI elements—like confidence scores and live alert colors—it empowers policymakers, farmers, and researchers to make data-driven decisions. The "Live Vegetation Suitability" feature, for instance, provides immediate drought-stress insights, while the "Sudden Change Detector" helps identify rapid environmental degradation.

Tools and Technologies Used:

  • Frontend: React.js, Vite, Recharts, React-Leaflet, Lucide-React, Axios.
  • Backend: Python, FastAPI, Uvicorn, Pydantic.
  • Data Science: Pandas, NumPy, SciPy, Statsmodels, PyMannKendall.
  • External APIs: NASA POWER, Open-Meteo, NOAA Coral Reef Watch (ERDDAP).
  • Reporting: ReportLab (for PDF generation).

Creativity and Considerations:
The design prioritizes "Scientific Honesty." We intentionally included data provenance, missing-data warnings, and statistical caveats (e.g., distinguishing correlation from causation) directly in the UI. The custom Alert Engine does not rely on fixed thresholds; instead, it dynamically calculates seasonal Z-score anomalies based on the specific location's 10-year history. The dark-themed, glassmorphic UI is designed to feel like a futuristic mission control dashboard, making the exploration of climate data engaging and intuitive.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Left Behind, Not Forgotten
projectDetails.summary: Left Behind, Not Forgotten is a presentation that tells the story of NASA’s discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars through the objects themselves. From the Apollo lunar rovers and descent stages to the Mars rovers and the Ingenuity helicopter, each piece of hardware “speaks” about its mission, what it achieved, and why it was left behind. The presentation includes a timeline of abandoned equipment, a comparison of what remains on the Moon versus Mars, and an explanation of why NASA leaves hardware behind, such as weight limits, fuel constraints, and mission completion. It also looks at what happens to this equipment over time in extreme environments like radiation, dust, and temperature swings. By turning technical mission data into human stories, the project makes space history easier to understand and more engaging. It reminds us that every piece of equipment left behind helped make exploration possible, and that these sites deserve to be remembered and protected.
projectDetails.details:
What it is: Left Behind, Not Forgotten is a 7-slide presentation that tells the story of NASA’s discarded equipment on the Moon and Mars. It treats each abandoned object as a character with a mission, an ending, and a legacy.

How it works: The presentation follows one story arc:

  1. Why NASA leaves hardware behind: mass and fuel limits, completed missions, lost contact, and the impossibility of recovery.
  2. The Moon: six Apollo landings, three Lunar Roving Vehicles, descent stages, science stations, and laser reflectors still used from Earth.
  3. Mars: the rovers Sojourner, Spirit and Opportunity, the InSight lander, and the Ingenuity helicopter, and how each mission ended.
  4. A chart comparing designed mission life with actual mission life for Spirit, Opportunity and Ingenuity.
  5. How the hardware slowly changes under radiation, temperature swings and dust, and why the sites deserve protection (NASA’s 2011 heritage guidelines and the Artemis Accords).
  6. A closing message, with sources and our AI-use disclosure.

Benefits and impact: The project turns technical mission data into human stories that students and the public can understand. It shows that “abandoned” equipment is not waste. Each piece made later exploration possible, and these sites are part of human history that should be remembered and protected.

Creativity: Instead of listing facts, we frame each object by what it was built to do and how long it actually lasted. The designed-versus-actual lifetime chart makes the story visible at a glance.

Tools: Microsoft PowerPoint and NASA’s public mission pages for facts. An AI assistant helped draft and structure the text, and the team reviewed it. No AI-generated images were used, and no NASA logos or mission patches appear.

Factors we considered: accuracy of facts from NASA sources, a clear story within the 7-slide limit, readability, and following all Space Apps rules on AI disclosure and NASA branding.

**The Last Footprint: A Learning Atlas of NASA’s Machines Beyond Earth**

The Last Footprint is an educational PowerPoint presentation that explores NASA’s spacecraft, landers, rovers, and scientific instruments left behind on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space. It introduces students to missions such as Apollo, Viking, Pathfinder, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight, and Voyager, explaining why these machines were sent, how they worked, what happened to them, and the scientific knowledge they contributed.

The project addresses the challenge by turning the history of space hardware into an engaging, student-friendly storytelling experience. Rather than simply listing abandoned equipment, it explores each machine’s purpose, journey, mission status, and scientific legacy. It also highlights that some equipment, such as lunar retroreflectors, continues to support scientific research.

This project is important because these machines represent human curiosity, engineering achievements, and scientific discovery. By sharing their stories, we aim to inspire school students to explore space science, technology, and the future of scientific discovery.
projectDetails.details:
The Last Footprint: A Learning Atlas of NASA’s Machines Beyond Earth

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

The Last Footprint is an educational PowerPoint presentation that takes students on a journey through NASA's history of space exploration. It explores spacecraft, landers, rovers, and scientific instruments left behind on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space.

Through mission-based storytelling, students learn about Apollo, Viking, Pathfinder, Spirit, Opportunity, InSight, and Voyager. Each mission is explained through its purpose, engineering, scientific instruments, journey, discoveries, mission status, and lasting legacy. The presentation also explains why some machines stopped working and why certain equipment remains scientifically useful.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Makes complex space science easier for school students to understand.
  • Introduces students to real NASA missions and scientific discoveries.
  • Explains robotics, engineering, planetary environments, and space exploration.
  • Encourages independent learning and scientific curiosity.
  • Provides an educational resource that can be used in classrooms and science clubs.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our goal is to change how students view abandoned space equipment. These machines are not simply forgotten objects; they are reminders of human exploration and scientific achievement. Even after a mission ends, its data, discoveries, and engineering contributions continue to benefit humanity.

We hope this project inspires students to develop an interest in astronomy, science, technology, engineering, and future space missions.

4. What tools and software were used?

The project was developed using:

  • Microsoft PowerPoint: Creating and organizing the educational presentation.
  • NASA official websites and mission resources: Researching spacecraft, mission histories, scientific instruments, and discoveries.
  • ChatGPT (OpenAI): Assisting with brainstorming, research organization, simplifying scientific explanations, structuring slide content, and improving written descriptions.

The final deliverable is a PowerPoint presentation. No custom hardware, programming language, or software application was developed.

5. How is the project creative?

Instead of presenting abandoned equipment as a technical list, we tell the stories behind the machines. We connect each object's original purpose with its journey, challenges, discoveries, and present status.

The concept of "The Last Footprint" represents the lasting mark of human exploration beyond Earth. We also distinguish between inactive equipment, completed missions, and hardware that continues to provide scientific value.

6. What factors did our team consider?

During development, we considered:

  • Scientific accuracy: Using reliable NASA resources and mission information.
  • Student accessibility: Explaining technical concepts in simple language.
  • Educational value: Making every mission a learning opportunity.
  • Global accessibility: Creating content that students from different backgrounds can understand.
  • Mission diversity: Including examples from the Moon, Mars, and deep space.
  • Historical importance: Showing how earlier missions contributed to modern space exploration.
  • Content reliability: Distinguishing confirmed scientific facts from explanations and interpretations.

Ultimately, The Last Footprint aims to demonstrate that a space mission's story does not end when its hardware stops functioning. Its discoveries and legacy continue to shape our understanding of the universe.

The system generates a suggested Marswalk route and presents information such as route distance, analysis zones, science targets, and mission locations. NASA mission and rover information provides additional scientific context.

Vaanora addresses the challenge by demonstrating how multiple Mars resources can be brought into one exploration interface instead of requiring explorers to work with separate datasets. It provides a single visual planning environment for evaluating routes and identifying areas of scientific interest.
projectDetails.details:
Vaanora is a web-based Martian surface intelligence and Marswalk planning interface designed to help future explorers plan safer and more scientifically valuable traverses on Mars. It brings planetary terrain information, mission locations, science targets, analysis zones, and route planning into a single interactive map.

Users can select a Martian region and destination, choose a mission priority such as Safety, Science, or Balanced, and generate a proposed Marswalk route. The interface displays route distance, science stops, analysis zones, mission locations, and relevant terrain context. The current prototype focuses on regions such as Gale Crater, Jezero Crater, and Elysium Planitia.

The project uses NASA Mars resources, including Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter (MOLA) topographic data and NASA Mars Trek resources, together with rover mission information. These resources provide the planetary and mission context, while Vaanora adds an explorer-focused planning and visualization layer.

I developed the project using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with the Leaflet mapping library. NASA map resources are integrated into the web interface, and the project is hosted publicly using GitHub Pages. No specialized hardware is required for the current prototype.

Vaanora's creative aspect is its combination of different types of Mars information into a simple mission-planning interface rather than presenting the resources separately. I considered route distance, terrain context, scientific value, potential analysis zones, mission locations, and the need for a clear interface that could be understood quickly during mission planning.

The intended impact is to demonstrate how publicly available planetary science and exploration resources can be transformed into an actionable visualization for human Mars exploration. Future versions could incorporate direct elevation and slope calculations, automated terrain-risk assessment, additional rover and orbital datasets, dynamic route optimization, and offline capabilities for mission operations.

projectDetails.name: Project Veloxio
projectDetails.summary:
Earth System Trend Detective is a web app that lets anyone investigate how Earth’s climate is changing at any location. It pulls 34 years of real NASA satellite data from the NASA POWER API and runs statistical analysis — OLS regression, Mann-Kendall trend test, and z-score anomaly detection — to answer all four challenge questions: trend direction, statistical significance, extreme anomaly years, and decade-by-decade comparison.

Users enter a latitude, longitude, and choose a variable — air temperature, precipitation, humidity, wind speed, solar radiation, or dew point — and get an instant verdict backed by real NASA data. No installation, no API key, no coding required. Works in any browser.
projectDetails.details:
Earth System Trend Detective is an interactive web application that empowers anyone to investigate how Earth’s climate variables are changing at any location on the planet. By pulling 34 years of real NASA satellite measurements from the NASA POWER API (Langley Research Center), the app runs rigorous statistical analysis and delivers a clear, detective-style verdict on what is changing, how fast, and whether it is real signal or random noise.

The app directly addresses all four challenge questions: it identifies whether a variable is trending up or down using OLS linear regression, determines statistical significance using both the OLS p-value and the Mann-Kendall trend test, flags extreme anomaly years using z-score detection at the ±2σ threshold, and compares decade-by-decade averages from the 1990s through the 2020s.

Users simply enter any latitude and longitude, choose from six Earth system variables — air temperature, precipitation, relative humidity, wind speed, solar radiation, or dew point temperature — and click Analyze. The app instantly fetches data from NASA POWER, computes the trend slope, R-squared value, Kendall tau, p-value, and anomaly years, then visualizes everything on an interactive trend chart with anomaly markers highlighted in red and green.

The tool requires no installation, no API key, no login, and no coding knowledge. It works in any browser and is fully open source. It was built to make NASA’s free and open Earth science data accessible to students, researchers, educators, and citizens worldwide.

challengeDetails.title: Be An Earth System Trend Detective!
challengeDetails.excerpt: Change is always occurring in the Earth’s interconnected environmental system, and when it runs in a consistent direction – rising or falling, increasing or decreasing, thickening or thinning – measured variables reflect it. But a measured Earth science data variable can trend one way in one region and the opposite way in another, even when the same process drives both. The multitude of Earth science data variables makes it difficult to select variables that could indicate change, and to then perform an analysis on the selected variables.  Your challenge is to create a tool that can select variables measured by Earth science missions or produced by Earth science models, visualize how they change over time, and determine what is changing, where it is changing, how much it is changing, and if these changes are what scientists call “significant.”

projectDetails.name: Project VYNTARA
projectDetails.summary: Earth System Trend Detective explores how Earth's climate system is changing by analysing four important environmental indicators: global surface temperature, atmospheric carbon dioxide, Arctic sea ice extent, and global sea-level rise. Using NASA datasets and partner scientific records, we examine long-term trends, compare independent observations, and identify patterns in Earth's changing climate. Our analysis reveals accelerated global warming, rising atmospheric CO₂ concentrations, declining Arctic winter sea ice, and increasing sea levels. We also propose an Earth Vital Signs dashboard that brings these indicators together in one accessible visual platform. VYNTARA aims to make complex Earth science data easier to understand and encourage informed environmental awareness through evidence-based analysis.
projectDetails.details:
VYNTARA is an Earth System Trend Detective project that investigates changes in Earth's climate using four independent environmental indicators: global surface temperature, atmospheric CO₂ concentration, Arctic sea ice extent, and global mean sea level.

The project uses NASA GISS GISTEMP v4 temperature records, NOAA Mauna Loa CO₂ measurements, NASA/NSIDC Arctic sea ice observations, and NASA/CNES satellite altimetry data.

We analyze long-term temperature and CO₂ records using statistical methods, including linear regression, trend comparison, and correlation analysis. Published NASA and NSIDC observations are used to examine Arctic sea ice and sea-level changes.

Our findings are presented through warming stripes, trend visualizations, statistical comparisons, and a proposed Earth Vital Signs dashboard.

The creative aspect of VYNTARA is its integration of four different Earth-system indicators into one understandable visual story. The project aims to improve climate awareness, communicate scientific evidence, and demonstrate how open Earth observation data can help people understand our changing planet.

The dashboard is currently a conceptual mock-up, with future plans for automated data updates and location-based exploration.

projectDetails.name: Earth Jukebox: Translating Earth Science Sight into Sound
projectDetails.summary:
Project Summary
Earth Jukebox is an interactive web application that turns NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) data into real time sound. Built by Walnut Space for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, it pairs visual climate indicators global sea level rise, atmospheric CO₂, tropical forest loss, and ice sheet mass change with dynamic sonification generated in the browser using the Web Audio API.
Users select a dataset, choose a musical scale and synth timbre, adjust tempo, and scrub a timeline from the 1990s to the present. Data values are mapped to pitch and pacing so rising seas climb in frequency, growing CO₂ increases harmonic tension, forest loss darkens into dissonance, and ice mass decline falls in descending arpeggios. A live Canvas waveform runs alongside the audio.
The project addresses the challenge by making complex Earth science multi-sensory and accessible especially for blind and low vision users while keeping the underlying science intact. Hearing planetary change, not only seeing it, strengthens engagement, memory, and emotional connection, supporting education, outreach, and inclusive climate communication.
projectDetails.details:
Project Details

 

 What it does and how it works   

Earth Jukebox is a browser-based application that turns NASA Earth Information Center (EIC) climate indicators into real-time sound. Users choose one of four datasets—global sea level rise, atmospheric CO₂, tropical forest cover loss, or ice-sheet mass change—then select a musical scale (pentatonic minor, major, harmonic minor, or chromatic), synthesizer timbre (sine, triangle, sawtooth, square), and tempo. A timeline scrubber moves from the 1990s to the present. As data values change, the Web Audio API maps them to pitch and pacing: rising sea level climbs in frequency, higher CO₂ increases harmonic tension, forest loss darkens into dissonance, and ice mass loss falls in descending arpeggios. A Canvas waveform updates live beside the audio so sighted users see and hear the same trend.

 

 Benefits and intended impact   

The project makes Earth science multi-sensory and more accessible, especially for blind and low-vision users who are often excluded by visualization-only tools. Hearing planetary change can strengthen emotional connection and memory compared with numbers or charts alone. It is suited to classrooms, museums, and public outreach, where an interactive “jukebox” of Earth’s data can support teaching and engagement without requiring specialized hardware.

 

 Tools and technologies   

Built entirely as a client-side web app using HTML5, Vanilla JavaScript, the Web Audio API (oscillators, gain envelopes, scheduling), HTML5 Canvas for the waveform, and Tailwind CSS for a dark cosmic interface. No server or extra hardware is required beyond a modern browser and speakers or headphones.

 

 Creativity and design considerations   

Creativity lies in assigning each dataset a distinct sonic character that reflects its physical meaning, and in giving users control over scale, timbre, and tempo so the same data can be explored as different musical moods. The team prioritized accessibility (clear labels, descriptive text, keyboard-friendly controls), scientific integrity (parameter mapping tied to real indicator trends), and simplicity (lightweight stack, no plugins) so the experience works widely and stays focused on hearing Earth’s change.

projectDetails.details:
Cosmic Pulse – Mission Health Command Center

Cosmic Pulse is a mission-health monitoring and management platform designed to support astronauts and ground medical teams during space missions. It acts as a centralised command centre that helps monitor astronaut health, identify potential health risks, and improve communication between astronauts and medical professionals on Earth.

The platform provides a mission overview displaying AURORA-7 mission status, flight day, crew status, relay signal, and mission progress. It monitors several important health indicators, including vital signs, sleep and recovery, mood and stress, exercise load, radiation exposure, bone health, and cardiovascular health. These readings are combined to calculate a composite health risk score, with alerts classified as Nominal, Watch, or Action. Historical trend charts help identify changes in astronaut health over time.

Cosmic Pulse includes two operating modes: Astronaut Mode and Ground Team Mode. Astronauts can review their health status, receive recommendations, and enter new health readings. Ground medical teams can review telemetry, monitor attention queues, and manage escalations. If a health concern is detected, astronauts can escalate it to ground support, where medical staff can acknowledge the issue.

The platform also uses automatically seeded mission data and stores new health readings and escalation records in a MongoDB database, ensuring that information remains available after refreshing the application.

Benefits and Intended Impact: Cosmic Pulse aims to support early identification of health concerns, improve medical coordination, and encourage proactive healthcare during long-duration space missions. By bringing multiple health indicators into one platform, it helps astronauts and ground teams make more informed decisions and respond to potential risks efficiently.

Tools and Technologies: The project was developed as a web-based digital prototype using frontend web technologies, backend integration, and MongoDB for persistent data storage. It combines interactive dashboards, health visualizations, role-based interfaces, and data management features.

Creativity and Innovation: The creative aspect of Cosmic Pulse is its combination of mission monitoring, astronaut health tracking, composite risk scoring, personalized recommendations, and two-way escalation management in a single platform. Instead of displaying health readings separately, it brings them together to provide a clearer picture of astronaut well-being.

Factors Considered: Our team considered astronaut safety, physical and mental well-being, radiation exposure, sleep quality, cardiovascular and bone health, exercise requirements, ease of use, reliable data storage, and effective communication between astronauts and ground medical teams.

Ultimately, Cosmic Pulse envisions a smarter and more proactive approach to astronaut healthcare, helping protect crew health and support safer, longer-duration space exploration.

Users can select a Moon or Mars mission and experience simulated space exploration tasks. They must monitor essential resources, including oxygen, food, water, and energy, while making decisions to handle unexpected mission challenges.

**Orbital Odyssey – An Interactive Space Mission Simulation Game**

Orbital Odyssey is an interactive space mission simulation game that allows players to experience the challenges of planning, building, and executing space missions. Players take the role of a space mission commander, selecting missions such as Lunar Dash, Mars Express, and Orbital Rescue.

The game features a spacecraft customization workshop where players select engines, fuel tanks, power systems, protective hulls, and mission-specific payloads while managing limited credits, spacecraft mass, and thrust requirements. Players then launch their spacecraft and navigate through space, avoiding asteroids, collecting fuel and energy resources, and responding to unexpected events such as solar flares and micrometeoroid swarms.

An asteroid mining mini-game allows players to earn additional credits. Each mission provides rewards based on performance, encouraging strategic decisions and resource management.

Orbital Odyssey combines interactive gameplay with space engineering concepts to make space mission planning an engaging learning experience.
projectDetails.details:
Orbital Odyssey – Interactive Space Mission Simulation Game

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Orbital Odyssey is an interactive space mission simulation game that allows players to experience the challenges of planning, designing and executing space missions. Players take the role of a space mission commander and choose between three missions: Lunar Dash, Mars Express and Orbital Rescue.

Players enter a spacecraft workshop where they customize their spacecraft by selecting engines, fuel tanks, power systems, protective hulls and mission-specific payloads. Each component has different costs, mass, thrust, fuel capacity and durability. Players must balance these factors and stay within their available budget to build a spacecraft capable of completing the selected mission.

After passing the launch requirements, players navigate through space while managing resources and responding to unexpected events, including solar flares and micrometeoroid swarms. Players can make strategic decisions, protect their spacecraft and earn credits through successful missions and an asteroid mining mini-game.

2. What are the benefits?

The game makes complex space mission concepts more accessible and engaging. It encourages players to understand spacecraft components, resource limitations, engineering trade-offs, mission requirements and risk management through interactive gameplay rather than only theoretical explanations.

3. What is the intended impact?

Our aim is to increase interest in space exploration, aerospace engineering and STEM education. By allowing players to experiment with spacecraft configurations and experience the consequences of their decisions, Orbital Odyssey promotes curiosity, creativity, logical thinking and problem-solving skills.

4. What tools and technologies were used?

The project was developed as a browser-based game using:

  • React: Building the interactive user interface and game components.
  • JavaScript: Implementing game logic, mission systems, resource management and interactions.
  • HTML: Structuring the web application.
  • CSS and Tailwind CSS: Designing the visual interface and styling the game.
  • Vite: Development environment and production build tool.
  • Lucide React: Icons and visual interface elements.
  • Browser Local Storage: Saving the player's credit balance between sessions.

The project runs in a web browser and does not require specialized hardware.

5. How is the project creative?

Orbital Odyssey combines spacecraft engineering and arcade-style space gameplay in a single interactive experience. Instead of simply presenting information about space missions, it allows players to make engineering decisions and immediately experience their consequences.

The combination of spacecraft customization, multiple mission objectives, random space events, resource management and asteroid mining creates an engaging experience that brings space mission planning into a game environment.

6. What factors did the team consider?

During development, we considered spacecraft mass, engine thrust, fuel consumption, power capacity, hull durability, payload requirements, available credits, mission difficulty and time limits.

We also considered gameplay accessibility, user engagement, balanced challenges and the importance of making engineering concepts understandable to players with different levels of space science knowledge.

Through Orbital Odyssey, we aim to make learning about space missions interactive, enjoyable and inspiring.

Our project, Orbital Odyssey, uses NASA's Near-Earth Object Web Service (NeoWs) API.

We integrated the NASA asteroid feed API (https://api.nasa.gov/neo/rest/v1/feed) to retrieve real near-Earth asteroid information for a seven-day period.

The game displays:

  • Asteroid names
  • Estimated maximum diameter
  • Close-approach dates
  • Distance from Earth
  • Potentially hazardous asteroid classification

Players can refresh the tracker to retrieve updated asteroid information. This NASA data integration helps connect the game's space exploration experience with real astronomical data.

NASA resource: NASA Near-Earth Object Web Service (NeoWs) – https://api.nasa.gov/

projectDetails.summary:
Abandoned, Not Forgottenhttps://github.com/King-of-the-Beast/Website.git

Our project is an interactive educational website that explores NASA's abandoned space equipment on the Moon and Mars. It features seven important pieces of equipment, including the Apollo 11 Retroreflector, Lunar Roving Vehicles, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, and InSight.

The website presents the history, purpose, scientific contributions, and current status of each machine through interactive mission cards, detailed information pop-ups, search and filtering options, and a historical timeline.

It addresses the challenge by transforming complex space exploration history into an engaging and easy-to-understand experience for school-age space enthusiasts. Rather than treating these machines as forgotten objects, the project highlights how they helped scientists understand the Moon and Mars.

This project is important because it demonstrates that space exploration does not end when a mission stops working. The equipment left behind represents human curiosity, technological achievement, and valuable scientific discoveries that continue to inspire future generations.
projectDetails.details: Project Details Abandoned, Not Forgotten 1. What does the project do and how does it work? Our project is an interactive educational website that tells the stories of NASA's equipment left behind on the Moon and Mars. It showcases seven important space exploration technologies, including the Apollo 11 Retroreflector, ALSEP Science Stations, Lunar Roving Vehicles, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, and InSight. Users can explore these machines through interactive cards, read detailed mission histories using pop-up windows, search for specific equipment, filter missions by location, and explore a historical timeline. 2. What are its benefits? - Makes space exploration history easier and more interesting to understand. - Provides scientific information in a simple, student-friendly format. - Encourages curiosity about astronomy, robotics, and space technology. - Demonstrates how abandoned equipment can continue contributing to scientific research. - Provides links to official NASA resources for further learning. 3. What is the intended impact? The main goal is to inspire school-age students to learn about space exploration and appreciate the scientific achievements behind NASA missions. We want students to understand that even when a spacecraft stops functioning, the discoveries and knowledge it provides remain valuable. 4. What tools and technologies were used? We developed the website using: - HTML5: Structure and content of the website. - CSS3: Styling, responsive layouts, animations, and visual design. - JavaScript: Interactive elements, search functionality, filters, and information pop-ups. - Web Browser: Testing and viewing the website. - NASA Official Websites: Research and scientific information. The project is software-based and does not require additional hardware. 5. How is the project creative? Instead of presenting information as ordinary paragraphs, we designed an interactive space-themed experience. The website uses a dark space-inspired interface, planetary illustrations, mission cards, interactive information windows, and a timeline. The storytelling approach presents each abandoned machine as an important part of humanity's space exploration journey. 6. What factors did the team consider? While developing the project, we considered: - Making the website simple and accessible for school-age students. - Ensuring scientific information is accurate and understandable. - Providing a responsive design for mobile phones and computers. - Making navigation easy through search and filtering options. - Using reliable NASA sources. - Creating an engaging experience without overwhelming users with technical information. Conclusion: Abandoned, Not Forgotten transforms the forgotten remains of space exploration into an engaging educational experience. It reminds us that although machines may be left behind, their contributions to science and humanity are never forgotten.

projectDetails.name: Project YOLO: Mission Echo
projectDetails.summary:
Abandoned but Not Forgotten is an interactive space exploration archive that brings the stories of nine historic space missions back into focus. From the Apollo lunar experiments and the Pioneer spacecraft venturing into deep space to the Mars rovers, Kepler, NEAR Shoemaker, and InSight, the project explores missions whose journeys ended, whose signals faded, or whose spacecraft were left behind.

Through immersive storytelling, authentic NASA imagery, mission timelines, scientific discoveries, and archival information, users can explore what each mission achieved, why contact or operations ended, and what humanity learned from it.

The project addresses the challenge by transforming space mission data and historical records into an engaging, accessible experience that encourages curiosity and scientific exploration. It highlights an important idea: a mission does not lose its significance when it stops operating. The knowledge, discoveries, and technological progress it leaves behind continue to shape our understanding of the universe.

Some explorers go silent. Their discoveries never do.
projectDetails.details:
Project title: Abandoned but Not Forgotten: The Stories We Left Behind

Live project: https://abandoned-but-not-forgotten-lake.vercel.app/

Summary: An interactive, narrated web experience that introduces school-age space enthusiasts to nine pieces of NASA hardware left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space. Visitors tune in to each machine’s “signal,” learn how it was built and what it discovered, and see where it is now.

What it does and how it works

The project opens like an incoming radio transmission. After a short introduction about the machines humanity has sent beyond Earth, a faint signal interrupts. The visitor tunes it in with a slider, then meets the explorer in plain language: what it is, where it is, when it flew and what its job was. Each story is told backwards. It starts with the final recorded evidence, such as the last signal received or the place the machine still rests, and then rewinds through the chapters: why we built it, how it was sent, what it discovered, and what came home to Earth.

Every screen carries one idea, one NASA image with its credit, and optional narration. Visitors tap or press a key to continue, so they read at their own pace. After each story, they return to a map of nine signals: Opportunity, Apollo 11 Eagle, Pioneer 10, the Lunar Roving Vehicles, Surveyor 3, ALSEP, InSight, Kepler and NEAR Shoemaker. They choose what to explore next and earn a rank as they listen. Once they have heard every signal, a final message about knowledge outliving the machines that gathered it opens. Each story ends with links to real NASA and JPL footage and images.

The engineering is always connected to the science. A visitor sees how Opportunity’s wheels, cameras and instruments led to evidence that Mars once held water, or how Pioneer 10’s flyby of Jupiter helped engineers design later spacecraft.

Benefits

  • It gives retired and silent machines a story. Young people mostly hear about active missions.
  • It needs no prior knowledge of astronomy, no account and no download. It works on a phone or a laptop.
  • It teaches evidence over legend. The Opportunity story includes a “fact or story” moment about the famous line “My battery is low and it’s getting dark.” Visitors learn that the rover actually sent numbers about dust and battery power, and a reporter turned them into a poem.
  • It is accessible. Narration is also on screen, narration and music can be turned off separately, the whole experience works with a keyboard, images have alt text, and animation is reduced when a device asks for it.

Intended impact

I want students to feel a personal connection to these robotic explorers without being asked to feel sorry for them. Each machine is a way into the people who built it and the questions they asked. A visitor should leave knowing the names of a few of these missions, understanding how a machine’s design produced the knowledge it brought home, and curious enough to open the NASA pages linked at the end of each story. The core message is: we may have left these machines behind, but we have not left their stories behind.

Tools, languages and software

  • React, Vite, JavaScript (JSX) and CSS, built as a static site with no backend
  • React Router for navigation
  • HTML Canvas for the drifting starfield, and SVG for the final constellation
  • Web Audio API for the original generated ambient music, the tuning static and soft chimes
  • Web Speech API for narration, with support for recorded voice files
  • Google Fonts: Cormorant Garamond and Inter
  • Visual Studio Code, Git and GitHub for development [add: GitHub Copilot, if you used it]
  • Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini for drafting story structure and code. I reviewed everything against NASA sources.
  • Vercel for hosting
  • Data and media sources: NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA), the NASA Image and Video Library, the NASA/JPL Photojournal, and NASA and JPL mission pages
  • Hardware: a personal laptop and phone for development and testing

How it is creative

  • The radio-signal premise. Visitors do not browse a catalogue. They tune a signal and discover an artifact, which turns learning into discovery.
  • Stories told in reverse. Each one begins with the last piece of evidence and rewinds, so the question “how did it get here?” drives the story.
  • A different dimension of curiosity for each machine. Opportunity is the will to keep going, Pioneer 10 is the courage to go farther, and Apollo 11 Eagle is the part that stayed.
  • No invented voices. I did not use talking-robot narration or made-up quotes. The emotion comes from documented history, such as engineers sending more than a thousand recovery commands over eight months.
  • A media-literacy moment built into a famous myth.
  • Sound design. The original ambient score and soft chimes create a calm, reflective mood, and the finale draws the nine signals into a constellation.
  • A restrained editorial look with serif headings and thin rules, so older students and adults are not talked down to.

Factors I considered

  • Accuracy: content is drawn from NASA and NSSDCA material, each story lists its sources, and every image carries its NASA credit. Machine-perspective text and invented quotes were removed.
  • Audience: ages 11 and up, plus casual space fans. Early versions changed screens on a timer and were too fast to read, so I rebuilt the experience around tap-to-continue, with short sentences and one idea per screen.
  • Tone and feel: early drafts used harsh sounds and a stressful look. I rebuilt the interface to feel calm and welcoming.
  • Accessibility and access: a static site with no accounts and no runtime API calls, so it loads quickly on phones and modest connections.
  • Attribution and copyright: NASA media is credited, nothing implies NASA endorsement, and the music is original rather than taken from any film score.
  • Scope: I chose a complete, polished flow across the Moon, Mars and deep space rather than a long list of shallow entries, and designed the map so more stories can be added.

projectDetails.name: AgriOrbit: Climate-Smart Crop Rotation Planning
projectDetails.summary: AgriOrbit is a crop-rotation decision-support web app that helps farmers compare multi-season rotation plans using NASA Earth observations, soil data and their own priorities. A farmer sets up a farm and its current rotation. AgriOrbit then pulls NASA POWER climate data, SoilGrids estimates and an uploaded Soil Health Card report. It screens 16 crops for soil pH, salinity, temperature, water and season-length limits, and ranks feasible rotations by net income, irrigation need, soil organic carbon change and pest-break benefit, with legume nitrogen fixation counted as a plan benefit. Farmers can adopt a plan, monitor it with NASA GIBS satellite layers, and ask an AI agronomist (English or Malayalam) whose answers are limited to computed project facts. Every data source is labelled live, cached, fixture or unavailable, so farmers see what the evidence is.
projectDetails.details:
THE PROBLEM

Farmers face shifting temperatures, uneven rainfall, water shortages and declining soil health, which makes it hard to choose rotations that protect soil, save water and still earn income. Evidence is scattered across weather sources, maps and lab reports, and goals such as income, water use and soil benefit pull in different directions.

WHAT AGRIORBIT DOES

AgriOrbit brings planning, monitoring and advice into one application:

- Set up a farm: location, growing zone, farm boundary and the existing "baseline" rotation, which is the reference for every proposed plan.

- Review data: NASA POWER agroclimatology (rainfall, temperature, radiation, humidity, wind) and SoilGrids soil estimates. Farmers can also upload a Soil Health Card (PDF or CSV). Values are shown in an editable preview before saving and are marked measured, estimated, missing or unsupported. Missing values are never invented.

- Check crops: each of 16 crops is labelled eligible, excluded (with a reason: soil pH, salinity, temperature, water, duration or region), not evaluated, or lacking data.

- Compare plans: a constrained multi-objective Pareto optimizer scores each plan on net income, irrigation required, change in soil organic carbon and pest-break score. Farmers can adjust objective weights. Constraints include a maximum number of cover crops, a minimum number of cash-crop seasons and a minimum income floor. Planning horizons (for example 1 year with 3 seasons, or 3 years with 1 season each) are matched to the climate zone.

- Adopt and monitor: NASA GIBS layers (NDVI, rainfall, root-zone soil moisture, land surface temperature), a 30-day water balance, an activity log, baseline-drift detection and plan-versus-baseline reports. The app works offline as a PWA.

- Ask the AI agronomist: answers in English and Malayalam are restricted to computed project facts, carry verified citation tags, and list missing evidence when data is thin.

HOW IT WORKS

Water physics uses FAO-56 Penman-Monteith reference evapotranspiration (ET0), crop water demand ETc = Kc x ET0, and a water balance of rainfall minus ET0. Drought (-30% rain), monsoon flood (+35% rain) and heat (+2.5 C) runs are labelled historical sensitivity stress tests, not forecasts. Plans are ranked with a weighted composite of normalized objectives; infeasible plans stay at rank 0.

SCIENTIFIC HONESTY

Each data source reports its status (live, cached, fixture or unavailable), version, resolution and last update, and fixtures are never presented as live. NASA NEX-GDDP-CMIP6 future projections are planned but not yet integrated. No physical sensors are connected, and the built-in test farms (Thrissur, Palakkad, Wayanad, Iowa, Fresno) are internal software checks, not field trials. AgriOrbit supports review of trade-offs; it does not replace local agronomic expertise or guarantee yield.

BENEFITS AND GOALS

Farmers get one transparent place to explore rotations that balance income, water and soil health under changing conditions, using free and open NASA data. Next steps: integrate CMIP6 climate projections, extend crop and regional coverage, and validate assumptions with agronomists and field data.

TOOLS

React 19, Vite, Tailwind CSS, TypeScript, Express (Node.js), Leaflet, Recharts, i18next (English/Malayalam), pdfjs-dist, TanStack Query, vite-plugin-pwa, Google Gemini API (@google/genai), hosted on Render.

SUPER INTELLIGENCE (SI) DISCLOSURE

The in-app AI agronomist uses the Google Gemini API, constrained to computed project data. [If you used AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude or Copilot to write or debug code, text or images, say so here, e.g. "Portions of the code and documentation were written with AI assistance and reviewed by the team." If you didn't use any, delete this line.]

projectDetails.name: TRADEOFF — Space Mission Design Lab
projectDetails.summary: TRADEOFF is a browser‑based mission design game for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It lets users design a science mission from the bus up: choose instruments, orbit, and launch vehicle, then live with the mass, power, data, and budget consequences. Every decision opens one door and closes another. The game runs entirely in the browser with no backend, using a provisional dataset compiled from public mission literature. It addresses the challenge by making trade‑offs visible and interactive, helping users understand the complexity of mission design. It is important because it lowers the barrier to entry for learning about space mission engineering, making it accessible to students, educators, and enthusiasts without requiring specialized software or expertise.
projectDetails.details: TRADEOFF is a browser-based mission design game that lets users design a science mission from the bus up. Choose instruments, orbit, launch vehicle, then live with mass, power, data, budget consequences. It implements a full mission design loop: briefing → spacecraft → orbit → launch → compatibility review → deterministic simulation → report → hangar. Includes 6 science objectives, 25 components, 15 orbits, 6 launch vehicles, 4 difficulty levels. A 1800-day simulation models eclipse, battery, downlink, degradation, science return. Review screen provides NASA-MDL-style compatibility check with JPL-CML-inspired maturity badge. Report includes score audit, science closure, margins, findings. Hangar stores runs locally with leaderboard and comparison. Sharing via URL-encoded links. Benefits: lowers barrier to entry for learning space mission engineering; makes trade-offs visible and interactive. Impact: educators, students, mission-design teams can iterate designs instantly without specialized software. Tools: React 19, TypeScript, Vite 8, Lucide icons, Fontsource, Puppeteer, Vitest. Creative: arcade-style UI with neon aesthetic, deterministic simulation with real telemetry, procedural mission patches. Factors considered: mass, power, data, pointing, lifetime, cost, radiation, coverage, eclipse, comms geometry.

projectDetails.name: Project ZeroG Flames
projectDetails.summary:
When humanity travels to the Moon and Mars, the greatest threat isn't just the vacuum of space—it's fire. While NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) database holds decades of vital combustion research, that massive volume of data can be overwhelming to navigate and apply.      

To solve this, we developed the ZeroG Flames Dashboard, an AI-powered platform that transforms raw microgravity combustion data into actionable intelligence. We built a custom Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline using Gemini 3.8-flash that directly ingests complex PSI research PDFs—like SAFFIRE and BASS—and presents insights through a highly intuitive interface.

ZeroG Flames directly addresses the challenge by evaluating fire scenarios across dynamic environments (ISS, Lunar, or Martian). It doesn't just summarize; it generates a relatability leaderboard that ranks the most relevant NASA investigations, provides match percentages, and links directly to official PSI repositories. It even highlights how this research improves terrestrial firefighter tech.

Fire behaves fundamentally differently in space, burning spherically without buoyancy. As we design next-generation habitats with elevated oxygen levels, understanding these dynamics is a matter of life and death. ZeroG Flames ensures critical safety data is instantly accessible, keeping our crews safe as we take the next giant leap.
projectDetails.details:
1. Overview: ZeroG Flames is an AI flight director for spacecraft fire safety. We built a RAG pipeline that ingests NASA PSI research. Users ask questions, and the AI retrieves physics-accurate data tailored to specific gravity environments (ISS, Lunar, Mars).
2. Benefits: It transforms overwhelming PDF archives into instant, actionable intelligence. It prevents AI hallucinations by grounding every answer exclusively in verifiable NASA experiments.
3. Impacts: It helps engineers design safer habitats for deep space, while accelerating the translation of microgravity research into better firefighter gear, smoke detectors, and extinguishers here on Earth.
4. Tools used: React, Tailwind CSS, Chart.js (Frontend); Python, FastAPI (Backend); Gemini 3.8-flash & 3.5 flash lite, LangChain, PyPDF2, ChromaDB (AI & Data).
5. Creativity: We created a closed-loop dashboard. Our code actively parses the AI's output to generate a visually animated "Relatability Leaderboard," automatically matching shorthand names to custom dictionaries to link directly to official NASA PSI source documents.
6. Factors considered: We prioritized strict zero-G physics accuracy (handling spherical flames and zero buoyancy) and engineered a high-stress, dark-mode UI with live data telemetry for professional aerospace use.

SPACE LEGACY: ABANDONED BUT NOT FORGOTTEN

Project: ZERO_GRAVITY6

Space exploration has given humanity remarkable achievements, from the first artificial satellites to missions exploring the Moon and Mars. However, many spacecraft, rovers, satellites and scientific instruments remain inactive or abandoned in space after completing their missions. Our project, Space Legacy: Abandoned but Not Forgotten, explores the stories behind these forgotten objects and highlights their historical, scientific and technological importance. Through our interactive website, ZERO_GRAVITY6, we present important space missions, their timelines, fascinating discoveries and educational quizzes. The platform aims to create awareness about humanity's achievements, the importance of preserving space heritage and the challenges of space debris. By connecting space science with digital technology, our project makes learning more engaging and accessible. We believe that even when a mission ends, its discoveries and contributions continue to inspire future generations.

Their missions may have ended, but their legacy lives forever.
projectDetails.details:
SPACE LEGACY – Abandoned but Not Forgotten

Space Legacy is an educational website created to explore and bring attention to forgotten and lesser-known space missions. The main aim of our project is to help people discover the history of space exploration, understand important space missions, and learn about the achievements and challenges faced during these missions.

Our website presents information about different space missions through images, descriptions, interesting facts, and a space mission timeline. It also includes sections explaining why these missions matter, references for further learning, and interactive quizzes to test visitors' knowledge. Users can explore the website easily and learn about space exploration in an interesting and engaging way.

Benefits:

Space Legacy makes learning about space exploration easier and more interesting. It helps students and space enthusiasts gain knowledge about historical missions, understand scientific achievements, and discover missions that are often forgotten. The interactive features also encourage visitors to explore and learn more.

Intended Impact:

Our goal is to create awareness about the history of space exploration and ensure that important missions and their contributions are not forgotten. We want to inspire curiosity among students, encourage interest in science and astronomy, and help people appreciate humanity's journey into space.

Creativity and Innovation:

The creative aspect of our project is the way we combine space history, visual storytelling, an interactive timeline, and quizzes in one website. Instead of presenting information like a traditional textbook, we provide an engaging experience that allows visitors to explore different missions and test their knowledge.

projectDetails.name: MARS BASE : SOL 30
projectDetails.summary: Mars Base: Sol 30 is a free browser game that teaches children aged 7–12 the real trade-offs of running a Mars outpost. Players manage a small base for 30 Martian days (sols), choosing one job each sol: research, recycling air and water, growing food, cleaning solar panels, or resting. Power, life support, food, crew health, research and radiation exposure are linked, so every choice has a cost. Events such as a dust storm, a water leak, a crop blight and a solar flare force hard decisions, and Earth’s replies arrive late, so players must decide for themselves. The solar flare event is built from a real NASA DONKI space weather record, clearly separated from simulated game values. After each choice, Buddy the robot explains the science. A final report scores crew safety, supplies and research and shows why a mission failed, encouraging replay with a new strategy. The game aims to show young learners that space exploration is about careful planning, not luck, and to make NASA science feel approachable. It runs in any modern browser with no account or install, includes saved NASA data as a fallback, and works on tablets and phones in landscape. Built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
projectDetails.details:
The player is the commander of a Mars base and plays 30 sols. Each sol, they tap a part of the base to do one job: the microscope for research, the recycler for air and water, the solar panels to clear dust, the sleeping pod to rest, and the control console to plant a greenhouse crop. Every job costs something. Research uses power, recycling uses power, and crops take five sols to grow, so players must plan ahead.

Six meters track the base: power, life support, food, crew health, research and radiation dose. Each sol, the crew uses air, water and food, and the base spends energy on heating and pumps. If power hits zero, life support drops faster. If life support or food runs out, the crew gets hurt.

Five story events break the routine: a dust storm that cuts solar power, a solar flare, a water leak, a crop blight and an ice discovery. Each has two choices, such as sheltering from a flare, which costs research time, or working outside, which gives more science but adds simulated radiation. Players can ask Earth for advice, but the reply takes two sols, so they must decide first.

After every action, Buddy the robot shows the changes and explains the science, for example why recycling and power are linked. At the end, a report gives star ratings and explains why a mission failed, such as running out of food, with a tip to try a different strategy.

NASA data

The solar flare event uses a real record from NASA’s DONKI space weather database: an X1.0 flare from Active Region 13664 on 8 May 2024, with its record ID and a link to NASA. The event card also cites the radiation that Curiosity measured on Mars during a solar storm in May 2024, as reported by Space.com. The game keeps real data and simulated values in two separate boxes. The radiation numbers used in play are labelled as game units, not Mars measurements. The deployed version also tries to load a recent strong flare live from the NASA DONKI API. If that fails, it uses the saved record, so the game always works.

Benefits and intended impact

Children learn that every choice on Mars has a trade-off. Saving power can hurt life support, and gathering more science can mean accepting radiation risk. They also learn why space weather matters to astronauts. The game needs no account, no install and no cost, so a classroom, library or home can use it right away. We hope it makes space science feel like a decision children can make, which encourages curiosity about careers in space and science.

Tools and technology

  • HTML5, CSS3 (grid layout) and plain JavaScript, with a custom turn-based game engine and no backend
  • NASA DONKI API through api.nasa.gov, with a local JSON-style fallback
  • Browser local storage for the best score
  • Google Fonts (Unbounded and Fredoka)
  • Python with Pillow and SciPy to prepare the artwork
  • A free metal texture by Magda Ehlers from Pexels
  • Claude, an AI assistant, helped write and test the code and text. I directed the design and checked the content.
  • Planned hosting: Vercel. No special hardware is needed.

Creativity

The base is a cutaway picture the player taps, so choosing a job feels like walking through a real habitat instead of picking from a menu. Buddy the robot reacts with different facts. The astronaut walks to each part of the base and waves. Earth’s late replies turn a real space-communication problem into a game choice. Clear labels separate NASA facts from game numbers, which models honest science for children.

Factors we considered

  • Age and language: short sentences, simple words, and emoji icons for each meter
  • Scientific honesty: real NASA data is separate from simulated values, with sources and a not-official-NASA note
  • Accessibility: large tap targets, readable colours, keyboard focus outlines, reduced-motion support, and text labels with every number
  • Reliability: works offline with saved data, and the game never crashes if the NASA API is down
  • Devices: works on computers and tablets, and phones in landscape, with a prompt to turn the phone sideways
  • Replayability: different choices give different endings
  • Safety and licensing: no accounts, no personal data, and credited image sources

projectDetails.name: CLPS Lunar Mission Browser
projectDetails.summary:
Codyseey is an open-source, interactive 3D WebGL lunar exploration browser built for NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative and Artemis program.

Addressing Challenge 4: CLPS Lunar Mission Browser, Codyseey integrates real NASA LRO LOLA elevation grids, LROC photographic basemaps, and JPL DE441 planetary ephemerides into a zero-install, real-time simulation. Users can inspect candidate South Pole landing sites (including Malapert Mountain and Nobile Crater), simulate powered descent, drive rovers (NASA VIPER and Griffin Rover 2) with physical 6-wheel terrain contact, and execute TRIDENT subsurface drill assays for volatile water-ice deposits.

The lunar South Pole presents extreme operational hazards—sub-degree solar grazing angles, prolonged night occultations, and cryogenic Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs). Codyseey replaces weeks of manual ephemeris scripting with an intuitive, multi-track synodic timeline (2026–2030), instantly calculating direct solar illumination corridors and Earth communications links. It democratizes mission planning for engineers, researchers, and students worldwide.
projectDetails.details:
Codyseey // Next-Generation CLPS Lunar Mission Browser

1. What Exactly Does It Do?

Codyseey is an open-source, zero-install, 3D lunar mission planning and ephemeris exploration platform built specifically for NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative and the Artemis campaign. It bridges the gap between raw planetary science datasets and actionable mission operations, allowing planners, scientists, and students to:

  • Explore Candidate Landing Sites: Inspect high-priority South Pole landing havens—such as Malapert Mountain, Shackleton Connecting Ridge, Mons Mouton, and Nobile Crater Rim—with authentic lunar topology.
  • Simulate Surface Operations: Drive robotic rovers (NASA VIPER and Astrobotic Griffin Rover 2) featuring dynamic 6-wheel rocker-bogie terrain contact physics, slope-hazard detection, and hazard-cam telemetry.
  • Execute Volatile Prospecting: Deploy the 1-meter TRIDENT rotary-percussive drill to simulate subsurface core sample extraction and geochemical volatile assays in Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs).
  • Track Synodic Sun & Earth Corridors (2026–2030): Calculate real-time line-of-sight communications with Earth and sub-degree solar illumination angles to ensure mission survival.

2. How Does It Work?

Codyseey runs entirely in the browser using a client-side, hardware-accelerated WebGL engine built on Three.js:

  1. Topographic Altimetry Pipeline: Integrates real elevation data from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) onboard NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO). The surface engine computes per-vertex heightfields and terrain normals to accurately render micro-craters, boulder fields, and ridge slopes.
  2. Planetary Ephemeris Engine: Ingests high-precision vectors derived from NASA JPL DE441 Planetary Ephemerides and NASA SPICE kernels. It computes the precise 3D vector positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the lunar South Pole across the entire synodic cycle from 2026 through 2030.
  3. Terrain & Wheel Contact Physics: Uses mathematical ground-plane contact constraints combined with rocker-bogie suspension articulation. As the rover navigates, each wheel independently tracks local elevation gradients, ensuring realistic physical interaction without floating or clipping into the regolith.
  4. High-Fidelity PBR Shader Engine: Utilizes physically-based rendering (PBR) calibrated with authentic Apollo 17 lunar sample specs (Sample 70017 vesicular basalt). Shaders dynamically account for zero-atmosphere direct solar glare, high-contrast harsh shadows, and subtle earthshine fill.

3. What Tools, Technologies & NASA Data Were Used?

  • Frontend & Core Engine: React 18, Vite, Three.js (r160+), WebGL 2.0.
  • Physics & Mathematical Modeling: Custom 6-wheel rocker-bogie suspension solver, raycasting collision detection, and spline-based traverse interpolation.
    • LRO LOLA: Global and polar DEMs (Digital Elevation Models) for elevation, slope hazard grading, and crater mapping.
    • LRO LROC (WAC & NAC): Global color basemaps and high-resolution Narrow Angle Camera imagery.
    • NASA JPL DE441: Ephemeris data providing exact Sun and Earth positions, sub-solar latitudes, and synodic luncation cycles.
    • Apollo 17 Station 6 Geochemistry: Vesicular basalt morphology and regolith albedo standards.

4. What Factors Did Our Team Consider & How Is It Creative?

  • The Harsh Reality of the Lunar South Pole: Unlike equatorial regions, South Pole solar grazing angles hover between 1.5° and −1.5°, casting immense, dynamic shadows. A rover that drives into a Permanently Shadowed Region (PSR) risks sudden battery freeze-out and cryogenic death at 40 Kelvin. Codyseey directly addresses this by providing instant line-of-sight solar and communications tracking.
  • Collapsible Minimalist Timeline: Designed a sleek, single-line collapsible synodic timeline (2026–2030) with faded gradient ends and an interactive Earth/Sun tracking bead, giving users both high-level overview and minute-by-minute tactical planning.
  • Zero-Barrier Accessibility: Rather than locking planetary mission planning behind specialized command-line scripts or proprietary GIS software, Codyseey packages full PBR physics into a lightweight, responsive web app that runs seamlessly on any standard laptop or desktop browser.

5. Intended Impact & Benefits

  • Accelerating CLPS Mission Trajectories: Enables commercial lander operators and science teams to prototype traverse routes and identify continuous sunlight survival corridors in seconds rather than weeks.
  • Risk Mitigation: Visualizes line-of-sight occultations to prevent catastrophic loss of signal (LOS) with NASA's Deep Space Network (DSN).
  • STEM Democratization: Empowers researchers, university students, and space enthusiasts worldwide with interactive access to authentic NASA planetary science.
