projectDetails.name: Project Revive The Unknown
projectDetails.summary:
For the NASA Space Apps Challenge, we developed Revive the Unknown, an immersive website providing real-time data and pure storytelling for historic hardware like the Apollo Lunar Module, Sojourner, Spirit, and Opportunity rovers.
Our application addresses the challenge by offering an interactive solar system observatory, curated video documentation of JPL launches, landings, and engineering challenges for missions like Voyager 1, Perseverance, Curiosity, and Pathfinder, alongside a dedicated spacecraft comparison tool and NASA image gallery. Finally, an interactive quiz challenges users to test their understanding, boosting curiosity and encouraging deeper exploration.
This project is important because it bridges complex aerospace engineering with engaging narrative and visual media. By transforming raw historical data and technical milestones into an interactive, educational experience, we honor humanity's past interplanetary achievements while inspiring a global audience to connect deeply with the legacy and ongoing future of space exploration.
projectDetails.details:
Revive the Unknown is an interactive web platform developed by team Revive The Unknown to bring historic off-world space hardware back into the spotlight. Rather than presenting dry encyclopedia facts, the website blends pure narrative storytelling with interactive features across six core sections:

  • Mission Archive & Storytelling: Detailed mission dossiers, authentic NASA imagery, and curated JPL documentary videos covering the engineering, launches, landings, and journeys of iconic hardware including the Apollo Lunar Module, Sojourner Rover, Spirit Rover, Opportunity Rover, Curiosity, Perseverance, Mars Pathfinder, and Voyager 1.
  • Interactive 3D Solar System Observatory: A live canvas-rendered simulation where users can drag, rotate, zoom, adjust orbital speeds, and inspect planetary data across our solar system.
  • Spacecraft Comparison Lab: A side-by-side technical specification tool allowing users to compare the design, power, and operating parameters of famous exploration machines.
  • NASA Visual Gallery & Mission Control Telemetry: A curated collection of official NASA mission imagery paired with a live-style simulated spacecraft telemetry dashboard.
  • Interactive Space Quiz: A six-question knowledge check designed to test comprehension, boost curiosity, and encourage users to revisit mission logs to master key concepts.

Raw aerospace data and engineering metrics can often feel overwhelming to general audiences. By framing historic space missions through gripping human storytelling alongside visual media, our platform makes planetary science accessible, emotional, and memorable for students, educators, and space enthusiasts worldwide. Instead of passive reading, the interactive observatory, comparison tool, and quiz encourage active exploration—honoring the silent machines left behind on the Moon and Mars while inspiring the next generation of explorers.

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Frontend: HTML5, CSS3 (custom dark-mode futuristic UI and responsive layouts), and JavaScript (interactive 3D solar system canvas rendering, dynamic comparison tables, modal dossiers, and quiz logic).
  • Backend & Data: Python and SQLite for structuring, managing, and seeding mission telemetry, hardware specifications, and archival metadata.
  • Media & Data Sources: Official NASA and JPL mission archives, public image libraries, and curated launch and landing documentary footage.
  • Development & Deployment: Built using Visual Studio Code on Windows laptops, version-controlled with GitHub, and deployed publicly to the cloud via Netlify.

Creativity & Key Factors Considered: Our team took a narrative-first creative approach—treating historic rovers and landers not as discarded space hardware, but as pioneering characters with real engineering challenges and dramatic touchdown stories. Technically, we prioritized zero-barrier public accessibility, fast browser performance, clean relative asset paths, and responsive layouts so anyone can explore the platform seamlessly on desktop or mobile without needing logins or specialized hardware.

projectDetails.name: FLARE-X: Flame Learning, Analysis, Risk & Extinction Explorer
projectDetails.summary:
As humanity prepares for long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars, spacecraft fire safety is a critical survival priority. Under microgravity, buoyancy disappears (Gr ∝ g), fundamentally altering flame behavior, boundary-layer dynamics, and extinction limits. While NASA has archived decades of microgravity combustion tests, these datasets have remained fragmented, qualitative, and difficult to translate into operational safety standards.

We developed FLARE-X: an open-science, interpretable Super Intelligence (SI) analytics platform and interactive web dashboard built on NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) BASS-II flight data. FLARE-X overcomes the fatal blind spot of conventional fire detectors—which fail when near-extinction flames turn dim and blue—by employing an extreme-value noise-gated radiance proxy. It extracts flow-axis morphological time series, pinpoints combustion regime transitions with sub-frame accuracy, and computes an auditable Extinction Proximity Index with exact closed-form attribution to safeguard deep-space habitats and terrestrial infrastructure.
projectDetails.details:
WHAT DOES IT DO OR HOW DOES IT WORK?

FLARE-X is an automated analytical and visualization platform for microgravity combustion data from NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository. The pipeline operates in five verifiable stages:

1. Extreme-Value Noise-Gated Segmentation: Microgravity flames near extinction lose soot and transition into dim, chemiluminescent blue emissions. Generic computer vision fire detectors filter on red/yellow hues and miss the flame entirely. FLARE-X segments on a soot-independent radiance proxy, V = max(R,G,B), with an extreme-value noise floor (σ√(2 ln N)) and dual-threshold hysteresis to prevent sensor noise flooding on empty frames.

2. Flow-Axis Morphology: Rather than using image-coordinate bounding boxes that distort when cameras tilt, FLARE-X projects all flame contours onto the fuel rod's physical flow vector, measuring axial length, width, standoff distance, perimeter circularity, and a decoupled sootiness index, χ = (R-B)/(R+B).

3. Multivariate Change-Point Detection: Combustion experiments in BASS-II follow an opposed-flow staircase. FLARE-X detects operational regime transitions using multivariate binary segmentation with a BIC penalty, aligning to commanded flow changes with 100% recall.

4. Extinction Proximity Index (EPI): Quantifies peer-reviewed qualitative indicators into a bounded linear metric (elongation, standoff, blueness, dimness, area contraction). Per-frame attribution is 100% mathematically exact without opaque neural networks.

5. Analytical Physics & Provenance: Integrates Grashof scaling (Gr ∝ g), buoyant velocity scales, and Damköhler numbers, binding every calculated floating-point value to cryptographic SHA-256 source file hashes.

WHAT BENEFITS DOES IT HAVE?

- Eliminates Black-Box Opacity: Features and attribution weights are closed-form, auditable, and interpretable by mission safety boards.

- Resilient to Color Shifts: Accurately tracks the yellow-to-blue chemiluminescent transition that blinds commercial fire detectors.

- Built-In Falsifiability: Scored directly against physical anemometer and fan voltage telemetry burned into NASA camera frames.

- Zero-Dependency Web Architecture: The compiled dashboard (index.html) runs entirely client-side in any modern browser without servers or cloud subscriptions.

WHAT IS THE INTENDED IMPACT OF THE PROJECT?

- Space Exploration (Galactic Impact): Directly informs safety protocols for Lunar Gateway, Artemis Basecamp, and multi-year crewed Mars transits where terrestrial flammability standards (like NASA-STD-6001 Test 1) can misjudge low-velocity microgravity flammability. Serves as an analytical bridge for upcoming NASA SoFIE (Solid Fuel Ignition and Extinction) flight data.

- Earth Safety (Local Impact): Low-speed opposed flows model horizontal flame propagation in ceiling-constrained environments like subway tunnels, mining shafts, and aircraft cargo compartments where buoyant updrafts are restricted.

- Open STEM Education: Provides an accessible, free tool for students and fire safety engineers worldwide to explore combustion transport physics without expensive wind tunnels or CFD clusters.

WHAT TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES, HARDWARE, OR SOFTWARE DID YOU USE?

- Languages: Python 3.11 / 3.12 / 3.14, HTML5, CSS3, Modern JavaScript (ES2022).

- Scientific Computing: NumPy, SciPy, Scikit-Image, Scikit-Learn, OpenCV (Headless), Matplotlib, Pandas.

- Verification & Testing: Pytest (24/24 unit and physics tests passing), Git, GitHub Pages, uv.

- Design: Custom IBM Plex Sans and IBM Plex Mono typography with SVG rendering.

HOW IS YOUR PROJECT CREATIVE?

FLARE-X turns the qualitative human story of fire—"the flame turning blue as it starves in freefall"—into the exact physical feature vector term χ = (R-B)/(R+B). Its user interface utilizes an authentic combustion emission palette: soot continuum orange , chemiluminescence blue , and duct slate, allowing users to scrub the timeline while contours, feature curves, and attribution bars animate in synchrony.

WHAT FACTORS DID YOUR TEAM CONSIDER?

- Data Commensurability: We reviewed 17 NASA PSI investigations and deliberately rejected FLEX (droplet) and ACME (gas) because pooling non-solid flames with spread flames creates misleading comparisons.

- Sensor Noise & Telemetry Artifacts: We masked burned-in camera telemetry overlays (+22.4% segmentation recovery) and enforced noise floors to eliminate false detections after extinction.

- Scientific Modesty & Honest Claim Levels: All outputs are categorized from L1 (NASA Fact) to L5 (Mission Concept). Where scale was unconfirmed, we recorded NOT_VERIFIED rather than inventing plausible numbers.

Multi-Scale & Multi-Dataset Synthesis (How These Datasets Power FLARE-X):

To solve the microgravity combustion challenge comprehensively, FLARE-X integrates across multiple NASA and international space agency flight datasets across spatial and physical scales:

• Micro-Scale Glovebox Flame Spread (NASA BASS & BASS-II): Primary benchmark for solid fuel rod pyrolysis, opposed forced flow velocities (0.4–8 cm/s), and camera burned-in telemetry change points.

• Large-Scale Vehicle Fire Safety (NASA Saffire I–VI): Informs compartment-scale flame growth, airflow interactions, and elevated oxygen concentrations (34% O₂, 8.2 psia) in automated Cygnus spacecraft before atmospheric disposal.

• Cool Flame Chemiluminescence (NASA FLEX & FLEX-2): Benchmarks low-temperature, invisible hydrocarbon reactions that persist after visible soot combustion stops, validating FLARE-X's soot-independent blue radiance proxy.

• Condensed Fuel Gas Emulation (NASA ACME BRE): Provides kinetic burn-rate validation by comparing gaseous diffusion burner outputs against solid-fuel pyrolysis models.

• Partial Gravity Lunar/Mars Extinction (JAXA FLARE on Kibo): Extends microgravity insights (10⁻⁶ g) to Lunar (0.166 g) and Martian (0.38 g) surface gravities, defining safe ventilation thresholds for Artemis Basecamp and Mars transit vehicles.

• Terrestrial Ground-Truth Modeling (NIST FDS & NASA FIRMS): Bridges spaceflight kinetics with terrestrial thermal sensor calibration, mine shaft ventilation, and subway tunnel fluid dynamics.

projectDetails.name: TERRAWATCH AI — NISAR Surface Change Explorer
projectDetails.summary:
TerraWatch AI is an evidence-first geospatial web application prototype for exploring surface-change signals in NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations. Users can define an area of interest, discover NISAR Level-2 GCOV acquisitions through NASA's Common Metadata Repository, inspect acquisition metadata, and review whether selected observations are compatible for comparison.

For compatible validated observations, its processing workflow compares calibrated HH/HV radar backscatter measurements in decibels over jointly valid pixels to identify candidate surface-change anomalies. The application is designed to visualize these results on an interactive map and export GeoTIFF, GeoJSON, CSV, and provenance records linking outputs to their source data and processing parameters.

TerraWatch AI aims to make radar-based Earth observation more accessible, transparent, and reproducible for researchers, students, and environmental analysts. It reports candidate backscatter anomalies rather than claiming to confirm floods, vegetation loss, or other physical events. Its authentic end-to-end NISAR processing still requires final verification.
projectDetails.details:
Project Overview

TerraWatch AI is an interactive geospatial research application developed in response to NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 — Dancing with the SARs.

Its primary objective is to make NASA–ISRO NISAR radar observations easier to discover, compare, analyze, and interpret through an evidence-first surface-change exploration workflow.

Unlike conventional satellite-image viewers, TerraWatch AI emphasizes acquisition compatibility, scientific processing, data quality, and traceable results.

How It Works

The application follows a structured workflow:

1. Area of Interest Selection

Users define an area of interest using geographic coordinates or a selected polygon.

2. NISAR Data Discovery

The backend searches NASA's Common Metadata Repository (CMR) for relevant NISAR Level-2 GCOV observations and retrieves their acquisition metadata.

3. Acquisition Compatibility Assessment

Users select reference and secondary observations. The application evaluates their product family, processing release, relative orbit, pass direction, frame, radar mode, polarization configuration, spatial overlap, and other relevant metadata before allowing analysis.

Incompatible observations are rejected rather than silently treated as comparable.

4. Radar Backscatter Analysis

For compatible observations, the Python processing pipeline reads calibrated GCOV backscatter measurements, respects product masks and native geospatial coordinates, converts power measurements into decibel values, and calculates temporal backscatter differences.

Configurable screening rules identify spatial regions containing candidate backscatter anomalies. Small connected components can be filtered, and candidate regions can be represented as geospatial features.

5. Interactive Visualization and Evidence

Analysis outputs are designed to be explored through an interactive geospatial interface, with source metadata, processing information, and scientific limitations available for inspection.

6. Data Export and Reproducibility

The application supports GeoTIFF, GeoJSON, CSV, and JSON provenance exports. The provenance information records source granule identifiers, checksums, and processing parameters to help users trace and reproduce an analysis.

Innovation and Creativity

The main differentiator is evidence-backed surface-change exploration.

TerraWatch AI does not treat radar imagery as ordinary optical images or rely on an unexplained AI-generated prediction. It uses a deterministic processing workflow and explicit compatibility checks to help ensure that comparisons are based on suitable observations.

Scientific limitations, data quality, processing metadata, and uncertainty are treated as important parts of the result rather than hidden implementation details.

Technology Stack

Frontend: Next.js, React, TypeScript, MapLibre GL JS.

Backend: Python, FastAPI, Pydantic.

Geospatial Processing: NumPy, SciPy, h5py, Rasterio, Shapely, and PyProj.

Data and Infrastructure: NASA Common Metadata Repository, NASA Earthdata Login, PostgreSQL/PostGIS, Redis, and Celery.

Data Access: NASA Earthdata and the Alaska Satellite Facility (ASF) NISAR data distribution infrastructure.

AI Usage

An optional evidence-grounded language-model component can assist in explaining already-computed analysis results. It does not generate radar measurements or perform the authoritative change-detection calculations.

The current processing pipeline is deterministic and does not depend on a custom-trained deep-learning model.

Intended Impact

TerraWatch AI aims to help Earth-science researchers, geospatial analysts, students, and environmental monitoring teams investigate changes in Earth's surface using NISAR observations.

By making data discovery, comparison, visualization, and provenance more accessible, the project can support research exploration and help prioritize locations for further investigation and independent validation.

Scientific Scope and Limitations

The current implementation focuses on validated NASA–ISRO NISAR L-band Level-2 GCOV products, specifically the supported P05036 processing release.

Its outputs represent candidate radar backscatter anomalies. They do not independently confirm flooding, deforestation, wetland loss, surface deformation, or other physical events.

The present implementation is not an InSAR phase/coherence processing system or an operational disaster-warning service. Physical interpretations require independent evidence and further scientific validation.

TerraWatch AI is an independent student-built challenge project and is not an official NASA or ISRO product or endorsement.

challengeDetails.title: Dancing with the SARs
challengeDetails.excerpt: Earth's surface is an endless dance of natural processes and human activities, but these changes are often difficult to visualize, understand, and communicate. From wetland loss to forest wildfires, earthquakes, farming activities, glacier movement, and more, Earth is in a constant waltz of surface changes. Your challenge is to build an interactive application that uses radar remote sensing data from the NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar (NISAR) mission to track and visualize one or more types of surface change at locations around the world.

challengeDetails.title: Space Mission Design Game
challengeDetails.excerpt: Designing a space mission requires careful consideration of competing demands, including mission objectives, spacecraft design, scientific instruments, launch vehicles, budgets, power, mass, communications, and orbital constraints. For students who  rarely get to experiment with an entire mission from concept to operation, these trade-offs often remain abstract. Your challenge is to create an interactive game that allows participants to design, manage, and simulate a complete space mission while making engineering decisions, managing limited resources, and evaluating how each choice shapes the success of their mission.
